records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that President Boyer had arrived at "the Gape." Additionally, it recorded the death of Duncan McIntosh at Aux Cayes on the 26th of the previous month, praising him for risking his life during the revolutionary troubles of 1793 in St. Domingo to save numerous inhabitants from the blacks.
records.summary_es: El periódico informó que el presidente Boyer había llegado a «the Gape». Además, registró el fallecimiento de Duncan McIntosh en Aux Cayes el día 26 del mes precedente, elogiándolo por arriesgar su vida durante los disturbios revolucionarios de 1793 en Santo Domingo para salvar a numerosos habitantes de los negros.

records.summary_en: An Aux Cayes correspondent, writing on March 3, makes no mention of any French fleet having sailed from Martinique, which casts doubt on the report of an expedition against St. Domingo. The correspondent reports that the Haitian government has raised the tonnage money on American vessels from half a dollar to one dollar per ton, and sends President Boyer's proclamation, which shows that Boyer was in possession of the city of St. Domingo early in February. The proclamation, dated at the National Palace of St. Domingo on February 9, 1822, in the nineteenth year of Haitian independence, begins: «Haytians—our national flag now displays itself upon every point of our island.» The paper holds the proclamation for translation and may publish it in its next issue.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal de Aux Cayes, en carta del 3 de marzo, no menciona ninguna flota francesa salida de Martinica, lo que pone en duda el informe de una expedición contra Santo Domingo. El corresponsal informa que el gobierno haitiano elevó el derecho de tonelaje de los buques estadounidenses de medio dólar a un dólar por tonelada, y envía la proclamación del presidente Boyer, que muestra que Boyer estaba en posesión de la ciudad de Santo Domingo a principios de febrero. La proclamación, fechada en el Palacio Nacional de Santo Domingo el 9 de febrero de 1822, en el decimonoveno año de la independencia de Haití, comienza: «Haitianos: nuestra bandera nacional se despliega ahora en todos los puntos de nuestra isla». El periódico guarda la proclamación para su traducción y podría publicarla en su próximo número.

records.headline: Arrivals from Santo Domingo bring accounts of the whole of the slave population of Spanish Santo Domingo having been emancipated
records.summary_en: Arrivals from Santo Domingo bring word that the whole of the enslaved population of Spanish Santo Domingo has been emancipated, a change the paper says could only have been expected from the political transformation that has so lately taken place in that territory. The emancipation is described as in perfect conformity with the constitution of Haiti, under which the territory now falls.
records.summary_es: Las llegadas procedentes de Santo Domingo traen la noticia de que toda la población esclavizada del Santo Domingo español ha sido emancipada, un cambio que, según el periódico, solo podía esperarse de la transformación política que tan recientemente ha tenido lugar en ese territorio. La emancipación se describe en perfecta conformidad con la Constitución de Haití, bajo la cual se encuentra ahora el territorio.

records.headline: St. Domingo.
records.summary_en: A letter from St. Pierre, Martinique, reprinted from the Curaçao Courant, reports that on February 13 a French force of a ship of the line, three frigates, three gabarras, four brigs and four schooners, carrying 2,000 men and 50 pieces of artillery, sailed for Samaná to throw up fortifications and, with reinforcements, attempt to retake Spanish St. Domingo from the Haitians. The same report says a French fleet was seen passing north of St. Thomas on February 14, and that emigrants were arriving daily at Martinique from St. Domingo, where planters were said to be ruined because the Haitian government had declared their slaves free. The paper is skeptical: a letter from its Aux Cayes correspondent, dated March 3, makes no mention of such a fleet, and it publishes Boyer's February 9 proclamation from the National Palace of St. Domingo, in which he declares the Haitian flag flies on every point of the island.
records.summary_es: Una carta de St. Pierre, Martinica, reproducida del Curaçao Courant, informa que el 13 de febrero una fuerza francesa compuesta por un navío de línea, tres fragatas, tres gabarras, cuatro bergantines y cuatro goletas, con 2.000 hombres y 50 piezas de artillería, zarpó hacia Samaná para levantar fortificaciones y, con refuerzos, intentar retomar el Santo Domingo español de manos de los haitianos. El mismo informe dice que una flota francesa fue vista pasando al norte de St. Thomas el 14 de febrero, y que emigrantes llegaban diariamente a Martinica desde Santo Domingo, donde se decía que los plantadores estaban arruinados porque el gobierno haitiano había declarado libres a sus esclavos. El periódico es escéptico: una carta de su corresponsal en Aux Cayes, fechada el 3 de marzo, no menciona tal flota, y publica la proclamación de Boyer del 9 de febrero desde el Palacio Nacional de Santo Domingo, en la que declara que la bandera haitiana ondea en todos los puntos de la isla.

records.summary_en: Mr. Granville, agent of the Haitian government, has arrived from Philadelphia with President Boyer's instructions for the emigration of 6,000 free Black people to Haiti during the present year, including 1,000 to Santo Domingo and 200 to Samaná. Those who form themselves into companies of twelve or more to cultivate the fertile lands assigned to them will have their passage and maintenance paid on arrival by the government, which will also provide subsistence for four months; those who travel on their own account will have their passage advanced but must repay it within six months. The president has sent coffee to a merchant in this city to fund the removal of emigrants from the interior to the ports of embarkation, and after a year's residence the emigrants will be entitled to all the civil and political rights of citizens, with liberty of conscience in matters of religion.
records.summary_es: El Sr. Granville, agente del gobierno haitiano, ha llegado desde Filadelfia con las instrucciones del presidente Boyer para la emigración de 6.000 personas negras libres a Haití durante el presente año, incluidas 1.000 a Santo Domingo y 200 a Samaná. Quienes se organicen en compañías de doce o más personas para cultivar las tierras fértiles que se les asignen tendrán su pasaje y manutención pagados a su llegada por el gobierno, que también les proporcionará sustento durante cuatro meses; quienes viajen por su cuenta tendrán el pasaje adelantado, pero deberán reembolsarlo dentro de los seis meses. El presidente ha enviado café a un comerciante de esta ciudad para financiar el traslado de los emigrantes del interior a los puertos de embarque, y tras un año de residencia los emigrantes tendrán derecho a todos los derechos civiles y políticos de los ciudadanos, con libertad de conciencia en materia de religión.

records.headline: A West India Parson.
records.summary_en: According to the *Phenix gazette* of June 26, 1826, Audain relocated to St. Domingo as a trader after abdicating his pulpit, where he subsequently shot two black general officers in a quarrel. When Christophe threatened to hang him if either man died, Audain escaped by night in an open boat to St. Eustatius. There, he resumed his role as a clergyman, offering his services to multiple religious sects by celebrating mass in French, reading the Church of England liturgy, and conducting the Dutch service.
records.summary_es: Según la *Phenix gazette* del 26 de junio de 1826, Audain se trasladó a Santo Domingo como comerciante tras renunciar al púlpito, donde posteriormente hirió de bala a dos oficiales generales negros durante una disputa. Cuando Christophe amenazó con ahorcarlo si alguno de ellos fallecía, Audain huyó de noche en un bote descubierto hacia San Eustaquio. Allí reanudó su ministerio religioso, ofreciendo sus servicios a diversas confesiones al celebrar misa en francés, leer la liturgia de la Iglesia de Inglaterra y oficiar el servicio holandés.

records.full_text:
A WEST INDIA PARSON.
[From Coleridge's Six Months in the West Indies.]
The church in Roseau is well situated and tolerably finished without, but the interior is in a miserable state. The common pitch pine, white unpainted, has a particularly unpleasant effect in a hot climate; it always oppressed me in a remarkable manner. About a hundred persons, chiefly colored, attended the morning service, they had few books, and apparently came for the purpose of seeing the bishop; certainly with one or two exceptions, they were entirely unacquainted with the ordinary ritual of the established religion. The Church of England indeed does not flourish in Dominica, which, considering the great capacity and spirituous affections of the people, is a matter of some character of surprise. I believe there are 2,000 protestants in this colony, of which number the Methodists form the larger part, about 16,000 are Papists, under the care of three Spanish priests; so that it is consolatory to the sympathies of obese and liquescent men to know that if true religion thrive not in Dominica, at least its minister does, since he is worth his salary, and just so much breathing exercise o' Sundays as may conduce to a good digestion for the rest of the week. Not that I would be thought to impeach the zeal of the rector of Roseau; very far from it; it is too well-known to be questioned, and it argues an unusual degree of apathy or stubbornness in those who are the daily witnesses of it, that its effects are not more perceptible.
Mr. Newman is great and remarkable; but he is not so great and remarkable as his predecessor Mr. Audain. This Mr. Audain was a patriot; few of his cloth like him; he was not content with praying against the enemies of his country—he fought against them also. St. Peter certainly owned a boat, and the authorized translation (Mr. Audain loved literal orthodoxy) intimates a partnership amongst some of the Apostles in a ship. So, Mr. Audain built a schooner, and carried on for many years a system of polemical politics with the disputants of the French school to his own abundant profit and notoriety. It is even yet fresh in the recollections of the inhabitants of Roseau, with how joyful a rapture this holy Dominican once broke off the service on a Sunday, unable to repress the emotions of his triumph on seeing the vessel of his faith sail into the bay with a dismantled bark laden with sugar, rum and other gallic vanities from Martinique.*
It was shortly after this event that the star of Audain began to wax dim. His zeal was equally great, his courage undaunted, but his evil destiny met him at every turn. An acquaintance of mine met him one day in the streets of Bassaterre, in St. Kitts, surrounded by negroes, to whom he was distributing plantains, yams, potatoes and other eatables, and holding private talk with them all by turns. Having caught my friend's eye, he came up to him and said, 'I am going to smuggle all these rascals this evening to Gaudaloupe.' He did so in his schooner, but remained himself on shore. A privateer of Nevis captured the smuggler before she could get to her market. Audain became furious, went himself to Nevis, and challenged the owner of the privateer to fight. The challenge was not accepted; and Audain immediately possessed the name of the recusant, as that of a scoundrel, on the court house. He himself for two days kept watch upon the platform with a sword by his side and four pistols stuck in his belt, to see if any one dared to touch the shields.
Audain fitted out another schooner and cruised in her himself. But fate was too heavy for him, though he struggled against it like a man. On the second day a large vessel was seen to leeward; he ascertained her to be worthy his armed, bore down on her as upon a certain prey. When he came within pistol shot, fourteen masked ports were opened and as many guns pointed at him through them. Audain was obliged to strike in an instant, and, with his carpenter, succeeded in secreting himself under the water casks in the hold of his schooner. The rest of the crew were taken out in the morning, upon further search their asylum was discovered. They were brought upon deck, and the Spaniards were on the point of sawing them by inches, when their captain exclaimed with rapidity, 'Hold all! this man's life is sacred, and the other's too for his sake.' Audain had formerly done the Spaniard great service at St. Thomas's, and it now saved his own and his carpenter's life.
Up to this time Audain, though occasionally and quietly for the above-mentioned, had continued the minister of Rosseau. He was a singularly eloquent preacher in the pathetic and suasory style, and he rarely failed to draw down tears from the cheeks of most of those who heard him. His manners were fine and gentle, and his appearance even venerable. He was hospitable to the rich and gave alms to the poor. But his repeated losses were such as to bear a royal merchant down, and the Dominicians became more scrupulous, and a governor came who knew not Audain. So Audain abdicated the pulpit of Rosseau.
Privateering and smuggling had lulled; so now he commenced honest trader. He went to St. Domingo with a cargo of Corn, sold it well, and lived on the island. But his star grew fainter and fainter. He quarrelled with two black general officers, challenged them both and shot them both severely. Christophe sent for him and told him that, if the men recovered, it was well, but if either of them died, he would hang him on the tamarind tree before his own door. Audain thought the men would die, and escaped from the tamarind tree by night in an open boat.
He now settled in St. Eustatius, put on his black coat again and recommenced clergyman—St. Eustatius is a fine place yet for the soul—his labor has made surprisingly slow advances in it. There were many religious, but no priest, in the island when Audain made his appearance there. He was become liberally minded by misfortune, and he was always actuated by a faith of such immense catholicity that it comprehended within its limits every variation of opinion from the centre of Christianity, as the jelly embraceth the spokes of a wheel. Audain offered to minister to all the sects respectively, which the free traders thankfully accepted. In the morning he celebrated mass in French, in the forenoon read the liturgy of the Church of England, in the afternoon spackened the Dutch service, and in the evening harangued the Methodists.
His star descended proner and proner, though he seemed to be gaining wealth and fame. Audain was a married man, but his wife resided and still resides at Bristol. A Dutch widow, rich, pious and large, cast a widow's eye on Audain; the rigor of creed violetly softened under the afternoon spackeneding of Audain, as Dutch butter melts under the kisses of Titan, and she told Audain that, if Heaven had made her such a man, she would have married twice. The hint was as broad as herself, but Audain liked it the better for its dimensions, and married her on the spot, spackening the service himself.
Audain has fought thirteen duels, and is a good boxer. Once upon a time, he fired twice without hitting; upon which he threw down his pistol on the ground, and said sternly to his second, 'Take care that does not happen again!' suggesting his pistol had not been charged with ball. A delay occurred; he fired again for the third time, upon which Audain went up to his antagonist, squared his body, saying 'Something however, sometimes between, good sir,' knocked him down with a flush hit on the nose.
Audain is now about sixty years of age, and has wholly reformed his manners. He loves his Dutch wife, and says his prayers so loud at night as to disturb his neighbors. His English wife sends him a Christmas box annually. He is a man of infinite talent, and has seen the world. I trust the report is true, that, like Lazarillo de Tormes and Gines de Pasamonte, he is writing a life of himself. It would be the most entertaining book of this age If he does not, these few lines may happily serve to rescue him from an oblivion which he does not seem to deserve.
* This is like the Cornish vicar. He was preaching one afternoon in a seaside church during a heavy southwest gale, when all on a sudden his audience began to leave, take down their hats, and push towards the door. The vicar, having the advantage of pulpit eminence and long experience, immediately perceived the cause, and, animated with a just indignation at their conduct, ordered them, as they valued their souls' welfare, to remain quiet till the end of the sermon. The good man in his eagerness to restrain them even left the pulpit, and, like Aaron, ran into the midst of the congregation, following and exhorting them, till he reached the porch; when, tucking up his gown under his arm, he shouted out, 'Now, my boys, let us start fair!' and immediately outran them all, as in his days of his heels, to administer Cornish relief to a distressed merchantman.
My friend Mr. Oxley, in Barbadoes, says he was present at a scene in Tortola, where Audain figured in the manner mentioned in the text; probably it happened twice.

records.headline: On Foreign Missions
records.summary_en: The *New-Hampshire Baptist register* reported on December 3, 1835, that new fields had been opened for missionaries in Africa and the Island of Hayti, alongside efforts to augment laborers in previously occupied fields. Additionally, the newspaper noted that on July 1, 1834, a reinforcement of 11 missionaries accompanied Brother Wade on his return to Burmah, with various individuals assigned to stations among the Karens, Siam, Arracan, Maulmein, and as a school teacher.
records.summary_es: El *New-Hampshire Baptist register* informó el 3 de diciembre de 1835 de la apertura de nuevos campos para misioneros en África y en la isla de Haití, junto con esfuerzos por incrementar los obreros en zonas previamente atendidas. Asimismo, el periódico consignó que el 1 de julio de 1834 un contingente de once misioneros acompañó al hermano Wade en su regreso a Birmania, asignándose diversas personas a estaciones entre los carenes, Siam, Arracán, Maulmein y en labores de maestro de escuela.

records.full_text:
Your committee on F. Missions present the following Report:—
The past year has been an eventful period in the history of F. Missionary operations.
While we have occasion to mourn the loss of some valuable Missionaries; the unparalleled success that has marked the proceedings of the Board, and that has attended the labours of the Missionaries, calls loudly for gratitude to Almighty God. Rostan of France, a "standard-bearer" indeed, has fallen. Miss Cummings of Burmah, O'Brynt and Mrs. Lewis of the Indian Stations, were "faithful unto death," and have all, doubtless, gone to the "rest that remaineth to the people of God." Still we have by far, greater reason to "sing of mercy" than of "judgment." Indeed, the past year may be said to have introduced a new era in the history of F. Missions, under the patronage of American Baptists. Many new and promising fields have come to light, inviting labourers to gather in the whitening harvest; China with her immense benighted population, now accessible at the nearest point of approach—the Bombay and Madras Presidencies, where are already scattered converts, both European and native, and where 40 millions of immortal souls are perishing for "lack of vision;"—Germany, where the leaven of Calvinistic Baptist sentiments, is already beginning powerfully to operate upon the putrid mass of neutralization; where Oncken, Lewis, and other kindred spirits are pouring light upon the surrounding darkness; Africa, ill fated and too long neglected, but now promising health, and successful effort, to our Missionaries; and the Island of Hayti with her numerous Catholic population.
Not only have these new fields been opened; but measures have been taken by the Board, to occupy most of them, and greatly to augment the number of labourers in fields previously occupied.
On the first of July 1834, a reinforcement of 11 missionaries, accompanied bro. Wade on his return to Burmah. Two of these with their wives were to be stationed among the Karens; one, with his wife, was to join the Siam Mission; another, with his wife, was to form a station in Arracan; Mr. Osgood, a printer, and his wife, were to remain at Maulmein; and sister Gardner was to reside in the family of bro. Wade, in the capacity of a School teacher. These missionaries had acquired a considerable knowledge of the language of the people where they were to be stationed, before they left this country, and have, doubtless, been successfully labouring in their respective spheres since the time of their arrival, the 1st of Dec. last.
On the 11th of July last, 3 Missionaries—Crocker, and Mylne and his wife, were sent out to Africa.
On the 21st of Sept. 14 other Missionaries embarked for the east. Five of these were destined for the Burman Mission; two others (one a printer) with their wives, were designated to Bankok, Siam there to prepare for laboring among the Chinese. The five others were to labor among the Talings on the Madras coast. With this last deputation, sailed Rev. Howard Malcom, appointed by the Board to visit the several Mission stations in the east, and to confer with the Missionary brethren on subjects pertaining to the interests of Eastern Missions.
Your committee hail with joy his appointment, as a measure promising great and important results.
Your committee learn with pleasure that the Board have secured the services of two valuable Missionaries, Willard and Shelden, with their wives, to join Porchat and Wilmarth in France; also, that they have designated a colored brother to Hayti.
The completion of the whole Bible in the Burman language, opens a wide field of labor, which ought thankfully and perseveringly to be cultivated; until every son and daughter of Burmah are permitted to read, how they may escape an "Eternal Hell." Viewing these enlarged operations, in connexion with the fact, that the Treasury is now, for the first time, almost empty, the inference is irresistible, that, while we are called upon by every consideration that is soul-stirring, to increase our contributions for Home Missions, Domestic Missions, and Ministerial Education, we must increase and greatly increase our contributions to the Foreign Mission Treasury.
Your committee feel, that the death of those Missionaries above mentioned, and the numerous instances in which the lives of others have been periled, ought forcibly to remind us of our dependence upon Him, "in whose hand our breath is," and of our duty to persevere in prayer for the lives, health, and success of those who are yet spared.
In closing their Report, your committee would offer the following resolutions:
Resolved, That this Convention cordially responds to the appeal of the Baptist General Convention, for the support and enlargement of their Mission in the heathen, and will use all suitable means in its power to carry into effect their resolution, to raise one hundred thousand dollars for Missionary purposes during the current year.
Resolved, That as the diffusion of authentic Missionary intelligence is a highly important means of calling forth the energies of the Christian church in extending the Redeemer's kingdom throughout the earth; And as the American Baptist Magazine is devoted specially to this object, and can now be furnished to subscribers at the very low price of one dollar a year; Therefore, be it further resolved, that we will use our efforts to secure its general circulation, and we do hereby cordially commend it to the patronage of all who are interested in the promotion of the glory of Christ, and the salvation of the heathen.
MARK CARPENTER, Chairman.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
LATE FROM HAYTI—By the schooner 'Baltimore' at this port, from Cape Haytien, intelligence has been received at the Merchants' Exchange as late as the 30th ult.
Tranquility was restored at Cape Haytien. where Guerrier had been accepted as President of the North, and accordingly proclaimed.
The different divisions of the Island are to be erected into States, somewhat after the plan of the United States. If the Dominicans reject this offer, another expedition will be sent against them.
There were five French brigs-of-war and a steamer off the island.
The additional duty of $10 per M. on coffee had been removed.
H. B. M. frigate Spartan, of 26 guns, Captain Elliott, arrived at the Cape on the 26th, from Port au Prince.
Port au Prince and the South was submissive to Guerrier's Government.
Ex-President Herard, and his kinsman, late President of the Assembly, had been ordered to leave the Island.
No new expedition was designed against the Dominicans, by whom Herard's troops had been beaten. The army had suffered from the small pox, hunger, nakedness, &c. in their retreat after the overthrow by the Dominicians.
The U. S. sloop Preble was at Aux Cayes a few days before the Baltimore sailed. She was expected at Port au Prince.
While there, the 'Baltimore' was at different times a means of shelter, not only to our American Consul, Mr. Usher, but at one time to as many as two hundred females whose lives were in danger during the late tumults; additionally to whom much of property, say $100,000, had been brought off to the Baltimore for safety. Even at midnight the vessel has been of service to the 'refugees'. The prospect of returning quiet caused the disembarkation of both persons and property.
Phil. Enq.

records.headline: Late from Hayti.
records.summary_en: According to the June 15, 1844 issue of the *Daily National Intelligencer*, Gurrier was proclaimed President of the North on the 18th, with plans to erect the island's divisions into States similar to the United States and potentially propose that the Dominicans join as a State. The newspaper reported that the ex-President and Herard Dumesle were ordered to be banished to Jamaica, that Aux Cayes and the South remained submissive, and that no new expedition was currently designed against the Dominicans, who had severely beaten Herard’s troops. Additionally, it noted unconfirmed talk of a treaty between the Dominicans and France, the arrival of the British frigate *Spartan* from Port au Prince, and the presence of the U.S. sloop *Preble* at Aux Cayes.
records.summary_es: Conforme al ejemplar del 15 de junio de 1844 del *Daily National Intelligencer*, Gurrier fue proclamado presidente del Norte el día 18, proyectando estructurar las demarcaciones insulares en estados a semejanza de Estados Unidos y plantear en su caso que los dominicanos se integrasen en calidad de estado. El periódico refirió que se dispuso el confinamiento en Jamaica del expresidente y de Herard Dumesle, que Aux Cayes y el Sur acataban la autoridad y que no se preparaba de momento ninguna expedición contra los dominicanos, quienes habían desbaratado a los destacamentos de Hérard. Además, aludió a negociaciones no confirmadas de un tratado dominicano con Francia, al arribo de la fragata británica *Spartan* desde Puerto Príncipe y a la estancia de la corbeta estadounidense *Preble* en Aux Cayes.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
The following intelligence, from the Philadelphia United States Gazette, confirms the reports which have previously reached us of another change of Government in Hayti. The intelligence is brought by the schooner Baltimore, which left Cape Haytien on the 30th ultimo. While there this vessel was at different times a means of shelter, not only to the American Consul, Mr. Usher, but at one time to as many as two hundred females whose lives were in danger during the late tumults. There was also a considerable amount of property placed on board of her for safety, but the prospect of returning quiet caused the disembarkation of both persons and property.
CAPE HAYTIEN, MAY 28, 1844.
This place has been rather quiet for the last week or two. The 'Council of State,' learning from Port au Prince that Rivera, or Herard, as he is called indifferently, had been deposed from office, and Gen. Guerrier appointed President in his place, concluded to accept Gurrier as President of the 'North' also, and he was accordingly proclaimed on the 18th. The Government is not to be consolidated, as heretofore; but it is in contemplation to erect the several divisions of the Island into States, somewhat in imitation of the United States Government, and Commissioners have gone to Port au Prince for that purpose. Their plans, however, do not appear to be very clearly developed at present. It is said this arrangement will be made to the Dominicans to join the new Government as a State, which, if they reject, another expedition will be sent against them. But it is the general opinion that they will be able to sustain their position as a distinct Government. There is some talk of their having made a treaty with France, but this wants confirmation.
The British frigate Spartan, 26 guns, Capt. Elliot, arrived here on the 26th instant from Port au Prince, whence she sailed the 23d. The officers report every thing quiet there. The ex-President has been ordered to leave the island, and his kinsman, Herard Dumesle, late President of the Constituent Assembly, has also been banished, and they are to retire to Jamaica.
Aux Cayes and the South generally continued submissive to the Government of Guerrier; and no new expedition is, at present, designed against the Dominicans, by whom Herard's troops were severely beaten. Both men and horses are said to have suffered extremely on the return march from hunger, nakedness, disease, and vermin.
The U. S. sloop Preble was at Aux Cayes a few days since, and when the Spartan left was daily expected at Port au Prince. The French force about the island consists of five frigates and a steamer.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
A Dominican man-of-war schooner, belonging to General Santa Ana, called the Separacion, formerly the pilot boat Romp, arrived off here to-day, with letters from General Santa Ana to Gen. Villanueve, informing him that he, Santa Ana, had been legally chosen by the legal Junta, President of the Republic, in the city of St. Domingo. Gen. Villanueve sent his son, and aid, Colonel Toutio, on board of her to invite the Captain to bring his vessel in, which he did. He saluted the town, which was returned by the fort. The same legal Junta that Gen. Santa Ana has reinstated, are the self-chosen or appointed, who wished to, or who in fact did cede Samana to the French. The party that President Duarte is the chief of, are opposed to the French protection. Since the deposition of the first named part of the Junta, the French have been actively employed in Port-au-Prince, to create there a diversion of the Black Government against the East. The same activity in intrigue has been displayed at Cape Haytien. It is not yet ascertained with what success.

At the time that Gen. Duarte was proclaimed President at La Vega and on this side of the island, Gen. Santa Ana was on the frontiers with his army. While there, he received a commission from Port-au-Prince, after which he commenced his march on St. Domingo—his army increasing on the route. Report says he appeared before the city with an army of 6,000 men, in a tolerable state of discipline, and was by them made President. He is in favor of French protection—so report says. Whether such protection would benefit the country is hard to say. On the principle that a powerful friend is a benefit, the protection of the French may possibly benefit these people, provided their commerce with other nations, and their own internal Government, are not interfered with.

As I before informed you, Gen. Duarte is a white man, about 30 years old; Gen. St. Ana is a Spanish white, about 55 years old. The last named has devoted all his fortune to this revolution; two of the man-of-war schooners are his private property. The existing difficulties may be amicably arranged; but I believe myself there will be some fighting, if the two Presidents can bring their followers up to it. The people don't like that sort of work.—N. Y. Jour. of Commerce.

records.headline: From Hayti.
records.summary_en: The newspaper reports that a French squadron was waiting at Port-au-Prince for an indemnity installment, though funds were scarce. It also states that General Accau, leader of the late revolution in Aux Cayes, was decoyed to Port-au-Prince by President Gurriere and made prisoner upon arrival. Additionally, patriots in the Spanish part of the island rejected French protection, while Dominican President General Santa Anna's movements suggested he might retain his post and form a confederacy with Gurriere's government.
records.summary_es: El diario refiere que una escuadra naval gala aguardaba en Puerto Príncipe la liquidación de una entrega de la indemnización pactada, si bien los caudales eran escasos. Da cuenta asimismo de que el general Accau, cabecilla del reciente levantamiento en Aux Cayes, fue conducido con ardides a Puerto Príncipe por el presidente Gurriere y puesto en prisión apenas desembarcó. Por su lado, los patriotas de la sección española repudiaban el protectorado francés, mientras que las resoluciones del presidente dominicano, el general Santana, presagiaban su permanencia en el mando y la concertación de un pacto federativo con el gobierno de Gurriere.

records.full_text:
The United States ship Vandalia, Commander JOHN S. CHAUNCEY, arrived at Pensacola, on the 25th ultimo, last from Port au Prince, via Aux Cayes, which latter port she left on the 12th ultimo.

Though the island of St. Domingo is in a very unsettled and precarious position, still all was quiet. At Port au Prince a French squadron, consisting of one frigate, a barque, and two brigs, was waiting for an instalment of the indemnity due the French Government; but, from all accounts, it was supposed they would have to await some time, as money was a scarce article in the market.

An arrival at New York in ten days from Port au Prince reports that General ACCAU, the leader of the late revolution in Aux Cayes, is now in Port au Prince, having been decoyed down by President GUERRIER, under a pretence of receiving the appointment of General of that part of the island, and, on his arrival, thrown into a prison. He was made prisoner immediately on his arrival.

The Patriots of the Spanish part of the island have declared against a French protection. The movements of Gen. Santa Anna, the President of the Dominicans, rendered it probable that he would retain his post, and unite his Government to that of Guerrier as a confederacy.

Additionally, authorities at Port au Platt arranged a treaty granting the French a patent for the Samana mines, though it was expected to fail due to popular opposition, while President Guerriere was on an island tour expected to reach Cape Haytien.

Paralelamente, las autoridades de Puerto Plata estipularon un convenio otorgando a los franceses la concesión minera de Samaná, cuya ratificación se juzgaba inviable por el rechazo popular, al paso que el presidente Guerrier recorría el país con destino a Cabo Haitiano.

records.full_text:
From St. Domingo.—We learn from Capt. Wilson of the brig Republic, just arrived from Port au Prince, that on the 12th of March the Haytien man of war Herard, in the schr. La Granada, had been seen off the South side of the Island, five miles off, by five gun boats. The whole coast was guarded by vessels of war, to prevent the ex-President and his adherents from landing. The government called out all the militia, and the whole of that part of the Island belonging to the Haytien government was under martial law. Several of the adherents of Herard had been taken and shot, and there was a great excitement throughout the Island. Coffee was very scarce and high on account of all the country men having been taken for soldiers, and no persons left to bring the Coffee to market. The markets were glutted with American produce.

Although numerous arrests were made in different parts of the Republic, judging from the tone of the journals, there was no general sympathy for Herard, nor any very serious apprehensions felt by the parties of government, that his attempts to revolutionize the country would be successful.

It was rumored at Port Republican, that a revolution had taken place at St. Domingo, which had resulted in the expulsion of Gen. Santana from the Presidency, and in the elevation to that office of Major Moru, a member of the numerous and highly respectable family of the Alvares de Zaguate (Saint Domingo) If true, this change of government in the Dominican Republic would be the triumph of an enlightened and liberal party over intrigue and demagogism personified in Santana and Bobadilla.

records.headline: The Daily National Intelligencer reprints a Commercial Advertiser item
records.summary_en: The Daily National Intelligencer reprints a Commercial Advertiser item from New York, clarifying the names of the island, to prevent common confusion. The notice explains that Columbus named the northern part of the island Hispaniola, the French later took possession of the western portion and called it St. Domingo, and after both Spaniards and French were ousted, the colored race gave the name Hayti to the whole island. Since the expulsion of President Boyer, the eastern and western portions have separated into the Dominican Republic, with its capital at the city of St. Domingo, and the Haytien Republic, with its capital at Port Republican, formerly Port au Prince. The paper notes that applying the name St. Domingo to the whole island is improper.
records.summary_es: El Daily National Intelligencer reproduce una nota del New York Commercial Advertiser que aclara los nombres de la isla para evitar una confusión frecuente. El texto explica que Colón dio el nombre de La Española a la parte norte de la isla, los franceses tomaron luego posesión de la porción occidental y la llamaron Santo Domingo, y tras la expulsión de españoles y franceses, la raza de color dio el nombre de Haití a toda la isla. Desde la expulsión del presidente Boyer, las porciones oriental y occidental se han separado en la República Dominicana, cuya capital es la ciudad de Santo Domingo, y la República Haitiana, cuya capital es Puerto Republicano, antes Puerto Príncipe. El periódico señala que aplicar el nombre de Santo Domingo a toda la isla es impropio.

records.summary_en: The Daily Union reprints a report from the Commercial Advertiser, which states that in a battle fought near Matsyaga, the Haytiens were totally defeated and lost their artillery and provisions. According to the account, a strong Dominican force was posted at Santiago and along the northern frontier, while great enthusiasm prevailed throughout the Dominican portion of the island and commerce remained uninterrupted. The inhabitants of Port-au-Platte and Santiago had purchased the American barque Alert and offered her to the Dominican government to be armed at the city of St. Domingo with 14 carronades and two 32-pounder pivot guns. The report adds that the Bridgewater left five Dominican men-of-war schooners at Port-au-Platte and that produce prices were extremely high.

records.headline: Under the heading "Recognition of St. Domingo," the New York Herald reports
records.summary_en: Under the heading "Recognition of St. Domingo," the New York Herald reports that the object of Mr. Hogan's recent mission on behalf of the United States to the island of San Domingo was to make inquiries and collect facts with a view toward the administration recognizing its independence. The paper disputes a statement by the Washington correspondent of the Commercial Advertiser claiming that recognizing the independence of the Dominican Republic would oblige the United States to receive a colored minister and colored consuls. The Herald asserts that out of a population of about 250,000 in the Spanish half of the island, more than half are whites of the Spanish race and the remaining half are mulattoes, arguing that its diplomatic representatives will therefore be whites. The editorial expresses hope that the administration will recognize the republic's independence during the ensuing session of Congress.
records.summary_es: Bajo el título «Reconocimiento de Santo Domingo», el New York Herald informa que el objeto de la reciente misión del Sr. Hogan en nombre de los Estados Unidos a la isla de Santo Domingo fue realizar indagaciones y recopilar datos con miras a que el gobierno reconozca su independencia. records.headline: The Liberator reprints an article discussing the fact-gathering
records.summary_en: The Liberator reprints an article discussing the fact-gathering and inquiries conducted with a view toward the United States administration recognizing the independence of the Dominican Republic. The reprinted text denies a statement by the Washington correspondent of the Commercial Advertiser that acknowledging Dominican independence would oblige the United States to receive a colored minister and colored consuls. It states that the Spanish half of the island of St. Domingo has a population of about 250,000—more than half whites of the Spanish race and the rest mulattoes—and contends that its representatives will therefore be whites, while urging recognition during the ensuing session of Congress. A concluding line by the Liberator begins to characterize the measure as the next thing to be attempted for the benefit of slavery.

records.headline: The Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: In 1845, the newspaper reported that Mr. Calhoun, while in the State Department, dispatched Mr. Hogan to investigate the resources of the Dominican Republic following a petition to have the United States acknowledge its independence. Hogan subsequently returned with a satisfactory account of the commonwealth. The publication advocated for the U.S. recognition of the Dominican Republic, citing racial sympathies with the white population struggling against Hayti, commercial interests in the West Indies, and strategic concerns regarding European monarchies holding territory in the region.

Hogan retornó consecuentemente con un balance favorable de aquella comunidad política. La publicación instaba a que Estados Unidos reconociese al Estado dominicano invocando afinidades de raza con la población blanca en conflicto contra Haití, conveniencias mercantiles en las Antillas e inquietudes de seguridad ante enclaves soberanos de coronas europeas en el área.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
Few of our readers are aware that a new Republic has been formed under this name in the island of St. Domingo. Yet such is the fact. Within two years past a revolution has been made, and successfully maintained against the negro government of Hayti. Our purpose is to give some new idea of this new Republic and its resources.
The Island of St. Domingo is the most flourishing and fertile of the West India Islands. There are two political divisions of the island. The formerly French portion is now the Haytien Republic, as it is called. From this nation are exported coffee, cotton, mahogany, dye wood, &c. The formerly Spanish portion of the island, or now the Dominican Republic, exports mahogany, wood, lignumvitæ, cocoa, honey, hides, gum guaiacum, and tobacco, equal to the best Havana in quality. Sugar is also raised. It unquestionably contains mineral wealth, as gold and copper mines have been discovered.
The climate of the island is that of the tropics—warm and damp. The heats, however, are tempered by the sea breeze, which sets in about 10 o'clock, A. M., and lasts until night, when it is followed by the land breeze. The soil of the island is exceedingly fertile.
The east end of the island of St. Domingo, formerly was known as the Spanish Possession, now forms the Dominican Republic. Its extent is 33,000 square leagues of 25 to a degree. This Republic has been formed by the white portion of the island rising in rebellion against the black Government of Hayti. For twenty years and upwards, the whites have submitted to a most humiliating oppression. In February, 1844, they successfully made a stand against the black government, and have since gallantly and efficiently maintained their independence. They sent commissioners to this country during the administration of Mr. Calhoun in the State Department, for the purpose of having the government of the United States take measures to acknowledge the independence of the Republic. Mr. Calhoun at once favored the idea, and despatched Mr. Hogan, of this State, to investigate the resources of the country. Mr. Hogan having faithfully executed his important trust, has returned and given, we hear, a most satisfactory account of the rising commonwealth.
We trust that steps will be taken to acknowledge the independence of the Dominican Republic. The sympathies of our race, Caucasian as it is, must be with the whites of the Dominican Republic struggling with the African race of Hayti.—The interests of the United States should also prompt us to feel a deep interest in this new nation, as our object is to extend our commercial relations with every country, but particularly with the West India islands. We wish to cultivate friendship with these, our next door neighbors. We cannot be insensible to the fact that England has her naval depots in one of these West India islands. That France has her home to fly to—that these little ocean gems of islands belong to European monarchies, except St. Domingo, (where a black government, with which we can have no sympathies, and certainly they have none for us,) rules with despotic sway. Does not our interest prompt us to cherish the effort of a white people to create an independent Republic in one of these islands? In case of a war with any European power, we should have a friendly naval power in the West Indies whose feelings, sympathies and government were all republican, and certainly more in favor of our system than any other power? The Dominican Republic has several fine harbors—good timber for ship building. Is it not right we should look for a refuge for our naval force in time of trouble?
The population of the Republic is about 220,000, and the country is capable of sustaining a population ten times beyond that which it now has.
There is very little doubt of the ability of the Dominican Republic to maintain its independence. It has cannon, military stores, about 7000 military men, and can in an emergency raise 25,000 capable of bearing arms. It also has a small naval force. There is reason to believe that the Haytiens will find it a difficult matter to attack the Dominicans. The negroes (Haytiens) are in disunion and incapable of making a vigorous assault on the whites of the Dominican Republic. Let not Congress hesitate to take the necessary steps to acknowledge the independence of the Dominican Republic.

records.headline: The harbors, commerce, and military defenses of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: The harbors, commerce, and military defenses of the Dominican Republic are described in numbered paragraphs in The New York Herald. The report highlights the Bay of Ocoa in the south and the Bay of the Peninsula of Samaná in the northwest as secure anchorages for formidable squadrons, names St. Domingo, Puerto de Plata, Azua, Samaná, and Monte Christi as the principal trade ports, and notes constant commerce with St. Thomas, Curaçao, the United States, France, England, and Germany in mahogany, tobacco, sugar, hides, wax, honey, and woods. It further states that St. Domingo, Santiago, and Puerto Plata are fortified with artillery, while fortifications are in progress at Azua and along the frontier to prevent aggression. Finally, the report credits the Republic with ample cannon, ammunition, a well-supplied arsenal, 18,000 men capable of bearing arms—half currently on duty—and four armed vessels built at Curaçao, consisting of one brig and three schooners.

records.full_text:
There has been an arrival at New York from St. Domingo, bringing dates to the 22d November.

A battle is reported to have taken place on the 27th of October, between the Dominican and Haytien armies. It commenced by attacking a fort, which the Haytiens occupied.

After a combat of two hours, the Dominicans entered and took possession of the fort, and completely destroyed the enemy, killing 350 Haytiens, and making a prize of two pieces of cannon, 8 drums, and all the musical instruments belonging to the 28th regiment of the Cape, 3 flags and more than 200 muskets.

The blockade promulgated on the 5th September, is a mere paper affair, there being not a solitary Haytien vessel to enforce it. A few vessels were preparing by the Dominicans to cruise around the coast, they appearing determined to sustain their independence, having been victorious in all the battles since the revolution last year.

records.headline: Effects of the News from Hayti.
records.summary_en: The *Anti-slavery Bugle* reported that letters published regarding St. Domingo caused widespread amazement and excitement in Congress and across the United States and Europe, completely overshadowing the Oregon and Texas questions. The published information claimed that 5,000 to 10,000 men could easily conquer the Black-occupied portion of the island within forty-eight hours to restore it to the white race, and that the Dominican government would accept such assistance from U.S. citizens.
records.summary_es: El *Anti-slavery Bugle* consignó que las cartas divulgadas sobre Santo Domingo provocaron general asombro y revuelo en el Congreso, en todo Estados Unidos y en Europa, opacando enteramente los litigios de Oregón y Texas. La información publicada sostenía que entre 5.000 y 10.000 hombres podrían subyugar con facilidad en cuarenta y ocho horas la porción de la isla ocupada por negros para devolverla a la raza blanca, y que el gobierno dominicano admitiría gustoso ese auxilio de ciudadanos estadounidenses.

records.full_text: Your number of yesterday, which arrived here this morning, containing the important news from your correspondents in Hayti and St. Domingo, fell like a bomb shell among all the politicians, from the Capitol to the White House, and throughout every hotel, tavern, and oyster cellar in the city.— 'Have you seen the Herald this morning?' said one. 'No; what is in it?' said the person spoken to—'Why the d—l,' the first would reply—'go get a copy, and read for yourself.' But alas, for his comfort, there were no Heralds to be found after nine o'clock. Every place where one could be found was secured in order to read the news from St. Domingo, which filled one entire page of interesting and important matter. In both Houses of Congress might be seen groups of members talking together upon the subject, perfectly amazed, and wondering at Bennett's industry in getting such information even in advance of the government. Nothing that has appeared on the tapis during the last ten years was calculated to cause more excitement throughout this country and Europe, than the information thrown before the public in those letters, respecting that island in your columns. Oregon and Texas are completely cast in the shade by them, and it would not surprise me much, were I to see 10,000 men in their way to that island before one month. They want such a force there at this time, in order to rescue the island from negro domination, and restore it to the white race, to whom it properly belongs. I have heard a gentleman say, who had just returned from there, that five thousand able-bodied men, in addition to the Dominican forces, would conquer, in forty-eight hours the whole of that part occupied by the blacks. There are no existing treaties between the United States and Hayti, to prevent our citizens from going there in any character they please, and I know from what I have learned on the subject, that assistance of this sort would be accepted by the Dominican government, and ample provision made for those who would emigrate there for the purpose of sustaining the white government and people against the black savages, with whom they are contending for liberty and independence.

records.headline: The paper presents a version of the island's recent history in which the eastern portion became a part and parcel of the Republic of Haiti
records.summary_en: The paper presents a version of the island's recent history in which the eastern portion became a part and parcel of the Republic of Haiti and, in the paper's words, the Dominicans adopted the Haitian government voluntarily. The same account says France, with an overwhelming force in Port-au-Prince harbor, demanded an indemnity of 150,000,000 francs and then acknowledged Haiti's independence, that a vigorous attempt to obtain similar acknowledgment from the United States failed because slaveholders' interests prevailed, and that about three years since, after Herard was elected President, the Spanish part declared itself independent.

records.summary_en: Under the headline "Restoration of St. Domingo to Spain," the Spirit of Jefferson reports that the Philadelphia U.S. Gazette quotes a recent Port au Prince newspaper stating that the Spanish fleet lately reported at Havana has arrived at St. Domingo. According to the report, the fleet established a protectorate over the Dominican Republic with the approbation of the Dominican President and Bishop Portes. The item adds that the Black government of the other part of the island, controlled by President Pierrot, is menaced by France over insults offered to the French Consul at the Cape, for which an indemnity is demanded.

records.headline: The New York Herald reports from Puerto Plata that the prisoners
records.summary_en: The New York Herald reports from Puerto Plata that the prisoners taken include a brother-in-law of President Pierrot, as well as a Dominican deserter who was condemned to death by court-martial and whose appeal for mercy was referred by the President to Congress, scheduled to convene on February 2. Citing El Dominicano of January 18, the paper states that some captured officers declared their instructions from President Pierrot were that, upon taking Samaná and Puerto Plata, all males regardless of age and all females under five were to be massacred, women over forty tied back-to-back and conveyed to the Cape, and younger women left to the captors' discretion. Meanwhile, the Dominican sloop-of-war Cibao (formerly the Alert) arrived from St. Thomas on the 15th ult. to proceed to Puerto Plata, and the newly purchased American schooner J. W. Failer and Danish brig Carlota were being equipped as men-of-war. The report adds that the Dominicans appeared settled in their policy and anxious for peace to pursue a career founded on encouraging foreigners and a liberal system of government.
records.summary_es: El New York Herald informa desde Puerto Plata que entre los prisioneros capturados se encuentran un cuñado del presidente Pierrot y un desertor dominicano condenado a muerte en consejo de guerra, cuya apelación de clemencia fue remitida por el presidente al Congreso, convocado para el 2 de febrero. Citando a El Dominicano del 18 de enero, el periódico señala que algunos oficiales capturados declararon que sus instrucciones del presidente Pierrot ordenaban que, una vez tomados Samaná y Puerto Plata, todos los varones sin excepción de edad y todas las niñas menores de cinco años fueran pasados a cuchillo, las mujeres mayores de cuarenta años atadas espalda con espalda y conducidas al Cabo, y las más jóvenes dejadas a discreción de los captores. Entretanto, la corbeta de guerra dominicana Cibao (antes Alert) llegó de San Tómas el día 15 del mes anterior para dirigirse a Puerto Plata, y la goleta estadounidense J. W. Failer y el bergantín danés Carlota, recién comprados por el gobierno dominicano, estaban siendo equipados como buques de guerra. El informe añade que los dominicanos parecían firmes en su política y ansiosos de paz para emprender una etapa fundada en el fomento de la inmigración extranjera y en un sistema liberal de gobierno.

records.full_text:
Here we have accounts from St. Domingo, the city, to the 10th of February. The Dominicans were expecting the attack of the Haytiens, with good courage and preparations. There was a report current that Acaau had been moving again and had massacred some mulattoes at the Anse d' Hainault. Also that a Dominican vessel, the Trinidad, had been chased to Turk's Islands by the French man-of-war Virginie, but that the English Governor of the islands had given her protection. Also, that a Haytien war schooner had been wrecked in going from Turk's Islands to Cape Haytien.

It was believed at St. Domingo that the U. S. Government had recognized the Dominican republic, and that a U. S. ship of war, with a consul on board, would soon arrive at St. Domingo.

The story prevailed, also, that a Spanish squadron from Cuba was coming to protect the Dominicans against the Haytiens.

records.headline: From Hayti.
records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported that news reached Cape Haytien that the people of St. Mark's and Port-au-Prince, as well as the southern part of the island, had revolted against President Perriot and refused to march against the Spanish portion of the island. The populace chose General Rishere as the new President, who marched toward Port-au-Prince while it was believed President Perriot would resign. Additionally, a Spanish fleet that sailed from St. Domingo city to Cape Haytien had settled matters to its satisfaction and returned to St. Domingo city.
records.summary_es: El *New York Herald* notificó que llegaron noticias a Cabo Haitiano de que los habitantes de Saint-Marc y Puerto Príncipe, así como los de la banda meridional de la isla, se sublevaron contra el presidente Pierrot y rehusaron emprender marcha contra la demarcación española. El vecindario proclamó mandatario al general Riché, quien avanzó hacia Puerto Príncipe entre rumores fundados de la inminente renuncia de Pierrot. Asimismo, una escuadra española que zarpó de la ciudad de Santo Domingo con rumbo a Cabo Haitiano compuso las diferencias a su entera satisfacción y tornó a la capital dominicana.

records.headline: Affairs in Mexico and Texas.
records.summary_en: The general in chief of the Spanish naval forces in the Antilles requested that the Dominican Republic respect the Spanish and exempt them from a supposed blockade. The Dominican government replied that no such blockade had been decreed by them, clarifying that any blockade had been declared by the Haytiens, and that Dominican naval demonstrations were intended only to prevent Haytien depredations and protect commerce. Following these exchanges of amity, the Spanish commanders and officers were invited ashore the next day, where they were received with profuse hospitality and departed with feelings of the warmest friendship.
records.summary_es: El general en jefe de las fuerzas navales españolas en las Antillas solicitó a la República Dominicana que respetara a los españoles y los exonerara de un pretendido bloqueo. El gobierno dominicano replicó que jamás había dictado semejante medida, aclarando que cualquier bloqueo procedía exclusivamente de los haitianos y que sus evoluciones navales sólo procuraban contener las depredaciones de aquéllos y resguardar el tráfico mercantil. Tras estos testimonios de concordia, los comandantes y oficiales hispanos bajaron a tierra al día siguiente por invitación, siendo agasajados con esmerada hospitalidad y despidiéndose en un clima de la más cordial amistad.

The news from the city of Mexico is to the 21st of March. It is of no importance. records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
ADDRESS TO THE COLORED PEOPLE OF
THE U. S. OF NORTH AMERICA.

SAINT DOMINGO, July 10, 1847.
Dear Friends—We being native Americans who emigrated to this country in 1824, being now in body assembled, have resolved to offer to our brethren of the United States the law of emigration passed by our House of Congress, on the 5th inst. It invites all strangers here to participate in our glorious liberty, without distinction of color; and all who will come by this invitation, will have their passage paid at the rate of $14 per head; and those who will come with the avowed intention of becoming farmers will have, in addition to the payment of their passage, fifty acres of land, as a donation to them forever, together with the implements of husbandry, and a regular maintenance until they are able to maintain themselves; and they will be entirely exempt from military service, as also their offspring, in order that they may attend to the agricultural pursuits. We presume that this law can fully be depended on by all who may feel disposed to embrace its offers, as it is founded on necessity. As we have a very healthy climate, and perhaps one of the best soils in the world, with a generous population, all we stand in need of is American society—or in other words, tillers of the ground; in fact, by the aid of foreigners, this might be made a paradisiacal garden. We have the full right of the liberty of conscience. We have a Methodist church in the city of Port Plat; and in Samana, and one in this city, where we worship God according to the dictates of our consciences, without the least molestation. Our friends may depend on this information as being strictly true; and up to the present time we have a majority of colored population of more than two-thirds. We expect that many white people will accept this offer, as they seem generally more disposed for adventure than the colored. However, we hope that our friends will not let this fine opportunity pass, without embracing it.

There is a vessel engaged to bring out emigrants. She is consigned to the house of Messrs Amar & Co., New York. Persons interested will do well to call on the above gentlemen. Furthermore, should it become a general desire, any merchant who would choose to fit out a vessel, for the purpose of bringing out emigrants, will be sure to receive $14 a head, including all expenses, for as many as they will land here. If any merchant should like to have a guaranty, they could, by writing to our President on the subject. His name is ‘Pedro Santana,’ President of the Dominican Republic. It will not be as inconvenient to new comers hereafter as it was with us. We can give them all the necessary information how to conduct themselves in this country.

We remain, dear brethren, yours.
Signed in behalf of the meeting,
REV. JAMES FALLS, Chairman.
ELIJAH B. GROSS, Secretary.

records.summary_en: *The Liberator* reported that the deck of the vessel *Esturra* carried destitute refugees—some formerly wealthy—who had fled following a political confrontation in Port-au-Prince. According to the account, a deputation of influential men questioned President Soulouque regarding the reigning constitution, and upon being told the 1816 constitution was in effect, Senator Celigne Ardoin asserted that Soulouque was not president. When immediate orders were given for his arrest, Ardoin drew a pistol and fired at Soulouque, though the shot missed its mark.
records.summary_es: *The Liberator* reportó que sobre la cubierta del buque *Esturra* viajaban refugiados desamparados —algunos acomodados en el pasado— que huyeron a consecuencia de una refriega política en Puerto Príncipe. Según el relato, una comisión de personalidades interpeló al presidente Soulouque sobre el régimen constitucional imperante, y al responderles éste que regía la carta de 1816, el senador Céligny Ardouin replicó que Soulouque carecía de investidura presidencial. Al dictarse su inmediata detención, Ardouin extrajo una pistola y descerrajó un tiro contra Soulouque, sin acertar en el blanco.

records.full_text: The report which reached this island of unfortunate Hayti being again the scene of more human massacres has been proved to be too true, by the arrival in this port on Sunday last of the Dutch schooner Estarra, having on board one hundred and twenty-seven refugees, who have fled the country of their birth to seek protection here. The greater number of these persons are females and children, many of them in the greatest state of destitution. We are told that the deck of the Estarra presented a most distressing appearance—men, women, and children, were lying about with scarcely raiment to cover them. Some of them are said to have been wealthy, but were glad to escape with but one suit of clothes on their persons.

HAYTI.
By the arrival of the brig H. D. Brookman, at this port, from Port-au-Prince, we have later accounts from that island. The colored people who had fled from Port-au-Prince, had taken a stand at a place called 'Croix de Bouquet,' four leagues from the former place, and were secure for the present, in the hope that the army on the borders of the Dominican side of the island would come to their assistance, and enable them to remove from the Presidency the tyrant who has been the cause of such bloodshed. It is the opinion of the present refugees, that there could not have been less than two thousand lives sacrificed at Port-au-Prince.

records.headline: Interesting from the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that the Spanish colony of St. Domingo was never primarily agricultural, as early colonists were drawn instead by gold mining. Due to a lack of agricultural enterprise, industry, and the departure of enterprise toward Mexico, the colony became isolated and stagnated. Consequently, the higher and richer classes lost their energy and ambition, sinking into intellectual and physical sloth while agriculture and wealth declined.
records.summary_es: El órgano noticioso refirió que la colonia española de Santo Domingo jamás tuvo un carácter preponderantemente agrícola, atrayendo más bien a los primeros pobladores la explotación aurífera. A consecuencia de la desatención del cultivo, el desmayo industrial y la emigración de hombres activos hacia México, la colonia quedó aislada y estancada. En consecuencia, las clases encumbradas y acomodadas perdieron el empuje y la ambición, sumiéndose en la incuria intelectual y material al compás de la postración del campo y la pérdida de caudales.

records.headline: Writing from Santo Domingo City on July 8, 1848, a correspondent describes the Dominican Republic's land in detail
records.summary_en: Writing from Santo Domingo City on July 8, 1848, a correspondent describes the Dominican Republic's land in detail, from the Los Llanos plain and the Ozama River in the south to the Vega Real plain and the Yuna River, which flows into the Bay of Samana, in the north. He praises the soil as able to grow sugar cane and nearly every tropical and temperate crop, notes the timber, gold, copper and marble, and puts the population at between 150,000 and 200,000 people spread thinly over some 30,000 square miles.
records.summary_es: Escribiendo desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo el 8 de julio de 1848, un corresponsal describe en detalle el territorio de la República Dominicana, desde la llanura de Los Llanos y el río Ozama en el sur hasta la llanura de la Vega Real y el río Yuna, que desemboca en la bahía de Samana, en el norte. Elogia el suelo como capaz de producir caña de azúcar y casi todos los cultivos tropicales y de clima templado, menciona la madera, el oro, el cobre y el mármol, y calcula la población entre 150,000 y 200,000 personas repartidas escasamente en unas 30,000 millas cuadradas.
records.passage: rivers and smaller streams, the principal of which is the Ozama, at whose mouth this city stands. On the northern slope of the mountains lie the table and prairie lands, known as the Vega Real or Royal Plain. Through this flows the Yuna, the principal river on the north side, which discharges itself into the spacious bay of Samana, on the northeast, a second San Francisco. This latter tract of country, as well as much of the former, is unsurpassed, in the general fertility and varied productive capacity of its soil, by any equal extent of country on the face of the globe. Besides every species of tropical production, its soil is capable of producing abundantly, almost all those which are more peculiar to the temperate zones. Speaking of these two tracts, in reference particularly to the sugar cane, Edwards, the English historian of the West Indies, says, in substance, that they are probably capable of producing more than all the British West Indies together. Besides the kinds of woods so well known as the staples of the commerce of this part of the island, the mountains are said to abound in the choicest pine and cedar. Its gold mines, now for many years unwrought, are celebrated not more on account of their productiveness in former times, than from the fact that, to work them, African negro slave labor was first introduced into the New World. records.summary_en: The newspaper reflects critically on Christopher Columbus, stating that the chains brought back with his ashes from Spain to St. Domingo were emblematic of the cruel slavery his enterprise entailed upon the hemisphere. It describes the indigenous people of Hispaniola as simple and happy islanders whom Columbus initially found and claimed could be converted through love rather than force, yet asserts that Columbus sowed the fatal seed from which a horrible system of slavery sprang. Additionally, the text addresses labor and subsistence questions regarding the state or republic, arguing that people, their wives, and their children ought to support themselves with their own hands rather than rely on the labor of Indians.
records.summary_es: Partiendo de las líneas extractadas, el periódico formula un juicio severo sobre Cristóbal Colón, aduciendo que las cadenas trasladadas con sus cenizas desde España a Santo Domingo simbolizaban la despiadada servidumbre que su empresa acarreó al continente. Retrata a los aborígenes de La Española como isleños sencillos y venturosos que Colón halló en un principio, aseverando que podían ganarse por el afecto y no por el rigor, aunque imputa a Colón el haber sembrado el germen funesto del cual brotó un atroz sistema de esclavitud. Asimismo, el texto ventila cuestiones de trabajo y subsistencia cívica, sosteniendo que los hombres, sus consortes e hijos deben procurarse el sustento con el propio esfuerzo de sus manos antes que depender del sudor indígena.

records.full_text: The great Genoese, like other original discoverers, was a fanatic. His zealous faith, turned in whatever direction, has the same intensity, and leaps over all intermediate and subordinate particulars to the result. One chief object which he proposed to himself in exploring what he supposed would be a shorter passage to Indies, was that, in this way an army might be conducted by an easier route to Jerusalem to prosecute a new Crusade. Could Columbus have had a prophetic vision of the horrible fleet, freighted with its cargoes of festering humanity, that was to follow in his track, could he have known that those chains which were brought back with his ashes from Spain to St. Domingo were emblematic of the cruel Slavery which his magnificent enterprise entailed upon the hemisphere he discovered, perhaps he would have died in Genoa, known only as a dreamer to a few intimates

records.headline: A correspondent writing from the City of St. Domingo
records.summary_en: A correspondent writing from the City of St. Domingo on July 15, 1848, reports on the president's decree of February 22 organizing the civic guard, which required foreigners resident in the country for three months to enroll and serve alongside citizens. He says the decree caused great excitement among foreign residents, that the French representative protested and told them not to comply, that the United States commercial agent at Puerto Plata also protested on behalf of American citizens, and that the president then modified the penalties for foreigners in a supplemental decree of March 28.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal que escribe desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo el 15 de julio de 1848 informa sobre el decreto presidencial del 22 de febrero que organizaba la guardia cívica, el cual exigía que los extranjeros residentes en el país desde hacía tres meses se inscribieran y sirvieran junto a los ciudadanos. Dice que el decreto causó gran excitación entre los residentes extranjeros, que el representante francés protestó y les indicó no cumplirlo, que el agente comercial de los Estados Unidos en Puerto Plata también protestó en nombre de los ciudadanos estadounidenses, y que el presidente entonces modificó las penas para los extranjeros en un decreto suplementario del 28 de marzo.

The French consular representative and the United States commercial agent at Puerto Plata both protested, and the President modified the decree on March 28 so that foreigners, who enjoy no political rights, could not be made part of the permanent army and would face only arrest and the small prescribed fines.

records.full_text:
Late from St. Domingo.
The schooner Mary and Elizabeth arrived here yesterday afternoon from Mariagone, St. Domingo, which place she left the 7th instant. Capt. Smith informs us that President Soulouque had, after a severe battle, taken from the Dominicans the towns of Las Matas and St. John, in which a great many of the Dominicans were killed and taken prisoners. Many of them escaped, abandoning five large pieces of artillery and a 6-pounder.

The above attack took place on the morning of the 18th March. Gens. Bobo, Vincent and Michel were left in possession of the captured towns, and the President with his troops left on the 19th for Port au Prince.

Three hundred troops from Jeremie passed through Mariagone on the 2d inst., on their way to Port au Prince to join the President. Men were gathering from all directions to join the President, who would shortly make another attack on the Dominicans.—N. Y. Tribune.

records.summary_en: The New York Herald reports a hotly contested battle in which the Haytiens reportedly lost 100 to 200 men and 300 to 400 Dominicans were killed, along with a number of women and children slain in Azua when the town fell to the conquerors, though accounts do not report general plunder or indiscriminate slaughter. A large quantity of provisions, 5,000 stand of arms, and many prisoners fell into Haytien hands, and from Azua, Soloque continued his march toward the city of St. Domingo, which the paper states would probably fall along with Santiago and the whole Spanish part of the island. A passenger from the Cape describes the portion of the Haytien army that started from that quarter as barefoot, ragged, penniless, and without food, obliged to live by forced contributions upon their own countrymen until reaching the frontier, adding that the Commanding General reportedly begged biscuits from a vessel in port before departing.

records.summary_en: The Daily National Intelligencer reports a hotly contested battle at Azua between the Haytiens and Dominicans that resulted in the rout of the Dominicans, with 100 to 200 Haytiens and 300 to 400 Dominicans killed. A number of women and children were also slain in Azua as the town fell into the conquerors' possession, though the accounts do not indicate general plunder or indiscriminate slaughter of its inhabitants. The Haytiens captured a large quantity of provisions, 5,000 stand of arms, and many prisoners. From Azua, President Solouque continued his march toward the city of St. Domingo, which the paper notes would probably fall into his hands along with Santiago and the entire Spanish part of the island.

Varias mujeres y niños también perecieron en Azua cuando la población cayó en poder de los conquistadores, aunque los relatos no señalan un saqueo general ni una matanza indiscriminada de sus habitantes. records.headline: Later from St. Domingo.
records.summary_en: *The Daily Crescent* reported via arrivals from the brig *Stephen G. Ross* that Haitian President Soulouque was advancing within 16 miles of Santo Domingo City with an army of 30,000 troops. Residents were fleeing the anticipated attack, with British vessels crowded with refugees and valuables deposited with American and British consuls for safekeeping. The city was largely deserted by women and children, and it was feared that Soulouque had already captured it with significant bloodshed.
records.summary_es: *The Daily Crescent* comunicó, con base en despachos traídos por el bergantín *Stephen G. Ross*, que el presidente haitiano Soulouque marchaba a unas dieciséis millas de la ciudad de Santo Domingo con un ejército de treinta mil hombres. records.summary_en: The *Daily National Intelligencer* reported that the Haitian army under President Soulouque was completely routed in the Dominican Republic, leaving behind numerous dead, artillery, munitions, and captured battle flags. Dominican forces recaptured Azua on April 21, with General Santana advancing across the border in aggressive pursuit. The report also reprinted a proclamation from Soulouque urging the eastern inhabitants to submit to the Haitian republic.

Las fuerzas dominicanas recuperaron Azua el 21 de abril, avanzando el general Santana a través de la frontera en decidida persecución. La reseña reprodujo asimismo una proclama de Soulouque exhortando a los habitantes del Este a someterse a la república de Haití.

records.headline: Soulouque, the Haytien President, and his forces from the town of Azera
records.summary_en: According to the *Arkansas State Gazette* reporting on information from the *Evening Post*, Dominican General Santa Anna defeated Haitian President Soulouque and his forces in a severe contest at the town of Azera, driving the Haitians completely out of Dominican territory. The report noted that the retreating Haitians burned Azera and suffered the loss of 500 troops and two principal generals, Geffrad and Paul Jean Jacque. Additionally, the newspaper reported that a severe earthquake had caused considerable damage at Maracaibo.
records.summary_es: A juicio de la *Arkansas State Gazette*, con base en informes del *Evening Post*, el general dominicano Santana derrotó al presidente haitiano Soulouque y a sus huestes en un encarnizado choque en la villa de Azua [nombrada Azera], arrojando enteramente a los haitianos fuera del suelo dominicano. La noticia puntualizaba que los invasores incendiaron Azua en su retirada, sufriendo la pérdida de quinientos soldados y de dos destacados generales, Geffrard y Paul Jean Jacques. Se añadía por otra parte que un violento terremoto ocasionó cuantiosos estragos en Maracaibo.
