records.headline: General Santa Anna then withdrew from the army, and retired to his plantation
records.summary_en: President Hernannes met troops on the outskirts of the city and claimed command, prompting General Santa Anna to briefly retire to his plantation before troops requested he lead them, leading him to march on the city after President Hernannes ordered the burning of Don Carlos. It was anticipated that Santa Anna would capture St. Domingo City and be declared President of the Dominican Government. Additionally, reports from the schooner *Silas E. Hand* noted that island affairs were discouraging for peace and commerce, and that the President falsely claimed victory in dispatches following an unsuccessful expedition against the Spanish part of the island where his army lost all its cannon.
records.summary_es: El presidente Jimenes [Hernannes] salió al encuentro de las fuerzas en los arrabales urbanos arrogándose el mando, induciendo al general Santana a retirarse brevemente a su hacienda hasta que la tropa le solicitó encabezarla, lo que le llevó a avanzar sobre la capital una vez que Jimenes decretó el incendio de San Carlos [Don Carlos]. Se calculaba que Santana reduciría la ciudad de Santo Domingo y sería aclamado presidente de la República Dominicana. Además, despachos traídos por la goleta *Silas E. Hand* pintaban un cuadro desalentador para la paz y el comercio insulares, señalando que el gobernante haitiano se atribuía falsas victorias tras una fallida expedición contra la banda española en la que su ejército perdió toda la artillería.

records.headline: The Daily Union first notes that President Soulouque has dispersed
records.summary_en: The Daily Union first notes that President Soulouque has dispersed the troops of the unsuccessful expedition against the Spanish part of the island and ordered the soldiers to return to their occupations. Under a subsequent heading from St. Domingo, intelligence brought by the brig L. W. Armstrong, 16 days from St. Domingo, reports that when the Haytiens were within one day's march of the city, Santana was called on by the Dominican government to lead the army and totally defeated them. The provinces then declared President Jimenes no longer fit to govern and empowered Santana to form a new government, whereupon Jimenes fortified the city of St. Domingo against Santana's army, firing 236 cannon against them at the walls and destroying the town of St. Carlos by fire. After the American consul refused Jimenes's demand to surrender the women, children, and refugees in his house, Jimenes attempted to arrest him with armed men—prevented by the French and English consuls—and directed two 32-pounder cannon against his house, prompting a consultation among the three consuls and the commanders of a French corvette-of-war and the 8-gun English sloop Hound.
records.summary_es: El Daily Union señala primero que el presidente Soulouque ha dispersado las tropas de la fallida expedición contra la parte española de la isla y ordenado a los soldados regresar a sus ocupaciones. Bajo un titular posterior sobre Santo Domingo, las noticias traídas por el bergantín L. W. Armstrong, a 16 días de Santo Domingo, informan que cuando los haitianos estaban a un día de marcha de la ciudad, Santana fue llamado por el gobierno dominicano para encabezar el ejército y los derrotó totalmente. Las provincias declararon entonces al presidente Jimenes incapaz de gobernar y otorgaron a Santana el poder de formar un nuevo gobierno, ante lo cual Jimenes fortificó la ciudad de Santo Domingo contra el ejército de Santana, disparando 236 cañonazos contra ellos en las murallas y destruyendo por el fuego el pueblo de San Carlos. Luego de que el cónsul estadounidense rechazara la exigencia de Jimenes de entregar a las mujeres, niños y refugiados alojados en su casa, Jimenes intentó arrestarlo con hombres armados —lo que fue impedido por los cónsules francés e inglés— y apuntó dos cañones de 32 libras contra su residencia, motivando una consulta entre los tres cónsules y los comandantes de una corbeta de guerra francesa y de la balandra inglesa de 8 cañones Hound.

records.summary_en: Under the headline "Late from St. Domingo," the Lynchburg Virginian reports via the brig L. W. Armstrong, 16 days from St. Domingo, that when the Haytiens were within one day's march of the city, Santana was called on by the Dominican government to lead the army and totally defeated them. The provinces then declared President Jimenes unfit to govern and authorized Santana to form a new government, prompting Jimenes to fortify the city of St. Domingo against Santana's army, fire cannon against them at the walls, and destroy the town of St. Carlos by fire. When the American consul refused Jimenes's demand to surrender the women, children, and refugees sheltered in his house, Jimenes attempted to arrest him with armed men—prevented by the French and English consuls—and directed two 35-pounder cannon against his house. In a consultation among the three consuls and the commanders of the French corvette Griffon and the 8-gun English sloop Hound, the French commander replied to the American consul's request for assistance that he could only protect his own consul and the inmates of his house.

Cuando el cónsul estadounidense rechazó la exigencia de Jimenes de entregar a las mujeres, niños y refugiados albergados en su casa, Jimenes intentó arrestarlo con hombres armados —lo que fue impedido por los cónsules francés e inglés— y apuntó dos cañones de 35 libras contra su residencia. En una consulta entre los tres cónsules y los comandantes de la corbeta francesa Griffon y la balandra inglesa de 8 cañones Hound, el comandante francés respondió a la solicitud de auxilio del cónsul estadounidense que solo podía proteger a su propio cónsul y a los ocupantes de su casa.

records.headline: The New York Herald reports from an arrival from Port au Platt
records.summary_en: The New York Herald reports from an arrival from Port au Platt that on the 18th ult. a Dominican man-of-war brig sailed from Port au Platt for St. Domingo carrying forty prisoners taken at Santiago during a rebellion, and that by the 24th ult. all was quiet and a large quantity of tobacco was arriving from the interior. An accompanying correspondence dated Port au Platt, July 28, 1849, under the headings of the Dominican Republic, President Soulouque, the expulsion of Ximenes, and reviving business, argues that the enemies of the Dominican Republic always deduce disastrous results from simple causes. The correspondent maintains that when a government enjoys popular feeling, suffrage, and the steady administration of justice based on wise and just laws, occasional popular effervescences do not signal the decay or destruction of the republic. The letter adds that the pompous denunciations and rhodomontades of Haytien President Soulouque during his invasion have met with failure.
records.summary_es: El New York Herald informa, a partir de una embarcación llegada de Puerto Plata, que el día 18 del mes anterior un bergantín de guerra dominicano zarpó de Puerto Plata hacia Santo Domingo con cuarenta prisioneros tomados en Santiago durante una rebelión, y que para el día 24 todo estaba en calma y llegaba una gran cantidad de tabaco desde el interior. Una correspondencia adjunta fechada en Puerto Plata el 28 de julio de 1849, bajo los epígrafes de la República Dominicana, el presidente Soulouque, la expulsión de Jimenes y la reanimación de los negocios, sostiene que los enemigos de la República Dominicana siempre deducen resultados desastrosos de causas simples. El corresponsal afirma que cuando un gobierno cuenta con el apoyo del sentimiento popular, el sufragio y la administración constante de la justicia basada en leyes sabias y justas, las efervescencias populares ocasionales no son señal de decadencia ni de destrucción de la república. La carta añade que las pomposas denuncias y fanfarronadas del presidente haitiano Soulouque durante su invasión han fracasado.

También informa de un comercio activo en el norte a través de Puerto Plata, con considerables envíos de tabaco esperados pese a que los cultivadores habían sido enrolados como soldados.

records.headline: The Richmond Enquirer questions what the Whigs will say to the "lust
records.summary_en: The Richmond Enquirer questions what the Whigs will say to the "lust for foreign territory" manifested by the Taylor administration, citing a rumor from Whig sources reprinted from the Turk's Island Royal Gazette of September 20. According to the Royal Gazette, an American ship-of-war had arrived at St. Domingo carrying Mr. Green, son of General Duff Green, on a mission from the United States Government to the Dominican general for the purpose of making overtures to annex the Dominicans to the United States, they having expressed a wish to be taken into the Union. The report adds that Mr. Green is fully authorized to treat with the Dominican Government on this subject and had just returned from Havana, where he had been on urgent business for his government.
records.summary_es: El Richmond Enquirer se pregunta qué dirán los whigs ante la «codicia de territorio extranjero» manifestada por la administración de Taylor, citando un rumor procedente de fuentes whigs reproducido de la Royal Gazette de Islas Turcas del 20 de septiembre. Según la Royal Gazette, un buque de guerra estadounidense había llegado a Santo Domingo con el Sr. Green, hijo del general Duff Green, en una misión del gobierno de los Estados Unidos ante el general dominicano con el propósito de realizar gestiones para anexar a los dominicanos a los Estados Unidos, habiendo ellos expresado el deseo de ser admitidos en la Unión. El informe añade que el Sr. Green está plenamente autorizado para tratar este asunto con el gobierno dominicano y que acababa de regresar de La Habana, donde había estado atendiendo asuntos urgentes de su gobierno.

records.headline: The Shepherdstown Register prints the concluding portion of a proclamation
records.summary_en: The Shepherdstown Register prints the concluding portion of a proclamation issued at St. Domingo by President Buenaventura Baez and countersigned by the Minister of War. In the statement, Baez declares that Dominican proposals for a mutual exchange of tobacco and other products for coffee have been rejected by the opposing rulers. He warns that all the horrors of war will consequently fall upon the heads of those rulers and upon the people who fail to compel them to adopt better measures.
records.summary_es: El Shepherdstown Register publica la parte final de una proclama emitida en Santo Domingo por el presidente Buenaventura Báez y refrendada por el ministro de Guerra. En la declaración, Báez afirma que las propuestas dominicanas para un intercambio mutuo de tabaco y otros productos por café han sido rechazadas por los gobernantes adversarios. Advierte que todos los horrores de la guerra recaerán en consecuencia sobre las cabezas de dichos gobernantes y sobre el pueblo que no los obligue a adoptar mejores medidas.

records.headline: A French paper states that Emperor Faustin I has dispatched a principal member of the Haitian Senate as envoy
records.summary_en: A French paper states that Emperor Faustin I has dispatched a principal member of the Haitian Senate as envoy extraordinary to the Holy See at Rome. It says he is sent to obtain from the Pope the creation of several bishopricks and two archbishopricks in the new empire, and the appointment of the Emperor's almoner Sylvester to one of the bishopricks.

records.headline: Under the headline "From St. Domingo," the Daily Richmond Times reprints
records.summary_en: Under the headline "From St. Domingo," the Daily Richmond Times reprints a report from the New York Commercial based on information from Captain Smith of the barque Nacochee, who left St. Domingo on February 16. According to Captain Smith, the Dominican Republic had a fleet of one ship, two brigs, and seven schooners ready for sea at the time of his departure. He further reported that on Sunday night, February 10, the Frenchman commanding one of the brigs of war, who had been promoted to commodore the previous day, was attacked on shore and beaten so severely by a Black man that he was not expected to recover, and that the assailant was scheduled to be shot on the morning of February 16.
records.summary_es: Bajo el titular «Desde Santo Domingo», el Daily Richmond Times reproduce un informe del New York Commercial basado en datos del capitán Smith, de la barca Nacochee, quien salió de Santo Domingo el 16 de febrero. Según el capitán Smith, al momento de su partida la República Dominicana contaba con una flota de una fragata, dos bergantines y siete goletas lista para hacerse a la mar. Informó además que en la noche del domingo 10 de febrero el comandante francés de uno de los bergantines de guerra, quien había sido ascendido a comodoro el día anterior, fue atacado en tierra y golpeado tan severamente por un hombre negro que no se esperaba que sobreviviera, y que el agresor iba a ser fusilado en la mañana del 16 de febrero.

records.headline: Under the heading "A Dominican Hero," the Lancaster Gazette reports
records.summary_en: Under the heading "A Dominican Hero," the Lancaster Gazette reports that General William Penson arrived at New York from St. Domingo aboard the schooner Dacoiah. The paper describes Penson as a Dominican who was educated and naturalized in the United States. According to the notice, during the recent invasion of the Dominican Republic by the Haytiens, Penson led fifty men in an attack against five hundred Haytiens, dispersing them with heavy losses and killing one general and three colonels with his own hand.
records.summary_es: Bajo el título «Un Héroe Dominicano», la Lancaster Gazette informa que el general William Penson llegó a Nueva York procedente de Santo Domingo a bordo de la goleta Dacoiah. El periódico describe a Penson como un dominicano educado y naturalizado en los Estados Unidos. Según la nota, durante la reciente invasión de la República Dominicana por los haitianos, Penson encabezó a cincuenta hombres en un ataque contra quinientos haitianos, dispersándolos con grandes pérdidas y dando muerte por su propia mano a un general y tres coroneles.

records.summary_en: The Daily Richmond Times reports advices from the Dominican Republic up to April 14, brought to New York by Captain Ogier of the schooner Cabot, stating that tranquility prevailed although fears of further invasion interfered with commercial activity. According to the report, the U.S. steamer Vixen arrived at the city of St. Domingo on March 28 and was expected to depart for Washington in a few days with Mr. Green, the American chargé, on board. Green brings home an elaborately carved solid mahogany altar weighing about ten tons and measuring 44 by 26 feet as a gift from the Roman Catholic Archbishop at St. Domingo to the Archbishop at Baltimore, while a Castilian family presented Dr. Bell, surgeon of the Vixen, with a Magdalen said to be painted by Murillo in acknowledgment of his surgical skill and attention at various ports.

records.full_text:
ST. DOMINGO.—Capt. Ogler, of the schooner Cabot, from the city of St: Domingo, the capital of the Dominican republic, April 14th, reports affairs there tranquil. Apprehension was entertained of further invasion from the blacks of the West End, which keeps the Dominicans in a constant attitude of defence and uncertainty, preventing productive labor, and destroying commerce.

The United States steamer Vixen, Lieutenant Commanding Ward, arrived at the city of St. Domingo on the 28th of March—all well. The Vixen was to sail for Washington in a few days with the United States chargé, Mr. Green. The Vixen takes home a magnificent altar, highly wrought with carved work, in solid mahogany—a present, through Mr. Green, from the Archbishop of St. Domingo to the Archbishop of Baltimore. It is in size 44 by 26 feet, weighs ten tons, and belonged to the ruined chapel of the Jesuit college. The Vixen has also a superb painting, a Magdalen, by “Murillo”—a present, from an ancient but decayed Castilian family, to the surgeon of the vessel, “Dr. Bell,” in token of gratitude for the numerous delicate and skilful professional operations performed among all classes of inhabitants who have come to him from various parts of the island.—New York Journal of Commerce.

records.headline: An editorial in the New York Herald promotes American emigration
records.summary_en: An editorial in the New York Herald promotes American emigration to the Dominican Republic—referred to in the passage as "Dominica" and the "republic of Dominica"—stating that there is room in St. Domingo for a hundred thousand agriculturists and no law preventing emigrants from going there as fast as they please for any purpose. The paper declares that the empire of Hayti has no political existence with the United States and is not recognized by it. Expressing a lack of faith in a cabinet it describes as composed mainly of avowed abolitionists, the Herald urges Congress to call for all State Department papers on the subject, including secret agents' reports and instructions, correspondence with the French and Spanish ministers, and the memorials, petitions, and 1841 ministerial letters from the people of "Dominica" placed on file under Secretaries Calhoun, Buchanan, and Clayton, so that Congress may take instant measures for recognition.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del New York Herald promueve la emigración estadounidense hacia la República Dominicana —llamada en el pasaje «Dominica» y «república de Dominica»—, afirmando que en Santo Domingo hay cabida para cien mil agricultores y que ninguna ley impide a los emigrantes dirigirse allí con cualquier propósito. El periódico declara que el imperio de Haití no tiene existencia política para los Estados Unidos ni cuenta con su reconocimiento. Expresando desconfianza hacia un gabinete al que describe como compuesto principalmente por abolicionistas declarados, el Herald insta al Congreso a solicitar todos los documentos del Departamento de Estado sobre la materia, incluidos los informes e instrucciones de agentes secretos, la correspondencia con los ministros de Francia y España, y los memoriales, peticiones y cartas ministeriales de 1841 del pueblo de «Dominica» archivados bajo los secretarios Calhoun, Buchanan y Clayton, a fin de que el Congreso tome medidas inmediatas para su reconocimiento.

records.headline: English abolitionists, it is said, are intriguing for the purpose of aiding the blacks to conquer the Spanish Dominicans
records.summary_en: The newspaper reported various speculations regarding the future of Hayti and the Spanish Dominicans, including plans by English abolitionists to aid blacks in conquering the Dominicans and buying Cuba, Spain intervening to conquer Faustin I. and bring St. Domingo under the Captain-generalship of Cuba, or United States adventurers aiding Dominicans to expel blacks and pursue annexation. Additionally, it noted that Hayti owes approximately $1,500,000 in original claims to U.S. citizens for past commercial depredations, as well as indemnities to France under a treaty with Charles X. Finally, the excerpt briefly mentioned that Mr. Clay appeared jaded and impatient regarding the adjustment bill due to fruitlessly discussed amendments.

Indicaba además que Haití adeudaba cerca de 1.500.000 duros en reclamaciones originarias a ciudadanos estadounidenses por pasados agravios mercantiles, amén de indemnizaciones a Francia dimanadas del tratado con Carlos X. Concluía refiriendo sumariamente que el Sr. Clay lucía fatigado e impaciente ante el debate estéril de enmiendas al proyecto de avenimiento.

records.headline: The New York Herald contrasts the alarming disorganization
records.summary_en: The New York Herald contrasts the alarming disorganization, diminishing exports, and outrages against inhabitants and foreign traders in Haiti with the condition of the Dominican Republic. According to the paper, the Spanish population created the 'republic of Dominica,' which holds two-thirds of the island's territory and the best-fortified towns, yet remains threatened by the troops of the Haitian emperor. Although the Dominicans broke away without means and almost without hope, they established a liberal commercial system and an honest, effective currency, and are now reaping the reward of their enterprise even as they face the threat of a disastrous invasion.

records.headline: Citing the New-York Tribune and advices from the brig Moselle
records.summary_en: Citing the New-York Tribune and advices from the brig Moselle, which left the island on the 3d instant, The Southern Press reports that the Haitian Emperor had not yet departed on his intended expedition to the Spanish part of the island, though he was still making preparations and his departure time remained uncertain. A second item from the Baltimore Sun notes that an earlier translation from a Havana paper suggesting that the difficulties between St. Domingo and Haiti had been finally settled is not fully borne out. According to a Kingston paper of the 14th instant, the British Government has ratified its treaty with the Dominican Republic and will mediate between that republic and Haiti, with the representatives of France and the United States also reportedly taking an interest in the settlement.
records.summary_es: Citando al New-York Tribune y noticias del bergantín Moselle, que partió de la isla el día 3 del corriente, The Southern Press informa que el emperador haitiano aún no había salido en su proyectada expedición hacia la parte española de la isla, aunque seguía haciendo preparativos y la fecha de su marcha permanecía incierta. Una segunda nota del Baltimore Sun señala que una traducción anterior de un periódico de La Habana, que daba a entender que las dificultades entre Santo Domingo y Haití se habían resuelto definitivamente, no se confirma del todo. Según un periódico de Kingston del día 14 del corriente, el Gobierno británico ha ratificado su tratado con la República Dominicana y mediará entre dicha república y Haití, habiéndose interesado también en el arreglo, según se dice, los representantes de Francia y de los Estados Unidos.

records.full_text: St. Lucia.—St. Lucia continued to be deluged with rain, accompanied at times with high winds. At other times a dead calm prevailed, with most oppressive heat. As the manufacturing process had closed on nearly all the sugar estates, the planters were not so much inconvenienced by the weather as they otherwise would have been. Attention was being paid to the young canes. Good accounts are given of the young cotton plants put in as an experiment in different places. The crop of sugar is estimated at 1500 hogsheads less than last year.

citizen died on the 18th instant at his residence in Greenville,

records.summary_en: According to the *Daily National Intelligencer*, the Dominicans were actively preparing to meet the Haytiens with an army formed under the chief command of Santanna and plentiful supplies of arms and ammunition, alongside a fleet of ten vessels of war. The Republic of St. Domingo also celebrated the ratification of a treaty in which England acknowledged its independence from Hayti, during which the British Consul stated that England would not interfere in the coming contest and noted that British vessels would pay fifty cents less tonnage duty than American vessels. Additionally, the newspaper reported on disturbances in Arkansas involving the "Everett clan" in Marion and Searcy counties, resulting in the killing of Mr. Tutt and an attack on Major Hensley.

records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported on articles of agreement between the British dominions and the Dominican Republic, establishing reciprocal freedom of commerce and equal protection for their respective subjects and citizens. Specifically, Article 2 grants British subjects the right to reside in, trade freely within, and buy and sell without monopolies in the Dominican Republic under most-favored-nation privileges, with corresponding rights granted to Dominican citizens in British dominions. records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported that the Dominican Republic declared the slave trade to be an act of piracy punishable by death. To help prevent this trade, the republic agreed to permit British warships—acting under specific treaty instructions—to visit vessels sailing under the Dominican flag that are reasonably suspected of slave trading within twenty leagues of the Dominican coast. If suspicions are confirmed, the detained vessel is to be sent to Santo Domingo and delivered to local authorities for prosecution under Dominican law.

De comprobarse el delito, la presa sería remitida a Santo Domingo y consignada a los tribunales de la República para su procesamiento conforme al derecho patrio.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
IN THE NAME OF THE MOST HOLY TRINITY.
Her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and the President of the Dominican Republic, being desirous to consecrate the formal recognition of the independence of the same, and to conclude a treaty of peace and friendship, and to regulate thereby the commercial intercourse between the dominions and subjects of her Majesty, and the territories and citizens of the Republic, they have for this purpose named as their respective Plenipotentiaries, that is to say:—
Her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, Sir Robert Hermann Schomburgk, Doctor of Philosophy, Knight of the Royal Prussian Order of the Red Eagle, of the Royal Saxon Order of Merit; of the Legion of Honor of the French Republic; Her Consul to the Dominican Republic;
And the President of the Dominican republic, Senor Jose Maria Medrano, Minister Secretary of State for the departments of police and the interior, and charged with those of Justice, Public Instruction, and Foreign Affairs;
Who, after having communicated to each other their respective full powers, found in good and due form, have agreed upon and concluded the following articles:—
Art. 1. There shall be perpetual peace and friendship between her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, her heirs and successors, and the Dominican republic, and between their respective subjects and citizens.
Art. 2. There shall be reciprocal freedom of commerce between the British dominions and the Dominican republic. The subjects of her Britannic Majesty may reside in and trade to any part of the territories of the republic, to which any other foreigners are or shall be admitted. They shall enjoy full protection for their persons and properties. They shall be allowed to buy from and sell to whom they like without being restrained or affected by any monopoly, contract, or exclusive privilege of sale or purchase whatever; and they shall moreover enjoy all other rights and privileges which are or may be granted to any other foreigners, subjects or citizens of the most favored nation.
The citizens of the Dominican republic shall, in return, enjoy similar protection and privileges in the dominions of Her Britannic Majesty.
Art. 3. No tonnage, import or other duties or charges shall be levied in the Dominican republic on British vessels, or on goods imported or exported in British vessels, than are or may be provided to be levied on national vessels, or on the like goods imported or exported in national vessels; and in the same manner, no tonnage, import, or other duties or charges shall be levied in the British dominions on vessels of the republic, or on goods imported or exported in those vessels, beyond what are or may be levied on national vessels, or on the like goods imported or exported in national vessels; or from the ports upon the commerce, without prejudice whatever to the provisions of the fourth article, exclusively reserved to national vessels of each of the the two countries respectively.
Art. 4. Merchandise or goods coming from the British dominions in any vessels, or coming from British vessels from any country, shall not be prohibited in the Dominican republic, nor be subjected to higher duties than are levied on the same kinds of merchandise or goods, coming from any other foreign country, or imported in any other vessels.
All articles, the produce of the republic, may be exported therefrom by British subjects and British vessels, on as favorable terms as by the subjects and citizens and vessels of any other foreign country.
Art. 5. The protection of the government of the republic shall be afforded to all British vessels, their crews and goods. If any British vessel should be wrecked on the coast of the republic, the local authorities shall afford them aid, and secure them from plunder, and shall cause all articles saved from the wreck to be restored to their lawful owners. The amount of salvage dues in such cases shall be settled, in case of dispute, by arbitrators chosen by both parties.
Art. 6. It being the intention of the two contracting parties to bind themselves by the present treaty, to treat each other on the footing of the most favored nation, it is hereby agreed between them, that any favor, privilege, or immunity whatever in matters of commerce and navigation, which either contracting party has actually granted, or may hereafter grant, to the subjects or citizens of any other State, shall be extended to the subjects or citizens of the other contracting party, gratuitously, if the concession in favor of that other State shall have been gratuitous, or in return for a compensation as nearly as possible of proportionate value and effect, to be adjusted by mutual agreement if the concession shall have been conditional.
Art. 7. Each contracting party may appoint Consuls for the protection of its trade, in the dominions or territories of the other; but no such Consul shall enter upon the exercise of his functions until he shall have been admitted and approved, in the usual form, by the government of the country to which he is sent.
The respective agents and Consuls of each of the two contracting parties residing within the dominions or territories of the other, shall enjoy the same rights, immunities, privileges and exemptions which are or may be granted to the diplomatic agents or Consuls of equal rank, of the most favored nation.
Art. 8. The subjects of her Britannic Majesty residing in the Dominican republic shall not be disturbed, persecuted, or annoyed on account of their religion, but they shall have perfect liberty of conscience therein, and exercise their creed either within their own private houses, or in the said or particular chapels. Liberty shall also be granted to them to bury in the Dominican republic, in the manner, they may freely establish and maintain, their subjects who may die in the territories of the said republic. In like manner, the citizens of the Dominican republic shall enjoy, within all the dominions of Her Britannic Majesty, a perfect and entire liberty of conscience, and shall be allowed to exercise their religion publicly or privately, within their own dwelling houses, or in the chapels and places of worship appointed for that purpose.
Art. 9. Slavery being perpetually abolished in the Dominican republic, and having been already declared by her an act of piracy punishable with the pain of death, the Dominican republic engages to permit any British vessel of war, which may be furnished with special instructions under the treaties between Great Britain and foreign powers, and with the formalities as are provided for in such cases by the said treaties relative to the prevention of the infamous slave trade, to visit any vessels sailing under the Dominican flag, which may, upon reasonable grounds, be suspected of being engaged in this vile trade in slaves; it being understood that the distances and places between which the right of visit shall be exercised as restricted as they are in the treaties with other powers, for Cuba and Porto Rico, shall likewise refer to the same distance of twenty leagues from the coasts of the Dominican republic; and if, by the result of the visit, it shall appear to the officer in command of such British vessel of war that the suspicions of the commander are well grounded, the vessel shall be sent, without delay, to the port of Santo Domingo, in the Dominican republic, and shall be delivered up to the local authorities, to be proceeded against according to the laws of the republic.
It is understood that the present article shall not be extended to other cases, which might occasion a vexatious and unnecessary visit to the Dominican vessels in their voyages and commercial enterprises; but that, with the aid of the Dominican authorities, authorized to expect protection and assistance; and, if the case should arise, which, however, is not to be supposed, that the Dominican republic should receive a conviction of having suffered a vexatious molestation, it rests with her to withdraw it, after having given a year's previous notice thereof.
Art. 10. In order that the two contracting parties may have the opportunity of hereafter treating and agreeing upon such other arrangements as may tend still further to the improvement of their mutual interests, and to the promotion of the commerce of their respective subjects and citizens, it is agreed that the present treaty shall remain in force for the term of ten years from the date of the exchange of the ratifications, and either of the contracting parties shall have the right of giving to the other party notice of its intention to terminate at the expiration of the said ten years the stipulations of the present treaty; and the present treaty shall cease to be binding after ten years, and all notice that might be given and amity shall remain obligatory to both nations.
Art. 11. The present treaty shall be ratified, and the ratifications shall be exchanged at Santo Domingo, within the space of eight months, or sooner, if possible, counted from the date of this treaty, or sooner, if shall be possible.
In witness whereof, the respective plenipotentiaries have signed the same, and affixed thereto the seals of their arms.
Done at Santo Domingo, the sixth day of March, in the year of our Lord eighteen hundred and fifty.
(L. S.) ROBERT H. SCHOMBURGK.
(L. S.) JOSE MARIA MEDRANO.

ADDITIONAL ARTICLES.
As the circumstances of the Dominican with the Haytien nation might oblige the Dominican republic to modify the third article, it is hereby especially understood and agreed between the two contracting parties, that the Dominican republic shall have perfect liberty of making during the space of ten years such changes as she may think fit in her duties, notwithstanding the stipulation of article 3 aforesaid; but the subjects of her Britannic Majesty shall not be restrained or affected by any monopoly, contract or exclusive privilege of purchase or sale; and as her disposition is constant to afford and protect commerce, it should enter in her views to adopt any measures of limited or except in the case that the existing laws should continue.
The present additional article shall have the same force and validity as if it were inserted, word for word, in the treaty signed this day. It shall be ratified at the same time. And in consequence of the exception it contains, it is equally understood that the sanction or disapprobation of the treaty is specially reserved to Her Britannic Majesty.
In testimony whereof the undersigned have, in virtue of their full powers, signed and sealed the present article.
Done at Santo Domingo, the sixth day of March, in the year of our Lord eighteen hundred and fifty.
(L. S.) ROBERT H. SCHOMBURGK.
(L. S.) JOSE MARIA MEDRANO.
Ratified in the city of St Domingo, September 10, 1850. BUENAVENTURA BAEZ.
DR. JOSE MARIA CAMINERO.

records.headline: News from Haiti to October 15 states that hostilities have actually commenced between the Haitians and Dominicans
records.summary_en: News from Haiti to October 15 states that hostilities have actually commenced between the Haitians and Dominicans, with about 500 Dominican troops driving back Soulouque's vanguard at the Pass of Bonica, and a Haitian brig of war with 200 men captured off Scott's Bay by two Dominican schooners and carried into Macao Roadstead. It adds that the Emperor marched on the 11th from Petit Goave, at the head of his staff and 400 guards, to take the field in person, and that the hostilities had disastrously affected the island's trade, with no coffee to be had and cutting of logwood and mahogany restricted.
records.summary_es: Noticias de Haití hasta el 15 de octubre afirman que las hostilidades han comenzado realmente entre haitianos y dominicanos, con unos 500 soldados dominicanos rechazando la vanguardia de Soulouque en el Paso de Bonica y un bergantín de guerra haitiano con 200 hombres capturado frente a Scott's Bay por dos goletas dominicanas y llevado a la rada de Macao. Añade que el emperador marchó el día 11 desde Petit-Goâve, al frente de su estado mayor y 400 guardias, para tomar el campo en persona, y que las hostilidades habían afectado desastrosamente el comercio de la isla, sin café disponible y con el corte de palo de tinte y caoba restringido.

records.headline: The New-York Daily Tribune reports, reprinting a Boston Traveller item of the 26th
records.summary_en: The New-York Daily Tribune reports, reprinting a Boston Traveller item of the 26th, that the people of the Dominican Republic were expecting a United States expedition to attack the Haitians, in which event a strong Dominican force would march to assist the enterprise. Under the heading 'From Hayti,' letters from Cape Haytien to the 2d instant state that all the laborers from that part of the country had joined the army against St. Domingo. The letters add that the Haitians were in high spirits because United States claims of about £300,000, which United States Agent Mr. Green had warned would be enforced by a naval fleet within six weeks, had not been backed by the appearance of any fleet, leading them to declare that the United States dared not send one and to denounce the affair as a humbug.
records.summary_es: Reproduciendo una nota del Boston Traveller del día 26, el New-York Daily Tribune informa que el pueblo de la República Dominicana esperaba una expedición de los Estados Unidos para atacar a los haitianos, en cuyo caso una fuerte tropa de dominicanos marcharía para apoyar la empresa. Bajo el encabezado 'From Hayti', cartas de Cabo Haitiano hasta el día 2 del corriente indican que todos los jornaleros de esa parte del país se habían unido al ejército contra Santo Domingo. Las cartas añaden que los haitianos estaban muy regocijados porque las reclamaciones por unas £300,000 a favor de ciudadanos estadounidenses, que el agente de los Estados Unidos, el Sr. Green, había advertido serían exigidas por una flota en seis semanas, no habían sido respaldadas por la aparición de ninguna escuadra, lo que los llevó a afirmar que los Estados Unidos no se atrevían a enviarla y a denunciar todo el asunto como una farsa.

records.headline: Late from St. Domingo—Peace Declared Between the Haytiens and Dominicans.
records.summary_en: According to an account from St. Domingo City received via the brig *George Otis* and reported from Boston on November 30, 1850, a treaty of peace between the Haytiens and Dominicans had been concluded through the intervention of the English and Americans, following some brief fighting that caused no serious loss. An English man-of-war was in port at the time of the treaty. The newspaper also reported on a separate railway collision near Batavia involving an emigrant train and an express train, which resulted in fatalities and injuries.

Un navío de guerra británico se encontraba fondeado en la rada al ajustarse el convenio. La gaceta daba cuenta por separado de un siniestro ferroviario cerca de Batavia entre un tren de emigrantes y un convoy expreso, saldado con víctimas mortales y heridos.

records.headline: Under the headline 'From St. Domingo,' the Daily National Intelligencer reports
records.summary_en: Under the headline 'From St. Domingo,' the Daily National Intelligencer reports that accounts from the city of San Domingo up to November 6 state that intelligence had arrived there that Emperor Souloque of Haiti was about to make a descent upon the Dominican Republic. In response, the Dominican Government was making extensive defensive preparations. The paper adds that rumors—which it characterizes as unfounded—had reached St. Domingo that the United States was fitting out an expedition against Haiti, in which case the Dominican Government intended to march a strong force into Souloque's territory to cooperate with the United States.
records.summary_es: Bajo el titular 'From St. Domingo', el Daily National Intelligencer informa que las noticias de la ciudad de Santo Domingo hasta el 6 de noviembre indican que se había recibido información allí de que el emperador Souloque de Haití estaba a punto de lanzarse sobre la República Dominicana. En respuesta, el Gobierno dominicano realizaba extensos preparativos de defensa. El periódico añade que habían llegado a Santo Domingo rumores —que califica de infundados— de que los Estados Unidos estaban preparando una expedición contra Haití, en cuyo caso el Gobierno dominicano tenía la intención de hacer marchar una fuerte tropa hacia los dominios de Souloque para cooperar con los Estados Unidos.

Additionally, a treaty with England acknowledging Dominican independence was celebrated at a public dinner attended by the British Consul—who stated England would not interfere in the contest—while no American consul or shipmasters were present. The barque Lysander, at Holmes's Hole, brings dates from Cape Haytien to the 24th of January inclusive. The country was tranquil. Coffee scarce.

The Lysander brings a new ordinance, published at the Cape, in the name of the Emperor, on the 22d of January, relative to important amendments of the law of 1838, on customs.

The fixed duties on customs shall be paid in Spanish money, at the rate of five per cent. on the gross proceeds on sales, without prejudice to the manifest, measuring and weighing. If the manifest is produced without the certificate of the Haytien consular agent at the port of departure, the master of the vessel shall pay one Spanish dollar per ton additional. Copies of every manifest, for verification, must be sent to the Haytien consular agent at the port of departure. Article 1st to go into effect on its publication

records.headline: What, therefore, could legally prevent a concentration of the vessels
records.summary_en: The *Wilmington Journal* reported on April 25, 1851, that because St. Domingo (the Dominican Republic) was unrecognized by the United States, it was regarded as a piratical government rather than a nation requiring an act of Congress for military action. The newspaper suggested that U.S. vessels fitted out at Norfolk and New York could join other American ships to demand redress from the "emperor" of Hayti or demolish his regime. Additionally, it noted rumors that expeditions from the Southern States purportedly bound for Cuba were likely intended to land on the Dominican part of the island to assist the Dominicans and revolutionize the social and political condition of the blacks.
records.summary_es: El *Wilmington Journal* comunicó el 25 de abril de 1851 que, por carecer de reconocimiento oficial por parte de Estados Unidos, Santo Domingo (la República Dominicana) era conceptuado más bien como un gobierno pirático que como una nación formal que demandase una ley del Congreso para emprender acciones militares. La hoja apuntaba que buques de guerra estadounidenses alistados en Norfolk y Nueva York podrían concurrir con otras unidades navales para exigir satisfacciones al «emperador» de Haití o derribar su régimen. Recogía además comentarios de que expediciones armadas procedentes de los estados del Sur, supuestamente destinadas a Cuba, tendrían por objeto desembarcar en la parte dominicana para auxiliar a los naturales y trastocar el ordenamiento político y social de las poblaciones negras.

It says Walsh, the American commissioner, has left the capital, that the result of his negotiations with the French and English consuls to induce Soulouque to settle the quarrel between the Haitians and Dominicans is not certainly known but is said to have entirely failed, and that Soulouque was generally thought never more powerful in the island.

Dice que Walsh, el comisionado estadounidense, ha dejado la capital, que el resultado de sus negociaciones con los cónsules francés e inglés para inducir a Soulouque a resolver la disputa entre haitianos y dominicanos no se conoce con certeza pero se dice que fracasó por completo, y que en general se pensaba que Soulouque nunca había sido más poderoso en la isla.

records.full_text:
ONE DAY LATER FROM HAYTI.—A letter from Porte-au-Prince, dated April 10, published in the New York Journal of Commerce, says that the Haytien Congress have not yet made a decision on the offer of mediation between the Haytiens and Dominicans, by the three commercial powers. This is one day later than the report that the offered mediation had been rejected. A Boston dispatch of the 1st inst. has the following:
The schooner October, from Porte-au-Prince, with advices to April 13, arrived here to-day. It is currently reported at St. Domingo that the Chambers had refused to comply with the demands of the American Commissioner, or to make peace. Emperor Soulouque was preparing to march on the Haytien to punish the black Prince Babo, who refused to comply with the imperial mandates. By the last accounts Babo was shut out from Cape Haytien, and had but few men with him who were willing to join in his rebellious acts.
The steamboat General Taylor arrived at Port-au-Prince on the 10th April, and was offered for sale.

records.headline: A correspondent signing 'AB.' writes to the New-York Daily Tribune
records.summary_en: A correspondent signing 'AB.' writes to the New-York Daily Tribune that Mr. Walsh is dissatisfied with the Haitian government's answer and is about to depart immediately on the French steamer Crocodile for the City of St. Domingo. The writer sees no reason to suppose that peace or a truce will be agreed to with the eastern part of the island on any basis other than incorporating both under one government, comparing foreign intervention there to British or French intervention if South Carolina were to secede from the United States. Nevertheless, the correspondent reports being informed that Soulouque, despite having made sufficient preparations for his planned expedition against 'Dominica' (the Dominican Republic), will delay it out of deference to the three powers engaged in the proposed mediation.

El autor no ve motivos para suponer que se acuerde la paz o una tregua con la parte oriental de la isla sobre otra base que no sea la incorporación de ambas bajo un solo gobierno, comparando la intervención extranjera allí con una intervención inglesa o francesa si Carolina del Sur se separara de los Estados Unidos. No obstante, el corresponsal informa haber sido enterado de que Soulouque, a pesar de haber hecho suficientes preparativos para su proyectada expedición contra 'Dominica' (la República Dominicana), la pospondrá por deferencia a las tres potencias comprometidas en la mediación propuesta.

records.headline: Summarizing an account from the Revue, the New-York Daily Tribune details
records.summary_en: Summarizing an account from the Revue, the New-York Daily Tribune details a proposed American colonization scheme in 'Dominica' (the Dominican Republic) under which settlers would import goods from the United States duty-free, own all mines on their grants exempt from taxation, and enjoy both Dominican citizenship rights and United States immunities. The colonists would form a special military corps under the Republic's authority with officers named by themselves or the Company, while the Republic would advance 30-year bonds at 10 percent interest to purchase two sea steamers to carry mails and emigrants between Santo Domingo and New York. Emigrants would receive free passage and freight, with the government paying the Company in 10 percent bonds £20 for each emigrant over 12 years old and $10 for each under, and retaining the right to take the steamers for war purposes upon repaying the Company's payments toward the original advance. The Tribune remarks that the Revue writer's aim is to excite France to annex the Dominican state.
records.summary_es: Resumiendo un relato de la Revue, el New-York Daily Tribune detalla un proyecto de colonización estadounidense en 'Dominica' (la República Dominicana) según el cual los colonos importarían mercancías de los Estados Unidos libres de derechos, serían propietarios de todas las minas en sus concesiones exentas de impuestos y gozarían tanto de los derechos de los ciudadanos dominicanos como de las inmunidades de los Estados Unidos. Los colonos formarían un cuerpo militar especial bajo la autoridad de la República con oficiales nombrados por ellos mismos o por la Compañía, mientras que la República adelantaría bonos a 30 años con un interés del 10 por ciento para comprar dos vapores marítimos destinados al transporte de correspondencia y emigrantes entre Santo Domingo y Nueva York. Los emigrantes recibirían pasaje y flete gratuitos, pagando el Gobierno a la Compañía en bonos al 10 por ciento £20 por cada emigrante mayor de 12 años y $10 por cada menor de esa edad, y reservándose el derecho de tomar los vapores en caso de guerra tras reembolsar a la Compañía lo abonado a cuenta del adelanto original. El Tribune observa que el propósito del autor de la Revue es incitar a Francia a anexarse el Estado dominicano.

records.summary_en: An envoy's failure to bring the Emperor at Port-au-Prince to reason is reported by The National Era. The envoy returned home, and the scheme was pursued with the Dominican Government through written proposals signed by Duff Green and B. B. Green at Washington on August 20, 1850. The proposals called for introducing a large body of American colonists into St. Domingo, granting 50 acres of land to each person and an additional square mile to each family of five. Settlers in 'Dominica' (the Dominican Republic) were to enjoy full Dominican civil rights as well as United States immunities, duty-free importation of goods from the United States, and tax-exempt ownership of all mines found on their grants. They were also to form a special military corps under the Republic's authority with officers named by themselves or the company, while the Republic would advance 30-year bonds bearing 10 percent interest to purchase two sea steamers for transporting mails and emigrants from Santo Domingo.

records.headline: The Vermont Watchman and State Journal reports that Sir Robert discovered
records.summary_en: The Vermont Watchman and State Journal reports that Sir Robert discovered aboriginal remains consisting of a circle containing a granite idol nearly six feet in length. According to the paper, he never encountered such a monument during all his travels in Guiana, and it indicates a much greater advancement than that possessed by the races currently inhabiting that territory or those who inhabited the island of St. Domingo when Columbus landed. Sir Robert made the discovery during one of the journeys undertaken under the command of the British government to acquaint himself with the capabilities and population of the Dominican Republic, and he is now preparing to travel to the province of Cabao, where Columbus landed.

records.headline: Citing the New York Sun and the June 15 issue of the Gaceta of St. Domingo
records.summary_en: Citing the New York Sun and the June 15 issue of the Gaceta of St. Domingo, The Daily Crescent reports on several official documents addressed to the Dominican people and army by President Buenaventura Baez. The documents concern an incursion by a column of Haitian infantry into the territory of St. Domingo on May 29, in violation of the existing truce between the Haitians and the Dominicans. According to the Gaceta, the Haitians were repulsed and tranquility has been restored to the frontier, while President Baez's spirited address to the army strongly denounces the conduct of the Haitian Government and the aims of Emperor Soulouque.
records.summary_es: Citando al New York Sun y la edición del 15 de junio de la Gaceta de Santo Domingo, The Daily Crescent informa sobre varios documentos oficiales dirigidos al pueblo y al ejército dominicanos por el presidente Buenaventura Báez. Los documentos se refieren a la incursión de una columna de infantería haitiana en el territorio de Santo Domingo el 29 de mayo, en violación de la tregua existente entre haitianos y dominicanos. Según la Gaceta, los haitianos fueron rechazados y la tranquilidad ha sido restablecida en la frontera, mientras que la enérgica alocución del presidente Báez al ejército denuncia duramente la conducta del Gobierno haitiano y las pretensiones del emperador Soulouque.

records.summary_en: According to the newspaper report dated July 19, 1851, dates from St. Domingo up to the 30th indicate that markets were glutted with American provisions, coffee was depressed, and an excessive issue of government paper money negatively impacted business while political affairs remained tranquil. The report also notes that the emperor's address had a grand effect, and his coronation would soon be solemnized with a general amnesty and the return of exiles.
records.summary_es: Con arreglo a la relación de prensa del 19 de julio de 1851, partes recibidos de Santo Domingo hasta el día 30 denotaban saturación de provisiones estadounidenses en plaza, cotizaciones deprimidas para el café y quebranto mercantil causado por emisiones desmedidas de papel moneda fiscal, en tanto la situación política discurría pacífica. La nota añade que el mensaje del emperador produjo viva impresión y que su unción imperial se solemnizaría en breve con indulto general y repatriación de desterrados.

Dice que los dominicanos, enfurecidos, se reunieron en fuerza y rechazaron a los haitianos con algunos muertos y heridos del lado haitiano, y que los comisionados renovarían sus esfuerzos por una paz permanente en el otoño.

records.headline: Reprinting an item from the London News, The Granite Farmer describes
records.summary_en: Reprinting an item from the London News, The Granite Farmer describes a granite monument nearly six feet in length discovered by Sir Robert during one of the journeys he undertook under the command of the British government to study the capabilities and population of the Dominican Republic. The paper notes that the monument indicates a much greater advancement than that possessed by the races currently inhabiting that territory or those who lived on the island of St. Domingo when Columbus landed. It adds that Sir Robert is preparing to travel to the provinces of Cibao, described as the most interesting district of the republic and the classical ground where Columbus landed.
records.summary_es: Reproduciendo una nota del London News, The Granite Farmer describe un monumento de granito de casi seis pies de largo descubierto por Sir Robert durante uno de los viajes que emprendió bajo las órdenes del Gobierno británico para conocer las capacidades y la población de la República Dominicana. El periódico señala que el monumento demuestra un adelanto mucho mayor que el que poseen las razas que habitan actualmente ese vasto territorio o las que habitaban la isla de Santo Domingo cuando desembarcó Colón. Añade que Sir Robert se prepara para realizar un viaje a las provincias del Cibao, descritas como el distrito más interesante de la república y el suelo clásico donde desembarcó Colón.

records.headline: The idea and the wish to dissolve the compulsory union
records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that after the expulsion of Boyer in 1843 and the accession of Gen. Riviere, the Dominicans seized an opportunity while the garrison was reduced to capture the remaining troops, proclaim a provisional independent government in early January 1844, and issue a revolutionary manifesto on January 16, 1844. It described the Dominican population as consisting of pure whites—who were the intellectually predominant and ruling class—and mixed races of various colors, all of whom were constitutionally declared equal citizens before the law. Additionally, the excerpt noted that Santana, the Dominican liberator and first President, resigned in 1848 and was succeeded by Jimenez, who was described as a traitor.
records.summary_es: El periódico relató que tras el derrocamiento de Boyer en 1843 y la exaltación del general Rivière, los dominicanos aprovecharon la mengua de la guarnición para reducir a las tropas restantes, proclamar un gobierno provisional independiente a principios de enero de 1844 y promulgar una manifestación revolucionaria el 16 de enero de 1844. Describía a la población dominicana integrada por blancos puros —que constituían la clase intelectualmente rectora y gobernante— y razas mixtas de diversos matices, proclamados todos constitucionalmente ciudadanos iguales ante la ley. Añadía el extracto que Santana, libertador dominicano y primer presidente, renunció en 1848 y fue sucedido por Jimenes, a quien se tildaba de traidor.

records.headline: The paper recounts that Soulouque never recognized the Dominican Republic, kept up a state of war and constantly
records.summary_en: The paper recounts that Soulouque never recognized the Dominican Republic, kept up a state of war and constantly threatened new expeditions, until the representatives of France, England and the United States intervened. It says he refused to make peace or agree to a ten-year truce but promised to suspend the war virtually and proclaimed that Dominicans could come in and trade with assurance of kind treatment, though a Haitian officer who crossed the frontier under a flag of truce to carry the proclamation was driven back with a few killed and wounded.
records.summary_es: El periódico relata que Soulouque nunca reconoció la República Dominicana, mantuvo un estado de guerra y amenazó constantemente con nuevas expediciones, hasta que intervinieron los representantes de Francia, Inglaterra y los Estados Unidos. Dice que se negó a hacer la paz o a aceptar una tregua de diez años, pero prometió suspender la guerra en la práctica y proclamó que los dominicanos podían venir a comerciar con garantía de buen trato, aunque un oficial haitiano que cruzó la frontera con bandera de tregua para llevar la proclamación fue rechazado con algunos muertos y heridos.

records.headline: The Turks Island Gazette reports that President Baez, after some months in retirement with his family at Azua
records.summary_en: The Turks Island Gazette reports that President Baez, after some months in retirement with his family at Azua, returned to Santo Domingo on Saturday the 6th and entered the city under a salute of guns, escorted by his life guards and four hundred dragoons to the National Palace. The same report describes General Santana, old and in poor health, making his slow way to Santiago, where the military guard turned out to salute him, on his way to assume command of the Dominican army assembled on the frontier, as Soulouque had joined his army at Port au Prince with the avowed purpose of invading Dominican territory.
records.summary_es: La Turks Island Gazette informa que el presidente Báez, después de algunos meses de retiro con su familia en Azua, regresó a Santo Domingo el sábado 6 y entró en la ciudad bajo una salva de cañonazos, escoltado por su guardia personal y cuatrocientos dragones hasta el Palacio Nacional. El mismo informe describe al general Santana, viejo y de salud quebrada, haciendo su lento camino hacia Santiago, donde la guardia militar salió a saludarlo, en ruta a asumir el mando del ejército dominicano reunido en la frontera, pues Soulouque se había unido a su ejército en Puerto Príncipe con el propósito declarado de invadir el territorio dominicano.
records.passage: President Baez, after spending some months in retirement with his family at Azua, returned to St. Domingo, on Saturday, the 6th inst. and entered the city under a salute of [illegible] guns. The elite of the Dominican army, newly accoutred and uniformed, received His Excellency, who was escorted by his life guards and four hundred dragoons from Azua, Bani, and San Cristobal; the body guard were in full dress, and wore their splendid new brass helmets, ornamented with horse tails; the cavalcade rode to the National Palace, through streets ornamented with flags, and followed by the troops. The triumphal entry into Rome of Scipio Africanus was less ostentatious than President Baez's appearance in the city of St. Domingo, on the morning of the 6th inst. and we may be allowed to remind our readers that Scipio subsequently lost his popularity with the Roman people when he claimed for himself and the Senators a station at public festivals which the laws of the republic did [illegible] either. As President Baez, thus escorted, was triumphantly hailed on his approaching the National Palace, an incident of a different description portrayed the respective characters of the actors in two distinct dramas; a mild looking elderly gentleman, whose military seat on horseback bespeaks the old soldier, notwithstanding the infirm appearance of the rider, is seen to wend his way slowly and with difficulty across the all but impenetrable passes met with between his farm and the direct road from it to St. Jago; the venerable old man is accompanied by a lady, evidently accustomed to that deference

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that Soulouque joined his army at Port-au-Prince with the avowed purpose of invading Dominican territory, prompting General Santana to proceed to the post of danger. While the British Consul desired to have Haytien ports blockaded, the French Consul opposed the measure in favor of a strong protest, which Soulouque might disregard. The publication also noted that the provided information was entirely one-sided.
records.summary_es: El periódico notificó que Soulouque se incorporó a su ejército en Puerto Príncipe con el manifiesto propósito de invadir el territorio dominicano, lo que indujo al general Santana a trasladarse al puesto de mayor peligro. Si bien el cónsul británico pretendía que se bloquearan los puertos haitianos, el cónsul francés se opuso a dicha providencia en favor de una enérgica protesta, la cual Soulouque bien podría desatender. La nota observaba asimismo que las informaciones recibidas eran enteramente parciales.

records.summary_en: The paper argues that unless a new system replaces the present mode of dealing with such questions, Soulouque will succeed in his project of subduing the Dominicans, a project it says is in reality warmly sustained by England. It argues that under Mr. Fillmore the United States lost what Mr. Calhoun's system had gained — holding Soulouque in check and upholding the Dominicans without direct intervention or protectorate — and has been trapped into a coalition with France and England in which it will exercise but nominal influence in Haitian affairs.
records.summary_es: El periódico argumenta que, a menos que un nuevo sistema reemplace el modo actual de tratar estas cuestiones, Soulouque tendrá éxito en su proyecto de subyugar a los dominicanos, un proyecto que, dice, en realidad es apoyado calurosamente por Inglaterra. Argumenta que bajo el Sr. Fillmore los Estados Unidos perdieron lo que el sistema del Sr. Calhoun había ganado —mantener a Soulouque a raya y apoyar a los dominicanos sin intervención directa ni protectorado— y han quedado atrapados en una coalición con Francia e Inglaterra en la que ejercerán solo una influencia nominal en los asuntos haitianos.

records.headline: The New York Herald reports that a colonel serving as a representative in the Congress of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: The New York Herald reports that a colonel serving as a representative in the Congress of the Dominican Republic has sailed for the United States on an important political mission to Washington. Explaining that 'Dominica' (the Dominican Republic) is a former Spanish colony and now a republic occupying the eastern and larger section of the island, the paper contrasts it with the western Empire of Haiti, whose recently crowned emperor is ambitious to control the entire island and whose designs—along with the policies of England and France—remain suspected. The Herald presumes the envoy's mission concerns these relations between the Haitian empire and the Dominican republic, and asks whether the Dominicans, whom it deems entitled to United States protection, will receive it from Mr. Webster.
records.summary_es: The New York Herald informa que un coronel que se desempeña como representante en el Congreso de la República Dominicana ha zarpado hacia los Estados Unidos en una importante misión política con destino a Washington. Explicando que 'Dominica' (la República Dominicana) fue originalmente una colonia española y es ahora una república que ocupa la sección oriental y más extensa de la isla, el periódico la contrasta con el Imperio de Haití en el extremo occidental, cuyo emperador recientemente coronado ambiciona toda la isla y cuyos designios —junto con la política de Inglaterra y Francia— siguen despertando sospechas. El Herald presume que la misión del enviado se refiere a estas relaciones entre el imperio haitiano y la república dominicana, y se pregunta si los dominicanos, a quienes considera con derecho a la protección estadounidense, la recibirán del Sr. Webster.

records.headline: The New-York Daily Tribune reports that the Haitian ruler has refused
records.summary_en: The New-York Daily Tribune reports that the Haitian ruler has refused to acknowledge the independence of the Dominican Republic and warned that unless the Haitian flag is hoisted there, he will march against the Dominicans in October. In response, the Dominicans are preparing to meet him on the frontier with a force of six thousand men and are busily repairing their frontier fortifications. Meanwhile, the Dominican Government guarantees land grants with indisputable title to all settlers, with five hundred Germans expected to settle at Cape Isabella, and is encouraging the cultivation of tobacco as the new crop comes in rapidly. A market report notes that American produce was in demand and lists St. Domingo coffee at $12 per hundredweight.
records.summary_es: El New-York Daily Tribune informa que el gobernante haitiano se ha negado a reconocer la independencia de la República Dominicana y ha advertido que, a menos que se ice allí la bandera haitiana, marchará contra los dominicanos el próximo mes de octubre. En respuesta, los dominicanos hacen preparativos para enfrentarlo en la frontera con una fuerza de seis mil hombres y reparan activamente sus fortificaciones fronterizas. Entretanto, el Gobierno republicano garantiza concesiones de tierras con título indisputable a todos los colonos, esperándose el asentamiento de quinientos alemanes en Cabo Isabela, y fomenta el cultivo de tabaco mientras la nueva cosecha entra con rapidez. Un informe de mercado señala que los productos estadounidenses tenían demanda y cotiza el café de Santo Domingo a $12 por quintal.

records.full_text: Advices from Port-au-Prince to the 28th May represent that public affairs were in an unsettled state. The Emperor Soulouque had refused to acknowledge the independence of the Dominican republic, and would not agree to an exchange of prisoners. He had threatened the messengers who went to Port-au-Prince to effect the exchange that unless the Haytien flag was hoisted he would march against them in October next. Arrangements were making to meet him on the frontier, under General Santana, with a force of 6,000 men. The Dominicans are also busily employed repairing their fortifications on the frontier, and are preparing to give him a warm reception.

Dice que la isla estaba tranquila pero Haití mantendría un ejército de 30,000 hombres en pie de guerra mediante conscripción.

records.headline: The Morning Star reports Mr. Green's statements concerning Boston merchants
records.summary_en: The Morning Star reports Mr. Green's statements concerning Boston merchants who held large contracts with Soulouque for ships, arms, and military supplies, and papers allegedly proving that persons in the United States were cooperating with the British and French governments in expectation that England and France would aid Soulouque to conquer the Dominicans and ultimately annex Cuba and the other West Indian islands. According to the account, Green protested against allowing Mr. Webster to sacrifice the Dominicans by withholding recognition of their independence; the President promised to inquire into the facts, professed his willingness to recognize both governments, and stated he could not legally prevent Green from obtaining a colonization contract from the Dominican government. After propositions sent to confidential persons in St. Domingo were intercepted by French agents and published in Paris and the United States, Green investigated conditions in St. Domingo and concluded that unless the United States counteracts British and French policy, the white population on the eastern part of the island will be compelled to acknowledge the dominion of Soulouque's government.

Según el relato, Green protestó contra permitir que el Sr. Webster sacrificara a los dominicanos al negarles el reconocimiento de su independencia; el Presidente prometió investigar los hechos, manifestó su disposición a reconocer a ambos gobiernos y declaró que no podía impedir legalmente que Green obtuviera un contrato de colonización del Gobierno dominicano. Después de que las propuestas enviadas a personas de confianza en Santo Domingo fueran interceptadas por agentes franceses y publicadas en París y en los Estados Unidos, Green indagó la situación real en Santo Domingo y concluyó que, a menos que los Estados Unidos contrarresten la política británica y francesa, los blancos de la parte oriental de la isla se verán obligados a reconocer el dominio del gobierno de Soulouque.

records.headline: The Rhode-Island Weekly Post reports that advices from St. Domingo
records.summary_en: The Rhode-Island Weekly Post reports that advices from St. Domingo to October 3 state that vague rumors of an expedition from the United States to St. Domingo caused considerable excitement in the republic for a time, though all had become quiet by the latest accounts. According to the report, the public believed that these unfounded rumors were circulated by persons seeking to foment internal trouble and aid schemes to overthrow the government. In response, Dominican President Baez issued a manifesto prohibiting foreigners from disembarking at any ports in the republic other than St. Domingo, Azua, and one other designated port except in cases such as shipwreck, closing La Romana and Samana for six months, and banning the importation of firearms and ammunition.
records.summary_es: El Rhode-Island Weekly Post informa que las noticias de Santo Domingo hasta el 3 de octubre indican que vagos rumores sobre una expedición procedente de los Estados Unidos hacia Santo Domingo causaron considerable agitación en la república por un tiempo, aunque según los últimos informes todo había vuelto a la calma. De acuerdo con la nota, el pueblo creía que esos rumores infundados eran difundidos por personas interesadas en fomentar disturbios internos y apoyar planes para destruir al gobierno. En respuesta, el presidente dominicano Báez emitió un manifiesto que prohíbe a los extranjeros desembarcar en cualquier puerto de la república salvo Santo Domingo, Azua y otro puerto habilitado, excepto en casos como naufragio, cierra La Romana y Samaná por seis meses y prohíbe la importación de armas de fuego y municiones.

records.headline: The New York Herald reports that several French warships have taken
records.summary_en: The New York Herald reports that several French warships have taken possession of a Dominican peninsula with designs to hold it as a naval station. Recalling an article it published the previous April, the paper states that an intrigue had been going on for years between Dominican President Buenaventura Baez and Major Reybaud, the French Consul to Haiti, aimed at allowing France to obtain a foothold in 'Dominica' (the Dominican Republic), conquer the western part of the island, extinguish Soulouque and his empire, and restore the entire island to French dominion. According to the Herald, the scheme had the cooperation of President Baez and a clique of French residents, whereas the mass of the citizens, being Spaniards, were hostile to any measure subjecting them to France. The paper adds that some two years earlier President Baez wrote to the French Consul General in Port-au-Prince offering to place the country under French protection at whatever sacrifice—which the April article hinted was the peninsula now seized—and more recently made an even stronger appeal to France.
records.summary_es: The New York Herald informa que varios buques de guerra franceses han tomado posesión de una península dominicana con el propósito de mantenerla como estación naval. Recordando un artículo que publicó en abril anterior, el periódico afirma que durante años venía desarrollándose una intriga entre el presidente de la República Dominicana, Buenaventura Báez, y el mayor Reybaud, cónsul francés en Haití, con el objeto de permitir que Francia obtuviera un punto de apoyo en 'Dominica' (la República Dominicana), conquistara posteriormente la parte occidental de la isla, extinguiera a Soulouque y su imperio, y restableciera toda la isla bajo el dominio francés. Según el Herald, el plan contaba con la cooperación del presidente Báez y de una camarilla de residentes franceses, mientras que la masa de los ciudadanos, siendo españoles, se mostraba abiertamente hostil a cualquier medida que los sometiera al poder de Francia. El periódico añade que unos dos años atrás el presidente Báez escribió al cónsul general francés en Puerto Príncipe ofreciendo poner al país bajo la protección francesa a cualquier sacrificio —el cual, según insinuaba el artículo de abril, no era otro que la península ahora ocupada— y que más recientemente dirigió un llamado aún más enérgico a Francia.

records.headline: An editorial in the Tribune addresses rumors that France has taken
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Tribune addresses rumors that France has taken possession of the peninsula of Samaná, criticizing rival newspapers for sensational bluster. The paper argues that the Dominican Republic is an independent government, virtually though not officially recognized by the United States, that has sought French protection or annexation of its own free will. The editorial maintains that the Monroe declaration contains no principle justifying American interference with the Dominican Republic's decisions, distinguishing its sovereign status from that of Cuba, which remains a Spanish dependency.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Tribune aborda los rumores de que Francia ha tomado posesión de la península de Samaná, criticando a los periódicos rivales por sus aspavientos sensacionalistas. El periódico sostiene que la República Dominicana es un gobierno independiente, virtual aunque no oficialmente reconocido por los Estados Unidos, que ha buscado la protección francesa o la anexión por su propia voluntad. El editorial afirma que la declaración de Monroe no contiene ningún principio que justifique la interferencia estadounidense en las decisiones de la República Dominicana, distinguiendo su condición soberana de la de Cuba, que sigue siendo una dependencia española.

records.headline: The Dispatch reports rumors that French warships have occupied
records.summary_en: The Dispatch reports rumors that French warships have occupied Samaná to establish a naval station. The paper recalls its earlier reporting on an intrigue between Dominican President Buenaventura Báez and the French consul to Haiti to secure France a foothold in "Dominica," from which French forces might conquer Haiti and restore the entire island to French rule. According to the article, while Báez and local French residents supported placing the country under French protection and offering Samaná, the Dominican population remained firmly hostile to French dominion.

Según el artículo, aunque Báez y los residentes franceses locales apoyaban poner el país bajo la protección francesa y ofrecer Samaná, la población dominicana se mantuvo firmemente hostil a la dominación francesa.

records.headline: A letter from envoy Robert Gloydan Walsh to Secretary of State Daniel Webster reports traveling from Port-au-Prince aboard
records.summary_en: A letter from envoy Robert Gloydan Walsh to Secretary of State Daniel Webster reports traveling from Port-au-Prince aboard the French war steamer Crocodile to Santo Domingo city to communicate the result of negotiations to the Dominican government. Walsh says the result relieved the Dominicans for the time from apprehension of attack but did not let them lay aside their arms, that they hoped the three powers would continue their interposition until Dominican independence was secured, and that they would prefer total extermination to falling again under the rule they had shaken off.

Walsh dice que el resultado libró por el momento a los dominicanos del temor a un ataque pero no les permitió deponer las armas, que esperaban que las tres potencias continuaran su interposición hasta que la independencia dominicana estuviera asegurada, y que preferirían el exterminio total a caer de nuevo bajo el dominio del que se habían librado.

records.headline: The paper prints instructions to Mr. Walsh
records.summary_en: The paper prints instructions to Mr. Walsh: on arriving at Port-au-Prince he is to seek a conference with his colleagues on inducing the Emperor Soulouque to consent to a lengthened truce or a permanent peace with the Dominicans. The instructions say the three governments are actuated by philanthropic views, direct him to keep his mind free from prejudice resulting from color or forms of government and to be impartial between the Haitian and Dominican governments, and note that France is a creditor of Soulouque's government to a large amount and cannot hope for discharge of her debt while its resources are consumed.
