records.headline: An editorial in the Daily Union discusses the reported surrender
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Daily Union discusses the reported surrender, by the Dominican president, of his country's independence to French domination under the pretext of protection against Haitian Emperor Faustin Soulouque. The paper contends that ceding Samaná and establishing a French naval depot would give France supreme control over the Dominican Republic. While expressing skepticism that France intends to conquer Haiti or the whole island, the editorial warns that Samaná possesses one of the world's finest natural harbors. Stationed there, the paper asserts, a French fleet would command the Mona Passage, threatening American trade routes and coasts.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Daily Union analiza los informes que indican que el presidente dominicano ha entregado la independencia de su país a la dominación francesa bajo el pretexto de protección frente al emperador haitiano Faustin Soulouque. El diario sostiene que la cesión de Samaná y el establecimiento de un depósito naval francés otorgarían a Francia un control supremo sobre la República Dominicana. Aunque expresa escepticismo de que Francia pretenda conquistar Haití o la isla entera, el editorial advierte que Samaná posee uno de los mejores puertos naturales del mundo. Estacionada allí, afirma el periódico, una flota francesa dominaría el paso de la Mona, amenazando las rutas comerciales y las costas estadounidenses.

records.headline: The paper prints the same mediating instructions and outcome as in the Walsh negotiation: agents were to require the Emperor
records.summary_en: The paper prints the same mediating instructions and outcome as in the Walsh negotiation: agents were to require the Emperor to conclude a permanent peace with the Dominican Government on a jointly prescribed basis or consent to a truce of not less than ten years. It says Great Britain and France instructed their agents to menace Soulouque with hostility if he refused, but he persisted in his designs against Dominica and would in no manner acknowledge its independence, so the utmost the mediating powers could effect was the prolongation of an existing truce, and it praises Mr. Walsh's mission.
records.summary_es: El periódico publica las mismas instrucciones de mediación y el mismo resultado que en la negociación de Walsh: los agentes debían exigir al emperador que concluyera una paz permanente con el Gobierno dominicano sobre una base prescrita conjuntamente o que consintiera una tregua de no menos de diez años. Dice que Gran Bretaña y Francia instruyeron a sus agentes a amenazar a Soulouque con hostilidad si se negaba, pero él persistió en sus designios contra Dominica y no quiso reconocer de ningún modo su independencia, por lo que lo máximo que las potencias mediadoras pudieron lograr fue la prolongación de una tregua existente, y elogia la misión del Sr. Walsh.

records.headline: The paper reports late news from Haiti: Soulouque has recruited and re-equipped his army and placed it on as effective a footing
records.summary_en: The paper reports late news from Haiti: Soulouque has recruited and re-equipped his army and placed it on as effective a footing as the empire's resources would permit, distributing eagles, crosses of the Legion of Honor, ranks and titles to ensure or reward the fidelity of his army. It summarizes the Emperor's address from the throne to the Senate as analyzing the condition of the empire — public works, the budget, internal and external trade, custom houses, the crops, the army and navy, foreign relations and public instruction — and as stating that the army and navy are on a respectable footing.
records.summary_es: El periódico informa noticias recientes de Haití: Soulouque ha reclutado y reequipado su ejército y lo ha puesto en un pie tan eficaz como lo permitían los recursos del imperio, distribuyendo águilas, cruces de la Legión de Honor, rangos y títulos para asegurar o recompensar la fidelidad de su ejército. Resume el discurso del emperador desde el trono ante el Senado como un análisis de la condición del imperio —obras públicas, presupuesto, comercio interno y externo, aduanas, cosechas, ejército y marina, relaciones exteriores e instrucción pública— y como una afirmación de que el ejército y la marina están en un pie respetable.

records.headline: The West-Jersey Pioneer describes defensive regulations issued
records.summary_en: The West-Jersey Pioneer describes defensive regulations issued by the Dominican government restricting passenger landings at Azua and Puerto Plata, requiring special permits at Santo Domingo, and barring the importation of arms and ammunition. The paper views these measures as an absurd overreaction to unfounded rumors of an impending filibustering expedition from the United States, which harms Dominican commerce. The editorial insists that no responsible American group has organized an invasion of the island, asserting that the United States government would promptly declare any such filibuster illegal and surrender the invaders to justice.
records.summary_es: El West-Jersey Pioneer describe las regulaciones defensivas emitidas por el gobierno dominicano que restringen el desembarco de pasajeros en Azua y Puerto Plata, exigen permisos especiales en Santo Domingo y prohíben la importación de armas y municiones. El periódico considera estas medidas como una reacción absurda y desmedida ante rumores infundados de una inminente expedición filibustera desde los Estados Unidos, lo que perjudica el comercio dominicano. El editorial insiste en que ningún grupo estadounidense respetable ha organizado una invasión de la isla, afirmando que el gobierno de los Estados Unidos declararía de inmediato ilegal cualquier intento filibustero y entregaría a los invasores a la justicia.

records.headline: Our National Reputation.
records.summary_en: The *West-Jersey pioneer* reported on December 18, 1852, that recurring American expeditions against Cuba and the Rio Grande caused neighboring regions—including St. Domingo, which barred its doors against foreigners—to view American commercial enterprises with extreme suspicion as disguised filibuster incursions. The newspaper lamented that these actions damaged the reputation of the United States, causing foreign nations to regard the American government as a piratical force rather than an honorable republic.

records.full_text: From the Saturday Gazette. OUR NATIONAL REPUTATION. The United States is rapidly becoming the bug-bear to frighten all the weaker nations, and colonies of weaker nations, whose territories lie within range of her commerce or whose resources can offer temptations to her speculators. New Grenada is alarmed at the infusion of our population into her territories, and last, of all, the little republic of St. Domingo has been in a panic about a report, received by way of Turks Island, to the effect that an American steamer had put into Puerto Plata, but had fled on sight of an English steamer, and that this solitary steamer was bound to land a force that would take possession of the Dominican Republic and straightway annex it to the dominions of Uncle Sam. However absurd such a report might be made, it is wild to suppose that the government of the United States would sanction it, or shoulder the responsibility of it. It would rather have declared the whole affair illegal and outrageous, and done every thing to give up the lawless invaders to the justice of the injured government. That such would have been the result, we have an assurance in the policy laid down by our government, in various administrations, when similar troubles have been menacing us with Canada, Cuba and Mexico. But neither the declared policy nor the actual practice of a government can give confidence to foreign powers, so long as the shameless spirit of encroachment, annexation and revolution exists as it does among so large a portion of the American people. The lawlessness of a class inspires more faith than the promises of a President, and the reputation of the nation suffers for the shamelessness of a faction. Thus it is that every commercial enterprise that is set on foot in an American port is at once looked upon as a Fillibuster expedition in disguise. Cuba shakes in her shores at the sight of an American steamer; St. Domingo bars her doors on all foreigners, lest a stray American invader may come in and upset her government, and we shall next have his High-colored Mightiness, the Emperor of Hayti, drawing a cordon across his land frontier and fortifying his ports, to prevent his Imperial domains from being carried off bobily to be annexed to the great American Republic. While we can laugh at the folly of these foreign fears, we cannot help lamenting that the name of the United States should have fallen into such an odium as to justify, in the slightest degree, such absurd alarms. But, thanks to the oft-repeated and shameless enterprises upon cuba and the Rio Grande, the government of the republic fought for by the fathers, and sanctified in all honor by Washington and those around him, has now come to be looked on as a species of piratical craft cruising in all seas, and ready to plunder and capture all foreign property. It is beginning to be a sort of national Rob Roy, whose policy is '—the simple plan, That they shall take who have the power, And they shall keep who can.' Right-minded citizens, who respect national honesty and deem acts of national wrong as shameful as pocket-picking, should set their faces against all movements that may tend to strengthen the opprobrium into which we have fallen among foreign governments. The mere fact of our being a nation of unexampled prosperity, and rapidly growing in wealth and power, should not satisfy us, so long as we are looked upon abroad as a lawless people, with a government incapable of checking the growing popular frenzy for annexation. There is something more than mere power and wealth to be attained by a nation—and that is the reputation as well as the fact of national integrity.

records.summary_en: The editorial calls it preposterous for The Union to talk of the United States assuming a protectorate over the Dominican Republic, or over any of the republics south of the United States, and says the true American policy is to keep clear of all protectorates. It argues that the Dominicans themselves would refuse and repudiate such protection, having instead solicited France for eight years, so that an American protectorate would have to be enforced at the cannon's mouth while France's would be welcomed.

records.headline: The Intelligencer reprints remarks from the New York Tribune
records.summary_en: The Intelligencer reprints remarks from the New York Tribune. They concern rumors that France had taken possession of the peninsula of Samaná. According to the quoted extract, American diplomacy faced three choices: returning the Dominicans to Haitian rule, maintaining their independence only to see them annexed to France, or annexing them directly to the United States. The Tribune observed that the Dominican people rejected the third option attempted by the Greenes and preferred French annexation under Napoleon III. The Intelligencer comments that domestic slavery severely weakens American external influence, making appeals to the Monroe doctrine in Santo Domingo pointless.
records.summary_es: El Intelligencer reproduce comentarios del New York Tribune acerca de los rumores de que Francia había tomado posesión de la península de Samaná. De acuerdo con el extracto citado, la diplomacia estadounidense enfrentaba tres opciones: devolver a los dominicanos al dominio haitiano, mantener su independencia solo para verlos anexionados a Francia, o anexionarlos directamente a los Estados Unidos. El Tribune observó que el pueblo dominicano rechazó la tercera opción intentada por los Greene y prefirió la anexión francesa bajo Napoleón III. El Intelligencer comenta que la esclavitud interna debilita gravemente la influencia exterior estadounidense, haciendo inútiles las apelaciones a la doctrina Monroe en Santo Domingo.

records.summary_en: The *Daily National Intelligencer* reported that the 1851 mediation mission of R. M. Walsh, the United States special agent acting with the consuls of France and Great Britain, failed to persuade the Haitian Emperor Soulouque to sign a peace treaty or a ten-year truce with St. Domingo. Soulouque argued that the island was naturally one and indivisible, viewing the Dominicans as rebels who had no right to secede, and therefore peremptorily declined the propositions through his Senate. However, the Emperor's Minister of Foreign Affairs subsequently volunteered a positive assurance that hostilities against the Dominicans would not be renewed.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
Early in 1851 the Administration sent Mr. R. M. Walsh to Hayti, in the capacity of special agent, to co-operate with the Consuls of France and Great Britain for the purpose of producing amicable relations between the Emperor Soulouque and the Dominican Republic. The step was taken in compliance with the earnest solicitations of the Dominicans, who were under constant apprehension of outrage and slaughter at the hands of the Haytiens. The interests of commerce coincided with the dictates of humanity, and the united interference of the three Powers was resolved upon to aid the Dominicans in preserving an independence which they had themselves achieved, and to compel the negro Emperor to defer, if not to abandon, his threatened war of extermination.

Mr. Walsh and his coadjutors commenced their negotiations in February, 1851, at Port au Prince, and closed them late in the following April. They had frequent interviews with Soulouque and his Creole Minister of Foreign Affairs, but failed to accomplish the object of the mission. Neither persuasion nor argument could induce the Emperor to make a definite treaty of peace, or a truce of ten years, with the Government of St. Domingo, which he regarded as a rebel whose subjection was necessary to the maintenance of his own authority. He argued that nature had designed the whole island to be under one Government, that the constitution of 1813 proclaimed it one and indivisible, and that the Dominicans, having voluntarily annexed themselves, had no right to secede. After consultation with his Senate, Soulouque peremptorily declined both propositions, but subsequently, through his Minister of Foreign Affairs, volunteered a positive assurance that "notwithstanding the refusal of the Government to make peace with the Dominicans, hostilities against them would not be renewed."

So the affair ended. The course pursued by Mr. Fillmore's administration in relation to it appears to us to have been honorable throughout. It originated in none but pure motives; it sought to accomplish none but humane ends; and, though the effort for the time ended in failure, we cannot but think that it left a wholesome influence behind it in the court and cabinet of the Haytien Emperor.

The recent publication of the correspondence referring to the transaction has furnished the New York Evening Post and kindred prints with a pretext for assailing the Administration on the score of alleged inconsistency. True to its Freesoil instincts, the Post thinks it monstrous that the United States should have presumed to question the right of the negroes of Hayti to cut the throats of their Castilian neighbors; and it professes to discover in this act of the Administration a flagrant departure from the professed policy of non-intervention. "Mr. Fillmore a Filibuster" is the phrase with which the Post made its start. Against these attacks the Administration needs no defence other than that which is afforded by the facts we have recapitulated. They may not convince those whose Abolitionist affinities blind them to the truth in any controversy in which color is concerned; but by the country generally they will be pronounced not merely satisfactory, but honorable in a high degree. Upon other points involved it were useless to reason with an opponent who will not distinguish between intervention to preserve peace between independent Powers and intervention to aid recognised subjects in a quarrel with their rulers. The journal which can find no other term for a mission of peace than "fillibusterism" can scarcely be capable of candor or justice while the merits of that mission are in dispute.

We are gratified to learn that the central organ of the Democratic party renders no help to the assailants of the Administration upon this question. The following article, which we transfer from the Union of yesterday, will be read with a great deal of pleasure. It presents important facts in a clear light, and extends a strong meed of praise to Mr. Fillmore and his advisers for their action in the premises:

"In general, the foreign policy of President Fillmore's administration has not been in accordance with our notion of what the foreign policy of this country should be, and we have been constrained in some instances to express an emphatic disapprobation of negotiations which seemed to us to compromise the dignity and to surrender the rights of the United States. For this reason, any instances of an energetic or wise administration of the foreign affairs of the country by an Executive whose general policy we have been constrained to condemn will the more readily command our warmest commendation. Such an instance of wise diplomacy do we regard the efforts of this Government, in conjunction with Great Britain and France, to arrest the sanguinary designs of the negro emperor of Hayti against the republic of Dominica.

"By some means publicity has been given to the correspondence between the State Department and Mr. Robert M. Walsh, its agent in the negotiation for the pacification of Hayti. In the various papers which constitute this correspondence the motives and purposes of the Administration in proffering its good offices in behalf of the Dominican republic are frankly and clearly set forth.

"In 1821 the Spanish portion of the Island of St. Domingo voluntarily subjected itself to the Government of Hayti, then presided over by Boyer. On the expulsion of Boyer, and on account of the wrongs and grievances which they had endured, with a repetition of which they were menaced, the Dominicans threw off the subjection of negro government, and established an independent republic. To this step the Spanish inhabitants of St. Domingo were driven by the necessity of self-preservation. Not only were their political rights and their liberty invaded and trampled upon by the black barbarians of Hayti, but the doom of indiscriminate slaughter and extermination was incessantly held before them in the threats of the Macaya and Dessalines.

"By the most imperious necessity, then, were the Dominicans impelled to set up an independent Government. Nevertheless, their act of separation was regarded as a revolt by the negroes of Hayti, who prepared to reduce the rebel whites to subjection by the strong arm of force. All the efforts of the Haytien Government were unequal, however, to the reconquest of Dominica. The Spaniards defended themselves with valor and energy, and, despite the disparity of numbers, successfully repelled the invasions of their foes. They achieved and established their independence. France formally recognised the Republic of Dominica. England and the United States recognised it by their acts. Still Soulouque refused to acknowledge the independence of the Dominicans, and persisted in his efforts to reduce them to subjection. In this juncture, under the apprehension of a very formidable attack by Soulouque, the Dominican Government solicited the mediation of the United States, Great Britain, and France, to restore, if possible, peaceable relations with its savage neighbors. Great Britain and France promptly acceded to the proposition, impelled thereto by every consideration of justice and humanity. Without reluctance the United States followed their example. The Government dispatched Mr. Walsh to the Haytien court, to co-operate with the representatives of Great Britain and France in the humane endeavor to persuade the Emperor Soulouque to abandon his hostile designs against the Dominicans. The nature of Mr. Walsh's commission may be gathered from the following extracts from Mr. Webster's instructions:

"'When, therefore, you shall have held free and full conferences with your colleagues, and shall have ascertained the reciprocal claims of the parties to the war, if the Emperor Soulouque shall insist upon maintaining a belligerent attitude until all his demands shall have been satisfied by the opposite party, you will unite with your colleagues in remonstrating against this course on his part. If the remonstrance should prove to be unavailing, you will signify to the Emperor that you shall give immediate notice to your Government that the President, with the concurrence of Congress, may adopt such measures, in co-operation with the Governments of England and France, as may cause the intervention of the three Powers to be respected; and you will lose no time in communicating the result to this Department. The Emperor should be made properly aware of the dangers which he and his country may encounter if he should be unfortunately advised to reject reasonable terms of pacification; but you will stop at remonstrance until further notice.

"'If, however, your joint and concurrent representations should induce the Emperor Soulouque to make an abatement of his demands, which you and your colleagues may deem reasonable, you will, in concert with them, make this known to the Dominican Government, and will recommend their adoption of a peace on that basis. You will, however, give a patient hearing to any objections which that Government may advance; and if you and your colleagues should deem those objections solid, you will communicate them to the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Hayti, and will require from him an answer to them. If this answer should not be given within a reasonable time, or if when given it should not prove to be satisfactory, you will then, conjointly with your colleagues, require the Emperor to conclude a permanent peace with the Dominican Government upon the basis which you may jointly prescribe to him, or to consent to a truce with that Government of not less than ten years.'

"Great Britain and France went even further, and formally instructed their agents to menace Soulouque with their hostility in the event of his refusal to accede to their proposition. Persuasion could not appease his ferocious wrath, nor could threats drive him from his bloody purposes. He persisted in his designs against Dominica, and would in no manner acknowledge its independence. The utmost the mediating Powers could effect was the prolongation of an existing truce.

"And this was the issue of a negotiation for which the Administration deserves credit. It originated in an impulse of humanity, and sought to protect a civilized community from the oppression and ferocity of a bloodthirsty savage. The mission of Mr. Walsh was a mission of peace and true philanthropy."

records.headline: The National Era publishes diplomatic instructions for an American commissioner
records.summary_en: The National Era publishes diplomatic instructions for an American commissioner to act impartially in mediating the conflict between Haiti and the Dominican Republic. The envoy is instructed not to deny justice to Haitian Emperor Faustin Soulouque because of his African race and monarchical system, nor to favor the Dominican government solely for its Castilian lineage and republican form. The dispatch explains that the commercial interests of France, Great Britain, and the United States require regional peace, enabling Haiti to repay French debts and opening expanded markets for all three powers.
records.summary_es: The National Era publica instrucciones diplomáticas que ordenan a un comisionado estadounidense actuar con imparcialidad al mediar en el conflicto entre Haití y la República Dominicana. El despacho explica que los intereses comerciales de Francia, Gran Bretaña y los Estados Unidos requieren la paz regional, lo que permitiría a Haití pagar sus deudas francesas y abriría mercados más amplios para las tres potencias.

records.summary_en: The newspaper criticizes United States policy toward Hayti, attributing it to slavery-dominated diplomacy and the failure to recognize Hayti's independence. It reports that, following domestic interference and joint bullying with foreign governments, the French have taken possession of Samana as a naval station under the pretext of intervening for Dominica. La publicación previene que dicho enclave consentirá a Francia vigilar las rutas mercantiles norteamericanas y propiciar acometidas bélicas contra Estados Unidos en coyunturas de guerra.

But we have not yet reached the final result of our indefensible conduct towards Hayti. As we have already said, had we recognised her independence, and exchanged with her the usual international courtesies, we should have enjoyed the largest portion of her valuable trade, and obtained an influence over her, beneficial to her internal interests, and protective against foreign aggression. In obedience to a blind and bigoted sectional Interest, we have pursued an opposite policy, and now retribution is about to overtake us. We have interfered impertinently in her domestic affairs, we have united with foreign Governments in bullying her—and now, one of these Governments, if the latest intelligence be correct, has taken possession of a most important station on the island, on pretence of making its intervention for Dominica more effective, but in reality with a view to secure a most important naval station, close upon our shores. Samana has been taken possession of by the French, by whom, it is stated, it is to be held as a naval station. And its positien is such, that it will enable France to keep an eye upon our commerce, and, in the event of war, facilitate hostile movements against our shores. And this is the result of negro-phobia—of Slavery domination—of pro-slavery diplomacy—of the base policy which we have pursued towards that important island.

records.summary_en: The *Wilmington Journal* reported on December 24, 1852, that the Dominican Republic had long sought French protection and offered annexation, a step the current French Emperor was taking to secure a strategic point for monitoring American movements regarding Cuba under existing treaties. The newspaper contrasted the history of the former Spanish portion—which achieved independence without a servile insurrection and retained a white and mixed population superior in society and education—with the former French portion (Hayti), where a violent slave uprising had occurred.
records.summary_es: El *Wilmington Journal* comunicó el 24 de diciembre de 1852 que la República Dominicana procuró largamente el patronato de Francia y propuso su anexión, resolución que el actual soberano galo aprovechaba para guarecer un apostadero estratégico desde el cual observar las maniobras norteamericanas respecto a Cuba al amparo de las convenciones vigentes. El diario contrastaba los antecedentes de la antigua sección española —que conquistó su autonomía sin insurrecciones de esclavos y preservó un vecindario blanco y mestizo más encumbrado en cultura y letras— con la antigua colonia francesa (Haití), teatro de un sangriento levantamiento servil.

records.headline: The paper defends the Fillmore administration's mediation, arguing that the Monroe declaration was aimed at European colonization
records.summary_en: The paper defends the Fillmore administration's mediation, arguing that the Monroe declaration was aimed at European colonization and aggressive intervention, not at France and Great Britain cooperating with the United States to pacify Haiti. It says the Dominicans besought the mediating powers to protect them, and that the powers interfered only to shield a feeble community from destruction.

Dice que los dominicanos suplicaron a las potencias mediadoras que los protegieran, y que las potencias intervinieron solo para escudar a una comunidad débil de la destrucción.

records.headline: The Daily Union prints an item from the New Orleans Picayune
records.summary_en: The Daily Union prints an item from the New Orleans Picayune. It summarizes news from the Santiago newspaper Correo del Cibao. The Dominican journal denounces the licensing of cockpits in central Santiago as a remnant of barbarism and features theological debates between Catholic clergy and Protestant missionaries. A correspondent in the Dominican paper also complains of irregular postal deliveries and a serious lack of physicians in many towns. In addition, the Portuguese schooner Ceres was detained at Puerto Plata for alleged involvement in the slave trade and sent to Santo Domingo for judicial proceedings.
records.summary_es: The Daily Union publica una nota del New Orleans Picayune que resume noticias del periódico santiagués Correo del Cibao. El periódico dominicano denuncia la autorización de galleras en el centro de Santiago como un vestigio de barbarie y presenta debates teológicos entre el clero católico y misioneros protestantes. Un corresponsal en el diario dominicano también se queja de las entregas postales irregulares y de una grave falta de médicos en muchas localidades. Además, la goleta portuguesa Ceres fue detenida en Puerto Plata por presunta participación en la trata de esclavos y enviada a Santo Domingo para procedimientos judiciales.

Además, ni la embarcación ni los despachos del 30 del mes anterior desde Santo Domingo por la vía de Nueva Orleans mencionan toma francesa alguna de la península de Samaná.

records.headline: The Dominican Republic appears to have come under the protection of France
records.summary_en: The Dominican Republic appears to have come under the protection of France against Emperor Faustin Soulouque of Haiti, an article in the Eastern Times observes. The paper notes that a French naval depot has been established at the Dominican port of Samaná, affording an advantageous position to observe Cuban developments. The editorial expresses surprise that France, having recently replaced its own republic with an imperial regime, would protect a West Indian republic whose inhabitants have previously demonstrated their ability to defend themselves.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en el Eastern Times observa que Francia parece haber asumido la protección de la República Dominicana frente al emperador Faustin Soulouque de Haití. El periódico señala que se ha establecido un depósito naval francés en el puerto dominicano de Samaná, lo que brinda una posición ventajosa para observar los acontecimientos en Cuba. El editorial expresa sorpresa de que Francia, habiendo sustituido recientemente su propia república por un régimen imperial, proteja a una república antillana cuyos habitantes han demostrado anteriormente su capacidad para defenderse por sí mismos.

records.headline: The Liberator denounces an unnamed New York filibustering newspaper
records.summary_en: The Liberator denounces an unnamed New York filibustering newspaper for endorsing Duff Green's project of colonizing the "Republic of Dominica" with armed emigrants under the guise of protection. Quoting the rival editor, William Lloyd Garrison's paper highlights the argument that because Washington never recognized Haiti, its citizens are outlaws whom armed American companies may rightfully dispossess by seizing the empire portion of the island. The editorial condemns the writer as an unmasked villain and scoundrel while warning against such predatory schemes of national robbery.
records.summary_es: The Liberator denuncia a un periódico filibustero no identificado de Nueva York por respaldar el proyecto de Duff Green de colonizar la «República de Dominica» con emigrantes armados bajo el pretexto de protección. Al citar al editor rival, el periódico de William Lloyd Garrison destaca el argumento de que, como Washington nunca reconoció a Haití, sus ciudadanos son forajidos a quienes las compañías armadas estadounidenses pueden legítimamente despojar apoderándose de la porción imperial de la isla. El editorial condena al autor como un villano y canalla confeso, al tiempo que advierte contra tales planes predatorios de despojo nacional.

records.summary_en: The *Pawtucket Gazette and Chronicle* reported that Haitian Emperor Soulouque rejected Dominican independence, insisting the island was indivisible, though he offered assurances that hostilities would not resume. The ongoing truce was attributed in part to the depletion of the Haitian treasury following Soulouque’s lavish coronation ceremonies. An observer, Mr. Walsh, concluded that Dominican independence could ultimately only be maintained by force of arms against Haiti.

Un observador, el comisionado Walsh, dedujo que la independencia dominicana sólo podría asegurarse a la postre por la vía de las armas contra Haití.

records.headline: Past diplomatic negotiations between France and the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Past diplomatic negotiations between France and the Dominican Republic are recounted in a French newspaper report translated by The Texas Republican. According to the article, protracted negotiations resulted in a treaty drafted in December 1843 to establish French protection over the emerging state. The reported terms bound France to support Dominican independence, required the Dominican Republic to cede the peninsula of Samaná for a permanent French establishment, and made the French governor of Samaná the representative of the protectorate. The paper adds that the agreement was accepted by Ferdinand Barrot and supported by the French naval squadron.
records.summary_es: The Texas Republican traduce un informe de un periódico francés que relata negociaciones diplomáticas pasadas entre Francia y la República Dominicana. Según el artículo, prolongadas negociaciones dieron como resultado un tratado redactado en diciembre de 1843 para establecer la protección francesa sobre el naciente Estado. Los términos consignados obligaban a Francia a respaldar la independencia dominicana, requerían que la República Dominicana cediera la península de Samaná para un establecimiento francés permanente y convertían al gobernador francés de Samaná en el representante del protectorado. El periódico añade que el acuerdo fue aceptado por Ferdinand Barrot y respaldado por la escuadra naval francesa.

records.headline: Under the heading "France and St. Domingo," the Tribune translates
records.summary_en: Under the heading "France and St. Domingo," the Tribune translates an article from the Courrier du Havre responding to American and British complaints over rumored French designs on Samaná. The French paper questions Anglo-American objections to foreign acquisitions and provides historical context regarding Dominican independence. The account states that during the 1844 independence movement against Haitian rule, Dominican leader Pedro Santana sought a foreign protector and turned to France, initiating long and difficult negotiations with a hesitant French cabinet.
records.summary_es: Bajo el encabezado «Francia y Santo Domingo», el Tribune traduce un artículo del Courrier du Havre que responde a las quejas estadounidenses y británicas sobre supuestos planes franceses en Samaná. El diario francés cuestiona las objeciones angloamericanas a las adquisiciones extranjeras y aporta contexto histórico sobre la independencia dominicana. El relato afirma que durante el movimiento de independencia de 1844 contra el dominio haitiano, el líder dominicano Pedro Santana buscó un protector extranjero y recurrió a Francia, iniciando negociaciones largas y difíciles con un indeciso gabinete francés.

The newspaper also noted that Mr. Brooke withdrew a resolution regarding the suspension of official relations with Nicaragua's minister for later introduction in Executive session. La gaceta registró asimismo que el Sr. Brooke retiró una moción tendiente a interrumpir los lazos diplomáticos con el ministro de Nicaragua a fin de someterla en sesión secreta. records.summary_en: Letters from France dated in late November make no mention of a pretended occupation of Saint Domingo, noting instead that French vessels were stationed at Port-au-Prince to watch Soulouque's movements. The report also states that no peace treaty has been signed between the Dominican Republic and the Haytian Empire, raising expectations that hostilities would resume following the expiration of the armistice. Additionally, M. Max. Raybaud's May mission as French Plenipotentiary was to sign a Treaty of Commerce and Navigation with the Dominican Republic, which has now been ratified.

El parte advierte asimismo que no se había firmado ningún tratado de paz formal entre la República Dominicana y el Imperio haitiano, avivándose el temor de que se reanudaran los enfrentamientos al fenecer el armisticio. Por lo demás, la misión de mayo de M. Max Raybaud como plenipotenciario consistió en suscribir un Tratado de Comercio y Navegación con la República Dominicana, el cual quedó ratificado.

records.headline: The Weekly National Intelligencer cites French press accounts
records.summary_en: The Weekly National Intelligencer cites French press accounts explaining naval movements that sparked American rumors regarding the occupation of Samaná. According to the semi-official paper La Patrie, the frigate La Sibylle left Martinique after an epidemic merely to cruise the Antilles for crew health, and its appearance in Dominican waters generated false reports of military occupation. Meanwhile, the Journal des Débats dismissed reports that France seized the eastern part of the island, though it deemed a French protectorate over the Dominican Republic plausible. The Débats recalled that the republic previously offered Louis Philippe the protectorate before the 1848 revolution intervened.
records.summary_es: El Weekly National Intelligencer cita reseñas de la prensa francesa que explican movimientos navales que suscitaron rumores en los Estados Unidos sobre la ocupación de Samaná. Según el diario semioficial La Patrie, la fragata La Sibylle abandonó Martinica tras una epidemia simplemente para realizar un crucero por las Antillas por la salud de su tripulación, y su presencia en aguas dominicanas generó falsos reportes de ocupación militar. En tanto, el Journal des Débats desestimó que Francia se hubiera apoderado de la parte oriental de la isla, si bien consideró verosímil un protectorado francés sobre la República Dominicana. El Débats recordó que la república había ofrecido anteriormente el protectorado a Luis Felipe antes de que sobreviniera la revolución de 1848.

records.headline: The Daily Union comments that Dominican offers of a protectorate
records.summary_en: The Daily Union comments that Dominican offers of a protectorate, previously rejected by King Louis Philippe and the Second Republic, have been renewed to Emperor Napoleon III with greater prospects of acceptance. The paper reprints an extract from the Congressional Globe copying a Kingston letter to the Courrier des États-Unis that welcomes French protection over the Dominican Republic. The correspondent argues that French control would safeguard Cuba from American filibusters and shield the fertile eastern part of the island against aggressive Haitian incursions, urging the French Empire to accept what earlier governments declined.

El corresponsal sostiene que el control francés resguardaría a Cuba de los filibusteros estadounidenses y protegería la fértil parte oriental de la isla frente a agresivas incursiones haitianas, instando al Imperio francés a aceptar lo que gobiernos anteriores declinaron.

records.headline: A Paris correspondent examines a French press article arguing that France had missed chances to extend its influence
records.summary_en: A Paris correspondent examines a French press article arguing that France had missed chances to extend its influence in America. The article says the peninsula of Samana and the whole Dominican Republic were offered to the French government in exchange for its flag and protection, and the correspondent suspects Napoleon III is now seriously considering a larger French role in America.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal en París examina un artículo de la prensa francesa que sostiene que Francia había perdido oportunidades de extender su influencia en América. El artículo dice que la península de Samaná y toda la República Dominicana fueron ofrecidas al gobierno francés a cambio de su bandera y su protección, y el corresponsal sospecha que Napoleón III está considerando ahora seriamente un papel francés mayor en América.

records.headline: The National Intelligencer publishes a translation of a French essay
records.summary_en: The National Intelligencer publishes a translation of a French essay discussing the expansion of French influence in the Americas. The writer recalls that the peninsula of Samaná and the entire Dominican Republic were previously offered to the French government in exchange for its flag and naval protection. The author explains that this proposal was rejected not because of Spanish or British opposition, but because of parliamentary timidity and opposition within the French Chambers under earlier regimes. Under the Empire, the essay concludes, the French government is finally liberated from legislative indecision.
records.summary_es: El National Intelligencer publica la traducción de un ensayo francés que examina la expansión de la influencia francesa en las Américas. El autor recuerda que la península de Samaná y toda la República Dominicana fueron ofrecidas anteriormente al gobierno francés a cambio de su bandera y protección naval. El texto explica que esta propuesta fue rechazada no por oposición española o británica, sino por la timidez parlamentaria y la resistencia de las Cámaras francesas bajo regímenes anteriores. Bajo el Imperio, concluye el ensayo, el gobierno francés se encuentra finalmente liberado de la indecisión legislativa.

records.headline: An editorial in the National Era censures American diplomacy
records.summary_en: An editorial in the National Era censures American diplomacy for interfering as a partisan in Hispaniola to resist Haitian supremacy while disregarding the Monroe Doctrine. The paper argues that Washington's policy achieved nothing—gaining neither a foothold in "Dominica," nor the favor of the Dominican government, nor colonial opportunities in that white republic, while opening the door to French influence at Samaná. The editorial then quotes a paragraph from the National Intelligencer reporting the arrival of the Spanish steamer Isabel II at Havana from Santo Domingo, where the vessel was warmly received, confirming that rumors of Samaná's cession to France were unfounded.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el National Era censura a la diplomacia estadounidense por intervenir como partidaria en La Española para oponerse a la supremacía haitiana, ignorando la doctrina Monroe. El periódico sostiene que la política de Washington no logró nada: no obtuvo ni un punto de apoyo en «Dominica», ni el favor del gobierno dominicano, ni oportunidades colonizadoras en esa república blanca, al tiempo que abrió la puerta a la influencia francesa en Samaná. Luego, el editorial cita un párrafo del National Intelligencer que reporta la llegada a La Habana del vapor español Isabel II procedente de Santo Domingo, donde fue recibido con entusiasmo, confirmando que los rumores de la cesión de Samaná a Francia carecían de fundamento.

records.summary_en: A vessel claimed as a prize by the Dominican government was declared piracy under republic laws, resulting in prison sentences of two years for the captain, mate, and pilot, and one year for the rest of the crew. Court proceedings revealed a questionable letter involving Senor Jose Maria Pando, the Spanish commercial agent at Curacao, regarding instructions and financial advances for the ship via a merchant in Porto Plata. Additionally, the Dominican Republic celebrated the February 15 inauguration of General Santana as president.

records.headline: The Republic reports that the Archbishop of Santo Domingo was summoned
records.summary_en: The Republic reports that the Archbishop of Santo Domingo was summoned before the Dominican National Congress for refusing to take the required constitutional oath of fidelity. When the archbishop declared he preferred banishment over sanctioning a heretical constitution, President Pedro Santana furnished him with passports, placed a national ship at his disposal, and granted him four thousand dollars for travel expenses. Touched by this unexpected generosity, the prelate withdrew his refusal and agreed to swear allegiance. The president ordered the oath ceremony conducted with full religious pomp in the Cathedral, followed by a Te Deum across all churches.
records.summary_es: The Republic informa que el arzobispo de Santo Domingo fue citado ante el Congreso Nacional dominicano por negarse a prestar el juramento constitucional de fidelidad requerido. Cuando el arzobispo declaró que prefería el destierro antes que sancionar una constitución herética, el presidente Pedro Santana le entregó sus pasaportes, puso un buque nacional a su disposición y le otorgó cuatro mil dólares para gastos de viaje. Conmovido por esta inesperada generosidad, el prelado retiró su negativa y aceptó jurar lealtad. El presidente ordenó que la ceremonia de juramento se celebrara con toda la pompa religiosa en la Catedral, seguida de un Te Deum en todas las iglesias.

records.headline: The Watchman and Observer reports that Dominican President Pedro Santana summoned
records.summary_en: The Watchman and Observer reports that Dominican President Pedro Santana summoned Archbishop Don Tomás de Portes before the National Congress for ecclesiastical interference in civil functions. When called upon to swear allegiance, the prelate refused to take the oath to what he termed an accursed and heretical constitution, stating he would choose exile instead. President Santana promptly provided him with a passport, a national vessel, and $4,000 for his journey, though the archbishop subsequently reconsidered, took the constitutional oath, and was restored to his ecclesiastical duties.

The archbishop initially refused the oath of fealty, declaring he would rather accept exile than swear to a heretical constitution. records.headline: The New York Herald publishes official documents brought to Boston
records.summary_en: The New York Herald publishes official documents brought to Boston from Santo Domingo aboard the schooner Arcturus. The papers include an executive decree issued under the national motto "God, Country and Liberty" by President Pedro Santana, General-in-Chief and Liberator of the Republic. The decree concerns offenses committed by Father Francisco Vionet, a Barcelona-born curate; while Santana affirms that such actions fall under ordinary judicial tribunals pursuant to the constitution and penal code, he defers to the Archbishop's request for executive clemency to avoid public scandal.
records.summary_es: El New York Herald publica documentos oficiales traídos a Boston desde Santo Domingo a bordo de la goleta Arcturus. Los papeles incluyen un decreto ejecutivo promulgado bajo el lema nacional «Dios, Patria y Libertad» por el presidente Pedro Santana, general en jefe y libertador de la República. El decreto se refiere a las faltas cometidas por el padre Francisco Vionet, cura oriundo de Barcelona; aunque Santana afirma que tales actos corresponden a los tribunales ordinarios conforme a la constitución y al código penal, acoge la solicitud del arzobispo de conceder clemencia ejecutiva para evitar el escándalo público.

records.headline: An article reprinted from the National Democrat in the Washington Sentinel highlights
records.summary_en: An article reprinted from the National Democrat in the Washington Sentinel highlights the geopolitical and commercial significance of Santo Domingo, situated at the nexus of major trade routes near Cuba and Jamaica. The piece rebukes the United States for maintaining an attitude of cruel indifference toward a country capable of providing immense wealth or serious political vexation. Describing the island as divided between a Black empire and a white republic, the article recounts how the Dominicans threw off Haitian oppression through heroic struggle. The author laments that Washington offered no assistance to the suffering republic during its contest for independence.
records.summary_es: Un artículo reproducido del National Democrat en el Washington Sentinel resalta la importancia geopolítica y comercial de Santo Domingo, situada en el nexo de las principales rutas comerciales cerca de Cuba y Jamaica. El escrito recrimina a los Estados Unidos por mantener una actitud de cruel indiferencia hacia un país capaz de proporcionar inmensas riquezas o graves complicaciones políticas. Al describir la isla como dividida entre un imperio negro y una república blanca, el artículo relata cómo los dominicanos se sacudieron la opresión haitiana mediante una lucha heroica. El autor lamenta que Washington no haya ofrecido auxilio a la sufrida república durante su contienda por la independencia.

records.headline: An editorial in the Daily Union highlights the ongoing dangers
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Daily Union highlights the ongoing dangers confronting the Dominican Republic from the neighboring Haitian empire. The paper asserts that European powers share an interest in aiding Haitian efforts to crush the Dominican republic and eliminate independent republican governance in the West Indies. Noting that the Dominican Republic is the only territory along this island perimeter aligned with American principles, the editorial argues that the safety and independence of "Dominica" represents a vital United States interest. The paper calls on Washington to offer protection, alliance, and formal recognition.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Daily Union destaca los continuos peligros que enfrenta la República Dominicana ante el vecino imperio haitiano. El diario sostiene que las potencias europeas tienen interés en respaldar los esfuerzos haitianos para aplastar a la república dominicana y eliminar el gobierno republicano independiente en las Antillas. Al advertir que la República Dominicana es el único territorio en ese perímetro insular afín a los principios estadounidenses, el editorial afirma que la seguridad y la independencia de «Dominica» representan un interés vital para los Estados Unidos. El periódico pide a Washington ofrecer protección, alianza y reconocimiento formal.

records.headline: The Richmond Enquirer quotes a New York Sun review of an article
records.summary_en: The Richmond Enquirer quotes a New York Sun review of an article in the New York paper La Verdad regarding the Dominican Republic. The piece contends that the United States government acts against its own interests by neglecting to cultivate a close alliance with its sister republic. According to the article, such an alliance would foster the extension of republican institutions throughout the island and thwart British-backed designs to "Africanize" the West Indian archipelago against the influence of the American republic.
records.summary_es: El Richmond Enquirer cita una reseña del New York Sun sobre un artículo publicado en el diario neoyorquino La Verdad en relación con la República Dominicana. El artículo sostiene que el gobierno de los Estados Unidos actúa en contra de sus propios intereses al descuidar el cultivo de una estrecha alianza con su república hermana. Según el texto, dicha alianza promovería la extensión de las instituciones republicanas por toda la isla y frustraría los planes auspiciados por los británicos para «africanizar» el archipiélago antillano en detrimento de la influencia de la república estadounidense.

records.headline: Reprinting an item from the New York Sun, the Weekly National Intelligencer notes
records.summary_en: Reprinting an item from the New York Sun, the Weekly National Intelligencer notes that a recent issue of La Verdad of New York contains an article examining the Republic of St. Domingo, its relations with the United States, and its position toward the Empire of Faustin I in Haiti. According to the report, the article argues that the U.S. government and people are neglecting their own interests by failing to foster their sister republic and form a closer alliance and community of interests with her. It points out that the rational result of such an alliance would be the extension of republican institutions over the Haitian portion of the island and the prevention of a British-protected scheme to "Africanize the Columbian Archipelago" as a bulwark against the spread of U.S. principles and institutions.
records.summary_es: Reproduciendo una nota del New York Sun, el Weekly National Intelligencer señala que un número reciente de La Verdad de Nueva York contiene un artículo que examina la República de Santo Domingo, sus relaciones con los Estados Unidos y su posición frente al Imperio de Faustin I en Haití. Según el informe, el artículo sostiene que el pueblo y el gobierno estadounidenses descuidan sus propios intereses al no fomentar a su república hermana ni procurar formar una alianza más estrecha y una comunidad de intereses con ella. Señala como resultado racional de dicha alianza la extensión de las instituciones republicanas sobre la parte haitiana de la isla y la prevención de un plan protegido por el gabinete británico para «africanizar el archipiélago colombino» como baluarte contra el avance de los principios e instituciones de los Estados Unidos.

records.summary_en: The paper gives a dramatic, racially framed period account of an attack on a Dominican village by a party led by one of Soulouque's captains after Santana raised the flag of Dominican independence, and of local horsemen rallying residents to a hand-to-hand fight. It says the account ended with a truce said to be consolidating into peace.

Dice que el relato terminaba con una tregua que se consolidaba en paz.

records.headline: The New York Herald reports that after two French Haitians were expelled
records.summary_en: The New York Herald reports that after two French Haitians were expelled from the country, the French demanded that President General Santana dismiss his cabinet and appoint another more favorable to French interests. The article predicts that French intrigue may bring about Santana's downfall in January or February and reinstate ex-President Báez—whom it characterizes as thoroughly French in feeling and sentiment—as dictator. The paper asks whether the U.S. government will permit this violation of its professed principles and urges the cabinet in Washington to investigate and compel the French to desist if proved to be "filibustering with the Dominican republic." It adds that the greatest excitement prevailed in the City of St. Domingo on the 25th of the previous month.
records.summary_es: El New York Herald informa que, tras la expulsión de dos haitianos franceses del país, los franceses exigieron al presidente general Santana la destitución de su gabinete y el nombramiento de otro más acorde con los intereses franceses. El artículo pronostica que la intriga francesa podría provocar la caída de Santana en enero o febrero y restituir como dictador al expresidente Báez, a quien describe como completamente francés en sentimiento. El periódico pregunta si el gobierno de los Estados Unidos permitirá esta violación de sus principios profesados e insta al gabinete en Washington a investigar el asunto y obligar a los franceses a desistir si se demuestra que están «filibusteando con la República Dominicana». Añade que la mayor agitación reinaba en la ciudad de Santo Domingo el día 25 del mes anterior.

records.passage: Still later, when Santana, the Liberator, unfurled the flag of Dominican independence, a party of negroes, led by one of Soulouque's black captains, attacked the neighboring village, with the war-cry of "death to the whites." This ominous cry, which has so often carried terror and destruction to the whites of eastern Hayti, sent the frightened inhabitants to the mountain dells for refuge, but as they fled they were met near the ruined church by a little band of horsemen, coming to their rescue. The young leader unfurled the white cross of Dominica under the light of their blazing homes, and rallied them to battle in their own defence. It was a deadly, desperate strife. They were not many, but they fought hand to hand with all the cherished bitterness of hostile races, until the morning — the glorious, gorgeous morning of the tropics — dawned on the field, and revealed the victory of the whites. records.headline: An editorial in the New York Herald argues that a reply in La Patrie fully
records.summary_en: An editorial in the New York Herald argues that a reply in La Patrie fully confirmed the impression that France contemplated serious steps against the independence of the Dominican Republic. According to the Herald, La Patrie passed over in silence the specific charges made by the Herald's correspondent and instead claimed that the inhabitants of St. Domingo had frequently demanded annexation to France or a French protectorate. The Herald counters that M. Mouttet conveniently omitted that those demands were made under the direct influence of ex-President Báez, a partisan of French interests who was subsequently expelled from the island for his anti-national tendencies. The editorial concludes that the object of the French hostile demonstration was to restore Báez and establish a French protectorate, which aroused indignation among the Dominican people.

El editorial concluye que el objeto de la demostración hostil francesa era restaurar a Báez y establecer un protectorado francés, lo cual despertó indignación entre el pueblo dominicano.

records.headline: Reporting from Santo Domingo newspaper files up to February 18
records.summary_en: Reporting from Santo Domingo newspaper files up to February 18, the New York Herald states that the Constituent Assembly was in session and spiritedly debating proposed constitutional amendments drafted by a select committee. Citing El Orden, the paper notes that Andrés Aybar, Alcalde of the capital, has undertaken vigorous municipal reforms in San Domingo, including the immediate construction of an extensive market house. Additionally, the Santo Domingo papers announce the death on January 23 of José Joaquín Delmonte at the age of eighty-four, noting that he devoted sixty-two years to public service and most recently served as President of the Supreme Court of Justice in the republic.
records.summary_es: Informando a partir de periódicos de Santo Domingo hasta el 18 de febrero, el New York Herald señala que la Asamblea Constituyente se encontraba en sesión y debatía animadamente varias enmiendas constitucionales propuestas y redactadas por una comisión selecta. Citando a El Orden, el diario indica que Andrés Aybar, alcalde de la capital, ha emprendido vigorosas reformas municipales en Santo Domingo, entre ellas la construcción inmediata de un amplio mercado. Asimismo, los periódicos anuncian el fallecimiento, el 23 de enero, de José Joaquín Delmonte a los ochenta y cuatro años de edad, destacando que dedicó sesenta y dos años al servicio público y que su último cargo fue el de presidente de la Suprema Corte de Justicia de la república.

records.summary_en: According to the *New-York daily tribune* on April 21, 1854, martial law was declared in Santiago following a conspiracy, with five ringleaders before the court and over forty persons under arrest. Meanwhile, the revision of the Dominican Constitution was completed, featuring an increased number of representatives and senators, the creation of a vice president, and changes reducing the naturalization time periods required for foreigners to become eligible as representatives and senators. Additionally, while the standard presidential and vice-presidential term was set at four years, actual President General Santana was granted two terms in office, allowing him to hold the chair until February 1861.
records.summary_es: Con arreglo al *New-York daily tribune* del 21 de abril de 1854, se declaró el estado de sitio en Santiago a raíz de una conspiración, encausándose ante los jueces a cinco cabecillas y permaneciendo más de cuarenta sujetos en prisión. Entre tanto, concluyó la reforma de la Constitución dominicana, elevándose la representación en el cuerpo legislativo con mayor número de diputados y senadores, estableciéndose la magistratura de vicepresidente y abreviándose los plazos de avecindamiento para que los forasteros optasen a ser elegidos representantes y senadores. Asimismo, fijándose en cuatro años el mandato ordinario del presidente y vicepresidente, al actual mandatario, general Santana, se le concedieron dos períodos sucesivos, autorizándosele a regir la presidencia hasta febrero de 1861.

records.headline: An editorial in the Washington Sentinel criticizes the failure of the United States
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Washington Sentinel criticizes the failure of the United States to recognize the independence of the Dominican Republic. Recounting twenty-two years of Haitian rule over the Spanish portion of the island of Santo Domingo, the paper states that the sons of the colonists in the plains of Seybo and Vega rose under Pedro Santana, fought three or four decisive battles, and drove Soulouque and his forces back to the west, where they have been kept for ten consecutive years. Having maintained the Dominican Republic under a liberal constitution, the Dominicans ask the United States for the moral aid of friendly recognition as what the paper calls the only free white self-governing American state in the West Indies. The editorial laments that after nine years this request remains unanswered, neglecting an opportunity to bring the republic into the American system as a center of resistance to the European policy of "Africanizing" the islands.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Washington Sentinel critica la negativa de los Estados Unidos a reconocer la independencia de la República Dominicana. Al relatar veintidós años de dominio haitiano sobre la parte española de la isla de Santo Domingo, el periódico afirma que los hijos de los colonos en las llanuras de El Seibo y La Vega se levantaron bajo el mando de Pedro Santana, libraron tres o cuatro batallas decisivas y rechazaron a Soulouque y sus fuerzas hacia el oeste, donde han sido contenidos durante diez años consecutivos. Habiendo mantenido la República Dominicana bajo una constitución liberal, los dominicanos solicitan a los Estados Unidos el apoyo moral de un reconocimiento amistoso para lo que el diario denomina el único Estado americano libre, blanco y autónomo en las Antillas. El editorial lamenta que, al cabo de nueve años, esta solicitud siga sin respuesta, desaprovechando la oportunidad de integrar la república al sistema americano como núcleo de resistencia frente a la política europea de «africanizar» las islas.

records.headline: An editorial in the Washington Sentinel argues that the Dominicans
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Washington Sentinel argues that the Dominicans, having established their republic and defended their territory from the Haitian government at the west end of the island for ten years, are entitled to U.S. recognition by all rules of international comity. The paper contends that "Dominica" is already forced to contend with Haiti as directed by the diplomacy of France and England, and that U.S. passivity and refusal to distinguish the Dominican Republic from Haiti aids European aims in the West Indies. It concludes that the mere act of acknowledging the Dominican Republic and establishing diplomatic relations with her would save the country from European machinations and preserve a valuable state for the American system.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Washington Sentinel sostiene que los dominicanos, tras haber establecido su república y defendido su territorio frente al gobierno haitiano en el extremo occidental de la isla durante diez años, tienen derecho al reconocimiento de los Estados Unidos según todas las normas de cortesía internacional. El periódico argumenta que «Dominica» ya se ve obligada a enfrentarse a Haití bajo la dirección de la diplomacia de Francia e Inglaterra, y que la pasividad estadounidense y su negativa a distinguir a la República Dominicana de Haití favorecen los propósitos europeos en las Antillas. Concluye que el solo acto de reconocer a la República Dominicana y establecer relaciones diplomáticas con ella salvaría al país de las maquinaciones de Europa y preservaría un Estado valioso para el sistema americano.

According to the correspondent, the Dominicans are making active preparations to receive him, though it has been discovered that the cannonballs purchased for their warships are too large for the guns and that they lack both seamen and commanders. Nevertheless, the writer remarks that this makes no difference because the Dominicans rely on close combat against the Haitians and are always victorious.

records.headline: A contributor in the New-York Daily Tribune criticizes the Post
records.summary_en: A contributor in the New-York Daily Tribune criticizes the Post for treating the Dominican Republic—described as independent and self-sustaining for ten years—as revolted subjects of Haiti, and disputes the claim that "Dominica" is no less a Black government than Haiti or Liberia. The writer asserts that the President, the entire Cabinet, and all other high officials of the Dominican government whom the writer has met were white gentlemen, except for one naval officer of maternal Indigenous descent. The letter further contrasts the two nations, stating that the Dominicans maintain a liberal, progressive republic where foreigners may hold property and enjoy freedom of religious worship, whereas Haiti excludes white citizens under a harsh "Czarism." Finally, the writer denies that General Pierce or his administration have engaged in any intrigue regarding the young republic.
records.summary_es: Un colaborador del New-York Daily Tribune critica al Post por tratar a la República Dominicana —descrita como independiente y autosuficiente durante diez años— como súbditos sublevados de Haití, y refuta la afirmación de que «Dominica» no sea menos un gobierno negro que Haití o Liberia. El autor asegura que el presidente, todo el gabinete y todos los demás altos funcionarios del gobierno dominicano que ha conocido eran caballeros blancos, con la excepción de un oficial naval de ascendencia indígena por línea materna. Asimismo, la carta contrasta a ambas naciones, señalando que los dominicanos mantienen una república liberal y progresista donde los extranjeros pueden poseer propiedades y gozar de libertad de culto religioso, mientras que Haití excluye a los ciudadanos blancos bajo un severo «zarismo». Por último, el autor niega que el general Pierce o su administración hayan participado en intriga alguna respecto a la joven república.

records.headline: An editorial in the Washington Sentinel urges the United States
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Washington Sentinel urges the United States to recognize the independence of the Dominican Republic, emphasizing that San Domingo lies at America's doors and has established a form of government similar to that of the United States. The paper notes that the Dominican Republic invites commerce and emigration and is anxious to conclude commercial treaties that would benefit U.S. trade, whereas the refusal to grant recognition prevents both treaty-making and any effort to end the chronic hostilities on the island. Pointing out that the United States has refused to recognize the government of Haiti, the editorial asks why Washington should respect Haitian claims to Dominican territory. It concludes that only an act of Congress is needed for recognition and states that President Pierce takes a deep interest in the matter and would be pleased to sign such legislation.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Washington Sentinel insta a los Estados Unidos a reconocer la independencia de la República Dominicana, destacando que Santo Domingo se encuentra a las puertas de los Estados Unidos y ha establecido una forma de gobierno similar a la estadounidense. El periódico señala que la República Dominicana invita al comercio y a la emigración y desea celebrar tratados comerciales muy beneficiosos para el intercambio estadounidense, mientras que la negativa a otorgar el reconocimiento impide tanto la firma de tratados como cualquier gestión para poner fin al estado crónico de hostilidades en la isla. Al señalar que los Estados Unidos se han negado a reconocer al gobierno de Haití, el editorial pregunta por qué Washington habría de respetar las pretensiones haitianas sobre el territorio ocupado por los dominicanos. Concluye que solo se necesita una ley del Congreso para el reconocimiento y afirma que el presidente Pierce siente un profundo interés en el asunto y firmaría con agrado dicha ley.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
THE RECOGNITION OF DOMINICA.

We are gratified to perceive that the public journals throughout the country are discussing the propriety of recognizing the independence of Dominica. Almost all those we have noticed urge the recognition as a duty we owe to a brave people and to republican principles. Some, however, oppose that recognition; and being chiefly of the freesoil or abolition stamp, their opposition proves the soundness of the measure. All we desire is to have the subject brought to the attention of the people and of the representatives of people, feeling perfectly sure that when it is understood, every obstacle will vanish at once.

For ten years the whites of San Domingo have maintained their independence against the Haytian negroes, although many attempts have been made to subjugate them. Having maintained their independence thus long against the barbarous forces of a negro empire, they ask only that countenance and encouragement from the United States, which we have often extended to others whose situation did not appeal so strongly to our sense of justice or to our sympathies.

The descendants of the few whites left by the great San Domingo massacre, retired to the west portion of the island, and after declaring their independence, maintained the declaration and established a republican form of government. The negroes in the eastern portion of the island, after years of tumult, established an empire with a black emperor—as black as the ace of spades—who has tricked himself out in all the stars, and spangles, and gewgaws, of an eastern monarch. This negro empire of Hayti will give the white republic of Dominica no rest. Year after year it persists in acts of annoyance, and is constantly threatening to exterminate the whites or bring them under subjugation.

We cannot believe that the people of America, omitting a few crazy abolitionists, can look with unconcern upon such a spectacle, when it is presented to them in the proper light. It is abhorrent to every American sentiment, and more than that, it is an outrage on humanity. To see a brave, frugal, thrifty white race of Christians overrun by a miserable and debauched horde of black barbarians, is a sight too revolting to be contemplated. And the picture is not softened in any of its disgusting details by the knowledge that the whites have established a form of government similar to our own, and that their adversaries bear the banner of an infamous despotism.

It should be borne in mind that San Domingo is not far off. It does not belong to the other hemisphere. It is at our doors; and forms a part of the North American continent. Its fate is, therefore, a matter of great importance, and ought to be one of deep concern to us. The Dominican republic invites commerce and emigration. It is anxious to enter into commercial treaties with us which would be eminently beneficial to our trade. Its productions are extremely valuable and a confirmed peace would increase them an hundred fold, and that too within a short time. But whilst we fail or refuse to recognize the independence of the republic we can make no treaties with it, nor can we interfere in any manner to cure that chronic state of hostilities which has hitherto existed.

We have refused to recognise the negro government of Hayti. Why should we then respect its claim to the territory occupied by the Dominicans? What then stands in the way of the recognition we urge? An act of Congress, of which no one can complain, is all that is needed; for we feel no hesitation in saying that the President would be much pleased to be afforded the opportunity of attaching his signature to such an act. We do not, of course, speak by authority; but, yet, we may safely say that General Pierce feels a deep interest in this matter, and would give his influence, as far as he rightfully could, to carry out such a measure; for there is a multitude of reasons which urge its adoption, whilst not one can be brought against it. It is time, therefore, that the independence of Dominica should be acknowledged by the United States. That recognition costs us nothing, whilst it will be of incalculable benefit to a sister republic maintaining herself against a black despotism.

The moral force of such a recognition would have an immediate effect, and it would place us in a position to negotiate favorable treaties and avail ourselves of a valuable trade. We could then say to the Haytien negroes that they had annoyed the neighborhood long enough; that Dominica had achieved her independence; that the commercial interests of those dealing with her could not longer be injured by the hostility of black savages. The earth was made for use; and all authorities agree that nations have a right to put an end to protracted wars which annoy their trade and injure their interests without promising any definite result. But even if our government shall not go thus far—even if it should be willing to see the negroes of Hayti harass the whites of Dominica for ten years to come, still we urge the recognition of the republic as a measure due to justice and to the sympathies of the people. It is right and proper in itself, it is in accordance with our previous action, and it is demanded by the genius of our institutions and the position we occupy as the great republic of the western world. We were the first to urge this measure, and we will be abandon it.

records.headline: A correspondence from the City of St. Domingo, published in the New York Herald
records.summary_en: A correspondence from the City of St. Domingo, published in the New York Herald and signed "Felix," dated May 16, 1854, reports that circumstances regarding the anticipated war with Haiti have altogether changed. According to the writer, five French warships and one English warship went to Port-au-Prince to keep Emperor Soulouque quiet, and the English warship Trincomalee also sailed from Jamaica to Port-au-Prince for the same purpose. The correspondent adds that Emperor Napoleon sent President Santana a splendid set of porcelain, which Santana accepted. Expressing suspicion about why the French and English are so attentive to the Dominican Republic, the writer concludes that whenever the United States wishes to possess the island, "American valor will take it with as much ease as you would a pinch of snuff."
records.summary_es: Una correspondencia desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo, firmada por «Felix» y fechada el 16 de mayo de 1854, publicada en el New York Herald, informa que la situación respecto a la guerra prevista con Haití ha cambiado por completo. Según el autor, cinco buques de guerra franceses y uno inglés se dirigieron a Puerto Príncipe para mantener tranquilo al emperador Soulouque, y el buque de guerra inglés Trincomalee también partió de Jamaica hacia Puerto Príncipe con el mismo propósito. El corresponsal añade que el emperador Napoleón envió como obsequio una espléndida vajilla de porcelana al presidente Santana, la cual este aceptó. Tras expresar sospechas sobre la gran atención que franceses e ingleses prestan a la República Dominicana, el autor concluye que el día en que los Estados Unidos deseen poseer la isla, el valor estadounidense la tomará con tanta facilidad como quien toma una pizca de rapé.

It argues the United States should protect the Dominican Republic and says France was intriguing for its conquest.

records.headline: An editorial in the New-York Daily Tribune calls public attention
records.summary_en: An editorial in the New-York Daily Tribune calls public attention back to intelligence derived from the journals of St. Domingo City regarding General Cazneau's mission to the Dominican Republic. The paper states that Cazneau, the alleged U.S. Commissioner, is notoriously connected with a scheme for colonizing and annexing "Dominica," noting that when he sailed aboard the frigate Columbia, its avowed destination was Haiti at the other end of the island. Consequently, the Tribune argues that either Cazneau is falsely passing himself off as a U.S. Commissioner with a frigate aiding the deception, or the Executive under General Pierce and Mr. Marcy is carrying out a conspiracy against a weak neighbor to gratify "slave-drivers" who have long coveted the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del New-York Daily Tribune vuelve a llamar la atención del público sobre las noticias procedentes de los periódicos de la ciudad de Santo Domingo acerca de la misión del general Cazneau en la República Dominicana. El diario afirma que Cazneau, el supuesto comisionado estadounidense, está notoriamente vinculado con el plan de colonizar y anexar a «Dominica», y señala que cuando zarpó a bordo de la fragata Columbia, el propósito declarado del viaje era dirigirse a Haití, en el otro extremo de la misma isla. En consecuencia, el Tribune sostiene que o bien Cazneau se hace pasar allí por comisionado de los Estados Unidos sin autorización pero con una fragata que secunda el engaño, o bien el Ejecutivo bajo el general Pierce y el señor Marcy lleva adelante una conspiración contra un vecino débil para complacer a los esclavistas que desde hace mucho codician a la República Dominicana.
