records.headline: An editorial in the Burlington Free Press warns of comprehensive schemes of pro-slavery
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Burlington Free Press warns of comprehensive schemes of pro-slavery expansion, noting alongside designs on Mexico, the African slave trade, and Brazil that a U.S. Senator has broached the recognition of the Dominican Republic with an ulterior view to its annexation. Although the paper acknowledges that some of these designs are still embryonic and not shared by judicious men of any section, it argues that their mere conception among men of eminent station should awaken public vigilance. Because American plans are executed with "the rapidity of magnetism," the editorial urges timely watchfulness against the earliest beginnings of such pro-slavery projects.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Burlington Free Press advierte sobre amplios planes de expansión esclavista y señala, junto a proyectos relativos a México, el tráfico de esclavos africanos y Brasil, que un senador estadounidense ha planteado el reconocimiento de la República Dominicana con la mira ulterior de su anexión. Aunque el periódico reconoce que algunos de estos designios se encuentran aún en ciernes y no son compartidos por los hombres sensatos de ninguna región, sostiene que su sola concepción entre figuras de alta posición debe despertar la vigilancia pública. Dado que en la nación los planes se ejecutan con «la rapidez del magnetismo», el editorial insta a mantener una vigilancia oportuna frente a los primeros indicios de tales proyectos proesclavistas.

Informa que la Colombia llegó en cambio a la ciudad de Santo Domingo, donde se habían abierto negociaciones para un tratado que aseguraría un puerto para el gobierno estadounidense en la bahía de Samaná.

records.headline: "The Plot Against Dominica" heads a New-York Daily Tribune editorial
records.summary_en: "The Plot Against Dominica" heads a New-York Daily Tribune editorial recalling that more than three years earlier the paper first warned the American public of a conspiracy to acquire the eastern part of St. Domingo, aimed at the ultimate conquest and annexation of the island to the American confederation as two or more slave states. The article recounts the visit of a U.S. diplomat—whom President Báez described to France as having come as Chargé d'Affaires—whose public purpose never transpired. According to the Tribune, the real scope of his visit was revealed in certain "Propositions of Colonization" submitted by that diplomat and his father, General Duff Green, which offered money, one or two steamers, and regular postal communication with the United States in exchange for permission for the Greens and their associates to introduce colonists.
records.summary_es: Bajo el titular «El complot contra Dominica», un editorial del New-York Daily Tribune recuerda que hace más de tres años el periódico advirtió por primera vez al público estadounidense sobre la existencia de una conspiración para adquirir la parte oriental de Santo Domingo, con miras a la conquista definitiva y anexión de la isla a la confederación estadounidense en forma de dos o más Estados esclavistas. El artículo relata la visita de un diplomático estadounidense —de quien el presidente Báez escribió a Francia que había llegado como encargado de negocios— cuyo propósito público nunca trascendió. Según el Tribune, el verdadero alcance de su visita se manifestó claramente en ciertas «Proposiciones de Colonización» presentadas por dicho diplomático junto con su padre, el general Duff Green, las cuales ofrecían dinero, uno o dos vapores y comunicación postal regular con los Estados Unidos a cambio de que se permitiera a los Green y sus asociados introducir colonos.

records.headline: The New-York Daily Tribune continues its critique of pro-slavery
records.summary_en: The New-York Daily Tribune continues its critique of pro-slavery interest in the Dominican Republic, arguing that appeals made on behalf of the people of "Dominica" by those who prioritize racial complexion are hypocritical and driven by "motives worthy only of robbers and slave-drivers." The editorial contends that it is difficult to see how the U.S. government can recognize "Dominica" while refusing the same courtesy to Haiti and Liberia, asserting that neither of the latter countries is more under the control of men of Black blood or less worthy in the character and abilities of its administrators. The passage also references B. E. Green's mission to St. Domingo City as a commissioner sent by President Polk and the propositions offering the Dominican government a loan and American colonists to carry on mining, concluding that selective diplomatic recognition depends on whether Northern freemen are willing to be used to spread slavery.
records.summary_es: Continuando su crítica al interés esclavista en la República Dominicana, el New-York Daily Tribune sostiene que los llamados hechos en nombre del pueblo de «Dominica» por quienes dan suma importancia al color de la piel son hipócritas y obedecen a «motivos dignos únicamente de ladrones y negreros». El editorial argumenta que resulta difícil comprender cómo el gobierno de los Estados Unidos puede reconocer a «Dominica» y negar esa misma cortesía a Haití y Liberia, afirmando que ninguno de estos dos últimos países está más bajo el control de hombres de sangre negra ni es menos digno en cuanto al carácter y capacidad de sus gobernantes. El pasaje también hace referencia a la misión de B. E. Green en la ciudad de Santo Domingo como comisionado enviado por el presidente Polk y a las proposiciones que ofrecían al gobierno dominicano un préstamo y colonos estadounidenses dedicados a la minería, concluyendo que el reconocimiento diplomático selectivo depende de hasta qué punto los hombres libres del Norte estén dispuestos a servir de instrumentos para extender la esclavitud.

records.summary_en: The paper confirms reports that General and Mrs. Cazneau succeeded in their mission to the Dominican Republic and that a treaty was made ceding the port of Samana, on the bay of that name, to the United States, along with a strip of land. The editorial describes Samana Bay, its entrance, islands and harbor, in detail, and denounces the acquisition as a foothold for a slavery-extending government and a first step toward annexation of the island.
records.summary_es: El periódico confirma los informes de que el general Cazneau y su esposa tuvieron éxito en su misión a la República Dominicana y de que se firmó un tratado que cede a los Estados Unidos el puerto de Samaná, en la bahía de ese nombre, junto con una franja de tierra. El editorial describe en detalle la bahía de Samaná, su entrada, sus islas y su puerto, y denuncia la adquisición como un punto de apoyo para un gobierno empeñado en extender la esclavitud y como un primer paso hacia la anexión de la isla.

records.summary_en: The *Liberator* reported that the Boston Post defended the United States government's disposition to recognize the independence of Dominica while ignoring the absence of any proposed recognition for Hayti and Liberia, despite stronger commercial and historical reasons to do so. The article argued that Dominica is of little commercial importance and would be politically united with Hayti—from which it rebelled due to religious differences—were it not for outside intrigues. Furthermore, the newspaper claimed that the American "Slave Power" has decided that the prosperity of Dominicans and Haytiens of African descent would injure its "peculiar institution."
records.summary_es: *The Liberator* refirió que el *Boston Post* justificó la inclinación del gobierno de Washington a reconocer la independencia dominicana al tiempo que ignoraba la falta de reconocimiento hacia Haití y Liberia, no obstante mediar motivos históricos y comerciales de mayor peso para hacerlo. La columna aducía que Santo Domingo poseía escaso relieve mercantil y permanecería unido políticamente a Haití —de donde se desgajó por disidencias religiosas— de no mediar intrigas foráneas. Aseveraba además el periódico que el «Poder Esclavista» norteamericano determinó que el florecimiento de dominicanos y haitianos de ascendencia africana perjudicaría a su «peculiar institución».

records.full_text:
From the Boston Commonwealth.
THE SLAVE POWER AND ST. DOMINGO.

Filibustering Manifest Destiny has proclaimed that the Slave Power must have ‘our Southern islands,’ and that the negroes of Cuba, Hayti, &c., must be doomed to perpetual slavery, and ‘kept at work under white republican masters.’ When this language was used in the Democratic Review, Hayti was named particularly, and it expressed no more than the Slave Power actually means and is now planning to accomplish. The purpose is to get possession of Hayti by means of filibusterism cunningly introduced into Dominica. One insidious attempt has been made upon Dominica, but failed. Duff Green was concerned in that affair, and his son was the agent employed in Dominica by our government. The conspirators sought to make an arrangement with the Dominican authorities, which should secure filibusters the privilege of ‘colonizing’ on that part of the island, with a separate and independent military organization of their own. Ostensibly, they were to be cutters of mahogony and dye woods, but really a filibustering army designed for the subjugation of the island when strong enough in numbers. But the Dominicans were suspicious, and the negotiation fell through.

Recently, Mrs. Cazneau, the ‘Cora Montgomery’ of some of the newspapers, and Gen. Cazneau, her husband, have been sent to Dominica to negotiate, plot, and intrigue, in behalf of this scheme of the Slave Power; and ‘Cora,’ it is said, has far more genius for the business than the General. It is reported that they have made some progress, that our Government will make a formal treaty with Dominica, and recognize its independence as a nation, and that the matter will soon be in shape to come before Congress. Of course, all this will not be done without such provisions in the treaty as will give our Slave Power that foothold in the island which it seeks. The whole purpose, on the part of our Government, is a filibustering invasion of both Dominica and Hayti. It means nothing else. It is seeking to execute that decree which says the African race in that island must be reduced to slavery, and ‘kept at work under white republican masters.’ If what is reported is true, (and it is fully credited by those likely to be best informed on the subject,) this is one of the next forms in which the slavery question is to be presented to the country, and the people should take it to their thoughts and feelings. The following statement in regard to this Cazneau treaty shows what is on foot:—

‘As far as could be collected from the first proceedings, the treaty is to have for one of its various ostensible objects, to stipulate for certain rights in the ports of the Republic, and especially in the spacious and secure bay of Samana, for the armed vessels of the United States, in case of war, and in time of peace, for the establishment of a kind of colonization, black or white, of individuals from the United States, in some part of the Dominican Republic.’

The Boston Post has already begun its defence of this villany, in a characteristic parrgraph of three or four lines, full of hypocritical wonder that anti-slavery men should put forth hostile criticism on the disposition of our government to recognize the independence of Dominica. Of course, that paper will never intimate to its readers, that, if this disposition of our Government were honest—if it is not, in fact, full of plotting piracy—it would also propose a recognition of the independence of Hayti and Liberia. There are more and stronger reasons for recognizing either of these gevernments than can be invented for this negotiation with Dominica. We have a large commerce with Hayti, and Liberia has grown up under American influences. Dominica is of little or no importance commercially, and would now be politically united with Hayti, if it had not rebelled and withdrawn, because that government proclaimed free toleration of all religious sects. The Dominicans have the religious training and bigotry of Spanish Catholics. They occupy what was the Spanish portion of the island, and the Haytiens that part which was held by the French. But they are all of African descent, and would constitute but one people, if not interfered with by the rascally intrigues of outsiders.

Our Slave Power has decided that it will injure the peculiar institution to allow the Dominicans and Haytiens, whose parents were slaves, to realize a prosperous and happy fortune. It will not do to let the world see them work out for themselves such a fortune; and, moreover, the slaveholders hope to prepare that island for annexation to the Union as a slave State. ‘Our Southern islands,’ they say; and how much that signifies!

records.headline: The Daily National Intelligencer reports news from St. Thomas
records.summary_en: The Daily National Intelligencer reports news from St. Thomas and states that U.S. diplomatic agents to the Dominican Republic have succeeded in their mission to secure the Bay of Samaná for a United States naval station. According to the report, President Santana is inclined to accept the friendship of the United States in the hope of finding a permanent barrier for the Dominicans against the ambition of the neighboring Haitian Emperor. The paper describes the Bay of Samaná, near the eastern end of the north side of the island, as one of the largest and most commodious harbors in the world, capable of accommodating the largest naval or merchant vessels and commanding both the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea more advantageously than any harbor in Cuba.
records.summary_es: El Daily National Intelligencer informa sobre noticias procedentes de San Tomás. Según éstas, los agentes diplomáticos de los Estados Unidos en la República Dominicana han tenido éxito en su misión de asegurar la bahía de Samaná para una estación naval estadounidense. Según el informe, el presidente Santana se inclina a aceptar la amistad de los Estados Unidos con la esperanza de encontrar en ella una barrera permanente para los dominicanos frente a la ambición del vecino emperador haitiano. El periódico describe la bahía de Samaná, situada en la costa norte cerca del extremo oriental de la isla, como uno de los puertos más grandes y cómodos del mundo, capaz de albergar a los mayores buques de guerra o mercantes y con dominio sobre el golfo de México y el mar Caribe en condiciones más ventajosas que cualquier puerto de Cuba.

records.headline: A letter in the New York Post says Soulouque, who was not worth a sous when chosen Emperor of Haiti, now owns
records.summary_en: A letter in the New York Post says Soulouque, who was not worth a sous when chosen Emperor of Haiti, now owns property valued at $2,000,000. It lists six large distilleries with sugar plantations attached for the manufacture of tafia and rum, fifty to seventy stores and houses, mostly in Port-au-Prince, and a new plantation bought recently for $60,000 with the intention, it is said, of attempting the manufacture of sugar.
records.summary_es: Una carta en el New York Post dice que Soulouque, que no valía un sou cuando fue elegido emperador de Haití, posee ahora propiedades valoradas en 2.000.000 de dólares. Enumera seis grandes destilerías con plantaciones de azúcar anexas para fabricar tafía y ron, entre cincuenta y setenta tiendas y casas, en su mayoría en Puerto Príncipe, y una nueva plantación comprada recientemente por 60.000 dólares con la intención, se dice, de intentar fabricar azúcar.

records.headline: Reprinting an item from the New York Herald, the Cecil Whig notes
records.summary_en: Reprinting an item from the New York Herald, the Cecil Whig notes a rumor that the U.S. diplomatic emissaries have succeeded in their mission to the Dominican Republic and that the port of Samaná has been ceded to the United States. The article expresses skepticism and calls for more authentic evidence before giving the report credence, asking why the Dominicans would be in such a hurry to part with their best seaport when the United States has no particular claim on their regard. Instead, the paper suggests it is more likely that the envoys followed in the steps of Louis-Philippe and obtained from the Dominicans the same privileges previously granted to that monarch.
records.summary_es: Reproduciendo una nota del New York Herald, el Cecil Whig recoge el rumor de que los enviados diplomáticos estadounidenses han tenido éxito en su misión ante la República Dominicana y que el puerto de Samaná ha sido cedido a los Estados Unidos. El artículo expresa escepticismo y pide pruebas más auténticas antes de dar crédito implícito a la noticia, preguntando por qué los dominicanos tendrían tanta prisa en desprenderse de su mejor puerto marítimo cuando los Estados Unidos no tienen ningún título particular sobre su consideración. En cambio, el periódico sugiere que parece más probable que los enviados hayan seguido los pasos de Luis Felipe y obtenido de los dominicanos los mismos privilegios que fueron concedidos a dicho monarca.

records.headline: Under the heading "The Republic of Dominica," the Anti-Slavery Bugle reports
records.summary_en: Under the heading "The Republic of Dominica," the Anti-Slavery Bugle reports that United States agents to the Dominican Republic have received from the Dominican president a guarantee granting the United States exclusive occupancy and use of the Bay of Samaná and adjacent land for a term of one hundred years. The paper characterizes this arrangement as a successful move against the independence and liberty of Haiti.
records.summary_es: Bajo el titular «La República de Dominica», el Anti-Slavery Bugle informa que los agentes de los Estados Unidos en la República Dominicana han recibido del presidente dominicano una garantía que otorga a los Estados Unidos la ocupación y el uso exclusivos de la bahía de Samaná y las tierras adyacentes por un plazo de cien años. El periódico califica este acuerdo como una maniobra exitosa contra la independencia y la libertad de Haití.

records.headline: The Athens Post notes that the St. Thomas correspondent of the New-York Tribune reports
records.summary_en: The Athens Post notes that the St. Thomas correspondent of the New-York Tribune reports a rumor current there that President Pierce's diplomatic agents to the Dominican Republic, Mr. and Mrs. Cazneau, have succeeded in their mission at least so far as to secure the Bay of Samaná for a United States naval station. The report also states that President Santana is inclined to accept the friendship of the United States, hoping to find in it a permanent barrier for "Dominica" against the ambition of the neighboring Emperor of Haiti.
records.summary_es: El Athens Post señala que el corresponsal del New-York Tribune en San Tomás informa sobre un rumor circulante allí según el cual los agentes diplomáticos del presidente Pierce en la República Dominicana, el señor y la señora Cazneau, han tenido éxito en su misión, al menos hasta el punto de asegurar la bahía de Samaná para una estación naval de los Estados Unidos. El informe también indica que el presidente Santana se inclina a aceptar la amistad de los Estados Unidos, esperando encontrar en ella una barrera permanente para «Dominica» frente a la ambición del vecino emperador de Haití.

records.headline: After denouncing American efforts to perpetuate and extend slavery
records.summary_en: After denouncing American efforts to perpetuate and extend slavery, the Anti-Slavery Bugle reprints from the Tribune a geographical description of the Bay of Samaná and the surrounding region in the northeastern corner of the island of St. Domingo. According to the account, the bay's entrance on the Atlantic is about twenty-four miles wide, its waters extend fifty miles inland, and two mile-long islands—the Grand Levantados Keys, situated fifteen miles from Cape Raphael on the south and twelve miles from Cape Samaná on the north—break the force of the winds and waves to create a secure anchorage. North of the bay stretches the hilly Samaná peninsula, which varies from four to ten miles in width, while the Port of Samaná, reported to be ceded to the United States, is formed by a cove extending from the bay into the peninsula.
records.summary_es: Tras denunciar los esfuerzos estadounidenses por perpetuar y extender la esclavitud, el Anti-Slavery Bugle reproduce del Tribune una descripción geográfica de la bahía de Samaná y la región adyacente en el extremo nororiental de la isla de Santo Domingo. Según la reseña, la entrada de la bahía hacia el Atlántico tiene unas veinticuatro millas de ancho, sus aguas se adentran cincuenta millas tierra adentro y dos islas de aproximadamente una milla de largo —los cayos Levantados, situados a quince millas del cabo Rafael al sur y a doce millas del cabo Samaná al norte— rompen la fuerza de los vientos y las olas para brindar un fondeadero seguro. Al norte de la bahía se extiende la montañosa península de Samaná, cuyo ancho varía entre cuatro y diez millas, mientras que el puerto de Samaná, que según se afirma ha sido cedido a los Estados Unidos, está formado por una ensenada que se adentra desde la bahía hacia la península.

records.headline: In a letter to the editor of the New-York Daily Tribune dated
records.summary_en: In a letter to the editor of the New-York Daily Tribune dated New York, October 20, 1854, a writer signing as "G." calls attention to what he terms a gross error in a St. Domingo correspondent's letter dated Santiago, September 14. The correspondent had claimed that the British Consul had more than once advised the Dominicans to strike the white cross and raise the Haitian tricolor, enraging the Dominican President. Asserting personal acquaintance with Sir Robert Schomburgh, the British Consul at St. Domingo, the letter writer declares that this allegation is a complete mistake and that the consul's actual course throughout has been the reverse of what was attributed to him.
records.summary_es: En una carta al director del New-York Daily Tribune fechada en Nueva York el 20 de octubre de 1854, un autor que firma como «G.» llama la atención sobre lo que califica de grave error en una carta del corresponsal en Santo Domingo fechada en Santiago el 14 de septiembre. El corresponsal había afirmado que el cónsul británico había aconsejado más de una vez a los dominicanos arriar la cruz blanca e izar el tricolor haitiano, enfureciendo al presidente dominicano. Asegurando conocer personalmente a Sir Robert Schomburgh, cónsul británico en Santo Domingo, el autor de la carta declara que dicha afirmación es un completo error y que la conducta seguida en todo momento por el cónsul ha sido exactamente la contraria a la que se le atribuye.

records.headline: An editorial in the Worcester Daily Spy warns that while northern
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Worcester Daily Spy warns that while northern freemen remain indifferent to the question of human freedom, pro-slavery forces are advancing plans to extend American slavery. According to the paper, agents of President Franklin Pierce have obtained from the Dominican government the right to establish naval and military stations in the northern part of the island of St. Domingo, including the mineral-rich mountainous region of Samaná, along with privileges for Americans to mine and trade in the Dominican Republic without naturalization. The editorial argues that the partial cession of the department of Cibao in "Dominica" is intended to facilitate the conquest of Haiti, Cuba, and Central America on behalf of the "Slaveocracy."
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Worcester Daily Spy advierte que mientras los hombres libres del Norte permanecen indiferentes ante la cuestión de la libertad humana, las fuerzas esclavistas avanzan en sus planes para extender la esclavitud estadounidense. Según el periódico, los agentes del presidente Franklin Pierce han obtenido del gobierno dominicano el derecho de establecer estaciones navales y militares en la parte norte de la isla de Santo Domingo, incluida la región montañosa y rica en minerales de Samaná, junto con privilegios para que los estadounidenses exploten minas y comercien en la República Dominicana sin necesidad de naturalizarse. El editorial sostiene que la cesión parcial del departamento del Cibao en «Dominica» tiene el propósito de facilitar la conquista de Haití, Cuba y Centroamérica en beneficio de la «esclavocracia».

records.summary_en: The *New-York Daily Tribune* reported on Dominican resistance to Haitian control, noting that memories of severe mistreatment and violence during past Haitian rule deterred locals from favoring Haitian dominance. Despite rumors circulated that Americans intended to enslave the population, both white and mixed-race residents remained fearful of a Haitian return. The correspondent urged the United States to counter British diplomatic influence by officially recognizing the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Daily Tribune* dio cuenta de la irreductible resistencia dominicana a la hegemonía haitiana, observando que la memoria de atropellos y rigores padecidos durante el régimen anterior apartaba a los naturales de cualquier simpatía hacia el dominio haitiano. Pese a las patrañas propaladas de que los norteamericanos proyectaban esclavizar a la población, tanto los moradores blancos como los de color temían sobremanera la restauración del yugo haitiano. El corresponsal encarecía a Estados Unidos a contrarrestar la injerencia diplomática británica mediante el reconocimiento oficial de la República Dominicana.

records.headline: A correspondent reports that it is generally understood in both
records.summary_en: A correspondent reports that it is generally understood in both official circles and among the public that General Cazneau, the United States Commissioner accredited to the Dominican Republic, has secured for the United States the right to establish military and naval depots on the northern coast of the island. According to the writer, these depots are regarded as essential for acquiring Cuba and Puerto Rico by force of arms, after which Dominican territory would also be colonized and annexed to the Union as a slave state. The correspondent adds that the broader plan contemplates dividing Cuba into two states so that, together with St. Domingo and Puerto Rico, four additional slaveholding states would be added to the Union.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal informa que se da por sentado, tanto en los círculos oficiales como entre el público en general, que el general Cazneau, comisionado de los Estados Unidos acreditado ante la República Dominicana, ha asegurado para los Estados Unidos el derecho de establecer depósitos militares y navales en la costa norte de la isla. Según el autor, dichos depósitos se consideran esenciales para asegurar la adquisición de Cuba y Puerto Rico por la fuerza de las armas, tras lo cual el territorio dominicano también sería colonizado y anexado a la Unión como un estado esclavista. El corresponsal añade que el plan contempla dividir a Cuba en dos estados para que, junto con Santo Domingo y Puerto Rico, se sumen cuatro estados esclavistas adicionales a la Unión.

records.headline: Citing a Tribune correspondent writing from St. Thomas, the Perrysburg Journal reports
records.summary_en: Citing a Tribune correspondent writing from St. Thomas, the Perrysburg Journal reports that United States diplomatic agents Mr. and Mrs. Cazneau have succeeded in their mission to the Dominican Republic to secure the Bay of Samaná for a U.S. naval station. The report states that President Santana is inclined to accept American friendship in hopes of establishing a permanent barrier for "Dominica" against the ambitions of the Haitian Emperor. Located near the eastern end of the northern coast, Samaná Bay is described as one of the largest and most commodious harbors in the world, capable of receiving the largest naval or merchant vessels and commanding both the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea better than any harbor in Cuba.
records.summary_es: Citando a un corresponsal del Tribune que escribe desde San Tomás, el Perrysburg Journal informa que los agentes diplomáticos de los Estados Unidos, el señor y la señora Cazneau, han tenido éxito en su misión ante la República Dominicana para asegurar la bahía de Samaná como estación naval estadounidense. El informe señala que el presidente Santana se inclina a aceptar la amistad estadounidense con la esperanza de establecer una barrera permanente para «Dominica» frente a las ambiciones del emperador haitiano. Situada cerca del extremo oriental de la costa norte, la bahía de Samaná es descrita como uno de los puertos más grandes y cómodos del mundo, capaz de recibir a los mayores buques navales o mercantes y de dominar tanto el golfo de México como el mar Caribe mejor que cualquier puerto de Cuba.

records.headline: A correspondent in the New-York Daily Tribune quotes a skeptical statement
records.summary_en: A correspondent in the New-York Daily Tribune quotes a skeptical statement arguing that President Santana would not be so improvident as to dispose of so important a maritime position as the peninsula of Samaná on his own without first consulting the governments of France and England, which would undoubtedly use every means in their power to refuse their consent. Responding to that view, the Tribune writer asks by what right France or England should be consulted by independent St. Domingo regarding whether it chooses to transfer a portion of its territory to the United States. The writer contends that the United States might just as well demand to be consulted on the balance of power in Europe and offer unsolicited aid to Russia against England and France.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal en el New-York Daily Tribune cita una declaración escéptica según la cual el presidente Santana no sería tan imprudente como para disponer por sí solo de una posición marítima tan importante como la península de Samaná sin consultar primero a los gobiernos de Francia e Inglaterra, los cuales sin duda emplearían todos los medios a su alcance para negar su consentimiento. En respuesta a esa postura, el autor del Tribune pregunta con qué derecho Francia o Inglaterra habrían de ser consultadas por un Santo Domingo independiente acerca de si decide o no transferir una parte de su territorio a los Estados Unidos. El articulista sostiene que, con igual razón, los Estados Unidos podrían exigir ser consultados sobre el equilibrio de poder en Europa y prestar ayuda no solicitada a Rusia contra Inglaterra y Francia.

records.summary_en: Reprinting an item from the New York Herald titled "Annexation of Samana," the Nevada Journal notes rumors that Mr. and Mrs. Cazeneau have succeeded in their mission to the Dominican Republic and that the fine port of Samaná has been ceded to the United States. The paper asks for more authentic evidence before giving the report full credence, questioning why the Dominicans would be in such haste to part with their best seaport when the United States holds no special claim on their regard. Instead, the article suggests it is more likely that the American envoys have obtained from the Dominicans the same privileges previously granted to a French monarch.
records.summary_es: Reproduciendo una nota del New York Herald titulada «Anexión de Samaná», el Nevada Journal recoge los rumores de que el señor y la señora Cazeneau han tenido éxito en su misión ante la República Dominicana y de que el excelente puerto de Samaná ha sido cedido a los Estados Unidos. El periódico pide pruebas más auténticas antes de dar entero crédito a la noticia, cuestionando por qué los dominicanos tendrían tanta prisa en desprenderse de su mejor puerto marítimo cuando los Estados Unidos no tienen ningún derecho particular a su favor. En cambio, el artículo sugiere que es más probable que los enviados estadounidenses hayan obtenido de los dominicanos los mismos privilegios concedidos anteriormente a un monarca francés.

records.headline: The Alexandria Gazette reports a formal protest by General Cazneau
records.summary_en: The Alexandria Gazette reports a formal protest by General Cazneau, the United States Commissioner, to the French and English consuls at St. Domingo, noting that four French warships are currently in the port and an English fleet is shortly expected. In the protest, dated at St. Domingo on November 17, Cazneau declares that French and British agents, aided by a menacing display of armed force before the capital, have overawed and controlled the free action of the Dominican Republic in its relations with the United States. Protesting against this encroachment on the sovereign rights of an independent American power, he affirms the determined purpose of the United States to oppose any measure intended to subject an American nation to the arbitrary will of a foreign power, whether strong or weak among its sister republics.
records.summary_es: La Alexandria Gazette informa que el comisionado de los Estados Unidos, el general Cazneau, ha dirigido una enérgica protesta a los cónsules de Francia e Inglaterra en Santo Domingo, señalando que cuatro buques de guerra franceses se encuentran actualmente en el puerto y que se espera en breve la llegada de una flota inglesa. En la protesta, fechada en Santo Domingo el 17 de noviembre, Cazneau declara que los agentes franceses y británicos, apoyados por un despliegue amenazante de fuerza armada frente a la capital, han intimidado y controlado la libre acción de la República Dominicana en sus relaciones con los Estados Unidos. Al protestar contra esta usurpación de los derechos soberanos de una potencia americana independiente, reafirma el firme propósito de los Estados Unidos de oponerse a cualquier medida destinada a someter a una nación americana a la voluntad arbitraria de una potencia extranjera, sin hacer distinción entre las repúblicas hermanas fuertes y las débiles.

records.headline: This long article describes the peninsula and bay of Samana, at the eastern end of the island of St. Domingo
records.summary_en: This long article describes the peninsula and bay of Samana, at the eastern end of the island of St. Domingo, guarding the Mona Passage between St. Domingo and Porto Rico. It details the bay's narrow entrance, its sheltered anchorage, and the veins of bituminous coal, iron, copper and gold found on the peninsula, and notes that the United States Government is in treaty for part or all of the territory, whose small population of 1,721 already includes some 300 Black emigrants from the United States and their descendants.
records.summary_es: Este extenso artículo describe la península y la bahía de Samaná, en el extremo oriental de la isla de Santo Domingo, que guarda el Paso de la Mona entre Santo Domingo y Puerto Rico. Detalla la estrecha entrada de la bahía, su fondeadero protegido y las vetas de carbón bituminoso, hierro, cobre y oro que se encuentran en la península, y señala que el Gobierno de los Estados Unidos negocia un tratado por parte o la totalidad del territorio, cuya pequeña población de 1,721 habitantes ya incluye a unos 300 emigrantes negros procedentes de los Estados Unidos y sus descendientes.

records.full_text:
SAMANA.

"This remarkable peninsula and bay is," says Mr. St. Remy, "one of those maritime positions not often met with in a survey of the map of the world. It is to the Gulf of Mexico what Mayotta is to the Indian Ocean. It is not only the military, but the commercial key of the Gulf." He elsewhere calls it the tete du pont, the "head of the bridge," of the highway from the Atlantic to the Caribbean Sea and the Isthmus of Darien, called the Mona Passage, between St. Domingo on the west, and Porto Rico on the east.

The Bay of Samaná is an indentation, thirty miles long and about eight miles wide, in the eastern end of the Island Hispaniola or St. Domingo. When Columbus first opened this bay, in 1493, on his return from his first voyage, he thought it was a strait separating the southern part of the Island along which he had been coasting from some other land. Samaná is in the peninsula at the north of this bay. The isthmus connecting it with the main is so low that at some time, within written history, there has been really a channel through it, practicable for boats. This channel called the Gran Estero, is now choked up with sand. Mountain chains rise suddenly from this low isthmus; and the peninsula extends from west to east about thirty miles. Its greatest width is eleven miles; the swampy land at the isthmus, its narrowest part, is five miles wide. Sir R. Schomburgh estimates the area of the whole peninsula at 225 square miles.

It has been said, not yet on good authority, however, that this whole peninsula has been transferred to our Government. We conceive it to be by no means improbable that the Republic of Dominica if asked to cede a spot for a Navy Yard should be willing to surrender the whole of it, as its population is small, and its whole extent is inconsiderable.

The Bay of Samaná is protected from the seas which would enter with north and east winds, by a formidable reef, which makes of it almost a landlocked basin. This reef extends from Cape Rafael, the south-eastern promontory of the mouth of the bay, W. N. W. to Pascual Key, which is but a mile from the main land of Samaná. The passage for vessels into this bay is wholly through the mile-wide strait which thus separates Pascual Key from Point Cacao on the main. This channel is further impeded by a shoal with only twenty four feet on it, lying only six cables' length north-west from the key—an obstruction which makes it difficult for vessels to leave with the sea breeze, and renders it advisable for vessels to stand out with the land-breeze. This narrowness of the channel gives to the immense harbor within a singular defense against enemies. The Point Cacao, which makes the northern side of the narrow channel of entrance, is a projecting, bold bluff, where a battery would entirely command the whole passage to the little sea within. Jack Bannister, the somewhat-celebrated pirate of the 16th century, availed himself of this position to drive off two English frigates which were in pursuit of him and his consort Lageroe.

Within, the bay affords good anchorage almost everywhere, and of course affords shelter and protection to the largest fleets. The French fleet sent out by Napoleon, to carry out his outrage on Toussaint, anchored here, and Le Clerc's army landed here. This fleet consisted of 60 vessels, of which 36 were ships of the line. The peculiar advantage which the bay here offers, however, as a naval station, consists of its veins of coal. Near the rivulet Almaçen are large veins of bituminous coal, which have also been met with farther east. The Almaçen flows into the bay near its west end. It is said that the coal, which has been tried, has proved "too bituminous" for the use of steamers. But the experiments have not been followed up with any energy, and the veins have not in any place been wrought to the depth of ten feet. The geological structure of the country is such that there may be coal of a better quality below. Iron, copper, and small quantities of gold, are also found on this little peninsula.

Now that our Government is in treaty for a part or the whole of this territory, it is a fact somewhat curious that a sixth part of the population is already furnished from our own country. The total population in 1851 was 1,721, of whom a considerable part were negroes from this country, who emigrated in 1824, when Boyer was President of Hayti, and this part of the island formed part of his dominions. These people, with their descendants, now number about 300—and it is a gratifying fact that they distinguish themselves by the cleanliness of their provision grounds, and their industry. They form the principal part of the congregation of the Missionary of the London Wesleyan Missionary Society, who resides at Puerto Plata, but occasionally visits this place, where is a Wesleyan chapel.

The population has been varied since the discovery of the Island. Columbus found on this peninsula a warlike tribe, and thought it to be thickly settled. The first blood shed in America in fight between the Indians and whites, was in a skirmish between his men and these Indians. Columbus gave the bay the name of the Bay of Arrows, in consequence. The peninsula was afterward made a station by French Buccaneers, whose settlement there was in a flourishing state, with the single want of women. D'Ogeron, the French Governor of Tortuga, supplied this want by sending to them a party, who had been sent to him from St. Malo, and the settlement thrived till near the end of the 17th century, when an attack from the Spaniards almost annihilated it, and in 1700, the straggling remnant was withdrawn by the French Government. Till 1756 the peninsula was neglected, but in that year the Spanish Government planted a colony from the Canaries there. Afterward some of the refugees from French St. Domingo took refuge there. The peninsula has been in the last century under the various dominion of Spain France, the Haytien Republic and Empire, the insurgent republic of "Spanish Hayti" of 1821, and the present Dominican Republic, which has held, since 1844, the eastern half of this beautiful island.

records.headline: Reprinting a January 3 article titled "The Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Reprinting a January 3 article titled "The Dominican Republic and the United States," the New York Herald reports that the measure of annexing Santo Domingo does not find general approbation even in the United States and meets complete opposition in the place most interested in the question. To illustrate domestic opposition, the writer quotes a manifesto to the American people issued at a June 20 meeting in Washington chaired by Representative Solomon Foot of Vermont on behalf of members of Congress opposed to the Nebraska bill. That manifesto warns of "unmistakable indications" of a design to annex the eastern part of San Domingo, subjugate the entire island, and restore it to slavery, followed by an alliance with Brazil to extend slavery into the valley of the Amazon. The writer praises these words as coming from Americans moved by the natural rights of mankind rather than the desire for territorial aggrandizement prevailing in the Southern states.
records.summary_es: Al reproducir un artículo del 3 de enero titulado «La República Dominicana y los Estados Unidos», el New York Herald informa que la medida de anexar a Santo Domingo no cuenta con la aprobación general ni siquiera en los Estados Unidos y encuentra una oposición total en el lugar más interesado en la cuestión. Para ilustrar la oposición interna, el autor cita un manifiesto dirigido al pueblo estadounidense emitido en una reunión celebrada el 20 de junio en Washington bajo la presidencia del representante Solomon Foot, de Vermont, en nombre de los miembros del Congreso opuestos al proyecto de ley de Nebraska. Dicho manifiesto advierte sobre «indicios inequívocos» de un propósito de anexar la parte oriental de Santo Domingo, subyugar toda la isla y restituirla al dominio de la esclavitud, seguido de una alianza con Brasil para extender la esclavitud hacia el valle del Amazonas. El articulista elogia estas palabras por provenir de estadounidenses movidos por los derechos naturales de la humanidad y no por el afán de engrandecimiento territorial que prevalece en los estados del Sur.

records.headline: Continuing its report on the Dominican Republic, an article
records.summary_en: Continuing its report on the Dominican Republic, an article in the New York Herald observes that nine-tenths of Santo Domingo's population of about 140,000 are Black or people of color. The writer states that France has taken measures to counteract American propensities toward annexing West Indian colonies, while Spain has been awakened to the imminent danger threatening Cuba and Puerto Rico should Americans take possession of Samaná or any other locality in Santo Domingo. According to the dispatch, the French chargé d'affaires and consul general at Haiti arrived in the capital and worked in concert with the English consul to warn President Santana's administration of the danger of permitting Americans to settle at Samaná. His effort was backed by the arrival of a division of the French West Indies squadron consisting of a 40-gun frigate, the 20-gun l'Oreste, and the 6-gun steam sloop l'Ardent.

records.summary_en: A Dominican writes from Santo Domingo (Dec. 19, 1854) on the French and English consuls' seizure of his government: their written protest against the Cazneau treaty, the threat that Faustin would land Báez with an army, and Santana's silent resistance.

Presently the American plenipotentiary enters the palace, in his plain black suit, and passes quite calmly into the President's private cabinet, where he remained so late that an officer had to be sent to the St. Carlos, or Gonde gate, to order it kept open for General Cazneau (who lives in the country), to pass out after the interview. The morning after this conference, their consular majesties were notified that their objections to the American treaty must be put in writing. The French consul, Duresse, had already sent an express to Hayti for [illegible] Raybaud, and declined doing anything more until he came; but the British consul was [illegible] enough to fall into the snare and expose all the plans of his government to the prejudice of the United States, in a [flaming?] protest. He plainly tells President Santana that the French and English governments must give their consent before he can make any treaty whatever, and particularly with such a dangerous power as the United States, which, he says, Lord Clarendon and the British Cabinet are convinced has some suspicious design on the Dominican people. records.headline: European Interference at St. Domingo.
records.summary_en: According to the *Thibodaux Minerva* of February 10, 1855, the French and British consuls cautioned the Dominican government against allowing Americans to settle at Samana, a warning reinforced by the arrival of a French naval division under Captain Fournier. The newspaper also noted public speculation regarding this naval demonstration, anticipated arrivals of English and Spanish warships, and reported that the Spanish government intended to send an accredited agent to Santo Domingo.

El rotativo reflejaba las conjeturas populares ante semejante despliegue marítimo, la inminente llegada de unidades de guerra británicas y españolas, y la resolución de Madrid de comisionar a un representante acreditado ante Santo Domingo.

records.full_text: EUROPEAN INTERFERENCE AT ST. DOMINGO.—London news, says the Baltimore Sun, furnishes further evidence of the fact that the British and French consuls did interfere to prevent the adoption by the Dominican Government of a treaty with the United States. It describes a 'stormy' interview the British consul had with the President of the Dominican Republic, which it says 'may be taken as the first direct opposition to the American designs upon Samana,' the direct opposition we suppose having been found unavailing. The French consul subsequently joined the British consul in impressing upon the Dominican Government the dangerous step of permitting the Americans to settle at Samana. The means which were taken to make this impression are very complacently dwelt upon as follows: 'Raybaud is renowned for the energetic manner with which he knows how to make a powerful impression upon such weak minds as those that compose President Santa Anna's administration, and in this position he was powerfully sustained by the arrival of a division of the French squadron at the West Indies, consisting of the frigate Penelope, 40; l'Oreste, 20; and the steam sloop l'Ardent, 6, under the command of the Chef de Division, Capt. Fournier. The object of this demonstration is not yet known, and the surmises of the public are various. It is likewise rumored that one or more English men-of-war are daily expected to join the French division, while the arrival of a large Spanish war steamer is equally looked for. It has been authentically reported from Porto Rico, that the Spanish Government intended to send an accredited agent to Santo Domingo.'

records.headline: The Western Democrat publishes a letter stating that the population of the Dominican Republic consists of whites
records.summary_en: The Western Democrat publishes a letter stating that the population of the Dominican Republic consists of whites, persons of mixed white and Indian blood, and mulattoes, similar to all the Spanish American republics, and noting that President Santana and his secretaries are white men. The writer remarks that the Dominican people have been misrepresented by some American newspapers and urges greater commercial and political interest in the country on the part of the people and government of the United States. Arguing that St. Domingo is much richer than Cuba, he cites its mines of silver, gold, coal, copper, and quicksilver, its ship timber, mahogany, and other precious woods, and declares that the Bay of Samaná is the key to the Caribbean Sea just as Cuba is the key to the Gulf of Mexico. The writer adds that he is not a Dominican, having been born in Puerto Rico, educated at Havana, and later naturalized in the United States.
records.summary_es: El Western Democrat publica una carta en la que se afirma que la población de la República Dominicana se compone de blancos, personas de sangre mestiza blanca e indígena, y mulatos, de manera similar a todas las repúblicas hispanoamericanas, y señala que el presidente Santana y sus secretarios son hombres blancos. El autor observa que el pueblo dominicano ha sido tergiversado por algunos periódicos estadounidenses e insta a que el pueblo y el gobierno de los Estados Unidos presten mayor interés comercial y político al país. Sosteniendo que Santo Domingo es mucho más rico que Cuba, destaca sus minas de plata, oro, carbón, cobre y azogue, sus maderas aptas para embarcaciones, la caoba y otras maderas preciosas, y declara que la bahía de Samaná es la llave del mar Caribe así como Cuba es la llave del golfo de México. El autor añade que no es dominicano, pues nació en Puerto Rico, se educó en La Habana y posteriormente se incorporó a los Estados Unidos.

records.summary_en: A brief notice in the Springfield Weekly Republican states that St. Domingo is in some respects preferable to Cuba and is much richer in natural resources. According to the paper, the island possesses mines of silver, gold, coal, copper, and quicksilver, along with various kinds of timber suitable for shipbuilding, mahogany, and other precious woods. The item concludes that if Cuba is the key to the Gulf of Mexico, the Bay of Samaná in the Dominican Republic is undoubtedly the key to the Caribbean Sea.

El artículo concluye que si Cuba es la llave del golfo de México, la bahía de Samaná en la República Dominicana es, sin duda, la llave del mar Caribe.

records.headline: Under the headline "The Dominican Republic," the Richmond Daily Dispatch reports
records.summary_en: Under the headline "The Dominican Republic," the Richmond Daily Dispatch reports that the country's population consists of whites, persons of mixed white and Indian blood, and mulattoes, corresponding to the population of the other Spanish American republics. Quoting a letter, the paper states that President Santana and his secretaries are white men and argues that Cuba is by no means preferable to the island of St. Domingo. Instead, the letter describes St. Domingo as much richer than Cuba, possessing silver, gold, coal, copper, and quicksilver mines as well as ship timber, mahogany, and other precious woods, while characterizing the Bay of Samaná in the Dominican Republic as the key to the Caribbean Sea.
records.summary_es: Bajo el titular «La República Dominicana», el Daily Dispatch de Richmond informa que la población del país se compone de blancos, personas de sangre mestiza blanca e indígena, y mulatos, en correspondencia con la población de las demás repúblicas hispanoamericanas. Citando una carta, el periódico señala que el presidente Santana y sus secretarios son hombres blancos y sostiene que Cuba no es de ningún modo preferible a la isla de Santo Domingo. Por el contrario, la carta describe a Santo Domingo como mucho más rico que Cuba, dotado de minas de plata, oro, carbón, cobre y azogue, así como de maderas para embarcaciones, caoba y otras maderas preciosas, al tiempo que califica a la bahía de Samaná en la República Dominicana como la llave del mar Caribe.

records.headline: The Dominican Congress rejected the Cazneau Treaty because it offered no reciprocity: Dominicans visiting the United States
records.summary_en: The Dominican Congress rejected the Cazneau Treaty because it offered no reciprocity: Dominicans visiting the United States could be imprisoned in the Southern States for no crime other than the color of their skin, while all the advantages were on the American side. The American plenipotentiary answered by giving the government twenty-four hours to reconsider, and the United States sloop-of-war Falmouth, which had been lying at Samana, stayed on instead of leaving for Jamaica.

records.headline: An article in the Green-Mountain Freeman reports that the American plenipotentiary in Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: An article in the Green-Mountain Freeman reports that the American plenipotentiary in Santo Domingo has openly hinted at the risk of filibustering expeditions like those that have threatened Cuba, suggesting that Greytown is not the only place Americans can lay in ashes and that the city of St. Domingo is within their reach. According to the paper, his countrymen immediately provoked a quarrel in the roadstead of St. Domingo, which quickly brought two British steam sloops, a French frigate, and two war brigs to the scene. The article adds that the Americans seek to establish a foothold at Samaná, where a watch is being maintained against invaders, and remarks that the Dominicans are likely aware that any invasion of their coasts will depend in part on the course of the war in the Crimea.
records.summary_es: Un artículo del Green-Mountain Freeman informa que el plenipotenciario estadounidense en Santo Domingo ha insinuado abiertamente el riesgo de expediciones filibusteras como las que han amenazado a Cuba, sugiriendo que Greytown no es el único lugar que los estadounidenses pueden reducir a cenizas y que la ciudad de Santo Domingo está a su alcance. Según el periódico, sus compatriotas provocaron de inmediato una disputa en la rada de Santo Domingo, lo que atrajo rápidamente al lugar a dos corbetas de vapor británicas, una fragata francesa y dos bergantines de guerra. El artículo añade que los estadounidenses desean establecer una posición en Samaná, donde se mantiene la vigilancia ante la llegada de invasores, y observa que los dominicanos probablemente saben que cualquier invasión de sus costas dependerá en parte del curso de la guerra en Crimea.

records.headline: A correspondent's letter from the City of Santo Domingo describes a military commission that sentenced General Pelletier
records.summary_en: A correspondent's letter from the City of Santo Domingo describes a military commission that sentenced General Pelletier, General Aybar, Francisco Ruiz and others accused of conspiracy to death, with others sentenced to expatriation, imprisonment or banishment. After the condemned men's children pleaded for grace, the prisoners were led to the execution ground on May 21, knelt while their sentence was read and faced the firing party, until General Santana cried halt and had a pardon for the three read aloud; Ruiz rose from his knees having lost his reason under the horror. The letter adds that the pardoned men received passports to leave the country and that upwards of fifty individuals were banished, including women and children and the sisters of ex-President Baez.
records.summary_es: La carta de un corresponsal desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo describe una comisión militar que condenó a muerte al general Pelletier, al general Aybar, a Francisco Ruiz y a otros acusados de conspiración, mientras otros fueron condenados a expatriación, prisión o destierro. Después de que los hijos de los condenados suplicaran gracia, los prisioneros fueron llevados al lugar de ejecución el 21 de mayo, se arrodillaron mientras se leía su sentencia y quedaron frente al pelotón de fusilamiento, hasta que el general Santana gritó alto e hizo leer en voz alta un indulto para los tres; Ruiz se levantó de rodillas habiendo perdido la razón por el horror. La carta añade que los indultados recibieron pasaportes para salir del país y que más de cincuenta personas fueron desterradas, incluidas mujeres y niños y las hermanas del expresidente Báez.

records.summary_en: Under the headline "Instructions to Mr. Buchanan," the Daily Comet of Baton Rouge reports that the Cabinet in Washington has instructed Mr. Buchanan, the United States Minister to the government of Great Britain, to intimate that the Monroe Doctrine will be strictly enforced by the United States. Según la nota, dicha aplicación se refiere de manera particular a la República Dominicana en la isla de Santo Domingo, así como a Greytown, Cuba y las Islas de la Bahía.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that the Dominican government discovered and crushed a revolutionary plot, but French and English consuls protected the conspirators from punishment by granting them asylum and refusing Dominican demands for their trial. records.full_text: France and England conspired with the negro party, headed by Baez, the secret ally of Solouque, to excite a war of races. Their prospect was to murder the heads of the government, overthrow the constitutional republic, and establish a negro despotism on the ashes of the white race. I was told weeks beforehand the co-operation of a French and English squadron was promised, and it actually presented itself at the appointed time before the city of Santo Domingo, and at certain indicated points in the vicinity. But when the squadron arrived it found the Dominican government had already discovered and crushed the plan of revolution and massacre, and the French and English consuls had to content themselves for the present with using the squadron and their diplomatic flags to protect the conspirators from punishment. records.headline: From the Union of Friday last. Our Relations with Dominica—The Interest taken by France and England in General Cazneau's Mission.
records.summary_en: According to the October 23, 1855 *Washington Sentinel*, agents of France and England conspired with a negro party led by Báez to incite a war of races, overthrow the Dominican government, and establish a despotism. Although French and English squadrons arrived to support the plot, the Dominican government crushed the plan beforehand, prompting the foreign consuls to use their flags and consulates to harbor the conspirators and deny the Dominican authorities custody of them for trial. Furthermore, the article claims that these foreign powers are usurping territory and extending semi-colonies and protectorates at points commanding the American coast and isthmus trade.

Si bien escuadras navales galas y británicas arribaron para secundar la sedición, el gobierno dominicano sofocó a tiempo la trama, lo que movió a los cónsules a valerse de sus banderas e inmunidades consulares para cobijar a los conjurados y rehusar su entrega a las cortes del país. records.full_text:
The anti-American journals of Europe have largely occupied themselves, in concert with their faithful allies—the disunion press of this country—in misrepresenting the motives and circumstances of the treaty which I had concluded with the Dominican republic, but which was afterwards set aside by the hostile interference of France and England. This was to be expected; for the enemies of American progress instinctively favor any attack on the internal peace or national greatness of our republic; and as naturally oppose whatever tends to give the United States pre-eminence over the European kingdoms of their idolatry.
If such a thing exists as an "American system of policy," the Dominican republic had the strongest claims on the friendly notice of our government, and, at the solicitation of many Spanish-American friends who felt the importance of the crisis, I caused those claims and the condition of that country to be laid before President Pierce at the commencement of his administration.
Its geographical vicinity and central position were urged in behalf of interests common to both nations, as well as its desirable harbors; its valuable products—exactly what our country does not produce, and must purchase; its wants—exactly what our people can supply on the best terms; its commanding situation at the intersection of the great and growing lines of American commerce; its free and liberal institutions; its expressed wish to enter into closer relations with its "great neighbor of the north; and, not least among those considerations, the significant fact—which no American patriot can, and which no American statesman will, overlook—that this neglected republic is the only territory in the whole circle of West India islands under American rule.
This solitary foothold of American nationality is struggling for life against the attempts of Solouque to reduce it to a negro despotism. He claims for the negroes, under the title they acquired by their former massacres of the whites, the right to hold the remnant of the race in subjection, and to blot out civil and religious liberty at their pleasure. France and England secretly foment these pretensions, and they are sustained, more or less openly, by the leading disunion journals in the United States.
The Dominicans asked nothing but to be left in the peaceful possession of their own patrimony, and to receive from the United States the moral aid of a national recognition and the encouragement of a fair reciprocal treaty. Their object was a stable and independent nationality, with free security of person, property and religion for all creeds, classes, and races; and to serve the Dominican people in this necessity was also the soundest course of policy for the United States.
In plain terms, these are the questions before us: Shall the entire West Indies, with their one hundred thousand square miles of territory, and their three millions of inhabitants, be wholly Africanized and made the instruments of European opposition to American progress, or shall we encourage the Dominican republic to maintain an independent nationality and become the nucleus of an American system in the Antilles? Shall the allied powers, who boast that their position at the gates of the Gulf of Mexico enables them "at any time to cut in twain the commerce between the Northern and Southern States" of the Union, be permitted to increase this power by new encroachments, to exclude us altogether, while they usurp Samana, the key of the Caribbean sea, as they have before usurped the control of San Juan, the invaluable inlet of the Nicaragua route, and the Ruatan archipelago, the general outpour of our isthmus transit to California, or shall we be allowed to obtain by fair negotiation one haven of refuge in our own American seas where we can treat guaranteed all the rights of trade, travel, and residence conceded to the citizens of the most favored nations, under the same universal and applicable conditions of obedience to the laws of the country while within their jurisdiction.
The wise liberality of the Dominican laws enabled me to engraft in the permanent conditions of amity perfect freedom and security of conscience, worship, and property; and this, with its eminent advantages of soil and climate, was so well calculated to invite American industry and capital to settle in the country and enhance its prosperity, not to excite the active opposition of the allies.
The governments of France and England injure their own people in obstructing the prosperity of the American republics, for we are their best customers. The richer we are, the more largely we shall buy of their fabrics, unless they drive us into tariffs of exclusion by way of reprisal for their attacks on our interests.
In this jealous dread of American progress, the agents of France and England conspired with the negro party, headed by Baez, the secret ally of Solouque, to excite a war of races. Their prospect was to murder the heads of the government, overthrow the constitutional republic, and establish a negro despotism on the ashes of the white race. I was told weeks beforehand the co-operation of a French and English squadron was promised, and it actually presented itself at the appointed time before the city of Santo Domingo, and at certain indicated points in the vicinity. But when the squadron arrived it found the Dominican government had already discovered and crushed the plan of revolution and massacre, and the French and English consuls had to content themselves for the present with using the squadron and their diplomatic flags to protect the conspirators from punishment. Their consulates were made the rendezvous and asylum of the negro leaders of the frustrated plot; and when the Dominican authorities demanded these notorious criminals for trial, the consuls replied with the same insolent contempt of the sovereign rights of the Dominican republic which they had displayed in the American negotiations—that the rebels were "under the protection of France and England, and none of them should be (and none of them were) punished."
Every intelligent observer is aware that not only in Santo Domingo, but at all the points commanding our coast and isthmus trade, these powers are usurping territory and extending their semi-colonies and contraband protectorates; but no President can put an end to European encroachment on our side of the Atlantic until he is sustained by a Congress that has the nerve and patriotism to plant itself on American principles.
England and France have violated the laws of neutrality towards us, and it would be no more than a just act of self-protection if Congress were to repeal the neutrality laws of 1818, so far as they apply to the encroaching powers, but not in any form to enlarge the safety of unoffending neighbors; or suspend them until the allies shall have evacuated their usurpations on American soil and sovereignty, and shall give better guarantees for the future than evasive diplomatic explanations.
WILLIAM L. CAZNEAU.

records.summary_en: A United States representative reported that Dominican officials expressed concern that both their legislative and executive powers were under European duress and asked if the U.S. would defend their negotiations from European dictation. While the representative expressed confidence in the U.S. Executive and noted that resisting European encroachment is a fundamental doctrine of the American system, they acknowledged that past passive behavior regarding England in Nicaragua and Honduras might mean the U.S. would remain passive regarding France colonizing the Bay of Samana. Despite the representative's efforts to encourage resistance, they admitted the Dominican government was pressed on all sides by France and England.
records.summary_es: Un enviado de Estados Unidos comunicó que las autoridades dominicanas exteriorizaron su zozobra de que tanto el poder legislativo como el ejecutivo se hallasen bajo coacción europea, indagando si Washington ampararía sus deliberaciones frente a imposiciones del Viejo Mundo. Aunque el comisionado manifestó confianza en el gobierno norteamericano y recordó que repeler intromisiones europeas era principio medular de la doctrina continental, admitió que la pasividad anterior frente a Inglaterra en Nicaragua y Honduras hacía temer una inacción semejante ante la colonización francesa de la bahía de Samaná. Pese a sus exhortaciones a la firmeza, reconoció que el régimen dominicano se encontraba acosado por doquier por Francia y Gran Bretaña.

records.headline: From Dominica the papers announce that Soulouque, so recently at the head of a formidable force against the Dominicans
records.summary_en: From Dominica the papers announce that Soulouque, so recently at the head of a formidable force against the Dominicans, has returned without firing a shot at his adversaries. It says a courier from a French man-of-war was dispatched to the Emperor with sealed dispatches, on perusal of which he immediately gave orders to turn right about and march back again, and that it is rumored and generally believed that France will not permit the Haitians to invade or molest the Dominicans.
records.summary_es: Desde Dominica los periódicos anuncian que Soulouque, que recientemente estaba al frente de una fuerza formidable contra los dominicanos, ha regresado sin disparar un tiro contra sus adversarios. Dice que un correo de un buque de guerra francés fue enviado al emperador con despachos sellados, tras leer los cuales ordenó de inmediato dar media vuelta y marchar de regreso, y que se rumora y se cree en general que Francia no permitirá que los haitianos invadan o molesten a los dominicanos.

records.headline: Reprinting an item from the Chicago Press, the Canton Weekly Register explains
records.summary_en: Reprinting an item from the Chicago Press, the Canton Weekly Register explains that the eastern portion of the island, called "St. Domingo or Dominica," was settled by Spaniards, whereas the people of Haiti descend from slaves held by the French on the western coast. Although the Dominicans are described as nearly all of mixed blood, including "Gen. Santander," the paper states that they call themselves Spaniards, cling tenaciously to their separate independence, and rely on steep mountain barriers to defend their population of about 175,000 against a Haitian population more than double that size. The Register also cites advices brought to the Philadelphia Exchange by Captain Burnaby of the schooner Ellen, which left Port-au-Prince on January 1, confirming the complete defeat of Emperor Faustin's 30,000-man march against the eastern side of the island, with Haitian losses of 200 to 300 soldiers, many officers, munitions, provisions, and the Emperor's military chest.
records.summary_es: Al reproducir un artículo del Chicago Press, el Canton Weekly Register explica que la porción oriental de la isla, llamada «Santo Domingo o Dominica», fue colonizada originalmente por españoles, mientras que los habitantes de Haití descienden de los esclavos mantenidos por los franceses en la costa occidental. Aunque se describe a los dominicanos como casi todos de sangre mestiza, incluido el «general Santander», el periódico señala que se llaman a sí mismos españoles, se aferran con tenacidad a su independencia separada y cuentan con escarpadas barreras montañosas para defender a su población de unos 175,000 habitantes frente a una población haitiana que supera el doble de esa cifra. El Register cita además informes llevados al Philadelphia Exchange por el capitán Burnaby, de la goleta Ellen, que zarpó de Puerto Príncipe el 1 de enero, los cuales confirman la completa derrota de la marcha de 30,000 hombres del emperador Faustin contra la parte oriental de la isla, con bajas haitianas de entre 200 y 300 soldados, numerosos oficiales, municiones, provisiones y la caja militar del emperador.

records.headline: Accounts conflict over Soulouque's campaign against the Dominicans: one says his army was thrown into confusion by the enemy's
records.summary_en: Accounts conflict over Soulouque's campaign against the Dominicans: one says his army was thrown into confusion by the enemy's first fire, about 1,000 men fled to Cape Haytien with the Emperor, the balance of 30,000 were unaccounted for, and he lost $200,000 as well as ammunition, provisions and most of the arms. A letter from Port-au-Prince discredits that defeat, saying the most reliable report was that he was at Banica, in the Dominican part of the island, after a repulse but nothing like the rout described.
records.summary_es: Los relatos difieren sobre la campaña de Soulouque contra los dominicanos: uno dice que su ejército fue puesto en confusión por el primer fuego enemigo, que unos 1.000 hombres huyeron a Cabo Haitiano con el emperador, que el resto de 30.000 estaba desaparecido y que perdió 200.000 dólares además de municiones, provisiones y la mayoría de las armas. Una carta de Puerto Príncipe desacredita esa derrota y dice que el informe más fiable era que estaba en Banica, en la parte dominicana de la isla, tras un rechazo pero nada parecido a la derrota descrita.

records.summary_en: The paper narrates Soulouque's rise after he was firmly seated in the presidential chair, saying he intrigued through the army, the rival factions and the two branches of the Legislature to transform the state into an empire. It says that after two years the imperial crown was placed on his head by the vote of the Senate and Representatives, making him Faustin the First, Emperor of Haiti and its dependent isles.
records.summary_es: El periódico narra el ascenso de Soulouque después de que se afianzó en la silla presidencial, diciendo que intrigó a través del ejército, las facciones rivales y las dos cámaras de la Legislatura para transformar el Estado en un imperio. Dice que después de dos años la corona imperial fue colocada en su cabeza por voto del Senado y de los Representantes, convirtiéndolo en Faustin Primero, emperador de Haití y sus islas dependientes.

records.headline: The paper profiles Faustin Soulouque, lately routed by the Dominican troops under Santana, describing his rise from servant
records.summary_en: The paper profiles Faustin Soulouque, lately routed by the Dominican troops under Santana, describing his rise from servant to a distinguished general to a military chieftain regarded as a man of moderate abilities but undoubted bravery. The writer describes seeing him ride on Sunday mornings through Port-au-Prince on a fine grey horse imported from the United States, accompanied by a hundred or more lifeguards, dressed far more richly than American officers in a blue broadcloth coat overlaid with heavy gold trimmings.

El autor describe haberlo visto cabalgar los domingos por la mañana por Puerto Príncipe en un fino caballo gris importado de los Estados Unidos, acompañado por cien o más guardias, vestido con mucho más riqueza que los oficiales estadounidenses, con una casaca de paño azul cubierta de pesados adornos de oro.

records.headline: The New-York Daily Tribune publishes an official notice from British Consul Robert H. Schomburgk
records.summary_en: The New-York Daily Tribune publishes an official notice from British Consul Robert H. Schomburgk, dated at the British Consulate in Santo Domingo on December 17, 1855. Schomburgk informs the authorities of the Turks Islands Presidency that the Dominican government has declared the Dominican Republic in a state of siege and closed Samaná and other ports to commercial intercourse. Noting the existing trade between the Turks Islands and Samaná, he requests that this measure be made known to the inhabitants to prevent disappointment and commercial losses, adding that only two Dominican ports, including Santo Domingo, remain open at present to foreign trade.

Schomburgk informa a las autoridades de la Presidencia de las Islas Turcas que el gobierno dominicano ha declarado a la República Dominicana en estado de sitio y ha cerrado Samaná y otros puertos al tráfico comercial. Señalando la existencia de comercio entre las Islas Turcas y Samaná, solicita que esta medida se dé a conocer a los habitantes para evitar contratiempos y pérdidas comerciales, y añade que solo dos puertos dominicanos, incluido Santo Domingo, permanecen abiertos actualmente al comercio exterior.

records.headline: An editorial in the Athens Post argues that it is hopeless to sustain
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Athens Post argues that it is hopeless to sustain an independent Black government on the same island as one largely composed of the Caucasian race, dismissing a New York Post correspondent's account of the defeat of 18,000 Haitian troops by four hundred Dominicans with cannon as the work of a "negro sympathizer." Claiming that General Walker's power in Nicaragua is now an established fact that will soon produce a Central American confederation infused with American energy and institutions, the paper predicts that these influences will extend to "Dominica" and cover the island of San Domingo, converting it into a republic within that Central American constellation. The editorial adds that the Cuba question will be resolved by the same process unless peaceful annexation brings the island into the United States first, declaring that "Manifest destiny" points to a brilliant career for filibusterism.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Athens Post sostiene que es inútil intentar mantener un gobierno negro independiente en la misma isla junto a otro compuesto en gran parte por la raza caucásica, y desestima el relato de un corresponsal del New York Post sobre la derrota de 18,000 soldados haitianos frente a cuatrocientos dominicanos con cañones por considerarlo obra de un «simpatizante de los negros». Afirmando que el poder del general Walker en Nicaragua es ya un hecho consumado que pronto dará lugar a una confederación centroamericana imbuida de energía e instituciones estadounidenses, el periódico predice que estas influencias se extenderán a «Dominica» y cubrirán la isla de Santo Domingo, convirtiéndola en una república dentro de esa constelación centroamericana. El editorial añade que la cuestión de Cuba se resolverá mediante el mismo proceso, a menos que una anexión pacífica incorpore primero la isla a los Estados Unidos, y declara que el «destino manifiesto» señala una brillante carrera para el filibusterismo.
