records.headline: Reviewing recent Dominican newspapers, the New York Herald notes
records.summary_en: Reviewing recent Dominican newspapers, the New York Herald notes a leading article describing the public enthusiasm and joy in the city of Santiago following the victory over the Haitians. A second article by a contributor discusses the Dominican-Haitian question and concludes that the Republic of St. Domingo will either see peace established through the mediation of French and British agents or refuse to lay down its arms until the Haitian forces are completely defeated. The papers also contain communications praising Dominican valor in the December battle, an address by the inhabitants of Santiago eulogizing General Domingo Mallol for his bravery during the recent campaign, and more than a page of official dispatches on the recently concluded war signed by Generals Juan L. F. Uldo and Domingo Mallol. The Herald remarks that although the press in "Dominica" is entirely free, it badly needs improvement and none of the journals list the names of their proprietors or editors.
records.summary_es: Al reseñar periódicos dominicanos recientes, el New York Herald destaca un artículo principal que describe el entusiasmo y el júbilo público en la ciudad de Santiago tras la victoria sobre los haitianos. Un segundo artículo de un colaborador analiza la cuestión dominico-haitiana y concluye que la República de Santo Domingo verá establecida la paz mediante la intervención de los agentes de Francia e Inglaterra o, de lo contrario, no depondrá las armas hasta haber derrotado por completo a las fuerzas haitianas. Los periódicos incluyen además comunicaciones que elogian el valor dominicano en la batalla de diciembre, un mensaje de los habitantes de Santiago en alabanza al general Domingo Mallol por su bravura durante la última campaña, y más de una página de despachos y documentos oficiales sobre la guerra recién terminada firmados por los generales Juan L. F. Uldo y Domingo Mallol. El Herald observa que, aunque la prensa en «Dominica» es completamente libre, necesita mejoras urgentes y ninguno de los periódicos mencionados indica los nombres de sus propietarios o editores.

English and French interest in Faustin I. was suspected to stem from jealousy of United States progress, while Dominican authorities ratified a treaty with the United States identical to the one negotiated by Cazneau. Asimismo, el presidente Mota promulgó bando de pena de muerte contra facciosos o filibusteros que hollasen el territorio —apuntando principalmente al expresidente Báez, a quien alentaban presuntamente Francia, Inglaterra y España—, arribando entretanto a Kingston el transporte militar estadounidense *Supply* con treinta y cinco animales traídos del Mediterráneo.

records.full_text: We have advices from Port au Prince to the 14th and from St. Domingo City to the 8th ult. Our correspondent at the first named place gives a retrospective summary of the governors who ruled and the policy which prevailed on the island anterior and subsequent to the servile revolution. He states that the Emperor in engaging in the late contest depended too much on the interested representations of disaffected Dominicans; but, although defeated, he was not disposed to listen to dictation from a foreign Power as to his future action in the affairs of his government. It was suspected that the interest shown by the English and French officials towards Faustin I. proceeded solely from jealousy of the progress and influence of the United States both in the Congress and Cabinet. The Dominican authorities had ratified a treaty with the United States. It is identical with the one negotiated by Gen. Cazeneau. President Mota had proclaimed death to all outlaws or filibusters landing on the island. The decree is mainly directed against ex-President Baez, as it was reported that he was encouraged by France, England and Spain, to attempt a revolutionary demonstration from St. Thomas.

records.headline: An Anglo-Africa Contraband Treaty.
records.summary_en: According to the *New-York dispatch* on May 4, 1856, England and France previously forced the Dominican Republic to cancel the Laznean treaty and insisted that a black population representative be appointed to the government, resulting in the nomination of an educated negro named Bobadilla to the Council of State. To avoid difficulty with England, President Pierce instructed the U.S. Commercial Agent at St. Domingo to revise or renegotiate the treaty using Bobadilla, and this new treaty was reportedly in the hands of the President for submission to the Senate around May 8th or 9th. Additionally, the Secretary of the Navy informed the President of the Pacific Mail Steamship Company that the U.S. ship *Cyane* had been ordered to Aspinwall to investigate the robbery and outrage against American citizens at Panama.
records.summary_es: Según el *New-York dispatch* del 4 de mayo de 1856, Inglaterra y Francia habían compelido en su momento a la República Dominicana a revocar el tratado de Cazneau [citado como Laznean], reclamando que se nombrase en el gobierno a un representante de la población de color, lo que derivó en la incorporación de Bobadilla al Consejo de Estado. Para solventar diferendos con Londres, el presidente Pierce dio orden al agente comercial en Santo Domingo de renegociar el pacto recurriendo a Bobadilla, hallándose dicho flamante texto en manos del mandatario para su elevación al Senado hacia el 8 o 9 de mayo. El secretario de Marina participó por otra parte al presidente de la Pacific Mail Steamship Company que la corbeta *Cyane* recibió orden de zarpar hacia Colón para indagar atropellos cometidos contra norteamericanos en Panamá.

records.full_text: An Anglo-Africa Contraband Treaty.—The Dominican Republic and our Government have received a new humiliation from England. When that Power, in conjunction with France, sent a fleet to St. Domingo, to order the Laznean treaty to be canceled, it also insisted, in behalf of the negroes, that the black population should be represented in the Cabinet or Senate. In obedience to this behest, an educated negro, named Bobadilla, was nominated to the Council of State. Rather than have any difficulty with England, Mr. Pierce thought proper to send private orders to our Commercial Agent at St. Domingo to revise the Laznean treaty, or make a new one to which England would not object; and this same negro, Bobadilla, was appointed to revise or negotiate a treaty. This precious Anglo-African mutilation of the original treaty is now in the hands of the President, and will probably be submitted to the Senate about the 8th or 9th of May.

records.headline: General Quitman's speech, quoted by The Anti-Slavery Bugle
records.summary_en: General Quitman's speech, quoted by The Anti-Slavery Bugle, surveys Nicaragua, Cuba, and San Domingo, in which he characterizes the Haitian government as a "strange and grotesque power" under whose rule a strategic Caribbean island is relapsing into barbarism while supported by European influences in attempting to exterminate the "small white Dominican Republic" that still holds part of the island. Observing that the rest of "insular America" is European or African, Quitman warns American statesmen that a "world-startling drama" is approaching in which the development, greatness, and safety of the United States are deeply concerned. In commentary following the excerpt, the Bugle ridicules the phrase "Insular America" as alien to the history and traditions of the American people, contrasting it with the "Continental America" that resisted George III.

records.full_text:
I write you under circumstances very dull for this republic. We are on the eve of a political hurricane; and I use this Indian word in this case, because it means wind from the four points, and the revolution which we expect every moment, will come from four points, viz:—France, England, Hayti and Spain, all combined, all united in the execution of two ideas—either to put down the present administration and to bring in Baez as chief magistrate, because it committed the crime of concluding a treaty with the United States, or, if not possible, to destroy the Dominican nationality by means of another Soulouque invasion, helped by those three nations.

On the 6th of June last, Senor Segovia, the Spanish Charge d'Affaires in this republic, went back to the capital from Puerto Rico, via St. Thomas, and soon after it was rumored there, as well as here, that he had received from the Cabinet of Madrid, by the Spanish mail steamer touching at Puerto Rico, full, arbitrary powers to act against the republic, under any pretext, no matter how light, in order to carry on their combined opposition to the American treaty, and in every way to prevent its exchange. And at the same time, the Spaniards in that city commenced to boast that a Spanish fleet was coming, and that the treaty would not be consummated.

By article 7th of the Dominican-Spanish treaty it was agreed that those Spaniards who have resided in the republic, and obtained Dominican nationality would be able to become again Spanish subjects, in which case their sons of age would have the same right. Senor Segovia, making a very wrong use of that stipulation, began to admit in his books as Spaniards some Dominicans, enemies of Santana's administration and friends of Baez, merely because their ancestors were Spaniards, in which point of law the great majority of the country might likewise be considered Spanish. The government, foreseeing the fatal consequences of this violent misinterpretation of the article, opposed Senor Segovia's action, and he closed the register of Spaniards until the two contracting parties would agree on its proper interpretation. Consequently, the Dominican government appointed an Extraordinary Envoy and Minister Plenipotentiary to the Court of Madrid to settle the difficulty; and as, almost at the same time, the American treaty was ratified, the Charge went in a hurry to St. Thomas in a British steam frigate of war, from which visit to that island and St. Martin he returned last month. Now, since his arrival he has been working the propaganda in favor of the interpretation which he gives to the above article, and has been propagating through his agents, in the interior as well as in the capital, that he has authority to register as Spaniards all those who declare their wish to be, giving them to understand, giving them a guarantee that no one who has once been registered in his consular office will be compelled by the Dominican government to carry arms. Consequently, the more ignorant, just with a view to relieve themselves from the military service, are running daily to the Spanish consulate by hundreds, and registering themselves as subjects of her Catholic Majesty.

By such conduct as this, Senor Segovia beyond question tramples on Dominican rights and independence, for it is plain, according to international law, that he cannot proceed on the admission of Dominican citizens as Spaniards, unless the question previously agreed by mutual agreement between Spain and the young republic. And what is more alarming, is the fact that on the 26th June last, General Blasco de Garay and the brig Gravina, of the Spanish navy, arrived in San Domingo, and no doubt the Dominicans believe that the only solution for the friends of Dominican nationality from this dark situation, was that Santana left the capital on that same day, with one hundred cavalry, and that every day are entering, little by little, a great many infantry, without beating the drums, in order, it seems, not to alarm the public. The government is no doubt adopting some great measure to be ready at the moment when the conspiracy is to explode; but it is impossible to ascertain what they propose to do.

President Mota, his ministers, the Senators, and several generals, go every day, and often twice a day, to visit the Liberador, as he is the commander-in-chief of the army, and because his opinion is always heard with respect by the cabinet. Certainly, as a means of mortification, the produce of the public revenue in cash is scarce. But, according to the first circular of the Minister for Foreign Relations, the revenue was increasing, not being burdened with unnecessary expenses or onerous contracts, and the hope was indulged that within a short time it would be exempted from transitory drawbacks, brought on by deplorable errors and the recent unfortunate events.

records.summary_en: Based on a letter from the schooner *Marietta Smith* arriving from Port-au-Platt, *The Daily Union* reported on August 20, 1856, that a revolution had broken out in the capital of the Dominican Republic following a treaty with Old Spain. The treaty's 11th article allowed Spanish descendants to become Spanish citizens, leading thousands of citizens and soldiers to register with Spanish consuls, which caused the suspension of business, the closure of tribunals, and the intended resignation of the President and his cabinet. Additionally, a city newspaper editor shot a Spaniard in broad daylight over a political dispute and escaped, prompting the Spanish consul to offer a $5,000 reward for his capture.

La cláusula undécima facultaba a los descendientes de españoles a recobrar la nacionalidad de sus mayores, empujando a millares de ciudadanos y tropa a inscribirse ante los cónsules hispanos, lo que ocasionó el cese de transacciones, la clausura de audiencias judiciales y la dimisión del presidente y su ministerio. Un redactor periodístico hirió de muerte a tiros a un peninsular a plena luz del día por motivos de facción dándose a la fuga, ofreciendo el cónsul español 5.000 duros de recompensa por su captura.

records.headline: Addressing the Chairman, the speaker in a speech printed by The Daily National Intelligencer surveys
records.summary_en: Addressing the Chairman, the speaker in a speech printed by The Daily National Intelligencer surveys San Domingo and describes the power ruling the island as a "caricature of government" under whose sway an island holding the same strategic relation to the Caribbean Sea as Cuba holds to the Gulf of Mexico is rapidly relapsing into barbarism. The speaker asserts that this regime is sustained by powerful European influences in its efforts to exterminate the "small white Dominican republic" that still retains part of the island, while all the rest of insular America is European or African. Warning that a "world-startling drama" is about to unfold affecting the development, greatness, and safety of the United States, he calls on American statesmen to act boldly and vigorously to fulfill the nation's destiny.
records.summary_es: El Daily National Intelligencer publica un discurso en el que el orador, dirigiéndose al presidente de la sesión, examina la situación de Santo Domingo y describe al poder que domina la isla como una «caricatura de gobierno» bajo cuyo mando una isla que guarda con el mar Caribe la misma relación estratégica que Cuba con el golfo de México está recayendo rápidamente en la barbarie. El orador afirma que dicho régimen es sostenido por poderosas influencias europeas en sus intentos de exterminar a la «pequeña república dominicana blanca» que aún conserva una parte de la isla, mientras que todo el resto de la América insular es europea o africana. Advirtiendo que está por desarrollarse un «drama que asombrará al mundo» y que atañe al desarrollo, la grandeza y la seguridad misma de los Estados Unidos, exhorta a los estadistas estadounidenses a actuar con audacia y vigor para cumplir el destino asignado a su república.

records.headline: Citing the Havana correspondent of the New York Herald, the Alexandria Gazette reports
records.summary_en: Citing the Havana correspondent of the New York Herald, the Alexandria Gazette reports that the Spanish government is engaging in what it characterizes as wholesale filibustering. According to the report, Spanish naval expeditions were preparing to depart Havana for San Domingo City and Vera Cruz. One fleet was to be sent to assist a movement against the territorial integrity of the Dominican Republic, while the other was to be dispatched to support Spanish claims in Mexico.
records.summary_es: Citando al corresponsal en La Habana del New York Herald, la Alexandria Gazette informa que el gobierno español se está embarcando en lo que califica como filibusterismo a gran escala. Según el informe, se estaban preparando expediciones navales españolas para zarpar de La Habana hacia la ciudad de Santo Domingo y Veracruz. Una flota sería enviada para apoyar el movimiento contra la integridad de la República Dominicana, mientras que la otra sería despachada para respaldar las pretensiones del gobierno español en México.

records.headline: Under the headline "Later from San Domingo — Martial Law in Dominica,"
records.summary_en: Under the headline "Later from San Domingo — Martial Law in Dominica," the Richmond Daily Dispatch reports advices received via Havana from both portions of the island up to mid-January. In the Dominican Republic, the longstanding conflict between Santana and President Báez, described as representing Spanish and French ideas respectively, continued to distract the country throughout its territory. While Santana held his position firmly in the mountains of Neyba, martial law was proclaimed in the name of the President and Senate. From Haiti, the paper adds that the anniversary of Haitian independence was celebrated with addresses involving Emperor Soulouque, and that Augustin Soulfrant, Prince of Jacmel and Grand Marshal of the Empire, died on January 9.
records.summary_es: Bajo el titular «Últimas noticias de Santo Domingo — Ley marcial en Dominica», el Daily Dispatch de Richmond informa sobre noticias recibidas vía La Habana procedentes de ambas partes de la isla hasta mediados de enero. En la República Dominicana, la antigua disputa entre Santana y el presidente Báez, descritos como representantes de las ideas españolas y francesas respectivamente, continuaba perturbando al país en toda su extensión. Mientras Santana mantenía firmemente su posición en las montañas de Neiba, se proclamó la ley marcial en nombre del presidente y del Senado. Desde Haití, el periódico añade que se celebró el aniversario de la independencia haitiana con discursos del emperador Soulouque, y que Augustin Soulfrant, príncipe de Jacmel y gran mariscal del Imperio, falleció el 9 de enero.

records.summary_en: During March, the American schooner *Charles Hill*, commanded by Captain Smith, collided with a Dominican packet, leading to the captain's imprisonment in San Domingo for failing to pay a $3,000 fine for willful damage. Captain Smith has abandoned his schooner to the government, prompting a correspondent in San Domingo City to demand redress from the Cabinet at Washington. Additionally, the excerpt briefly notes that no further outbreaks occurred yesterday following an incident where individuals arriving at a location found only a doorman.

El capitán Smith desamparó su embarcación dejándola en manos del fisco dominicano, induciendo a un corresponsal en la capital a clamar desagravio ante el gabinete de Washington. El suelto añadía sucintamente que no se registraron nuevas alteraciones en la víspera tras un incidente donde varios sujetos acudieron a un paraje hallando únicamente a un portero.

records.headline: The Revolution in St. Domingo.
records.summary_en: A private letter published in the *Turks Island Standard* reports that a revolution has broken out in the Dominican Republic. According to the excerpt, the primary cause of the uprising was an attempt by the government to depreciate the paper currency or alter the rate of exchange by twenty percent, alongside grievances regarding the central government's appropriation of provincial resources. Additionally, the revolutionists' manifesto—modeled after the American Declaration of Independence—complains of oppressive administrations, despotism, violations of personal liberty, arbitrary arrests, and the suppression of the press.
records.summary_es: Una misiva particular divulgada en el *Turks Island Standard* expone el estallido de un alzamiento revolucionario en la República Dominicana. Según el relato, el detonante principal consistió en la pretensión oficial de devaluar el papel moneda o alterar en un veinte por ciento el tipo de cambio, aunada a los agravios por la incautación de recursos provinciales por el poder central. Se añade que el manifiesto de los sublevados —inspirado en el Acta de Independencia de Estados Unidos— denunciaba administraciones vejatorias, tiranía, conculcación de la libertad individual, prisiones arbitrarias y clausura de la imprenta.

records.full_text: THE REVOLUTION IN ST. DOMINGO.—A private letter, dated Porto Plata, July 20th, which is published in the Turks Island Standard of August 1st, gives the principal cause of the revolution which has recently broken out in the Dominican republic as an attempt made by the government to alter the present rate of exchange or to depreciate the value of the paper currency of the country some twenty per cent. Another rumor was to the effect that the authorities of the city of St. Domingo have been drawing upon the resources of the provinces, and appropriating them without allowing a reasonable proportion to be spent in improvement and for other purposes of a local nature. Other causes are also assigned. The manifesto of the revolutionists is very nicely copied after our own Declaration of Independence, stating the preliminary dogmas about the uses of government, the reserved rights of the governed, &c., precisely in the same style, and giving that body to complain of a succession of devouring and rapacious administrations which have oppressed the republic and despoiled the people of property and happiness. The rebels charge that the paper currency, most of the years 1844 and 1854 have been nothing but the means of giving strength, support &c., to despotism and plunder. They allege the violation of personal liberty, the arbitrary arrest of citizens, tyranical judgements, the destruction of the liberty of the press, and of the nation, and the dissolution of the national representative bodies by insidious and artful intrigues.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that after the arrival of reinforcements and a subsequent battle, General Puello was taken prisoner and a colonel reportedly killed himself to avoid the same fate, while the provisional government offered pardons to partisans of President Baez. According to the correspondence, President Baez was obliged to leave St. Domingo, and the provisional government was selecting a competent chief, though letters from Port-au-Prince also noted that the insurgents appealed to Emperor Faustin for aid and sought annexation to the empire of Hayti.

Conforme a la correspondencia, el mandatario Báez se vio obligado a desamparar Santo Domingo, abocándose el gobierno provisorio a elegir un jefe idóneo, si bien epístolas remitidas desde Puerto Príncipe advertían que los insurrectos imploraron socorro al emperador Faustino demandando la incorporación al Imperio de Haití.

records.headline: The Alexandria Gazette reports that a revolution is in progress
records.summary_en: The Alexandria Gazette reports that a revolution is in progress in the Dominican Republic, on recent accounts from St. Domingo, aimed at removing President Báez and restoring Santana to power. According to the notice, the Báez faction, finding itself hard pressed by the insurgents, has formed an alliance with Emperor Soulouque of Haiti, who has dispatched assistance to his ally.
records.summary_es: La Alexandria Gazette informa que hay una revolución en curso en la República Dominicana, según noticias recientes procedentes de Santo Domingo, con el propósito de destituir al presidente Báez y restituir a Santana en el poder. Según la nota, el bando de Báez, al verse fuertemente acosado, ha formado una alianza con el emperador Soulouque de Haití, quien ha enviado ayuda a su aliado.

In the fiscal year ending June 30,1856, out of the total
exports from this country to foreign ports the propor
tion of New Orleans was $80,576,652. During the year
ending June 30, 1857, her exports amounted to $04,
514,286—an increase of nearly eleven millions in a year.
If we add the exports to domestic ports, the total value
of produce, &e. shipped from New Orleans during the
year ending June 80, 1857, amounts to 3119,222,615.
This is an enormous amount for a single port. and gives
some idea of the scale on which business is transacted in
the Crescent City. For a port whose trade was thought
to be declining a few years ago, and sure to decline still
more with the extension of the Northern system of rail
roads, such an exhibit of prosperity is remarkable.

records.headline: The New York Herald reports news brought by the schooner Mary Jane
records.summary_en: The New York Herald reports news brought by the schooner Mary Jane from Puerto Plata, reprinting items from the Turks Islands Gazette of October 7, regarding hostilities in San Domingo. A translated September 17 bulletin from the official paper at Santo Domingo announces that the English schooner Merillen arrived from Samaná with dispatches from a government general reporting that his forces attacked and routed the Cibao garrison at Savannah la Mar, inflicting heavy losses in killed and wounded while suffering only one soldier wounded and a slight shoulder contusion to the general himself. The official bulletin hails this victory as proof that Providence protects the loyal armies from Mojarra to this latest engagement and adds that the northern flotilla opened fire on the 11th against a group of men assembled near Matanzas. The Turks Islands Gazette remarks that although civil war is raging in the Dominican Republic, it has not yet been able to ascertain the aims of the contending parties.
records.summary_es: Al reproducir notas de la Turks Islands Gazette del 7 de octubre, el New York Herald informa sobre las noticias llevadas desde Puerto Plata por la goleta Mary Jane acerca de las hostilidades en Santo Domingo. Un boletín traducido del 17 de septiembre del periódico oficial de la ciudad de Santo Domingo anuncia que la goleta inglesa Merillen llegó procedente de Samaná con despachos de un general del gobierno en los que informa haber atacado y derrotado a la guarnición cibaeña en Savannah la Mar, causando numerosas bajas entre muertos y heridos, mientras que sus tropas solo tuvieron un herido además de una leve contusión en el hombro sufrida por el propio general. El boletín oficial celebra este triunfo como prueba de que la Providencia protege a los ejércitos leales desde Mojarra hasta este último encuentro, y añade que la flotilla que opera en el norte abrió fuego el día 11 contra un grupo de hombres reunidos cerca de Matanzas. La Turks Islands Gazette observa que, aunque la guerra civil hace estragos en la República Dominicana, aún no ha podido determinar los objetivos de los bandos en pugna.

records.headline: News from Saint Domingo.
records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported that an expedition of 1,000 men was marching against Samaná, the last location holding out for Báez, while business in Port au Plata and Santiago remained safe despite all provincial military forces being under arms. The Cibao government sought to purchase two small clipper schooners and other armaments, including an 18-inch mortar, to blockade Santo Domingo. Additionally, the newspaper noted local astonishment that the U.S. government had not sent a warship to demand satisfaction regarding the seizure of the American schooner *Charles Hill* by Báez.

El gobierno del Cibao procuraba adquirir dos goletas de casco fino y otros pertrechos, comprendido un mortero de dieciocho pulgadas, para estrechar el bloqueo sobre Santo Domingo. El diario hacía constar la sorpresa de los pobladores ante la omisión del gobierno de Washington de comisionar un buque de guerra para reclamar reparaciones por el embargo de la goleta estadounidense *Charles Hill* dispuesto por Báez.

records.full_text:
News from Saint Domingo.
THE LIBERTY PARTY ORGANIZING A CONSTITUTION—
ELECTIONS ORDERED—SIEGE OF SAN DOMINGO CITY
—TWO WAR VESSELS AND A LARGE MORTAR WANTED
—BAEZ’S FRIENDS FALLING OFF—THE AMERICAN
SCHOONER CHARLES HILL.

The schooner City Belle, Captain Pendleton, arrived at this port yesterday from Port au Plata, with news dated at that place on 29th of October.

The authors of the revolution of the liberty party in the Dominican republic are fast organizing a new government very different from that of Senor Baez.

The election for the deputies of the nation was to take place on the 10th of November, and the members were to meet at the town of Moca on the 1st of December.

General Santana and several other valiant Generals were besieging the city of St. Domingo with a force of 8,000 men. The besiegers are very moderate in their fire against the city, as it was momentarily expected that Baez would be forced to capitulate. An expedition of 2,000 men strong were marching against Samana, the only place holding for Baez.

Business in Port au Plata and Santiago continued quite safe and easy, although all the military in the province of Cibao were under arms.

The Cibao government wish to purchase two small clipper schooners of 150 to 180 tons, to blockade the port of St. Domingo; vessels that are staunch and strong, that will be able to carry a twenty-four pounder upon a pivot, besides small guns of smaller calibre. There being no vessels in port suitable, any American speculator might find a good offer from the government, if quickly attended to, in Port au Plata.

News had reached Port au Plata that many of the first families had lately left the city of St. Domingo, besides natives that Baez has sent away.

The people and foreign residents were very much astonished that the American government did not send a vessel of war to St. Domingo, to demand satisfaction in the case of the American schooner Charles Hill, which was seized by Baez (valued at $10,000), and as yet not claimed by the American government. The American Consul at St. Domingo had sent all the documents relative to this affair in May last to Washington.

Fighting men, friends to the republic, would be well received. Arms and ammunition were in good demand, and they were in want of an 18-inch mortar, for which the highest rates would be paid.

records.headline: Dispatches from the South American naval station report that conditions
records.summary_en: Dispatches from the South American naval station report that conditions in the Dominican Republic required the French admiral to intervene for the protection of French residents. Additionally, the Paris Moniteur issues a caution to emigrants, noting that after a group recently departed France for St. Domingo and another departure was announced, unfavorable accounts of the first settlers prompted advice that French colonists postpone establishing themselves in the republic.
records.summary_es: Despachos desde la estación naval de América del Sur informan que las condiciones en la República Dominicana obligaron al almirante francés a intervenir para la protección de los residentes franceses. Asimismo, el Moniteur de París emite una advertencia a los emigrantes, señalando que, tras la reciente partida de un grupo desde Francia hacia Santo Domingo y el anuncio de otra salida, los informes desfavorables sobre la situación de los primeros colonos aconsejan que los colonos franceses pospongan sus planes de establecerse en la república.

records.headline: The Tribune reprints a report from the Turks Islands Standard based
records.summary_en: The Tribune reprints a report from the Turks Islands Standard based on the arrival of the Dominican sloop Isabel from Puerto Plata. At the vessel's departure, the capital had not yet surrendered to the besieging army under General Santana, while General E. Puello commanded 1,500 men before Samaná against forces facing a shortage of provisions. Meanwhile, the mail schooner Nineteenth of March surrendered under a flag of truce with $22,000 Spanish in provisions, leading to the capture of President Baez's correspondence from Europe and St. Thomas, with private letters forwarded to British Consul Hood for delivery. The Isabel then embarked General F. Sosa and other refugees who had fled Baez's persecution to transport them to Puerto Plata.
records.summary_es: El Tribune reproduce un informe del Turks Islands Standard basado en la llegada de la balandra dominicana Isabel desde Puerto Plata. A la salida de la embarcación, aún no se sabía que la capital se hubiera rendido al ejército sitiador del general Santana, mientras que el general E. Puello comandaba 1,500 hombres frente a Samaná contra fuerzas que enfrentaban escasez de víveres. Entretanto, la goleta correo Diecinueve de Marzo se rindió bajo bandera de tregua con provisiones valoradas en 22,000 pesos fuertes españoles, lo que condujo a la captura de la correspondencia del presidente Báez desde Europa y Saint Thomas, enviándose las cartas privadas al cónsul británico Hood para su entrega. Posteriormente, la Isabel embarcó al general F. Sosa y a otros refugiados que habían huido de la persecución de Báez para trasladarlos a Puerto Plata.

records.headline: The English, French, and Spanish Consuls met in the camp of Santana
records.summary_en: Baez and his party are reported to be hard-pressed by Santana, leading to official steps to procure peace through the mediation of English, French, and Spanish consuls. Santana has rejected their initial terms and insists that Baez submit a written proposition for the capitulation of San Domingo. Meanwhile, Santana's forces have occupied the peninsula of Samana, and the war-brig *Nineteenth of March*, carrying munitions, provisions, and documents implicating Baez in the misuse of public funds, has surrendered to the Provisional Government.

Santana desechó las condiciones preliminares y exigió que Báez presentase una propuesta formal y por escrito para la capitulación de Santo Domingo. records.summary_en: Following the expiration of a deadline, a bombardment of Port au Plate commenced, though fire from the fort forced the attackers out of range. The St. Jago government stated it would seek foreign aid before yielding to Baez, whose fleet's movements were favored by English and French consuls, leaving the United States as the sole government to depend upon. Additionally, the American schooner *Wing of the Wind* successfully ran the blockade with a cargo from New York on the 27th, while the U.S. Consul at St. Domingo, Mr. Elliott, remained imprisoned in his house for fear of his life without the presence of U.S. warships.
records.summary_es: Expirado el plazo otorgado, dio principio el cañoneo sobre Puerto Plata, aunque la réplica de artillería del fuerte obligó a los atacantes a retirarse fuera de tiro. El gobierno radicado en Santiago previno que antes recabaría auxilio foráneo que someterse a Báez, a cuyos buques amparaban los cónsules británico y francés, restando Estados Unidos como el único amparo confiable. Asimismo, la goleta estadounidense *Wing of the Wind* burló el bloqueo con cargamento de Nueva York el día 27, en tanto el cónsul norteamericano en Santo Domingo, Sr. Elliott, permanecía encerrado en su morada temiendo por su vida ante la ausencia de buques de guerra de su nación.

records.headline: A dispatch reports that the U.S. steamer Colorado arrived at Aspinwall
records.summary_en: A dispatch reports that the U.S. steamer Colorado arrived at Aspinwall from St. Domingo on the 17th. The vessel brought intelligence that the President of the Dominican Republic had capitulated to General Santana, printed in the report as Santa Anna, and was scheduled to depart San Domingo on the 13th for Curaçao after most of his followers left the previous day. Santana gave Commodore McIntosh the strongest assurances regarding the protection of American citizens and expressed a desire to maintain amicable relations with the United States government. Commodore McIntosh was also reported to have secured from President Baez all the official documents for which he had been dispatched.
records.summary_es: Un despacho informa que el vapor estadounidense Colorado llegó a Aspinwall procedente de Santo Domingo el día 17. La nave trajo noticias de que el presidente de la República Dominicana había capitulado ante el general Santana, identificado en el informe como Santa Anna, y tenía previsto partir de Santo Domingo el día 13 rumbo a Curazao, habiendo salido la mayoría de sus seguidores el día anterior. Santana ofreció al comodoro McIntosh las más firmes garantías sobre la protección de los ciudadanos estadounidenses y manifestó su deseo de mantener relaciones amistosas con el gobierno de los Estados Unidos. Asimismo, se informó que el comodoro McIntosh logró obtener del presidente Báez todos los documentos oficiales que había sido enviado a conseguir.

records.headline: A report brought by the U.S. frigate Colorado details the political crisis
records.summary_en: A report brought by the U.S. frigate Colorado details the political crisis in the Dominican Republic following the warship's arrival at Santo Domingo on May 24. The dispatch states that President Baez held the capital with 250 soldiers through French and Spanish consular intrigues, while General Santana besieged the city with 5,000 to 10,000 native troops, reducing the inhabitants to near starvation. Commodore McIntosh secured assurances for the protection of American citizens and received the official records regarding the case of Charles Hill. The presence of the Colorado reportedly hastened the capitulation of Baez, who agreed to surrender his naval squadron and prepare for departure to Curaçao on June 13.
records.summary_es: Un informe traído por la fragata estadounidense Colorado detalla la crisis política en la República Dominicana tras la llegada del buque de guerra a Santo Domingo el 24 de mayo. El despacho afirma que el presidente Báez sostenía la capital con 250 soldados gracias a las intrigas consulares francesas y españolas, mientras el general Santana sitiaba la ciudad con 5,000 a 10,000 soldados nativos, reduciendo a los habitantes a un estado cercano a la inanición. El comodoro McIntosh obtuvo seguridades para la protección de los ciudadanos estadounidenses y recibió los expedientes oficiales sobre el caso de Charles Hill. La presencia del Colorado presuntamente aceleró la capitulación de Báez, quien acordó entregar su escuadra naval y prepararse para partir hacia Curazao el 13 de junio.

records.headline: The editorial looks back on the eleven-month civil war just ended in the Republic of San Domingo, describing it as largely
records.summary_en: The editorial looks back on the eleven-month civil war just ended in the Republic of San Domingo, describing it as largely a geographical contest between the northern and southern sections, led by the rival cities of Santiago and San Domingo under Pedro Santana. It sketches the two cities and the republic's history: independence declared in 1821, twenty-two years united with Haiti under Boyer, the proclamation of the Dominican Republic in 1844, Haitian invasions beaten back by Santana, who received the title of Liberator, and the dissatisfaction that followed under President Jimenez.
records.summary_es: El editorial repasa la guerra civil de once meses que acaba de terminar en la República de Santo Domingo, describiéndola como en gran parte una contienda geográfica entre las secciones norte y sur, encabezada por las ciudades rivales de Santiago y Santo Domingo bajo Pedro Santana. Esboza las dos ciudades y la historia de la república: la independencia declarada en 1821, veintidós años unida a Haití bajo Boyer, la proclamación de la República Dominicana en 1844, las invasiones haitianas rechazadas por Santana, quien recibió el título de Libertador, y el descontento que siguió bajo el presidente Jiménez.

records.headline: The Herald publishes the text of a convention negotiated by the consuls of France
records.summary_en: The Herald publishes the text of a convention negotiated by the consuls of France, England, and Spain between President Buenaventura Baez and General Pedro Santana to terminate the Dominican civil war. Under the agreement, Baez consents to vacate the presidency and leave the country immediately upon signing. General Santana solemnly pledges that no individual will be persecuted or molested for having sustained Baez's government, and promises passports to all officers wishing to depart after the surrender. Santana also undertakes to maintain order in and around the city of Santo Domingo, which is to be delivered to his authority along with its forts, arsenals, and naval squadron.
records.summary_es: El Herald publica el texto de una convención negociada por los cónsules de Francia, Inglaterra y España entre el presidente Buenaventura Báez y el general Pedro Santana para poner fin a la guerra civil dominicana. En virtud del acuerdo, Báez acepta abandonar la presidencia y salir del país inmediatamente después de la firma. El general Santana se compromete solemnemente a no perseguir ni molestar a ninguna persona por haber respaldado al gobierno de Báez, y promete pasaportes a todos los oficiales que deseen marcharse tras la capitulación. Santana se compromete asimismo a mantener el orden dentro y fuera de la ciudad de Santo Domingo, la cual será entregada a su autoridad junto con sus fuertes, arsenales y escuadrilla naval.

records.headline: The Tribune publishes the concluding lines of a valedictory proclamation
records.summary_en: The Tribune publishes the concluding lines of a valedictory proclamation issued by President Buenaventura Baez to the Dominican people upon his departure from office. Baez charges the citizens to render obedience to the new authorities governing in the name of the law and entreats them to shun political turmoil, describing factional fury as deplorable even in victory. He urges his compatriots to embrace fraternally, forget past discords, and find peace after their bitter sufferings, expressing a fervent hope for national stability. The document was signed at the National Palace of Santo Domingo on June 12, 1858, during the fifteenth year of Dominican independence.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica las líneas finales de una proclama de despedida dirigida por el presidente Buenaventura Báez al pueblo dominicano al dejar el poder. Báez encomienda a los ciudadanos prestar obediencia a las nuevas autoridades que han de gobernar en nombre de la ley y les suplica evitar las convulsiones políticas, calificando el furor de las facciones como deplorable aun cuando se corone con la victoria. Exhorta a sus compatriotas a abrazarse fraternalmente, olvidar las discordias pasadas y alcanzar la felicidad tras sus amargos sufrimientos, manifestando su ferviente deseo de estabilidad nacional. El documento fue firmado en el Palacio Nacional de Santo Domingo el 12 de junio de 1858, en el décimo quinto año de la independencia dominicana.

records.summary_en: The *New-York daily tribune* reported that Baez has been overthrown and Santana has taken power in the Republic of Dominica. While Southern journals view this as a triumph of the white over the black race and urge the U.S. government to formally recognize the Dominican Republic, the newspaper supports recognition regardless of racial distinctions. However, the publication questions whether the U.S. government and its Washington court circle would tolerate diplomats or future presidents of darker complexions in a country where the vast majority of the population is of African lineage.

Con todo, la hoja se pregunta si el gabinete estadounidense y las tertulias de Washington consentirían a diplomáticos o futuros mandatarios de tez morena oriundos de una nación cuya gran mayoría desciende de linaje africano.

records.headline: The Bugle quotes an article from a proslavery paper styled The South
records.summary_en: The Bugle quotes an article from a proslavery paper styled The South, which argues that the United States must restrain French intrigue in St. Domingo and assert its influence in the Dominican Republic following the rejection of an American treaty. The Southern journal asserts that obtaining a foothold on the island is advisable for self-protection and essential for future aggrandizement in relation to the question of slavery. In response, the Bugle contends that the South's interest in the country it calls Dominica has been frankly exposed as an effort to make the island subservient to the ambitions of Southern slavery agitators.

records.headline: The paper reports, on intelligence from the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: The paper reports, on intelligence from the Dominican Republic, the entry of General Santana, whom the dispatch calls Santa Anna, into Santiago on September 1. Following his entry, the sitting government was dissolved and President Valverde fled to Turk's Island. The dispatch states that the country had fallen into anarchy, with commercial business entirely suspended and government currency discredited. Observers were said to be anxiously awaiting the general's next movements.
records.summary_es: El periódico publica noticias de la República Dominicana que anuncian la entrada del general Santana, a quien el despacho llama Santa Anna, en Santiago el 1 de septiembre. Tras su entrada, el gobierno establecido fue disuelto y el presidente Valverde huyó a la isla Turca. El despacho señala que el país había caído en la anarquía, con las actividades comerciales completamente suspendidas y la moneda gubernamental desacreditada. Se añade que se aguardaban con inquietud las próximas medidas del general.

records.headline: A Washington letter discusses European diplomatic policy on the West Indies
records.summary_en: A Washington letter discusses European diplomatic policy on the West Indies and the preservation of European equilibrium in the Western Hemisphere. The writer cites statements that the Dominican Republic must be submerged by the Haitian empire because an independent republic with American sympathies endangers European colonial supremacy in the region. The correspondent further reports claims that an Anglo-French alliance is pressing Spain to alter Cuba's status, possibly through a confederation with Puerto Rico and St. Domingo, to place it beyond the reach of the United States. Although European ministers in Washington deny these plans, the writer insists that concerted European efforts aim to block American influence across the Antilles.
records.summary_es: Una carta desde Washington analiza la política diplomática europea sobre las Antillas y la preservación del equilibrio europeo en el hemisferio occidental. El autor cita declaraciones según las cuales la República Dominicana debe ser absorbida por el imperio haitiano, debido a que una república independiente con simpatías estadounidenses pone en peligro la supremacía colonial europea en la región. El corresponsal informa además sobre versiones de que una alianza anglo-francesa presiona a España para alterar el estatus de Cuba, posiblemente mediante una confederación con Puerto Rico y Santo Domingo, a fin de colocarla fuera del alcance de los Estados Unidos. Aunque los ministros europeos en Washington niegan dichos planes, el redactor insiste en que los esfuerzos concertados europeos procuran cerrarle el paso a la influencia estadounidense en las Antillas.

records.headline: A political history of the republic traces the rivalry of Baez and Santana, beginning with Baez, twice called to the presidency
records.summary_en: A political history of the republic traces the rivalry of Baez and Santana, beginning with Baez, twice called to the presidency, as Santana's intimate friend and able co-operator in securing independence after Soulouque, the Emperor of Haiti, twice invaded and was beaten back. It recounts an embassy to Port au Prince that found Soulouque would accept nothing but the complete subjugation of Dominica and produced only an exchange of prisoners, the fight over ratifying a treaty with the United States, Santana's election and the friendship turning to bitter hostility, and Baez being sworn in again amid the demands of the naturalization party.
records.summary_es: Una historia política de la república recorre la rivalidad de Baez y Santana, comenzando con Baez, llamado dos veces a la presidencia, como amigo íntimo y capaz colaborador de Santana en asegurar la independencia después de que Soulouque, el emperador de Haití, invadiera dos veces y fuera rechazado. Relata una embajada a Port au Prince que descubrió que Soulouque no aceptaría nada más que la completa subyugación de Dominica y que solo produjo un intercambio de prisioneros, la lucha por la ratificación de un tratado con los Estados Unidos, la elección de Santana y cómo la amistad se convirtió en hostilidad amarga, y la nueva juramentación de Baez en medio de las exigencias del partido de la naturalización.

records.headline: Patriotism is not extinct among the Dominicans-on the contrary, it always
records.summary_en: Forty-five Dominican officers and civilians signed a manifesto from Baní on October 27, 1858, expressing indignation over a memoir by Senor Maximo Reybaud that proposed sacrificing their nationality to Hayti. The signatories declared that patriotism among Dominicans remains strong, asserting their readiness to defend the freedom and independence won in 1844 rather than submit again to Hayti.
records.summary_es: Cuarenta y cinco jefes militares y próceres civiles dominicanos estamparon su firma en un manifiesto fechado en Baní el 27 de octubre de 1858, exteriorizando su viva indignación ante una memoria de Maxime Raybaud que proponía el sacrificio de la nacionalidad patria en provecho de Haití. Los signatarios proclamaban que el sentimiento patrio permanecía inalterable entre los dominicanos, jurando hallarse resueltos a empuñar las armas para defender la libertad e independencia conquistadas en 1844 antes que someterse de nuevo a la servidumbre haitiana.

records.headline: The paper quotes an article from the Paris Union recalling that Emperor Soulouque
records.summary_en: The paper quotes an article from the Paris Union recalling that Emperor Soulouque had invaded the Dominican Republic three years earlier, suffered defeat, and subsequently concluded an armistice with General Santana guaranteed by France and England. The French journal reports that this truce is set to expire on February 15, and Soulouque has already formally denounced it to the government at Santo Domingo. In consequence, a renewal of hostilities is considered probable, and Santana is reported to be actively preparing for war.
records.summary_es: El periódico cita un artículo del Paris Union en el que se recuerda que el emperador Soulouque había invadido la República Dominicana tres años antes, sufrió una derrota y concluyó posteriormente un armisticio con el general Santana bajo la garantía de Francia e Inglaterra. El diario francés informa que dicha tregua expirará el 15 de febrero próximo y que Soulouque ya la ha denunciado formalmente ante el gobierno de Santo Domingo. En consecuencia, se considera probable la reanudación de las hostilidades, y se informa que Santana se prepara activamente para la guerra.

records.headline: The paper quotes the Paris Union regarding the impending expiration of the peace
records.summary_en: The paper quotes the Paris Union regarding the impending expiration of the peace agreement between Haiti and the Dominican Republic. Three years after Emperor Soulouque's invasion was repulsed, the armistice concluded with General Santana under the guarantee of France and England is set to expire on February 15. Soulouque has already notified the Dominican government that the agreement will not be renewed, making a resumption of war appear probable as Santana prepares his forces for defense.

records.summary_en: A letter from Hayti published in the *Journal du Havre* contradicts reports of a declaration from Emperor Soulouque, though the Dominican nation remains ready to resist any potential invasion while its country is tranquil and preparing for a January 1 presidential election. The article notes that General Geffrard's reported successful insurrection could open a new chapter in the island's wars, and provides geographic and demographic statistics for the island, which is divided between Hayti and the Dominican republic. Additionally, it describes the island's capital, military forces, climate, and soil, noting that productiveness has declined due to corrupt rule.
records.summary_es: A tenor del fragmento reproducido, una correspondencia procedente de Haití inserta en el *Journal du Havre* desmiente la versión de un bando atribuido al emperador Soulouque, persistiendo la nación dominicana en firme apresto para rechazar cualquier intento de invasión, al tiempo que el país goza de sosiego y se prepara para los comicios presidenciales del 1 de enero. El suelto apunta que el triunfo insurreccional del general Geffrard podría abrir una nueva etapa en las guerras de la isla, consignando cifras demográficas y geográficas de la partición territorial entre Haití y la República Dominicana. Describe finalmente la capital insular, su fuerza militar, el clima y los suelos, haciendo notar que la fecundidad de la tierra había decaído bajo gobiernos viciados.

records.headline: An imperial bulletin treats the revolution from Soulouque's point of view as a mere temporary riot, reporting the seizure of a small
records.summary_en: An imperial bulletin treats the revolution from Soulouque's point of view as a mere temporary riot, reporting the seizure of a small French boat, the Emperor's inspection of the army and of ramparts built overnight, and insurgents fleeing and leaving their ammunition. The paper also prints the Emperor's January 1 proclamation calling his loyal subjects to his aid and vowing strict dealing with persistent insurgents, and notes a December 27 decree declaring the port of Gonaives blockaded.
records.summary_es: Un boletín imperial trata la revolución desde el punto de vista de Soulouque como un mero disturbio temporal, informando de la captura de un pequeño bote francés, de la inspección del ejército y de las murallas construidas durante la noche por el emperador, y de insurgentes que huyeron dejando su munición. El periódico también publica la proclamación del emperador del 1 de enero, que llama a sus súbditos leales en su ayuda y promete tratar con rigor a los insurgentes persistentes, y señala un decreto del 27 de diciembre que declara bloqueado el puerto de Gonaïves.

records.full_text: REVOLUTION IN HAYTI. The schooner North Wind, Capt. Higgins, from Gonaives Jan. 1st, reports that a revolution broke out in Hayti, Dec. 22d, between the Haytien Government and a party of Republicans headed by General Goffard, one of the Haytien Generals. He took the city of Gonaives, and was proclaimed President. He entered the city with only four men. The inhabitants are joining Gen. Goffard wherever he goes. Aux Cayes, Jacmel and all the South have declared in his favor. Capt. Higgins passed St. Marks on the night of January 1st, and saw the place in flames, on account probably of a division of opinion of the inhabitants (St. Marks is a small fortified town). Goffard was to enter that place on that day, and probably did so, but met with some opposition from a party of Solouque’s adherents.

records.headline: A statistical account describes the island of Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: A statistical account describes the island of Santo Domingo, whose 29,000 square miles are divided between the Empire of Haiti on one-third and the Dominican Republic on two-thirds. The paper records Haiti's population at 650,000 and that of what it calls the republic of Dominica at 150,000, nine-tenths being of African descent and the remainder of Spanish and Indigenous origin. The Dominican capital of St. Domingo was founded by Bartholomew Columbus in 1496, and the Dominican army is placed at 12,000 men against Soulouque's 40,000 troops. While praising the island's fertile soil and delightful climate, the article asserts that agriculture has severely declined under misrule, reducing exports of coffee and tobacco to almost nothing and requiring sugar imports from the United States.
records.summary_es: Una reseña estadística describe la isla de Santo Domingo, cuyas 29,000 millas cuadradas están divididas entre el Imperio de Haití en un tercio y la República Dominicana en los dos tercios restantes. El periódico cifra la población de Haití en 650,000 habitantes y la de la entidad que denomina república de Dominica en 150,000, de los cuales nueve décimas partes se describen como de ascendencia africana y el resto de origen español e indígena. La capital dominicana, Santo Domingo, fue fundada por Bartolomé Colón en 1496, y el ejército dominicano se estima en unos 12,000 hombres frente a los 40,000 de Soulouque. Pese a elogiar el suelo fértil y el clima deleitable, el artículo afirma que la productividad agrícola ha decaído profundamente por el mal gobierno, reduciendo las exportaciones de café y tabaco a casi nada y obligando a importar azúcar desde los Estados Unidos.

ST. DOMINGO AND THE UNITED STATES—THE IMPORTANT SERVICES OF MONSIEUR REYBAUD BALDERDASH.

records.headline: The Liberator reprints a London Anti-Slavery Reporter letter
records.summary_en: The Liberator reprints a London Anti-Slavery Reporter letter. The letter discusses foreign diplomacy in the Caribbean under the heading "American Intrigues in St. Domingo." The correspondent states that the island, described by the writer as having once been united under President Boyer for twenty-two years, is now divided between the Dominican Republic in the east and the empire of Soulouque in the west. This division and mutual antagonism, the letter argues, created severe vulnerability and invited aggressive intrigue from the representatives of England, France, Spain, and the United States. The writer particularly condemns American emissaries, alleging they have been guided by the most unscrupulous motives in exploiting local weaknesses.

records.full_text:
To the Editor of the Anti-Slavery Reporter.'

SIR,—The island of St. Domingo, once united under the firm administration of Boyer for a period of twenty-two years, is now divided into two parts; the East, or Spanish part, forming the Dominican Republic, and the West, or French part, being constituted into the empire of Soulouque. It is not, at present, my intention to enter into the history of the civil war in the eastern province which led to the separation, nor is it necessary to show to any one who has studied the recent history of the country, that this separation has occasioned much present weakness and past ruin to both, and surrounded both with perils of incalculable magnitude. The existence of two independent states on so small an island, necessarily influenced by mutual jealousies and hatreds, and each looking to foreign aid for protection against a foreign power and a revolted province, could not fail to invite foreign aggression and intrigue. The great representatives of England, France, Spain, and the United States, have, in turn, taken advantage of the weakness of the local governments to play the game of their respective countries, but the aggressions of the latter power appear to have been influenced by the most evil motives, and to have a direct tendency to encourage new attacks on the liberty and independence of the island. These intrigues doubtless form a part of a systematic plan of American encroaching policy, holding propaganda, which aims to extend the ‘blessings of the peculiar institution’ over Hayti, Central America, and Cuba. The first-fruits of American diplomacy in the Dominican Republic were gathered in 1854, when, by dint of intrigues with Santana, the President, and, as it is asserted, heavy bribes to the petty representatives of the Dominican Republic, the United States’ Commissioner, General Cazneau, obtained the cession of Navaza, in the splendid peninsula bay of Samana, together with other privileges to which I need not more particularly allude, further than to say that they included a right to establish factories on land and to construct railways to the interior, and, in short, to work mines. This object of this treaty was, doubtless, to allure large numbers of American adventurers into the country, who, dazzled by the certainty of immediate profit and the prospect of far more substantial rewards, would form a powerful nucleus. Fortunately, this plot was not carried out, owing, in a great measure, to the exertions of the French and English Consuls, who, by showing to the Dominican Congress the danger of making such important concessions to the United States, prevented its ratification. The agent of General Santana, however, still refused to encourage American interests, and shortly afterwards the invasion of Dominican territory in 1855 by the Emperor Soulouque, whose fears were not unnaturally excited by the prospect of an American occupation of St. Domingo. This war turned out to be disastrous to Santana, however, which took place in 1856, when he was compelled to resign the presidential office amid the execrations of his countrymen. In his flight through the streets of San Domingo, *A bas le tyran! A bas les Americains!* rang from every lip. Baez, the former President, was compelled to leave the country; but he returned after a short absence, and by decree of the Senate succeeded in capturing the city of San Domingo, and restoring himself to power.

It is not difficult to discover what political advantages the possession of territorial rights in the Dominican Republic, together with the important bay of Samana, would have conferred upon the Americans; nor is it more difficult to see that, had it come to pass, they would have been able to prevent that union of the two sections of the island which alone can give a fair chance of success to the great experiment of negro self-government, and thereby prove the falseness of those theories of the natural and inherent inferiority of the African race, which form the sole justification for American slavery. This would have given them a pretext, of which they would not have been slow to avail themselves, to interfere by force in the domestic affairs of the whole island; and if no worse result happened, they would, at least, have placed the Haytian Government and Dominican President in a position of abject dependence upon the United States; while the bay of Samana might have formed a point from which to carry on filibustering operations against Cuba, and even our West India possessions; thus giving a new lease of life to slavery, if not a new field of action. No doubt all these considerations were well weighed by the Cabinet of Washington in instructions to their commissioners, and by Santana and his confederates bought with American gold, and to whose standard every enemy of his country seemed by destiny to rally. Happily, however, the temporary overthrow of Santana put an end to these projects, or at least suspended their execution; but their revival is not unlikely, now that Santana, by the defeat of Baez, has been restored to power. General Cazneau, it is true, has retired from the scene, but his party still continues in the ascendant at Washington, and Mr. Buchanan, like his predecessor, is its creature and instrument, rather than its director.

That a change of Presidents in the United States has produced no change of policy is but too evident from the proceeding of Mr. Buchanan in regard to the island of Navaza. This island, which forms a part of the Dominican territory, is small and uninhabited, situated between the south-western extremity of Hayti and the island of Jamaica, and is about thirty miles from Cape Tiburon. That the island belongs to Hayti is proved by incontrovertible historical evidence. A French authority, Moreau de St. Mery, is agreed on this point. Herrera says, in his ‘Descripcion de las Occidentales,’ chap. vi. p. 7, Madrid, 1730:—‘The harbors, &c., and the isles belonging to the coast of that island (Hispaniola) are found several small isles that are annexed to her, and that may still be very useful to her. The most considerable are the Saona besides Navaza and Mona, the first being ten leagues from Cape Tiburon towards Jamaica.’ Several months ago the Haytian Government learnt that this island, which contains extensive deposits of guano, had been invaded by a party of American adventurers, who had established themselves there for the purpose of digging and exporting the guano, without making any attempt to obtain the permission of the authorities at Port-au-Prince. The Haytian Government immediately forwarded a statement of the facts of the case to the Cabinet at Washington, soliciting their intervention as a medium of communication with the American adventurers occupying Navaza, because, up to the present time, no diplomatic relations had been established between the two countries. They also dispatched two Commissioners to Navaza to report upon the actual state of affairs in the island. The Commissioners, on their return, reported that they discovered on the northern side of the island three distinct establishments for the exportation of guano. This establishment consisted of about fifty persons, together with a wharf, boats, and houses, and two four-pounders. The whole party was under the management of Mr. John L. Frazier, who acted as agent for the officers of an association at Baltimore which had entered into a treaty with the leaders of the pirate party in the Caribbean Sea, for the exportation of guano from such of them as might be found to contain that valuable manure. It is scarcely necessary to say that no such treaty had ever been made with the Haytian Government, and that Mr. Frazier’s statement was an invention of his own.

As might be expected, the remonstrances of the Haytian Government have failed to produce any effect upon the American Cabinet. The protest sent through the American commercial agent was answered by Mr. Cass to the effect that the President had ordered the appearance, at Port au Prince, of two American men-of-war. The American commodore notified to the Haytian Government that he had not come to vindicate the sovereign rights of Hayti, but to raise the flag of the United States, and protect the intruders at Navaza, who, he alleged, had a clear right by virtue of an Act of Congress passed on the 18th of August, 1856, which authorized the President to protect American citizens who may discover guano on any island not within the lawful jurisdiction of any other Government. The Haytian commodore, not being empowered to discuss the question,—for in all likelihood, the very size of his vessel formed the principal reason why he was susceptible of too easy a proof—sailed off without making any reply. The Haytian Government have addressed a new protest to Washington, and there, for the present, the matter rests. It will be remembered that this is not the first case of a similar difficulty that arose between the United States and Peru, when the island of Lobos was invaded by a party of American citizens. Then the Cabinet at Washington was compelled, after a brief show of bluster, to respect the rights of Peru. Why, then, should America treat Peru with respect, and refuse to render equal justice towards Hayti? The reason would certainly appear to be, either that she cares no longer to recognize the rights of weak nations, or that, in the particular case of Hayti, she has ulterior designs to accomplish. It is certainly more than probable that this aggression, like most others of a similar character, has for its ultimate object, not the mere possession of guano, which, according to report, is of such an inferior quality, that it was impossible to find a market, and the vessel in which it was loaded was compelled to take it back again, thereby involving the speculators in a serious loss. But although America may not be able to turn the guano of Navaza to profitable account, she may, nevertheless, retain possession of the island for more important purposes. What could be easier than for her to erect on the island a small fort, and garrison it with soldiers? or to use it as a coaling station for American steamers? But whether the act of 1856 be made by America or not, the principle involved in the question remains precisely the same: If an American is allowed to retain possession of Navaza without protest, what is to prevent him from seizing on the numerous other islands which dot the Haytian coast, and, under similar pretexts, erect a fort upon such of them as he may please to occupy?

Clearly it is the duty of England to interpose her powerful influence, and to exert all the influence she can exert, to protect the rights of a feeble ally. St. Domingo may have fallen, and Hayti may have fallen, under the hand of Lord Malmesbury; but as this is necessarily a matter of truth and importance to humanity, we cannot but hope that the influence of Lord Brougham and of other distinguished friends of the negro in both Houses of Parliament, will be exercised to accomplish this most desirable object.

With your permission, in a future communication I shall call attention to another and a later phase which American designs against St. Domingo have assumed.

I am, Sir, your obedient servant,
F. W. CHESSON.

records.headline: A private letter of January 10 from Port-au-Prince, received via St. Thomas
records.summary_en: A private letter of January 10 from Port-au-Prince, received via St. Thomas and Havana, says Soulouque had been defeated by General Geffrard and the imperial troops were running back to the city. The writer says Soulouque himself was expected every moment, Geffrard was only a few leagues in his rear, and the contest was nearly ended, with the republic expected to be in full force in a day or two.

El autor dice que se esperaba a Soulouque en cualquier momento, que Geffrard estaba a pocas leguas detrás de él y que la contienda estaba casi terminada, con la república en pleno vigor en uno o dos días.

records.summary_en: The paper says its latest intelligence from Haiti leaves scarcely room for doubt that Soulouque has been compelled to abdicate and is probably on his way to a foreign land for safety. It gives a biographical sketch: about sixty-eight years of age, born a slave on Mr. Vallet's property and freed by him, entered the army under General Dessalines at the French evacuation, rose to colonel by the fall of President Boyer, and was admitted into the secrets of the political conspiracies that followed from 1843 to 1847.
records.summary_es: El periódico dice que su información más reciente de Haití apenas deja lugar a dudas de que Soulouque se ha visto obligado a abdicar y probablemente está en camino a una tierra extranjera en busca de seguridad. Ofrece un esbozo biográfico: unos sesenta y ocho años de edad, nacido esclavo en la propiedad del Sr. Vallet y liberado por él, entró en el ejército bajo el general Dessalines en la evacuación francesa, ascendió a coronel para la caída del presidente Boyer y fue admitido en los secretos de las conspiraciones políticas que siguieron de 1843 a 1847.

Our latest intelligence from Hayti leaves
scarcely room for a doubt that his Royal High
ness, Faustin Soulouque, the black Republican
Emperor of Hayti, who for the past seven

is at the present time about sixty-eight years of

records.summary_en: The account describes Geffrard's revolution in Haiti: after a church ceremony and speeches promising thorough reform, he established himself at St. Marc, towns across the north acknowledged him, and the two armies faced each other without an engagement. It says Soulouque's army gradually lost confidence in him, and he abdicated and fled, leaving the popular party in bloodless possession of the country.
records.summary_es: El relato describe la revolución de Geffrard en Haití: tras una ceremonia en la iglesia y discursos que prometían una reforma profunda, se estableció en Saint-Marc, las ciudades del norte lo reconocieron y los dos ejércitos se enfrentaron sin llegar a combatir. Dice que el ejército de Soulouque perdió gradualmente la confianza en él, y que abdicó y huyó, dejando al partido popular en posesión incruenta del país.

records.headline: A retrospective article on the overthrow of Emperor Soulouque recounts
records.summary_en: A retrospective article on the overthrow of Emperor Soulouque recounts his past conflicts with the Dominican Republic. The Herald notes that Soulouque never recognized Dominican independence, insisting the territory belonged to his empire, and eventually marched an army to what the paper terms the frontiers of Dominica. General Santana, referred to as the Liberator, met the invading troops with an inferior force and defeated Soulouque in several engagements. The article reports that the three-year armistice agreed upon after the campaign expired this month, and rumors suggested Soulouque was preparing a new offensive against the Dominicans just as the revolution erupted that drove him from power.
records.summary_es: Un artículo retrospectivo sobre el derrocamiento del emperador Soulouque pasa revista a sus antiguos conflictos con la República Dominicana. El Herald señala que Soulouque nunca reconoció la independencia dominicana, insistiendo en que el territorio pertenecía a su imperio, y llegó a marchar con un ejército hacia lo que el diario denomina las fronteras de Dominica. El general Santana, a quien se llama el Libertador, enfrentó a las tropas invasoras con una fuerza numéricamente inferior y derrotó a Soulouque en varios combates. El artículo añade que el armisticio de tres años pactado tras la campaña venció este mes, y circulaban rumores de que Soulouque preparaba una nueva ofensiva contra los dominicanos justo cuando estalló la revolución que lo expulsó del poder.

records.headline: An editorial in the Herald contends that a change of government
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Herald contends that a change of government in Haiti will not extinguish the animosity rooted in racial prejudice and memories of past persecution on the island of St. Domingo. The paper observes that genuine progress remains impossible so long as the Dominican Republic, which it refers to as Dominica occupying two-thirds of the island, remains hostile to the western third and poised for armed collision. While celebrating the island's natural wealth—including its salubrious climate, rich soil suited for sugar, coffee, tobacco, and cotton, and excellent harbors—the editorial laments that commerce has been ruined and finances thrown into confusion by despotic rule and internal strife.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Herald sostiene que un cambio de gobierno en Haití no extinguirá la profunda animosidad nacida de los prejuicios raciales y los recuerdos de persecuciones pasadas en la isla de Santo Domingo. El periódico advierte que el verdadero progreso resulta imposible mientras la República Dominicana, a la que llama Dominica al ocupar dos tercios de la isla, se mantenga enemistada con el tercio occidental y lista para un choque armado. Pese a elogiar las riquezas naturales de la isla —como su clima saludable, sus suelos productivos aptos para el azúcar, el café, el tabaco y el algodón, y sus magníficos puertos—, el editorial lamenta que el comercio se haya arruinado y las finanzas se encuentren en desorden a causa del despotismo y las luchas internas.

The population of Haiti is given as 650,000, while that of what the item calls the republic of Dominica is listed as 150,000, nine-tenths of whom are reported to be of African descent. The notice notes the founding of Santo Domingo in the 1490s and praises the island's fertile soil, while observing that agricultural production has decayed so substantially that sugar is imported from the United States.

records.headline: The island of Santo Domingo, whose 29,000 square miles are divided
records.summary_en: The island of Santo Domingo, whose 29,000 square miles are divided between the Empire of Haiti on one-third and the Dominican Republic on two-thirds, is described by the paper, citing the New York Herald. Haiti's population is reported at 650,000 and that of what the article calls the republic of Dominica at 150,000, nine-tenths being of African descent and the rest of Spanish and Indigenous ancestry. The capital, St. Domingo, was established by Bartholomew Columbus in 1496, and the Dominican army is estimated at 12,000 men compared to Soulouque's 20,000 troops. While praising the island's fertile soil and delightful climate, the account laments that corrupt rule has ruined coffee and tobacco exports and forced the country to import American sugar.
records.summary_es: Citando al New York Herald, el periódico describe la isla de Santo Domingo, cuyas 29,000 millas cuadradas se dividen entre el Imperio de Haití en un tercio y la República Dominicana en dos tercios. La población de Haití se cifra en 650,000 habitantes y la de lo que el artículo llama república de Dominica en 150,000, siendo nueve décimas partes de ascendencia africana y el resto de origen español e indígena. La capital, Santo Domingo, fue fundada por Bartolomé Colón en 1496, y el ejército dominicano se calcula en 12,000 hombres frente a los 20,000 soldados de Soulouque. Pese a elogiar el suelo fértil y el clima deleitable, el informe lamenta que el gobierno corrupto haya arruinado las exportaciones de café y tabaco y obligado al país a importar azúcar estadounidense.

records.headline: A dispatch reports that a Danish envoy supported by a war vessel
records.summary_en: A dispatch reports that a Danish envoy supported by a war vessel peremptorily demanded $150,000 from the Dominican government as indemnity for two Danish ships seized by President Baez during the recent revolution in Dominica. President Santana offered to submit the dispute to arbitration, but the Danish official refused and delivered a twenty-four-hour ultimatum backed by the threat of a naval blockade. The Dominicans resolved to resist and immediately began manning their coastal batteries against the single Danish warship in port. A local postscript adds that prior to the Danish ultimatum, French naval authorities in port had demanded concessions over all gold, silver, and copper mines in the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: Un despacho informa que un enviado danés respaldado por un buque de guerra exigió perentoriamente al gobierno dominicano 150,000 dólares como indemnización por dos embarcaciones danesas incautadas por el presidente Báez durante la reciente revolución en Dominica. El presidente Santana propuso someter la disputa a un arbitraje, pero el funcionario danés lo rechazó y dio un ultimátum de veinticuatro horas bajo amenaza de bloqueo naval. Los dominicanos decidieron resistir y comenzaron de inmediato a artillar sus baterías costeras frente al único buque danés surto en el puerto. Una nota local añade que, antes del ultimátum danés, las autoridades navales francesas en puerto habían exigido concesiones sobre todas las minas de oro, plata y cobre de la República Dominicana.
