records.summary_en: A dispatch in The Daily Dispatch reports that a Danish functionary peremptorily demanded $50,000 in indemnity for the seizure of two Danish vessels during the recent revolution in the Dominican Republic. President Santana offered to refer the dispute to arbitrators, but the Danish envoy refused and gave the Dominicans 24 hours to comply under threat of a port blockade. With only one Danish vessel in port, the Dominicans decided in favor of war and immediately began manning their batteries. Private advices received at Washington confirm the report and add that a French commander in port had previously demanded the concession of all gold, silver, and copper mines in the Dominican Republic, while a second dispatch from New York notes that the Herald's St. Domingo correspondent says Santana may send a commissioner to the United States to issue privateer commissions.

records.full_text: HOSTILITIES BETWEEN DENMARK AND DOMINICA.—New York, April 6.—Letters from St. Domingo of the 15th of March announce hostilities between Dominica and Denmark. A Danish Envoy, who recently arrived in a war vessel, peremptorily demanded $150,000 as indemnity for the seizure of two Danish vessels by President Baez during the recent revolution in Dominica. President Santana offered to refer the matter to arbitrators, but the Danish functionary declined, giving the Dominicans only twenty-four hours to comply with his demands, with the understanding that a refusal would be followed by a blockade of the port.

records.headline: The Nevada Journal reports that war has broken out between Denmark
records.summary_en: The Nevada Journal reports that war has broken out between Denmark and the Dominican Republic (referred to as "Dominica") after the Danish government sent a diplomatic agent with two war steamers to demand $150,000 in indemnity for the seizure of two Danish vessels by Dominican authorities. Upon the steamers' arrival at San Domingo, the Danes made a peremptory demand, and when President Santana offered to refer the dispute to arbitration, they refused and threatened to blockade the port. Santana chose war and immediately began manning the Dominican batteries, while the report adds that it is hinted he will issue commissions to privateers in the United States.
records.summary_es: The Nevada Journal informa que ha estallado la guerra entre Dinamarca y la República Dominicana (denominada «Dominica») después de que el gobierno danés enviara un agente diplomático con dos vapores de guerra para exigir una indemnización de $150,000 por la incautación de dos buques daneses por las autoridades dominicanas. A la llegada de los vapores a Santo Domingo, los daneses formularon una exigencia perentoria y, cuando el presidente Santana ofreció someter la disputa a arbitraje, se negaron y amenazaron con bloquear el puerto. Santana optó por la alternativa bélica y comenzó de inmediato a guarnecer las baterías dominicanas, mientras que el informe añade que se insinúa que emitirá patentes de corso en los Estados Unidos.

The paper also prints President Santana's decree granting a French and English company, for forty years, the right to explore and work mines and state forests in the republic.

El periódico también publica el decreto del presidente Santana que concede a una compañía francesa e inglesa, por cuarenta años, el derecho de explorar y explotar minas y bosques del Estado en la república.

records.headline: Port-au-Prince correspondence dated May 15, 1859, reports great political agitation in Haiti: the President proposed
records.summary_en: Port-au-Prince correspondence dated May 15, 1859, reports great political agitation in Haiti: the President proposed that the Chambers expel Soulouque and his family, and General Delva, for life, the Chambers refuse, and deputations are coming from all quarters to have the proposition retaken. The correspondent predicts that on the 17th the President will drive out the Senators and Representatives and will be sustained by every honest citizen, and mentions the sale of the brig African's arms to the government.

El corresponsal predice que el día 17 el presidente expulsará a senadores y diputados y será apoyado por todo ciudadano honesto, y menciona la venta de las armas del bergantín African al gobierno.

records.headline: Writing from St. Domingo on May 17, 1859, the New York Herald's correspondent
records.summary_en: Writing from St. Domingo on May 17, 1859, the New York Herald's correspondent reports under the heading "News from Dominica" that the Dominican government's refusal to redeem its obligations to resident foreigners has compelled the foreign consuls to protest, strike their flags, and request their passports. According to the correspondent, the United States consul is the only one who has not struck his flag, supposedly because his government does not sustain him in protecting the interests of U.S. citizens. Taking issue with other accounts of the Danish question, the correspondent asserts that the recent boarding and robbery of Danish vessels on the open sea—carried out with the republic's Secretary of War as commander-in-chief of the operation—was an outrageous and piratical insult to the Danish flag.
records.summary_es: Escribiendo desde Santo Domingo el 17 de mayo de 1859, el corresponsal del New York Herald informa bajo el título «Noticias de Dominica» que la negativa del gobierno dominicano a redimir sus obligaciones con los extranjeros residentes ha obligado a los cónsules extranjeros a protestar, arriar sus banderas y solicitar sus pasaportes. Según el corresponsal, el cónsul de los Estados Unidos es el único que no ha arriado su bandera, supuestamente porque su gobierno no lo respalda en la protección de los intereses de los ciudadanos estadounidenses. Discrepando de otras versiones sobre la cuestión danesa, el corresponsal sostiene que el reciente abordaje y robo de buques daneses en alta mar —llevado a cabo con el Secretario de Guerra de la república como comandante en jefe de la operación— fue un insulto pirático e indignante a la bandera danesa.

records.headline: The New York Herald prints diplomatic correspondence addressed
records.summary_en: The New York Herald prints diplomatic correspondence addressed to the President of the Dominican Republic by European monarchs in March 1859. The first item is the conclusion of a letter from Emperor Napoleon, counter-signed by A. Walewski at the Palace of the Tuileries in March 1859, expressing lively interest in the country and feelings of esteem and goodwill. It is followed by a letter from Queen Victoria of Great Britain, counter-signed by Malmesbury at Buckingham Palace in March 1859, congratulating the Dominican president on being elevated to the presidency for the third time and expressing satisfaction with his intention to maintain and draw nearer the friendly relations between Great Britain and the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: El New York Herald publica correspondencia diplomática dirigida al presidente de la República Dominicana por monarcas europeos en marzo de 1859. El primer documento es la conclusión de una carta del emperador Napoleón, refrendada por A. Walewski en el Palacio de las Tullerías en marzo de 1859, en la que expresa un vivo interés por el país y sentimientos de estima y buena voluntad. Le sigue una carta de la reina Victoria de Gran Bretaña, refrendada por Malmesbury en el Palacio de Buckingham en marzo de 1859, en la que felicita al presidente dominicano por haber sido elevado por tercera vez a la presidencia y expresa satisfacción por su intención de mantener y estrechar las relaciones amistosas entre Gran Bretaña y la República Dominicana.

records.headline: The Richmond Enquirer reports that the government of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: The Richmond Enquirer reports that the government of the Dominican Republic has entered into a serious quarrel with the consular representatives of the European governments accredited to the republic. According to the paper, the current Dominican administration refuses to receive for dues the paper money issued under a previous administration, which is held principally by foreign merchants. Because of the dispute, the representatives of England, Spain, Sardinia, and Holland have departed for Europe, leaving the United States flag as the only one afloat in the city of St. Domingo at last accounts, where little doubt was entertained that U.S. claims on the government would be speedily adjusted.
records.summary_es: El Richmond Enquirer informa que el gobierno de la República Dominicana ha entrado en una seria disputa con los representantes consulares de los gobiernos europeos acreditados ante la república. Según el periódico, la actual administración dominicana se niega a recibir para el pago de derechos el papel moneda emitido bajo una administración anterior, el cual se encuentra principalmente en manos de comerciantes extranjeros. Debido al conflicto, los representantes de Inglaterra, España, Cerdeña y Holanda han partido hacia Europa, dejando la bandera de los Estados Unidos como la única que ondeaba en la ciudad de Santo Domingo según los últimos informes, donde cabía poca duda de que las reclamaciones estadounidenses ante el gobierno se ajustarían prontamente.

El informe señala además que la emisión de papel moneda irredimible por Báez durante su administración había provocado considerables problemas con los representantes de gobiernos extranjeros residentes en Santo Domingo.

It also quotes an emigrant of 1824 who said great numbers were swindled by agents sent out by Boyer to induce emigration, including one who hired many on his estate on shares and then turned them off before the crop was ripe to evade paying their wages.

records.headline: An article in the Memphis Daily Appeal reports that foreign consuls
records.summary_en: An article in the Memphis Daily Appeal reports that foreign consuls brought produce down the coast under the consular flag and sold it to the starving inhabitants of St. Domingo at exorbitant prices, accumulating millions in spurious paper money issued by Báez. After President Santana entered the city and Báez fled, the consuls demanded that Santana redeem this currency at fifteen times what they had paid for it, and when Santana refused—offering instead to appoint commissioners to ascertain and pay what had actually been allowed—the consuls rejected the offer out of anger over his opposition to their scheme of annexing the Dominican Republic to Haiti, struck their flags, and left the country together. The writer adds that British Consul Hood is reportedly returning to present the alternative of irretrievable financial ruin or immediate acceptance of the Haitian constitution, which encourages colored immigration while excluding whites, and asks whether the twenty-five million white inhabitants of the United States and their government will remain passive and see Samaná lost.

records.full_text:
INTERESTING FROM ST. DOMINGO.

Our St. Domingo Correspondence.
ST. DOMINGO, Dec. 13, 1859.
A French and English Squadron Before the City—Peremptory Demands—The Depreciated Paper Currency—Requisition for Its Redemption at Extravagant Rates—History of Its Issue—Venality of European Consuls—Their Efforts to Crush the Liberal Government—Probable Ultimate Designs of the Present Demonstration, &c.

We have now four European ships of war on parade before this city. They have come to St. Domingo on a mission so strange and scandalous that it almost staggers belief. There are two French vessels, one English and one Spanish steamer engaged in bullying this government into sanctioning a stupendous swindling operation, but the moneyed profits of the speculation will remain to the exclusive benefit of two or three British officials.

To begin at the beginning, and make a clear statement, we must go back to 1857-8, when—thanks to European intervention—Baez became the despotic ruler of the Dominican republic. Baez has the warm support of a large portion of the negroes, who wish to unite with Hayti on the basis of holding the white race in absolute subjection to the black; but when left to themselves, this party is much the weaker, and can only keep the control while European vessels of war are on hand to sustain them in the possession of the capital and other seaports.

Baez, with his staff of ministers and officers, being thus backed, were disposed to shear as large a fleece as the closest cutting could collect from the backs of the poor Dominicans while he had them in hand. They had many ways of fleecing the people, but the one in which they operated the most extensively was in the issue of paper money. During the whole of his administration, Baez kept the government press hotly at work manufacturing paper dollars, until the whole country was swamped with it. Millions of it was employed by Baez and his agents in buying up property of every kind on speculation? Among other friends and partners in these operations, some members of the British consular corps became deeply interested in the Baez money, or as the people here call it, “Mangolino papeletes.”

There are limits to everything, and the issue of forty or fifty millions of “papeletes” banished specie circulation to such a degree that not even a copper coin was visible in trade—necessarily the Baez paper went down to nothing. The poor people who had received it for their rice, sugar and tobacco; for their corn, cattle, wax, honey, yams, cocoanuts, &c., were dismayed to see their little all melting away into bits of waste paper. They had sold the fruits of their labor for this “government currency,” because it was the only circulating medium of the country, and there was no help.

While Baez yet held the supreme power in St. Domingo, his “Mangolino papeletes” sunk down to the rate of two thousand to the dollar under his own eyes; yet he went on printing it off by millions, and sent it into the interior to buy up produce for shipment to Europe on his own account.

At last the whole country rose against the Baez government and his iniquitous nest of money-makers. The whole concern, except the foreign consuls, were forced to leave the Dominican territory, but not without the “spoils,” for the European consuls used their official position to cover their own and their partners’ ill-gotten wealth. The French Consul, who governs the other consuls here just as his master—Napoleon—governs their masters at home, abetted and sustained Baez and all his corruptions in their most offensive forms, although no one accuses him of any personal interest in the papelete speculation.

This may be perhaps explained by considering this support the reward of Baez’s disposition to carry out the Anglo-French plan of annexing this republic to Hayti.

When General Santana succeeded to the Presidency this proposition of accepting the negro rule of Hayti, was pressed upon the Dominican Cabinet with such disrespectful urgency that the Executive sent Mr. Raybaud his passports. This gentleman was the late Charge d’Affairs of France at the court of Soulouque, but is now the special annexation agent of France, England and Hayti. While Santana was battling with the European scheme of Haytien supremacy, the Consular speculators in Baez’s paper were pressing him to recognise the “Mangolino papeletes” as government currency. This Santana had no right to do, for, by an act of Congress, provision had already been made to call in and cancel this paper at a fixed price. This was at the highest rate at which it was circulating before Baez went out of power—that is, at 2,000 papeletes to the dollar. But this liberal law did not satisfy the demands of the European Consuls, and they officially informed the government that they would be “treated as null and void.” None of them pretend that a rag of the millions of it they have on hand cost either of them more than the government offers to allow and it is known that they have bought nine-tenths of it at 3,500 and 4,000 “papeletes” to the dollar. Yet, in the face of these admitted facts, they have brought a fleet to “insist” upon this poor and friendless government allowing them twenty times as much as they paid for their 18,000,000 mangolino papeletes.

After an official correspondence full of dictatorial arrogance on the part of the French, English, and Spanish Consuls, these gentlemen informed the Dominican government that they would close their consulates and leave the country in a body if their demands were not acceded to at once. They were answered that the Dominican executive had not the right or power to annul an act of Congress, and they were reminded that the act was in itself most just and liberal, as it provided for the acceptance of the Mangolino papaletes at a much better rate than its makers had left it in circulation; the government therefore could do no more in the premises.

On this the Consuls of France, Spain and England struck their flags with a great deal of parade, and left the country. The Dominican government despatched agents to Paris, London and Madrid, with full statements of the case, but all those courts have united in the plan of suppressing—that is, of crushing out the Dominican republic—and refused to entertain the question.

This republic has not an ally on this continent, and the European Powers take advantage of its friendless, unsupported position to oppress it outrageously. Revenons a nos moutons. The French, English, and Spanish squadron now pointing its guns on our city, has brought back our consular masters with a list of new demands, amounting in fact to an unconditional surrender of the independence of the Dominican republic.

Some of these demands are secret, but there is scarcely room for a doubt that it is a repetition of the old alternative—negro rule or ruin. Be certain that American commerce, American enterprise and American citizens must be forbidden the Dominican territory, or the Dominican republic must be “suppressed,” and the white race driven out if it does not yield submission to Hayti.

This is the sum and substance of the old quadruple alliance of France, England, Spain and Hayti, and it will not be changed until this republic is recognized by the United States, or the negroes of Hayti are put in full possession of the whole island.

It is the cue of the consuls to let the Dominicans understand that the Anglo-French alliance no longer consider it an independent nationality. Spain and Hayti are but passive tails to this kite, although they are counted in as equal Powers in the quadruple alliance. Since Faustin has dropped out of the square, his imperial brother, Napoleon, and his august sisters, Victoria and Isabella, may only stand for a triangle, though it is very far from a right angled triangle. The square of the French base is a good deal more than equal to the square of the British and Spanish sides which Napoleon subtends, and, what is more than Euclid knew how to reduce to geometry, extends at his pleasure without increasing their power. Before they landed the consuls sent a note to the Dominican Executive ordering that a salute of twenty-one guns should be given within twenty-four hours to each of their flags. The Dominican Cabinet felt and said that such an order would only be issued to a dependent, or in chastisement of some wrong inflicted, and outside of the “Mangolino Papelete question” no offence had been alleged. The consuls only replied by commanding the salutes to be given within six hours.

The Dominican government complied, though under protest that it yielded to force, for they could not expose the city to the horrors of a bombardment for a form. After this preliminary the French consul carried his British colleague to the palace, that he might repeat after him, and endorse in the name of the English government, the recent orders of the Emperor Napoleon. What these are no one knows positively, but enough has leaked out to justify the belief that they relate to Hayti, and contain a death blow to this republic.

After this was attended to, the British consul had his turn, and was let loose on his Papelete business. John Bull is not to be balked of his pennies, and the allied squadron is here to see everything settled to their mind.

John Bull’s fight for the opium smugglers was a noble and honest war by the side of this bullying a weak republic into bankruptcy in support of a fraudulent paper issue; and the Anglo-French exploits in doctoring “sick Turkeys” to death and robbing bits of “broken China,” become in comparison fair business transactions.

POSTSCRIPT.
DECEMBER 14.
The government has surrendered to the consuls at discretion. It agrees to redeem all the Mangolino papelites at 500 to the Spanish dollar, and pledges the custom house and all other resources for principal and interest. The eighteen or twenty millions of it stored at the British consulate was bought at 2,500, 3,000 and 4,000 to the dollar. To buy 18,000,000 papelites at an average of 3,500 to the dollar and sell them off at 500 is a very good spec for a couple of these consular worthies; but that is the way John Bull uses his navy to take care of his children.

records.headline: Writing on April 9, 1860, from the chief commercial town of the Dominican Republic (dated
records.summary_en: Writing on April 9, 1860, from the chief commercial town of the Dominican Republic (dated from "Dominica"), a correspondent of the New-York Daily Tribune remarks that three weeks of residence have revealed few features in the mode of life of the natives worthy of a letter for publication. The writer compares life in the town to an abortive attempt to realize the world of Tennyson's poem "The Lotos-Eaters," substituting the plantain for the lotus because it yields the maximum of food with the minimum of exertion, and observing that it seems always late afternoon from the inhabitants' languid movements. Although the correspondent describes the residents as irascible and light-hearted rather than mild-eyed or melancholy, the writer states that the climate, scenery, and people have ceased striving for a better state of things, before explaining that the purpose of writing is to send a sketch of a visit to the nearby farm of a fugitive slave from Florida.

El autor compara la vida en la localidad con un intento fallido de realizar el mundo del poema «Los comedores de loto» de Tennyson, sustituyendo el loto por el plátano porque produce el máximo de alimento con el mínimo de esfuerzo, y observando que allí siempre parece ser tarde por los movimientos lánguidos de los habitantes. Aunque el corresponsal describe a los residentes como irascibles y alegres en lugar de melancólicos, afirma que el clima, el paisaje y la gente han dejado de esforzarse por mejorar su situación, antes de explicar que el propósito de su carta es enviar un bosquejo de su visita a la pequeña finca cercana de un esclavo fugitivo de la Florida.

records.headline: There is a coalition of the French, Spanish and English diplomatists
records.summary_en: The *Holmes County Republican* reported on May 31, 1860, that a coalition of French, Spanish, and English diplomats was conspiring to force the Dominican Republic to unite with Haiti. According to the article, England sought to prevent white emigration to stop American progress, Spain desired to keep Americans away from Cuba, and France aimed to extend its 100-million-franc mortgage over the entire island to eventually colonize it using coolie labor.

records.full_text:
News from St. Domingo.
REVIVAL OF COMMERCE—IMPORTANT DECREE—EDUCATION—IMMIGRATION—CURRENCY.

Files of St. Domingo papers have been received in Havana to May 17. We translate the following from the Diario de la Marina of the 14th inst.:—

Judging from the tone of the press the country is visibly recovering the low condition it has been in, consequent upon the frequent upheavings it has suffered from, and the government, as well as private individuals, were busy with administrative and other reforms relative to commerce and agriculture. Amongst the measures adopted by the former is the annexed decree, which we publish entire for the benefit of our commercial readers:—

The Senate, at the instance of the Executive power, considering that the advancement of commerce is one of the most important causes of national wealth, and being desirous of attracting to to the ports of the republic, by immunities and privileges of every kind, the flags of all commercial and friendly nations, to increase our revenue and develope the elements of prosperity which our privileged soil possesses, has resolved, in the name of the nation, to issue the following

DECREE.

Article 1. From and after the day of the publication of this decree, the vessels of those friendly nations with which the republic has not had treaties will be placed on a similar footing with respect to the payment of import, export, tonnage, or lighthouse dues, and everything else relating to the commerce of the most favored nations.

Art. 2. The vessels of those nations which, after the lapse of a year from the publication of this decree, shall not have granted to the vessels of this republic equal advantages shall be deprived of the benefits of this measure.

Art. 3. This decree repeals every other act that may be contrary to it, and shall be transmitted to the executive power for constitutional purposes.

Given at the National Palace of the Senate, on the 8th day of May of the year 1860, and the 17th of the Country.

On the following day it was signed by Vice President Alfan, in the absence of President Santanna, and by the Minister of Commerce and Finance.

We see, besides, that they are not unmindful of other useful branches. The subject of public instruction is prominently spoken of, thanks to the spirit of progress which animates the government. In addition to the opening of various free schools, we read in the Gazette that the High Directing Junta of Education was occupied with praiseworthy interest in drawing up the project of a law on the restoration of the old University, to be submitted to the Senate, and it was hoped that that body would sanction it before the close of the present session.

records.summary_en: The Dominican Senate requested the President to demand explanations and immediate reparation from Venezuela regarding the shooting of several Dominicans, warning that recourse would otherwise be taken. The President replied that no expostulations or reprisals were warranted because the individuals had abandoned their nationality and entered the enemy's ranks, noting further that letters from Venezuela asserted those men had actually been killed in battle rather than executed. Additionally, the press advocated for establishing a bank to suppress paper money, and the value of the gold ounce was fixed at 4,000 national dollars.
records.summary_es: El Senado dominicano solicitó al presidente que exigiera explicaciones y reparación inmediata a Venezuela con respecto al fusilamiento de varios dominicanos, advirtiendo que de lo contrario se recurriría a otras medidas. El presidente respondió que no se justificaban protestas ni represalias dado que tales individuos habían renunciado a su nacionalidad y se habían sumado a las filas enemigas, señalando además que cartas procedentes de Venezuela aseguraban que esos hombres en realidad habían muerto en combate y no fusilados. Por otra parte, la prensa abogó por la fundación de un banco para retirar el papel moneda, y el valor de la onza de oro se fijó en 4.000 pesos nacionales.

country for political opinions; and by another from the Senate, the port of Romana will be opened to foreign commerce from the 1st of June, 1861. The same body had approved, unanimously, the second reading of the decree which proposes opening the ports of Montecristo for the exportation of cattle.

The question of immigration from the Canaries, of those who were forced to fly from Venezuela on account of the revolution in that republic, was occupying the attention not only of the press but of the government of St. Domingo. Vessels had been provided for bringing them over, and those who had arrived from Laguayra, to the number of seventy-six, had been provided with excellent lands. This humane conduct of the Dominican government had produced an unfavorable feeling in Venezuela, where the periodicals cry down Dominican nationality, as we gather from an energetic article on this subject, published in the Dominican Semi-Monthly Review.

The shooting of several Dominicans in Venezuela was also engaging the attention of the government. The Senate addressed a letter to the President, in which the Executive was requested, in view of the compromise of national honor, to demand explanations from the goverment of Venezuela, and if immediate reparation for those outrages "to the nation, the rights of persons, and the very laws of humanity," was not made, recourse would be had, as a last resource, to the right of reprisal, and the Venezuelans residing in St. Domingo would be treated in like manner. His Excellency replied, reminding the Senate that they were not treating of a general measure of the Venezuelan government against every Dominican, but of a chastisment inflicted on individuals who had abandoned their nationality and had entered the enemy's ranks, on which account there could be neither expostulations nor reprisals. This reply had called forth a vote of thanks from the resident Venezuelans; and, moreover, it appears that letters received from Venezuela assert that the Dominicans in question were not executed, but had been killed in battle, with the exception of one who was assassinated by a party of marauders.

Finally, the press warmly advocates the establishment of a bank as the best means for suppressing the paper money in circulation, which occasions serious inconvenience to the government and citizens. To regulate the operations of the public administration, the value of the gold ounce is fixed at 4,000 national dollars each.

records.headline: A travel narrative describes approaching Santo Domingo by sea and entering Puerto Plata, whose harbor the writer
records.summary_en: A travel narrative describes approaching Santo Domingo by sea and entering Puerto Plata, whose harbor the writer calls a poor one surrounded by sublime scenery. It recounts the coming of the pilot and the custom-house officers, some white and some colored, along with Mr. Collins, an American gentleman to whom the writer was addressed.
records.summary_es: Un relato de viaje describe la aproximación a Santo Domingo por mar y la entrada a Puerto Plata, cuyo puerto el escritor califica de malo rodeado de un paisaje sublime. Relata la llegada del piloto y de los oficiales de aduana, algunos blancos y otros de color, junto con el Sr. Collins, un caballero estadounidense a quien el escritor venía recomendado.

records.headline: The Daily Exchange cites a letter from Porto Plata dated November 10
records.summary_en: The Daily Exchange cites a letter from Porto Plata dated November 10 reporting that the Dominican Republic (referred to as "the little Republic there known as Dominica") has been sold to Spain for half a million dollars. According to the letter, the bargain was made in March but kept secret for three months to smooth matters with the population and to see whether the people of the United States would object to this violation of the Monroe Doctrine. The report adds that the Dominican commissioner who negotiated the sale took his family to Spain and sold his property on the island as soon as the business was settled, and that Minister of Foreign Relations Don Miguel Lavastida and Minister of War and Marine Don Felipe de Castro have done the same and stand ready to flee at a moment's notice.
records.summary_es: The Daily Exchange cita una carta de Puerto Plata fechada el 10 de noviembre que informa que la República Dominicana (denominada «la pequeña República allí conocida como Dominica») ha sido vendida a España por medio millón de dólares. Según la carta, el trato se cerró en el mes de marzo pero se mantuvo en secreto durante tres meses para suavizar la situación con el pueblo y ver si el pueblo de los Estados Unidos objetaría esta violación de la doctrina Monroe. El informe añade que el comisionado dominicano que negoció la venta llevó a su familia a España y vendió sus propiedades en la isla tan pronto como se concretó el negocio, y que el ministro de Relaciones Exteriores, don Miguel Lavastida, y el de Guerra y Marina, don Felipe de Castro, han hecho lo mismo y están listos para huir en cualquier momento.

records.headline: Under the heading "From Hayti," The Daily Exchange reports that various rumors
records.summary_en: Under the heading "From Hayti," The Daily Exchange reports that various rumors are circulating concerning relations between Haiti and the Dominican Republic. According to the item, progress under the Geffrard administration has reportedly led many Dominicans to desire annexation, while other accounts state that the Spanish flag is flying at several important points in the eastern part of the island. The report also notes that Geffrard was preparing to set out on a journey to the interior early in February.

El informe añade que Geffrard estaba por emprender un viaje hacia el interior a principios de febrero.

records.headline: Following a passenger list that includes Mariano Alvarez, Spanish Consul-General
records.summary_en: Following a passenger list that includes Mariano Alvarez, Spanish Consul-General at San Domingo and bearer of dispatches for his government, the New-York Daily Tribune publishes correspondence from Havana dated March 25, 1861, under a headline announcing that Spain is taking possession of the Dominican Republic and preparing to acquire the whole island. The correspondent reports that the Spanish home government has ordered the reinforcement of its Antilles fleet with the ship-of-the-line Rey Don Francisco de Asis, the screw-propeller frigate Princesa de Asturias, the sloops Cortes, Colon, and Mazaredo, and the gunboat Cruz, while official circles in Havana report that five or six thousand troops are to be added to the regular force. According to the correspondent, the ministerial explanation that these reinforcements are made necessary by the recent political change in the U.S. administration is merely a cover for Spain's real designs.
records.summary_es: Tras una lista de pasajeros que incluye a Mariano Álvarez, cónsul general de España en Santo Domingo y portador de despachos para su gobierno, el New-York Daily Tribune publica una correspondencia desde La Habana fechada el 25 de marzo de 1861, bajo un titular que anuncia que España está tomando posesión de la República Dominicana y preparándose para adquirir toda la isla. El corresponsal informa que el gobierno español ha ordenado reforzar su flota de las Antillas con el navío de línea Rey Don Francisco de Asís, la fragata de hélice Princesa de Asturias, las corbetas Cortés, Colón y Mazarredo, y la cañonera Cruz, mientras que en los círculos oficiales de La Habana se informa que se sumarán cinco o seis mil soldados a la fuerza regular. Según el corresponsal, la explicación ministerial de que estos refuerzos son necesarios debido al reciente cambio político en la administración de los Estados Unidos es solo un pretexto para encubrir los verdaderos designios de España.

records.summary_en: Following years of division and subsequent invasion and occupation under Boyer, the Dominican population rose in insurrection against Haytian ascendancy and chose Pedro Santana as president. After Santana's term expired in 1849, Jimenes was elected Chief Magistrate while Santana was banished due to suspicions of intriguing with Madrid; however, Jimenes soon conspired with Hayti's Emperor Soulouque to unite the island, prompting the Dominicans to recall Santana from exile and invest him with dictatorial power.

records.headline: The Daily National Intelligencer describes the geography of the island of Haiti
records.summary_en: The Daily National Intelligencer describes the geography of the island of Haiti, noting that the western third forms the Republic of Haiti with its capital at Port-au-Prince, while the more mountainous eastern division constitutes the Dominican Republic (also referred to as the "Republic of Dominica" and "San Domingo"), with San Domingo as its capital. Pointing out that the island is separated from Cuba by the twenty-five-mile Windward Passage and from Puerto Rico by the twenty-five-mile Mona Passage, the paper observes that any power holding all three islands would command the ocean gateways to the Gulf of Mexico, the Caribbean Sea, and Central America. The editors explain that they detail this geography because intelligence from Havana states that Spain has seized the Dominican Republic and is about to re-annex it to the Spanish Crown, a report they consider not at all improbable.
records.summary_es: El Daily National Intelligencer describe la geografía de la isla de Haití, señalando que el tercio occidental forma la República de Haití con su capital en Puerto Príncipe, mientras que la división oriental, mucho más montañosa, constituye la República Dominicana (también denominada «República de Dominica» y «Santo Domingo»), con Santo Domingo como capital. Al destacar que la isla está separada de Cuba por el Paso de los Vientos, de veinticinco millas, y de Puerto Rico por el Canal de la Mona, también de veinticinco millas, el periódico observa que cualquier potencia que posea las tres islas dominaría las vías marítimas de acceso al Golfo de México, el Mar Caribe y Centroamérica. Los editores explican que detallan esta situación geográfica porque informes procedentes de La Habana indican que España se ha apoderado de la República Dominicana y está a punto de reanexarla a la Corona española, noticia que consideran nada improbable.

records.passage: FROM HAYTI — APPEAL TO THE PEOPLE. By the arrival of the brig Echo at New York we are placed in possession of Hayti files to March 9th. The Dominicans have issued the following proclamation against the Spanish invasion. APPEAL TO THE NATION. Dominicans! The country is in danger, and there is but one way to save it — by revolution. — Santana, since his last elevation to power, has sold the Republic. The price of the Yankees did not suit him. To-day he has adjudged it to Spain, and is preparing to crush the Dominican people under the colonial yoke for the vile price of a few puerile dignities, and of the gold which will be distributed to him and five or six principal accomplices. To-morrow the Tartars will enjoy in quiet the riches gained by this criminal bargain, and will welcome us with an ironical smile on hearing the clank of our chains. To-morrow shame will settle on our hearthstones, and the stigma of ignominy will soil our brows. To-morrow, our wives will fly from our arms, our mothers will refuse their caresses, and our children their smiles — a degenerate people merit them not. To-morrow we shall be able to leave to our families neither country, glory, honor, prosperity, nor even the repose of the domestic hearth. To-morrow — to express it once for all — we shall have changed the noble aegis of the Cross for the livery of slavery. What, then, shall be the way of restoration? "Revolution. A revolution, holy, noble, just, grand, because it has for its object the preservation of a nationality created

records.summary_en: According to *The National Republican* on April 5, 1861, Spain sent a representative to the Dominican Republic, while Santana's policies fueled opposition by provoking claims that he was selling the country to whites. Santana sought foreign aid to secure his government's perpetuity and repay a loan, which he used to counter the ongoing intrigues of the opposition and the exiled Baez. Additionally, the newspaper noted Mr. Redpath's view that suggestions of a French reconquest of Hayti are absurd and could harm efforts to colonize Hayti with colored Americans, noting that France has recognized Hayti's independence and draws revenue from it.
records.summary_es: Según *The National Republican* del 5 de abril de 1861, España envió un representante a la República Dominicana, mientras que las políticas de Santana alimentaban a la oposición al suscitar acusaciones de que estaba vendiendo el país a los blancos. Santana buscó ayuda extranjera para asegurar la permanencia de su gobierno y pagar un préstamo, el cual empleó para contrarrestar las continuas intrigas de la oposición y del desterrado Báez. Además, el periódico consignó la opinión del Sr. Redpath de que las insinuaciones de una reconquista francesa de Haití eran absurdas y podían perjudicar las gestiones para colonizar Haití con afroestadounidenses, destacando que Francia había reconocido la independencia haitiana y obtenía rentas de ella.

records.headline: The New-York Dispatch contrasts the two nationalities of the island
records.summary_en: The New-York Dispatch contrasts the two nationalities of the island, identifying the eastern part as the Dominican Republic—also called St. Domingo or the Spanish part—and the western part as the Republic of Haiti. According to the article, the Dominican Republic has a population of 120,000, chiefly Spanish-speaking mulattoes who were formerly subjects of Spain, and is ruled by President Santana, whom it describes as a nearly white leader whose sympathies have always favored reuniting his country with Spain. By contrast, Haiti has a French-speaking population estimated at 600,000 to 1,200,000 and is ruled by President Geffrard, whose aim is to establish an independent nationality composed exclusively of men of African descent. The paper concludes that there is no probability either that the Dominicans will submit to Spanish domination or that the Haitians will allow French whites to become their masters.
records.summary_es: El New-York Dispatch contrasta las dos nacionalidades que ocupan la isla, identificando la parte oriental como la República Dominicana —también llamada Santo Domingo o la parte española— y la parte occidental como la República de Haití. Según el artículo, la República Dominicana tiene una población de 120,000 habitantes, principalmente mulatos hispanohablantes que fueron súbditos de España, y está gobernada por el presidente Santana, a quien describe como un gobernante casi blanco cuyas simpatías siempre han favorecido la reunión de su país con España. En contraste, Haití tiene una población francófona estimada entre 600,000 y 1,200,000 habitantes y está gobernada por el presidente Geffrard, cuyo objetivo es establecer una nacionalidad independiente compuesta exclusivamente por hombres de ascendencia africana. El periódico concluye que no hay probabilidad alguna de que los dominicanos se sometan a la dominación española ni de que los haitianos permitan que los blancos franceses se conviertan en sus amos.

records.headline: The Springfield Weekly Republican remarks on a sensational report of the week
records.summary_en: The Springfield Weekly Republican remarks on a sensational report of the week, which claims a Spanish colony has instigated a revolution in St. Domingo and that a Spanish fleet has sailed from Havana to subjugate and re-annex the whole island to Spain with France's consent. The paper argues that any attempt to subjugate the Haitian Republic is improbable and would be opposed by both France and England, suggesting instead that the affair likely stems from an internal outbreak against Dominican President Santana, who is heavily indebted to Spain, has previously tried to sell out to the Spanish government, and probably obtained aid from Spanish forces in Cuba against domestic resistance. The editorial concludes that such a situation hardly warrants anxiety over an infraction of the Monroe Doctrine, adding that rumors of a united British and French fleet sailing for American waters under sealed orders likely refer only to a routine fleet of observation.
records.summary_es: El Springfield Weekly Republican señala que una noticia sensacionalista de la semana afirma que una colonia española ha promovido una revolución en Santo Domingo y que una flota española ha zarpado de La Habana para subyugar y reanexar toda la isla a España con el consentimiento de Francia. El periódico sostiene que cualquier intento de subyugar a la República de Haití es improbable y contaría con la oposición de Francia e Inglaterra, sugiriendo en cambio que el asunto probablemente se debe a un levantamiento interno contra el presidente dominicano Santana, quien está fuertemente endeudado con España, ha intentado anteriormente vender el país al gobierno español y probablemente obtuvo ayuda de las fuerzas españolas en Cuba frente a la resistencia interna. El editorial concluye que tal situación difícilmente justifica inquietud por una infracción de la doctrina Monroe, y añade que los rumores sobre una flota conjunta británica y francesa rumbo a aguas americanas bajo órdenes selladas probablemente se refieren solo a una habitual flota de observación.

records.summary_en: According to the *Chicago Daily Tribune* on April 6, 1861, Santana failed in his desperate effort to induce white emigration from the United States despite the support of U.S. consuls. The newspaper reported that Santana previously borrowed a million dollars from Spain, and failing to repay it, offered a mortgage on the Custom House, resulting in a small band of Spaniards arriving at St. Domingo to act as collectors and mechanics. This policy fueled the opposition by prompting claims that he was "selling the country to the whites," leading to revolutionary circulars and proclamations as early as last December.

El periódico informó que Santana había tomado prestado previamente un millón de dólares de España y, al no poder devolverlo, ofreció una hipoteca sobre las aduanas, lo que resultó en la llegada a Santo Domingo de una pequeña partida de españoles para desempeñarse como recaudadores y artesanos. Esta política alimentó a la oposición al dar pie a acusaciones de que estaba «vendiendo el país a los blancos», provocando circulares y proclamas revolucionarias ya desde el pasado diciembre.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that the Dominican Republic, covering an area of 1,000 square miles with a population of 136,000, declared its complete independence from the French portion, though Spain had never formally admitted its independence after forty years out of its possession. According to Mr. James Redpath, officially connected with the Republic of Hayti, the Dominican Republic has been divided between two alternating parties represented by Santana and Baez, whose policies indicate re-union and independence. Redpath explained that after Santana failed to repay a million-dollar loan borrowed from Spain and offered a mortgage on the custom-houses, a small band of eighty Spaniards arrived in St. Domingo last summer to work as custom collectors and mechanics, which fueled the opposition's revolutionary claims that Santana was selling the country.
records.summary_es: El periódico informó que la República Dominicana, con una superficie de 1.000 millas cuadradas y una población de 136.000 habitantes, declaró su completa independencia de la porción francesa, aunque España nunca había reconocido formalmente su independencia tras cuarenta años fuera de su dominio. Según el Sr. James Redpath, vinculado oficialmente a la República de Haití, la República Dominicana ha estado dividida entre dos facciones alternantes representadas por Santana y Báez, cuyas directrices apuntaban respectivamente a la anexión y a la independencia. Redpath explicó que, tras no poder Santana amortizar un empréstito de un millón de dólares solicitado a España y ofrecer en garantía las aduanas, un reducido contingente de ochenta españoles llegó a Santo Domingo el verano anterior para ejercer como recaudadores aduaneros y artesanos, lo que avivó las denuncias revolucionarias de la oposición de que Santana vendía la patria.

records.headline: Under the headline "Spain and the Dominican Republic," the Daily Whig of Richmond observes
records.summary_en: Under the headline "Spain and the Dominican Republic," the Daily Whig of Richmond observes that rumors concerning Spain's designs against the Dominican Republic (referred to as "the Republic of Dominica") draw attention to the military and naval strength of the Madrid government. Citing a statement from the New York World, the article notes that in 1860 the Spanish navy numbered 137 vessels—including 49 ships-of-war, war steamers, and other war vessels—in addition to smaller coast-service craft, three ships-of-the-line with 1,000-horse auxiliary steam-power on the stocks, and five steam frigates. The piece also points to the size of Spain's regular army organization, including 10 captain-generals and 148 major-generals, and reports that in Cuba Spain maintains eight regiments of veterans, one regiment of artillery, a brigade of five batteries, one company of workmen, two regiments of cavalry, one battalion of engineers, and a large militia force across the principal ports and towns.
records.summary_es: Bajo el titular «España y la República Dominicana», el Richmond Daily Whig observa que los rumores sobre los designios de España contra la República Dominicana (denominada «la República de Dominica») llaman la atención sobre la fuerza militar y naval del gobierno de Madrid. Citando un informe del New York World, el artículo señala que en 1860 la armada española contaba con 137 buques —incluidos 49 buques de guerra, vapores de guerra y otras embarcaciones bélicas—, además de embarcaciones menores para el servicio costero, tres navíos de línea con potencia auxiliar de vapor de 1,000 caballos en astillero y cinco fragatas de vapor. records.headline: The Wilmington Journal comments on the reported intention of Spain
records.summary_en: The Wilmington Journal comments on the reported intention of Spain to reconquer the Dominican Republic, noting that it is a former Spanish colony whose independence the Spanish government has never formally acknowledged. The paper mocks a Dominican call to arms declaring that the inhabitants would "make a fight of giants which will astonish the whole world, and make the earth tremble under our feet," contrasting the boast with the republic's total population of 126,500. Despite denials by the Spanish minister, the article states that Spain genuinely appears to intend to assert authority over San Domingo, predicting that Spain will take the eastern part of the island, known as the Dominican Republic, while France will take the western part, known as the Republic of Haiti.
records.summary_es: El Wilmington Journal comenta la anunciada intención de España de reconquistar la República Dominicana, señalando que se trata de una antigua colonia española cuya independencia el gobierno español nunca ha reconocido formalmente. El periódico ironiza sobre un llamado a las armas dominicano que declara que sus habitantes harían «una lucha de gigantes que asombrará al mundo entero y hará temblar la tierra bajo nuestros pies», contrastando la proclama con la población total de la república de 126,500 habitantes. A pesar de los desmentidos del ministro español, el artículo afirma que España realmente parece tener la intención de imponer su autoridad sobre Santo Domingo, y predice que España tomará la parte oriental de la isla, conocida como la República Dominicana, mientras que Francia tomará la parte occidental, conocida como la República de Haití.

records.headline: A correspondent in the Orleans Independent Standard reports
records.summary_en: A correspondent in the Orleans Independent Standard reports that no more than eighty Spaniards in all arrived at St. Domingo, consisting of mechanics and three officials who immediately assumed duties as port collectors, which the writer states represents the entirety of the "emigration" sent to the Dominican Republic by Spain, alongside the customary influx of South American exiles fleeing revolutions in Venezuela and neighboring countries. According to the writer, President Santana's policy nevertheless enabled his opponents to unite behind the charge that he was "selling the country to the whites," and as early as the previous December revolutionary circulars and proclamations were in type in St. Domingo, with a copy of the proofs shown to an ambassador in Paris. Although that plot was suppressed and Báez remains in exile, the writer reports that growing opposition intrigues have led Santana to call for outside aid both to perpetuate his own government and to repay his loan.

records.summary_en: Following the 1844 secession of the Dominican Republic, two alternating political parties led by Santana and Baez emerged, representing reunion and independence policies respectively. Santana repeatedly and unsuccessfully sought to place the republic under the control of Spain, France, or Venezuela, and also failed in his efforts to induce white emigration from the United States.
records.summary_es: Tras la separación de la República Dominicana en 1844 surgieron dos partidos políticos rivales encabezados por Santana y Báez, partidarios respectivamente de la anexión y de la independencia. De forma reiterada e infructuosa, Santana procuró colocar la república bajo el control de España, Francia o Venezuela, fracasando igualmente en sus tentativas de atraer inmigración de colonos blancos procedentes de los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: The Anti-Slavery Bugle reprints "The Dominican Republic," an article
records.summary_en: The Anti-Slavery Bugle reprints "The Dominican Republic," an article from the New-York Tribune, noting that for nearly seventy years the island of Haiti—formerly called Hispaniola and later St. Domingo—has been a theater of revolutions since the first African slave was brought there. Situated fifty-four miles from Cuba and once known as the "Garden of the Antilles," the island was divided almost equally at the outbreak of the French Revolution into a French and a Spanish colony. According to the article, the wealthy white slaveholding proprietors of the French colony initially embraced principles of liberty and equality for themselves, before those principles spread downward through society. The account adds that in 1791 the French National Assembly decreed civil freedom for persons of color born of free parents, that universal freedom was proclaimed to the slaves in 1793, and that the Spanish colony was subsequently ceded to France.
records.summary_es: Reproduciendo un artículo titulado «La República Dominicana» del New-York Tribune, el Anti-Slavery Bugle señala que durante casi setenta años la isla de Haití —antes llamada La Española y luego Santo Domingo— ha sido escenario de revoluciones desde que fue llevado allí el primer esclavo africano. Situada a cincuenta y cuatro millas de Cuba y conocida en otro tiempo como el «Jardín de las Antillas», la isla estaba dividida casi en partes iguales al estallar la Revolución Francesa en una colonia francesa y otra española. Según el artículo, los ricos propietarios blancos de esclavos de la colonia francesa abrazaron inicialmente los principios de libertad e igualdad para sí mismos, antes de que dichos principios penetraran hacia los estratos inferiores de la sociedad. El relato añade que en 1791 la Asamblea Nacional Francesa decretó la libertad civil para las personas de color nacidas de padres libres, que en 1793 se proclamó la libertad universal para los esclavos y que posteriormente la colonia española fue cedida a Francia.

records.headline: Following the closing lines of a proclamation dated Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: Following the closing lines of a proclamation dated Santo Domingo, March 10, 1861, and signed by Santana with cries of long live Doña Isabel II and liberty, The Daily Green Mountain Freeman presents an account of the Dominican portion of the island in view of intelligence that it has been re-annexed to Spain. The paper describes the island of Haiti as the largest, richest, and most important of the West India islands next to Cuba, noting that since its independence it has been divided into Haiti, a former French colony occupying about two-fifths of its area, and the "republic of Dominica" (the Dominican Republic), a former Spanish colony holding the remaining three-fifths. According to the report, the Dominican Republic has a population of about 105,000, roughly one-tenth of whom are white, and maintains an army of 20,000 men and a navy of seven small vessels. In 1852, its total exports—chiefly mahogany, ebony, and other precious woods—amounted to one and a half million dollars, while its imports, largely from the United States, totaled slightly more.
records.summary_es: Tras las líneas finales de una proclama fechada en Santo Domingo el 10 de marzo de 1861 y firmada por Santana con vivas a Doña Isabel II y a la libertad, The Daily Green Mountain Freeman presenta una reseña de la parte dominicana de la isla ante la noticia de que ha sido reanexada a España. El periódico describe la isla de Haití como la más grande, rica e importante de las Antillas después de Cuba, señalando que desde su independencia se ha dividido entre Haití, antigua colonia francesa que ocupa cerca de dos quintas partes de su superficie, y la llamada «república de Dominica» (la República Dominicana), antigua colonia española que posee las tres quintas partes restantes. Según el informe, la República Dominicana tiene una población de unos 105,000 habitantes, de los cuales aproximadamente una décima parte son blancos, y mantiene un ejército de 20,000 hombres y una armada de siete embarcaciones pequeñas. En 1852, sus exportaciones totales —principalmente caoba, ébano y otras maderas preciosas— ascendieron a un millón y medio de dólares, mientras que sus importaciones, procedentes en gran parte de los Estados Unidos, superaron ligeramente esa cifra.

records.headline: A correspondent in the Holmes County Republican reports that since
records.summary_en: A correspondent in the Holmes County Republican reports that since the independence of the Dominican Republic, two parties led respectively by Santana and Baez have divided and alternately governed the country under policies represented by the words "reunion" and "independence." Some years earlier, Santana borrowed a million dollars from Spain and, failing to repay the loan according to its terms, offered a mortgage on the custom houses, resulting in the arrival the previous summer of no more than eighty Spaniards at St. Domingo, including three officials who immediately assumed duties as port collectors while the rest were mechanics. According to the writer, that group constituted all the "emigration" Spain had sent to the Dominican Republic, and Santana's policy united the opposition against his government with accusations that he was selling the country to the whites. Although revolutionary circulars and proclamations were in type in St. Domingo as early as December and proofs were shown to the ambassador at Paris, the project was nipped in the bud, Baez remains in exile, and Santana has called for aid as opposition intrigues continue and increase.

Algunos años atrás, Santana tomó prestado un millón de dólares de España y, al no poder pagarlo según los términos del préstamo, ofreció una hipoteca sobre las aduanas, lo que dio lugar a la llegada el verano anterior de no más de ochenta españoles a Santo Domingo, entre ellos tres funcionarios que asumieron de inmediato sus cargos como recaudadores en los puertos mientras que el resto eran mecánicos. Según el autor, ese grupo constituía toda la «emigración» enviada por España a la República Dominicana, y la política de Santana unió a la oposición contra su gobierno bajo la acusación de que estaba vendiendo el país a los blancos. Aunque ya en diciembre circulaban en imprenta proclamas y circulares revolucionarias en Santo Domingo cuyas pruebas fueron mostradas al embajador en París, el proyecto fue sofocado en ciernes, Báez permanece en el exilio y Santana ha solicitado ayuda ante el continuo aumento de las intrigas opositoras.

records.headline: The transfer was to be effected by a coup it main
records.summary_en: According to *The New York herald* on April 19, 1861, three members of the Dominican cabinet orchestrated a transfer of power to Spain through a coup, supported by secret agents landed from the war steamer *Don John de Austria* and Spanish vessels arriving from Cuba and Porto Rico with paid emigrants, arms, and soldiers. When local authorities questioned these arrivals, they were officially told that the soldiers came to help repel Haytian invasions and the emigrants to till the ground, explanations that the people eventually came to believe after several months passed without further movements.
records.summary_es: Según *The New York Herald* del 19 de abril de 1861, tres miembros del gabinete dominicano orquestaron la entrega del poder a España mediante un golpe de Estado, secundados por agentes secretos desembarcados del vapor de guerra *Don John de Austria* y por navíos españoles procedentes de Cuba y Puerto Rico con inmigrantes pagados, armas y tropas. Cuando las autoridades locales inquirieron sobre estos desembarcos, se les contestó oficialmente que la tropa llegaba para ayudar a rechazar invasiones haitianas y los colonos para labrar la tierra, explicaciones que la población terminó por creer al cabo de varios meses sin que se registraran nuevos movimientos.

records.headline: A correspondent in the New-York Dispatch laments what he calls
records.summary_en: A correspondent in the New-York Dispatch laments what he calls the funeral obsequies of the Dominican Republic, asserting that Spain has bought up and intimidated President Santana and the heads of the Dominican forces so that the Spanish flag of "blood and gold" now floats from the bastions of Santo Domingo. According to the writer, the only free and constitutional state in the West Indies was stifled on March 18, 1861, by a select corps of traitors backed by a force of Spanish soldiers and Spanish bribe-money. The correspondent states that the late President of the United States had been informed of the plan to end the Dominican Republic by high-ranking Cubans and must also have been apprised of it by his own envoys at Madrid and Santo Domingo, yet took no notice of it. Two years earlier, La Presse and La Patrie of Paris had published articles on suppressing the Dominican Republic as semi-official feelers to gauge international reaction to converting a free state on the borders of the American Union into a Spanish coolie colony, while the Spanish press began patronizing its former colony as rich in natural wealth but lacking the political strength required of a nation.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del New-York Dispatch lamenta lo que denomina las exequias fúnebres de la República Dominicana, afirmando que España ha comprado e intimidado al presidente Santana y a los jefes de las fuerzas dominicanas, de modo que la bandera española de «sangre y oro» ondea ahora en los bastiones de Santo Domingo. Según el autor, el único Estado libre y constitucional de las Antillas fue sofocado el 18 de marzo de 1861 por un grupo selecto de traidores respaldados por una fuerza de soldados españoles y dinero de sobornos españoles. El corresponsal señala que el anterior presidente de los Estados Unidos había sido informado del plan para poner fin a la República Dominicana por cubanos de alta posición y que también debió haber sido advertido por sus propios enviados en Madrid y Santo Domingo, pero no le prestó atención. Dos años antes, La Presse y La Patrie de París habían publicado artículos sobre la supresión de la República Dominicana como sondeos semioficiales para medir la reacción internacional ante la conversión de un Estado libre cercano a la Unión Americana en una colonia española de culíes, mientras la prensa española comenzaba a referirse con condescendencia a su antigua colonia como rica en recursos naturales pero carente de la fuerza política propia de una nación.

records.headline: Continuing its report on the Spanish takeover, a correspondent
records.summary_en: Continuing its report on the Spanish takeover, a correspondent signed "E. D." in the New-York Dispatch states that Spain had been secretly landing men and supplies for three weeks while the entire population was disarmed before anyone suspected the cause. In the towns of Neyba, Azua, and San Cristobal, single officers collected all weapons under the pretext of replacing them with a better class, and popular patriotic leaders were lured inside the walls of Santo Domingo and detained as prisoners. At six in the morning on the 18th, the President, the three members of his cabinet, and a half-dozen high officers who had managed the affair raised the Spanish flag over the forts and proclaimed Isabella II Queen of the Dominican territory. The correspondent reports that the people received the notification in silent consternation and that scarcely a single Dominican outside the paid officials responded to the Spaniards' shout of "long live the Queen," despite double pay and lavish promises distributed overnight to the garrison and police, adding that desperate resistance is expected in the interior even though Dominicans say Spain will send 20,000 soldiers to crush the republic.

A las seis de la mañana del día 18, el presidente, los tres miembros de su gabinete y media docena de altos oficiales que habían dirigido el asunto izaron la bandera española sobre los fuertes y proclamaron a Isabel II reina del territorio dominicano. records.headline: The New-York Daily Tribune, commenting on United States relations
records.summary_en: The New-York Daily Tribune, commenting on United States relations with Spain, remarks that there remains the chance of a collision, or rather of a diplomatic coolness and alienation, resulting from Spain's recent "reannexation" of the Dominican Republic (referred to in the passage as "Dominica"). The editorial characterizes the Spanish move as a rapacious and foolish act, though not nearly so unjustifiable as the United States' own kindred appropriation of Texas. The paper argues that had the United States ever treated the Dominican Republic with common decency or formally recognized its existence, Washington might now with reason interpose an energetic protest against the new Spanish blunder. As matters stand, the Tribune asks how the United States can protest when "Dominica," so far as appears on the surface, has chosen to merge its independent existence into a return to colonial dependence on Spain.
records.summary_es: Al comentar las relaciones de los Estados Unidos con España, el New-York Daily Tribune señala que subsiste la posibilidad de un choque, o más bien de un enfriamiento y distanciamiento diplomático, como resultado de la reciente «reanexión» española de la República Dominicana (denominada en el pasaje «Dominica»). El editorial califica la medida española de acto rapaz y necio, aunque ni de lejos tan injustificable como la apropiación similar de Texas por parte de los propios Estados Unidos. El periódico sostiene que si los Estados Unidos hubieran tratado alguna vez a la República Dominicana con decencia elemental o hubieran reconocido formalmente su existencia, Washington podría ahora interponer con razón una enérgica protesta contra el nuevo desacierto español. Tal como están las cosas, el Tribune se pregunta cómo pueden protestar los Estados Unidos cuando «Dominica», por lo que aparenta en la superficie, ha optado por fundir su existencia independiente en un retorno a la dependencia colonial de España.

records.summary_en: Forty-three notable persons from Cibao were arrested and sent under escort to St. Domingo, while Padre Moya hoisted the Spanish flag in Vega despite public opposition and subsequently escaped the pursuing populace. The nation is described as indignant over being sold and betrayed through annexation, with unarmed citizens struggling in Moca following disarmament, a movement resulting in seven persons being shot in Azua, and reinforcements requested from Porto Rico. Consequently, Spain finds herself engaged in an unforeseen labyrinth of trouble stemming from the annexation.

Por consiguiente, España se encuentra atrapada en un imprevisto laberinto de dificultades derivado de la anexión.

records.headline: Presenting a Spanish account of the annexation of St. Domingo
records.summary_en: Presenting a Spanish account of the annexation of St. Domingo, The New York Herald states that the United States had always been a powerful obstacle to Spain opening her arms to her former colony, as Spain knew that the North Americans wanted St. Domingo for themselves just as they wanted Cuba, and delayed acquiring the former so as not to imperil the latter. Meanwhile, the Dominicans endeavored to counteract North American influence by becoming increasingly Spanish, opposing the continuous drafts of workmen sent by New York filibusters by encouraging the immigration of Spanish colonists and artisans at great sacrifice and appointing to their reduced army all Spanish officers who wished to enter the republic's service. Perceiving this, the North Americans redoubled their efforts, with one of Walker's former lieutenants operating in St. Domingo in a semi-official character to organize and receive the workmen sent from New York and establishing supplementary operations in Samana and Puerto Plata. According to the writer, two events rapidly changed the situation, including the war sustained by Spain in Africa, which gave Spain a consideration in the eyes of the Dominicans and Haitians that it had formerly lacked when they supposed Spain too weak to counteract North American influence.
records.summary_es: Al presentar un relato español sobre la anexión de Santo Domingo, The New York Herald afirma que los Estados Unidos habían sido siempre un poderoso obstáculo para que España abriera los brazos a su antigua colonia, pues España sabía muy bien que los norteamericanos querían Santo Domingo para sí mismos tal como querían a Cuba, y demoró la adquisición de la primera para no poner en peligro la segunda. Entretanto, los dominicanos procuraron contrarrestar la influencia norteamericana volviéndose cada vez más españoles, oponiendo a los continuos envíos de trabajadores mandados por los filibusteros de Nueva York la inmigración de colonos y artesanos españoles, fomentada a costa de grandes sacrificios, así como el nombramiento en su reducido ejército de todos los oficiales españoles que desearan entrar al servicio de la república. Al percibir esto, los norteamericanos redoblaron sus esfuerzos, hallándose uno de los antiguos lugartenientes de Walker en Santo Domingo con carácter semioficial para organizar y recibir a los trabajadores enviados desde Nueva York y estableciendo operaciones auxiliares en Samaná y Puerto Plata. Según el autor, dos acontecimientos cambiaron rápidamente la situación, entre ellos la guerra sostenida por España en África, la cual revistió a España ante los ojos de dominicanos y haitianos de una consideración que antes no tenía cuando la suponían demasiado débil para contrarrestar la influencia norteamericana.

records.headline: The New York Herald reviews a newly published pamphlet titled
records.summary_en: The New York Herald reviews a newly published pamphlet titled "French and European Interests in St. Domingo," noting that its author examines the question not merely from a political point of view but from the standpoint of liberal and democratic principles. Quoting the pamphlet, the article states that if principles are not words devoid of meaning in Europe, Spain will not be permitted to consummate its attempt against the Dominican Republic, where the author says liberty has reigned since 1822, nor against the Republic of Haiti, where it has reigned since the beginning of the century. The pamphlet argues that the people of Haiti are called upon to resolve the great question of the extent to which the Black race is susceptible of progress and civilization, noting that philosophers and politicians of all countries study their course while populations of African blood throughout the New World turn their eyes toward them. According to the author, they stand in the Antilles as a beacon pointing the road of liberty to eight million Black people who still groan under the lash and the stick in the nineteenth century, which he presents as their title to the protection of civilized nations.

Citando el folleto, el artículo afirma que si los principios no son en Europa palabras vacías de sentido, no se permitirá a España consumar su intento contra la República Dominicana, donde según el autor reina la libertad desde 1822, ni contra la República de Haití, donde reina desde principios del siglo. El folleto sostiene que el pueblo de Haití está llamado a resolver el gran problema de saber hasta qué punto la raza negra es susceptible de progreso y civilización, apuntando que filósofos y políticos de todos los países estudian con solicitud sus distintas fases mientras las poblaciones de sangre africana esparcidas por el Nuevo Mundo vuelven sus ojos hacia ellos. Según el autor, parecen haber sido colocados en las Antillas como un faro para señalar el camino de la libertad a ocho millones de negros que en pleno siglo XIX aún gimen bajo el látigo y el garrote, lo cual constituye su título a la protección de las naciones civilizadas.

records.headline: The Daily Exchange reports that letters from Kingston, Jamaica
records.summary_en: The Daily Exchange reports that letters from Kingston, Jamaica, indicate that the recent annexation of St. Domingo to Spain has been received there with very great alarm. A public meeting was recently held in Jamaica to consider the subject and to memorialize the British Queen. Among the resolutions adopted was a declaration that the attempt at annexation without the approval and concurrence of the popular vote of the Dominican Republic is contrary to every sentiment of justice and right, involves a gross outrage upon popular liberty, violates the principle held sacred by leading European powers that a people have the inalienable right to settle their own form of government, and could not be consummated without reflecting disgrace upon the Spanish flag. According to the report, the resulting memorial to the Queen has received not less than 3,500 signatures, making it the most numerously signed petition forwarded from the island with the exception of one on behalf of the late Governor Sir Lionel Smith.
records.summary_es: The Daily Exchange informa que cartas procedentes de Kingston, Jamaica, indican que la reciente anexión de Santo Domingo a España ha sido recibida allí con grandísima alarma. Recientemente se celebró una asamblea pública en Jamaica para examinar el asunto y elevar un memorial a la reina británica. Entre las resoluciones aprobadas figuraba una declaración según la cual el intento de anexión sin la aprobación y concurrencia del voto popular de la República Dominicana es contrario a todo sentimiento de justicia y derecho, entraña un grave atropello contra la libertad popular, viola el principio tenido por sagrado por las principales potencias europeas de que es derecho inalienable de un pueblo establecer su propia forma de gobierno, y no podría consumarse sin arrojar deshonra sobre la bandera española. Según el informe, el memorial dirigido a la reina ha recibido no menos de 3,500 firmas, convirtiéndose en el más numeroso enviado desde la isla con excepción de uno en favor del difunto gobernador Sir Lionel Smith.

records.summary_en: Under the headline "Revolution in St. Domingo," The Daily Dispatch reports advices received from St. Domingo up to June 9 stating that a fierce reactionary movement against the renewal of Spanish rule is progressing in the country. According to the report, General Santana had established a reign of terror in support of Queen Isabella's annexation project, but the Dominicans had taken up arms against him in Moca, the Cibao, Vega, and every important standpoint of the country. A reinforcement had been sent from Puerto Rico to the Spanish army, and it was believed that 20,000 soldiers would be required in order to sustain Santana and the Spanish Queen. The dispatch adds that a severe mortality existed in the Spanish regiments.
records.summary_es: Bajo el titular «Revolución en Santo Domingo», The Daily Dispatch informa sobre despachos recibidos de Santo Domingo hasta el 9 de junio según los cuales avanza en el país un feroz movimiento de reacción contra el restablecimiento del dominio español. De acuerdo con el informe, el general Santana había instaurado un verdadero régimen de terror en apoyo del proyecto de anexión de la reina Isabel, pero los dominicanos se habían levantado en armas contra él en Moca, el Cibao, La Vega y todos los puntos importantes del país. Se había enviado un refuerzo desde Puerto Rico al ejército español, y se estimaba que serían necesarios 20,000 soldados para sostener a Santana y a Su Majestad Católica. El despacho añade que existía una grave mortandad en los regimientos españoles.

records.headline: Reporting on congressional proceedings, the Daily National Intelligencer notes
records.summary_en: Reporting on congressional proceedings, the Daily National Intelligencer notes a message from the President of the United States stating, through the Secretary of State, that the Executive Department of the Government did not deem it advisable at that time to communicate the diplomatic correspondence that had taken place between the United States Government and that of Her Catholic Majesty of Spain touching the annexation of the Dominican Republic to Spain. Following the message, the House of Representatives adjourned until twelve o'clock the next day.
records.summary_es: Al informar sobre las sesiones del Congreso, el Daily National Intelligencer reseña un mensaje del presidente de los Estados Unidos en el que declaró, por conducto del secretario de Estado, que el Departamento Ejecutivo del Gobierno no consideraba conveniente en ese momento comunicar la correspondencia diplomática mantenida entre el Gobierno de los Estados Unidos y el de Su Majestad Católica de España en torno a la anexión de la República Dominicana a España. Tras el mensaje, la Cámara de Representantes levantó la sesión hasta las doce del día siguiente.
