records.headline: In correspondence from Havana, the Daily Ohio Statesman reports
records.summary_en: In correspondence from Havana, the Daily Ohio Statesman reports that General Serrano returned in an unpleasant mood from his trip to St. Domingo, having found everything in great confusion there and convinced himself that the inhabitants are dissatisfied with the way in which they are to be governed. According to the report, when the Dominicans annexed themselves to Spain, they insisted on being considered Spaniards and governed by the laws of Spain, but instead the Constitution there, as in Cuba, is a dead letter; although there is no slavery, the Dominicans aspire to possess as much political freedom as Spaniards have in Spain. When Serrano arrived aboard the Isabel la Catolica and signal guns announced his approach while troops lined the streets and fort artillery prepared a grand salute, a signal from the steamer ordered the troops back to their garrisons and directed that no public demonstrations be made. Serrano landed around twelve o'clock, walked to the palace for ten minutes, and rode off on horseback with officers to the villa "Los Molinos," where his wife, the Condesa de San Antonio, was awaiting him.
records.summary_es: En una correspondencia desde La Habana, el Daily Ohio Statesman informa que el general Serrano regresó de mal humor de su viaje a Santo Domingo, tras haber encontrado todo en gran confusión allí y haberse convencido de que los habitantes no están satisfechos con la forma en que van a ser gobernados. records.headline: Publishing the provisions of a Spanish royal decree in its Havana
records.summary_en: Publishing the provisions of a Spanish royal decree in its Havana correspondence, The New York Herald outlines the judicial arrangements scheduled to take effect on the first day of the coming year in the annexed territory of St. Domingo. Under Articles 2 through 4 of the decree, criminal proceedings will be adjusted in conformity with the laws and practice before the tribunals of the Spanish peninsula, while the civil code, the laws emanating from the legitimate powers of the former Dominican Republic, and the traditions and customs admitted by the tribunals of the territory will continue to be observed and applied in the meantime, with common law governing whenever there is no precedent under those codes, laws, and traditions. The correspondent adds that by subsequent decrees the Queen appoints judges and executive officers for the Supreme Court to be established at St. Domingo city, noting that many of them are respectable citizens of the acquired territory in a measure calculated to strengthen the bonds of union with the crown.
records.summary_es: Al publicar las disposiciones de un real decreto español en su correspondencia de La Habana, The New York Herald expone las normas judiciales que entrarán en vigor el primer día del año entrante en el territorio anexado de Santo Domingo. Conforme a los artículos 2 a 4 del decreto, los procesos penales se ajustarán a las leyes y prácticas vigentes ante los tribunales de la península española, mientras que el código civil, las leyes emanadas de los poderes legítimos de la antigua República Dominicana y las tradiciones y costumbres admitidas por los tribunales del territorio seguirán observándose y aplicándose entretanto, rigiendo el derecho común cuando no exista precedente bajo dichos códigos, leyes y tradiciones. El corresponsal añade que, mediante decretos posteriores, la reina nombra jueces y funcionarios ejecutivos para la Corte Suprema que habrá de establecerse en la ciudad de Santo Domingo, señalando que muchos de ellos son ciudadanos respetables del territorio adquirido, en una medida destinada a estrechar los lazos de unión con la corona.

records.headline: O'Donnell, in a recent meeting of the Senate, defended the annexation
records.summary_en: According to the newspaper, Spanish Prime Minister Gen. O'Donnell defended Spain's annexation of the Dominican Republic during a Senate meeting. He claimed that if Spain had not occupied that part of the island of Hayti, the Americans would have done so and established a republican community near Cuba and Porto Rico, thereby disturbing those colonies.
records.summary_es: Según el diario, el presidente del Consejo de Ministros de España, el general O'Donnell, defendió la anexión de la República Dominicana durante una sesión del Senado. Afirmó que si España no hubiese ocupado dicha parte de la isla de Haití, los estadounidenses lo habrían hecho, estableciendo una comunidad republicana en las proximidades de Cuba y Puerto Rico que habría perturbado la tranquilidad de esas colonias.

Citing writers and James Redpath's "Guide to Hayti," the article highlighted the region's agricultural productiveness—particularly for coffee, sugar, and cotton, noting that tree cotton grows with extraordinary facility and yields two crops annually.

records.headline: The republic was virtually dead, and the island was openly presented
records.summary_en: According to a January 13 dispatch reported by *The New York Herald* correspondent in San Domingo, the Dominican Republic was virtually dead and openly presented to the world as a Spanish province ruled by General Santana as the commissioned Captain-General for Queen Isabella. Spain promised numerous reforms as part of its policy of absorption—including declaring Samana a free port, inviting universal emigration, reducing tariffs on foreign-imported goods, proclaiming full religious toleration, and abolishing slavery—while it was also thought Queen Isabella would invite President Lincoln to send surplus negroes and contrabands to San Domingo. Additionally, the city's streets were enlivened with foreign carriages, buggies, drays, and new toilets, and the new United States Consul had not held any official intercourse with the government.
records.summary_es: Según un despacho del 13 de enero remitido por el corresponsal de *The New York Herald* en Santo Domingo, la República Dominicana había prácticamente dejado de existir, mostrándose abiertamente al mundo como provincia española gobernada por el general Santana como capitán general comisionado de la reina Isabel. España prometía múltiples reformas como parte de su política de absorción —incluida la declaración de Samaná como puerto libre, la invitación a la inmigración general, la rebaja de aranceles a las importaciones foráneas, la proclamación de una entera libertad de cultos y la abolición formal de la esclavitud—, al tiempo que se suponía que la reina Isabel cursaría una invitación al presidente Lincoln para asentar en Santo Domingo a los libertos negros rescatados de la Confederación («contrabands»). Asimismo, las calles de la capital se veían animadas con carruajes, calesas y carretas foráneas y novedades en el vestir, mientras que el nuevo cónsul de los Estados Unidos se abstenía de mantener trato oficial alguno con las autoridades.

records.summary_en: The Dominican Republic has ended and been annexed by Spain, though Spain finds the acquisition less than a bargain and is constrained by Castilian pride from backing out. No great powers have recognized the island as a Spanish province, while the consulates of France, England, and the United States maintain a modest presence. Spain is proposing several measures—including a new tariff, making Samana a free port, exercising religious tolerance, and encouraging global emigration—while the city has materially benefited from the change in government.
records.summary_es: A tenor del extracto periodístico, la República Dominicana dejó de existir y fue anexionada por España, si bien esta última encuentra la adquisición poco provechosa y se ve refrenada por el orgullo castellano para desistir de ella. Ninguna de las grandes potencias ha reconocido la isla como provincia española, en tanto que los consulados de Francia, Inglaterra y los Estados Unidos mantienen una discreta presencia. España proyecta varias medidas —entre ellas un nuevo arancel, habilitar Samaná como puerto franco, garantizar la tolerancia religiosa y fomentar la inmigración internacional—, mientras que la ciudad se ha beneficiado materialmente con el cambio de gobierno.

records.full_text:
IMPORTANT FROM ST. DOMINGO.

Our St. Domingo City Correspondence.

St. Domingo City, May 17, 1862.

Grand Industrial Progress Under the New Rule of Spain—Enterprise of Every Description Fostered—Openings for American Capital—The Tariff—Fine Chance for the Negro Contrabands of the United States—Slavery in the Spanish Colonies Nearly at an End—Advance in Dominican Property—Trade Report, &c., &c.

Although our news is tame and trivial compared with your grand march of events, yet I will send you the few items afloat.

Spain is making her mark here. By her liberal and enlightened policy she has silenced the few remaining malcontents. The Dominicans have certainly no reason to complain of her occupation. Indeed, the benefits bestowed have been thus far like the jug handle—all on one side—for poor St. Domingo has had nothing but acquiescence and gratitude to render on its part. The officials of her Majesty's government are free to express their avowed desire to foster enterprise, and especially to welcome and protect foreign capital and labor. There will be plenty of fat contracts to be had, and as Spain pays up in solid rocks we may expect to see the "Yanks" along here in the natural course of things.

The railroad from Santiago to Angelina, on the Yuna, is decided upon. This will give an outlet for the productions of the splendid valley of the Yuna, known as the Vega Real, to the Bay of Samana. Already propositions for navigating the Yuna from its mouth, at Samana Bay, to Angelina, have been presented by an American company and favorably considered.

The new tariff, reducing the rate of duties from thirty to twenty per cent ad valorem, it is said, will take effect in July. All articles necessary for the personal use of the colonists, except provisions, are to be admitted free of duty. I enclose a copy of the new decree regulating the terms for the payment of duties.

Our accounts from Hayti as to the practical working of the colonization of American blacks there are favorable, and Spain is not unwilling to take a leaf out of Hayti's book. Indeed the authorities here have already taken the initiative in the matter, and I understand expect shortly large arrivals of "contrabands." There is no fear that they will be other than well treated. There is no country on the face of the earth where the irrepressible darkey blooms as he does here. They hold high offices, both in the civil and military departments, and possess the same political and religious, if not social, status as the whites. This is a peculiar feature of Spanish policy. It is well known that the home government favors emancipation in the colonies, and every year sees a new condition imposed on slavery. The institution in the Spanish West Indies is now so hampered with restrictions, bearing heavily upon the master and operating to the proportionate advantage of the slave, that the planters of Cuba and Porto Rico are seriously considering the propriety of proposing to the home government the policy of emancipation, with compensation.

Spain evidently intends to build up in these waters a powerful free black empire. She distrusts the loyalty of her white Creole subjects. They are a little too much exposed to the captivating influences of Secessia; and, seeing what the progress of the age demands, and will not be cheated of, she wisely determines to have her best bower out to windward. So her policy is towards emancipation, and not only this, but she treats free blacks with marked respect and partiality. In Havana you will see a regiment of a thousand free black volunteers parading with the troops of the line or keeping guard in the Obra Pia. This service, it is to be borne in mind, is not allowed to the whites of Creole birth, except as special cases of favor. Thus the blacks are educated to the use of arms, while the whites grow up in ignorance of this accomplishment—a wrinkle which the non-slaveholding States of the United States may make a note of. In point of civil privileges the free blacks are in every respect the equal of whites. In courts of law their testimony is considered quite as good, and they have the same rights as to the holding of lands and other property. The government reserves to itself the right to dissolve the connection of master and slave on proof of cruel treatment, &c. One quarter of the blacks in Cuba are free, and many of them are rich. It may be mortifying to acknowledge that Spain is leading us in wisdom and progress; but such is the melancholy fact.

Since the annexation, real estate in and about the city has increased in value several hundred per cent. Houses rent at Fifth avenue rates. The large property of Gen. Cazneau, which adjoins the city walls, is now a splendid fortune to its lucky owner. Land in the interior has not perceptibly increased in value, as but few agriculturists have yet arrived.

At Samana great improvements are being made. The Royal West India Mail Company's steamships will probably make this port their terminus, in lieu of St. Thomas. If the coal is as good and abundant as represented, it will doubtless be the favorite resort for steamships plying in these waters. All such vessels may enter and depart free of duties and port charges. It is probable that Samana will be declared a free port for all nations in July. Then farewell to the glory and prosperity of St. Thomas. It would be well for Uncle Sam to secure a good location for a coal and naval depot at this port before the speculators get their clutches on every point.

Business is lively. House carpenters, masons and painters command good wages. Lumber continues in demand. No American vessels now in port. Health of the city good.

records.summary_en: According to the *New-York daily tribune*, the Dominican Republic was unexpectedly annexed to Spain on March 12, 1861, through the treason of President Santana without consulting the public, and the annexation was formally accepted by the Queen of Spain on May 20, 1861. While resident Spaniards and their descendants favored the change, citizens of African or mixed descent opposed it and desired to retain a republican form of government. Cuban papers report that the national party subsequently made an attempt to regain their independence.
records.summary_es: Según el *New-York daily tribune*, la República Dominicana fue anexionada inesperadamente a España el 12 de marzo de 1861 debido a la traición del presidente Santana sin consultar a la ciudadanía, y dicha anexión fue aceptada formalmente por la reina de España el 20 de mayo de 1861. Aunque los españoles residentes y sus descendientes favorecieron el cambio, los ciudadanos de ascendencia africana o mestiza se opusieron y desearon conservar la forma de gobierno republicana. Los diarios cubanos señalan que el partido nacionalista intentó posteriormente recuperar la independencia.

records.summary_en: In correspondence from Havana, The New York Herald reports that the rebellion in St. Domingo still continues and that Spanish troops are being dispatched to Puerto Plata. According to the dispatch, the screw corvette Santa Lucia left Santiago again on the 4th with troops, and the Ulloa sailed from Nuevitas on the 7th with a battery of artillery in company with the Isabel la Catolica, which had put in from stress of weather. The report further states that 216 soldiers of the Second Battalion San Marcial were found in Haiti by the Haitian government, disarmed, and delivered to the Spanish Consul at Port-au-Prince, who has sent to General Dulce for a vessel to take them away. The Haitian steamer Esther arrived at Santiago on the 3d, supposedly carrying the Spanish consul's dispatches for General Dulce, while more troops are scheduled to leave on Monday and the militia is expected to be called out.

records.full_text:
FROM SANTO DOMINGO.

Positive Information on the Progress of the Insurrection—The Destruction of Puerto Plata.

By the arrival on the 31st of October of the Bremen brigantine Santiago from Puerto Plata, we have received at last positive information of the political events in St. Domingo up to the 6th of the same month. The news reached us through the kind intermediation of various refugees, foreign merchants of said place.

After the destruction by fire of the inland and principal town of Santiago de les Caballeros, the Spanish garrison stationed there, together with reënforcements of about two thousand Spanish troops, began their retreat to the seaport of Puerto Plata on the 13th of September, joined by a great part of the foreign and native residents.

Shortly after their departure the insurgents began to harrass their march by continuous guerrilla fire, keeping the same up until their final arrival, on the 16th, causing them thereby a severe loss, estimated at from one thousand to one thousand two hundred killed and wounded, and some pieces of field artillery and a considerable amount of cash belonging to the regiment. Fresh arrivals of troops from Cuba and Puerto Rico reënforced the garrison in Puerto Plata up to four thousand men; nevertheless the insurgents succeeded in compelling the Spaniards to keep within the narrow limits of the town, and although they were not more in number than one thousand, not the slightest effort of repulsing the Dominicans was made by the Spanish garrison, and even small foraging bodies, dispatched to obtain food and grass, were driven back with considerable loss of life.

Intrenchments having been erected at the outskirts of the town, the Spaniards limited themselves to defend the same against the small assailing pickets who occasionally threatened to invade the town. This state of affairs continued up to the 2d of October, when preparations were made to evacuate the town, in order to retire to the fortifications dominating the port and town, which plan was executed on the dawn of the following day, by abandoning the intrenchments and retiring with the whole of the Spanish forces to the fort. Great dismay prevailed among the population in witnessing this unexpected and shameful event—the greater part of the same refuging on board the foreign vessels anchored in the port and in the fort, where, however, admittance was refused so much so that the distressed inhabitants were obliged to quarter themselves on the sea shore before the intrenchments erected there for the better protection of the fort.

The reason given for the evacuation of the town is that orders had been received to send the greater part of the troops to the City of San Domingo, where a new basis of operations is to be commenced, and not being able to defend all the barricades with the force remaining. It is, however, generally believed that the Spaniards evacuated the town either because of their inability to defend it, or because they wished to plunder it. The latter seems to have been their motive, as on the same day Spanish troops and Chinese laborers attached to the regiments, who were sent from the fort into the town without their officers engaged until sunset in pillaging the stores and houses. None of the Spanish officers attempted to stop their men from plundering. In the afternoon of the same day about four battallions of the Spanish troops embarked in the Spanish war steamers Herman Cortez, Velasco and Isabella la Catolico, their probable destination being the City of St. Domingo, reducing the garrison to about 1,500 men.

On the morning of the 4th of October the Spaniards began to pillage the town again. The Dominicans, finding that the Spaniards were bent on sacking the whole town, began to plunder also, and, while both parties were pillaging, there was some hot skirmishing going on, the Spaniards wishing to rival the Dominicans in securing the booty. In the afternoon every store and house, save one or two stores on the sea-beach, were emptied of their contents, and whatever objects the Spaniards could not remove they wantonly destroyed. The remaining garrison is under the command of Brigadier Rafael Prime de Rivera. About 4 o'clock p. m. a sally was made from the fort by 600 Spaniards against the insurgents, the number of whom was not known. A severe fight ensued, and the Dominicans were driven out of the town.

The Spaniards were protected by their guns on the fort, throwing shells to the center of the town, and about 5 o'clock p. m. a fire broke out in town, in the vicinity of the market, in the direction where the shells had fallen, it being the general belief that the fire was occasioned by the missiles thrown from the fort into the town. A weak attempt to check the fire was made by a company of sappers, which proved unsuccessful. The fire soon spread with great rapidity, and continued up to the moment the Bremen Bergantin Santiago left the harbor, being the 6th of October, in the evening, destroying among others the valuable stores of the considerable body of foreign merchants residing there.

In fact the whole town, with the exception of the Wesleyan Mission-House and a few small buildings in the eastern suburbs, has been destroyed completely by fire, and it is fully believed that the few remaining buildings will be destroyed equally. The losses on property, &c., from the firing of Santiago and Porto Plata exceed the sum of $5,000,000. The whole population of Porto Plata has fled to foreign countries, and thousands of foreigners, as well as natives, have sought refuge on the islands of St. Thomas, Curacoa, and Turks Island, and some of the principal merchants on the hospitable shores of the United States of North America. No notification whatever has been give to the representative of foreign Powers, and consequently the whole consular body consisting of the United States commercial agent, the French and British vice consuls, the consuls for Austria, Prussia, Hanoveria, Oldenburg, Denmark, and the free Hanseatic towns of Hamburg and Bremen, finding no protection either for their persons, residences or their nationality, have been forcibly compelled to leave the country and seek refuge on foreign shores, leaving behind their properties, wantonly destroyed, and saving nothing but their lives. It is to be hoped that ample and energetic measures will be taken by their respective governments to claim from Spain the just indemnification they are entitled to for the heavy losses sustained.

On the 21st the British war steamer Barracouta called at the port of Puerto Plata, but finding no necessity to afford protection to British and foreign property, viewing the strength of the Spanish soldiery sufficient for cases of emergency, left the harbor on the next day for Jamaica.

records.summary_en: According to *The Lancaster gazette* on November 5, 1863, fighting and fires in the Dominican Republic resulted in the destruction of the Government House, the Roman Catholic Church, and the American and British Consuls' residences, the latter of whom arrived at Grand Turk. Reports indicated that the entire south side of the island was in actual rebellion with 40,000 Dominicans in the neighborhood, and that Spanish soldiers pillaged the town before 600 Spaniards sortied from the fort and drove the Dominicans away with the aid of the fort's guns. The resulting fires destroyed numerous stores and properties belonging to foreign merchants, with losses in Santiago and Port-au-Platte expected to reach several millions of dollars.
records.summary_es: Según *The Lancaster Gazette* del 5 de noviembre de 1863, los combates e incendios en la República Dominicana ocasionaron la destrucción de la Casa de Gobierno, la iglesia católica y las residencias de los cónsules británico y estadounidense, habiendo llegado este último a Gran Turca. Los informes indicaban que toda la vertiente sur del territorio se hallaba en rebelión abierta con unos 40.000 dominicanos en las proximidades, y que la soldadesca española saqueó la población antes de que 600 peninsulares salieran de la fortaleza y rechazaran a los dominicanos con el auxilio de los cañones del fuerte. Los incendios resultantes destruyeron numerosos comercios y propiedades de comerciantes extranjeros, previéndose pérdidas millonarias en Santiago y Puerto Plata.

records.summary_en: According to the newspaper excerpt, eight to ten thousand Dominicans were in arms against Spanish troops, having burned Santiago to dislodge the Spaniards, while Spaniards burned Puerto Plata to deny refuge to natives. Foreigners reportedly handled all the business for both sides and stood to be the only ones with money when the war ended. Additionally, a report at San Cristobal stated the United States consul had a document that would benefit the U.S., following a failed Spanish military movement where the occupying force turned back upon hearing the enemy was accumulating ahead.
records.summary_es: Entre ocho y diez mil dominicanos se encontraban en armas contra las tropas españolas tras haber incendiado Santiago para desalojar a los peninsulares, mientras que los españoles quemaron Puerto Plata para privar de refugio a los patriotas. Trascendió que los extranjeros canalizaban el comercio de ambos contendientes y apuntaban a ser los únicos beneficiados económicamente al concluir la guerra. Además, un informe de San Cristóbal señalaba que el cónsul de los Estados Unidos poseía un pliego favorable a su nación, tras un fallido repliegue militar español donde la fuerza expedicionaria retrocedió al conocerse la concentración de tropas enemigas al frente.

records.headline: A correspondent in The New York Herald states that after the country
records.summary_en: A correspondent in The New York Herald states that after the country was handed over to Spain by a couple of Dominican leaders headed by General Santana, the people initially accepted the annexation quietly while hoping for the best, but have now risen in rebellion upon seeing that Spain is oppressing them. Disputing another writer's claims that the island's commerce has vastly improved since becoming a Spanish province and that real estate worth hundreds in Dominican times was worth thousands in Spanish times, the letter asserts that commerce has actually diminished over the last two years and that real estate values have shown no difference. Furthermore, the correspondent states that Spain merely exchanged the Dominican paper currency for its own paper without introducing the gold or silver promised at the time of annexation. Endorsing the remark that it is a paradox to say Spain has fattened upon the blood of the island, the writer asks whether the acknowledged fact that annexation has proved a bad speculation for Queen Isabella authorizes her government to act so shamefully and to destroy a town where the property of many foreigners as well as her own subjects is deposited.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal de The New York Herald afirma que, después de que el país fue entregado a España por un par de líderes dominicanos encabezados por el general Santana, el pueblo aceptó inicialmente la anexión en silencio esperando lo mejor, pero ahora se ha levantado en armas al ver que España lo oprime. Rebatiendo las afirmaciones de otro autor en el sentido de que el comercio de la isla ha mejorado enormemente desde que se convirtió en provincia española y de que los bienes raíces que valían cientos en tiempos dominicanos valían miles en tiempos españoles, la carta sostiene que el comercio en realidad ha disminuido en los últimos dos años y que el valor de los bienes raíces no ha registrado diferencia alguna. Además, el corresponsal señala que España simplemente cambió el papel moneda dominicano por su propio papel sin introducir el oro ni la plata prometidos en el momento de la anexión. Suscribiendo la observación de que es una paradoja decir que España ha engordado con la sangre de la isla, el autor pregunta si el hecho reconocido de que la anexión ha resultado ser una mala especulación para la reina Isabel autoriza a su gobierno a actuar tan vergonzosamente y a destruir una población donde se hallan depositadas las propiedades de muchos extranjeros además de las de sus propios súbditos.

records.headline: In The New York Herald, a pro-Spanish correspondent asserts
records.summary_en: In The New York Herald, a pro-Spanish correspondent asserts the absence of any well-founded complaint against Spanish rule in St. Domingo. The sole exception is the conduct of a single official who was summoned to answer charges and reportedly tried to kill himself on the passage. The writer claims that all the respectable, industrious, and wealthy people of the island have remained loyal to Spain, while characterizing the insurrectionists as the vagabond class, professional revolutionists, and idle wretches with nothing to lose. According to the letter, St. Thomas opposes Spanish rule in St. Domingo out of pecuniary interest, alleging that its population of Jewish shopkeepers formerly sold wares to the natives at enormous profits during the days of the Dominican Republic when others would not trade with them. The correspondent argues that when Spain came in to protect life and property, threw open the island to foreign enterprise, and proposed making Samana a free port, those merchants lost their market.
records.summary_es: En The New York Herald, un corresponsal proespañol sostiene la ausencia de toda queja bien fundada contra el dominio español en Santo Domingo. La única excepción es la conducta de un solo funcionario que fue citado a responder cargos y que según se dice intentó quitarse la vida durante la travesía. El autor afirma que todas las personas respetables, laboriosas y adineradas de la isla han permanecido leales a España, mientras califica a los insurrectos como la clase vagabunda, revolucionarios de oficio y miserables ociosos que no tienen nada que perder. Según la carta, Saint Thomas se opone al dominio español en Santo Domingo por interés pecuniario, alegando que su población de comerciantes judíos vendía anteriormente sus mercancías a los nativos con enormes ganancias en los días de la República Dominicana, cuando otros no se dignaban comerciar con ellos. El corresponsal argumenta que cuando España intervino para dar protección a la vida y la propiedad, abrió la isla a la empresa extranjera y propuso convertir a Samaná en puerto libre, dichos comerciantes perdieron su mercado.

records.headline: The New York Herald reports that St. Domingo advices to the Turks Island Standard represent
records.summary_en: The New York Herald reports that St. Domingo advices to the Turks Island Standard represent the Spaniards as making little progress against the Dominicans. According to the dispatch, the town of Samana had been plundered by the Spaniards, and the Wesleyan Mission House and chapel had been burned. Meanwhile, the merchants of St. Thomas have closed all accounts with Puerto Rico, Haiti, and Cuba, refusing to transact any further business with those places except for cash. The report concludes by noting that Spanish forces under their commander were completely surrounded by the Dominicans at Bani, and that the Dominicans have erected a battery commanding the entrance to the harbor of Porto Platte.
records.summary_es: The New York Herald informa que las noticias de Santo Domingo recibidas por el Turks Island Standard presentan a los españoles logrando muy pocos avances frente a los dominicanos. Según el despacho, el pueblo de Samaná había sido saqueado por los españoles, y la casa de la Misión Wesleyana y su capilla habían sido incendiadas. Entretanto, los comerciantes de Saint Thomas han cerrado todas las cuentas con Puerto Rico, Haití y Cuba, y no realizarán más negocios con esas plazas sino al contado. El informe concluye señalando que las fuerzas españolas bajo su comandante se hallaban completamente rodeadas por los dominicanos en Baní, y que los dominicanos han levantado una batería que domina la entrada del puerto de Puerto Plata.

records.headline: Wer harrassed terribly by Dominican guerrillas; and on reaching a defile at the river Jomera
records.summary_en: The *Worcester Daily Spy* reported that Spanish forces suffered defeats and heavy casualties against Dominican guerrillas, including losses at the river Jomera and a severe battle on December 20th at Puerto Plata. The report noted that Dominicans held St. Christobal, cut off Spanish land communications, captured various supplies and equipment, and placed Santanna in a critical position. Additionally, the newspaper included a brief dispatch from Fairfax Court House regarding a minor skirmish with rebels near Flint hill.
records.summary_es: El *Worcester Daily Spy* informó que las tropas españolas sufrieron derrotas y copiosas bajas frente a las guerrillas dominicanas, incluidos reveses en el río Jomera y una recia batalla librada el 20 de diciembre en Puerto Plata. El parte señalaba que los dominicanos dominaban San Cristóbal, habían cortado las comunicaciones terrestres de los españoles, capturado diversos pertrechos y provisiones y colocado a Santana en una situación sumamente comprometida. Además, el periódico incluyó un breve parte de Fairfax Court House relativo a una escaramuza menor con rebeldes confederados cerca de Flint Hill.

records.full_text:
Twelve hundred Spaniards left St. Domingo city Jan. 9, to capture St. Christobal, but were harrassed terribly by Dominican guerrillas; and on reaching a defile at the river Jomera, were driven back helter-shelter to the city, losing some 200 killed and wounded. The Dominicans still hold St. Christobal, thus preventing all land communications with the places occupied by the Spaniards. Some 200 Spaniards, 300 rifles, 40,000 rounds of cartridges, and a field piece, had been captured by the Dominicans.

Santanna's position is critical, and it is thought the Dominicans might inflict a fatal blow on him. Two native regiments have been ordered to be formed in St. Domingo.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that Dominicans captured Spanish supplies and a field piece at Yabacoa, while Spanish forces under Santana remained unable to move forward near San Guino due to reinforcements of 700 men being offset by over 700 sick in camp. Additionally, a severe battle occurred on December 20th at Puerto Plata, resulting in the defeat of the Spaniards, who lost 100 out of 600 men and a cannon to the gallantly fighting Dominicans. The *Standard* characterized the contest as unprofitable and dishonorable for Spain, noting that the Spaniards only hold the ground they stand on, while a separate weather report from Toronto noted a fierce snowstorm stopping railroad trains.
records.summary_es: El diario consignó que los dominicanos capturaron suministros y una pieza de campaña española en Yabacoa, mientras que las columnas peninsulares al mando de Santana permanecían inmovilizadas cerca de San Guino, toda vez que la llegada de 700 hombres de refuerzo quedó neutralizada por más de 700 enfermos en el campamento. Además, el 20 de diciembre se libró una cruenta batalla en Puerto Plata que concluyó con la derrota de los españoles, quienes perdieron 100 de sus 600 efectivos y un cañón ante el denodado arrojo dominicano. El *Standard* describió la lucha como estéril y deshonrosa para España, señalando que los españoles solo dominan el terreno que pisan, al tiempo que un parte meteorológico independiente desde Toronto daba cuenta de una feroz tormenta de nieve que paralizó los trenes.

A train of eighty mules laden with ammunition for Santannas' army was captured Dec. 9th by the Dominicans.

Twelve hundred Spaniards left St. Domingo city Dec. 9th to capture St. Christobal, but were harrassed terribly by the Dominican guerrillas, and on reaching a defile at the river Jaina were driven back hilter skilter to the city, losing some 200 in killed and wounded. The Spaniards are strengthening the fortifications of St. Domingo by two redoubts.

records.headline: Reporting on the war in St. Domingo, the Cleveland Morning Leader states
records.summary_en: Reporting on the war in St. Domingo, the Cleveland Morning Leader states that the Dominicans still hold St. Christobal, preventing all communication with Spanish-occupied places, and have captured some 2,000 Spaniards, 300 rifles, 4,000 rounds of cartridges, and a field piece at the army supply depot at Yaba Coa. While the Spaniards are strengthening the fortifications of St. Domingo with two redoubts and two native regiments have been ordered there, the Spanish commander near San Girno, despite recently receiving 1,500 reinforcements, has more than 700 sick in his camp, is unable to move his army forward, and remains in a critical position. On December 20, a severe battle took place at Puerto Plata in which the Dominicans fought with great gallantry, captured a cannon, and defeated the Spaniards with a loss of 150 out of 600 men. Summarizing the situation, the Standard remarks that the sooner Spain withdraws from these dishonorable and unprofitable contests the better, as the Spaniards are masters only of the ground they stand upon and will acquire only a cemetery rather than vanquish the Dominicans.
records.summary_es: Al informar sobre la guerra en Santo Domingo, el Cleveland Morning Leader señala que los dominicanos aún mantienen San Cristóbal, impidiendo toda comunicación con los lugares ocupados por los españoles, y que han capturado a unos 2,000 españoles, 300 rifles, 4,000 cartuchos y una pieza de campaña en el depósito de suministros del ejército en Yabacoa. Mientras los españoles refuerzan las fortificaciones de Santo Domingo con dos reductos y se ha ordenado el envío de dos regimientos nativos, el comandante español cerca de San Girno, pese a haber recibido recientemente 1,500 hombres de refuerzo, tiene más de 700 enfermos en su campamento, no puede hacer avanzar su ejército y se encuentra en una posición crítica. El 20 de diciembre tuvo lugar un recio combate en Puerto Plata en el que los dominicanos lucharon con gran valentía, capturaron un cañón y derrotaron a los españoles, quienes sufrieron 150 bajas de un total de 600 hombres. En un resumen de la situación, el Standard observa que cuanto antes se retire España de estas contiendas deshonrosas e infructuosas será mejor, pues los españoles solo son dueños del terreno que pisan y, en vez de vencer a los dominicanos, solo adquirirán un cementerio.

records.headline: Assisted by the artful management of his Secretaries of War and Marine
records.summary_en: According to the newspaper, a leader deceived the Dominican people by inviting in Spanish forces under the guise of assistance and instruction, subsequently collecting their arms, declaring the Republic extinct, and proclaiming the Queen of Spain as ruler. After being oppressed by Spanish officials and failing twice in armed resistance, the Dominicans achieved victory on their third attempt, restoring their free constitution while retreating Spanish forces burned towns in vengeance. The report notes that the Spanish navy subsequently maintained a strict blockade of most of the seaboard with six thousand Spanish soldiers.
records.summary_es: Según el periódico, un caudillo engañó al pueblo dominicano llamando a las fuerzas españolas con el pretexto de ayuda e instrucción militar, para luego confiscarles el armamento, declarar extinguida la República y proclamar soberana a la reina de España. Tras padecer la opresión de los funcionarios coloniales y sucumbir en dos tentativas armadas, los dominicanos alcanzaron la victoria en su tercer alzamiento, restableciendo su constitución libre mientras las tropas españolas en retirada quemaban poblados por venganza. El informe agrega que la escuadra española impuso subsiguientemente un riguroso bloqueo sobre la mayor parte del litoral apoyada por seis mil soldados peninsulares.

records.headline: England’s Recognition of the Dominicans.
records.summary_en: Following public concern over an announcement, English Ambassador Sir John Crampton requested instructions from Earl Russell regarding the Spanish blockade of the Dominican coasts. The English government consulted the legal advisers of the crown, whose opinion was favorable to recognizing the Dominicans as belligerents because Spain was bound by the maritime law of the Treaty of Paris to maintain a real and effective blockade. Earl Russell communicated this legal opinion to the Spanish representative in London, who promptly informed the Spanish government.
records.summary_es: A raíz de la inquietud pública ante una proclama oficial, el embajador británico Sir John Crampton solicitó instrucciones a Earl Russell sobre el bloqueo español de las costas dominicanas. El gobierno británico consultó a los asesores jurídicos de la Corona, cuyo dictamen fue favorable a reconocer la beligerancia de los dominicanos, por cuanto España estaba obligada en virtud del derecho marítimo del Tratado de París a mantener un bloqueo real y efectivo. Earl Russell trasladó este dictamen jurídico al representante español en Londres, quien lo puso de inmediato en conocimiento del gobierno de Madrid.

ENGLAND’S RECOGNITION OF THE DOMINICANS.
[From the Madrid Epoca, Dec. 18.]
In consequence of the effect produced upon the public mind by this announcement, Sir John Crampton, the English Ambassador at this Court, felt bound to request explanations from his government upon a matter in which he was without official instructions. Earl Russell lost no time in replying, and his despatch reached the English representatives yesterday evening, at the same time that the First Secretary of State received the despatches from our Minister Plenipotentiary in London, previously announced by telegraph to the Spanish Cabinet. These despatches contained ample details of all that had occurred. On account of certain questions arising from events that have taken place in consequence of the blockade of the Dominican coasts by the Spanish squadron, the English government considered it necessary to take the opinion of the legal advisers of the crown, following its practice in all matters of this kind. Their opinion was favorable in a certain manner to the recognition of the Dominicans as belligerents—Spain being bound, according to their view, by the maritime law laid down in the treaty of Paris, to maintain a real and effective blockade of all the points of the island where she undertook to prevent the entry of supplies destined for the rebels. Earl Russell communicated this opinion to our representative in London, who in his turn considered it urgently necessary to acquaint the Spanish government with the same. Hence the origin of a news which, having come to the knowledge of the telegraphic agents of various periodicals in this city, was transmitted by them with the urgency which its importance dictated, although the want of the details above mentioned caused some exaggeration in their communications. The reply of Earl Russell to the English Ambassador could not be expressed in more satisfactory terms. The English Minister confirmed the explanations given by Senor Comyn, and, wishing to afford a proof of the friendly attitude of England in questions so greatly affecting the prestige of our country, he authorized the English Ambassador to acquaint the Spanish Cabinet with his determination to indefinitely postpone any act which might be considered hostile, or as tending to exercise any sort of influence in the settlement of our internal affairs. We, who cannot be accused of being ardent admirers of the English policy, have satisfaction in declaring that its conduct in the present circumstances has been worthy of a great Power, and therefore merits our most sincere eulogies.

records.headline: An editorial headed "St. Domingo" argues that Spain's attempt
records.summary_en: An editorial headed "St. Domingo" argues that Spain's attempt to recover Dominica has ended in confusion and failure. It recounts that the island stood divided between Dominica and Hayti, that the Haytian government ruled the whole island from 1822 until the Dominicans threw off its authority and formed a republic of their own, and that Spain, which obtained possession again in 1861, met an insurrection it never overcame and now withdraws after heavy losses in men and money. The paper offers the episode as a warning on the unwisdom and injustice of the original sale of the country to Spain.
records.summary_es: Un editorial titulado «St. Domingo» sostiene que el intento de España de recuperar Dominica ha terminado en confusión y fracaso. Recuerda que la isla estaba dividida entre Dominica y Haití, que el gobierno haitiano gobernó toda la isla desde 1822 hasta que los dominicanos se libraron de su autoridad y formaron una república propia, y que España, que volvió a obtener la posesión en 1861, encontró una insurrección que nunca venció y ahora se retira tras grandes pérdidas de hombres y dinero. El periódico ofrece el episodio como advertencia sobre la imprudencia y la injusticia de la venta original del país a España.

records.summary_en: According to *The New York Herald* on April 30, 1865, European monarchies were described as quaking with fear over the growing strength of the United States and its potential impact on Spanish possessions like Cuba and Porto Rico. The article specifically cited a fearful argument presented by the "Conqueror of Africa," which claimed the United States planned to send thousands of freed colored people to St. Domingo to form a negro nationality and army to ultimately attack and destroy Cuba. The newspaper dismissed this theory as a "raving of an imagination entirely possessed by fear," asserting that no dilatory measures would be needed if the United States truly intended to conquer European possessions.

records.headline: Advices from San Domingo to April 9 announce that the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Advices from San Domingo to April 9 announce that the Dominican Republic has been completely re-established. The sessions of the National Convention came to an end in late March, and a decree of amnesty was published, with exceptions that include the high functionaries who took part in the intrigues that produced the annexation, the officers and soldiers who fought under the Spanish flag, and the public writers who opposed the restoration in the newspapers. A Spanish steamer had arrived with the order from Madrid for the evacuation, and the Spanish troops left the island on March 30.

Un vapor español había llegado con la orden de Madrid para la evacuación, y las tropas españolas salieron de la isla el 30 de marzo.

records.headline: An editorial sets out the geography and population of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: An editorial sets out the geography and population of the Dominican Republic and the failure of Spain's attempt to hold the country. The republic occupies the eastern and larger portion of the island, some 17,500 square miles, with a population estimated at between 120,000 and 200,000. Since the summer of 1863 the Spaniards have been confined to a few seaport towns, and the paper argues that Spain, whose bill before the Cortes admits that the inhabitants were unanimously opposed to her government, is now compelled to withdraw her troops and recognize the independence of the republic.
records.summary_es: Un editorial expone la geografía y la población de la República Dominicana y el fracaso del intento de España de retener el país. La república ocupa la porción oriental y mayor de la isla, unas 17,500 millas cuadradas, con una población estimada entre 120,000 y 200,000 habitantes. Desde el verano de 1863 los españoles han estado confinados a unos pocos puertos, y el periódico sostiene que España, cuyo proyecto ante las Cortes admite que los habitantes se opusieron unánimemente a su gobierno, se ve ahora obligada a retirar sus tropas y reconocer la independencia de la república.

records.headline: An editorial traces the political history of Santo Domingo in defense of the principle
records.summary_en: An editorial traces the political history of Santo Domingo in defense of the principle that all races have equal rights before the law. It recalls the fall of President Boyer, the separation of the Dominican Republic in 1844, and some fifteen years of Haitian attacks that the Dominicans always defeated. The writer holds that if the Dominicans remain true to themselves and to their principles of liberty and equality, they will be secure in their independence forever.
records.summary_es: Un editorial recorre la historia política de Santo Domingo en defensa del principio de que todas las razas tienen iguales derechos ante la ley. Recuerda la caída del presidente Boyer, la separación de la República Dominicana en 1844 y unos quince años de ataques haitianos que los dominicanos siempre derrotaron. El autor sostiene que si los dominicanos se mantienen fieles a sí mismos y a sus principios de libertad e igualdad, estarán seguros en su independencia para siempre.

records.headline: An editorial hails the triumph of the Dominican Republic over Spain
records.summary_en: An editorial hails the triumph of the Dominican Republic over Spain as the most mortifying rebuke yet given to the schemes of European conquest in America. It describes the republic as occupying the eastern part of the island, some 17,500 square miles with a population put at between 120,000 and 200,000, recalls that Santana sold San Domingo to Spain, and notes that the Spaniards, confined since 1863 to a few seaport towns, have been compelled to withdraw and to recognize the independence of the country.

records.headline: The Dominican government refuses to sanction the acknowledgment
records.summary_en: The Dominican government refuses to sanction the acknowledgment Spain demands in return for its withdrawal from the island. Spain asks the republic to admit that she took possession at the spontaneous desire of the people, that her conduct while there was grandly generous, and that she leaves entirely of her own free will. Rather than sign such an admission, the government faces the blockade General Gandara has declared on all the coasts and harbors of the republic, while his officers talk in the streets of San Domingo of laying the city in ashes.
records.summary_es: El gobierno dominicano se niega a sancionar el reconocimiento que España exige a cambio de su retirada de la isla. España pide que la república admita que tomó posesión por deseo espontáneo del pueblo, que su conducta allí fue grandemente generosa y que se marcha enteramente por su propia voluntad. Antes que firmar tal admisión, el gobierno afronta el bloqueo que el general Gándara ha declarado sobre todas las costas y puertos de la república, mientras sus oficiales hablan en las calles de Santo Domingo de reducir la ciudad a cenizas.

records.summary_en: Intelligence from the Dominican Republic, whose official documents have been laid before the State Department, reports that by the act of the Spanish Cortes of May 1, 1865, the military occupation of the island was formally abandoned. The paper calls the attempt to convert an American state into a European colony a terrible failure, defeated by the brave and unceasing resistance of the Dominicans, and says Spain leaves San Domingo, as she left her other American colonies, because it was beyond her power to stay. As a last shot in the magazine, General Gandara demands from the republic a false and self-accusing acknowledgment that Spain came at the people's desire and behaved with generosity while there.

records.summary_en: According to the *New-York Daily Tribune* of August 22, 1865, the *Boletin Oficial* of Santiago reported on July 7 that departing Spanish troops were taking Dominican cannon and property, while a few Spanish troops still lingered in St. Domingo because Gen. Gándara and the Dominicans had not agreed on a final evacuation treaty. The Dominican government rejected a drafted treaty because Gándara's preferred language made the agreement appear to be a Spanish concession rather than a surrender, and Gándara subsequently refused to receive new commissioners unless they confirmed the objectionable treaty. Consequently, the Dominican government officially expressed its determination not to yield, signifying that the war had not ceased.

El gobierno dominicano rechazó el borrador del convenio porque los términos exigidos por Gándara hacían figurar el acuerdo como una concesión graciosa de España y no como una capitulación en regla, negándose luego Gándara a recibir nuevos comisionados si no convalidaban dicho documento objetado. records.full_text:
The Revolution in Hayti—President Jeffrard preparing to Escape—Suffering among the Negroes on the Island of Jamaica—An outbreak Feared—San Domingo Affairs.

NEW YORK, Sept. 1.—The Herald's Kingston, Jamaica, correspondent says, that the headway which the revolutionists are making in Hayti, has been deemed by President Jeffrard sufficiently alarming to induce him to make preparations for escape from his country. A mail steamer has therefore been chartered at Kingston to proceed to Port au Prince and there remain till the time arrives for him to seek safety in flight or till the danger of such an event has passed.

Owing to the severe drought of the present summer in the Island of Jamaica, the heavy taxes and other causes, the negro laborers there have been reduced to the most abject poverty and great suffering, and thousands of them are on the verge of starvation. They blame the governor and his officers as the cause of their afflictions, and so strong and bitter is their feeling against the local government that an outbreak on their part is feared in the western part of the Island, in consequence of which two gunboats have been dispatched to that locality.

The Herald's Santiago correspondent says, notwithstanding the havoc and destruction of the Spaniards during their invasion of San Domingo, the crops are now coming forward which promise ample subsistence for the inhabitants, and that the sacrifices which the war has compelled the people to endure have made them more united and determined to maintain their independence. The latter statement is hardly borne out by reports which we have already published of threatened hostilities between two native chiefs, Gen'ls Penisutal and Cotral. It is said that the Spaniards stole and destroyed large quantities of fine wools, principally the property of American merchants, which had been stored at different places, and now Gen. Gandana, the Spanish commander, having withdrawn his troops from the interior, has blockaded the principal forts of the Republic because the Dominican Government will not submit to his haughty and unreasonable demands in the peace treaty, thus preventing the exportation of large stocks of tobacco belonging to Americans as well as Europeans. To offset this blockade the Dominicans have determined to commission privateers to prey on Spanish commerce and an agent authorized to issue letters of marque has already left for the United States and Europe.

records.summary_en: The latest advices from San Domingo report that the last of the Spaniards have left the island, and the Dominicans are sole masters of their territory. One of their military chiefs has been appointed Protector General of the republic, and the citizens are busily reorganizing the various departments of government. A national convention for the formation of a permanent constitution and government is announced, patriot journals have been established at important points, and the people are everywhere rejoicing over the prospect of future independence and freedom undisturbed.

records.headline: An editorial surveys recent European aggressions upon the republics of America
records.summary_en: An editorial surveys recent European aggressions upon the republics of America, and numbers Spain's attack on the Dominican Republic among them. Spain, on a pretext like the one that served in Mexico, attacked the republic with a view of subjugating it and bringing it under colonial rule, and threatened at the same time the republics of South America on the Pacific. She proceeded no further, the paper argues, because she met an unexpected stubborn resistance in the Dominicans, and because the progress of events in the United States warned her off.

No fue más lejos, sostiene el periódico, porque encontró una inesperada y tenaz resistencia en los dominicanos, y porque el curso de los acontecimientos en Estados Unidos la disuadió.

records.headline: News from St. Domingo
records.summary_en: News from St. Domingo to September 9 describes Dominicans celebrating the second anniversary of their liberation from Spain, after eighteen months of fighting forced Spain to evacuate the island. General Pimentel, elected provisional president in March, became unpopular for harsh and unlawful acts, and after citizens in the capital repudiated him he resigned, while General J. M. Cabral was commissioned as Protector of the republic to summon a National Convention.

records.summary_en: Advices received from St. Domingo to the 19th of September report that President Cabral has prohibited all further issues of paper money, and efforts are making to restore the currency to a specie basis. A large quantity of copper money is expected from Porto Rico, and a terrific hurricane had visited the coast, doing great damage. records.summary_en: The *Daily National Intelligencer* reported on November 13, 1865, that Don Pedro Valverde, a member of the "Yankee party," supports opening Dominican gold mines, mahogany forests, and pearl fisheries to immigrants under a liberal colonization law, and proposes establishing free and neutral ports jointly with President Geffrard of Hayti. In contrast, the newspaper noted that General Cabral has intimate relations with European consuls while the United States is unrepresented, and suggested that Cabral might pursue a close union with Hayti that could threaten the white race in the eastern part of the island. Additionally, the article stated that if Valverde is elected, the Dominican Republic would respond to Spanish demands for the repayment of conquest costs with a counter-demand.

records.headline: A report on the colored Americans of Santo Domingo, emigrants
records.summary_en: A report on the colored Americans of Santo Domingo, emigrants from the United States, tells how they formed a mutual assistance society for their own members and for any unfortunate stranger from the United States cast helpless on the Dominican shore, and how they took a ruined Bethel church and repaired and roofed it by their own exertions. When the Spanish forces took formal possession of Santo Domingo in 1861 they were deprived of the church, and the public exercise of the Protestant religion was not allowed them during the four years of Spanish rule. After the Spaniards evacuated the country and the republic was restored, General Cazneau, formerly United States commissioner at Santo Domingo, obtained the building again for them, and on the first Sunday of October it was reopened with a well-attended jubilee of thanksgiving for the restoration of equal rights to all races and of perfect freedom of conscience under the laws of the Dominican Republic.

Cuando las fuerzas españolas tomaron posesión formal de Santo Domingo en 1861 fueron privados de la iglesia, y el ejercicio público de la religión protestante no les fue permitido durante los cuatro años de dominio español. Después de que los españoles evacuaron el país y la república fue restaurada, el general Cazneau, antiguo comisario de Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo, recuperó el edificio para ellos, y el primer domingo de octubre fue reabierta con un concurrido jubileo de acción de gracias por la restauración de la igualdad de derechos para todas las razas y de la perfecta libertad de conciencia bajo las leyes de la República Dominicana.

records.summary_en: An armed man abruptly entered a session of the Dominican Congress to announce the impending arrival of revolutionary forces and proclaim General Baez as president, causing the ministers to flee in terror. Following this confusion, General Pedro Guillermo was appointed dictator until Baez could arrive, and an election on December 14th unanimously named Buenaventura Baez President of the Dominican Republic. Meanwhile, Cabral accepted a military position under the new government, which Guillermo practically headed.
records.summary_es: Un individuo armado irrumpió súbitamente en una sesión del Congreso dominicano para anunciar la inminente llegada de huestes revolucionarias y proclamar presidente al general Báez, haciendo que los ministros huyeran despavoridos. En medio del desconcierto subsiguiente, el general Pedro Guillermo fue investido como mandatario provisorio hasta la llegada de Báez, y en los comicios del 14 de diciembre se proclamó unánimemente a Buenaventura Báez presidente de la República Dominicana. Entretanto, Cabral aceptó un cargo militar bajo el nuevo régimen, que de facto encabezaba Guillermo.

records.summary_en: A narrative of the crisis at the capital describes how the ministers, in the confusion, abandoned their seats and sought protection in the houses of the French, Italian and English consuls. Cabral appeared in public and declared that if the popular voice and welfare demanded the rule of Baez he would gladly give his consent; the popular feeling then turned in favor of Cabral, and he retained power for several weeks. The mysterious man who had frightened the Congress proved to be General Pedro Guillermo, who managed to have himself appointed dictator until Baez should arrive; and an election held on the 14th of December by the Constitutional Assembly unanimously appointed Buenaventura Baez President of the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: Una narración de la crisis en la capital describe cómo los ministros, en la confusión, abandonaron sus escaños y buscaron protección en las casas de los cónsules de Francia, Italia e Inglaterra. El hombre misterioso que había asustado al Congreso resultó ser el general Pedro Guillermo, quien logró hacerse nombrar dictador hasta que Báez llegara; y una elección celebrada el 14 de diciembre por la Asamblea Constitucional nombró por unanimidad a Buenaventura Báez presidente de la República Dominicana.

records.headline: A coup d'etat effected his elevation to the Presidency through the treason of General Cabral
records.summary_en: According to *The Evening Telegraph* of January 30, 1866, Mr. Baez attained the presidency through a coup d'état aided by General Cabral's relinquishment of power and Pedro Guillermo's armed force. The article reports that the majority of the nation opposes Baez's administration due to his service as a Spanish Field Marshal during the independence struggle, and notes that his regime is currently jailing and persecuting suspected opponents of a thwarted uprising at Puerto Plata.
records.summary_es: Según *The Evening Telegraph* del 30 de enero de 1866, el Sr. Báez ascendió a la presidencia mediante un golpe de Estado facilitado por la declinación del poder del general Cabral y el respaldo armado de Pedro Guillermo. La crónica refiere que la mayoría de los ciudadanos rechaza el gobierno de Báez en razón de su pasado como mariscal de campo al servicio de España durante la guerra de independencia, señalando asimismo que el régimen persigue y encarcela a presuntos desafectos involucrados en un frustrado alzamiento en Puerto Plata.

La nota se publica con un extracto del Tidende de Santo Tomás que anuncia la llegada del vapor de guerra De Soto con el secretario de Estado a bordo.

The newspaper noted that the U.S. government had recognized the independence of Dominica and that the President nominated General Cazenau, who was engaged as a merchant there, as Minister to that republic. Additionally, the excerpt briefly reported on a fire that broke out in a closet of a building on Chatham Street between 12 and 1 o'clock on Sunday morning.

records.headline: A letter from San Domingo reports a January 14 conversation
records.summary_en: A letter from San Domingo reports a January 14 conversation at the national palace between Secretary Seward and President Báez, at which the Dominican cabinet was present. Báez told the Secretary that the revolution had been made in the republic and accepted by the whole people, and that his government lacked nothing for its stability but the recognition of the United States. Seward answered that General Cabral — who, he said, had most loyally been the obstacle to recognition — had headed the republic when Spain's power was cast off, and that the United States, satisfied that the revolution was as successful as it was just and permanently established under Cabral, had instructed its consul to recognize the republic without hesitation; before those instructions could be executed, a change had taken place.
records.summary_es: Una carta de Santo Domingo reseña una conversación del 14 de enero en el palacio nacional entre el secretario Seward y el presidente Báez, con asistencia del gabinete dominicano. Báez dijo al secretario que la revolución se había consumado en la república y había sido aceptada por todo el pueblo, y que a su gobierno nada le faltaba para su estabilidad sino el reconocimiento de los Estados Unidos. Seward respondió que el general Cabral —quien, dijo, había sido muy lealmente el obstáculo para el reconocimiento— había encabezado la república cuando se derrocó el poder de España, y que los Estados Unidos, satisfechos de que la revolución era tan exitosa como justa y de que se había establecido permanentemente bajo la dirección de Cabral, habían instruido a su cónsul para que reconociera la república sin vacilación; antes de que esas instrucciones pudieran ejecutarse, había sobrevenido un cambio.

records.summary_en: In an exchange printed by the paper, a Dominican speaker pleads for recognition by the United States, calling the enjoyment of American favor essential to Dominica's stability and peace and hoping that the proclamation of general liberty in the United States had removed the obstacles to recognition. Secretary Seward replies by recounting how the United States established itself as a republic on the principle of the equality of men while African slavery still existed under state laws.
records.summary_es: En un intercambio publicado por el periódico, un orador dominicano suplica el reconocimiento de Estados Unidos, y califica el disfrute del favor estadounidense de esencial para la estabilidad y la paz de Dominica, con la esperanza de que la proclamación de la libertad general en Estados Unidos hubiera eliminado los obstáculos para el reconocimiento. El secretario Seward responde relatando cómo Estados Unidos se estableció como república sobre el principio de la igualdad de los hombres mientras la esclavitud africana aún existía bajo las leyes estatales.

records.summary_en: President Baez provided a concise view of the contest and struggle on the island of St. Domingo, while Secretary Seward outlined U.S. progress following the rebellion that crushed the pro-slavery power. Seward explained that the abolition of slavery removed barriers to recognizing Liberia and Hayti and enabled the United States to extend fellowship to the republic of Dominica, which had been fighting monarchical influences.

Por otra parte, el puerto dominicano de Montecristi ha quedado clausurado al comercio extranjero.

records.headline: The Herald argues that the Dominican republic should be accepted
records.summary_en: The Herald argues that the Dominican republic should be accepted without further delay as an outpost of the United States, and says that since Mr. Seward's visit to the island the republic of St. Domingo, conducted by President Báez, has been recognized, as has that of Hayti. It accompanies the argument with a sketch of the republic: the eastern portion of the island of Hayti, comprising nearly three-fifths of it, its name derived from the Spanish name of the island, Santo Domingo; an area estimated at 17,500 square miles and a population of about 136,000, of whom one tenth claim to be whites and the rest are of African descent or of mixed African and European descent; a boundary with the Haytian republic running from the mouth of the river Massacre, on the north coast, to the Pedernales river on the south; and an interior of mountain ranges six to eight thousand feet high, covered with tropical forests, with large plains watered by numerous streams stretching toward the coast.

records.headline: From St. Domingo, the Crescent prints paragraphs from the Havana papers
records.summary_en: From St. Domingo, the Crescent prints paragraphs from the Havana papers on conditions in the republic. In Puerto Plata, commerce is reported pretty brisk; the whole island was prospering, perfect tranquility reigned throughout the country, Spaniards continued to be very well treated, and General Báez was generally well liked, from which it was hoped the government would very soon be consolidated under his presidency. Another paragraph gives an unconfirmed report that some of the interior provinces had sent communications to the President calling on him to declare war against the Haytians for the injuries they were committing on the frontier. An earthquake of great severity had thrown down several houses and badly damaged others.

records.headline: Until last September, Cabral held the supreme power, a Herald review of the Dominican struggle
records.summary_en: Until last September, Cabral held the supreme power, a Herald review of the Dominican struggle relates; a general election was then held for president. A large majority, it says, is known to have been given for Báez, particularly in Azua, Baní, Santo Domingo, Higüey, Moca and Macorís; but Cabral had Báez's votes thrown out on the ground that, being away from the country, Báez could not be considered a candidate, and Cabral, fraudulently elected, continues to hold tyrannical power. Several hundred of the friends of Báez have been arbitrarily banished from the island and are now destitute in Panama, Puerto Rico, Colón and Chagres, along the Spanish Main and in the United States, and a brother of General Báez has lain chained in a dungeon at Santo Domingo since last June, for fear of some attempt to reinstate him.
records.summary_es: Hasta septiembre pasado, Cabral mantuvo el poder supremo, relata una reseña del Herald sobre la lucha dominicana; se celebraron entonces elecciones generales para presidente. Una gran mayoría, afirma, se sabe que fue dada a Báez, particularmente en Azua, Baní, Santo Domingo, Higüey, Moca y Macorís; pero Cabral hizo anular los votos de Báez con el argumento de que, por hallarse fuera del país, Báez no podía ser considerado candidato, y Cabral, fraudulentamente electo, continúa ejerciendo un poder tiránico. Varios cientos de amigos de Báez han sido desterrados arbitrariamente de la isla y hoy se encuentran desamparados en Panamá, Puerto Rico, Colón y Chagres, a lo largo de la costa firme española y en los Estados Unidos, y un hermano del general Báez permanece encadenado en una mazmorra de Santo Domingo desde junio pasado, por temor a algún intento de reponerlo.

records.headline: A French account of the bay of Samana, printed in translation
records.summary_en: A French account of the bay of Samana, printed in translation, describes a bay whose fine situation has always caught the eye of navigators: several rivers flow into it, one of them, the Yuna, navigable for over fifty miles; it is surrounded by forests abounding in the finest building timbers, and the country around it contains mines of iron, copper and lead, and, still more valuable, mines of coal. Had France kept St. Domingo, the writer says, Samana would long ago have become one of the busiest centres of European trade with America. He recounts the French attempts on the bay: a settlement founded in 1673, renewed attempts in 1699 and under the Count d'Estaing, and the plan's revival in 1822 and under Louis Philippe, when it failed because of the formal opposition of the British Cabinet, who argued that France, having lost her colony of St. Domingo, had no real claim to occupy Samana. The writer turns at last to the recent attempt of the United States, to be judged, on the question of right, in the same light.
records.summary_es: Un relato francés sobre la bahía de Samaná, publicado en traducción, describe una bahía cuya excelente situación siempre ha llamado la atención de los navegantes: varios ríos desembocan en ella, uno de ellos, el Yuna, navegable por más de cincuenta millas; está rodeada de bosques que abundan en las mejores maderas de construcción, y el país que la rodea contiene minas de hierro, cobre y plomo y, aún más valiosas, minas de carbón. Si Francia hubiera conservado a Santo Domingo, dice el autor, Samaná se habría convertido hace mucho en uno de los centros más activos del comercio europeo con América. Refiere los intentos franceses sobre la bahía: una fundación en 1673, nuevos intentos en 1699 y bajo el conde d'Estaing, y la reactivación del plan en 1822 y bajo Luis Felipe, cuando fracasó por la oposición formal del gabinete británico, que alegó que Francia, habiendo perdido su colonia de Santo Domingo, no tenía derecho real a ocupar Samaná. El autor se vuelve por último hacia el reciente intento de los Estados Unidos, que debe juzgarse, en cuanto a la cuestión de derecho, bajo la misma luz.

records.headline: An American execution of the Samana project would be viewed
records.summary_en: An American execution of the Samana project would be viewed with regret by France, the French writer whose account the Herald prints in translation concludes, for it could not fail to become a cause of lasting disquiet to France, Spain, England and the republic of Hayti. He recalls that the French consul general at Port-au-Prince had the honor of baffling the project before the annexation of the Dominican republic to Spain, and asks whether France could succeed so well now, if the United States really have the intentions attributed to them.

records.headline: The Haytian government was about to establish friendly relations
records.summary_en: The Haytian government was about to establish friendly relations with the Dominican republic, the Herald reports from news of a late date: a circular of the Secretary for the Interior, addressed to the commandants of the frontier territories, recommended them to adopt the necessary measures to prevent all persons with arms or warlike stores from crossing the borders or in any way endangering the peace between the two republics; the government would enforce the regulations in the strictest terms as soon as the Dominican government adopted similar measures, and persons travelling from one republic to the other would be duly provided with passports. The paper also prints a translation of the message of General Salnave to the people and army of Hayti: called to the presidency by a decision of the National Assembly of June 14, 1867, he vows that the law will be the strength of the government, that the public liberties established by the constitution will be respected, and that the public welfare will be the supreme law of his administration.

El periódico publica además una traducción del mensaje del general Salnave al pueblo y al ejército de Haití: llamado a la presidencia por decisión de la Asamblea Nacional del 14 de junio de 1867, promete que la ley será la fuerza del gobierno, que las libertades públicas establecidas por la constitución serán respetadas y que el bienestar público será la ley suprema de su administración.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported that the bay and a portion of the peninsula of Samaná, located on the northeast coast of the island of Hayti, possess great natural facilities for repairing vessels and occupy an important strategic position relative to inter-oceanic routes. The article stated that possession of Samaná would be of incalculable value to the United States for commercial purposes and as a naval station, comparing its potential importance to that of Gibraltar. Additionally, the excerpt described the area as having a fertile soil, a salubrious tropical climate, and being reachable from New York in four days by steamer.

El artículo aseveró que la posesión de Samaná revestiría un valor inestimable para los Estados Unidos con fines mercantiles y como base naval, comparando su trascendencia potencial con la de Gibraltar. Además, el extracto describió la zona dotada de un suelo feraz y un saludable clima tropical, accesible desde Nueva York en cuatro singladuras por vapor.

records.headline: The naval station made over to the United States by the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: The naval station made over to the United States by the Dominican Republic is described by the Evening Post, in a description the Press reprints under the heading 'Our Newest Possessions.' It is situated on the south side of the peninsula of Samana, in the island of Hayti. The bay of Samana is almost completely land-locked, forty-three miles long by eight in width, with an entrance but three miles wide; it is capacious enough to contain any fleet that might be collected, and its shape affords a harbor where vessels can anchor with perfect safety. The Yuna, the largest river of Hayti, empties into its western end, and the small town of Santa Barbara stands on its northern shore.
records.summary_es: La estación naval cedida a los Estados Unidos por la República Dominicana es descrita por el Evening Post, en una descripción que la Press reproduce bajo el título «Our Newest Possessions». Está situada en el lado sur de la península de Samaná, en la isla de Haití. La bahía de Samaná está casi completamente cerrada por tierra, con cuarenta y tres millas de largo por ocho de ancho y una entrada de solo tres millas; es lo bastante capaz para contener cualquier flota que pudiera reunirse, y su forma ofrece un puerto donde los buques pueden anclar con perfecta seguridad. El Yuna, el río más grande de Haití, desemboca en su extremo occidental, y el pequeño pueblo de Santa Bárbara se encuentra en su costa norte.
