records.headline: The acquisition of the bay of Samana is the subject of an editorial
records.summary_en: The acquisition of the bay of Samana is the subject of an editorial recounting that the obvious intent was to acquire the bay with its valuable coal mines, which, with the development of steam navigation in the Pacific after the discovery of the treasures of California, were regarded as one of the most valuable properties that could be opened up; the population of the country is estimated at only about 200,000. At that period, it says, France was represented as having designs upon the republic, and a futile attempt was made to raise a Dominican loan of £750,000 in London; afterwards the temporary reoccupation of San Domingo by Spain and the exigencies of the American civil war diverted attention from the subject. Its resumption at the present moment, the writer holds, may in its commercial bearings be regarded with satisfaction: the bay is among the finest harbors in the world, its coal supply alleged to be virtually inexhaustible and so situated that vessels may even load alongside the mines, and the station would prove of incalculable importance to the United States in a naval sense, whatever mixture of motives produced the acquisition.
records.summary_es: La adquisición de la bahía de Samaná es el tema de un editorial que refiere que la intención evidente era adquirir la bahía con sus valiosas minas de carbón, las cuales, con el desarrollo de la navegación a vapor en el Pacífico tras el descubrimiento de los tesoros de California, eran consideradas una de las propiedades más valiosas que pudieran explotarse; la población del país se estima en solo unos 200,000 habitantes. En aquella época, dice, se representaba que Francia tenía designios sobre la república, y se hizo un intento inútil de levantar en Londres un empréstito dominicano de £750,000; después, la reocupación temporal de Santo Domingo por España y las exigencias de la guerra civil americana desviaron la atención del asunto. records.summary_en: According to the *New-York Tribune* on October 4, 1867, the peoples of Hayti and the Dominican Republic recognized that union was necessary to maintain their independence and prosperity, following past experience and Spanish intervention. A treaty—awaiting only the ratification of the Dominican Congress—had its preliminaries signed six days after the arrival of six delegates sent by President Balnave, amidst great enthusiasm from the government and people. The treaty's articles provided for the suppression of frontier brigandage and the extradition of political refugees, a commitment by both parties to preserve the inviolability of their respective territories (ruling out any United States purchase of the Bay of Samaná), and the settlement of claims arising from injuries sustained during the 1844 separation.

Se firmaron las bases de un tratado —pendiente solo de la ratificación del Congreso dominicano— a los seis días del arribo de seis delegados comisionados por el presidente Salnave, en medio del fervor popular y oficial. records.summary_en: The Avis reprints an editorial on the acquisition of the bay of Samana and its valuable coal mines: the obvious intent, it says, was to acquire the bay with those mines, regarded — as steam navigation in the Pacific was developed by the newly discovered treasures of California — as one of the most valuable properties that could be opened up; the population of the country is estimated at only about 200,000. It recalls that France was then represented as having designs upon the republic, and that a futile attempt was made to raise a Dominican loan of £750,000 in London, before the temporary reoccupation of San Domingo by Spain and the exigencies of the civil war in America diverted attention from the subject. Its resumption now may in its commercial bearings be regarded with satisfaction, for the bay is among the finest harbors in the world and its coal supply is alleged to be virtually inexhaustible, so situated that vessels may even load alongside the mines.

records.headline: A Dominican concession printed by the Tribune settles its disputes
records.summary_en: A Dominican concession printed by the Tribune settles its disputes in the courts of the Dominican Republic: disputes between the grantee and the government, or between the grantee and any other party, are to be settled by those courts. Another camel road is to be opened from Santiago de los Caballeros to the port of Monte Cristo, to expedite the transfer of copper ore from the mines of the interior to the coast; the constructors may open branch roads in any direction, extend the road to Santo Domingo City, and navigate the river Yaque by steamers, and they hold the right of converting the camel road into a railroad at a future period. Messrs. Joseph W. Fabens and James R. Young, of New York City, are the principals in the undertaking. The paper also prints a correspondence between Mr. Martin F. Hood, of London, and the Secretary of the Interior on the conditions under which foreigners will be allowed to work the mines in Santo Domingo: the old law that required foreigners going to St. Domingo to work in the mines to become naturalized citizens has been abrogated, and they are now as free to work in the mines as the natives, without changing their nationality.

Se abrirá otro camino de camellos desde Santiago de los Caballeros hasta el puerto de Monte Cristi, para facilitar el traslado del mineral de cobre desde las minas del interior hasta la costa; los constructores podrán abrir caminos ramales en cualquier dirección, extender el camino hasta la ciudad de Santo Domingo y navegar el río Yaque en vapores, y tienen asegurado el derecho de convertir el camino de camellos en ferrocarril en el futuro. records.full_text:
HAVANA, Nov. 17—We have the announcement that St. Domingo City has been destroyed, probably by an earthquake. I have telegraphed for details, which I shall forward at once.

The news of the insurrection in Hayti is confirmed. On the 12th of October the scene in the legislative chambers was very violent, and the language used was of the most threatening character. It all arose from a motion made to relieve Montes, who is in a Cape Haytien dungeon. The members all spoke in his defence. It is said Prince Salnave became so audacious as to secretly incite a rabble of women and boys to attack the House of Assembly. This they did with loud vivas for Salnave and cries of “Down with the Assembly,” hurling at the same time bricks, bottles, sticks, &c. The dwellings of many were vigorously stoned. The American consul was fired at, but escaped unhurt. A unanimous protest of the diplomatic corps has been presented against any further repetition of such scenes, and demanding of the government to see to it that the like does not again occur. At last accounts the city of Port au Prince was quieting. The treaty with the United States is as yet in suspense.

Destruction of St. Domingo.

NEW YORK, Nov. 18.—The Herald's Havana special, of the 17th, says: We have an announcement that St. Domingo City has been destroyed, probably, by an earthquake. I have telegraphed for details, which I shall forward at once.

records.headline: The hurricane lasted four hours and destroyed nearly all the shipping
records.summary_en: A Havana press dispatch reported that a tremendous hurricane struck St. Domingo on October 30, lasting four hours, destroying nearly all harbor shipping and Commerce street in St. Domingo city, and causing two hundred deaths, though no American vessels were reported lost. Additionally, a dispatch from Havana stated that the treaty with St. Domingo had been annulled, the Haytian Minister had returned, revolutionary movements were rife with Dominican forces on the Haytian frontier, and an intended issue of $600,000 in bonds was unpopular.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de prensa desde La Habana comunicó que un tremendo huracán azotó a Santo Domingo el 30 de octubre durante cuatro horas consecutivas, destruyendo la casi totalidad de las embarcaciones del puerto y la calle del Comercio en la capital, con un saldo de doscientos muertos, sin registrarse pérdidas de navíos estadounidenses. Además, un parte habanero indicó la anulación del tratado con Santo Domingo, el regreso del ministro haitiano, la proliferación de movimientos revolucionarios con destacamentos dominicanos en la frontera con Haití y el unánime repudio hacia una proyectada emisión de bonos de 600.000 pesos.

ST. DOMINGO.

SPECIAL TELEGRAM TO THE HERALD.

Terrific Hurricane—Destruction of Property on Land and Afloat.

HAVANA, Nov. 18, 1867.

A terrible hurricane blew over the island on the 30th of October. It desolated the capital and destroyed two hundred lives. The hurricane lasted four hours and destroyed nearly all the shipping in harbor. No American vessels are reported. Comercio street, St. Domingo city, is in ruins. There was no news from the interior.

records.headline: The Spy, discussing the sister republic of St. Domingo, holds
records.summary_en: The Spy, discussing the sister republic of St. Domingo, holds that the spirit of the Dominican population is decidedly opposed to American aggression, on account of the past treatment of the colored race in this country, and that on that account alone the efforts of the State Department to purchase the bay of Samana have proved abortive: the financial difficulties of the Dominican government would long ago have induced it to dispose of a portion of its territory but for a public opinion that would at once become a deadly enemy of the administration, and even the cause of rebellion against it. In this dilemma, it relates, the Dominican cabinet entered into negotiation with the Paris banking house of Erlanger & Co.: the firm was to open a subscription in France for a loan of two millions and a half of dollars in gold, one tenth of the amount to be guaranteed by the house if the subscription had little success in Europe, its advances to be guaranteed in securities on the custom-house duties of the republic. The government of Cabral indignantly refused to accept the proposition, though the country's financial difficulties may yet compel the administration to come to terms.
records.summary_es: El Spy, al tratar de la república hermana de Santo Domingo, sostiene que el espíritu de la población dominicana se opone decididamente a la agresión americana, a causa del trato pasado dado a la raza de color en este país, y que solo por esa razón han resultado infructuosos los esfuerzos del Departamento de Estado por comprar la bahía de Samaná: las dificultades financieras del gobierno dominicano lo habrían inducido hace mucho a desprenderse de una porción de su territorio si no fuera por una opinión pública que se convertiría de inmediato en enemiga mortal de la administración, e incluso en causa de rebelión contra ella. En este dilema, refiere, el gabinete dominicano entró en negociación con la casa bancaria parisina Erlanger & Co.: la casa abriría una suscripción en Francia para un empréstito de dos millones y medio de dólares en oro, cuya décima parte garantizaría la propia casa si la suscripción tuviera poco éxito en Europa, y sus anticipos serían garantizados con valores sobre los derechos de aduana de la república. El gobierno de Cabral se negó indignado a aceptar la proposición, aunque las dificultades financieras del país podrían aún obligar a la administración a llegar a un acuerdo.

records.headline: Conflicting reports of Cabral's defeat and Báez's proclamation
records.summary_en: Conflicting reports of Cabral's defeat and Báez's proclamation are printed in the Herald's St. Domingo telegrams of December 23–24. A press telegram from Santo Domingo of December 20 announces that Cabral's government has been defeated, owing to the defective organization of his troops; that a pronunciamiento of the people against him has been issued and Báez proclaimed President; and that a commission is going to Washington to complete arrangements for the transfer of the bay of Samana to the United States. Later advices from Santiago de Cuba report that well-informed persons there doubt the news of the defeat of General Cabral's forces, as well as the announcement of a pronunciamiento in favor of ex-President Báez. From Santo Domingo City the paper also reports that Señor Pujol, still at Santiago, was expected there and is to offer the lease of Samana for ninety-nine years; that in the Legislative Chamber the ten-million-franc loan recently negotiated in Paris was approved; and that Consul Savage, on a telegram from the American consul at Santiago de Cuba, has telegraphed Secretary Seward advising him to defer further proceedings in relation to the St. Thomas purchase.
records.summary_es: Informes contradictorios sobre la derrota de Cabral y la proclamación de Báez se publican en los telegramas del Herald sobre Santo Domingo, de fechas 23 y 24 de diciembre. Un telegrama de prensa de Santo Domingo, del 20 de diciembre, anuncia que el gobierno de Cabral ha sido derrotado, a causa de la defectuosa organización de sus tropas; que se ha emitido un pronunciamiento del pueblo en su contra y Báez ha sido proclamado presidente; y que una comisión va a Washington a ultimar los arreglos para la transferencia de la bahía de Samaná a los Estados Unidos. Avisos posteriores de Santiago de Cuba reportan que personas bien informadas allí dudan de la noticia de la derrota de las fuerzas del general Cabral, así como del anuncio de un pronunciamiento en favor del expresidente Báez. Desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo el periódico informa además que el señor Pujol, todavía en Santiago, era esperado allí y va a ofrecer el arrendamiento de Samaná por noventa y nueve años; que en la Cámara Legislativa fue aprobado el empréstito de diez millones de francos negociado recientemente en París; y que el cónsul Savage, a raíz de un telegrama del cónsul americano en Santiago de Cuba, ha telegrafiado al secretario Seward aconsejándole diferir las gestiones relativas a la compra de Santo Tomás.

records.headline: A Dominican mission has arrived at Washington from New York
records.summary_en: A Dominican mission has arrived at Washington from New York, the Herald's correspondent reports: Colonel Juan Macías, of the Dominican army, is among them, and General Pujol informed the correspondent that he is vested with plenary powers to negotiate. The object of the visit is to lay before Secretary Seward, by instructions from President Cabral, a proposition to sell the peninsula and bay of Samana to the United States. The terms of the purchase are two million dollars cash down and three hundred thousand dollars per annum for fifty years, the government of St. Domingo reserving to itself one fifth of the proceeds from the various mines on the peninsula — a stipulation General Pujol has the option of waiving if the sale can be better facilitated by it. At the expiration of the fifty years the peninsula becomes the fee-simple property of the United States, the total cost being seventeen millions.
records.summary_es: Una misión dominicana ha llegado a Washington procedente de Nueva York, reporta el corresponsal del Herald: el coronel Juan Macías, del ejército dominicano, figura entre sus miembros, y el general Pujol informó al corresponsal que está investido de plenos poderes para negociar. El objeto de la visita es presentar al secretario Seward, por instrucciones del presidente Cabral, una proposición para vender la península y la bahía de Samaná a los Estados Unidos. Los términos de la compra son dos millones de dólares en efectivo de contado y trescientos mil dólares anuales durante cincuenta años, reservándose el gobierno de Santo Domingo una quinta parte de los productos de las distintas minas de la península, estipulación que el general Pujol tiene la opción de renunciar si con ello se facilita mejor la venta. Al expirar los cincuenta años, la península pasará a ser propiedad plena y absoluta de los Estados Unidos, con un costo total de diecisiete millones.

records.headline: An American steamer had arrived at St. Thomas from New York
records.summary_en: An American steamer had arrived at St. Thomas from New York with a large sum in specie to be placed at the disposal of the Dominican envoy, Mr. Pujol, a Herald press telegram from Havana of March 23 reports; Pujol was to proceed to St. Domingo with the money to secure the lease of the bay of Samana for the United States from the new Báez government — a story the telegram itself notes has no good authority and is given for what it is worth. The United States steamer Palos had arrived at St. Domingo, where she met a very favorable reception. A deputation of Dominicans had gone to Curaçao to bring President Báez to the capital, and Hungría, Luciano and Gómez were acting as administrators of the government pending his arrival. The cholera had entirely disappeared from St. Domingo, and business was very dull. A companion telegram reports a great battle in Hayti on March 7, at Savanna-la-Grande, in which the Cacos were totally destroyed, the national troops taking possession of Fort Liberté; a general amnesty has been proclaimed, President Salnave is still at the Cape, and paper money stands at thirty-one for the silver dollar.

SANTO DOMINGO.

SPECIAL TELEGRAM TO THE HERALD.

Baezist Policy—Samana to be a Free Port—An Alliance with Hayti.

HAVANA, April 27, 1868.

The steamer Pajaro del Oceano, Captain Ochoa, has arrived here with advices from St. Domingo to the 20th inst.

Although General Baez had taken the usual oath as President of the republic, Congress was endeavoring so to amend the Constitution during its present session as to confirm the leading points of General Baez' policy. These were the following:— To make Samaná a free port of entry and a general foreign mail station. To arrange the mail and trade service at Samaná so that it should form a neutral station and become the centre of the Caribbean telegraphic cable service.

A brother of General Baez and General Caminero had gone to Hayti to negotiate for a permanent alliance between both republics. According to the proposed terms of the new alliance all disputed territory shall contribute *provisionally* a line of division. But such neutral provinces shall be bound to complete the geological and mineralogical survey of their respective limits. The general survey of the respective republics thus completed shall specify the situation and value of the gold and silver mines and of the debts secured by guaranties of such mines.

The general banker, Jesurun, and Colonel Fabens have been charged with the negotiation of a loan to be secured by the revenues from customs of the Dominican republic.

records.headline: A letter from Santo Domingo City, dated April 18, reports the March session of Congress
records.summary_en: A letter from Santo Domingo City, dated April 18, reports the March session of Congress, at which Generals Hungría and Luciano appeared and resigned the ample faculties entrusted to them by the interior towns, after the Secretary of the Interior had read to the body their message declaring the calamities brought upon the republic by the administration of Cabral. Congress at once reinvested the generals with the same faculties, to continue until the arrival and induction into office of President Báez — a sequence the writer says entirely refutes the misrepresentations sent from the capital to certain journals of the island of Cuba, stating that President Báez would not return. The letter adds that the government of the United States is about to get the Bay of Samaná on its own terms, and will not, therefore, take over the island of St. Thomas as it intended.
records.summary_es: Una carta desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo, fechada el 18 de abril, informa de la sesión de marzo del Congreso, en la que los generales Hungría y Luciano comparecieron y renunciaron a las amplias facultades que les habían sido confiadas por los pueblos del interior, después de que el secretario del Interior hubiera leído ante la cámara el mensaje de los generales en el que declaraban las calamidades traídas a la república por la administración de Cabral. El Congreso volvió a investirlos de inmediato con las mismas facultades, para que continuaran hasta la llegada y toma de posesión del presidente Báez, secuencia que, según el corresponsal, refuta por completo las falsas versiones enviadas desde la capital a ciertos periódicos de la isla de Cuba, según las cuales el presidente Báez no regresaría. La carta añade que el gobierno de los Estados Unidos está a punto de obtener la bahía de Samaná en sus propios términos y que, por tanto, no tomará la isla de Santo Tomás como se había previsto.

records.headline: The Free Trader recounts the history of the guano claims at Alto Velo.
records.summary_en: The Free Trader recounts the history of the guano claims at Alto Velo. Americans who had been taking guano from the island were ejected by the Dominican government, which asserted its jurisdiction, and the parties then sought a contract with that government for permission to ship guano and claimed damages. Secretary of State Jeremiah S. Black refused to notice the claim for damages until the United States agent at St. Domingo should have ascertained and reported the grounds upon which the Dominican government had asserted its jurisdiction; before the answer was received, Black had ceased to be Secretary of State and had been succeeded by Mr. Seward, and the rebellion and the war, various revolutions in the Dominican Republic, and war between that government and Hayti postponed any consideration of the claims. When the question was raised again, the department answered that two parties of Americans had claimed the island as discoverers, that St. Domingo had asserted a title and ejected the claimants, and that it declined to give any encouragement to Americans to resort there for guano without first obtaining the consent of St. Domingo.
records.summary_es: El Free Trader relata la historia de las reclamaciones por el guano de Alto Velo. Los estadounidenses que extraían guano de la isla fueron expulsados por el gobierno dominicano, que afirmó su jurisdicción, y los interesados buscaron entonces un contrato con ese gobierno para obtener permiso de embarcar guano, reclamando además daños y perjuicios. El secretario de Estado Jeremiah S. Black se negó a atender la reclamación de daños hasta que el agente de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo averiguara e informara sobre los fundamentos en que el gobierno dominicano había basado su jurisdicción; antes de que llegara la respuesta, Black había cesado como secretario de Estado y había sido sucedido por el señor Seward, y la rebelión y la guerra, varias revoluciones en la República Dominicana y la guerra entre ese gobierno y Haití pospusieron toda consideración de las reclamaciones. Cuando la cuestión se planteó de nuevo, el departamento respondió que dos grupos de estadounidenses habían reclamado la isla como descubridores, que Santo Domingo había afirmado un título y expulsado a los reclamantes, y que se negaba a dar estímulo alguno a los estadounidenses para acudir allí por guano sin obtener primero el consentimiento de Santo Domingo.

records.headline: An editorial in the Republican reviews the Alto Velo guano claim
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Republican reviews the Alto Velo guano claim: parties from Baltimore say they discovered guano upon the island of Alto Velo, lying about twenty miles south of the southernmost promontory of the island of San Domingo or Hayti, claimed it as not at the time the property or under the sovereignty of any government, and began to open and remove the valuable deposits, until in October an armed vessel of the Dominican Republic removed them. Their attorney, Judge Jeremiah S. Black, has ever since been urging their claims at Washington, either to obtain compensation or to induce the government to take forcible possession of the island, in defiance of the weak and distracted republic which assumes sovereignty over it. The Republican attributes Black's break with President Johnson — his withdrawal from the President's defense in the impeachment trial, and his present war on Mr. Seward — to the refusal of both to interfere in his behalf in this claim; it notes that the Court of Claims has likewise decided that the case is without any merit, and warns that four of the impeachment managers have committed themselves to a recommendation of what it calls this preposterous claim.

Su abogado, el juez Jeremiah S. Black, ha urgido desde entonces las reclamaciones en Washington, ya sea para obtener una indemnización o para inducir al gobierno a tomar posesión forzosa de la isla, en desafío de la débil y atribulada república que asume la soberanía sobre ella. El Republican atribuye la ruptura de Black con el presidente Johnson — su retiro de la defensa del presidente en el juicio político y su guerra actual contra el señor Seward — a la negativa de ambos a intervenir en su favor en esta reclamación; observa que la Corte de Reclamaciones ha decidido igualmente que el caso carece por completo de mérito, y advierte que cuatro de los fiscales del juicio político se han comprometido a recomendar lo que califica de reclamación disparatada.

records.full_text:
ST. DOMINGO.

The Reactionary Forces at Work Against Baez—His Brother Held by the Haytien Cacos—Interesting Review of the Situation—Dominican Speculators on Their Way to the United States.

ST. DOMINGO, May 20, 1868.

Several Dominican generals recently made the island of St. Thomas a rendezvous. Among them were Cabral, Luperon, Embert, Adon, Pina, Ricardo, Fernandez and Pimentel. They concerted a plan of operations against Baez. The result was that ex-President Cabral sailed for Jacmel May 15 on board the English steamer. He is to take command of the revolutionists along the southern frontier—in San Juan, Neyba, Las Matas, Cercao, Barahona, &c. The chieftains Timsteo and Andres Ogando, Sico Moreno, Damian Castillo and Mariano Rodriguez sent a young man named Abelard Dubreuil through Haytien territory to meet General Cabral. Baez and his partisans, as well as Cazneau, represent that this movement in the south is in favor of President Salnave. This is like what such would report to carry out their own schemes.

General Luperon went to Turks Island so as to operate against the north of this republic—the provinces of Cibao—whither the people call him as their leader. He will there meet Generals Palanco, Alvarez and many others who await his arrival to pronounce against General Baez.

General Pimentel is to go from Curaçao in company with General Castillo, Linares, Valverde and others to operate against Seybo and St. Domingo provinces, in which neighborhood they are to meet the brave General Manzueta, whom Baez has been unable to put down, either with threats or promises or by the imprisonment of his family. He kept in the vicinity of Llamasá, a district in St. Domingo province, and never ceased fighting the Baezists.

General Baez does not know how to get his government into working order, as the employes resign almost immediately after appointment. They all regard Baez's government as illegal and transitory, and no one is willing to compromise himself therewith. This is the reason why Señor F. M. Delmonte has not accepted the portfolio that Baez has tendered him, although he has been urged and besought to accept it.

By letters from St. Thomas we have learned that the Cacos hold Carlos Baez a prisoner. He was on his way to Salnave's government for the purpose of selling that portion of Dominican territory bounded on the south by the Rio Yaqui. This sale was the condition by which Baez agreed with Salnave's Minister, Delorme, for the aid which the latter would give in overthrowing Cabral. The western portion of the island, the Haytien side, has no savannas nor pasture lands to raise cattle. From the Rio Pedernales, whence the dividing line goes, according to the Aranjuez treaty of 1777, to the Rio Yaqui there are magnificent bays, which the Haytiens have always coveted without ever having taken the measures to secure so valuable a portion of our island. To fulfil this part of his engagements Baez has had to mutilate our constitution by dropping the article which points out the limits of the republic as well as the clause which creates the office of Vice President. Baez wants absolute power, and as the constitution of 1865 is very liberal and controlled the President's action while it abolished the death penalty in political cases, he has substituted the constitution of 1854, which makes him master and lord over the Dominicans and imposes capital punishment for political offences. This same substitution he attempted in 1865, when he came to power, but before he could carry it out he was overthrown and had to take refuge in the French Consulate.

Baez has also presented to Congress a bill of his expenses during the revolution that has just brought him to power, but out of decorum they have not made public the amount. The following is the only allusion to it made in the reply of Congress to the President's message:—"As to the detailed accounts of the revolutionary outlays which have been presented by the worthy General Buenaventura Baez, they are entirely approved, as well as the agreement entered into with Señores J. A. Jesurun & Zoons of the neighboring island of Curaçao, which amounts to $37,145 80, which is approved in all its tenor and conditions."

So many documents and mortgages will be secured by Baez in the names of Jesurun, Fabens and Cazneau that, even if the peninsula of Samana were sold for ten times its value, the proceeds could not liquidate all the claims that he will have on the treasury of the republic. In connection with this trio of speculators it is very positively asserted here that Jesurun and Fabens are authorized by Baez to raise a loan of $200,000 in the United States, on account of Samana. This money is needed to improve Baez's situation, at least until such time as the bay and peninsula of Samana can be disposed of for good. I do not think these rumors can be well founded, as Jesurun and Fabens left here on April 20 and Baez was inaugurated only on May 2. The Boletin Oficial of that date attacked such a project, and brought severe charges against ex-President Cabral for having sought to alienate Samana. What is certain, however, is, that whatever engagements those gentlemen make in the United States are null and of no validity, as they are not authorized by government legally constituted. Baez has been proclaimed by a faction who overthrew Cabral without electing Baez in a constitutional manner through popular suffrage, as the constitution then in force required. The latter has seated himself in the Presidential chair in spite of the will of the majority, and has imprisoned, exiled and persecuted the most distinguished citizens of the republic.

records.headline: A letter from St. Domingo City, dated July 4, reports the campaign
records.summary_en: A letter from St. Domingo City, dated July 4, reports the campaign against Báez in the north and in the south, under headlines that also speak of threats against the lives of those who negotiate the sale or lease of Samaná. General Polanco has taken the field against President Báez, while besides him Generals Ogando, Andújar, Moreno and others are operating in the south under the immediate command of ex-President Cabral himself; the government troops that are encamped at Azua make no attack upon them, but keep strictly on the defensive, and meanwhile the insurgents are doing all they can to make a connection with the northern rebels, so as to commence a combined movement forwards. General Luperón, who is commander-in-chief of the revolutionists, left St. Thomas June 30 for Jacmel, accompanied by General Pedro Valverde and Colonel Antonio Madrigal, intending to take command in the north; Generals Pimentel and others also sailed from St. Thomas on the 30th for Turk's Island. In Seibo and San Cristóbal some attempts at insurrection have taken place, and Báez has sent commissioners to see if he can succeed in putting a stop to the trouble.
records.summary_es: Una carta desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo, fechada el 4 de julio, informa de la campaña contra Báez en el norte y en el sur, bajo titulares que hablan también de amenazas contra la vida de quienes negocien la venta o el arrendamiento de Samaná. El general Polanco ha entrado en campaña contra el presidente Báez, mientras que, junto a él, los generales Ogando, Andújar, Moreno y otros operan en el sur bajo el mando inmediato del propio expresidente Cabral; las tropas del gobierno acampadas en Azua no los atacan y se mantienen estrictamente a la defensiva, y mientras tanto los insurgentes hacen todo lo posible por enlazar con los rebeldes del norte para iniciar un movimiento combinado de avance. El general Luperón, comandante en jefe de los revolucionarios, salió de Santo Tomás el 30 de junio hacia Jacmel, acompañado del general Pedro Valverde y el coronel Antonio Madrigal, con la intención de tomar el mando en el norte; los generales Pimentel y otros zarparon también de Santo Tomás el día 30 hacia la isla Turca. En Seibo y San Cristóbal ha habido algunos intentos de insurrección, y Báez ha enviado comisionados para ver si logra poner fin a los disturbios.

records.headline: A letter from Santo Domingo City dated July 4, 1868 reports a spreading insurrection against President Baez, with General Polanco
records.summary_en: A letter from Santo Domingo City dated July 4, 1868 reports a spreading insurrection against President Baez, with General Polanco in the field in the south under ex-President Cabral and General Luperon, the revolutionists' commander-in-chief, sailing from St. Thomas to take command in the north. Government troops at Azua stay on the defensive while towns desert, prisoners are taken at Higuey, and the capital lives in alarm as money runs out and Baez cannot find men willing to fight.
records.summary_es: Una carta desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo fechada el 4 de julio de 1868 informa de una insurrección creciente contra el presidente Baez, con el general Polanco en campaña en el sur bajo el mando del expresidente Cabral y el general Luperon, comandante en jefe de los revolucionarios, zarpando de Santo Tomás para tomar el mando en el norte. Las tropas del gobierno en Azua se mantienen a la defensiva mientras los pueblos quedan desiertos, se toman prisioneros en Higuey y la capital vive en alarma porque se acaba el dinero y Baez no encuentra hombres dispuestos a luchar.

records.headline: The Tribune's special correspondent writes from Puerto Plata
records.summary_en: The Tribune's special correspondent writes from Puerto Plata, July 5, that the threatened invasion of St. Domingo by ex-President Cabral and the exiled generals of his party, Luperón, Polanco and others, has taken place: Cabral, after passing through Hayti under shelter of the arms of the Cacos, has crossed the frontiers and is at Banica with a considerable force of men, while General Ramírez Báez and Colonel Le Mar, each at the lead of a large body of troops, have been sent against him, and in Santiago, which has been threatened by Polanco, the authorities are rapidly organizing a military force to resist him. The correspondent reports the manifesto the malcontent generals have published, addressed to the people of St. Domingo, setting forth that the revolutionists are not animated by a spirit of vengeance, but that it is absolutely necessary to the peace and prosperity of the country that Báez should be removed from the presidency — that should he abdicate power, dissensions may speedily be healed, but if he resists their demands a general civil war is imminent. In the city of St. Domingo great disquiet prevails in consequence of the imminency of another desperate struggle; the prisons, it is said, are full, and one of the prisoners has been tried by a council of war and sentenced to death, but an appeal has been made to the Supreme Court, where it is expected the sentence will be reversed.
records.summary_es: El corresponsal especial del Tribune escribe desde Puerto Plata, el 5 de julio, que la amenazada invasión de Santo Domingo por el expresidente Cabral y los generales exiliados de su partido, Luperón, Polanco y otros, ya se ha producido: Cabral, tras pasar por Haití al amparo de las armas de los cacos, ha cruzado la frontera y se encuentra en Banica con una considerable fuerza de hombres, mientras que el general Ramírez Báez y el coronel Le Mar, cada uno al frente de un numeroso cuerpo de tropas, han sido enviados contra él, y en Santiago, amenazada por Polanco, las autoridades organizan rápidamente una fuerza militar para resistirlo. El corresponsal reproduce el manifiesto publicado por los generales descontentos, dirigido al pueblo de Santo Domingo, en el que exponen que los revolucionarios no están animados por un espíritu de venganza, pero que es absolutamente necesario para la paz y la prosperidad del país que Báez sea apartado de la presidencia: que si abdica del poder, las disensiones podrán curarse pronto, pero que si se resiste a sus demandas, una guerra civil general es inminente. En la ciudad de Santo Domingo reina gran inquietud ante la inminencia de otra lucha desesperada; se dice que las cárceles están llenas, y uno de los prisioneros ha sido juzgado por un consejo de guerra y sentenciado a muerte, pero se ha presentado una apelación ante la Corte Suprema, donde se espera que la sentencia sea revocada.

records.headline: An account reprinted in the Avis, beginning in the middle of the report
records.summary_en: An account reprinted in the Avis, beginning in the middle of the report, describes the forces gathered together for the purpose of overthrowing the government: in the centre stands a general in command of a column, and he is one of the most implacable enemies of Báez; on the frontiers of the south General Ogando, Moreno and others have risen; on the frontiers of the north General Polanco had also taken up arms against the government. There is no doubt that Báez will fall very soon, the account says, for public opinion is very unfavorable to him, and he is detested on account of his tendency to sell the country to the Spaniards or Americans. The revolution is imminent, and it is very probable that General Luperón, who is the chief of the movements in operation in the Dominican Republic, will come to power; Luperón is now in Christiansted on his way to St. Domingo, and is attended by some of his friends.
records.summary_es: Un relato reproducido en el Avis, que comienza a mitad del informe, describe las fuerzas reunidas con el propósito de derrocar al gobierno: en el centro se halla un general al mando de una columna, uno de los enemigos más implacables de Báez; en las fronteras del sur se han sublevado los generales Ogando, Moreno y otros; y en las fronteras del norte el general Polanco también ha tomado las armas contra el gobierno. No hay duda de que Báez caerá muy pronto, dice el relato, pues la opinión pública le es muy desfavorable y es detestado por su tendencia a vender el país a los españoles o a los estadounidenses. La revolución es inminente, y es muy probable que el general Luperón, jefe de los movimientos en curso en la República Dominicana, llegue al poder; Luperón se encuentra ahora en Christiansted, de camino a Santo Domingo, acompañado de algunos de sus amigos.

records.headline: A column of advices reports that a battle took place on the 24th of July
records.summary_en: A column of advices reports that a battle took place on the 24th of July, between the revolutionists and the forces of Salnave, which ended in a victory for the former; that the revolutionists have concentrated 4,000 troops, well provided with provisions and ammunition, around the city of Port-au-Prince, and are pressing on with renewed vigor; that General Lynch, a revolutionary commander, has issued a manifesto protesting against the cession of any Haytien territory to the United States; that the Dominican troops have crossed the frontier and commenced the invasion of Hayti; and that a general and his son had been murdered, with robberies and depredations reported in various parts of the country. Advices from St. Domingo represent the revolutionary movement against Báez as steadily progressing, under the leadership of General Luperón; a decisive victory has been gained by one of his generals, and the speedy fall of Báez, and the expulsion of his government, is anticipated.
records.summary_es: Una columna de noticias informa que el 24 de julio tuvo lugar una batalla entre los revolucionarios y las fuerzas de Salnave, que terminó con la victoria de los primeros; que los revolucionarios han concentrado 4.000 tropas, bien provistas de víveres y municiones, alrededor de la ciudad de Puerto Príncipe, y avanzan con renovado vigor; que el general Lynch, comandante revolucionario, ha publicado un manifiesto en el que protesta contra la cesión de cualquier territorio haitiano a los Estados Unidos; que las tropas dominicanas han cruzado la frontera y comenzado la invasión de Haití; y que un general y su hijo habían sido asesinados, con robos y depredaciones reportados en varias partes del país. Las noticias de Santo Domingo presentan el movimiento revolucionario contra Báez en progreso constante, bajo la jefatura del general Luperón; uno de sus generales ha ganado una victoria decisiva, y se anticipa la pronta caída de Báez y la expulsión de su gobierno.

records.headline: A dispatch from St. Domingo
records.summary_en: A dispatch from St. Domingo City, dated July 11, 1868, reports that rebel General Timoteo Ogando routed the government forces at Ceiba, killing General Brigman, and that an alarmed President Baez placed two cannons before his house and ordered forty prominent citizens, including men he had held in prison, to leave the country. It also reports aid and money reaching Baez from Curacao, Dominican exiles sailing from there under General Aybar, government troops living off the cattle of private owners, and whole companies deserting on the march.
records.summary_es: Un despacho desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo, fechado el 11 de julio de 1868, informa que el general rebelde Timoteo Ogando derrotó a las fuerzas del gobierno en Ceiba, dando muerte al general Brigman, y que un alarmado presidente Báez colocó dos cañones ante su casa y ordenó a cuarenta ciudadanos prominentes, incluidos hombres que había tenido presos, que abandonaran el país. También informa de ayuda y dinero que llegaban a Báez desde Curazao, de exiliados dominicanos que zarparon de allí bajo el mando del general Aybar, de tropas gubernamentales que vivían del ganado de propietarios privados y de compañías enteras que desertaban en la marcha.
records.passage: from Curacao to the Rebels? Crimes and Atrocities? Summary of Events. St. Domingo City, July 11, 1868. Yesterday there was great alarm in this city. The news which government has received in relation to its first reverses are deplorable. As I told you in my last letter, General Ramirez Baez had gone from Azua with a body of troops to take San Juan; but he put more reliance on the bravery of a German officer named General [Brightman?], as none of the Baez family—the President included—has ever been in an engagement. When the rebel commander, General Timoteo Ogando, learned this movement he advanced to meet General [Brightman?], and attacked him at Ceiba and completely routed his troops, leaving General [Brightman?] among the dead on the field. Immediately after having received news of this defeat the President ordered two cannons to be placed before the door of his house, as if the danger threatened him very closely. He also sent passports to forty prominent citizens, with orders to leave the country. He also banished Señores J. M. Perez, M. M. Santamaria, A. Brua, S. de Castro, R. Santin, T. Aguero, B. Medina, D. Henriquez, F. Duluc, F. Chain, and W. de Costa Gomez, whom he had held in prison. The Baezists state that government is preparing to send the families of the exiled [illegible] if this barbarous measure be carried out the city will be largely thinned of its population, as there are now scarcely eight thousand inhabitants here,

records.headline: A private letter from Santo Domingo denounces the Baez administration, saying its efforts to obtain gold through the Samana
records.summary_en: A private letter from Santo Domingo denounces the Baez administration, saying its efforts to obtain gold through the Samana negotiation, a Spanish protectorate and foreign loans have failed, while ruinous contributions are exacted from the people. It describes cattle seized in the province of La Vega and sold in Santiago, with the money then presented in La Vega as part of a foreign loan, and it lists arrests, forced contributions, the exile of 22 political prisoners on the schooner Dos Hermanos, and executions in Azua.
records.summary_es: Una carta privada desde Santo Domingo denuncia a la administración de Báez y dice que sus esfuerzos por obtener oro mediante la negociación de Samaná, un protectorado español y préstamos extranjeros han fracasado, mientras se exigen contribuciones ruinosas al pueblo. Describe ganado incautado en la provincia de La Vega y vendido en Santiago, cuyo dinero fue presentado después en La Vega como parte de un préstamo extranjero, y enumera arrestos, contribuciones forzadas, el exilio de 22 presos políticos en la goleta Dos Hermanos y ejecuciones en Azua.

records.summary_en: Under the head of Santo Domingo, the Avis reports intelligence received by the Solent from the Dominican Republic: by the Spanish steamer Pelayo came passenger Mr. John P. O'Sullivan, to enter into a convention with the authorities for the establishment of a line of steamers to run between New York and New Orleans, and the various ports of the Dominican Republic. This gentleman, the paper says, has filled several high diplomatic posts under the American government, and is accompanied by General Cazneau, who for some time was a resident of St. Croix. Mr. David Cohen, Postmaster-General and acting British consul at St. Domingo, was named by the government as a special commissioner to treat, and settle matters with, the American gentleman.
records.summary_es: Bajo el encabezado de Santo Domingo, el Avis informa de noticias recibidas por el Solent desde la República Dominicana: en el vapor español Pelayo llegó como pasajero el señor John P. O'Sullivan, para celebrar un convenio con las autoridades para el establecimiento de una línea de vapores que correría entre Nueva York y Nueva Orleans y los distintos puertos de la República Dominicana. Este caballero, dice el periódico, ha ocupado varios altos cargos diplomáticos bajo el gobierno estadounidense, y viene acompañado del general Cazneau, que durante algún tiempo fue residente de Santa Cruz. El señor David Cohen, administrador general de Correos y cónsul británico en funciones en Santo Domingo, fue nombrado por el gobierno comisionado especial para tratar y arreglar los asuntos con el caballero estadounidense.

records.headline: The Tribune reprints a Washington story from the Boston Post
records.summary_en: The Tribune reprints a Washington story from the Boston Post on the proposed Samana purchase: Mr. Seward's star is again in the ascendant, and the United States is likely to become the owner of the Bay of Samana, the purchase of which Frederick Seward failed to accomplish during his secret mission to the island of St. Domingo last winter. The difficulty in his way, the story says, was the exhibition of too great an anxiety to purchase, which induced Cabral, then at the head of the Dominican government, to become exorbitant, hoping thereby to get vast wealth with which to leave the island. Buenaventura Báez was called to the presidency of the republic in 1865, but Cabral succeeded in holding on until the spring of the present year, when he was driven from the country and Báez regularly installed in office; Báez is described as highly educated and immensely wealthy, most of his wealth invested in France, where he has spent many years of his life. He has just communicated to Secretary Seward his desire to transfer the Bay of Samana to the United States on Mr. Seward's own terms, provided these terms shall stipulate for a lease only and not for an actual sale of the property — Báez proposing to respect the bitter prejudices existing among the Dominicans against selling territory by leasing the bay for ninety-nine years to the United States.
records.summary_es: El Tribune reproduce una versión de Washington del Boston Post sobre la propuesta compra de Samaná: la estrella del señor Seward vuelve a estar en ascenso, y es probable que los Estados Unidos lleguen a ser dueños de la bahía de Samaná, cuya compra Frederick Seward no logró realizar durante su misión secreta a la isla de Santo Domingo el invierno pasado. La dificultad en su camino, dice la versión, fue la exhibición de un excesivo afán de comprar, que indujo a Cabral, entonces al frente del gobierno dominicano, a mostrarse exorbitante, esperando obtener así una vasta riqueza con la que abandonar la isla. Buenaventura Báez fue llamado a la presidencia de la república en 1865, pero Cabral logró mantenerse hasta la primavera del presente año, cuando fue expulsado del país y Báez instalado regularmente en el cargo; Báez es descrito como muy educado e inmensamente rico, con la mayor parte de su fortuna invertida en Francia, donde ha pasado muchos años de su vida. Acaba de comunicar al secretario Seward su deseo de transferir la bahía de Samaná a los Estados Unidos en los propios términos del señor Seward, siempre que esos términos estipulen solo un arrendamiento y no una venta efectiva de la propiedad, proponiéndose Báez respetar los amargos prejuicios existentes entre los dominicanos contra la venta del territorio mediante un arrendamiento de la bahía a los Estados Unidos por noventa y nueve años.

records.summary_en: According to the newspaper report, government troops in the Dominican Republic actively pursued and dispersed the Orgando faction while elections progressed quietly throughout the country, and a revival of trade at Puerto Plata helped restore public confidence. Meanwhile, foreign residents in Havana joined active-service volunteers for the seat of war, prominent individuals denied Mexican involvement in the rebellion, and military battalions prepared to sail for Gibara and take the field in Cuba.

records.full_text: HAVANA, Nov. 30.—Late advices from St. Domingo report all quiet on the Haytien frontier. The rebel General Orgando was severely wounded in the recent skirmish. Colonel Hevin, another rebel, was a prisoner, and had been sentenced to be shot, at Azua.

records.headline: The Tribune prints Havana advices of November 30 from St. Domingo
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints Havana advices of November 30 from St. Domingo under the head 'Restoration of Peace and Revival of Trade': all was quiet on the Haytian frontier; the rebel General Ogando was severely wounded in a recent skirmish; Colonel Hevia, another rebel, was a prisoner, and had been sentenced to be shot at Azua; the government troops continued to pursue with great activity the dispersed bands of the Ogando faction, and had taken rebel prisoners; and the elections were progressing quietly throughout the country. Santa Anna intended to proceed from Puerto Plata to the capital; Colonel Fabens, and Messrs. O'Sullivan and Prime, had arrived at St. Domingo from New York; and the revival of trade at Puerto Plata had restored public confidence throughout the republic, and hopes were entertained of future peace and prosperity.

Santa Anna se proponía pasar de Puerto Plata a la capital; el coronel Fabens y los señores O'Sullivan y Prime habían llegado a Santo Domingo desde Nueva York; y la reactivación del comercio en Puerto Plata había restaurado la confianza pública en toda la república, y se abrigaban esperanzas de paz y prosperidad futuras.

records.headline: The Herald's Havana advices of November 30 report that all was quiet
records.summary_en: The Herald's Havana advices of November 30 report that all was quiet on the Haytian frontier. Drawn from government sources, the advices add that the rebel General Ogando was reported severely wounded in a recent skirmish; that Colonel Hevia, another rebel, was a prisoner and had been sentenced to be shot at Azua; that the government troops continued to pursue with great activity the dispersed bands of the Ogando faction and had taken many rebel prisoners; that the elections were progressing quietly throughout the country; that Santa Anna intended to proceed from Puerto Plata to the capital; that Colonel Fabens and Messrs. O'Sullivan and Prime had arrived at St. Domingo from New York; and that the revival of trade at Puerto Plata had restored public confidence throughout the republic, and hopes were entertained of future peace and prosperity.

records.headline: The Herald prints the prospectus of the Samana Bay Company
records.summary_en: The Herald prints the prospectus of the Samana Bay Company, published in New York for private circulation only. The passage opens in the middle of the Samaná affair, with word that Báez's own party is determined not to let him consummate anything of the kind. An opportunity is now being presented, the prospectus says, through the confidential agent of the Dominican Republic in New York, to secure a lease of the bay and peninsula of Samana, with all the eminent domain, rights and prerogatives of sovereignty now held and enjoyed by the republic, for a period of twenty years, paying for the same the sum of one hundred thousand dollars in gold annually in advance — it being understood that at the expiration of that period, or on the payment of the whole amount of the lease, to wit, two million dollars, the territory shall be finally transferred in fee and become the absolute property of the company. During the period of the lease the company will enjoy all privileges and immunities of sovereignty under the joint protection of the republics of St. Domingo and the United States; and in furtherance of the scheme the company proposes to raise at once the sum of one hundred thousand dollars in gold, and despatch its agent therewith to St. Domingo to tender the same to the Dominican authorities as the first instalment under the lease, and receive from them a formal ratification of the terms and conditions of the contract entered into with the Dominican agent in New York.

records.headline: In an editorial on the new political combinations now germinating
records.summary_en: In an editorial on the new political combinations now germinating in the countries south of the United States, the Ledger treats the Dominican Republic as an element in the complication: there the anti-Spanish party is on the eve of triumph over the government of President Báez, and the island, lying as it does between the Spanish islands of Cuba and Porto Rico, possesses ready means of danger to the Spanish forces which promise to be brought into play at an early day. In Mexico the question is already put forward as one of annexation of Cuba to the Mexican republic, the editorial says, while among the Dominicans, at home and in the revolutionary service in Cuba, it assumes the form of a West Indian confederation. No word of annexation to the United States is breathed by the Cuban revolutionists, and thus far President Céspedes seems to have carefully abstained from sending an authorized agent to Washington — a reserve the editorial traces to the opinion prevalent in Cuba that in former efforts to attain independence, whenever Cubans have confided their hopes and views to members of the Washington cabinet, from Fillmore's time down to that of Buchanan, they have been betrayed to the Spanish government. Whether the new combinations will crystallize into something effective and tangible, the Ledger concludes, yet remains to be seen.
records.summary_es: En un editorial sobre las nuevas combinaciones políticas que ahora germinan en los países al sur de los Estados Unidos, el Ledger trata a la República Dominicana como un elemento de la complicación: allí el partido antiespañol está en vísperas de triunfar sobre el gobierno del presidente Báez, y la isla, situada como está entre las islas españolas de Cuba y Puerto Rico, posee medios prontos de peligro para las fuerzas españolas que prometen entrar en juego en fecha temprana. En México la cuestión ya se plantea como la anexión de Cuba a la república mexicana, dice el editorial, mientras que entre los dominicanos, en el país y en el servicio revolucionario en Cuba, asume la forma de una confederación de las Indias Occidentales. Los revolucionarios cubanos no pronuncian palabra alguna de anexión a los Estados Unidos, y hasta ahora el presidente Céspedes parece haberse abstenido cuidadosamente de enviar un agente autorizado a Washington, reserva que el editorial atribuye a la opinión prevaleciente en Cuba de que en anteriores esfuerzos por alcanzar la independencia, cada vez que los cubanos han confiado sus esperanzas y pareceres a miembros del gabinete de Washington, desde los tiempos de Fillmore hasta Buchanan, han sido traicionados ante el gobierno español. Si las nuevas combinaciones cristalizarán en algo efectivo y tangible, concluye el Ledger, aún está por verse.

records.headline: Under the head 'What San Domingo Is,' the Spy describes the island of San Domingo
records.summary_en: Under the head 'What San Domingo Is,' the Spy describes the island of San Domingo and its resources. It has an area, with the smaller ones under its jurisdiction, of about 30,000 square miles, and is in extent about the size of Scotland. Every product of tropical and temperate climes can be grown there; it is known to be enormously rich in mineral wealth — for many years, while under the dominion of Spain, its annual tribute from the gold mines, consisting of one-fourth of the product, was about $5,000,000 — and in timber it is exceedingly rich, having every variety of cabinet woods; the flora includes the most valuable medicinal plants known to man. The Dominican territory could sustain in comfort at least ten million inhabitants, probably twice as many; there is an abundant water power; and it is geographically in the very centre of the Antilles. Commercially speaking, its position is worth everything to us, the writer says: we acquire Samana, one of the only half dozen harbors in the world in which the Great Eastern can ride, and secure the key and controlling position in the Gulf. The outlines given are, in the writer's judgment, what seems now the most honest in effort and most promising in result of all annexation schemes lately had before the public.
records.summary_es: Bajo el encabezado «Lo que es Santo Domingo», el Spy describe la isla de Santo Domingo y sus recursos. Tiene una superficie, con las islas menores bajo su jurisdicción, de unas 30.000 millas cuadradas, y en extensión es comparable a Escocia. Allí puede cultivarse todo producto de climas tropicales y templados; es conocida por su enorme riqueza mineral — durante muchos años, bajo el dominio de España, su tributo anual de las minas de oro, consistente en la cuarta parte del producto, fue de unos $5.000.000 — y en maderas es sumamente rica, con toda variedad de maderas preciosas; su flora incluye las plantas medicinales más valiosas que conoce el hombre. El territorio dominicano podría sostener con comodidad al menos a diez millones de habitantes, probablemente al doble; hay abundante fuerza hidráulica; y se halla geográficamente en el centro mismo de las Antillas. Comercialmente hablando, su posición lo vale todo para nosotros, dice el autor: adquirimos Samaná, uno de los escasos seis puertos del mundo en los que puede flotar el Great Eastern, y aseguramos la posición clave y dominante en el Golfo. Las líneas expuestas son, a juicio del autor, lo que parece ahora el esfuerzo más honesto y el resultado más prometedor de todos los planes de anexión presentados últimamente ante el público.

records.headline: An editorial in the Crescent argues for American expansion in the West Indies.
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Crescent argues for American expansion in the West Indies. It is intimated, the editorial says, that evidence may be produced to show that the populations of the most desirable of the West India islands, including Cuba and Porto Rico, are eager to solve the troublesome and at present gloomy problem of their destiny by annexation to the United States, and it dwells on the richness of the island of St. Domingo in mineral and agricultural resources. It is not to be supposed, the Crescent argues, that if the Dominican republic were annexed, Hayti would be content to remain, or would in any case long remain, outside of American jurisdiction. Dominica occupies the larger part of the territory, and contains the greater portion of the population, of the island of St. Domingo, of which the whole area is 28,000 square miles and the whole population 1,250,000; next to Cuba in point of population, this island is also, next to Cuba, the most beautiful and productive of the West Indies. And the value to American commerce of the trade which would be developed by the opening of this island to American enterprise by annexation is only less, the editorial says, than that which would result from the annexation of Cuba. The Crescent has no idea that any definite programme for these ends will be carried in the present Congress, but it expects that the subject will be a subject of increasing agitation during the incoming administration.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Crescent defiende la expansión estadounidense en las Indias Occidentales. Se sugiere, dice el editorial, que podrá producirse evidencia de que las poblaciones de las más deseables de las islas de las Indias Occidentales, incluidas Cuba y Puerto Rico, ansían resolver el problema trabajoso y actualmente sombrío de su destino mediante la anexión a los Estados Unidos, y se detiene en la riqueza de la isla de Santo Domingo en recursos minerales y agrícolas. No debe suponerse, argumenta el Crescent, que si la república dominicana fuera anexada, Haití se contentaría con permanecer, ni en ningún caso permanecería mucho tiempo, fuera de la jurisdicción estadounidense. Dominica ocupa la mayor parte del territorio, y contiene la mayor parte de la población, de la isla de Santo Domingo, cuya superficie total es de 28.000 millas cuadradas y cuya población total es de 1.250.000 habitantes; después de Cuba en población, esta isla es también, después de Cuba, la más bella y productiva de las Indias Occidentales. Y el valor para el comercio estadounidense del comercio que se desarrollaría con la apertura de esta isla a la empresa estadounidense mediante la anexión solo es menor, dice el editorial, que el que resultaría de la anexión de Cuba. records.headline: An item in the National Republican, beginning in mid-argument
records.summary_en: An item in the National Republican, beginning in mid-argument, denies the report that advices have been received from the highest official sources that President Báez and the Dominican people would accept unconditional annexation: no such proposition, it says, has been made. The mission of Mr. Angenard is a plain one, the item continues, with which he alone is entrusted, and its object is sought to be attained by none of the dubious ways of diplomacy; it is free from disguise or concealment, and is in no wise, directly or indirectly, connected with any of the speculations with which efforts are made to associate it. The envoy says the interference of any one with his purpose is wholly unwarranted, and as damaging as it is manifestly indelicate and improper. But it is asserted by several prominent Congressmen, the item adds, that the commission now here treating for an annexation of San Domingo are humbugs, and are in the interest of Dominicans and Americans who wish annexation in order to make money out of it.
records.summary_es: Una nota en el National Republican, que comienza a mitad de la argumentación, niega la versión de que se han recibido noticias de las más altas fuentes oficiales de que el presidente Báez y el pueblo dominicano aceptarían la anexión incondicional: no se ha hecho, dice, proposición alguna en ese sentido. La misión del señor Angenard es sencilla, continúa la nota, confiada a él únicamente, y su objeto se busca alcanzar por ninguna de las vías dudosas de la diplomacia; está libre de disfraz u ocultamiento, y no está conectada en modo alguno, directa ni indirectamente, con ninguna de las especulaciones con las que se intenta asociarla. El enviado afirma que la interferencia de cualquiera en su propósito es enteramente injustificada, y tan dañosa como manifiestamente indelicada e impropia. Pero varios congresistas prominentes aseguran, añade la nota, que la comisión que se encuentra aquí tratando de una anexión de Santo Domingo son unos farsantes, al servicio de dominicanos y estadounidenses que desean la anexión para enriquecerse con ella.

records.headline: A letter to the editor attacks Secretary of State Seward's shifting plans for St. Domingo
records.summary_en: A letter to the editor attacks Secretary of State Seward's shifting plans for St. Domingo, arguing that whether the form is intervention, a protectorate or annexation, the result would be enormous wealth for certain private individuals. The writer says President Baez, entrenched in his capital with civil wars to look after and exiles including Cabral returning, proposes through Seward to transfer to the United States the parts of his country over which he has no control.
records.summary_es: Una carta al editor ataca los cambiantes planes del secretario de Estado Seward para Santo Domingo, argumentando que, ya sea bajo la forma de intervención, de protectorado o de anexión, el resultado sería una riqueza enorme para ciertos particulares. El autor dice que el presidente Báez, atrincherado en su capital con guerras civiles que atender y exiliados como Cabral de regreso, propone por medio de Seward transferir a los Estados Unidos las partes de su país sobre las que no tiene ningún control.

[illegible] THE DOMINICAN QUESTION To the Editor of The Tribune SIR: The plans of the Secretary of State in regard to St. Domingo are many and various, but all tend in the same direction. When one form of action is ignominiously defeated in the House, he has substantially the same thing (at least so far as the interests of private parties are concerned) proposed in another shape. It makes little difference to him whether it is intervention, a protectorate," or annexation," which finally succeeds. Either will give enormous wealth to certain private individuals for whom Mr. Seward's benevolent nature seems to be painfully excited. I mean no reflection upon the persons who have secured Mr. Seward's very active assistance. records.headline: An editorial in the Tribune opens in mid-argument against the cession of St. Domingo
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Tribune opens in mid-argument against the cession of St. Domingo to the United States, holding that the beleaguered chief who pretends to cede the island has no more power to transfer it than Queen Isabella has at this moment to transfer Spain, and that the scheme would thus compel them to conquer the island. In the mean time, the editorial says, there is the 'Samana Bay Company' and the 'Alta Vela Guano Company,' rich and powerful in both countries: while the ceding and giving away is going on, land grants, gold mines, and guano islands may be made over to these gentlemen under the seal of the nation, and the President, too, his country being so ungrateful, might seek an honest recompense for all his toils by becoming a partner in the speculations of these good people. Besides all this, one of the conditions of the transfer is understood to be, as international law requires, that the United States shall pay the public debt of St. Domingo, and so soon as the former is made liable, the gentlemen of the ring will turn up with certificates of indebtedness. When the vaunted evidence of the willingness of the people of St. Domingo to be annexed comes to be produced, the Tribune predicts, it will likely be found to consist of nothing but the mutual assurances of these high contracting parties — of the waning President and 'his friends' on the one hand, and of the waning Secretary of State on the other.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Tribune se abre a mitad de la argumentación contra la cesión de Santo Domingo a los Estados Unidos, sosteniendo que el asediado caudillo que pretende ceder la isla no tiene más poder para transferirla que el que tiene en este momento la reina Isabel para transferir España, y que el plan obligaría así a conquistar la isla. Mientras tanto, dice el editorial, están la «Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná» y la «Compañía del Guano de Alta Vela», ricas y poderosas en ambos países: mientras sigue la cesión y la entrega, podrán hacerse a estos caballeros, bajo el sello de la nación, traspasos de concesiones de tierras, minas de oro e islas de guano, y el propio presidente, su país siéndole tan ingrato, podría buscar una honesta recompensa por todos sus trabajos haciéndose socio de las especulaciones de esta buena gente. Además de todo esto, se entiende que una de las condiciones de la transferencia es, como exige el derecho internacional, que los Estados Unidos paguen la deuda pública de Santo Domingo, y en cuanto aquel quede obligado, los caballeros de la camarilla aparecerán con certificados de deuda. Cuando se presente la tan pregonada evidencia de la disposición del pueblo de Santo Domingo a ser anexado, predice el Tribune, probablemente se encontrará que consiste únicamente en las mutuas seguridades de estas altas partes contratantes: del presidente en decadencia y «sus amigos», por una parte, y del secretario de Estado en decadencia, por la otra.

records.headline: A Washington letter attacks Secretary Seward's scheme for St. Domingo
records.summary_en: A Washington letter attacks Secretary Seward's scheme for St. Domingo, which shifted within weeks from a protectorate to annexation with no explanation offered for either. The writer argues that President Baez, entrenched in his capital with several civil wars to look after, has no more right to give his country to the United States than Seward would have to give the United States to Great Britain, and warns that the Samana Bay Company and the Alta Vela Guano Company would gain land, mines and guano while the United States took on the Dominican public debt.
records.summary_es: Una carta desde Washington ataca el plan del secretario Seward para Santo Domingo, que en pocas semanas pasó de un protectorado a la anexión sin que se ofreciera explicación alguna de ninguno de los dos. El autor sostiene que el presidente Báez, atrincherado en su capital con varias guerras civiles que atender, no tiene más derecho a entregar su país a los Estados Unidos que el que tendría Seward de entregar los Estados Unidos a Gran Bretaña, y advierte que la Samana Bay Company y la Alta Vela Guano Company ganarían tierras, minas y guano mientras los Estados Unidos asumían la deuda pública dominicana.

records.headline: A letter printed in the Herald gives an account, beginning in mid-course
records.summary_en: A letter printed in the Herald gives an account, beginning in mid-course, of Secretary Seward's Caribbean diplomacy: kings, who were disposed to negotiate for a free and neutral port at Samaná as a great steam centre, he made a dash for St. Thomas: he would have bought Samana also, but until the Dominican President was reduced to extremity he dared not attempt the dismemberment of the republic. That failed, the letter continues, and we now hear of annexation. Báez has purposely secured his loan in such a way as to keep up his government for two years, and by the end of that term he trusts to the development of the mining and industrial interests of the country for maintaining it without sacrificing Samana. The idea of annexation failed to alarm the people, the letter says, because it came in the form of a fraternal invitation, highly flattering to their self-respect, and if the project is followed up in that guise there will be no opposition worth mentioning to the measure. The country is quiet, though many arrests were made after the Seibo fiasco, and some twenty persons are held for examination on a charge of conspiracy; it is said that henceforth such attempts will be treated with the utmost rigor of the law, but before this system is put into effect Báez will proclaim a general amnesty, and only those who renew seditious efforts are to suffer the death penalty. The roads are bad beyond description; and before signing the drafts for the first $200,000 instalment of the loan, two engineers, brought from Europe for the purpose, made a scientific reconnaissance of the gold districts, to see whether there was sufficient promise of mineral wealth to secure the payment.
records.summary_es: Una carta publicada en el Herald ofrece un relato, que comienza a mitad de su curso, de la diplomacia caribeña del secretario Seward: reyes que estaban dispuestos a negociar un puerto libre y neutral en Samaná como gran centro de vapores, él se lanzó sobre Santo Tomás: también habría comprado Samaná, pero hasta que el presidente dominicano no se viera reducido al extremo, no se atrevía a intentar el desmembramiento de la república. Aquello fracasó, continúa la carta, y ahora oímos hablar de anexión. Báez ha asegurado su empréstito deliberadamente de manera que su gobierno se mantenga dos años, y al final de ese plazo confía en el desarrollo de los intereses mineros e industriales del país para sostenerlo sin sacrificar Samaná. La idea de la anexión no alarmó al pueblo, dice la carta, porque vino en forma de una invitación fraternal, muy halagadora para su amor propio, y si el proyecto se sigue en esa forma no habrá oposición digna de mención a la medida. El país está tranquilo, aunque se hicieron muchos arrestos tras el fiasco de Seibo y unas veinte personas están detenidas para ser examinadas por un cargo de conspiración; se dice que en adelante tales intentos serán tratados con el máximo rigor de la ley, pero antes de que este sistema entre en vigor Báez proclamará una amnistía general, y solo quienes renueven los esfuerzos sediciosos sufrirán la pena de muerte. Las carreteras están malas más allá de toda descripción; y antes de firmar los giros de la primera cuota de $200.000 del empréstito, dos ingenieros, traídos de Europa con ese fin, hicieron un reconocimiento científico de los distritos auríferos, para ver si había suficiente promesa de riqueza mineral que asegurara el pago.

records.headline: An editorial in the Herald lays down conditions for annexation
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Herald lays down conditions for annexation: if they mean business in this annexation scheme, the annexationists must discuss the affair at home and show that a valid majority of the people of the Dominican Republic desire the step to be taken: when this is done the Dominican government can make its application, and it will be considered without fear or favor. The Dominican Republic will be the great gainer by the step if it is ever taken, the editorial says, and we have no need to pay a high price for a very small article. As for Samaná, it has been in the market for sale under every administration St. Domingo has had since it separated from Hayti, and has not found a purchaser, and it has been before the world for settlement and population ever since Columbus struck the New World, in 1492, and its pestilential shores are as solitary now as they were three hundred and fifty years ago. Let the Dominican spoilsmen agitate at home, the editorial concludes: they can get nothing out of the United States Treasury under the new regime of honesty that rules there.
records.summary_es: Un editorial del Herald establece condiciones para la anexión: si hablan en serio en este plan de anexión, los anexionistas deben discutir el asunto en su propio país y demostrar que una mayoría válida del pueblo de la República Dominicana desea que se dé el paso: cuando eso se haya hecho, el gobierno dominicano podrá presentar su solicitud, y será considerada sin temor ni favor. La República Dominicana será la gran beneficiada por el paso, si alguna vez se da, dice el editorial, y no tenemos necesidad de pagar un precio alto por un artículo muy pequeño. En cuanto a Samaná, ha estado en venta bajo todas las administraciones que Santo Domingo ha tenido desde que se separó de Haití, y no ha encontrado comprador, y ha estado ante el mundo para su población y colonización desde que Colón llegó al Nuevo Mundo en 1492, y sus costas pestilentes están tan desiertas ahora como hace trescientos cincuenta años. Que los expoliadores dominicanos agiten en su país, concluye el editorial: no sacarán nada del Tesoro de los Estados Unidos bajo el nuevo régimen de honestidad que allí impera.

records.headline: The Herald prints what it says may be relied upon as exact and authentic
records.summary_en: The Herald prints what it says may be relied upon as exact and authentic — in point of fact, in sense and letter, the translation of Mr. Fabens' last official instructions. Báez so firmly believes that his views are also the accepted views in Congress, and he so firmly believes that they are also the accepted views of President Grant, that he has instructed Minister Fabens to confer with the incoming Secretary of State at as early a day as possible on the subject, and to take an early occasion to manifest to President Grant personally, and without the slightest reserve, the actual situation of the Dominican Republic, and to solicit the co-operation of the Washington Cabinet in the policy of creating a free and neutral centre of commerce in the Antilles. This knowledge, the Herald says, was imparted to the French, Italian and Danish consuls, if not officially at least distinctly, from the lips of the Dominican Secretary of State, in the course of a long conversation respecting various incorrect reports of revolutionary movements under the Ogandos, Marcos Adón and Luperón, which had never had existence, and from that the Secretary slid adroitly to the contradictory statements about the sale of Samana. 'None of you, Messieurs les Consuls, believe that there is any question of dismembering the republic,' said the Minister, with some warmth; 'and it is scarcely a secret from any of you that liberal propositions have been made to us to declare Samana a free and neutral port.' Such a measure, the French Consul replied, should command the sympathies of every maritime power.
records.summary_es: El Herald publica lo que dice que puede tenerse por exacto y auténtico: de hecho, en sentido y letra, la traducción de las últimas instrucciones oficiales del señor Fabens.
