records.headline: Continuing his account of St. Domingo, a Herald correspondent
records.summary_en: Continuing his account of St. Domingo, a Herald correspondent lists the island's strong places as the paper prints them: the fort of San Luis at Santiago de los Caballeros, the castle of San Felipe at Puerto Plata, the fort of San Francisco at Monte Cristi, the fort of Santa Barbara at Samaná and another fort at the same place, whose name is not legible in the passage; the custom houses at St. Domingo and its dependencies and at Samaná; the ports of St. Domingo, Azua, Samaná and Puerto Plata, licensed for commerce with foreigners; and numerous other ports and bays that could be used, among them Monte Cristi, Barahona, Las Calderas, La Romana and Manzanillo. The concessions granted by the government, he continues, are for a geological survey of the island; a steam line between New York and New Orleans and the ports of the island; the right to ship guano from Alta Vela; the right to build a railroad from Monte Cristi to Santiago, or from Santiago to the Yuna river, with a grant of land; the right to build a wagon road from Santiago to the coast; and a steamship line from the island to New York. The value of St. Domingo to the United States would unquestionably be incalculable, he writes, but the country, however willing it may be to become part of the North American confederation, is certainly at present in no condition to assume the important duties which attach to such relations, its institutions being entirely unknown to the people; it would therefore first be a wise policy to give them time to become familiar with them, where the window ends.

Las concesiones otorgadas por el gobierno, continúa, son para un estudio geológico de la isla; una línea de vapores entre Nueva York y Nueva Orleans y los puertos de la isla; el derecho a embarcar guano desde Alto Velo; el derecho a construir un ferrocarril de Monte Cristi a Santiago, o de Santiago al río Yuna, con una concesión de tierras; el derecho a construir un camino de carretas de Santiago a la costa; y una línea de vapores de la isla a Nueva York. records.headline: Writing from Porto Plata on September 6, 1869, the correspondent recalls that Columbus founded Isabella, the first European town
records.summary_en: Writing from Porto Plata on September 6, 1869, the correspondent recalls that Columbus founded Isabella, the first European town in the New World, near here, and that only ruins remain where it stood. He describes a country whose trade has been almost annihilated, with Porto Plata and St. Domingo City as its principal outlets and small trade also at Azua and Samana, and reports an unusually large tobacco crop, estimated at 100,000 quintals for export, shipped almost exclusively to Hamburg, with talk of a railroad from Santiago to carry it to the sea.
records.summary_es: Escribiendo desde Puerto Plata el 6 de septiembre de 1869, el corresponsal recuerda que Colón fundó cerca de aquí La Isabela, la primera ciudad europea del Nuevo Mundo, y que solo quedan ruinas donde estuvo. Describe un país cuyo comercio ha sido casi aniquilado, con Puerto Plata y la ciudad de Santo Domingo como sus principales salidas y un pequeño comercio también en Azua y Samaná, e informa de una cosecha de tabaco inusualmente grande, estimada en 100.000 quintales para la exportación, embarcada casi exclusivamente a Hamburgo, mientras se habla de un ferrocarril desde Santiago para llevarla al mar.
records.passage: of a primitive and feeble effort at agriculture satisfy the small demands for money. PORTO PLATA AND THE OPEN PORTS. The result of this condition of things is almost an entire annihilation of trade. This port and St. Domingo City are the only two principal outlets to the island. A very small trade is accomplished also at the open ports of Azua and Samana. Porto Plata is now the only port on the northern side of the island, and the proceeds of the Custom House here are the main source of revenue to the government. The town itself is small and very uninviting; it has a small harbor well protected by reefs; a vessel anchors some distance from the shore: all cargo is put on board the vessels or taken off by lighters, which cannot themselves approach the shore within fifty yards, owing to the shallowness of the water on the beach which sweeps in front of the town. The shippers have a very novel mode of conveying cargo from shore to lighters and vice versa. This is done by means of carts drawn into the water a sufficient depth by bullocks which are manoeuvred by ropes passing through the cartilage of the nose. All this trouble, inconvenience and expense could be saved by a pier run out to a sufficient depth of water to allow vessels to lie alongside. Although Porto Plata is one of the early towns of the Island the Spaniards, upon being driven out of the country, completely destroyed it. records.headline: In a statistical account of the Dominican republic's commerce
records.summary_en: In a statistical account of the Dominican republic's commerce that begins in mid-item, the Herald reports that American vessels freighted on the island and five British vessels also loaded; the value of the importation of provisions, flour and petroleum from the United States under the British flag was $40,000, and during the year 162 vessels, including those carrying the Dominican flag, arrived at St. Domingo, with a total of 12,203 tons. Its table for the year ending June 30 — the year itself is not legible in the passage — gives Puerto Plata exports of $696,463 against imports of $354,808, and totals of $788,838 in exports with an excess of exports of $53,471; several of the table's other figures are not legible in the passage and are not stated here. In the same year, the item adds, seven American vessels arrived in port with cargoes valued at $22,600; and during the quarter ending March 31, 1869, two American vessels arrived from St. Thomas in ballast and four British vessels from Boston, with cargoes valued at $20,000, the exports by the two American vessels being valued at $19,364 and by three British vessels at $14,855. The production of the island by the hand of man is small, the Herald continues, and the foreign trade is also limited, owing to the smallness of the population, which numbers not more than 200,000 souls; the territory under the jurisdiction of the Dominican republic embraces about two-thirds of the island of St. Domingo, or nearly 20,000 square miles.

Su tabla para el año terminado el 30 de junio — el año mismo no es legible en el pasaje — da para Puerto Plata exportaciones de $696.463 frente a importaciones de $354.808, y totales de $788.838 en exportaciones con un excedente de exportaciones de $53.471; varias de las demás cifras de la tabla no son legibles en el pasaje y no se consignan aquí. En el mismo año, añade la nota, llegaron a puerto siete buques estadounidenses con cargamentos valorados en $22.600; y durante el trimestre terminado el 31 de marzo de 1869, llegaron dos buques estadounidenses desde Santo Tomás en lastre y cuatro buques británicos desde Boston, con cargamentos valorados en $20.000, valorándose las exportaciones de los dos buques estadounidenses en $19.364 y las de tres buques británicos en $14.855. La producción de la isla por mano del hombre es pequeña, continúa el Herald, y el comercio exterior también es limitado, debido a la escasa población, que no pasa de 200.000 almas; el territorio bajo la jurisdicción de la República Dominicana abarca unas dos terceras partes de la isla de Santo Domingo, o cerca de 20.000 millas cuadradas.

records.headline: A letter from St. Domingo dated
records.summary_en: A letter from St. Domingo dated October 8, 1869 says the summary of Dominican feeling on annexation is 'ready and eager,' but that a painful fear lingers that Congress might refuse to receive the country. If Dominicans offered their country and were turned away, the writer warns, Baez and his party would be swept from power, so the invitation, he argues, must come from the United States.
records.summary_es: Una carta de Santo Domingo fechada el 8 de octubre de 1869 dice que el sentimiento dominicano sobre la anexión se resume en estar 'listos y deseosos', pero que persiste el temor doloroso de que el Congreso pudiera negarse a recibir al país. Si los dominicanos ofrecieran su país y fueran rechazados, advierte el autor, Báez y su partido serían barridos del poder, por lo que la invitación, sostiene, debe venir de los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: The dispatch gives the case of Mr. Davis
records.summary_en: The dispatch gives the case of Mr. Davis Hatch, a United States citizen who was living at Barahona as agent of a New York company interested in working salt mines. When government troops evacuated the port at the end of August, Hatch was taken with them to Azua and arrested, then brought to the capital and held in close confinement, then taken back to Azua, tried by court martial and sentenced to be shot. A messenger was at once sent back to Azua with a pardon for Hatch, and the dispatch says the anxiety of five days of suspense had a severe effect on his mind and health.
records.summary_es: El despacho expone el caso del señor Davis Hatch, ciudadano de los Estados Unidos que vivía en Barahona como agente de una compañía de Nueva York interesada en explotar minas de sal. Cuando las tropas del gobierno evacuaron el puerto a finales de agosto, Hatch fue llevado con ellos a Azua y arrestado, luego trasladado a la capital y mantenido en estricto confinamiento, y después devuelto a Azua, juzgado por un consejo de guerra y condenado a ser fusilado. De inmediato se envió un mensajero de regreso a Azua con un indulto para Hatch, y el despacho dice que la angustia de cinco días de suspense tuvo un efecto grave en su mente y su salud.

records.headline: In an editorial fragment that begins in mid-argument, the Herald argues
records.summary_en: In an editorial fragment that begins in mid-argument, the Herald argues for the bay of Manzanillo as the site for an American naval station: Monte Cristi and the noble bay of Manzanillo are on the dividing line, it argues, and the presence of a United States steamer would protect both governments in the act of transition; President Grant has it in his power to accept the use of a naval station at Manzanillo, which is peculiarly safe from hurricanes, is about as central as Samaná, and is the key to the great agricultural and mining regions of the east and the mountains of Cibao. The Stars of the Union, the paper continues, would not float a month over a naval station at Manzanillo before the chief provinces of the Dominican republic would openly declare for annexation, and the nearest half of the republic of Hayti would lose no time in profiting by the example; while these sections were passing a brief period of preparation under a provisional government as a Territory of the United States, the window ends. The fragment's Haytian half concerns the friends of Salnave, president of that division, against the partisans of Pimentel, who assert that their chief would put the question to a vote any day a United States agent will call to salute his flag and recognize his government.
records.summary_es: En un fragmento editorial que comienza a mitad de un argumento, el Herald aboga por la bahía de Manzanillo como sitio para una estación naval estadounidense: Monte Cristi y la noble bahía de Manzanillo están en la línea divisoria, sostiene, y la presencia de un vapor de los Estados Unidos protegería a ambos gobiernos en el acto de transición; el presidente Grant tiene en su poder aceptar el uso de una estación naval en Manzanillo, que es peculiarmente segura contra los huracanes, es casi tan céntrica como Samaná, y es la llave de las grandes regiones agrícolas y mineras del este y de las montañas del Cibao. Las estrellas de la Unión, continúa el periódico, no flotarían un mes sobre una estación naval en Manzanillo sin que las provincias principales de la República Dominicana se declararan abiertamente por la anexión, y la mitad más cercana de la república de Haití no perdería tiempo en aprovechar el ejemplo; mientras estas secciones pasaban un breve período de preparación bajo un gobierno provisional como Territorio de los Estados Unidos, termina la ventana. records.headline: In a historical essay on the island's two republics, the Herald explains
records.summary_en: In a historical essay on the island's two republics, the Herald explains that the republic of Hayti, which comprises the western third of the island, that being the area of the ancient French colony, displaced the name of St. Domingo for the more distinctive and historic appellation of Hayti, by which the natives introduced their island to Columbus. This uniformity of name between the island as a whole and the separate government of the western portion, the essay observes, often leads careless inquirers into confounding the Dominican republic with that of Hayti, though there is a wide difference between them: the Dominicans are Spanish in language, customs and habits of thought, though more democratic in sentiment and more tolerant in religion than the corresponding social levels usually found in the mother country. The Dominican republic, it adds, was the first American state which made the absolute equality of all races before the law a fundamental principle of its constitution, where the window ends. Of Hayti itself the essay recounts that its French section was the scene of the first successful struggle of the black race for political equality with the whites, and that the newly emancipated slaves discarded the colonial name of St. Domingo and restored the one known to the red race.
records.summary_es: En un ensayo histórico sobre las dos repúblicas de la isla, el Herald explica que la república de Haití, que comprende el tercio occidental de la isla, siendo esa el área de la antigua colonia francesa, desplazó el nombre de Santo Domingo por el apelativo más distintivo e histórico de Haití, con el que los nativos presentaron su isla a Colón. Esta uniformidad de nombre entre la isla en su conjunto y el gobierno separado de la porción occidental, observa el ensayo, lleva a menudo a los indagadores descuidados a confundir la República Dominicana con la de Haití, aunque hay una amplia diferencia entre ellas: los dominicanos son españoles en lengua, costumbres y hábitos de pensamiento, aunque más democráticos en sentimiento y más tolerantes en religión que los niveles sociales correspondientes que suelen hallarse en la madre patria. La República Dominicana, añade, fue el primer estado americano que hizo de la igualdad absoluta de todas las razas ante la ley un principio fundamental de su constitución, donde termina la ventana. De Haití mismo el ensayo relata que su sección francesa fue el escenario de la primera lucha exitosa de la raza negra por la igualdad política con los blancos, y que los esclavos recién emancipados desecharon el nombre colonial de Santo Domingo y restauraron el conocido por la raza indígena.

records.headline: Traordinary preparations now going on in the 'navy yards arc not
records.summary_en: According to the *Nashville Union and American*, extraordinary preparations in navy yards were reported to be for guarding the annexation of the Dominican Republic to the United States rather than for war with Spain over Cuba. The article stated that General Babcock, a confidential officer on Grant's staff, had settled the annexation conditions with San Domingo authorities, and the treaty—modeled after the Texas annexation—would be submitted to the Senate. Additionally, warships were sent to West Indies ports at President Baez's request to be present when the U.S. flag was hoisted, with opposition anticipated only from a revolutionary faction aided by Cabral.
records.summary_es: Según el *Nashville Union and American*, los extraordinarios aprestos en los astilleros navales respondían al propósito de asegurar la anexión de la República Dominicana a los Estados Unidos antes que a un conflicto armado con España a causa de Cuba. El artículo exponía que el general Babcock, edecán de confianza en el estado mayor de Grant, había acordado las cláusulas de anexión con las autoridades dominicanas, previéndose remitir al Senado el tratado —calcado del modelo de incorporación de Texas—. Se agregó asimismo que varios buques de guerra zarparon hacia las Antillas a requerimiento del presidente Báez para asistir al acto de izamiento del pabellón estadounidense, aguardándose resistencia tan solo de la facción rebelde auxiliada por Cabral.

records.full_text: THE New York Sun has discovered something out of which to manufacture a sensation. That paper says, editorially, in its issue of the 11th inst., that the extraordinary preparations now going on in the navy yards are not in expectation of war with Spain about Cuba, but simply to keep guard over the annexation of the Dominican Republic to the United States. The conditions of annexation have been fully settled between Gen. Babcock, confidential officer of Grant's staff, and the authorities of San Domingo. The treaty is similar to that for the annexation of Texas, and will be laid before the Senate when Congress opens. All members of the Dominican government and leading men among the people are anxious for annexation, and the approval of the Senate is confidently expected. The ships of war now going to the West Indies are sent at the request of President Baez and his advisers, so that there may be one or more in each port when the United States flag is hoisted. No trouble is expected from the people generally, and the only opposition would be from a revolutionary faction aided by Cabral. This may be something more than a mere sensation.

records.headline: A Washington letter in the Herald recounts the earlier course of the St. Domingo
records.summary_en: A Washington letter in the Herald recounts the earlier course of the St. Domingo negotiations, in which the annexation was on the eve of completion in 1865, having been wisely and prudently negotiated by Mr. J. Somers Smith, United States Commercial Agent at St. Domingo City; Mr. Frederick Seward was sent out in a United States war vessel with the necessary power and funds to arrange the preliminaries of the acquisition, but that gentleman made himself so absolutely offensive to Báez and his Cabinet that these gentlemen summarily declined to consider any of the propositions he had to lay before them. It is considered here, the letter continues, that the course being pursued in the negotiation is hardly that which should be adopted between two independent nations engaged in a matter of so great moment to both; it is thought that General Báez should send a commissioner to Washington to be a party to the negotiation here and to witness the ratification of the treaty — such gentlemen as the Minister of War, without doubt the most popular man on the island; the Minister of Justice, conversant with our language; and Gautier, Minister of Foreign Affairs, a gentleman of culture — where the window breaks off in the middle of the list. The St. Domingo question, the letter indicates, is now in a fair way of speedy and practical solution, both in the hands of the United States government and in the administration of Báez.

records.headline: A descriptive item on the island in the Marshall County Republican reports
records.summary_en: A descriptive item on the island in the Marshall County Republican reports that the imports to the United States for 1868 were valued at 760,000 from Hayti and $33,000 from San Domingo, the principal articles being raw cotton, sugar, coffee, dye woods, gum arabic, hides and cocoa. San Domingo is divided into five provinces; there is an army of 20,000 troops of all arms, and a small navy; the language of the people is Spanish, and the religion Roman Catholic; the government is that of a president, with a Congress consisting of two branches. Hayti and Dominica were several times united, the item recounts, but were divided by revolution, and the country has been for twenty years in a state of chronic revolution, the Dominicans having long since concluded that there can be no peace until they are taken under the flag of the United States; for several years they have proposed to cede the Bay of Samana to the United States, and now offer the whole republic. The other part of the island, the Republic of Hayti, contains 10,000 square miles and a population of 600,000; in considering the question of the acquisition of Dominica, the item concludes, it is necessary to consider also the probable acquisition of Hayti, where the window ends.

records.headline: In an editorial on the annexation of St. Domingo, the Herald argues
records.summary_en: In an editorial on the annexation of St. Domingo, the Herald argues from the letter it published yesterday from its Washington correspondent that the St. Domingo question, both in the hands of the United States government and in the administration of Baez, at the head of affairs in the Dominican republic, is in a fair way towards a speedy and practical solution. The project of annexation, the editorial continues, has long been entertained by the two contending parties in that republic, and the small faction of Cabral revolutionists who oppose it would doubtless favor it, as they favored it when in power a few years ago, if they were now in power. The people generally are reported to be well disposed to the step: President Baez was assured during last summer that the inhabitants of Porto Plata, Santiago, Lavega and Cotuy are agreed on this point. Baez, of course, could not with propriety initiate this annexation scheme any more than he could consent to the leasing of the Bay of Samana or to the plan of a protectorate to be exercised by the United States government, unless that government, as well as his own people, were unquestionably willing and ready to accomplish it; and without entering into the details of the preliminary negotiations which have from time to time been informally conducted between the two independent governments, the editorial expresses the opinion that it is now highly probable — where the window breaks off in mid-sentence, the editorial continuing beyond it.

Se informa que el pueblo en general está bien dispuesto hacia la medida: el presidente Báez recibió seguridades el verano pasado de que los habitantes de Puerto Plata, Santiago, La Vega y Cotuy están de acuerdo en este punto. records.headline: In a later window of the same Herald editorial on annexation
records.summary_en: In a later window of the same Herald editorial on annexation, the paper argues that the abolition of slavery in the United States and the establishment of civil and political equality have removed certain objections which used to stand in the way of annexation, and there will be no difficulty on this score in governing Dominica and Hayti as territories until they shall have ripened into States. It will not be long, the editorial continues, before American capital, which has already turned its eye towards the incalculable, undeveloped resources of this beautiful and fertile island, and American enterprise, which has established Dominican banking, railway and steamship companies — in fact, actually laying the egg out of which annexation seems about to be hatched — and, in due time, emigration from the United States, from Europe and, perhaps, from China, will redeem the island of St. Domingo from revolutionary chaos and open multiplied markets to its increased productions. Moreover, the annexation of St. Domingo carries the consideration that Cuba is within but a few hours' sail of the waters in which a really formidable American fleet is now being gathered; whatever may be the upshot of the Cuban insurrectionary movement, the editorial concludes by asking how long it will be before all the West India islands shall form the encircling belt of the Gulf of Mexico as an inland lake of the United States — this is merely a question of time.

No pasará mucho tiempo, continúa el editorial, antes de que el capital estadounidense, que ya ha vuelto su mirada hacia los incalculables y no explotados recursos de esta hermosa y fértil isla, y la empresa estadounidense, que ha establecido compañías dominicanas de banca, ferrocarriles y vapores — de hecho, poniendo realmente el huevo del que la anexión parece a punto de salir — y, a su debido tiempo, la emigración desde los Estados Unidos, desde Europa y, tal vez, desde China, rediman a la isla de Santo Domingo del caos revolucionario y abran mercados multiplicados a sus aumentadas producciones. records.headline: In a narrative of the annexation negotiations that begins in mid-item
records.summary_en: In a narrative of the annexation negotiations that begins in mid-item, the Tribune relates that Mr. Seward was pleased at the prospect of having the great Bay of Samana for the United States, and supposed that its acquisition would be pregnant of good results; the people of Santo Domingo did not relish the project and were at one time on the point of driving Baez out of power, and he deemed it the more prudent course to suspend for a season all negotiations. But as soon as General Grant was introduced to power, Mr. O'Sullivan began to work again, and in a short time has encouraged President Baez to perfect a scheme for the annexation of the island. The people of San Domingo have, on divers occasions of late years, manifested, in a remarkable degree, their love of liberty and independence: they resisted the last invasion of Spain for two years, until, in fact, the Spanish Treasury became poorer by some twenty-four millions and 15,000 of the soldiers of the Peninsula had died of disease and in battle; the natives, it is said, fought like heroes, and, on one occasion, 5,000 Spanish troops were terribly harassed by about 50 Dominicans. The Government of Spain became so hard pressed for money that they were compelled to appeal to the liberality of the rich men of Havana, where the window ends.

records.headline: The Evening Telegraph reprints a Havana despatch: all the Dominican leaders
records.summary_en: The Evening Telegraph reprints a Havana despatch: all the Dominican leaders are anxious for annexation to the United States in consideration of a reasonable amount of money. Baez, Pimentel, and Cabral, however much they may disagree on other points, are united on this, and the only question is which shall get the money: Baez is the constitutional President of the republic, and it is stated that he is ready to open negotiations whenever the Congress of the United States shall make the necessary appropriations; his rivals, however, are equally well disposed, the partisans of Pimentel scattering among the people handbills favoring annexation with the United States, and Cabral hoping to be in power when the bargain is concluded, so that he may get the money. In Hayti, the despatch adds, the only opponents to selling out to the United States are parties under European influence, while Salnave and Saget, the rival Presidents, both are willing and anxious to dispose of their claims; the entire island, it is said, can be purchased for $2,000,000, where the window ends. The despatch is set against Spain's refusal to sell Cuba, which the paper says we really have a longing for, on any terms.

records.headline: The Herald prints a letter received at Havana from St. Domingo
records.summary_en: The Herald prints a letter received at Havana from St. Domingo, dated the 10th, showing that all the Dominican leaders, including Baez, Pimental and Cabral, are pledged to the annexation of the island to the United States. President Baez is ready to open negotiations when assured that the Congress of the United States is ready to make the necessary appropriation to meet the requirements of the occasion; the people of St. Domingo are opposed to the dismemberment of the republic, and favor the annexation of the country in its entirety. The partisans of Pimental are scattering handbills throughout the island favoring the project of annexation, and the only opposition exhibited is that derived from European sources. The republic of Hayti is following suit as regards annexation, the letter adds, and Salnave and Saget are loud in its favor; it is said the entire island can be purchased by the United States for $2,000,000, the same figure other papers of the week printed for the same report.
records.summary_es: El Herald imprime una carta recibida en La Habana desde Santo Domingo, fechada el día 10, que muestra que todos los líderes dominicanos, incluidos Báez, Pimental y Cabral, están comprometidos con la anexión de la isla a los Estados Unidos. El presidente Báez está listo para abrir negociaciones cuando tenga la seguridad de que el Congreso de los Estados Unidos está listo para hacer la asignación necesaria para cubrir las exigencias de la ocasión; el pueblo de Santo Domingo se opone a la desmembración de la república, y favorece la anexión del país en su totalidad. Los partidarios de Pimental reparten hojas sueltas por toda la isla a favor del proyecto de anexión, y la única oposición manifestada es la derivada de fuentes europeas. La república de Haití sigue el ejemplo en cuanto a la anexión, añade la carta, y Salnave y Saget se pronuncian ruidosamente a su favor; se dice que la isla entera puede ser comprada por los Estados Unidos por $2.000.000, cifra que es la misma impresa para el mismo informe en otros periódicos de la semana.

records.headline: In an editorial, the Herald looks forward to the annexation of St. Domingo
records.summary_en: In an editorial, the Herald looks forward to the annexation of St. Domingo as an accomplished fact within six months: General Grant is heartily in favor of the proposed annexation, it declares, and from this fact, and his unmistakable sympathy in behalf of Cuban independence, and from his desire to see the Darien Canal a thing accomplished under his administration, we have the landmarks of a projected American policy of the grandest proportions. We shall not in the least degree be surprised, the editorial continues, if before the expiration of six months the annexation of the magnificent island of St. Domingo, or Hayti, shall be an accomplished fact. The recent departure of General Babcock, accompanied by General Rufus Ingalls, on board the United States steamer Albany, from New York, bound for the island with instructions from President Grant regarding the course he shall pursue in the pending negotiations of our government with President Baez, of the Dominican republic, assures us of the energetic prosecution of the purpose; and within the same period we look first for the independence of Cuba, and secondly for an application from the republic, a la Texas, for admission into the Union, which will not be denied, where the window ends.

records.chapter_es: La lucha por la anexión estadounidense
records.full_text:
ST. DOMINGO.

The steamer Tybee, Captain Delanoy, from St. Domingo the 16th and Porto Plata the 19th, arrived here yesterday. She brings letters and papers up to date of sailing. The compliments of the purser are acknowledged.

Political Affairs—The Position of President Baez—What Is Thought of Annexation—European Influence at Work.

ST. DOMINGO, Nov. 16, 1869.
There is a party here so deeply implicated in the interior complication of the Dominican republic and so well situated to convey false statements to the foreign press that it is nearly impossible for the simple truth to obtain a hearing. For example, it went from here, on "consular" authority and endorsement, that the important and central town of Santiago had declared against Baez and that this government was on the eve of downfall. Your correspondent happened to be in company with the very general who was named as the leader of this fictitious revolution, and at that very date he was on his way to this city with a committee of the leading men of La Vega, Santiago and Puerte Plata, who came to this city to congratulate President Baez on the advance of public industry "which had resulted from the perfect tranquillity which for two years has reigned throughout the country." "We do not count the Caco guerillas on the frontier as a serious disturbance of the public peace." General Luccano went on to say although the labors and the vigilance demanded for their repression has caused the government some inconvenience, as everywhere in the great body of our territory enterprise has taken root and the general products of the country largely increased.

Speaking of enterprises, the proposal for introducing 2,000 German emigrants in the coffee and mining regions is not yet acted upon, but it most probably will be, as it is believed that M. Landais, the French Consul, gives it his warm though secret support, and he is a strong man with the Baez Cabinet, and is also a man of liberal ideas. It is reported, or rather whispered cautiously inside the consular ring, that Mr. Martin Hood, the former British Consul here, is to be sent back "to cure the Dominicans of the annexation fever." He is and was of old very obnoxious to the whole Baez party, for various personal as well as political reasons, and some members of the Senate have advised the President in advance not to receive him officially.

Major K. H. Perry, the newly appointed United States Consul, arrived in the Tybee last week, and raises his flag to-day. He was warmly welcomed by Baez.

I have heretofore attempted to explain the curious triangular antagonism of Baez, Cabral and Pimentel, each of whom accuses the other of an "intrigue to dismember the republic by selling its most precious section"—the peninsula of Samaná—to the United States, and all of whom are, more or less, openly working and praying for annexation.

The proposition of the English Company for a free port at Manzanilla with all the public lands within ten leagues of it for colonization, is probably a movement to head off annexation. The proposal is to establish the Germans, "or other European immigrants" in parties of thirty families, in a continuous chain of settlements, giving to each man a three acre block in the village or a twenty acre farm in its vicinity. These villages, beginning at their fine seaport of Manzanilla and taking in some sites with fine water power for manufacturing purposes, would extend to the old gold mines of San Rafael, which the French and Spanish governments agreed should be closed about a century ago. The promoters of this colonization project forget that German immigrants to America are almost invariably intensely loyal to the land of their adoption and would be more likely to swell than to oppose the vote for annexation. They also forget when debating on the "unwieldy expansion" of the United States—a favorite European phrase—that the telegraph and railways have compacted our national limits into much firmer and more manageable bounds than the Union exhibited at the beginning of this century, before either Florida or the States of the lower Mississippi were added to the old thirteen. Baez himself put it rather neatly at the introduction of the new United States Consul, Major Perry, to the Ministers and consular corps, at the President's morning reception. "San Francisco is now very much nearer the government at Washington," he observed, "than Mobile or New Orleans was forty years past, and all these islands are within easier reach of the commerce (he did not say arms, but he thought it) of all its seaboard States than those of the Atlantic with those of the Gulf of Mexico or either of them with the States of the Pacific."

This remark shows that Baez has looked at the map and reflected upon the beauties of a free exchange of products.

The Tybee takes on 3,000 bales of tobacco in transit for Europe, that is if the horrible roads will allow of getting down to port in time.

The London Alta Vela Company have made their arrangements for taking out from 1,000 to 5,000 tons of guano per month. The works started by the Baltimore firm, which Spain turned adrift so unceremoniously, come in very nicely for the London company. It pays a royalty of five dollars per ton on all the guano exported, and the magnitude of its arrangements is the best proof of the value of the American discovery. There can be no mistake about it, for, as I wrote you at the time, Mr. Lawson, one of the present owners, made a careful exploration of the island, accompanied by a chemist and other guano savans, with laborers and all other appliances for a thorough examination. On this he offers a royalty of one pound per ton and takes the island.

It is hardly worth the space to say that for the last six weeks the Cacos have had an uncomfortable time on the Dominican frontier. Two of their officers—Curul and Volla—have been captured, and their great Dominican leader, the brave but misguided General Cabral, narrowly escaped by leaving his horse and throwing himself down an almost impracticable ravine.

These border raids are amplified into undue importance by the St. Thomas and Jamaica press, out of spite for Baez's supposed intention to cede Samaná to the United States for a naval station, which, of course, is regarded as the entering wedge of annexation.

No American vessel in port except the steamer Tybee. Europe does all the business here.

records.headline: Under the heading "Dominica," the Chicago Tribune writes that the departure of General Babcock
records.summary_en: Under the heading "Dominica," the Chicago Tribune writes that the departure of General Babcock for San Domingo, with sealed instructions from the President, in response to the proposition of President Baez to submit the question of annexation to the people of the Dominican Republic, indicates a belief on the part of our administration that a thirty-eighth star is soon to be added to the National cluster. The Dominican Republic, comprising the eastern three-fifths of the island, has maintained during nearly its whole history a separate political existence, whether as colony or republic, owing to its original settlement by the Spanish, while the remainder of the island was French; its area is stated in the passage in a comparison — about half as large as the State of Indiana, and more than twice the size of Massachusetts — the square mileage itself not being legible. Its population numbers 140,000, of whom one-tenth are whites and the rest are of African descent and mixed; the country is chiefly valuable for magnificent mountain forests of cabinet woods, ebony, mahogany, and live-oak. Its constitution as a republic was modelled upon that of the United States; it abolished slavery on achieving independence, and has never made any political distinction on account of color. Secret negotiations for the cession of the island to the United States were made during Pierce's administration, with Santana, the predecessor of Baez; indeed, the dissatisfaction with Santana, fomented — where the window breaks off.
records.summary_es: Bajo el encabezado «Dominica», el Chicago Tribune escribe que la partida del general Babcock para Santo Domingo, con instrucciones selladas del presidente, en respuesta a la proposición del presidente Báez de someter la cuestión de la anexión al pueblo de la República Dominicana, indica una creencia por parte de nuestra administración de que pronto se añadirá una trigésimo octava estrella al conjunto nacional. La República Dominicana, que comprende los tres quintos orientales de la isla, ha mantenido durante casi toda su historia una existencia política separada, ya como colonia o república, debido a su asentamiento original por los españoles, mientras que el resto de la isla era francés; su área se expresa en el pasaje en una comparación — cerca de la mitad del tamaño del estado de Indiana, y más del doble del tamaño de Massachusetts — no siendo legible la cifra misma de millas cuadradas. Su población asciende a 140.000, de los cuales una décima parte son blancos y el resto son de ascendencia africana y mixtos; el país es valioso principalmente por magníficos bosques montañosos de maderas preciosas, ébano, caoba y roble vivo. Su constitución como república fue modelada sobre la de los Estados Unidos; abolió la esclavitud al lograr la independencia, y nunca ha hecho distinción política alguna por motivo de color. Negociaciones secretas para la cesión de la isla a los Estados Unidos se hicieron durante la administración de Pierce, con Santana, predecesor de Báez; en efecto, la insatisfacción con Santana, fomentada — donde la ventana se interrumpe.

records.headline: In the Chicago Tribune's long descriptive feature, Port au Prince
records.summary_en: In the Chicago Tribune's long descriptive feature, Port au Prince, sometimes called Port Republican, stands at the hinge of two bays, and Baez's capital, the city of Santo Domingo, is on the south side. Yet, while Dominica is the more eligible and open country and far larger than its mountain rival, Hayti has as many people as New Jersey, while Dominica has no more than Rhode Island, the writer observing that the cause of this difference lies in the superior energy and fecundity of the French race, as the passage puts it. Under the heading "Dominica and its people," the feature relates that the eastern, superior, and yet weaker half of the island contains the historical relics: the first colony founded in the New World was Isabella, on its north coast, near the present town of Puerto Plata, founded by Columbus himself; his brother, Bartholomew Columbus, founded the city of Santo Domingo in 1494, as the passage dates it; Columbus' son Diego built the cathedral here. It rose into importance and riches long prior to the greater conquests of Spain; here Cortez was a notary before he dreamed of Mexico; the Spanish made the island the key to the whole of their possessions in the New World, and it entered upon a wonderful career of gold and silver mining, stock raising, sugar and coffee growing, and commerce. The original people, called the Caribs, were all killed off speedily, and this prosperity only ceased when Peru and greater conquests on the mainland were achieved, where the window ends.

Sin embargo, mientras Dominica es el país más elegible y abierto y mucho más grande que su rival montañoso, Haití tiene tanta gente como Nueva Jersey, mientras que Dominica no tiene más que Rhode Island, observando el autor que la causa de esta diferencia radica en la energía superior y la fecundidad de la raza francesa, según lo expresa el pasaje. Bajo el encabezado «Dominica y su pueblo», el reportaje relata que la mitad oriental, superior y sin embargo más débil de la isla contiene las reliquias históricas: la primera colonia fundada en el Nuevo Mundo fue Isabella, en su costa norte, cerca de la actual ciudad de Puerto Plata, fundada por el propio Colón; su hermano, Bartolomé Colón, fundó la ciudad de Santo Domingo en 1494, según lo fecha el pasaje; Diego, hijo de Colón, construyó aquí la catedral. Surgió en importancia y riquezas mucho antes que las mayores conquistas de España; aquí Cortés fue notario antes de soñar con México; los españoles hicieron de la isla la llave de todas sus posesiones en el Nuevo Mundo, y entró en una maravillosa carrera de minería de oro y plata, cría de ganado, cultivo de azúcar y café, y comercio. El pueblo original, llamados los caribes, fueron todos extinguidos rápidamente, y esta prosperidad solo cesó cuando se lograron el Perú y mayores conquistas en el continente, donde termina la ventana.

records.headline: The Chicago Tribune's descriptive feature continues: Puerto Plata
records.summary_en: The Chicago Tribune's descriptive feature continues: Puerto Plata is the chief place of resort for American vessels, for we do the majority of the trade both for Hayti and Dominica. The cattle of Dominica are celebrated; its mahogany and sandal wood are the best in the tropics; many American colored men have settled in this republic, and, but for the civil war, none would ever have quitted it. The bay of Samana, the feature continues, is the outlet of the Yuna River, and is fifty miles long and from fifteen to twenty miles wide; the ocean entrance to it is only a mile wide, and is commanded by an old fort, while high mountains enclose both shores. Twenty-five miles up the bay, upon an inlet to the north, is the town of Samana, the inlet very deep and almost land-locked; the bay has been compared both to the Bay of Naples and to the Chesapeake, to the former for its dazzling tropical and mountain scenery, to the latter for its innumerable wild fowl. This bay has been pronounced the key to the Gulf of Mexico; fine beds of coal surround it, and navigators say that the future route to Darien and Mexico will be by the Mona Passage, just outside of Samana. Samana town, the passage adds, is no town at all, a mere semi-detached peninsula with town vestiges upon it, and the site is swampy; Bonaparte planned a city near Samana, to be called Napoleon, and had the site surveyed. The window ends as the feature turns toward Hayti, mid-sentence: while the State of Dominica contains all the most ancient and hallowed relics of St. Domingo, Hayti —

records.headline: An unnamed speaker tells the Chicago Tribune, in its final window
records.summary_en: An unnamed speaker tells the Chicago Tribune, in its final window, that "we have been besieged from the Spanish end of the island these four or five years, to annex Domingo, bodily, and twice or thrice during the same period we have been asked to extend our protectorate over Hayti." Baez has offered to use the whole influence of his party to make the United States proprietors of Dominica, accepting it as a territory of the United States, to be, in course of time, a candidate for admission into the Union as a State, and for no other price than the assumption of its small debt; this offer is open to us at present. With a foothold established there, the Haytian end of the island would be soon anxious for annexation, and Salnave would be only too glad to be the instrument of consigning Hayti to a place among the United States. Asked whether there is any party in either end of St. Domingo violently opposed to annexation, the speaker answers: none; the Jacmel party of Hayti have been, at times, incensed with us for permitting our Consuls and Agents to take sides with Salnave, and we have reason to believe that the enemies of Baez are the enemies of the United States; but everybody in St. Domingo who owns a foot of land wants us to come. The offer, the speaker adds, is not entirely from the natives: there are many Americans, with large interests, in both republics — merchants, planters, and lumber-sawyers — whose property would appreciate immensely if the United States shielded the land, where the window ends.
records.summary_es: «Hemos sido asediados desde el extremo español de la isla estos cuatro o cinco años, para anexar a Domingo corporalmente, y dos o tres veces durante el mismo período se nos ha pedido extender nuestro protectorado sobre Haití», dice un orador sin nombre al Chicago Tribune en la ventana de cierre de su reportaje descriptivo. Báez ha ofrecido usar toda la influencia de su partido para hacer a los Estados Unidos propietarios de Dominica, aceptándola como territorio de los Estados Unidos, para ser, con el tiempo, candidata a la admisión en la Unión como estado, y por ningún otro precio que la asunción de su pequeña deuda; esta oferta nos está abierta al presente. Con un punto de apoyo establecido allí, el extremo haitiano de la isla pronto estaría ansioso por la anexión, y Salnave estaría más que contento de ser el instrumento de consignar a Haití a un lugar entre los Estados Unidos. Preguntado si hay algún partido en cualquiera de los extremos de Santo Domingo violentamente opuesto a la anexión, el orador responde: ninguno; el partido de Jacmel, en Haití, ha estado, en ocasiones, indignado con nosotros por permitir que nuestros cónsules y agentes tomen partido con Salnave, y tenemos razones para creer que los enemigos de Báez son los enemigos de los Estados Unidos; pero todo el que en Santo Domingo posee un pie de tierra quiere que vengamos. records.summary_en: In a historical sketch of the Dominican leaders, the Herald relates that Pimentel, Provisional President in the war of deliverance, deputed Don Pablo Pujol to Washington to proffer a naval station at Samaná, and that Mr. Seward would not receive Pujol, nor recognize the restored Dominican republic even as a belligerent. Cabral, who had shared the struggle with Pimentel, is the sketch's Putnam of Dominican history, as Báez is its Talleyrand; the window traces his breach with Pimentel, his entry into St. Domingo city with the title of Protector when the Spaniards retired to their ships, his resignation in favor of Báez in 1866 and his later succession to the presidency, and breaks off in mid-sentence as it turns to the Samaná offer he was induced to accept at a price.

Cabral, que había compartido la lucha con Pimentel, es en el bosquejo el Putnam de la historia dominicana, como Báez es su Talleyrand; la ventana sigue su ruptura con Pimentel, su entrada en la ciudad de Santo Domingo con el título de Protector cuando los españoles se retiraron a sus barcos, su renuncia a favor de Báez en 1866 y su posterior sucesión en la presidencia, y se interrumpe a mitad de frase cuando pasa a la oferta de Samaná que se le indujo a aceptar a un precio.

records.headline: A United States Navy lieutenant writing from the island reports that he has travelled some two hundred miles since
records.summary_en: A United States Navy lieutenant writing from the island reports that he has travelled some two hundred miles since leaving Santo Domingo, crossing the mountains and now working on the northern side under his instructions, keeping a full journal of what he has seen. He says that wherever he went he received the kindest attention, even in the mountains, and that he might have travelled with any amount of money without fear of being molested, though he also saw misery and destitution that would make the heart ache; the island's resources, he writes, are inexhaustible and want only population and a more industrious people to develop them.
records.summary_es: Un teniente de la Marina de los Estados Unidos que escribe desde la isla informa que ha viajado unas doscientas millas desde que salió de Santo Domingo, cruzando las montañas y trabajando ahora en el lado norte según sus instrucciones, llevando un diario completo de lo que ha visto. Dice que dondequiera que fue recibió la atención más amable, incluso en las montañas, y que podría haber viajado con cualquier cantidad de dinero sin temor de ser molestado, aunque también vio una miseria y una indigencia que daban dolor al corazón; los recursos de la isla, escribe, son inagotables y solo necesitan población y un pueblo más industrioso para desarrollarlos.

records.headline: A special despatch reports that the United States steamer Albany sailed
records.summary_en: A special despatch reports that the United States steamer Albany sailed for Santo Domingo on Wednesday afternoon carrying three commissioners who go to take formal possession of Samaná Bay as an American station; the Albany was loaded with heavy ordnance for coast fortifications, and will take nearly a regiment of infantry and a company of artillery at the Dry Tortugas. The sending of the commissioners, the despatch adds, is looked upon as paving the way for the annexation of the Dominican Republic, the negotiations entered into last August having progressed so far as to substantially provide that San Domingo shall be annexed as a State, without going into Territorial form.
records.summary_es: Un despacho especial informa que el vapor estadounidense Albany zarpó hacia Santo Domingo el miércoles por la tarde con tres comisionados que van a tomar posesión formal de la bahía de Samaná como estación americana; el Albany iba cargado de artillería pesada para fortificaciones costeras, y recogerá en las Dry Tortugas casi un regimiento de infantería y una compañía de artillería. El envío de los comisionados, añade el despacho, se considera el paso que abre el camino a la anexión de la República Dominicana, pues las negociaciones entabladas en agosto pasado han avanzado hasta el punto de disponer sustancialmente que Santo Domingo sea anexado como Estado, sin pasar por la forma territorial.

records.headline: The President's views come in a Herald account that begins in mid-item
records.summary_en: The President's views come in a Herald account that begins in mid-item with the choice between the sale of Samaná and a lease of it for from fifty to one hundred years. The President does not think an immediate acquisition of St. Domingo desirable, for various reasons, among them the great difference in the habits and tastes of the people of that country and our own. Under a trial lease of the bay for a term of years, he believes, the Dominicans would within three or four years be so convinced of the superiority of the American style of government that they would be not only willing but clamorous for annexation, which would then follow. The account adds that the lease, with the possession of the entire Dominican portion of the island in prospect, meets with great favor in official circles, and that the bay of Samaná commands one of the main avenues between the Atlantic Ocean and the Caribbean Sea; the window ends in mid-sentence on the peninsula's valuable woods and its vein of coal.

records.full_text:
Policy of the Administration in the West Indies.

We published yesterday a glowing account of the reported lease of the Bay of Samana, island of St. Domingo, by the United States government, which was communicated to us, and also a letter from Washington of the same tenor, announcing the arrival at New York of General Babcock and the Dominican Commission on board the United States steamer Albany, for the purpose of negotiating a fifty years' lease with our government for the Bay of Samana. There is some discrepancy between the two statements. One has it that the bargain has been completed, and that the United States flag now floats over that portion of the Dominican territory; while the other says the Commission has arrived for the purpose of negotiating a lease. Then, again, it is stated the territory embraces an area of two thousand five hundred square miles; when it appears from a reliable communication from our correspondent at Samana that it is only estimated at two hundred and twenty-five to two hundred and forty square miles—that is, the length is about thirty miles and the breadth eight miles, including the islands along the coast.

It is particularly worthy of notice, too, that in the same paper in which these statements appear, that is, in our issue of yesterday, was published the news of St. Domingo having negotiated a loan with British capitalists, for seven hundred and fifty-seven thousand pounds sterling, on the condition that St. Domingo hypothecates the entire proceeds of receipts from imports and exports at the ports of St. Domingo and Puerto Plata, as well as the royalties from the working and export of guano from the island of Alta Vela, and in addition to the revenues arising from coal and other minerals, and mahogany and other woods, from the peninsula of Samana. If this be true the cunning Dominicans are playing a nice game with both the United States and the British, and all on this strip of territory called Samana, with its bays, harbors and islands. If they would only sell out some other, or some of the same privileges to France, Spain and other European countries, it would make as nice a muddle in the future as any one could wish to see. This Samana business has all the appearance of a big job or, may be, a number of jobs.

But why lease the Bay of Samana at all? Why give a hundred and fifty thousand dollars in gold a year for fifty or a hundred years for a lease? It may be said, and indeed it is said, this is only an entering wedge for the ultimate acquisition of Samana or the whole island. What a miserable policy for a mighty republic like this to enter upon! What wretched peddling! It is utterly unworthy any great nation, and particularly the United States, which is the dominating Power of this hemisphere. If we want Samana, or any part of the island of St. Domingo, let us buy it and have no further trouble about the matter, or any possible dispute hereafter. Our government appears to be the tool of any insignificant ruler or country or clique of speculators. It seems incapable of a comprehensive policy, of acting with foresight with regard to the future or of appreciating the commanding position this republic holds over all questions pertaining to the countries of America. Its peddling, narrow-minded and timid course is enough to make every American citizen feel ashamed of his government.

The most curious and significant thing about this Samana business is that the administration, or rather the Secretary of State, appears very desirous of making a great fuss about it just now, and of representing that leased possession as more important than the island of Cuba. If we relied upon the glowing accounts given of the Bay of Samana and the official action so far concerning it, we might suppose it the most valuable possession in the Antilles. Indeed, it has been stated that this bay would be of more advantage to the United States than the annexation of Cuba. Is this absurd statement another dodge to cover up the weakness and miserable policy of the administration relative to Cuba? Does the government suppose it can blind the American people by any such wretched subterfuge? Yes, let us have the Bay of Samana; but let us get it in a proper way; let us buy it, and not pay tribute to a few negroes or mulattoes for permission to use it. Yes, let us have the whole island if that suits our policy and it can be made useful. We go as far as the farthest in our desire to extend the area and usefulness of our country. But let it be remembered that St. Domingo is sparsely settled by little more than a hundred thousand negroes and mulattoes, while Cuba has a million and a half inhabitants, and out of that number seven or eight hundred thousand of the white European race. Let it be remembered that the island of St. Domingo is desolated and produces little, while Cuba is one of the most, if not the most, productive country on the globe. The Bay of Samana may be a fine harbor, and may prove of value to us; but it lies on the eastern and outer verge of the whole of the West Indies, and is almost fifteen hundred miles from the nearest point of the United States. Cuba has many as fine or finer harbors, and some of them are almost within sight of the United States. The whole island stretches along and faces our border. It commands the entrance to the Gulf of Mexico; it dominates the channel of Yucatan, which connects the gulf with the Caribbean Sea, and it controls the windward passage at the east end, and consequently nearly all the navigation of the West Indian group. The idea of comparing the value of Samana with Cuba is simply ridiculous. Cuba, for its productions and trade, and from its important position, geographically considered, is worth far more to the United States than the whole of the rest of the West Indies put together. So much, then, for the speculative and glowing accounts of Samana and the supremely absurd comparison of it with the rich and highly important island of Cuba.

In connection with this subject it will not be out of place to notice the peculiar position the administration occupies at present on the Cuban question. Looking at the refusal of the Secretary of State to give Congress the information asked for about Cuba, we are compelled to infer that negotiations are still going on or have been revived with Spain for the cession of the island. The conduct of Mr. Fish cannot be accounted for on any other ground. We hope it may be so, and that the terrible, bloody drama and work of devastation now going on in Cuba may be soon stopped. Of course our government is honest in the matter, should we be right in this supposition. But is Spain honest? Are not Prim and his associates humbugging our Minister at Madrid and our weak Secretary of State? Do they not still cling to the hope of crushing the Cubans, and that by temporizing with the United States? And then, if successful, would they not tell their faithful ally that, the trouble being over, Spanish honor and pride would forbid any further negotiation for the cession of Cuba? In short, would they not laugh at us for our folly, and should we not have to coolly pocket the insult? Mr. Fish may have confidence in his Spanish friends, but we have not. We hope Congress, therefore, will stand no nonsense or unnecessary palaver, but will bring this question to a practical issue at once, and that in favor of Cuban independence and annexation.

records.full_text:
SAMANA BAY. OUR FOOTHOLD IN THE ANTILLES. Full Description of Samana Bay and the Land Adjoining—Capacity, Extent, Climate, Soil and Productions of the Prospective Territory.

SAMANA, Dec. 16, 1869.

The Stars and Stripes are floating to-day over the Gibraltar of the Antilles, in token and testimony of sovereign possession. Leaving to other pens the details of the brief but impressive ceremony of assuming dominion in the name and behalf of the United States, let us take a rapid survey of our new acquisition.

FIRST IMPRESSION.

Entering the Bay of Samana with the United States steamer Albany, whose commander, Captain George B. Balch, had the pleasant charge of planting the Flag of the Union on this latest addition to its territory, a long succession of bold and verdant heights charm the eye by their varied and romantic beauty. Deep coves, each a fine harbor in itself, indent and divide into picturesque promontories these lofty and rounded hills, and back of them tower, like giant sentinels on eternal guard over this outpost of American supremacy in the Antilles, the mountains of Pilon and Diavolo, the one nearly 2,000 feet, the other fully 1,300 feet in height, and forming striking landmarks for the mariner. The soft climate, which “has no winter in its year,” and the never fading verdure, always glowing with the rich tints and breathing the sweet fragrance of rosy June, lent a finishing charm to the enchanting effect of the beautiful landscape. To one fresh from the leafless dreariness of Northern coast scenes in November this delicious atmosphere and lavish variety of graceful forms and vivid colors was like a vision of Arcadia, and a closer observation only serves to confirm the impression that Samana will soon become a favorite resort for invalids and pleasure hunters fleeing from the cold and windy rigors of a northern winter. The placid bay, with its winding shores and numerous islands offer eloquent invitation to boating, bathing and fishing parties.

NUMEROUS HAVENS.

The bay shore of Samana is so rich in fine sheltered coves, protected by boldly projecting headlands, that the Dominicans love to say that “every farmer in Samana may have a good seaport of his own;” but there are several of such marked excellence that they demand special notice. We are no sooner fairly within the bay, with its enclosing shores visibly defined on both sides from the deck of a ship, than the port of Cacao rounds back into an inviting sweep under the commanding heights of the same name, on which the Spaniards, during their last occupation, had traced out the plan of a strong fortification. “A battery and a monitor would hold this point, protect the bay and keep out the whole fleet of Spain,” said an officer of some experience not long since, when dilating on the value of this outpost to American progress; but he did not state the number and calibre of the guns of the proposed battery.

Passing Cacao and leaving behind the “coal depots” of former negotiations, another beautiful cove opens to view, having Punta del Serio (Lily Point) as its western arm of demarcation. This is the Carenero Chiquito, a famous and favorite resort of pirates in the reign of the buccaneers in these seas for the repair of their vessels. Hence its name of Carenero—careening place.

Between Punta Serio and Punta Garda sets back the deep, well sheltered and easily defended inlet which General (then Major) McClellan selected for a United States naval station. A cay, or inlet, off the entrance of this inner bay is called—and the bay itself as well—Careneo Grande, which the Spaniards used as a coal depot, and protected by a battery, which vanished with them.

Passing Punta Gorda, with the Paloma islet on the other hand, we come suddenly on the town of Santa Barbara, the capital, so to speak, of the Peninsula of Samana. It is a straggling village, built too much on the crescent of low ground at the edge of the bay, but it has a pretty tree-embowered effect when seen from the bay, as many cottages, surrounded by fruit trees, have been planted on the hill sides, and seem to look cosily out on the sparkling waters, the bright little islands and the long embracing arms of their own bay shores with dreamy satisfaction. Beyond Santa Barbara are several other fine coves, of which those of Capuza and Corozo are as much distinguished for their healthy position and crystal springs as for their safe and commodious landing places.

EXTENT OF CESSION.

The territory ceded to the United States may be stated in round numbers as averaging eight miles in breadth by a length of nearly thirty miles. The area has been variously estimated at from 225 to 240 square miles—the latter calculation including the islands along the coast. Counting in some superior landing places on these islands, which the Spaniards valued very highly as general depots, the peninsula of Samana has a seaboard line of nearly 100 miles, presenting a series of good harbors that can scarcely be matched in any similar space in all tropical America for the general service of our growing trade. Our new domain is so nearly an island that up to the close of the last century coasting craft passed from Samana Bay to the Atlantic through the Gran Estero, at the head of what has become a peninsula by the filling up of the channels which formerly traversed the low isthmus now connecting it with the main island. This isthmus is about five miles across, and forms the western limit of Samana, and one who knew how such things are done declares that two companies from any of our colored regiments would reopen the channel in one season if commanded by an officer of the engineer corps, and so complete the water boundary of our new possession, besides cutting off ninety miles of navigation around the peninsula for vessels from the Yuna region, bound to Puerto Plata or Monte Cristi. The river Yuna falls into the head of Samana bay and the side channels of its delta interlace with the outlet of the old canal tracks that formerly cut through the isthmus and brought the navigation of that river and one of the most fertile districts in the Antilles directly to a port on the Atlantic. Within ten miles of this delta, down the bay, the much debated coal formations of Samana crop out in numerous places, but they seem to have never had a careful scientific examination.

SOIL AND PRODUCTION.

For its limited extent the country presents a great diversity of feature and a large range of production. A range of hills run down the centre of the peninsula from west to east, growing more sharp and lofty as it nears and passes Santa Barbara, until it finally culminates in the two great mountain peaks before named of El Diavolo and Pilon. From these hills issue abundant springs of purest water, and there are few indeed, so rugged as not to produce full crops of fruit and coffee. The rapid and hardy growth of limes and oranges astonishes even those familiar with the luxuriance of tropical vegetation. It would be a superior orchard that would yield as many bushels of apples to the acre as the same area in Samana will produce of oranges. Its pineapples are celebrated and its cocoanuts for abundance, but the whole island is rich in fruits, and it is not in Samana alone that clusters of fifty or sixty full grown cocoanuts may be taken three times a year from a single tree. They thrive on the poorest soil and require next to no trouble in planting and rearing. Sugar, indigo, cocoa (for chocolate), make generous returns. Almost every family gathers coffee enough for its own use from little gardens, and often have two or three hundred pounds picked by the children for sale. In these patches of half-tilled ground one sees a dozen or two neglected coffee bushes struggling for life with a wilderness of corn, sweet potatoes, squash, corn, ocra, egg plant, beans and tomatoes, planted any how and at all seasons, yet contriving to bear and furnish a supply of fruits and vegetables the year around to its thriftless owners. What system and industry might do for human comfort in this coffee garden of ours, only five days' steam from New York, it is pleasant to contemplate. Some American settlers declare that ten acres in coffee, with an extra five acres for a cow pasture and provision field, will keep a family as comfortably as a one hundred acre farm in New England. However that may be, there is now an open chance to make a fair trial at Samana, where the best of new land for coffee planting can be had within five miles of a seaport for from three to five dollars per acre.

THE CLIMATE

of Samana is much like the benign, uniform temperature of the south side of Cuba. From Janury to June it is one long period of bloom and bright weather, with an occasional shower in the first and last weeks of this pleasant season. Through the summer and fall months they have copious rains in Samana, rather a larger quantity than the general average in Cuba and Hayti, say the settlers from other parts of the island, but two or three days together of heavy rain and clouds is considered a hard and unusual visitation. Frost and the sharp chilling northeasters of New York and New England March weather is wholly unknown. There are plenty of people in Samana who have never seen ice except as a matter of commerce for table luxury.

THE AMERICAN FREEDMEN AT SAMANA

number about 400 souls all told, and form at least one third of the entire population of our new territory. They are delirious with joy at the idea of their coffee kingdom being taken up by Uncle Sam. On the 6th December, 1492, Columbus landed on the western coast of the island of Hayti, and on the anniversary of that day, 377 years afterwards, the free flag of the United States was raised over the long oppressed country; but perhaps not one descendant of the old Indian possessors was alive to be present at this auspicious day. The whole race was exterminated by Spanish oppression in all the Antilles.

SAMANA BAY. OUR FOOTHOLD IN THE ANTILLES. Full Description of Samana Bay and the Land Adjoining—Capacity, Extent, Climate, Soil and Productions of the Prospective Territory.

SAMANA, Dec. 16, 1869.

The Stars and Stripes are floating to-day over the Gibraltar of the Antilles, in token and testimony of sovereign possession. Leaving to other pens the details of the brief but impressive ceremony of assuming dominion in the name and behalf of the United States, let us take a rapid survey of our new acquisition.

FIRST IMPRESSION.

Entering the Bay of Samana with the United States steamer Albany, whose commander, Captain George B. Balch, had the pleasant charge of planting the Flag of the Union on this latest addition to its territory, a long succession of bold and verdant heights charm the eye by their varied and romantic beauty. Deep coves, each a fine harbor in itself, indent and divide into picturesque promontories these lofty and rounded hills, and back of them tower, like giant sentinels on eternal guard over this outpost of American supremacy in the Antilles, the mountains of Pilon and Diavolo, the one nearly 2,000 feet, the other fully 1,300 feet in height, and forming striking landmarks for the mariner. The soft climate, which “has no winter in its year,” and the never fading verdure, always glowing with the rich tints and breathing the sweet fragrance of rosy June, lent a finishing charm to the enchanting effect of the beautiful landscape. To one fresh from the leafless dreariness of Northern coast scenes in November this delicious atmosphere and lavish variety of graceful forms and vivid colors was like a vision of Arcadia, and a closer observation only serves to confirm the impression that Samana will soon become a favorite resort for invalids and pleasure hunters fleeing from the cold and windy rigors of a northern winter. The placid bay, with its winding shores and numerous islands offer eloquent invitation to boating, bathing and fishing parties.

NUMEROUS HAVENS.

The bay shore of Samana is so rich in fine sheltered coves, protected by boldly projecting headlands, that the Dominicans love to say that “every farmer in Samana may have a good seaport of his own;” but there are several of such marked excellence that they demand special notice. records.summary_en: A letter from St. Thomas dated December 10, 1869 reports that President Baez has leased the Bay of Samana to the United States for fifty years at $160,000 a year, with $60,000 a year more to Baez personally as secret service money, wherever he may be. It says the first year's rent has been paid, United States colors were hoisted on December 6 and saluted by the war steamer Albany, Baez received $150,000 as three years of his salary in advance, and his government received $80,000 worth of arms and munitions, to be deducted from the rent in yearly installments.

records.headline: The Evansville Journal's account, beginning in mid-report, states
records.summary_en: The Evansville Journal's account, beginning in mid-report, states that when the matter was satisfactorily settled and the agreed payment made, the Albany, with the commissioners and one of President Báez's staff, sailed to the Bay of Samaná to take formal possession of the waters and peninsula in the name of the United States, and that on the 6th of December the United States flag was hoisted on the island of Corenero, in the bay, amidst general joy on the part of the inhabitants. The lease of Samaná is already stated for fifty years, at $130,000 in gold per annum, and the Journal notes the heavy freight the hold of the Albany contained. The same column carries the Herald's report that the government of St. Domingo has negotiated a loan for nearly $4,000,000 in gold, for the repayment of which the revenues of the ports of St. Domingo and Puerto Plata, to the amount of $53,000 per annum, and the royalties produced from the export of guano from the island of Alta Vela, and the duties from coal and mahogany from the peninsula of Samaná are pledged.
records.summary_es: El relato del Evansville Journal, que comienza a mitad de la noticia, afirma que cuando el asunto quedó satisfactoriamente resuelto y se hizo el pago acordado, el Albany, con los comisionados y un miembro del estado mayor del presidente Báez, zarpó hacia la bahía de Samaná para tomar posesión formal de las aguas y la península en nombre de los Estados Unidos, y que el 6 de diciembre la bandera estadounidense fue izada en la isla de Corenero, en la bahía, en medio del regocijo general de los habitantes. El arrendamiento de Samaná se fija ya en cincuenta años, a $130,000 en oro por año, y el Journal señala la pesada carga que contenía la bodega del Albany. La misma columna trae el informe del Herald de que el gobierno de Santo Domingo ha negociado un empréstito de casi $4,000,000 en oro, para cuyo pago están pignorados los ingresos de los puertos de Santo Domingo y Puerto Plata, hasta la suma de $53,000 por año, y las regalías producidas por la exportación de guano de la isla de Alta Vela, y los derechos sobre el carbón y la caoba de la península de Samaná.

records.headline: The closing window of the Herald's long essay on the island
records.summary_en: The closing window of the Herald's long essay on the island gives the terms on which, it says, the United States is to assume the possession of the Dominican republic: a Territorial government identical with the other Territorial governments within the jurisdiction of the United States, the Dominican people first deciding by vote to allow such possession, the United States assuming the public debt and other obligations of the Dominican government, amounting to one million dollars, and paying for their State property one million dollars more. The essay recalls that our government sent out commissioners in July last, who returned in October expressing their belief that the Dominicans are desirous of annexation and that the island is worth possessing, and predicts that, 'Dominica once a Territory of the United States, Hayti will soon seek our protection,' Salnave already looking with favor upon annexation and having several times sought the protection of the American flag, while the newly accredited Minister from Hayti, General Alexander Tate, is said to favor annexation — the man who, in 1861, offered his services to Mr. Lincoln to aid in the organization of colored troops. The window ends in mid-sentence, on the peace that possession will bring 'to a people long distracted.'
records.summary_es: La ventana final del largo ensayo del Herald sobre la isla ofrece los términos en que, dice, los Estados Unidos han de asumir la posesión de la república dominicana: un gobierno territorial idéntico a los demás gobiernos territoriales bajo la jurisdicción de los Estados Unidos, decidiendo primero el pueblo dominicano por voto permitir tal posesión, y asumiendo los Estados Unidos la deuda pública y demás obligaciones del gobierno dominicano, que ascienden a un millón de dólares, y pagando un millón de dólares más por sus propiedades estatales. El ensayo recuerda que nuestro gobierno envió comisionados en julio pasado, que regresaron en octubre expresando su convicción de que los dominicanos desean la anexión y de que la isla merece ser poseída, y predice que, «siendo Dominica territorio de los Estados Unidos, Haití pronto buscará nuestra protección», pues Salnave ya mira con favor la anexión y ha buscado varias veces la protección de la bandera americana, mientras que el recién acreditado ministro de Haití, el general Alexander Tate, según se dice, favorece la anexión: el hombre que, en 1861, ofreció sus servicios al Sr. Lincoln para ayudar en la organización de tropas de color. La ventana termina a mitad de frase, con la paz que la posesión traerá «a un pueblo largo tiempo agitado».
