records.full_text:
A DOMINICAN OFFICER'S REPLY TO GEN. TATE.

Col. G. X. Franco, a Dominican officer, writes to THE TRIBUNE in reply to to Gen. Tate, who, as the embassador of Salnave, he regards as the natural enemy of Gen. Cabral. Regarding the annexation vote he says: "That the vote in favor of annexation is legal is false. This is proved by the insurrection of the people at Puerto Plata, their manifesto against annexation, and the blood that flowed upon the occasion." Col. Franco further says the statement made by Gen. Tate that "Cabral has only a few hundred men" is false. "Cabral has thousands of the best men of the Republic in his ranks, and holds the whole of the Province of the South, which contains from 35,000 to 40,000 inhabitants. In that part of the Republic there are 14 different communities. In the North, Gens. Pimentel, Cabrera, Valerio, and others are operating, and now hold eight settlements. They have, likewise, a large number of soldiers. In the East there are many political refugees, who are, every now and then, fighting the Government troops. In the Homenage Fortress at San Domingo are imprisoned more than 235 persons. Does Gen. Tate think that a country can be legally annexed under such circumstances? The movement begun at Puerto Plata is the most important that has occurred in the Republic, and it has ramifications in all parts of the Republic. I will guarantee that in a very short time Buenaventera Baez will be away from San Domingo City."

records.headline: A San Domingo annexation bill failed again to gain consideration
records.summary_en: A San Domingo annexation bill failed again to gain consideration in Washington, and its sponsor was to make another attempt the next day under a suspension of the rules: the bill provides for the annexation of St. Domingo as the Territory of Dominica, with the consent of the Dominicans, and for the payment of $1,850,770, and no more, to liquidate the debt of the new Territory.
records.summary_es: Un proyecto de anexión de Santo Domingo volvió a no lograr consideración en Washington, y su autor haría otro intento al día siguiente bajo suspensión de las reglas: el proyecto dispone la anexión de Santo Domingo como Territorio de Dominica, con el consentimiento de los dominicanos, y el pago de $1,850,770, y no más, para liquidar la deuda del nuevo Territorio.

records.summary_en: Mr. Fabens, the new Minister Plenipotentiary from St. Domingo, brings the recent annexation election returns complete, the Herald reports on information from J. W. Currier, the Dominican Consul General at New York: the acts contain 15,110 signatures for annexation to 111 against, the largest vote cast in the republic for twenty-six years; the only material opposition, it says, is on the Haytian frontier, where lawless bands are accused of guerrilla tactics and of being instigated by the British and Spanish consuls at Port au Prince to defeat annexation.

GRANT ASSUMES THE RESPONSIBILITY. Hayti was desolating the Dominican frontiers with lawless guerilla raids, and the Dominican forces were worn out with harassing marches and irregular payments. Baez was forced to choose between Europe and the United States. European friends, and even European mediation for his relief from Hayti, were certainly within his reach, but not compatible with the proposed relations at Washington. In this dilemma President Grant assumed the responsibility of retaining the Dominican State within the American system. Samana was to be put into the possession of the United States, and one year's rent ([illegible]) paid over at once to the Dominican Executive. The [plebiscite?] was immediately to follow the receipt of this aid from Washington, and the declared will of the Dominican people would govern the action of the Dominican Executive. records.headline: The translated Dominican presidential message in this window
records.summary_en: The translated Dominican presidential message in this window argues that existing interests point to the United States as the natural protector of the Dominican republic, that the desire of leading political figures in the provinces brought the two cabinets into closer union and led to two contracts with a Washington commission, and that selling Samaná alone could not secure the country's future: whatever sum it brought would assure only a short existence and might awaken claims that, if satisfied, would frustrate economic salvation or, if thwarted, breed rebellion — a point the large property-holders and lovers of peace understood.
records.summary_es: El mensaje presidencial dominicano traducido en esta ventana sostiene que los intereses existentes señalan a los Estados Unidos como protector natural de la república dominicana, que el deseo de figuras políticas importantes de las provincias acercó a los dos gabinetes y condujo a dos contratos con una comisión de Washington, y que vender Samaná por sí sola no podría asegurar el futuro del país: cualquier suma obtenida garantizaría solo una existencia breve y podría despertar pretensiones que, de satisfacerse, frustrarían la salvación económica o, de frustrarse, engendrarían rebeliones — punto que entendieron los grandes propietarios y los amantes de la paz.

records.summary_en: Mr. Perry's long communication to Secretary Fish was read to the Senate's special committee, in which Perry said he had acted only for the interests of the United States and of President Grant's policy. He reported being told that Cazneau was running the whole Dominican government and represented large land interests, and he described the negotiations with President Baez, including a proposal, which he protested, to draw up two separate papers, one to control the election in St. Domingo and another for the United States government.

records.summary_en: This editorial fragment, opening in mid-argument, urges annexation as a war measure against Spain: with St. Domingo annexed, Spanish Cuba will be flanked by American guns, and the acquisition of Samaná, a strategic point commanding the Antilles, will show Spain that the United States is prepared for war; once St. Domingo is under the American flag, the paper argues, even Spanish arrogance will hardly venture a quarrel, the surest way to prevent war being to show that you are prepared for it.

records.summary_en: This window opens with Senate testimony on Dominican sentiment: an unnamed witness says he mingled with the people at Samaná, Puerto Plata and twenty or thirty miles back from St. Domingo City to learn their sentiment; that Cabral and all his party are in favor of annexation but want to have a hand in it, a judgment he bases on conversations with Cabral's strongest friends in the city; and that any party opposing annexation in possession of the island would be too weak to make organized opposition, two-thirds or three-fourths of the inhabitants being in favor; the window then opens the testimony of Babcock, a United States engineer officer stationed at Washington since the close of the war, who went to St. Domingo first in July as a special agent with written instructions from the State Department.

records.headline: Baez, Fablos, and Cazeneau proposed to make Babcock a grant of land at Samana
records.summary_en: The *Chicago Tribune* reported on the negotiations involving Babcock, Sackett, Fablos, Cazeneau, and Baez, noting that the final treaty closely resembled the one drafted in the U.S. State Department. According to the excerpt, Babcock and Sackett rejected Cazeneau's proposal for a secret treaty, and Babcock declined a land grant at Samana offered to him by Baez, Fablos, and Cazeneau. The report also details Babcock's correspondence with Cazeneau—shared with President Grant—and actions regarding the American flag and coaling station at Samana following the treaty's signing.
records.summary_es: El *Chicago Tribune* dio cuenta de las negociaciones mantenidas entre Babcock, Sackett, Fabens [Fablos], Cazneau [Cazeneau] y Báez, señalando que el texto final del tratado concordaba sustancialmente con el redactado en el Departamento de Estado de los Estados Unidos. Conforme al extracto, Babcock y Sackett desestimaron la propuesta de Cazneau de concertar un tratado secreto, en tanto que Babcock declinó una concesión de tierras en Samaná que le brindaron Báez, Fabens y Cazneau. La relación detalla además la correspondencia sostenida entre Babcock y Cazneau —elevada al presidente Grant— y las resoluciones sobre el izamiento del pabellón estadounidense y la instalación del apostadero de carbón en Samaná tras la firma del convenio.

records.headline: The Herald editorializes on the Senate inquiry into Mr. Hatch's claim
records.summary_en: The Herald editorializes on the Senate inquiry into Mr. Hatch's claim against the Báez government, an inquiry that has brought up the whole Dominican question and the overtures for annexation: whatever Hatch's guilt or innocence of opposing annexation among the Dominicans, the prominent fact, it argues, is that an American citizen was imprisoned, tried and sentenced to death without cause yet shown, while prominent officials knew of it by written and verbal notice and apparently winked at the outrage; had he been a British subject, Báez would never have imprisoned him, and the editorial closes by noting Hatch's arrival on the steamer De Soto from Havana, suffering nervous prostration from his incarceration.

records.headline: President Grant's letter of June 27, printed here, answers an inquiry
records.summary_en: President Grant's letter of June 27, printed here, answers an inquiry about General Babcock's mission: Babcock did not exceed Grant's written or verbal instructions in connection with the Confidential Basis; he was sent to San Domingo to ascertain the wishes of the Dominican people and government as to annexation and, if he found them favorable, the terms on which they desired it; the Confidential Basis he brought back was not binding on either government unless each chose to continue the negotiations, and was null and void unless accepted and carried into effect; Grant also directed the Navy Secretary to have the commander of the United States steamer Seminole seize the Telegrafo on the high seas and send her to Baltimore for adjudication, she having interfered with American merchant shipping, and he closes that Babcock's conduct meets his entire approval.
records.summary_es: La carta del presidente Grant del 27 de junio, aquí impresa, responde a una consulta sobre la misión del general Babcock: Babcock no excedió las instrucciones escritas ni verbales de Grant en relación con la Base Confidencial; fue enviado a Santo Domingo a averiguar los deseos del pueblo y del gobierno dominicanos en cuanto a la anexión y, si los hallaba favorables, los términos en que la deseaban; la Base Confidencial que trajo consigo no obligaba a ninguno de los dos gobiernos salvo que cada uno decidiera continuar las negociaciones, y era nula si no se aceptaba y se llevaba a efecto; Grant también ordenó al secretario de Marina que el comandante del vapor estadounidense Seminole apresara al Telégrafo en alta mar y lo enviara a Baltimore para adjudicación, por haber interferido con la navegación mercante estadounidense, y cierra afirmando que la conducta de Babcock merece su aprobación entera.

records.headline: A war in Dominica might embroil the world, the Herald argues
records.summary_en: A war in Dominica might embroil the world, the Herald argues in this editorial fragment: opening in mid-argument, it denies as untrue an offensive and defensive alliance between China and Hayti — in which case Russia, the friend and ally of St. Domingo because of Dominican friendliness to the United States, would make a demonstration on China's northern boundary — professes no opinion on Hindustan, and argues that with the great numbers of Chinese and Japanese immigrants in the West Indies the question of war in Dominica deserves grave consideration, the window closing in mid-sentence.

records.headline: Ample power to renew negotiations with the American Government for a treaty of annexation
records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on August 4, 1870, that the Dominican government retained ample power to renew annexation negotiations with the United States and propose modifications to address opponents' objections. It noted that the U.S. protectorate had been extended for one year from July 1, 1870, providing the Dominicans with a guaranteed shield against internal revolution, tensions with Hayti, and European intervention. Additionally, the newspaper stated that President Baez and his ministers expressed regret over attacks against President Grant and General Babcock regarding the affair, while dismissing charges made against themselves by unfamiliar critics.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó el 4 de agosto de 1870 que el gobierno dominicano conservaba plenas facultades para reanudar las negociaciones de anexión con los Estados Unidos y proponer modificaciones encaminadas a salvar los reparos de la oposición. Destacó que el protectorado estadounidense había sido prorrogado por un año a partir del 1 de julio de 1870, brindando a los dominicanos un escudo garantizado frente a revoluciones intestinas, desavenencias con Haití e intervenciones europeas. Además, el periódico consignó que el presidente Báez y sus ministros lamentaron los ataques dirigidos contra el presidente Grant y el general Babcock a propósito de este asunto, desestimando los cargos que detractores desconocidos formularon en su contra.

records.full_text: Col. Fabens (who was the bearer to this Government of the news of the rejection of the treaty) returns in the Tybee to the United States, and in his capacity of Dominican Minister to Washington he is clothed with ample power to renew negotiations with the American Government for a treaty of annexation, and to propose such modifications of the old treaty as circumstances may demand, in order to meet within reasonable limits the objections of the opponents of the measure. It is some consolation to the Dominicans, under the disappointment which naturally they feel at the turn things have unexpectedly taken, that the United States protectorate of this country has been extended for one year from the 1st July, 1870; for this is a guarantee to them of immunity thus far, both from intestine revolutionary troubles and foreign invasion. Their relations with Hayti are not at present of the most friendly kind, but they feel that while this protectorate lasts they are safe from troubles in that quarter, and also that no European Power will presume to repeat the experiment which Spain tried a few years ago.

records.headline: The Herald's remedy for St. Domingo's troubles is annexation
records.summary_en: The Herald's remedy for St. Domingo's troubles is annexation: Cabral is doing his utmost to embarrass President Báez, with President Saget of Hayti expected to aid Cabral because Báez favors the Salnave party against Saget, and the only way to end these bloody dissensions, the paper argues, is the annexation of either one or both of the island's republics to the United States; the lost opportunity to acquire St. Domingo on fair terms is regretted, and with it under the American flag, the paper claims, the disturbances convulsing Haytians and Dominicans would finally end and a rich, fruitful tract be added to the Union.
records.summary_es: El remedio del Herald para los trastornos de Santo Domingo es la anexión: Cabral hace todo lo posible por embarazar al presidente Báez, con la expectativa de que el presidente Saget, de Haití, ayude a Cabral porque Báez favorece al partido de Salnave contra Saget, y el único modo de poner fin a estas sangrientas disensiones, sostiene el diario, es la anexión de una o de ambas repúblicas de la isla a los Estados Unidos; lamenta la oportunidad perdida de adquirir Santo Domingo en términos justos y afirma que, bajo la bandera estadounidense, cesarían por fin los trastornos que convulsionan a haitianos y dominicanos y se añadiría a la Unión una tierra rica y fructífera.

records.headline: A letter from Don Apolinar de Castro quotes the latest advices from the capital, Santo Domingo, dated the 14th
records.summary_en: A letter from Don Apolinar de Castro quotes the latest advices from the capital, Santo Domingo, dated the 14th, confirming the arrival of Cabral on the northern frontier, where he was received with enthusiasm. The advices report the firm position of Generals Adon and the Ogandos, who will soon march on Azua, a deepening division in Baez's party since Hungria's withdrawal from the ministry, and an irreparable lack of means to carry on the government.
records.summary_es: Una carta de don Apolinar de Castro cita las últimas noticias de la capital, Santo Domingo, fechadas el día 14, que confirman la llegada de Cabral a la frontera del norte, donde fue recibido con entusiasmo. Las noticias informan de la firme posición de los generales Adón y los Ogando, que pronto marcharán sobre Azua, de una división cada vez mayor en el partido de Báez desde la retirada de Hungría del ministerio, y de una falta irreparable de medios para sostener el gobierno.

records.summary_en: Secretly aided by President Báez, plots against the Saget administration open the Herald's survey of Haitian and Dominican troubles — grave frauds and counterfeited national bank notes in Hayti, with counterfeiters sentenced to death, and Spanish intrigue stirring up the enemies of annexation in St. Domingo — from which it asks why Congress acted so blindly on Dominican annexation: President Grant's West Indian policy, it argues, is wise and deserves fair consideration, the American people and merchants favor it, and when it is next taken up the legislature should respect the people's desires.

records.headline: In the Senate on December 9, Mr. Sumner of Massachusetts submitted
records.summary_en: In the Senate on December 9, Mr. Sumner of Massachusetts submitted a resolution asking the President to send the Senate all papers and correspondence relating to the proposed annexation of the Dominican portion of the island of St. Domingo or the purchase of any part of it. The resolution also calls for an account of the Dominican government's debt and liabilities, especially to Haiti, the constitutional provisions on selling the national domain, communications from Haiti, the instructions given to the American naval squadron, and information on President Baez's position and on how far he has been maintained in power by United States vessels of war; on Mr. Conkling's suggestion it was laid over temporarily and ordered printed.
records.summary_es: En el Senado, el 9 de diciembre, el señor Sumner de Massachusetts presentó una resolución pidiendo al Presidente que enviara al Senado todos los documentos y la correspondencia relativos a la anexión propuesta de la parte dominicana de la isla de Santo Domingo o a la compra de cualquier parte de ella. La resolución pide también una relación de la deuda y las obligaciones del gobierno dominicano, especialmente con Haití, las disposiciones constitucionales sobre la venta del dominio nacional, las comunicaciones de Haití, las instrucciones dadas a la escuadra naval estadounidense e información sobre la posición del presidente Báez y sobre hasta qué punto ha sido mantenido en el poder por buques de guerra de los Estados Unidos; a sugerencia del señor Conkling quedó sobre la mesa temporalmente y se ordenó su impresión.
records.passage: Washington, Dec. 9—Mr. Sumner (Mass.) submitted the following: Resolved, That the President of the United States be requested to communicate to the Senate, if in his opinion not incompatible with the public interests, copies of all papers and correspondence relating to the proposed annexation of the Dominican portion of the island of St. Domingo, or the purchase of any part thereof, including the original and all subsequent instruction to any agent or consul of the United States, with the correspondence of such agent or consul; also, any protocol or convention signed by such agent or consul. Also, an account of the debt and liabilities of the Dominican Government, especially its obligations to the neighboring republic of Hayti. Also, the provisions of the existing Constitution of Dominica, so far as the same relate to the sale or transfer of the national domain. records.headline: A Washington correspondent traces the history of the scheme to annex San Domingo, which the President is pressing
records.summary_en: A Washington correspondent traces the history of the scheme to annex San Domingo, which the President is pressing again, with General Butler expected to introduce the annexation resolutions in the House. He recounts how General Cazeneau had long promoted annexation, how General Babcock's treaty failed in the Senate, and how Secretary Fish had warned Babcock against Cazeneau because of the vast land concessions Cazeneau was known to have secured in the Bay of Samana and elsewhere.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal en Washington traza la historia del plan de anexionar Santo Domingo, que el presidente está impulsando de nuevo, y se espera que el general Butler presente las resoluciones de anexión en la Cámara. Cuenta cómo el general Cazeneau había promovido la anexión durante mucho tiempo, cómo el tratado del general Babcock fracasó en el Senado, y cómo el secretario Fish había advertido a Babcock contra Cazeneau por las vastas concesiones de tierras que se sabía que Cazeneau había conseguido en la bahía de Samaná y en otros lugares.

records.headline: This Rutland Herald editorial window, opening in mid-argument
records.summary_en: This Rutland Herald editorial window, opening in mid-argument, urges the annexation of the Dominican Republic to the United States as recommended by the President: American vessels in the West Indies and on the passage to and from the Gulf will find a port under their own flag, San Domingo will become the depot of the West India islands' wealth and the central point of their intercourse and prosperity, and, looking at the question in all its bearings, the paper expects the people and the press to favor annexation in some form.
records.summary_es: Esta ventana editorial del Rutland Herald, que se abre a mitad de un argumento, insta a la anexión de la República Dominicana a los Estados Unidos, tal como la recomienda el presidente: los buques estadounidenses en las Indias Occidentales y en la travesía hacia y desde el Golfo hallarán un puerto bajo su propia bandera; Santo Domingo se convertirá en depósito de la riqueza de las islas antillanas y punto central de su intercambio y prosperidad; y, mirando la cuestión en todos sus aspectos, el diario espera que el pueblo y la prensa favorezcan la anexión en alguna forma.

records.headline: This Chicago Tribune editorial window, opening in mid-argument
records.summary_en: This Chicago Tribune editorial window, opening in mid-argument, argues against annexation: if the Republic of Dominica cannot last six weeks without civil war, if no authority is recognized there but the bayonet and life and liberty depend on the will of the faction leader of the moment, what invites the United States to incorporate so distant and squabbling a republic, when it has enough of reconstruction on its hands; it asks why Americans should incorporate a foreign people it describes in contemptuous terms as degraded, ignorant and speaking a different language, and it says the attempt to force the annexation of this Dominican Republic is being made as an administration measure at a present cost of several millions and a perpetual annual cost of twice as many, with the President, his official family, the Vice President and influential senators and representatives behind it — the window closing in mid-list.
records.summary_es: Esta ventana editorial del Chicago Tribune, que se abre a mitad de un argumento, se pronuncia contra la anexión: si la República de Dominica no puede durar seis semanas sin guerra civil, si allí no se reconoce autoridad alguna sino la bayoneta y la vida y la libertad dependen de la voluntad del caudillo de la facción dominante, ¿qué invita a los Estados Unidos a incorporar una república tan distante y pendenciera, cuando tiene bastante reconstrucción entre manos?; pregunta además por qué habría de incorporarse a un pueblo extranjero al que describe en términos despectivos como degradado, ignorante y de lengua distinta; y afirma que el intento de forzar la anexión de esta República Dominicana se impone como medida de la administración, a un costo presente de varios millones y un costo anual perpetuo del doble, con el presidente, su familia oficial, el vicepresidente y senadores y representantes influyentes detrás — y la ventana se cierra a media enumeración.

records.headline: The Spy prints the Senate's Santo Domingo commission resolution
records.summary_en: The Spy prints the Senate's Santo Domingo commission resolution, in its closing sections: the commissioners are to learn what grants, concessions and franchises have been given, and to whom, the terms on which the Dominican government desires annexation as a territory, and such other information as bears on the republic's future incorporation into the United States; they are to report to the President, who shall lay their report before Congress, and they are to serve without compensation beyond their expenses and a secretary's pay fixed by the Secretary of State with the President's approval. The Senate then adjourned at 6:45 in the morning until twelve, and on reassembling went into executive session after receiving the credentials of Mr. Jewett of Missouri, presented by Mr. Schurz, to fill temporarily the vacancy left by Mr. Drake's resignation.

records.headline: The Senate debate on the Santo Domingo commission resolution
records.summary_en: The Senate debate on the Santo Domingo commission resolution is reported by the Tribune: Mr. Schurz's amendment, to postpone all investigation until three months after the withdrawal of the United States naval force from San Domingo waters, was supported by Mr. Sumner on the ground that an expression of the popular will of the Dominican Republic, for or against annexation, should be uninfluenced by a pressure of bayonets — he cited with approval the English law forbidding a military force within a certain limit of an election poll, and argued that the amendment involved a great principle of constitutional liberty. Mr. Thurman of Ohio retorted that the principle had not been appreciated by the Senator from Massachusetts when he voted for the Fifteenth Amendment enforcement and naturalization bills authorizing the presence of the military at the polls in New-York and other states; and in a personal controversy that followed, Mr. Sumner admitted to Mr. Edmunds that when at the last session he became satisfied he could not support the treaty he ought to have communicated the fact to the President, and regretted not having done so — the extent, he said, of his offending, which did not justify the denunciation heaped upon him.
records.summary_es: El debate del Senado sobre la resolución de la comisión de Santo Domingo es reseñado por el Tribune: la enmienda del Sr. Schurz, de posponer toda investigación hasta tres meses después de la retirada de la fuerza naval de los Estados Unidos de las aguas de Santo Domingo, fue apoyada por el Sr. Sumner con el argumento de que una expresión de la voluntad popular de la República Dominicana, a favor o en contra de la anexión, debía estar libre de la presión de las bayonetas; citó con aprobación la ley inglesa que prohíbe una fuerza militar dentro de cierto límite de un colegio electoral, y sostuvo que la enmienda entrañaba un gran principio de libertad constitucional. El Sr. Thurman de Ohio replicó que el principio no había sido apreciado por el senador de Massachusetts cuando votó a favor de las leyes de ejecución de la Decimoquinta Enmienda y de naturalización que autorizaban la presencia de militares en los colegios electorales de Nueva York y otros estados; y en una controversia personal que siguió, el Sr. Sumner admitió ante el Sr. Edmunds que cuando en la sesión pasada se convenció de que no podía apoyar el tratado debió haber comunicado el hecho al Presidente, y lamentó no haberlo hecho: esa era, dijo, la medida de su falta, que no justificaba la denuncia acumulada sobre él.

records.headline: The catalogue of inquiries in the Santo Domingo commission resolution
records.summary_en: The catalogue of inquiries in the Santo Domingo commission resolution is printed by the Intelligencer, in a window opening midway through it: the physical, mental and moral condition of the Dominican people and their material wealth and industrial capacity; the country's resources in minerals, agriculture, the products of its waters and forests, the character and cultivable extent of its soil; its climate and health, its harbors and rivers, its meteorological character and remarkable phenomena; the government's debt and obligations, funded and admitted or unadjusted and in dispute; its treaties and engagements with other powers; the extent of its boundaries and territory, and what proportion is covered by foreign claimants or by grants of concessions, and generally what concessions or franchises have been granted, with the names of the grantees; the terms on which the Dominican government may desire annexation as a territory of the United States; and such other information as bears on the Dominican republic's future incorporation. By the resolution's second section the commissioners are to report to the President as soon as conveniently may be, and he shall lay their report before Congress.
records.summary_es: El catálogo de indagaciones de la resolución sobre la comisión de Santo Domingo es publicado por el Intelligencer, en una ventana que se abre a mitad del texto: la condición física, mental y moral del pueblo dominicano y su riqueza material y capacidad industrial; los recursos del país en minerales, agricultura, los productos de sus aguas y bosques, el carácter y la extensión cultivable de su suelo; su clima y salubridad, sus puertos y ríos, su carácter meteorológico y fenómenos notables; la deuda y las obligaciones del gobierno, consolidadas y reconocidas o no ajustadas y en disputa; sus tratados y compromisos con otras potencias; la extensión de sus límites y territorio, y qué proporción está cubierta por reclamantes extranjeros o por donaciones de concesiones, y en general qué concesiones o franquicias se han otorgado, con los nombres de los concesionarios; los términos en que el gobierno dominicano pueda desear la anexión como territorio de los Estados Unidos; y cuanta otra información se refiera a la futura incorporación de la república dominicana. Por la segunda sección de la resolución, los comisionados deberán informar al Presidente tan pronto como sea conveniente, y él presentará su informe ante el Congreso.

records.headline: The Spy traces the annexation scheme to the Cazneaus, heard of again
records.summary_en: The Spy traces the annexation scheme to the Cazneaus, heard of again in San Domingo after the collapse of the Confederacy and making propositions to Mr. Seward for its fulfilment, in an editorial window opening mid-sentence: the matter fell through then, and was revived on General Grant's accession, when a convention was drawn up under General Babcock, one of the President's young military secretaries, with Admiral Porter, in the Spy's phrase, as wet nurse, and Cazneau as interpreter. Mr. Fish, the editorial says, had particularly warned Babcock against Cazneau as a dangerous man mixed up in private schemes and speculations, who wanted only to make a cat's-paw of the United States to realize on the vast concessions of lands in the bay of Samaná and elsewhere that he had secured; but Babcock, ignorant of Spanish, gladly accepted the services of Cazneau, who was master of the situation and said what he liked — the window closing mid-sentence as it turns to Babcock's liking for the bay of Samaná.
records.summary_es: El Spy atribuye el plan de anexión a los Cazneau, de quienes se vuelve a oír en Santo Domingo tras el colapso de la Confederación, haciendo proposiciones al Sr. Seward para su realización, en una ventana editorial que se abre a mitad de una frase: el asunto fracasó entonces, y revivió con el ascenso del general Grant, cuando se redactó una convención bajo el general Babcock, uno de los jóvenes secretarios militares del Presidente, con el almirante Porter, en la expresión del Spy, como nodriza, y Cazneau como intérprete. El Sr. Fish, dice el editorial, había advertido particularmente a Babcock contra Cazneau por ser un hombre peligroso, mezclado en planes y especulaciones privadas, que solo quería hacer de los Estados Unidos un instrumento para realizar las vastas concesiones de tierras en la bahía de Samaná y otras partes que había asegurado; pero Babcock, que ignoraba el español, aceptó gustoso los servicios de Cazneau, quien era dueño de la situación y decía lo que quería: la ventana se cierra a mitad de una frase cuando pasa a la afición de Babcock por la bahía de Samaná.

records.headline: Discussing Mr. Sumner's charges, this Tribune editorial window
records.summary_en: Discussing Mr. Sumner's charges, this Tribune editorial window — which opens by answering an imputation against him, that he intended no injury or oppression of any race nor to deprive men of chances to vindicate their capacity for self-government — reports his allegations: that the President's proceedings in reference to San Domingo are a menace to the Republic of Hayti, which embraces four-fifths of the population of the island; that threats of violence have been openly made against Hayti by the United States naval forces in those waters; and that the President in his annual message referred no less than nine times to the Dominican Republic as the whole island, entirely ignoring the existence of Hayti. Senator Morton calls the last an inadvertence, and the Tribune thinks it very likely was; but, it argues, the annexation of San Domingo would be only a step to the annexation of Hayti, whose thrifty portion the President's commercial advantages cannot be attained without; that the Haytians are strongly opposed to the annexation of Dominica, and still more strongly to the annexation of themselves, is not disputed — the window closing as the editorial turns to Mr. Gerrit Smith's argument.

records.headline: Inquiries about Báez and Cabral are answered in a speech against the annexation
records.summary_en: Inquiries about Báez and Cabral are answered in a speech against the annexation printed by the Freeman, from one described as bound to be well informed, in a window opening mid-course: Cabral, the speaker is assured, once favored the sale of the bay of Samaná to the United States but has never favored annexation, and his policy is to bring the two governments of Dominica and Hayti together again, as they were down to the revolution and war that ended in the uncertain independence of the Dominican part of the island. The evidence, the speaker says, is not that the two chieftains agree but that they differ — one seeking unity for the two governments, the other seeking to sell his country for a price; and whatever the people's sentiment, Báez has been maintained in power by the naval force of the United States: 'Deny it, if you can.' He then supposes Louis Napoleon, in an evil hour, setting up Jefferson Davis as head of the United States government and treating with him to yield Texas to become part of Mexico, itself to become more or less part of France — the window closing inside the supposition.
records.summary_es: Las preguntas sobre Báez y Cabral se responden en un discurso contra la anexión publicado por el Freeman, de alguien descrito como necesariamente bien informado, en una ventana que se abre a mitad del discurso: Cabral, se le asegura al orador, favoreció una vez la venta de la bahía de Samaná a los Estados Unidos pero nunca ha favorecido la anexión, y su política es volver a unir los dos gobiernos de Dominica y Haití, como estuvieron hasta la revolución y la guerra que terminaron en la incierta independencia de la parte dominicana de la isla. La evidencia, dice el orador, no es que los dos caudillos estén de acuerdo sino que difieren: uno busca la unidad de los dos gobiernos, el otro busca vender su país por un precio; y cualquiera que sea el sentimiento del pueblo, Báez se ha mantenido en el poder por la fuerza naval de los Estados Unidos: «Niéguenlo, si pueden». records.headline: Under the head 'San Domingo,' the Gazette states its own position
records.summary_en: Under the head 'San Domingo,' the Gazette states its own position: it has taken little interest in the question, and regards it as one on which honest men and good patriots may fairly differ. The primary question is one of fact — do the people of the Dominican Republic really desire annexation to the United States? If they do, the Gazette inclines to receive them into the Union; if they do not, it strongly objects to annexing them by force, wanting no acquisitions of territory whose people prefer to keep apart. It has heartily supported Senator Morton's proposition, because its adoption seemed calculated to shed light on the vital question.
records.summary_es: Bajo el encabezado «San Domingo», el Gazette expone su propia posición: se ha interesado poco en la cuestión, y la considera una de esas sobre las que hombres honestos y buenos patriotas pueden diferir justamente. La cuestión primaria es de hecho: ¿desea realmente el pueblo de la República Dominicana la anexión a los Estados Unidos? Si la desea, el Gazette se inclina a recibirlo en la Unión; si no la desea, se opone firmemente a anexarlo por la fuerza, pues no quiere adquisiciones de territorio cuyo pueblo prefiera mantenerse aparte. Ha apoyado de corazón la proposición del senador Morton, porque su adopción parecía calculada para arrojar luz sobre la cuestión vital.

records.headline: A conference of the Democratic members of Congress at the capital
records.summary_en: A conference of the Democratic members of Congress at the capital on the San Domingo question, reported under the head 'The Democrat, and San Domingo,' decided unanimously to oppose the annexation project: they admitted that the acquisition of territory had been the manifest destiny and doctrine of the Democratic party, but held the objections to San Domingo too great to be overcome — that Dominica represented only half of the island, that its population was, in the conference's characterization, a half-civilized and ignorant race, and that the scheme was shrouded in corruption.
records.summary_es: Una conferencia de los miembros demócratas del Congreso en la capital sobre la cuestión de Santo Domingo, reseñada bajo el encabezado «The Democrat, and San Domingo», decidió por unanimidad oponerse al proyecto de anexión: admitieron que la adquisición de territorio había sido el destino manifiesto y la doctrina del partido Demócrata, pero sostuvieron que las objeciones a Santo Domingo eran demasiado grandes para ser superadas: que Dominica representaba solo la mitad de la isla, que su población era, en la caracterización de la conferencia, una raza semicivilizada e ignorante, y que el plan estaba envuelto en corrupción.

records.headline: In a despatch from Port-au-Prince the Herald prints General Cabral's manifesto
records.summary_en: In a despatch from Port-au-Prince the Herald prints General Cabral's manifesto announcing the defeat of Báez: 'Baez is faithless to us. In exchange for gold he wants to sacrifice our independence, and our independence we must maintain as the only thing we have, and as the most precious jewel we can bequeath to future generations.' The manifesto's concluding paragraph, as the Herald quotes it, looks past the revolution to 'the election of men of known honesty to fill the offices of public administration,' and ends: 'Citizens, union and we will save the Dominican Republic.' The Herald calls the manifesto's language pointed, strong, and meaning business.
records.summary_es: En un despacho desde Puerto Príncipe, el Herald publica el manifiesto del general Cabral que anuncia la derrota de Báez: «Báez nos es infiel. A cambio de oro quiere sacrificar nuestra independencia, y nuestra independencia debemos mantenerla como lo único que tenemos, y como la joya más preciosa que podemos legar a las generaciones futuras». El párrafo final del manifiesto, tal como lo cita el Herald, mira más allá de la revolución hacia «la elección de hombres de honradez conocida para desempeñar los cargos de la administración pública», y termina: «Ciudadanos, unión y salvaremos la República Dominicana». El Herald califica el lenguaje del manifiesto de incisivo, fuerte y que va en serio.

records.headline: A Washington item explains that the Seward-Stevens West India fund is now exhausted: Seward spent most of $100,000 of it
records.summary_en: A Washington item explains that the Seward-Stevens West India fund is now exhausted: Seward spent most of $100,000 of it on his West Indies trip, and General Babcock took the remaining $150,000 to lease the Bay of Samana. It reports that Mr. Dawes, chairman of the House Committee on Appropriations, refused two senators' request for a bill to pay the rent now due to Envoy Fabens, saying he could only make appropriations authorized by law, and that Senator Sumner calls the whole proceeding without the shadow of law.

Informa que el señor Dawes, presidente del Comité de Asignaciones de la Cámara, rechazó la petición de dos senadores de un proyecto de ley para pagar la renta ya vencida al enviado Fabens, diciendo que solo podía hacer asignaciones autorizadas por la ley, y que el senador Sumner califica todo el procedimiento como carente de toda sombra de legalidad.

records.summary_en: The Sun reports that the money expended by the President in the Dominican job is drawn from an appropriation of $250,000 made in 1868: of this, $100,000 is said to have been spent by Mr. Seward in various investigations and negotiations respecting San Domingo, and the other $150,000 was used to pay the first year's rent of the bay of Samaná; for the second year's rent, the Sun says, there is no appropriation, nor, so far as now appears, any likelihood of getting one.

records.headline: The Tribune prints the closing numbered objections of an argument
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints the closing numbered objections of an argument against the annexation, in a window opening on the tail of the ninth — a settled principle of public law, that when one sovereign succeeds to another by purchase it takes all its just obligations as well as all its rights. The tenth objection is that Báez, the present President of the Dominican Republic, has no authority to dispose of his country: its constitution is its fundamental law, and its seventh article provides, 'The territory of the Republic is inalienable. No person or authority can transfer the whole or any portion of it to any other Power'; no amendment voiding the provision has been adopted, nor any legal or valid consent of the people obtained, and Báez's consent is 'the dernier resort of a ruined tyrant' who sells his country for a moneyed consideration, cash down, in advance. The eleventh is that this is no time to enlarge the national territory at so fearful a cost, with hundreds of millions of acres of the finest agricultural and mineral lands still untitled and unproductive and a burden of taxation heavier than can readily be borne — the window closing as it urges reducing existing obligations first.

records.headline: The Dominican Resolution
records.summary_en: The report covers the debate in both chambers on the joint resolution to appoint commissioners to Dominica. In the Senate, Senator Sumner protested against the whole measure as involving a bloody lawsuit, presented General Cabral's proclamation as evidence of civil war in the country, and proposed that the commissioners be required to inquire into that war and into the relations between Dominica and Hayti. In the House, Mr. Cox of New York denounced the scheme as a private, corrupt job, saying the annexation would be that of husks, because the kernels had already gone to private parties. Mr. Hoar of Massachusetts said he did not concur in the idea that respect for the President required them to support the measure, while Mr. Stevenson of Ohio favored acquiring Dominica for its minerals, harbors and fertile soil. A dispatch was read announcing that the Indiana Senate had instructed its senators, and requested its representatives, to vote against annexation. The House agreed to Mr. Ambler's amendment, declaring that nothing in the resolution committed the government to annexation, and then passed the resolution, 123 to 63.

records.full_text:
Senate · Washington, Jan. 10, 1871

When Mr. Trumbull concluded his remarks, Mr. Morton moved to take up the Senate Dominican joint resolutions as returned from the House, with an amendment providing that nothing contained in them shall be held, understood or construed as committing Congress to the policy of the annexation of the said republic of Dominica.

Mr. Sumner asked whether the Senator was aware that there would be some discussion. He submitted whether the consideration of the amendment could be proceeded with except by unanimous consent.

The Vice President replied that he was not aware of any rule which would prevent it from being taken up, except the pendency of the present bill.

Mr. Morton's motion was then agreed to, yeas 26, nays 16.

The House amendment to the Senate resolution was read, when Mr. Morton moved that the Senate concur.

Mr. Sumner asked for the yeas and nays. He knew not if Senators were aware of the painful news received since the debate on this subject, showing more than ever why we should hesitate in this business. It might be remembered that he protested against the whole measure as involving a bloody lawsuit. As prudent citizens we should not buy a lawsuit, especially one flowing with blood. Since the last discussion a proclamation of General Cabral had been received. He held in his hand an original copy in Spanish, printed on the island, against the usurper Baez, who, he had once said, was retained in power by the republic of the United States, a republic standing before the world to maintain the power of a pretender. Truly a sad part for a republic to play. The proclamation commenced with the words “God, country and liberty,” and was signed “Cabral, General of a division of the army,” in which he states “that the South was still in arms; that lately the enemy was beaten and routed; that reinforcements had reached the advanced posts, and without waiting for the infantry he vigorously attacked and defeated the foe,” &c. The proclamation is dated November 15, 1870. Mr. Sumner asked whether he was wrong when he called this a bloody lawsuit? This opened a melancholy picture; it was a picture of civil war. Here was a chief in the mountains, and another chief on the seashore, the latter sustained in power by the United States, and we were asked to proceed still further in this business. Better say with Macbeth, “I'll proceed no further in this business.” When this subject was formerly before the Senate he (Mr. Sumner) discussed the character of the President's Message as a menace to the people of Hayti. He did not then so soon anticipate a report from that republic; he did not at that time know how promptly he would be confirmed in his fears. He had before him a paper which, for its news, had not its superior in the country, the New York Herald. It was a paper known to be in no respect in sympathy with him or his conclusions. He thought proper to present this paper, bearing date January 5, 1871, as it gave news direct from Hayti. The letter is dated “Port au Prince, December 22, 1870,” with the heading:

Hayti—How the Haytiens receive the annexation news—Intense excitement on receipt of President Grant's Message—A guerilla warfare to be carried on—The Haytiens will fight to the death in support of their independence, and they threaten to burn the towns and then to take to the mountains—Demands on the government.

Mr. Sumner said that Senators smiled. He read it from an important newspaper, differing from him in sentiment. It did not seem unnatural that there was in the human heart a love of independence. When our independence is assailed we are aroused. He could not complain of the humble Haytiens, because their independence is assailed. It was a painful matter to think that this great country of ours, which should be a benediction, should become a terror and violence.

Mr. Pomeroy asked the Senator to yield the floor, so that he might suggest, by unanimous consent, that a vote be taken at two or three o'clock to-morrow.

Mr. Morton asked whether it would not be better to take a recess until this evening.

Mr. Sumner wished to offer an amendment to the resolution by adding at the end that the commissioners shall inquire specially of the alleged pendency of civil war in Dominica, the extent of the territory occupied by the respective parties; also the relations existing between Dominica and Hayti, and the claims of the latter on the former, and if there is a war or a menace of war between these countries.

Mr. Wilson wanted to adjourn and take up the subject to-morrow.

Mr. Trumbull hoped there would be no more excitement. If they should go into discussion now the session would be protracted. It would be better for them all to adjourn until to-morrow, and resume the matter at one o'clock. There was at this moment no attempt to prevent the action of the Senate. Should such an attempt be made to-morrow he trusted that every Senator would sit it out. He should not expect any Senator to try to prolong the proceedings.

Mr. Conkling asked Mr. Trumbull whether, after the measure had been once fully debated in the Senate and came back with an amendment tending to dilute it, an intention to reopen the whole subject afforded evidence to his mind of a factious opposition and a desire to delay and procrastinate.

Mr. Trumbull replied he never entered into an enterprise of that kind. He hoped the time would never come when he would enter into a factious opposition.

Mr. Stewart remarked that on a former occasion he stayed there all night; if he remembered correctly, the Senator relieved himself by going home. If this thing was to be repeated he would rather stay here to-night than any other night.

Mr. Warner sincerely trusted that no difficulty would arise. He thought the friends of the resolution would be glad to agree that the vote on the question should be taken at three or four o'clock to-morrow.

Mr. Pomeroy said he should be glad if the Senate by unanimous consent would agree to vote on the question to-morrow at four o'clock.

Mr. Saulsbury objected to the introduction, in effect, of the previous question by fixing an hour for the termination of the debate and taking a vote. Heretofore discussion was freely allowed. There never had been a more serious and important question than this. For the first time the Senator from Massachusetts is right. (Laughter.) He hoped the Senate would therefore allow the fullest discussion.

The Senate agreed to close the discussion at four o'clock to-morrow, when, at a quarter to five o'clock, an adjournment took place.

House of Representatives · Washington, Jan. 10, 1871

St. Domingo

The House resumed the consideration of the joint resolution for the appointment of commissioners to Dominica.

Mr. Willard (rep.) of Vt., a member of the Committee on Foreign Affairs, explained why he was found voting yesterday with so few of his republican colleagues against taking the resolution from the Speaker's table. He was opposed to the acquisition of the republic of Dominica by treaty or by joint resolution, and therefore he was opposed to taking any step looking to that acquisition. He was unwilling to authorize the friends of acquisition in working this machinery in aid of their scheme. It was charged, and not denied, that the commission was to return to Washington in time for Congress to act on its report at this session. What opportunity, then, would the Commission have for obtaining the information directed? Were the commissioners to inquire only from Fabens or Baez or Cazneau, or were they to traverse the republic and ascertain facts for themselves? If the latter they would require not two weeks, but six months or a year. The scope of the investigation was so broad that the idea that the commission was to bring back any plausible information was absurd. It was impossible for the commissioners to report anything from their own observation, but a report would be made and would be given to the country as the report of the commissioners.

Mr. Cox (dem.) of N.Y. opposed the joint resolution. After discussing the details of the measure he said the proviso of Mr. Ambler may not pass. It is sugar-coating. This measure is a pretence for information. It is annexation, in fact. If annexation is accomplished there is no need of this commission. If it is not to be accomplished what need is there, then? The information is already here, all we want. It was sent in last night late. Let us print and read what we have. It is voluminous; but does it give the list of grants and jobs attached to the treaty? I assert there is such a list; it was not sent to the Senate. It was called for by a resolution I drew last session. The annexation will be that of husks. The kernels are already gone to private parties. What do you want the annexation for—a port for commerce? Had you not better first revive commerce? How our phantom ships and ghostly steamers will sail into Samana! Oh, but it is Manifest Destiny! Democrats are invited to our old policy and charged with inconsistency by those who always opposed us. So you radicals are copying the despised democracy, are you? Is Saul also among the prophets? Remember that no one but Prince Arthur could wield the prince's magic sword. I am not against this scheme because it adds territory, but because it is a private, wicked scheme. Jefferson was for extended empire, but, as he said, “with self-government.” We are departing in many ways from the Jeffersonian standard and policies. I find but one precedent for this, and that hardly analogous. Not the Puritan way of taking the land of the Pequods, but Joshua sending spies to go over Jordan and search out the land. They went into Jericho and kept bad company. Is Baez your Rahab? I do not object because the territory is not coterminous. It is as near as California was. And because we swallow 200,000 colored people, after taking in 4,000,000, we can digest a few. The man who swallowed a pumpkin worried down a peach. I oppose the scheme because it is a specious, prearranged, corrupt job, and no commission can deodorize its putrescence. It is not to be compared to the achievements of the democracy in their expanding policy. When the democracy obtain power they will take care of the Monroe doctrine and territorial expansion.

Mr. Hoar (rep.) of Mass. explained the reasons which led him to differ from the majority of his colleagues. He did not concur in the idea that respect for the President of the United States required them to support this measure. The Committee on Foreign Affairs had refused to report a proposition for the appointment of commissioners to form a treaty, but instead of that had reported a proposition for the perpetration of a farce as great as had ever been enacted on such a subject. He was not willing to annex to a self-governing republic an island which would be filled with the scum of the tropics, the adventurers of all lands, who would come to influence the government of this country. In eleven States there was a rebellious element striking hands with Tammany Hall and striving to obtain possession of the government for the next four years. He was not willing to do anything to add to that danger.

Mr. Stevenson (rep.) of Ohio spoke in favor of the acquisition of Dominica and of its admission as one of the Territories of the Union. He did not want any information about the island. He found it crystallized in books. He found the island was rich in mines of gold and silver, copper, iron and coal. He found that it was rich in bays and harbors, one of which was the key of the Gulf. He found that the climate, though tropical, was less unwholesome than elsewhere in the West Indies. Its soil was exceedingly fertile, producing sugar, coffee, cotton and tropical fruits, and he found that its political constitution was modelled after that of the United States.

Mr. Voorhees (dem.) of Ind. sent to the Clerk's desk and had read a telegraphic despatch, stating that the Senate of Indiana had just passed a joint resolution instructing the Senators and requesting the Representatives from that State to vote against the annexation of St. Domingo. (Laughter.)

Mr. Orth (rep.) of Ind. remarked that those who knew how the democratic party in Indiana had obtained control of the Senate would not be surprised at the action of that body.

Mr. Potter (dem.) of N.Y. spoke against the acquisition of Dominica.

Mr. Swann (dem.) of Md., a member of the Committee on Foreign Affairs, also spoke against the joint resolution. He regarded the vote about to be taken as one involving important and vital issues. They all knew that before the making of the treaty oppressed Cuba was knocking at the doors of the American republic, but that the President of the United States, by his power and influence, defeated the proposition of the Committee on Foreign Affairs in aid of Cuba. He would not assail the President of the United States, but he would ask why did the President manifest such interest in this matter? Why did they see Senators and Cabinet officers lobbying in the House in favor of this measure? If the Postmaster General had no more influence in the House than he had in his own State of Maryland he should have been kept in his department attending to its business, which was sadly in need of attention, instead of coming to the House to try to influence its legislation.

Mr. Fitch (rep.) of Nev. said that he should vote for the pending resolution and against the eviscerating amendment of the gentleman from Ohio (Mr. Ambler). He should vote for it because he believed it would be followed by the annexation of Dominica, and then of Hayti and Cuba. He should have preferred to vote directly for a joint resolution of annexation.

Mr. Ela (rep.) of N.H. opposed the joint resolution as one tending to entangling alliances with a foreign people having no common interest with the people of the United States, who have already in their midst enough of conflicting elements. It meant the expenditure of vast sums of money for fortifications, navy yards and ships-of-war. He believed that the policy would end in disaster, and therefore he opposed it.

Mr. Farnsworth (rep.) of Ill. declared that he was opposed to the annexation of Dominica; that his constituents were opposed to it, and that, in his belief, nine-tenths of the constituents of every member were opposed to it. He was not so much of a manifest destiny man as his friend from Nevada (Mr. Fitch). He believed that the wings of the American Eagle might be spread too much, to the injury of that national bird. He would rather wait and people the territory already possessed. He would rather wait until Nevada got some population. (Laughter.) If the amendment offered by Mr. Ambler was agreed to he would vote for the joint resolution; but otherwise he would vote against it.

Mr. Butler (rep.) of Mass. sustained the joint resolution, and opposed the amendment of Mr. Ambler as only tending to produce delay, and thus kill the investigation.

Mr. Ambler (rep.) of Ohio denied having offered the amendment with any such intention.

Mr. Butler accepted the statement, but always attributed to a man's act its natural consequences.

Mr. Dawes (rep.) of Mass. asked him if the subject would not stand debate.

Mr. Butler replied that it would stand debate even from the false friend of the party. He had heard many painful things, but none more painful than the telegraphic despatch from Indiana, not that the Senate, organized through fraud, should send such a message, but that it should have been sent to the honored and revered Senator from Massachusetts (Mr. Sumner).

Since he's misnamed the Morning Star,
Nor man nor fiend hath fallen so far.

Mr. Voorhees remarked that a majority of republicans had been elected to the Indiana Senate, but that enough of them had been disgusted by the course of the party in Congress to induce them to vote as they did.

Mr. Butler went on to say that the political party which would set itself up against annexation of territory would come to naught. It was the doctrine of Jefferson, of Jackson, of Polk and of every democratic administration, and had now come to be accepted as the doctrine of the country.

Mr. Bingham (rep.) of Ohio sustained the joint resolution and opposed Mr. Ambler's resolution as unnecessary and only tending to promote delay. He pointed with pride to the vast acquisition of territory by this government in the past, and to the emigration from the north of Europe promoted by that territorial expansion. He was for an honorable acquisition of Dominica if it could be made and it were for the interest of the people, and it was to ascertain the facts that these commissioners were to be sent out. The only way to obtain knowledge of the facts was by inquiry. The resolution proposed an inquiry. He was for the resolution without the amendment.

At the conclusion of Mr. Bingham's remarks Mr. Garfield (rep.) of Ohio proposed a further extension of fifteen minutes of the time allowed for discussion.

Mr. Butler objected.

Mr. Garfield: Listen to the gentleman who cracks a whip objecting to debate! (Excitement.)

Mr. Butler: And listen to the man whose back smarts! (Laughter.)

Mr. Garfield: The gentleman's lash can hurt nothing but the cause in which he wields it.

Mr. Morgan (dem.) of Ohio: The House is under the domination of a whip-cracker.

Mr. Shanks (rep.) of Ind. supported the resolution as one which proposed to obtain information which would show the false position in which its opponents placed themselves and which would furnish an answer to the Senator from Indiana.

Mr. Poland (rep.) of Vt. also supported the resolution and opposed the amendment.

Mr. Kellogg (rep.) of Conn. said he would vote for the resolution and against the amendment.

The discussion was closed by Mr. Orth in support of the resolution. He declared that nothing could be discovered in the resolution, when honestly examined, which could deter any member, much less a member of his own side of the House, from giving it his support. It contained but the single proposition that the President of the United States, a man in whom a large majority of the House had confidence, should appoint three commissioners to proceed to the island of St. Domingo, and there acquire certain information to be laid before the American Congress and the American people. He knew nothing about the character of those commissioners, but he entertained no doubt as to the result of their report on the acquisition of that island. There was nothing in the resolution which committed the government to the rejection or acceptance of the report. If he had been honored by a seat in the next Congress he would not consider himself bound to vote for the adoption of the report which the commission would make to the next Congress, for he had no hope that the commission could proceed to its destination and accomplish its object in time for action at this Congress. He opposed the amendment offered by Mr. Ambler as one which would only cause delay and reopen in the Senate a quarrel which no friend of the union and harmony of the republican party would desire to see reopened. The adoption of the resolution, pure and simple, was due to the President, who had been unjustly assailed by political enemies and by political friends.

Mr. Brooks (dem.) of N.Y. asked Mr. Orth to allow him to offer an amendment that the Commissioners be appointed by the Speaker of the House and the President of the Senate.

Mr. Orth declined to do so.

Mr. Brooks reminded him of his promise to allow it to be offered at some time during the session.

Mr. Orth replied that the promise meant at some time during the present session. (Laughter.)

The House then proceeded to vote on Mr. Ambler's amendment, declaring that nothing in the resolution was to be construed as committing the government to the annexation of Dominica.

The amendment was agreed to, yeas 106, nays 76.

The joint resolution as amended was then passed, yeas 123, nays 63. The democrats voted solidly in the negative, and the following named republicans also voted no: Messrs. Beatty, Boyd, Finkelnburg, Hoar, Peters and Willard.

The joint resolution goes back to the Senate for action on the amendment.

records.headline: A Washington article traces the money behind the Samana lease to a West India fund obtained by Thaddeus Stevens
records.summary_en: A Washington article traces the money behind the Samana lease to a West India fund obtained by Thaddeus Stevens, saying Seward took $100,000 of it on his West Indies trip and General Babcock took the balance of $150,000, with which he leased the Bay of Samana. With that fund now exhausted, the article says, Senators friendly to the administration asked Representative Dawes to bring in a bill appropriating $150,000 for the payment now due to Fabens, but Dawes refused because there is no law for it, and Senator Sumner is quoted as saying the whole proceeding is without a shadow of law.
records.summary_es: Un artículo de Washington atribuye el dinero del arrendamiento de Samaná a un fondo para las Indias Occidentales obtenido por Thaddeus Stevens, y dice que Seward se llevó 100.000 dólares de ese fondo en su viaje a las Indias Occidentales y que el general Babcock se llevó el resto, 150.000 dólares, con los que arrendó la bahía de Samaná. Agotado ya ese fondo, dice el artículo, senadores afines a la administración pidieron al representante Dawes que presentara un proyecto para asignar 150.000 dólares para el pago que ahora se debe a Fabens, pero Dawes se negó porque no existe ley que lo autorice, y se cita al senador Sumner diciendo que todo el procedimiento carece de la menor base legal.
records.passage: appropriated, and soon after Seward, with his son and Admiral Porter, started for the West Indies. They took with them $100,000 out of Thad's West India fund, and spent the most of it. As is well known, this trip did not result in anything. When General Babcock went to St. Domingo he took the balance of this Seward -Stevens fund, 150,000, with which he leased the Bay of Samana. This fund is now exhausted, so that Envoy Fabens will not be able to collect his rent from that source. It is stated that a couple of Senators, friends of the administration, visited Mr. Dawes, chairman of the House Committee on Appropriations, and requested him to bring in a bill appropriating [illegible] for the payment now due. Dawes, who is a very careful fellow, and who does not seem to be aware of the existence of the "extra article" of the treaty, positively refused to comply with the request, for the reason, as he alleged, that there is no law for it. He told the Senators that he could only make appropriations which are authorized by law. Should Mr. Dawes adhere to his determination it is difficult to see where Mr. Fabens will get his rent. It might be taken out of the State Department Secret Service fund, but of late years this fund has been limited. Last year it was cut down from [illegible] to [illegible]. This year Judge Kelsey, who has charge of the Diplomatic and Consular appropriation bill, says he intends to keep it down to $100,000. This will not be sufficient for the payment of Mr. Fabens little bill. Senator Sumner

records.headline: This pro-annexation Herald editorial takes up both ends of the island
records.summary_en: This pro-annexation Herald editorial takes up both ends of the island, Dominica the Spanish and Hayti the French, and declines to repeat the financial, commercial, political and military reasons of President Grant's annual message: annexation, it says, is no new idea, for twenty-six or twenty-seven years ago John C. Calhoun was mixed up with intrigues for the island's acquisition in the interest of Southern African slavery. In the last year of the French dominion, it recalls, the Haytian end exported 47,500,000 pounds of clayed sugars, nearly 77,000,000 pounds of coffee and 7,000,000 pounds of cotton; as in St. Domingo African slavery was first established on American soil, so there it was first abolished in a deluge of blood. The material advantages of possessing the island are clear enough, the editorial says, provided its colored freemen can be brought to work; it puts the population of Dominica at about 140,000 and of Hayti at 575,000 — the window closing mid-sentence on the scheme of annexation.

records.headline: Under the rubric 'Commission of 1871,' the Tribune prints a geographical and historical account of the island
records.summary_en: Under the rubric 'Commission of 1871,' the Tribune prints a geographical and historical account of the island, in a window opening mid-argument: the island of Hayti, or San Domingo, lies between Cuba on the north-west, Porto Rico on the south-east and Jamaica on the south-west, with an area of 27,000 square miles and a population of 703,500; San Domingo proper, or the Dominican Republic, has an area of 17,500 square miles and a population of 136,800, according to the Geographisches Jahrbuch — the two republics so connected, the article says, that in discussing the one it is almost discussing the other. The island was called Hayti, the Highland Country, by the natives, and Hispaniola, or Española, and also San Domingo, by the Spaniards; its bold coast is a succession of rugged limestone mountains, and three great ranges traverse it from west to east, the highest summit of the central range rising 7,200 feet. The island was discovered by Columbus in 1492, and the Spaniards established their first permanent settlement on its northern coast — the window closing as it turns to their disappointment in the yield of gold.

records.full_text:
Misrule and oppressive taxation brought about the revolution of 1863, the restoration of the republic in 1865, and of Baez as President, but no cessation of the intrigues of Cabral, who, though much inferior in intelligence to Baez, who was educated in Paris, has many partisans in the interior, the principal strength of Baez being at the capital and the large seaports.

San Domingo is one of the richest in natural resources of the West India Islands, though thus far little has ever been done to develop them, notwithstanding the unusual mildness of its tropical climate and its many fine harbors. The soil is generally fertile in the highest degree, the soil of the mountain slopes being almost as fertile as that of the plains and valleys. The south part of the island is intersected and watered by many rivers, which not only increase the natural productiveness of the soil, but afford a means of communication with the interior districts.

records.headline: A Washington despatch reports the commission's delayed sailing
records.summary_en: A Washington despatch reports the commission's delayed sailing: because of the delay in forming it, the expedition will not sail until Tuesday; the commission as now formed is generally spoken of with favor: Dr. Samuel G. records.headline: The Santo Domingo commissioners mustered in strong force at the Astor House
records.summary_en: The Santo Domingo commissioners mustered in strong force at the Astor House yesterday, the Herald reports under the head 'The Commission in New York,' with their secretaries, interpreters, stenographers and representatives of the press: Ex-Senator Wade and Professor White arrived early in the morning, accompanied by Secretary Burton and Assistant Secretary Fred Douglass, and Commissioner Howe later in the day; Secretary Robeson, General Porter, the President's secretary and Commodore Alden, Chief of the Bureau of Navigation, had also come on from Washington to speed the parting commissioners and superintend the arrangements on board the Tennessee, which is to convey the three commissioners, the two secretaries, two stenographers and the press representatives — General Sigel and Fred Douglass, Jr., also accompanying the expedition. A meeting announced for the afternoon, to examine the credentials of the journalists to be granted passage, waited until evening for the last of them to appear; and it remains uncertain, the Herald says, whether the Tennessee can accommodate the whole party, a second vessel of war to be detailed if necessary — the window closing mid-sentence on the method of the investigation.

records.headline: The Herald reprints testimony summed up in six points on Dominica
records.summary_en: The Herald reprints testimony summed up in six points on Dominica, the Spanish portion of St. Domingo: first, that it was thinly populated — the estimates varied widely, their endpoints not legible in this printing, and those who appeared to have the best opportunities for correct information fixed the number at less than 200,000; second, that its soil was rich, of a productive power beyond any corresponding extent of Cuba; third, that its actual production was greatly diminished by the disturbed state of its civil and political society, caused partly by the Spanish invasion, partly by the character of the population, and largely by the aggressive policy of the neighboring republic of Hayti; fourth, that all parties with equal unanimity sought refuge in a more intimate connection with the United States, regarded as the natural protector of republican institutions in the Western Hemisphere; fifth, that to this end all desired to lease the bay and peninsula of Samaná to the United States for a naval station, as a first step toward ultimate annexation; and sixth, that the bay of Samaná was the key to the Mona Channel, the 'Gate to the Caribbean Sea and the Isthmus of Panama.'
records.summary_es: El Herald reproduce un testimonio resumido en seis puntos sobre Dominica, la parte española de Santo Domingo: primero, que estaba escasamente poblada —las estimaciones variaron ampliamente, sus extremos no legibles en esta impresión, y quienes parecían haber tenido las mejores oportunidades de información correcta fijaron el número en menos de 200,000—; segundo, que su suelo era rico, de un poder productivo superior a cualquier extensión correspondiente de Cuba; tercero, que su producción real estaba muy disminuida por el estado perturbado de su sociedad civil y política, causado en parte por la invasión española, en parte por el carácter de la población, y en gran medida por la política agresiva de la vecina república de Haití; cuarto, que todos los partidos con igual unanimidad buscaban refugio en una conexión más íntima con los Estados Unidos, considerados el protector natural de las instituciones republicanas en el Hemisferio Occidental; quinto, que con ese fin todos deseaban arrendar la bahía y la península de Samaná a los Estados Unidos como estación naval, como primer paso hacia la anexión definitiva; y sexto, que la bahía de Samaná era la llave del canal de la Mona, la «Puerta al mar Caribe y al istmo de Panamá».

records.headline: The Tribune prints Mr. Fabens telling a story against himself
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints Mr. Fabens telling a story against himself — a stranger denouncing 'Fabens' to him as the wretch at the bottom of the San Domingo job, and opening his eyes when told, 'I am that Fabens exactly' — and then answering questions about the debt of the Dominican Republic: it was, he alleged, a very small debt, a part owing to Hayti, a part to a celebrated banking house of Curaçao, described as the Rothschilds of the West Indies, and besides some debt owing to Peabody & Company in London. The two marplots in the whole business, he said, were St. John, a British consul, and a former Spanish consul at San Domingo city, who had brought about the Spanish occupation: the Spaniard opposes the annexation of San Domingo by the Americans because Spain had failed in it, and St. John's conduct he attributed to the general cussedness of the British character in any matter of territorial emulation. Saget, the present usurper of Hayti in Fabens's word, he described with racial contempt, while Salnave, who had been killed at Cape Haytien, he called a hero; Saget, he said, had Salnave's body dragged behind an ox cart before the American consul's residence, where the wife and family of the dead President remained, as a token of his contempt of the United States.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica al Sr. Fabens relatando una anécdota en su contra —un desconocido que le denunciaba a «Fabens» como el miserable que estaba en el fondo del asunto de Santo Domingo, y a quien se le abrieron los ojos cuando se le dijo: «Yo soy exactamente ese Fabens»— y respondiendo luego preguntas sobre la deuda de la República Dominicana: era, alegó, una deuda muy pequeña, una parte debida a Haití, otra parte a una célebre casa bancaria de Curazao, descrita como los Rothschild de las Indias Occidentales, y además alguna deuda debida a Peabody & Company en Londres. Los dos entorpecedores de todo el asunto, dijo, eran St. John, un cónsul británico, y un antiguo cónsul español en la ciudad de Santo Domingo, que habían provocado la ocupación española: el español se opone a la anexión de Santo Domingo por los americanos porque España fracasó en ella, y la conducta de St. John la atribuyó a la general maldad del carácter británico en cualquier asunto de emulación territorial. A Saget, el actual usurpador de Haití en la palabra de Fabens, lo describió con desprecio racial, mientras que a Salnave, que había sido muerto en Cabo Haitiano, lo llamó un héroe; Saget, dijo, hizo arrastrar el cuerpo de Salnave detrás de una carreta de bueyes ante la residencia del cónsul americano, donde permanecían la esposa y la familia del presidente muerto, como muestra de su desprecio hacia los Estados Unidos.
