records.headline: The Tribune reprints the report of an Assistant Secretary of State
records.summary_en: The Tribune reprints the report of an Assistant Secretary of State on an earlier Samaná negotiation: the Dominican government, he reported, said it could not consent to an absolute sale of territory without violating an express provision of the constitution of the Dominican Republic just adopted, and that it would be inconvenient to await amendments to the constitution; it proposed instead a lease of Cayo Levantado, which commands the entrance of the bay of Samaná, with the use of the adjacent waters and certain specified privileges on the mainland and the peninsula. This, the Assistant Secretary said, would not answer the purpose of the United States: he declined to entertain the proposition, stating frankly that the United States wanted no place at all unless it was one it should have absolute control over while it owned it, large enough for its use, and one it could hold, fortify and maintain against all enemies; and he reported as the result of all the discussions that it was impracticable to conclude any arrangement at that time on the basis of the Department's instructions, the Dominican government offering only such privileges as it needs no treaty to obtain in any part of the civilized world — space for yards, wharves and buildings, to be paid for with United States money but not to be under its flag or protected by its guns — the window closing mid-sentence on the project's commendation by leading minds.
records.summary_es: El Tribune reproduce el informe de un subsecretario de Estado sobre una negociación anterior de Samaná: el gobierno dominicano, informó, dijo que no podía consentir en una venta absoluta de territorio sin violar una disposición expresa de la constitución de la República Dominicana recién adoptada, y que sería inconveniente esperar enmiendas a la constitución; propuso en cambio un arrendamiento de Cayo Levantado, que domina la entrada de la bahía de Samaná, con el uso de las aguas adyacentes y ciertos privilegios especificados en tierra firme y en la península. Esto, dijo el subsecretario, no respondería al propósito de los Estados Unidos: declinó aceptar la proposición, declarando francamente que los Estados Unidos no querían lugar alguno a menos que fuera uno sobre el que tuvieran control absoluto mientras lo poseyeran, suficientemente grande para su uso, y que pudieran ocupar, fortificar y mantener contra todos los enemigos; e informó como resultado de todas las discusiones que era impracticable concluir arreglo alguno en aquel tiempo sobre la base de las instrucciones del Departamento, ofreciendo el gobierno dominicano solo los privilegios que no necesita tratado alguno para obtenerse en cualquier parte del mundo civilizado —espacio para astilleros, muelles y edificios, a pagarse con dinero de los Estados Unidos pero sin estar bajo su bandera ni protegido por sus cañones—: la ventana se cierra a mitad de una frase sobre la recomendación del proyecto por las mentes principales.

records.headline: Mr. Somers Smith's letters to the Department, reprinted by the Tribune
records.summary_en: Mr. Somers Smith's letters to the Department, reprinted by the Tribune, open on December 9, 1868: he wrote that he had had repeated interviews for the past fortnight with President Báez — General Luperón had protested against any kind of arrangement between the United States and the Dominican Republic, and had written to President Salnave saying it was necessary to forbid all negotiations, to protect the negroes, 'the only caste that must govern this island'; Salnave refused to agree with him, and sent Mr. Báez the communication of General Luperón; General Pimentel had likewise protested; and the only true government that possesses power and popularity, and wishes to be under the protection of the United States, is that of Mr. Báez. On December 10 he wrote that Mr. Delmonte had called, at the special instance of the President, to inform him that Báez had addressed letters to the different authorities throughout the republic on the question of seeking the protection of the United States, and had received replies from all quarters affirming that such measure is most highly approved of, and is very popular in all parts of the country; and on December 19 he wrote again, that Báez is well aware that the Congress of the United States may not be inclined to bring about the annexation of any state or country by an act of war — the window closing inside the third letter.
records.summary_es: Las cartas del Sr. Somers Smith al Departamento, reproducidas por el Tribune, se abren el 9 de diciembre de 1868: escribió que había tenido repetidas entrevistas durante las últimas dos semanas con el presidente Báez —el general Luperón había protestado contra toda clase de arreglo entre los Estados Unidos y la República Dominicana, y había escrito al presidente Salnave diciendo que era necesario prohibir todas las negociaciones, para proteger a los negros, «la única casta que debe gobernar esta isla»; Salnave se negó a estar de acuerdo con él, y envió al Sr. Báez la comunicación del general Luperón; el general Pimentel había protestado igualmente; y el único gobierno verdadero que posee poder y popularidad, y desea estar bajo la protección de los Estados Unidos, es el del Sr. Báez. El 10 de diciembre escribió que el Sr. Delmonte había acudido, por instancia especial del Presidente, para informarle de que Báez había dirigido cartas a las diferentes autoridades de toda la república sobre la cuestión de buscar la protección de los Estados Unidos, y había recibido respuestas de todas partes afirmando que tal medida es muy altamente aprobada, y es muy popular en todas las partes del país; y el 19 de diciembre escribió de nuevo, que Báez es bien consciente de que el Congreso de los Estados Unidos puede no estar inclinado a realizar la anexión de ningún estado o país mediante un acto de guerra: la ventana se cierra dentro de la tercera carta.

records.headline: The News reprints two San Domingo items: a statement of position
records.summary_en: The News reprints two San Domingo items: a statement of position introduced as the Tribune's, and a special telegram on the commission's personnel. The first, from a writer of little previous interest in the question, holds that honest men and good patriots may fairly differ, and that the primary question is one of fact — do the people of the Dominican Republic really desire annexation to the United States? If they do, the writer inclines to receive them into the Union; if they do not, he strongly objects to annexing them by force, wanting no acquisitions of territory whose people prefer to keep apart; and he has heartily supported Senator Morton's proposition, because its adoption seemed calculated to shed light on the vital question. The second reports the commission now complete: Mr. Wade is to be chairman, and Professor Andrew White, of Cornell University, and Dr. Samuel G. Howe, of Boston, are the other members; Dr. Howe was notified by telegraph to-day of his appointment and directed, in case of acceptance, to repair to New York in time to sail on Tuesday, and it is understood he has since notified the President of his acceptance; General Sigel had accepted a place with the commission but has since given it up, for reasons not given — the window closing inside the item.

Si la desea, el escritor se inclina a recibirlo en la Unión; si no la desea, se opone firmemente a anexarlo por la fuerza, pues no quiere adquisiciones de territorio cuyo pueblo prefiera mantenerse aparte; y ha apoyado de corazón la proposición del senador Morton, porque su adopción parecía calculada para arrojar luz sobre la cuestión vital. records.headline: A correspondent who travelled extensively through the island reports that in Santiago, Puerto Plata, La Vega
records.summary_en: A correspondent who travelled extensively through the island reports that in Santiago, Puerto Plata, La Vega, Macoris and Moca the universal sentiment was in favour of annexation, with people heartily tired of war and the better class of merchants and property holders enthusiastically endorsing President Baez and his policy. He reports that the election at Azua resulted in an unprecedented majority in favour of annexation, and denies the charge that grants had been given to those sent to negotiate the treaty. A further dispatch adds that news of the appointment of a United States commission was generally favourably received at St. Domingo.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal que viajó extensamente por la isla informa que en Santiago, Puerto Plata, La Vega, Macorís y Moca el sentimiento universal era favorable a la anexión, con un pueblo muy cansado de la guerra y la clase alta de comerciantes y propietarios apoyando con entusiasmo al presidente Báez y su política. Informa que la elección en Azua dio una mayoría sin precedentes a favor de la anexión, y niega la acusación de que se hubieran dado concesiones a los enviados a negociar el tratado. Otro despacho añade que la noticia del nombramiento de una comisión de los Estados Unidos fue recibida en general favorablemente en Santo Domingo.
records.passage: lar inquiries as to the sentiments of all classes on the subject. In the towns of Santiago, Puerta Plata, La Vega. Macoris and Moca the universal sentiment expressed was in favor of the measure. The people are heartily sick and tired of war, and look to annexation as the sound way to put a stop to such petty factions as that now held by Cabral. All the better class of merchants and property holders are enthusiastic in their endorsement of President Baez and his policy, and esteem him as a statesman and a patriot. The election at Azua resulted in an UNPRECEDENTED MAJORITY IN FAVOR OF ANNEXATION. and their voice was re-echoed all over the island. As to the charge that the [illegible] here to negotiate the treaty were interested in plantations, and that grants had been given them, it is like the balance of the Senator's statements? simply untrue. Your correspondent has had access to the records in the Department of the Interior, and knows that no grant ever has been given or offered to further this or any similar movement. He has, further, in the official handwriting of Minister Delmont, a specific denial of the charges made. This fact will be shown conclusively to the new Commission coming on its arrival. It is to be hoped in the future those opposing the proposed annexation will deal in facts, and not risk their reputations, as the Hon. Senator from Massachusetts has done, by making assertions unbecoming and unmanly.

records.headline: The Herald presents a legend from the childhood of President Báez.
records.summary_en: The Herald presents a legend from the childhood of President Báez. It recounts that upon his baptism as Bonaventura, his father was so moved by a dream that his son would deliver his people that he built a church to commemorate it. The paper observes that the fulfillment of the dream is well known to the people of the country it calls Dominica, where Báez has proven himself a statesman and patriot. A separate dispatch from Santo Domingo dated January 10 reports that news of the appointment of a United States commission was received favorably and with enthusiasm, though public improvements remain halted awaiting congressional action. It adds that agents of German, English, and American capitalists are investigating investment opportunities in anticipation of annexation, while Cabral continues depredations and writes proclamations without confronting Báez's troops.
records.summary_es: El Herald presenta una leyenda de la infancia del presidente Báez. Relata que, tras su bautismo con el nombre de Buenaventura, su padre quedó tan impresionado por un sueño según el cual su hijo sería el libertador de su pueblo que construyó una iglesia para conmemorarlo. El periódico observa que el cumplimiento de ese sueño es bien conocido para el pueblo del país que llama Dominica, donde Báez ha demostrado ser un estadista y patriota. Un despacho por separado desde Santo Domingo fechado el 10 de enero informa que la noticia del nombramiento de una comisión de los Estados Unidos fue recibida favorablemente y con entusiasmo, aunque las mejoras públicas permanecen paralizadas a la espera de la acción del Congreso estadounidense. Añade que agentes de capitalistas alemanes, ingleses y estadounidenses investigan oportunidades de inversión a la espera de la anexión, mientras Cabral continúa sus depredaciones y redacta proclamas sin enfrentarse a las tropas de Báez.

records.full_text:
I have not ascertained satisfactorily what is the situation here, but I will briefly state my belief on the subject.

President Baez, as a statesman and patriot, sincerely desires the annexation of Dominica to America. Delay in accomplishing this is attended by financial trouble, anxiety and risk of insurrection. There is a very rich and large extent of valley country on the western frontier of Dominica, watered by the affluents of the Antibonite, containing some small towns, bearing Spanish names, but of which the Dominicans have not had the complete possession. It is here that Cabral operates with a small predatory party, which President Baez believes is procured and supported by Hayti. Cabral is now at San Juan, say forty miles east of the boundary line between Dominica and Hayti, according to the treaty between Spain and France, with his followers, variable in numbers, but always small, whence he makes raids and retreats as occasion requires. His last operation, noised about as a movement to defeat annexation, was very insignificant and amounted to a few persons killed, wounded and captured by his followers. At Azua and at the posts on several roads leading westward from it the Dominicans have some 1,000 or 1,500 troops. These seem to be in position for defence against incursion from without or insurrection from within. They appear to form the main organization of troops, though there are some troops here and in other places. Though the ordinary expenses of the military, which is the chief administration, are estimated at about $7,000 monthly, the revenue is so small and the paper money of the country is of so little value that the employés of the government have been a long time unpaid, and measures are now proposed looking to treating the paper money like our Continental currency and the French assignats, and providing for receiving some real money for duties wherewith to carry on the government.

records.headline: The Herald's correspondent reports that a British flying squadron
records.summary_en: The Herald's correspondent reports that a British flying squadron has been ordered to rendezvous at Kingston, Jamaica, alongside other British naval movements in the region. The correspondent visited the USS Severn, flagship of the West India squadron, whose admiral reported that the Dominicans are unanimous in favor of annexation. The dispatch attributes the British naval precautions to London's apprehension over expanding United States influence and territorial foothold in the West Indies should Santo Domingo be annexed. It also notes that Admiral S. P. Lee, commanding the North Atlantic Squadron, was entertained at dinner by the Governor of Jamaica.

El corresponsal visitó el buque estadounidense Severn, nave capitana del escuadrón de las Antillas, cuyo almirante informó que los dominicanos son unánimes a favor de la anexión. El despacho atribuye las precauciones navales británicas al recelo de Londres ante la expansión de la influencia y la presencia territorial de los Estados Unidos en las Antillas si se anexa Santo Domingo. También señala que el almirante S. P. Lee, al mando del Escuadrón del Atlántico Norte, fue agasajado en una cena por el gobernador de Jamaica.

records.full_text:
JAMAICA. Herald Special Report from Kingston. England Jealous of the Possible Annexation of St. Domingo. The British Squadron to be Increased and Additional Troops Sent to the Island. A Great Military and Naval Station to be Established.

TELEGRAM TO THE NEW YORK HERALD.

By special telegram from the HERALD'S correspondent at Jamaica we have the important intelligence that England intends to form at Kingston a great military and naval station. This action is, no doubt, in view of the possible annexation of St. Domingo by the United States.

KINGSTON, Jam., Jan. 23, 1871.

We have the important intelligence that the British government has telegraphed the Governor of Jamaica to-day that the island is at once to be placed in a state of complete defence, or, in other words, it is to be made the great military and naval station of the Caribbean Sea. A very large number of troops, in addition to those already here, have been ordered to the island. They will be under the command of General Monroe, and have been ordered from Barbados for the purpose. A British flying squadron is to rendezvous at Kingston, and the flagship is expected to arrive shortly. Your correspondent has visited the United States ship Severn, flagship of the West India squadron, and the admiral reports that the Dominicans are unanimous for annexation. It is the possibility of the annexation of St. Domingo to the United States that has doubtless caused this action on the part of the British government. It fears the extended influence of the United States by getting a foothold among the West India islands, and it deems it best to be ready for any emergency that may arise.

Admiral S. P. Lee, commanding the North Atlantic Squadron, has been entertained at a dinner by the Governor of Jamaica.

records.headline: A published list of inquiries signed 'Bache' outlines the subjects of investigation
records.summary_en: A published list of inquiries signed 'Bache' outlines the subjects of investigation concerning the Dominican Republic. The questions propose examining the physical, moral, and intellectual condition of the Dominicans, their wealth and industrial capacity, and the country's agricultural, forest, marine, and mineral resources. They further call for investigating the climate, soil, harbors, public debt, foreign treaties, and the names of individuals holding territorial grants and concessions. The writer also asks about the meteorological character of the country it calls Dominica, including its exposure to hurricanes and earthquakes, and concludes by asking on what terms the Dominican government desires annexation to the United States.
records.summary_es: Una lista publicada de interrogantes firmada por «Bache» detalla los temas de investigación relativos a la República Dominicana. Las preguntas plantean examinar la condición física, moral e intelectual de los dominicanos, su riqueza y capacidad industrial, así como los recursos agrícolas, forestales, marinos y minerales del país. Piden además indagar sobre el clima, el suelo, los puertos, la deuda pública, los tratados extranjeros y los nombres de las personas que poseen concesiones y mercedes territoriales. El autor pregunta asimismo sobre el carácter meteorológico del país que denomina Dominica, incluyendo su exposición a huracanes y terremotos, y concluye indagando bajo qué términos desea el gobierno dominicano la anexión a los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: The Reporter notes a common mistake in referring to the country
records.summary_en: The Reporter notes a common mistake in referring to the country sought by the United States as 'Dominica.' The paper clarifies that the proper geographical designation is San Domingo and that the formal name of the nation is the Dominican Republic. It explains that the island of Dominica belongs to the British, situated in the Leeward group twenty-two miles north of Martinique and fully five hundred miles east of San Domingo, with another island of that name located in the Marquesas group of the South Pacific.
records.summary_es: El Reporter señala un error muy común al denominar «Dominica» al país al que aspiran los Estados Unidos. El periódico aclara que la designación geográfica correcta es Santo Domingo y que el nombre formal de la nación es República Dominicana. Explica que la isla de Dominica pertenece a los británicos, situada en el grupo de Sotavento a veintidós millas al norte de Martinica y a más de quinientas millas al este de Santo Domingo, y que existe otra isla con ese mismo nombre ubicada en el grupo de las Marquesas en el Pacífico Sur.

records.headline: An article in the Telegraph reviews the historical prosperity
records.summary_en: An article in the Telegraph reviews the historical prosperity and current agricultural potential of the island. It recounts that prior to the revolution of 1789–1790 San Domingo was the wealthiest colonial possession in the Americas, with prosperous French and Spanish sections exporting sugar, coffee, tobacco, and cocoa. Turning to the present, the paper asserts that the territory belonging to the Dominican Republic could support five million people, yet trade remains depressed and the people of Dominica lack even basic implements. It states there is not a single iron plow or sawmill within the republic, despite rich exports of mahogany, lignum-vitae, logwood, and other valuable timbers.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en el Telegraph examina la prosperidad histórica y el potencial agrícola actual de la isla. Recuerda que con anterioridad a la revolución de 1789-1790 Santo Domingo fue la posesión colonial más rica de las Américas, con partes francesa y española prósperas que exportaban azúcar, café, tabaco y cacao. Al abordar el presente, el periódico afirma que el territorio perteneciente a la República Dominicana podría sostener a cinco millones de habitantes, pero el comercio sigue deprimido y la población de Dominica carece incluso de herramientas básicas. Afirma que no existe un solo arado de hierro ni aserradero dentro de la república, a pesar de sus ricas exportaciones de caoba, guayacán, campeche y otras maderas preciosas.

records.headline: The Manchester Journal details the agricultural, forest, and mineral
records.summary_en: The Manchester Journal details the agricultural, forest, and mineral wealth of Santo Domingo. It reports that Dominican tobacco is exported in large quantities to Bremen and Hamburg, with the best quality grown on the great plain near La Vega, marketed in Santiago, and transported across the mountains to Puerto Plata for shipment. The article also notes extensive forests of superior mahogany, logwood, oak, ebony, and mountain pine suitable for shipbuilding, alongside abundant crops of plantains, fruits, and spices. In addition, it describes diverse mineral resources, including deposits of gold, silver, copper, iron, platinum, quicksilver, marble, and rock salt.
records.summary_es: El Manchester Journal detalla la riqueza agrícola, forestal y mineral de Santo Domingo. Informa que el tabaco dominicano se exporta en grandes cantidades hacia Bremen y Hamburgo, cultivándose la mejor calidad en la gran llanura cerca de La Vega, comercializándose en Santiago y transportándose a través de las montañas hasta Puerto Plata para su embarque. El artículo destaca además extensos bosques de caoba superior, campeche, roble, ébano y pino de montaña adecuado para la construcción naval, junto con abundantes cosechas de plátanos, frutas y especias. Asimismo, describe diversos recursos minerales, entre ellos yacimientos de oro, plata, cobre, hierro, platino, azogue, mármol y sal de roca.

records.headline: The Yorkville Enquirer sketches the Dominican Republic's geography
records.summary_en: The Yorkville Enquirer sketches the Dominican Republic's geography and history, noting that it comprises nearly three-fifths of the island, with an area of about 17,500 square miles and a population of roughly 136,000, of whom one-tenth claim to be white. The paper recounts early settlement from Columbus's first colony at Isabela and the founding of Santo Domingo in 1496, followed by French settlement in the west. It states that the whole island was reunited under President Boyer in 1822, until the inhabitants of the eastern part rose against the Haitians and established the independent Dominican Republic in 1844. The article contrasts this with the western section, describing Hayti as historically the richer and more populous portion, which once supplied Europe with half its sugar.
records.summary_es: El Yorkville Enquirer esboza la geografía y la historia de la República Dominicana, y señala que abarca casi tres quintas partes de la isla, con una superficie de unas 17,500 millas cuadradas y una población de aproximadamente 136,000 habitantes, de los cuales una décima parte afirma ser blanca. El periódico relata los primeros asentamientos desde la colonia inicial de Colón en La Isabela y la fundación de Santo Domingo en 1496, seguidos por el establecimiento francés en el oeste. Afirma que toda la isla fue reunificada bajo el presidente Boyer en 1822, hasta que los habitantes de la parte oriental se levantaron contra los haitianos y establecieron la República Dominicana independiente en 1844. El artículo contrasta esto con la sección occidental, describiendo a Haití como la porción históricamente más rica y poblada, que en el pasado abasteció a Europa con la mitad de su azúcar.

records.headline: The Tribune reports that Dominican insurgents under Cabral and other leaders
records.summary_en: The Tribune reports that Dominican insurgents under Cabral and other leaders are determined to challenge the United States protectorate over the Báez government, declaring themselves ready to engage American gunboats. General Pimentel landed near Monte Cristi with 500 Dominicans from St. Thomas and Turks Island, equipped from El Seibo, and is threatening Puerto Plata, while Cabral marches toward Azua. The dispatch notes that Santiago de los Caballeros is set to join the uprising, naming prominent figures of the restoration struggle, including Luperón and Sánchez, among the rebel leaders. It adds that while the insurgent forces are prepared to resist vigorously, the forces of Pimentel and El Seibo are expected to make overtures to the visiting United States commissioners.
records.summary_es: El Tribune informa que los insurgentes dominicanos bajo el mando de Cabral y otros caudillos están decididos a desafiar el protectorado de los Estados Unidos sobre el gobierno de Báez, y se declaran dispuestos a enfrentarse a las cañoneras estadounidenses. El general Pimentel desembarcó cerca de Montecristi con 500 dominicanos procedentes de Santo Tomás y las Islas Turcas, pertrechados desde El Seibo, y amenaza Puerto Plata, mientras Cabral marcha hacia Azua. El despacho señala que Santiago de los Caballeros se apresta a sumarse al levantamiento, y menciona entre los jefes rebeldes a destacadas figuras de la gesta de la Restauración, como Luperón y Sánchez. Añade que, aunque las fuerzas insurgentes están dispuestas a ofrecer una enérgica resistencia, se prevé que las tropas de Pimentel y de El Seibo presenten propuestas a los comisionados estadounidenses que visitan el país.

records.summary_en: The editorial argues that Dominican annexation, if accomplished at all, should be accomplished honorably, and that it cannot be while the U.S. fleet lies in the waters of Santo Domingo after threats conveyed to the president of the Haitian republic by the American minister and admiral. It calls the recall of the ships the first necessity of the situation and says an admiral who threatened to open fire on the Haitian chief should be called before a court of inquiry, as that was an act of war Congress had not declared.

Califica la retirada de los buques de primera necesidad de la situación y dice que un almirante que amenazó con abrir fuego contra el jefe haitiano debería ser llamado ante un tribunal de investigación, pues aquello fue un acto de guerra que el Congreso no había declarado.

records.headline: The Chicago Tribune analyzes the absence of news from the frigate
records.summary_en: The Chicago Tribune analyzes the absence of news from the frigate Tennessee, which departed carrying the United States commissioners to Santo Domingo. The paper explains that the vessel faced head winds, sluggish engines, and a limited twelve-day coal supply, leading its commander to rely largely on sail. Calculating the 1,600-mile voyage from New York to Samaná Bay, along with intended stops at Samaná and Santo Domingo City and transit to Havana, the article estimates that at least twenty-two days would be required before reports could reach the United States. It concludes that there is no real foundation for the prevailing rumors of disaster, and notes that officials in Washington remain confident of the expedition's safety.
records.summary_es: El Chicago Tribune analiza la falta de noticias sobre la fragata Tennessee, que zarpó con los comisionados estadounidenses rumbo a Santo Domingo. El periódico explica que la nave enfrentó vientos contrarios, un rendimiento deficiente de sus máquinas y un suministro de carbón limitado a doce días, lo que llevó a su comandante a navegar principalmente a vela. Al calcular la travesía de 1,600 millas desde Nueva York hasta la bahía de Samaná, junto con las escalas previstas en Samaná y la ciudad de Santo Domingo y el traslado a La Habana, el artículo estima que se requerirían al menos veintidós días para recibir informes en los Estados Unidos. Concluye que no existen motivos reales para los rumores de siniestro y señala que los funcionarios en Washington confían en la seguridad de la expedición.

records.headline: The Evening Telegraph publishes an explanation discounting concerns
records.summary_en: The Evening Telegraph publishes an explanation discounting concerns over the lack of intelligence from the frigate Tennessee and the Dominican commission. It notes that the commissioners had not decided whether to sail directly to Santo Domingo City or visit Samaná Bay first, which would alter the eight-to-ten-day sailing schedule. The report stresses that no regular commercial or telegraphic communication exists at this season from Dominican ports to points linked to the United States, and that no news should be expected until the steamer Tybee returns to New York in about ten days. It reassures the public by describing the Tennessee as a staunch, newly built vessel of nearly three thousand tons, fully capable of weathering the voyage.
records.summary_es: El Evening Telegraph publica una explicación para disipar la inquietud por la falta de noticias de la fragata Tennessee y de la comisión para Santo Domingo. Señala que los comisionados no habían resuelto si navegarían directamente a la ciudad de Santo Domingo o si visitarían primero la bahía de Samaná, lo que modificaría el tiempo de navegación estimado de ocho a diez días. El informe subraya que en esta época del año no existen líneas regulares comerciales ni telegráficas desde los puertos dominicanos hacia puntos conectados con los Estados Unidos, por lo que no deben esperarse noticias hasta el regreso a Nueva York del vapor Tybee en unos diez días. Tranquiliza al público describiendo al Tennessee como un buque nuevo, sólido y de casi tres mil toneladas, plenamente capacitado para la travesía.

records.headline: A satirical squib in The Spirit of Democracy pretends to anticipate
records.summary_en: A satirical squib in The Spirit of Democracy pretends to anticipate the findings of the Dominican commission report while it is still in the pocket of commissioner Wade at Samaná Bay. The paper mockingly predicts the commission will report that the Dominican Republic is the original Garden of Eden with modern improvements, and that its inhabitants possess such moral and intellectual perfection that they seemingly escaped the fall of man. It further lampoons annexation arguments by suggesting that the United States cannot pay its debts, earn a living, or keep out of the poorhouse without annexing San Domingo.

El periódico predice en tono de burla que la comisión dictaminará que la República Dominicana es el Jardín del Edén original con mejoras modernas, y que sus habitantes poseen tal perfección moral e intelectual que aparentemente escaparon a la caída del hombre. Satiriza además los argumentos anexionistas al sugerir que los Estados Unidos no podrán pagar sus deudas, ganarse el sustento ni evitar la bancarrota sin la anexión de Santo Domingo.

records.headline: An official dispatch in The Portland Daily Press gives assurance of no alarm
records.summary_en: An official dispatch in The Portland Daily Press gives assurance of no alarm regarding the frigate Tennessee and the Dominican commission. The dispatch states that the vessel's route between Santo Domingo City and Samaná Bay remained undecided at departure, making the exact duration of the voyage variable beyond the baseline of eight to ten days under steam. It emphasizes that no regular telegraphic or shipping channels connect Dominican ports to points in contact with the United States at this season, meaning news cannot be expected until the steamer Tybee arrives in New York in about ten days. The statement adds that the Tennessee is a staunch vessel of nearly 3,000 tons, larger than any American warship in the West Indies.
records.summary_es: El Portland Daily Press publica un despacho oficial con respecto a la fragata Tennessee y a la comisión dominicana. El despacho explica que no debe cundir la alarma. El despacho indica que la ruta del buque entre la ciudad de Santo Domingo y la bahía de Samaná no estaba decidida al momento de zarpar, lo que hacía variable la duración de la travesía más allá de los ocho a diez días normales a vapor. Subraya que en esta temporada no existen canales telegráficos ni marítimos regulares que comuniquen los puertos dominicanos con puntos en contacto con los Estados Unidos, por lo que no pueden esperarse noticias hasta que el vapor Tybee arribe a Nueva York en unos diez días. La declaración añade que el Tennessee es un navío sólido de casi 3,000 toneladas, más grande que cualquier buque de guerra estadounidense en las Antillas.

records.summary_en: Commander John Irwin reports how, at President Baez's request, he sent Lieutenant Commander McCook and the Nantasket to Azua, where partisans of Cabral, accompanied by Haitians, were causing trouble, and then to Puerto Plata when Baez warned that Luperon's partisans, aided by men from Turks Island, intended to seize that place. records.headline: The Weekly Ottumwa Courier prints an authoritative statement
records.summary_en: The Weekly Ottumwa Courier prints an authoritative statement on the frigate Tennessee, dispelling rumors concerning its safety. It explains that whether the commissioners proceeded directly to Santo Domingo City or stopped first at Samaná Bay, the voyage would require eight to ten days under steam, with additional time for any port call. The paper underscores that there are no regular winter communication lines connecting Dominican ports to telegraphic centers, so that news should not be anticipated until the steamer Tybee reaches New York in about ten days. It assures readers of the vessel's seaworthiness, describing the Tennessee as a newly built ship of nearly 3,000 tons, larger than any other in the West India squadron and commanded by an experienced officer.
records.summary_es: El Weekly Ottumwa Courier publica una declaración oficial sobre la fragata Tennessee, para disipar los rumores sobre su seguridad. Explica que, ya fuera que los comisionados se dirigieran directamente a la ciudad de Santo Domingo o hicieran escala previa en la bahía de Samaná, el viaje requeriría de ocho a diez días a vapor, con tiempo adicional por cualquier parada en puerto. El periódico subraya que no existen líneas regulares de comunicación invernal que conecten los puertos dominicanos con centros telegráficos, por lo que no deben anticiparse noticias hasta que el vapor Tybee llegue a Nueva York en unos diez días. Asegura a los lectores la navegabilidad del buque, describiendo al Tennessee como una nave de reciente construcción de casi 3,000 toneladas, más grande que cualquier otra en el escuadrón de las Antillas y comandada por un oficial experimentado.

records.headline: The New National Era publishes official naval correspondence
records.summary_en: The New National Era publishes official naval correspondence, outlining United States operations in Dominican waters. The instructions direct American naval commanders to secure United States authority at Samaná Bay and the capital, ordering them to capture or destroy any Haitian ships that might attack the Dominicans. The paper notes exchanges between Admiral Poor and Haitian officials regarding these orders, as well as an instance where President Báez requested an American warship to carry mails to St. Thomas. A concluding dispatch from Admiral Lee, dated January 16 at Santo Domingo, reports that he ordered the Swatara to provision at Samaná, directed the Nantasket from Puerto Plata to assist the arriving commission, and designated the commander of the Yantic as senior officer.
records.summary_es: El New National Era publica correspondencia naval oficial, que detalla las operaciones de los Estados Unidos en aguas dominicanas. Las instrucciones ordenan a los comandantes navales estadounidenses asegurar la autoridad norteamericana en la bahía de Samaná y en la capital, disponiendo capturar o destruir cualquier buque haitiano que ataque a los dominicanos. El periódico da cuenta de intercambios entre el almirante Poor y funcionarios haitianos sobre estas órdenes, así como de una ocasión en que el presidente Báez solicitó un buque de guerra estadounidense para transportar correspondencia a Santo Tomás. Un despacho final del almirante Lee, fechado el 16 de enero en Santo Domingo, informa que ordenó a la Swatara abastecerse en Samaná, envió al Nantasket desde Puerto Plata para asistir a la comisión entrante y designó al comandante del Yantic como oficial superior.

records.summary_en: The lack of communication from the frigate Tennessee is explained in an official report carried by The New Orleans Republican. It states that the commissioners had not determined whether to land first at Santo Domingo City or visit Samaná Bay or another northern Dominican port, an itinerary that would extend the baseline voyage of eight to ten days. It reassures the public by describing the Tennessee as a staunch ship of nearly three thousand tons burden, launched since the close of the war and larger than any American vessel in the West Indies.
records.summary_es: El New Orleans Republican publica un informe oficial sobre la fragata Tennessee. El informe explica la falta de comunicación de la fragata. Señala que los comisionados no habían determinado si desembarcarían primero en la ciudad de Santo Domingo o si visitarían la bahía de Samaná u otro puerto del norte dominicano, itinerario que prolongaría la travesía estimada de ocho a diez días. Dado que durante esta época no existe comunicación regular entre los puertos dominicanos y las estaciones telegráficas, el despacho indica que razonablemente no pueden esperarse noticias hasta el regreso del vapor Tybee a Nueva York en unos diez días. Tranquiliza al público describiendo al Tennessee como un barco resistente de casi tres mil toneladas de porte, botado tras el fin de la guerra y más grande que cualquier buque estadounidense en las Antillas.

records.headline: The Chicago Tribune recalls a previous naval mission to examine
records.summary_en: The Chicago Tribune recalls a previous naval mission to examine public sentiment regarding annexation across all ports of the Dominican Republic. It recounts that the USS Nipsic lost her screw propeller three days out and had to put into Port-au-Prince, Haiti, under sail, leading Commander Selfridge to report that strong trade winds and currents made it impossible for a sailing vessel to beat to windward and forced him to abandon his Dominican orders. The paper suggests that if the frigate Tennessee suffered an engine breakdown in these same waters, she would face similar navigation difficulties, though it maintains there is still no evidence that any accident has occurred.
records.summary_es: El Chicago Tribune recuerda una misión naval previa destinada a examinar el sentimiento público hacia la anexión en todos los puertos de la República Dominicana. Relata que el buque estadounidense Nipsic perdió su hélice propulsora a los tres días de navegación y tuvo que arribar a vela a Puerto Príncipe, Haití, lo que llevó al comandante Selfridge a informar que los fuertes vientos alisios y las corrientes hacían imposible que un velero navegara contra el viento, obligándolo a abandonar sus órdenes respecto a Santo Domingo. El periódico sugiere que, de haber sufrido la fragata Tennessee una avería en sus máquinas en esas mismas aguas, enfrentaría dificultades de navegación semejantes, aunque sostiene que aún no existe prueba de que haya ocurrido accidente alguno.

records.headline: In a review of recent magazine literature, the New-York Tribune notices
records.summary_en: In a review of recent magazine literature, the New-York Tribune notices 'My Mission to San Domingo,' an article by Robert M. Walsh published in a monthly periodical. The review states that the work recounts Walsh's experiences as a special agent of the United States government sent to cooperate with British and French commissioners in negotiating peace between the Dominican Republic and the Empire of Hayti. While noting that the article presents many interesting observations on the social condition of the island, the paper criticizes the author's tone as too flippant for so serious a subject, marked by occasional touches of Wall Street slang.
records.summary_es: En una reseña de literatura periódica reciente, el New-York Tribune comenta «My Mission to San Domingo», artículo de Robert M. Walsh publicado en una revista mensual. La reseña señala que la obra relata las vivencias de Walsh como agente especial del gobierno de los Estados Unidos enviado a cooperar con comisionados británicos y franceses para negociar la paz entre la República Dominicana y el Imperio de Haití. Si bien destaca que el artículo aporta numerosas observaciones de interés sobre la condición social de la isla, el periódico censura el tono del autor por considerarlo demasiado frívolo para un tema tan serio, con ocasionales dejes de la jerga de Wall Street.

records.summary_en: A letter describes the annexation commissioners' planned route through Azua and the north side of the island, probably stopping at Port-au-Prince and Puerto Plata, and lists the questions regarded as most important, including whether a war with Haiti would soon follow annexation and whether the U.S. treasury could stand the required appropriation. It expects the commission's report to give a favorable summing up of the island's material resources and a strong commendation of Samana as a naval station.

Espera que el informe de la comisión haga un balance favorable de los recursos materiales de la isla y una firme recomendación de Samaná como estación naval.

records.headline: A correspondent of the New Orleans Republican describes the northern
records.summary_en: A correspondent of the New Orleans Republican describes the northern approach to the island, remarking that while the land remains uncultivated owing to Haitian incursions over the past half century, its picturesque beauty enchanted voyagers long at sea. The dispatch recalls Columbus’s first sight of the island and compares the harbor of Cape François with those of St. Nicolas and Samaná. It notes that Cape François sits at the western end of the great Vega Real, a fertile plain extending far into the Spanish or Santo Domingo part of the island. The writer highlights a historical tie to Louisiana, recalling that explorer Iberville organized naval operations there after establishing French settlements under Sauville and Bienville.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del New Orleans Republican describe la aproximación a la isla desde el norte y señala que, aunque la tierra permanece inculta debido a las incursiones haitianas durante el último medio siglo, su pintoresca belleza cautivó a los viajeros tras una larga travesía marítima. El despacho recuerda la primera impresión de Colón al avistar la isla y compara el puerto de Cabo Francés con los de San Nicolás y Samaná. Observa que Cabo Francés se ubica en el extremo occidental de la gran Vega Real, fértil llanura que se adentra profundamente en la parte española o de Santo Domingo. El autor resalta un lazo histórico con Luisiana al recordar que el explorador Iberville organizó allí operaciones navales tras establecer los primeros asentamientos franceses dirigidos por Sauville y Bienville.

records.headline: Writing from aboard the frigate Tennessee at sea, a special
records.summary_en: Writing from aboard the frigate Tennessee at sea, a special correspondent of the Herald assesses the political stakes surrounding the commission sent to Santo Domingo. The correspondent argues that President Grant has staked his administration and West Indian policy on annexation, meaning the expedition's outcome may make or unmake his presidency. If the commissioners and the journalists accompanying them report favorably on the territory, annexation would satisfy the American desire for expansion and bolster Grant's re-election prospects. Conversely, should the commission or the press report unfavorably, the scheme could collapse and strengthen the formidable opposition already mounted against the administration in Congress.
records.summary_es: Desde la fragata Tennessee en alta mar, un corresponsal especial del Herald evalúa la trascendencia política que rodea a la comisión enviada a Santo Domingo. El corresponsal sostiene que el presidente Grant ha apostado su administración y su política hacia las Antillas a la anexión, por lo que el resultado de la expedición podría consagrar o arruinar su presidencia. Si los comisionados y los periodistas que los acompañan emiten un informe favorable sobre el territorio, la anexión satisfaría el anhelo estadounidense de expansión y fortalecería las perspectivas de reelección de Grant. Por el contrario, si la comisión o la prensa informan desfavorablemente, el proyecto podría fracasar y robustecer la formidable oposición ya entablada contra la administración en el Congreso.

records.headline: A Herald dispatch from Samana reports local claims that there is no sickness there worth speaking about, while
records.summary_en: A Herald dispatch from Samana reports local claims that there is no sickness there worth speaking about, while cautioning that the people have every motive to make a favorable impression on the Commission. The writer finds the climate agreeable and the breezes on the bay balmy, the soil rich and the vegetation luxuriant with palms and coconut groves, but notes that little is raised for market except a few oranges and coconuts, and that improving the country is above all a question of labor.
records.summary_es: Un despacho del Herald desde Samaná recoge las afirmaciones locales de que allí no hay enfermedades de las que valga la pena hablar, advirtiendo a la vez que la gente tiene todos los motivos para causar una impresión favorable a la Comisión. El autor encuentra el clima agradable y las brisas de la bahía templadas, el suelo rico y la vegetación exuberante con palmeras y cocotales, pero señala que poco se cultiva para el mercado salvo unas cuantas naranjas y cocos, y que mejorar el país es ante todo una cuestión de mano de obra.

records.headline: The Herald profiles the leadership of the Dominican commission
records.summary_en: The Herald profiles the leadership of the Dominican commission under a display heading surveying the geography of Santo Domingo. The correspondent characterizes former Senator Benjamin F. Wade, the president of the commission, as an honest investigator who nonetheless believes firmly in manifest destiny and the eventual union of all North American lands with the United States. Noting Wade's longstanding support for Cuban independence and its ultimate incorporation into the Union, the dispatch considers him General Grant’s ideal choice to head the mission and command the confidence of Congress. It introduces Andrew D. White as another commissioner, describing him as a learned university president free from political prejudice against annexation.
records.summary_es: Bajo un encabezado ilustrado que examina la geografía de Santo Domingo, el Herald traza una semblanza del liderazgo de la comisión dominicana. El corresponsal caracteriza al expresidente del Senado Benjamin F. Wade, presidente de la comisión, como un investigador íntegro que, no obstante, cree con firmeza en el destino manifiesto y en la unión final de todas las tierras norteamericanas con los Estados Unidos. Al recordar el respaldo constante de Wade a la independencia de Cuba y a su eventual incorporación a la Unión, el despacho lo considera la elección ideal del general Grant para encabezar la misión y concitar la confianza del Congreso. Presenta además a Andrew D. White como otro de los comisionados, describiéndolo como un erudito presidente universitario exento de prejuicios políticos contra la anexión.

records.headline: The Herald analyzes appointments to the Dominican commission
records.summary_en: The Herald analyzes appointments to the Dominican commission and the political and racial strategy behind them. The correspondent describes the inclusion of a colored father and son in an official role on the commission as an adroit stroke of policy designed to satisfy domestic radicals and propitiate the colored citizens of the Dominican Republic. By displaying Black officials on an equality with distinguished white commissioners and naval officers, the paper argues that Dominicans will see proof of equal rights under the American flag and be encouraged to accept annexation. It observes that such integration illustrates the profound social revolution experienced by the United States over the previous decade, before noting the inclusion of German-American figures such as General Franz Sigel.
records.summary_es: El Herald analiza la estrategia política y racial tras las designaciones en la comisión para Santo Domingo. El corresponsal califica la inclusión de un padre e hijo de color con carácter oficial en la comisión como una hábil maniobra destinada a satisfacer a los radicales en el país y a ganarse a los ciudadanos de color de la República Dominicana. El periódico sostiene que, al mostrar a funcionarios negros en pie de igualdad con distinguidos comisionados y oficiales navales blancos, los dominicanos verán una prueba de igualdad de derechos bajo la bandera estadounidense y se sentirán inclinados a aceptar la anexión. Observa que dicha integración ilustra la profunda revolución social experimentada por los Estados Unidos durante la última década, antes de señalar la presencia de personalidades germano-estadounidenses como el general Franz Sigel.

records.headline: A Herald dispatch dated January 21 from aboard the frigate Tennessee announces
records.summary_en: A Herald dispatch dated January 21 from aboard the frigate Tennessee announces the arrival of the United States commissioners at Samaná Bay following a seven-day voyage. The correspondent reports a smooth passage without storms, noting that the ship relied on favorable winds and auxiliary steam, which was limited to four or five miles an hour because one boiler had been removed. Captain Temple is commended for his skillful navigation and courteous care of the expedition's members. Describing Samaná Bay, the dispatch notes its bold shoreline, deep entrance waters, and the small settlement of Santa Bárbara de Samaná, which it describes as an impoverished village of two to three hundred inhabitants situated on an inner bay inaccessible to large warships.
records.summary_es: Un despacho del Herald fechado el 21 de enero a bordo de la fragata Tennessee anuncia la llegada de los comisionados estadounidenses a la bahía de Samaná tras una travesía de siete días. El corresponsal informa de un viaje tranquilo y sin tormentas, señalando que el buque aprovechó vientos favorables y vapor auxiliar, limitado a cuatro o cinco millas por hora debido a que se le había desmontado una de las calderas. Se elogia al capitán Temple por su diestra navegación y sus esmeradas atenciones hacia los miembros de la expedición. Al describir la bahía de Samaná, el despacho destaca sus costas escarpadas, las aguas profundas en la entrada y el pequeño poblado de Santa Bárbara de Samaná, al que describe como una aldea modesta de doscientos a trescientos habitantes ubicada en una rada interior inaccesible para buques de guerra de gran calado.

records.headline: The dispatch reports that the officials at Samana pray for annexation, and explains that Colonel Abreu, whom the commissioners
records.summary_en: The dispatch reports that the officials at Samana pray for annexation, and explains that Colonel Abreu, whom the commissioners had honoured as the chief man there, is only the special agent and military commander of the Dominican government, while the governor of this section is General Acosta. The commission, with its geologists, botanists, naturalists and correspondents, has been sending parties out to explore the country bordering the bay and up to the mouths of the Yuna River, and going ashore daily to talk with the people and examine their plantations.
records.summary_es: El despacho informa que los funcionarios de Samaná ruegan por la anexión, y explica que el coronel Abreu, a quien los comisionados habían honrado como el hombre principal del lugar, es solo el agente especial y comandante militar del gobierno dominicano, mientras que el gobernador de esta sección es el general Acosta. La comisión, con sus geólogos, botánicos, naturalistas y corresponsales, ha estado enviando grupos a explorar el país que bordea la bahía y hasta las bocas del río Yuna, y desembarcando a diario para hablar con la gente y examinar sus plantaciones.

records.headline: A Herald correspondent reports arriving at St. Domingo City
records.summary_en: A Herald correspondent reports arriving at St. Domingo City on February 3 after a thirty-five hours' passage from Samana, and describes the so-called harbor as a poor roadstead the Tennessee could not leave, where vessels roll heavily even in a light land breeze. In the morning the ship fired a salute of twenty-one guns, which the Dominican fort returned, and the correspondent describes St. Domingo as a quaint, ancient and dilapidated town of seven or eight thousand inhabitants, the oldest place built by Europeans in America.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del Herald informa de su llegada a la ciudad de Santo Domingo el 3 de febrero tras una travesía de treinta y cinco horas desde Samaná, y describe el llamado puerto como una mala rada que la Tennessee no podía abandonar, donde los buques se balancean pesadamente aun con una ligera brisa de tierra. Por la mañana el buque disparó una salva de veintiún cañonazos, que el fuerte dominicano devolvió, y el corresponsal describe Santo Domingo como una ciudad pintoresca, antigua y derruida de siete u ocho mil habitantes, el lugar más antiguo construido por europeos en América.

records.headline: The Tennessee arrived at Santo Domingo from Samana, a few hours after the Nantasket, and the United States commissioners
records.summary_en: The Tennessee arrived at Santo Domingo from Samana, a few hours after the Nantasket, and the United States commissioners came ashore. The dispatch recounts how President Baez's offer of an unoccupied palace for the commissioners was declined by their secretaries, who instead rented a smaller house belonging to Baez and then had to ask him for cots and other necessities, while the correspondents accepted the palace. That day the commission paid a formal visit to Baez, presenting President Grant's autograph letter, and Baez replied that he desired a closer union of the two republics and offered every facility for inquiry, including hearing opponents of annexation.
records.summary_es: El Tennessee llegó a Santo Domingo desde Samaná, pocas horas después del Nantasket, y los comisionados de los Estados Unidos bajaron a tierra. El despacho cuenta cómo el ofrecimiento del presidente Báez de un palacio desocupado para los comisionados fue rechazado por los secretarios de estos, que en su lugar alquilaron una casa más pequeña perteneciente a Báez y luego tuvieron que pedirle catres y otros artículos necesarios, mientras que los corresponsales sí aceptaron el palacio. Ese día la comisión hizo una visita formal a Báez, presentándole la carta autógrafa del presidente Grant, y Báez respondió que deseaba una unión más estrecha de las dos repúblicas y ofreció todas las facilidades para la investigación, incluida la de escuchar a los opositores de la anexión.

M., having been preceded a few hours by the Nantasket. The Commissioners sent for the American Consul, Dr. Ames, to come on board, and this morning they all came ashore. A MISUNDERSTANDING. An unpleasant incident has occurred, which shows either great ignorance and mismanagement on the part of those who conduct matters for the Commissioners or else great cowardice on their part. The messengers who came across country from Samana, after presenting their despatches to President Baez, received from him an offer of an unoccupied palace for the accommodation of the Commissioners and suite. This offer was not to include provisioning them, but simply to afford them proper accommodations. As it was extended through courtesy, and as quarters for such a large party were difficult to be obtained, the offer was accepted on behalf of the Commissioners. When the latter arrived, however, their private secretaries in their wisdom deemed that public opinion in the United States would frown upon such an undemocratic proceeding, and vetoed the whole arrangement. Wise philosophers! They declined the kind offer and hired, for a small price, a smaller house, which, however, belongs to President Baez as his private property; and then, not being able otherwise to procure cots and many other necessary articles, they were compelled finally to ask President Baez to furnish them. records.headline: An editorial in the Chicago Tribune discusses the investigations of the United States Commissioners
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Chicago Tribune discusses the investigations of the United States Commissioners in the Dominican Republic. The paper observes that the Commissioners will hardly determine whether the population genuinely favors annexation until completing their tour of the interior, while noting their inquiries into whether Dominicans will accept American internal revenue laws. It reports that fortifying Samaná is estimated to equal the cost of fortifications around New York, and dismisses the island's mountain scenery as of little value to productive industry. Presuming that Dominicans desire annexation mainly because the Haitians oppose it, the paper cites President Báez's assertion that Cabral's band consists of predatory Haitians operating near the border, and notes that the Commission is inquiring whether annexing Dominica will ultimately require the purchase or conquest of Haiti.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Chicago Tribune comenta las investigaciones de los comisionados de los Estados Unidos en la República Dominicana. El periódico observa que los comisionados difícilmente determinarán si la población favorece genuinamente la anexión hasta que concluyan su recorrido por el interior, al tiempo que señala sus indagaciones sobre si los dominicanos aceptarán las leyes estadounidenses de rentas internas. Informa que se estima que fortificar Samaná igualaría el costo de las fortificaciones alrededor de Nueva York, y desestima el paisaje montañoso de la isla como de escaso valor para la industria productiva. Al presumir que los dominicanos desean la anexión principalmente porque los haitianos se oponen a ella, el periódico cita la afirmación del presidente Báez de que la banda de Cabral está compuesta por haitianos depredadores que operan cerca de la frontera, y señala que la comisión averigua si la anexión de Dominica requerirá en última instancia la compra o conquista de Haití.

records.headline: A dispatch in the Chicago Tribune reports that President Grant received
records.summary_en: A dispatch in the Chicago Tribune reports that President Grant received congratulations in Washington following the safe arrival of the frigate Tennessee in the Dominican Republic. The paper reprints a New-York Tribune correspondence dated Samaná Bay, January 27, describing the voyage of the vessel conveying the annexation Commissioners. The correspondent recounts that after fine initial weather, the ship encountered heavy seas and persistent discomfort off Cape Hatteras. Although the vessel made a moderately quick passage using both steam and sail, the writer notes that its machinery suffered from serious defects, contrasting its poor performance under steam with its faultless sailing qualities before sighting land on the morning of January 24 amid blistering heat.
records.summary_es: Un despacho en el Chicago Tribune informa que el presidente Grant recibió felicitaciones en Washington tras la llegada segura de la fragata Tennessee a la República Dominicana. El periódico reproduce una correspondencia del New-York Tribune fechada en la bahía de Samaná el 27 de enero, que describe la travesía del buque que transportaba a los comisionados de la anexión. El corresponsal relata que, tras un buen clima inicial, el barco encontró mares agitados y persistentes incomodidades frente al cabo Hatteras. Aunque el buque realizó una travesía moderadamente rápida utilizando vapor y velas, el autor señala que su maquinaria sufría de graves defectos, contrastando su deficiente desempeño a vapor con sus impecables cualidades de navegación a vela antes de avistar tierra la mañana del 24 de enero en medio de un calor abrasador.

records.headline: A Santo Domingo dispatch says President Baez emphatically denies reports that he intended to leave the country, and that because of reported
records.summary_en: A Santo Domingo dispatch says President Baez emphatically denies reports that he intended to leave the country, and that because of reported troubles at Azua the United States steamer Nantasket would probably sail for that port. The commission had a long interview with Baez and his cabinet, and Baez offered guides, interpreters and, if needed, a guard, and agreed to grant safe conduct to the city even to Cabral or any of his partisans whom the commission wished to consult.

La comisión tuvo una larga entrevista con Báez y su gabinete, y Báez ofreció guías, intérpretes y, si fuera necesario, una guardia, y aceptó conceder salvoconducto hasta la ciudad incluso a Cabral o a cualquiera de sus partidarios a quienes la comisión deseara consultar.

records.headline: A correspondent for the New-York Tribune reports on agricultural
records.summary_en: A correspondent for the New-York Tribune reports on agricultural practices and tobacco culture in the Dominican Republic. The dispatch notes that local sugarcane remains strong and healthy for decades with minimal cultivation, while plows remain entirely unheard of in the area. The writer pronounces the tobacco grown near Samaná far superior to American varieties, judging a one-cent Samaná cigar superior to cigars selling for ten or fifteen cents in New York, and notes that local smoking tobacco brings twenty cents a pound compared to $1.50 or $2.00 in the United States. He adds that local inhabitants of both sexes frequently chew tobacco and share cigars socially from person to person, considering it wasteful to smoke an entire cigar alone.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del New-York Tribune informa sobre las prácticas agrícolas y el cultivo del tabaco en la República Dominicana. El despacho señala que la caña de azúcar local se mantiene vigorosa y saludable durante décadas con un cultivo mínimo, mientras que los arados son completamente desconocidos en la zona. El autor califica el tabaco cultivado cerca de Samaná como muy superior a las variedades estadounidenses, juzgando que un cigarro de un centavo de Samaná es mejor que los cigarros que se venden por diez o quince centavos en Nueva York, y señala que el tabaco para fumar local cuesta veinte centavos la libra frente a $1.50 o $2.00 en los Estados Unidos. Agrega que los habitantes locales de ambos sexos mastican tabaco con frecuencia y comparten los cigarros socialmente de persona a persona, considerando un despilfarro fumar un cigarro entero en solitario.

records.headline: A correspondent for the New-York Tribune reports on Dominican
records.summary_en: A correspondent for the New-York Tribune reports on Dominican public opinion regarding annexation, stating that Captain McCook found the inland town of Baní, with its 1,800 inhabitants, largely in favor of the measure. According to the dispatch, annexationist sentiment prevailed generally across the country except at Puerto Plata, where English and German merchants feared their commercial interests would suffer. The writer observes that residents around Samaná hold an abiding faith that annexation will make them wealthy, causing land prices to rise so high that no land can be purchased within five miles of the town. Under the heading "The Government," the report states that local magistrates disregard established legal codes, administering summary justice according to their own crude concepts of equity.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del New-York Tribune informa sobre la opinión pública dominicana respecto a la anexión, señalando que el capitán McCook encontró que el poblado interior de Baní, con sus 1,800 habitantes, está ampliamente a favor de la medida. Según el despacho, el sentimiento anexionista prevalecía en general en todo el país, excepto en Puerto Plata, donde los comerciantes ingleses y alemanes temían que sus intereses comerciales se vieran afectados. El autor observa que los habitantes de los alrededores de Samaná mantienen una fe inquebrantable en que la anexión los enriquecerá, provocando que los precios de la tierra suban tanto que no se puede adquirir ninguna parcela a menos de cinco millas del pueblo. Bajo el título «El Gobierno», el informe señala que los magistrados locales ignoran los códigos legales establecidos y administran justicia sumaria según sus propias nociones rudimentarias de equidad.

records.headline: The New-York Tribune's correspondent reports from Samaná on the activities of the United States Commission
records.summary_en: The New-York Tribune's correspondent reports from Samaná on the activities of the United States Commission to Santo Domingo. The dispatch states that on the morning of January 26, the Commissioners sent Captain Henry Wade, son of Commission President Benjamin F. Wade, overland with journalists on an eighty-mile journey to deliver an official communication to President Báez in Santo Domingo City. It reports that the Commissioners toured Samaná and its surrounding district in person, taking shorthand testimony from prominent local residents for submission to President Grant. Among those examined were Provincial Governor José Silvano Acosta, military commandant Enrique Abren, local magistrate Eugenio García, council member Benito García, and planter Benjamin Burr.
records.summary_es: El corresponsal del New-York Tribune informa desde Samaná sobre las actividades de la comisión de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo. El despacho señala que la mañana del 26 de enero los comisionados enviaron al capitán Henry Wade, hijo del presidente de la comisión Benjamin F. Wade, por tierra junto a varios periodistas en un viaje de unas ochenta millas para entregar una comunicación oficial al presidente Báez en la ciudad de Santo Domingo. Informa que los comisionados recorrieron personalmente Samaná y su distrito circundante, tomando testimonios taquigráficos de destacados residentes locales para presentarlos al presidente Grant. Entre los examinados figuraron el gobernador provincial José Silvano Acosta, el comandante militar Enrique Abren, el magistrado local Eugenio García, el miembro del concejo Benito García y el hacendado Benjamin Burr.

records.headline: An editorial in The New York Herald announces the safe arrival of the frigate
records.summary_en: An editorial in The New York Herald announces the safe arrival of the frigate Tennessee at Samaná Bay, Santo Domingo, on January 24, following a seven-day voyage from New York with all on board reported well. The paper denounces rival journals for fabricating sensational rumors questioning the vessel's seaworthiness or reporting it lost at sea. It asserts that the Herald never entertained any doubt regarding the ship's safety, having consistently maintained that the Commissioners had arrived at their destination to inspect the country and enjoy the tropical scenery. The editors declare satisfaction that their steady reporting allayed public anxiety, claiming that the paper's statements can always be relied upon as factual.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en The New York Herald anuncia la llegada segura de la fragata Tennessee a la bahía de Samaná, Santo Domingo, el 24 de enero, tras una travesía de siete días desde Nueva York con todos a bordo en buen estado. El periódico denuncia a los diarios rivales por inventar rumores sensacionalistas que cuestionaban las condiciones de navegación del buque o lo daban por perdido en el mar. Afirma que el Herald nunca albergó duda alguna sobre la seguridad del barco, habiendo sostenido constantemente que los comisionados habían llegado a su destino para inspeccionar el país y disfrutar del paisaje tropical. Los editores manifiestan satisfacción de que sus continuas informaciones calmaran la inquietud pública, asegurando que siempre se puede confiar en la veracidad de las afirmaciones del periódico.

records.summary_en: President Baez tells the commission he himself held an election with a perfectly free vote to obtain the true sentiment of the people. A Tribune correspondent's account of Santa Barbara de Samana follows, describing a poor village of 80 or 90 bamboo and palm-thatched buildings along half a mile of shore, with about 250 inhabitants in the village and about 3,000 on the whole peninsula, a majority of the villagers speaking English.

Sigue el relato de un corresponsal de la Tribune sobre Santa Bárbara de Samaná, que describe un pueblo pobre de 80 o 90 edificios de bambú y techo de palma a lo largo de media milla de costa, con unos 250 habitantes en el pueblo y unos 3.000 en toda la península, hablando inglés la mayoría de los vecinos.

During the stay of the commission at Samana Bay the Tribune correspondent wrote as follows: Samana is a poor little dirty place enough, for all its romantic and picturesque appearance. It is built in a random haphazard sort of way along half-a-mile of curving shore at the foot of a ridge of high wooded hills, and what with its rambling lanes and grotesque huts, I think it is one of the most absurd places I ever saw. There are [illegible] or [illegible] buildings, all told, consisting for the most part of a light framework of scantlings brought from the States, and clapboarded with bamboos split in half and pressed flat by piling stones upon them while wet. The rude planking made in this primitive manner is from four to six inches wide and a half a quarter of an inch thick. Paint is almost unknown, but most of the huts are whitewashed. The roofing is of cocoa leaves bound together with vines. The flooring, when there is any, which is not often, consists of rough-hewn wood, or bark, or boughs, or the same leaves that are used for thatch. records.headline: A Tribune correspondent describes the San Domingo expedition's voyage to Samana Bay: charming weather for two days
records.summary_en: A Tribune correspondent describes the San Domingo expedition's voyage to Samana Bay: charming weather for two days, then stormy seas from the latitude of Hatteras onward, until land was sighted on the morning of January 24. Rounding Cape Cabron and entering the bay, the party saw the roofs of Santa Barbara de Samana, palm tops, green hills and small farm patches, and dropped anchor in the outer harbor at two o'clock that afternoon.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal del Tribune describe el viaje de la expedición a Santo Domingo hasta la bahía de Samaná: tiempo encantador durante dos días y luego mares tormentosos desde la latitud de Hatteras en adelante, hasta que se avistó tierra en la mañana del 24 de enero. Al doblar el Cabo Cabrón y entrar en la bahía, el grupo vio los techos de Santa Bárbara de Samaná, las copas de las palmas, las colinas verdes y pequeños pedazos de tierra cultivada, y echó el ancla en el puerto exterior a las dos de esa tarde.

Writing in the Bay of Samana, on January 27, the Tribune correspondent says: We had charming weather for the first two days out cold, indeed, but bright and clear, with fresh and favoring winds, and every prospect of a pleasant voyage. But toward evening of the second day, in the rough latitude of Hatteras, our troubles began, and from that time until we neared our destination we experienced abundant discomfort and many stormy seas, though without any specially severe test of the seagoing qualities of the frigate. Using generally both steam and sails, we have made a moderately quick passage; but the behavior of the vessel under steam is far from satisfactory, and the machinery is found to be full of serious defects. As a sailer, however, the ship is pronounced faultless. We had been out of sight of land six days and a half, when on the morning of the 24th we heard from the look-out in the maintop the welcome cry of "Land ho!" and the passengers rushed upon deck. Thick clouds hung heavily over a dark line about two points off our starboard bow, hardly discernible at first; but as we came nearer we gradually traced the outline of the mountain range which stretched westward to the mainland from Cape Cabron at the extremity of the peninsula of Samana. The ship anchored in the outer harbor about two miles from the village, where the American flag floated over the property leased by the United States and the steamer Nantasket lay, and the commissioners landed to visit the local authorities.

El barco ancló en el puerto exterior, a unas dos millas del pueblo, donde la bandera americana ondeaba sobre la propiedad arrendada por los Estados Unidos y se encontraba el vapor Nantasket, y los comisionados desembarcaron para visitar a las autoridades locales.

Behind this mountain barrier and opening to the east lies the bay to which we were bound. The morning was the hottest we had yet felt. A burning sun blistered the deck. The brass work of the frigate glowed like fire, and the waters glittered like burnished metal under the blazing heavens. There was hardly a breath of air, and as we steamed through the calm sea the sails hung useless from the yards. Long before noon the whole country around the mouth of the bay was distinctly visible in outline. There were the hills rising abruptly close to the shore, the palisade-like rocks almost surrounding the peninsula, the irregular and picturesque profile of the range stretching back as far as the eye could reach. We could discover no table-land; we saw no beach; and at first there was no sign of life except in the waters, from which a flying fish darted now and then; nor was there much appearance of vegetation. records.headline: The correspondent describes sailing into Samana Bay on the 24th, rounding Cape Cabron to find Santa Barbara de Samaná
records.summary_en: The correspondent describes sailing into Samana Bay on the 24th, rounding Cape Cabron to find Santa Barbara de Samana coming into view, and anchoring in the outer harbour near the United States steamer Nantasket, with the American flag flying over the property leased by the United States. Ashore the next day, the party inspected the town's few public buildings, its Catholic church, a Methodist church being built, and schools whose pupils include descendants of the coloured colony sent here from Philadelphia, whose textbooks are all in English.

Al día siguiente en tierra, el grupo inspeccionó los pocos edificios públicos del pueblo, su iglesia católica, una iglesia metodista en construcción, y escuelas cuyos alumnos incluyen descendientes de la colonia de color enviada aquí desde Filadelfia, cuyos libros de texto están todos en inglés.
records.passage: It was not until we had rounded Cape Cabron and entered the mouth of the bay that the dingy aspect of the landscape changed, and we realized something of that tropical luxuriance and freshness upon which travellers have loved to dilate. In the distance, we soon descried, peeping above the horizon, the roofs of Santa Barbara de Samana, and little by little the whole scene broke upon us in its delicious beauty. One by one appeared the spreading tops of the palms. The brown hue of the hills changed to the most brilliant shades of green, their sides showed here and there a little patch of farm-land shut in by waving forest, and over all the country was a mantle of that soft, beautiful verdure which we never see at home except after the showers of early summer. We could appreciate now the rapture with which Columbus (and we were sailing so they say in the very track of the discoverer) painted the beauties of this island paradise. Close to the shore, in a little gully through which a stream of water ran singing to the sea, stood a hut, with round thatched roof and a single window looking out upon the ocean. Waving palms shaded it in front and rear; blooming hills sheltered it from the winds, and close by was a huge ragged rock against which the lazy surf beat perpetual music. This perfect picture was succeeded by views of larger houses, with patches of cleared land and groves of cocoonuts and bananas. records.headline: A correspondent at Samana describes landing with the commissioners and inspecting the town's public buildings
records.summary_en: A correspondent at Samana describes landing with the commissioners and inspecting the town's public buildings, including its Catholic church, a Methodist church being built, and its schools, where the textbooks are all in English and published in Philadelphia. He also describes the barefoot, half-clad troops guarding the jail, their varied knives, swords and muskets, and a village where more than half of the eighty houses are in some way devoted to trade.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal en Samaná describe el desembarco con los comisionados y la inspección de los edificios públicos del pueblo, incluidos su iglesia católica, una iglesia metodista en construcción y sus escuelas, donde los libros de texto están todos en inglés y publicados en Filadelfia. También describe a las tropas descalzas y semivestidas que guardan la cárcel, con sus variados cuchillos, espadas y mosquetes, y un pueblo donde más de la mitad de las ochenta casas se dedican de algún modo al comercio.
