records.headline: The Tribune publishes an extract from Senator Charles Sumner's speech
records.summary_en: The Tribune publishes an extract from Senator Charles Sumner's speech citing official dispatches from U.S. Commercial Agent Raymond H. Perry in Santo Domingo to show executive intervention. In a dispatch dated January 20, 1870, Perry reported that the warship Nantasket was visiting Puerto Plata and Samaná Bay, stating that Báez needed a man-of-war before public opinion on annexation was expressed. Sumner argues that Báez urgently requested naval forces because he feared the Dominican people would pronounce for his overthrow rather than for annexation. Sumner also cites a February 8, 1870 dispatch in which Perry reported that Báez complained daily that the United States had failed to fulfill its promise to send warships to the coast.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica un extracto del discurso del senador Charles Sumner en el que cita despachos oficiales del agente comercial estadounidense Raymond H. Perry en Santo Domingo para demostrar la intervención del ejecutivo. En un despacho fechado el 20 de enero de 1870, Perry informó que el buque de guerra Nantasket visitaba Puerto Plata y la bahía de Samaná, señalando que Báez necesitaba un buque de guerra antes de que se expresara la opinión pública sobre la anexión. Sumner sostiene que Báez pedía con urgencia fuerzas navales porque temía que el pueblo dominicano se pronunciara por su derrocamiento en lugar de la anexión. Sumner cita también un despacho del 8 de febrero de 1870 en el que Perry informó que Báez se quejaba a diario de que los Estados Unidos no habían cumplido su promesa de enviar buques de guerra a la costa.

records.headline: This account of Dominican history relates that after Baez was overthrown, General Jose Maria Cabral became lawful president
records.summary_en: This account of Dominican history relates that after Baez was overthrown, General Jose Maria Cabral became lawful president by the direct vote of the people in September 1866, the first time a question had been submitted to a direct vote in the country's history, and that peace ensued. It says Cabral, embarrassed by financial difficulties, turned to the United States offering a lease of the bay of Samana, while the exiled Baez denounced the sale of his country, organised a hostile force with the help of Salnave of Hayti, and compelled Cabral's capitulation on February 8, 1868, after which a convention named Baez Grand Citizen with unlimited powers and his enemies were exiled or executed.
records.summary_es: Este relato de la historia dominicana cuenta que, tras la caída de Báez, el general José María Cabral llegó a ser presidente legítimo por el voto directo del pueblo en septiembre de 1866, la primera vez que una cuestión se sometía al voto directo en la historia del país, y que sobrevino la paz. Dice que Cabral, agobiado por dificultades financieras, se dirigió a los Estados Unidos ofreciendo el arrendamiento de la bahía de Samaná, mientras Báez, desde el exilio, denunciaba la venta de su patria, organizaba una fuerza hostil con la ayuda de Salnave, de Haití, y obligaba a Cabral a capitular el 8 de febrero de 1868, tras lo cual una convención nombró a Báez Gran Ciudadano con poderes ilimitados y sus enemigos fueron exiliados o ejecutados.
records.passage: also manifesto of Cabral, assigning at still greater length reasons for the overthrow of Baez, and holding him up as the enemy of peace and union; also a manifesto by the Triumvirate, constituting the Provisional Government, declaring his infractions of the Constitution; also a manifesto from the General in command of the City of Santo Domingo, where, after denouncing the misdeeds of one man, it says, "this man, this monster, this speculator, this tyrant is Buenaventura Baez." Soon after the disappearance of Baez, his rival became lawful President by the direct vote of the people, according to the requirement of the Constitution. Different numbers of the official journal now before me contain the election returns in September, 1866, where the name of Gen. José Maria Cabral appears at the head of the poll. This is memorable as the first time in the history of Dominica when a question was submitted to the direct vote of the people. By that direct vote Cabral became President, and peace ensued. records.headline: The Chicago Tribune prints an extract from Secretary of the Navy Robeson's letter
records.summary_en: The Chicago Tribune prints an extract from Secretary of the Navy Robeson's letter explaining the administration's actions regarding the Dominican Republic. The letter asserts that the right of revolution does not empower insurgents to treat agents of foreign nations as enemies while they act under existing laws. Robeson states that neither the United States nor its executive has taken part in internal Dominican conflicts. He argues that the President holds the constitutional authority to initiate treaties, and that Congress appropriated funds in 1866 to lease or purchase territory on the island of San Domingo. Robeson maintains that the bay and peninsula of Samaná were deemed most suitable for a naval station, justifying the negotiation of treaties for cession and annexation.
records.summary_es: El Chicago Tribune publica un extracto de la carta del secretario de la Armada Robeson en la que explica las acciones del gobierno respecto a la República Dominicana. La carta asevera que el derecho de revolución no faculta a los insurgentes para tratar a los agentes de naciones extranjeras como enemigos mientras actúen bajo las leyes vigentes. Robeson declara que ni los Estados Unidos ni su ejecutivo han intervenido en los conflictos internos dominicanos. Sostiene que el presidente posee la facultad constitucional para iniciar tratados y que el Congreso asignó fondos en 1866 para arrendar o comprar territorio en la isla de Santo Domingo. Robeson mantiene que la bahía y península de Samaná se consideraron las más adecuadas para una estación naval, justificando la negociación de tratados de cesión y anexión.

records.headline: A Washington dispatch in the Daily Kennebec Journal reports
records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch in the Daily Kennebec Journal reports that Senate discussion of the San Domingo question drew a large crowd to the galleries, attracting House members after adjournment to hear General Carl Schurz. Schurz, standing near Senator Sumner and receiving frequent suggestions from him, was announced to speak the next day in criticism of Secretary Robeson's March 21 letter to Admiral Lee. The dispatch further notes that the San Domingo Commissioners have agreed upon their report, with the exception of the subjects of public health and the debts of the Dominican Republic. It adds that the commissioners may not be ready to submit their findings until Thursday.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Washington en el Daily Kennebec Journal informa que el debate en el Senado sobre la cuestión de Santo Domingo atrajo a una multitud a las galerías, congregando a miembros de la Cámara tras el receso para escuchar al general Carl Schurz. Schurz, ubicado cerca del senador Sumner y recibiendo constantes sugerencias suyas, fue anunciado para hablar al día siguiente criticando la carta del 21 de marzo del secretario Robeson al almirante Lee. El despacho señala además que los comisionados de Santo Domingo han acordado su informe, a excepción de los temas de salud pública y la deuda de la República Dominicana. Añade que los comisionados tal vez no estén listos para presentar sus conclusiones hasta el jueves.

records.headline: Senator Morton's reply to Sumner: the commission could not negotiate, Haiti itself assured Minister Bassett it would not interfere
records.summary_en: Senator Morton's reply to Sumner: the commission could not negotiate, Haiti itself assured Minister Bassett it would not interfere with the Dominicans' free will, and the United States merely warned Haiti - which had given Cabral passage and war vessels - not to make war during the negotiations.
records.summary_es: La respuesta del senador Morton a Sumner: la comisión no podía negociar, Haití mismo aseguró al ministro Bassett que no interferiría con la libre voluntad de los dominicanos, y Estados Unidos solo advirtió a Haití - que había dado a Cabral paso y buques de guerra - que no hiciera la guerra durante las negociaciones.
records.passage: Mr. Morton then had read by the Secretary a dispatch to United States Minister Bassett, from the Haytien Secretary of Foreign Affairs, assuring him that Hayti had no disposition or desire to interfere with the free will of the Dominicans. As a further reply to Mr. Sumner, he reminded the Senator, as evidence, that the Administration had not proposed to take any immediate action upon annexation; that Commission had no authority to negotiate a treaty, and that no one went with them who could take a single step in that direction. The Haytien Government, in violation of the law of nations, had given free passage across its territory to Cabral, and had furnished him with war vessels to attack Dominica, and the United States had merely notified Hayti that while our negotiations were pending with Dominica we would not allow him to make war on the island. This the United States had an undoubted right to do, because our Government had information of organizations on foot in Hayti to defeat annexation. No one need tell him (Morton) that the Senator from Massachusetts was a friend of liberty or the colored man when he so industriously spent his time in an effort to put the Democratic party in power, for to destroy the President is to destroy the great party of which he is the head (applause), and we know the terrible effect upon the liberties of this country if the Democratic party comes into power.

records.headline: The Kentucky Gazette reports that Secretary of the Navy Robeson addressed
records.summary_en: The Kentucky Gazette reports that Secretary of the Navy Robeson addressed a letter to Rear-Admiral Lee defending the administration's naval posture toward Haiti during the San Domingo negotiations. Robeson maintained that in executing United States policy, not a single shot had been fired nor had any armed men landed in hostility on the island of San Domingo. He insisted that the government had neither interfered in the internal conflicts of the Dominican Republic nor coerced any foreign power. Instead, Robeson explained that the administration simply announced its intention to protect its acquired interests in the republic against external attacks until the annexation treaties were decided, thereby preserving its right of pre-emption.
records.summary_es: The Kentucky Gazette informa que el secretario de la Armada Robeson dirigió una carta al contraalmirante Lee defendiendo la postura naval del gobierno frente a Haití durante las negociaciones sobre Santo Domingo. Robeson sostuvo que, al ejecutar la política de los Estados Unidos, no se había efectuado un solo disparo ni desembarcado hombres armados en actitud hostil en la isla de Santo Domingo. Insistió en que el gobierno no había intervenido en los conflictos internos de la República Dominicana ni coaccionado a ninguna potencia extranjera. Por el contrario, Robeson explicó que la administración simplemente anunció su intención de proteger contra ataques externos los intereses adquiridos en la república hasta que se resolvieran los tratados de anexión, preservando así su derecho de prelación.

records.headline: The Evening Telegraph prints a Washington report headed 'Cabral
records.summary_en: The Evening Telegraph prints a Washington report headed 'Cabral Goes Back on His Friend Sumner,' citing a letter from General José María Cabral obtained by the San Domingo Commission in Port-au-Prince. The correspondent writes that Cabral's authentic letter upsets Senator Charles Sumner's calculations regarding Santo Domingo. In the letter, addressed to the President of the United States Senate on February 18, 1871, Cabral refers to Sumner's December 21, 1870 speech. Cabral quotes Sumner's assertion that Cabral's actual policy was to reunite the two governments of Dominica and Haiti as they existed before 1844, a claim Cabral seeks to correct.
records.summary_es: The Evening Telegraph publica un informe de Washington titulado «Cabral le da la espalda a su amigo Sumner», citando una carta del general José María Cabral obtenida por la comisión de Santo Domingo en Puerto Príncipe. El corresponsal escribe que la auténtica carta de Cabral desbarata los cálculos del senador Charles Sumner respecto a Santo Domingo. En la misiva, dirigida al presidente del Senado de los Estados Unidos el 18 de febrero de 1871, Cabral hace referencia al discurso pronunciado por Sumner el 21 de diciembre de 1870. Cabral cita la aseveración de Sumner de que su verdadera política era reunir nuevamente los dos gobiernos de Dominica y Haití como estaban antes de 1844, afirmación que Cabral busca rectificar.

records.summary_en: Washington telegrams on the commission's return: rumor that the administration will drop San Domingo for party harmony; the commissioners' view that annexation means war with Haiti; Báez's admission that a thousand square miles along the Haitian line are held by Cabral; Wade, White and Howe arrive with Douglass.

records.passage: Annexation Means War with Hayti. Another Washington correspondent telegraphs that it seems to be the general opinion of the Commissioners that annexation cannot take place without involving the United States in a war with Hayti. Baez admitted to the Commissioners that one thousand square miles of territory belonging to the Dominican republic, and lying contiguous to Hayti, are under control of Cabral and his followers. It is stated that Baez did not make any effort to allow the Commissioners to meet Cabral, but on the contrary assured them that he could not afford them any protection if they visited the part of the island that Cabral controlled. All speak in the highest terms of the island, its climate and productions, but appear to entertain a very poor opinion of the people, who are described as indolent, superstitious and exceedingly undesirable in their present condition as an addition to the population of the United States. records.headline: The Nashville Union and American reports that the San Domingo Commissioners met
records.summary_en: The Nashville Union and American reports that the San Domingo Commissioners met with President Grant at the Executive Mansion, though their formal report was not submitted. The item notes that the commissioners are scheduled to dine with the President on Thursday. Under the heading 'Reconstructing Their Report,' a separate brief states that the commissioners have agreed upon the main contents of their report, except on the subjects of health and the debt of the Dominican Republic. It adds that because of these pending questions, the commissioners may not be able to deliver their final report until Thursday.
records.summary_es: El Nashville Union and American informa que los comisionados de Santo Domingo se reunieron con el presidente Grant en la Mansión Ejecutiva, aunque no presentaron su informe oficial. La nota señala que los comisionados tienen programado cenar con el presidente el jueves. Bajo el título «Reconstruyendo su informe», una breve nota aparte indica que los comisionados han acordado los aspectos principales de su informe, excepto en lo relativo a la salud y la deuda de la República Dominicana. Añade que, debido a estos temas pendientes, es posible que los comisionados no puedan entregar su informe definitivo hasta el jueves.

records.headline: A Washington dispatch in the Worcester Daily Spy recounts Senate debate
records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch in the Worcester Daily Spy recounts Senate debate following Charles Sumner's speech against the administration. Senator Oliver P. Morton argued that the executive had not violated international law, maintaining that Haiti had routinely breached the law of nations in its relations with Dominica by permitting its territory to serve as a base for hostile incursions and supplying domestic insurgents with money and weapons. Morton asserted that American naval intervention to protect San Domingo from Haitian hostility during pending treaty negotiations was an exercise of legitimate rights under international law. The correspondent adds that Senator Howe of Wisconsin subsequently attacked Sumner with great intensity, comparing his course to historical party apostates.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Washington en el Worcester Daily Spy reseña el debate en el Senado tras el discurso de Charles Sumner contra el gobierno. El senador Oliver P. Morton sostuvo que el ejecutivo no había violado el derecho internacional, afirmando que Haití había infringido sistemáticamente el derecho de gentes en sus relaciones con Dominica al permitir que su territorio sirviera de base para incursiones hostiles y al suministrar dinero y armas a los insurgentes locales. Morton aseveró que la intervención naval estadounidense para proteger a Santo Domingo de la hostilidad haitiana durante las negociaciones del tratado constituía un ejercicio de derechos legítimos bajo el derecho internacional. El corresponsal añade que el senador Howe de Wisconsin atacó luego a Sumner con notable vehemencia, comparando su conducta con la de conocidos apóstatas de la historia.

records.headline: A Senate report in the Portland Daily Press covers Carl Schurz's response
records.summary_en: A Senate report in the Portland Daily Press covers Carl Schurz's response to Senator Frelinghuysen regarding Secretary Robeson's dispatch to Admiral Lee. Schurz condemned as brazen Robeson's assertion that the Executive had not taken part in internal Dominican affairs, citing naval orders under which American commanders at Dominica protected President Báez against both Haiti and his own citizens. Schurz stated that a United States warship carried Báez's troops from Azua to Santo Domingo, and that the Tennessee conveyed Báez and his staff so he could direct his forces. Schurz further charged that Báez's troops carried the American flag against Cabral to deceive opponents, and noted that rockets were supplied to Báez during a threatened attack by Luperón.
records.summary_es: Una crónica del Senado en el Portland Daily Press cubre la respuesta de Carl Schurz al senador Frelinghuysen respecto al despacho del secretario Robeson al almirante Lee. Schurz calificó de descarada la afirmación de Robeson de que el ejecutivo no había intervenido en los asuntos internos dominicanos, citando órdenes navales bajo las cuales comandantes estadounidenses en Dominica protegieron al presidente Báez tanto de Haití como de sus propios ciudadanos. Schurz declaró que un buque de guerra de los Estados Unidos transportó tropas de Báez desde Azua hasta Santo Domingo, y que el Tennessee trasladó a Báez y a su estado mayor para que dirigiera sus fuerzas. Schurz denunció además que las tropas de Báez llevaron la bandera estadounidense contra Cabral para engañar a sus adversarios, y señaló que se suministraron cohetes a Báez ante una amenaza de ataque de Luperón.

records.headline: The New York Herald reports on Senator Carl Schurz's speech
records.summary_en: The New York Herald reports on Senator Carl Schurz's speech challenging Secretary Robeson's dispatch to Admiral Lee, which Senator Frelinghuysen had introduced. Schurz denounced Robeson's claim that the executive had refrained from participating in Dominican internal affairs, contending it contradicted official Navy Department orders. Under those orders, Schurz argued, naval commanders at Dominica intervened to uphold Báez against both Haiti and domestic opposition. He cited evidence that an American war vessel transported Báez's troops from Azua to Santo Domingo, that the Tennessee carried Báez and his staff to command military operations, and that Dominican government forces carried the United States flag against Cabral to deceive insurgents into believing they faced American soldiers.
records.summary_es: El New York Herald informa sobre el discurso del senador Carl Schurz en el que impugnó el despacho del secretario Robeson al almirante Lee, presentado previamente por el senador Frelinghuysen. Schurz denunció la afirmación de Robeson de que el ejecutivo se había abstenido de participar en los asuntos internos dominicanos, sosteniendo que contradecía las órdenes oficiales del Departamento de la Armada. Bajo tales órdenes, argumentó Schurz, los comandantes navales en Dominica intervinieron para sostener a Báez tanto contra Haití como contra la oposición interna. Citó pruebas de que un buque de guerra estadounidense transportó tropas de Báez de Azua a Santo Domingo, que el Tennessee trasladó a Báez y a su estado mayor para dirigir operaciones militares, y que las fuerzas del gobierno dominicano portaron la bandera de los Estados Unidos contra Cabral para hacer creer a los insurgentes que se enfrentaban a soldados estadounidenses.

records.headline: (Jacques ler.) 1805—A proclamation of Dessalines, of April 28th, orders the massacre of all French residents
records.summary_en: The newspaper excerpt details a chronological timeline of events in the island from 1804 to 1812, including the declaration of Hayti's independence under Dessalines, subsequent leadership changes, conflicts, and massacres. It notes that Spain recovered possession of the eastern part of the island in 1806 and the colony in 1808, followed by Dominicans declaring their independence, abolishing slavery, and driving the French out of Santo Domingo in 1809. The timeline concludes with leadership divisions between Christophe, who was crowned King Henry I, and President Petion of Haiti up to 1812.
records.summary_es: El extracto periodístico detalla una relación cronológica de los sucesos acaecidos en la isla entre 1804 y 1812, que abarca la proclamación de la independencia de Haití bajo Dessalines, las consiguientes alternancias de mando, guerras y degüellos. Refiere que España recobró la posesión de la parte oriental de la isla en 1806 y de la colonia en 1808, sucediéndose la expulsión de los franceses de Santo Domingo por los dominicanos en 1809, junto con declaraciones emancipadoras y de libertad. La cronología concluye con las escisiones de mando entre Christophe, coronado rey Enrique I, y el presidente Petion de Haití hacia 1812.

records.full_text:
Hayti and Santo Domingo.

Chronological Epitome.

1795—By the treaty of Basle, the Spanish portion of Santo Domingo is ceded to France.

1798—Hedouville lands at French Cape, and sends Toussaint L'Ouverture, an emancipated slave, to France. On the 8th of May, the English leave the island, and civil war between Toussaint L'Ouverture and Rigaud.

1801—Toussaint L'Ouverture takes the Spanish portion of the island, and assumes the title of Governor General for life.

1802—The French squadron, under Leclerc, arrives at Port au Prince in February; takes the Cape and burns the town, Dessalines opposing. A truce concluded May 1st.

1803—In April, L'Ouverture dies in France, having been taken prisoner during the truce. The French are driven into Cape Haytien, where, November 30th, they surrendered to English commanders.

1804—1st of January, Hayti is declared independent, and Dessalines made Governor General for life. October 8th he is crowned Emperor, with the title of James I. (Jacques 1er.)

1805—A proclamation of Dessalines, of April 28th, orders the massacre of all French residents, and the order is at once put in force. Those spared are subsequently assembled on the Place d'Armes to receive certificates of protection, and the little remnant of survivors are then shot.

1806—Dessalines is executed as a tyrant October 17th, at Pont Rouge. The east part of the island repossessed by Spain.

records.headline: The Worcester Daily Spy prints a report of Senator Carl Schurz's Senate speech
records.summary_en: The Worcester Daily Spy prints a report of Senator Carl Schurz's Senate speech condemning American naval intervention in the Dominican Republic. Schurz argued that Secretary Robeson's denial of executive interference was refuted by instructions under which naval officers at Dominica upheld Báez against Haiti and his own people. He highlighted instances where a U.S. warship carried Báez's troops from Azua to Santo Domingo, the Tennessee transported Báez and his staff, and Dominican troops flew the American flag against Cabral's forces. Schurz further recounted that when Luperón threatened Báez's faction, rockets were supplied from the warship Congress to summon aid; when one was fired, an armed boatload of sailors immediately put off toward shore.
records.summary_es: El Worcester Daily Spy publica una crónica del discurso del senador Carl Schurz en el Senado en el que condena la intervención naval estadounidense en la República Dominicana. Schurz sostuvo que la negativa del secretario Robeson sobre una injerencia del ejecutivo quedaba desmentida por las instrucciones bajo las cuales los oficiales navales en Dominica respaldaron a Báez frente a Haití y su propio pueblo. Destacó casos en que un buque de guerra estadounidense trasladó tropas de Báez de Azua a Santo Domingo, el Tennessee transportó a Báez y a su estado mayor, y las tropas dominicanas enarbolaron la bandera estadounidense frente a las fuerzas de Cabral. Schurz relató además que cuando Luperón amenazó a la facción de Báez, se suministraron cohetes desde el buque de guerra Congress para pedir auxilio; al dispararse uno, un bote con marineros armados zarpó de inmediato hacia la orilla.

records.headline: An editorial in the New-York Tribune examines the Dominican border
records.summary_en: An editorial in the New-York Tribune examines the Dominican border conflict, describing an ill-defined boundary and disputed territory between the Dominican Republic and Haiti. The paper notes that the entire island was originally Spanish and had previously been united, in the paper's phrasing, under Haitian rule for a few years half a century earlier. It reports that José María Cabral, operating in the debatable border region with quiet backing from Haitian men and munitions, seeks to overthrow President Buenaventura Báez by appealing to Dominican patriotism against annexation. The Tribune defends President Grant's directive providing moral naval support to Báez, arguing it simply warns Haiti and Cabral not to subvert the Dominican government by force while treaty negotiations remain pending.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el New-York Tribune examina el conflicto fronterizo dominicano, describiendo un límite impreciso y un territorio en disputa entre la República Dominicana y Haití. El periódico señala que toda la isla fue originalmente española y había estado previamente unida, según la formulación del diario, bajo dominio haitiano durante algunos años medio siglo antes. Informa que José María Cabral, operando en la zona fronteriza disputada con el respaldo encubierto de hombres y pertrechos haitianos, procura derrocar al presidente Buenaventura Báez apelando al patriotismo dominicano contra la anexión. El Tribune defiende la disposición del presidente Grant de brindar apoyo naval moral a Báez, argumentando que simplemente advierte a Haití y a Cabral que no derroquen por la fuerza al gobierno dominicano mientras las negociaciones del tratado sigan pendientes.

records.headline: The Rutland Weekly Herald comments editorially on the removal of Charles Sumner
records.summary_en: The Rutland Weekly Herald comments editorially on the removal of Charles Sumner from the chairmanship of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations. The Herald expresses skepticism that Sumner's displacement will result in the annexation of San Domingo or damage foreign relations, asserting that other able senators can adequately fill the position. Citing the Montpelier Freeman, the paper dismisses predictions of party rupture, noting that whether the action is viewed as an administration victory regarding the Santo Domingo annexation scheme or prompted by other motives, it need not disturb Republican harmony. The Freeman emphasizes that although Vermont's two senators took opposing stances, no division within the state's party will follow.
records.summary_es: El Rutland Weekly Herald comenta en su editorial sobre la destitución de Charles Sumner de la presidencia del Comité de Relaciones Exteriores del Senado. El Herald manifiesta su escepticismo de que el relevo de Sumner conduzca a la anexión de Santo Domingo o perjudique las relaciones exteriores, afirmando que otros senadores competentes pueden ocupar adecuadamente el cargo. Citando al Montpelier Freeman, el periódico descarta los pronósticos de una ruptura partidaria, señalando que, ya sea vista la medida como una victoria de la administración respecto al plan de anexión de Santo Domingo o motivada por otras razones, no tiene por qué perturbar la concordia republicana. El Freeman recalca que, aun cuando los dos senadores de Vermont adoptaron posturas opuestas, no se derivará división alguna dentro del partido en el estado.

records.headline: The Daily Kennebec Journal prints an extract from Secretary of the Navy Robeson's official
records.summary_en: The Daily Kennebec Journal prints an extract from Secretary of the Navy Robeson's official letter defending executive actions concerning the Dominican Republic. Robeson states that the Republic of San Domingo, with its advantageous position, natural wealth, and friendly population, was deemed highly desirable for American commerce and naval stations at Samaná. He maintains that the President held the constitutional power to initiate and negotiate treaties for the cession of Samaná and annexation with the established de facto and de jure Dominican government. While acknowledging that these treaties remained subject to ratification by the Senate and the Dominican people, Robeson argues that the Executive had a clear duty to protect this newly acquired interest against foreign interference.
records.summary_es: El Daily Kennebec Journal publica un extracto de la carta oficial del secretario de la Armada Robeson en defensa de las acciones del ejecutivo relativas a la República Dominicana. Robeson manifiesta que la República de Santo Domingo, con su ventajosa posición, riqueza natural y población amistosa, se consideraba muy conveniente para el comercio estadounidense y para estaciones navales en Samaná. Sostiene que el presidente poseía la facultad constitucional para iniciar y negociar tratados de cesión de Samaná y de anexión con el gobierno dominicano establecido de facto y de jure. Si bien reconoce que dichos tratados estaban sujetos a la ratificación del Senado y del pueblo dominicano, Robeson afirma que el ejecutivo tenía el claro deber de proteger este interés recién adquirido frente a cualquier injerencia extranjera.

records.headline: The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer reprints a New York Times dispatch
records.summary_en: The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer reprints a New York Times dispatch, under the heading 'Fred Douglass' Views on San Domingo and Sumner,' reporting an audience between Frederick Douglass and President Grant, attended by Secretary Robeson and Attorney General Akerman. When questioned by the President, Douglass reported his impressions of Dominica and Haiti, describing the Dominicans as far superior to the Haitians and characterizing Haiti's government as an oppressive despotism devoid of republicanism. Douglass expressed regret over Senator Charles Sumner's opposition, hoping the forthcoming commissioners' report would convince him to change his views. Douglass stated that if Sumner continued his resistance, he would consider him 'the worst foe the colored race has on this continent,' while affirming his own support for annexation.
records.summary_es: Bajo el título «Opiniones de Fred Douglass sobre Santo Domingo y Sumner», el Wheeling Daily Intelligencer reproduce un despacho del New York Times que informa sobre una audiencia entre Frederick Douglass y el presidente Grant, en presencia del secretario Robeson y el fiscal general Akerman. Al ser consultado por el presidente, Douglass transmitió sus impresiones sobre Dominica y Haití, calificando a los dominicanos de muy superiores a los haitianos y describiendo el gobierno de Haití como un despotismo opresivo carente de republicanismo. Douglass lamentó la oposición del senador Charles Sumner, esperando que el próximo informe de los comisionados lo indujera a rectificar su postura. Douglass declaró que si Sumner persistía en su resistencia, lo consideraría «el peor enemigo que tiene la raza de color en este continente», reafirmando su propio respaldo a la anexión.

records.headline: A Senate debate report in the Springfield Weekly Republican covers
records.summary_en: A Senate debate report in the Springfield Weekly Republican covers Carl Schurz's speech denouncing Secretary Robeson's dispatch to Admiral Lee. Schurz challenged Robeson's written assertion that the Executive had not taken part in Dominican internal affairs, maintaining that naval commanders at Dominica actively intervened to uphold Buenaventura Báez against both Haiti and Dominican citizens. Schurz stated that a United States warship carried Báez's troops from Azua to Santo Domingo, and that the Tennessee conveyed Báez and his staff so he could assume command of his forces. He further asserted that Báez's troops carried the American flag against Cabral to deceive opponents into believing they were engaging United States forces.
records.summary_es: Una crónica del debate en el Senado en el Springfield Weekly Republican cubre el discurso de Carl Schurz denunciando el despacho del secretario Robeson al almirante Lee. Schurz rebatió la afirmación escrita de Robeson de que el ejecutivo no había intervenido en los asuntos internos dominicanos, sosteniendo que los comandantes navales en Dominica intervinieron activamente para respaldar a Buenaventura Báez tanto frente a Haití como ante los propios ciudadanos dominicanos. Schurz declaró que un buque de guerra de los Estados Unidos trasladó tropas de Báez de Azua a Santo Domingo, y que el Tennessee transportó a Báez y a su estado mayor para que asumiera el mando de sus fuerzas. Afirmó además que las tropas de Báez portaron la bandera estadounidense contra Cabral para hacer creer a sus opositores que se enfrentaban a fuerzas de los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: The Springfield Weekly Republican prints an extract from Secretary of the Navy Robeson's official
records.summary_en: The Springfield Weekly Republican prints an extract from Secretary of the Navy Robeson's official letter to Rear-Admiral Lee. Robeson addresses a published letter concerning the San Domingo Commission, warning that it misleads the public and authorities of San Domingo regarding the spirit of executive orders to naval vessels. He rejects the premise that anyone connected with the commission captured within rebel lines could be treated as a spy on the theory that the United States had chosen to intervene in Dominican domestic conflicts. Robeson terms this assertion unfounded in fact and law, insisting that the United States was dealing with the regularly constituted government of the Dominican Republic in accordance with international law.
records.summary_es: El Springfield Weekly Republican publica un extracto de la carta oficial del secretario de la Armada Robeson dirigida al contraalmirante Lee. Robeson se refiere a una carta divulgada relativa a la comisión de Santo Domingo, advirtiendo que induce a error al público y a las autoridades de Santo Domingo sobre el verdadero sentido de las órdenes del ejecutivo a los buques navales. Rechaza la premisa de que cualquier persona vinculada a la comisión capturada tras las líneas rebeldes pudiera ser tratada como espía bajo la teoría de que los Estados Unidos habían resuelto intervenir en los conflictos internos dominicanos. Robeson califica dicha aseveración de infundada en los hechos y en el derecho, insistiendo en que los Estados Unidos trataban con el gobierno legítimamente constituido de la República Dominicana conforme al derecho internacional.

records.headline: A Herald letter from aboard the frigate Tennessee, off Port-au-Prince on March 1871, describes the Santo Domingo Commission's return
records.summary_en: A Herald letter from aboard the frigate Tennessee, off Port-au-Prince on March 1871, describes the Santo Domingo Commission's return journey, with the steamer Nantasket arriving from Puerto Plata bringing Professor White and the parties who had rendezvoused there after traversing the country. The commissioners are shown quarreling over the journey home: Ben Wade wants to make the most direct course home now that their business is done and their report almost completed, while Dr. Howe and Professor White outvote him, to the general dissatisfaction of everyone on board, and the letter doubts the three will even settle on a joint report.
records.summary_es: Una carta del Herald desde a bordo de la fragata Tennessee, frente a Puerto Príncipe en marzo de 1871, describe el viaje de regreso de la Comisión de Santo Domingo, con la llegada del vapor Nantasket desde Puerto Plata trayendo al profesor White y a los grupos que se habían reunido allí tras recorrer el país. Los comisionados aparecen discutiendo sobre el regreso: Ben Wade quiere tomar el rumbo más directo a casa ahora que su trabajo está hecho y su informe casi terminado, mientras el doctor Howe y el profesor White lo superan en votos, para disgusto general de todos a bordo, y la carta duda que los tres lleguen siquiera a acordar un informe conjunto.

records.headline: In a letter from his headquarters dated March 5, 1871, General Jose Maria Cabral tells the United States
records.summary_en: In a letter from his headquarters dated March 5, 1871, General Jose Maria Cabral tells the United States Commissioners, Wade, White and Howe, that he has no power to enter into any negotiations on the annexation of his country, that he has protested against it and that his people have been protesting with arms in their hands for more than a year. He invites the Commissioners to visit the people and his headquarters, but White and Howe reply that a visit is not convenient for the present, while Mr. Wade declines to sign the reply; the correspondent adds that Cabral in fact holds only a small strip of mountainous land along the Neyba River.
records.summary_es: En una carta desde su cuartel general fechada el 5 de marzo de 1871, el general José María Cabral dice a los comisionados de los Estados Unidos, Wade, White y Howe, que no tiene poder para entrar en ninguna negociación sobre la anexión de su país, que ha protestado contra ella y que su pueblo lleva más de un año protestando con las armas en la mano. Invita a los comisionados a visitar al pueblo y su cuartel general, pero White y Howe responden que la visita no es conveniente por el momento, mientras el señor Wade se niega a firmar la respuesta; el corresponsal añade que Cabral en realidad solo ocupa una pequeña franja de tierra montañosa a lo largo del río Neyba.

Howe, members of the Commission of the United States: GENTLEMEN: I have read the contents of your communication, dated on the 21st of the past month, with an additional note dated on the 28th of the same month in Azua, and have duly countered them. records.headline: The New York Herald prints a formal letter from General José María Cabral addressed
records.summary_en: The New York Herald prints a formal letter from General José María Cabral addressed to the President of the United States Senate. Cabral protests a statement made in Senator Charles Sumner's December 21, 1870 speech, which attributed to Cabral a policy of reuniting the two governments of Dominica and Haiti as they existed prior to 1844. Cabral denies that he or his party pursues such a policy, declaring that his protest fulfills a sacred duty as party leader to reflect the true stance of his associates. The passage also includes a subsequent shipboard report describing the commissioners' voyage from Port-au-Prince to Kingston, noting that the departure was reached as a compromise with Commissioner Ben Wade.
records.summary_es: El New York Herald publica una carta oficial del general José María Cabral dirigida al presidente del Senado de los Estados Unidos. Cabral protesta contra una afirmación hecha en el discurso del senador Charles Sumner del 21 de diciembre de 1870, en la cual se atribuía a Cabral la intención de unificar los dos gobiernos de Dominica y Haití como estaban organizados antes de 1844. Cabral niega que él o su partido sostengan semejante política, declarando que su protesta cumple con el deber sagrado de líder partidario al reflejar la verdadera posición de sus correligionarios. El pasaje incluye además una crónica posterior a bordo que describe el viaje de los comisionados desde Puerto Príncipe hasta Kingston, señalando que la partida se acordó como una fórmula de compromiso con el comisionado Ben Wade.

records.headline: An editorial paragraph in The Sun discusses Washington dispatches
records.summary_en: An editorial paragraph in The Sun discusses Washington dispatches reporting Commissioner Ben Wade's view that Congress must act immediately on the annexation of Santo Domingo. Wade reportedly argued that unless annexation is promptly agreed upon, President Buenaventura Báez will be unable to maintain power and will be overthrown by revolution. The Sun mocks this assertion, contrasting it with Wade's claims that Dominicans enthusiastically favor annexation, asking how the public could despise Báez if they adore the measure he embodies. The paper concludes that the United States would do best to leave Báez and the Dominicans to paddle their own canoe, along with General Grant and his speculative associates.
records.summary_es: Una nota editorial en The Sun analiza los despachos de Washington que informan sobre la opinión del comisionado Ben Wade de que el Congreso debe actuar de inmediato sobre la anexión de Santo Domingo. Según los informes, Wade sostuvo que, a menos que se apruebe prontamente la anexión, el presidente Buenaventura Báez no podrá sostenerse en el poder y será derrocado por una revolución. The Sun ridiculiza esta afirmación, contrastándola con las declaraciones de Wade de que los dominicanos apoyan con entusiasmo la anexión, y preguntando cómo el pueblo podría rechazar a Báez si idolatra la medida que él personifica. El periódico concluye que lo mejor para los Estados Unidos sería dejar a Báez y a los dominicanos remar su propia canoa, junto con el general Grant y sus allegados especuladores.

records.headline: A Washington letter in the Pawtucket Gazette and Chronicle criticizes
records.summary_en: A Washington letter in the Pawtucket Gazette and Chronicle criticizes Senator Charles Sumner for delivering his speech before the San Domingo Commission made its report. The correspondent argues that candor, patriotism, and gratitude toward President Grant should have restrained Sumner from weakening the administration while it struggled with southern disturbances. Under the heading 'The San Domingo Commission,' the letter reports that the commissioners arrived in Washington the previous evening by rail directly from Charleston. The correspondent notes that while no official results of their visit to the Dominican Republic have been made public, reports circulating in the press indicate that the forthcoming commission report will be favorable.
records.summary_es: Una carta de Washington en el Pawtucket Gazette and Chronicle critica al senador Charles Sumner por pronunciar su discurso antes de que la comisión de Santo Domingo presentara su informe. El corresponsal sostiene que la franqueza, el patriotismo y la gratitud hacia el presidente Grant debieron frenar a Sumner de debilitar al gobierno mientras enfrentaba disturbios en el sur. Bajo el título «La comisión de Santo Domingo», la carta informa que los comisionados llegaron a Washington la noche anterior por ferrocarril directamente desde Charleston. El corresponsal señala que, aunque no se ha hecho público ningún resultado oficial de su visita a la República Dominicana, los informes que circulan en la prensa indican que el próximo informe de la comisión será favorable.

records.headline: The Springfield Weekly Republican publishes an excerpt from Senator Charles Sumner's speech
records.summary_en: The Springfield Weekly Republican publishes an excerpt from Senator Charles Sumner's speech recounting Dominican political history. Sumner relates that José María Cabral attained the presidency through direct popular vote, and that during Báez's exile in Washington, Secretary Seward referred Báez to Sumner. Sumner states that Báez visited his residence seeking money and arms to overthrow the Dominican government, but received no encouragement, though Sumner expressed his hope that America would assist Dominica. He explains that when Cabral later offered to lease Samaná Bay to relieve financial distress, Báez denounced the proposal as a sale of his country, but subsequently organized a force backed by President Salnave of Haiti that forced Cabral's capitulation on February 8, 1868.
records.summary_es: El Springfield Weekly Republican publica un extracto del discurso del senador Charles Sumner en el que repasa la historia política dominicana. Sumner relata que José María Cabral alcanzó la presidencia mediante el voto popular directo y que, durante el exilio de Báez en Washington, el secretario Seward remitió a Báez ante Sumner. Sumner señala que Báez visitó su casa en busca de dinero y armas para derrocar al gobierno dominicano, sin obtener apoyo alguno, aunque Sumner expresó su deseo de que los Estados Unidos ayudaran a Dominica. Explica que cuando Cabral ofreció más tarde arrendar la bahía de Samaná para aliviar dificultades financieras, Báez denunció la propuesta como una venta de su patria, pero luego organizó una fuerza respaldada por el presidente Salnave de Haití que forzó la capitulación de Cabral el 8 de febrero de 1868.

records.headline: The paper reports Senator Sumner repeating his allegations that Báez was maintained in power by the U.S. Navy
records.summary_en: The paper reports Senator Sumner repeating his allegations that Báez was maintained in power by the U.S. Navy to carry out the sale of his country and that Haiti was menaced by an American admiral to assure that sale, both of which he called breaches of public law. Sumner said he now presented the charges on documentary evidence from government officers.

Sumner dijo que ahora presentaba los cargos con pruebas documentales de oficiales del gobierno.

records.headline: An article cites dispatches from Commercial Agent Perry at Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: An article cites dispatches from Commercial Agent Perry at Santo Domingo to argue that President Buenaventura Báez was kept in power only by United States naval force. In a dispatch dated January 20, 1870, Perry reported that the warship Nantasket was visiting Puerto Plata and Samaná Bay in Dominica, noting that American naval protection was urgently needed before public opinion on annexation was expressed. The writer asserts that Báez actually feared the Dominican people would pronounce for his overthrow without warships present. Dispatches from February 8 and February 20 further report that Báez complained daily of delays in sending warships and warned that if American ships were withdrawn, he could not maintain his government in the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: Un artículo cita despachos del agente comercial Perry en Santo Domingo para sostener que el presidente Buenaventura Báez se mantenía en el poder únicamente por la fuerza naval de los Estados Unidos. En un despacho fechado el 20 de enero de 1870, Perry informó que el buque de guerra Nantasket visitaba Puerto Plata y la bahía de Samaná en Dominica, señalando que la protección naval estadounidense era sumamente necesaria antes de que se expresara públicamente la opinión sobre la anexión. El articulista afirma que Báez en realidad temía que el pueblo dominicano se pronunciara por su derrocamiento si no había buques de guerra presentes. Los despachos del 8 y 20 de febrero informan además que Báez se quejaba a diario de los retrasos en el envío de buques de guerra y advertía que, si se retiraban los barcos estadounidenses, no podría sostener su gobierno en la República Dominicana.

records.headline: Under the heading "Dominica," the paper reports that the report of the San Domingo Commissioners
records.summary_en: Under the heading "Dominica," the paper reports that the report of the San Domingo Commissioners is nearly completed. According to the summary of its findings, the Dominican government was found in full operation, with President Báez in peaceable possession of the entire country except along the Haitian border. The report states that Báez enjoys the respect of the great majority of the population and that the president, cabinet, legislature, and judiciary all favor relinquishing their power to the United States. It adds that years of commotion have paralyzed industry and left the Dominican Republic unable to pay its expenses, while an insurgent leader holds only three or four mountain villages and Luperon stirs disturbances in the north.

records.headline: A correspondent recounts arriving at Samaná aboard the steamer
records.summary_en: A correspondent recounts arriving at Samaná aboard the steamer Tybee, noting that officers boarded from naval vessels in the bay and passengers landed at a dock built by Spofford Brothers near Santa Barbara. After departing Samaná in the afternoon, the writer arrived off Santo Domingo City the following night and entered the capital early the next morning. The correspondent reports being presented to President Buenaventura Báez and his brother Damien, the governor of Santo Domingo City, describing both as refined gentlemen who offered saddle-horses for the visitor's use. The letter describes warm summer weather, abundant tropical fruits, and plans to write further once rested and acclimated.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal relata su llegada a Samaná a bordo del vapor Tybee, señalando que los oficiales abordaron desde los buques de guerra en la bahía y que los pasajeros desembarcaron en un muelle construido por Spofford Brothers cerca de Santa Bárbara. Tras partir de Samaná por la tarde, el autor llegó frente a la ciudad de Santo Domingo la noche siguiente y entró a la capital temprano a la mañana siguiente. El corresponsal informa haber sido presentado al presidente Buenaventura Báez y a su hermano Damián, gobernador de la ciudad de Santo Domingo, describiendo a ambos como caballeros refinados que pusieron caballos de montar a su disposición. La carta describe el clima veraniego, las abundantes frutas tropicales y los planes de escribir con mayor detalle una vez que haya descansado y se haya aclimatado.

records.full_text:
ST. DOMINGO REPORT.

The report of the Santo Domingo commissioners was read in the Cabinet meeting to-day, and will probably be submitted to Congress on Monday. It will be accompanied by a brief message from the President, in which, it is reported, he will inform Congress that while their official report is merely confined to answering the inquiries proposed by Congress, he has, nevertheless, been informed by them that they are in favor of the immediate annexation of Santo Domingo. It remains to be seen whether the President thus proposes to travel outside of the official record. If so, his only excuse will be the opinion expressed to him by the commissioners that Baez's condition is such that the annexation question must necessarily be disposed of at the earliest practicable moment. Several Republican Senators favor disposing of the question by passing a resolution now declaring Congress opposed to annexation, and thus obviate the negotiation and subsequent discussion of a new treaty. A Republican Senator has prepared such a resolution, and is only awaiting events before offering it.

records.headline: An article reviews the Dominican rebellion led by Cabral against Spain
records.summary_en: An article reviews the Dominican rebellion led by Cabral against Spain and the political upheavals in Dominica that followed it. It recounts that after the Spanish withdrawal, Cabral served as protector before Báez was restored to power, only for another revolution to reinstate Cabral, who then offered the United States a lease of Samaná Bay. Following another convention, Báez assumed executive power while Cabral withdrew to the interior to wage war, prompting Báez to seek foreign protectorate aid after European powers refused his half of the island. The paper sharply criticizes the Grant administration for sending an inexperienced young officer to negotiate with Báez, and condemns the American promoter Cazneau for securing lucrative concessions in the Dominican Republic while remaining disloyal to the United States.
records.summary_es: Un artículo examina la rebelión dominicana encabezada por Cabral contra España y las convulsiones políticas que la siguieron en Dominica. Relata que, tras la retirada española, Cabral fungió como protector antes de que Báez fuera restablecido en el poder, solo para que otra revolución reinstalara a Cabral, quien luego ofreció a los Estados Unidos el arrendamiento de la bahía de Samaná. Tras una nueva convención, Báez asumió el poder ejecutivo mientras Cabral se retiraba al interior para hacer la guerra, lo que llevó a Báez a buscar ayuda extranjera después de que las potencias europeas rechazaran su mitad de la isla. El periódico critica severamente al gobierno de Grant por enviar a un joven oficial inexperto a negociar con Báez, y condena al promotor estadounidense Cazneau por asegurarse lucrativas concesiones en la República Dominicana mientras se mostraba desleal a los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: The Star publishes a translation of a letter to Allan A. Burton
records.summary_en: The Star publishes a translation of a letter to Allan A. Burton, secretary of the Santo Domingo Commission in Washington, sent by the Secretary of War of the Dominican Republic and dated Santo Domingo, March 29, 1871. The Dominican official states that the country is entirely tranquil and increasingly anxious for speedy annexation to the United States as the only salvation against the intrigues of Haiti. He further reports that President Buenaventura Báez has returned to the capital from Azua after decisively routing Cabral, leaving that district in complete order.
records.summary_es: El Star publica la traducción de una carta a Allan A. Burton, secretario de la Comisión de Santo Domingo en Washington, enviada por el ministro de Guerra de la República Dominicana y fechada en Santo Domingo el 29 de marzo de 1871. El funcionario dominicano afirma que el país se encuentra en completa tranquilidad y cada vez más ansioso por una pronta anexión a los Estados Unidos como única salvación frente a las intrigas de Haití. Informa además que el presidente Buenaventura Báez regresó a la capital desde Azua tras derrotar contundentemente a Cabral, dejando ese distrito en perfecto orden.

records.passage: THE SANTO DOMINGO REPORT NOT READY YET — NO DISAGREEMENT AMONG THE COMMISSIONERS — SPECULATIONS CONCERNING THE PRESIDENT'S INTENTIONS — THE NEW-YORK APPOINTMENTS. [BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.] WASHINGTON, Monday, April 3, 1871. The Santo Domingo report is not yet finished, but those who have been most familiar with the views of the Commissioners believe that there is not the slightest variation in the general views of the members, and that the report, when finally finished and signed, will be as favorable to annexation as the first report prepared by Mr. Wade. The report which will be presented to the President will be more full in details, will embrace more subjects, and give more space to discussion of the subjects laid down in the resolutions of Congress than the report which was first considered. It seemed doubtful yesterday that the Commissioners were in full accord, but the intimate friends of all the Commissioners say that there will be no disagreement, and that the report will be mainly straightforward and emphatic, and not meaningless recital of what was seen and heard by Commissioners in making their investigation. One of the Commissioners says that any one who reads the report cannot be in doubt as to the opinions and views of the members. The report is now [finishing?], and a meeting of Commissioners to-morrow will determine the whole subject. A sufficient number of clerks are now engaged in arranging the documentary evidence and testimony of witnesses, which the investigation elicited, and all the documents and testimony, enough to make a large book, will be ready for the printer by time the report shall be handed in.

records.headline: Under the heading "San Domingo Altogether Lovely," a New York telegraphic
records.summary_en: Under the heading "San Domingo Altogether Lovely," a New York telegraphic dispatch reports on a letter dated March 20th from the Secretary of War of the Dominican Republic to the secretary of the San Domingo Commissioners. The Dominican minister reports that the country remains entirely tranquil and is increasingly eager for annexation to the United States to be speedily accomplished. Quoting the letter directly, the dispatch notes that the writer sees annexation as the only salvation against the insidious intrigues of Haiti, and announces that President Báez has returned to the capital after routing Cabral at Azua.
records.summary_es: Bajo el título «Santo Domingo del todo encantador», un despacho telegráfico de Nueva York informa sobre una carta fechada el 20 de marzo enviada por el ministro de Guerra de la República Dominicana al secretario de los comisionados de Santo Domingo. El funcionario dominicano comunica que el país permanece en total tranquilidad y se muestra cada vez más deseoso de que la anexión a los Estados Unidos se concrete con prontitud. Citando directamente la carta, el despacho señala que el autor considera la anexión como la única salvación frente a las insidiosas intrigas de Haití, y anuncia que el presidente Báez ha regresado a la capital tras derrotar a Cabral en Azua.

During the conversation, Mr. Sumner asked Fabens if he thought that annexation would stop with Santo Domingo. "Oh, no!" replied the Dominican Envoy, "you must have Hayti too." And is that all, continued the Senator. Fabens thought that we could not stop with Hayti, but must, in the nature of things, finally absorb Porto Rico, Jamaica, Cuba, the Windward Islands, and, indeed, all of the West Indies. Mr. Sumner then called the attention of Fabens to the fact that the treaty involved not only the question of the annexation of the little republic of Santo Domingo, but an entirely new foreign policy for the United States. He professed his friendship for the people of the island, and his willingness to aid them by every means in his power; but while he doubted that Santo Domingo would in the end gain by annexation, he was sure that the United States would lose. Mr. Sumner believes that the West India Islands are destined to be the home of the black race. records.headline: Reprinting an editorial from the New York World, the paper denounces
records.summary_en: Reprinting an editorial from the New York World, the paper denounces conditions in Santo Domingo, asserting that paper currency has collapsed to where $1,000 is needed to buy a pound of tea and claiming the country had three revolutions and 4,000 major generals in five years. The piece claims that Commissioners Benjamin Wade, Dr. Howe, and Frederick Douglass regard the situation as a failure, pointing to widespread ignorance and asserting that the populace does not understand republican government. It cites an unnamed gentleman with the Commission who saw no improvement since visiting thirty years earlier, judging the Haitians to be better and wiser. The excerpt concludes that the Commission will nonetheless urge annexation to please President Grant.
records.summary_es: Al reproducir un editorial del New York World, el periódico denuncia las condiciones en Santo Domingo, afirmando que su moneda de papel ha colapsado hasta el punto de requerirse 1,000 dólares para comprar una libra de té, y alegando que el país tuvo tres revoluciones y 4,000 mayores generales en cinco años. El artículo afirma que los comisionados Benjamin Wade, el Dr. Howe y Frederick Douglass consideran la situación un fracaso, señalando una ignorancia generalizada y asegurando que la población no comprende el gobierno republicano. Cita a un caballero no identificado vinculado a la Comisión que no vio mejora alguna desde que la visitó treinta años antes, considerando a los haitianos más capaces y prudentes. El extracto concluye que, pese a todo, la Comisión instará a la anexión para complacer al presidente Grant.

records.headline: The paper publishes an excerpt from the San Domingo Commission's report
records.summary_en: The paper publishes an excerpt from the San Domingo Commission's report reviewing the career and legitimacy of President Buenaventura Báez. The report notes that Báez presided over Congress following the overthrow of Haitian rule and that his initial term was the only one in Dominican history to complete its full constitutional period before Gen. Pedro Santana succeeded him in 1853. Following subsequent upheavals and Spanish rule, Báez was repeatedly recalled to establish provisional authority, once on the invitation of a delegation including Gen. Cabral. The Commissioners find that in his third year of office, Báez has maintained as much liberty as circumstances allowed, with no rival holding a superior title to power.
records.summary_es: El periódico publica un extracto del informe de la Comisión de Santo Domingo que examina la trayectoria y legitimidad del presidente Buenaventura Báez. El informe señala que Báez presidió el Congreso tras el derrocamiento del dominio haitiano y que su período inicial fue el único en la historia dominicana en cumplir todo su mandato constitucional antes de que el general Pedro Santana lo sucediera en 1853. Tras los trastornos subsiguientes y la dominación española, Báez fue llamado repetidamente para establecer una autoridad provisional, en una ocasión por invitación de una delegación que incluía al general Cabral. Los comisionados determinan que, en su tercer año de mandato, Báez ha mantenido tanta libertad como permitían las circunstancias, sin que ningún rival ostente un derecho superior al poder.

records.headline: The Commission reports finding extensive evidence that insurgent
records.summary_en: The Commission reports finding extensive evidence that insurgent forces under Cabral received direct assistance from Haiti, citing examinations of Haitian prisoners captured with Haitian-stamped muskets. Near Manzanillo Bay, insurgent leader Luperón commands a small guerrilla band described by local witnesses as having only the strength of a desperado. According to the Commissioners, both movements would have collapsed without foreign intriguers and the support of Haiti, a nation with nearly five times the population and revenue of the Dominican Republic. The report adds that internal instability is compounded by long-standing regional jealousy between the northern provinces, including Santiago and Puerto Plata, and the southern district.
records.summary_es: La Comisión informa haber hallado amplias pruebas de que las fuerzas insurgentes dirigidas por Cabral recibieron auxilio directo de Haití, citando interrogatorios a prisioneros haitianos capturados con fusiles que llevaban el cuño haitiano. Cerca de la bahía de Manzanillo, el líder insurgente Luperón comanda una pequeña partida guerrillera calificada por testigos locales de poseer solo la fuerza de un forajido. De acuerdo con los comisionados, ambos movimientos habrían fracasado sin la ayuda de intrigantes extranjeros y el respaldo de Haití, país que cuenta con casi cinco veces la población y los ingresos de la República Dominicana. El informe agrega que la inestabilidad interna se agrava por el arraigado recelo regional entre las provincias del norte, incluidas Santiago y Puerto Plata, y el distrito sur.

records.headline: Under the heading "The Bay of Samana," the Commission's report
records.summary_en: Under the heading "The Bay of Samana," the Commission's report surveys the harbors of the Dominican Republic, noting that while Ocoa and Manzanillo accommodate large vessels, neither possesses major military significance. The report singles out Samaná Bay as the most important harbor in the West Indies, describing it as thirty miles long by ten miles wide and capable of sheltering the largest naval fleets. Citing a survey by General McClellan, the Commissioners state that simple fortifications at the bay's entrance and at Port Jackson would provide complete defense. They add that the bay commands the Mona Passage and would acquire immense strategic value upon the opening of a canal route across the Isthmus of Darien.
records.summary_es: Bajo el subtítulo «La bahía de Samaná», el informe de la Comisión examina los puertos de la República Dominicana y señala que, aunque Ocoa y Manzanillo admiten embarcaciones de gran calado, ninguno posee gran importancia militar. El informe destaca la bahía de Samaná como el puerto más importante de las Antillas, describiéndola con una extensión de treinta millas de largo por diez de ancho y capacidad para albergar las mayores flotas navales. Citando un estudio del general McClellan, los comisionados señalan que fortificaciones sencillas en la entrada de la bahía y en Port Jackson bastarían para defenderla por completo. Añaden que la bahía domina el paso de la Mona y adquiriría un inmenso valor estratégico si se abre una ruta canalera a través del istmo de Darién.

records.headline: The Commission's report details trade routes from Samaná Bay
records.summary_en: The Commission's report details trade routes from Samaná Bay. It observes that the Yuna River could accommodate light-draft steamers and that the surrounding valley offers favorable conditions and abundant timber for a railroad. While at the capital, the Commissioners learned that although the United States had continuously occupied Samaná Bay as a naval station, its rental payments were in default for more than a year. Under the heading "Public Debt," the report outlines an exhaustive inquiry into the liabilities of the Dominican Republic. The Commissioners collected data from public financial records, interviewed official custodians, examined private claimants, and received detailed itemized claims from the Dominican Senate and President Báez.
records.summary_es: El informe de la Comisión detalla las rutas comerciales desde la bahía de Samaná. Observa que el río Yuna podría admitir vapores de poco calado y que el valle circundante ofrece condiciones propicias y abundante madera para un ferrocarril. Estando en la capital, los comisionados se enteraron de que, si bien los Estados Unidos habían ocupado de forma continua la bahía de Samaná como estación naval, el pago del alquiler presentaba un retraso de más de un año. Bajo el subtítulo «Deuda pública», el informe expone una minuciosa investigación sobre las obligaciones financieras de la República Dominicana. Los comisionados recopilaron datos de los registros contables oficiales, entrevistaron a funcionarios encargados, examinaron a reclamantes privados y recibieron listas detalladas de reclamaciones del Senado dominicano y del presidente Báez.

records.headline: The Commission reports that it examined the originals of the annexation treaty and the Samana lease in the archives of the Dominican Government
records.summary_en: The Commission reports that it examined the originals of the annexation treaty and the Samana lease in the archives of the Dominican Government in Santo Domingo City, in the presence of the President and his Cabinet on February 18, 1871, and found no particle of evidence of any secret clause or concession favoring any United States official. President Baez told the commissioners his government was willing to stand by the 1869 treaty, but asked whether the Samana rent for the nearly two years of delay might fairly be paid without deduction, and he agreed to modify the treaty to devote one-fifth of the public lands to common schools if the United States would add land for colleges of agriculture, mining and engineering.
records.summary_es: La Comisión informa que examinó los originales del tratado de anexión y del arrendamiento de Samaná en los archivos del Gobierno dominicano en la ciudad de Santo Domingo, en presencia del Presidente y su Gabinete el 18 de febrero de 1871, y no encontró ni la menor evidencia de cláusula secreta o concesión alguna en favor de ningún funcionario de los Estados Unidos. El presidente Báez dijo a los comisionados que su gobierno estaba dispuesto a mantener el tratado de 1869, pero preguntó si no sería justo que la renta de Samaná por los casi dos años de demora se pagara sin deducción, y aceptó modificar el tratado para dedicar una quinta parte de las tierras públicas a escuelas comunes si los Estados Unidos añadían tierras para colegios de agricultura, minería e ingeniería.

records.headline: The Herald publishes an extract detailing mining concessions
records.summary_en: The Herald publishes an extract detailing mining concessions and land grants made to foreign individuals, from the report of the San Domingo Commission and corporations. The list enumerates rights to copper and coal deposits in San Cristóbal and Samaná, including concessions awarded to William L. Cazneau, Cambiaso and Company, and the San Domingo Company. The Commissioners affirm that the Dominican government has made no grant or concession of public land to any foreign government other than the United States. In addition to national concessions, the report notes municipal grants made to American citizens in the village of Santa Bárbara on Samaná Bay, including a waterfront parcel granted to J. P. O'Sullivan.
records.summary_es: El Herald publica un extracto del informe de la Comisión de Santo Domingo, que detalla las concesiones mineras y de tierras otorgadas a personas y corporaciones extranjeras. La lista enumera derechos sobre yacimientos de cobre y carbón en San Cristóbal y Samaná, incluidas concesiones otorgadas a William L. Cazneau, Cambiaso y Compañía, y la San Domingo Company. Los comisionados afirman que el gobierno dominicano no ha otorgado ninguna cesión ni concesión de tierras públicas a ningún gobierno extranjero con excepción de los Estados Unidos. Además de las concesiones nacionales, el informe menciona cesiones municipales otorgadas a ciudadanos estadounidenses en la villa de Santa Bárbara en la bahía de Samaná, incluida una parcela frente al mar concedida a J. P. O'Sullivan.

records.headline: Under the heading "St. Domingo," the Herald reports Havana telegraphic
records.summary_en: Under the heading "St. Domingo," the Herald reports Havana telegraphic dispatches describing recent clashes between Dominican government forces under President Báez and insurgents commanded by Cabral and Luperón. The dispatches state that the insurgent forces were defeated in two separate engagements, though casualties and prisoner counts were apparently light. The paper notes that the insurgents likely lost their entire cavalry force, with fourteen horses captured in the first action and fifteen in the second. Approximately eight hundred men and ten general officers participated in the initial encounter, though the Herald observes that these government victories provide no guarantee of lasting peace.
records.summary_es: Bajo el título «Santo Domingo», el Herald informa sobre despachos telegráficos desde La Habana que describen recientes enfrentamientos entre las fuerzas del gobierno dominicano bajo el presidente Báez y los insurgentes comandados por Cabral y Luperón. Los despachos indican que las tropas insurgentes fueron derrotadas en dos combates distintos, aunque el número de bajas y prisioneros aparentemente no fue elevado. El periódico señala que los insurgentes probablemente perdieron toda su caballería, habiéndose capturado catorce caballos en la primera acción y quince en la segunda. Alrededor de ochocientos hombres y diez oficiales generales participaron en el choque inicial, aunque el Herald advierte que estas victorias gubernamentales no ofrecen garantía alguna de una paz duradera.

The commissioners state that acquiring Samana Bay would give the United States a powerful military and naval station, and the report, which also gives the total of the Dominican government's debt and claims, was transmitted by the President to Congress.

records.summary_en: Summary of the commissioners' report: a government in full operation and Báez in peaceable possession except on the Haitian border; the country's resources, Samaná Bay as a naval station, the debt and claims reckoned at over $156 million against resources of $79 million, and a people who have discussed annexation and call it their only hope.

records.headline: Under the heading "San Domingo: The Annexation Fever," dispatches
records.summary_en: Under the heading "San Domingo: The Annexation Fever," dispatches report that President Grant transmitted the report of the San Domingo Commissioners to Congress just before the House adjourned. A telegram from St. Thomas dated April 1 announces that President Báez has defeated Cabral's forces near Azua, while Luperón's troops are reported to be advancing in the northern provinces. The dispatch notes that the Dominican public remains anxious for a final resolution of the annexation question. A dispatch from Havana adds that intense public excitement over the American annexation project persists in neighboring Haiti, though that country otherwise remains quiet.
records.summary_es: Bajo el título «Santo Domingo: La fiebre de la anexión», los despachos informan que el presidente Grant transmitió el informe de los comisionados de Santo Domingo al Congreso poco antes de que la Cámara levantara la sesión. Un telegrama de Saint Thomas, fechado el 1 de abril, comunica que el presidente Báez derrotó a las fuerzas de Cabral cerca de Azua, mientras se reporta que las tropas de Luperón avanzan en las provincias del norte. El despacho señala que el público dominicano sigue ansioso por una resolución definitiva de la cuestión de la anexión. Por su parte, un despacho de La Habana añade que persiste una intensa agitación pública sobre el proyecto de anexión estadounidense en el vecino Haití, aunque ese país por lo demás permanece tranquilo.

records.headline: An excerpt from the report of the San Domingo Commission estimates
records.summary_en: An excerpt from the report of the San Domingo Commission estimates the population of the republic at 150,000, of whom more than nineteen-twentieths are native Dominicans, noting that white blood largely preponderates. The report surveys the country's mineral wealth, finding abundant iron ore, moderately rich copper deposits, extensive salt beds near Neyba, and coal in Samaná and Puerto Plata, though of inferior quality to Pennsylvania coal. The Commissioners divide the territory into five classes of land, including rich mountain valleys, pasture prairies, and the fertile agricultural plains of La Vega. They conclude that almost the entire country is cultivable and exceptionally fertile, observing that sugar cane yields fifteen annual cuttings from a single root.
records.summary_es: Un extracto del informe de la Comisión de Santo Domingo estima la población de la república en 150,000 habitantes, de los cuales más de diecinueve vigésimos son dominicanos nativos, señalando que la sangre blanca predomina ampliamente. El informe examina las riquezas minerales del país, destacando abundantes minerales de hierro, depósitos de cobre de regular riqueza, extensos yacimientos de sal cerca de Neyba y carbón en Samaná y Puerto Plata, aunque de calidad inferior al carbón de Pensilvania. Los comisionados dividen las tierras en cinco clases, entre ellas fértiles valles montañosos, llanuras de pastoreo y las ricas tierras agrícolas de La Vega. Concluyen que casi todo el territorio es cultivable y sumamente fértil, observando que la caña de azúcar produce quince cortes anuales a partir de una misma raíz.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that an investigation found no land grants or franchises given to any U.S. official regarding the treaty, and that the Dominicans reaffirmed their willingness to be annexed under the terms of the 1869 treaty, with additional requests regarding Samana Bay rent and educational funding. The Commissioners concluded that Dominican independence has never been a reality and that union as a State is the republic's only chance to secure its freedom and independence, though they made no formal recommendation on whether to adopt that course.

Los comisionados concluyeron que la independencia dominicana nunca había sido una realidad y que la incorporación como Estado de la Unión constituía la única vía para afianzar sus libertades e independencia, aun cuando se abstuvieron de formular una recomendación explícita sobre dicho camino.
