HAYTI.
—
Another of our Consuls in Trouble.
NEW YORK, April 13.—Haytien advices report the arrest and imprisonment of the American Consul at Port au Prince, because of his having given protection to Gen. Batellia, insurrectionary leader who escaped the custody of the guard and sought refuge in the Consul's office while on his way to be imprisoned. The Consul has conferred with Minister Bassett on the subject, who, it is understood, will apply to the Haytien government for redress.

Threat of War with San Domingo.
PORT AU PRINCE, April 13.—The invasion from Monte Christo consisted of 140 men. Eight Haytiens, five Dominicans, and one Frenchman were captured and executed. It is reliably reported that the Haytien Government will probably declare war against Baez, who is charged with an attempt to overthrow President Saget.

records.full_text:
And yet, again: Here at Santo Domingo City other popular ideas, propagated by Congressional speeches, are found to have no basis save in the distempered imaginations of political leaders.

How often have our people been assured that our Executive was guilty of maintaining a fleet in these waters, at vast expense, without necessity, and "solely to maintain a usurper in power!"

How confidently, how earnestly, how frequently have our orators asserted that the Baez administration was kept in power mainly by our naval forces, and that it could not stand a day after their withdrawal!

How have our orators thundered against this abuse of national power, this degrading service of our navy; and how have weak-kneed Republicans shaken their heads in disapproval of the supposed error and wrong! But what is the truth about it? We must have a squadron in the West Indies. The Dominican ports are capacious and convenient, and thither our ships frequently resort. But at this time there is not one of our war vessels in Dominican waters! The last one, the "Nantasket," sailed away some time ago, to return no one knows exactly when. But yet President Baez has not fallen nor fled! He sits more firm in the saddle than ever, and his administration has the confidence and the almost unanimous support of the people!

History will show, what all in these regions admit, that the moral effect of the presence of our fleet in Dominican and Haytian waters has been blessed indeed, because it has helped greatly to deter fillibusters, and to maintain peace and order.

records.headline: A report summarizes ten charges brought against President Grant's administration
records.summary_en: A report summarizes ten charges brought against President Grant's administration in a political speech comparing him with Horace Greeley. The third charge denounces Grant's negotiations for the annexation of the Dominican Republic without a minister approved by the Senate, along with his undignified lobbying of senators to secure ratification of the treaty. The indictment further condemns Grant for appointing unqualified cabinet members and relatives, forcing the resignation of Interior Secretary Cox, improperly enforcing congressional enforcement acts with troops, and mismanaging foreign relations.

El pliego condena además a Grant por nombrar ministros del gabinete y parientes no cualificados, forzar la renuncia del secretario del Interior Cox, aplicar indebidamente las leyes de ejecución mediante el ejército y gestionar deficientemente las relaciones exteriores.

The writer maintains that patronage was actively employed by the White House to promote the annexation of the Dominican Republic among members of Congress. He states that while the Santo Domingo treaty was pending, two gentlemen intimately connected with the administration separately approached him, offering him whatever patronage he desired if he would support the project. The author notes that after being taunted on the Senate floor, he asked one of those emissaries whether the patronage offer had been authorized by the President.

records.full_text: Soon after his accession to power, he gave his mind, not to the great problems the solution of which the people so anxiously looked for, but to a project of his own—the acquisition of Santo Domingo. A subject of such importance as the incorporation with our political system of a tropical country with an utterly heterogeneous people, called for the most careful and earnest consideration. It is believed that the Secretary of State did not favor the scheme, and the State Department, whose office it is to conduct all the diplomatic affairs of the Government, was unceremoniously set aside. The President commenced a personal negotiation with Baez, the ruler of Santo Domingo, which he intrusted to one of his young aides de camp, whose zeal he had reason to believe equal to his own. The extraordinary character of this proceeding did not trouble him. He wanted to have the thing done; and to do it, an aide de camp was better than a Secretary of State. The aide de camp made a sort of a personal treaty between the two potentates, in which the President was pledged to propitiate the favor of Congress for the scheme of the lobby influence. This disgraceful engagement would have revolted the sensibilities of any President having the dignity of his high office and the honor of the nation at heart.

records.headline: A correspondent defends President Grant against charges of racial
records.summary_en: A correspondent defends President Grant against charges of racial prejudice regarding the Santo Domingo Commission's return to Washington. The writer explains that the official duties of Frederick Douglass and General Sigel terminated immediately upon submitting their respective reports on American colored emigrants in the Dominican Republic and the fortification of Samaná Bay. Both men departed that night to reunite with their families, while the commissioners remained and were invited to dine with President Grant after paying their respects. The author argues that had Douglass been present he would certainly have been invited, asserting that Grant had completely rejected color prejudice in his treatment of Douglass.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal defiende al presidente Grant contra acusaciones de prejuicio racial tras el regreso de la Comisión de Santo Domingo a Washington. El autor explica que las funciones oficiales de Frederick Douglass y del general Sigel terminaron de inmediato al entregar sus respectivos informes sobre los emigrantes de color estadounidenses en la República Dominicana y sobre la fortificación de la bahía de Samaná. Ambos partieron esa misma noche para reunirse con sus familias, mientras que los comisionados permanecieron y fueron invitados a cenar con el presidente Grant tras presentarle sus respetos. El autor sostiene que de haber estado presente Douglass habría sido invitado sin duda, afirmando que Grant había desechado por completo el prejuicio racial en su trato hacia él.

Among the specific indictments, the third charge attacks Grant's negotiations for the annexation of the Dominican Republic, asserting that no minister was approved by the Senate and that Grant engaged in improper lobbying to secure ratification. The remaining charges accuse Grant of nepotism, appointing unqualified cabinet secretaries, forcing the removal of Interior Secretary Cox, using troops to carry out the enforcement acts, and mismanaging American foreign policy.

records.summary_en: A legal notice issued by the clerk of the circuit court at Enterprise, Volusia County, Florida, orders non-resident defendants to appear and answer the partition complaint of Samuel Benlisa. The notice recites that none of the defendants are residents of Florida, citing defendant Elias Benlisa as residing in Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic, alongside co-defendants residing in Saint Thomas and New York City. The proceeding concerns the division of specified tracts of land located across Marion, Sumter, Orange, and Volusia counties.
records.summary_es: Un aviso legal expedido por el secretario del tribunal de circuito en Enterprise, condado de Volusia, Florida, ordena a los demandados no residentes comparecer y responder a la demanda de partición presentada por Samuel Benlisa. El aviso hace constar que ninguno de los demandados reside en Florida, señalando que el demandado Elias Benlisa reside en Puerto Plata, República Dominicana, junto a otros codemandados que residen en Santo Tomás y en la ciudad de Nueva York. El procedimiento se refiere a la división de parcelas determinadas de tierras ubicadas en los condados de Marion, Sumter, Orange y Volusia.

records.headline: A Tribune court notice directs non-resident defendants to appear
records.summary_en: A Tribune court notice directs non-resident defendants to appear and respond to a bill filed by Samuel Benlisa in the circuit court at Enterprise, Volusia County, Florida, for the partition of real property. The notice states that defendant Elias Benlisa resides in Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic, while his fellow defendants reside in Saint Thomas, West Indies, and New York. The property subject to partition encompasses described acreages in Marion, Sumter, Orange, and Volusia counties, including a river grant opposite Volusia.

El aviso indica que el demandado Elias Benlisa reside en Puerto Plata, República Dominicana, mientras que sus codemandados residen en Santo Tomás, Antillas, y en Nueva York. La propiedad sujeta a partición comprende extensiones determinadas en los condados de Marion, Sumter, Orange y Volusia, incluida una concesión fluvial frente a Volusia.

records.headline: Iiayti has been the bully Hayt tas alway been the hawk
records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that Hayti has historically acted as a bully and a constant threat to the progress and independence of Dominica, treating it as its lawful prey while possessing a much larger population. The publication defended U.S. actions regarding San Domingo—asserting it was under U.S. protection and duty-bound to prevent outside pressure—while accusing the Haytien government of aiding opponents of the legal executive of San Domingo, including Cabral, with men-of-war, arms, and mountaineer forces. Additionally, it recounted that an American admiral in the Gulf sailed to Port-au-Prince to quietly inform the Haytien minister of state about pending negotiations involving San Domingo.
records.summary_es: A partir del extracto, el periódico aseveró que Haití ha obrado históricamente de manera prepotente y como constante amenaza para el desenvolvimiento y la soberanía dominicana, considerándola su legítima presa al gozar de una población muy superior. El rotativo defendió la conducta de los Estados Unidos con respecto a Santo Domingo —sosteniendo que se hallaba bajo amparo estadounidense y en el deber de atajar coacciones foráneas—, inculpando a la vez al gobierno haitiano de secundar a los enemigos del gobernante constitucional dominicano, en especial a Cabral, facilitándoles buques de guerra, armamento y combatientes monteros. Añadió que un almirante estadounidense en el Golfo fondeó en Puerto Príncipe para advertir discretamente al ministro de Estado haitiano acerca de las negociaciones pendientes relativas a Santo Domingo.

records.full_text:
Sajet, I say, showed at once his desire to continue the usual Haytien policy of bullying San Domingo. Fabre Geffrard and Salnave were the only Haytien executives who had not sought to embroil or invade the feebler republic. Four times the Haytiens have swept over the Dominican territory. Only once have their troops entered it on a mission of friendship and good faith, and that was when Salnave’s army, under General Alexandre Tate, (the accomplished soldier and diplomat, who for a brief space represented Hayti here,) aided the Dominicans, in 1864, to recover their independence from Spain. Mr. Sumner knows he cannot plead ignorance—that the claims of Hayti upon the territory of Dominica have always been a leading cause of the want of progress and prosperity therein. Hayti has been the bully! Hayti has alway been the hawk sailing in the air and ready to swoop upon Dominica, which it has always insisted was

ITS LAWFUL PREY.

Hayti has 800,000, San Domingo less than 200,000, inhabitants. Hayti is nearly all black, made up of slaves from over sixty African tribes, whose descendants have nobly, and savagely, too, fought and won their personal freedom and national independence. But, though they may be honored in this, there’s nothing in their history for sixty years past to go in ecstacies over. When Mr. Sumner says we bullied them, San Domingo was, in diplomatic usage, under our protection. We had the right, and it was our duty, to prevent outside pressure. The Haytien government was doing all it dared do to create this pressure. Its men-of-war were loaned to Luperon and others to make war on Baez—not a usurper, but the legal executive of San Domingo.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that Hayti repeatedly sought to subjugate Santo Domingo, whose government eventually appealed to the United States for protection amidst an imminent crisis. In response, the U.S. administration notified Haytian authorities that, pending a decision by Congress on the preliminary annexation treaty, any foreign invasion of Dominican territory would be considered an unfriendly act toward the United States. The author defended this action as a necessary duty in the interest of peace and humanity rather than a violation of international law.
records.summary_es: El diario consignó que Haití procuró en reiteradas ocasiones sojuzgar a Santo Domingo, cuyo gobierno acabó solicitando la protección de los Estados Unidos ante una crisis inminente. Como réplica, la administración de Washington notificó a las autoridades haitianas que, mientras el Congreso deliberase sobre las bases del tratado de anexión, toda invasión foránea al territorio dominicano se consideraría un acto hostil hacia los Estados Unidos. El autor justificó dicho proceder como una obligación ineludible en aras de la paz y de la humanidad, y no como una transgresión del derecho internacional.

records.full_text:
1. The alleged outrage upon Hayti occurred as follows: No sooner was it known that a negotiation for annexation was pending than preparations were made by the Haytian authorities to invade their feeble neighbor, instigated to this course by the diplomatic representatives of certain European Powers, who were jealous of American supremacy. Hayti, which comprises less than one-third of the island, (10,000 square miles,) has repeatedly sought to subjugate the whole (32,000 square miles.) She feared that Santo Domingo would forever escape from her clutches. The population of Hayti (500,000) is four-fold that of Santo Domingo, (125,000,) and is governed by a military despotism under the forms of a republic. Hayti was possessed of an armed steamer. The seaports of Santo Domingo, protected by only two small schooners, were liable to bombardment. The crisis was imminent, and the Government of Santo Domingo appealed to our Government for protection against a danger growing out of this very negotiation.

What did the Administration do? Just this: in the interest of peace and humanity it notified the Haytian authorities that a preliminary treaty of annexation had been negotiated, and that, until Congress should have expressed its decision, an invasion of the Dominican territory by any foreign Power would be regarded as an act unfriendly to the United States.

records.headline: An article from the Chicago Inter-Ocean, reprinted in the New National Era
records.summary_en: An article from the Chicago Inter-Ocean, reprinted in the New National Era, reports that Germany may seek the cession of Manzanilla Bay from Haiti following an extraction of £15,000 by a German naval squadron. The report compares Manzanilla to Samaná Bay at the opposite end of the island, which had been sought by the United States. While white colonization is reportedly abhorred by the Haitian populace, the account notes that upper classes recognize little prospect of stability unless a strong foreign power intervenes to compel Haiti and the Dominican Republic into peaceful relations. It adds, however, that many fear foreign protection would lead to complete subjugation, citing the prior experience of the Dominicans under Spanish rule.
records.summary_es: Un artículo del Chicago Inter-Ocean, reproducido en el New National Era, informa que Alemania podría procurar la cesión de la bahía de Manzanilla por parte de Haití tras la exacción de 15.000 libras por una escuadra naval alemana. El informe compara Manzanilla con la bahía de Samaná en el extremo opuesto de la isla, la cual había sido pretendida por los Estados Unidos. Aunque la colonización de personas blancas es supuestamente aborrecida por la población haitiana, el relato señala que las clases acomodadas reconocen pocas probabilidades de estabilidad a menos que una potencia extranjera fuerte intervenga para obligar a Haití y a la República Dominicana a mantener relaciones pacíficas. Añade, sin embargo, que muchos temen que la protección extranjera conduzca a una subyugación total, citando la experiencia previa de los dominicanos bajo el dominio español.

records.headline: Says that lo ro-clcct tho President after such conduct is to condone the most flagrant and perilous violation of the Constitution
records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that the Dominican Republic, facing perpetual aggressions and an impending invasion by Hayti, proposed annexation to the United States in exchange for the assumption of its debt. Following an inquiry by a confidential agent, the President submitted an annexation treaty to the Senate. When Hayti prepared to invade the helpless Dominican Republic, the Dominican Government appealed to the United States for protection, prompting the Executive to notify Hayti that a treaty was pending and that an invasion would not be permitted while the Senate acted.
records.summary_es: A tenor del extracto periodístico, la República Dominicana, víctima de continuos amagos y de una inminente invasión por parte de Haití, propuso su incorporación a los Estados Unidos a cambio de que estos asumieran su pasivo financiero. Tras una misión de pesquisa a cargo de un agente confidencial, el presidente elevó el tratado de anexión al Senado. Ante los aprestos haitianos para asaltar a la indefensa República Dominicana, las autoridades dominicanas solicitaron socorro a los Estados Unidos, moviendo al Ejecutivo a advertir formalmente a Haití de que existía un tratado en trámite y que no consentiría agresión alguna mientras el Senado resolviese.

records.chapter_es: La lucha por la anexión estadounidense
records.full_text: We were at one time inclined to think the action of the Administration in sending ships into the waters of San Domingo was, at least, questionable. Mr. Schurz says that to re-elect the President after such conduct is to condone the most flagrant and perilous violation of the Constitution, and to invite despotism. That is an extravagance at which a man can only smile. For never was anything more frank and fair than the position of the President upon the whole subject. Indeed, nothing has commended him to the confidence of the country more than his entire candor upon this question. For the satisfactory truth about the ships is told by Mr. Blackwell. The Dominican republic, helpless and hopeless under the perpetual aggressions of Hayti, proposed annexation to the United States upon condition of our assumption of its debt, which was about a million and a half of dollars. The President, who was not at first inclined to the project, at last sent a confidential and honorable agent to ascertain the precise facts. Satisfied with the inquiry, a treaty was prepared and submitted to the Senate. But as soon as Hayti knew that a negotiation was pending, she prepared to invade her neighbor, undoubtedly instigated by European influence.

The action seeks the partition of several specified parcels of real estate in Marion, Sumter, Orange, and Volusia counties.

La acción pretende la partición de varias parcelas determinadas de bienes raíces en los condados de Marion, Sumter, Orange y Volusia.

records.summary_en: The *Fremont weekly journal* reported on December 13, 1872, that a group of prominent American businessmen and merchants, independent of the government, raised money to secure territory in Santo Domingo—including the Bay of Samaná—that Congress had previously refused to fund. According to Mr. C. K. Garrison, the steamer *Tybee* was dispatched with this money and valuable cargo for the Báez Government to pursue the enterprise as a business venture.

De acuerdo con el Sr. C. K. records.full_text:
SAMANA OURS.

The Money Sent to Baez by New York Merchants—Trade With Santo Domingo Secured.

From the New York World, Dec. 7.
It is now three and a half years since President Grant took up the subject of the annexation of Santo Domingo. The main idea urged in favor of the plan was that it was indispensible to the prosperity of American commerce for the United States to have in their possession a substantial territory in the West Indies. In June, 1869, the President appointed an agent to obtain information about the Dominican Republic, and General Babcock was finally sent out there. In September, 1869, he negotiated a preliminary treaty, which was approved by President Grant, and in November a regular treaty with President Baez was concluded. The matter was debated in Congress, a commission was sent to the island in January, 1871, and finally in April of that year President Grant relinquished the plan.

But it has since been taken up by prominent business men of this country, who were persuaded that it would be profitable to them to secure what the Government had rejected. Some of them had visited Santo Domingo, and the result is that the steamer Tybee has just taken out, with other valuable cargo, the money required by the Baez Government for a certain specified amount of territory, including the Bay of Samana and for which Congress refused an appropriation. It is reported in business circles that one gain that will accrue to the new company will be in the shape of the port dues.

The following coloquy with Mr. C. K. Garrison gives all the particulars upon the matter that are now obtainable:

Mr. Garrison, when found at his office at the Bowling Green, was at first unwilling to communicate what he knew upon this important subject, but finding that the main facts were already known to his visitor became more communicative.

When asked, "Is it really true, that the Tybee has gone out with important lading connected with the new enterprise of the mercantile association that proposes tofollow up the Santo Domingo project?" he replied in substance, "Yes, a number of us, merchants and others, have concluded that we will accept the bargain that the government has refused. This is apart from all political considerations; is a mere matter of business."

"What shape has your action taken?"

"We have raised the money demanded and sent it out in the Tybee, and will thus gain control of the Port of Samana, the finest in the West Indies, and capable of holding the navies of the world."

"You will have special rights and privileges, I suppose—be a sort of western 'East India Company?'"

"Well, we are paying out a great deal of money, and of course we are not giving it for nothing, but expect ample returns."

"Will not this first outlay need to be followed by other large expenditures for warehouses, etc.?"

"We don't know much about what will come after. We shall move cautiously, and be governed by circumstances."

"Are only New York capitalists in the enterprise?"

"No; there are capitalists of Boston, Philadelphia and other towns in the movement."

"It appears to be a legitimate transaction. I suppose that many of you have long had mercantile dealings with those regions?"

"Yes; I, for one, have been running steamers to those islands, as far down as Brazil. I have no connection with the administration, and it is a matter of business with us all."

"This is certainly a good way to settle a vexed question, and prevent further political controversy on the subject. But what is the condition of the island? Is there much industrial activity there?"

"There is a large export trade of coffee and other tropical products; but the point of the greatest importance will be the possession by Americans of such a fine port in the West Indies?

records.chapter_es: La lucha por la anexión estadounidense
records.full_text:
The annexation of the eastern portion of Santo Domingo, known as Dominica, and formerly a colony of Spain, was very actively discussed by the public and Congress. The following are the facts of the early negotiations and treaties: Two treaties between the governments of the United States and Dominica were signed. The first was known as the Samana treaty. By this Dominica cedes the entire domain of the district described therein, which includes the Peninsula and Bay of Samana, for a term of fifty years, reserving the free navigation, for an annual rental of $15,000 gold. Four months are stipulated for ratification, during which the United States protects Dominica from foreign intervention. One year's rent was paid down, and possession duly taken.

The second, known as the annexation treaty, provides for a renunciation of sovereignty in favor of the United States, and that the Dominican Republic be incorporated on the footing of a territory, eligible to admission into the Union in the discretion of Congress. Dominica cedes her property, as specified in a schedule, but reserves all other property not scheduled; delivery not to be made nor consideration paid until Congress shall have appropriated the money. This is $1,500,000 in gold; and is in consideration of property only. Its disposition is provided for—Dominica is to apply it to her debts. But the application is to be made by a commission which the United States is to respect and protect, to be appointed by those who at the signing of the treaty constituted the present actual Dominican Government. For all debt, liquidated and unliquidated, in excess of such sum, public bonds of Dominica shall stand as security; likewise all the public lands and other property reserved from cession. After the execution of the treaty no grants or concessions of lands, or of rights in lands, were to be made, or any debt contracted. Franchises other than those are not prohibited. It is also agreed that the United States is in no event liable for Dominican debts or obligations. The cession was not to be valid unless ratified by a vote of the people.

Both treaties were signed at the city of Santo Domingo November 29, 1869, on behalf respectively of President Grant and President Baez. In execution of anticipatory instructions, an adequate naval force under the direction of a representative of the army immediately carried into effect the protection clauses. This protection has never been remitted. Hayti, either as a foreign nation or as the government de jure of the whole island, as they claim, ostensibly remonstrated.

In March, 1870, the result was received of an election held in Dominica during a fortnight, beginning under a decree of President Baez and his Senate, dated February 16, 1870. The returns indicated a general approval of the treaty. About eighty days, however, had intervened before an election was found "possible." In appropriate localities an official registry was opened, in which citizens were invited to inscribe their suffrages. On the first day of opening the polls a citizen recorded himself in the negative. He was seized on the spot and sent out of the city by the military guard, present in strong force. Several, afterwards expelled from the country by President Baez, found refuge from violence in the house of the Italian consul. President Baez, in presence of the commercial agent of the United States, threatened influential citizens with banishment if they opposed the treaty, and frequently expressed the like intolerance.

The unanimity thus obtained was so suspicious as to require negative votes by invitation. The Dominican President habitually declared the dependence of his authority upon that of the United States in force, and said that the death or expulsion of himself and his cabinet could be averted only by this annexation.

The public property of Dominica in the main was to be left to her, with the corresponding burden of her own debts and liabilities, necessarily, without prejudice to third parties. Encumbrances then became matter of essential consequence. Beyond the fact that they were large, only the most obscure and meagre data were before the United States government concerning them previous to the report of the commissioners. A person named Fabens, resident in Dominica, made, as agent of the United States, a report placing the aggregate at $600,000. With some additions since it has been reckoned at some millions. It was reported that mortgages of enormous scope, grants of public lands—of which a single one to Fabens absorbed one-fifth—perpetual navigation and commercial franchises and other monopolies, mining right, banking privileges, right to valuable woods, guano, &c., land grants and charters for railroads, for immigration societies, &c., existed; and thus there was excited the belief that by way of grant or lien all the appropriable resources of the country have fallen under private control.

Subsequent to the signing of the treaty grants and concessions of every description were solicited of the Dominican government, against zealous remonstrances of their regular United States diplomatic agent, made without encouragement from Washington. The President, on sending the report of the commissioners to Congress, accompanied it with a message, in which he took strong ground for annexation, but, as is well known, without success.

records.headline: An editorial in the Tribune discusses the Samaná Bay enterprise
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Tribune discusses the Samaná Bay enterprise and disputes the assertions of Dr. Samuel G. Howe. The paper agrees that the undertaking points to the establishment of controlling American influence in the Republic of Santo Domingo and throughout the West Indies, and will be favored so far as it remains a legitimate business project. It cautions, however, that serious complications will arise, as the new owners of Samaná will demand greater protection than President Báez can supply. The editorial concludes that Washington will ultimately be required to defend American citizens, effectively placing the Samaná establishment under the United States flag.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Tribune analiza la empresa de la bahía de Samaná y refuta las afirmaciones del doctor Samuel G. Howe. El periódico coincide en que la iniciativa apunta al establecimiento de una influencia estadounidense preponderante en la República de Santo Domingo y en todas las Antillas, y que será vista con agrado en la medida en que siga siendo un proyecto comercial legítimo. Advierte, sin embargo, que surgirán graves complicaciones, ya que los nuevos propietarios de Samaná exigirán mayor protección de la que el presidente Báez puede brindar. El editorial concluye que el gobierno de Washington se verá finalmente obligado a defender a los ciudadanos estadounidenses, colocando prácticamente el establecimiento de Samaná bajo la bandera de los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: An article in the Dispatch quotes commentary on the Samaná concession
records.summary_en: An article in the Dispatch quotes commentary on the Samaná concession, observing that whatever productive wealth the Dominican side of the island possesses will belong to the men who obtained the grant. The quoted analysis likens the project to the historic English and Dutch East India trading companies, suggesting that the acquisition of land titles may serve as the first step toward the transfer of sovereignty and the establishment of dominant American influence in the Republic of Santo Domingo. The Dispatch remarks upon the historic irony that this commercial enterprise originates in the very region once heavily engaged in the transatlantic slave trade.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en el Dispatch reproduce un comentario sobre la concesión de Samaná, observando que cualquier riqueza productiva que posea la parte dominicana de la isla pertenecerá a los hombres que obtuvieron la concesión. El análisis citado compara el proyecto con las históricas compañías comerciales inglesa y holandesa de las Indias Orientales, sugiriendo que la adquisición de títulos de propiedad sobre la tierra puede servir como el primer paso hacia la transferencia de soberanía y el establecimiento de una influencia estadounidense dominante en la República de Santo Domingo. El Dispatch destaca la ironía histórica de que esta empresa comercial tenga su origen en la misma región que en el pasado participó activamente en la trata transatlántica de esclavos.

records.headline: A Tribune reporter interviews Mr. Hazard regarding the plans of the newly
records.summary_en: A Tribune reporter interviews Mr. Hazard regarding the plans of the newly chartered Samaná Bay Company. Hazard disclaims annexation as the company's objective, stating that maintaining separate status while exercising its granted rights is far more profitable, even if populating the territory with Americans might ease future annexation. Asked whether the enterprise could establish a model republic in Santo Domingo, Hazard affirms there is opportunity for free trade, suffrage, and general improvements. The paper notes reports that the company has already subleased a maritime privilege in Samaná Bay for an amount equaling its entire annual payment obligation, leaving nearly all of its resources untouched.
records.summary_es: Un reportero del Tribune entrevista al señor Hazard sobre los planes de la recién constituida Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná. Hazard descarta que la anexión sea el objetivo de la compañía, señalando que mantener una condición separada en ejercicio de los derechos otorgados resulta mucho más provechoso, aun cuando poblar el territorio con estadounidenses pudiera facilitar una anexión futura. Preguntado sobre si la empresa podría establecer una república modelo en Santo Domingo, Hazard afirma que existe la oportunidad de instituir el libre comercio, el sufragio y mejoras generales. El periódico menciona informes de que la compañía ya ha subarrendado un derecho marítimo en la bahía de Samaná por una suma equivalente a toda su obligación de pago anual, dejando casi todos sus recursos intactos.

records.headline: In a letter extract on the ratification of the Samaná lease
records.summary_en: In a letter extract on the ratification of the Samaná lease, Dr. Samuel G. Howe details the sovereign powers secured by the Samaná Bay Company. The corporation holds eminent domain over the entire peninsula and bay of Samaná, possessing authority to enact laws, appoint police and judicial officers, collect customs duties, establish a bank, and construct roads, canals, and telegraph lines across the Dominican Republic in return for alternate leagues of public land. The company has bought out all prior government concessions, whose holders formally renounced their claims, and retains a virtual monopoly barring the Dominican government from chartering any rival enterprise without offering the same terms to the company.
records.summary_es: En un extracto de carta sobre la ratificación del arrendamiento de Samaná, el doctor Samuel G. Howe detalla los poderes soberanos obtenidos por la Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná. La corporación ejerce dominio eminente sobre toda la península y la bahía de Samaná, gozando de facultades para promulgar leyes, designar funcionarios policiales y judiciales, recaudar derechos aduaneros, fundar un banco y construir caminos, canales y líneas telegráficas a través de la República Dominicana a cambio de leguas alternas de tierras públicas. La compañía ha adquirido todas las concesiones gubernamentales previas, cuyos titulares renunciaron formalmente a sus derechos, y conserva un monopolio virtual que prohíbe al gobierno dominicano autorizar empresas rivales sin antes ofrecer las mismas condiciones a la compañía.

records.headline: A despatch announces the completion of a treaty between the Samana Bay Company and the Republic of St. Domingo
records.summary_en: A despatch announces the completion of a treaty between the Samana Bay Company and the Republic of St. Domingo under President Baez, ceding the peninsula of Samana with the waters of the bay, its islands and reefs. Under the treaty the company may acquire and sell property, carry on any kind of business, issue bonds, establish banks, collect port dues and taxes in its possessions, keep its own police and other forces, and sail vessels under its own flag, with the stated object of building up a free state and a great centre of trade at Samana Bay.
records.summary_es: Un despacho anuncia la conclusión de un tratado entre la Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná y la República de Santo Domingo bajo el presidente Báez, que cede la península de Samaná con las aguas de la bahía, sus islas y arrecifes. Según el tratado, la compañía puede adquirir y vender propiedades, ejercer cualquier clase de negocio, emitir bonos, establecer bancos, cobrar derechos portuarios e impuestos en sus posesiones, mantener su propia policía y otras fuerzas, y hacer navegar barcos bajo su propia bandera, con el propósito declarado de construir un estado libre y un gran centro de comercio en la bahía de Samaná.

records.summary_en: According to *The New York Herald* on January 17, 1873, a business or stock-jobbing scheme involving St. Domingo gained thousands of dollars in free advertising through press coverage. The newspaper stated that while American enterprise abroad is acceptable provided the government is not dragged into defending land grants, the President must define the administration's position to prevent annexation or complications. Finally, the article expressed strong opposition to annexing St. Domingo, describing it as a distant tropical island with little trade and a sparse population, while asserting that the United States already has sufficient territory.
records.summary_es: Según *The New York Herald* del 17 de enero de 1873, un tinglado especulativo de bolsa centrado en Santo Domingo cosechó miles de dólares en publicidad gratuita mediante la cobertura periodística. El diario opinó que, si bien la iniciativa privada estadounidense en el exterior es lícita con tal de que no comprometa al gobierno en la defensa de mercedes de tierras, el presidente debe deslindar la postura oficial para precaver anexiones o conflictos. Finalmente, el artículo expresó una enérgica repulsa a incorporar a Santo Domingo, caracterizándola como una remota isla tropical de precario comercio y escaso vecindario, concluyendo que los Estados Unidos gozan ya de suficiente extensión territorial.

These facts may create a suspicion that General Grant is not only "deeply interested" in this private enterprise of American citizens—as Mr. Hazard, the secretary of the company, says, though not in a personal sense, we presume—but that this scheme is favored by him with the ulterior view of bringing about annexation in an indirect manner—thus accomplishing his long-cherished object which the Senate mercilessly squelched. We do not think the President would act in such a surreptitious manner. We believe he honestly thinks that the possession of the territory of St. Domingo, or the Samana portion of it, by an American company, would be a benefit to the trade of the country. This, we imagine, is the "deep interest" he takes in the project, and for no other reason. Still, the American people will be disposed to believe that the President has the ulterior object of annexation in view, and he should at once remove such an impression by disavowing any purpose of the nature.

The new St. Domingo Company, like the old one, if, indeed, it be not the old one revived and reorganized, shows a great deal of tact in the initiation of its project. It has obtained, to begin operations, a systematic and extensive advertisement in the press of this city and of the country gratuitously. This cunningly planned dodge, like a skilful coup d'etat, has aroused public attention generally. A mere business operation, and, perhaps, a stockjobbing one, has obtained all the notoriety desired without costing the parties a cent. The advertising is worth many thousands of dollars if the scheme is worth anything at all. records.headline: The Samaná Bay Company agreement is criticized in a Herald editorial
records.summary_en: The Samaná Bay Company agreement is criticized in a Herald editorial, which observes that company revenues will prove a windfall to President Báez following the loss of United States payments for a naval wharf at Samaná. The paper condemns Báez as a dictator and usurper, challenging his authority to alienate Dominican territory and warning American investors to scrutinize the legitimacy of any titles he confers. While conceding that genuine commercial development of Dominican trade would be welcome under valid title, the Herald emphatically protests against using the project as a pretext for annexation, urging Americans not to be misled by promotional misrepresentations.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Herald critica el acuerdo con la Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná, observando que los ingresos de la empresa serán un alivio providencial para el presidente Báez tras la pérdida de los pagos de los Estados Unidos por el arrendamiento de un muelle naval en Samaná. El diario condena a Báez calificándolo de dictador y usurpador, cuestionando su autoridad para enajenar el territorio dominicano y advirtiendo a los inversionistas estadounidenses que examinen la legitimidad de cualquier título que otorgue. Aunque admite que el desarrollo comercial genuino del comercio dominicano sería bienvenido si contara con títulos válidos, el Herald protesta enfáticamente contra el uso del proyecto como pretexto para la anexión, instando a los estadounidenses a no dejarse engañar por presentaciones engañosas de promoción.

records.full_text:
SAMANA BAY. What Mr. Hazard Says of the New Company—It Will Have to Protect Itself—Everybody Bound To Be Friendly to It—Prospects for the Future. The Enterprise Growing in Importance.

The Samana Bay Company seems, as time runs on—and even twenty-four hours are a sufficient allowance for a popular judgment to be formed upon a scheme so vast in its pretensions—to more and more fulfil the first judgment of the HERALD upon its aspirations, and to confirm the impression that it is in its aims and purposes a copy of the British East India Company. There is this difference, however, between it and its English prototype—the latter, either from craft or from ignorance of the possibilities of its own future fortunes, disclosed, only as necessity forced it from its lips, the confession of its ultimate designs. On the other hand, the American corporation starts with a

FAIR, FRANK, OPEN AND ABOVE BOARD

declaration of all that it means to do, unless untoward events or influences should intervene. Listen, for instance, to the following brief but pointed interview yesterday between a representative of the HERALD and Mr. Hazard, the Secretary of the coming "Power of the West Indies":—

"I suppose, Mr. Hazard," said the reporter, "that our guess as to the company being in its general character modelled upon the pattern of the English East India Company, which contrived in the course of a century or so to gobble up an empire of a couple of hundred millions of people and the fairest section of the largest and richest of the five continents, is correct?"

"Well, yes; they are in many respects alike in their general ultimate objects," replied Mr. Hazard.

"But are you clear as to

THE POWER OF CITIZENS

of the United States to establish outside of their own country an independent State?"

"I think that we are tolerably secure in our position. We have such a right, in my judgment."

"And I believe you are reported to have stipulated for the privilege of maintaining your own armaments and troops and the rest of it?"

"Yes, that is substantially the case. We shall have to protect ourselves from outside interference if necessary."

"Interference, for instance, from Great Britain, or France, or Spain or from the other great Powers of Europe?"

"From most of those Powers we count upon sympathy and aid, not opposition. It is to

THEIR INTEREST

to protect and assist us. But, should they protest and attempt to enforce their protest by force, we should have the right to protect ourselves as we best could."

"Why should you count upon sympathy and aid from them?"

"Because it is to their interest that this marvellously fertile land, capable of supporting easily 10,000,000 people in comfort and plenty, should be brought within the pale of civilization. Besides, one of our first acts will be to declare Samana Bay a free port, open to the flags of all nations, just as the country itself will be thrown open at our invitation to the industry and enterprise of the whole world. We shall find our best interest in

SHARING WHATEVER BENEFITS

may accrue from our acquisition with all comers."

"And you are quite confident as to the resources of St. Domingo, or rather of your end of it, being sufficiently large to be shared without any one being the worse off?"

"It is the richest portion of the world for its size, not only agriculturally, but minerally. There are gold mines within the tract ceded to us which alone yielded to the Spaniards $20,000,000 per annum; and the other riches of the island will, I am confident, speedily be developed under the intelligent supervision of this company."

"But how do they intend to bring about this process of development?"

"Partly by themselves and their own efforts and partly by the aid of the immigration which will quickly flow thither under their auspices. Under the general company numerous other minor companies will be formed, seeking the development and utilization of the various resources of the island. Everything that pertains to the highest form of civilization will be introduced, and we are confident that Samana will become one of the great trading entrepôts of the world. The prospects of the company are, in my opinion, as bright as any one can well imagine."

For a day or so the text of

THE CONTRACT

entered into between Baez and the company cannot be obtained; but when it is we shall be better able to estimate what the powers and possible developments of this company may be. At present, however, it is pretty clear that the powers conceded to it under the contract are believed to be almost limitless, and that it has practically acquired absolute control of the island. Should this prove the case the parallel between the East India Company and this new American copy of it will be complete.

The following circular was sent out by the promoters of the scheme to induce the co-operation of capitalists, and is worth careful perusal:—

[Strictly private.]

No. 110 BROADWAY,

New York, Oct. 29, 1872.

Since the failure of the proposed Treaty of Annexation of the Republic of St. Domingo to the United States a convention has been prepared, with the approbation of leading citizens of that Republic, which concedes to individuals, to be organized into an association under the name of the "Samana Bay Company of St. Domingo," all the rights, privileges and immunities over and in the bay and peninsula of Samana which were ceded to the United States by the said proposed treaty; to hold all the public lands on said peninsula of Samana, the waters of Samana Bay and the islands and reefs therein, without taxation, with ample powers over said lands and waters, and special privileges to establish commercial lines; a bank of issue, with branches; to construct railways, common roads and telegraph lines; to acquire vast tracts of the richest mineral lands on the globe, and of agricultural lands of wonderful fertility—in fee, for nominal considerations.

It is understood that our government looks with favor upon an enterprise directed toward an increase of our national commerce with this free people, and approves an effort to stimulate the cultivation of staple tropical productions so largely imported into this country by free labor, and under the direction of our own citizens.

It is evident that this fertile island will soon become a part of the United States.

The President, in his message to the Forty-first Congress, says:—"I was thoroughly convinced that the best interests of this country, commercially and materially, demanded its ratification (the Treaty of Annexation). Time has only confirmed me in this view. I now firmly believe * * * that a free port will be negotiated for by European nations. In the Bay of Samana a large commercial city will spring up, to which we will be tributary without receiving corresponding benefits, and then will be seen the folly of our rejecting so great a prize. St. Domingo, with a stable government, under which her immense resources can be developed, will give remunerative wages to tens of thousands of laborers not now upon the island. This labor will take advantage of every available means of transportation to abandon the adjacent islands and seek the blessings of freedom and its sequence, each inhabitant receiving the reward of his own labor."

The Commissioners, in their report, say:—"St. Domingo is capable of supporting millions of people. Land is cheap. In fertility it certainly equals, and probably surpasses, the neighboring islands, and it is even better suited to the production of sugar and coffee. It could supply the entire market of the United States with these great West India staples."

Dr. Samuel G. Howe, of Boston, one of the Commissioners, in a recent letter, says:—"No commercial enterprise upon record ever gave promise of so much good to the enslaved races and to oppressed native races, such development of internal resources, such expansion of commercial relations and such rich returns to those who first enter upon it as does this one. I say so, mindful of the grand old companies of the East Indies and other great enterprises of past ages." History shows that during the first half century after it was possessed by the Spaniards it sprang suddenly into such wealth and importance as to be the wonder of the world. * * * It has now all the immense resources and capabilities which the Spaniards failed to develop."

Mr. S. L. M. Barlow, who has devoted great attention to the subject, writes:—"The power of such a combination would control the island, its lands and commerce. It will build up a State and make every acre of land on the island not only as good as that of Cuba, but as that of Illinois."

It is proposed to organize this company by associating fifteen gentlemen of high character, who will receive the concession from the Dominican government, and it is indispensable to the success of the great enterprise that they should take some personal interest in the formation of the State, and contribute in some direction to its development and prosperity.

Immediate action is indispensable to secure these valuable grants. It will afford me pleasure to explain the details to you, if you have any desire to participate in what must be regarded as an exceptional opportunity for doing a great public service and reaping a great pecuniary reward. Very respectfully,

ROWLAND R. HAZARD, JR.

records.headline: The Samana Bay Company persistently refused to give the press a copy of its treaty with the Dominican government
records.summary_en: The Samana Bay Company persistently refused to give the press a copy of its treaty with the Dominican government, even as its officers freely praised the resources and prospects of their acquired possession. The Herald prints the treaty's full text and reports that the commissioners, after weeks of daily sessions with President Baez in the Executive Palace, obtained concessions more favorable than they had hoped for, and that the Dominican Senate accepted the treaty after about a week of debate, stipulating only that it be submitted to the people for ratification.

The company is entitled to emit bonds for railroad, canal, telegraph and highroad constructions, with the faculty of guaranteeing payment there-against, and further, shall have the right to hypothecate the bonds emitted for the purpose of raising funds to carry on the work, and shall further have the right to emit further stock for the completion of said work.

Neither:—Emigrants who shall purchase land of the company or the agents of said company, or merchants who shall be engaged in commercial pursuits between Samana and other points of the Dominican Republic shall be compelled to pay higher imposts than Dominican citizens. It is also further understood that no taxes shall be levied by the Dominican government upon works of public utility, or the banking establishments—and, in a word, the company shall be treated as the most favored of Dominican citizens.

The company shall have the privilege of authorizing the formation of other companies, and has the right of ceding land to them upon such terms and stipulations as may be considered most advantageous, and, by so doing, carry out the aims and objects for which the company was organized.

The aforesaid smaller companies shall have their names designated by the said Samana Bay Company, and shall be under the superintendence and inspection of the said company, which shall have the privilege of holding shares in the said smaller companies.

The privileges and concessions accorded to this company shall be without prejudice to privileges and concessions accorded to any other person or persons by the Dominican government, for, up to the present time, no such privileges or concessions have been granted similar to those now conceded to the Samana Bay Company, which is now empowered, for the space of thirty days, to accept or refuse said treaty.

ART. 10.—These concessions, rights, privileges and immunities shall take effect on the first day of January, in the year eighteen hundred and seventy-three, and will continue in force and will remain in force for ninety-nine years from the said date (with the exception of a certain time that is to be conceded to the company for the purpose of taking possession, on the condition that the said company, its successors or representatives, pay or cause to be paid, to the Dominican government the sum of $150,000, in American gold, in advance, to the Dominican government. The said sum to be charged in advance to the company on the 1st day of January of each year, and the payment thereagainst to be made in the capital city of St. Domingo on the same, or at any place that may be designated by the Dominican government.

The first of these annual advance payments shall be made on the 1st of January, in the year 1873, unless it has been made before. The company and its territories shall remain under the united protection of the Dominican Republic and the United States of America, and the company and its agents, when they deem it necessary, shall ask the protection and intervention of either of these nations or of both.

ART. 11.—For the purposes of ratifying this convention a vote will be taken on the subject by the Dominican nation and the Dominican Senate. The non-payment of the annual rent alluded to in article 10 or the breaking out of war or other circumstances of force majeure will cause the said convention to be considered null and void after thirty days' notice has been given by the Dominican government.

The Herald says: "It is absurd to speak of a vast trade with St. Domingo. One little steamer making monthly trips does the principal trade with the United States. There is hardly any other. The Company speaks of a prospective trade amounting to hundreds of millions. This is ridiculous. San Domingo has scarcely any production in itself. However rich the soil may be, there is not the labor, nor do we think it can be carried there to make the soil productive. Then it is an error to say that the island has a commanding position for trade with the Antilles and South America. It lies on the outer verge of the whole group, and is not properly in the track of commerce."

The Company, however, say they will make Samana virtually a free port, and gradually absorb all the trade of the West Indies. Governor Fabens has posted the Company's flag at Samana, and the steamship Tybee, at Pier No. 4, North River, floats the same emblem from her fore. It is a combination of the Dominican and United States flags. From edge to edge across its centre, lengthwise and crosswise, is a broad white band, dividing the flag into four other parts. In the upper left-hand corner is the union jack, a blue field and white stars. The upper right-hand corner is red, the lower right blue, and the lower left-hand corner red. The negotiations with Baez for the purchase of Samana extended through two weeks. Audiences were given daily in the Executive Palace, the hours being from 8:30 a. m. to 4:30 p. m., with an intermission for dinner. The negotiations were conducted in Spanish, and during their progress the Commissioners had no relations of intimacy with the members of the Government, living on board the ship, and not seeing the Dominicans except in business hours. When the negotiations were completed, and the treaty ratified, the President gave a grand ball in honor of the Commissioners, who returned the compliment by a dinner on the Tybee.

Several times the negotiations were nearly broken off. On one occasion the Commissioners retired to their steamer, got up steam, blew their whistle, and were nearly off, and then they were recalled. Whether the Dominicans were frightened by the steam whistle is not known, but the negotiations were resumed, and finally the President and his Ministers ratified the contract. It was then referred to the Senate, which comprises nine members. The Senate discussed the Convention several days, during which the members of the Government were invited before that body to explain the various provisions of the treaty. The result of these deliberations was the ratification by the Senate. That branch of the Government agreed with the Executive, that a treaty, which was such an innovation on the laws of the country, and which granted such unusual and extraordinary powers to a private company, should not be finally and wholly carried into effect without its ratification by the people at the polls. This has doubtless been accomplished before the present date. Perhaps nine-tenths of the population, altogether about 240,000, are uneducated and ignorant. The voters of this class are expected to have no opinion but to vote as their superiors direct. The educated and wealthier classes favor the scheme and therefore the Company have no doubt that the Convention will be overwhelmingly ratified at the polls.

records.headline: The secretary of the Samana Bay Company says the company was to protect itself from outside interference but counted
records.summary_en: The secretary of the Samana Bay Company says the company was to protect itself from outside interference but counted upon the sympathy and aid of foreign governments, and that it would first declare Samana Bay a free port to the whole world. A Washington dispatch adds that congressmen considered the Samana Bay scheme impracticable, and that the Haitian minister thought the American purchasers would find they had made a bad speculation, the bay being fit for nothing but a naval station.
records.summary_es: El secretario de la Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná dice que la compañía debía protegerse de la interferencia externa pero contaba con la simpatía y la ayuda de gobiernos extranjeros, y que primero declararía la bahía de Samaná puerto libre para todo el mundo. Un despacho de Washington añade que los congresistas consideraban el plan de la bahía de Samaná impracticable, y que el ministro haitiano pensaba que los compradores estadounidenses descubrirían que habían hecho una mala especulación, pues la bahía no servía para nada más que para una estación naval.

records.full_text:
SAMANA BAY.

Further Details of the Sale to the American Company—Creation of a Sovereign Power—Speculations and Surmises Regarding the Future Action of the New Nation.
Special Despatch to The Chicago Tribune.
NEW YORK, Jan. 18.—The full text of the Samana purchase convention confirms the fact that the Company has obtained absolute sovereignty over the peninsula, with its inhabitants and private interests. The sovereignty conceded to the Company is greater than that of the State of New York, or any other State in the Union, for it includes the right to levy and collect custom duties, and to do many other things which can only be done by a sovereign nation. Baez not only sells them these extraordinary privileges, but he sells them the flag of the Republic of St. Domingo to use as they may see proper. Besides all this, the Company can build railroads and telegraphs in any part of the island, obtaining grants as extraordinary as those accorded to the Union Pacific and other railroads when Congress was giving away the public domain. Every league of railroad constructed by the Company brings its square league of land, and every three leagues of telegraph, a square league grant. The Company promised Baez to use all their influence with Congress to bring Dominican products into the ports of the United States, free of duty, which would be a singular discrimination against other tropical countries.

A most extraordinary feature of the treaty is that it frees the men composing the Company from the operation of our Register and Navigation laws. Under the acts of Congress, American merchants cannot buy ships abroad. This Company, though composed mostly of Americans, can buy ships where it can buy them cheapest, for it has bought a flag under which to run them.

The Herald says on this head: "A few judicious alliances with American railway monopolies would make the Company as powerful in the United States as in St. Domingo, and in the end it might rule us as effectually as our tan-colored brethren in the West Indies."

[To the Associated Press.]
NEW YORK, Jan. 18.—A great deal of speculation is rife in this city as to the Samana Bay Company seeking aid from the United States Government in furthering its objects. It is thought that the Company will endeavor first to obtain the formal protection of our Government, and, if possible, to lease it a naval station in the bay, and, further, to agitate the idea of annexation. Already it is stated that powerful lobby interests are to be created with these ends in view, and that Congress will be asked soon to pass exceptional tariff laws applying to the trade from San Domingo.

records.headline: The News outlines how the Samana Bay Company of Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The News outlines how the Samana Bay Company of Santo Domingo was organized, formed by American capitalists after negotiations between the United States and the Dominican Republic broke off. Prominent corporators include S. L. M. Barlow, Alden B. Stockwell of the Pacific Mail Company, Dr. Samuel G. Howe, Henry Clews, Oliver Ames, and William G. Fargo. Capitalized at $20,000,000 in one-hundred-dollar shares, the company is governed by five to thirteen directors elected annually. The corporation is empowered to buy, sell, mortgage, and lease property of every description in Santo Domingo and elsewhere, as well as issue bonds.
records.summary_es: El News detalla la organización de la Samana Bay Company of Santo Domingo, constituida por capitalistas estadounidenses después de que se interrumpieran las negociaciones entre los Estados Unidos y la República Dominicana. Entre los socios destacados figuran S. L. M. Barlow, Alden B. Stockwell de la Pacific Mail Company, el Dr. Samuel G. Howe, Henry Clews, Oliver Ames y William G. Fargo. Capitalizada en $20,000,000 en acciones de cien dólares, la empresa estará gobernada por entre cinco y trece directores elegidos anualmente. La corporación está facultada para comprar, vender, hipotecar y arrendar propiedades de toda clase en Santo Domingo y otros lugares, además de emitir bonos.

records.headline: An editorial in the Tribune argues that the Samana Bay Company
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Tribune argues that the Samana Bay Company has obtained an unprecedentedly broad charter that renders it a sovereign government rather than a mere commercial corporation. Because the company assumes governing functions, the paper contends the United States Government must not extend special protection to it, leaving the enterprise to face the ordinary risks of war and revolution on its own. The editorial questions President Báez's legal authority to convey Dominican territory to private capitalists, suggesting the deal may provoke resistance from Haiti, objections from Spain, or revolution from dispossessed concession holders.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Tribune sostiene que la Samana Bay Company ha obtenido una concesión de una amplitud sin precedentes que la convierte en un gobierno soberano y no en una simple corporación comercial. Debido a que la empresa asume funciones de gobierno, el periódico afirma que el gobierno de los Estados Unidos no debe extenderle una protección especial, dejando que la compañía enfrente por su cuenta los riesgos habituales de guerra y revolución. El editorial cuestiona la autoridad legal del presidente Báez para transferir territorio dominicano a capitalistas privados, señalando que la transacción podría provocar la resistencia de Haití, objeciones de España o una revolución de titulares de concesiones despojados.

records.headline: An editorial in the Herald criticizes a clause in the Samana Bay Company's convention
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Herald criticizes a clause in the Samana Bay Company's convention requiring vessels flying the American or Dominican flag to be manned and commanded by citizens of either nation. The paper warns that this provision appears designed to evade United States registry and navigation laws by intertwining American shipping with Santo Domingo under a private corporation exercising governmental powers. It questions whether President Grant is aware of the arrangement and urges the American public to investigate the scheme thoroughly rather than be misled by the company's extravagant claims.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Herald critica una cláusula del convenio de la Samana Bay Company que exige que las embarcaciones que naveguen bajo bandera estadounidense o dominicana sean tripuladas y comandadas por ciudadanos de cualquiera de las dos naciones. El periódico advierte que esta disposición parece concebida para evadir las leyes de registro y navegación de los Estados Unidos al entrelazar la navegación estadounidense con Santo Domingo bajo una corporación privada que ejerce poderes gubernamentales. Cuestiona si el presidente Grant tiene conocimiento del acuerdo e insta al público estadounidense a examinar minuciosamente el proyecto en lugar de dejarse engañar por las extravagantes pretensiones de la compañía.

records.headline: A message from the commissioners at Puerto Plata announces the ratification by the Dominican Senate of the convention
records.summary_en: A message from the commissioners at Puerto Plata announces the ratification by the Dominican Senate of the convention leasing the Bay of Samana to a company, on terms similar to those once offered to the United States administration. In addition, the company is allowed to build railroads, construct canals and telegraphs in return for land grants, and for its privileges, which could let it monopolize the commerce and port duties of the island, it will pay the Dominican Government $150,000 in gold annually.
records.summary_es: Un mensaje de los comisionados en Puerto Plata anuncia la ratificación por el Senado dominicano del convenio que arrienda la bahía de Samaná a una compañía, en términos similares a los ofrecidos en su día a la administración de los Estados Unidos. Además, la compañía podrá construir ferrocarriles, canales y telégrafos a cambio de concesiones de tierras, y por sus privilegios, que podrían permitirle monopolizar el comercio y los derechos portuarios de la isla, pagará al Gobierno dominicano 150.000 dólares en oro al año.

records.headline: The Tribune introduces an exposé. It regards the political scheming
records.summary_en: The Tribune introduces an exposé. It regards the political scheming behind the Dominican annexation project and the subsequent lease of Samaná Bay to American capitalists. Warning that the transaction may prove a costly burden on the United States Treasury to bail out English speculators, the paper publishes a communication titled "For Sale, a Republic." The correspondent opens with a biographical sketch of Buenaventura Báez in 1865 and 1866, describing him living near poverty in Bordeaux while planning to recoup power in Santo Domingo.
records.summary_es: El Tribune presenta una denuncia sobre las intrigas políticas detrás del proyecto de anexión dominicana y el posterior arrendamiento de la bahía de Samaná a capitalistas estadounidenses. Tras advertir que la transacción podría resultar una costosa carga para el Tesoro de los Estados Unidos con el fin de rescatar a especuladores ingleses, el periódico publica una comunicación titulada «Se vende una república». El corresponsal inicia con un bosquejo biográfico de Buenaventura Báez en 1865 y 1866, describiéndolo viviendo cerca de la pobreza en Burdeos mientras planeaba recuperar el poder en Santo Domingo.

records.headline: Continuing a letter in the Tribune, a correspondent alleges
records.summary_en: Continuing a letter in the Tribune, a correspondent alleges that financial speculator Hartmont, backed by the English firm of Lawsons, lobbied Washington for two years before helping engineer the Samaná Bay concession under various aliases. Turning to describe the Dominican Republic, the writer characterizes the country as an earthly paradise of unparalleled tropical scenery and natural wealth. He notes that the island produces exceptional mahogany, supplies abundant lignum vitae to England and the United States, and possesses soils capable of yielding unsurpassed sugar cane, oranges, lemons, and citrons.
records.summary_es: Al continuar una carta en el Tribune, un corresponsal afirma que el especulador financiero Hartmont, respaldado por la firma inglesa de los Lawson, ejerció presión en Washington durante dos años antes de ayudar a urdir la concesión de la bahía de Samaná bajo diversos alias. Al pasar a describir la República Dominicana, el autor califica al país como un paraíso terrenal de paisajes tropicales y riqueza natural sin igual. Señala que la isla produce una caoba excepcional, suministra abundante guayacán a Inglaterra y a los Estados Unidos, y posee tierras capaces de producir caña de azúcar, naranjas, limones y cidras inigualables.

records.headline: The Tribune reports on the Samana Bay Company's plans to establish
records.summary_en: The Tribune reports on the Samana Bay Company's plans to establish a weekly steamship line between New York and Samaná, contracting for three vessels and chartering a steamer to carry tourists to the island. It then prints the formal report submitted to Chairman Alden B. Stockwell by the commissioners dispatched to negotiate the concession. Appointed on December 4, the commissioners sailed on the Tybee and arrived at Santo Domingo City on December 14. Finding President Báez forty miles away at Azua commanding the army observing the Haitian frontier, they presented their credentials to Secretary of State Gautier.
records.summary_es: El Tribune informa sobre los planes de la Samana Bay Company para establecer una línea semanal de vapores entre Nueva York y Samaná, mediante la contratación de tres embarcaciones y el fletamento de un vapor para llevar turistas a la isla. Luego publica el informe formal presentado al presidente de la junta, Alden B. Stockwell, por los comisionados enviados a negociar la concesión. Nombrados el 4 de diciembre, los comisionados zarparon en el Tybee y llegaron a la ciudad de Santo Domingo el 14 de diciembre. Al hallar al presidente Báez a cuarenta millas de distancia en Azua al mando del ejército que observaba la frontera haitiana, presentaron sus credenciales al secretario de Estado Gautier.

records.headline: An editorial in the Republican analyzes the sweeping privileges
records.summary_en: An editorial in the Republican analyzes the sweeping privileges granted to the Samana Bay Company, describing the leased territory as highly fertile for sugar cane, coffee, and cocoa, and rich in minerals such as iron. Beyond territorial jurisdiction, the company receives rights to establish a bank of issue whose paper is legal tender for internal taxes, a practical monopoly on future railways, canals, and telegraphs with extensive land grants, and immunity from burdensome taxation. The paper cautions that the venture assumes ultimate annexation by the United States, warning that the speculators face ruin if annexation fails to occur or if the Dominican population resists.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en el Republican analiza los amplios privilegios otorgados a la Samana Bay Company, y describe el territorio arrendado como sumamente fértil para la caña de azúcar, el café y el cacao, y rico en minerales como el hierro. Más allá de la jurisdicción territorial, la empresa recibe derechos para establecer un banco emisor cuyo papel moneda sea de curso legal para los impuestos internos, un monopolio práctico sobre futuros ferrocarriles, canales y telégrafos con extensas concesiones de tierras, y exención de impuestos gravosos. El periódico advierte que la empresa da por sentada la anexión final por parte de los Estados Unidos, señalando que los especuladores enfrentan la ruina si la anexión no llega a concretarse o si la población dominicana se resiste.

records.headline: The Appeal questions the financial and legal foundations of the Samana Bay Company's agreement
records.summary_en: The Appeal questions the financial and legal foundations of the Samana Bay Company's agreement with President Báez. The paper doubts that the enterprise can generate the required $150,000 annual payment in advance without speculative stock sales, noting that Báez shrewdly insisted on payment in American gold on pain of nullifying the contract. It further warns that treaty provisions authorizing company vessels to fly the American or Dominican flag, manned by citizens of either country, appear designed to circumvent United States registry and navigation laws while entangling the federal government in the company's private rule.
records.summary_es: El Appeal cuestiona los fundamentos financieros y legales del acuerdo de la Samana Bay Company con el presidente Báez. El diario duda de que la empresa pueda generar el pago anual requerido de $150,000 por adelantado sin recurrir a la venta especulativa de acciones, y señala que Báez insistió astutamente en recibir pagos en oro estadounidense bajo pena de anulación del contrato. Advierte además que las cláusulas del tratado que autorizan a los buques de la compañía a enarbolar la bandera estadounidense o la dominicana, tripulados por ciudadanos de cualquiera de los dos países, parecen diseñadas para eludir las leyes de registro y navegación de los Estados Unidos al tiempo que involucran al gobierno federal en el régimen privado de la empresa.

records.headline: Reprinting an editorial from the New York Herald, the Appeal scrutinizes
records.summary_en: Reprinting an editorial from the New York Herald, the Appeal scrutinizes article ten of the convention between the Dominican government and the Samana Bay Company. The clause specifies that the company and its territories shall remain under the joint protection of the Dominican Republic and the United States, with the company authorized to solicit intervention from either or both nations. The paper asks whether President Grant or Congress authorized this guarantee, or whether the speculators inserted it without sanction to market their stock and bonds while President Báez safeguarded his personal financial interests.
records.summary_es: Al reproducir un editorial del New York Herald, el Appeal examina el artículo diez del convenio entre el gobierno dominicano y la Samana Bay Company. La cláusula establece que la empresa y sus territorios permanecerán bajo la protección conjunta de la República Dominicana y los Estados Unidos, autorizando a la compañía a solicitar la intervención de cualquiera de las dos naciones o de ambas. El periódico cuestiona si el presidente Grant o el Congreso autorizaron esta garantía, o si los especuladores la introdujeron sin autorización para colocar sus acciones y bonos mientras el presidente Báez resguardaba sus intereses financieros personales.

records.headline: An editorial headed "The Samana Bay Purchase" traces President Báez's efforts
records.summary_en: An editorial headed "The Samana Bay Purchase" traces President Báez's efforts to monetize Dominican territory following his victory over Cabral. The paper asserts that after failing to secure a French loan, Báez's agent Hartmont engaged the English firm of Lawson & Son for £80,000, prompting the British financiers to seek reimbursement through United States annexation. When Senators Sumner and Schurz helped defeat that scheme, the English investors and Báez turned to New York bankers and speculators, who have now agreed to lease the territory and supply the sought-after funds.
records.summary_es: Un editorial titulado «The Samana Bay Purchase» describe las gestiones del presidente Báez para monetizar el territorio dominicano tras su victoria sobre Cabral. El periódico afirma que, tras fracasar en la obtención de un préstamo francés, el agente de Báez, Hartmont, comprometió a la firma inglesa Lawson & Son por unas £80,000, lo que impulsó a los financieros británicos a buscar su reembolso mediante la anexión a los Estados Unidos. Cuando los senadores Sumner y Schurz contribuyeron a derrotar dicho plan, los inversionistas ingleses y Báez recurrieron a banqueros y especuladores neoyorquinos, quienes ahora han acordado arrendar el territorio y suministrar los anhelados fondos.
