records.headline: The New-York Tribune reports that Buenaventura Baez, the deposed
records.summary_en: The New-York Tribune reports that Buenaventura Baez, the deposed President of the Republic of Santo Domingo, arrived in New York from St. Thomas aboard the steamer South America on Thursday. Noting that it had already published a complete history of the events that led to his downfall and the progress of the revolution, the paper states that a Tribune reporter called on the ex-President at the Brevoort House yesterday to ascertain his views regarding the revolution and the condition and prospects of the Republic of Santo Domingo. The reporter describes General Baez as a man of short stature and slight figure, with regular and comely features framed by gray whiskers and a gray mustache, an alert air, and a brisk courtesy in his manners far removed from Spanish formality. According to the Tribune, Baez is fluent and emphatic in speech and shows an eager desire to put forward his own explanation of his career and recent loss of power, though the writer remarks that his defense has much wordiness and repetition and that his positive assertions do not always meet the precise point in question.
records.summary_es: El New-York Tribune informa que Buenaventura Báez, el depuesto presidente de la República de Santo Domingo, llegó a Nueva York procedente de Saint Thomas a bordo del vapor South America el jueves. Señalando que ya había publicado una historia completa de los acontecimientos que condujeron a su caída y del desarrollo de la revolución, el periódico indica que un reportero del Tribune visitó ayer al expresidente en la Brevoort House para conocer sus opiniones respecto a la revolución y a la situación y perspectivas de la República de Santo Domingo. El reportero describe al general Báez como un hombre de baja estatura y complexión más bien delgada, de facciones regulares y agradables enmarcadas por patillas y bigote grises, porte alerta y una cortesía viva en sus modales muy distante de la solemne formalidad española. Según el Tribune, Báez es fluido y enfático al hablar y muestra un vivo deseo de exponer su propia explicación de las circunstancias de su carrera y su reciente pérdida del poder, aunque el redactor observa que en su defensa abundan la verbosidad y la repetición y que sus rotundas afirmaciones no siempre responden al punto preciso en cuestión.

records.headline: The Tribune's interview with ex-President Baez carries his account of the revolution
records.summary_en: The Tribune's interview with ex-President Baez carries his account of the revolution that overthrew him: Gen. Gonzalez, he said, still lacked two years of the thirty-eight required of a candidate for the Presidency, yet was determined to grasp the chief power by means of a revolution, though he owed his standing to Baez, who had made him Collector at Puerto Plata and afterward Governor. The pretext chosen by the agitators, Baez said, was the alleged unconstitutionality and impropriety of the alienation of Samana Bay; and the strongest proof of their bad faith was that, after the outcry against him for the sale of Samana to a foreign company, on gaining power they sent an agent to the Samana Bay Company assuring it of their good will and their desire to confirm all the arrangements previously made, and to enter into any new ones of mutual advantage. Of the Puerto Plata manifesto of November 25, with its long list of charges and its many signatures — Batista, Du Rocher, Leyba and more — Baez said the most prominent names had been used without their bearers' consent, and that several had written to the Government disavowing all connection with the agitators: the window closes as 150 men march on Santiago.
records.summary_es: La entrevista del Tribune con el expresidente Báez trae su relato de la revolución que lo derrocó: el general González, dijo, aún carecía de dos años de los treinta y ocho requeridos a un candidato a la Presidencia, y sin embargo estaba decidido a apoderarse del poder supremo por medio de una revolución, aunque debía su posición a Báez, que lo había nombrado colector en Puerto Plata y después gobernador. El pretexto escogido por los agitadores, dijo Báez, fue la supuesta inconstitucionalidad e impropiedad de la enajenación de la bahía de Samaná; y la prueba más fuerte de su mala fe fue que, tras el clamor contra él por la venta de Samaná a una compañía extranjera, al llegar al poder enviaron un agente a la Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná asegurándole su buena voluntad y su deseo de confirmar todos los arreglos hechos anteriormente y de celebrar cualesquiera nuevos de mutua ventaja. Del manifiesto de Puerto Plata del 25 de noviembre, con su larga lista de cargos y sus muchas firmas —Batista, Du Rocher, Leyba y más—, Báez dijo que los nombres más prominentes habían sido usados sin el consentimiento de sus titulares, y que varios habían escrito al Gobierno desautorizando toda conexión con los agitadores: la ventana se cierra cuando 150 hombres marchan sobre Santiago.

records.headline: After the insurgent commander obtained a four-day armistice and President Baez had made his arrangements for leaving
records.summary_en: After the insurgent commander obtained a four-day armistice and President Baez had made his arrangements for leaving the country, Baez sent the Senate a message on January 2, 1874 laying down the presidency, recalling that he had been called in 1868 when paper money had brought bankruptcy and public credit had vanished. That same afternoon Baez left Santo Domingo for St. Thomas on the French war vessel Kersaint, declaring he was in no sense an exile, having left voluntarily, and that he was tired of office and wished to rest and consult physicians about his eyes.
records.summary_es: Después de que el comandante insurgente obtuviera una tregua de cuatro días y el presidente Báez hubiera hecho sus arreglos para salir del país, Báez envió al Senado un mensaje el 2 de enero de 1874 en el que renunciaba a la presidencia, recordando que había sido llamado en 1868 cuando el papel moneda había traído la bancarrota y el crédito público había desaparecido. Esa misma tarde Báez salió de Santo Domingo hacia Saint Thomas en el buque de guerra francés Kersaint, declarando que no era en ningún sentido un exiliado, pues había salido voluntariamente, y que estaba cansado del cargo y deseaba descansar y consultar a médicos sobre sus ojos.

Paper money had brought about bankruptcy; public credit had vanished, and not a single element of social reconstruction remained. records.headline: Ex-President Baez denies he is an exile in a second Tribune interview
records.summary_en: Ex-President Baez denies he is an exile in a second Tribune interview window: he left Santo Domingo voluntarily, he said, and no sentence of banishment has been pronounced against him; he had grown somewhat tired of office, of its cares and responsibilities, and desired rest and an opportunity to recruit his health and to consult the best physicians about a threatening trouble of the eyes. Of projects of regaining office he desired to say nothing, and he was chary of speech about the new Government's prospects; he still regards the men now in power as his personal friends, though they have supplanted him, and declines to say anything against them, though he hinted that stirring news about the new Government might be expected soon. For himself, he had been called four times to the Presidency, each time from a foreign country. Asked how the change of rulers might affect the interests of the Samana Bay Company, Baez replied that there is no prospect of injury to it by the revolution — the party in power will be glad enough to receive the rent from that enterprise — and that the revolutionary leaders, once in a position to declare their real views, had sent a messenger to the Company to say that the charges against him for favoring that enterprise had been only pretext: the window closes mid-sentence.
records.summary_es: El expresidente Báez niega ser un exiliado en una segunda ventana de la entrevista del Tribune: abandonó Santo Domingo voluntariamente, dijo, y no se ha pronunciado contra él sentencia alguna de destierro; se había cansado un poco del cargo, de sus cuidados y responsabilidades, y deseaba descanso y la oportunidad de recuperar su salud y de consultar a los mejores médicos sobre una afección amenazante de los ojos. De proyectos de recuperar el cargo no deseaba decir nada, y fue parco al hablar de las perspectivas del nuevo Gobierno; sigue considerando amigos personales suyos a los hombres hoy en el poder, aunque lo han suplantado, y se niega a decir nada contra ellos, aunque insinuó que pronto podrían esperarse noticias agitadas sobre el nuevo Gobierno. En cuanto a él, había sido llamado cuatro veces a la Presidencia, cada vez desde un país extranjero. Preguntado sobre cómo el cambio de gobernantes podría afectar los intereses de la Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná, Báez respondió que no hay perspectiva de daño para ella por la revolución —el partido en el poder estará muy contento de recibir la renta de esa empresa— y que los jefes revolucionarios, una vez en posición de declarar sus verdaderas opiniones, habían enviado un mensajero a la Compañía para decir que los cargos contra él por favorecer esa empresa habían sido solo un pretexto: la ventana se cierra a mitad de una frase.

records.headline: The Herald visited ex-President Baez at the Brevoort House
records.summary_en: The Herald visited ex-President Baez at the Brevoort House, where he had arrived late on Thursday from Santo Domingo, and prints the interview under heads promising what the recent ruler says — the causes of his fall, his betrayal by friends, the doubtful stability of the provisional Government, the Samana Bay Company, and his errand off for Washington to lobby annexation. Baez, General of Division and lately President of the republic, is described as a man of nearly sixty, short and stoutish in build, with strongly marked, war-worn features, dressed in a plain suit of black without much display of jewelry. The bloodless revolution that ousted him, the statement begins, was the result of an election agitation among the progressive party which he had represented very successfully in the Presidency for the last six years; Baez was a candidate for re-election, and Generals Villanueva, Gonzalez and others, whom he had appointed to places of trust — the window closes as their part begins.
records.summary_es: El Herald visitó al expresidente Báez en el Brevoort House, adonde había llegado tarde el jueves desde Santo Domingo, y publica la entrevista bajo encabezados que prometen lo que dice el reciente gobernante: las causas de su caída, su traición por amigos, la dudosa estabilidad del Gobierno provisional, la Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná y su viaje a Washington para gestionar la anexión. Báez, general de división y hasta hace poco presidente de la república, es descrito como un hombre de casi sesenta años, bajo y algo corpulento, de facciones fuertemente marcadas y curtidas por la guerra, vestido con un traje negro sencillo sin mucha exhibición de joyas. La revolución sin sangre que lo derrocó, comienza la declaración, fue el resultado de una agitación electoral entre el partido progresista que él había representado con mucho éxito en la Presidencia durante los últimos seis años; Báez era candidato a la reelección, y los generales Villanueva, González y otros, a quienes había nombrado para puestos de confianza —la ventana se cierra cuando comienza su parte.

records.summary_en: The *New York Herald* reported on a past scheme led primarily by England and Spain to establish a new power called the Confederation of the Antilles, which would unite St. Domingo, Cuba, Jamaica, and other West India islands to counter rapidly developing American interests. According to the article, General Báez expressed sympathy for the islanders' independence and noted that while St. Domingo harbored sympathies for Spain, Cubans living in St. Domingo opposed his government because he refused to violate neutrality laws by fitting out expeditions against Spain.
records.summary_es: El *New York Herald* informó sobre un proyecto anterior encabezado principalmente por Inglaterra y España para establecer una nueva potencia denominada la Confederación de las Antillas, la cual uniría a Santo Domingo, Cuba, Jamaica y otras islas de las Antillas para contrarrestar el rápido crecimiento de los intereses estadounidenses. Según el artículo, el general Báez expresó simpatía por la independencia de los isleños y señaló que, si bien Santo Domingo albergaba simpatías hacia España, los cubanos residentes en Santo Domingo se oponían a su gobierno porque se negaba a infringir las leyes de neutralidad pertrechando expediciones contra España.

As to the probabilities of who may be called to the Presidential chair, General Baez thinks that Caceres has at present the best chance. He says that the new men in power dare not come before the people to ask their suffrages, for then there is no doubt he would be recalled at once.
Another cause of trouble to Baez was the opposition which he suffered from the Haytiens because of his friendship for the United States. In Hayti there is a law which prohibits white men from holding or becoming possessed of real estate, and the people of that black Republic think that if Americans once got a foothold on the lovely and fertile island of St. Domingo the colored race would go to the wall. Had Baez determined upon using force to maintain himself in power (which, he asserts, might easily have been done), the worst passions of the people belonging to both Republics would have been appealed to by such freebooters and bandits as Luperon, and a sanguinary war must have ensued. The Dominicans like foreigners, especially Americans; while the Haytiens abhor all white men, particularly those of the United States.
About the ability of the Samana Bay Company to comply with the conditions of their contract there appears to be no doubt. Last year the company paid up the yearly rent of $150,000 for which the bay and its dependencies are leased. This term the rent has not been delivered over because there was no stable or legitimate government to receive it.
General Baez remembers very well the project that was set on foot some years ago with the object of establishing a new Power, to be called the Confederation of the Antilles. It was not decided whether this new nation in embryo should be a kingdom or a republic. That was to be left to the decision of an inter-insular convention of notables. records.summary_en: 'An illustrious exile': a sketch of Buenaventura Báez on his arrival in New York after his fourth banishment, recapitulating his presidencies, his resistance to Santana, his expulsions by Cabral, and his negotiations to annex the island to the United States.

Baez is a remarkable man in many respects, and is deserving of more than a passing notice. He is a mulatto, about [illegible] years of age, and was born in Hayti. He gained great influence in San Domingo on account of his talents and his wealth, and after the expulsion of [Jiminez?] from the presidency was called to fill that position. At the next election, however, Santana was chosen president, but Baez refused to surrender the reins of power into his hands, and for two years successfully resisted the installation of Santana, who, up to his election to the presidency, had been Baez's warmest personal friend. Exiled on the accession of Santana, in 1858, he did not allow his restless nature to repose, but continued his intrigues for control of the island. In [illegible] he again returned to the island, was elected president a third time, but was almost immediately expelled by Cabral, his life-long enemy. Three years subsequently he again landed on his native shores, was again proclaimed president, and has retained his hold on the position till last month, when another reverse of fortune compelled his abdication. His negotiations to secure the annexation of the island to the United States are matters of public notoriety. records.headline: Ex-Senator Wade, president of the late Commission of Inquiry
records.summary_en: Ex-Senator Wade, president of the late Commission of Inquiry to San Domingo, Judge Burton, its secretary and Spanish interpreter, Frederick Douglass, Senator Cameron and Representative Orth called the night before at Willard's Hotel to pay their respects to ex-President Baez, the Ledger's Washington despatch of February 27 reports. The conversation was cordial and unrestrained, the ex-President expressing deep regret over the fate of the offer of the annexation of Dominica to the United States, as the interest and destiny of the two peoples are identical, and making dark forecasts for the island: the Haytiens, he said, under the lead of renegade Dominicans, are constantly harassing the Dominicans, murdering and robbing on the borders, while the island has always been coveted by the European powers. The Chronicle, as quoted here, remarks that the arrival in Washington of so many gentlemen connected with the San Domingo commission at the same moment as Baez may be quite significant, and possibly meant business.

La conversación fue cordial y sin reservas, expresando el expresidente su profundo pesar por la suerte de la oferta de anexión de Dominica a los Estados Unidos, pues el interés y el destino de ambos pueblos son idénticos, y haciendo sombríos pronósticos para la isla: los haitianos, dijo, bajo la dirección de dominicanos renegados, hostigan constantemente a los dominicanos, asesinando y robando en las fronteras, mientras la isla siempre ha sido codiciada por las potencias europeas. El Chronicle, tal como se le cita aquí, observa que la llegada a Washington de tantos caballeros vinculados con la comisión de Santo Domingo en el mismo momento que Báez puede ser bastante significativa, y posiblemente signifique negocios.

records.headline: A sworn statement accusing ex-President Baez, by an American citizen
records.summary_en: A sworn statement accusing ex-President Baez, by an American citizen whose name this window does not reach, is printed by the Herald in its opening charges: that during 1869 and 1870, while Baez was President of the Dominican Republic, the plaintiff was arrested at his residence at Barahona, in August 1869, by an armed force under Gen. Frederico Garcia on Baez's orders, and held upwards of five months on a charge of conspiracy with armed resistance to Baez's rule; that he was then tried by a court martial of Baez's officers, upon the testimony, the filing says, of mainly convicted felons, and sentenced to be shot; that Baez pardoned him of the offence, yet required him to depart forthwith from the republic, and thereafter detained and imprisoned him for six months more: the window closes as the third charge begins.
records.summary_es: Una declaración jurada que acusa al expresidente Báez, de un ciudadano estadounidense cuyo nombre esta ventana no alcanza, es publicada por el Herald en sus cargos iniciales: que durante 1869 y 1870, siendo Báez presidente de la República Dominicana, el demandante fue arrestado en su residencia de Barahona, en agosto de 1869, por una fuerza armada bajo el general Frederico García por órdenes de Báez, y retenido más de cinco meses bajo un cargo de conspiración con resistencia armada al gobierno de Báez; que fue entonces juzgado por un consejo de guerra de oficiales de Báez, sobre el testimonio, dice la demanda, de principalmente delincuentes convictos, y sentenciado a ser fusilado; que Báez lo indultó del delito, pero le exigió partir de inmediato de la república, y después lo detuvo y encarceló por seis meses más: la ventana se cierra cuando comienza el tercer cargo.

records.headline: The case of ex-President Baez of St. Domingo
records.summary_en: The case of ex-President Baez of St. Domingo was again up in Brooklyn on a motion to vacate the order of arrest issued by Judge Pratt. An affidavit submitted by his counsel states that the complainant Hatch was an active participant in an insurrection, was captured and sentenced to death, but that the sentence was commuted to exile as a favor to the United States Government, and Baez maintains that the capture and sentence were merely the proper exercise of his powers and duties as president of the republic and denies the jurisdiction of the court.
records.summary_es: El caso del expresidente Báez de Santo Domingo volvió a verse en Brooklyn en relación con una moción para anular la orden de arresto dictada por el juez Pratt. Una declaración jurada presentada por su abogado afirma que el demandante Hatch fue participante activo en una insurrección, fue capturado y condenado a muerte, pero que la sentencia fue conmutada por el exilio como un favor al gobierno de los Estados Unidos, y Báez sostiene que la captura y la sentencia fueron simplemente el ejercicio debido de sus facultades y deberes como presidente de la república y niega la jurisdicción del tribunal.

records.headline: The Tribune's editorial on the revocation of the Samana Bay Company's lease
records.summary_en: The Tribune's editorial on the revocation of the Samana Bay Company's lease calls it another semi-tropical bubble burst: with the expiration of the troubled official life of Baez, it says, began the real difficulties of the American company; the new Government was hostile and, it is alleged, under British influence — an assertion the Tribune itself warns will probably need examination. Provisional President Gonzalez, claiming that the company is delinquent in its dues, revokes the contract and annuls the lease; and the Tribune expects next to hear of the company as a claimant for damages, with a brief in the State Department.
records.summary_es: El editorial del Tribune sobre la revocación del arrendamiento de la Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná lo llama otra burbuja semitropical reventada: con la expiración de la atribulada vida oficial de Báez, dice, comenzaron las verdaderas dificultades de la compañía estadounidense; el nuevo Gobierno era hostil y, se alega, estaba bajo influencia británica —una afirmación que el propio Tribune advierte que probablemente necesitará examen. El presidente provisional González, alegando que la compañía está en mora en sus pagos, revoca el contrato y anula el arrendamiento; y el Tribune espera oír a continuación de la compañía como reclamante de daños, con un alegato en el Departamento de Estado.

records.full_text:
The United States mail steamship Tybee, Captain Delanoy, from St. Domingo 30th ult. at this port reports the following important intelligence:—
Soon after leaving Samana Bay the Tybee fell in with the Dominican man-of-war Capotillo, bound in.

BRITISH DIPLOMACY AND TREATY MAKING.
Mr. St. John, British Consul General at Port au Prince, had been on a tour of observation to Samana Bay in Her Majesty's ship Woodlark, where he spent several days in informing himself as to the great natural advantages of the position, and had afterwards visited St. Domingo with propositions from the Haytian government for a treaty between the two republics. Among the conditions of the proposed treaty, it is said, were the cession to Hayti of the disputed territory on the frontier and the annulment of the Samana Bay Convention, made with citizens of the United States. These conditions being admitted by the Dominican government, Hayti (or England) was to loan a considerable sum to St. Domingo, payable at convenience and without interest.
The discussion of this measure was causing great excitement throughout the island.

CONSTITUTIONAL DIFFICULTIES.
The President elect, Ignacio M. Gonzalez, who styles himself "General of the National Armies and Supreme Chief of the Republic," had not yet been installed in office, as the Convention called for the purpose of framing a new constitution was still unable to agree upon the articles thereof.

THE SAMANA BAY COMPANY IN A DIFFICULTY.
The Special Commission of the Samana Bay Company, composed of Dr. Samuel G. Howe, of Boston; Captain Samuels, of Dreadnaught celebrity, and Governor Fabens, of Samana, have not succeeded in obtaining an amicable settlement of the question pending between the government and the Company, including outstanding and overdue accounts against the government, and the provisional government has declared the Samana bay Convention null and void.

AN APPEAL TO WASHINGTON.
The Commissioners have protested against this summary act as arbitrary and illegal, and, on being instigated by British-Haytian influence, demanded an arbitration upon the matters in dispute according to the terms of the Convention. The company will, in the meantime, call upon the United States government for protection against any violent proceedings on the part of the Dominican authorities.
The inhabitants of Samana, most of whom are Americans or of American descent, were at first greatly incensed against the Gonzalez government on receipt of the news of the annulment of the lease, and declared their determination to resist any attempt at enforcing it. The Commissioners explained to them that such a course would retard and perhaps defeat a just and equitable settlement of the question, and enjoined upon them to deport themselves in a peaceable manner, to pay their taxes, and, if necessary, to pay them under protest.
The paper money of the Gonzalez government was being issued in large quantities, and was already at a discount of 50 per cent. Business was entirely suspended, and the prospect for trade was very poor.

WHAT GOVERNOR FABENS SAYS.
Governor Fabens—ex-President Baez is a warm friend of the United States, and is desirous to promote the annexation of St. Domingo to this country. Baez is the representative of American ideas and Gonzales is not, the latter being strongly imbued with Haytian-English proclivities. Now, with reference to what you ask about Baez and the news from St. Domingo, I cannot tell you, for I have, as you know, just landed from my trip.
REPORTER—Governor, do you find the Americans in your troubles, seeing that there is no established government in St. Domingo?
GOVERNOR FABENS—Well (musingly) I think the United States government ought to step in and aid, in answer to our appeal, and we rely upon it to protect our interests against any over-acts of the Dominican authorities.

The Proclamation Annulling the Contract.
IGNACIO MARIA GONZALEZ, General of the National Armies, &c.:—
Whereas, in conformity with article 10 of the contract for the lease of the peninsula and bay of Samana and its islets, made in the city of St. Domingo, on the 28th of December, 1872, between the Minister of the Interior and Police and Foreign Relations, Citizens Manuel Maria Gautier and Messrs. Samuel Samuels, T. Scott Stewart and Burton S. Harrison, Commissioners of the Company styled "The Samana Bay Company," and by decree dated 19th February, 1873, of the Dominican Executive is called the "Samana Bay Company of St. Domingo," it was stipulated and decreed that the amount of rent fixed at $150,000 annually should be paid each year in advance on the 1st day of January;
Whereas, according to article 11 of the aforesaid contract, the non-payment of the annual rent at the time fixed upon, and, in case of war or other circumstance of force majeure, finally proven one month after that date at furthest, incurs the rescinding of the Convention, it being so expressly stipulated;
Whereas, when the provisional government, under date of 2d of December, 1873, ordered the withholding of the annual payment due on the 1st January of the present year, because, in virtue of the proclamation of the 25th of November previous, it had ignored the authority of General Baez, it did so solely with the object of avoiding future difficulties with the company if it should pay the late administration;
Whereas, in the official notice that it gave to the company, on the above mentioned date of 2d December, the Provisional government assured the company that it would respect the Samana Bay Company convention so far as it should be in the interest of the country and the conditions that were being fulfilled;
Whereas the company, through its Vice President, Mr. Paul Spofford, under date of 13th January of the present year, advises the Minister of Foreign Relations that the annual payment has been withheld, thus conforming to the order of the said Minister, while at the same time he states that he is awaiting official communications upon the subject;
Whereas, in virtue of the advice to which the preceding paragraph refers, the Treasury Department, by resolution of the government and by order of the Secretary of the Treasury, drew in favor of several merchants of the capital and the Minister of Foreign Affairs and Finance drafts for the sum of $147,224.14, on account of the rent due since the 1st of last January, the said drafts being presented for acceptance, and the company, in the meantime, told the government that they would not be accepted;
Whereas at the time the government drew against the company it gave it official notice of its establishment in this capital, and through the Minister of Foreign Affairs and Finance granted the company a prolongation, responding to the annual rental due, the reasons which until then it might have had for withholding the payment;
Whereas the non-payment of the amount said in advance is a sufficient cause for declaring the convention rescinded, as stipulated in the eleventh clause of the same, there being no cause on the part of the company for its inability to withhold the payment at the time mentioned;
Whereas the propositions that, verbally and in writing, have been made to the government on the 21st, 23d and 24th of the present month by the Commissioners, Samuel Samuels and Samuel G. Howe, in the name of the company, tending to modify the contract, grant extensions for the payment of the rent and to reduce the amount of said rent, are not and cannot be accepted by the government, since they would impose upon the nation a responsibility from which it could not release itself;
Whereas the Dominican government, in virtue of the communication of the 10th of January, signed by the Vice President of the company, and of the perfect right that it has as a depositor to the rent due, ought to consider said rent paid, and as such it was accepted by the government when it drew against the company, which reason it drew a portion for the amount of $147,224, and the drafts having been presented for non-acceptance, costs and damages are due, apart from the liquidation of the respective accounts of reclamation;
Whereas the company called the "Samana Bay Company of St. Domingo" has enjoyed the advantages of the lease of said bay, peninsula and keys for the time elapsed since the last payment, it is not allowed, up until the date of this decree, making use of the benefits which said lease may have produced;
Whereas, according to the terms of the mentioned eleventh clause of the convention, the right is reserved to the Dominican government of declaring null or rescinding the contract whenever the company fails to make the payment of the rent;
Whereas the government, after having taken into account the opinion of the Council of the Secretaries of State and the Council of the Government, has decreed and does hereby decree:—
ARTICLE 1.—The convention made in this city, under date of 28th of December, 1872, between the Dominican government and the company entitled the "Samana Bay Company of St. Domingo," for the lease of the peninsula and bay of Samana and of the islands and quays in those waters, is and is hereby declared from this date, in virtue of the non-fulfillment of its conditions in all its parts and null and of no value nor effect.
ART. 2. The Peninsula and Bay of Samana and the islands and keys of its waters will again from this date, as before the celebration of the Convention of the 28th of December, 1872, be ruled by the Dominican laws and authorities in the same form and manner as the provinces and districts of the Republic and islands adjacent to its territory.
ART. 3. The company will make good the amount of the account of damages incurred through the bills protested through its fault, and what concessions to the portion of the rent due since the first of January up to the date of this decree for the time that it has had the control of the said bay, peninsula and keys, until the same date.
ART. 4. The respective departments charged with the direction of the different branches of public administration will name the authorities that are to be installed in the peninsula and bay of Samana, and will take the necessary measures for the fulfillment of this decree.
Given in the National Palace of St. Domingo, the 25th of March, 1874, the 31st year of the Independence and the 11th of the Restoration.
(Signed) IGNACIO MARIA GONZALEZ.
Countersigned:—
The Minister of the Interior and Police, (Signed) P. G. ESPAILLAT.
The Minister of Foreign Relations, (Signed) J. DE LA C. ALFAU.
The Minister of Justice and Public Instruction, (Signed) T. C. DE CASTRO.
The Minister of Finance and Commerce, (Signed) J. M. COHEN.
The Minister of War and Marine, (Signed) M. M. CASTILLO.

records.full_text:
INTERVIEW WITH GOVERNOR FABENS.
Two members of the Samana Bay Commission returned to this city yesterday by the Tybee, and upon Governor Fabens, at Messrs. Spofford’s office, the following description of his visit was received.
Mr. Fabens was very courteous, but evidently very much chagrined at the unhappy fate of the enterprise. The following dialogue ensued:—
REPORTER—It is reported down town that the Samana Bay Company is dead; is that so?
GOVERNOR FABENS (hesitating)—Well, I hardly think we can say that; we have hopes of yet coming to an amicable arrangement with the Dominican government. I do not think the company can be called defunct; it is merely suffering under temporary embarrassment. When we receive proper recognition from the Dominican government we will pay over the $150,000 in gold due last 1st January. In addition to this we have claims upon that country for provisions furnished to the government, and, in addition to that, we have to receive payment for the regular performance of the mail service, &c. Our claims in the aggregate amount to about $50,000.
HIS INTERVIEW WITH THE PRESIDENT ELECT.
I had a long interview with Gonzalez, who I consider to be the head of the revolutionary party, and not the legitimate representative of the Dominican people. He has not taken the oath of office, and I therefore cannot consider him at present as the accepted Chief Magistrate. The proclamation of Gonzalez must therefore be taken for what it is worth. A new constitution, I may here remark, is being framed at St. Domingo City.
Dr. Howe has written a long letter to President Grant on the subject, while the United States Consul has also made a full report to Secretary of State Mr. Hamilton Fish, touching the occurrence.
WHERE THE SHOE PINCHES.
The publication of the decree of Gonzalez has a most prejudicial effect upon our company, for it prevents our placing on the commercial centres a loan for the company which we have had in contemplation. “Yes, sir,” said Mr. Fabens, with animation, “I think we have been very unfairly dealt with.

The same advices report that President-elect Gonzalez had not been installed because the constitutional convention could not agree, and that the Provisional Government has declared the Samana Bay Convention null and void, while the company's commissioners protested and demanded arbitration and United States protection.

records.full_text:
The Samana Bay Company have succeeded as ill as President Grant in their efforts at the annexation of Santo Domingo. They have failed, however, from contrary reasons to those which caused the defeat of the Babcock treaty. An unusual conscientiousness induced the Senate to reject that instrument, and a far from unusual lack of conscience has instigated Señor Gonzales to abrogate his predecessor's concession to the American Company. An attempt will be made by the projectors to involve the Government in their quarrel, and this attempt will be met according to the logical habit of a portion of the press by efforts to defeat this scheme through abuse of the enterprise and those interested in it. We see no necessity for siding with either party in this matter. When the enterprise was set on foot, we rendered full justice to the motives and purposes of the capitalists who were endeavoring in this way to open up a new highway of commerce. But while we saw nothing objectionable in their scheme and hoped for its success, we could not refrain from the prediction that sooner or later the exigencies of Dominican politics would give rise to trouble which would call for the intervention of the United States, and that this would be refused, no matter under what pretext it was asked. The gentlemen who went into this business were not born yesterday. They knew what risks they were taking. They knew the character of those ex-officio brigands who make their living out of revolutions in that island. It was the business of the buyers to look carefully at their bargain, and not to look to the Government to avenge them in case they were cheated. They have no more right to ask the Government to defend them against the scoundrels who are trying to rob them.
It is not worth while to complicate the question by bringing in the supposed influence of the British Government in inducing Gonzales to take his recent course. It was an old maxim of art that a god should not be brought out of the flies, unless the matter on the stage were important enough to call for his assistance. In this case the cruise of the Woodlark is not a necessary explanation of Gonzales's action. We need not look any further than the dictator's cabinet for a motive. No one suspects Señor Baez of any very lofty motives in making the original concession. When he and Captain-General Gonzales arranged the recent farcical revolution by which he gave up the Government to him, there is no question that the annual rental of Samana Bay was the principal resource the new rulers looked to for furnishing their empty treasury. But it is stated that Gonzales did on arriving at his capital warn the Company not to pay their rent to anybody else, and to assure them of his friendly regard. While they were waiting for official information of his inauguration, which did not come, and were naturally hesitating about paying $150,000 to a usurper who might be driven out to-morrow, he took their silence for a refusal or for a notice, and they allowed his drafts to be protested. After this, nothing he could do ought to surprise them. In common with statesmen of his class, if he has no money, he has no quantity of any dignity. He needed no further incentive, from Consul-General St. John, the British Government, or anybody else, to resent the prudent suspicions of the Yankees, and to answer them by an act as public and as thorough as possible.
The cause of the Company's failure was inherent in this enterprise from the beginning. They had no right to expect honest and fair dealing from the Dominican Government, and it was not reasonable to hope for any permanency in the occupants of power at Santo Domingo. Their scheme was in most respects an admirable one, but it has been mismanaged from the start. It could only have succeeded by making a sufficient force of Americans on the place against the greedy and treacherous "statesmen" who made the grant. This was the only course to adopt if the enterprise was a genuine one. If it was merely intended for a piece of stock jobbing, it might as well die now as later, and in either case it has no just claim that we can see to come upon the United States for protection or indemnification.

THE PROCLAMATION ANNULLING THE CONTRACT.
Ignacio Maria Gonzalez, General of the National Armies:
WHEREAS, In conformity with Article 10 of the contract for the lease of the Peninsula and Bay of Samana and its keys, made in this city on the 28th December, 1872, between the Government of the Republic represented by the then Minister of the Interior and Police and Foreign Relations, Citizen Manuel Maria Gautier, and Messrs. Samuel Samuels, T. Scott Stewart, and Burton N. Harrison, Commissioners of the Company which was called and by decree dated 19th February, 1873, of the Dominican Executive is called the “Samana Bay Company of St. Domingo,” it was stipulated and decreed that the amount of rent fixed at $150,000 annually should be paid each year in advance on the 1st day of January.
WHEREAS, According to Art. 11 of the aforesaid contract, the non-payment of the annual rent at time fixed upon, and, in case of war or other circumstance of fuerza mayor, legally proved one month after that date at furthest incurs the rescinding of the Convention, it being so expressly stipulated.
WHEREAS, When the Provisional Government, under date of 7th December, 1873, ordered the withholding of the annual payment due on the 1st January of the present year, because in virtue of the proclamation of the 23d of November previous, it had ignored the authority of Gen. Baez, it did so solely with the object of avoiding future difficulties with the Company if it should pay the late administration.
WHEREAS, In the official notice that it gave to the Company, on the above mentioned date of the 7th December, the Provisional Government signified to the Company that it would respect the Samana Bay Company Convention in the form stipulated by the late Government and under the conditions laid down therein.
WHEREAS, The Company, through its Vice-President, Mr. Paul Spofford, under date of 10th January of the present year, advises the Minister of Foreign Relations that the annual payment has been delayed, thus conforming to the order of the said Minister, while at the same time he states that he is awaiting official communications upon the subject.
WHEREAS, In virtue of the advices to which the preceding paragraph refers the Treasury Department, by resolution of the Government and by order of the Secretary of the Treasury, drew in favor of several merchants of this and other places in the Republic and abroad for the sum of $11,084 upon the Company and on account of the rent due since the 1st of last January, the bills having been protested for non-acceptance, notwithstanding the assurances that the Government had that they would be accepted.

records.summary_en: The expelled Samana Bay Company's expected demand for indemnity is taken up by the Tribune's editorial from the Dominican authorities, which it will doubtless expect the United States to support — their interests, they say, being to a certain extent identical with our Government's, because the United States is a tenant of theirs, having accepted a lease of the island of Levantado as a naval station. The Tribune doubts the company is entitled to the consideration it is likely to receive at Washington: unlike American citizens who pursue a regular business in a foreign land, it says, the company virtually renounced its nationality and attempted to set up a little independent state of its own, with its own laws, its own governor, its own police, its own custom-house, its own system of taxation, its own navy and, if it chose to use it, its own flag, under a purchase that stipulated arbitration of disputes between buyer and seller; it entered into this speculation with its eyes wide open, knowing the character of the men with whom it dealt: the window closes mid-argument.

records.headline: Pocket the loss in silence, concludes the Tribune's Samana Bay editorial
records.summary_en: Pocket the loss in silence, concludes the Tribune's Samana Bay editorial in this second window on the same page: a company which did business with a landlord utterly incapable of making good his agreements, and has now been swindled, should pocket the loss: the plain truth of the whole matter, it says, is that a little knot of New-York speculators have been cheated — not by the Dominican people nor by the Dominican Republic, but by Mr. Buenaventura Baez — and there is not the shadow of a reason why the United States should interfere to help them. records.headline: A court report describes an application for a receiver for the Samana Bay Company, which was incorporated in 1873 by a special
records.summary_en: A court report describes an application for a receiver for the Samana Bay Company, which was incorporated in 1873 by a special act of the Dominican government, with all its stockholders citizens of the United States and its headquarters in New York, to promote mining, agriculture and railways. Creditor William Rowland argued that General Gonzales's decree had dissolved the company, while director Paul Spofford, himself a creditor for $50,000, argued that Gonzales's act was not the act of the republic; Judge Donohue reserved his decision.
records.summary_es: Un informe judicial describe una solicitud de un síndico para la Samana Bay Company, que fue incorporada en 1873 por un acto especial del gobierno dominicano, con todos sus accionistas ciudadanos de los Estados Unidos y su sede en Nueva York, para promover la minería, la agricultura y los ferrocarriles. El acreedor William Rowland argumentó que el decreto del general Gonzáles había disuelto la compañía, mientras que el director Paul Spofford, él mismo acreedor por 50.000 dólares, argumentó que el acto de Gonzáles no era un acto de la república; el juez Donohue reservó su decisión.

records.headline: Under the head 'Samana Bay Company,' the Herald reports an application
records.summary_en: Under the head 'Samana Bay Company,' the Herald reports an application for the appointment of a receiver for the company incorporated in 1873 by special act of the Dominican government as the Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná de Santo Domingo, whose stockholders were all citizens of the United States, mainly of New York, where its headquarters were established and still continue; among the leading stockholders named are Paul V. Spofford, A. B. Stockwell and Leonardo Del Monte. The company's objects were to promote mining and agriculture, build railways, and otherwise develop the resources of the republic, but it has not, it is claimed, been very successful, and its affairs have for some time been the subject of inquiry in the courts, first in the United States court and yesterday in a new shape in Supreme Court Chambers: a petition by William Rowland, a creditor, for a receiver, on the grounds that the incorporation being the work of the Dominican Republic, the decree of General Gonzalez has actually dissolved the company, and that nothing now remains — the window closes within the petition's grounds.

Spofford, A. B. Stockwell y Leonardo Del Monte. Los objetos de la compañía eran promover la minería y la agricultura, construir ferrocarriles y desarrollar de otro modo los recursos de la república, pero no ha sido, se afirma, muy exitosa, y sus asuntos han sido desde hace tiempo objeto de indagación en los tribunales, primero en el tribunal de los Estados Unidos y ayer en una nueva forma en las sesiones de la Corte Suprema: una petición de William Rowland, un acreedor, para un síndico, sobre la base de que, siendo la incorporación obra de la República Dominicana, el decreto del general González ha disuelto de hecho la compañía, y de que ahora nada queda —la ventana se cierra dentro de los fundamentos de la petición.

records.headline: The Sun looks back on the annexation schemes with open sarcasm
records.summary_en: The Sun looks back on the annexation schemes with open sarcasm: first, it says, a protectorate over San Domingo was asked, because the Dominicans were so extremely jealous of their autonomy and would be so thankful if the United States would undertake to preserve it for them; then, when Congress had voted this down, annexation was straightway proposed, because the Dominicans were so heartily tired of their autonomy and so clamorous to be rid of it that they were worrying the life out of Mr. Seward by their incessant appeals to be bought and annexed. Meanwhile the guano, whose existence and commercial value the Americans had discovered and demonstrated, became to San Domingo what cotton was to the Confederate States: it was her only basis of credit, the foundation of nearly all the building loans by which Baez attempted from time to time to raise money, and the pledge of its royalties the only thing of value upon which the Hartmont bonds were secured; and it was merely to foreclose on those bonds, in the Dominican fashion, that the Samana Bay Company attempted some time ago to get possession of them: the window closes as the narrative reaches Mr. Seward.
records.summary_es: El Sun repasa los planes de anexión con abierto sarcasmo: primero, dice, se pidió un protectorado sobre Santo Domingo, porque los dominicanos eran tan extremadamente celosos de su autonomía y estarían tan agradecidos si los Estados Unidos se encargaran de preservarla por ellos; luego, cuando el Congreso había rechazado esto, se propuso directamente la anexión, porque los dominicanos estaban tan de corazón cansados de su autonomía y tan clamorosamente deseosos de deshacerse de ella que estaban matando a fuerza de preocupaciones al Sr. Seward con sus incesantes apelaciones a ser comprados y anexados. Mientras tanto, el guano, cuya existencia y valor comercial los estadounidenses habían descubierto y demostrado, se convirtió para Santo Domingo en lo que el algodón fue para los Estados Confederados: era su única base de crédito, el fundamento de casi todos los préstamos para construcción con los que Báez intentó de vez en cuando recaudar dinero, y la prenda de sus regalías lo único de valor sobre lo que se aseguraron los bonos Hartmont; y fue meramente para ejecutar la hipoteca sobre esos bonos, a la manera dominicana, que la Compañía de la Bahía de Samaná intentó hace algún tiempo apoderarse de ellos: la ventana se cierra cuando el relato llega al Sr. Seward.

records.headline: Germany's designs on Caribbean bays did not cease with President Grant's Monroe-doctrine
records.summary_en: Germany's designs on Caribbean bays did not cease with President Grant's Monroe-doctrine message, the Herald's feature argues: the message of December 1870 had declared the acquisition of St. Domingo an adherence to that doctrine, to be agreed to by the Senate lest the people of St. Domingo look for foreign support — and still Germany pressed on: according to the diplomatic correspondence, Germany has been anxious to secure the Bay of Limon, in Costa Rica, and the Bay of Samana, in St. Domingo, for the benefit of her people and her navy. In proof of the first, this window prints the United States legation's despatch from San Jose, Costa Rica, of March 8, 1868, transmitting the correspondence on the visit of the Prussian steam sloop-of-war Augusta to the bay of Limon: Captain Kinderling's letter to the Prussian consul residing there, the consul's letter to the Costa Rica government, and that government's reply — the window closes within the despatch's own introduction of the papers.
records.summary_es: Los designios de Alemania sobre las bahías del Caribe no cesaron con el mensaje sobre la doctrina Monroe del presidente Grant, argumenta el reportaje del Herald: el mensaje de diciembre de 1870 había declarado que la adquisición de Santo Domingo era una adhesión a esa doctrina, que el Senado debía aprobar para que el pueblo de Santo Domingo no buscara apoyo extranjero —y aun así Alemania siguió adelante: según la correspondencia diplomática, Alemania ha estado ansiosa por asegurarse la bahía de Limón, en Costa Rica, y la bahía de Samaná, en Santo Domingo, en beneficio de su pueblo y su marina. Como prueba de lo primero, esta ventana publica el despacho de la legación de los Estados Unidos en San José, Costa Rica, del 8 de marzo de 1868, que transmite la correspondencia sobre la visita del vapor de guerra prusiano Augusta a la bahía de Limón: la carta del capitán Kinderling al cónsul prusiano residente allí, la carta del cónsul al gobierno de Costa Rica y la respuesta de ese gobierno —la ventana se cierra dentro de la propia introducción de los documentos por el despacho.

records.headline: The special agent of the Dominican Government at Samana was examined
records.summary_en: The special agent of the Dominican Government at Samana was examined by the Commissioners, a second window of the Herald's feature shows, and they elicited that the man duly accredited as German consul, though a citizen of St. Domingo, had not received his exequatur, the Dominican Government having its own reasons for not receiving him in the capacity of Prussian consul — so that what a German consul had been authorized to do at San Jose toward the acquisition of the bay could not be done in St. Domingo, the Government refusing to recognize him. Germany's second step, the Herald argues, was bolder than the first, taken in the very teeth of the Monroe doctrine against the weakness of an independent government on the American continent. After all this, it asks, does the reported proposed cession of Porto Rico, temporarily or definitively, to Germany look so absurd as Secretary Fish says it does? — and the window closes as it turns to what was proposed, according to the confidential information of the Freeman's Journal.
records.summary_es: El agente especial del Gobierno dominicano en Samaná fue examinado por los comisionados, muestra una segunda ventana del reportaje del Herald, y obtuvieron de él que el hombre debidamente acreditado como cónsul alemán, aunque ciudadano de Santo Domingo, no había recibido su exequátur, teniendo el Gobierno dominicano sus propias razones para no recibirlo en calidad de cónsul prusiano —de modo que lo que un cónsul alemán había sido autorizado a hacer en San José hacia la adquisición de la bahía no podía hacerse en Santo Domingo, negándose el Gobierno a reconocerlo. El segundo paso de Alemania, argumenta el Herald, fue más audaz que el primero, dado en los propios dientes de la doctrina Monroe contra la debilidad de un gobierno independiente en el continente americano. Después de todo esto, pregunta, ¿parece tan absurda la propuesta cesión de Puerto Rico, temporal o definitiva, a Alemania como dice el secretario Fish? —y la ventana se cierra cuando pasa a lo que se propuso, según la información confidencial del Freeman's Journal.

AFFAIRS IN THE WEST INDIES.
NEGOTIATIONS FOR A TREATY OF COMMERCE BETWEEN SANTO DOMINGO AND HAYTI—DISGRACEFUL SCENE DURING A FUNERAL SERVICE.
ST. THOMAS, Sept. 16.—Santo Domingo dates of the 12th instant are at hand. President Gonzalez had just returned from his voyage to the northern provinces. The whole country is perfectly quiet. A Haytien steamer had arrived at Santo Domingo City, and by her the Dominican Commissioners will leave for Port-au-Prince to conclude the treaty of amity and commerce between the two republics.
Gen. Caceres has arrived here and met ex-President Baez of Santo Domingo.
The Haytien Government has imposed heavy taxation upon resident foreigners, including foreign clerks in the employment of Haytiens.
A disturbance recently occurred in the Catholic Cathedral at Jamaica. A priest tore the Cuban flag from the coffin of a patriot, refusing to permit the introduction of politics into the Catholic service. A riot ensued. The priest was assaulted and knocked off the platform on which the coffin rested.

Dominican commissioners were set to leave for Port-au-Prince aboard a Haytien steamer to conclude a treaty of amity and commerce, while the Haytien Government had imposed heavy taxation on resident foreigners and foreign clerks. Additionally, General Caeeres arrived and met with ex-President Baez of San Domingo.

Comisionados dominicanos estaban listos para partir hacia Puerto Príncipe a bordo de un vapor haitiano con el fin de concluir un tratado de amistad y comercio, en momentos en que el Gobierno haitiano había fijado fuertes tributos a los extranjeros residentes y a los dependientes comerciales extranjeros. records.headline: Affairs in Santo Domingo.
records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on April 5, 1875, that a treaty of peace, amity, extradition, and reciprocity between the two republics on the island had been ratified and exchanged, demonstrating an *entente cordiale*. Additionally, the newspaper stated that the Dominican Government was being pressed by about 2,000 citizens—victims of Báez's actions while under the protection of U.S. warships—to present a claim against the United States Government for £3,000,000 in losses and injuries. This prospective claim, drawing its foundation from Senator Sumner's March 27, 1871 speech, argues that Báez was maintained in power by U.S. troops and attempted to dispose of the country and the lease of Samaná.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó el 5 de abril de 1875 que se había ratificado y canjeado un tratado de paz, amistad, extradición y reciprocidad entre las dos repúblicas de la isla, evidenciando una *entente cordiale*. Asimismo, el periódico indicó que el Gobierno dominicano sufría presiones de cerca de 2.000 ciudadanos —víctimas de las acciones de Báez mientras este se hallaba bajo la protección de buques de guerra estadounidenses— para que presentara una reclamación contra el Gobierno de los Estados Unidos por 3.000.000 de dólares en daños y perjuicios. Dicha reclamación proyectada, fundamentada en el discurso pronunciado por el senador Sumner el 27 de marzo de 1871, argumentaba que Báez fue sostenido en el poder por tropas estadounidenses e intentó disponer del país y del arrendamiento de Samaná.

records.full_text:
AFFAIRS IN SANTO DOMINGO.
THE PRESIDENT IN FAVOR OF FREE SPEECH—
AMICAL RELATIONS WITH HAYTI—CLAIMS FOR
INDEMNITY AGAINST THE UNITED STATES.

SANTO DOMINGO, March 22.—The yacht Tarolinta of the New-York Yacht Club arrived here on the 19th inst. from Porto Rico, having on board Mr. Kent, her owner, and a party of friends who have been making a tour of the islands. Yesterday they called on President Gonzales, who returned the visit in the afternoon, accompanied by two of the ministers and other dignitaries. The President in a speech on the yacht said he was determined to try the experiment of free speech, a free press, and as much liberty as existed in the United States, even though he should perish in the attempt. No one had been exiled but Baez and a few of his family, and they were at liberty to return here now if they wished. The Tarolinta left here this morning for Kingston, Jamaica, from which place she will proceed to Havana, and thence home.

President Gonzales, accompanied by three of his ministers, his staff and some friends, returned a few days since from the province of Azua, where he had a conference with President Domingue of Hayti. The meeting was near the boundary line, and, by preconcert, took place on February 27, the anniversary of the separation of the two Republics in 1844, which is another proof of the entente cordiale now existing between the two Governments and people of the island. The treaty of peace, amity, extradition, reciprocity of trade guarantees to each other that neither any part nor the whole of the territory of either shall be alienated, has been ratified and exchanged.

It is stated that this Government is now being hard pressed by about 2,000 of its citizens, victims of Baez’s action, while under the immediate protection of the United States ships of war, to prepare and present a claim on the United States Government for losses and injuries to the Government and people arising therefrom. The foundation of this claim has been taken from the speech of Senator Sumner, of March 27, 1871, on violations of international law and usurpations of war powers. The Government intends, it is said, to present a claim for $5,000,000, but has not yet decided how or by whom they will present it, having no diplomatic representative in Washington. The argument which it is said the Dominican Government will submit in support of this claim recites the facts in connection with Baez’s accession to power, his attempt to dispose of the country, and the lease of Samana; declares that he was maintained in power by the United States troops, and was compelled to fly when they ceased to support him, and that, while occupying the Presidency, protected by United States ships, he plundered the Treasury of a large portion of its revenue, and ill-treated the citizens; alludes to many other facts in regard to the relations between the United States and Santo Domingo which have occupied attention during several years, and asserts that the acts of the United States Government were in violation of international law, and that it is responsible for the losses and injuries occasioned by the protection of Baez.

records.headline: Immediate protection of the United States, during the negotiations for the purchase of the island
records.summary_en: The Dominican Government submitted a claim arguing that the United States Government is responsible for losses and injuries caused by its protection of Baez during his presidency. According to the claim, Baez forced a loan from citizens, plundered the treasury, and ill-treated people while maintained in power by U.S. troops and ships, making the U.S. actions a violation of international law.
records.summary_es: El Gobierno dominicano presentó una reclamación alegando que el Gobierno de los Estados Unidos es responsable de las pérdidas y daños causados por la protección brindada a Báez durante su presidencia. records.summary_en: Based on advices from Santo Domingo City dated March 22, the Dominican government is reportedly being pressed by about two thousand citizens—who claim they were victims of Baez's actions while under the protection of U.S. warships—to present a $3,000,000 claim against the United States government. records.summary_es: Conforme a despachos procedentes de la ciudad de Santo Domingo con fecha 22 de marzo, el gobierno dominicano se encuentra presionado por unos dos mil ciudadanos —quienes aseguran haber sido víctimas de las acciones de Báez mientras gozaba de la protección de buques de guerra estadounidenses— para elevar un reclamo de 3.000.000 de dólares contra el gobierno de los Estados Unidos. El reclamo se sustenta en un discurso del senador Sumner pronunciado el 27 de marzo de 1871 sobre la vulneración del derecho internacional y la usurpación de prerrogativas bélicas, esgrimiendo que tropas estadounidenses sostuvieron a Báez en el poder y responsabilizaron a los EE. records.headline: A Washington dispatch reports fresh disclosures from a British parliamentary inquiry into foreign loans placed in London
records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch reports fresh disclosures from a British parliamentary inquiry into foreign loans placed in London, centered on the Dominican loan floated by Hartmont and Company in the fall of 1869. It says Hartmont was connected with Fabens and Cazneau and their concessions from the Baez government, including railroad rights, large estates near Samana Bay and commercial privileges there, and that annexation of San Domingo to the United States was necessary to make those concessions immensely valuable, with money spent in New York and Washington to promote President Grant's scheme.

records.headline: Of this the Government of San Domingo received only $230,000
records.summary_en: According to the *Clarksville Weekly Chronicle*, a British House of Commons committee investigated the negotiation of foreign loans in England, hearing testimony from Mr. Edward Hertzberg Hartmont regarding a Dominican loan nominally valued at $3,788,500. Hartmont testified that he received only $1,800,415 in cash—of which the San Domingo government received merely $230,000—with the remainder spent on arms in Berlin and disbursed in Washington, where Hartmont was sent to work for annexation. The newspaper questions whether the unaccounted-for funds were paid to General Grant's military favorites, such as Babcock, who became suddenly prosperous and invested in real estate, and suggests that the next Congress should investigate the matter.

Hartmont declaró haber recibido únicamente 1.800.415 dólares en efectivo —de los cuales el gobierno de Santo Domingo recibió tan solo 230.000 dólares—, destinándose el resto a la compra de armas en Berlín y a desembolsos en Washington, a donde Hartmont fue enviado para gestionar la anexión. El diario cuestiona si los fondos no rendidos fueron pagados a los militares predilectos del general Grant, tales como Babcock, quien se enriqueció repentinamente e invirtió en bienes raíces, y sugiere que el próximo Congreso debería investigar el asunto.

records.full_text:
SAN DOMINGO.
The Facts About the Annexation Job Coming to Light—Disgraceful Revelations Before a House of Commons Committee.
New York Sun.
The boldest and by odds the most infamous scheme of pillage organized under the first administration of Grant was that for the annexation of San Domingo. It was in its very inception lawless and cruel and base beyond any-thing in the history of the Western world, since Cortez and Pizarro. Baez had usurped the Presidency of San Domingo without a decent pretext of an election; and finding that his barbarous murders, confiscations and treasons would be borne no longer, he deliberately determined to sell the country and divide the price with his accomplices. These were the camp followers and personal intimates of the two Presidents, Grant and Baez.
Grant's dependents, Babcock, Porter, Ingalls, and the rest, were to have spoils so rich and tempting that Grant actually stipulated in terms to lobby the scheme through Congress. But Baez in the meantime was in evil ease. He frankly declared that he had no popular strength in the country he had proposed to sell, and that he could not hold out long enough to consummate the sale without extraordinary aid of money, and a fleet from the United States. Thereupon Grant ran his hand into the Treasury and seized certain unappropriated moneys for the use of Baez, and sent them down by Babcock, with a fleet large enough to keep this savage wretch in power until the temper of the American Congress could be tried.
We recur to this shameful history now only to ask how much of the proceeds of the British loan which Baez about that time put upon the London market was used at Washington? The House of Commons has appointed a committee to ascertain and report the methods by which foreign loans are negotiated in England. One of the witnesses on the 15th of April last was Mr. Edward Hertzberg Hartmont, who negotiated in 1869 a Dominican loan for the nominal amount of $3,788,500. He confessed that he received in cash only $1,860,445. Of this the Government of San Domingo received only $250,000, and the remainder was expended in England and the United States.
Hartmont was sent to Washington to work for annexation, where he testifies a large amount of the money was expended. Who got it? For his loan of $3,788,500, Harmont received in cash $1,860,445. The difference between $1,860,445 and $250,000 is rather startling. “A part” of it, Mr. Hartmont swears, was sent to “Berlin for arms;” but the rest was disbursed in Washington.
It was a great sum. To whom was it paid? About that time several of Gen. Grant's military favorites became suddenly prosperous, and invested their money in the real estate pool which throve so fabulously under the two bosses, Shepard and Grant. One of these was Babcock. Is it possible that Hartmont could have paid him any part of this vast sum yet unaccounted for? If not, to whom? The next Congress might profitably follow the example of the House of Commons and inquire.

records.full_text:
General Brutus Brice was a man of great repute and intelligence. He was a son of a distinguished general under the Emperor Soulouque, bearing the same name. The subject of this sketch was born at Miragoane, in Hayti. At an usually early age he graduated as bachelor of arts in the National College of Port-au-Prince. Shortly afterward he became one of President Geffrard's private secretaries. In the year 1860 he became one of President Salnave's aids-de-camp with the honorary rank of lieutenant colonel. Shortly afterward he was elected deputy to the Legislature, representing Port-au-Prince, and became one of the most prominent leaders of the opposition against Salnave. In 1868 he commanded the revolutionary forces at Jeremie, and withstood a siege of a year's duration, the town being bombarded by the Haytian fleet. After the revolutionary forces became victorious he was elected to the position of commandant-in-chief, and with that grade effected a landing at Port-au-Prince at the head of the troops and captured the capital city of Port-au-Prince in December, 1869. In consideration of his brilliant services he was elected Speaker of the Legislature. The next position he held was that of envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary to the courts of the Tuileries and St. James in the years 1871 and 1872.
In the year 1873, after his return to Hayti, he was sent on a special mission to the court of Berlin with reference to the outrage committed by Commandant Basch, who had threatened to bombard Port-au-Prince with the Prussian corvettes Augusta and Gazelle, and in addition to this had seized two Haytian gunboats, for the reason that Hayti had not paid her debts to some German citizens of Hayti. His mission to Berlin on this subject was a successful one, and Commandant Basch was censured for hasty and unwarrantable conduct. Shortly after his return he was again elected deputy for Port-au-Prince. About this time he obtained a concession from the government for the construction of a railroad from Port-au-Prince to the Dominican frontier. He also erected a large manufactory in the neighborhood of the capital for the extract of dyes from logwood, to compete with the three great similar establishments in the United States. Since the advent of President Domingue to power, the General retired to private life, and has been known as an avowed enemy of Domingue, although he took an active part in the election and held a prominent position in the army.
SKETCH OF GENERAL PIERRE.
General Montplaisir Pierre, of the Republic of Hayti, who committed suicide on May 3, at Port-au-Prince, in Hayti, after being captured in a revolutionary uprising on that date by the government troops, was a native of Anse-a-Veaux, in the south side of Hayti. He was formerly minister of war under President Nessage Saget, and was an old soldier. Upon the occasion of the recent presidential election in Hayti he ran against President Domingue, the present chief magistrate, and was largely defeated. He has been Speaker of the Assembly and was a man of literary tastes and had traveled considerably in this country and Europe. During the presidential terms of Salnave and Geffrard he held important offices.—New York Herald.

records.headline: Leniency to the rebels, but to secure peace and submission
records.summary_en: A traveler arriving from Port-au-Platte on August 24 reported that recent telegrams from Havana concerning a revolution in Santo Domingo were entirely false. According to the source, the rumor was fabricated and circulated by a banished individual named Barrera upon his arrival in Porto Rico. Furthermore, the traveler stated that no general disaffection existed and the government was fully capable of handling any conspirators.
records.summary_es: Un viajero arribado desde Puerto Plata el 24 de agosto informó que los recientes telegramas enviados desde La Habana respecto a una revolución en Santo Domingo carecían enteramente de veracidad. Según la fuente, el rumor fue fraguado y puesto a circular por un individuo desterrado de apellido Barrera tras su llegada a Puerto Rico. Asimismo, el testigo manifestó que no existía descontento generalizado y que el gobierno gozaba de plena capacidad para contener a cualquier conspirador.
records.passage: leniency to the rebels, but to secure peace and submission to the Government at all hazards. A gentleman who arrived in this city yesterday from Port-au-Platte, which he left on Aug. 24, said that if there had been any such revolution as was stated by the telegrams from Havana he would have heard of it before he left. According to advices received by the Dominican Consul and statements from Capt. records.headline: The National Republican charges Spain with complicity in a revolutionary programme
records.summary_en: The National Republican charges Spain with complicity in a revolutionary programme for the restoration of Baez: the Spaniards, its editorial says, have not forgiven San Domingo the severe handling they got from the brave Dominicans and their expulsion from the island, while Baez was a man after their own heart, a bloodthirsty and lawless tyrant, and they tolerated him; the present President, Gonzales, a man of more liberal views who tolerates the residence of pacific Cuban exiles in the republic, has stirred their ire, and they are underhandedly endeavoring to displace him. As proof it prints a private letter from Puerto Plata of August 23, 1875: the country is under the pressure of a revolutionary movement whose consequences cannot yet be predicted, and the Spaniards are playing into the hands of the party opposed to the constituted Government, in favor of Baez; the most prominent Spaniard of the city, Senor Barreras, one of its leading merchants, was ordered the day before to leave the country within two hours, after a package of correspondence addressed to him by General Sanz, Captain-General of Porto Rico, had been seized, disclosing the plot and the services already rendered to the conspiracy; Barreras, the letter says, cowed and confessed, and fell on his knees at the feet of the Governor: the window closes within the letter.

records.summary_en: A professed agent of the Government of Santo Domingo made overtures to the President regarding the annexation of the island to the United States, though the President initially suspected the agents might be adventurers. records.full_text:
THE SANTO DOMINGO QUESTION.
After a lapse of six years since the President submitted to the Senate a treaty for the annexation of Santo Domingo to the United States, we venture to refer again to the subject for the purpose of reaching other matters. In justification of the President, however, it might be stated that the question of acquiring insular possession never occurred to him until the matter was forced upon him by circumstances. Soon after his first inauguration he was waited upon by a professed agent of the Government of Santo Domingo, who explained very vividly the topography, climate, products, &c., of that part of the island under the Dominican Government, the number and character of its population, the desire of the people and authorities to become a part of the United States, and that he was authorized and directed to make overtures to our Government for the purpose of bringing about annexation. The President listened to all that was said without venturing a remark that could in any way be interpreted as an indication favorable to the proposition. In fact, his whole judgment at the time was against the proposition. But later a second agent appeared, making substantially the same statements as the first, and was listened to and treated in a like manner. The President seemed to feel no assurance that these parties were not adventurers, anxious to make something for themselves out of the transfer. In view, however, of the close proximity of the island to our shores and of the oft-repeated Monroe doctrine on our part, he believed it his duty to ascertain the real feelings of the people and Government of Santo Domingo in relation to the question of annexation. For this purpose he dispatched a confidential agent who visited nearly every portion of the island, held free intercourse with both officials and non-officials, and found that it was the enthusiastic desire of all to become a part of “the Great Republic.” Under these circumstances a treaty was entered into and submitted to the Senate for ratification. Furthermore, the President believed that annexing Santo Domingo would have honorably resolved the ongoing Cuban revolution and its associated issues regarding slavery, U.S. commercial interests, and international obligations.

Sostenía además el presidente que la anexión de Santo Domingo habría zanjado con honor la contienda revolucionaria cubana y sus repercusiones respecto a la esclavitud, los intereses comerciales estadounidenses y las obligaciones internacionales.
