records.full_text:
The Revolution in San Domingo.

A correspondent of the New York Sun, writing from Puerto Platte under date of February 23, says:

As most of your readers are probably aware, the real cause which precipitated the fall of President Baez was that after the Fabens-Babcock treaty for the annexation of this republic to the United States had been killed in the United States Senate, Baez received money from Spain to enter into a treaty for the deportation to Cuba of refugees from the latter island.

When the revolution which drove Baez into exile had been consummated, Gonzales, who had hitherto been the champion of the Cubans and anti-annexationists, was raised to the Presidency. His promise to protect the integrity of Dominican territory, and carry out the constitution in every detail, were very ample and satisfactory.

The last Spanish occupation of this republic has unfortunately left here an element most pernicious to all republican governments. Under the sway of this element President Gonzales fell. The political action of this element originated in the animosity evinced by Spanish residents of the capital against the publication in this city of two papers which warmly and logically advocated the cause of the independence of Cuba, and it may be said to have culminated in the consent of Gonzales to issue a decree for their suspension. Subsequently money was sent to Gonzales from Havana, and he was induced to sign a treaty with Spain which bound San Domingo to return to Cuba all refugees against whom Spain might trump up a charge of incendiarism. The treaty was cleverly worded, because it carefully avoided comprising in its stipulations the rendition of political prisoners. But of course it virtually included every Cuban exile, for Spain could easily accuse any of them of complicity, at least, with incendiaries.

As soon as it was known here that the treaty had really been signed, the Cuban population not unreasonably felt alarmed. The Governor of this city increased this alarm by issuing a decree that if more than three Cuban exiles embarked for foreign ports on board any one vessel, they should be seized and delivered over to Spanish war vessels as intending to form part of a filibustering expedition against the peace of Spain.

The Cubans held sundry meetings on the subject, and a final one was to have been held on Sunday, the twenty-third ultimo, when a radical change occurred, the details of which I will condense from my note book.

At 4:30 P. M., January 23, shots were heard in the little plaza in front of the Protestant church, in the neighborhood of the government house, and at the residence of General Luperon. The latter, who was in his house with two friends, returned the fire. The whole city was excited. The common council assembled, sent for the foreign consuls, and forwarded propositions to Governor Ortea and General Luperon, which were declined. Ortea insists on capturing Luperon dead or live, Luperon resists, and all hope of a peaceful solution seem at an end. Everybody expected a fearful night of fire and blood, but luckily it passed in alarms only. The laborantes avail of the opportunity to spread thousands of rumors against Ortea and President Gonzales.

Monday, twenty-fourth.—The Governor accedes to the protest of the common council and consuls, and offers guarantees to General Luperon until the receipt of fresh orders from the government. Outside the city several cantons assemble opposed to the government; committees are sent out by the common council to confer with the cantons, but the latter refused to yield; reports are circulated that everything will be settled without having recourse to arms. But the laborantes work hard; they manage to induce the troops to desert, and fraternization between the soldiers and the Cubans in the shape of drinks and handshaking is the order of the day. A lieutenant whom I met in the bodeja of Concha Rey said to me, "Look out to-night, at twelve we meet at the end of the Plaza del Mercado to attack the commandancia where Ortea is shut up." They are more than on time; firing commenced at eleven o'clock. One man was killed, and they disperse. Many families leave the city; men go out into the country, and the Cuban families seek and find refuge in the English, American and German consulates. None go the French consulate, for the consul is supposed to be in league with the Spaniards.

Tuesday, twenty-fifth—Three guns are discharged from the fort as a signal of alarm, but nobody comes in from the country. A proclamation is read at the street corners calling on the citizens to arms, and declaring every one an enemy who does not repair to the government house. All stores and private houses are closed, and the city wears a mournful aspect. One meets nobody but groups of Cubans in the streets.

Wednesday, twenty-sixth—The city is declared in a state of siege, and citizens are prohibited from carrying arms. More excitement.

Thursday, twenty-seventh—Groups of more than three people are prohibited from assembling in the streets.

Friday, twenty-eight—A committee arrives from Santiago de los Caballeros with a protest against the abuses of Ortea. An impeaching board had been appointed in Santiago, and the people of this place give in their adhesion to the accusation there made before the Legislature against President Gonzalez.

Saturday, twenty-nine—A committee goes to Santiago, composed of the President of the Common Council and other prominent citizens. To-day two barricades are completed at the fort.

Thirtieth—Nothing but alarms.

Monday, thirty-first—A bando (proclamation by town crier) is issued, declaring that Governor Ortea did not attempt to escape last night by flight. It states that he relies on 800 armed men and on public opinion. This announcement is made as usual, accompanied by music, and is read out aloud at the corner of every two or three blocks. The reason whereof is that the majority of the people here can not read.

Tuesday, February 1.—At 5 A. M. crowds began to assemble in the streets shouting, "Hurrah for the constitution!" Down with the treaty!" and not a few added "Death to Spain!" Luperon rides through the streets on horseback with a considerable following mounted and on foot. He takes the Comandancia and the house of the municipality. At 7 A. M. the common council assembles a committee from this body, to which are added Messrs. Francisco Colis and Pedro Recio, both Cubans, and Ponce de Leon, of Porto Rico, is appointed and sent to Ortea, demanding his surrender and the capitulation of the fort, with guarantee of life to everybody. The people indorsed the impeachment of Gonzales, as demanded by the citizens of Santiago.

At 8:30 the whole population was gathered in front of the government house, the protest from Santiago was read, and it was unanimously indorsed. General Luperon addresses the crowd, and sketches the abuses of the administration of Gonzales and of subalterns, Ortea in particular. He adds that he is in possession of letters from several generals, who assure him that the entire province of Cibao has "pronounced."

Ortea requests that in his surrender the consular body should accompany the committee which waited on him. This request is granted, he surrenders, and at 12 M., in company with General Luperon, takes refuge in the British consulate. At 10 A. M. General Arceno enters the city at the head of fifty men. At eleven, General Lithgow and others, who some days previously had been imprisoned by Ortea, are set at liberty.

At 4 P. M. a proclamation is issued announcing that Senor Segundo Ymben had been appointed Governor and General Lithgow commander of the city. Until Senor Ymben's return he is represented by General Telesforo Pelegrin. The families who had taken refuge in the consulates return to their homes. A loose sheet detailing the occurrences is published. It is stated that President Gonzales is in the vicinity of Santiago, and refuses to submit to trial. Santiago is the centre of the movement. End of my note book.

Since then there has been nothing important in this city except the sending of soldiers into the country. President Gonzales collected some cantons, who helped him to resist, and a few people were killed. On the seventeenth he surrendered to a committee from the capital, and he has repaired thither. The Baezistas meanwhile have not been idle, and have managed to raise a few cantons in one or two places. It seems now as if everything might pass off without the horrors of a civil war, although these people belong to the last person who may harangue them.

The English steamer arrived to-day from the capital, and brought the news that Gonzales, impeached as he was, has resigned. I am inclined to think that this was the best way to settle matters.

records.full_text:
THE DOMINICAN PRESIDENCY.
The election in St. Domingo for President to succeed Gonzalez, resigned, will be held on March 24. Señor Espaillott and General Luperon are prominent candidates. Ex-President Gonzalez has arrived at Port au Prince and been well received by the people.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that the American Government issued an ultimatum to the Haytian Government demanding the return of any exactions made upon American subjects, backed by a threat of war if the treaty's execution is opposed. In the Dominican Republic, Mr. Espaillat was successfully elected to the presidency by an overwhelming majority, a reported rising in Azua proved to be a minor riot, and the nation remains in perfect tranquility while organizing the new government.

records.summary_en: According to the newspaper report, the Dominican government ordered the arrest of a general aboard the steamship *Tyhee* on the grounds of attempting to foment a revolution from the Haytian frontier, but American Consul Paul Jones decided the general was entitled to remain on board under the protection of the American flag. Despite the Consul's protests and Captain Kuhl's preparations to defend the vessel—which included displaying American flags—Dominican authorities brought a field piece to the wharf and sent fifty armed soldiers who tore away the flags and boarded the ship.

records.summary_en: On June 28, a ship arrived at Cap Haitien and took on board Pablo Villanueva, the former Minister of War and Marine under Dominican President Rousales, who carried a Dominican passport bound for St. Domingo City. Upon arriving at the capital, officials recognized Villanueva, but he was subsequently warned that he would be arrested if he came ashore, prompting him to seek the assistance of American Consul Mr. Paul Jones to explain his non-political intentions of visiting his family and collecting money. The following day, the first notification of hostilities by the Dominicans occurred when a cannon was brought down to the wharf.
records.summary_es: El 28 de junio, un buque arribó a Cap-Haïtien y recibió a bordo a Pablo Villanueva, antiguo ministro de Guerra y Marina del presidente dominicano González, quien portaba un pasaporte dominicano con destino a la ciudad de Santo Domingo. Al recalar en la capital, los funcionarios identificaron a Villanueva, a quien seguidamente se advirtió de que sería apresado si saltaba a tierra, lo que le llevó a impetrar el auxilio del cónsul estadounidense, Sr. Paul Jones, a fin de explicar sus propósitos estrictamente pacíficos de ver a su familia y cobrar un dinero. Al día siguiente se produjo la primera muestra de hostilidad por parte de los dominicanos al emplazar un cañón en el muelle.

records.headline: The Dominican Insult to the American people in boarding the steamship
records.summary_en: *The New York Herald* reported that the Dominican Republic committed an insult to the American people by boarding the steamship *Tybee* and forcibly removing a passenger. The newspaper asserted that this action by the "half-clothed barbarians of St. Domingo" ought to be speedily and sternly punished to teach them that they cannot bring their petty political warfare onto the deck of an American ship.
records.summary_es: A tenor del extracto de prensa facilitado, *The New York Herald* denunció que la República Dominicana perpetró un ultraje contra el pueblo estadounidense al abordar el vapor *Tybee* y retirar por la fuerza a un pasajero. El periódico sostuvo que esta conducta de los «bárbaros semidesnudos de Santo Domingo» debía ser reprimida con rapidez y severidad para escarmentarles de que no podían trasladar sus mezquinas rencillas políticas a la cubierta de un buque estadounidense.

records.summary_en: The American steamship *Tybee*, commanded by C. J. F. Kuhl, arrived in San Domingo on June 7th with passenger Gen. Pablo Villanueva, a former Minister of War under Báez and González who sought to retire on his estates. Although the local government demanded his surrender, Capt. Kuhl refused and claimed the protection of the American flag, while the U.S. Consul protested the forcible removal during an interview at the consulate. Ultimately, soldiers boarded the vessel, tied Villanueva to a chair with ropes, and handed him over the ship's side while Capt. Kuhl spread the Stars and Stripes on the deck, leading to current reports that a U.S. man-of-war has been sent to exact reparation.

records.full_text:
AN INSULT TO BE RESENTED
WHERE THE UNITED STATES WILL DEMAND REPARATION.
Our Flag Dishonored by a Power that Probably has not yet Employed the Son-in-Law of the Secretary of State as Counsel.
SAN DOMINGO, June 29.—The Stars and Stripes have been insulted by the Government of this country in the roadstead of this capital. The Baezist General, Villanueva, has, since the election of Espallart to the Presidency of this republic, been endeavoring, on the Haytian frontier, in the neighborhood of Cape Hayti, to foment a revolution against the existing Government of this republic, and several skirmishes have occurred on the border line in the northwestern part of the territory, resulting in the killing of fifty or sixty Dominicans. For a purpose which has not hitherto transpired—Gen. Villanueva says, for the purpose of settling some private business affairs in this capital—he took passage in the steamer Tybee from this place. He touched at Puerto Plata and Samana, but did not land. On his arrival here, the Government, knowing of his presence on board, demanded his surrender.
Capt. Kuhl declined to deliver the General, and claimed the protection of his flag. An interview followed in the United States Consulate between the Consul and the emissaries of this Government, and the Consul protested against the forcible removal of Gen. Vellanueva from the deck of the Tybee. At length a file of soldiers was sent on board, and as Villianueva refused to move from the chair on which he was sitting on the quarter deck, he was tied to it with ropes and handed over the ship's side. Capt. Kuhl spread the Stars and Stripes on the deck so that the men who were carrying Gen. Vellanueva had to step over the flag.
It is currently reported that a United States man-of-war has been sent for to exact reparation.

records.summary_en: The steamer Tybee lost her passenger Villanueva, the ex-Minister of War, to soldiers at San Domingo, the National Republican reports: the Tybee arrived at San Domingo in the latter part of June from Cape Haytien, where Villanueva, who had been minister of war under Gonzales, took passage under a properly vised passport; at San Domingo a party of soldiers, under orders of the military governor, planted cannon on the wharf within sixty feet of the steamer, went on board notwithstanding that the United States consul had placed the American flag across the gangway and in the name of the United States protested against the outrage, and forcibly took Villanueva away. He was probably shot, the despatch adds. Consul Jones sent the details of the outrage to Secretary Fish, which probably reached him the day the paper went to press; at the State Department there were as yet no advices of its own.

records.headline: Detail of the occurrence furnished by several of the crew of the steamship Tybee
records.summary_en: According to the *Morning Herald* of July 10, 1876, crew members of the steamship *Tybee* reported that Pablo Villanueva, ex-Minister of War and Marine under Dominican President Gonzales, boarded the vessel at Cape Haytien with a valid Dominican passport and arrived at St. Domingo City. Upon arrival, Villanueva was warned that the newly elected President would order his arrest if he came ashore, prompting Villanueva to summon American Consul Mr. Paul Jones to state that his only intentions were to reunite with his family, collect a debt of $5,000, and depart for New York without causing political strife. Following this conversation, Consul Jones went ashore.
records.summary_es: Según el *Morning Herald* del 10 de julio de 1876, tripulantes del vapor *Tybee* informaron que Pablo Villanueva, exministro de Guerra y Marina del presidente dominicano González, embarcó en Cap-Haïtien con pasaporte dominicano en regla y llegó a la ciudad de Santo Domingo. A su arribo, se advirtió a Villanueva que el recién electo presidente ordenaría su detención si bajaba a tierra, lo que indujo a Villanueva a llamar al cónsul estadounidense, Sr. Paul Jones, para manifestarle que su único propósito era reunirse con su familia, cobrar una acreencia de 5.000 dólares y viajar a Nueva York sin provocar disturbios políticos. Concluida la conversación, el cónsul Jones marchó a tierra.

records.full_text:
OUR FLAG INSULTED
The Steamship Tybee Boarded by Dominican Troops—Forcible Removal of One of Her Passengers.
An insult to the American flag that calls for prompt redress was recently committed in St. Domingo. The following are the details of the occurrence furnished by several of the crew of the steamship Tybee, now lying at the foot of Congress street, Brooklyn, in the absence of Captain Kuehl:—
On the 20th of June we arrived at Cape Haytien, in Hayti, where we took on board a passenger named Pablo Villanueva, ex-Minister of War and Marine under President Gonzales of the Republic of St. Domingo. He was provided with a Dominican passport, duly visited by the Haytien authorities, and was bound for St. Domingo City, the capital of St. Domingo. In due course we arrived there and came to anchor in the port, where we were boarded by the Captain of the Port and other officials, several of whom spoke and recognized Villanueva. A few hours afterwards word was sent to Villanueva from the recently elected President of the Republic that if he should come ashore he would be arrested. Villanueva, feeling safe under the protection, sent for the American Consul, Mr. Paul Jones, and told him in English, which he speaks very fluently, that he came to St. Domingo City to see his wife and child, as all the letters he wrote to them had been intercepted, and that he intended to take them away to New York, where he was going to reside for the future. He also said he came to claim some $5,000 due to him from different people, and, in conclusion, that he had no desire to cause any new political strife, his errand being simply as above stated.—After learning this the Consul left the Tybee and was rowed ashore.

records.headline: Incensed resident Americans and the consul's protest close the Morning Herald's Tybee report
records.summary_en: Incensed resident Americans and the consul's protest close the Morning Herald's Tybee report in this window: the Americans are terribly incensed over the matter, and hope that Secretary Fish will show some national feeling in it. It may be mentioned, the paper adds, that a British man-of-war caused the Dominicans at Puerto Plata, in St. Domingo, some time back to salute the British flag and pay an indemnity for having taken a Dominican by main force out of the British consulate at that place. Under the head 'The Consul's Protest,' it reports that Captain G. W. Brown has received information that Consul Paul Jones, of St. Domingo City, has sent a protest to Secretary Hamilton Fish by the Tybee, in charge of Purser Van Duzen, which will doubtless reach Washington this morning.
records.summary_es: Los estadounidenses residentes indignados y la protesta del cónsul cierran el informe del Morning Herald sobre el Tybee en esta ventana: los estadounidenses están terriblemente indignados por el asunto, y esperan que el secretario Fish muestre algo de sentimiento nacional en él. Puede mencionarse, añade el periódico, que un buque de guerra británico obligó hace algún tiempo a los dominicanos en Puerto Plata, en Santo Domingo, a saludar la bandera británica y pagar una indemnización por haber sacado a un dominicano por la fuerza del consulado británico de ese lugar. Bajo el título 'The Consul's Protest', informa que el capitán G. W. Brown ha recibido información de que el cónsul Paul Jones, de la ciudad de Santo Domingo, ha enviado una protesta al secretario Hamilton Fish por el Tybee, a cargo del sobrecargo Van Duzen, que sin duda llegará a Washington esta mañana.

Our Flag Insulted.
THE STEAMSHIP TYBEE BOARDED BY DOMINICAN TROOPS—FORCIBLE REMOVAL OF ONE OF HER PASSENGERS—CONSUL JONES’S PROTEST.
NEW YORK, July 8.—On the 20th of June the steamer Tybee arrived at Cape Haytien, in Hayti, where we took on board a passenger named Pablo Villanueva, ex-Minister of War and Marine under President Gonzales, of the Republic of St. Domingo. He was provided with a Dominican passport, duly viséd by the Haytien authorities, and was bound for St. Domingo city, the capital of St. Domingo. In due course we arrived there and came to anchor in the port, where we were boarded by the Captain of the Port and other officials, several of whom spoke and recognized Villanueva. A few hours afterward word was sent to Villanueva from the recently-elected President of the republic that if he should come ashore he would be arrested. Villanueva, feeling safe under the protection, sent for the American consul, Mr. Paul Jones, and told him in English, which he speaks very fluently, that he came to St. Domingo City to see his wife and child, as all the letters he wrote to them had been intercepted, and that he intended to take them away to New York, where he was going to reside for the future. He also said he came to claim some $5,000 due to him from different people, and, in conclusion, that he had no desire to cause any new political strifes, his errand being simply as above stated. After learning this the consul left the Tybee and was rowed ashore.

From official advices received at the State Department to-day in relation to the reported insult to the American flag at San Domingo, it appears that ex-Minister of War Villenueva, formerly of Dominica, a fugitive from justice, took refuge on board the steamer Tybee, lying at San Domingo. The authorities there demanded his surrender, but the Captain of the Tybee refused to comply with the demand. When they went aboard and took him off no insult was offered to the American flag, the United States Consul or the Captain of the Tybee, and there was no violation of the international law or treaty stipulation. The Tybee carries Dominican mails under a subsidy from the Dominican government.
The President has signed the bill extending for ten days from to-day the late provision act.

records.full_text:
A DOUBLE-HEADED INSURRECTION IN SAN DOMINGO
HAVANA, August 12.—Advices from San Domingo of July 18th report that an insurrection has broken out in the Ciboa provinces, formerly the northern part of the Dominican republic. The insurgents may be said to be divided into two parties. Those east of Puerto Plata are fighting on account of their envy of or dislike for Cubans, who have emigrated in large numbers to that quarter of the island. This feeling of hostility has been intensified by the murder of a native, recently committed in Puerto Plata, by one of the Cuban emigrants. The other party appears to seek revolution for its own sake, calling now for the restoration of Baez and now for Gonzales, without knowing who they prefer or what they want.
President Espaillat has promptly taken vigorous measures to quell the insurrection. The whole republic has been declared in a state of siege, and troops have been dispatched from the capital to the scene of insurrection. At last accounts Puerto Plata was surrounded by insurgents, who had made several ineffectual attempts to enter the town.
The steamer Tybee had touched at Puerto Plata from New York, but was unable to land her cargo on account of fighting there, and left for San Domingo city.

SANTO DOMINGO.
Signs of Progress—Wonderful Resources of the Island.
The following is from the London Times: Holders of the Santo Domingo loan, who remember that Colonel Mendes, the diplomatic representative of Santo Domingo, expressed before the Foreign Loans Committee the willingness of his government to refund to those entitled the sum of £38,000, which the government had received out of the total proceeds of the loan, will read with interest Major Stuart’s hopeful report upon the resources of the Dominican Government. The report appears among the commercial papers recently issued by the Foreign Office. Major Stuart is Minister Resident at Hayti and Charge d’Affaires to the Dominican Republic. The imports in 1875 were £171,159 in value, the exports £97,936 at the port of Santo Domingo alone. The direct imports from Great Britain amounted to only £3,581, but British manufactures (cotton, hardware, crockery) to the value of £72,000 were imported through St. Thomas and Curacoa. This country is thus the leading state in the trade, the United States coming next with £48,000, while France, the next European state to ourselves, in this branch of commerce only sends goods to the value of £13,731. The principal exports are timber and sugar, and although the timber trade has declined, the result has been to direct labor to more profitable employment. records.headline: Dwelt especially upon the expenditure, by General Babcock, on San Domingo
records.summary_en: According to the newspaper, General Babcock expended a large sum from the Secret Service Fund regarding San Domingo, leading to a misunderstanding between President Grant and Senator Sumner, where the President intended to discuss the treaty for the acquisition of the Dominican Republic while Sumner believed they were discussing the expenditure. Sumner assured the President he was a Republican supporter and intended to examine the papers to sustain the expenditure, while Major Poore's statement purportedly resolves historical doubts regarding the cause of the difficulty between Grant and Sumner.

Sumner aseguró al presidente su lealtad republicana y su disposición a revisar los documentos para respaldar el desembolso, mientras que las declaraciones del mayor Poore esclarecen supuestamente las dudas históricas sobre el origen de las desavenencias entre Grant y Sumner.

Poore adds the opinion that Sumner thought the President had come to enlist his services in defending this expenditure by General Babcock, but the President meant the treaty for the acquisition of the Dominican Republic. records.full_text:
SUMNER AND GRANT.
Maj. Poore's Story of their Disagreement.
Washington, Oct. 26.—Maj. Ben. Perley Poore, who was Senator Sumner’s guest at the time of his estrangement from President Grant, has explained the cause of the trouble. He says the removal of Jas. M. Ashley, ex-Congressman from Ohio, from the governorship of Montana, and the appointment of Col. Potts, which had just happened, was the subject of a table conversation, and a letter from Ashley protesting against the change had been read, when the President was announced. He was received and shown Ashley’s letter, and became immediately excited, denouncing Ashley as a worthless mischief-maker. The next topic discussed was the San Domingo treaty. Sumner dwelt especially upon the expenditure by Gen. Babcock on San Domingo of a large sum taken from a secret service fund, for promoting intercourse with the West India Islands, which Seward had prevailed on Thad. Stevens to have inserted in an appropriation bill during the war, and the President impressed Sumner with the idea that he feared an attack in Congress for that expenditure. Poore adds his opinion that Sumner thought that the President had come to enlist his services in defending this expenditure by Gen. Babcock, but the President meant the treaty for the acquisition of the Dominican Republic. The President and the Senator misunderstood each other. After a while the President promised to send Gen. Babcock to call on the Senator the next day with copies of the papers, and left. As Sumner escorted him to the door, he told him that he was a Republican, and a supporter of the Republican administration, and that he should sustain the administration in this case if he possibly could, after he had examined the papers. He meant to sustain the expenditure of $100,000 in cash and $50,000 in a light battery and muskets purchased at New York, but the President meant the treaty.
Maj. Poore's statement thus removes a grave historical doubt, and seems to set at rest the stories recently published of the cause of the difficulty between Grant and Sumner.

CAUSE OF THE TROUBLE BETWEEN GRANT AND SUMNER.

CHICAGO, October 26.—A Tribune Washington special says: Major Ben. Perley Poore, who was Senator Sumner’s guest at the time of his estrangement from President Grant, has explained the cause of the trouble. He says the removal of James M. Ashley, ex-congressman from Ohio, from the governorship of Montana, and the appointment of Colonel Potts, which had just happened, was the subject of table conversation, and a letter from Ashley, protesting against the change, had been read when the President was announced. He was received, shown Ashley’s letter and became immediately excited, denouncing Ashley as a mischief-maker. The next topic discussed was the San Domingo treaty. Sumner dwelt especially upon the expenditure by General Babcock on San Domingo, of the large sum taken from the secret service fund for promoting intercourse with the West India islands, which Seward had prevailed on Thad. Stevens to have inserted in the appropriation bill during the war, and the President impressed Sumner with the idea that he feared an attack in congress for that expenditure. Poore adds: “My opinion is that Sumner thought that the President had come to enlist his services in defending this expenditure by General Babcock, but the President meant the treaty for the acquisition of the Dominican republic. The President and the senator misunderstood each other. After a while the President promised to send General Babcock to call on the senator next day with copies of the paper and left. As Sumner escorted him to the door he told him that he was a Republican, a supporter of the Republican administration, and that he should sustain the administration in this case, if he possibly could, after he had examined the papers. He meant to sustain the expenditure of $100,000 in cash ($50,000 in a light battery and muskets purchased at New York), but the President meant the treaty.” Major Poore’s statement thus removes a grave historical doubt, and seems to set at rest the stories recently published of the cause of the difficulty between Grant and Sumner.

records.summary_en: Following remarks by Wendell Phillips regarding General Grant's statements on the St. Domingo treaty, a *New York Herald* representative interviewed ex-Secretary of State Fish in Boston. Fish stated that Senate records show multiple drafts of treaties remained in the hands of the Foreign Affairs Committee under Senator Sumner for months—and in some cases over two years—whereas the entire batch was disposed of within four months after Sumner's retirement.
records.summary_es: A raíz de las manifestaciones de Wendell Phillips sobre las declaraciones del general Grant acerca del tratado de Santo Domingo, un reportero de *The New York Herald* entrevistó en Boston al exsecretario de Estado Fish. The Grant-Sumner Row.
WASHINGTON, October 26.—Major Ben Perley Poore, who was Senator Sumner’s guest at the time of his estrangement from President Grant, has explained the causes the trouble. He says the removal of Jas. M. Ashley, ex-Congressman from Ohio, from the Governorship of Montana, and the appointment of Colonel Potts, which had just happened, was the subject of table conversation, and a letter from Ashley protesting against the change had been read, when the President was announced. He was shown Ashley’s letter, and became immediately excited, denouncing Ashley as a worthless mischief maker. The next topic of conversation was the San Domingo treaty. Sumner dwelt especially upon the expenditure by Gen. Babcock in San Domingo of a large sum taken from a secret service fund for promoting intercourse with the West India islands, which Seward had prevailed on Thad Stevens to have inserted in the appropriation bill during the war, and the President impressed Sumner with the idea that he feared an attack in Congress for that expenditure. Poore adds the opinion that Sumner thought that the President had come to enlist his services in defending this expenditure by Babcock, but the President meant the treaty for the acquisition of the Dominican Republic. The President and the Senator misunderstood each other. After awhile the President promised to send Babcock to call on the Senator next day with copies of the papers, and left. As Sumner escorted him to the door he told him that he was a Republican—a supporter of the Republican Administration and that he should sustain the Administration in this case if he possibly could. After he had examined the papers, he meant to sustain the expenditure of $100,000 in cash, $50,000 in a light battery and muskets purchased at New York, but the President meant the treaty. Poore’s statement thus removes a grave historical doubt and seems to set at rest the stories recently published of the cause of the difficulty between Grant and Sumner.

records.full_text:
GRANT—SUMNER.
Maj. Ben Perley Poore Rises to an Explanation.
[Washington Cor. Chicago Tribune.]
Maj. Ben Perley Poore has at last given to the world an authentic statement of the causes of the estrangement between Sumner and President Grant. This explanation has been called out by the recent statements of Gen. Grant, Wendell Phillips, ex-Secretary Fish, and John W. Forney. Maj. Poore was the guest of Sumner at the time of the estrangement, and heard all of the conversation between President Grant and Sumner. Maj. Poore’s story, in substance, is this: The removal of James M. Ashley, ex-Congressman from Ohio, from the Governorship of Montana, and the appointment in his place of Col. Potts, which had just happened, was the topic of table conversation. A letter just received from Ashley, protesting against the change, had been read at table, when the servant announced that the President was at the door. He was received, and in the course of the conversation the letter from Ashley was handed to the President. The latter became immediately excited, and denounced Ashley as a mischief-maker and a worthless fellow.
The next topic discussed was the San Domingo treaty. Sumner, Maj. Poore says, dwelt especially upon the expenditure by Gen. Babcock on San Domingo of a large sum taken from a secret-service fund for promoting intercourse with the West India islands, which Seward had prevailed on Thad Stevens to have inserted in an appropriation bill during the war, and the President impressed Sumner with the idea that he feared an attack in Congress for that expenditure. Poore adds the opinion that Sumner thought that the President had come to enlist his services in defending this expenditure by Gen. Babcock, but the President meant the treaty for the acquisition of the Dominican republic. The President and the Senator misunderstood each other. After a while the President promised to send Gen. Babcock to call on the Senator the next day, with copies of the papers, and left. As Mr. Sumner escorted him to the door he told him that he was a Republican, a supporter of the Republican administration, and that he should sustain the administration in this case if he possibly could, after he had examined the papers. He meant, sustain the expenditure of $100,000 in cash, $50,000 in a light battery and muskets, purchased at New York, but the President meant the treaty.
Maj. Poore’s statement thus removes a grave historical doubt, and seems to set at rest the stories recently published of the cause of the difficulty between Grant and Sumner.

records.headline: American commercial interests in Puerto Plata have been lost
records.summary_en: American commercial interests in Puerto Plata have been lost sight of by the Administration, the Sun charges: the town, on the northern shore of the island, is one of the chief seaports of the Dominican Republic, with a population of about 8,000 inhabitants, and carries on a considerable trade with the United States; its trade had lately been regarded as important enough to justify the establishment of a full consulate where there had been only a consular agent, and to it, the Sun says, Frederick Douglass was appointed the first American consul. The commercial and political importance of the town has made it a prominent point of attack during the revolutionary contest which has now prevailed in San Domingo for many months: for sixty days past, by the latest despatches, the conflicts in the streets and the outlying districts had been almost incessant, and scarcely a day passed without more or less musketry firing among the warehouses and dwellings of the foreign merchants, whose families had been compelled to take refuge on the shipping in the harbor. At such a place as this, if anywhere — the editorial is arguing as the window closes — the visits of a man-of-war would seem to be called for.
records.summary_es: Los intereses comerciales estadounidenses en Puerto Plata se han perdido de vista por la Administración, acusa el Sun: la ciudad, en la costa norte de la isla, es uno de los principales puertos marítimos de la República Dominicana, con una población de unos 8,000 habitantes, y mantiene un comercio considerable con los Estados Unidos; su comercio había sido considerado últimamente lo bastante importante para justificar el establecimiento de un consulado pleno donde antes solo había un agente consular, y para él, dice el Sun, fue nombrado Frederick Douglass primer cónsul estadounidense. La importancia comercial y política de la ciudad la ha convertido en un punto prominente de ataque durante la contienda revolucionaria que ha prevalecido ya en Santo Domingo por muchos meses: durante los últimos sesenta días, según los últimos despachos, los conflictos en las calles y los distritos periféricos habían sido casi incesantes, y apenas pasaba un día sin más o menos fuego de mosquetería entre los almacenes y viviendas de los comerciantes extranjeros, cuyas familias se habían visto obligadas a refugiarse en los barcos del puerto. En un lugar como este, si en alguno —argumenta el editorial cuando la ventana se cierra—, parecerían necesarias las visitas de un buque de guerra.

records.summary_en: According to the *Daily press and Dakotaian* on January 12, 1878, an incessant revolutionary conflict had prevailed in San Domingo for months, putting foreign merchants and their families in danger while no American naval vessel had appeared at Puerto Plata since the outbreak began over three months prior. Consequently, U.S. Consul Douglass departed, leaving a native Dominican and relative of President Baez's minister of war as vice consul—a succession that alarmed American residents who feared partisan bias and opposition to potential U.S. naval assistance.

Ante ello, el cónsul estadounidense Douglass se ausentó de la plaza, delegando la vicecancillería en un nativo dominicano emparentado con el ministro de Guerra del presidente Báez, relevo que sobresaltó a los residentes norteamericanos ante el temor a sesgos partidistas y trabas a un eventual auxilio naval de los EE. records.full_text:
St. Louis Journal.

One of the objects for which the United States maintain a costly naval establishment in time of peace is presumably to protect American commercial interests in foreign countries. Intelligence from the West Indies indicates that the administration at Washington has lost sight of this object in one important instance at least. On the northern shore of Hayti or San Domingo is the town of Puerto Plata, one of the chief seaports of the Dominican republic. It has a population of about three thousand inhabitants, and carries on a considerable trade with the United States. Formerly our government was represented there by a consular agent but more recently the trade with the United States has been regarded as important enough to justify the establishment of a full consulate, and a son of Frederick Douglas was appointed the first American consul.

This action certainly indicates that there are American interests of some consequence in Puerto Plata. The commercial and political importance of the town has made it a prominent point of attack and defense during the revolutionary contest, which has now prevailed in San Domingo for many months. For sixty days preceding the date of our latest dispatches the conflict in the outlying districts had been almost incessant, and scarcely a day passed without more or less musketry firing among the warehouses and dwellings of the foreign merchants. The families of many of them had been compelled to take refuge on the shipping in the harbor, It would seem that at such a place as this, if anywhere, the presence or occasional visits of a man-of-war would have some effect to secure the lives and property of alien residents against needless perils and destruction; yet we are informed that no vessel of the American navy has made her appearance at Puerto Plata since the last outbreak began, now more than three months ago.

Under these circumstances, even Mr. Douglass, the consul, has found the country too uncomfortable to remain in it any longer, and has come away, leaving behind him as vice consul a native of San Domingo, who is a relative of the minister of war under President Baez. It is anything but pleasing to the American residents of Puerto Plata to find themselves represented by a man who must needs be influenced in its acts by his adherence to one of the two parties now at war for the possession of San Domingo; and the fear is expressed that even if an American man-of-war should come into the harbor, this vice consul would try to convince the commander that she was not needed.

records.full_text:
CONTINUANCE OF THE DOMINICAN REVOLUTION--LOOKING FOR THE BODY OF COLUMBUS.
ST. DOMINGO, Jan. 17, 1878.
Political affairs continue complicated. Neither the government troops nor the revolutionists are advancing.

SEARCH FOR THE BODY OF COLUMBUS.
On the 26th ult. the Spanish steamer Alcantara arrived here from Havana, bringing a commission appointed by the Spanish government to examine a box supposed to contain the remains of Christopher Columbus. The examination was permitted after many formalities had been gone through with. The box was removed from the place of its deposit, the seals broken and the inscription closely examined. The bones were scrupulously inspected and photographs taken of the remains. Several physicians were present.

records.headline: Rumor of a New Treaty with Spain--a Spanish Protectorate Feared.
records.summary_en: A Havana dispatch of January 25, 1878, sent via Key West on January 26, reports a rumor that Spain will sign a treaty with St. Domingo at the end of this month, assuming a protectorate over the island. The rumor causes great excitement in St. Domingo and Hayti and serves to further increase the unpopularity of President Baez. The report adds that the rumor is somewhat strengthened by the appointment of new Spanish consuls at several ports of the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de La Habana del 25 de enero de 1878, enviado vía Cayo Hueso el 26 de enero, informa de un rumor de que España firmará un tratado con Santo Domingo a finales de este mes, asumiendo un protectorado sobre la isla. records.headline: The Sun's editorial on a reported Spanish protectorate over San Domingo holds
records.summary_en: The Sun's editorial on a reported Spanish protectorate over San Domingo holds that the belief in it is strengthened by the appointment of new Spanish consuls in several of the ports of the Dominican Republic: it is not at all unlikely, it says, that the unscrupulous usurper who tried to bargain away his country to the United States, under an arrangement with Cazneau, is equally ready to sell it to Spain. If such a sale has been or is being made, the question is, will the people of San Domingo bear it? Crushed and cowed as they may be, the prospect of being brought under the Spanish yoke must kindle any spark of liberty latent in their breasts. But even should the citizens of San Domingo tamely submit to a Spanish protectorate, other American republics could not look quietly on: interference to prevent such an outrage would be an inevitable duty.

Si tal venta se ha hecho o se está haciendo, la pregunta es: ¿lo soportará el pueblo de Santo Domingo? Aplastado e intimidado como pueda estar, la perspectiva de ser puesto bajo el yugo español debe encender cualquier chispa de libertad latente en su pecho. Pero aun si los ciudadanos de Santo Domingo se sometieran dócilmente a un protectorado español, las demás repúblicas americanas no podrían mirar tranquilamente: interferir para impedir tal ultraje sería un deber inevitable.

Pueblo, (Col.,) January 28. - Last Saturday evening a west bound train on the Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railroad was boarded a few miles east of Dodge City by four men, who attempted to rob the express messenger. Two of the robbers jumped on the engine and directed the engineer and fireman to do as directed, while the other two boarded the express car. The express messenger, however, proved too plucky and repulsed them. He thinks he shot one of the robbers, as he was only three feet off and dropped when the messenger fired. The robbers escaped, but are hotly pursued by a competent party, and as the trail is plain there is little doubt of their capture. The robbers had previously bound and gagged the agent of a small station east of Dodge City and ransacked his safe. [illegible]

records.summary_en: The *Public Ledger* reported on August 3, 1878, that proponents of the annexation of St. Domingo failed to demonstrate that Dominicans were largely in favor of the project, which hindered their case in Congress and among the U.S. public. Additionally, the newspaper stated that the separate project of annexing Canada could never be accomplished without an earnest petition from Canadians and specific governmental guarantees.
records.summary_es: El *Public Ledger* consignó el 3 de agosto de 1878 que los partidarios de la anexión de Santo Domingo no consiguieron acreditar que los dominicanos respaldaran mayoritariamente la iniciativa, lo que entorpeció su acogida parlamentaria y el favor del público en los Estados Unidos. Declaró además la publicación que el proyecto independiente de incorporar el Canadá jamás fructificaría sin mediar una sincera petición del pueblo canadiense y expresas garantías constitucionales.
records.passage: matter of such minute consideration, that there is no need of trying to exhibit the moral or political principle of the transaction except under a microscope. The price we had to pay for it is big enough to see without common spectacles. If the authors of the project for annexing St. Domingo had been able to show that the Dominicans were largely in favor of it, they would have been able to make a much better show in Congress and among the people of the United States. The other project so often broached, of annexing Canada to the Union, a most undesirable thing, as we have always thought, can never be accomplished except on the earnest petition of the Canadians, and then only with guarantees that the Federal government shall not be bound by the restrictions of the old treaty between Great Britain and France, which maintains a wealthy and powerful hierarchy inside of a political authority, and leads to the chief disorders that are continually occurring in the Dominion.
records.full_text: Annexation of foreign territory to another nation ought never to take place except by a common agreement between the annexer and the annexed. The annexations to the United States have not been conducted on such principles, unfortunately for our principles. The monarchs of Spain and France sold us their possessions at the South without consulting their inhabitants, because they wanted to get rid of them, as they cost them more than they were worth. The people of Texas generally did desire annexation, but it would not have been accomplished when it was but for the determination of the Democratic party to procure more territory in which to extend slavery and create larger representation in the senate and house for the slave holding aristocracy. A bloody war had to be fought to secure this end, which might, at a later period, have been secured without war and with the deliberate and formal consent of Mexico as well as that of the people of Texas. When Alaska was annexed, there were no people to consult worth speaking of, and the advantage or disadvantage to the United States or the Alaskans is a matter of such minute consideration, that there is no need of trying to exhibit the moral or political principle of the transaction except under a microscope. The price we had to pay for it is big enough to see without common spectacles. If the authors of the project for annexing St. Domingo had been able to show that the Dominicans were largely in favor of it, they would have been able to make a much better show in congress and among the people of the United States. The other project so often broached, of annexing Canada to the Union--a most undesirable thing, as we have always thought--can never be accomplished except on the earnest petition of the Canadians, and then only with guarantees that the Federal government shall not be bound by the restrictions of the old treaty between Great Britain and France, which maintains a wealthy and powerful hierarchy inside of a political authority, and leads to the chief disorders that are continually occurring in the Dominion.

records.full_text:
Two Dominican Conspirators Shot.

NEW YORK, Jan. 18.--A rumor prevailed throughout the city today to the effect that two well known Spanish subjects had been forcibly taken from a steamer in San Domingo, and cruelly put to death, and it created no little excitement among our Spanish and Cuban population. Senor H. Bellini, Dominican Consul in this city, when spoken to on the subject, said that General Valentine Perez and Manuel Cammino, both of whom were Dominicans and not Spanish subjects, had taken passage from Mayaguez, Porto Rico, for Porto Platte, San Domingo, on the Spanish steamer Manuel, after having combined with General Baez, ex-President of the San Domingo Republic, in a revolutionary movement for the overthrow of the existing government. Governor Lithgood, of Porto Platte, learned of the conspiracy, and when the vessel touched there demanded the men of her captain. They were delivered up under protest, both claiming to be Spanish citizens, and were taken to the office of the Minister of War, when the form of trial was gone through, lasting about two hours. They were found guilty of conspiracy to overthrow the government and sentenced to be shot, and four hours after they left the vessel their bodies were riddled with bullets. They appealed for respite, but their judges were inexorable. General Perez was at one time Governor of Azua, San Domingo.

records.summary_en: According to a dispatch from U.S. Consul Mr. Soutier at Cape Haytien, San Domingo is experiencing considerable distress because its tobacco crop cannot be sold, largely due to a new German tariff that closed that market. This loss costs Dominicans over a million dollars and the government $75,000 in duties, leading some planters to consider substituting sugar and coffee crops. Additionally, a private letter from Minister Resident and Consul General John M. records.full_text:
SPAIN AND ST. DOMINGO.

THE PRESENT TROUBLE BETWEEN THE TWO GOVERNMENTS--AN EXPLANATION BY THE DOMINICAN CONSUL GENERAL.
CONSULADO DE LA REPUBLICA DOMINICANA,
NEW YORK, August 8, 1879.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE HERALD:--
SIR--For some time the press of this city has been giving some reports respecting the trouble between Spain and St. Domingo, and yesterday some private information received in this city set forth that "should Spain bombard, as she threatens to do, the capital of St. Domingo the Dominican government will issue letters of marque for vessels to prey on Spanish shipping." I am not aware that Spain has made any direct threat to the Dominican government, nor have I learned that a Spanish squadron is expected at St. Domingo; but regarding the letters of marque, the Dominican Republic not having marine forces, its constitution authorizes the Executive to issue letters of marque in case of war with any foreign nation. I have not commenced to buy arms and ammunition, as has been reported. Since the election and inauguration of General Cesarea Guillermo as President his government has been regularly buying arms and ammunition merely to equip the army. The cause of the dispute between the two nations has been more or less misrepresented. The facts are simply these:--About six months ago, on the arrival of the regular Spanish mail steamer at Puerto Plata, information was received that there were on board two Dominican Generals members of the Bay party who were about to start a revolution on the Dominican frontier against the existing government. The authorities of Puerto Plata interviewed the Spanish Consul, asking him to give the necessary orders for the surrender of the said generals, which the captain of the steamer did, thus following the instructions of his Consul, protesting, at the same time, against the orders of the Consul, and not against the Dominican government. It is as well to state here that when making his custom house entry at Puerto Plata the captain did not mention, either in the bill of health or in the passenger list, the presence on board of the two generals. As everybody knows, they were courtmartialled and shot.

My government has done nothing against Spain, nor has it been the habit of the Dominican Republic to disregard the law of nations. In all international questions it always has behaved with moderation and dignity. In the present instance President Guillermo and his Cabinet will know how to maintain their dignity. Owing to our political commotions it is generally believed that foreign residents and their properties are not respected. This is, indeed, a great injustice. Never has a foreigner suffered any inconvenience, nor has his property been violated by any government or revolutions. The country is enjoying now perfect tranquillity, foreigners are settling down every day in the Republic, and with the franchises the government has given in favor of all agricultural establishments large sugar, coffee and other plantations are rising up. The government has asked authority of Congress to propose to the United States a treaty of reciprocity, and the Dominican press has been for some time and is yet discussing that question. The Dominican Republic has no doubt entered into an era of happiness and peace. I hope you will have the kindness to insert this letter in your valuable paper and oblige your obedient servant,
H. BILLIN, Dominican Consul.

records.full_text:
THE SCANDALS OF GRANTISM.

The San Domingo Job—Its Inception, Prosecution, and Final Failure.
I.

“If Gen. Grant, Gen. Babcock, and others high in office in Washington are so well satisfied with the real value of our prospects, and feel safe in lending their names and influence to carry them out, I cannot for the life of me see why you should hesitate. It was our intention to have sent 1,200 shares of the stock of the San Domingo Copper Company to you, as soon as Knapp shall have signed the certificates, to be distributed among officials of influence in Washington. But from the tone of your letters I suppose we shall have to do our business through some other party.”

These words, which seem like the idle boast of a confidence operator, are in reality the statement of a scandalous fact. They were written on the 21st of December, 1866, by Joseph W. Currier, then of New York, to a friend in Washington, who hesitated to embark in a scheme which looked to the raising of a million of dollars for the avowed purpose of mining copper in the island of San Domingo. Currier had been a quartermaster in the Union Army. He was speculative by nature, and circumstances made him impecunious. He was enthusiastic and credulous, but perhaps not deliberately dishonest. At this time, however, he was in the clutches of two unscrupulous knaves, who, years before, had gone from Massachusetts to the West Indies to teach the Dominicans tricks of which they never dreamt before. These were Joseph W. Fabens and William L. Cazneau. They were both natives of the Bay State. In 1863, Fabens, Cazneau, and Currier established the Great American West India Company, with an office at 5 Pine street, New York. Their rooms were fitted up in sumptuous style, and by the free use of printers’ ink they succeeded in disposing of their worthless stock to the amount of $160,000. Then they closed their doors and disappeared. But they came again in 1866, scattering far and wide their prospectus of the Great San Domingo Copper Company. They were accompanied this time by Buenaventura Baez, the deposed President of the Dominican Republic, who had been driven from the island and was ready for any sort of a job which promised him a good living without work. These conspirators explained that Cabral’s revolution had destroyed the Great American West India Company, but that the present corporation rested on a secure basis. To all doubting inquirers they whispered, “Gen. Grant is in it!” On the strength of his name they raised money from investors. Fabens took $30,000 and started for Africa to buy camels for the copper mines. He was accompanied by Baez. The 1,200 shares of stock were duly distributed among “officials of influence in Washington,” and $200,000 was raised by the sale of shares. Then the doors of the office were closed again, and the adventurers sought safety in flight. They returned to San Domingo, where Baez reëstablished himself in the Presidency. There they remained till President Grant was inaugurated, and then they began once more their swindling operations in good earnest.

Armed with this document, Babcock set out for San Domingo. He also took with him an order from Robeson, Secretary of the Navy, placing at his disposal the United States ship-of-war Seminole, and directing her commander to seize the Telegraph, a little vessel belonging to Cabral, which was to be brought as a prize into the port of Baltimore. She was to be seized as a pirate, but an examination before the British Consul showed that the charge of piracy could not be sustained. But even after this decision Robeson directed Commander Queen to sail in the Tuscarora to San Domingo and place himself under Babcock's orders, that he might help to capture the Telegraph. All this gratuitous service was rendered to Baez, against his enemy Cabral, that the annexation scheme might not fall through.

Babcock remained in San Domingo till August, when he returned to Washington, received further instructions from Grant, and departed almost immediately to complete his arrangements with Baez.

III.

Davis Hatch was a citizen of Connecticut who went to San Domingo in 1862 to act as agent of a New York company organized to work a salt mine in that island. The required concessions were made by the Spanish Government in 1864, but in 1865 Spain abandoned the country, and Baez, who set up as President, annulled the grants. But when Cabral overthrew and succeeded Baez, in 1866, he reconfirmed the concessions of Spain to the salt company. In 1868 Baez defeated Cabral, through an insurrection, and returned to power. In May, 1869, the city of Barahona, where Hatch resided, was deserted by Baez, and taken possession of by Cabral's forces. It was retaken in the following August by Baez, who thereupon caused the arrest of Hatch on the ground that he had sided with Cabral. He was condemned to death by a court martial, and was then pardoned by Baez on condition that he should immediately leave the island. He was quite willing to go, but was not permitted to do so. He was kept a close prisoner from the 29th of August, 1869, till the 15th of March, 1870, in flagrant violation of his rights as an American citizen. A PEACEFUL ELECTION IN SAN DOMINGO.

HAVANA, July 6.--News from Puerto Plata, San Domingo, to June 22 has been received. Order prevailed during the elections for President of San Domingo. The Rev. Fernando Arturo Merino obtained a majority of the votes cast. The party of the "Blues" expected the realization of their political programme by the nomination of the Rev. Mr. Merino.

General Caman, the Haytian Commissioner, was in Puerto Plata with the object of arranging for the expulsion of Dominican political refugees from the Haytian frontiers, whence they continually infest the territory of San Domingo. The building of a railroad from Santiago to Samana was to be begun at an early day. The Republic was prospering.

VARIOUS.

HAYTI.
HAVANA, Cuba, Aug. 21.--There is great curiosity here to know in what shape and manner the Haytien Government will proceed to fulfill the clause of the treaty it recently concluded with the neighboring Republic of San Domingo. According to that treaty all political refugees from the Dominican Republic who inhabit Hayti, where they constantly concoct revolutionary plans and schemes, are to be driven out from that Republic. It is expected that Gen. Solomon, the Haytien President, will enforce the treaty, inasmuch as he is a friend of Father Padre Merino, who has just been installed as President of the Dominican Republic.

records.summary_en: *The Indianapolis Leader* described the historical impact of educated, affluent refugees of color from Saint-Domingue who settled in Louisiana, particularly New Orleans, after fleeing the island. Their arrival stimulated the local free colored Creole population to establish new schools and send their children to France for higher education. It is strongly believed here that something is going on with reference to San Domingo. There was a treaty for the acquisition or lease, November 29, 1869, of Samana Bay to the United States. It was discovered that these two parts of the island of Santa Domingo had been in chronic revolution, and it was thought that through these Spanish and French concessions the Americans would not only utilize the entire island, but would also make such a showing, by enterprise and energy, as would make Cuba and Porto Rico drop like a ripe apple into the lap of the new empire, and make the West Indies a part of the United States. A few years before this, the Samana Bay Company, a company chartered at Albany, under the laws of the State of New York, led by men who run the steamer “Tybee,” for instance—such men as Marshall O. Roberts, Wm. R. Grace, the present Mayor of New York, Commodore Garrison, and others—undertook to make a trade between New York and San Domingo City, for the purpose of developing San Domingo and bringing hence to this country the products of that island, which were principally mahogony, coffee, and tobacco equal to the best produced and called Vuelra Abajo in the Cincho Vias of Cuba. The company had a concession from the Dominican Government, taking in the waters and islands and the frontage of Samana Bay, and a railroad grant reaching from Samana to Santa Domingo. The opposition to this scheme of the government to acquire the island brought about the well-known fight against the administration of Charles Sumner which resulted in his deposition from the Chairmanship of the Foreign Relations Committee of the United States Senate, and which fight, created a commission, consisting of Benjamin F. Wade, of Ohio, as Chairman, Professor Howe, Frederick Douglass, and a number of specialists, who were directed to proceed to Santa Domingo and investigate and report upon the character of its climate, its agricultural productions, and upon the general resources of the country. They were further directed to report upon the financial condition of the government, debts and obligations due to foreign governments or creditors, giving in detail a full statement of such debts or obligations. This commission was further instructed to report fully as to the character of all grants and concessions of whatever nature given by the Government of Dominica to any individual or corporation, particularly with respect to concessions granting lands upon the Bay of Samana. The committee's report is well known. There is a little island around there somewhere which has been bought up by a syndicate of New York speculators, who seem to have an object just now, knowing all these facts, to make a coaling station for American vessels. They are trying their best to have our government purchase it in expectation of the annexation of the West Indies. This idea is in connection with the Isthmus canal. Their agents are here and have secured already the detailing of a vessel from the North Atlantic squadron to make a thorough survey of Samana Bay. This bay was surveyed in 1870 or thereabouts, but the survey was only partial. The English Government made a survey for their own use some years ago.

At the Hydrographic Office in this city, where the navy records are kept, they say that this is a preliminary affair simply to the survey of the harbors of the world that have not been surveyed, for purposes of general information. I do not think there is anything in the statement of the Hydrographic Office in this matter of exploring West Indian harbors beyond a desire to establish a coaling station somewhere down there. Whether it be in the Bay of Samana, the Bay of St. Nicholas la Mole, or the Island of St. Thomas, or a point in Cuba, is, with the proposed coaling station itself, a matter of the future.

records.full_text:
SAN DOMINGO.

A PRONUNCIAMENTO BY GENERAL DON CESAREO GUILLERMO.
HAVANA, May 19.--The Herald's correspondent writes that the general of division in the national army and ex-president of the Dominican Republic, Don Cesareo Guillermo, has issued a revolutionary manifesto addressed to his fellow citizens. The document itself does not show where it was promulgated, and its date can only be presumed from the fact that it bears the impress of April, 1882. General Guillermo claims to have been urgently called upon by many men best known in the national political parties of the country to place himself at the head of the revolution, which he at once initiated in the Eastern province. In consequence of the evils imposed upon the nation through the dictatorship of Marino, which commenced in June, 1881, General Guillermo considers himself justified in the course he has taken, and also in deciding upon forming an expedition to open the campaign. The general refers back to the triumphs which placed the present government in power, and says that if it were possible for him to blot from the pages of history all the abominable acts which have happened since those triumphs, he would efface them at the cost of his life. The manifesto goes on in a strain of fierce denunciation against the obnoxious government which is the object of General Guillermo's wrath. He is not, however, explicit in naming the particular act of misgovernment that might justify revolution. He is no doubt a brave soldier, for his paper says for him: "All Dominicans! Here you have my sword and my life! Here I am, disposed to shed, even to the last drop, my blood, to be the first in danger and the last after victory! Therefore study my words! Long live all the parties regulated by law! Hurrah for national reconciliation!"

records.full_text:
A Suspended Law.

Since 1861 that statute of the United States known as the "Guano act" has been a dead letter, so far as the State Department is concerned. No American citizen, we believe, when he desired to avail himself of the benefit of its provisions, has ever been allowed to invoke them against unlawful interference with his business by any other power.

In order to encourage and build up an extensive and valuable domestic trade, Congress declared that whenever a citizen of the United States should discover guano on any derelict island or key, beyond the maritime jurisdiction of any other nation, he might raise the flag of the United States over it, and proceed to dig and ship the guano to this country under the laws of the coastwise trade. Such islands became by reason of such occupation appendages of the United States, subject to its jurisdiction, and entitled to its protection. They were registered in the Treasury Department, upon certain proofs of the facts, and the Treasury certificate was a conclusive and final adjudication in favor of the parties making the discovery, and adventuring their capital and labor in the business into which they were expressly invited by the public policy of the nation.

The "Guano act" was plain. Several times its provisions were submitted to the Attorney-General, and received each time the same interpretation, both as to the municipal law and the public law of the world. In a case with Venezuela it was diplomatically enforced. In a case with Hayti it was enforced by the navy, under instructions of the State Department. But Mr. SEWARD, for reasons of his own, chose to disregard it. American citizens had discovered a rich deposit of guano upon a barren and derelict islet lying in the high seas off the coast of San Domingo. They occupied it peacefully for seven months, had complied with all the conditions of the law, and established a large business. At the end of that time an armed Dominican vessel called, tore down the flag, and carried the men away prisoners. There never was a more flagrant insult to a nation, or a more indefensible outrage upon the rights of our private citizens. But Mr. SEWARD declined to seek any redress, and from that day to this there has been no instance in which the Guano act has been successfully invoked against a foreign aggressor. It appears that a case almost exactly similar to the above has been recently brought to the attention of the State Department. This time it is Mexico which sends an armed force to tear down the American flag, and carry off American citizens engaged in lawful business, in which they were by statute specially promised the protection of their country. Will Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN follow the remarkable precedent of 1861? Will he follow those set by Gen. CASS, and enforce the law not merely as he finds it in every writer from VATTEL to WHEATON, but as it is written in plain English on the statute book of the United States? If the newspaper reports of the facts is correct, the case is too clear for any dispute, and the people will be glad to see some evidence of old-time spirit and vigor in our dealings with this class of questions.

records.full_text:
Threatened Invasion of San Domingo.

ST. THOMAS, Feb. 4.—Gen. Guillermo, ex-President of San Domingo, with eleven other exiles from that republic, left here on the 29th ult. on board the British steamer Yucatan with the avowed purpose of organizing in Jamaica a formidable party to invade San Domingo and Hayti. It is reported that he has purchased the Victoria, a small steamer, which will form part of a fleet of four vessels. He is said to have in his possession letters of credit to the amount of $80,000. The Dominican Consul here has chartered the British schooner Lillie to convey to the Government of San Domingo intelligence of Gen. Guillermo’s designs.

records.headline: The Haytian Rebels.
records.summary_en: E. Nadale, an emissary of the Haytian Government, arrived in New York on Monday on a secret mission. He said that the rebels under Bazelais and La Forestre numbered nearly 1,000 and were composed mostly of exiled Haytians, Cubans and Dominicans. Bazelais, he said, is a very brave man who would fight to the last before giving up the port of Miragoane; La Forestre, who was Inspector of Prisons under the late Emperor Soulouque, once caused all the State prisoners to be shot, saying that it was cheaper to kill than to feed them. A stubborn and prolonged struggle may be expected, but Nadale seemed confident that the insurgents would finally be overthrown by the Government troops.

To the Editor of the Indianapolis Journal:
What kind of revolution is going on in Hayti, and is Hayti a negro republic?
FRANKLIN, Ind. A READER.
During the past ninety years the island of Hayti, or Santo Domingo, has been in a chronic state of insurrection, and it would require the patience of a Philadelphia lawyer to figure out all the abortive rebellions that have been inaugurated there. The result of all these disturbances, however, has been to secure to the island its independence. The western half is known as the Republic of Hayti, while the eastern half is known as the Dominican Republic, each independent of the other. There is now an insignificant insurrection in the former, the fighting being carried on in a desultory and ineffectual manner.

records.summary_en: The *Cleveland Gazette* reported on the life and character of Toussaint, praising his devotion to his race, original opinions, and austere sobriety while in power. The newspaper noted that without formal education or military training, the former slave rose to become a valiant soldier, General, Governor, and victor over Napoleon's experienced forces, earning renown in both St. Domingo and the National Councils of France.

Resaltó la publicación que, sin ilustración académica ni instrucción militar, el antiguo esclavo descuella como esforzado combatiente, general, gobernador y vencedor de los aguerridos ejércitos de Napoleón, granjeándose celebridad imperecedera tanto en Santo Domingo como en las asambleas nacionales de Francia.
records.passage: devotion to the welfare of his unhappy race. Like most men of energetic temperament his habits were thoughtful, in speech he arrived at his meaning by the shortest methods. So profound and original were his opinions that they have been adopted by all the chiefs who survived him. His maxims are still the guidance of the rulers of Hayti. His thoughts were vigorous as well as copious, and whatever he could not express in his native "patois" appeared tame and insipid in the polished language of France, which he was compelled to employ in official business. While at the height of power, Toussaint himself practiced an austere sobriety bordering on abstemiousness, though his subordinate officers' were reveling in luxury. Veneration for his character was not confined to Ste. Domingo, but penetrated to the heart of Europe. In generous France his name, his fame and his incomparable virtues were often pronounced in the National Councils. Toussaint, without an hour's education in the science of arms, became a valiant soldier, baffled the skill and conquered Napoleon's most experienced followers! Without a syllable of military knowledge he fought like one born on the field! Without means he prosecuted the war for the emancipation of his race, beat his enemies in battle and, turned their deadly weapons against themselves. From ignorance he became educated by his own inherent energies. From a slave he rose to a soldier, a General and a Governor, and might, if he would, have been King or Emperor of the people his bravery had redeemed
records.full_text:
WRITTEN FOR THE GAZETTE.
L'HISTOIRE DES HEROS D'AFRIQUE.
Dans L'Ile de Ste. Domingo.
BY PAUL GASTON.
No V.—Toussaint L'Ouverture.
Vincent Beaupre, in his celebrated "Reflections on the Tragical Drama of the Dominican Insurrection," says: "Toussaint L'Ouverture, at the head of an army, was the embodiment of the most active and the most indefatigable man that it is possible for the human mind to form a conception. His great sobriety, combined with the faculty which none but himself possessed, of never reposing, the facility with which he resumes the affairs of the cabinet after the most disastrous reverses on the field of battle, render him so eminently superior to those around him that their respect and submission were carried to the verge of fascination, and it is certain that no man of modern times ever possessed such an influence over a body of men as Toussaint exercised over his brethren of Ste. Domingo."
Such is the testimony of an enemy who had lost all his earthly possessions through the instrumentality of our hero.
Toussaint was of a prepossessing and commanding appearance, of medium stature, but of an iron frame. His dignified, calm and unaffected features, broad and well developed forhead would under any circumstances, designate him as one born to rule. Endowed by nature with lofty qualities of mind, he owed his elevation to his own energies and devotion to the welfare of his unhappy race. Like most men of energetic temperament his habits were thoughtful. In speech he arrived at his meaning by the shortest methods. So profound and original were his opinions that they have been adopted by all the chiefs who survived him. His maxims are still the guidance of the rulers of Hayti. His thoughts were vigorous as well as copious, and whatever he could not express in his native "patois" appeared tame and insipid in the polished language of France, which he was compelled to employ in official business.
While at the height of power, Toussaint himself practiced an austere sobriety bordering on abstemiousness, though his subordinate officers were reveling in luxury. Veneration for his character was not confined to Ste. Domingo, but penetrated to the heart of Europe. In generous France his name, his fame and his incomparable virtues were often pronounced in the National Councils.
