records.full_text:
YELLOW FEVER ON A FRENCH WAR VESSEL.
HAMILTON, Ont., Nov. 11.—The French war steamer Le Chasseur, Captain E. Courrequelle, arrived here on October 24 from Port au Prince, Hayti. On October 9 she received on board a distressed merchant crew of eight men in a boat from St. Marcs. One of the men was ill, and died next day of yellow fever. The remainder were put ashore at Port au Prince, and the Chasseur came north to prevent the development of yellow fever. No sickness appeared. She left Bermuda on October 27 for Guadaloupe and Martinique.

records.headline: John Mercer Langston's arrival aboard the U. S. S. Galena is announced
records.summary_en: John Mercer Langston's arrival aboard the U. S. S. Galena is announced to the Globe by a correspondent: Langston, Minister Resident and Consul General to the Republic of Hayti and Charge d'Affaires to the Dominican Republic, was given a pleasant reception by the American citizens there, of which a fuller account is promised in another communication: it was a grand sight, he writes, to see America's greatest Negro leader and San Domingo's greatest Negro President, Ulises Heureaux, clasped hand in hand, as the representatives of their common country. The letter then holds Mr. Langston up as the central figure to whom the race must turn at this eventful epoch — a crisis in the nation's history, in which, it says, the tribunal that will sit at Chicago on the third of June next will pronounce its verdict, with the Republican party and the Negro himself sitting as judges.

La carta presenta luego al Sr. Langston como la figura central a la que la raza debe volverse en esta época trascendental —una crisis en la historia de la nación, en la que, dice, el tribunal que se reunirá en Chicago el 3 de junio próximo pronunciará su veredicto, con el partido Republicano y el propio negro sentados como jueces.

records.summary_en: According to dispatches from Santo Domingo brought by a steamer from St. Thomas, the Dominican Congress passed a bill establishing free trade with the United States, and Senor Galvan was appointed Commissioner to finalize arrangements in Washington. Negotiations were also reported to be proceeding with Washington regarding the lease of Samaná Bay, with bondholders of the Samana Bay Company slated to receive the first claim on the lease money. Additionally, the newspaper reported on a dynamite scare affecting English Island and St. Vincent, yellow fever deaths on a vessel at Barbados, and the withdrawal of insurance agencies in Trinidad.

records.full_text:
SANTO DOMINGO PASSES THE FREE TRADE BILL.
HAVANA, May 13.—The British mail steamer from St. Thomas, May 5, brings Santo Domingo dispatches to May 1. According to these, the bill establishing free trade with the United States has been passed by the Dominican Congress. Senor Galvan had been appointed Commissioner, and was to proceed to Washington on the 7th inst., for the purpose of making the final arrangements. It is again ascertained that negotiations are proceeding with Washington for the lease of Samana Bay. It is reported that the government will give the bondholders of the Samana Bay Company the first claim on the money part for the lease. Advices from Cape Hayti of April 24 say that the refugees of the British Consulate there have been pardoned. A change in the entire Haytien administration is anticipated.

The Thibodaux Sentinel, SATURDAY, JULY 5 1884.
TARIFF LEGISLATION BY THE PRESIDENT.
The ease with which the Hawaiian and Mexican reciprocity treaties have been carried through the Senate has given our State Department an entirely new field of activity. By acting in conjunction with New York interests, it can contrive a new reciprocity treaty at any time providing for the free admission of certain articles agreed upon. St. Domingo, which Grant tried to annex, has been pitched upon as the proper scene of the third experiment in executive tariff legislation. It is situated with especial reference to the conveniences demanded by the exigencies requiring more free admission. Just east of it lies Spanish Port Rico. The British Bahama Islands are north-west, and Jamaica west by north. Cuba is west-north-west, and the Central and South American coasts, the Lesser Antilles, and a great number of inlets belonging to the Nether land, Denmark, France, Spain and Great Britain, etc., are accessible.
This treaty, like the Mexican, is one sided in appearance. The list of articles to be admitted free into St. Domingo is so much longer than that of articles to be admitted free into the United States, that it seems as though the United States must have got the best of the bargain, and the Dominicans must have been asleep. But since we exported to St. Domingo only $1,179,200 worth of domestic merchandise during the fiscal year ended June 30, 1883, and since we can scarcely hope to build up very much of a market among 250,000 people, it is not a matter of great consequence, except to her treasury, whether we gain free entrance for a long list of our products or not.
But short as is the list of articles which we care to admit free from San Domingo, it contains sugar and molasses. The sugar is not to be above No. 16 Dutch standard—a fact to be explained by the necessities of our refiners, who need reciprocity treaties in abundance for the procurement of raw material, and need the exclusive possession of our home market for the sugars which are fit to put on table for use. THE TREATY WITH SPAIN.
This Government has more than once been called upon of late to take action in fulfillment of international obligation with Spain. Agitation in the Island of Cuba hostile to the Spanish crown having been fomented by persons abusing the sacred rights of hospitality which our territory affords, the officers of the Government have been instructed to exercise vigilance to prevent infractions of our neutrality laws at Key West and at other points near the Cuban coast. I am happy to say that in the only instance where those precautionary measures were successfully eluded, the offenders, when found in our territory, were subsequently tried and convicted.
The growing need of close relationship of intercourse and traffic between the Spanish Antilles and their natural market in the United States led to the adoption in January last of a commercial agreement looking to that end. This agreement has since been superseded by a more carefully framed and comprehensive convention, which I shall submit to the Senate for approval. It has been the aim of this negotiation to open such a favored reciprocal exchange of productions carried under the flag of either country as to make the intercourse between Cuba and Porto Rico and ourselves scarcely less intimate than the commercial movement between our domestic ports, and to insure a removal of the burdens on shipping in the Spanish Indies, of which masters have so often had cause to complain. The negotiation of this convention has, for a time, postponed the prosecution of certain claims of our citizens, which were declared to be without the jurisdiction of the Spanish-American Claims Commission, and which we therefore remitted to diplomatic channels for adjustment. The speedy settlement of these claims will now be urged by this Government.
Negotiations for a treaty of commercial reciprocity with the Dominican Republic have been successfully concluded, and the result will shortly be laid before the Senate.

The last session of the present Congress assembled on Monday last, and will remain in session until the 4th of March next, and then adjourn and give way to the new Congress elected on the 4th of November.
The first day was occupied with the reading of President Arthur's message, which presents nothing of any great importance. It is in the usual common-place style, as the following synopsis will show:
The President says nothing could more strikingly illustrate the temper of the American citizens, his love of order and his loyalty to law, than the quiet way the election excitement passed off. Nothing could more singularly demonstrate the strength and wisdom of our political institutions.
Eight years have passed since a controversy concerning the result of a National election sharply called the attention of Congress to the necessity of providing more precise and definite regulations for counting the Electoral vote.
Our relations with all foreign powers continue to be amicable.
The most important subject referred to in the message is the treaty with Nicaragua for the construction of an interocean canal through the territory of that country by the Government of the United States.
In addition to the commercial treaty negotiated with Spain, providing for reciprocal trade between the United States and the islands of Cuba and Porto Rico, the President reports that a similar treaty has been concluded with the Dominican republic.
He recommends that the neutrality laws shall be amended so as to prohibit and punish acts against neutrality committed within this country and aimed against the peace of a friendly nation.

Whitthorne Not a Cabinet Seeker.
WASHINGTON, Dec. 6.—"They say you are to be Secretary of the Navy," said a reporter to ex-Congressman Whitthorne, of Tennessee. "They don't know what they are talking about," he replied. "I ask for nothing except that we shall have a wise, economical and progressive Democratic administration. I firmly believe that we will have such an administration under President Cleveland, but personally I expect nothing."

records.full_text:
THE ST. DOMINGO TREATY.
COMMERCIAL RECIPROCITY PROPOSED.
SCHEDULES OF TARIFF CHANGES—A LONG FREE LIST OF AMERICAN PRODUCTS.
A treaty aiming at the advancement of trade between this country and St. Domingo—entitled "A convention for commercial reciprocity between the United States of America and the Dominican Republic"—is now before the United States Senate, awaiting consideration, having been negotiated and signed at Washington, December 4, 1884, by Secretary Frelinghuysen and Manuel De J. Galvin, the Dominican Minister to this country. It consists, according to the full text printed in The New-York Herald, of twenty-eight articles, of which the first provides that the following named articles of Dominican production shall be admitted into the United States free from duty:

records.headline: Ben Perley Poore recounts how the ill feeling between President Grant and Senator Sumner grew out of a misunderstanding
records.summary_en: Ben Perley Poore recounts how the ill feeling between President Grant and Senator Sumner grew out of a misunderstanding on the evening the San Domingo treaty was sent to the Senate: Sumner thought Grant wanted his help defending General Babcock's expenditures in Santo Domingo, while Grant meant the treaty for acquiring the Dominican Republic. When Babcock read the treaty to Sumner the next day, Sumner objected to the stipulation that Grant would use his influence to make annexation popular in Congress, and became the enemy of the whole scheme.
records.summary_es: Ben Perley Poore relata cómo el resentimiento entre el presidente Grant y el senador Sumner nació de un malentendido la noche en que el tratado de Santo Domingo fue enviado al Senado: Sumner creyó que Grant quería su ayuda para defender los gastos del general Babcock en Santo Domingo, mientras que Grant se refería al tratado para adquirir la República Dominicana. Cuando Babcock le leyó el tratado a Sumner al día siguiente, Sumner objetó la estipulación de que Grant usaría su influencia para hacer popular la anexión en el Congreso, y se convirtió en enemigo de todo el proyecto.

What did not appear to be wrong to the General the Senator regarded as criminal. records.headline: Lucas Gibbs, Minister of Finance and Commerce of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: *The New York Freeman* reported on a meeting in the Dominican Republic presided over by Hon. Lucas Gibbs, Minister of Finance and Commerce, with Hon. Richard Alexander Gross serving as secretary, alongside several appointed vice-presidents and officials. Following his opening remarks, Mr. Gibbs introduced the evening's speaker, Hon. John Mercer Langston, an American citizen who expressed surprise before briefly addressing commercial relations and a reciprocal treaty.

records.headline: A speech printed by the Freeman urges the commercial treaty
records.summary_en: A speech printed by the Freeman urges the commercial treaty then pending between the Dominican Republic and the United States: San Domingo, Hayti, Venezuela and the South American republics, the speaker argues, should be made commercially great and prosperous without divesting them of their sovereignty or nationalities, so that the continent's commercial and diplomatic relations triumph as American against European competition. 'We want your products, and in exchange we want you to have ours exclusive of all others upon a reciprocal basis.' The country, he tells his hearers, is largely undeveloped and in its infancy — forests of valuable woods unexplored for want of transportation, immense virgin fields unapproachable for the same reason and for lack of capital and labor — and a new administration, just inaugurated, is about to construct its foreign policy and will be especially interested in such a measure: the window closes as the speaker recalls the steamboat's passage along the coast.

records.summary_en: According to the *St. Paul daily globe* of December 9, 1885, a commercial treaty signed with the Dominican Republic was subsequently withdrawn from the Senate for re-examination. The official concluded that entering into such engagements was inexpedient because the treaties required the United States to surrender large revenues on sugar for inadequate advantages, provided only illusory relief to consumers, risked raising embarrassing questions under favored-nation clauses, and diminished independent control over national revenues.

On taking office I withdrew for re-examination the treaties signed with Spain and Santo Domingo, then pending before the senate. The result has been to satisfy me of the inexpediency of entering into engagements of this character not covering the entire tariff. These treaties contemplated the surrender, by the United States, of large revenues for inadequate considerations. Upon sugar alone duties were surrendered to an amount far exceeding all the advantages offered in exchange. Even were it intended to relieve our consumers, it was evident that, so long as the exemption but partially covered our importation, such relief would be illusory. To relinquish a revenue so essential seemed highly improvident at a time when new and large drains upon the treasury were contemplated. Moreover, embarrassing questions would have arisen under the favored nation clauses of treaties with other nations. As further objection it is evident that tariff regulation by treaty diminished that independent control over its own revenues which is essential for the safety and welfare of any government. records.summary_en: The *Gloucester County Democrat* reported on December 10, 1885, that a commercial treaty had been signed by the Dominican republic following steps taken to establish less obstructed traffic with Cuba and Porto Rico. The newspaper also noted that subsequent overtures for a similar mutual extension of commercial intercourse were made by Her Britannic Majesty's government regarding British West Indian and South American dependencies, but these efforts yielded no result. Consignó asimismo la publicación que gestiones posteriores formuladas por el gobierno de Su Majestad Británica para ensanchar recíprocamente el comercio con las dependencias británicas antillanas y sudamericanas resultaron infructuosas. THE DIPLOMATIC AND CONSULAR SERVICE. I earnestly urge that Congress recast the appropriations for the maintenance of the diplomatic and consular service on a footing commensurate with the importance of our national interests. At every post where a representative is necessary, the salary should be so graded as to permit him to live with comfort. With the assignment of ade[illegible] salaries, the so-called notarial extra-official fees, which our officers abroad are now permitted to treat as personal perquisites, should be done away with. Every act requiring the certification and seal of the officer should be taxable at schedule rates, and the fee therefore returned to the treasury. By restoring these revenues to the public use the consular service would be self-supporting, even with a liberal increase of the present low salaries. In further prevention of abuses a system of consular inspection should be instituted.

records.headline: The Sun surveys the Dominican presidential succession: the men
records.summary_en: The Sun surveys the Dominican presidential succession: the men spoken of for President include the ex-Minister of Finance, the ex-Vice-President, a general of Azua and a general of Puerto Plata, but the controlling elements are Gen. W. Heureux, commander-in-chief of the army, and Gen. Gregorio Luperon, Government delegate for the district of the Cibao, and which of the two is now more powerful is disputed. Luperon has been recognized as leader of the Blue party from the overthrow of the Baez administration and has been virtually the dictator of the republic's politics since; Heureux, his lieutenant and friend, has gradually increased in popularity and strength, and his prompt suppression of the recent Guillermo revolution, driving its leader to suicide, has helped place him where he stands. Now, for the first time, the two seem at cross purposes: Luperon is determined to dictate the nomination in the person of Gen. Pedro Bono, and if Bono declines, as at the last election, to select another; Heureux favors the ex-Minister of Finance, to whom Luperon is greatly opposed because of his affiliation with the Baez or Red party, and will oppose him even to war: the window closes as Heureux's own intentions begin.

records.headline: The report describes the Dominican government's costly borrowing, including a recent loan of $150,000 made in Puerto Plata
records.summary_en: The report describes the Dominican government's costly borrowing, including a recent loan of $150,000 made in Puerto Plata at a stated two per cent a month, of which the government actually received far less, and the Puerto Plata syndicate's plan to issue $500,000 in paper currency. It says the country's only hopes of relief are a commercial treaty with the United States or American capital at a reasonable rate, and praises United States Consul H. C. C. Astwood for settling American claims, including a $63,000 indemnity for the widow of Piatt, an American carpenter shot by government troops.

Astwood, por resolver reclamaciones estadounidenses, incluida una indemnización de $63,000 para la viuda de Piatt, un carpintero estadounidense muerto a tiros por tropas del gobierno.

To deceive the public a recent loan was effected in Puerto Plata of $150,000 at, it was stated, two per cent. per month. The Government received from the syndicate $130,000, less seven per cent., and then agreed to pay two per cent. per month on the $150,000. so that it might appear to the public that only interest at that reduced rate was being paid. The Puerto Plata syndicate has become emboldened by its success, and is now planning to issue $500,000 in paper currency under its own guarantee, and proposes for the present making this the circulating medium of the country. This scheme has gone so far that it is understood that a well-known New York house has by this time got the order for the printing of the bills. Notwithstanding this fact, Congress and the merchants of the city of San Domingo will oppose the matter. The latter, with the assistance of Mr. Alexander [Bird?], the English capitalist who is building the railroad here, have established a bank with a cash capital of $75,000. Their rates of interest are proportionate with the risk, and can be estimated when it is seen that the Government, on as good security as the country affords, has to pay all the way from 24 to 30 per cent. per annum. records.headline: The Dominican Consulship.
records.summary_en: *The New York Freeman* reported on February 20, 1886, that Mr. Astwood's name was submitted for Presidential consideration for reappointment as United States Consul to San Domingo, whose affairs were described as unsettled with an anticipated upheaval due to the presidential succession. The newspaper also stated that recent reports of the assassination of President Salomon of Hayti were unfounded, praising him as a wise and discreet leader. Additionally, the excerpt criticized a note from the *Norfolk Virginian* regarding a statement made by a colored brother, Rev. Hooper Jolly, at a Methodist conference in Philadelphia.

records.full_text:
The Hon. H. C. C. Astwood, United States Consul to San Domingo, arrived in New York last Monday, and proceeded immediately to Washington.
In the New York Sun of Tuesday, we find a communication from San Domingo City, the closing paragraph of which, bearing upon the Dominican Consulship, is here given:
H. C. C. Astwood, the United States Consul, who is on confidential terms with the Government and very popular with the American residents here, has left for New York. Mr. Astwood's success in negotiating and settling American claims against the Dominican Government leads people here to hope that his efforts with his own people on behalf of his country here may prove fruitful.
Mr. Astwood succeeded in having the repudiated claims of Messrs. Remington of New York, Wanamaker & Brown of Philadelphia, and others, recognized. It was he who obtained an indemnity of $33,000 for the widow of Platt, the American carpenter, who was shot by the Government troops here in June last. The underwriters of New York, Philadelphia and Boston, in recognition of his services in breaking up and preventing numerous frauds attempted upon them, have together with Messrs. Clyde of New York and many others, petitioned the President, praying that he be continued in office. His knowledge of the language and people renders him almost indispensable to the Americans here. When the immense amount of American capital invested in sugar plantations and otherwise is considered, it is important that a suitable representative of the United States Government should be here.
It is very gratifying to note this high endorsement of Mr. Astwood's diplomatic labors. We have no doubt that President Cleveland will recognize in Mr. Astwood a capable officer of the diplomatic service, and grant the petition of those Americans who have business relations with San Domingo to reappoint Mr. Astwood.
We understand that Mr. Astwood is not anxious to retain the post, but allows his name to go before the President for consideration at the earnest solicitation of the parties above cited, who recognize in him a public servant whose place it would not be very easy to supply.
We trust the President will reappoint Mr. Astwood United States Consul to San Domingo.
The Sun's correspondent states that the affairs of San Domingo are in a very unsettled condition, and anticipates that there will be an upheavel consequent upon the Presidential succession.

records.headline: The Capital retells how Senator Sumner turned against the annexation
records.summary_en: The Capital retells how Senator Sumner turned against the annexation scheme: the stipulation was read aloud by an officer styled in the protocol 'aide-de-camp of His Excellency Gen. Ulysses S. Grant,' and when the reading reached the words by which President Grant promised 'perfectly to use all his influence in order that the idea of annexing the Dominican Republic to the United States may acquire such a degree of popularity among the members of Congress as will be necessary for its accomplishment,' Sumner showed signs of disapprobation — from that reading, the piece says, Sumner became the enemy of the whole scheme. The anecdote is printed inside a larger appeal for harmony between the President and Congress and for a united, forgiving Republican party.

La anécdota viene impresa dentro de un llamamiento más amplio a la armonía entre el Presidente y el Congreso y a un Partido Republicano unido y dispuesto a perdonar.

Additionally, the source stated that the island's primary need is capital, noting that New York capitalists are currently considering propositions to establish a local bank and build a railroad to develop the interior.

Tuthill's Successor.
WASHINGTON CITY, May 22.—The president informed Congressmen Ward and Lawler, Thursday, that District Attorney Tuthill's successor would not be named for at least six weeks. He assured the two representatives that the new district attorney should be a resident of Chicago, and hoped that he might see his way clear to the appointment of their candidate, Mr. Jamieson. Mr. Ward says all the Illinois congressmen with the exception of Col. Townshend have agreed to sign a petition favoring Mr. Jamieson's appointment, and that this will be presented to the president by Col. Morrison.
Consul Recognized.
WASHINGTON CITY, May 22.—The president has recognized Carlos Lemale as consul of the Dominican republic at Chicago.

records.full_text:
SAN DOMINGO SUGAR.
Judge Coxe Decides that it Cannot be Brought In Free of Duty.
Judge Coxe of the United States Court decided yesterday in favor of the Government the suit of Joseph Netherclift & Co., one of a number of similar suits, in which San Domingo sugar importers seek to recover customs duties aggregating many hundred thousand dollars which their counsel argue was levied in violation of treaty obligations and of the tariff act of 1883. The treaty made with San Domingo in 1867 said that "no higher or other duties shall be imposed on the importations into the United States of any articles, the growth, produce, or manufacture of San Domingo, than are or shall be payable in like articles, the growth of any foreign country."
The treaty with Hawaii of 1873 made sugar free, and it was claimed that San Domingo sugar ought also to be free. Judge Wallace decided otherwise in the Bartram case, now before the Supreme Court. Congress, in 1883, declared that nothing in the Tariff act should "in any way change or impair the force or effect of any treaty between the United States and any other Government," and it was under this act that the present suits were brought.
Judge Coxe says that at the date of the act Congress found the Hawaiian treaty in full operation, a treaty which made the ports of the United States free to a group of Pacific Ocean islands, upon the express condition, however, that the island ports should be open to a much larger number of articles of United States growth and manufacture. No other similar treaty was in operation. San Domingo sugar had paid duty for sixteen years. The aim of the lawmakers was to have unchanged and unimpaired the existing state of things.
"It is hardly supposable," says the Judge, "that it was their purpose to make sweeping changes in the law, to open our ports without advantage or consideration to the industry of many countries, to destroy a vast source of revenue, and to encourage fraud by making the Dominican republic the dumping ground for the sugar and molasses of the West Indies."
District Attorney Walker and Assistant District Attorney Thomas Greenwood appeared for the Government.

records.full_text:
AFFAIRS IN SAN DOMINGO.
The Revolution is Over and Gen. Herreux is Complete Master of the Situation.
The San Domingo revolution is over, and Gen. Herreux, for the Government, has again been victorious. The leaders of the revolution are all fugitives. Gens. Moza and Moncion, with some of the others, are in Fort aux Paix, Hayti, where they are held prisoners by the Haytian Government, and Gen. Pablo Villeneuve is in the south trying to make some conditions for surrender.
Herreux was too strong for them. Besides being better supplied with arms, money, and men, he had such a reputation as a fighter that it appears when he personally was in the field it was impossible to make the revolutionists stand their ground. In the beginning the revolutionists gained some important victories, and many thought that the issue was doubtful. With very few exceptions, the white and better class of the people were in sympathy with the Moza or revolutionary party. The latter part of last month and the beginning of this signaled a series of successes for the Government troops. While matters were at the worst for the Mozaists, a number of the young men in the city of Santo Domingo began securing arms and making arrangements for the seizing of the city. A boy, who was employed as messenger, and who was thoroughly in the confidence of the conspirators, was arrested by the authorities, who had some information or suspicion as to what was in progress. He was taken to the fort, a file of soldiers was told off, and he was informed that he had the alternative of confessing all that he knew or being shot in half an hour. He confessed, and that evening the Government authorities arrested about sixty young men who were implicated.

records.headline: THE DOMINICAN REVOLUTION. CONSUL H. C. C. ASTWOOD’S ESTIMATE OF PRESIDENT CLEVELAND. He Thinks Blaine the Republican Giant—Cleveland Alone Can Stand against Him—Description of the Dominican Election and the Subsequent Revolution.
records.summary_en: Writing from Santo Domingo on December 3, 1886, United States Consul H. C. C. Astwood gives T. Thomas Fortune of The Freeman his reading of American politics—Cleveland's fairness to Black citizens, Blaine's strength for 1888—and then a full account of the Dominican election: Heureaux, the candidate of the masses, beat Casimiro N. de Moya by twenty thousand votes; Moya's party rose in arms under Benito Monción, and Heureaux's march through La Vega, Moca and Santiago ended the revolt. Astwood notes that the color line appeared in a Dominican contest for the first time.
records.summary_es: En carta desde Santo Domingo, el 3 de diciembre de 1886, el cónsul de los Estados Unidos H. C. C. Astwood ofrece a T. Thomas Fortune, de The Freeman, su lectura de la política estadounidense—la equidad de Cleveland hacia los ciudadanos negros, la fuerza de Blaine para 1888—y luego un relato completo de la elección dominicana: Heureaux, el candidato de las masas, venció a Casimiro N. de Moya por veinte mil votos; el partido de Moya se alzó en armas bajo Benito Monción, y la marcha de Heureaux por La Vega, Moca y Santiago puso fin a la revuelta. Astwood observa que la línea de color apareció por primera vez en una contienda dominicana.

records.full_text:
THE DOMINICAN REVOLUTION.

CONSUL H. C. C. ASTWOOD'S ESTIMATE OF PRESIDENT CLEVELAND.

He Thinks Blaine the Republican Giant—Cleveland Alone Can Stand against Him—Description of the Dominican Election and the Subsequent Revolution.

The following personal letter from United States Consul H. C. C. Astwood was received in November. There were so many things of interest in it that we wrote to Mr. Astwood asking his permission to publish the same which was given in a letter just received dated San Domingo, Dec. 3, 1886. Mr. Astwood said:

"My Dear Friend Fortune:--I received your communication by last mail and noted its contents; my not writing to you before was caused by a combination of circumstances, over which I had no control, principally my recent illness of more than a month's duration and of which I have just recovered. I receive THE FREEMAN regularly; it is a welcome visitor, I like its manly tone and I am glad of the increasing favor which it seems to be gathering and the favorable criticism it receives from many of the white journals, but I do not want you to think that I endorse its politics; because you know I am a Republican—I do not mean a slave to the party but that I am an adherent to its principles.

Of course I think with you that the day of sentimentalism is past and that the Negro must stand or fall upon his merits just as any other American citizen. He cannot do anything by dividing up in factions. He must learn the art of organization and cohesion and fight for his rights; by the force of the unity which alone can give force.

The present Democratic administration is not a fair test of the policy of that party. Mr. Cleveland is an extraordinary man, and would be an exceptional one in the ranks of any party. The individual who does not admire him is simply blind to all reason and fairness. I think he has gone further in demonstrating his partiality to the Negro than any President that I have known since Grant. There does not seem to be anything truckling or mean about him. He is outspoken and candid. His letter to Stewart was a manly demonstration of this fact; his action in the Matthews' case was surprising, looking at it from a general political standpoint; the courtesies he extended to Douglass, the acknowledged leading Negro of the country, were so marked that it must have caused our white Republican brethren to blush with shame. I have learned to admire and respect the man, but I think that these actions are the outcoming of the individual honesty of the man rather than the principles of his party. I have in my experience only come in contact with one other individual like him in any party. That is Governor Porter, present Assistant Secretary of State. These men at heart are Republicans of Republicans.

The political outlook in our country is becoming complicated. The many organizations which are developing strength will cause the two great parties to be very circumspect in their actions, and there is none that seems to be more alarming than that of the labor organizations. Powderly, the chief of the Knights of Labor, heretofore an obscure man, is becoming to be a central figure. His action at the recent Richmond Convention cannot fail to bear fruit. What a lesson to the colored brother!

The contest of '88 will be a remarkable one, in my judgment. Notwithstanding your criticisms, and you know I respect them as I do you, yet I see the handwriting on the wall, that Blaine will be the nominee of the Republican party. There is no good of being prejudiced against facts. He is the brainiest and most astute statesman in our political ranks. You know I have always been an anti-Blaine man; but facts are facts. Looking over the field and comparing all of our great Republican lights, Conkling and Arthur being out of the way, the latter would have been strong for his Grant proclivities, the former for his great ability—leaves Blaine alone as the great giant of the Republican party. I predict that he will go into the convention with three-fourths of the colored delegations from the South. In the Democratic party, he can find only one opponent—that is Cleveland. Can Cleveland be nominated? If he can then comes the tug of war, because, if he makes no mistakes between this and election day, he will draw from all parties; and I think he will be a stronger independent candidate than he could possibly be from the convention of any party. The working man's position in the next campaign will be the perplexing one; the party which can secure it in its entirety will certainly be the successful one.

The recent political contest here was interesting, and for the first time and unfortunately so the color-line made its appearance. The young men of this city have learned in recent years by foreign association to consider themselves white, and they have been learning gradually to discriminate. They are the educated class. The masses, who are in the majority blacks, neglected this important factor in making the nominations recently. General Heureaux, the most popular and able man of this country and a valiant military chief, was nominated as the representative of the masses. General Casimira N. de Moya was nominated as the elite candidate. Electoral committees were formed all over the country and the largest latitude possible was allowed by the Government to these committees. You know that the election here is by popular vote. The Moya crowd made large and expensive demonstrations by processions and otherwise, and it did seem from these demonstrations that their candidate would have been elected by an overwhelming majority. They laid great stress upon the fact that the time had come when the country could be no longer ruled by the Negro. Heureaux refused to make a single demonstration, but organized quietly, and it did seem like a wet blanket. In this city the so-called whites have a large majority. On election day Moya took up his headquarters in the inland city of La Vega and Heureaux established his in this city. During the three days of election the greatest enthusiasm prevailed, and when the result was declared it was found that Heureaux had carried the country by twenty thousand majority. Moya and his principal followers were so much surprised and chagrined, that they refused to accept the result and before Congress could meet to count and declare the vote, they resorted to arms as a means of gaining the control of the Government. The city of La Vega revolted on the 21st of July. It was immediately followed or responded to by the District of Monti Christi and the Haytien Frontiers, under the lead of the great Chief Benito Muncion, whose will no Government had heretofore dared to question, or even to inquire into his gubernatorial actions. This of course gave the revolution at once formidable proportions and its success did seem inevitable.

General Heureaux, the daring, mounted his horse on the 29th of the same month, followed by one thousand men. His ranks were swelled all along the route and in the early days of August he surrounded the city of La Vega. The night preceding his well planned attack upon that city Moya and his followers became alarmed and evacuated the city, taking refuge in the Mountains of Jarabacoa. Heureaux entered the city the next morning without firing a shot. The contest then became fearful, almost a hand to hand struggle, but this daring man pushed on; the enemy fleeing before him in every direction. He passed through the city of Moca, reached Santiago and then encountered Muncion with all of his forces in front of this important city, the largest and wealthiest of the country. Moncion fought desperately. He was fighting for his home and his fortune and the district that he had so despotically ruled ever since the dawn of this Republic; but he was forced to fly and took refuge across the Haytien frontiers, from which country he has gone into exile. He has by his foolish ambition lost all of the prestige he had gained in a lifetime. Heureaux's victory is complete and he stands before the country as one of the most remarkable men in connection with its history. I am glad of this. It is another evidence of the Negro's superior ability and tact whenever an equal chance is afforded him. I have written you at such great length that I must now bring my communication to a close. With my best regards to you and yours, I am with great respect, your friend,

H. C. C. ASTWOOD."

records.summary_en: President Grant and Senator Sumner misunderstood each other during a meeting, with Grant referring to the treaty for the acquisition of the Dominican Republic while Sumner believed they were discussing General Babcock's expenditures of $100,000 in cash and $24,000 for a light battery. The following morning, General Babcock visited Senator Sumner with a copy of the treaty, but Sumner showed immediate signs of disapproval upon hearing the preamble and the stipulation regarding President Grant's influence to secure congressional popularity for the annexation.
records.summary_es: El presidente Grant y el senador Sumner sufrieron una confusión recíproca durante una reunión: Grant aludía al tratado para la adquisición de la República Dominicana, en tanto que Sumner entendió que deliberaban acerca de las erogaciones del general Babcock, ascendentes a 100.000 pesos en efectivo y 24.000 para una batería ligera. A la mañana siguiente, Babcock entregó al senador Sumner un ejemplar del convenio, manifestando el legislador su inmediata repulsa nada más conocer el preámbulo y la estipulación relativa al influjo presidencial para concitar el respaldo legislativo a la anexión.

records.full_text:
The recent publications by General Badeau on the relations of Grant and Sumner give especial pertinency to the following episode of the San Domingo difficulty. The evening before the treaty was sent to the Senate, General Grant called at Sumner's house and found the Senator at dinner with John W. Forney and Major Poore. The President joined the party at table:
After some preliminary conversation, General Grant began to talk about San Domingo, but he did not have the treaty or any memorandum of it with him. He dwelt especially upon the expenditures of General Babcock at San Domingo of a large sum taken from a secret service fund for promoting intercourse with the West India Islands, which Mr. Seward, when Secretary of State, had prevailed on Representative Thad Stevens to have inserted in an appropriation bill during the war. The President impressed Mr. Sumner with the idea that he looked for an attack in Congress on the manner in which much of that money had been spent. Mr. Sumner unquestionably thought that General Grant had come to enlist his services in defending the expenditure by General Babcock of $100,000 in cash, and $50,000 for a light battery purchased at New-York. The President meant, as Colonel Forney and the writer thought, the treaty for the acquisition of the Dominican Republic. The President and the Senator misunderstood each other. After awhile General Grant promised to send General Babcock to the Senator the next day with copies of the papers, and then left. While escorting the President to the door, Mr. Sumner assured him that he was a Republican and a supporter of the Republican Administration, and that he should sustain the Administration in this case if he possibly could, after he had examined the papers. He meant the expenditure of General Babcock, but the President meant the treaty.

records.headline: Condensed Despatches.
records.summary_en: The president recognized Carlos Jumion as consul of the Dominican Republic at New York. This was reported alongside various other national and international news items in the February 4, 1887 issue of *The Evening Telegram*.
records.summary_es: El dignatario reconoció a Carlos Jumion en calidad de cónsul de la República Dominicana en Nueva York. La reseña se publicó entre diversas noticias del ámbito nacional y foráneo en la edición del 4 de febrero de 1887 de *The Evening Telegram*.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on the Santo Domingo Central Railroad Company, a corporation organized by New York businessmen under the Foreign Railroad Act of 1883 with a capital of $500,000, which secured valuable concessions and a twenty-year tax exemption from the Dominican Government. General Horatio C. King serves as president, with General King and Henry L. Bean conducting most of the negotiations for the franchise, which was recently amended by the Dominican National Congress to require construction to begin within two years and finish within ten.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* dio cuenta de la fundación de la Santo Domingo Central Railroad Company, corporación constituida por financieros neoyorquinos al amparo de la Ley de Ferrocarriles Extranjeros de 1883 con un capital social de 500.000 dólares, la cual obtuvo del Gobierno dominicano valiosas franquicias y una exención impositiva por veinte años. El general Horatio C. King ocupa la presidencia, habiendo gestionado junto a Henry L. Bean la mayor parte de las cláusulas de la concesión, modificada hace poco por el Congreso Nacional dominicano para estipular que la explanación de las vías se inicie en el plazo de dos años y concluya en un decenio.

Its officers and stockholders are mostly business men of this city. General Horatio C. King is the president, George Ward, of the Commercial Cable Company, vice president, Philip I. Harris, treasurer, [James?] E. Coleman, secretary, and Henry L. Bean, president of the Santo Domingo Rock Salt Company, general superintendent. Among its trustees are General John S. Woodward, Ogden P. Pell, Henry W. Alden, of the Fourth National Bank, William H. Bibby and Daniel [illegible] Wood. General King and Mr. Bean have conducted most of the negotiations with the Dominican Government, and it was to them, in behalf of the company, that the concessions were granted. The franchise was really obtained nearly a year ago, but as it was not entirely satisfactory to the company, some of its clauses were changed at the company's request by the late National Congress of the Dominican Republic. As amended, the franchise provides that the work of constructing the road shall be started inside of two years and finished within ten years. WHAT THE DOMINICAN GOVERNMENT IS WILLING TO GIVE—RESOURCES OF THE ISLAND.
For some time negotiations have been carried on between the Government of Santo Domingo and a company organized under the laws of this State for the purpose of building a railroad through that island. The company sought certain concessions from the Santo Domingo authorities, which have at last been granted. They embody a gift of each alternate section of land four miles square along the line of the proposed road (about 500,000 acres in all), besides several other valuable privileges, such as the exemption of the company from the payment of import and export duties or, in fact, taxes of any kind for at least twenty years.
The Santo Domingo Central Railroad Company, as the corporation that has obtained these grants is called, was organized under the Foreign Railroad act...

records.summary_en: A speaker at an event, identifying as a fifty-year-old Democrat, publicly praised Mr. Astwood and expressed a desire for him to remain in his position as United States Consul at San Domingo. The speaker also asserted that the colored race can demonstrate the capability to occupy any position held by a white man, and that existing prejudices among white people can be easily overcome.
records.summary_es: Un orador, que se proclamó demócrata de cincuenta años, encomió públicamente al Sr. Astwood e hizo votos por su confirmación en el cargo de cónsul de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo. Proclamó además que la raza negra reúne sobrada capacidad para desempeñar cualquier dignidad detentada por el hombre blanco y que las prevenciones raciales de estos últimos se pueden disipar con facilidad.
records.passage: am, when I became acquainted with this gentleman on my left (Mr. Astwood) it gave me very great pleasure to write to the President, although he was a Republican, he was the right man in the right place, and that it would be a personal favor to me if he continued him in the position of United States Consul at San Domingo. (Applause.) A longer and better acquaintance with him has assured me that he is still the right man in the right place, and though I am a Democrat of the Democrats, fifty years old and [illegible] a Democrat, I have not changed my opinion in regard to Mr. Astwood, and I am ready and shall always be ready to stand by him, as I have done from the first instance. (Voices: "Hear, hear.") Now I suppose it might be excusable in me on an occasion of this kind to say exactly what I feel, and I think that I can say with a better grace, because I belong to that party which is supposed to be opposed to the advancement of the colored race in this country, that I think that there is but one thing for the colored race to show, and that is that they are capable to occupy any of the positions in this country which a white man can occupy. records.full_text:
Mr. Langston spoke as follows:
Gentlemen: I understand that the object of this occasion is to honor my friend who sits opposite to me, whom I have known a long time; whom I have known very intimately. I have known him in Louisiana, I have known him in the walks of political life in this country, I have known him in the ways of religion, as a pulpit orator, as the pastor of a flourishing church; I have known him as I have seen him, as I have been with him in his work as United States Consul at San Domingo; I have eaten in his house, I have slept in his house; I have seen him in his office, I have seen him with Presidents, I have seen him with diplomats, I have seen him with Consular officers, I have seen him in war, and I have seen him in peace. I have seen him defending American citizens and I have seen him caring for them after they have been abused; I have known of his winding up their cases with honor to himself and with credit to his Government, maintaining in dignity the authority and the power of his Government, and those great chiefs who stood over him.

records.headline: Honoring Consul Astwood
records.summary_en: The author of the article states that San Domingo is the finest island in the Antilles and the only republic in the island group—aside from Hayti—that maintains its sovereignty free from European dictation. Despite being portrayed in American journals as a revolutionary and barbarous country, the author argues that its political revolutions are less destructive to life and property than United States labor strikes. Furthermore, the writer notes that the island possesses a vast territory with a population under 400,000, and aims to correct misrepresentations regarding the commerce between the two countries.
records.summary_es: El articulista califica a Santo Domingo como la isla más rica de las Antillas y la única república insular —fuera de Haití— que preserva su soberanía exenta de tutela europea. Frente a la estampa que la prensa estadounidense divulga como comarca bárbara y sediciosa, arguye el autor que sus revueltas políticas ocasionan menos estragos a la vida y la propiedad que las huelgas obreras de los Estados Unidos. Subraya por añadidura que la isla encierra un vasto suelo patrio con una población inferior a los cuatrocientos mil habitantes, teniendo por propósito su escrito rectificar los falsos juicios esparcidos sobre el comercio entre ambos países.

San Domingo, which in my judgment is the very finest island in the Antilles or New World, is little known to the majority of our people, although it is the first island upon which Columbus, the great discoverer, founded a city in the New World; and, strange to say, it is the only Republic on this continent in the group of islands outside of Hayti which maintains its sovereignty free from all encumbrances of foreign or European dictation. My friends, I cannot find words to express to you my thanks for this very high compliment paid to me, in my official capacity, by you gentlemen, and the honor you do me in bringing me on an occasion like this in relations with the honorable gentlemen that surround this board, and inviting me to speak upon a subject so important as the commercial relations between San Domingo and the United States. records.summary_en: According to *The New York Freeman* on May 14, 1887, a speaker at a meeting credited President Heureux of the Dominican Republic, Minister of Foreign Nations M. M. Guetieu, and the Minister of Public Improvements for offering inducements to United States capitalists to develop the Dominican Republic's resources. The speaker asserted that erroneous reports had been circulated by designing individuals to discredit the country and maintain a monopoly, to the detriment of commercial relations between San Domingo and the United States.
records.summary_es: Según *The New York Freeman* del 14 de mayo de 1887, un orador ensalzó al mandatario Heureaux de la República Dominicana, al ministro de Relaciones Exteriores M. M. Gautier y al ministro de Fomento por brindar garantías a los capitalistas estadounidenses para la explotación de las riquezas dominicanas. Aseveró el tribuno que individuos malintencionados propagaban especies falsas para desprestigiar a la nación y perpetuar un monopolio comercial, con grave quebranto de las relaciones mercantiles entre Santo Domingo y los Estados Unidos.

I trust, gentlemen, that this meeting here to-night will be the means of the beginning of an investigation which will go far in determining and developing all of these great enterprises now contemplated by our people, and in which a great many here present are positively interested. If I have done anything, gentlemen, to merit the high honor conferred upon me by you in tendering me this compliment to-night, it has been by the humble efforts which I have put forth in behalf of my country and people, in developing that happy condition of affairs, both commercial and otherwise, existing to-day between the people of the United States and San Domingo. Too much cannot be said in behalf of the efforts put forth by President Heureux of the Dominican Republic and its Minister of Foreign Nations, the Hon. M. M. Guetieu, and the Minister of Public Improvements, in holding out inducements to our capitalists to assist in developing the rich resources of the Dominican Republic, and I trust that the erroneous reports which have been circulated dully by designing individuals, who are not anxious to see capitalists of the United States invest in this important country, but are doing all in their power to discredit the country, to maintain a strict and meagre monopoly to the detriment of the commercial relations not only of San Domingo but of the United States — I hope that these schemers will be unmasked and that our people will be led to see the true condition of affairs as has
records.full_text: The many American enterprises now undertaken by our people, if carried into effect in good faith, cannot fail to build up a large business within a very few years. The San Domingo Central Railroad, whose President and Vice-President sit at this board, starting in at the point of Barahona, crossing the Great Salt Mountains twenty-one miles from the terminus, passing through the District of Neiba with its immense mahogany forests and other valuable woods, thence through the fertile region known as the St. John's Valley, crossing the mountain range over to Sabanata, going through the fertile district of Guyabin with its immense pine, log-wood and other forests, would be an immense outlet to the commodities of this country, to say nothing of the hundreds of thousands of acres of land that would be thrown open to emigrants from this and other countries for the production of tropical fruits, cotton, etc., in great abundance. The fruit industry to be established at Samana Bay by the Bay State Fruit Company of Boston, of which Willis M. Snow is president, and the other Northern ports of the Island, will be a great factor in connection with its commerce, to say nothing of the immense tract of land contracted for by a Boston syndicate upon the Romana Cumayasa and Chabon Rivers, in the District of Seybo, represented by Hiram Newcomb and Edgar R. Champlin, where a Winter resort will be established upon the most picturesque and fertile region known in the New World. Negotiations are also being effected with capitalists of the United States for bettering the financial condition of the country which if successfully carried out will at once establish the commercial destiny of San Domingo, and in the course of a very few years the business will be increased from a few millions to scores of millions.

records.headline: Honoring Consul Astwood
records.summary_en: Mr. Langston delivered a speech at an event honoring a longtime friend and former subordinate who served as the United States Consul at San Domingo. In his remarks, Langston praised the consul's extensive work in politics, religion, war, and peace, specifically highlighting his defense and care of American citizens in San Domingo while maintaining the dignity and authority of the United States government.
records.summary_es: El Sr. Langston pronunció una alocución con motivo de un homenaje rendido a un antiguo allegado y subalterno que se desempeñó como cónsul de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo. En sus consideraciones, Langston ensalzó las dilatadas ejecutorias del cónsul en la política, la religión, la guerra y la paz, ponderando singularmente su desvelo en la guarda de los ciudadanos estadounidenses en Santo Domingo sin menoscabo del decoro y la soberanía del gobierno norteamericano.
