records.full_text:
The handsomely furnished ladies' parlor of the Stevens House, No. 27 Broadway, New York City, on Friday evening, May 6, was draped with national and Dominican flags, from the folds of which hung in a frame of plush a genial looking picture of Hon. H. C. C. Astwood, United States Consul at San Domingo, to whom the Rev. Wm. B. Derrick, D D., and Editor T. Thos. Fortune had tendered a complimentary reception and banquet. Covers were laid for twenty and an extra table for the press representatives was provided in a side room. The menu was as follows:

MENU.

Little Neck clams — Sauterne

Potages

Green turtle — Consomme a la royale — Sherry

Varies — Hors d'oeuvre — Varies

Brissotins au supreme

Poisson

Broiled brook trout a la meuniere — Claret

Stuffed olives — Parisian potatoes

Releve

Tenderloin of beef a la financiere

Tomates farcies

Entree

Supreme of spring chicken a la Chambord

Potatoes en surprise — French green peas

Niersteiner

Sorbet

Punch a la romaine

Game

English snipe sur canape — Macon

Asparagus, hollandaise

Roast

Spring lamb, mint sauce — Salad

String beans — Champagne

Cold

Foie-gras aux truffes — Aspic of lobster

Entremets sucres

Cream diplomate — Pudding a la Montpensier

Omelette soufflee a la rouennaise

Fruits and dessert — Cafe

Liqueurs and cigars.

About this table, laden with the rarest viands and fragrant with the perfume of a profusion of variegated floral designs and boutonnieres, sat men noted in every walk of life, and the sparkling speeches that fell from the lips of renowned orators carried the hotel back to the days of its glory, in the Dutch epoch of Manhattan Island. At the head of the table sat Editor Fortune; on his right Mr. Astwood, followed by Gen. Horatio C. King, President of the San Domingo Railway. On Mr. Fortune's left was Hon. Chas. Julian, Consul of the Dominican Republic at New York; next came Hon. John Mercer Langston, ex-Minister to Hayti and President of the Virginia Normal and Collegiate Institute. At the other end of the table was Dr. Derrick, on whose left sat Hon. E. D. Bassett, Consul-General of the Haytian Government at New York; Prof. H. M. Joseph of Antigua, W. I.; Lawyer T. McCants Stewart, Prof. Chas. L. Reason, Dr. B. W. Arnett, member of the Ohio Legislature, Prof. C. A. Dorsey, H. L. Bean, R. Henri Herbert of Trenton, N. J.; Jerome B. Peterson of THE FREEMAN, James Grant of Wanamaker & Co., Philadelphia; Rev. Wm. H. Dickerson, pastor of Siloam Presbyterian Church, Brooklyn; Charles Julian, Jr., and E. G. Morrell of the Dominican Consulate, and N. McKay. When ample justice had been done the gastronomic feast, toasts were proposed and responded to, Mr. Fortune acting as master of ceremonies.

In response to the toast of "Our Guest," Mr. Astwood delivered the following speech on the subject of commercial relations between San Domingo and the United States:

Mr. Derrick and Mr. Fortune:

My friends, I cannot find words to express to you my thanks for this very high compliment paid to me, in my official capacity, by you gentlemen, and the honor you do me in bringing me on an occasion like this in relations with the honorable gentlemen that surround this board, and inviting me to speak upon a subject so important as the commercial relations between San Domingo and the United States. Time would fail me to handle this important subject in all its details and in which the interests of the two countries are so much involved, but I will as briefly as possible present a few facts which, I hope, will go far toward explaining away a great many misrepresentations and misstatements in connection with the commerce of the two countries.

San Domingo, which in my judgment is the very finest island in the Antilles or New World, is little known to the majority of our people, although it is the first island upon which Columbus, the great discoverer, founded a city in the New World; and, strange to say, it is the only Republic on this continent in the group of islands outside of Hayti which maintains its sovereignty free from all encumbrances of foreign or European dictation. Although when first discovered this beautiful island contained an inhabitance of several millions of people, yet to-day the Dominican Republic with its vast area of territory, with its fertile and unexplored forests of valuable woods and minerals, has a population of less than four hundred thousand. Its commercial relations with the United States are little known, as I have already stated, to a majority of our people. San Domingo is often considered in the columns of our journals as a revolutionary and barbarous country. This is an error; they have their periodical political troubles, and sometimes they resort to the sword or to war to settle these difficulties; but these revolutions are less destructive to life and property than our labor strikes. History cannot show a single instance where the Dominicans have ever molested foreign property, or have ever maltreated the person of a foreigner during their political upheavals. The name of San Domingo is often mixed up with that of other countries. This is unfortunate as far as the people of that Republic are concerned. A more friendly, docile and magnanimous people cannot be found anywhere in the world; with a government as liberal as that of the United States, the foreigner having every facility and right given by any civilized government.

The principal products of San Domingo are the valuable woods of its native forests, such as mahogany, lignum vitæ, fustic, satin wood, and too many others to mention; tobacco, sugar, beeswax, honey, rum, hides, coffee, cocoa, etc., etc., and the largest number of tropical fruits imaginable. Its soil is fertile in the extreme, capable of the most extensive production, and it only requires capital, railroads and immigration to make it the very finest and wealthiest island in the West Indies. Its government is liberal in the extreme, and I was pleased to  meet in the city to-day one of its representative men in the person of General Luperon, who has left no stone unturned to encourage and protect the interests of the foreigner in the Dominican Republic; and no abler executive can be found than General Heureaux, the present President of that country, who is especially friendly and interested in the commercial relations with the United States.

In dealing with this question it would be necessary to give a few figures to see how, or to what extent, the trade has increased. Ten years ago importations from the United States were in a measure small, most of the trade then being with the little Danish Island of St. Thomas, from which all the provisions and merchandise were brought, the principal markets being Germany, Spain, England and Italy. I think by actual statistics the business between San Domingo and the United States at that period was less than half a million of dollars for the whole Republic; the value exported to the United States being really nothing but a few cargos of wood, the entire tobacco crop being shipped to Europe. Since that time trade has increased immensely, and in my District alone, we find the following figures:

In the year 1884—Merchandise, $86,802.28; machinery, $48,857.73; provisions, $253,883.45; hardware, $24,424.70; sundries, $30,000; liquors, $4,278.65; lumber, $31,818.53; lime, $6,948.27; bricks, $4,060; specie, $69,980; making a total $561,064.11 imported from the United States. Imports from foreign countries: In the year 1884—Merchandise, $213,611.91; provisions, $117,816.10; liquors, $33,847.44; lumber, $3,740.25; machinery, $22,312.63; hardware, $37,726.80; zinc and copper, $28,896.71; bricks, $2,214.70; sardines, $54,553.35; total, $521,692.89, leaving, you see, a considerable balance in favor of the United States. Since then, these figures have increased quite 50 per cent., which will be seen by the next official report.

The imports and exports varied as follows during the years 1881, 1882, 1883 and 1885: 1881—imports, $683,700.45; exports, $808,349.54. 1882—imports, $936,154.42; exports, $1,084,379.64. 1883—imports, $1,235,887.96; exports, $1,422,665.83. 1885—imports, $1,118,759.01; exports, over a million and a half of dollars.

The statistics for the whole island will show about the same proportion as that of the Consular District of San Domingo, and it can be seen at once that closer commercial relations between San Domingo and the United States are desirable for our people. The Reciprocal Treaty proposed by that Government and celebrated by it and Secretary Frelinghuysen about three years ago, if ratified, would build up an immense commerce between San Domingo and the United States and would be the stepping stone to a monopoly of all the business between the West Indies and South American Republics. And, besides, its fine harbors, notably that of Samana Bay, would be a splendid coaling and commercial station for our naval, as well as commercial fleet, and I am certain if a treaty of reciprocity was celebrated between these two countries, such an acquisition would be feasible on the part of the United States. This would be the gateway or the key of the world's commerce with the Isthmus of Panama.

The many American enterprises now undertaken by our people, if carried into effect in good faith, cannot fail to build up a large business within a very few years. The San Domingo Central Railroad, whose President and Vice-President sit at this board, starting in at the point of Barahona, crossing the Great Salt Mountains twenty-one miles from the terminus, passing through the District of Neiba with its immense mahogany forests and other valuable woods, thence through the fertile region known  as the St. John's Valley, crossing the mountain range over to Sabanata, going through the fertile district of Guyabin with its immense pine, log-wood and other forests, would be an immense outlet to the commodities of this country, to say nothing of the hundreds of thousands of acres of land that would be thrown open to emigrants from this and other countries for the production of tropical fruits, cotton, etc., in great abundance. The fruit industry to be established at Samana Bay by the Bay State Fruit Company of Boston, of which Willis M. Snow is president, and the other Northern ports of the Island, will be a great factor in connection with its commerce, to say nothing of the immense tract of land contracted for by a Boston syndicate upon the Romana, Cumayasa and Chabon Rivers, in the District of Seybo, represented by Hiram Newcomb and Edgar R. Champlin, where a Winter resort will be established upon the most picturesque and fertile region known in the New World. Negotiations are also being effected with capitalists of the United States for bettering the financial condition of the country which if successfully carried out will at once establish the commercial destiny of San Domingo, and in the course of a very few years the business will be increased from a few millions to scores of millions.

I trust, gentlemen, that this meeting here to-night will be the means of the beginning of an investigation which will go far in determining and developing all of these great enterprises now contemplated by our people, and in which a great many here present are positively interested. If I have done anything, gentlemen, to merit the high honor conferred upon me by you in tendering me this compliment to-night, it has been by the humble efforts which I have put forth in behalf of my country and people, in developing that happy condition of affairs, both commercial and otherwise, existing to-day between the people of the United States and San Domingo. Too much cannot be said in behalf of the efforts put forth by President Heureux of the Dominican Republic and its Minister of Foreign Nations, the Hon. M. M. Guetieu, and the Minister of Public Improvements, in holding out inducements to our capitalists to assist in developing the rich resources of the Dominican Republic, and I trust that the erroneous reports which have been circulated daily by designing individuals, who are not anxious to see capitalists of the United States invest in this important country, but are doing all in their power to discredit the country, to maintain a strict and meagre monopoly to the detriment of the commercial relations not only of San Domingo but of the United States—I hope that these schemers will be unmasked and that our people will be led to see the true condition of affairs as has been represented from time to time in our reports to the Department of State at Washington. You will be astonished when I tell you, gentlemen, that foreign capitalists to-day are controlling the finances of San Domingo and forcing that government to pay an interest of from three per cent. to five per cent. a month, and they have been willing for the last eight or ten years to carry on this unmerciful and shylock speculation, and yet when the attention of foreign capitalists is called to the fact that they might invest safely and securely at a reasonable rate of interest, these people are always ready to raise the hue and cry that to invest in San Domingo is worse than throwing your money into the sea; but still they are contented to remain themselves and feast upon the fatted calf. I have done all in my power to destroy these base influences, and I feel that the time is fast approaching when our people, upon a close investigation will see the underlying causes for these discrediting reports, and will at once come to the rescue of this struggling and meritorious country. Hoping, gentlemen, that what I have said will be sufficient to cause a deeper interest to be taken by our commercial men in the development of the commercial relations between San Domingo and the United States, and that our eminent divine, Dr. Derrick, and our fearless and independent editor, Mr. Fortune, will be participants in gathering of the golden harvest to be reaped from our commercial, religious, educational and industrial progress which might possibly be precipitated by this important private gathering so happily brought about by their laudable efforts.

When the health of the President of the Dominican Republic was proposed, Consul Chas. Julian arose and said: "I beg to express myself in Spanish and to toast to 'Do your best and leave the rest.'" He then spoke in Spanish, and half the gentlemen being versed in that tongue, expressed their approval by constant applause.

The toast "The President of the United States" was then proposed and Lawyer T. McCants Stewart on rising to respond to this sentiment, said:

Gentlemen, I am too full for utterance (laughter); and yet I am not alone, for we have all freely indulged in a flow of spirits (laughter). Of course, I mean animal spirits not liquid spirits (laughter); for following the example of my esteemed friend, Editor Fortune, I have confined myself to water on this occasion (laughter). We certainly have had a rich feast. It has been enjoyable from the Little Neck clams clear down to the "toast" (laughter); and if the "toast" which we are now having should prove as excellent as the other dishes, I shall adopt the language of a good old hymn and say:

"My willing soul would stay In such a place as this."

(Great laughter).

Speaking as I do in the presence of Republicans, Democrats, Mugwumps and Negrowumps, I have to guard well my language and have an eye to the proprieties of the occasion; but gentlemen, it seems to me that in drinking the health of the President of the United States as we have done, we have risen above the narrow limits of  party and passed into the broad field of patriotism (applause). The Presidency of the United States is a great office, made so by the vastness of the country and the strength of the people. Think of what a vast area of territory stretches between ocean and ocean, and between where the lakes with their beauty lie on the North to where the Gulf rolls dark heaving on the South. Think of the variety of climate, the fertility of soil, the richness of resources; and think of the millions of citizens who are strong in their intelligence, stronger in their virtue, and stronger still in the aspirations which they feel in the battle of life, and then unite with me in declaring that the first citizen among such citizens and in such a country is a king among kings (applause).

The glory and strength of our political system whose centre is the President lies in the fact that the humblest boy may aspire to be President of the United States (applause). The bootblack, the paper-seller—anybody; and they see both their hope and inspiration in the fact that Lincoln was a rail splitter; that Grant was a tanner; that Garfield was a driver of mules on the canals of Ohio; and that Cleveland is of the people and from the people, having been a poor boy, the son of an humble minister of the Gospel.

No matter, gentlemen, what our nationality, our citizenship, our politics—be we West Indians, or Republicans, or Democrats, or Mugwumps, let us at this moment be Americans one and all, and let us rejoice that the President of the United States is an honest conscientious patriot, who is administering the government with wisdom and with justice (applause). He has kept the United States at peace with all the world without sacrificing one iota of our national manhood and self-respect; and if he continues the good work we shall remain at peace with the rest of mankind, using the language of President Taylor, I think, who in an annual message unwittingly said, "We are at peace with all the world, and we hope to maintain amicable relations with the rest of mankind" (laughter)—reminding us of the deacon who prayed—"Let the power of the Gospel be felt everywhere; let it extend to earth's remotest bounds; let this precious power be felt where the foot of man or beast never trod" (great laughter).

President Cleveland has strengthened commercial and business confidence by a sound financial policy; he has purified the public service; he has secured general and hearty admiration because of his habits of industry and earnest toil in the public service, and because all along the line of his administration there is honesty and cleanness (applause). But if we differ here, there is one act of President Cleveland that we all approve. It is the act entitled, "An act making a noble and gifted woman the first lady of the land." My reference to the President of the United States would be materially defective if I should fail to say, "All hail" to the President's wife, whose influence emanating from a noble soul is felt throughout the United States, and is destined to leap the limits of our Republic, and like that of the good Queen Victoria to be felt throughout the earth (applause).

Permit me, Mr. President, before sitting, to express my appreciation of the honor which you have done me in inviting me to join these distinguished gentlemen in meeting on this festive occasion the eminent Consul from the United States to San Domingo, our friend, Mr. Astwood. By force of character, by strength of intellect, by conscientious devotion to duty, our honored guest has won the respect and esteem of his countrymen and of the Dominicans, and he has forced even his opponents to feel and to express the highest admiration for him (applause). As I listened to  his able and instructive speech, and heard of the vast resources and growing prosperity of the island of San Domingo and Hayti, my mind reverted to the illustrious soldier and statesman, Toussaint L'Ouverture (great applause), who declared as he was borne an unwilling captive to the dungeons of the treacherous Napoleon, "I have planted the tree of liberty and independence so deep in my native soil that all France cannot root it up" (continued applause). That utterance was prophetic; for during all these generations there have stood strong and immovable the Republic of Hayti and the Republic of San Domingo, combining their light with that of our native country and illuminating the politically dark places of the earth, strengthening democracy in France, and weakening aristocracy and monarchism in Great Britain and Germany, and hastening the day when governments of the people, for the people and by the people shall prevail throughout the earth (great applause). Sustaining, encouraging and inspiring these West Indian Republics will be for all time to come the aim and effort of our own great country through its Chief Magistrate; and we shall have the power as well as the disposition to do this work; for in the generations to come, here upon this soil, dedicated to Liberty by the tears and blood of the patriots of the Revolution, and saved forever to Union and Freedom by the blood of the heroes of the Rebellion—here upon this sacred soil there will flourish such a republic as hath not entered even into the imagination of men—a republic greater than Greece and stronger than Rome, mighty in war, glorious in peace and enshrined in the affections of the people (continued applause).

The master of ceremonies then introduced the Hon. John Mercer Langston in the following remarks:

The next gentleman whom I shall call upon to address you, refreshes in my memory that which is significant of the flight of time. Eleven years ago, then quite a lad, athirst for knowledge in the far Southland, I wended my way by hook or crook to the city of Washington with Howard University in my mind's eye. When I reached Howard University, like many another poor colored boy from the South, my pocket was very empty (like it is to-night) (applause). Of course the first thing that imperatively impressed itself upon me was "ways and means." I was directed to the President of Howard University. I called upon the gentleman, and I found in him the gentleman whom I shall next call upon to address you. I stated my case to him and he made provision for me temporarily; subsequently I made my own provision. When I went to this gentleman he said to me: "Young man, your case is extreme; we have many such, but none so exaggerated; I will look out for you." He provided a shelter for me, he went my credit to the Treasurer of the Institution, and I am happy to say that in the course of time I liquidated all my debts. Eleven years ago I sat at home at the feet of John Mercer Langston, at Howard University. I was then a young man of twenty years of age, and I now have the extreme pleasure of introducing him to a body of gentlemen representative of all the walks of life as seen in the United States, from that of the mechanic to that of the banker and the merchant (a voice "and the Editor"). Notwithstanding this, gentlemen, I hardly need say anything eulogistic of him as he is so well known to you. But I feel it necessary to say that as lawyer in the State of Ohio, as agent of the Freedman's Bureau, as dean of the law department of Howard University, as a member of the Board of Health of the District of Columbia, as an attorney for that Board, and as United States Minister Resident and Consul-General for eight years to Hayti—I feel that in introducing to you a man of such wide and varied and extensive experience and learning no better subject could be selected than that which I shall now propose, "The Necessity for a School of Training for Diplomacy."

Mr. Langston spoke as follows:

Gentlemen: I understand that the object of this occasion is to honor my friend who sits opposite to me, whom I have known a long time; whom I have known very intimately. I have known him in Louisiana, I have known him in the walks of political life in this country, I have known him in the ways of religion, as a pulpit orator, as the pastor of a flourishing church; I have known him as I have seen him, as I have been with him in his work as United States Consul at San Domingo; I have eaten in his house, I have slept in his house; I have seen him in his office, I have seen him with Presidents, I have seen him with diplomats, I have seen him with Consular officers, I have seen him in war, and I have seen him in peace. I have seen him defending American citizens and I have seen him caring for them after they have been abused; I have known of his winding up their cases with honor to himself and with credit to his Government, maintaining in dignity the authority and the power of his Government, and those great chiefs who stood over him.

As I approve of everything that I have known him to do, for I was many years his chief, I am here to say that there is one thing about him that I honor more than anything that is official, more than anything that has to do with his labors in the pulpit, more than anything with his public life, more than anything that has to do with his success in building a church in San Domingo, in maintaining that church according to Methodistic usages, that which I applaud more than any success that he has had in his labors in the United States or in his labors abroad in developing commerce, in maintaining a national interest—a thing which does more to reveal to me his real character, making him worthy of this occasion, making him worthy of this high honor, than any other thing appertaining to his life, of which I have any knowledge. Do I betray domestic confidence, do I betray social intimacy, do I betray that secret of friendship and brotherly confidence that he expected of me when he invited me into his home, into his house, in the heart of his family, near to his  children, near to his wife, near to his mother, when I speak of a thing that I felt at midnight once as I never felt any other thing in my life. Shall I tell you how at midnight roused by his voice, aroused by the thing that he did, I heard him reading the sacred words of that Book to which my friend referred a few moments ago, to an aged mother; with explanations kind and just and agreeable, pointing to that Paradise which awaits after this life all the good—"the just made perfect"—in that world where fathers shall meet their children and where all the good shall meet and where we shall receive all the promise of the good, in a manner grander and closer than anything we can do here (applause). And after I had heard these words from that Sacred Book, read with such tones of voice, in such an impressive manner to an aged and blind mother on her bed aroused to hear those words, and then listened to the prayer that followed, an earnest, manly prayer that not only went to the heart of an aged mother but my own heart and made me love that man the better, and I said to myself "That is the paragon of real manhood;" a man who does not forget after the labors of the day, the labors for government, the labors for a great country, after discharging the blended duties—yielding himself to this influence, he kneels by the bedside of his aged mother and teaches her who is without eyes, how she may look up and gladly see all that is glorious shining in the Saviour who came to save the children of men (applause). And I said: "That is my man," and I say so to-day, and let me tell you that when you celebrate the ratification of a Democratic administration, do not forget to say that that administration had the sense and the honesty and the ability to keep in office a man who builds his inward character as he builds his official character, on that rock, "upon which if a man builds a house the storm may beat against it, and the rains may descend and the floods dash against it, and it stands, because it is founded on a rock," and that is the secret of that man's success (several voices, "very good, very good").

Now I said to him and he recognizes the prayer, and he can never forget, "Astwood, I always loved you; Astwood, I was always disposed to honor you, but, Sir, when I heard your voice pronouncing to your aged mother the sweet words of the New Testament last night, and then listened to that prayer of yours, I loved you like a brother and my love was intensified towards you," and so it is to-night. And he will recollect how night after night as we would come in at ten and eleven o'clock from the office, the business of the day ended, I would delight to hear his voice and to hear him read to his aged mother who could not read for herself, and join with him when he did not know it, in lifting up my voice in a silent way to the same throne beseeching God to bestow the same blessing on his family and on himself for his leadership in that prayer. ("Very good, very good.")

Now when we shall send abroad such paragons of American character to represent us in Europe, to represent us on the great continents, to represent us in the island government, you need not be afraid as to whether the interests of American citizens will be guarded and creditably cared for, for such a citizen will not only know how to care for the interests of the government near which he dwells, but will also know how to care for the welfare of the government which he represents. And so it has been with my friend, and it is perfectly natural for him to commence at his own government, while he cares for every interest attaching to the government of my distinguished friend, General Ulysses Heureaux, President of the Republic of San Domingo. And it is in this spirit that I will now speak, the spirit of my distinguished friend the officer of this Government, near the capital of another Republic—that is the spirit of a genuine diplomat. Diplomacy is not dishonesty. Diplomacy is intelligent honesty which defends at once the interests of the government you represent and is not unmindful of the government near which you dwell. And so in all the experience which I have had of my distinguished friend, and he knows how many times and how many affairs in the Island of San Domingo I have had occasion to meet him—as I have been carried across the sea on American men-of-war from my post of duty around to the capital of the Dominican Republic where my friend lives—I have always found him at home, always in his office, always mindful of his duty, always scrupulously diligent in discharging his duties, never forgetting American interests and never forgetting that he owed a debt to the greatest government on the face of the earth, and the only such, and after that to a smaller but important government. So has he represented the Christian spirit of a manly American, strong in the true Christian American spirit as right in diplomacy and consular service. For if you would find the rock on which international light is founded you must look for it in the strong and substantial and beautiful sentiments of Christianity. Christianity is the soul of diplomacy; Christianity is the rock on which diplomacy erects its temple and that temple stands forever. And if you need a school of diplomacy for any purpose, to begin with it is to infuse into your young men the Christian spirit looking to the proper discharge of diplomatic duties. We have an idea that a diplomat can be dishonest and some people have an idea that a lawyer ought to be dishonest, but if there is any man whose hands are to be clean, whose head is to be clear, the sentiments of whose soul are to be as pure as the hangings of Diana's temple, that man is the lawyer and no other man. When a man ceases, in the legal profession, to be the impersonation of honesty and integrity he is no longer a lawyer, and no matter what his abilities may be, he falls ignominiously from his high position. And so it is with a diplomat. The moment he ceases to be a man of honor, just as it is with the lawyer, all the confidence of his people in him is at once destroyed. Now the first thing for us to do is to impress upon the Ministers Resident and other officers in the service the great necessity of engrafting into our young men the principles of Christianity, which are the soul of manly existence and "without which they are nothing; a sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal." Go with me now to San Domingo and let the Sabbath Day come. Visit my friend and see how all the doors that lead to the ordinary business of the week are all closed, locked and barred. And nine o'clock in the morning he is in the Sabbath School teaching, not American children, but teaching in the Spanish language young San Dominicans; and you and I there with him to follow and not to lead. And when these Dominican children have been taught then will come the time for the sermon, and he who was a moment ago the superintendent of the school is now the pastor, the minister of the Gospel and in a church prepared through outlays taken from his own pocket (applause). And year by year he has nurtured that church until the only African Methodist Episcopal Church in San Domingo is the church erected, sustained and supported by the ministrations and outlays of our distinguished friend. Do you want further evidence that I testify the truth with regard to his character? Let the week commence; Monday is upon us and it is nine o'clock and he appears with me in the presence of the President in his business he appears with me before this Secretary of State in the foreign office; he goes with me to see great men in regard to matters of commercial importance, and while he is an American he would not see a single right of the Dominican government encroached upon. And everybody respects him accordingly. Why as he walks through the streets the women bow to him and the men stop and shake hands with him and of course all these men at home, and in official life address him as "Senor Consul." And so all through, whether in business life or in social life, good Americans of whatever class I meet, in the city and in the country, this is the manner in which our representative is regarded. When you are abroad and you look upon our representatives and you inquire about their character, it is not always the case that you find such men as this. I have never visited with my friend in San Domingo a single whiskey shop in my life. I have never been invited by him to go into a single drinking place, not once, and I need hardly say in the presence of my friend whether or not there are drinking places in San Domingo. Laughter.

I have been asked to speak on "The Necessity of a School of Diplomacy." I am in favor of that, and I think that it would do much to preserve the American people as such. A man who has had some experience in matters of this kind has stated that it is very hard to find men to send abroad as diplomats, as consular officers, and as commercial agents, and he begins to discover that the time is coming when we will have to take decisive steps, when young Americans are to be educated. I will favor him in that sort of Civil Service. The young man who is training for diplomacy should know law, should know languages, should know the usages of governments from the beginning of the world's history to the present hour, so that when he goes abroad he may know what the sovereignty and the independence and the power of the American government is; what American citizenship signifies and not allow any other government however great or however small to lay a finger's weight on the rights of American citizens. Do you think you can climb up to that? Almost all Americans who go abroad go with their hats in their hands in servile attitudes to foreign governments. As I said to an old Englishman once, when in the presence of a great Englishman, "Salter, put your hat on," so I would say to every man, and represent the power and dignity of the American government. Salter was my client and I was collecting a large sum of money for him in England from an estate that was looking for heirs; I collected the money and Salter still kept his hat in his hand. He took his money and went to be an Ohio farmer owning thousands of acres of land. Mr. Salter said to me, "Mr. Langston, I was a servant in the old country and served these men so long and so faithfully with my hat in my hand or under my arm in their presence, that when I went into the presence of this man I voluntarily took my hat off and put it under my arm and I could not help it." Yes, you see, the slavery spirit was still in his soul. That is the difficulty, that a touch of slavery still continues in the minds of these men. How long will it take the American Negro, how long will it take any man who has been 245 years in slavery to rid his soul of the slavery spirit? This is a great government of ours and a great country. You have got a President; you have a ruler, so you have. You have international usages and justice and honesty at home; all these—yes, and sixty millions of people, and why do we take our hats off in the presence of any government? The United States is the great master of nations, and we hold in our hands the key that will unloose and unlock international power. Charles Sumner said to me once—he had gone to the White House to have an interview with General Grant—"He asked me to wait fifteen minutes for him at the White House." "And did you wait, Senator?" "No, I did not. No sir, the Senator of Massachusetts wait fifteen minutes? Oh no, never should the Senator of Massachusetts be asked to wait one minute. And while Charles Sumner is Senator, he represents the power and dignity and the majesty of the great commonwealth of Massachusetts and he will not wait fifteen minutes for anybody." What do you think of that? Well, I looked at that great man towering up above me with his great broad shoulders as he used those words, and I said to myself, "If I were you I would not wait fifteen minutes myself for anybody," and because he was asked to wait he never went back to the White House any more while Grant was there as the President of the United States.

Now as to the education which the diplomat should have. Take the matter of language, as my friend said who addressed us in Spanish, the American youth ten years of age should know the Spanish language. Many of the men who represent us abroad do not know English, or French, or Spanish, or German and when they get to their places of duty they do not know how to address either the Secretary of State, or the Minister of Foreign Affairs, or the President of the Republic, or the King near whose kingdom they reside. And we do need to be taught languages and we must have them. Charles Sumner, while in the United States Senate was the master of French, to some extent the master of Spanish, to a certain extent the master of Italian and to a limited extent he understood all these languages, and was considered a prodigy among his people. But every Senator should have a knowledge of these languages. Why, you cannot even use the phrases of diplomatic uses without some knowledge of Greek and Latin. Latin and French and then all the modern languages, that is the order in which they come. Then you must also understand the law. I began my course in law in the backwoods and my first experience was on a Sunday when I undertook to defend twenty whiskey venders. And because I understood the law and was at home in it I am now teaching young men law in the schools, our law in our schools. And now who shall be the chief professor of this school of diplomacy, and who shall deliver the lectures; and shall these lectures be lectures worthy of the American citizen and the dignity of the calling of diplomats? Who shall it be? And now, whether our friend Astwood remains a long time in the country or goes hence to his duty at an early day, my benediction goes with him and my prayers follow him as he labors directly in behalf of American citizens, and I shall ever pray that whatever he does he may do it successfully and add honors yet to be won to the honors he has already gained, so that whether a Democrat or a Republican is President, his services may still be had to our government and to the country near whose capital he resides.

Mr. Fortune then introduced General Horatio C. King, who spoke as follows:

Mr. Chairman and Gentlemen: I find myself in a somewhat peculiar position to-night. You who were listening and apparently interested in the private conversation before the regular speech-making began, may have observed that I have had to combat the peculiar principles of Prof. Langston and Mr. Mackay in regard to the Civil Service features of the Democratic party. While on the one hand, as an old Democrat, born a Democrat, inculcated a Democrat, I never have been able to get the Democratic feeling out of my system, and in favor of Civil Service Reform I have had to combat the features of Mr. Langston's address and of Mr. Mackay's that "to the victors belong the spoils," which has heretofore been considered a feature of the Democratic party, nevertheless I feel very much as the man who said on one occasion when some one asked him whether he would rather go to heaven or to that other place below, he said it did not make much difference because he had friends in both places. Now, I understand that the object of this meeting is to pay honor to our friend Mr. Astwood, and Democrat as I am, when I became acquainted with this gentleman on my left (Mr. Astwood) it gave me very great pleasure to write to the President although he was a Republican he was the right man in the right place and that it would be a personal favor to me if he continued him in the position of United States Consul at San Domingo. (Applause). A longer and better acquaintance with him has assured me that he is still the right man in the right place, and though I am a Democrat of the Democrats, fifty years old and still a Democrat, I have not changed my opinion in regard to Mr. Astwood and I am ready and shall always be ready to stand by him as I have done from the first instance. (Voices: "Hear, hear"). Now I suppose it might be excusable in me on an occasion of this kind to say exactly what I feel, and I think that I can say with a better grace because I belong to that party which is supposed to be opposed to the advancement of the colored race in this country, that I think that there is but one thing for the colored race to show, and that is that they are capable to occupy any of the positions in this country which a white man can occupy. And I believe that in a short time those prejudices which have misled many, and we must confess they exist amongst the white people, can be easily overcome, if they could only see, as we have seen to-night, the magnificent ability which has been shown in this entertainment. Certainly where can you find among white people greater eloquence than has been manifested by Mr. Stewart, my friend opposite? [Applause]. Where among white men can you find a man better capable of expressing his sentiments than Prof. Langston, immediately opposite? [Applause]. Where in diplomacy can you find a better representative of the United States Government than is found in my friend on the left, Mr. Astwood? ["Hear, hear." Applause]. Especially in that notable instance where he secured the $33,000 to a man who was unjustly murdered in his country. Could we find a better man to represent the United States Government and to secure from the Dominican Government what they should pay in the case of such an atrocious murder as was committed at that time?

I suppose that I would be in fault to-night if I did not say something about what I think the Dominican Government needs. What it needs in my judgment, to make it a perfect Government, is the success of the Dominican Railroad which I represent. [Applause]. I think I may honestly claim that a railroad from the point of Barahona to the port of Mansanila will not only make that the finest Government in the world but it will annex it with the United States. My attention has been called to the Island of San Domingo since my connection with this company, and I think it will surprise every one in this country, as it has surprised me, to discover what the resources of that country are. And the only reason, as I understand it, why that country has not been developed as our own country has been developed, is because of the impression in this country that it has not a stable Government. There are magnificent resources there, woods, salts, and all the tropical fruits, the sugar, tobacco and everything of that character—but the thing that we have been unable to impress upon the capitalists of this country is the fact that they are not sure that the Government there is as stable as it should be. And yet, as I understand it, for more than twenty years there has been no serious uprising in that country except the little revolutionary tendencies there, a street riot as we would call it here, that they had last Summer. But I am not here to talk railroad, that is not my purpose whatever. I am here simply to honor the representative of the Government of the United States at San Domingo. I am very glad to add my testimony to his worth; I am very glad to say that in all the transactions that we have had with him he has proved himself to be an able administrator and a faithful friend. [Applause]. And I hope that the time may not come when it shall be necessary to plead further with President Cleveland and his Administration to retain him in the service of the Government. There comes in my Democratic principles again, which Mr. Langston and Mr. Mackay do not approve of. But the sentiments of these gentlemen as I understood them in a private conversation which was publicly stated, was that the party in power ought to clean out everybody who was not a Democrat, commencing at the top and ending with the scrub woman in the lowest office. As a Democrat I do not believe nor do I entertain such notions. I hold that the stability of this Government depends upon the faithfulness of its employees, and the faithfulness of its employees depends upon the security that they feel that if they do their duty well they shall be retained in the office to which they have been appointed. Certainly in my own business I do not ask a man who comes into my office, "Are you a Democrat or Republican?" I simply ask him, "Are you capable of performing the duties that are put before you?" And as long as he

performs those duties honestly and faithfully, I retain him in that employ. There is no great merchant in this country that ever asks a man who comes into his employ, “Are you a Republican or are you a Democrat?” but “Are you capable of performing the duties that are put before you?” And if they do not perform those duties then, and then only, are they dismissed from his employment. I regard this Government of the United States simply as a great business machine. I do not forget that Webster said more than thirty-five years ago that under the system then proceeding if this country ever had more than forty thousand employees and they were appointed on the system of political risks, that it would destroy the Government. Now we have more than a hundred and fifteen thousand employees of the Government, and if we were asked to change them every time that the Administration changes, I say to you, gentlemen, it is violating all the principles of business and it is leading our Government simply towards anarchy, and we are giving to every man his work simply for the party, no matter what his ability, whatever his power, or whatever his character; taking the place of an honest man who is doing his honest duty in the Government employ. [“Hear, hear.”]

I am sorry to differ from my Republican friends, but I am afraid President Cleveland has made this mistake, that while the previous Administrations have preached Civil Service Reform, he is the only man who has held the Presidency of the United States that has practiced Civil Service Reform. It is easy to put in your platforms, but it is more difficult to carry it out. And I point to this man [Mr. Astwood] as one of the evidences that President Cleveland has carried out—that he has not only preached but he has carried out the practice and kept the right man in the right place, and he intends to do the same thing again, and I have no doubt that Mr. Mackay and Mr. Langston will do all that they can for him at the next election.

Now let me say one other word which is somewhat personal, perhaps, but there is no color line in Brooklyn in the Board of Education which I have the honor to represent. Mr. Dorsey will excuse me if I point to him as an example of it. Mr. Dorsey is in the position that he holds in his colored school in Brooklyn not because he is a colored man, nor would he be in that position because he was a white man, but simply because he was capable of filling that place. A man whom every member of the Board of Education respects and who will retain his position despite of his color as long as he continues to be as able and excellent a principal as he is to-day. [Applause].

Mr. Fortune stated that he had received letters of regret from the following: Hon. John H. Smythe, ex-United States Minister to Liberia; Mr. James M. Trotter, Recorder of Deeds for the District of Columbia; Wm. E. Matthews, banker of Washington; Wm. Still of Philadelphia, of Underground Railroad fame; Geo. T. Downing of Newport, R. I.; Rev. Rufus L. Perry, editor of the National Monitor and author of “The Cushite.” A letter from Prof. Peter H. Clark, Trustee of the Ohio State University, contained this passage: “Honor to whom honor is due is a maxim worthy of all acceptation, and surely honor is due to your distinguished guest who has represented the whole country with ability and success and his colored fellow-citizens in a double sense; an American—a colored man.”

“After a quarter of a century, after a war which necessitated emancipation as a war measure, and without a pretence that it was for any other reason than to weaken the enemy; after the presentation of suffrage to our race for no other reason than that it came to the aid of the victors in governing the vanquished; after our race discovered that its support of a policy of oppression, of suspicion and hate was a failure; after seeing that a division of population into caste and classes separated by a color line was contrary to sound sense and to any enlightened idea of statesmanship—after all these experiences, many of us, with a majority of all the people, elected and placed in power a Democratic president. The party that had been in power had lived in declarations, had thrived and had its being on professions of its belief in the equality of man; it had quoted the Declaration of Independence until all professed to believe in that document—until perhaps some really did.

“The new President was an honest man who determined and whose party determined to blot out all political race distinctions and to obliterate the color line in politics. Behold! there stand opposed to him a Republican Senate who say, Not so; ours is the right to dictate the political creed of the colored nominee; the slave is freed, but he has become our political serf; we have set his body free, but we have enchained his mind, his soul, and we will drag his race at our party chariot wheels; a Negro Democrat is a monster, no colored man not a Republican can be confirmed by this Senate. These are the elevated sentiments of the Republican Senate of the United States. These are the statesmanlike views of the men who cling to the color line; who invite and insist upon political class distinctions; men who would deny the truth of the multiplication table, who cannot understand the last census on which is written in words that illuminate that whole document: 'In eighty years there will be in these United States one hundred millions of Negroes. In eighty years, aye in less, the great South will be the seat of industry and manufacture such as the world has never seen.' What fools and blind, to build up scorn and hatred, instead of love and confidence and mutual regard!

“And so the far-seeing statesmanship of the Democratic President of the Democratic party shall come to naught! I tell you not so; the truth shall prevail; the ephemeral insect of a day vanishes when his little day comes to an end, but the great orbs of God's universe march solemnly through the sky. Your honored guest, our friend and brother, stands this day an example of what is Democratic statesmanship. Appointed to an honorable position by a Republican President; performing the duties of that office so that he is this day praised of all men—was he rejected by the President by reason of his political faith and his color? Renominated—reappointed, he goes back to perform the duties of his place. No other test than, is he honest? Is he capable? Is he true to his creed, to his race? Compare, I pray you, the statesmanship of the words, of the actions of the chief of Democrats, of the chiefs of the Republicans. Compare, I pray you, the breadth of views, their depths of sagacity; their heights of views, their far-seeing wisdom. My friends, we are living in a new age; we are breathing a newer, a diviner air; heart beats are quicker, fuller, stronger; we cannot kneel and grovel as serfs to any political party; we are invited to a higher, a nobler destiny. We stand to-day God's freemen, freedmen no longer. Party ties rest lightly on all men. Let us see that we go where the best interests of our race call us—more, where the best interests of our native land call us; for we, too, can say to day, 'It is my proudest boast that I am an American citizen.'

* * * * *

“I am with President Cleveland and yourselves for the political equality of man and the advancement and elevation of the oppressed of every race, of whatever color, politics and religion.”

Mr. James Grant, representing one of the largest houses in the country, Wanamaker and Son of Philadelphia, responded to the toast of “Our Commercial Relations,” and said: “On account of the lateness of the hour, you will no doubt think a long address tiresome and I shall therefore tell you of my visit to Hayti.” He then told of the hospitality received at the hands of Consul Astwood and the high esteem in which that gentleman was held by the natives.

The chairman next introduced Dr. Benjamin W. Arnett, member of the Ohio Legislature, to respond to “The Church.” Dr. Arnett said: “I consider not the mere banquet but its object, a banquet where we can feel Christian intelligence and sagacity, and, as well said by the gentleman of Brooklyn, the time has now arrived for the brothers of American liberty, through ability, to promote the duties of life that they may contend with, in church and in state. And as friends have marked the successful American citizens of the African race, I also have noted. I am one of those American citizens that love my country; I am proud of her high mountains, proud of her grand rivers, proud of her institutions of learning, and excellent schools and teachers and churches. Aye, proud of her respectability; that which praises in your land, and by which an American of the African race may rise from the lowest to the highest.” After giving some church data, he terminated by paying a glowing tribute to Mr. Astwood, as a founder of a church in Hayti and a sincere and faithful devotee of that grand institution.

In response to the toast to the health of “The President of Hayti,” Hon. E. D. Bassett, Consul General of Hayti at New York, responded and spoke of the population of the Island of Hayti, stating that it was about four hundred thousand. In fact he knew that no statistics on the subject were thoroughly taken. Half of the population spoke the French language, and the insurrections were merely ephemeral and not of the frequency reputed. He gave an excellent description of President Salomon and recited how, after having been banished, he returned one morning and how enthusiastically the people received him.

At this juncture a vote of approval was proposed to Caterer Crocker, and Dr. Derrick made a brief yet eloquent speech telling how pleased he felt. Gen. Horatio C. King proposed and led the chorus “For he's a jolly good fellow.”

records.summary_en: In this window of the Freeman's banquet coverage, a speaker rises to praise the American consular officer at the Dominican capital — 'my distinguished friend, the officer of this Government, near the capital of another Republic': in all his experience of the man, across the many affairs in the island of San Domingo on which he has had occasion to meet him, carried across the sea on American men-of-war from his own post of duty to the capital of the Dominican Republic, he has always found him at home, in his office, scrupulously diligent, never forgetting American interests and never forgetting the debt owed to the government he serves. Diplomacy, the speaker declares, is not dishonesty but intelligent honesty, and Christianity is the soul of diplomacy, the rock on which it erects its temple: the window closes inside the oration.

records.full_text:
Involving Treaty Relations With Two Countries.
WASHINGTON, Dec. 14.—An important case, involving the treaty relations of the United States with Hawaii and San Domingo, was argued to-day in the United States supreme court. The case stands on the docket as No. 1,012, High Kelly, plaintiff in error, against Edward L. Hedden, collector, in error to the United States circuit court for the southern district of New York. The question presented is the alleged exemption from duty, under the existing tariff, of products of the Dominican republic which are identical in kind with products of the Sandwich islands admitted free of duty under the special act of congress, approved Aug. 15, 1876. About twenty years ago the United States entered into a treaty with the Dominican republic by the terms of which each country agreed not to charge higher import duties on the products of the other than were imposed upon like products from any other country. The importers, who are the plaintiffs in error in this and another similar case, claim exemption from duty for certain sugars and other products imported by them from San Domingo, upon the ground that the articles were of such a character that had they been imported from Hawaii they would have been admitted free of duty under the treaty between the United States and Hawaii and the act of Aug. 15, 1876, enforcing that treaty. The importers assert that if their contention is not sustained, the Dominican republic will be released from its treaty obligations by virtue of the failure of the United States to keep its engagements, and that San Domingo may then practically exclude United States manufacturers from her ports by exemptions and discriminating duties in favor of the European countries, which are seeking the trade of the island.
The United States government on the other hand maintains that the treaty with the Hawaiian islands was not a mere reciprocity treaty, but was in substance a commercial contract by virtue of which Hawaii pays a valuable consideration for the admission of certain merchandise to the ports of the United States. The importations from that country are not free, but the nation whence the articles came has made a special bargain by which the nation, and not the importer, pays the duties. It is furthermore contended by the United States that more than eleven years have passed since the promulgation of the Hawaiian treaty and that although the products of San Domingo have during all that time been charged with the duties now complained of, the Dominican government has never alleged a violation of her treaty rights, nor does it appear that any of her citizens either in this case or heretofore has complained of wrong.

records.headline: Suit Against the United States Which May Upset Existing Commercial Treaties.
records.summary_en: An importer named Hugh Kelly brought a legal suit against collector Edward L. Hedden, claiming an exemption from duty for products imported from the Dominican Republic under a past treaty guaranteeing equality with products from any other country, specifically referencing products admitted free from the Sandwich Islands under an 1876 act. The United States Government contested this, arguing that the Hawaiian arrangement was not a mere reciprocity treaty but a commercial contract involving valuable consideration, and that granting the exemption would violate existing trade terms and lead to foreign trade complications.

Suit Against the United States Which May Upset Existing Commercial Treaties.

WASHINGTON, December 14.—An important case involving the treaty relations of the United States with Hawaii and San Domingo was argued to-day in the United States Supreme Court. The case stands on the docket as Hugh Kelly, plaintiff in error, against Edward L. Hedden, collector. The question presented is an alleged exemption from duty under the existing tariff of products of the Dominican Republic which are identical in kind with the products of the Sandwich Islands and admitted free of duty under a special act of Congress, approved August 15, 1876. About twenty years ago the United States entered into a treaty with the Dominican Republic, by the terms of which each country agreed not to charge higher import duties on the products of the other than were imposed on like products from any other country. The importer claims exemption from duty for certain sugars and other products imported by him from San Domingo upon the ground that the articles were of such character that had they been imported from Hawaii they would have been

ADMITTED FREE OF DUTY,

under the treaty between the United States and Hawaii and the treaty of August 15, 1876, enforcing that treaty. The United States Government maintains that the treaty with the Hawaiian Islands was not a mere reciprocity treaty, but was in substance a commercial contract, by virtue of which Hawaii pays valuable consideration for the admission of certain merchandise to ports of the United States. Counsel for the importer say if the United States should be defeated in this case San Domingo might become the Honolulu of the Atlantic coast, while if the United States should succeed, Denmark, Brazil, Central America, Peru, Persia and other foreign governments would be at liberty to shut out American manufactures and products from their ports without giving the United States any cause for complaint for a violation of existing treaties placing the United States on an equality there with all other nations. This, they say, would upset nearly all our existing commercial treaties with foreign powers.

records.full_text:
Always Prevail Over Its Treaties.
Associated Press dispatches to the HERALD:
WASHINGTON, January 9.—Decision was rendered to-day in the case of James F. Whitney and others against William A. Robertson, formerly Collector of the Port of New York. The question raised was the scope and force of certain provisions contained in the treaties concluded between the United States and the Republic of San Domingo and the Kingdom of Hawaii, respectively. The plaintiffs who appeared are New York merchants who imported in 1882 from San Domingo a large quantity of molasses and sugars similar in kind to those imported from the Sandwich Islands. The Collector exacted duties on these San Domingo sugars amounting to $22,000, plaintiffs paying the same under protest. They then brought suit against the government to recover the amount exacted, on the ground that by virtue of article 9 of the treaty between the United States and San Domingo, the United States was debarred from imposing a higher duty, or any other duty, upon the products of San Domingo than is imposed upon similar products of other countries with which the United States might have commercial relations. Sugars similar to those in controversy were imported free of duty from the Sandwich Islands under the treaty provisions; therefore, it is contended, they should be admitted free from San Domingo.
THE COURT HOLDS
First, that the ninth article of the treaty between the United States and San Domingo is merely a pledge of the contracting parties that there should be no discriminating legislation against imported articles of either country. It was never designed to prevent special concessions like those granted Hawaii, and the clearest language is necessary to justify the conclusion that the United States Government intended to preclude itself from such engagements with other countries, which might become of highest importance to our interests.
Second: The act of Congress under which the duties in this case were collected, authorized their exaction. It was of general application, making no exception in the favor of the goods of any country, and passed after the treaty with the Dominican Republic, and if there is any conflict between laws and treaties the former must prevail. The country disatisfied with the action of the legislature must address its complaints to the executive head of the government, and take measures which it deems essential to protect its own interests. When the law is clear its validity cannot be assailed before courts for want of conformity with treaty stipulations.
The judgment of the United States Circuit Court in favor of the collection, is therefore affirmed.
A SIMILAR DECISION
Was rendered in the case of Hugh Kelly vs. Edward L. Hedden. Had these decisions been adverse to the Government, the United States would have had to pay out many millions of dollars as refunds for duties exacted, as the above suits were test cases. Justice Field wrote the above detailed decision.

records.headline: The Morning News prints a character sketch of an American colonel
records.summary_en: The Morning News prints a character sketch of an American colonel settled at Monte Christi: his ideal soldier during the civil war was Gen. Grant, and when, years after laying down arms, he learned of President Grant's Samana annexation scheme, he was seized with the desire to see the place from which his hero expected so much, packed his trunk and went down there — and the lazy, easy-going, sunny existence he found captured him at once. Since then he has lived in every section of the island: he has fought cocks with the high officials in San Domingo City, dug gold in the Cibao mountains, flirted outrageously with the girls in Puerto Plata, taken snapshots at revolutionary insurgents at Las Matas, danced with the Governor's wife at Guayubin, and been coy with tarantulas and scorpions along the Mao, gathering a little moss everywhere until he settled at Monte Christi with upward of 250 pounds of bone and muscle: the window closes as the sketch turns to his figure.

PROTESTS COME FROM HAYTI.
AMERICAN TRADERS IN THE INSURGENT NORTH WANT A CRUISER.
Hippolyte and Jimenes is the Presidential Ticket in the North—The Saginaw's Arms Going to Jimenes—Dutch Gold Greatly Soothe the Dominicans.
The steamship George W. Clyde of the Clyde line got here yesterday with news from the Haytian and Dominican republics. She left Santo Domingo city on Oct. 24, and touched at Samana, Porto Plata, Cape Haytien, Port de Paix, and Turk's Island. Two American merchants doing business at Gonaives and Cape Haytien have forwarded protests to this Government against the Haytian blockade on account of its effect on their business, and ask that a United States cruiser be sent to protect the interests of American citizens in the North of Hayti. The whole North is said to have risen in its might and demanded that Légitime withdraw from the Presidential candidacy and leave the island. The merchants say that there is now no Government of Hayti, and that, therefore, there can be no blockade. If Légitime will withdraw the North will then be ready for a real election. Meantime all business is neglected in the North, for everybody joined the army when the blockade was announced. The enthusiasm is so great that even old men and boys have joined the ranks. This army is only waiting for arms and ammunition to advance on Port-au-Prince and avenge what it terms the assassination of Seïde Thilemaque.
In regard to the arms shipped in the Saginaw, it is said that the Dominican Government may find itself in serious trouble if it allow these munitions of war to be smuggled across the Haytian frontier in the interest of the North. The Dominican Government has no war ships, and both Monte Criste and Santo Domingo could be bombarded by Légitime's little navy.
Another interesting bit of news brought by the George W. Clyde is to the effect that Juan F. Jimenes of the firm of Jimenes & Haustedt of this city is a candidate for the Vice-Presidency in the North, F. Hippolyte being at the head of the ticket. The cabalistic address
P.
Monte Criste
J.
on the Saginaw's consignment of arms is now understood to mean that the goods are intended for Gen. Papillon and Mr. Jimenes.
The relations between the Haytian and Dominican Governments are reported to be far from cordial. A Dominican merchant in this city said yesterday that there was little intercourse between the two countries. Légitime is thought to be backed up by French capital furnished by merchants interested in the Haytian trade. The Dominican republic is itself on the verge of the election of a new President. These elections have usually been followed by insurrections, the party defeated at the polls not caring to give up so easily. This election, however, bids fair to be a peaceable one. The present President is Ulysses Herreux, and the opposition candidate is Gen. Luperon. On the 22d of October Gen. Luperon cabled from Porto Rico to Santo Domingo that he should not run against Herreux. This news was received with great joy throughout the Dominican republic, and at the Dominican ports where the George W. Clyde put in bonfires illumined the hills far and near. Herreux is said to have arranged a loan of $4,000,000 with Holland, and before the Clyde left, £30,000 of Dutch gold had arrived at San Domingo. The Dominican republic has been in a very bad way, financially, and this money is greatly needed. Hence the bonfires, and hence Gen. Luperon's decision not to run against a man who can borrow money like that. The Royal Standard, an English paper published at Turk's Island, bearing the date of Nov. 3, says a United States war vessel had just left Cuba to investigate the seizure of the Haytian republic by one of Légitime's vessels.

REBELS DEFEAT GOVERNMENT TROOPS.
CASES OF RIFLES SHIPPED FOR HAYTI — THE STORY OF A MERCHANT ABOUT THE INSURRECTION.
Consul-General Bassett said yesterday that private advices had been received in this city, dated Port au Prince, November 12, which said that the port of St. Marc, which had been held by the insurgents, had been surrendered by them to the Haytien Government; but up to last night he had received no official communication to corroborate the information. The Clyde Line steamer George W. Clyde was cleared at the Custom House yesterday for Monti Christi, a small Dominican port near Cape Haytien. Her manifest showed that she had among her cargo 500 cases of rifles and ammunition on board. Consul Preston said that these goods were for the insurgents in Hayti and that among the passengers on the steamer were two rebel agents. He waited on the Customs authorities requesting them to stop the sailing of the ship, but as the vessel had cleared for a port outside of the Haytien Republic, they were powerless to act in the matter, and the vessel was expected to go to sea last night. William P. Clyde, one of her owners, yesterday acknowledged that the arms were on board the ship, but added that as the goods were consigned to a Dominican port his firm had no concern with their ultimate destination after they were landed from the steamer. Referring to the question of the alleged rebel agents being on board, he said that they sold tickets to any passenger applying and paying for them, without making inquiries as to their religion, politics or private affairs.
E. Lockwood, a merchant of New-Haven, Conn., who arrived here from Hayti on the George W. Clyde on November 10, said yesterday that he was on board the steamer Haytien Republic at Port de Paix when Captain Compton took on board 300 armed insurgents who were landed at Gonaives on October 18, where they encountered the Government troops. A battle ensued which lasted for some hours and resulted in a victory for the rebels. The general in command of the Government troops fled to the woods, where he was taken prisoner by the rebels and severely beaten. He subsequently swore allegiance to the rebels and is now fighting on their side.
Mr. Lockwood said that he had heard that Captain Compton had previously carried 500 armed men from Cape Haytien to Gonaives, and he told the captain when he boarded the ship that the Government troops were looking out to capture his vessel. The captain said that he had nothing to do with the men, as they were ordinary passengers and he was in no way responsible for their acts.
Notice has been given to the Haytien Government that the case of the Haytien Republic will be appealed to the higher Haytien courts, as the owners consider the confiscation of their vessel illegal. They say, furthermore, that the court was illegally constituted.

At half-past 6 last night Rear Admiral Luce was snugly ensconced in the cabin of the Richmond, although his flag flew on the Galena.
"Orders have been received from Washington," he said, "for the Galena and Yantic to set sail for Port-au-Prince to-morrow. I won't undertake to state the exact hour at which the vessels will sail, for if it should be fifteen minutes out of the way you newspaper men would pitch into the United States navy. It is quite certain that we won't go before 7 o'clock, and very likely not before 10. We thought we could get the Richmond ready to accompany the Galena, and so my flag was transferred to her. When we found that that was impossible the flag went back to the Galena, and I shall sail on that ship. The difficulty about the Richmond has been to get her decks properly calked. Our calkers have gone and got permanent jobs in New York. The Richmond can get her coal and ammunition on board in four or five days, and will then be ready for sea. She will follow on to Port-au-Prince, and if I am still there she will take me on board. Otherwise she will go on to St. Thomas, where we shall be waiting for her. Do I expect to bombard Port-au-Prince? Why, of course not. You surely wouldn't have us act so cruelly toward a weaker sister republic. The fact is I don't believe there will be any necessity for a bombardment, because I feel certain the Haytian Government will promptly release the Haytian Republic."
Some newspaper had printed an alarming report that the Galena was full of holes. Admiral Luce laughed as he encountered this weather-worn naval chestnut.
"Port holes," he chuckled. "You can depend upon it that the Galena is quite seaworthy or your uncle would not sail on her. Capt. Cooper, formerly of the Haytian navy and commander of the Dessalines, made me a brief call this morning and said that the Dessalines was a fine gunboat in good condition. Mr. Morse, one of the Boston agents of the Haytian Republic, will go with us by special permit to look after the interests of that steamer. There is plenty of coal stored on an island in the harbor of Port-au-Prince, the owner of which will be very glad to sell all the coal he can to the owners of the Haytian Republic, which can then be taken home by a crew sent out for the purpose. We take along a deck load of coal because we don't want to pay Port-au-Prince prices. Besides, yellow fever can be brought aboard ship with a load of coal. I take along no sealed instructions of any nature. That used to be the custom in the days of Paul Jones, but the last case that I know of personally was in 1853. Then the Captain of a ship might be ordered to proceed to a certain latitude and longitude before he could learn what his destination was to be."
The Yantic lay last night at the ordnance dock ready to sail at a moment's notice. On Monday night her Captain was surprised to get an order to take aboard the ship's powder. This was an unusual night's order, but all the lights were put out, and the powder was taken aboard in the dark.
Every one at the Haytian Consulate seemed to be in a good humor yesterday. Minister Preston laughed when he was asked whether there was any likelihood of the Galena's goat Billy striking terror into the hearts of the Haytian soldiers.
"I don't think there would be much chance of that," said the Minister. "Goats are one of the chief products of Hayti. We eat them in Hayti as you do mutton here, and the flavor very much resembles that of Welsh mutton. Besides, goat's milk is very highly esteemed in Hayti, and commands a high price."
Speaking of the reported revolution in San Domingo, a representative of the legation said: "We hear, unofficially, that affairs in San Domingo are in a rather serious condition. It appears that Gen. Luperon, one of the candidates for the Presidency of the Dominican Republic, published a manifesto about Nov. 1, withdrawing in favor of President Heraux, provided the election should be a fair one and express the will of the people. It seems that the election that followed was not satisfactory to Luperon or his adherents, and was followed by riots and a general uprising. The news now comes that the Dominican insurgents have seized all the arms they could get their hands on, and it is said that the arms brought by Papillon to Monte Cristi for the use of Hippolyte's followers were also taken by the Dominicans. If this proves to be true, it will be a great blow to the North."
Mr. J. S. Cameron of Clyde & Co. said:
"That is all nonsense. Gen. Luperon and M. Heraux are great personal friends, and Gen. Luperon was glad to withdraw in Heraux's favor. The fact is that after the election a lot of Gen. Luperon's friends got drunk at Porto Plata and captured the Captain of the port. Then they went to Luperon's house, and bade him lead them against Heraux and capture the city of Santo Domingo. Gen. Luperon came out, and told his misguided friends to go home and sleep it off. They kept up their demonstration until some of them were arrested and taken to Santo Domingo city to be tried. That is all there was in that alleged insurrection."

records.headline: The vessel is now seized and held by the Haytian gov
records.summary_en: The *Burlington weekly free press* reported on December 14, 1888, that the steamer *Haytian Republic* (also referred to as the *Saginaw*) had been seized and held as a prize by the Haytian government for allegedly carrying contraband of war, supplying munitions, and transporting rebel troops to aid insurgents. While the Haytian authorities claimed the vessel aided insurgents who subsequently defeated government troops, the ship's owners denied carrying insurgent supplies, stating the cargo was unloaded at ports under the Dominican government and that their responsibility ended once the goods left the ship.
records.summary_es: El *Burlington weekly free press* informó el 14 de diciembre de 1888 de que el vapor *Haytian Republic* (denominado asimismo *Saginaw*) había sido capturado y declarado presa de guerra por las autoridades haitianas bajo la imputación de transportar contrabando de guerra, proveer pertrechos y trasladar contingentes rebeldes para secundar la insurrección. En tanto el gobierno haitiano aseveraba que la nave prestó auxilio a sediciosos que luego vencieron a tropas oficiales, los armadores negaron haber conducido vituallas revolucionarias, manifestando que los cargamentos se desembarcaron en puertos bajo jurisdicción dominicana y que sus obligaciones fenecían una vez los fardos salían de a bordo.
