records.full_text:
An Important San Domingo Colony from the United States.
The New York World of Sunday contains a splendid article by Lieut. C. H. ROCKWELL of the American Navy, in which he describes with much eloquence and sympathy a visit he made to the colony of Afro-Americans who settled on the Bay of Samana in 1824 and 1825. About 2,000 of these people settled there upon the invitation of President BOYER.
Lieut. ROCKWELL found that the colonists had greatly increased in numbers, that they were prosperous, highly intelligent and hospitable, and that they had clung to the English language, while having acquired the Spanish language, which is generally spoken in Santo Domingo. Lieut. ROCKWELL draws the following picture of the condition of the people:
These sturdy elements of character have not failed to receive recognition even there. The present government estimates the whole colony very highly, and all the offices, from the governor down, are held by the descendants of the American emigrants. There is absolute peace and quietness in the district. The country is vigilantly patrolled, the people seem innocently happy and their hospitality is boundless. There is ample room for many thousands. The people are anxious to receive and welcome and help all who will come. The country is healthy, and its natural resources are boundless.
In conclusion he says:
Here is one emigration and colonization of colored people which has been a success. There is ample room for more; kind, willing hands and hearts to receive them, and a smiling paradise ready for occupancy. The political and social regeneration of the island of Santo Domingo is a possibility for the colored race of the United States.
If the Dominican Republic would offer such inducements to actual settlers as the United States offer to foreigners, we dare say that a very large number of Afro-Americans would take advantage of them, to their own and the betterment of the Dominican government. A hundred thousand could go of the most desirable of the people, and would go if offered fair inducements. We trust the matter will be looked into. What has the Afro-American press to say about the matter? Now is a good time to discuss it.

records.headline: A traveling Odd Fellow's letter in the Age describes the Odd Fellow lodges
records.summary_en: A traveling Odd Fellow's letter in the Age describes the Odd Fellow lodges in Puerto Plata and Santo Domingo: at Puerto Plata he stopped two days, was received by the local lodge, and a large committee waited on him to express their welcome and offer the lodge's hospitality whenever he might visit; at San Domingo he officiated under the vouching of the Honorable H. C. C. Astwood, who established the San Domingo Lodge and under whose direction the work was translated into the Spanish language. The lodge room there, he writes, puts their own old lodge room at home to shame — longer and wider by about ten feet in each dimension, its floor of tiles, its walls kalsomined sky blue, and its borders and ceiling decorated with the emblems of Odd Fellowship, the regalia, altars and insignia all imported from the United States.
records.summary_es: La carta de un viajero de la Orden de los Odd Fellows en el Age describe las logias de la orden en Puerto Plata y Santo Domingo: en Puerto Plata se detuvo dos días, fue recibido por la logia local, y una numerosa comisión lo visitó para expresarle su bienvenida y ofrecerle la hospitalidad de la logia siempre que la visitara; en Santo Domingo ofició bajo el aval del Honorable H. C. C. Astwood, quien estableció la Logia de Santo Domingo y bajo cuya dirección el ritual fue traducido al español. El salón de la logia allí, escribe, avergüenza a su antiguo salón en casa: más largo y más ancho por unos diez pies en cada dimensión, con piso de losetas, paredes encaladas de azul celeste, y bordes y techo decorados con los emblemas de la Odd Fellowship, con las insignias, altares y emblemas importados todos de los Estados Unidos.

records.summary_en: The *Springfield Weekly Republican* reported that Dominican representative Manuel de Jesús Galván was meeting in Washington with Secretary of State James G. Blaine to establish a commercial reciprocity agreement. The Dominican government expressed eagerness for closer ties and offered favorable trade concessions to expand commerce between the two nations.
records.summary_es: El *Springfield Weekly Republican* informó que el representante dominicano Manuel de Jesús Galván se encontraba reunido en Washington con el secretario de Estado James G. Blaine para establecer un acuerdo de reciprocidad comercial. El gobierno dominicano manifestó su vivo interés por estrechar lazos y ofreció concesiones comerciales favorables para expandir el comercio entre ambas naciones.
records.passage: enters the city of New York. The next reciprocity arrangements to be announced will be with the republic of San Domingo and the United States of Venezuela. The representative of the Dominican republic, Senor Galvan, who negotiated the reciprocity treaty of 1884 is here and has had several conferences with Secretary Blaine. The little black republic is anxious to promote the friendliest relations with this country and Senor Galvan seems willing to offer us very favorable terms. The entire trade of San Domingo is not of supreme importance, but the United States could probably easily obtain more than her present share under a favorable reciprocity arrangement. There have been some domestic difficulties in Venezuela which have made progress a little slow in the negotiation of an arrangement with that country, but the people at the state department are confident that an arrangement will soon be well under way. The president of the republic has communicated to the Congress the propositions of Secretary Blaine, and there is a wholesome fear of having the duty imposed upon coffee at the beginning of next year if no agreement is made in the meantime. Our imports of coffee from Venezuela during the fiscal year 1890 reached a value of $9,662,207, making her the most formidable competitor of Brazil, from whom we purchased $45,664,127 worth.

records.headline: The Tribune prints the Dominican special envoy's presentation of his credentials
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints the Dominican special envoy's presentation of his credentials at Washington: the envoy, accredited by an official letter from the President of the Dominican Republic as Minister Plenipotentiary on special mission, tells President Harrison he is charged to propose a commercial arrangement between the two countries in conformity with the recent tariff legislation of the United States, and expresses the sentiments and good disposition with which the Dominican Government and people are animated toward the United States. President Harrison replies that he does not doubt a friendly exchange of views will promptly lead to a conclusion of mutual advantage, and that it will give him great pleasure to promote not only this special work but everything tending to promote peace and good will, welcoming the minister cordially to the capital; a short but cordial exchange of views followed before the envoy took leave.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica la presentación de credenciales del enviado especial dominicano en Washington: el enviado, acreditado por una carta oficial del Presidente de la República Dominicana como ministro plenipotenciario en misión especial, dice al presidente Harrison que está encargado de proponer un arreglo comercial entre los dos países conforme a la reciente legislación arancelaria de los Estados Unidos, y expresa los sentimientos y la buena disposición con que el Gobierno y el pueblo dominicanos están animados hacia los Estados Unidos. El presidente Harrison responde que no duda de que un intercambio amistoso de pareceres conducirá prontamente a una conclusión de ventaja mutua, y que le dará gran placer promover no solo esta labor especial sino todo lo que tienda a promover la paz y la buena voluntad, dando al ministro una cordial bienvenida a la capital; siguió un breve pero cordial intercambio de pareceres antes de que el enviado se retirara.

records.full_text:
SAMANA AS A NAVAL STATION.
Santa Barbara Harbor May Possibly be a Substitute for Mole St. Nicolas.
WASHINGTON, May 27.—It would be strange if after twenty years of neglect the project for the acquisition of a foothold in Samana Bay should now be revived. President Baez, on receiving the news of the rejection by the United States Senate of the famous San Domingo treaty of 1869, put on record the prediction that it would some day be renewed. In the broad form of annexation the scheme is no nearer fruition now than then; but in the very limited particular of securing a repair and coaling station for our war vessels within the Dominican republic there is a prospect of its again coming to the front.
There is little doubt that the State and Navy departments were somewhat chagrined at Hayti's refusal to cede the use of Mole St. Nicolas as a naval station. The indirect but powerful aid which the affair of the steamship Haytian Republic gave to the cause of Hippolyte, when the latter was in arms against Légitime, had hardly been expected to lead up to the futile negotiations lately carried on by Admiral Gherardi and Minister Douglass. It is true that the action of our Government in that affair was directed to the interests of its own citizens and the maritime rights of neutrals in general rather than to interfering for one party in the civil war on the island. It is also probable that the promises of French help with which M. de Sesmaisons buoyed up the hopes of Légitime's followers were not grounded on any assurances from his Government, so that the counter-interference of our own country to prevent European control of Hayti would not have been called for. Still, Hippolyte's cause did undoubtedly receive much moral and some material strength from the United States. But the real ground of the disgust of the Washington authorities is doubtless rather the folly of Hayti in failing to see its own advantage in ceding the use of Mole St. Nicolas, with its resulting local and general benefits to her. Of course the ability of a great power like the United States to conquer and annex Hayti, if that were its object, is too obvious for dispute; while its willingness to take merely a lease of the desired lands and water privileges, and even to receive them through the medium of a private corporation, was a further guarantee of its moderate aims.
But the revival of the Samana project, which is believed to have begun when Admiral Gherardi was ordered a few weeks ago to visit that bay, where Gen. Ulises Heureaux, the President of San Domingo, held a long private interview with him on the flagship, is not to be ascribed to mere official pique. It is true that, should this substitute scheme be carried out, Hayti would probably soon recognize that she had thrown away an opportunity. But the Samana Bay project rests on its intrinsic merits. Situated at the northeastern end of the island, on the south side of Samana peninsula, the bay could hold the war fleets of the whole world. At the western end it receives the Yuma, the chief river of San Domingo. As a strategic position it is of great value, since it opens into the Mona Passage, the principal entrance to the Caribbean Sea for vessels from Europe, and is hardly a day's steaming from the Windward Passage at the other end of the island. As a sheltered place for repairs and coaling, no better need be asked in the West Indies, while it is sufficiently near the Nicaragua Canal to serve in keeping a watch upon that future highway of commerce.
The port of Santa Barbara, which would be the particular region leased, is on the north shore of Samana Bay. The entrance is narrow, from a line of reefs and islets parallel with the shore, but the harbor within is deep enough for large vessels. It could be perfectly covered by batteries, but the true defence would be at the entrance of Samana Bay, where the channel is less than a mile wide in consequence of a cluster of reefs and small islands. Batteries there placed would easily shut out any hostile ships from the entire bay. At the head of Santa Barbara harbor is a village from which a railroad runs westward, and there it is proposed to build a dry dock for repairs.
One thing tolerably clear is that if a reasonable proposal to lease the port of Santa Barbara is made to the Dominican republic it will be accepted. As is well known, this republic occupies the larger part of the island, having an area of about 18,000 square miles, of which only an insignificant part would be taken. Even as early as 1850, only half a dozen years after its independence of Hayti had been declared, San Domingo talked of annexation to the United States, and shortly after the close of our civil war its Government expressed willingness to lease Samana Bay, this being a rival proposition to the St. Thomas annexation project at that time mooted. In 1869 President Grant intrusted Gen. Babcock and Mr. R. H. Perry with negotiations, the result of which was a treaty signed on the 29th of November for the annexation of the whole republic. The money consideration named was $1,500,000, and Gen. Grant, in transmitting the treaty to the Senate, said that he had reason to believe that a European power stood ready to offer $2,000,000 for Samana Bay alone. He argued that the annexation would be in the line of the Monroe doctrine, especially in its aiding the United States to command the Isthmus of Darien. The treaty called for a popular vote in San Domingo, which proved to be almost unanimous for annexation; but it failed to secure the approval of our Senate. In 1873 the bay privileges and peninsula of Samana were ceded to a company formed in the United States, but the following year its rights were declared to be annulled for the non-payment of the stipulated rent. What seems clear is that if even the annexation project was so favored in the island, the present less objectionable form of a concession such as we already hold at Pago Pago from Samoa and at Pearl Island from Hawaii, could be easily procured.

records.full_text:
VIEWS UPON THE LITTLE REPUBLIC.
ADVANTAGES TO BE DERIVED FROM RECIPROCITY—FEATURES OF INTEREST.
Minister Galvan, who represents the Government of San Domingo in this country, and who is at work on a reciprocity treaty between the United States and his Government, is now in New-York, where he expects to remain until the treaty has been signed and the official announcement of it has been made.
A Tribune reporter found him yesterday at his hotel in Union Square. He speaks fairly good English, but his oldest son, who acts as his secretary, also fills the place of interpreter at times. The Minister received the reporter pleasantly, and signified his willingness to discuss San Domingo affairs as freely as the circumstances of his official place would permit.
"In what condition are the negotiations for reciprocity treaty between San Domingo and this country?" he was asked.
"I cannot say anything about that just at present," he replied. "The conditions are such now that I cannot discuss the matter. I will say, however, that the treaty as proposed will be a benefit to both countries. It will aid San Domingo, because if our sugar is let in here free of duty it will stimulate and extend the sugar-growing business of my country. Planters then will have the knowledge that in the United States they can find a steady market. The benefits to your country will come in the admission of American manufactures at such reduced rates of duty that your manufacturers can compete with the other foreign countries in the contest for trade."
"Is there any prospect of your Government ceding the United States a coaling station on Samana Bay?" he was asked.
"Of that I am unable to speak. Nothing has been said to me by my Government about it, and the subject has not been broached in any way by any of the representatives of your country. The bay is probably one of the finest on the globe. It has plenty of water for the largest ships.
"No, I do not think that there will be trouble between the Governments of Hayti and San Domingo. The two countries are not on good terms, owing to Hayti's breach of the treaty of 1874. The Haytians do not want to attack the Dominicans."
GENERAL U. HEUREAUX, President of Santo Domingo.
Everybody knows what a keen observer Nathaniel McKay is, and that he is well up in men, manners and customs as well as in figures. He recently made a voyage to San Domingo, and during his trip he collected many interesting facts and statistics. Mr. McKay had the other day a talk with a Tribune reporter about his journey and the information he had picked up by the way.
"The climate of San Domingo is pleasant, and a voyage to this ancient city in the winter would be one of the most enjoyable that a man could take for his health. The greatest distance out of sight of land is between New-York and Turks Islands; the rest of the time you sail among the islands, day and night. The sea voyage would be much preferable to a trip to Florida. The steamers of the Clyde line are fitted and furnished in the best manner; the food is in abundance and of the best kind; the beds on the ships are excellent."

records.headline: The Record prints a geographical description of Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Record prints a geographical description of Santo Domingo and its great bay: the cape and town of Isabella, where Columbus first established himself, are on the northern coast of the territory the description calls Dominica, and the city of San Domingo, where he finally planted his colony and where his body was deposited when returned from Spain — remaining 240 years until finally taken to Havana — is on the southern coast. The Bay of Samana is beyond doubt the grandest harbor of the Antilles, extending some thirty miles from east to west by nine or twelve from north to south; the peninsula that forms it is a grand promontory of steep, irregular hills ranging from a few hundred to 2,000 feet, covered with dense underbrush, vines and timber and watered by mountain streams that sometimes fall in beautiful cascades. The predominant rock is limestone, with schist, quartz and mica slate also occurring, and bituminous coal is found of exceeding richness; the harbor's entrance, for vessels drawing more than eight feet, is contracted to about 2,000 yards by a broad coral reef, north of which lie five small islands, the largest of about 100 acres.

La bahía de Samaná es sin duda el puerto más grandioso de las Antillas, con unas treinta millas de este a oeste por nueve o doce de norte a sur; la península que la forma es un gran promontorio de colinas escarpadas e irregulares que van de unos pocos cientos a 2,000 pies, cubiertas de densa maleza, enredaderas y bosques y regadas por arroyos de montaña que a veces caen en hermosas cascadas. La roca predominante es la caliza, con esquistos, cuarzo y mica también presentes, y se encuentra carbón bituminoso de extraordinaria riqueza; la entrada del puerto, para buques de más de ocho pies de calado, se estrecha a unas 2,000 yardas por un amplio arrecife de coral, al norte del cual hay cinco islotes, el mayor de unas 100 acres.

records.full_text:
The then recent experiences of the people, however, under foreign domination rendered the proposition inopportune. Although, as the Assistant Secretary reported, the measure commended itself to the better judgment of the leading minds of the Dominion republic, it would require time to satisfy the minds of the people that the occupation of Samana by the United States would be a far different matter from its recent temporary control by Spain, and that our presence and friendship would save them from the very evils which they dreaded, and bring peace and prosperity to take the place of their unhappy discords. The negotiations were, however, broken off; but on the 24th of November in the same year our commercial agent again wrote that an informal proposal had been made to him for a lease of Samana and the following month President Baez, after consulting the magnates of the republic, made arrangements for submitting a proposition for the protection of the United States to a popular vote.
Such was the condition of these negotiations when the administrtion of Mr. Johnson ceased and General Grant was elected President. General Babcock was now sent as a commissioner to act in conjunction with Mr. Perry, the commercial agent of the United States, to negotiate a treaty for the annexation of the whole territory of the republic to the United States, or for a lease of the peninsula and bay of Samana.
In February, 1870, the proposition for annexation was submitted to the people and was approved by an almost unanimous vote. Mr. Perry in his dispatches said: "The whole people desire annexation to the United States."
The treaty, however, failed to receive the requisite two-thirds of the United States Senate, and General Grant again called attention to it in his annual message at the next session of Congress. He said: "I now firmly believe that the moment it is known that the United States have entirely abandoned the project of accepting as a part of its territory the island of Santo Domingo a free port will be negotiated for by European nations. In the bay of Samana a large commercial city will spring up to which we will be tributary without receiving corresponding benefits, and then will be seen the folly of our rejecting so great a prize."
After referring to the fact that the Government and people of St. Domingo had voluntarily sought this annexation—that they were a weak power, yet possessing one of the richest territories under the sun, capable of suporting in luxury 10,000,000 of people—he presented at great length the commercial advantages to be secured, and finally argued that "the acquisition of St. Domingo is an adherence to the Monroe doctrine; that it is a measure of national protection; that it is asserting our just claim to a controlling influence over the great commercial traffic soon to flow from east and west by way of the isthmus—that it is to build up our merchant marine; that it is to furnish new markets for the products of our farms, shops, and manufactories; that it is to extend the area of freedom and to furnish our citizens with the necessaries of life at a cheaper rate than ever before." In fine, he concluded: "So convinced am I of the advantages to flow from the acquisition of St. Domingo and of the great disadvantage—I might say calamities—to flow from non-acquisition that I believe the subject has only to be investigated to be approved."
But this eloquent and patriotic appeal fell unheeded upon the dull ears of an unappreciative Senate, and the matter has strangely remained in abeyance through successive administrations from that day to this, until so disheartened had the authorities and the people of the little republic finally become that they plaintively referred to it in recently declining to be represented at the World's Fair in 1893.
It is true that President Baez and others prophesied that it would some day be renewed. And this has now come to pass. But the renewal now proceeds from the side of the United States, and not until our humble supplications at the other end of the island have been peremptorily rejected. The vigorous increase of our navy, our rapidly augmenting commerce with the southern republics, and the new impetus to be given to isthmian transit by the Nicaragua Canal, and soon, perhaps, by a ship railway at Tehuantepec, all so forcibly urged by General Grant in his repeated appeals to Congress, contribute to impress upon the mind as a matter of imminent importance.—Chicago Times.

records.summary_en: This historical article traces Dominican approaches to the United States from the republic's 1840s application for recognition, through Agent Hogan's 1845 report and Lieutenant D. D. Porter's 1846 survey of the island, to Captain George B. McClellan's 1854 survey of Samana Bay in the flagship Columbus for sites for a naval station and coal depot. It says President Santana was particularly anxious for a general treaty, that in 1856 the American commercial agent was authorized to offer the United States any location in Samana Bay plus its coal mines, that Spain's attempt to restore its power during the American Civil War was abandoned in 1865, and that in January 1867 the United States offered $2,000,000, half in cash and half in arms, for the proposed cession.

AFFAIRS IN SAN DOMINGO.
That Republic Has Not Been Affected by the Troubles in Haiti.
[SPECIAL TELEGRAM TO THE DISPATCH.]
NEW YORK, July 24.—Thomas Simpson, United States Consul at Puerto Plata, San Domingo, is at the Astor Hotel. He expects to return to San Domingo to-morrow afternoon. In an interview this morning he said: "The revolutionary disturbances in Haiti have had no apparent effect on San Domingo. Formerly there was a reciprocity treaty between the two republics, but this is in force no longer. Some months ago representatives of the two powers met at San Domingo and tried to frame a new treaty, but were not successful."
"The President of San Domingo is a native of the United States, and his son is my Vice Consul. However, they are not in favor of annexation with the United States. As far as reciprocity is concerned, I believe there is no particular interest, though the Dominicans are not opposed to it." Mr. Simpson said he believed that with the friendly relations existing between this country and San Domingo a sentiment could easily be created in the latter country in favor of leasing Samana to the United States.

records.headline: The Record-Visitor tells how Columbus's remains came to rest
records.summary_en: The Record-Visitor tells how Columbus's remains came to rest at Santo Domingo: in 1795, when the eastern part of the island came under French dominion, the Spaniards exhumed from the vaults of the cathedral a coffin they judged to contain the body of Columbus and transferred it to Havana. But in 1877 a new vault was discovered in San Domingo, near that opened in 1795, and the coffin found in it bore inscriptions showing that the mortal remains of Christopher Columbus were certainly contained in it; the body previously exhumed was that of his son Diego. At present the remains of the illustrious navigator still repose in the cathedral of San Domingo, capital of the Dominican Republic and one of the most ancient cities founded in America by Europeans; his principal descendant today, the Duke of Veragua, a grandee of Spain, has confided to the Academy of Madrid the task of awarding in 1892 a prize of $6,000 to the author of the best history of his immortal ancestor.
records.summary_es: El Record-Visitor cuenta cómo los restos de Colón llegaron a reposar en Santo Domingo: en 1795, cuando la parte oriental de la isla pasó a dominación francesa, los españoles exhumaron de las bóvedas de la catedral un ataúd que juzgaron contenía el cuerpo de Colón y lo trasladaron a La Habana. Pero en 1877 se descubrió en Santo Domingo una nueva bóveda, cerca de la abierta en 1795, y el ataúd hallado en ella llevaba inscripciones que demostraban que ciertamente contenía los restos mortales de Cristóbal Colón; el cuerpo exhumado anteriormente era el de su hijo Diego. En la actualidad, los restos del ilustre navegante reposan aún en la catedral de Santo Domingo, capital de la República Dominicana y una de las ciudades más antiguas fundadas en América por europeos; su principal descendiente hoy, el duque de Veragua, grande de España, ha confiado a la Academia de Madrid la tarea de premiar en 1892 con $6,000 al autor de la mejor historia de su inmortal antepasado.

records.headline: The Sun argues the strategic case for Samana Bay on expert testimony
records.summary_en: The Sun argues the strategic case for Samana Bay on expert testimony: according to the best testimony obtainable, the harbor might be fortified by a system of defenses not very costly to build, and it would have over St. Thomas the marked advantage of commanding the Mona Pass, one of the two chief strategic points in the Antilles. The two great nautical routes between Europe and the Gulf of Mexico and Central America, the Sun continues, are the Mona Pass, on the south side of the island of San Domingo, and the Mole St. Nicolas route, or Windward Passage, on the northern or Haytian side of the island; the power that occupies these two points and fortifies them will control the principal waterways between Europe and the Gulf of Mexico. Were an interoceanic canal built across Central America, the occupation of both the Mole St. Nicolas and Samana Bay would prove of invaluable importance to the United States, and the Mole lies barely thirty miles from the Cuban coast.

Las dos grandes rutas náuticas entre Europa y el golfo de México y la América Central, continúa el Sun, son el paso de la Mona, en el lado sur de la isla de Santo Domingo, y la ruta del Môle St. Nicolas, o paso de los Vientos, en el lado norte o haitiano de la isla; la potencia que ocupe esos dos puntos y los fortifique controlará las principales vías acuáticas entre Europa y el golfo de México. Si se construyera un canal interoceánico a través de la América Central, la ocupación tanto del Môle St. Nicolas como de la bahía de Samaná resultaría de inestimable importancia para los Estados Unidos, y el Môle dista apenas treinta millas de la costa cubana.

records.full_text:
RECIPROCITY WITH SAN DOMINGO.
President Harrison's Proclamation Giving the List of Duty-Free Articles.
WASHINGTON, Aug. 1.—The President to-day issued a proclamation announcing reciprocity with San Domingo, under the tariff act of last October, which, with a view to securing reciprocal trade, exempted from duty sugars, molasses, coffee and hides imported into the United States. By this treaty the following articles manufactured in the United States will be admitted free of duty into the Dominican republic from and after Sept. 1, 1891:
Live animals; meats of all kinds, excepting smoked corn; corn-meal and starch; oats, barley, rye and buckwheat, and flour of these grains; hay; bran and straw; trees; plants, vines and seeds; cotton-seed oil and meal-cake; pitch tar, turpentine and rosin; coal; mineral waters; ice machines; mining machinery; agricultural implements; railway material; wrought and cast-iron and steel, in pigs, bars, rods, beams, etc., and wire nails, screws and pipes; zinc, tin and lead, and roofing material; copper in bars, plates, nails, etc., and copper and lead pipe; bricks, cement, lime, stone, marble and paving tiles; fence wire, telegraph wire and apparatus; wood and lumber of all kinds; material for ship-building; school furniture; books, pamphlets, printed matter and paper for newspapers; inks, gold and silver coin and bullion.
The following articles are to be admitted into the Dominican republic at a reduction of duty of 25 per centum:
Butter, cheese and condensed milk; fish of all kinds; fruits and vegetables of all kinds; cotton, manufactured, spun or twisted, and in fabrics of all kinds, woven or knit, and the same fabrics mixed with other vegetable or animal fibres in which cotton is the equal or greater component part; boots and shoes; writing paper, blank books, wall paper, paper for wrapping and packing, for cigarettes in cardboard boxes and bags, sandpaper and pasteboard; tin-plate and tinware for arts, industries and domestic uses; cordage, rope and twine of all kinds; woodenware implements for household use
The proclamation closes with the following language: "And whereas, the special plenipotentiary of the United States has by my direction given assurance to the envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary of the Dominican republic at Washington that this action of the government of the Dominican republic in granting exemption of duties to the products and manufactures of the United States of America on their importation into the Dominican republic is accepted as a due reciprocity for the action of Congress as set forth in Section 3 of said act;
"Now, therefore, be it known that I, Benjamin Harrison, President of the United States of America, have caused the above-stated modifications of the tariff laws of the Dominican republic to be made public for the information of the citizens of the United States of America. In testimony whereof I have hereunto set my hand and caused the seal of the United States to be affixed. Done at the city of Washington, the first day of August, one thousand, eight hundred and ninety-one, and of the independence of the United States of America the one hundred and sixteenth.
"BENJAMIN HARRISON.
"William A. Wharton, Acting Secretary of State."
The correspondence preceding the proclamation of the treaty was brief, consisting of but two letters exchanged between Senor Galvan, Minister of the Dominican Republic, and Hon. John W. Foster, special plenipotentiary of the United States, both bearing date June 4, 1891. The schedules submitted by Senor Galvan were accepted with the exception of the following sentence, which is omitted from the treaty:
"It is understood that the packages or coverings in which the articles named in the foregoing schedules are imported shall be free of duty if they are usual and proper for the purpose."

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on specific assurances given by the Dominican government under the new reciprocity arrangement with the United States. Santo Domingo pledged not to raise export duties on free-list goods, to extend any future export duty reductions to American shipments, and to prevent discriminatory municipal taxes on United States products. The treaty permitted reasonable customs regulations to verify the origin of goods while protecting Dominican revenue without imposing undue restrictions on importers.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó sobre las garantías específicas brindadas por el gobierno dominicano bajo el nuevo arreglo de reciprocidad con los Estados Unidos. Santo Domingo se comprometió a no aumentar los aranceles de exportación sobre los artículos de la lista libre, a extender cualquier reducción futura de aranceles de exportación a los envíos estadounidenses y a evitar impuestos municipales discriminatorios sobre los productos de Estados Unidos. El tratado permitía reglamentaciones aduaneras razonables para verificar el origen de las mercancías protegiendo los ingresos fiscales dominicanos, sin imponer restricciones indebidas a los importadores.

RECIPROCITY.
Provisions of the New Trading Arrangement with San Domingo to go into Effect Sept. 1.
NEW YORK, July 30.—A Washington dispatch announces the conclusion of an important treaty of reciprocity between the United States and the republic of San Domingo. The treaty was negotiated by Maquel De J. Galvin, minister plenipotentiary and envoy extraordinary, on the part of San Domingo and John W. Foster, special commissioner, on the part of the United States, and was signed in Washington June 4. Under the terms of the McKinley bill the treaty does not require ratification by the senate. As Senor Galvin was specially authorized by his government to carry on the negotiations and was granted full power to sign the convention the treaty will go into force without delay. September 1 is the day fixed upon. The full text will be officially published within a few days. Both Secretary Blaine and the president have approved the treaty.
Secretary Suarez, of the Dominican legation, has just returned to this city from a flying trip to San Domingo, where he laid the text of the convention before President Heureaux and received his indorsement on July 4. The treaty follows closely the lines laid down in the convention with Brazil. In the opening sections the authority of the McKinley act for the free entry of sugar, molasses, coffee, cocoa and hides is referred to and in reciprocity for these concessions the admission into Dominican ports is authorized of goods enumerated in two schedules which are appended, the one schedule without any duty and the other with a reduction of 25 per cent. upon the duty now levied. In the free schedule are enumerated various breadstuffs, potatoes, hay and oats, pork and fish, cotton-seed oil, agricultural implements, mining and mechanical tools and material for the construction and equipment of railways.
The admission into Dominican ports of a large number of articles with a reduction of 25 per cent. on the present duty is authorized by a clause in the treaty and a schedule appended including cured and canned meats and vegetables, manufactures of cotton, iron and steel not included in the free schedule, unmanufactured leather, lumber, and manufactures of wood, etc.
In exchange for $1,715,000 worth of sugar the United States last year sent to San Domingo a trifle over $925,000 worth of goods which included wheat, flour, lard, cottons, iron and steel manufacture and wood manufactures. A good deal of New England capital is invested in the island.

records.headline: The Democrat prints a geographical description of Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Democrat prints a geographical description of Santo Domingo and its great bay: the Bay of Samaná, to which the United States has been invited, is at one extreme of the island, in the territory the description calls Dominica, commanding the Mona passage, the principal channel to the Caribbean Sea and the Spanish Main, while the island's northwesternmost point is in Haytian territory. The cape and town of Isabela, where Columbus first established himself, are on the northern coast of Dominica, and the city of Santo Domingo, where he finally planted his colony and where his body rested 240 years after its return from Spain before being taken to Havana, is on the southern coast. The bay is beyond doubt the grandest harbor of the Antilles, extending some thirty miles from east to west by nine or twelve from north to south; the peninsula that forms it is a grand promontory broken into exceedingly steep, irregular hills ranging from a few hundred to 2,000 feet, covered with a dense growth of underbrush, vines, and timber and watered by numerous mountain streams that sometimes fall in beautiful cascades. The predominant rock is limestone, with schistose rocks, quartz, and an abundance of mica slate also occurring, and bituminous coal is found of exceeding richness.

records.headline: The Times tells how the remains of Columbus came to rest in the cathedral of San Domingo
records.summary_en: The Times tells how the remains of Columbus came to rest in the cathedral of San Domingo in the Dominican Republic: in 1795, when the eastern part of the island came under French dominion, the Spaniards exhumed from the vaults of the cathedral a coffin they judged contained the body of Columbus and transferred it to Havana. But in 1877 a new vault was discovered in San Domingo, near that opened in 1795, and the coffin found in it bore inscriptions which showed that the mortal remains of Christopher Columbus were certainly contained in it; the body previously exhumed was that of his son Diego. At present the mortal part of the illustrious navigator still reposes in the cathedral of San Domingo, capital of the Dominican Republic and one of the most ancient cities founded in America by Europeans; his principal descendant today is the Duke of Veragua, a grandee of Spain, who has confided to the Academy of Madrid the task of awarding in 1892 a prize of $6,000 to the author of the best history of his immortal ancestor.

records.full_text:
THE TRADE TREATIES.
Representative STONE, of Kentucky, has introduced in Congress a resolution, which was adopted, calling upon the secretary of the treasury for a tabular statement of all goods imported into Porto Rico and the Dominican republic under the operation of the reciprocity treaty, and upon the secretary of state for copies of all communications between the United States and Spain, San Salvador and Brazil on the subject of reciprocal trade relations with the United States. The aim of this is to ascertain whether there has been any practical benefit to our people from reciprocity as applied to these nations.
The scope of the proposed inquiry is a limited one. It might very well be applied to all the Central and South American countries, and no doubt will eventually be extended to embrace the whole of them. There is little doubt that this country is paying, or is proposing to pay, dear for the much-vaunted reciprocity whistle, and that the reciprocal trade relations mean a market for manufactures and products of our coast states, without material benefits to western agriculturists, merchants and people generally.
The latest treaty is with San Salvador and gives it, free of duty, all kinds of machinery, agricultural implements, lumber, wagons, iron and steel products, furnaces, building material, coal, fruits, cereals, and preparations of flour, all of which when imported into the United States are taxed from 35 to 100 per cent. In none of the reciprocity treaties is taxation reduced upon articles brought to the United States.
It is to be hoped that a complete overhauling will be given by Congress to the whole business of negotiating these treaties and the effect they have had and are likely to have upon our commerce.

Hale explained that the executive power to impose retaliatory sugar tariffs had served as vital leverage to secure trade concessions for American agricultural and manufactured goods internationally.

Hale explicó que la facultad del poder ejecutivo para imponer aranceles de represalia al azúcar había servido como una herramienta de presión fundamental para obtener concesiones comerciales a escala internacional para los productos agrícolas y manufacturados estadounidenses.

However, the correspondent noted that complications existed because the Samaná Bay Company held prior treaty claims, necessitating that the State Department resolve the company's damage claims against the Dominican government before securing a title.

Sin embargo, el corresponsal señaló que existían complicaciones debido a que la Samaná Bay Company poseía reclamos derivados de tratados previos, lo que exigía que el Departamento de Estado resolviera los reclamos por daños y perjuicios de la compañía contra el gobierno dominicano antes de asegurar un título de propiedad.

Engineers have declared it to be the best place for a coaling station in the whole West Indies, as it is easily approached without danger from reefs or shoals, while it is a matter of peril to undertake to reach many of the other islands, so hemmed in are they by dangers to the navigator. The United States Buys Samana Bay.

PARIS, June 8.—A dispatch from Kingston, Jamaica, says great excitement was caused in San Domingo by the announcement that the port of Samana bay, in the western part of the island, had been ceded to the United States and the cession confirmed. The Haitian minister is alarmed, owing to the fact that American Minister Durham, of Haiti, who is in charge of affairs at San Domingo, has taken residence in the city of San Domingo. The German consul at Port-au-Prince has received instructions to come to an understanding with the representatives of France and England with regard to taking steps to safeguard the autonomy of San Domingo.

[Samana bay is on the south side of the peninsula of Samana. It is about forty-three miles in length from east to west, by about eight miles broad, and at its west end receives the Yuma, the largest river in the Dominican republic. It forms one of the finest harbors in the world, and may be regarded as a most important maritime position, in reference to the trade of the Gulf of Mexico and the interoceanic routes across Central America, both in a commercial and military point of view.]

records.full_text:
RECIPROCITY ATTACKED

Germany Secretly Working Against the United States.

BRIBERY AND COERCION EMPLOYED

The State Department Cognizant of the Overtures Made to the Pan-American Republics to Abrogate the Existing Treaties With This Country.

NEW YORK, Oct. 3.—That there is a conspiracy among the great European nations to force the Pan-American republics to abrogate their reciprocity treaties with this country seems to be a settled fact. All the means known to the diplomats of the Old World, from coercion to bribery, are being used without stint, and all the benefits which have resulted from reciprocal treaties to the manufacturers and producers of the United States are liable to be lost unless the most decisive steps are taken by this government.

That such steps will be taken may be regarded as certain, for Secretary of State John W. Foster, when approached by the representative of the president of one of these republics with the request that the United States outbid a bribe offered by Germany, replied:

"This country is neither to be blackmailed nor bullied. If your country breaks the treaty it must be prepared to bear all the consequences of that act, for in my mind the word 'reciprocate' is coupled with 'retaliation.'"

The moving cause for this action on the part of the European nations is that the trade which for years they have monopolized with the Pan-American countries has, since the reciprocal treaties with the United States went into effect, been fading away.

The republic which at present is considering offers of bribes is San Domingo. Although small she has heretofore done a large trade with European countries, particularly Germany.

Two months ago a formal protest was made to the Dominican government by the representatives of Germany, Italy and France against the further continuance of reciprocity with this country, and it was accompanied by a demand that the treaty be abrogated at once. The Dominican government stood firm, however, and the consul in New York, Francisco Leonte Vasquez, was instructed to visit Washington and consult with Secretary of State John W. Foster. He did so, and while nothing definite was decided upon he was assured that the United States would see that San Domingo was protected in her rights. With this assurance the consul returned to this city.

Germany the Moving Power.

As soon as it was found that bullying did not succeed another tack was taken. Germany was chosen as the moving power of the conspiracy, because her relations with the little republic are peculiar.

In 1885 a treaty was signed between the two, in which Germany was named as the "most favored of nations." Her goods were permitted to enter Dominican ports at extremely low imposts, and her citizens were to receive special favors and exemptions.

On the other hand, many Dominican products were given precedence in Germany, and under this treaty a large and valuable trade grew up between the two nations. Dominican tobacco especially found favor in Germany and soon crowded out the Sumatra product, and at present almost the entire product of Puerto Plata is used in Germany.

The loss of this market for its staple product would be a serious blow to the San Domingan people, and it was on this line that the conspirators went to work.

A special envoy was sent from Germany to San Domingo, and about two weeks ago he had an interview with President Ulises Heureaux, in which the harm which could be done his country should Germany close her ports to Dominican products was fully set forth. The German envoy then offered a personal subsidy of $50,000 a year to the president "to recompense him for any unpopularity he might incur" if the reciprocity treaty with the United States was abrogated.

President Heureaux at once dispatched an emissary to this country to see if he could not obtain $75,000 from the United States. The person chosen for this work was a merchant, who is a correspondent of the exporting and shipping firm of Eggers & Heinflein, of 5 South William street, this city. On his arrival he saw Mr. Eggers and explained his mission. He requested Mr. Eggers to accompanying him to Whshington to interview Secretary Foster. Mr. Eggers refused, and the San Domingan then visited other friends and requested their aid with a like result. About ten days ago he went to Washington alone and saw the secretary.

Only the Entering Wedge.

The answer he received from Mr. Foster is that quoted above. The San Domingan told friends here that he would go to Germany in hopes of getting that government to raise its offer. He sailed for Europe last Thursday.

When questioned about the transaction Mr. Heinlein, of the firm of Eggers & Heinlein, said: "I know little or nothing about it. I was away at the time, and my partner, Mr. Eggers, had charge of the business. However, I have known for a long time that the European nations would try to break up our reciprocal relations with the Pan-American countries.

"I have been to Germany this summer, and I know that country has been trying to force San Domingo to abrogate the treaty, and I expect she will be successful. You see the entire tobacco crop is used in Germany, and the commercial relations between the two countries are very close. For that reason she, of all other nations, is the one now to move in this matter, and if she can force San Domingo to abrogate the treaty, then an immediate attack will be made on all the other republics having reciprocal relations with this country to force them to follow her example.

"If the Dominican treaty is broken I fully expect to see all the others broken as well, and that within a very short time. The fact of the matter is that England, Germany, France and Italy all have large and valuable interests in South and Central America, and they cannot afford to have their trade with those points destroyed because of reciprocity with the United States. All of these countries have experience in handling such matters, and it is quite certain that nothing will be left undone to gain the end desired. Germany's step is but the entering wedge."

When questioned as to the name of the merchant who acted as the messenger in the attempt to blackmail the United States government he refused to give the slightest information.

San Domingo Asks Our Aid.

Consul Francisco Leonte Vasquez, of 31 Broadway, who represents the Dominican republic in this city, when seen by a reporter seemed very much surprised that the matter had become known. He said, "This affair is still in the hands of the state department at Washington and it was agreed that it should be kept secret for the present.

"The outlook for a practical monopoly of the Dominican trade was excellent until the present troubles began. When Germany, Italy and France made demand upon our government for the abrogation of the reciprocity treaty our government stood firm. Then they demanded to be placed on the same footing in all respects as the United States, which would have been a practical annullment of the treaty. It was then I was sent to Washington to see what could be done. Of course our small republic would be almost helpless with these three nations attacking us at once, and we wanted to be certain of the aid of the United States in case of trouble. I had a talk with Secretary Foster over the matter, but while he was most encouraging he wished the matter to remain in abeyance for a time.

An Envoy to Crespo.

"No course of action was decided upon, and the certainty that Germany would use our tobacco industry to force matters to a crisis has troubled me greatly. That Germany will try to produce this result unless we recede from our treaty obligations with the United States I have for a long time known.

"Another feature of this attempt of the European nations to cause the abrogation of all reciprocity treaties with Pan-American republics is that the present Venezuelan government is being aided with money and supplies by England, Germany and France. An offer was made and accepted shortly after Crespo's rebellion had begun, and the terms have been ratified by both parties since. The agreement was that the present government should refuse to ratify the reciprocity treaty with the United States and should refuse all overtures to that end while opening its ports freely to European trade.

"An envoy was sent to Crespo, and he agreed that on obtaining power his government would promptly ratify the treaty thrown aside by the present officials.

"On his pledge to this effect money was sent him and the South Portland and one other vessel, the name of which the members of the "junta" refuse to give, were sent down laden with arms.

records.summary_en: *The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer* reported that a German envoy threatened to embargo Dominican tobacco and offered President Ulises Heureaux an annual bribe of $50,000 to terminate the reciprocity treaty with the United States. In response, Heureaux sent a confidential emissary to New York merchants to determine whether the United States government would pay him $75,000 to preserve the treaty.

En respuesta, Heureaux envió a un emisario confidencial ante comerciantes de Nueva York para averiguar si el gobierno de los Estados Unidos le pagaría 75.000 dólares para mantener el tratado.

records.summary_en: *The National Tribune* reported that European nations lodged diplomatic protests against the United States-Dominican reciprocity treaty, demanding identical trade privileges under existing most-favored-nation pacts. The Dominican government defended the treaty, explaining that special concessions were necessary because the United States accounted for the majority of Dominican trade and provided essential markets for its sugar, coffee, and hides. Facing persistent European pressure, President Heureaux appealed to Washington for diplomatic backing.
records.summary_es: El *National Tribune* informó que varias naciones europeas presentaron protestas diplomáticas contra el tratado de reciprocidad entre los Estados Unidos y la República Dominicana, exigiendo privilegios comerciales idénticos en virtud de los pactos existentes de nación más favorecida. El gobierno dominicano defendió el tratado explicando que las concesiones especiales eran necesarias debido a que Estados Unidos representaba la mayor parte del comercio dominicano y ofrecía mercados fundamentales para su azúcar, café y cueros. Ante la persistente presión europea, el presidente Heureaux apeló a Washington en busca de respaldo diplomático.

The European powers mentioned above followed these negotiations with a jealous eye, as they were the only countries outside of the United States which had any considerable commerce with the island, and it was very manifest that the adoption of such a favorable treaty would give our country a practical monopoly of San Domingo's import trade. The paper characterized the international controversy as exaggerated, pointing out that total Dominican commerce was modest and that recent gains in American exports had merely displaced European competitors.

El periódico calificó la controversia internacional de exagerada, señalando que el comercio total dominicano era modesto y que los recientes incrementos en las exportaciones estadounidenses se limitaban a desplazar a los competidores europeos.

There the matter stands at present. After all, this tempest in a teapot over the concessions granted by the Dominican Government to the United States seems to be rather an absurd affair. records.summary_en: *The Kimball Graphic* published excerpts from President Benjamin Harrison's annual message to Congress reviewing foreign relations. Harrison reported that successful reciprocal trade agreements under Section 3 of the tariff act had been concluded with numerous countries, including the Dominican Republic, Brazil, Spain for its Caribbean colonies, and the German Empire.

records.headline: A railway between Puerto Plata and Santiago de Los Caballeros
records.summary_en: The *St. Paul Daily Globe* detailed the collapse of the Dutch Westendorp concession, which had issued millions in bonds to finance a railway between Puerto Plata and Santiago that remained largely unbuilt. Facing default and exhausted credit, the Dutch financiers negotiated a transfer of their Dominican debt claims and customs-collection rights to an American syndicate organized by New York financiers.

Ante la suspensión de pagos y el agotamiento del crédito, los financieros holandeses negociaron la transferencia de sus reclamaciones sobre la deuda dominicana y de sus derechos de recaudación aduanera a un consorcio estadounidense organizado por financistas neoyorquinos.

A railway between Puerto Plata and Santiago de Los Caballeros, an inland city, has long been the subject of discussion. The bonds were issued to complete and equip the railway. Only about eleven miles of road are finished, and in addition to the first $6,000,000 of bonds the country has become responsible for about $1,800,000 additional. The export and import duties amount to about $1,200,000 per annum. records.summary_en: A Madrid dispatch says the Captain-General of Cuba reported great popular excitement in Santo Domingo over the concession of the customs, with an accompanying grant of land, to an American syndicate, with President Heureaux fiercely denounced and every sign of an imminent revolution. A Spanish vessel had left Cuba for Santo Domingo to protect Spanish interests, amid fears the concession was only a prelude to a United States attempt on Dominican independence, and Madrid had asked for specific information before deciding whether to send a protest to Washington.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Madrid dice que el capitán general de Cuba informó de una gran agitación popular en Santo Domingo por la concesión de las aduanas, con una cesión de tierras que la acompañaba, a un consorcio estadounidense, con el presidente Heureaux fieramente denunciado y todos los indicios de una revolución inminente. Un buque español había salido de Cuba rumbo a Santo Domingo para proteger los intereses españoles, ante el temor de que la concesión fuera solo el preludio de un intento de los Estados Unidos contra la independencia dominicana, y Madrid había pedido información específica antes de decidir si enviaría una protesta a Washington.
records.passage: Madrid, Feb. 20. — The Minister of the Colonies has received a dispatch from Rodriguez Arias, Captain-General of Cuba, stating that great popular excitement prevails in Santo Domingo, in consequence of the concession of the customs, with an accompanying grant of land, to an American syndicate. General Heureaux, the President of Santo Domingo, is fiercely denounced by the people, and there is every sign of a revolution being imminent. A Spanish vessel has left Cuba for Santo Domingo to protect Spanish interests in the Republic. The excitement among the people of Santo Domingo is based on a fear that the concession to the syndicate is only a prelude to an attempt by the United States upon Dominican independence. The telegram from Captain-General Arias hints at interference by the United States in Dominican affairs. The Minister of the Colonies has sent a cable dispatch to the Captain-General asking for specific information as to any action [illegible] the United States [illegible] and the decision whether or not the Spanish Government will send a protest to Washington against any course on the part of the United States that intrenches upon or menaces the independence of Santo Domingo. records.summary_en: *The Indianapolis Journal* reported that Dominican President Ulises Heureaux moved ruthlessly to crush a suspected conspiracy by ordering the summary arrest and execution of prominent political opponents in the capital. In one raid, government troops surrounded the residence of Dr. Theick, fatally shooting his wife and servants, while Theick narrowly escaped through a window and fled abroad to Jamaica.
records.summary_es: *The Indianapolis Journal* informó que el presidente dominicano Ulises Heureaux actuó de manera despiadada para aplastar una supuesta conspiración al ordenar el arresto sumario y la ejecución de prominentes opositores políticos en la capital. En una redada, tropas gubernamentales rodearon la residencia del Dr. Theick, matando a tiros a su esposa y a sus sirvientes, mientras que Theick escapó milagrosamente por una ventana y huyó al extranjero rumbo a Jamaica.
records.passage: for some time that he would strike a blow which he hoped would crush the opposition and put an end to the plot against him. A few days ago President Heureaux discovered what he announced was a conspiracy against him, with which many leading men of the Dominican capital were alleged to be connected. President Heureaux ordered that all the leaders of the conspiracy be arrested and shot. Soldiers were sent to surround the residences of all the suspected persons. Dr. Theick's house was one of the first visited. When the soldiers appeared he knew their visit meant death to himself, and he hastened preparations to escape. The soldiers opened fire and riddled Mrs. Theick and the servants with bullets. The Doctor leaped from a window, mounted a horse and fled. He made his way to Cape Hayti, and from there sailed to Kingston, reaching here in safety. His own departure was so hurried that he did not learn the fate of the other men whom Heureaux had sentenced to death. Generals Arnaux and Momplasier, exiles from Hayti, have been arrested here by order of the government of Jamaica. They are accused of violating international law by fitting out and arming a vessel in August, 1893, to be employed in ousting Hippolyte from the presidency of the black republic. General Momplasier was formerly Minister of the Interior of Hayti. Senator Morgan Recovering. Southampton, March 7. The condition of Senator John T. records.summary_en: A Paris dispatch of March 20 in the Tribune reports the rumor of French troops and its denial: nothing is known in Paris to confirm the advices said to have been received in Madrid to the effect that French troops had landed in San Domingo. The concern felt in government circles at Madrid in regard to a French or American intervention in the Dominican Republic has been caused probably, the dispatch says, by the reading of dispatches published in a New-York paper on March 7, according to which a man whose nationality the dispatch does not indicate had arrived at Kingston, Jamaica, and related there that soldiers had been sent by President Heureaux to capture him, as he was accused of conspiring against the Dominican Government, and that he had succeeded in escaping by a back door while his wife and children were riddled by the bullets of the troops. This story has not yet been denied or confirmed; at any rate, the dispatch says, it is certain that no American intervention or 'aggression,' as the Madrid cable dispatch puts it, has occurred in Santo Domingo. records.summary_en: *The Sun* commented on Spanish apprehensions regarding the Dominican Republic, asserting that Spain could neither re-establish colonial control nor prevent voluntary annexation by the United States. The editorial noted that under the Monroe Doctrine, European powers—including Spain and France—were strictly barred from acquiring territory or interfering in the political destinies of New World republics.
records.summary_es: *The Sun* comentó sobre los temores españoles respecto a la República Dominicana, aseverando que España no podía restablecer el control colonial ni impedir una anexión voluntaria por parte de los Estados Unidos. El editorial señalaba que, en virtud de la Doctrina Monroe, a las potencias europeas —incluidas España y Francia— se les prohibía terminantemente adquirir territorios o intervenir en los destinos políticos de las repúblicas del Nuevo Mundo.
records.passage: troop to prevent that step from being consummated, or of her rallying Europe around her. The annexation of San Domingo is nowhere talked of or dreamed of here at the present time, but does Spain imagine that if the people of the United States and the people of San Domingo wished to join fortunes she would have the right or power to prevent it? On the other hand, if the secret of this otherwise inexplicable [illegible] in Madrid is the [illegible] on the part of Spain to regain her old control in San Domingo, she may as well abandon it. She could not be suffered to acquire as her own either the eastern or the western part of the Island. That would conflict with American policy as embodied in the Monroe doctrine. This policy and doctrine, however, may relieve Spain from her latest source of anxiety — the supposed designs of France upon San Domingo. For it does not even accord to France the right to transfer to herself Cuba, which is now not free but under European domination. Secretary Clay's letter of Oct. 25, [illegible], is clear on that point, while as to the republics of the New World, Monroe had declared that any interposition for the purpose of oppressing them, or controlling in any other manner their destiny, by any European power, would be regarded as the manifestation of an unfriendly disposition toward the United States. This view is not essentially altered by the fact that France, then a monarchy, is now a republic. records.headline: Sage to Congress after the rejection of the Annexation treaty
records.summary_en: The *St. Croix Avis* revisited President Grant's arguments for annexing the Dominican Republic, emphasizing its heightened relevance with the planned construction of the Nicaragua Canal. The article argued that acquiring Santo Domingo and its strategic harbor at Samaná Bay would enable the United States to safeguard the Mona Passage and counterbalance British naval influence in the Caribbean.
records.summary_es: El *St. Croix Avis* retomó los argumentos del presidente Grant a favor de la anexión de la República Dominicana, destacando su creciente relevancia ante la proyectada construcción del canal de Nicaragua. El artículo sostenía que la adquisición de Santo Domingo y de su puerto estratégico en la bahía de Samaná permitiría a los Estados Unidos proteger el paso de la Mona y contrarrestar la influencia naval británica en el Caribe.
records.passage: sage to Congress after the rejection of the Annexation treaty, President Grant said: The acquisition of San Domingo is an adherence to the Monroe Doctrine; it is a measure of national protection; it is asserting our just claim to a controlling influence over the great commercial traffic soon to flow from west to east by way of the Isthmus of Darien. So convinced am I of the advantage to flow from the acquisition of San Domingo, and of the great disadvantages — I might almost say calamities — to flow from non-acquisition, that I believe the subject has only to be investigated to be approved. The building and control of the Nicaragua Canal by this government immensely increases the importance of the consideration urged by the patriotic President in favour of bringing the Dominican republic under the Stars and Stripes. Great Britain has Jamaica to command that waterway. With San Domingo in our possession we could promptly checkmate any hostile designs against the canal in case of war. It commands Mona Passage, through which lies the direct route of European commerce from the Atlantic to the Caribbean Sea and the coasts of South and Central America. Samana Bay offers a safe and commodious harbour, one of the finest in the world, whose entrance is guarded by cliffs and coral reefs on all sides. To obtain San Domingo would be to cut in two the cordon of fortified stations drawn by England from Halifax via the Bermudas and the Bahamas, around our Eastern and Southern coasts. records.summary_en: *The Morning Call* reviewed early United States diplomatic and naval missions to the Dominican Republic, including Lieutenant David D. Porter's 1846 survey of Dominican finances and Samaná Bay's strategic harbors. The paper also recalled the 1851 joint mission of Robert M. Walsh alongside British and French commissioners to negotiate an end to Haitian military incursions against the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: *The Morning Call* examinó las primeras misiones diplomáticas y navales de los Estados Unidos en la República Dominicana, incluida la inspección efectuada en 1846 por el teniente David D. Porter sobre las finanzas dominicanas y los puertos estratégicos de la bahía de Samaná. El diario también recordó la misión conjunta de 1851 de Robert M. Walsh junto con comisionados británicos y franceses para negociar el cese de las incursiones militares haitianas contra la República Dominicana.
records.passage: [illegible] dropped anchor off the ancient city of San Domingo, May 6, [illegible]. Lieutenant Porter found the Dominican finances in a deplorable condition. The small amount of specie in the country was in the hands of usurers. The currency consisted of paper and copper tokens, and twenty paper dollars were equivalent to one [illegible] silver. On his return to Washington, Porter made a full report in duplicate, one for the State and the other for the Navy Department, but both of these papers disappeared from the departments prior to the breaking out of the Civil War in 1861. The report was highly favorable in tone, commending the excellent harbor at Samana Bay, and pointing to its strategical advantages as a naval station. In 1851 President Fillmore and Secretary of State Webster commissioned Robert M. Walsh as special agent of the Government to Hayti and San Domingo to co-operate with the British and French commissioners in bringing about a cessation of the warfare that the Haytians had been waging on the peacefully inclined and numerically inferior San Dominicans. The United States steamer Saranac conveyed Commissioner Walsh to Port-au-Prince, where he met the French and English commissioners, and during a stay of some weeks had two interviews with Emperor Faustin I. With the French and English commissioners he then went to San Domingo and reported the results of their negotiations at Hayti to President Baez of the Dominican republic. records.summary_en: *The Seattle Post-Intelligencer* reported that an armed insurgent force led by General Pablo Reyes and Horacio Vásquez crossed from Haiti into Dajabón on March 10 to invade the Dominican Republic. Dominican government forces commanded by Governor Anderson repulsed the invasion, resulting in twelve deaths during the combat. Haitian President Florvil Hyppolite cooperated by disarming the retreating insurgents and deporting their leaders aboard the steamer *Ozama* to Turks Island.
records.summary_es: *The Seattle Post-Intelligencer* informó que una fuerza insurgente armada encabezada por el general Pablo Reyes y Horacio Vásquez cruzó desde Haití hacia Dajabón el 10 de marzo para invadir la República Dominicana. Las fuerzas gubernamentales dominicanas, comandadas por el gobernador Anderson, repelieron la invasión, con un saldo de doce muertos durante el combate. El presidente haitiano Florvil Hyppolite cooperó desarmando a los insurgentes en retirada y deportando a sus líderes a bordo del vapor *Ozama* hacia las islas Turcas.
records.passage: AN EPHEMERAL REVOLUTION. How the Late Invasion of San Domingo Was Squelched. NEW YORK, April 2. — Advices from Cape Haytien, under the date of March 26, say: An invasion of Santo Domingo occurred at Dajabon, on the borders between Santo Domingo and Haiti, on March 10. The attacking force consisted of [illegible] men, under the insurgent leaders, Gen. Pablo Reyes, R. Vasquez and others. Two men were killed. The insurgents were repulsed by a force of 200 Dominican soldiers, led by Gov. Anderson, of Samana, and aides, and ten of the Dominicans lost their lives. By order of President Hyppolite, of Haiti, the insurgents were disarmed and brought here. The rebels, including Gens. Pablo Reyes and H. AN EPHEMERAL REVOLUTION. How the Late Invasion of San Domingo Was Squelched.

NEW YORK, April 2.—Advices from Cape Haytien, under the date of March 26, say: An invasion of Santo Domingo occurred at Dejabon, on the borders between Santo Domingo and Haiti on March 10. The attacking force consisted of 160 men, under the insurgent leaders, Gen. Pablo Reyes, H. Vasques and others. Two men were killed. The insurgents were repulsed by a force of 200 Dominican soldiers, led by Gov. Anderson, of Samana, and aides, and ten of the Dominicans lost their lives.

By order of President Hippolyte, of Haiti, the insurgents were disarmed and brought here. The rebels, including Gens. Pablo Reyes and H. Vasquez and others, were forced to leave the country by being put aboard the steamer Ozama to be left at Turk's Island.

records.headline: The Bee prints news from Santo Domingo of an insurrection against President Heureaux
records.summary_en: The Bee prints news from Santo Domingo of an insurrection against President Heureaux and of the issue the insurrectionists raise: a statement quoted in the report says that troops are massed on the border of Santo Domingo, but that the writer is also officially informed this is only a measure of caution and there is no danger of a battle. News of a more serious nature has been received, however, from Santo Domingo: it is said that under the leadership of General Ygnacio Ma. Gonzales, the discontented citizens of that republic have started an insurrection against President Heureaux. Gonzales was secretary of foreign affairs under the previous administration, which retired February 27. The issue raised by the insurrectionists is opposition to the supposed policy of annexation to the United States: Gonzales had circulated reports that President Heureaux is scheming for the annexation of the republic. The majority of the citizens of Santo Domingo, the report adds, oppose any change of government.
records.summary_es: El Bee publica noticias de Santo Domingo sobre una insurrección contra el presidente Heureaux y sobre la cuestión que los insurrectos plantean: una declaración citada en el informe dice que hay tropas apostadas en la frontera de Santo Domingo, pero que el autor está también informado oficialmente de que esto es solo una medida de precaución y que no hay peligro de batalla. Sin embargo, se han recibido noticias de naturaleza más grave de Santo Domingo: se dice que, bajo la dirección del general Ygnacio Ma. Gonzales, los ciudadanos descontentos de esa república han iniciado una insurrección contra el presidente Heureaux. Gonzales fue secretario de Relaciones Exteriores bajo la administración anterior, que se retiró el 27 de febrero. La cuestión planteada por los insurrectos es la oposición a la supuesta política de anexión a los Estados Unidos: Gonzales había hecho circular noticias de que el presidente Heureaux trama la anexión de la república. La mayoría de los ciudadanos de Santo Domingo, añade el informe, se opone a cualquier cambio de gobierno.

records.summary_en: The *Omaha Daily Bee* reported that Haiti and the Dominican Republic settled their diplomatic disputes after Haitian President Hyppolite apologized and offered indemnity for border raids linked to General Luperón. Presidents Heureaux and Hyppolite formed an alliance barring political exiles from organizing in either nation and pledged to coordinate against foreign aggression. The agreement also stipulated that neither republic would cede naval bases like Samaná Bay or Môle Saint-Nicolas to foreign powers without mutual consent.
records.summary_es: El *Omaha Daily Bee* informó que Haití y la República Dominicana resolvieron sus disputas diplomáticas luego de que el presidente haitiano Hyppolite se disculpara y ofreciera una indemnización por las incursiones fronterizas vinculadas al general Luperón. Los presidentes Heureaux y Hyppolite conformaron una alianza que prohibía a los exiliados políticos organizarse en cualquiera de las dos naciones y se comprometieron a coordinar acciones contra agresiones extranjeras. El acuerdo estipulaba además que ninguna de las dos repúblicas cedería bases navales como la bahía de Samaná o Môle Saint-Nicolas a potencias extranjeras sin consentimiento mutuo.
records.passage: between the two republics were settled. On behalf of Hayti President Hippolyto formally apologized for the encouragement Hayti had given General Luperon in his raid over the Santo Domingo border. He promised to pay indemnity. President Heureaux was satisfied with this apology and promise of indemnity. He has issued orders for the withdrawal of his troops from the border line. Traffic is thus reopened. An alliance was entered into between the two republics by which they agree to deny the right of refuge in either republic to political exiles from the other. Heureaux also enters into alliance to operate with Hayti on all questions of foreign interferences. President Heureaux and the war ship El Presidente have gone to the city of Santo Domingo. Hippolyto's forces that were massed about Cape Haytien have started on their return to Port-au-Prince. Hippolyte, his cabinet and his family will remain at Cape Haytien and return the visit of Heureaux in August. The German man-of-war [Gneisenau?] has sailed for Cuba. The United States ship Kearsarge is the only foreign war vessel now in these waters. Under the agreement between Presidents Hippolyto and Heureaux all hope of Europe securing either Samana Bay or the Mole St. Nicholas as a coaling station is lost. The treaty has been revised, and under the terms the presidents of the republics are bound not to cede either port without the consent of the other. records.headline: The Sun argues in an editorial against Spain attacking Dominica
records.summary_en: The Sun argues in an editorial against Spain attacking Dominica over the Cuban recruits: we would not like to see Spain attack Dominica because recruits for the Cuban revolutionary force have been raised there. Spain has the right to drive away, capture, or destroy any hostile vessel that may approach Cuban shores from any quarter, but she had better not attack Dominica for failing to prevent the departure from Samaná of an unfriendly transport, any more than she would attack Jamaica for a like failure, or Mexico, or the United States. The Dominican Republic is a very feeble institution, but if it were attacked by any foreign government, that government might find itself involved in serious complications; Spain can work her will in Cuba and Porto Rico, but nowhere else on this side of the sea.
