records.headline: Under the head 'Columbus' Remains,' the Courier prints the letter of F. L. Vasquez of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Under the head 'Columbus' Remains,' the Courier prints the letter of F. L. Vasquez of the Dominican Republic to the American press, dated at New York, May 2: in reference to the story from Chicago that an attempt had been made to steal the ashes of Columbus, said to be deposited in the convent of La Rabida, Vasquez declares it officially that the precious remains of Columbus are now in the city of San Domingo, honored and guarded with jealous reverence and care as a sacred obligation by the government he has the honor to represent. His government, he writes, has rejected with indignation several propositions to remove the remains, and will always look upon any suggestion of that kind as unworthy of serious consideration; a magnificent monument in the principal plaza of San Domingo, in front of the cathedral, is to be erected, where it is hoped the sacred relic will rest undisturbed for many centuries to come. That the remains of Columbus are in San Domingo, he concludes, is indisputable, the evidence therefor being so ample and conclusive that no intelligent person who examines it can thereafter entertain the slightest doubt.

Su gobierno, escribe, ha rechazado con indignación varias proposiciones de trasladar los restos, y siempre considerará cualquier sugerencia de esa clase como indigna de seria consideración; un magnífico monumento en la plaza principal de San Domingo, frente a la catedral, habrá de erigirse, donde se espera que la sagrada reliquia descanse sin perturbación por muchos siglos venideros. Que los restos de Colón están en San Domingo, concluye, es indiscutible, siendo la evidencia al respecto tan amplia y concluyente que ninguna persona inteligente que la examine podrá abrigar después ni la menor duda.

records.headline: The Eagle reprints an extract by Carl Schurz from Harper's Magazine
records.summary_en: The Eagle reprints an extract by Carl Schurz from Harper's Magazine, carrying the expansionist argument in its own terms: if we do not take Cuba, some other power will take it, and that power may be hostile; let us take it ourselves. Santo Domingo is only a few miles distant from Cuba, also a country of rich resources; other powers several times tried to get it; if in the hands of a hostile power it would 'threaten' Cuba; it also 'commands' the Caribbean Sea; the Dominican Republic, occupying the larger part of the island, offered to join us once, and will wish to do so again; to acquire the Haitian Republic we shall have to fight; it will cost men and money, but we can easily beat the negroes. We must have Santo Domingo; Puerto Rico will come as a matter of course with Cuba. All the more necessary will it be to have possession of the mainland bordering and 'commanding' the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea on the western side: we must have all the 'keys' to the seas and to the land, or at least as many as we can possibly get, one to protect another, and once well launched on this course we shall hardly find a stopping-place north of the Gulf of Darien, and we shall have an abundance of reasons, one as good as another, for not stopping even there.

records.summary_en: The Times reprints the same extract from Harper's Magazine, in which Carl Schurz carries the expansionist argument in its own terms: if we do not take Cuba, 'some other power will take it'; that power may be hostile; let us take it ourselves. Santo Domingo is only a few miles distant from Cuba, also a country of rich resources; other powers several times tried to get it; if in the hands of a hostile power it would 'threaten' Cuba; it also 'commands' the Caribbean Sea; the Dominican Republic, occupying the larger part of the island, offered to join us once, and will wish to do so again; to acquire the Haitian Republic we shall have to fight; it will cost men and money, but we can easily beat the negroes. We must have Santo Domingo. Puerto Rico will come as a matter of course with Cuba; the British possessions of Jamaica will still be there to 'threaten' and 'command' everything else, and it will be difficult to get it and the other little islands from the clutch of the British lion. All the more necessary, the extract argues, to have possession of the mainland bordering and 'commanding' the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea on the western side: we must have all the 'keys' to the seas and to the land, or at least as many as we can possibly get, one to protect another, and once well launched on this course we shall hardly find a stopping-place north of the Gulf of Darien, with an abundance of reasons, one as good as another, for not stopping even there.

Santo Domingo está a solo unas pocas millas de Cuba, también un país de ricos recursos; otras potencias trataron varias veces de obtenerlo; si estuviera en manos de una potencia hostil «amenazaría» a Cuba; también «domina» el mar Caribe; la República Dominicana, que ocupa la mayor parte de la isla, se ofreció una vez a unirse a nosotros, y deseará hacerlo de nuevo; para adquirir la República Haitiana tendremos que luchar; costará hombres y dinero, pero podemos vencer fácilmente a los negros. Debemos tener Santo Domingo. Puerto Rico vendrá como cosa natural con Cuba; las posesiones británicas de Jamaica seguirán allí para «amenazar» y «dominarlo» todo lo demás, y será difícil obtenerlo a él y a las otras islitas de las garras del león británico. Tanto más necesario, argumenta el extracto, tener posesión de la tierra firme que bordea y «domina» el golfo de México y el mar Caribe por el lado occidental: debemos tener todas las «llaves» de los mares y de la tierra, o al menos cuantas podamos obtener, una para proteger a otra, y una vez bien lanzados en este curso, difícilmente encontraremos un punto de parada al norte del golfo de Darién, con abundancia de razones, una tan buena como otra, para no detenernos ni siquiera allí.

records.headline: The Tribune notes new financial arrangements in Europe for the Dominican debt
records.summary_en: The Tribune notes new financial arrangements in Europe for the Dominican debt and the conversion of its railroad bonds: the financial agent of the San Domingo Government at Brussels, Belgium, has issued a circular inviting the holders of the Dominican Railroad 6 per cents of 1888 to present their titles for conversion into bonds of the Dominican 4 per cent loan. The old coupons, which have not been paid, will be converted into scrip of the same loan. The note comes at a time when cable dispatches announce the approaching triumphal visit of President Heureaux of the Dominican Republic to his former enemy and now great friend, General Hyppolite, President of Hayti.
records.summary_es: El Tribune señala los nuevos arreglos financieros en Europa para la deuda dominicana y la conversión de sus bonos ferrocarrileros: el agente financiero del Gobierno de San Domingo en Bruselas, Bélgica, ha emitido una circular invitando a los tenedores de los bonos del 6 por ciento del Ferrocarril Dominicano de 1888 a presentar sus títulos para su conversión en bonos del empréstito dominicano del 4 por ciento. Los cupones antiguos, que no han sido pagados, se convertirán en scrip del mismo empréstito. La nota llega en un momento en que despachos cablegráficos anuncian la próxima visita triunfal del presidente Heureaux, de la República Dominicana, a su antiguo enemigo y ahora gran amigo, el general Hyppolite, presidente de Haití.

records.headline: The Press prints the latest advices on the reported uprising
records.summary_en: The Press prints the latest advices on the reported uprising in Santo Domingo and Consul Vasquez's account of it: the latest advices received are to the effect that the movement is well under way and the government has not as yet succeeded in suppressing it, and a general exiled by President Heureux has gone back to San Domingo for the purpose of aiding the insurgents. At New York, December 22, F. L. Vasquez, consul from the Dominican Republic, was asked about the reported uprising against President Ulysse Heureux at San Domingo: he admitted that there was some trouble there, thought it was caused principally by a number of American exiles who are continually plotting against the government, and said he received a cable yesterday afternoon stating that the revolt had taken place but that it has been quickly suppressed and the government is stronger than ever before; the cable, he said, gave no further details, and from an authoritative source he was sure the trouble was at an end.

records.summary_en: *The Jersey City News* reported that Dominican soldiers fired upon a landing boat from the American schooner *Henry Crosby* near Azua, critically wounding a sailor and injuring the first officer. The schooner's captain sailed to Azua and filed a formal report with the United States Consul General in Santo Domingo, who forwarded the complaint to Washington. The unprovoked attack was believed to have resulted from soldiers mistaking the crew for insurgents attempting to land and overthrow President Heureaux.
records.summary_es: *The Jersey City News* informó que soldados dominicanos abrieron fuego cerca de Azua contra un bote de desembarco de la goleta estadounidense *Henry Crosby*, hiriendo de gravedad a un marinero y lesionando al primer oficial. El capitán de la goleta navegó hacia Azua y presentó un informe formal ante el cónsul general de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo, quien remitió la queja a Washington. Se creía que el ataque no provocado se debió a que los soldados confundieron a la tripulación con insurgentes que intentaban desembarcar para derrocar al presidente Heureaux.

records.summary_en: France is pressing the Dominican government with its ships off the coast and the threat of suspending diplomatic relations, while President Heureaux keeps a French merchant in prison whose only crime, it is said, is that he started a soap factory in competition with one in which the President had an interest. The article also reports that the Dominican revenues, which were stated as amounting to 1,500,000 and fell to $1,205,101 in 1892, are collected by an American syndicate that acquired the rights of a concession granted in 1888 to Amsterdam bankers who had lent the government £710,068 on those revenues as guarantee.

records.summary_en: The *Weekly Union* reported that a boat crew from the American schooner *Henry Crosby* was fired upon by Dominican troops while approaching the beach near Azua, resulting in severe wounds to the first officer and the fatal shooting of a sailor. The captain reached Azua to lodge an official protest with the United States Consul General, who transmitted the findings to the State Department. Dominican troops reportedly mistook the American boat for an insurgent expedition sent to unseat President Heureaux.
records.summary_es: El *Weekly Union* informó que la tripulación de un bote perteneciente a la goleta estadounidense *Henry Crosby* fue atacada a tiros por tropas dominicanas mientras se aproximaba a la playa cerca de Azua, lo que causó graves heridas al primer oficial y la muerte por disparos de un marinero. El capitán llegó a Azua para presentar una protesta oficial ante el cónsul general de los Estados Unidos, quien transmitió las averiguaciones al Departamento de Estado. Según trascendió, las tropas dominicanas confundieron la embarcación estadounidense con una expedición insurgente enviada para derrocar al presidente Heureaux.

records.full_text:
DASTARDLY OUTRAGE On the Crew of the American Schooner Henry Crosby. Wantonly Fired Upon and Wounded by Soldiers of the Dominican Government at Old Azua.

NEW YORK, December 28—The steamship G. W. Clyde, from Turk's Island, which arrived here today, brings a report of an outrage inflicted on the crew of the American schooner Henry Crosby, which, having lost her bearings, put into the port of Old Azua, San Domingo. The first officer and four seamen got into the boat and pulled for the shore. When about three hundred yards out a file of soldiers in the uniform of the Dominican government came running down to the beach and leveling their carbines at the men in the small boat fired. One of the rowers threw up his hands and fell over into the bottom of the boat. The others paused in surprise and affright, when suddenly another volley was sent among them by the soldiers on shore. This time the first officer was struck. The other three sailors turned the boat about and desperately pulled for the schooner.

The men were taken on board, when it was found the first officer had received a bullet in the shoulder and the seamen were struck by several balls. A bad wound in the back made it doubtful if one man could recover.

A report of the affair has been made to the United States government by the Consul-General at San Domingo City.

records.headline: The Star reviews the quarrel between President Heureaux and France
records.summary_en: The Star reviews the quarrel between President Heureaux and France over the Banco Nacional: it had been declared that the president had broken open the bank and abstracted the cash therein, about 200,000 francs, but the Santo Domingo authorities assert that no money was touched and that the documents abstracted consisted merely of securities deposited against a contract never executed; the president said that he had demanded the return of these documents from the French authorities of the bank and that his application had been refused, and later he himself refused the proposition of the French admiral, De Libran, to deposit the money or the securities in the hands of a responsible third party until arbitration should have decided upon the merits of the case. France, the Star says, was satisfied with sending occasionally one or two men-of-war to maneuver off the Dominican coast and with suspending diplomatic relations; meanwhile Heureaux keeps in prison a French merchant named Bolmare, whose only crime, it is said, is that he started a soap factory in competition with one in which the president had an interest. Heureaux is the more interested in picking no quarrel with the United States on account of the decrease in his financial resources: in 1888 the customs revenues were given in guarantee at Amsterdam to Dutch bankers, who took up a loan whose amount the window does not print legibly; the revenues were stated then as amounting to $1,500,000, they fell to $1,305,101 in 1892, and they are collected by an American syndicate, which has acquired the rights and the concession granted in 1888 to the Amsterdam bankers.

Francia, dice el Star, se contentó con enviar de vez en cuando uno o dos buques de guerra a maniobrar frente a la costa dominicana y con suspender las relaciones diplomáticas; mientras tanto, Heureaux mantiene en prisión a un comerciante francés llamado Bolmare, cuyo único crimen, se dice, es haber establecido una fábrica de jabón en competencia con una en la que el presidente tenía interés. Tanto más interesado está Heureaux en no buscar disputa con los Estados Unidos a causa de la disminución de sus recursos financieros: en 1888 los ingresos aduaneros fueron dados en garantía en Ámsterdam a banqueros holandeses, que tomaron un empréstito cuyo monto la ventana no imprime legiblemente; los ingresos se declararon entonces como ascendentes a $1,500,000, cayeron a $1,305,101 en 1892, y son recaudados por un sindicato estadounidense, que ha adquirido los derechos y la concesión otorgados en 1888 a los banqueros de Ámsterdam.

records.summary_en: *The Abbeville Press and Banner* reported that Captain Stubbs of the American schooner *Henry Crosby* anchored near Old Azua after losing his bearings and dispatched a longboat to determine their location. Dominican soldiers on the beach opened fire without warning, striking a sailor in the back of the head and wounding the chief officer. Captain Stubbs proceeded to Azua and lodged a formal complaint with the American consul for transmission to Washington.
records.summary_es: *The Abbeville Press and Banner* informó que el capitán Stubbs, de la goleta estadounidense *Henry Crosby*, fondeó cerca de Azua Vieja tras perder el rumbo y envió un bote para determinar su ubicación. Soldados dominicanos apostados en la playa abrieron fuego sin previo aviso, alcanzando a un marinero en la parte posterior de la cabeza e hiriendo al primer oficial. El capitán Stubbs se dirigió a Azua y presentó una queja formal ante el cónsul estadounidense para su transmisión a Washington.
records.passage: December 11, but the populace of San Domingo City, which is eighty-four miles from Azua, were still talking of the affair when the Clyde came away, two days later. Old Azua harbor is ten miles away from Azua, and in approaching the first named Captain Stubbs, of the Crosby, lost his bearings. His schooner dropped anchor and the captain ordered four of his sailors in the long boat in charge of the chief mate to ascertain the exact position of the craft. As the boat drew near the beach a dozen soldiers in Dominican uniform were seen running toward the surf. Without warning of any kind the men leveled their carbines at the occupants of the long boat and fired. A bullet from the first volley hit one of the rowers in the back of the head, and a second shot from another round laid low the chief officer. The uninjured men then hurried back to the Crosby with their mates. All were thoroughly frightened, but Captain Stubbs was beside himself in anger. He was for going ashore and dealing vengeance then and there. But he weighed anchor instead and went to Azua, where he sent a complaint to the American Consul at St. Domingo City. records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on an official communication from Dominican President Ulises Heureaux to Vice President Figuereo announcing the summary execution of several political opponents. Heureaux stated that General Eugenio Generoso Marchena and five associates were executed at La Clavellina for the murder of a government delegate, while three others were shot at Los Jovillos for attempting to assassinate Heureaux. Seven other accused conspirators were spared execution and transferred to prison in the capital.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó sobre una comunicación oficial del presidente dominicano Ulises Heureaux al vicepresidente Figuereo en la que anunciaba la ejecución sumaria de varios opositores políticos. Heureaux declaró que el general Eugenio Generoso Marchena y cinco colaboradores fueron fusilados en La Clavellina por el asesinato de un delegado gubernamental, mientras que otros tres fueron pasados por las armas en Los Jovillos por intentar atentar contra la vida de Heureaux. Otros siete acusados de conspiración se salvaron de la ejecución y fueron trasladados a prisión en la capital.

The document says, among other things: "Having carefully sifted the facts and reached the full conviction of the guilt of the accused of the said ambushes and assassinations, acting with justice and with the consciousness of duty, which impose now hard and painful measures, I gave the order to shoot, in the place called 'La Clavellina,' where General Joaquin Campos, Delegate of the General Government, had been assassinated, General Eugenio Generoso Marchena, José Concha, Oliverio Reyes, José Maria Guzman, José Reyes and Carlos Baez Figueroa. And in the place called 'Los Jovillos,' where was the ambush of those who sought to assassinate me on my journey from Neiba to this city (Azua), I have given orders that José Pérez, Pablo Baez and Lorenzo Brito shall be executed. "Although important documents referring to those occurrences incriminate Senors Alfredo Blandino, Abraham Ortiz, Antonio Romano, Manuel [illegible], Prospero [Freites?], Agapito [Felix?] and José Polin [Reyes?], yet, believing that a sufficient example has been made, I have felt bound not to have them executed, and I have put them in the jail of the capital, where they shall remain until otherwise disposed of." records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on escalating authoritarian measures by President Heureaux, who restricted foreign travel and arrested suspected political opponents across the country. Following Heureaux's armed seizure of $60,000 from a French bank, the bank’s Dominican attorney, Jacinto de Castro Peynado, was imprisoned for his arguments during legal proceedings against the government. Additionally, Dominican troops blocked the son of a former Spanish consul from landing in Santo Domingo, threatening him with rifles until he departed on the steamer.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó sobre la escalada de medidas autoritarias adoptadas por el presidente Heureaux, quien restringió los viajes al extranjero y arrestó a presuntos opositores políticos en todo el país. Tras la incautación armada por parte de Heureaux de 60.000 dólares de un banco francés, el abogado dominicano de la entidad bancaria, Jacinto de Castro Peynado, fue encarcelado a causa de sus alegatos en los procedimientos judiciales contra el gobierno. Además, tropas dominicanas impidieron el desembarco en Santo Domingo del hijo de un excónsul español, amenazándolo con fusiles hasta que abandonó el lugar a bordo del vapor.

records.headline: The Tribune reports the release of the French soap manufacturer
records.summary_en: The Tribune reports the release of the French soap manufacturer held in San Domingo: the Paris papers say that the French citizen whose case was mentioned in the Tribune of February has been set at liberty after more than one year of imprisonment. He was a soap manufacturer, and consequently a competitor of President Heureaux, who is interested in a soap factory, and he had not done any act justifying his arrest. He was released through the efforts of the Spanish Consul, who has had charge of French affairs in San Domingo since the suspension of diplomatic relations between that Republic and France. President Heureaux, meanwhile, is desirous of avoiding the conflict which threatened to cause a war between his Government and France, while the latest telegraphic dispatches from the Republic of San Domingo report the possibility of a conflict with Spain; he has not yet surrendered the 950,000 francs which he took arbitrarily from the safe of the Banco Nacional, a Franco-Dominican establishment.

Era un fabricante de jabón, y por consiguiente un competidor del presidente Heureaux, que tiene interés en una fábrica de jabón, y no había hecho ningún acto que justificara su arresto. Fue liberado gracias a las gestiones del cónsul español, que se ha hecho cargo de los asuntos franceses en San Domingo desde la suspensión de las relaciones diplomáticas entre esa República y Francia. El presidente Heureaux, mientras tanto, desea evitar el conflicto que amenazaba con causar una guerra entre su Gobierno y Francia, mientras los últimos despachos telegráficos de la República de San Domingo informan de la posibilidad de un conflicto con España; aún no ha entregado los 950,000 francos que tomó arbitrariamente de la caja fuerte del Banco Nacional, un establecimiento franco-dominicano.

records.headline: The Tribune prints a story from San Domingo, received by way of Panama
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints a story from San Domingo, received by way of Panama and dated March 2, reporting that the two sons of ex-President Baez had been shot by order of President Heureaux: the elder son had previously been sentenced to imprisonment for life for plotting to overthrow the existing government, and when the younger was also discovered to be implicated, Heureaux determined that both should die; soon after the younger Baez's arrest, the President sent word to the Baez family that the two had need of two broadcloth suits. Among the victims, the story adds, was Francis Pintado, an alleged dynamiter, brother of the Spanish consul to San Domingo, who was himself ejected from the island without recourse to diplomatic formalities.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica un relato de San Domingo, recibido por vía de Panamá y fechado el 2 de marzo, según el cual los dos hijos del expresidente Báez habían sido fusilados por orden del presidente Heureaux: el hijo mayor había sido condenado antes a prisión perpetua por conspirar para derrocar al gobierno existente, y cuando se descubrió que el menor también estaba implicado, Heureaux determinó que ambos debían morir; poco después del arresto del menor de los Báez, el presidente hizo saber a la familia Báez que los dos necesitaban dos trajes de paño fino. Entre las víctimas, añade el relato, estaba Francis Pintado, presunto dinamitero, hermano del cónsul español en San Domingo, quien fue expulsado de la isla sin recurso a formalidad diplomática alguna.

records.summary_en: The Times prints a story of the execution of the two Baez brothers in the Dominican Republic: when the younger was also discovered to be implicated in the plot to overthrow the existing government, President Heureaux determined that both should die; soon after the younger's arrest, the President sent word to the Baez family that the two brothers had need of two broadcloth suits — this was on February 2 — and the clothes were sent, and the next morning the youths were told to put the black suits on, and when they had complied they were told that the freedom of the jail yard was given them, and in the yard a squad of soldiers' bullets speedily put an end to their lives. This, it is said, makes twelve martial executions in the Dominican Republic in sixty days; among the twelve was that of Francis Pintado, an alleged dynamiter, brother of the Spanish consul to San Domingo, the consul himself having been ejected from the island without recourse to any of the diplomatic formalities.
records.summary_es: El Times publica un relato de la ejecución de los dos hermanos Báez en la República Dominicana: cuando se descubrió que el menor también estaba implicado en el complot para derrocar al gobierno existente, el presidente Heureaux determinó que ambos debían morir; poco después del arresto del menor, el presidente hizo saber a la familia Báez que los dos hermanos necesitaban dos trajes de paño fino —esto fue el 2 de febrero— y los trajes fueron enviados, y a la mañana siguiente se dijo a los jóvenes que se pusieran los trajes negros, y cuando hubieron obedecido se les dijo que se les concedía la libertad del patio de la cárcel, y en el patio las balas de un pelotón de soldados pusieron fin rápidamente a sus vidas. Esto, se dice, eleva a doce las ejecuciones militares en la República Dominicana en sesenta días; entre los doce estaba la de Francis Pintado, presunto dinamitero, hermano del cónsul español en San Domingo, habiendo sido el propio cónsul expulsado de la isla sin recurso a formalidad diplomática alguna.

records.headline: May Bombard San Domingo.
records.summary_en: *The Lusk Herald* reported imminent conflict between France and the Dominican Republic after French warships appeared off Santo Domingo City to take soundings. The French government delivered an ultimatum demanding the return of $60,000 seized from a French-backed bank along with a $20,000 indemnity, threatening bombardment if President Heureaux failed to pay. Heureaux reportedly responded that the Dominican treasury lacked the money to meet the demand.

records.full_text:
MAY BOMBARD SAN DOMINGO.

France Demands Indemnity for Confiscation of a French Bank.
New York special: A dispatch to the World, dated Puerto Plat, San Domingo, January 18, says:
“Trouble seems imminent between France and the Dominican Republic. A French man of war appeared off San Domingo City a few days ago and began to take soundings. Soon after she departed another appeared. The latter was boarded by a pilot, who was informed that his services were not needed, and when he asked the commander his intention, he was told it was none of his business.”

The San Domingo authorities had a dispute with a bank a few years ago, and eventually took $60,000 from it. The bank was backed by French capitalists, and the bankers laid the case before the French Government. France demanded that the money be returned to the bank, but diplomatic negotiations seem to have resulted in nothing. The World correspondent learns upon trustworthy authority that the French ultimatum has already been sent in and demands the restoration of the $60,000 and $20,000 as indemnity. President Heuraux, it is said, has declared that he has no money to pay it with.

Dispatches for the British Admiral at Jamaica passed this port probably asking him to look after British interests in case of bombardment.

records.headline: The Republican takes the Dominican affair of twenty-five years
records.summary_en: The Republican takes the Dominican affair of twenty-five years ago as its text in an editorial against annexation and the pending Hawaii proposition: the doctrine of the true grandeur of nations, it says, was preached where that other crime against San Domingo and against the principles of republican government was defeated, the hot and inconsiderate defense of the doctrine of national greed and conquest which the junior senator from Massachusetts has given to the country in the parallel case of Hawaii. We predict for these imperialists, the editorial says, the same fate which overtook the jingoists in the Dominican affair 25 years ago: if the proposition to annex an island adjacent to the American coast was then regarded as hostile to republican principles and ruled out of order, what must be said of this pending proposition to reach out 2,000 miles into the Pacific for more territory? It is something not to be listened to by any person who has regard for the safety of republican institutions, and the editorial quotes Washington's Farewell Address against quitting our own ground to stand upon foreign ground.

Es algo que no debe escuchar ninguna persona que se preocupe por la seguridad de las instituciones republicanas, y el editorial cita el discurso de despedida de Washington contra abandonar nuestro propio suelo para pisar suelo extranjero.

records.summary_en: *The Indianapolis Journal* reported on the diplomatic dispute arising from French threats to forcibly collect an indemnity from Dominican customs houses pledged to the San Domingo Improvement Company of New York. records.summary_en: The Courier prints a travel sketch of San Domingo, opening with the approach to the city from the sea: as the city of San Domingo, the capital of the Dominican Republic, is approached from the sea, one is struck by the quaintness of an old, dilapidated tower which rises up from a formidable-looking stone wall along the beach, and on coming nearer the wall and tower become plainly noticeable as only a harmless mass of ruins. In order to become thoroughly interested in the place and its ruins, the sketch — printed under the head 'Where Columbus Is Buried' — says, one must go ashore and meet one of the old inhabitants and hear some of his blood-curdling yarns dating back to the times when pirates were bold; and after he has told all the stirring stories he has ever heard, and the relative merits of cock-fighting and bull-fighting have been discussed, and a hope has been expressed that there would soon be another revolution, it becomes comparatively easy to draw the conversation toward Columbus. The window closes in the sketch's opening movement, with the old inhabitant beginning to point out and explain.
records.summary_es: El Courier publica un relato de viaje de San Domingo, que se abre con la aproximación a la ciudad desde el mar: al acercarse a la ciudad de San Domingo, la capital de la República Dominicana, desde el mar, llama la atención la singularidad de una torre vieja y dilapidada que se alza desde una muralla de piedra de aspecto formidable a lo largo de la playa, y al acercarse más la muralla y la torre se revelan claramente como una masa de ruinas inofensiva. Para interesarse a fondo en el lugar y sus ruinas, dice el relato —publicado bajo el título «Where Columbus Is Buried»—, hay que bajar a tierra y conocer a uno de los viejos habitantes y oír algunos de sus relatos escalofriantes que datan de los tiempos en que los piratas eran audaces; y después de que haya contado todas las historias emocionantes que haya oído jamás, y se hayan discutido los méritos relativos de las peleas de gallos y las corridas de toros, y se haya expresado la esperanza de que pronto hubiera otra revolución, resulta comparativamente fácil llevar la conversación hacia Colón. La ventana se cierra en el movimiento inicial del relato, cuando el viejo habitante comienza a señalar y explicar.

records.summary_en: *The Anaconda Standard* recounted the political fallout from President Grant’s attempt to annex Santo Domingo, highlighting the favorable report by commissioners Benjamin Wade, Samuel Gridley Howe, and Andrew D. White. The proposal provoked a fierce Senate battle led by Charles Sumner, causing the treaty’s defeat, a lasting personal breach between Grant and Sumner, and Sumner's removal as chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

La propuesta provocó una encarnizada batalla en el Senado liderada por Charles Sumner, lo que ocasionó el fracaso del tratado, un distanciamiento personal duradero entre Grant y Sumner y la destitución de este último como presidente del Comité de Relaciones Exteriores del Senado.

There followed in the senate one of the most ill-tempered debates ever heard in congress. Charles Sumner led in the opposition — he made a terrific attack on the president's conduct; he went farther than most of the senators felt was right. The annexation scheme failed, and the smoke of the battle hung heavily and long. Thereafter General Grant and Senator Sumner had no personal intercourse. A few months afterward, by action of the senate, Sumner lost the chairmanship of the committee on foreign relations, and he refused committee appointments to which he was assigned. From that time until the close of his life Senator Sumner, brilliant as had been his career and splendid his ability, was in an uncomfortable place, although, just as the end was approaching, he appeared to be treated by the republican senators with renewed friendliness. He died three years and a day after his chairmanship was taken from him; meanwhile, the San Domingo annexation scheme had passed out of the minds of the people. records.headline: The Tribune prints the first part of a published statement by a Dominican exile
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints the first part of a published statement by a Dominican exile: the barbarous executions ordered by 'the little tyrant Heureaux' in the department of Cibao and the district of Monte Cristi, where universal discontent is openly manifested against the President of the Dominican Republic, who is prolonging unconstitutionally the presidential period from four to eight years with the criminal object of obtaining re-election and continuing in power against the wish of the majority of the nation, resolved the writer at once to go to Hayti, with the idea of crossing over the frontier and uniting himself with the many friends of recognized political importance who have taken refuge in those places, to decide what would be best to do under the circumstances. He therefore embarked, incognito, at Ponce in the steamer Manuela on November 25 last, reaching Puerto Plata on the 26th at 3 p.m., on the same day that the man-of-war Independencia was expected with General Heureaux on board from Sanchez and Samana; continuing his voyage that same afternoon to Cape Haytien, he reached that port on the morning of the 27th and disembarked without inconvenience, and though he had to present himself at the office of the commandant of the port, a strong partisan of Heureaux on account of relationship, he managed to pass through undiscovered, but unfortunately in crossing over from the office to the hotel he was seen and recognized by one of the numerous spies of the Dominican Government who infest that port. The window closes there.

Se embarcó, pues, de incógnito, en Ponce, en el vapor Manuela, el 25 de noviembre pasado, llegando a Puerto Plata el 26 a las 3 p.m., el mismo día en que se esperaba el buque de guerra Independencia con el general Heureaux a bordo, procedente de Sánchez y Samaná; continuando su viaje esa misma tarde hacia Cabo Haitiano, llegó a ese puerto en la mañana del 27 y desembarcó sin inconveniente, y aunque tuvo que presentarse en la oficina del comandante del puerto, un fuerte partidario de Heureaux por razón de parentesco, logró pasar inadvertido, pero desafortunadamente, al cruzar de la oficina al hotel, fue visto y reconocido por uno de los numerosos espías del Gobierno dominicano que infestan ese puerto. La ventana se cierra ahí.

records.headline: The Tribune prints the conclusion of the statement of A. F. Morales
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints the conclusion of the statement of A. F. Morales, dated at St. Thomas in December 1895: it was stated that it was not desirable that the writer should be allowed to go to 'the little English island so near to San Domingo,' and he was therefore kept in prison at the Cape until the next morning, when the German steamer arrived in which they decided to embark him for St. Thomas; but as that steamer had to remain in port several days receiving cargo, the commandant of the port took him on board in the custody of two officers, who conducted him from the prison to the Suevia under a numerous escort. It remains now, he writes, publicly to thank the many Dominicans who came to see him in prison, placing themselves entirely at his service, and also the inhabitants of the Cape for their cordial manifestation of sympathy, accompanying him in great number from the port office to the door of the prison and back again, with many marks of respect and significant murmurs of disapprobation for the servile attitude assumed by the government of Hyppolite in favor of his worthy colleague Heureaux.

records.headline: The friendship of Gen. Heureaux toward the Spanish Government, especially in regard to Cuban affairs
records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported that the Spanish government awarded the Grand Cross of Isabel the Catholic to Dominican President Ulises Heureaux in recognition of his friendly neutrality during the Cuban insurrection. Spanish officials valued Heureaux's cooperation in preventing Dominican ports from being used as staging grounds for insurgent filibustering expeditions to Cuba.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó que el gobierno español otorgó la Gran Cruz de Isabel la Católica al presidente dominicano Ulises Heureaux en reconocimiento a su neutralidad amistosa durante la insurrección cubana. Las autoridades españolas valoraron la cooperación de Heureaux para evitar que los puertos dominicanos fueran utilizados como puntos de partida de expediciones filibusteras insurgentes hacia Cuba.

records.full_text:
MANY CUBANS KILLED

SPANISH ACCOUNTS OF RECENT FIGHTS WITH INSURGENTS.

Several Hundred of the Iatter Said to Have Been Slaia and Wounded in Havana Province.

FORCED TO MOVE WESTWARD

THE PATRIOT ARMY UNABLE TO ENTER MATANZAS IN FORCE.

No Prisoners Yet Executed by Weyler —An American's Observations While Visiting the Island.

HAVANA, Feb. 22.—The Spanish columns which have been operating against the insurgents have been engaged with the enemy under Maximo Gomez and others commanding the main forces of the insurgent army. Several fights have taken place during the last few days on the limits of the province of Havana and the province of Matanzas. The insurgents have lost seventy killed and over three hundred wounded. It is asserted that only a small portion of the insurgent forces has been able to enter Matanzas. The main body, it is added, has been obliged to retreat westward. A dispatch from San Felipe says that a severe skirmish has taken place at the plantation of Aguacata, resulting in the insurgents being compelled to retire with the loss of twenty-five killed and thirty-seven wounded. Among the killed was an insurgent colonel. This body of insurgents is said to have lost during the recent fighting about two hundred men in killed and wounded. Advices just received from Aguacita say that the sound of continued rifle and artillery firing has been heard from there, and it is supposed that the column of Spanish troops under Colonel Hernandez has again been engaged with the insurgents.

Colonel Periz reports having been engaged with 1,200 insurgents between Penon and Dolorita. The insurgents left eleven killed, among them being Major Morejon. Three soldiers were seriously wounded. Major Cabelo, telegraphing from the front, announces that his column of troops has been engaged with the insurgents under Mestre and Rojas, at the plantation of Buena Vista. The insurgents lost five killed.

The insurgent leader Cartagena has attacked a detachment of Spanish troops at Tanamo, province of Santiago de Cuba. The enemy was repulsed. Cartagena was wounded and two of his folowers were killed. The insurgents have attacked the village of Casigua, province of Havana, but they were repulsed with loss.

MACEO'S DEFEAT.

A telegram from San Jose de las Lajas says that when the column of troops commanded by Colonel Tort was leaving that place, firing was heard in the direction of Zenea and Luz, and detachments were pushed in those directions, it being believed that the insurgents were retreating before Generals Linares and Aldecoa. When the troops reached Zenea it was found that Maceo and other inusrgent leaders had been defeated in an attempt to capture Jaruco, and General Linares reported that he had defeated the insurgents at Morales and was countermarching towards Catalina. Colonel Tort saw a great fire in the direction of Catalina, and, making a forced march to that place, he found that Colonel Hernandez had dislodged the insurgents there. Hernandez and Tort met at the passage of the river Ojo de Agua, and soon afterwards their columns exchanged shots for thirty minutes with the insurgents, six of whom were killed and many wounded.

At Catalina the insurgents encamped at the plantation of El Gato for forty-five minutes only before being dispersed by the troops. The insurgent advance guards advanced shortly upon the enemy, although the latter kept up a well-sustained fire from behind fences and ruined houses, which formed a semicircular defense. The insurgents were estimated to number about five thousand, but they were dislodged by the artillery, after defending their position with tenacity. Four companies of Spanish infantry and a squadron of the Pizarro cavalry charged the enemy after the artillery had done its work, and the insurgents retreated leaving ten killed and a great many wounded on the field. The main body of the insurgents retreated towards the Esperanza mountains, where Maximo Gomez was awaiting them. At Catalina the insurgents were under the leadership of Zavas, Cardenas and Miro. In the figthing at El Gato the Spaniards lost Capt. Antonio Serra, and eighteen privates wounded.

A telegram from Perdoso announces that a column of infantry, cavalry and civil guards has been engaged there with an insurgent force commanded by Gomez. The latter is said to have lost thirty, killed.

A detachment of civil guards, commanded by a lieutenant, has had a skirmish with the insurgents, commanded by Francisco Collado, at the plantation of Tinguaro, near Colon, in the province of Matanzas. The guards captured Callado, his lieutenant, Eliseo Campo, and nine privates.

JARUCO PARTLY BURNED.

Although the insurgents were defeated at Jaruco, it is now known that they burned 132 brick and fifty wooden houses, in addition to forty huts, and plundered all the buildings except those on Real street, which was fortified. The garrison of the fort and the firemen surrendered to the insurgents after having exhausted their ammunition. Three of the garrison elected to remain with the insurgents, but the rest refused to do so, and were set at liberty. Among the houses burned at Jaruco was the city hall and the fine residence of Pedro Rodriguez. The insurgents took all the money they could find in the town. The troops lost four wounded, and the insurgents left two killed on the field and retired with their wounded.

The insurgents have attacked the village of Rio Blanco and plundered the stores.

A dispatch from Bolondron, province of Matanzas, announces that a band of 200 insurgents passed there yesterday going in the direction of the swamps of the Grand Cienega Occidental de Zapata. On the other hand a dispatch from Sabanilla, in the same province, says that several insurgent bands have passed that place, going in the direction of the province of Havana.

Official advices from Madruga, on the borders of the province of Havana, say that a band of insurgents, comanded by Pedro Castillo, has crossed the frontier, coming from the province of Matanzas, and plundered the stores of a village, Santa Ana. The insurgents have also plundered a store between Palp and Vega and have burned two culverts and destroyed two bridges two miles from Guanabacoa, which is not far from this city. Near Matanzas, the insurgents have destroyed the railroad and at Banaguises they have cut the telegraph lines. In addition, the insurgents have burned a railroad bridge between Rodrigo and Liticeto la Sagua, and have also derailed an exploring engine.

In the province of Pinar del Rio, the insurgents have burned the villages of Santa Cruz de los Pinos, including the church.

A telegram received here from Matanzas, this evening, says that the insurgent leader, Tavares, has been killed near Cardenas, that province.

PARDONS FOR INSURGENTS.

General Weyler announces that he will pardon those insurgents who will surrender at once to the government officials. If those who surrender are found armed a second or third time, he gives warning in his statement just issued, they will be subject to proceedings which may result in their being punished for a capital offense.

The Spanish consul at Santo Domingo has succeeded in obtaining from the Dominican government the detention of a number of filibusters, who, it is claimed, intended to capture the Spanish steamer Maria Herrara, in order to embark on an expedition to this island.

The casino of the colored population has elected Captain General Weyler honorary president of that organization as a token of their gratitude for the kind words he uttered regarding the colored population on the day of his arrival here. It is reported that the Captain General is preparing a circular which will cause a great impression.

The insurgents have burned the railroad bridge at Jiqui, and have twice attacked Fort Monte Alto, at San Jose de Los Ramos, but they were repulsed with loss. The insurgent force commanded by the well-known leader, Perico Delgado, is reported to be moving in the vicinity of Cabanas, province of Pinar del Rio.

The insurgents have burned the house, machinery and plantation of Dolores, in the district of Santo Domingo, province of Santa Clara.

The Cayo Confiles police have captured a band of counterfeiters engaged in putting out spurious notes of the Bank of Spain.

Troops captured near Guines several important insurgent leaders, among them being General Ynglesito and Colonel Nunez. The insurgent officers captured were immediately court-martialed. Near Jaruco, the Spanish forces recently fought a battle with a band of insurgents. Eleven of the insurgents were left dead on the field of battle.

A band of 150 insurgents attacked the village of Hoye Colorado, eleven miles from Havana. Colonel Cavestany hurried to the assistance of the Spanish forces, and the insurgents retreated, leaving nine dead and wounded on the field of battle.

records.summary_en: The *Wheeling Register* reported the executions of Dominican Minister of War General Ramón Castillo and General José Estay, Governor of San Pedro de Macorís. Castillo had obtained 1,000 rifles from President Ulises Heureaux under false pretenses to arm his own presidential conspiracy, leading Heureaux to discover the plot and order the execution of the rebel leaders.
records.summary_es: El *Wheeling Register* informó sobre las ejecuciones del ministro de Guerra dominicano, el general Ramón Castillo, y del general José Estay, gobernador de San Pedro de Macorís. Castillo había obtenido 1.000 fusiles del presidente Ulises Heureaux mediante engaños para armar su propia conspiración presidencial, lo que llevó a Heureaux a descubrir el complot y ordenar la ejecución de los cabecillas rebeldes.
records.passage: [illegible]ister of War. El Listin Diario, a newspaper supposed to be inspired by the government, published with details an account of the shooting of Gen. Castillo and also of Gen. Jose Estay, governor of the district of Macori. Great excitement was produced by the news among the Dominicans established in New York, and nearly all of them attributed the double execution to personal revenge of the president of San Domingo, Gen. Heureaux. Private letters received since explain the affair in the following manner: Gen. Ramon Castillo, Minister of War, asked President Heureaux some months ago for 1,000 rifles and the necessary ammunition to suppress, as he said, an outbreak against the president, which was going to occur in the province of San Pedro Macori. He described so vividly the importance of the conspiracy, and the urgency of suppressing it with a strong hand, that the 1,000 rifles were given to him, and, besides, he was ordered to go directly to San Pedro Macori and take command of the government forces. He did so, but time passed, and President Heureaux heard no more of the rebel movement. Instead of that, what he heard was that Gen. Castillo himself was conspiring against him with the aim of supporting, by means of arms, his own candidacy for the presidency of the republic. Moreover, the president learned that his 1,000 rifles had been distributed among disloyal persons in the province of Macori. Immediately after the news reached the capital orders were sent to Gen. records.summary_en: The Register prints a full account of the shootings of Castillo and of General Jose Estay in the Dominican Republic: 'That is impossible,' answered Castillo. 'How can I be sentenced to death without a trial? How can I be sentenced without my judge first hearing my defense?' All his pleading was of no avail; the soldiers of El Pacificador fired on him and he fell dead, pierced by several bullets. 'At last justice is done,' exclaimed Jose Estay, when a doctor certified the death of Castillo. 'Not yet, sir,' answered President Heureaux, approaching him. 'Another sentence has to be executed before we can say that justice is satisfied. That sentence is yours, Gen. Jose Estay.' After these words the unfortunate Estay was carried to the place where Castillo was shot and the soldiers of El Pacificador again did their duty. The observer stated that the Dominican government was actively opposed to filibustering and exerted every effort to prevent unauthorized expeditions from sailing to Cuba from Dominican territory.

records.summary_en: The *Waterbury Democrat* reported on a high-profile political libel trial in Port-au-Prince concerning financial corruption by Haiti's former finance minister in state telegraph transactions and scrip speculation. The paper also noted diplomatic friction between Haiti and France resulting from Haitian reluctance to pay compensation for damages suffered by a French citizen.

El periódico señaló asimismo las fricciones diplomáticas entre Haití y Francia derivadas de la renuencia haitiana a pagar una compensación por los perjuicios sufridos por un ciudadano francés.

Charmant on the other, whereby the inland telegraph system was purchased for $37,600 and sold to the government of Haiti for $100,000. records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported on historical precedents for United States diplomatic recognition of foreign nations, including Haiti, Liberia, and the Dominican Republic. It noted that the U.S. recognized Dominican independence by issuing an exequatur to J. W. Currier as Consul-General in New York on September 1, following earlier special diplomatic missions in 1845 and 1851. The article also reviewed American recognition of Korea, Germany, and the Congo Free State.

Currier como cónsul general en Nueva York el 1 de septiembre, luego de misiones diplomáticas especiales previas en 1845 y 1851. El artículo repasó además el reconocimiento estadounidense de Corea, Alemania y el Estado Libre del Congo.

records.headline: The Tribune prints an account of the arrangement by which Spanish consuls
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints an account of the arrangement by which Spanish consuls in the Bahamas act for the government of Santo Domingo: if Spanish consuls in the Bahamas were authorized to act in the name of the Santo Domingo government, they would be able to detect and stop more easily any filibustering expedition organized under Dominican colors, given the known pro-Cuban sympathies of all Dominicans. General Heureaux was much praised by the Havana papers for his devotion to Spanish interests, but the fact is that he was merely using Spanish consuls as his own spies; the Dominican dictator is aware that the people of the island are thoroughly tired of his rule, and that revolutionary attempts will not be delayed much longer, being about to sally forth from some of the Bahama islands, and Heureaux has made the Spanish consuls his own agents and informers, since they act as Dominican consuls and are bound to report to Santo Domingo any information of interest to his government; while the Spaniards proclaim that they have secured an effective ally in the person of General Heureaux, who transfers to them his consular service, the Spanish consular service in the Bahamas will act henceforth for the Dominican dictator, who will be the only one benefited by the arrangement.

records.headline: THE PROTOCOL, “In answer to your direct question, and with a knowledge of the deep interest you manifest in everything affecting the foreign relations of the United States
records.summary_en: The *Richmond Dispatch* published an account from a former American diplomat concerning an unfinished protocol submitted by Dominican President Ulises Heureaux as the basis for a new treaty. After verbally briefing Secretary Sherman in Washington, the diplomat decided to disclose the details following the acceptance of his resignation. He explained that Heureaux had requested his visit to Santo Domingo in March to receive the proposed terms and related memoranda.
records.summary_es: El *Richmond Dispatch* publicó el relato de un exdiplomático estadounidense acerca de un protocolo inconcluso presentado por el presidente dominicano Ulises Heureaux como base para un nuevo tratado. Tras informar verbalmente al secretario Sherman en Washington, el diplomático decidió revelar los detalles luego de que se aceptara su renuncia. Explicó que Heureaux había solicitado su visita a Santo Domingo en marzo para recibir los términos propuestos y los memorandos pertinentes.
records.passage: THE PROTOCOL. "In answer to your direct question, and with a knowledge of the deep interest you manifest in everything affecting the foreign relations of the United States, I will give you an outline of the unfinished protocol submitted to me by General Heureaux, President of the Dominican republic, for presentation to my government as the basis of a new treaty between the two countries. On my arrival in Washington I made a verbal report to Secretary Sherman, because I had not arranged the memoranda submitted by President Heureaux, and hastily taken in a note-book on the eve of my departure, and the Secretary, who appeared interested in the matter, suggested that I go home, and after I had recruited my strength, make him a formal report as to the proposed convention and the general conditions in Haiti and San Domingo. Now, inasmuch as the acceptance of my resignation, tendered the [illegible] of March, has released me from the obligations of my position, I deem it at least permissible to give you for the press the information you desire, although I can only surmise the source from which you acquired a knowledge of the matter in question. records.summary_en: The *San Francisco Call* reported that former minister Smythe negotiated the outline of a treaty with President Heureaux granting the United States a coaling station in Santo Domingo free of charge. In return, the Dominican government requested reciprocal coaling privileges in American ports and the removal of U.S. import duties on Dominican sugar. The report highlighted naval experts' views on the strategic necessity of acquiring West Indian coaling stations.

A cambio, el gobierno dominicano solicitaba privilegios recíprocos de aprovisionamiento de carbón en puertos estadounidenses y la eliminación de los derechos de importación de Estados Unidos sobre el azúcar dominicano. El informe destacó la opinión de expertos navales sobre la imperiosa necesidad estratégica de adquirir estaciones carboneras en las Antillas.

The sole condition attached to the concession was that Dominican naval vessels be granted coaling facilities in American ports.

records.headline: In order that this independence of the Congress shall be complete
records.summary_en: The *Evening Bulletin* analyzed legal questions regarding the proposed annexation of Hawaii, citing the Dominican precedent for provisionally maintaining local governance machinery until Congress legislates for a newly incorporated territory. The report outlined how treaties, local statutes, and labor systems would be adapted under American authority. It specifically noted provisions safeguarding congressional authority and prohibiting the entry of Chinese laborers.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Bulletin* analizó cuestiones jurídicas relativas a la proyectada anexión de Hawái, citando el precedente dominicano para mantener de manera provisional la estructura del gobierno local hasta que el Congreso legisle sobre un territorio recién incorporado. El informe describió cómo se adaptarían los tratados, estatutos locales y regímenes laborales bajo la autoridad estadounidense. Señaló específicamente disposiciones que salvaguardaban la autoridad del Congreso y prohibían la entrada de trabajadores chinos.
records.passage: of the annexed territory, the citizenship and elective franchise of its inhabitants and the manner in which laws of the United States are to be extended to the islands. In order that this independence of the Congress shall be complete and unquestionable, and pursuant to the recognized doctrine of public law that treaties expire with the independent life of the contracting state, there has been introduced out of abundant caution an express proviso for the determination of all treaties heretofore concluded by Hawaii with foreign nations and the extension to the islands of the treaties of the United States. This leaves Congress free to deal with such especial regulation of the contract labor system of the islands as circumstances may require. There being no general provision of existing statutes to prescribe the form of Government for newly incorporated territory, it was necessary to stipulate, as in the Dominican precedent, for continuing the existing machinery until provision shall be made by law for the Government, as territory of the United States, of the dominion thus incorporated into the union, but having in view the peculiar status created in Hawaii by laws enacted in execution of the treaties heretofore concluded between Hawaii and other countries, only such Hawaiian laws are thus provisionally continued as shall not be incompatible with the Constitution or the laws of the United States or with the provisions of this treaty. records.headline: The Tribune reprints a Chicago Times-Herald item on the coinage
records.summary_en: The Tribune reprints a Chicago Times-Herald item on the coinage the United States mint makes for foreign governments: the work is being done for the Dominican Republic, and the dollars will be sent to Santo Domingo; the design for the coins was furnished by the Dominican treasury department and in no respect, excepting shape, resembles the dollar of the United States. It has long been the custom of the United States to make the money of several South American countries, the item says, and as an act of comity and good will the work is done at the actual cost of labor and material; the present order from Santo Domingo also includes 800,000 half dollars, 875,000 quarter dollars, and 750,000 dimes; the mint bureau has just filled an order from Costa Rica for a large quantity of gold coins, and so pleased is Costa Rica that it has ordered through its minister at Washington 40,000 more coins of gold; and the first work of this kind done by the United States was in 1876, when $100,000 worth of minor coins were turned out for the government of Venezuela.

Hace mucho que es costumbre de los Estados Unidos hacer el dinero de varios países sudamericanos, dice la nota, y como un acto de cortesía y buena voluntad el trabajo se hace al costo real de la mano de obra y el material; el pedido actual de Santo Domingo incluye también 800,000 medios dólares, 875,000 cuartos de dólar y 750,000 monedas de diez centavos; la oficina de la moneda acaba de cumplir un pedido de Costa Rica de una gran cantidad de monedas de oro, y tan complacida está Costa Rica que ha ordenado, por medio de su ministro en Washington, 40,000 monedas de oro más; y el primer trabajo de esta clase hecho por los Estados Unidos fue en 1876, cuando se produjeron $100,000 en monedas menores para el gobierno de Venezuela.

records.headline: The Union prints an item on the foreign coinage of the United States
records.summary_en: The Union prints an item on the foreign coinage of the United States mint, the work for the Dominican Republic being already begun at Philadelphia: already the work has been started at the mint in Philadelphia, and within a few days 300,000 of them will be turned out; they will be only 35 per cent silver, the balance being copper and nickel, but they will circulate at full value. Happily they are not intended for circulation in this country; the work is being done for the Dominican Republic, and the dollars will be sent to Santo Domingo; the design of the coins was furnished by the Dominican treasury department and in no respect, excepting shape, resembles the dollar of the United States. records.full_text:
REVOLUTION FOR SAN DOMINGO.

It Is Being Brewed in New York by Enemies of President Hereaux.

New York, Oct. 21.—The Journal and Advertiser says: Efforts to crystalize the opposition to President Hereaux of San Domingo, the Spanish speaking republican that shares with the French speaking republic of Hayti the West Indian island of Hayti, into a revolution, are said to be nearing completion in this city.

The leader of the movement in New York is given Moscoso, who arrived here last July and is said to have been constantly busy ever since with secret meetings with the purpose in view. He is one of Hereaux's implacable foes and his friends here declare that he is the most available man to lead a revolt against the Dominican ruler. Moscoso was long ago recognized by Hereaux as a dangerous man and Hereaux was scheming to put him in prison and thus get him where he could not endanger the administration, when Moscoso got wind of his intention and promptly skipped out of the country. He went to the neighboring island of Porto Rica, the usual refuge of Dominican exiles, and was nearly assassinated there shortly after. Moscoso's friends openly declare their belief that the would-be assassins were in the pay of President Hereaux, the desperate method having been resorted to, they claim, because Moscoso was rapidly effecting his plans to return secretly to San Domingo and start an uprising, which Hereaux wanted to prevent by any means. Moscoso's assailants in Pence, Porto Rica, came very near killing him. He was taken unawares and stabbed once before he realized his danger, and then managed to escape only because one of the men thinking a fatal blow had been struck ran away, and the other was too scared and bewildered at the flight of his companion to follow up his attack. Moscoso is barely 35 years of age. He was educated in this country and speaks languages with fluency. His personal bravery is extolled as highly as his mental accomplishments, and his following at home is declared to be large and enthusiastic. He refuses to discuss his plans, but talks readily when President Hereaux's administration is mentioned. He makes no secret of his opposition to the president, whom he freely denounces.

Dominican exiles are not numerous in New York but they make up in determination what they lack in numbers. They declare they mean to stake their all in Mocoso's movement and basing their hopes on recent advices chief seaport, are confident that it will be successful.

Hereaux has been president of Santo Domingo three terms, a much longer period than any of his predecessors. His enemies declare that he has been able to retain the reins of president so long because he has been unscrupulous in carrying out his secret intention of making himself dictator for life by stifling opposition by means of bribery and intimidation. In consequence the best and most influential of the country have either been stultified or banished. It is even charged that a number have been unlawfully put to death at the president's instigation.

records.headline: The Sun doubts that San Domingo has made any stipulation whatever
records.summary_en: The Sun doubts that San Domingo has made any stipulation whatever in regard to the possession of Samana Bay: it recalls a time when the customs duties of San Domingo, then pledged to the American syndicate, were seized in the prosecution of some claims of a foreign power's citizens — the United States Government itself having claims of long standing against San Domingo which it had not sought to settle by force — and says the difficulty, it believes, was amicably smoothed over, though for a time it caused uneasiness. Yet the strategic importance of the bay, from its opening upon the Mona Passage, makes its future an object of watchfulness for the United States Government, and since the collection of the export and import duties of San Domingo is to pass from an American to an English syndicate, American authorities, after Mr. Powell's letter, will naturally await assurances that no political or territorial control can thereby pass to the British Government.

Sin embargo, la importancia estratégica de la bahía, por su apertura sobre el paso de la Mona, hace de su futuro un objeto de vigilancia para el gobierno de los Estados Unidos, y como el cobro de los derechos de exportación e importación de San Domingo va a pasar de un sindicato americano a un sindicato inglés, las autoridades americanas, tras la carta del Sr. Powell, esperarán naturalmente seguridades de que ningún control político o territorial pueda pasar con ello al gobierno británico.

records.summary_en: The *San Francisco Call* reported that the warship *Detroit* was ordered to Samana Bay, where U.S. officials had previously negotiated for a coaling station. While naval authorities claimed the visit was merely to display the American flag, the deployment was also expected to expedite the arbitration of a contract claim by American citizen Nathaniel McKay against the Dominican government. The report also mentioned pending arbitration proposals regarding American claims in Haiti.

It has long been the custom of the United States to make the money of several South American countries, and as an act of comity and good will the work is done at the actual cost of labor and material; the present order from Santo Domingo also includes 800,000 half dollars, 875,000 quarter dollars and 750,000 dimes. The mint bureau has just filled an order from Costa Rica for a large quantity of gold coins, and Costa Rica, so pleased with the coinage, has ordered through its minister at Washington 40,000 more coins of gold; and the first work of this kind done by the United States was in 1876, when $100,000 worth of minor coins were turned out for the government of Venezuela.

records.headline: About thirty years ago an attempt was made by the Grant
records.summary_en: *The Saint Paul Globe* published a letter comparing the proposed annexation of Hawaii to President Grant's unsuccessful effort to annex Santo Domingo in 1869 and 1870. The writer recalled that despite strategic arguments, joint resolution efforts, and a favorable commission report, the annexation treaty failed in the Senate. The author argued that past fears of foreign powers absorbing Santo Domingo proved unfounded and hoped Hawaii would avoid annexation.
records.summary_es: *The Saint Paul Globe* publicó una carta en la que comparaba la proyectada anexión de Hawái con la infructuosa tentativa del presidente Grant de anexionar Santo Domingo en 1869 y 1870. El autor recordaba que, a pesar de los argumentos estratégicos, de los esfuerzos por lograr una resolución conjunta y de un informe favorable de la comisión, el tratado de anexión fracasó en el Senado. El autor sostuvo que los temores pasados de que potencias extranjeras absorbieran a Santo Domingo resultaron infundados y expresó su deseo de que Hawái evitara la anexión.
records.passage: HISTORY REPEATS. Similarity in Hawaiian and Santo Dominican Cases. To the Editor of the Globe. About thirty years ago an attempt was made by the Grant administration to annex Santo Domingo, the second largest island in the West Indies, which ingloriously failed, as I hope the present administration will fail in its attempt to annex the Hawaiian islands. Then, as now, a treaty had been signed for annexation between President Grant and the president of the Santo Domingo republic on Sept. 9, 1869, which treaty was rejected by the senate. In December, 1870, inspired by the president's annual message, another attempt was made to annex said island by passing a joint resolution, which then, as it is now claimed, could be accomplished by a majority vote. This was met and it was held that no territory could be annexed without a treaty which must be ratified by a two-thirds vote of the senate. Finally, a commission of visiting statesmen was appointed, who, in due time, reported favorably, but the whole thing was abandoned in the long run, and no "foreign power" has thus far expressed any desire to absorb that republic. Then, as now, it was strongly urged how indispensable that island was to us for military and naval reasons. Then, as now, certain great patriots were much distressed lest some foreign power would absorb that island and its dusky inhabitants. records.headline: An American company held land in the neighborhood many years Ago
records.summary_en: *The Sun* highlighted the strategic value of Samana Bay as a coaling station along the Mona Passage between Santo Domingo and Puerto Rico, citing its sheltered anchorage and defensible geography. The article reviewed the rejection of President Grant's annexation project 28 years prior, which led the Dominican Republic to refuse any sale, cession, or lease of its territory. It emphasized that current American interest did not contemplate territorial annexation or permanent fortifications.
records.summary_es: *The Sun* destacó el valor estratégico de la bahía de Samaná como estación carbonera en el paso de la Mona, entre Santo Domingo y Puerto Rico, señalando su fondeadero protegido y su ventajosa geografía defensiva. El artículo repasó el rechazo al proyecto de anexión del presidente Grant ocurrido 28 años atrás, lo que llevó a la República Dominicana a negarse a cualquier venta, cesión o arrendamiento de su territorio. Subrayó que el interés estadounidense en ese momento no contemplaba anexiones territoriales ni fortificaciones permanentes.
records.passage: desired coaling station during the various negotiations for acquiring a foothold there. An American company held land in the neighborhood many years ago, and a coal pile was established on Carenero Island. Samana Bay not only gives anchorage enough for the fleets of the world, but it is exceedingly well situated for our purpose. It is true that Mole St. Nicolas, on the Windward Passage, between Hayti and Cuba, has strategic advantages, that route being shorter from our ports to the Isthmus, but Samana Bay lies on the Mona Passage, a route which is taken by the merchant vessels that go to South America between San Domingo and Porto Rico. It is healthful, under the trade winds which blow into it, and it is capable of defence, its narrow entrance being commanded by Levantada Island, while the bold headlands on the north shore give a plunging fire. But we are to assume that there is no question whatever of fortifications now, since no annexation of territory is undertaken, nor even any lease from the Dominican Government. It will be remembered that the old project of acquiring Samana Bay as a coaling station, under President Grant's Administration, about twenty-eight years ago, developed into the form of annexing all San Domingo, and this the Senate did not approve. But afterward the little republic took the ground not only that she would not be annexed, but that she would not sell, cede, or even lease us any territory at all. records.headline: The Graphic prints part of a survey of the West Indies in wartime
records.summary_en: The Graphic prints part of a survey of the West Indies in wartime: the passage opens with the closing words of the story of Christophe's citadel — that the secrets of the citadel they had just completed should never be divulged. There are quite a million people on the island, the survey says, but they dally on the way to civilization; there is no army, and Hayti's only use to the United States would be in lending it a harbor: there are no harbors on the north coast, but Port au Prince, in the republic of Hayti, is a well-protected port lying behind the island of Gonave; in the Dominican Republic there are the harbors of Santo Domingo and Puerto Plata, which would make convenient bases for operations in the Caribbean. The Mona Passage, only 60 miles wide, separates Hayti from the beautiful island of Porto Rico, which the survey calls a valuable possession and, taken altogether, the most important of all the West Indies after Cuba, its exports estimated at more than a quarter of a million dollars a few years ago and its staples sugar and coffee.

records.headline: The Gazette prints a quoted argument for American coaling harbors
records.summary_en: The Gazette prints a quoted argument for American coaling harbors: of harbors in the Atlantic, the best the United States could probably secure is St. Thomas, or, if not this, then Samana Bay, in the Dominican Republic; in the great Pacific, north of the equator, there is only one, Pearl Harbor, near Honolulu. The writer of this has been in all these three places, the argument continues, and knows of what he is speaking; certainly, no time should be lost in securing one harbor in the Atlantic and one in the Pacific as stepping stones on the line of the American coast, of immense value in connection with the isthmian canal; then comes the canal itself, and the question of dry docks large enough for the greatest vessels of today.
records.summary_es: El Gazette publica un argumento citado en favor de puertos americanos de carboneo: de los puertos del Atlántico, el mejor que los Estados Unidos probablemente podrían asegurarse es Santo Tomás, o, si no este, la bahía de Samaná, en la República Dominicana; en el gran Pacífico, al norte del ecuador, solo hay uno, Pearl Harbor, cerca de Honolulu. El autor de esto ha estado en estos tres lugares, continúa el argumento, y sabe de lo que habla; ciertamente, no debe perderse tiempo en asegurarse un puerto en el Atlántico y uno en el Pacífico como escalones en la línea de la costa americana, de inmenso valor en conexión con el canal ístmico; luego viene el propio canal, y la cuestión de los diques secos, lo bastante grandes para los mayores buques de hoy.

records.headline: The Standard prints a survey of the West Indies in wartime
records.summary_en: The Standard prints a survey of the West Indies in wartime: the island's two republics, it says, are the only countries in the West Indies whose form of government is like the United States' own, except, of course, the republic of Cuba. Toussaint L'Ouverture's successful struggle against France and his capture by treachery, followed by the complete expulsion of the French, is one of liberty's favorite tales; the Spanish invaded San Domingo in 1861, and their defeat left the islanders free. The Haytians have experimented with kings and discarded them; the treasure of one of these despots, Christophe, remains buried under the rank vegetation among the ruins of a stronghold he built, whose architect and workmen, the story goes, were thrown from the parapets so that the secrets of the citadel they had just completed should never be divulged. There are quite a million people on the island, but they dally on the way to civilization; there is no army or fortification worthy the name, and Hayti's only use to the United States would be in lending it a harbor: there are no harbors on the north coast, but Port au Prince, in the republic of Hayti, is a well-protected port lying behind the island of Gonave; in the Dominican Republic there are the harbors of Santo Domingo and Puerto Plata, which would make convenient bases for operations in the Caribbean. The Mona Passage, only 60 miles wide, separates Hayti from the beautiful island of Porto Rico, a valuable possession which Spain risks losing on a turn of the war cards.
records.summary_es: El Standard publica un estudio de las Indias Occidentales en tiempo de guerra: las dos repúblicas de la isla, dice, son los únicos países de las Indias Occidentales cuya forma de gobierno es como la de los propios Estados Unidos, excepto, por supuesto, la república de Cuba. La exitosa lucha de Toussaint L'Ouverture contra Francia y su captura por traición, seguida de la completa expulsión de los franceses, es uno de los relatos favoritos de la libertad; los españoles invadieron San Domingo en 1861, y su derrota dejó libres a los isleños. Los haitianos han experimentado con reyes y los han desechado; el tesoro de uno de esos déspotas, Christophe, permanece enterrado bajo la espesa vegetación entre las ruinas de una fortaleza que construyó, cuyo arquitecto y cuyos obreros, según el relato, fueron arrojados desde las murallas para que los secretos de la ciudadela que acababan de completar no fueran divulgados jamás. Hay en la isla cerca de un millón de personas, pero se demoran en el camino de la civilización; no hay ejército ni fortificación digna de ese nombre, y el único uso de Haití para los Estados Unidos sería prestarles un puerto: no hay puertos en la costa norte, pero Puerto Príncipe, en la república de Haití, es un puerto bien protegido situado detrás de la isla de Gonave; en la República Dominicana están los puertos de Santo Domingo y Puerto Plata, que harían bases convenientes para las operaciones en el Caribe. El paso de la Mona, de solo 60 millas de ancho, separa a Haití de la hermosa isla de Puerto Rico, una posesión valiosa que España arriesga perder en una vuelta de las cartas de la guerra.
