records.headline: The Sentinel prints a survey of the West Indies in wartime
records.summary_en: The Sentinel prints a survey of the West Indies in wartime: the island's two republics, it says, are the only countries in the West Indies whose form of government is like the United States' own, except, of course, the republic of Cuba. Toussaint L'Ouverture's successful struggle against France and his capture by treachery, followed by the complete expulsion of the French, is one of liberty's favorite tales; the Spanish invaded San Domingo in 1861, and their defeat left the islanders free. The Haytians have experimented with kings and discarded them; the treasure of one of these despots, Christophe, remains buried under the rank vegetation among the ruins of a stronghold he built, whose architect, a European, and all of the workmen were thrown from the parapets so that the secrets of the citadel they had just completed should never be divulged. There are quite a million people on the island, but they dally on the way to civilization; there is no army or fortification worthy the name, and Hayti's only use to the United States would be in lending it a harbor: there are no harbors on the north coast, but Port au Prince, in the republic of Hayti, is a well-protected port lying behind the island of Gonave; in the Dominican Republic there are the harbors of Santo Domingo and Puerto Plata, which would make convenient bases for operations in the Caribbean. The Mona Passage, only sixty miles wide, separates Hayti from the beautiful island of Porto Rico, a valuable possession which Spain risks losing on a turn of the war cards.

The editorial protests that for the increasing needs of the United States the government is minting no additional silver dollars: the people of South American states get the benefit, and the trade of those distant republics, not America's own, is stimulated thereby.

records.headline: The Graphic reprints the closing passage of a Chicago Times-Herald item
records.summary_en: The Graphic reprints the closing passage of a Chicago Times-Herald item on the coinage the United States mint makes for foreign governments: happily, the coins are not intended for circulation in this country; the work is being done for the Dominican Republic, and the dollars will be sent to Santo Domingo; the design for the coins was furnished by the Dominican treasury department and in no respect, excepting shape, resembles the dollar of the United States. It has long been the custom of the United States to make the money of several South American countries, and as an act of comity and good will the work is done at the actual cost of labor and material; the present order from Santo Domingo also includes 800,000 half dollars, 375,000 quarter dollars and 750,000 dimes. The mint bureau has just filled an order from Costa Rica for a large quantity of gold coins, and Costa Rica, so pleased with the coinage, has ordered through its minister at Washington 40,000 more coins of gold; and the first work of this kind done by the United States was in 1876, when $100,000 worth of minor coins were turned out for the government of Venezuela.

Hace mucho que es costumbre de los Estados Unidos hacer el dinero de varios países sudamericanos, y como un acto de cortesía y buena voluntad el trabajo se hace al costo real de la mano de obra y el material; el pedido actual de Santo Domingo incluye también 800,000 medios dólares, 375,000 cuartos de dólar y 750,000 monedas de diez centavos. La oficina de la moneda acaba de cumplir un pedido de Costa Rica de una gran cantidad de monedas de oro, y Costa Rica, tan complacida con la acuñación, ha ordenado, por medio de su ministro en Washington, 40,000 monedas de oro más; y el primer trabajo de esta clase hecho por los Estados Unidos fue en 1876, cuando se produjeron $100,000 en monedas menores para el gobierno de Venezuela.

records.headline: Among the Herald's war dispatches: a copyrighted cablegram of the World
records.summary_en: Among the Herald's war dispatches: a copyrighted cablegram of the World from its correspondent George Bronson Rea, dated Puerto Plata, San Domingo, May 8: Dominican officials report heavy cannonading off the north of Monte Cristi, about 50 miles from here, and it is believed there that Rear Admiral Sampson's squadron is engaging the Spanish Cape Verde fleet; the firing began about 9 o'clock this morning and was terrific. Sampson came here, the cablegram continues, with orders to find the fleet and reduce it, and after destroying the Spanish ships will begin a strict blockade and, if necessary, will bombard and capture Porto Rico; and a St. Thomas dispatch of May 8, printed in the same columns, reports that the American fleet under Rear Admiral Sampson has not yet arrived off Porto Rico and no fighting has yet occurred in that quarter.

records.headline: A Haitian deputy, who professes to be well informed on all
records.summary_en: *The Indianapolis Journal* reported from Haiti regarding proposed constitutional changes concerning foreign property rights. Haitian Foreign Minister Brutus St. Victor denied claims that the government intended to repeal Article 6 of the constitution, which prohibited alien ownership of real estate, stating the public was not prepared for such reform. St. Victor also declined to disclose specific government plans to address the rising premium on paper currency.
records.summary_es: *The Indianapolis Journal* informó desde Haití sobre las propuestas de reforma constitucional relativas a los derechos de propiedad de los extranjeros. El ministro de Asuntos Exteriores haitiano, Brutus St. Victor, desmintió las versiones de que el gobierno pretendiera derogar el artículo 6 de la constitución, que prohibía a los extranjeros la propiedad de bienes inmuebles, afirmando que la opinión pública no estaba preparada para tal cambio. St. Victor declinó asimismo revelar planes gubernamentales específicos para hacer frente al creciente sobreprecio del papel moneda.

Her officers would like to serve in her under the American flag. Her second officer is an American, who was in the federal navy during the civil war. A Haitian deputy, who professes to be well informed on all political matters, said yesterday that the government was certain to favor the elimination of Article 6 from the Constitution at the session of the Chambers, which will probably begin this week. The correspondent of the Associated Press derived from Brutus St. Victor, the secretary of state for foreign relations, to-day, an entirely different view of the parliamentary programme. records.full_text:
HAITI'S FUTURE MAY DEPEND ON THE OUTCOME OF THE HISPANO-AMERICAN WAR. Bulldozing Germans Waiting for an Opportunity to Wrest the Place from Its Black Owners, CONCESSION TO AMERICANS THAT MAY INVOLVE THE LITTLE REPUBLIC IN NO END OF TROUBLE. Europeans, and Especially Germans, Will Expect Same Commercial Privileges as Yankee Traders. MANY CUBANS NOW IN HAITI SEEM TO CARE LITTLE ABOUT WHAT IS GOING ON AT HOME. Minister Powell's Warning to the Haitian Administration—Interview with Brutus St. Victor.

(Copyright, 1898, by the Associated Press.)

PORT-AU-PRINCE, May 8.—German war ships some time ago made soundings in the principal ports of Haiti—Port-au-Prince, the Mole St. Nicholas, Cape Haiti, St. Marie, Jeremie and Jacmel. What Germany might undertake to do in this part of the world, in the event of a general conflict of the nations, a dread of which Lord Salisbury is said to have expressed in a recent speech, is a question that is occupying the attention of the public men of Haiti. Well-informed observers residing here do not doubt that if America were involved on one side, Germany would send a fleet to seize the island. German traders fervently cherish this hope. Their feeling against the Haitians since the Luders incident has been intense and, so far as a volatile people is capable of cherishing old scores, the animosity is reciprocal.

Of all the masters of vessels coming to Haitian ports, the Germans treat the native officials and stevedores with the least consideration, often with unconcealed contempt. The wonder is that their attitude does not oftener provoke conflicts. If you walk the streets here and a lower class native hurls after you a certain epithet, you may be sure it is because of the ill will towards the Germans and not on general principles. Yet the Germans are by far the most numerous class of traders here. It may be that this has not a little to do with the action of the government in conceding the amendment of Article 5 of the treaty with the United States, about which I cabled you this week, granting to Americans the same commercial rights as that enjoyed by the Haitians. However this may be, it is certain that the concession will involve the Haitian government in vexatious difficulties with other nations, unless it does the same by them. Whether M. Brutus St. Victor, the able minister of foreign affairs, has looked so far ahead as this I cannot say, though it is very reasonable to assume that he has.

By the concession to the Americans, Haiti loses about $50,000 in gold a year in revenue. In order to afford to treat other foreigners with like liberality, she must devise new taxation. It looks very much as if, counting on the protection of the United States in case of need, the foreign minister expected to refuse an equal concession to other nations, on the ground that the treaty of 1864 is purely reciprocal, each party making to the other a specific return for specific privileges granted. But such an excuse is likely to have little force if the West India waters become the principal naval battlefield in a general war.

WAR ECHOES FROM HAITI.

Cuban Refugees—Minister Powell's Warning to the Government.

(Copyright, 1898, by the Associated Press.)

PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti, May 8.—It is estimated that there are about 1,000 Cuban refugees in Haiti, the great majority, of course, in this city. A singular absence of enthusiasm among them over the intervention of America in behalf of their people has been remarked. If hope is at the fever point they do not show it. At one special resort in Port-au-Prince Cubans of nearly every class congregate in the evening, drink, smoke, play cards, sing and talk of the war. They evince by far less excitement over the hostilities than do the Haitians, who group themselves daily, a little before and a little after the hour of the siesta, in front of the restaurant De la Paix and the Hotel Central and divide their attention between the movements of the gold premium and the achievements, actual and prospective, of the Americans. The wildest and strangest and most absurd rumors find ready currency in the city. Not one in ten, when traced anywhere near its source, can readily be made to have a serious foundation. Whether the Cubans invent the majority of these, in competition with the Spaniards at Havana, it is impossible to say.

The chairman of the Cuban Junto in Haiti is Dr. J. E. Nunez, who declares himself an American citizen. Another leader of the Junto is Dr. E. Heraux. Dr. Nunez is seriously considering the suggestion that if the Cubans in Haiti would secretly organize a force to join the insurgents the United States would undoubtedly send arms and munitions down to some convenient point of the eastern end of Cuba for their use. They could pass from here to Cuba in a sailing vessel without much danger of capture. A recent rumor that a Spanish cruiser had taken an American three-master off the Mole St. Nicholas was received in Port-au-Prince with absolute incredulity, and thus far there has been no confirmation of it. It is hardly believed that any single Spanish war-ship would venture within reaching distance of the American squadron in the West Indies.

About a week ago a former Haitian general, Dorsainville, called on the American minister and offered to raise a battalion of 500 men to serve under the American flag in Cuba. He was informed that the American government would not authorize or sanction the recruiting of an armed force in a foreign country, as that would be a flagrant violation of international law. Of course, to equip and provision such a force after it had landed in Spanish territory would be a different thing.

The report that the United States government has negotiated with the Haitian government for the purchase of the gunboat Crete A. Pierrot, the finest vessel in the latter's navy, has been persistently circulated. Admiral Killeck, the highest naval officer of Haiti, told the correspondent of the Associated Press yesterday that it was true, and that the Haitian government had refused the offer made to it for the express reason that it could not spare the vessel. The Crete A. Pierrot, named after one of Haiti's famous battlefields, is built on handsome lines, and when she is in the harbor always attracts more than any other Haitian war ship the attention of strangers. She has an imposing ram and her armament is excellent, her guns being of the latest type. She has an entire complement of rapid-fire ordnance. With only one boiler, she is said to make sixteen knots an hour. She has a triple expansion engine, and, with a double boiler, which could be put into her at short notice, could make, her engineer declares, about twenty knots an hour. Her officers would like to serve in her under the American flag. Her second officer is an American, who was in the federal navy during the civil war.

A Haitian deputy, who professes to be well informed on all political matters, said yesterday that the government was certain to favor the elimination of Article 6 from the Constitution at the session of the Chambers, which will probably begin this week. The correspondent of the Associated Press derived from Brutus St. Victor, the secretary of state for foreign relations, an entirely different view of the parliamentary programme. Mr. St. Victor denied categorically that the government contemplated any project for the removal of the prohibition of alien ownership of real property. Such a step, he said, if ever taken, must be yet a very great way off. "The people," he continued, "are not ready to accept such a change. There must be a gradual preparation of public sentiment before the government could even suggest it. There is, no doubt, such an opinion favorable to it, but it has as yet manifested itself chiefly in the cities, and it must be remembered that the mass of the Haitian population is rural, and that it is strongly wedded to national traditions."

Mr. St. Victor would not speak definitely as to the means which the government intended to take to check the increase of the premium on paper money; but he admitted that this was, perhaps, the most urgent business which would claim the attention of the chambers. He mentioned the contract recently entered into by the government with the Bank of Haiti to burn publicly every month a certain percentage of the paper money received in payment of customs duties. This would reduce the volume of paper currency quite rapidly. "The real chief cause of the premium on gold, however," said Mr. St. Victor, "is the low price of coffee. It has begun to rise again, and it is hoped will be restored in a few months to its normal value."

The correspondent asked the foreign minister whether the stories which had been printed about the distressed condition of the people in the interior had been exaggerated. He replied that among the country people there was some distress, but no actual want of the necessaries of life. Nobody could starve in the interior of Haiti who was industrious enough to scratch the soil ever so little by way of cultivation. It was in the cities that the real misery existed, and there was danger that the Hispano-American war would render it worse. The city folk could not live without money as the country people could. They had been dependent for many cheap articles of food upon the American trade. This supply had been largely reduced, and with the premium and prices generally going up, the small wage earners were threatened with dire need.

Mr. St. Victor also said that Haiti was resolved to maintain the strictest neutrality as between Spain and America, but, when questioned as to the special privileges granted to American ships of war in the treaty of 1864, he evaded a direct answer. He confirmed Minister Powell's statement of a few days ago to the Associated Press correspondent, to the effect that Americans and Haitians in this country were hereafter to be upon an equal commercial footing. Whatever view critics may take on the policy of the American government in persisting in sending men of color to represent it in the island of Haiti, they will not be able to find fault with the present minister at Port-au-Prince, William F. Powell, on account of a lack of energy. A man of seemingly very deliberate action and of extremely quiet manners, he yet seems to have made a noteworthy impression on the powers that rule at either end of the island.

These dispatches have already called attention to the steps which Mr. Powell has taken, in pursuance of instructions from Washington, to commit the Haitian government to the literal fulfillment of all the provisions of the treaty of 1864 with the United States, which give to that country in time of war special advantages which cannot be enjoyed by other nations and also the article which purports to place Americans on an equal footing with Haitians as to the privileges of local trade. The former achievement was less difficult than the latter, which follows some twenty years of unsuccessful effort in the same direction, beginning at the time when Hamilton Fish was secretary of state. It is easy to believe, however, that the increased martial prestige of America, consequent upon that country's going to war with Spain for the deliverance of a west Indian people from oppression, has impressed Haitian statesmen and the Haitians in general much more effectively than any amount of forcible diplomacy could have done. Mr. Powell, nevertheless, so far as one can discern at this moment, deserves full credit for having "risen to the height of the occasion." His language to the minister of the exterior on the treaty obligations has been of no uncertain meaning. He has several times strongly stated that the fate of Haiti as a nation depended in a large degree upon the attitude of the government towards America during the present war. The Haitian administration already realized this fact, but in an alternative

However virile and worthy of respect may be the present disposition of Brutus St. Victor, the foreign minister, President Sam himself is inclined to choose the less decisive course whenever the other presents a chance of danger. It was not difficult, however, to convince the Haitian government that to provoke resentment on the part of the American people in the present emergency would be to jeopardize the benevolent friendship which they have exhibited towards the former since the days of Dessalines. The Haitians are rightly indifferent to the friendship of the Spaniards, though they have some fear of reprisal upon the part of the latter if the special privileges accorded to Americans should be so freely used as to provoke a declaration that they contravene the laws of neutrality. To cut short any possible period of vacillation on the part of the Haitian government it was necessary for the American minister to assume a tone which had been rarely, if ever, used by his predecessors. He caused the government to understand that now was the opportunity to assure forever the substantial support of the United States or to invite their lasting aversion and enmity.

Another negotiation has been in progress at Santo Domingo for some time. It involves the project of a treaty between the United States and the Dominican republic granting to the former even a broader preference over other nations than accorded in the Haitian treaty. One of its articles has a political significance which will astonish and may dismay some of the Europeans, who are anxious to achieve something of consequence in this island. The correspondent hopes soon to be at liberty to be more explicit on this subject.

Simon Sam’s Birthday.

(Copyright, 1898, by the Associated Press.)

PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti, May 15.—The second anniversary of the election of Gen. Tiresias Simon Sam as president of the republic of Haiti, was celebrated here to-day. There was a brilliant review of troops and there was an imposing religious ceremony at the cathedral, where a Te Deum was chanted. All the members of the diplomatic corps were present. President Sam made a tour of the city, which was in holiday attire, and was warmly acclaimed by the population.

records.headline: The Plain Dealer prints part of a West Indies survey in wartime
records.summary_en: The Plain Dealer prints part of a West Indies survey in wartime: a moment's consideration of the history of the two republics, Hayti in the west and San Domingo in the east, the only countries in the West Indies whose form of government is like our own, except, of course, the republic of Cuba. Toussaint L'Ouverture's successful struggle against France and his capture by treachery, followed by the complete expulsion of the French, is one of liberty's favorite tales; the Spanish invaded San Domingo in 1861, and their defeat left the islanders free; the Haytians have experimented with kings and discarded them, and the treasure of one of these despots, Christophe, remains buried under the rank vegetation among the ruins of a stronghold he built, whose architect and all the workmen were thrown from the parapets so that the secrets of the citadel they had just completed should never be divulged. There are quite a million people on the island; there is no army, or Hayti's only use to us would be in lending us a harbor: there are no harbors on the north coast, but Port au Prince, in the republic of Hayti, is a well-protected port lying behind the island of Gonaive, while in the Dominican republic there are the harbors of Santo Domingo and Porto Plata, which would make convenient bases for operations in the Caribbean; and the Mona passage, only 60 miles wide, separates Hayti from Porto Rico.

records.headline: The Jersey City News prints the closing passage of the Associated Press dispatch
records.summary_en: The Jersey City News prints the closing passage of the Associated Press dispatch on the steamer Fanita: she was to touch at Monte Cristi, Dominican Republic, or at the keys just outside, to fill up the empty portion of her hold, and she has on board Chris Roberts, of Great Inagua, the most famous pilot of the West Indies. The captain of the Fanita, when that vessel was here, said the portion of her cargo which was not landed consisted of coal, but there is good reason to suppose that it is something very different from coal; and proof that the Fanita is under serious suspicion was afforded this morning by the excited conduct of the Spanish consul here, who denounces the taking on board the steamer of Spanish-speaking roustabouts and the sudden sailing of the vessel without the permission of the Dominican consul, classes this as a great outrage and an act of piracy, and has entered a formal protest with the Haytien authorities and telegraphed to his diplomatic chief at Santo Domingo this morning about the Fanita. There are large numbers of Cubans in Santo Domingo who eagerly desire to return to Cuba and take part in the war, and the correspondent here of the Associated Press is informed that the Spaniards of this place believe that it may be part of the mission of the Fanita to afford these Cubans transportation, at the same time furnishing them with arms and ammunition.

records.headline: Among the El Paso Herald's dispatches is a report on the Jiminez expedition
records.summary_en: Among the El Paso Herald's dispatches is a report on the Jiminez expedition: a revolutionary expedition from Hayti landed at Monte Cristi, San Domingo, on Thursday under the leadership of Senor Jiminez, formerly a New York merchant; the Dominican government had been advised of the movement of the troops and was waiting to capture the party; General Augustin Morales, a leader of the expedition, was shot without ceremony; and the whole party will probably be executed.

records.headline: The Intelligencer prints part of the Associated Press feature
records.summary_en: The Intelligencer prints part of the Associated Press feature on the revolution the steamer Fanita carried to Monte Cristi: General Villanueva, who fought bravely against President Heureaux's alleged usurpation and was exiled, has been living at Great Inagua for some time past, and the Fanita is said to have stopped there in order to take him on board. The preparations for the revolution are said to have been very elaborate, and there is a strong belief there that the revolutionists are sure of success; but, on the other hand, the Dominican consul there says he has a report that the revolutionists have been defeated at Monte Cristi, a report not generally believed. The advices received there on the subject say that the Fanita arrived at Monte Cristi at 3 o'clock yesterday afternoon, and that the revolutionists had no difficulty in taking the town; the most circumstantial reports have it that the revolutionists are now in considerable force, and that under Generals Morales and Villanueva they are marching on Puerto Plata, while another detachment is moving against Santiago de los Caballeros, on the Yaque river, one hundred miles east of there; General Garcia, another important Dominican leader, is said to be taking part in the revolution, and it is expected there will be a rising at Santo Domingo, the capital of the republic; and General Jimenez is a merchant who has business houses there, at Monte Cristi, at Puerto Plata and at Hamburg, in his youth he served in the army, and for many years he has been very popular in the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: El Intelligencer publica parte del reportaje de la Associated Press sobre la revolución que el vapor Fanita llevó a Monte Cristi: el general Villanueva, que peleó valientemente contra la alegada usurpación del presidente Heureaux y fue exiliado, ha estado viviendo en Gran Inagua desde hace algún tiempo, y se dice que la Fanita se detuvo allí para recogerlo a bordo. Se dice que los preparativos de la revolución fueron muy elaborados, y hay una fuerte creencia allí de que los revolucionarios están seguros del éxito; pero el cónsul dominicano allí dice que tiene un reporte de que los revolucionarios han sido derrotados en Monte Cristi, reporte que no es creído en general. Los avisos recibidos allí sobre el asunto dicen que la Fanita llegó a Monte Cristi a las 3 de la tarde de ayer, y que los revolucionarios no tuvieron dificultad en tomar la ciudad; los reportes más circunstanciados sostienen que los revolucionarios están ahora en fuerza considerable, y que bajo los generales Morales y Villanueva marchan sobre Puerto Plata, mientras otro destacamento se mueve contra Santiago de los Caballeros, sobre el río Yaque, cien millas al este de allí; el general García, otro importante líder dominicano, se dice que toma parte en la revolución, y se espera que haya un levantamiento en Santo Domingo, la capital de la república; y el general Jimenez es un comerciante que tiene casas de negocio allí, en Monte Cristi, en Puerto Plata y en Hamburgo, en su juventud sirvió en el ejército, y por muchos años ha sido muy popular en la República Dominicana.

records.summary_en: *The News & Observer* reported that an armed uprising against Dominican President Heureaux had begun at Monte Cristi, near the Haitian border. The Clyde Line steamer *Fanita* reportedly departed Cape Haitien carrying 150 Dominican insurgents concealed in its hold, alongside rebel leaders General Juan Isidro Jimenes and General Villanueva. Observers in Haiti described the revolutionary expedition as well prepared and expressed strong confidence in its potential success.
records.summary_es: *The News & Observer* informó que se había iniciado un levantamiento armado contra el presidente dominicano Heureaux en Monte Cristi, cerca de la frontera con Haití. Se informó que el vapor *Fanita*, de la Clyde Line, zarpó de Cabo Haitiano transportando a 150 insurgentes dominicanos ocultos en sus bodegas, junto a los cabecillas rebeldes, los generales Juan Isidro Jimenes y Villanueva. Observadores en Haití describieron la expedición revolucionaria como bien preparada y manifestaron gran confianza en su posible éxito.

Cape Haytien, Hayti, June 3. — 11:40 a. m. — The mystery surrounding the movements of the Clyde Line steamer Fanita is now said to be fully explained. It appears established beyond a doubt that the reports of an uprising in the republic of Santo Domingo against the power of President Heureaux are correct. The initial blow was struck at Monte Cristo, on the borders of Hayti, the nearest Dominican port to Cape Haytien. It would appear as though the Fanita had 150 Dominicans on hand while here, who remained in the hold of the ship so as to escape attention. records.headline: The Salt Lake Herald prints part of the Associated Press feature
records.summary_en: The Salt Lake Herald prints part of the Associated Press feature on the Fanita revolution: the reports of an uprising in the republic of Santo Domingo against the power of President Heureaux are correct; the initial blow was struck at Monte Cristi, on the borders of Hayti, the nearest Dominican port to Cape Haytien. It would appear that the Fanita, instead of having on board only 17 Dominicans, probably had 330 on board; she arrived at Cape Haytien on June 1 half empty, bringing from New York provisions for the navy, which she landed at Matthewtown, in the Bahama Islands, and slipped away about 10 o'clock the same night, to fill up the empty portion of her hold; she had on board Chris Roberts, the most famous pilot of the West Indies. General Ysidro Jimenez and General Pablo Villanueva are believed to have been on board; Jimenez has long been in the public eye in Santo Domingo as a desirable man for the presidency, and Villanueva fought bravely against President Heureaux's alleged usurpation and was exiled. The preparations for the revolution are said to have been very elaborate, and there is a strong belief there that the revolutionists are sure of success.
records.summary_es: El Salt Lake Herald publica parte del reportaje de la Associated Press sobre la revolución de la Fanita: son correctos los reportes de un levantamiento en la república de Santo Domingo contra el poder del presidente Heureaux; el golpe inicial fue dado en Monte Cristi, en los límites de Haití, el puerto dominicano más cercano a Cabo Haitiano. Parecería que la Fanita, en lugar de tener a bordo solo 17 dominicanos, probablemente tenía 330 a bordo; llegó a Cabo Haitiano el 1 de junio medio vacía, trayendo de Nueva York provisiones para la marina, que desembarcó en Matthewtown, en las islas Bahamas, y escapó cerca de las 10 de esa misma noche, para llenar la parte vacía de su bodega; llevaba a bordo a Chris Roberts, el piloto más famoso de las Indias Occidentales. Se cree que el general Ysidro Jimenez y el general Pablo Villanueva iban a bordo; Jimenez ha estado por largo tiempo ante la vista pública en Santo Domingo como un hombre deseable para la presidencia, y Villanueva peleó valientemente contra la alegada usurpación del presidente Heureaux y fue exiliado. Se dice que los preparativos de la revolución fueron muy elaborados, y hay una fuerte creencia allí de que los revolucionarios están seguros del éxito.

records.summary_en: The Times prints the closing passage of the Associated Press feature on the Fanita revolution, with the consul's report of its defeat: the revolutionists are now in considerable force, and under Generals Morales and Villanueva they are marching on Puerto Plata, while another detachment is moving against Santiago de los Caballeros, on the Yaque river, 103 miles east of there; and General Garcia, another important Dominican leader, is said to be taking part in the revolution, and there is said to be a rising at Santo Domingo, the capital of the Dominican republic. President Heureaux, according to a common saying among the Dominicans, has killed off all the prominent men on whom he could lay hands and who might be rivals, and is said to have recently resumed the arbitrary execution of his opponents, sometimes openly, sometimes stealthily, the tragic disappearances of men of political note having been frequent of late in the republic. This afternoon the Dominican consul there received a dispatch from President Heureaux saying that an attempted revolution at Monte Cristi had been defeated, that General Jiminez fled at the first fire of the government troops, taking refuge on board the Fanita, and that all the others who landed, with the exception of three, had been killed; two of the prisoners are Pablo Villanueva, son of General Villanueva, and a laborer, and they will be executed today with other prisoners; General Morales, the Haytian general, and several Dominicans who shipped there are among the killed, and another person was killed on board the steamer Fanita.

El presidente Heureaux, según un dicho común entre los dominicanos, ha eliminado a todos los hombres prominentes a los que pudo echar mano y que pudieran ser rivales, y se dice que recientemente ha reanudado la ejecución arbitraria de sus oponentes, a veces abiertamente, a veces a escondidas, habiendo sido frecuentes en los últimos tiempos en la república las trágicas desapariciones de hombres de nota política. Esta tarde el cónsul dominicano allí recibió un despacho del presidente Heureaux diciendo que un intento de revolución en Monte Cristi había sido derrotado, que el general Jiminez huyó al primer fuego de las tropas del gobierno, refugiándose a bordo de la Fanita, y que todos los demás que desembarcaron, con la excepción de tres, habían sido muertos; dos de los prisioneros son Pablo Villanueva, hijo del general Villanueva, y un jornalero, y serán ejecutados hoy con otros prisioneros; el general Morales, el general haitiano, y varios dominicanos que se embarcaron allí están entre los muertos, y otra persona fue muerta a bordo del vapor Fanita.

records.summary_en: The *Indianapolis Journal* reported that insurgent forces led by Generals Morales and Villanueva were advancing on Puerto Plata and Santiago de los Caballeros against Dominican President Heureaux. The report profiled revolutionary leader General Juan Isidro Jimenes, an established merchant with business houses in Europe and the Caribbean who had organized the movement from New York. It noted that Jimenes enjoyed wide popularity and had previously resided in Paris to escape Heureaux's hostility toward political rivals.
records.summary_es: El *Indianapolis Journal* informó que fuerzas insurgentes encabezadas por los generales Morales y Villanueva avanzaban sobre Puerto Plata y Santiago de los Caballeros contra el presidente dominicano Heureaux. El informe trazó un perfil del líder revolucionario general Juan Isidro Jimenes, un consolidado comerciante con casas comerciales en Europa y el Caribe que había organizado el movimiento desde Nueva York. Señalaba que Jimenes gozaba de amplia popularidad y que previamente había residido en París para escapar de la hostilidad de Heureaux hacia sus rivales políticos.

According to an official dispatch from Heureaux, insurgent leader General Jimenes fled aboard the steamer *Fanita* under fire, while Haitian General Morales and several others were killed. Dominican authorities captured several prisoners, including General Villanueva's son, who were slated for execution.
records.summary_es: El *Richmond Dispatch* informó que un intento de revolución contra el presidente dominicano Heureaux fue rápidamente derrotado en Monte Cristi. Según un parte oficial de Heureaux, el líder insurgente general Jimenes huyó bajo fuego a bordo del vapor *Fanita*, mientras que el general haitiano Morales y varios otros perecieron. Las autoridades dominicanas capturaron a varios prisioneros, entre ellos el hijo del general Villanueva, quienes estaban destinados a ser ejecutados.

records.summary_en: The Globe prints part of the Associated Press feature on the Fanita revolution: there is a strong belief at Cape Haytien that the revolutionists are sure of success, though the Dominican consul there says he has a report that the revolutionists have been defeated at Monte Cristi. According to the impression which prevails at Cape Haytien, the Fanita, when she left there, had a tried and resolute body of men on board, and also carried a heavy supply of arms and ammunition; it is charged that she skilfully worked up the impression that she was engaged in an expedition to Cuba, and was going to Monte Cristi to take on more men. The advices received there on the subject say that the Fanita arrived at Monte Cristi at 3 o'clock yesterday afternoon, and that the revolutionists had no difficulty in taking the town; the most circumstantial reports have it that the revolutionists are now in considerable force, and that under Generals Morales and Villanueva they are marching on Puerto Plata, while another detachment is moving against Santiago de los Caballeros, on the Yaque river, 100 miles east of Cape Haytien; General Garcia, another important Dominican leader, is said to be taking part in the revolution, and it is expected there will be a rising at Santo Domingo, the capital of the Dominican republic; and General Jiminez is a merchant who has business houses at Cape Haytien, at Monte Cristi, at Puerto Plata and at Hamburg, in his youth he served in the army, and for many years he has been very popular in the Dominican Republic.

records.summary_en: The Post-Intelligencer prints the closing passage of the Associated Press feature on the Fanita revolution: General Jiminez, a man of mild temperament, has several times been a candidate for the presidency, and his father was formerly president of the republic. A correspondent of Puerto Plata cables the confirmation of the accounts of the repulse of the revolutionary party at Monte Cristi: General Augustin Morales and another officer were killed, five of the insurgents were taken prisoners and shot this morning, and the others escaped in the steamer Fanita; President Heureaux left the capital this morning with three men-of-war, and the correspondent, in concluding his dispatch, says the revolutionary movement is regarded in Puerto Plata as of no consequence. The Dominican consul at Cape Haytien reasserts that Jiminez escaped on the Fanita, saying that had Jiminez been killed President Heureaux would have informed him of the fact; and this afternoon the consul received a dispatch from President Heureaux saying that the attempted revolution at Monte Cristi had been defeated, that Jiminez fled at the first fire of the government troops, taking refuge on board of the Fanita, and that all the others who landed, with the exception of three, had been killed, two of the prisoners being Pablo Villanueva, son of General Villanueva, and a laborer, who will be executed with the other prisoners.
records.summary_es: El Post-Intelligencer publica el pasaje final del reportaje de la Associated Press sobre la revolución de la Fanita: el general Jiminez, hombre de temperamento apacible, ha sido varias veces candidato a la presidencia, y su padre fue anteriormente presidente de la república. Un corresponsal de Puerto Plata cablegrafía la confirmación de los relatos de la repulsa del partido revolucionario en Monte Cristi: el general Augustin Morales y otro oficial fueron muertos, cinco de los insurgentes fueron tomados prisioneros y fusilados esta mañana, y los demás escaparon en el vapor Fanita; el presidente Heureaux salió de la capital esta mañana con tres buques de guerra, y el corresponsal, al concluir su despacho, dice que el movimiento revolucionario es considerado en Puerto Plata como de ninguna consecuencia. El cónsul dominicano en Cabo Haitiano reafirma que Jiminez escapó en la Fanita, diciendo que si Jiminez hubiera sido muerto el presidente Heureaux se lo habría informado; y esta tarde el cónsul recibió un despacho del presidente Heureaux diciendo que el intento de revolución en Monte Cristi había sido derrotado, que Jiminez huyó al primer fuego de las tropas del gobierno, refugiándose a bordo de la Fanita, y que todos los demás que desembarcaron, con la excepción de tres, habían sido muertos, siendo dos de los prisioneros Pablo Villanueva, hijo del general Villanueva, y un jornalero, que serán ejecutados con los demás prisioneros.

records.headline: The Leader prints part of the Associated Press feature on the Fanita revolution
records.summary_en: The Leader prints part of the Associated Press feature on the Fanita revolution: Jimenez has long been in the public eye in Santo Domingo as a desirable man for the presidency, and General Villanueva, who fought bravely against President Heureaux's alleged usurpation and was exiled, has been living at Great Inagua for some time past, and the Fanita is said to have stopped there in order to take him on board. The preparations for the revolution are said to have been very elaborate, and there is a strong belief at Cape Haytien that the revolutionists are sure of success, but, on the other hand, the Dominican consul there says he has a report that the revolutionists have been defeated at Monte Cristi, a report not generally believed. According to the impression which prevails at Cape Haytien, the Fanita, when she left there, had a tried and resolute body of men on board and also carried a heavy supply of arms and ammunition, and it is charged that she skilfully worked up the impression that she was engaged in an expedition to Cuba and was going to Monte Cristi to take on more men. The advices received there on the subject say that the Fanita arrived at Monte Cristi at 3 o'clock Thursday afternoon, and that the revolutionists had no difficulty in taking the town; the most circumstantial reports have it that the revolutionists are now in considerable force, and that under Generals Morales and Villanueva they are marching on Puerto Plata, while another detachment is moving against Santiago de los Caballeros, on the Yaque river, 100 miles east of Cape Haytien; and General Garcia, another important Dominican leader, is said to be taking part in the revolution.
records.summary_es: El Leader publica parte del reportaje de la Associated Press sobre la revolución de la Fanita: Jimenez ha estado por largo tiempo ante la vista pública en Santo Domingo como un hombre deseable para la presidencia, y el general Villanueva, que peleó valientemente contra la alegada usurpación del presidente Heureaux y fue exiliado, ha estado viviendo en Gran Inagua desde hace algún tiempo, y se dice que la Fanita se detuvo allí para recogerlo a bordo. Se dice que los preparativos de la revolución fueron muy elaborados, y hay una fuerte creencia en Cabo Haitiano de que los revolucionarios están seguros del éxito, pero, por otro lado, el cónsul dominicano allí dice que tiene un reporte de que los revolucionarios han sido derrotados en Monte Cristi, reporte que no es creído en general. Según la impresión que prevalece en Cabo Haitiano, la Fanita, cuando salió de allí, tenía a bordo un cuerpo de hombres probados y decididos y también llevaba un pesado suministro de armas y municiones, y se le imputa haber trabajado hábilmente la impresión de que estaba ocupada en una expedición a Cuba y que iba a Monte Cristi a recoger más hombres. Los avisos recibidos allí sobre el asunto dicen que la Fanita llegó a Monte Cristi a las 3 de la tarde del jueves, y que los revolucionarios no tuvieron dificultad en tomar la ciudad; los reportes más circunstanciados sostienen que los revolucionarios están ahora en fuerza considerable, y que bajo los generales Morales y Villanueva marchan sobre Puerto Plata, mientras otro destacamento se mueve contra Santiago de los Caballeros, sobre el río Yaque, 100 millas al este de Cabo Haitiano; y el general García, otro importante líder dominicano, se dice que toma parte en la revolución.

records.headline: The Dominican consul here at Cape Haytien reasserts positively
records.summary_en: The *Daily Morning Journal and Courier* reported that Dominican President Heureaux mobilized three warships after insurgent leader General Jimenes escaped aboard the steamer *Fanita* following the defeat at Monte Cristi. The report highlighted Jimenes's past role in financing President Hyppolite in Haiti and noted the significant use of a Clyde Line steamer in the conspiracy. It also reported that Heureaux had resumed arbitrary executions and forced disappearances of prominent political opponents.
records.summary_es: El *Daily Morning Journal and Courier* informó que el presidente dominicano Heureaux movilizó tres buques de guerra luego de que el líder insurgente general Jimenes escapara a bordo del vapor *Fanita* tras la derrota en Monte Cristi. El informe resaltó el papel pasado de Jimenes en la financiación del presidente Hyppolite en Haití y señaló el uso significativo de un vapor de la Clyde Line en la conspiración. Asimismo, informó que Heureaux había reanudado las ejecuciones arbitrarias y las desapariciones forzadas de destacados opositores políticos.
records.passage: ers escaped in the steamer Fanita. President Heureaux left the capital this morning with three men-of-war. The correspondent, in concluding his dispatch, says the revolutionary movement is regarded at Puerto Plata as of no consequence. The Dominican consul here at Cape Haytien reasserts positively that General Jimenes escaped on the Fanita. He says that had Jimenes been killed President Heureaux would have informed him of the fact. General Jimenes was regarded as the wheelhorse of the revolution which put Hippolyte in power in Hayti, managing the financial end of the movement. When he was here the last time it was understood that President Heureaux warned him to leave Dominica for his own safety. Last April his principal partner came here from Hamburg to replace him in the direction of the business. The fact that the Clyde company furnished the conspirators with a steamer is regarded as very significant of the completeness of the preparations and the prospect of their success, since the Clyde steamship concession is the most valuable held under the Dominican government. President Heureaux is said to have recently resumed the arbitrary execution of his opponents, sometimes openly, sometimes stealthily. records.summary_en: The *Waterbury Evening Democrat* reported on the clandestine expedition of the steamer *Fanita*, which picked up exiled General Villanueva and pilot Chris Roberts at Great Inagua while concealing insurgent troops in its hold. Led by General Juan Isidro Jimenes, the expedition aimed to overthrow President Heureaux following extensive preparations. Although early observers expected success, the Dominican consul reported that the insurgent force had been defeated upon landing at Monte Cristi.

Encabezada por el general Juan Isidro Jimenes, la expedición tenía por objetivo derrocar al presidente Heureaux tras minuciosos preparativos. Aunque los primeros observadores auguraban el éxito, el cónsul dominicano informó que la fuerza insurgente había sido derrotada al desembarcar en Monte Cristi.

records.summary_en: The *Wichita Daily Eagle* reported conflicting accounts regarding an armed expedition led by General Juan Isidro Jimenes against Dominican President Heureaux. While the Dominican consul claimed the insurgents were defeated at Monte Cristi, other reports stated the rebels had landed munitions from the *Fanita* and were marching toward Puerto Plata and Santiago de los Caballeros. The paper described Jimenes as an influential merchant and former presidential heir who had long avoided Heureaux's violent crackdowns on political rivals.
records.summary_es: El *Wichita Daily Eagle* informó sobre versiones contradictorias relativas a una expedición armada encabezada por el general Juan Isidro Jimenes contra el presidente dominicano Heureaux. Mientras el cónsul dominicano aseguraba que los insurgentes habían sido derrotados en Monte Cristi, otros informes señalaban que los rebeldes habían desembarcado pertrechos desde el *Fanita* y marchaban hacia Puerto Plata y Santiago de los Caballeros. El diario describió a Jimenes como un influyente comerciante e hijo de un antiguo mandatario que durante largo tiempo había evadido las violentas represalias de Heureaux contra sus rivales políticos.

Two of the prisoners are Pablo Villanueva, son of General Villanueva, and a laborer named Calderon. They will be executed to-day with the other prison[illegible]. records.headline: An editorial on the Spanish-American republics: they are republics
records.summary_en: An editorial on the Spanish-American republics: they are republics only in name, in the throes of revolutions, liberty is nominal, and the presidents are more like military dictators than anything else, the inhabitants speaking French in the republic of Hayti and Spanish in the republic of Santo Domingo. An attempt to overturn President Heureaux's government in Santo Domingo has recently been foiled, and its leading instigators have been executed, and this is only one of a long series of similar revolts on the island; and the editorial, rating the native people of Cuba as considerably superior in intelligence and ability to the Haytians and Dominicans, doubts whether a stable government can be secured for the Cubans in a short space of time without the aid and protection of the United States.
records.summary_es: Un editorial sobre las repúblicas hispanoamericanas: son repúblicas solo en el nombre, en medio de revoluciones, la libertad es nominal y los presidentes son más parecidos a dictadores militares que a otra cosa, hablando los habitantes francés en la república de Haití y español en la república de Santo Domingo. Un intento de derrocar el gobierno del presidente Heureaux en Santo Domingo ha sido frustrado recientemente, y sus principales instigadores han sido ejecutados, y esto es solo una de una larga serie de revueltas similares en la isla; y el editorial, que estima a los nativos de Cuba como considerablemente superiores en inteligencia y habilidad a los haitianos y los dominicanos, duda que pueda asegurarse un gobierno estable para los cubanos en poco tiempo sin la ayuda y protección de los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: The Tribune prints the assassination rumor from Cape Haytien
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints the assassination rumor from Cape Haytien: it is rumored there that President Heureaux of San Domingo has been assassinated, and the Associated Press correspondent at Monte Cristi, San Domingo, gives further confirmation of the failure of the attempted revolution there. The son of Señor Jiminez, the wealthy merchant who took part in the revolution in San Domingo, at 11 o'clock this morning was still without news from the revolutionists as to the result of the attempt to overthrow President Heureaux, but he is disposed to believe the worst; he ascribes the supposed defeat of the revolutionists to the lack of opportunity to land from the Fanita at Monte Cristi, to the failure to seize Señor Galito, the Governor of the province, as had been planned, and to the death at the first fire of the two foremost military leaders.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica el rumor de asesinato desde Cabo Haitiano: se rumora allí que el presidente Heureaux de Santo Domingo ha sido asesinado, y el corresponsal de la Associated Press en Monte Cristi, Santo Domingo, da confirmación adicional del fracaso del intento de revolución allí. El hijo del señor Jiminez, el rico comerciante que tomó parte en la revolución en Santo Domingo, a las 11 de esta mañana aún estaba sin noticias de los revolucionarios en cuanto al resultado del intento de derrocar al presidente Heureaux, pero está dispuesto a creer lo peor; atribuye la supuesta derrota de los revolucionarios a la falta de oportunidad para desembarcar de la Fanita en Monte Cristi, al fracaso en capturar al señor Galito, el gobernador de la provincia, como se había planeado, y a la muerte al primer fuego de los dos principales jefes militares.

records.headline: The Tribune prints the captain's account of the Monte Cristi landing
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints the captain's account of the Monte Cristi landing: General Jiminez again went ashore, returning to the ship with ten men, who, he told the captain, were laborers engaged by him to unload the cargo as soon as the vessel reached Cuba, and he added that his advices were still to the effect that it was unsafe to land an expedition in Cuba just yet, and that he desired to touch at Monte Cristi, San Domingo, where important news was awaiting him. Monte Cristi was reached on Thursday, June 2; on casting anchor the captain was surprised to see General Jiminez come on deck in uniform and fully armed, followed by General Morrillo and the other two officers, similarly equipped; they ordered thirty-seven rifles and two cases of ammunition to be put aboard the long boat that was to row them ashore, and then commanded the ten alleged laborers to take their seats in the boat, 'Chris' Roberts remaining on board the Fanita. The captain understood that something was wrong, but he was reassured by Roberts and General Jiminez, and shortly after 6 o'clock in the morning the boat was rowed ashore by three sailors and the second mate of the Fanita; no sooner had they reached the wharf, where General Jiminez and his party landed, than a volley of musketry was heard and three of the men fell wounded, the first to fall being General Morrillo, pierced through the breast by a bullet; troops were seen advancing in large numbers, and the little band of fourteen was soon cut down to five, and the sailors in the Fanita's boat shoved off from the wharf amid a rain of bullets.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica el relato del capitán sobre el desembarco de la Fanita en Monte Cristi: el general Jiminez bajó de nuevo a tierra, regresando al buque con diez hombres, quienes, según dijo al capitán, eran jornaleros contratados por él para descargar el cargamento tan pronto como el buque llegara a Cuba, y añadió que sus avisos seguían siendo en el sentido de que todavía no era seguro desembarcar una expedición en Cuba, y que deseaba tocar Monte Cristi, Santo Domingo, donde le esperaba noticia importante. Se llegó a Monte Cristi el jueves 2 de junio; al echar el ancla el capitán se sorprendió de ver al general Jiminez salir a cubierta en uniforme y completamente armado, seguido por el general Morrillo y los otros dos oficiales, igualmente equipados; ordenaron poner a bordo de la lancha que los llevaría a tierra treinta y siete rifles y dos cajas de municiones, y luego mandaron a los diez supuestos jornaleros tomar sus asientos en la lancha, quedando 'Chris' Roberts a bordo de la Fanita. El capitán entendió que algo andaba mal, pero fue tranquilizado por Roberts y el general Jiminez, y poco después de las 6 de la mañana la lancha fue remada a tierra por tres marineros y el segundo oficial de la Fanita; apenas llegaron al muelle, donde desembarcaron el general Jiminez y su grupo, se escuchó una descarga de fusilería y tres de los hombres cayeron heridos, siendo el primero en caer el general Morrillo, atravesado el pecho por una bala; se vieron tropas avanzando en gran número, y la pequeña banda de catorce pronto quedó reducida a cinco, y los marineros de la lancha de la Fanita se alejaron del muelle en medio de una lluvia de balas.

records.headline: The Call prints word of the arrest of Señor Jiminez at Inagua
records.summary_en: The Call prints word of the arrest of Señor Jiminez at Inagua and an interview with President Heureaux: Señor Jiminez, the leader of the revolutionary expedition which recently landed in Santo Domingo from Hayti, on his arrival at Inagua from Monte Cristi, Santo Domingo, was arrested by the British authorities for a violation of the navigation laws in flying a Clyde line flag, though the Fanita, the vessel in which the expedition sailed, had been sold by the Clyde line company six months before; Chris Roberts, the pilot of the expedition, made a complaint on the above ground, and the American Consul also prosecuted Señor Jiminez, alleging that the expedition was illegal, inasmuch as the Fanita's papers were ostensibly for service in Cuban waters. From Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic, June 6, the correspondent reports an interview with President Heureaux, who proceeds to Monte Cristi to-night on board a warship; he declares the country quiet, and has confiscated all the property of Jiminez.
records.summary_es: El Call publica la noticia del arresto del señor Jiminez en Inagua y una entrevista con el presidente Heureaux: el señor Jiminez, el líder de la expedición revolucionaria que recientemente desembarcó en Santo Domingo procedente de Haití, a su llegada a Inagua desde Monte Cristi, Santo Domingo, fue arrestado por las autoridades británicas por una violación de las leyes de navegación al enarbolar una bandera de la línea Clyde, aunque la Fanita, el buque en que zarpó la expedición, había sido vendida por la compañía de la línea Clyde seis meses antes; Chris Roberts, el piloto de la expedición, presentó una denuncia por ese motivo, y el cónsul americano también procesó al señor Jiminez, alegando que la expedición era ilegal, ya que los papeles de la Fanita eran ostensiblemente para servicio en aguas cubanas. Desde Puerto Plata, República Dominicana, el 6 de junio, el corresponsal informa de una entrevista con el presidente Heureaux, quien parte hacia Monte Cristi esta noche a bordo de un buque de guerra; declara que el país está tranquilo, y ha confiscado toda la propiedad de Jiminez.

FEW MELONS AT LODI.
Crop Will Be Small Because of the
Spring Drought.
STOCKTON, June 6.— The watermelon
crop will, no doubt, be the lightest the
Lodi section has known in years— possibly
since Lodi became famous for the size and
succulence of its melons. The absence of
late rains worked havoc. The acreage is
small, and the few who are successful
with watermelons this season will have
a small Klondike. Lodi will have to sup
ply the entire melon market this time, for
if reports be true, rival melon centers
have been blighted by the drought.

records.headline: The Press prints a dispatch on the aftermath of the Monte Cristi landing
records.summary_en: The Press prints a dispatch on the aftermath of the Monte Cristi landing: three prisoners were taken in the recent abortive revolutionary attempt headed by Jiminez and Morales, and Commodore Jansen landed to receive the report of the Dominican consul on the illegal shipments of men from this point by the two leaders to participate in the landing at Monte Cristi. The warships left Monte Cristi at eleven o'clock this morning, and a rumor is current that after they left President Heureaux was made a prisoner in a new uprising and was shot, the report having it that Joaquin Taveras, Lieutenant Commander at Monte Cristi under Governor Galito, led the new movement; the story is not believed, although no explicit reply is forthcoming from Monte Cristi to cabled inquiries. It appears that General Jiminez was transferred from the Fanita, on which he escaped from Monte Cristi, to another steamer before landing at Great Inagua, and it is said that he has been released on bail of 200 pounds; the Fanita did not venture within the jurisdiction of the island authorities on her return voyage.
records.summary_es: El Press publica un despacho sobre las consecuencias del desembarco de Monte Cristi: tres prisioneros fueron tomados en el reciente intento revolucionario abortado encabezado por Jiminez y Morales, y el comodoro Jansen desembarcó para recibir el informe del cónsul dominicano sobre los embarques ilegales de hombres desde este punto por los dos líderes para participar en el desembarco en Monte Cristi. Los buques de guerra salieron de Monte Cristi a las once de esta mañana, y corre el rumor de que después de su salida el presidente Heureaux fue hecho prisionero en un nuevo levantamiento y fusilado, sosteniendo el reporte que Joaquín Taveras, teniente comandante en Monte Cristi bajo el gobernador Galito, encabezó el nuevo movimiento; la historia no es creída, aunque no llega de Monte Cristi respuesta explícita alguna a las indagaciones cablegráficas. Parece que el general Jiminez fue transferido de la Fanita, en la que escapó de Monte Cristi, a otro vapor antes de desembarcar en Gran Inagua, y se dice que ha sido liberado bajo fianza de 200 libras; la Fanita no se aventuró dentro de la jurisdicción de las autoridades de la isla en su viaje de regreso.

records.headline: The Journal prints the New York Herald dispatch from Puerto Plata
records.summary_en: The Journal prints the New York Herald dispatch from Puerto Plata: a revolutionary expedition was landed at Monte Cristi from Hayti under Señor Jiminez, who was formerly a merchant in New York; the government had been advised of the movement and troops were in waiting for the party, and all were captured; the leader, Jiminez, was reserved for examination, but a subordinate, General Augustin Morales, was shot without delay, and it is almost certain that the whole party will be shot.

records.headline: The Enterprise prints the Fanita's story, a filibustering voyage
records.summary_en: The Enterprise prints the Fanita's story, a filibustering voyage: so far from being engaged in peaceful traffic, she had been for two weeks on a filibustering expedition, and from Tampa the Fanita was ordered to Mobile, ostensibly to take an expedition to Cuba under the charge of Jiminez and Morrillo, both Dominicans, but strongly sympathetic with the movement for Cuban independence. Monte Cristi, San Domingo, was reached on June 2; on casting anchor the captain was surprised to see Jiminez come on deck in uniform, fully armed, and the others similarly equipped; they ordered 37 rifles and two cases of ammunition to be put aboard the boat that was to row them ashore, and then commanded the ten alleged laborers on board to take their seats in the boat; the captain understood that something was wrong, but the boat was rowed ashore. No sooner had they reached the wharf, where Jiminez and his party landed, than a volley of musketry was heard and three of the party fell wounded, the first to fall being Morrillo, pierced through the breast by a bullet; troops were seen advancing in large numbers, and the little band of 14 was soon cut down to five; the sailors in the Fanita's boat were seized with terror and shoved off from the wharf amid a rain of bullets; Jiminez jumped into the boat just in time and, seizing an oar, joined the crew in pulling for dear life, and the last seen of the landing party was the figures of two men covered with blood struggling desperately against superior odds in the face of blazing muskets; Jiminez reached the Fanita in safety.

Se llegó a Monte Cristi, Santo Domingo, el 2 de junio; al echar el ancla el capitán se sorprendió de ver a Jiminez salir a cubierta en uniforme, completamente armado, y a los demás igualmente equipados; ordenaron poner a bordo de la lancha que los llevaría a tierra 37 rifles y dos cajas de municiones, y luego mandaron a los diez supuestos jornaleros a bordo tomar sus asientos en la lancha; el capitán entendió que algo andaba mal, pero la lancha fue remada a tierra. Apenas llegaron al muelle, donde desembarcaron Jiminez y su grupo, se escuchó una descarga de fusilería y tres del grupo cayeron heridos, siendo el primero en caer Morrillo, atravesado el pecho por una bala; se vieron tropas avanzando en gran número, y la pequeña banda de 14 pronto quedó reducida a cinco; los marineros de la lancha de la Fanita fueron presa del terror y se alejaron del muelle en medio de una lluvia de balas; Jiminez saltó a la lancha justo a tiempo y, empuñando un remo, se unió a la tripulación remando con todas sus fuerzas, y lo último que se vio del grupo desembarcado fueron las figuras de dos hombres cubiertos de sangre luchando desesperadamente contra fuerzas superiores frente a mosquetes en llamas; Jiminez llegó a la Fanita a salvo.

records.headline: The State Journal prints a Cape Haytien dispatch on President Heureaux's pursuit of Jiminez
records.summary_en: The State Journal prints a Cape Haytien dispatch on President Heureaux's pursuit of Jiminez: some mystery was observed regarding the visit of the Dominican gunboat Restoracion to that port last evening, and it transpired that President Heureaux of San Domingo was aboard the vessel, and that from there he goes to Inagua, where Señor Jiminez was last known to be located, the Restoracion having left Cape Haytien before 5 o'clock this morning. Commodore Jansen, who came ashore shortly after the arrival of the Restoracion to receive the report of the Dominican consul on the alleged illegal shipment of men from that point by Señor Jiminez and his fellow leader to take part in the landing of the revolutionists at Monte Cristi, spent the greater part of the night with the consul. The Dominican gunboat Independencia did not enter the port in company with the Restoracion, as cabled last night; she proceeded to Port de Paix in order to investigate the report of Jiminez's presence at that place, just before the revolutionary attempt at Monte Cristi; and it is understood that if President Heureaux finds that Jiminez is still there he will make an effort to induce the authorities to deliver the insurgent to him on the charge of piracy.
records.summary_es: El State Journal publica un despacho de Cabo Haitiano sobre la persecución de Jiminez por el presidente Heureaux: se observó cierto misterio en torno a la visita del cañonero dominicano Restoracion a ese puerto anoche, y se supo que el presidente Heureaux de Santo Domingo iba a bordo del buque, y que desde allí va a Inagua, donde se supo por última vez que estaba el señor Jiminez, habiendo la Restoracion salido de Cabo Haitiano antes de las 5 de esta mañana. El comodoro Jansen, que bajó a tierra poco después de la llegada de la Restoracion para recibir el informe del cónsul dominicano sobre el alegado embarque ilegal de hombres desde ese punto por el señor Jiminez y su compañero líder para tomar parte en el desembarco de los revolucionarios en Monte Cristi, pasó la mayor parte de la noche con el cónsul. El cañonero dominicano Independencia no entró al puerto en compañía de la Restoracion, como se cablegrafió anoche; procedió a Port de Paix para investigar el reporte de la presencia de Jiminez en ese lugar, justo antes del intento revolucionario en Monte Cristi; y se entiende que si el presidente Heureaux encuentra que Jiminez todavía está allí hará un esfuerzo para inducir a las autoridades a entregarle al insurgente bajo el cargo de piratería.

records.summary_en: The Sun prints a letter on the Dominica and Santo Domingo names: a correspondent protests against the name Dominica given to the island he has known as Hayti, of which San Domingo is one of the political divisions; the island of Dominica, as he has known it, is one of the Windward group near Martinique, owned by Great Britain, and the people of that island are known as Dominicans, while San Domingo, which should properly be called Santo Domingo — the original Española of Columbus, for centuries after its discovery known by the Latinized form of Hispaniola — is quite a different country from Dominica, and the Santo Domingoans are an entirely different people from the Dominicans. Dominica is the ecclesiastical form of Domingo, the Spanish for Sunday, and was applied to the island which bears the name because Columbus discovered it on that day; the island was later settled by the French and ultimately passed into the hands of the English, and the writer thinks it important to call attention to these facts in these days when Americans are obtaining such rapid lessons in West India geography. He has also seen in the press many allusions to the meaning of the word morro, which some have confused with 'Moro,' the Spanish for 'Moor'; the Spaniards employed the word morro to signify any round-shaped projection, whether horizontal like a promontory or perpendicular like a circular butte or mountain, or for a round fortification like Castle Williams.

Dominica es la forma eclesiástica de Domingo, el nombre español del domingo, y fue aplicada a la isla que lleva el nombre porque Colón la descubrió en ese día; la isla fue después colonizada por los franceses y en última instancia pasó a manos de los ingleses, y el escritor cree importante llamar la atención sobre estos hechos en estos días en que los americanos están obteniendo tan rápidas lecciones de geografía de las Indias Occidentales. También ha visto en la prensa muchas alusiones al significado de la palabra morro, que algunos han confundido con 'Moro', la palabra española para moro; los españoles empleaban la palabra morro para significar cualquier proyección de forma redonda, ya fuera horizontal como un promontorio o perpendicular como una loma circular o montaña, o para una fortificación redonda como Castle Williams.

records.headline: The Republican prints the June 10 dispatch from Cape Haytien
records.summary_en: The Republican prints the June 10 dispatch from Cape Haytien: President Ulysses Heureaux, of the Dominican Republic, believes he has discovered proof that the steamer Fanita, formerly of the Clyde line, which was used by Señor Jiminez and Morales in their unsuccessful attempt to overthrow the Dominican government, left the United States with the countenance of the American government, under a mere pretense of taking munitions of war to Cuba. President Heureaux arrived there yesterday on the Dominican gunboat Restauracion, from Great Inagua; while there he personally made a charge of piracy against Señor Jiminez, who had previously been released on bail under a charge of having violated the navigation laws, and a Dominican agent was left at Matthew Town to look after the case until an advocate can be sent there from San Domingo to push the prosecution. General Heureaux talked with the greatest apparent freedom about the recent revolutionary attempt, ridiculing Jiminez and the preparations the latter had made; he told how the revolution was nipped in the bud, and how he had executed nearly all the prisoners, reserving only those who, he thought, might be useful in obtaining further information about the conspiracy; and he said distinctly that he could make no charge against the United States government, believing that the government had been misled, and that a feeble country could not enforce a demand against so strong a neighbor.

El presidente Heureaux llegó allí ayer en el cañonero dominicano Restauracion, procedente de Gran Inagua; mientras estuvo allí presentó personalmente un cargo de piratería contra el señor Jiminez, quien había sido anteriormente liberado bajo fianza bajo un cargo de haber violado las leyes de navegación, y un agente dominicano quedó en Matthew Town para atender el caso hasta que pueda enviarse allí un abogado desde Santo Domingo para impulsar la acusación. records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported that President Heureaux traveled to Great Inagua to lodge piracy charges against General Juan Isidro Jimenes following the failed Monte Cristi invasion. In an interview aboard his gunboat, Heureaux dismissed Jimenes as a skilled merchant but an inept politician whose revolutionary schemes were childish and thoroughly penetrated by government informants. Heureaux also exhibited seized documents and papers taken from insurgent casualties to demonstrate that the conspiracy was completely neutralized.

records.headline: The Tribune prints President Heureaux's words in interview
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints President Heureaux's words in interview: he spoke of the interpretation the State Department at Washington would give of the 'moral support' it had promised in the event of European Powers demanding the same privileges under the most-favored-nation clause, and of San Domingo's refusing compliance. 'I have always been,' he said, 'and am still desirous of favoring foreign investment in my country to the greatest extent possible. We are at a pass where we must continue to progress or we will recede as rapidly as Hayti is doing.' President Heureaux denied the reported wholesale shooting of the employes of Jimenez, asserting that the only two shot were those found with arms in their hands; Chuchu Mercado, a prisoner on the gunboat, was spared as an informer, and the younger Villanueva was spared because of the friendship of the Governor for his father.

'Siempre he sido', dijo, 'y sigo siendo partidario de favorecer la inversión extranjera en mi país en la mayor medida posible. Estamos en un punto en que debemos continuar progresando o retrocederemos tan rápidamente como lo está haciendo Haití'. El presidente Heureaux negó el reportado fusilamiento en masa de los empleados de Jimenez, afirmando que los únicos dos fusilados fueron los encontrados con armas en las manos; Chuchu Mercado, prisionero en el cañonero, fue perdonado como informante, y el joven Villanueva fue perdonado por la amistad del gobernador con su padre.

records.headline: The Republican sums up the past week's reports of the San Domingo revolution
records.summary_en: The Republican sums up the past week's reports of the San Domingo revolution: President Heureaux has been reported assassinated, and the report denied; however, the revolutionary attempt appears to have been unsuccessful, and its originators are now fugitives. The two principal leaders of the revolutionary attempt in the Dominican republic, J. I. Jiminez and General Agustin Morales, are well known in this country, particularly in New York city and Washington, says the New York Tribune; both of them have been conspicuous in their efforts in favor of the Cuban cause, which they rightly considered as intimately connected with that of the liberal party in their native country, San Domingo; while General Heureaux, president of that republic, ever evidenced strong pro-Spanish proclivities, for which he was rewarded with a decoration by the Madrid government.

records.headline: The Record-Union prints the Cape Haytien dispatch of June 13
records.summary_en: The Record-Union prints the Cape Haytien dispatch of June 13: officials of the Dominican Government have seized at Monte Cristi, San Domingo, a business house formerly belonging to Señor Jiminez, leader of the recent abortive revolutionary attempt, but now the property of a German company, and the German Consul General has asked Germany to send a warship to protect the company's interests. records.headline: The Times prints a feature on Santiago de Cuba and its antiquity
records.summary_en: The Times prints a feature on Santiago de Cuba and its antiquity: as General Shafter's army approaches Santiago, citizens of the United States will take new interest in that ancient city, the oldest standing city in the new world, except Santo Domingo, which was established by Columbus four hundred years ago, Santiago itself having been founded only eighteen years after Santo Domingo. Santiago was the former capital and is the third city of commercial importance on the island of Cuba; it is the residential town of the archbishop and is the seat of several yearly religious festivals which are celebrated with pomp and ceremony; it is the terminus of two railroad lines, one of which is the outlet of Lomas de Cobre, the celebrated copper mines, situated several miles inland, and the second passes through the rich sugar country, affording transportation for that staple article of exportation; the exports from Santiago are said to reach the sum of $8,000,000 annually, tobacco, honey, rum, cocoa and mahogany being also exported in great quantities, and the city is inclosed on three sides by hills rising rapidly from the bay to mountains of great height and beauty.

records.headline: The Olivia, a small sloop, is passing along the northern coast
records.summary_en: The *Waterbury Evening Democrat* reported that Dominican dissidents were organizing a renewed attempt to overthrow President Heureaux using the sloop *Olivia* to recruit men along Haiti's northern coast for attacks on Monte Cristi or Puerto Plata. records.headline: The Tribune prints part of its correspondent's account of President Heureaux
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints part of its correspondent's account of President Heureaux at Cape Haytien: Heureaux entertained a good deal of suspicion of the Haytian authorities, which may not be entirely allayed, and the correspondent judges his ambition not unequal to an attempt to consolidate the whole island under his sway, if ever a fair excuse and a fairer opportunity offered, rating Hayti, though a little stronger in the armament of her gunboats and in the paper strength of her army, greatly inferior to Santo Domingo in the warlike qualities of her people, as also in their capacity for culture and industrial and commercial advancement. One of the notable traits of Heureaux's conversation while in the port of Cape Haytien the second time, last Thursday, the 9th, was his contempt, not the least bit concealed, for the Haytians; nevertheless, on this visit he ordered the regulation salute of twenty-one guns to be fired, and it was returned after the usual lazy fashion by the Haytians from the two or three small field-pieces of ancient type which constitute about the whole of the serviceable artillery there. Under the head 'Night Excursions in Disguise,' the account adds that Heureaux is a man of mystery and of mystification, as well as of promptitude and blood, and that after each of his departures from Cape Haytien it was reported he had been ashore in the evening in disguise, and thus, for purposes of his own, had made a tour of the city.

Uno de los rasgos notables de la conversación de Heureaux durante su segunda visita al puerto de Cabo Haitiano, el jueves pasado, día 9, fue su desprecio, nada disimulado, por los haitianos; sin embargo, en esta visita ordenó disparar la salva reglamentaria de veintiún cañonazos, que fue contestada en la forma perezosa acostumbrada por los haitianos desde las dos o tres pequeñas piezas de campaña de tipo antiguo que constituyen casi toda la artillería útil de allí. records.headline: A report on Dominican politics under President Heureaux describes Emmanuel Jimines as a young man of pleasing
records.summary_en: A report on Dominican politics under President Heureaux describes Emmanuel Jimines as a young man of pleasing manners who has much sympathy, but calls his Monte Cristi attempt one of the worst planned and feeblest ever known. It recounts how Heureaux employs a large number of spies, many of them women, yet is his own best spy, telling of him disguised as a laborer learning of a conspiracy, confronting conspirators in their own meeting, and pardoning a hired assassin who revealed who sent him, while thousands of dollars have secretly been offered for his assassination and the common people believe he leads a charmed life.
records.summary_es: Un reportaje sobre la política dominicana bajo el presidente Heureaux describe a Emmanuel Jimines como un joven de modales agradables que despierta mucha simpatía, pero califica su intento de Monte Cristi como uno de los peor planeados y más débiles que se hayan conocido.
