records.headline: The Tribune prints the close of a dispatch on the revolution
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints the close of a dispatch on the revolution in Santo Domingo and a Kingston item of August 3 headed 'Meant to Capture Heureaux': later advices from the Dominican Republic indicate that the revolution is growing in strength; at Santiago de la Cruz five hundred well armed men have risen under the command of General Ramon Pacheco, and General P. Reyes, who is very influential in certain districts, has joined the insurgents with several other generals, each commanding fairly important forces. The Kingston item says that, owing to the efforts of the Government of Santo Domingo to suppress news and information about the recent assassination of President Heureaux and the reported revolution in Santo Domingo, the facts in the case are difficult to obtain; but a dispatch received by a messenger who has passed through Hayti indicates that the assassination of President Heureaux was not on the programme, the purpose of the revolutionists being to capture Moca, with the President, thus decapitating the Dominican Government at the first blow, the insurgents not possessing the means of prosecuting a protracted conflict; the premature departure of President Heureaux threatened to frustrate this scheme, whereupon an enthusiast, who was watching the President's movements, committed the act; a subsequent attack on Moca being repulsed, the insurgents withdrew into the fastnesses between Moca and Porto Plata, hoping to secure sufficient accessions of men and arms to attack Porto Plata and prosecute the movement, in spite of its initial failure.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica el cierre de un despacho sobre la revolución en Santo Domingo y una nota de Kingston del 3 de agosto titulada «Meant to Capture Heureaux»: noticias posteriores procedentes de la República Dominicana indican que la revolución crece en fuerza; en Santiago de la Cruz se han levantado quinientos hombres bien armados bajo el mando del general Ramón Pacheco, y el general P. Reyes, muy influyente en ciertos distritos, se ha unido a los insurrectos con varios otros generales, cada uno al mando de fuerzas bastante importantes. La nota de Kingston dice que, debido a los esfuerzos del Gobierno de Santo Domingo por suprimir las noticias y la información sobre el reciente asesinato del presidente Heureaux y la reportada revolución en Santo Domingo, los hechos del caso son difíciles de obtener; pero un despacho recibido por un mensajero que ha pasado por Haití indica que el asesinato del presidente Heureaux no estaba en el programa, siendo el propósito de los revolucionarios capturar Moca, con el Presidente, decapitando así al Gobierno dominicano al primer golpe, al no poseer los insurrectos los medios para sostener un conflicto prolongado; la partida prematura del presidente Heureaux amenazó con frustrar este plan, ante lo cual un entusiasta, que vigilaba los movimientos del presidente, cometió el acto; rechazado un ataque posterior contra Moca, los insurrectos se retiraron a las asperezas entre Moca y Puerto Plata, con la esperanza de conseguir suficientes refuerzos de hombres y armas para atacar Puerto Plata y proseguir el movimiento, a pesar de su fracaso inicial.

records.headline: The Expositor completes a Puerto Plata dispatch on the critical situation
records.summary_en: The Expositor completes a Puerto Plata dispatch on the critical situation in Santo Domingo: the situation is critical and an outbreak is expected at any time; the friends of the government are under arms and ready for action to protect property and preserve peace; a feeble attempt was made to seize the body of President Heureaux by the assassins Ramon Caceres, Manuel Caceres, Horacio Vasquez and Domingo Pichardo, who are in the country about Moca with their followers; Gov. Pepin has assembled troops in Moca, and the governor of La Vega Real has 1,000 men; the government is taking steps for the protection of business and the finance of the country, and expects to carry out the contemplated cancellation of the state bank notes; in Puerto Plata there is an urgent demand that the government send a sufficient force to Moca to hunt down the assassins of the president.
records.summary_es: El Expositor completa un despacho de Puerto Plata sobre la situación crítica en Santo Domingo: la situación es crítica y se espera un estallido en cualquier momento; los amigos del gobierno están en armas y listos para actuar a fin de proteger la propiedad y preservar la paz; se hizo un débil intento de apoderarse del cuerpo del presidente Heureaux por parte de los asesinos Ramón Cáceres, Manuel Cáceres, Horacio Vásquez y Domingo Pichardo, que se encuentran en los campos alrededor de Moca con sus seguidores; el gobernador Pepín ha reunido tropas en Moca, y el gobernador de La Vega Real tiene 1,000 hombres; el gobierno está tomando medidas para la protección de los negocios y las finanzas del país, y espera llevar a cabo la cancelación contemplada de los billetes del banco estatal; en Puerto Plata hay una demanda urgente de que el gobierno envíe una fuerza suficiente a Moca para perseguir a los asesinos del presidente.

records.headline: The Union prints a Cape Haytien dispatch of July 28 with the details of the murder
records.summary_en: The Union prints a Cape Haytien dispatch of July 28 with the details of the murder: General Ulysses Heureaux, president of the Dominican republic, was killed by an assassin at Moca, Santo Domingo, at half past 4 o'clock yesterday afternoon; the name of the murderer is Ramon Caceros, and he succeeded in escaping. Details of the murder received here are to the effect that the president was assassinated as he was about to leave on horseback for Santiago de las Caballeros; the assassin, Ramon Caceros, surrounded by several accomplices, approached the president as he was talking with some friends and fired twice with a revolver; the first bullet struck the president in the left side and penetrated the heart, causing instant death; the second bullet killed an old man who was standing near the president; the assassin and his accomplices then fled to avoid the shots fired at them by the president's friends; it is not known whether any of them was wounded; the body of the president was taken to the palace of the governor of Moca; President Heureaux's death has caused a panic; it is said that Juan Isidoro Jiminez, who took part in the attempted insurrection of last year, is a candidate for the presidency; Jiminez landed from the Fanita, but was driven off with the loss of most of his band of ten men; the dispatch is headed 'Revenge on a President.'

records.headline: A report on President Heureaux's assassination at Moca says his death caused a panic, that Juan Isidoro Jiminez, who
records.summary_en: A report on President Heureaux's assassination at Moca says his death caused a panic, that Juan Isidoro Jiminez, who took part in the attempted insurrection of the previous year, is a candidate for the presidency, and that General Maximo Gomez is also reported to aspire to it. It notes that the father of Caceres, the assassin, was put to death by order of Heureaux in 1884, that Vice President Wenceslao Figuereo at once assumed the direction of affairs, and that President McKinley sent Figuereo a cable of condolences in the name of the American people.
records.summary_es: Un informe sobre el asesinato del presidente Heureaux en Moca dice que su muerte causó pánico, que Juan Isidoro Jiminez, que tomó parte en el intento de insurrección del año anterior, es candidato a la presidencia, y que también se informa que el general Máximo Gómez aspira a ella. Señala que el padre de Cáceres, el asesino, fue ejecutado por orden de Heureaux en 1884, que el vicepresidente Wenceslao Figuereo asumió de inmediato la dirección de los asuntos, y que el presidente McKinley envió a Figuereo un cable de condolencias en nombre del pueblo americano.
records.passage: Isidoro Jiminez, who took part in the attempted insurrection of last year, is a candidate for the presidency, Jiminez landed from the Fanita, but was driven off with the loss of most of his band of ten men. It is reported that General Maximo Gomez, formerly president of the Cuban insurrectionists, who is a native of Santo Domingo, also aspires to the presidency. The father of Caceros, the assassin, was put to death by order of President Heureaux in 1884. Vice President Wenceslao Figuereo, immediately upon the announcement of the president's death, assumed the direction of affairs. It has long been expected that Heureaux would be assassinated. He used to boast that he was a more absolute ruler than any czar or emperor in the world. His ability and shrewdness made a great impression on Europeans and Americans who met him. His daring was remarkable and his shrewdness was said to be equal to that of the most experienced European diplomats. The president was frequently reported assassinated. He had numerous enemies. As a political mystifier he had great talent and boldness. He himself caused reports to be circulated that he had been seized by revolutionists, imprisoned and subsequently shot. This was done to draw out his enemies. When they appeared, Heureaux would ride up, followed by his army, and capture them. They were usually put to death at once. records.headline: The Union prints the McKinley condolence telegram in a Washington item of July 28
records.summary_en: The Union prints the McKinley condolence telegram in a Washington item of July 28: official confirmation of President Heureaux's death was communicated to the President at Lake Champlain by the State Department, and the following cable message was sent by his direction, under the head 'M'Kinley's Telegram': 'Lake Champlain, via Washington, July 27. — His Excellency Wenceslao de Figuereo, president of the Dominican Republic, Santo Domingo: In the name of the American people and in my own I offer to Your Excellency and the Dominican nation most sincere condolences by reason of the death of President Heureaux. — William McKinley.'

records.headline: The Call prints the closing words of a dispatch on the revolution
records.summary_en: The Call prints the closing words of a dispatch on the revolution in Santo Domingo — 'has joined the insurgents with several other generals, each commanding fairly important forces' — a Havana interview of August 3 with Juan Isidro Jiminez, and a Washington item of August 3: in conversation with a Herald correspondent to-day, Juan Isidro Jiminez, candidate for the dictatorship of San Domingo, said: 'For the last few years I have been working against President Heureaux. I have worked among foreign powers, I have landed filibustering expeditions, and at last my plans are successful. They were my agents who killed President Heureaux, and I am going to the United States in a day or so to organize another party who will go with me to San Domingo, and if necessary, take forcible possession of the Government. The people do not want Figuereo; they want me and they shall have me.' General Jiminez will be accompanied to the United States by Captain Piedra of the police force, and several prominent Cuban army men who sympathize with him; the correspondent saw cables to-day that General Jiminez sent to his agents in San Domingo, saying that unless the present Government retired before the 15th of this month he would lead a general uprising and take forcible possession of the island; his movement is attracting attention here because of the number of prominent men concerned in it, and Gomez is said to favor Jiminez. The Washington item says administration officials here are not disposed to take the Havana interview with Jiminez seriously.
records.summary_es: El Call publica las palabras finales de un despacho sobre la revolución en Santo Domingo —«se ha unido a los insurrectos con varios otros generales, cada uno al mando de fuerzas bastante importantes»—, una entrevista de La Habana del 3 de agosto con Juan Isidro Jiménez y una nota de Washington del 3 de agosto: en conversación hoy con un corresponsal del Herald, Juan Isidro Jiménez, candidato a la dictadura de San Domingo, dijo: «Durante los últimos años he estado trabajando contra el presidente Heureaux. He trabajado entre las potencias extranjeras, he desembarcado expediciones filibusteras, y por fin mis planes han tenido éxito. Fueron mis agentes quienes mataron al presidente Heureaux, y voy a los Estados Unidos dentro de un día o dos para organizar otro grupo que irá conmigo a San Domingo, y si es necesario, tomará posesión del Gobierno por la fuerza. El pueblo no quiere a Figuereo; me quiere a mí y me tendrá». El general Jiménez será acompañado a los Estados Unidos por el capitán Piedra, de la policía, y varios prominentes militares cubanos que simpatizan con él; el corresponsal vio hoy cables que el general Jiménez envió a sus agentes en San Domingo, diciendo que a menos que el Gobierno actual se retire antes del 15 de este mes, él encabezará un levantamiento general y tomará posesión de la isla por la fuerza; su movimiento está atrayendo atención aquí por el número de hombres prominentes involucrados en él, y se dice que Gómez favorece a Jiménez. La nota de Washington dice que los funcionarios de la administración aquí no están dispuestos a tomar en serio la entrevista de La Habana con Jiménez.

records.headline: The Transcript prints the statement of Señor Adriano Grullon
records.summary_en: The Transcript prints the statement of Señor Adriano Grullon, of the firm of Huttlinger Vivié, New York, headed 'Not an Act of Revenge': Señor Grullon, the representative in the United States of the Santo Domingo revolutionists and formerly the business partner of Señor Jiminez, the leader of the insurrection, has made public the following statement of the reasons for the recent assassination of President Heureaux: 'The assassination of President Heureaux was not an act of revenge for the murder of Caceres' father, but the signal for the commencement of the uprising against the existing government there. Caceres is a cousin of General Horacio Vasquez and was with him at the time of the shooting. General Vasquez is a member of one of the best families of Moca and was for some years a partner in the house of Cosmo Batile, a firm well known there, and former agents of the Clyde Steamship company. Neither Mr. Caceres nor General Vasquez can be considered common assassins, as their motives were patriotic. They attacked the president in broad daylight and in an open space and not from an ambush of any kind nor even in the dark, although their little party was outnumbered 2 to 1 by the president and his bodyguard. For 14 years Heureaux has held power by a system of tyrannism. Persons were sent to prison without the slightest pretense of law and more than 300 were clandestinely shot.'
records.summary_es: El Transcript publica la declaración del señor Adriano Grullón, de la firma Huttlinger Vivié, de Nueva York, titulada «Not an Act of Revenge»: el señor Grullón, representante en los Estados Unidos de los revolucionarios de Santo Domingo y antiguo socio comercial del señor Jiménez, líder de la insurrección, ha hecho pública la siguiente declaración de las razones del reciente asesinato del presidente Heureaux: «El asesinato del presidente Heureaux no fue un acto de venganza por el asesinato del padre de Cáceres, sino la señal para el comienzo del levantamiento contra el gobierno existente allí. Cáceres es primo del general Horacio Vásquez y estaba con él en el momento del tiroteo. El general Vásquez es miembro de una de las mejores familias de Moca y fue durante algunos años socio de la casa de Cosmo Batile, firma muy conocida allí, y antiguos agentes de la Clyde Steamship Company. Ni el señor Cáceres ni el general Vásquez pueden ser considerados asesinos comunes, pues sus motivos fueron patrióticos. Atacaron al presidente a plena luz del día y en un espacio abierto, y no desde emboscada alguna ni siquiera en la oscuridad, aunque su pequeño grupo era superado 2 a 1 por el presidente y su guardia. records.summary_en: The Transcript prints a Puerto Plata dispatch of August 2: the assassins of President Heureaux and their friends are in the mountainous district twenty miles from Moca; Señor de Cordero, former minister of the interior under President Heureaux, has taken the field against them with a large force of men; the acting president, in view of the anxiety of the commercial classes with regard to the paper currency, has suspended the issue and asks that the business men be patient; it is suspected that Jiminez is in the neighborhood of Quebras; news from Moca and Santiago indicate a calmer feeling; and the United States gunboat Machias has arrived at Santo Domingo, the capital. records.headline: The Herald completes a Kingston dispatch on the plot against President Heureaux
records.summary_en: The Herald completes a Kingston dispatch on the plot against President Heureaux and prints the Gleaner's comment on American intervention: the assassination of President Heureaux was not on the programme, the purpose of the revolutionists being to capture Moca with the president, thus decapitating the Dominican government at the first blow, the insurgents not possessing the means of prosecuting a protracted conflict; the premature departure of President Heureaux threatened to frustrate this scheme, whereupon an enthusiast who was watching the president's movements committed the act; a subsequent attack on Moca being repulsed, the insurgents withdrew into the fastnesses between Moca and Porto Plata, hoping to secure sufficient accessions of arms and ammunition to attack Porto Plata and prosecute the movement in spite of its initial failure. Commenting on a London cablegram relative to possible American intervention in Santo Domingo, the Gleaner to-day says it anticipates the finding of an excuse 'to tie the string of Antillian gems on the new colonial diadem,' and invokes the powers to 'curb America's ambition.'

records.headline: The Times prints the closing part of the Havana interview with Juan Isidro Jiminez
records.summary_en: The Times prints the closing part of the Havana interview with Juan Isidro Jiminez: the general claims the assassination as his agents' work: '...working against President Heureaux. I have worked among foreign powers; I have landed filibustering expeditions, and at last my plans are successful. They were my agents who killed President Heureaux, and I am going to the United States in a day or so to organize another party who will go with me to San Domingo, and if necessary, take forcible possession of the government. The people do not want Figuereo; they want me, and they shall have me.' General Jiminez will be accompanied to the United States by Captain Piedra, of the police force, and several prominent Cuban army men who sympathize with him; the correspondent saw cables to-day that General Jiminez sent to his agents in San Domingo, saying that unless the present government retired before the 15th of this month he would lead a general uprising and take forcible possession of the island; his movement is attracting attention here because of the number of prominent men concerned in it, and Gomez is said to favor Jiminez.

records.headline: The Leader prints a sketch of the late president, Gen. Heureaux
records.summary_en: The Leader prints a sketch of the late president, Gen. Heureaux, with the story of his life: immediately upon the announcement of the president's death, Vice-President Gen. Wenceslao Figuereo assumed control of the government; several attempts have been made before to take the life of President Heureaux, but they were frustrated — on one occasion, while passing through the arched entrance to the palace between lines of guards, his quick eye caught one of the soldiers, who appeared to lower his rifle in his direction; quickly pulling a revolver he shot the man dead in his tracks, and passed on to his private office, where he gave orders to remove a dead man lying at the main entrance. Gen. Heureaux was born in Porto Plata in 1846 and served in the war against Spain from 1868 to 1874; later he was put at the head of the advanced Dominicans, who sought to improve their country by inducing foreign capital to locate on the island; as he advanced, all the wealthy inhabitants joined his forces, and when he arrived at the gates of the historic city of Santo Domingo he was chosen president of the republic and served his term of four years; at the expiration of every four years an electoral college assembles in the city to vote for a president for the following term, but owing to Gen. Heureaux's popularity and ability he has always been unanimously re-elected, and was serving his fifth term.
records.summary_es: El Leader publica una semblanza del difunto presidente, el general Heureaux, con la historia de su vida: inmediatamente después del anuncio de la muerte del presidente, el vicepresidente, el general Wenceslao Figuereo, asumió el control del gobierno; antes se habían hecho varios intentos de quitar la vida al presidente Heureaux, pero fueron frustrados: en una ocasión, al pasar por la entrada abovedada del palacio entre filas de guardias, su ojo rápido percibió a uno de los soldados, que pareció bajar su fusil en su dirección; sacando rápidamente un revólver, lo mató en el acto y siguió hasta su despacho privado, donde dio órdenes de retirar a un hombre muerto que yacía en la entrada principal. El general Heureaux nació en Puerto Plata en 1846 y sirvió en la guerra contra España de 1868 a 1874; después fue puesto al frente de los dominicanos avanzados, que buscaban mejorar su país atrayendo capital extranjero a la isla; a medida que avanzaba, todos los habitantes acaudalados se unieron a sus fuerzas, y cuando llegó a las puertas de la histórica ciudad de Santo Domingo fue elegido presidente de la república y sirvió su período de cuatro años; al expirar cada cuatro años, un colegio electoral se reúne en la ciudad para votar por un presidente para el período siguiente, pero debido a la popularidad y la capacidad del general Heureaux siempre ha sido reelegido por unanimidad, y servía su quinto período.

records.headline: The Gazette prints an editorial on Santo Domingo: the country
records.summary_en: The Gazette prints an editorial on Santo Domingo: the country, it says, is subject to insurrections, and a president there will not be scrupulous about the use of force, since his subjects must have a fear of him to deter them from plots, and if he would retain his power he must often use what in an established republic like ours would be called rigor. Present reports affirm that the assassin of President Heureaux was the son of an offender whom he had put to death over a dozen years ago; the young man's name was Caceros, and he came to our country shortly after his father's death, attended one of our higher literary institutions, but seems to have brooded over his father's death and fostered revenge; he shot his victim as he was preparing to mount his horse, and the whole land is convulsed. The population is about six hundred thousand; Vice President Figuereo assumes control of public affairs, but how long he may have peaceable supremacy is uncertain; and it is asserted that Gen. Gomez is designing to leave Cuba to see if he can obtain authority in San Domingo. The Dominican republic and Hayti, the editorial says, occupy different parts of the island formerly called by the latter name: Hayti has control of the western part, while San Domingo claims the eastern section; the republic contains not far from twenty thousand square miles of territory, of great fertility, its area about equal to the combined area of New Hampshire and Vermont; it used to produce a great deal of coffee, though of an inferior quality, and it furnishes mahogany.
records.summary_es: La Gazette publica un editorial sobre Santo Domingo: el país, dice, está sujeto a insurrecciones, y un presidente allí no será escrupuloso en el uso de la fuerza, ya que sus súbditos deben temerle para disuadirlos de conspiraciones, y si quiere conservar su poder a menudo debe usar lo que en una república establecida como la nuestra se llamaría rigor. Los informes actuales afirman que el asesino del presidente Heureaux era hijo de un delincuente a quien él había hecho ejecutar hacía más de una docena de años; el joven se llamaba Caceros y vino a nuestro país poco después de la muerte de su padre, asistió a una de nuestras instituciones literarias superiores, pero parece haber rumiado la muerte de su padre y fomentado la venganza; disparó contra su víctima cuando se preparaba a montar su caballo, y todo el país está convulsionado. La población es de unos seiscientos mil habitantes; el vicepresidente Figuereo asume el control de los asuntos públicos, pero es incierto cuánto tiempo podrá mantener la supremacía en paz; y se afirma que el general Gómez se propone salir de Cuba para ver si puede obtener autoridad en San Domingo. La república dominicana y Haití, dice el editorial, ocupan partes diferentes de la isla llamada antiguamente por este último nombre: Haití controla la parte occidental, mientras que San Domingo reclama la sección oriental; la república contiene cerca de veinte mil millas cuadradas de territorio, de gran fertilidad, con una superficie aproximadamente igual a la superficie combinada de New Hampshire y Vermont; antes producía mucho café, aunque de calidad inferior, y suministra caoba.

records.headline: The Capital completes the Washington item on the warship orders
records.summary_en: The Capital completes the Washington item on the warship orders for Santo Domingo and prints an item on the creditors of San Domingo: orders were issued also to the Machias, at St. Thomas, to proceed to Santo Domingo city by way of San Juan; these orders were made at the instance of the State Department, and as a precautionary measure owing to the disturbed conditions following the assassination of President Heureaux of San Domingo. The trouble between the Government of San Domingo and its creditors has reached an acute stage; the creditors, who are almost entirely Americans, have begun to clamor for an American protectorate, which would necessarily be the first step in the direction of annexation; political plots are already shaping themselves; the adherents of Gen. Jiminez seek to put him at the head of affairs, while the friends of Gen. Maximo Gomez are talking of making him the ruler of the republic; and it is said by officers who have recently been in San Domingo that interference by this Government would be welcomed by a large proportion of the inhabitants of the island.
records.summary_es: El Capital completa la nota de Washington sobre las órdenes a los buques de guerra para Santo Domingo y publica una nota sobre los acreedores de San Domingo: también se dieron órdenes al Machias, en Saint Thomas, de dirigirse a la ciudad de Santo Domingo pasando por San Juan; estas órdenes se dieron a instancias del Departamento de Estado, y como medida de precaución debido a las condiciones perturbadas tras el asesinato del presidente Heureaux de San Domingo. El problema entre el gobierno de San Domingo y sus acreedores ha llegado a una etapa aguda; los acreedores, que son casi en su totalidad americanos, han comenzado a clamar por un protectorado americano, que necesariamente sería el primer paso en dirección a la anexión; ya se están formando complots políticos; los partidarios del general Jiminez buscan ponerlo al frente de los asuntos, mientras que los amigos del general Máximo Gómez hablan de hacerlo gobernante de la república; y oficiales que han estado recientemente en San Domingo dicen que una intervención de este gobierno sería bien recibida por una gran proporción de los habitantes de la isla.

records.headline: The Sentinel prints an editorial on the Monroe Doctrine and Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Sentinel prints an editorial on the Monroe Doctrine and Santo Domingo: the doctrine, it is alleged, makes it necessary for us to warn Europe to keep its hands off, since we are the 'paramount power' in this part of the world, and if the revolutionists of the Dominican Republic do not behave themselves the United States alone has the right to restrain them; the doctrine sustained a very severe shock, it argues, when the United States became a 'world power' and established itself in the 'Far East,' but the imperialists maintain that it is our mission to take whatever is desirable in any part of the world, while not recognizing the right of Europe to adopt the same principle on this side of the world. With a reasonable pretext for intervention in Santo Domingo, it is not unlikely that the annexation scheme of President Grant's administration will be revived; we should not gain anything by annexation, the editorial says, and all depends upon the syndicate which has been financing the island: if these gentlemen can exploit Santo Domingo to advantage as an American possession, they may get their imperialist friends in and out of Congress to boom an annexation project.
records.summary_es: El Sentinel publica un editorial sobre la Doctrina Monroe y Santo Domingo: la doctrina, se alega, hace necesario que advirtamos a Europa que mantenga las manos fuera, ya que somos la 'potencia suprema' en esta parte del mundo, y si los revolucionarios de la República Dominicana no se comportan, solo los Estados Unidos tienen el derecho de contenerlos; la doctrina sufrió un golpe muy severo, argumenta, cuando los Estados Unidos se convirtieron en una 'potencia mundial' y se establecieron en el 'Lejano Oriente', pero los imperialistas sostienen que es nuestra misión tomar lo que sea deseable en cualquier parte del mundo, sin reconocer el derecho de Europa a adoptar el mismo principio en este lado del mundo. Con un pretexto razonable para intervenir en Santo Domingo, no es improbable que se reviva el plan de anexión de la administración del presidente Grant; no ganaríamos nada con la anexión, dice el editorial, y todo depende del sindicato que ha estado financiando la isla: si estos caballeros pueden explotar Santo Domingo con ventaja como posesión americana, quizá consigan que sus amigos imperialistas dentro y fuera del Congreso promuevan un proyecto de anexión.

records.headline: The Dispatch prints part of an interview with General Jiminez
records.summary_en: The Dispatch prints part of an interview with General Jiminez and an item headed 'Funeral of Heureaux': 'I did hear,' he continued, 'that Heureaux was sending men to Cuba to kill me, but I knew nothing whatever regarding the plot to kill him. I had no connection with Ramon Caceres, who did the shooting. I do not believe that the United States will interfere with my government in San Domingo, which will be a government peaceful and helpful to all, for the United States did not interfere with the government of Heureaux, who robbed and murdered for fourteen years.' General Jiminez admits that he has often been to the United States incognito, but says he has not had interviews with official persons; he considers that there is no need of promoting expeditions to land in San Domingo, as there are already a thousand men waiting for him, a force which he deems quite sufficient for his purpose; referring to the future relations of San Domingo with the United States, he expressed a desire to be on friendly terms with Washington, and said he believed he could count upon American sympathy; Gomez he referred to as 'esteemed by all classes of Dominicans, but not sought for as President'; and the people of San Domingo, he declares, are impetuous, and are urging him to come to them at once, but for a time he prefers delay, as 'each day is worth a battle won.' The funeral item, from San Domingo, August 4, says solemn funeral services in memory of the late President Heureaux were held in the Cathedral to-day, and the diplomatic and consular bodies were present.
records.summary_es: El Dispatch publica parte de una entrevista con el general Jiminez y una nota titulada 'Funeral of Heureaux': 'Sí oí', continuó, 'que Heureaux enviaba hombres a Cuba para matarme, pero no supe absolutamente nada del complot para matarlo a él. No tuve ninguna relación con Ramón Cáceres, que hizo los disparos. No creo que los Estados Unidos vayan a interferir con mi gobierno en San Domingo, que será un gobierno pacífico y útil para todos, porque los Estados Unidos no interfirieron con el gobierno de Heureaux, que robó y asesinó durante catorce años'. La nota fúnebre, desde San Domingo, el 4 de agosto, dice que hoy se celebraron en la Catedral solemnes servicios fúnebres en memoria del difunto presidente Heureaux, y que estuvieron presentes los cuerpos diplomático y consular.

records.summary_en: The Sentinel prints an item on Ramon Caceros, the assassin of President Heureaux: General Ulises Heureaux, president of the Dominican Republic, was assassinated at Moca, Santo Domingo, on July 26 by Ramon Caceros, a man 25 years of age, connected with one of the best and richest families of that republic; he completed his education at the Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute at Troy, where he graduated about four years ago; Caceros often said that as soon as the opportunity offered he would go to Santo Domingo and inaugurate a revolution; he started on his mission a few weeks ago; and those who know Caceros well are confident that he laid his plans well and had taken precautions to escape.

records.headline: The Journal and Courier prints the closing part of the Jiminez interview
records.summary_en: The Journal and Courier prints the closing part of the Jiminez interview: he replied that he had not made the statement attributed to him — that he would proceed to the United States to organize an expedition against the existing government of San Domingo; he said that it was quite unnecessary for him to proclaim himself hostile to the present government, as it could not possibly last beyond the 15th of this month. 'I did hear,' he continued, 'that Heureaux was sending men to Cuba to kill me, but I knew nothing whatever regarding the plot to kill him. I had no connection and have no connection with Ramon Caceres, who did the shooting. I do not believe that the United States will interfere with my government in San Domingo, which will be a government peaceful and helpful to all, for the United States did not see fit to interfere with the government of Heureaux.' General Jiminez admits that he has often been to the United States incognito, but says he has not had interviews with official persons; he considers that there is no need of promoting expeditions to land in San Domingo, as already there are a thousand men waiting for him, a force which he deems quite sufficient for his purposes; referring to the future relations of San Domingo with the United States, he expressed a desire to be on friendly terms with Washington and said he believed he could count upon American sympathy; Gomez, he referred to as 'esteemed by all classes of Dominicans, but not sought for as president'; and the people of San Domingo, he declared, are impetuous, and are urging him to come to them at once.
records.summary_es: El Journal and Courier publica la parte final de la entrevista con Jiminez: respondió que no había hecho la declaración que se le atribuía —que se dirigiría a los Estados Unidos para organizar una expedición contra el gobierno existente de San Domingo—; dijo que era bastante innecesario que se declarara hostil al gobierno actual, ya que este no podría durar en modo alguno más allá del 15 de este mes. 'Sí oí', continuó, 'que Heureaux enviaba hombres a Cuba para matarme, pero no supe absolutamente nada del complot para matarlo a él. No tuve ni tengo ninguna relación con Ramón Cáceres, que hizo los disparos. No creo que los Estados Unidos vayan a interferir con mi gobierno en San Domingo, que será un gobierno pacífico y útil para todos, porque los Estados Unidos no consideraron oportuno interferir con el gobierno de Heureaux'. El general Jiminez admite que ha estado a menudo en los Estados Unidos de incógnito, pero dice que no ha tenido entrevistas con personas oficiales; considera que no hay necesidad de promover expediciones para desembarcar en San Domingo, ya que ya hay mil hombres esperándolo, una fuerza que juzga bastante suficiente para sus propósitos; al referirse a las relaciones futuras de San Domingo con los Estados Unidos, expresó su deseo de mantener relaciones amistosas con Washington y dijo que creía poder contar con la simpatía americana; de Gómez se refirió como 'estimado por todas las clases de dominicanos, pero no buscado como presidente'; y el pueblo de San Domingo, declaró, es impetuoso y lo insta a ir junto a ellos de inmediato.

records.headline: The Citizen prints the closing part of a dispatch on the burial of President Heureaux
records.summary_en: The Citizen prints the closing part of a dispatch on the burial of President Heureaux and the situation at Santiago: the remains are to be buried at Santiago de las Caballeros, and orders for the carrying out of this plan have been given to the governor of Santiago; it is currently reported that this course was decided upon in order to avoid the excitement and manifestations which would be the result of the removal of the remains to the city of Santo Domingo; foreseeing the possibility of disturbances, and in order to be prepared for any emergency, General Pepin, governor of Santiago, has taken important precautionary measures and has decided to demand that arms and ammunition be forwarded to him from Santo Domingo; advices from Santiago report that the situation there is becoming more serious; the governor of Santiago confirms the general opinion that the assassination of President Heureaux was a political crime; it is reported that the assassin's party is gathering forces preparatory to an attack on the government troops; it has been learned that Caceros' companions when President Heureaux was killed were Juan Pichardo and Horacio Vasquez, the latter the brother of a deputy in parliament; a financial crisis having arisen in Santo Domingo, and an insurrection being feared owing to the number of malcontents, President Heureaux went to the north and west of the island to prepare for what might happen, and was about to leave Moca for Santiago de las Caballeros when he was killed. Under the head 'Bullet Straight to the Heart,' the dispatch closes: booted and spurred, ready to mount his horse, he sat under the gallery of a house in the Rue Colon, talking with two friends, at 4:30 in the afternoon.
records.summary_es: El Citizen publica la parte final de un despacho sobre el entierro del presidente Heureaux y la situación en Santiago: los restos serán enterrados en Santiago de los Caballeros, y se han dado órdenes para la ejecución de este plan al gobernador de Santiago; se informa corrientemente que este curso se decidió para evitar la excitación y las manifestaciones que resultarían del traslado de los restos a la ciudad de Santo Domingo; previendo la posibilidad de disturbios, y para estar preparado ante cualquier emergencia, el general Pepín, gobernador de Santiago, ha tomado importantes medidas de precaución y ha decidido exigir que se le envíen armas y municiones desde Santo Domingo; noticias de Santiago informan que la situación allí se está volviendo más grave; el gobernador de Santiago confirma la opinión general de que el asesinato del presidente Heureaux fue un crimen político; se informa que el partido del asesino está reuniendo fuerzas en preparación de un ataque contra las tropas del gobierno; se ha sabido que los compañeros de Caceros cuando fue asesinado el presidente Heureaux fueron Juan Pichardo y Horacio Vásquez, este último hermano de un diputado del parlamento; habiendo surgido una crisis financiera en Santo Domingo, y temiéndose una insurrección por el número de descontentos, el presidente Heureaux fue al norte y al oeste de la isla para prepararse ante lo que pudiera suceder, y estaba a punto de salir de Moca hacia Santiago de los Caballeros cuando fue asesinado. Bajo el título 'Bullet Straight to the Heart', el despacho cierra: con botas y espuelas, listo para montar su caballo, estaba sentado bajo la galería de una casa en la calle Colón, hablando con dos amigos, a las 4:30 de la tarde.

records.headline: The Leader prints a Cape Haytien dispatch on the Dominican revolt
records.summary_en: The Leader prints a Cape Haytien dispatch on the Dominican revolt and a Washington item: an armed insurrection has broken out at La Vega, a town 78 miles northwest of Santo Domingo, in favor of Jiminez, who aspires to the presidency in succession to the late President Heureaux; later advices from the Dominican republic indicate that the revolution is growing in strength; at Santiago de la Cruz well-armed men have risen under the command of General Ramon Pacheco, and General P. Reyes, who is very influential in this district, has joined the insurgents, with several other generals, each commanding fairly important forces. The Washington item says the cruiser New Orleans has arrived at Santo Domingo City, where she was sent to protect American interests in case of an outbreak.

Reyes, muy influyente en este distrito, se ha unido a los insurgentes, junto con varios otros generales, cada uno al mando de fuerzas bastante importantes. La nota de Washington dice que el crucero New Orleans ha llegado a la ciudad de Santo Domingo, adonde fue enviado para proteger los intereses americanos en caso de un estallido.

records.headline: The Times prints the opening of its feature 'The Character of Santo Domingo's Assassinated Ruler.'
records.summary_en: The Times prints the opening of its feature 'The Character of Santo Domingo's Assassinated Ruler.' From a New York item of August 4: 'Ulisses Heureaux was a peculiar figure in modern history, in many respects,' said a merchant whom long years of travel and trade in the West Indies have enabled to be entertainingly reminiscent, 'not, perhaps, so very different from the average successful politician of the smaller Spanish-creole republics, but still a decided anomaly in this nineteenth century and within such a short distance of a civilization like ours. For years he held his post with a tact and finesse that would have done credit to a finished diplomat; threatening one man, paying hush money to another, alternately disgracing and rewarding friends and enemies alike; securing vast sums for his personal expenditure, and through it all managing somehow to keep the national credit from falling utterly, while he boasted openly, and with that peculiar bonhomie that he sometimes chose to affect, that "no five men in the island could kill him." Three of them did it, however, the other day, but, if the reports are to be believed, not in open fight.'
records.summary_es: El Times publica el inicio de su reportaje 'The Character of Santo Domingo's Assassinated Ruler'. De una nota de Nueva York del 4 de agosto: 'Ulises Heureaux fue una figura peculiar en la historia moderna, en muchos aspectos', dijo un comerciante a quien largos años de viajes y comercio en las Antillas le han permitido ser entretenidamente evocador, 'no, quizá, muy diferente del político exitoso promedio de las repúblicas hispanocriollas más pequeñas, pero aun así una decidida anomalía en este siglo diecinueve y a tan corta distancia de una civilización como la nuestra. Durante años mantuvo su puesto con un tacto y una fineza que habrían hecho honor a un diplomático consumado; amenazando a un hombre, pagando dinero por el silencio de otro, alternativamente deshonrando y recompensando a amigos y enemigos por igual; asegurando vastas sumas para su gasto personal, y a través de todo ello arreglándoselas de algún modo para evitar que el crédito nacional cayera por completo, mientras se jactaba abiertamente, y con esa peculiar jovialidad que a veces elegía afectar, de que "ningún grupo de cinco hombres en la isla podría matarlo". Sin embargo, tres de ellos lo hicieron el otro día, pero, si los informes son de creer, no en pelea abierta'.

records.headline: The Times prints the continuation of its feature 'The Character of Santo Domingo's Assassinated Ruler'
records.summary_en: The Times prints the continuation of its feature 'The Character of Santo Domingo's Assassinated Ruler': the merchant says Heureaux was shrewd, crafty, and remorseless if thwarted, and that under his rule human life was held cheaper than he ever believed could be possible; to say that he had friends would hardly be possible, but he had many adherents, for disloyalty meant, sooner or later, death to the transgressor. A friend of his, an English merchant, told him last January that while in conversation with Heureaux the latter had alluded to his own quickness in suppressing crime, instancing a case where, some years before, a man adjudged guilty of burning a sugar cane plantation had been seized, quietly carried across the river from San Domingo City to a place called Pajarito, and there hung to a tree, to remain for three days, a warning to the people at large; the fact that no form of legal trial had been gone through mattered little — the President, as a man of decisive action, had sustained his reputation. The feature adds that Heureaux, born of a Haitian father and a mother who came from St. Thomas, took part in Santo Domingo's early struggles against Spain, and during the war of liberation in 1853-'63 rose to the post of colonel of staff; later he served in the uprisings under Cabral, and held one minor office after another until 1871, when President Merino made him his Minister of the Interior; when Merino's term of office ceased, Heureaux was made President for the then constitutional term of two years, at the close of which he retired to private life.
records.summary_es: El Times publica la continuación de su reportaje 'The Character of Santo Domingo's Assassinated Ruler': el comerciante dice que Heureaux era astuto, artero e implacable si se le contrariaba, y que bajo su gobierno la vida humana se tenía por más barata de lo que él jamás creyó posible; decir que tenía amigos difícilmente sería posible, pero tenía muchos partidarios, porque la deslealtad significaba, tarde o temprano, la muerte para el transgresor. Un amigo suyo, un comerciante inglés, le contó en enero pasado que, mientras conversaba con Heureaux, este aludió a su propia rapidez para suprimir el crimen, citando un caso en el que, algunos años antes, un hombre juzgado culpable de quemar una plantación de caña de azúcar había sido apresado, llevado en silencio al otro lado del río desde la ciudad de San Domingo a un lugar llamado Pajarito, y allí colgado de un árbol, para permanecer durante tres días, como advertencia para el pueblo en general; el hecho de que no se hubiera seguido ninguna forma de juicio legal importaba poco: el presidente, como hombre de acción decisiva, había sostenido su reputación. El reportaje añade que Heureaux, nacido de un padre haitiano y una madre que vino de Saint Thomas, tomó parte en las primeras luchas de Santo Domingo contra España, y durante la guerra de liberación de 1853-'63 ascendió al puesto de coronel de estado mayor; después sirvió en los levantamientos bajo Cabral, y ocupó un cargo menor tras otro hasta 1871, cuando el presidente Merino lo nombró su ministro de lo Interior; cuando cesó el período de Merino, Heureaux fue nombrado presidente por el entonces período constitucional de dos años, al cabo del cual se retiró a la vida privada.

records.headline: The Tribune prints a traveler's narrative of Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints a traveler's narrative of Santo Domingo: the city of Santo Domingo, the capital of the republic, was again reached after spending a month in visiting Samana Bay and the north coast, scaling the lofty Cibao range, descending into La Vega Real, where Christopher Columbus had explored, and journeying across the roadless, bridgeless island, swimming rivers or ferrying across them in dugouts, and sleeping nights in hammocks swung between giant mahogany trees in pristine forests. Before departing on this cruise along the coast and starting on an overland ride from the north to Santo Domingo City on the south, the Government furnished letters to the governors of the districts, which everywhere received the most respectful consideration. At the time a rival named Cabral was cruising in Samana Bay on an ancient ferryboat called the Telegrafo, mounting several smooth-bores; the Dominican navy could muster a fleet of four or five one- and two-masted schooners, each carrying an 8-inch Spanish gun of the seventeenth century. The same afternoon Señor Manuel Mona Gautier, Secretary of State, called at the hotel with an invitation to dine with the President, Buenaventura Baez, and the members of his official household, at his own residence, the Palace not being occupied at the time; United States Consul Somers Smith was also a guest.

Antes de partir en este crucero por la costa e iniciar una cabalgata por tierra desde el norte hasta la ciudad de Santo Domingo, en el sur, el gobierno facilitó cartas para los gobernadores de los distritos, que en todas partes recibieron la más respetuosa consideración. records.headline: The Tribune continues its description of the republic's products
records.summary_en: The Tribune continues its description of the republic's products and climate: honey, molasses, cocoanuts, dyewoods and many other articles are exported, the records showing that about £5,000,000 worth of various products leave the republic every year. As to the climate, a writer says: 'It must be healthful when one may see by the records that the death rate is only eight to the thousand inhabitants. There are no densely populated places, yellow fever is unknown, and intermittent fevers may be avoided, as in Europe, with the smallest precautions. There is scarcely a section of the republic where the trade winds do not blow all day long; the mountain ranges run east and west, and the valleys between them, as well as the mountain sides, receive the trade winds, which blow continually from the east in that latitude. The city of Puerto Plata, on the north coast, and the interior cities of La Vega, Moca and Santiago, in the Royal Plain (Vega Real) of Columbus, are kept healthful and comfortable all the year by this wind, which removes miasmatic emanations. On the south the great sugar-raising plains are between the mountains and the Caribbean Sea. Although Santo Domingo city, the capital, is situated only 18½ degrees from the equator, and Puerto Plata, the northern port, 20 degrees, and the temperature in winter is quite mild, the thermometer does not rise high in midsummer.'
records.summary_es: El Tribune continúa su descripción de los productos de la república y el clima: se exportan miel, melaza, cocos, maderas tintóreas y muchos otros artículos, y los registros muestran que cada año salen de la república productos por valor de unas 5.000.000 de libras. En cuanto al clima, un escritor dice: 'Debe de ser saludable cuando se puede ver en los registros que la tasa de mortalidad es de solo ocho por cada mil habitantes. No hay lugares densamente poblados, la fiebre amarilla es desconocida, y las fiebres intermitentes pueden evitarse, como en Europa, con las más pequeñas precauciones. Apenas hay una sección de la república donde los vientos alisios no soplen durante todo el día; las cordilleras corren de este a oeste, y los valles entre ellas, así como las laderas de las montañas, reciben los vientos alisios, que soplan continuamente desde el este en esa latitud. La ciudad de Puerto Plata, en la costa norte, y las ciudades del interior de La Vega, Moca y Santiago, en la Vega Real de Colón, se mantienen saludables y confortables todo el año gracias a este viento, que elimina las emanaciones miasmáticas. En el sur, las grandes llanuras azucareras están entre las montañas y el mar Caribe. Aunque la ciudad de Santo Domingo, la capital, está situada a solo 18½ grados del ecuador, y Puerto Plata, el puerto del norte, a 20 grados, y la temperatura en invierno es bastante suave, el termómetro no sube mucho en pleno verano'.

records.headline: The Register prints the Havana dispatch on the departure of Gen. Juan Isidro Jiminez
records.summary_en: The Register prints the Havana dispatch on the departure of Gen. Juan Isidro Jiminez: the general, accompanied by six Cubans and four natives of Santo Domingo, is believed to have left here this afternoon for the Dominican republic; it has not yet been ascertained how the party left, but if, as it is thought, they went on one of the Herrera line steamers for the north coast, expecting to obtain a schooner at Nuevitas, they will probably be arrested or prevented from continuing their journey; Gen. Jiminez claimed to be ill yesterday, but the many visitors whom he received this morning led to the belief that the movement was on foot; one thing only is certain, and that is that he has gone, taking his baggage with him, as did also his companions; and the authorities are making a close investigation in order to discover in which direction the party went. The dispatch is headed 'General Jiminez.'

records.summary_en: The Post-Intelligencer prints the close of a Washington item and a New York special to the Herald from Havana of August 5: Minister Powell has cabled the State Department that the presence of a United States warship may be required, if the present threatening condition continues, to insure the safety of the United States legation and consulates. General Jiminez to-day displayed a cipher cablegram which he received from an agent in Santo Domingo, reading: 'Revolution commences to-day in Dajabon and La Vega. records.full_text:
HEUREAUX'S BLOODY RULE.

HIS END A BEFITTING ONE FOR HIS CAREER.

Held the Nominal Republic in Iron Grasp, and Conquered His Foes With Knife, Bullet and Rope, Instead of by Finesse or Intrigue.

THERE was dramatic justice in the tragic end of the Dominican president, Ulysses Heureaux, who died by an assassin's hand last Wednesday. Out of a modern republic he had wrought a medieval empire, and from the intrigues and cruelties he had fostered grew his own undoing. He was shot to death by the son of a man whom he had sent fifteen years before to an untimely end. When Ramon Caceres, at Moca, on Wednesday afternoon, fired the shots which ended Heureaux's life, he avenged not only the murder of his father, but that of scores of others who had been killed at the dictator's word—some with a feint show of legal trial, others by cold-blooded and undisguised assassination. Throughout his career Heureaux showed a contempt for human life which was scarcely matched in the days of the Huguenot struggle in France. He conquered his foes with knife and bullet, ignoring modern diplomacy and political intrigue for the surer methods of hired assassin or firing squad. Ostensibly the president of a republic, he was, in fact, as absolute a monarch as ever wore a crown, and he held the life of every citizen of his beautiful island country in his hand.

Heureaux was unique in his generation. Of unbending will, endowed with much intellectual force, and possessed of great courage, he strove honestly for the people of his fatherland, but with methods which found their only counterpart in the middle ages. In the less than fifty years of his life he rose from a half-breed peasant to the dictatorship of Santo Domingo, and in the thirteen years of his administration he materially advanced the country in civilization, welding out of a mass of half savage brigands an army of considerable strength, and building up a financial system which brought prosperity to his people. He established schools, compelled a degree of education in the cities, and fostered a commerce which increased a hundred fold under his care. His people looked upon him either with a devotion akin to idolatry, or with horror and fear, for his vigorous personality admitted of no lukewarm sentiment. Whether they loved or hated him, they obeyed him without question.

Thirty years ago, an ill-clad, half-starved mulatto boy from the hills of the interior, he joined as a private the so-called army. It was a lawless, impotent mob when Private Heureaux found it, controlled by corrupt politicians and incompetent generals. Despite a withered arm, which was almost useless, Heureaux developed into a good soldier, and soon rose from the ranks to an under officership. His genius for organization developed, and by rapid promotions the young officer advanced until he became commander-in-chief. Then came the turbulent days of 1883-84, and in the disorder of the time Heureaux found his opportunity. With his power as head of the army, he forced his election as president, and thenceforth, to the hour of his death, despite dozens of desperate attempts to displace him, he firmly maintained his position.

His political career abounded in stirring episodes. He established an elaborate secret service and through it his life was saved many times. Many of his spies were women, and through them he was able, time and again, to crush incipient rebellions and stamp out plots against his life. He administered himself "the high justice, the middle and the low," and the luckless plotter found in him judge and jury. When he deemed it unwise to order a military execution, the victim of his displeasure met his fate at home or in a dark street at the hands of one of the President's secret agents.

The visitor to Santo Domingo, the capital of the republic, found evidence of the terror-inspiring character of Heureaux' rule on every hand. From the moment of landing the footsteps of the tourist were dogged night and day by detectives. The residents were shy in their intercourse with strangers, and it was almost impossible to secure from them expressions of opinion on any subject touching the president or his policy. When it was possible, however, to find a Dominican who was willing to talk of the life of Heureaux, the stories told had the flavor of old-time romance. One of the striking instances of the president's personal courage is to be found in the story of his supression of the "Santiago" rebellion a few years ago. Santiago is inland from the famous Samana bay, and at a distance from the capital which made it possible for the residents to foment trouble with the possibility of escaping immediate punishment. Here a band of malcontents from all parts of the island gathered and soon succeeded in enlisting the sympathies of almost the entire population of the town. Encouraged by the fact that the terrible president was several days' journey distant, the ringleaders finally became bold enough to issue a manifesto declaring Heureaux a monstrous tyrant, and urging an uprising. Great posters were printed bearing the picture of a coffin and calling on all patriots to aid in ridding the fatherland of its oppressor.

The government secret service soon apprised the president of the affair, and in his usual picturesque manner he proceeded with preparations for revenge. He ordered made a rough, black coffin, and putting it aboard his little armored yacht, he took a detail of soldiers and sailed around the coast for Santiago. Landing with thirty soldiers, he started on the twenty-five-mile horseback journey inland, and, arriving within a few miles of the town, halted his company and spent the night. Just before dawn, with two soldiers bearing the coffin, he entered the city, leaving the troops behind. The town bugler was aroused, and, at the point of the bayonet, was compelled to sound the alarm, which, in Dominican cities, calls the residents together. Half-dressed and heavy with sleep, the townspeople rushed to the little palm-shaded plaza, and there, all alone under a great tree, upon which was nailed one of the revolutionary posters, the president stood, his arms folded across his uniformed breast. Terrified, the people huddled together. Heureaux called to the bearers to bring the coffin and place it at his side. As the rapidly coming day revealed the faces of the people before him, the president turned to the manifesto and read it aloud.

"Well," he said, as he paused at conclusion; "well; why do you not act? Here is the tyrant. Here is the coffin. Why do you not make good your glorious purpose? Is there no man here? No; half a man?"

Then he burst into a tirade of abuse which reduced his hearers to the last stage of terror. Finally, he strode towards the crowd and pointed out man after man of those whom his spies had declared to be ringleaders.

"Stand out there," he cried. "You—and you—and you," and when he had finished eighteen wretches stood in line awaiting their doom.

"Now march," he ordered, and out through the gates of the city the eighteen men went, the two soldiers with the coffin at their head, and of all the friends and neighbors who saw them go, not one dared raise a finger to oppose the black warrior who stalked behind. When the camp was reached the conspirators were placed in line opposite a file of soldiers. Ten minutes later Heureaux and his soldiers had gone, and eighteen dead men were all that remained of the Santiago rebellion.

Heureaux's heartlessness in the discharge of what he believed to be his duty was never better shown than in the execution, for conspiracy, of his brother-in-law. With the president lived a half sister, much younger than he, and the one person in the world for whom he seemed to have a real affection. The girl met and married a young Dominican merchant. Heureaux soon took the young man into the government service and advanced him rapidly. But the young official was soon deep in the councils of a group of conspirators who had for their object the assassination of the president and the overthrow of the government. The all-wise secret service soon knew all about it, and Heureaux, for his sister's sake, contented himself with warning his brother-in-law that a repetition of his offense would cost him his life. The man's treachery was kept from the public and he was allowed to retain his government position on promise of future good behavior. In less than six months, however, he was again at work plotting against his chief's life, and again his guilt was reported to the president. Heureaux carefully concealed his knowledge of the treachery and issued orders for a state breakfast at his palace. With the noon hour officials of army and state gathered, and with them came the young conspirator. He arrived without his uniform, and Heureaux ordered him to go and don it.

"This breakfast is in your honor," he said, "and I wish you to appear as you should." When the breakfast party was seated at the table the young man was given the place of honor at the president's right, and the officials and their wives wondered at the great show of favor. As the repast was finished and the people rose, the president turned to his brother-in-law and asked if he had enjoyed himself.

"I have, indeed, your excellency," the young man replied.

"I hope you have," returned Heureaux, still smiling, "for you are going to be shot in five minutes." He touched a bell and two black soldiers entered and seized the doomed official. The momentary silence was broken by the screams and frantic pleadings of the president's sister, but he ignored her and calmly led the way down the great flagged stairway and out into the shade of the tropical foliage of the court. The young man met his end bravely, refusing to open his lips as he was led beneath the window of the banquet room and faced about before a file of soldiers. Heureaux, with his sister's screams ringing from the windows above him, coolly gave the order to fire, and stood by, with his cigarette, while the uncoffined body was quickly buried in a flower garden.

Several months after this incident the president received word one stormy evening that a number of conspirators were meeting in a deserted house a mile outside the city to devise a plan for the ruler's assassination. Heureaux ordered a horse and started alone for the house. He dismounted a short distance away, crept up to the door, and suddenly forced an entrance. As he strode among them the score or so of men, who had even then been swearing to take his life, quailed as though before a fully equipped battery.

"I wished to show you," Heureaux said, "that you are not nearly so anxious for my life as you believed. I know you all but I shall take no action. You are free." And he turned and went away. He kept his word and none of the conspirators was punished, but the majority of them left the country.

Heureaux had the features of a full-blooded negro. His manner was polished and his conversation entertaining. The aristocratic Dominicans, who are of pure Spanish blood, refused to admit him to their social circles because of his negro blood, and he felt their slight keenly. Little was known of his family history or his parentage, and he was always reticent about the incidents of his life before he became famous. His palace in Santo Domingo is a three-story building covering a block, and built in the typical style of the tropics. Its plaster walls and green window slats are all that can be seen by the tourist.—Chicago Tribune.

records.headline: The paper reports Dominican revolutionary troops assembled at Ouanaminthe crossed the frontier and took Dajabón, its garrison
records.summary_en: The paper reports Dominican revolutionary troops assembled at Ouanaminthe crossed the frontier and took Dajabón, its garrison retiring to Fort Belair and the foreign population and Haitian consul leaving. records.headline: The Journal prints the close of a Cape Haytien dispatch and a Puerto Plata dispatch of August 7
records.summary_en: The Journal prints the close of a Cape Haytien dispatch and a Puerto Plata dispatch of August 7 headed 'Trying to Keep Order': General Guellito, governor of Monte Cristi, is thus placed in a dangerous position and is unable to attack the revolutionists, and it is added that he will be obliged to capitulate; numbers of Dominicans are arriving in Hayti by sea in order to reach the revolutionary army by crossing the frontier, thus augmenting the force of General Pacheco. The Puerto Plata dispatch says Minister of Finance Señor Alvarez and Senator Cordero, with 100 men, went to Monte Cristi yesterday, where they united with 700 men who had been assembled in behalf of the government for the restoration of order; American steamships are also watching the coast to prevent the landing of an insurrectionary expedition, should any such attempt be made; it is claimed the governor of Monte Cristi has 3,000 men under arms for the preservation of the peace, but the situation is considered very grave; and the United States gunboat Machias has left the port of Santo Domingo for Punta Macoris, but the cruiser New Orleans still remains here.

AS WASHINGTON VIEWS IT. WASHINGTON, [illegible] — Notwithstanding the growing turbulence in San Domingo, as disclosed in Press dispatches, neither the State nor Navy Departments had received anything up to the close of office hours today to show that our officials there were apprehensive over the developments. The authorities here are proceeding on the theory that the existing order of affairs is regular, and this will continue to be the course observed. Only in the event that the insurrection becomes strong enough to establish a de facto form of government is there any likelihood that its claim could be taken into consideration as against the de jure government.

records.headline: The Messenger prints a Cape Haytien dispatch of August 3 on the Dominican revolt
records.summary_en: The Messenger prints a Cape Haytien dispatch of August 3 on the Dominican revolt: it has just become known that an armed insurrection has broken out at La Vega, a town seventy-eight miles northwest of Santo Domingo, in favor of Jiminez, who aspires to the presidency in succession to the late President Heureaux; later advices from the Dominican republic indicate that the revolution is growing in strength; and at Santiago de la Cruz 500 well armed men have risen under the command of General Ramon Pacheco, and General Reyes, who is very influential in those districts, has joined the insurgents with several other generals, each commanding fairly important forces. The dispatch is headed 'Unrest in West India Republics.'
records.summary_es: The Messenger publica un despacho de Cabo Haitiano del 3 de agosto sobre la revuelta dominicana: se acaba de saber que ha estallado una insurrección armada en La Vega, pueblo situado a setenta y ocho millas al noroeste de Santo Domingo, a favor de Jiminez, quien aspira a la presidencia en sucesión del fallecido presidente Heureaux; informaciones posteriores de la República Dominicana indican que la revolución gana fuerza; y en Santiago de la Cruz se han levantado 500 hombres bien armados bajo el mando del general Ramón Pacheco, y el general Reyes, muy influyente en esos distritos, se ha unido a los insurgentes con varios otros generales, cada uno al mando de fuerzas bastante importantes. El despacho lleva por título 'Unrest in West India Republics'.

records.headline: The Weekly Post prints a Puerto Plata dispatch of August 7

The capital dispatch, headed 'Situation at the Capital', says the United States gunboat Machias has left here for Punta Macoris; news from the interior indicates that tranquillity prevails, but business continues depressed and the want of drafts is greatly felt; the government is endeavoring to ameliorate the financial condition; advices that a hurricane is approaching have been received from various parts of the republic of Dominica, and the barometer here is falling rapidly; the Dominican warships have sailed for Caldera, a port of refuge on the south coast; the United States cruiser New Orleans is still here, with steam up and ready to leave at any moment; the American steamer Carib, from New York July 28 for Turks Island, which is now at Samana, is anxiously expected; and as provisions are very scarce and prices high, the poor people are suffering severely, their earnings not being in proportion to the prices now asked for the necessaries of life.

records.headline: The Post prints the Cape Haytien, Puerto Plata, and Santo Domingo dispatches of August 7
records.summary_en: The Post prints the Cape Haytien, Puerto Plata, and Santo Domingo dispatches of August 7 in heavily degraded type: partisans of Don Juan Jiminez have taken up arms in Santo Domingo on the plains of Chaguel and San Jose de las Matas and in the towns of Guayabin, Sabaneta, Manzanillo and Dajabon, abandoned by the troops of the government of Santo Domingo; more than half of these troops are said to have gone over to the camp of General Pacheco; General Guellito, governor of Monte Christo, who it is claimed has lost half his troops, who have gone over to the enemy, it is believed will capitulate; and numbers of Dominicans are arriving in Hayti by sea, crossing the frontier to join the force of General Pacheco. The Puerto Plata dispatch says Señor Alvarez, the minister of finance, and Señor Cordero, with a hundred men, went to Monte Christo yesterday and united there with 700 men assembled in behalf of the government for the restoration of order; steamers are watching the coast to prevent the landing of an insurgent expedition, should such a thing be attempted; and the governor of Monte Christo has 3,000 men under arms for the preservation of the peace, the situation being considered grave. The Santo Domingo dispatch says the United States gunboat Machias has left here for Punta Manacoris; the United States cruiser New Orleans remains here; advices from the interior indicate that tranquillity prevails, but business continues depressed and the want of drafts is generally felt, and the government is endeavoring to ameliorate the prevailing condition. A Washington item of August 7 adds that, notwithstanding the growing turbulence in Santo Domingo as disclosed in press dispatches, neither the State nor the Navy Department had received anything up to the close of office hours to-day.
records.summary_es: The Post publica los despachos de Cabo Haitiano, Puerto Plata y Santo Domingo del 7 de agosto, en tipos muy degradados: partidarios de don Juan Jiminez han tomado las armas en Santo Domingo en las llanuras de Chaguel y San José de las Matas y en los pueblos de Guayabín, Sabaneta, Manzanillo y Dajabón, abandonados por las tropas del gobierno de Santo Domingo; se dice que más de la mitad de esas tropas se han pasado al campamento del general Pacheco; el general Guellito, gobernador de Monte Christo, de quien se afirma que ha perdido la mitad de sus tropas, pasadas al enemigo, se cree que capitulará; y numerosos dominicanos están llegando a Haití por mar, cruzando la frontera para unirse a la fuerza del general Pacheco. El despacho de Puerto Plata dice que el señor Alvarez, ministro de Hacienda, y el señor Cordero, con cien hombres, fueron ayer a Monte Christo y se unieron allí a 700 hombres reunidos a favor del gobierno para el restablecimiento del orden; vapores vigilan la costa para impedir el desembarco de una expedición insurgente, si tal cosa se intentara; y el gobernador de Monte Christo tiene 3,000 hombres en armas para la preservación de la paz, considerándose grave la situación. El despacho de Santo Domingo dice que el cañonero estadounidense Machias ha salido de aquí hacia Punta Manacoris; el crucero estadounidense New Orleans permanece aquí; avisos del interior indican que prevalece la tranquilidad, pero el comercio continúa deprimido y la falta de letras de cambio se siente en general, y el gobierno se esfuerza por mejorar la situación prevaleciente. Una nota de Washington del 7 de agosto añade que, a pesar de la creciente turbulencia en Santo Domingo revelada en los despachos de prensa, ni el Departamento de Estado ni el de Marina habían recibido nada hasta el cierre de las oficinas hoy.

records.passage: FIRST MOVE in the New Haytian Revolution — Jiminez Shows His Hand. Port-au-Prince, Hayti, Aug. [illegible] — The revolutionary Dominican troops, which assembled at [Ouanaminthe?], have crossed the frontier and taken possession of Dajabon. The garrison at that place retired to Fort Blair, a strategic position commanding the town. The foreign population and Haytian consul have left the place. It is considered probable that Jiminez, the leader of the revolution, will attempt to make a landing on the island shortly in order to join the revolutionary troops at Dajabon and take direct command of the movement. The Haytian government is taking measures to prevent Jiminez from landing in its territory

records.headline: The Messenger prints the closing part of the Havana interview
records.summary_en: The Messenger prints the closing part of the Havana interview with General Jiminez: the present government, he had said, could not possibly last beyond the 15th of this month. 'I did hear,' he continued, 'that Heureaux was sending men to Cuba to kill me, but I knew nothing whatever regarding the plot to kill him. I had no connection and have no connection with Ramon Caceres, who did the shooting. I do not believe that the United States will interfere with my government in San Domingo, which will be a government peaceful and helpful to all, for the United States did not interfere with the government of Heureaux, who robbed and murdered for fourteen years.' General Jiminez admits that he has often been to the United States incognito, but says he has not had interviews with official persons; he considers that there is no need of promoting expeditions to land in San Domingo, as there already are a thousand men waiting for him, a force which he deems quite sufficient for his purposes; referring to the future relations of San Domingo with the United States, he expressed a desire to be on friendly terms with Washington, and said he believed he could count upon American sympathy; Gomez he referred to as esteemed by Dominicans, but not sought for as president; and the people of San Domingo, he declares, are impetuous, and are urging him to come to them at once, but for a time he prefers delay, as 'each day is worth a battle won.'

records.headline: The News prints a dispatch from Santo Domingo on the revolution
records.summary_en: The News prints a dispatch from Santo Domingo on the revolution: the revolutionary Dominicans have crossed the frontier and have taken possession of Dajabon; the garrison at that place retired to Fort Belair, a strategic position commanding the town; the foreign population and the Haytian consul left the place; it is considered that Jiminez, the leader of the revolution, will attempt to make a landing on the island shortly in order to join the revolutionary troops at Dajabon and take direction of the movement; the Haytian government is taking measures to prevent Jiminez from landing in its territory; it is very difficult at present to obtain information regarding the events transpiring in the Dominican Republic; and it is reported that the exiled Dominicans assembled at Ouanaminthe, Hayti, crossed the frontier of Santo Domingo and captured the town of Dajabon.
