records.headline: Reporting on Jiminez's movements, the Omaha Daily Bee notes
records.summary_en: Reporting on Jiminez's movements, the Omaha Daily Bee notes that after receiving dispatches from friends in Santo Domingo, he departed unarmed accompanied by two friends to meet a private yacht placed at his disposal at or off Santiago, declining to name the vessel's owner. In an August 17 Havana dispatch, Jiminez is quoted as claiming that he will bring what the text calls 'all the islands of Santo Domingo' under a single strong administration to the benefit of all parties, asserting that plenty of honest, competent men are available for public office and that conditions in neighboring Hayti—which he describes as bordering on revolution—favor the plan. His son is remaining in Havana to wind up his affairs and expects to join his father shortly should the Santo Domingo venture succeed.

records.headline: In an editorial comment signed "DEM.," the Washington Standard warns
records.summary_en: In an editorial comment signed "DEM.," the Washington Standard warns that the recent assassination of President Heureaux of the Dominican Republic and the disputed succession there are likely to bring new problems to the United States. Noting allegations that a powerful American syndicate practically controls the country's finances and affairs, the item reports that two warships have been ordered to San Domingo to protect American interests. The writer remarks ironically that syndicates have been well cared for by the present Administration and argues that if the seizure of the Philippines can be justified, there is no reason not to take in San Domingo as well, since all territorial syndicates should look alike to Mr. McKinley and "manifest destiny" ought not to discriminate among friends.
records.summary_es: En un comentario editorial firmado «DEM.», el Washington Standard advierte que el reciente asesinato del presidente Heureaux de la República Dominicana y la disputada sucesión en ese país probablemente traerán nuevos problemas a los Estados Unidos. Tras señalar versiones de que un poderoso sindicato estadounidense controla en la práctica las finanzas y los asuntos del país, la nota informa que dos buques de guerra han recibido órdenes de dirigirse a San Domingo para proteger los intereses estadounidenses. El autor observa con ironía que los sindicatos han sido muy bien atendidos por la actual Administración y sostiene que, si puede justificarse la toma de las Filipinas, no hay razón para no incorporar también a San Domingo, pues todos los sindicatos territoriales deberían parecerle iguales al señor McKinley y el «destino manifiesto» no debería hacer distinciones entre amigos.

records.headline: Reporting from Havana, a dispatch in the New-York Tribune states
records.summary_en: Reporting from Havana, a dispatch in the New-York Tribune states that General Jiminez, after reportedly receiving dispatches from friends in San Domingo, departed unarmed with two companions to meet a private yacht placed at his disposal at or off Santiago, though he declined to name the vessel's owner. According to the dispatch, Jiminez declares that he will place the entire island of San Domingo under a single strong government staffed by honest and competent men, asserting that the situation in neighboring Hayti—described as a country bordering on revolution—favors the plan. His son is remaining in Havana to settle his affairs and plans to join him shortly if the San Domingo expedition succeeds. Although Chief of Police Detectives Colonel Bacallao told General Ludlow shortly before 9 o'clock that evening that Jiminez was still in Havana, an Associated Press correspondent saw him depart by train that morning, and after detectives watched his house until 6 o'clock the "Heraldo" issued an extra announcing that he had gone.

Según el despacho, Jiminez declara que pondrá toda la isla de San Domingo bajo un solo gobierno fuerte integrado por hombres honestos y competentes, afirmando que la situación en el vecino Hayti —descrito como un país al borde de una revolución— favorece dicho proyecto. Su hijo permanece en La Habana para liquidar sus asuntos y piensa reunirse pronto con él si la expedición a San Domingo tiene éxito. Aunque el coronel Bacallao, jefe de detectives de la policía, informó al general Ludlow poco antes de las 9 de esa noche que Jiminez seguía en La Habana, un corresponsal de The Associated Press lo vio partir en tren esa mañana, y después de que dos detectives vigilaran su casa hasta las 6 en punto el «Heraldo» publicó una edición extraordinaria anunciando su salida.

records.headline: The Houston Daily Post, concluding an item on Jiminez's expedition
records.summary_en: The Houston Daily Post, concluding an item on Jiminez's expedition plans, reports that a vessel placed at his disposal will meet him at or off Santiago, that he proposes to place all of Santo Domingo under one strong government—claiming that conditions in neighboring Hayti, a country bordering on revolution, favor the idea—and that his son will join him shortly if his Santo Domingo expedition succeeds. A separate New York dispatch dated August 17, citing a Herald report from Santo Domingo under the headline "Dominican Uprising," states that another invasion from Hayti was attempted on Tuesday, when government forces met and dispersed the insurgents near Monte Cristo after severe fighting and reportedly captured some of them. Because the revolutionary movement lacks organization and has waged only sporadic guerrilla warfare, the government is undismayed; interior reports describe everything as quiet, several leaders have been arrested, and despite lingering discontent the public generally hopes the civil troubles will soon be settled.
records.summary_es: The Houston Daily Post, al concluir una nota sobre los planes expedicionarios de Jiminez, informa que una embarcación puesta a su disposición se reunirá con él en Santiago o frente a esa costa, que se propone poner todo Santo Domingo bajo un solo gobierno fuerte —afirmando que la situación en el vecino Hayti, país al borde de una revolución, favorece la idea— y que su hijo se le unirá pronto si su expedición a Santo Domingo prospera. Un despacho aparte fechado en Nueva York el 17 de agosto, que cita un informe del Herald desde Santo Domingo bajo el titular «Dominican Uprising», señala que el martes se intentó otra invasión desde Hayti, cuando las fuerzas gubernamentales enfrentaron y dispersaron a los insurgentes cerca de Monte Cristo tras recios combates y, según se informa, capturaron a algunos de ellos. Dado que el movimiento revolucionario carece de organización y solo ha librado una guerra de guerrillas esporádica, el gobierno no se muestra alarmado; los informes del interior indican que todo está tranquilo, varios cabecillas han sido arrestados y, pese al descontento persistente, la población espera en general que pronto se resuelvan los disturbios civiles.

records.headline: Opening a feature article on Dominican politics, The Indianapolis Journal states
records.summary_en: Opening a feature article on Dominican politics, The Indianapolis Journal states that General Don Juan Isidro Jiminez claims to be the real leader of the Dominicans, asserts that his agents murdered President Heureaux, and declares that he is going to take possession of the government. Alluding to an earlier episode in which Jiminez allegedly deceived the United States government and nearly drew it unwittingly into his schemes, the paper asks whether the Navy Department has hurriedly dispatched the New Orleans and the Machias southward out of fear that Jiminez will gain the presidency of San Domingo, or whether the administration wishes to see him seated and secure the annexation of San Domingo. Adopting a satirical tone, the writer adds that the island had room for only one "big man" at a time—the late President Heureaux—alongside Jiminez, a wealthy merchant and frequent traveler owning vast island plantations as well as warehouses and commercial branches in New York, Hamburg, and other cities, joking that whenever Jiminez landed the island sagged toward the coast and tilted Heureaux's inland palace forty-five degrees.
records.summary_es: Al iniciar un artículo especial sobre la política dominicana, The Indianapolis Journal señala que el general Don Juan Isidro Jiminez afirma ser el verdadero líder de los dominicanos, asegura que sus agentes asesinaron al presidente Heureaux y declara que va a tomar posesión del gobierno. Aludiendo a un episodio anterior en el que Jiminez supuestamente engañó al gobierno de los Estados Unidos y casi lo involucró sin saberlo en sus planes, el periódico pregunta si el Departamento de Marina ha enviado a toda prisa al New Orleans y al Machias hacia el sur por temor a que Jiminez ocupe la presidencia de San Domingo, o si la administración desea verlo instalado para asegurar la anexión de San Domingo. En tono satírico, el autor añade que en la isla solo cabía un «gran hombre» a la vez —el difunto presidente Heureaux— frente a Jiminez, acaudalado comerciante y gran viajero dueño de inmensas plantaciones en la isla así como de almacenes y sucursales comerciales en Nueva York, Hamburgo y otras ciudades, bromeando que cada vez que Jiminez desembarcaba la isla se hundía hacia la costa e inclinaba cuarenta y cinco grados el palacio interior de Heureaux.

records.headline: Under the subheading "Warning to Jiminez," The Indianapolis Journal presents
records.summary_en: Under the subheading "Warning to Jiminez," The Indianapolis Journal presents a satirical champagne scene in which President Heureaux—after a servant opens a third bottle of champagne with a machete—tells General Don Juan Jiminez that the presidency views his growing popularity and his friendly standing at the custom house with apprehension. Declaring that the island is growing poorer while Jiminez grows richer, Heureaux announces plans to float a multi-million-dollar loan with Americans, rebond the customs of San Domingo as security, and place a foreigner in charge of the customs. Heureaux warns Jiminez to curb his popularity before it proves fatal, boasting that during sixteen years of rule no fewer than 400 gentlemen on the island have been eliminated because of their growing popularity, and adding that Heureaux and Jiminez can remain on the island together only if one of them stays quiet.
records.summary_es: Bajo el subtítulo «Warning to Jiminez», The Indianapolis Journal presenta una escena satírica con champán en la cual el presidente Heureaux —después de que un sirviente destapa con machete una tercera botella de champán— dice al general Don Juan Jiminez que la presidencia observa con creciente recelo su popularidad en aumento y sus buenas relaciones en la aduana. Tras declarar que la isla se empobrece mientras Jiminez se enriquece, Heureaux anuncia planes de colocar un empréstito de muchos millones de dólares con los estadounidenses, volver a comprometer las aduanas de San Domingo como garantía y sentar a un extranjero al frente de las aduanas. Heureaux advierte a Jiminez que frene su popularidad antes de que le resulte fatal, jactándose de que durante sus dieciséis años de mando no menos de 400 caballeros de la isla han sido eliminados a causa de su creciente popularidad, y añadiendo que un Heureaux y un Jiminez solo pueden permanecer al mismo tiempo en la isla si uno de los dos se mantiene callado.

records.headline: Continuing its narrative of General Jiminez's earlier expedition
records.summary_en: Continuing its narrative of General Jiminez's earlier expedition, The Indianapolis Journal relates that Jiminez had sent word ahead counseling General Garcia at Monte Christi to have at least a thousand men ready to take arms, attack the forts, slaughter the garrisons, and march on San Domingo city and Heureaux's palace, though that message never reached Garcia. When the vessel arrived off Monte Christi at daybreak and neither Garcia nor the thousand men could be seen on shore, the ship anchored and lowered two boats carrying Jiminez and some eighteen armed fighting men. Upon landing, Jiminez shouted "Viva, San Domingo libre!" and fired the first shot into the air; finding the governor absent from his palace, the party dragged an astonished Garcia from bed by the heels at his home, returned to seize the governor at his palace, and moved toward the fortress at Jiminez's command.

Cuando la embarcación avistó Monte Christi al amanecer y ni Garcia ni los mil hombres aparecieron en la costa, el buque echó anclas y arriaron dos botes con Jiminez y unos dieciocho combatientes armados. Al tocar tierra, Jiminez gritó «Viva, San Domingo libre!» y disparó al aire el primer tiro; al no hallar al gobernador en su palacio, el grupo sacó por los talones de la cama a un atónito Garcia en su casa, regresó al palacio para apresar de inmediato al gobernador y avanzó hacia la fortaleza a la voz de Jiminez.

records.headline: In a concluding section on Dominican-American friction, The Indianapolis Journal notes
records.summary_en: In a concluding section on Dominican-American friction, The Indianapolis Journal notes that the attempt to overthrow Heureaux occurred two months earlier and states that two weeks ago the Dominican president was stabbed to death in Moca. Recounting the aftermath of Heureaux's earlier failure to put Jiminez behind bars, the paper describes the Dominican president's outrage that a U.S. government vessel flying the Stars and Stripes, loaded with government arms, and officered by Americans had engaged in a filibustering expedition against an island at peace with the United States, while the War Department in Washington fumed that Jiminez had tricked Uncle Sam by diverting an expedition intended for Cuba. Assistant Secretary Meiklejohn telegraphed the leaders of the financial syndicate that had loaned President Heureaux a vast sum secured by the island's customs; after a secret Washington conference produced mutual explanations and closed the incident, the Fanita was later sent to Cuba with her cargo for Gomez.
records.summary_es: En un pasaje final sobre las fricciones domínico-estadounidenses, The Indianapolis Journal señala que el intento de derrocar a Heureaux ocurrió dos meses atrás y afirma que hace dos semanas el presidente dominicano fue muerto a puñaladas en Moca. Al relatar las secuelas del fracaso previo de Heureaux en encarcelar a Jiminez, el diario describe la indignación del mandatario dominicano ante el hecho de que un buque del gobierno estadounidense que enarbolaba la bandera de las barras y las estrellas, cargado con armas oficiales y al mando de oficiales estadounidenses, participara en una expedición filibustera contra una isla en paz con los Estados Unidos, mientras el Departamento de Guerra en Washington rabiaba porque Jiminez había engañado al Tío Sam desviando una expedición destinada a Cuba. El subsecretario Meiklejohn telegrafió a los jefes del sindicato financiero que había prestado al presidente Heureaux una cuantiosa suma garantizada con las aduanas; tras una conferencia secreta en Washington que dio lugar a explicaciones mutuas y cerró el incidente, el Fanita fue enviado posteriormente a Cuba con su cargamento para Gomez.

records.headline: Opening with reaction to Jiminez's arrest, The Beatrice Daily Express reports
records.summary_en: Opening with reaction to Jiminez's arrest, The Beatrice Daily Express reports general sentiment that authorities had no right to arrest him as an unarmed citizen apparently traveling to Santiago de Cuba, and that even if bound for San Domingo he would merely be returning to his native country. Under the headline "Searching for Jiminez," an August 19 dispatch from Kingston cites advices from Santo Domingo stating that the Dominican government is desperately apprehensive of the momentarily expected arrival of revolutionary leader Jiminez, which would sway undecided popular opinion, and has ordered armed vessels patrolling the coast to search every strange ship and capture him under any flag, armed or not. An accompanying August 19 dispatch from Santiago de Cuba adds that American representatives are rapidly recruiting expeditions on the north coast, that Havana ordered the men recently captured at Baracoa held pending investigation, and that although several expeditions have escaped without interference, General Leonard Wood is determined to enforce neutrality.
records.summary_es: Al iniciar con las reacciones al arresto de Jiminez, The Beatrice Daily Express recoge la opinión generalizada de que las autoridades no tenían derecho a detenerlo como ciudadano desarmado que viajaba aparentemente hacia Santiago de Cuba, y de que aun si se dirigiera a San Domingo solo estaría regresando a su país natal. Bajo el titular «Searching for Jiminez», un despacho de Kingston fechado el 19 de agosto cita informes de Santo Domingo según los cuales el gobierno dominicano teme desesperadamente la llegada inminente del líder revolucionario Jiminez, que inclinaría por completo a la opinión pública indecisa, y ha ordenado a buques armados que patrullan la costa registrar toda embarcación extraña y capturarlo bajo cualquier bandera, armado o no. Un despacho adjunto desde Santiago de Cuba, también del 19 de agosto, añade que representantes estadounidenses reclutan rápidamente expediciones en la costa norte, que La Habana ordenó retener bajo investigación a los hombres capturados recientemente en Baracoa y que, aunque varias expediciones han logrado salir sin interferencia, el general Leonard Wood está decidido a hacer cumplir la neutralidad.

records.headline: Writing editorially, The Magnolia Gazette contends that the recent
records.summary_en: Writing editorially, The Magnolia Gazette contends that the recent assassination of President Heureaux of the Dominican Republic and the disputed succession there are likely to bring new problems to the United States. The paper notes allegations that a powerful American syndicate practically controls the country's finances and affairs, and states that two warships have been ordered to San Domingo to protect American interests. Observing sarcastically that syndicates have been well looked after by the current administration, the editorial remarks that there is no reason not to take in San Domingo if the seizure of the Philippines can be justified, adding that all territorial syndicates should look alike to Mr. McKinley and "manifest destiny" ought not to discriminate between friends.
records.summary_es: En un comentario editorial, The Magnolia Gazette sostiene que el reciente asesinato del presidente Heureaux de la República Dominicana y la disputada sucesión en ese país probablemente traerán nuevos problemas a las puertas de los Estados Unidos. El periódico recoge versiones de que un poderoso sindicato estadounidense controla prácticamente las finanzas y los asuntos de esa nación, e informa que dos buques de guerra han recibido órdenes de dirigirse a San Domingo para proteger los intereses estadounidenses. Observando con sarcasmo que los sindicatos han sido muy bien atendidos por la actual administración, el editorial señala que no hay motivo para no incorporar a San Domingo si puede justificarse la toma de las Filipinas, y añade que todos los sindicatos territoriales deberían parecerle iguales al señor McKinley y que el «destino manifiesto» no debería discriminar entre amigos.

records.summary_en: The *Passaic City Record* reported that while official tranquillity prevailed in Santo Domingo following President Heureaux's assassination, trade remained depressed due to public reluctance to withdraw paper currency. In addition, a devastating hurricane caused severe flooding and property destruction across San Pedro de Macoris, Samana, and Puerto Plata. In Cuba, American customs officers at Baracoa intercepted an arms shipment of 143 rifles and 18,000 rounds of ammunition bound for Dominican rebels.
records.summary_es: El *Passaic City Record* informó que, si bien prevalecía una aparente tranquilidad en Santo Domingo tras el asesinato del presidente Heureaux, el comercio continuaba deprimido debido a la renuencia del público a aceptar el papel moneda. Además, un devastador huracán provocó graves inundaciones y destrucción material en San Pedro de Macorís, Samaná y Puerto Plata. En Cuba, agentes de aduanas estadounidenses en Baracoa interceptaron un cargamento clandestino de armas de 143 fusiles y 18.000 proyectiles con destino a los rebeldes dominicanos.

The problem of taking up the paper currency has not yet been solved, as the people in general do not wish it taken up. This is the real cause of dullness in business. Once the matter has been arranged, affairs should take on a different aspect. Many families had abandoned their houses for the time and boats were used in the streets to carry people from one point to another. records.summary_en: The New York Journal and Advertiser, citing State Department denials, reports that proposed additional U.S. precautions were not prompted by representations from the Santo Domingo government, but rest on the duty of preventing filibustering against a friendly nation—a stance already shown by military orders barring filibustering expeditions from leaving Cuba. Asking the Navy to assist is viewed as an indication that efforts in Cuba to aid the Dominican insurgents are more active than reports from Havana and Santiago suggest. An accompanying August 18 dispatch from Santiago de Cuba states that Dominican agents are rapidly recruiting expeditions, especially on the north coast; orders arrived from Havana that day to hold recently captured men pending investigation, trading schooners are closely watched, the tug Adonis was armed the previous day and sent to Guantanamo to patrol the coast, and despite several expeditions having escaped unhindered, Military Governor General Wood is determined to enforce neutrality.

El hecho de haberse solicitado el auxilio de la Marina se interpreta como indicio de que en Cuba hay mayor actividad en apoyo de los insurgentes dominicanos de lo que reflejan los informes de La Habana y Santiago. Un despacho adjunto de Santiago de Cuba fechado el 18 de agosto señala que agentes dominicanos reclutan rápidamente expediciones, sobre todo en la costa norte; ese día llegaron órdenes de La Habana de retener bajo investigación a hombres capturados recientemente, las goletas mercantes son vigiladas de cerca, el remolcador Adonis fue armado la víspera y enviado a Guantanamo para patrullar la costa y, aunque varias expediciones lograron partir sin tropiezos, el gobernador militar general Wood está decidido a hacer cumplir la neutralidad.

records.headline: A feature on Santo Domingo describes its minerals, including rock salt, petroleum found near Azua, abundant copper
records.summary_en: A feature on Santo Domingo describes its minerals, including rock salt, petroleum found near Azua, abundant copper and great masses of iron ore in the interior, and explains that the president is chosen by an electoral college for four years with a cabinet of six. It says sugar, tobacco, cacao and coffee are the leading exports, that the United States led all other countries in trade with the republic, that most sugar estates are owned by Americans with the crop estimated at 65,000 tons, and that steamers of the Samana Bay Fruit Company carry fifteen to eighteen thousand bunches of bananas on each trip to the United States.

records.headline: This account describes the Republic of Santo Domingo, which covers 18,045 of the island's 28,240 square miles, its rivers
records.summary_en: This account describes the Republic of Santo Domingo, which covers 18,045 of the island's 28,240 square miles, its rivers, its gold washings, the rock-salt hills of the Neyba valley, petroleum near Azua and other minerals, and a government headed by a president chosen by an electoral college for four years. Its four leading exports are sugar, tobacco, cacao and coffee; the sugar crop this season is estimated at 65,000 tons and most sugar estates are owned by Americans, tobacco goes chiefly to Germany, and the Samana Bay Fruit Company's steamers carry fifteen to eighteen thousand bunches of bananas on each trip to the United States.
records.summary_es: Esta descripción presenta la República de Santo Domingo, que cubre 18.045 de las 28.240 millas cuadradas de la isla, sus ríos, sus lavaderos de oro, las colinas de sal de roca del valle de Neyba, el petróleo cerca de Azua y otros minerales, y un gobierno encabezado por un presidente elegido por un colegio electoral por cuatro años. Sus cuatro principales productos de exportación son el azúcar, el tabaco, el cacao y el café; la cosecha de azúcar de esta temporada se estima en 65.000 toneladas y la mayoría de las haciendas azucareras son propiedad de americanos, el tabaco va principalmente a Alemania, y los vapores de la Samana Bay Fruit Company llevan de quince a dieciocho mil racimos de plátanos en cada viaje a los Estados Unidos.

Tobacco is extensively grown and much of it is said to be of a quality nearly equal to the celebrated Havana product. Germany is the chief market for this crop. The banana industry is a growing one. The steamers of the Samana Bay Fruit Company make three or four trips a month to the United States, and on each trip between fifteen and eighteen thousand bunches of the fruit are carried. THE BISHOP A BORROWER. Church Mortgages to Be Raised With English Money. New York, Aug. 19—Bishop Wigger, of the Catholic Diocese of Newark, has confirmed the report that he proposes to accept a loan of $1,500,000 from an English syndicate to be used in taking up mortgages on the churches in his diocese, upon which 5 per cent interest is exacted. Under the new arrangement only 3 1-2 per cent interest will be charged by the foreign syndicate. The Bishop of Madison yesterday said he would probably have the money next week. It is estimated that Catholic Church property in this diocese, which is worth about 10,000,000, is mortgaged for nearly $2,000,000. The syndicate considers the property gilt-edged security, and is willing to advance another million if the loan of $1,500,000 does not prove sufficient.

records.headline: The Marietta Daily Leader prints advices from Santo Domingo via Kingston, Jamaica, dated August 20
records.summary_en: The Marietta Daily Leader prints advices from Santo Domingo via Kingston, Jamaica, dated August 20, stating that the Dominican government is growing desperately apprehensive of the momentarily expected arrival of revolutionary leader Jiminez, which reportedly would completely turn partly undecided popular opinion. To intercept him, armed vessels are patrolling the coast under orders to search every strange ship and capture Jiminez under any flag, armed or not. An accompanying August 19 dispatch from Santiago de Cuba reports that Dominican agents are rapidly recruiting expeditions, particularly along the north coast; Havana sent orders on Friday to hold recently captured men pending an investigation, trading schooners are closely watched, the tug Adonis was armed on Thursday and sent to Guantanamo to patrol the coast, and although several expeditions have gotten away without interference, Military Governor General Leonard Wood is determined to enforce neutrality.

Con el fin de interceptarlo, embarcaciones armadas patrullan la costa con órdenes de registrar todo buque extraño y capturar a Jiminez bajo cualquier bandera, esté armado o no. Un despacho adjunto desde Santiago de Cuba fechado el 19 de agosto informa que agentes dominicanos reclutan con rapidez expediciones, sobre todo en la costa norte; el viernes se recibieron órdenes de La Habana para retener bajo investigación a hombres capturados recientemente, las goletas comerciales son vigiladas estrechamente, el jueves fue armado el remolcador Adonis y enviado a Guantanamo para patrullar la costa y, aunque varias expediciones han logrado zarpar sin interferencia, el gobernador militar general Leonard Wood está decidido a hacer cumplir la neutralidad.

records.headline: Dispatches in The San Francisco Call report that Santo Domingo government
records.summary_en: Dispatches in The San Francisco Call report that Santo Domingo government forces trying to suppress the revolution have been defeated and driven back at Monte Cristi, while the province of San Pedro Macoris has enthusiastically proclaimed a revolution in favor of presidential aspirant General Juan Isidro Jiminez. An August 19 dispatch from Port-au-Prince adds that a revolutionary band gathered between Cupey and Esterovasa in Santo Domingo dispersed without fighting and re-entered Haitian territory, while a thousand men under Minister Cordero guard Fort Belair and watch the frontier as warships patrol the coast to prevent Jiminez from landing. Under the headline "Neutrality Laws Are to Be Enforced," an August 19 Washington dispatch reports Secretary Root's statement that General Jiminez was arrested by the collector of customs at Cienfuegos—presumably on orders from General Brooke under recent instructions to prevent U.S. neutrality violations from Cuba and keep Jiminez under close surveillance—and notes that Washington has heard nothing of his release and will send Brooke no instructions unless requested.
records.summary_es: Despachos publicados en The San Francisco Call informan que las fuerzas del gobierno de Santo Domingo empeñadas en sofocar la revolución han sido derrotadas y rechazadas en Monte Cristi, mientras que la provincia de San Pedro Macoris ha proclamado con gran entusiasmo la revolución en favor del aspirante presidencial general Juan Isidro Jiminez. Un despacho de Puerto Príncipe fechado el 19 de agosto añade que un grupo revolucionario reunido entre Cupey y Esterovasa, en Santo Domingo, se dispersó sin combatir y reingresó en territorio haitiano, en tanto que mil hombres al mando del ministro Cordero resguardan el fuerte Belair y vigilan la frontera mientras buques de guerra patrullan la costa para impedir el desembarco de Jiminez. Bajo el titular «Neutrality Laws Are to Be Enforced», un despacho de Washington del 19 de agosto recoge las declaraciones del secretario Root de que el general Jiminez fue arrestado por el administrador de aduanas en Cienfuegos —presumiblemente por orden del general Brooke conforme a instrucciones recientes para impedir violaciones de las leyes de neutralidad estadounidenses desde Cuba y mantener estrecha vigilancia sobre Jiminez—, e indica que en Washington no consta su liberación ni se enviarán instrucciones a Brooke salvo que las solicite.

records.headline: Commenting editorially on Cuban and Dominican affairs, The Times of Washington dismisses
records.summary_en: Commenting editorially on Cuban and Dominican affairs, The Times of Washington dismisses the suggestion advanced by U.S. authorities in Cuba—seeking, in the paper's view, to escape blame for persecuting "so good an Administration man"—that Maximo Gomez is responsible for the affair involving Jiminez. Even if Gomez and Jiminez are reportedly no longer friendly, the editorial argues that Gomez must be counted out for financial reasons, observing pointedly that he is not worth fourteen million dollars, has no one-million-dollar cash Dominican campaign fund, and has no New York partner traveling to Lake Champlain to see the President. The paper predicts that Jiminez will likely sail again successfully and soon sit upon Heureaux's "throne," guarding the remains of Christopher Columbus in the cathedral at San Domingo City while also looking after the interests of the Smith M. Weed syndicate.
records.summary_es: En un comentario editorial sobre asuntos cubanos y dominicanos, The Times de Washington descarta la idea promovida por las autoridades estadounidenses en Cuba —en un intento, según el diario, de eludir culpas por perseguir a «tan buen hombre de la Administración»— de que Maximo Gomez sea responsable de todo el asunto relacionado con Jiminez. Aun si según se dice Gomez y Jiminez ya no mantienen amistad, el editorial sostiene que hay que descartar a Gomez por razones financieras, señalando con mordacidad que este no posee catorce millones de dólares, carece de un fondo de campaña dominicano de un millón en efectivo y no tiene un socio neoyorquino que viaje a Lake Champlain para ver al Presidente. El periódico pronostica que con toda probabilidad Jiminez volverá a zarpar con éxito y pronto ocupará el «trono» de Heureaux, custodiando los restos de Cristóbal Colón en la catedral de la ciudad de San Domingo sin olvidar tampoco velar por los intereses del sindicato de Smith M. Weed.

records.headline: A dispatch from Santiago, Cuba, in the New York Journal and Advertiser states
records.summary_en: A dispatch from Santiago, Cuba, in the New York Journal and Advertiser states that General Juan Isidro Jiminez is expected to arrive at Santiago or Manzanillo within a day or two, and reports that an American passenger aboard the steamer when Jiminez was arrested at Cienfuegos overheard him offering Dominican army commissions to two Cuban army officers. Jiminez's agents are said to be very active among Cubans in Santiago, where two Cubans believed to be in his pay are under surveillance. An accompanying August 21 dispatch from Havana adds that former Cuban soldiers and Italians continue offering their services as would-be filibusters to Jiminez's son despite his repeated statements that he does not wish to organize an expedition, while rumors say an independent group of twenty to thirty men will leave that day to fight for Jiminez in Santo Domingo if his cause prospers.
records.summary_es: Un despacho desde Santiago, Cuba, publicado en el New York Journal and Advertiser señala que se espera la llegada del general Juan Isidro Jiminez a Santiago o a Manzanillo en uno o dos días, e informa que un pasajero estadounidense que viajaba en el vapor con Jiminez cuando fue arrestado en Cienfuegos escuchó una conversación en la que este ofreció grados en el ejército dominicano a dos oficiales del ejército cubano. Se afirma que los agentes de Jiminez despliegan gran actividad entre los cubanos en Santiago, donde dos cubanos que se cree están a su sueldo se hallan bajo vigilancia. Un despacho adjunto de La Habana fechado el 21 de agosto añade que exsoldados cubanos e italianos siguen ofreciendo sus servicios como aspirantes a filibusteros al hijo de Jiminez pese a la insistencia de este en que no desea organizar ninguna expedición, mientras se rumora que un grupo independiente de entre veinte y treinta hombres partirá ese día para combatir por Jiminez en Santo Domingo si su causa prospera.

records.headline: The Denison Review, following a comment that authorities had no right
records.summary_en: The Denison Review, following a comment that authorities had no right to arrest Jiminez as an unarmed citizen apparently going to Santiago de Cuba—and that even if bound for San Domingo he would only be returning to his native country—prints an August 19 Kingston dispatch under the headline "Searching for Jiminez." Citing advices from Santo Domingo, the dispatch reports that the government there is desperately apprehensive of the momentarily expected arrival of revolutionary leader Jiminez, which would completely turn partly undecided popular opinion, and has ordered armed vessels patrolling the coast to search every strange ship and capture him under any flag, armed or not. A partially garbled August 19 dispatch from Santiago de Cuba below it notes expeditions being recruited on the north coast, orders to hold recently captured men, several expeditions getting away without interference, and a determination to enforce neutrality.

Citando informes de Santo Domingo, el despacho señala que el gobierno dominicano teme desesperadamente la llegada inminente del líder revolucionario Jiminez, la cual volcaría por completo a la opinión pública parcialmente indecisa, y ha ordenado a buques armados que patrullan la costa registrar toda embarcación extraña y capturarlo bajo cualquier bandera, armado o no. Más abajo, un despacho parcialmente mutilado desde Santiago de Cuba del 19 de agosto menciona el reclutamiento de expediciones en la costa norte, órdenes de retener a hombres capturados recientemente, la salida sin interferencia de varias expediciones y la determinación de hacer cumplir la neutralidad.

records.headline: Following a brief report via Puerto Plata, San Domingo, that Sanchez Blanco
records.summary_en: Following a brief report via Puerto Plata, San Domingo, that Sanchez Blanco and Moca have declared for the revolution and that Santiago—whose governor, General Pepin, left earlier to march against the insurgents—is expected to rise and march on La Vega, the New-York Tribune publishes a statement from Jiminez's representative in the United States, of No. 143 East Fifty-fifth Street. Speaking to a Tribune reporter, the representative expresses surprise that the prudent revolutionary chief was arrested in Cienfuegos while peacefully traveling to Santiago de Cuba, contrasting the arrest with the freedom enjoyed by liberators in monarchical London. Although Jiminez was subsequently liberated, the representative states that the moral effect has somewhat disappointed the masses, describing Jiminez as a patriot who has abandoned family, business, and everything to free his country from despotism.

records.headline: The San Francisco Call and the New York Herald, by special cable
records.summary_en: The San Francisco Call and the New York Herald, by special cable from Porto Plata dated August 24, report that the Jiminez revolution is expanding even though the uprising in Monte Christi was suppressed. Revolutionary chiefs Ramon Caceres, Horacio Vasquez, and Jose Brache—alleged to have taken part in the killing of President Heureaux—have captured San Francisco de Macoris, Lavega, and a third city under the war cry 'Vive Jiminez! Down with Paper Currency!' Rebels five miles outside Santiago plan to intercept Governor Pedro Pepin on his return from Monte Christi, while a strong government column from Cotui is advancing against the insurgents and the acting president has telegraphed that Americans in Havana arrested Jiminez. Appearing before Macoris with 500 revolutionists, Caceres, Vasquez, and Brache left their main force at the city entrance and advanced with twenty men to Governor Castillo's house to demand surrender.
records.summary_es: The San Francisco Call y el New York Herald, mediante cable especial desde Porto Plata fechado el 24 de agosto, informan que la revolución de Jiminez sigue creciendo pese a haber sido sofocado el levantamiento en Monte Christi. Los jefes revolucionarios Ramon Caceres, Horacio Vasquez y Jose Brache —a quienes se atribuye participación en la muerte del presidente Heureaux— han tomado San Francisco de Macoris, Lavega y una tercera ciudad bajo el grito de guerra «Vive Jiminez! Down with Paper Currency!». Un grupo rebelde situado a cinco millas de Santiago intentará interceptar al gobernador Pedro Pepin a su regreso de Monte Christi, mientras una fuerte columna gubernamental avanza desde Cotui contra los insurrectos y el presidente interino ha telegrafiado que los estadounidenses arrestaron a Jiminez en La Habana. Al presentarse ante Macoris con 500 revolucionarios, Caceres, Vasquez y Brache dejaron el grueso de sus tropas a la entrada de la ciudad y avanzaron con veinte hombres hasta la casa del gobernador Castillo para exigir la rendición.

records.headline: Concluding an earlier dispatch that notes no check on the eastern
records.summary_en: Concluding an earlier dispatch that notes no check on the eastern boundary and scant news from Monte Christi, where government troops and General Pepin remain, The Saint Paul Globe prints an August 24 telegram from Cape Haytien relaying word from Puerto Plata, Santo Domingo. According to this dispatch, Sanchez Blanco, near Puerto Plata, and Moca have declared in favor of the revolution, and Puerto Plata expects Santo Domingo—whose governor, General Bona, left the province earlier to march against the insurgents—to rise as well and march on La Vega. At the foot of the column, a separate headline announces that Cuban soldiers have offered their services to Jiminez.

Según este despacho, Sanchez Blanco, cerca de Puerto Plata, y Moca se han declarado a favor de la revolución, y en Puerto Plata se espera que Santo Domingo —cuyo gobernador, el general Bona, salió hace algún tiempo de la provincia para marchar contra los insurrectos— también se levante y marche sobre La Vega. Al pie de la columna, un titular aparte anuncia que soldados cubanos han ofrecido sus servicios a Jiminez.

records.headline: Quoting General Moscoso in The Evening Times, this passage recounts
records.summary_en: Quoting General Moscoso in The Evening Times, this passage recounts an 1893 mission in which Generals Morales, Moya, Luperas, and Moscoso traveled to Paris during a crisis between the Dominican government and France—sparked by the imprisonment of a French officer and a French indemnity demand of a million and a half francs—to urge Jiminez to head a revolution. Although they secured French sympathy and potential aid, needing only Jiminez's declaration and about half a million dollars, Jiminez—then at the height of his prosperity with twenty-three business houses in Santo Domingo, the United States, and Europe—refused to risk his private interests. Moscoso adds that Jiminez was ruined when President Heureaux withdrew his concessions, and State Department observers note that because the influential Moscoso has threatened to fight Jiminez to a finish, a bloody complication may follow.
records.summary_es: Citando al general Moscoso en The Evening Times, este pasaje relata una gestión de 1893 en la que los generales Morales, Moya, Luperas y el propio Moscoso viajaron a París durante una grave crisis entre el gobierno dominicano y Francia —provocada por el encarcelamiento de un oficial francés y una exigencia de indemnización de un millón y medio de francos— para instar a Jiminez a encabezar una revolución. Aunque obtuvieron la simpatía y la posible ayuda del gobierno francés, faltando solo el pronunciamiento de Jiminez y cerca de medio millón de dólares, Jiminez —entonces en la cúspide de su prosperidad con veintitrés casas comerciales en Santo Domingo, Estados Unidos y Europa— se negó a poner en riesgo sus negocios privados. Moscoso añade que Jiminez quedó arruinado cuando el presidente Heureaux le retiró sus concesiones, y en el Departamento de Estado se comenta que, dada la considerable influencia de Moscoso en Santo Domingo y su amenaza de combatir a Jiminez hasta el final, podría sobrevenir una sangrienta complicación.

records.headline: Continuing an account of insurgents taking delivery of a park
records.summary_en: Continuing an account of insurgents taking delivery of a park, fort, arsenal, and government buildings without resistance and occupying the surrounding countryside unopposed, the Richmond Dispatch describes the revolution as humane and peaceful, seemingly assuring victory for Jiminez, with no check on the eastern boundary and little known of Monte Christi, where government troops and General Pepin remain. A following Cape Haitien dispatch dated August 21 reports news from Puerto Plata, Santo Domingo, that Sanchez Blanco, near Puerto Plata, and Moca have declared for the revolution. With General Pepin, Governor of Santiago, having left the province earlier to march on the insurgents, observers in Puerto Plata expect Santiago to rise and march on La Vega.
records.summary_es: Continuando un relato sobre la entrega sin resistencia de un parque, fuerte, arsenal y edificios gubernamentales a los insurrectos y la ocupación pacífica de los alrededores, el Richmond Dispatch describe el avance de la revolución como humano y pacífico, lo que parece asegurar el triunfo de la causa de Jiminez, sin freno en la frontera oriental y con pocas noticias de Monte Christi, donde siguen las tropas del gobierno y el general Pepin. Un despacho posterior desde Cabo Haitiano, fechado el 21 de agosto, transmite noticias de Puerto Plata, Santo Domingo, según las cuales Sanchez Blanco, cerca de Puerto Plata, y Moca se han declarado a favor de la revolución. Dado que el general Pepin, gobernador de Santiago, partió hace tiempo de la provincia para marchar contra los insurrectos, en Puerto Plata se cree que Santiago se levantará y marchará sobre La Vega.

records.headline: Advices from Santiago, Cuba, dated August 21 in the Chariton Courier state
records.summary_en: Advices from Santiago, Cuba, dated August 21 in the Chariton Courier state that General Leonard Wood, governor of Santiago province, has been instructed from Washington to hold until further orders the Dominican filibuster captured at Baracca. Following reports that an expedition bound for Santo Domingo is expected to depart near the eastern extremity of Cuba, the government tug Adonis at Guantanamo will patrol the Cuban coast to block this and other expeditions. Because the Dominicans possess only sailing vessels, the dispatch adds, they cannot maintain an effective guard against invaders.
records.summary_es: Noticias procedentes de Santiago de Cuba, fechadas el 21 de agosto en el Chariton Courier, indican que el general Leonard Wood, gobernador de la provincia de Santiago, ha recibido instrucciones de Washington de retener hasta nueva orden al filibustero dominicano capturado en Baracca. Ante informes de que se espera la salida de una expedición hacia Santo Domingo desde las inmediaciones del extremo oriental de Cuba, el remolcador gubernamental Adonis, surto en Guantánamo, patrullará la costa cubana para impedir la partida de esta y otras expediciones. El despacho añade que, como los dominicanos solo disponen de embarcaciones de vela, no pueden establecer una vigilancia eficaz contra los invasores.

records.summary_en: The Boletín Mercantil de Puerto Rico, within a column of English-language news briefs, reports a declaration by President Tiresias Simón Sam of the Republic of Hayti regarding the conflict in Santo Domingo. records.headline: Opening with word of fighting in which government troops reportedly
records.summary_en: Opening with word of fighting in which government troops reportedly suffered heavy casualties while well-positioned insurgents sustained only slight loss and continued receiving reinforcements, the New-York Tribune prints an August 25 dispatch from Kingston, Jamaica, summarizing Dominican mail advices. According to those dispatches, the government of San Domingo is paralyzed while the revolutionary movement has achieved strong organization, broad popularity, and enthusiasm across the republic, with Santiago preparing to declare for Jiminez and even loyal Santo Domingo experiencing revolutionary demonstrations, passport confiscations, and arrests. Describing the movement as national rather than merely political, the report states that the public awaits only Jiminez's arrival for many remaining generals and much of the army to join him, leaving the government reliant solely on the navy to capture Jiminez and break up the revolt.
records.summary_es: Tras iniciar con noticias de combates en los que las tropas gubernamentales habrían sufrido fuertes bajas mientras los insurrectos, bien posicionados, tuvieron pérdidas leves y seguían recibiendo refuerzos, el New-York Tribune publica un despacho del 25 de agosto desde Kingston, Jamaica, que resume informes recibidos por correo dominicano. Según dichos informes, el gobierno de San Domingo se encuentra paralizado mientras el movimiento revolucionario ha alcanzado gran organización, amplia popularidad y entusiasmo en toda la república, con Santiago preparándose para declararse por Jiminez e incluso la leal Santo Domingo registrando manifestaciones revolucionarias, confiscación de pasaportes de viajeros y varios arrestos. Al calificar el movimiento de nacional y no meramente político, el despacho señala que el pueblo solo aguarda la llegada de Jiminez para que muchos de los generales restantes y gran parte del ejército se le unan, dejando a la marina como único apoyo del gobierno para capturar a Jiminez y desarticular la revolución.

records.headline: The Santa Fe New Mexican, gathering August 28 dispatches from several points
records.summary_en: The Santa Fe New Mexican, gathering August 28 dispatches from several points, tracks rebel advances in the Dominican Republic, beginning with reports that insurgents are cutting off communication with Monte Christo and that General Patino, the Dominican government minister sent into the Cibao territory, has joined the partisans of revolutionary leader Jiminez. Advices from Puerto Plata via Martinique note that although Santiago de Los Cabelleros has not surrendered, its townspeople oppose the government, while a New York item reports that revolutionary representative Andriano Grullon received a Santiago de Cuba cablegram signed by La Marche—identified here as the Jiminez representative at Santo Domingo—claiming that revolutionists are in the capital and the government has surrendered. A separate dispatch from Santo Domingo states that insurgents led by Ramon Caceres and Horacio Vosquez hold San Francisco de Macoris, 'La Vegal, Real,' and Cotuy and are marching on the capital, prompting the government to send a commission including C. N. Moya, Leonte, Reynoso, and three other members whose names are garbled in print to ascertain their demands.

records.summary_en: The Santa Fe New Mexican, continuing its coverage of the Dominican crisis, reports that pending the return of a mission, not a single shot has yet been fired, though if no agreement is reached the government is expected to take energetic measures and serious trouble may follow. Both the United States cruiser New Orleans and the French cruiser Cecille are in port, along with all of the Dominican warships, which may depart at any moment. Meanwhile, Puerto Plata, Santiago, Mora, and Monte Christo are reported quiet, the revolutionists are said not to have proclaimed any special candidate, and telegraph communication is generally interrupted.

records.headline: In the Evening Star, an opening report from the Dominican Republic notes
records.summary_en: In the Evening Star, an opening report from the Dominican Republic notes that although Santiago de los Caballeros has not surrendered, its townspeople openly oppose the government, while at the correspondent's location General Juan Garrido's government troops are entrenched on two hills about eight kilometers from the city as well-equipped sympathizers—including Dr. Dionicio—leave to join the insurgents and more than 100 of Garrido's men desert with arms and supplies. The dispatch adds that the revolution is advancing rapidly and bloodlessly in Monte Christi while flourishing crops make rural residents anxious for a quick end to the conflict. A following August 28 dispatch from Cape Haytien, Hayti, reports that General Pepin, returning from relieving Santiago, was defeated by Dominican revolutionists and forced back to Monte Christi, that Mao and part of Guayacanes have declared for the revolution and cut off communication with Monte Christi, and that Dominican minister General Patino, sent into the Cibago territory, has joined Jiminez's partisans.
records.summary_es: En el Evening Star, un primer informe desde la República Dominicana señala que, aunque Santiago de los Caballeros no se ha rendido, sus habitantes se oponen abiertamente al gobierno, mientras que en la localidad del corresponsal las fuerzas gubernamentales del general Juan Garrido están atrincheradas en dos colinas a unos ocho kilómetros de la ciudad, al tiempo que simpatizantes bien equipados —entre ellos el doctor Dionicio— salen para unirse a los insurrectos y más de 100 hombres de Garrido han desertado con armas y provisiones. El reporte añade que la revolución avanza con rapidez y sin derramamiento de sangre en Monte Christi, mientras la prosperidad de las cosechas lleva a la población rural a desear un pronto desenlace. Un despacho posterior del 28 de agosto desde Cabo Haitiano, Haití, informa que el general Pepin, al regresar de socorrer a Santiago, fue derrotado por los revolucionarios dominicanos y obligado a replegarse hacia Monte Christi, que Mao y una sección de Guayacanes se declararon por la revolución cortando la comunicación con Monte Christi, y que el ministro dominicano general Patino, enviado al territorio del Cibago, se unió a los partidarios de Jiminez.

An opening continuation notes that General Juan Guarrido's troops are entrenched on two hills eight kilometers outside the city while well-equipped sympathizers, including a physician, leave to join the insurgents, more than 100 of Guarrido's men desert with arms and supplies, and the revolution advances bloodlessly in Monte Christi amid flourishing crops. Up until noon not a single shot had been fired, while the U.S. cruiser New Orleans, the French cruiser Cecille, and all Dominican warships lie in port, and Puerto Plata, Santiago, Mora, and Monte Christi are reported quiet.

records.headline: Three dispatches in The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer cover naval
records.summary_en: Three dispatches in The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer cover naval precautions, General Juan Isidro Jimines's arrival in Cuba, and rebel gains in Santo Domingo. An opening segment reports that no shot has yet been fired at the port, where the U.S. cruiser New Orleans, a French cruiser, and all Dominican warships are anchored, while Puerto Plata, Santiago, Mora, and Monte Christi are quiet, the insurgents have proclaimed no special candidate, and telegraph lines are generally interrupted. A dispatch from Santiago de Cuba relates that General Juan Isidro Jimines, revolutionary aspirant to the Santo Domingo presidency, arrived with his two sons on the south coast boat but was barred from landing—refusing a press interview out of annoyance—while a large crowd of Dominican sympathizers and refugees was indignantly denied permission to board and salute him. Finally, an August 28 dispatch from Cape Haytien, Hayti, reports General Pepin's defeat and retreat to Monte Christi after relieving Santiago, the declaration of Mao and part of Guayacanes for the revolution, and a subhead noting that another general has joined the insurgents.
records.summary_es: Tres despachos en The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer abordan precauciones navales, la llegada del general Juan Isidro Jimines a Cuba y avances rebeldes en Santo Domingo. Un primer fragmento informa que aún no se ha disparado un solo tiro en el puerto, donde se encuentran el crucero estadounidense New Orleans, un crucero francés y todos los buques de guerra dominicanos, mientras se reporta calma en Puerto Plata, Santiago, Mora y Monte Christi, los insurrectos no han proclamado candidato especial y las comunicaciones telegráficas están generalmente interrumpidas. Un despacho desde Santiago de Cuba relata que el general Juan Isidro Jimines, aspirante revolucionario a la presidencia de Santo Domingo, llegó con sus dos hijos en el vapor de la costa sur pero no se le permitió desembarcar —negándose molesto a conceder una entrevista de prensa—, mientras a una numerosa multitud de simpatizantes y refugiados dominicanos se le impidió abordar el buque para saludarlo, provocando su indignación. Por último, un despacho del 28 de agosto desde Cabo Haitiano, Haití, informa la derrota del general Pepin y su retirada hacia Monte Christi tras socorrer a Santiago, el pronunciamiento de Mao y parte de Guayacanes por la revolución, y un subtítulo que señala el paso de otro general a las filas insurrectas.

records.headline: The Saint Paul Globe prints an August dispatch from Cape Haitien
records.summary_en: The Saint Paul Globe prints an August dispatch from Cape Haitien, Haiti, reporting rebel gains in Santo Domingo, after a brief closing fragment noting that an indignant crowd of Dominican sympathizers was refused permission in an attempt to board a steamer and salute Jiminez. According to this account, General Poppy, returning from relieving Santiago, was defeated by Dominican revolutionists and forced to retreat to Monte Cristo, Maio and a section of Guayacanos have declared for the revolution and cut off communication with Monte Cristo, and General Patento, the minister sent by the Dominican government into the Cibao territory, has joined Jiminez's partisans. A following August 28 New York dispatch adds that revolutionary representative Andriano Grullon has received an August 27 cablegram from La Marche, the Jiminez representative at Santiago de Cuba, reporting revolution in the capital and the government's surrender, though Grullon has received no further details.
records.summary_es: The Saint Paul Globe publica un despacho de agosto desde Cabo Haitiano, Haití, sobre avances rebeldes en Santo Domingo, tras un breve fragmento final que señala la negativa de permiso y la consiguiente indignación de una multitud de simpatizantes dominicanos que buscaba subir a un vapor para saludar a Jiminez. Según este relato, el general Poppy, al regresar de socorrer a Santiago, fue derrotado por los revolucionarios dominicanos y obligado a retirarse hacia Monte Cristo, Maio y una sección de Guayacanos se han declarado a favor de la revolución cortando la comunicación con Monte Cristo, y el general Patento, ministro enviado por el gobierno dominicano al territorio del Cibao, se unió a los partidarios de Jiminez. Un despacho posterior del 28 de agosto desde Nueva York añade que el representante revolucionario Andriano Grullon recibió un cablegrama del 27 de agosto enviado por La Marche, representante de Jiminez en Santiago de Cuba, informando revolución en la capital y la rendición del gobierno, aunque Grullon aún no cuenta con más detalles.

records.headline: Dispatches in The Times of Richmond report the defection of a Dominican
records.summary_en: Dispatches in The Times of Richmond report the defection of a Dominican minister, growing opposition to the government, and a rumored surrender. Opening lines state that revolutionists are cutting off communication with Monte Christi and that General Patino, the minister sent into the Cibao territory by the Dominican government, has joined Jiminez's partisans. A Puerto Plata dispatch of August 21 sent via Martinique adds that townspeople in Santiago de Los Caballeros openly oppose the government, that General Juan Garruido's forces are entrenched on two hills about eight kilometers from Puerto Plata while local sympathizers leave to join the insurgents, and that the revolution advances bloodlessly in Monte Christi amid flourishing crops. Finally, a New York dispatch reports that revolutionary representative Andriano Grullon received an August 27 cablegram from La Marche at Santiago de Cuba announcing revolution in the capital and the surrender of the government, with no details yet received.
records.summary_es: Despachos publicados en The Times de Richmond informan sobre la defección de un ministro dominicano, la creciente oposición al gobierno y una supuesta rendición. Las líneas iniciales señalan que los revolucionarios cortan la comunicación con Monte Christi y que el general Patino, ministro enviado al territorio del Cibao por el gobierno dominicano, se ha unido a los partidarios de Jiminez. Un despacho de Puerto Plata del 21 de agosto, transmitido vía Martinica, añade que los habitantes de Santiago de Los Caballeros se oponen abiertamente al gobierno, que las fuerzas del general Juan Garruido están atrincheradas en dos colinas a unos ocho kilómetros de Puerto Plata mientras simpatizantes locales salen a unirse a los insurrectos, y que la revolución avanza sin derramamiento de sangre en Monte Christi entre cosechas florecientes. Por último, un despacho de Nueva York indica que el representante revolucionario Andriano Grullon recibió un cablegrama del 27 de agosto enviado por La Marche desde Santiago de Cuba anunciando revolución en la capital y la rendición del gobierno, sin que aún se hayan recibido detalles.

records.headline: Three reports in the Evening Times-Republican describe spreading
records.summary_en: Three reports in the Evening Times-Republican describe spreading insurgency and rebel territorial control in the Dominican Republic. An opening segment states that insurgents have cut all telegraph lines to the island's interior, Governor Llonas of the La Vega district has gone over to the revolutionists with many soldiers, Dominican gunboats have entered the river amid rumors that the president and cabinet may flee to Porto Rico in an emergency, and the U.S. cruiser New Orleans and a French cruiser stand ready to land marines to protect the consulate if rioting erupts. A Cape Haytien dispatch of August 29 reports that General Peppin was defeated while returning from relieving Santiago and retreated to Monte Christi, that Mao and part of Guayacanes have declared for the revolution and cut off Monte Christi, and that Dominican minister General Patino in the Cibao territory has joined Jiminez's partisans. Finally, an August 29 Washington dispatch quotes a cable from Consul Simpson at Porto Plata, Santo Domingo, stating that Porto Plata surrendered and that all towns in his district except Monte Christi are held by the revolutionists.
records.summary_es: Tres informes publicados en el Evening Times-Republican describen la expansión de la insurgencia y el control territorial rebelde en la República Dominicana. Un fragmento inicial señala que los insurrectos han cortado todas las líneas telegráficas hacia el interior de la isla, que el gobernador Llonas del distrito de La Vega se pasó a los revolucionarios con numerosos soldados, que cañoneras dominicanas entraron en el río entre rumores de que el presidente y el gabinete huirían a Porto Rico en caso de emergencia, y que el crucero estadounidense New Orleans y un crucero francés están listos para desembarcar infantes de marina a fin de proteger el consulado si estallan disturbios. Un despacho desde Cabo Haitiano del 29 de agosto informa que el general Peppin fue derrotado al regresar de socorrer a Santiago y se retiró a Monte Christi, que Mao y parte de Guayacanes se declararon por la revolución aislando a Monte Christi, y que el ministro dominicano general Patino en el territorio del Cibao se unió a los partidarios de Jiminez. Por último, un despacho de Washington del 29 de agosto cita un cable del cónsul Simpson en Porto Plata, Santo Domingo, según el cual Porto Plata se rindió y todos los pueblos de su distrito, salvo Monte Christi, están en poder de los revolucionarios.

records.headline: Well-equipped sympathizers left an unnamed city to join insurgents
records.summary_en: Well-equipped sympathizers left an unnamed city to join insurgents positioned in the hills about eight kilometers away, dispatches in The Record-Union report, while more than 100 men with arms and supplies deserted to the enemy. In Monte Christi the revolution is advancing rapidly without battles as the insurgents wish to avoid bloodshed, and with crops flourishing, rural residents want a quick end to the uprising so agriculture will not suffer. An August 28 dispatch from San Domingo adds that revolutionists—some led by Horacio Vasquez and another commander—hold three towns, including San Francisco de Macoris and Cotuy, and are marching on the capital, where not a single shot has yet been fired and the government has sent a commission to learn their demands before taking action. The U.S. cruiser New Orleans, the French cruiser Cecille, and all Dominican warships are in port at San Domingo, where Puerto Plata, Santiago, and Monte Christi are among the places reported quiet and the revolutionists are said not to have proclaimed any special candidate.
records.summary_es: Simpatizantes bien equipados salieron de una ciudad no identificada para unirse a los insurrectos apostados en las colinas a unos ocho kilómetros de distancia, informan despachos publicados en The Record-Union, mientras más de 100 hombres con armas y pertrechos desertaron hacia el enemigo. En Monte Christi la revolución avanza con rapidez sin combates, pues los insurrectos desean evitar el derramamiento de sangre, y ante la abundancia de las cosechas la población rural desea un pronto fin del levantamiento para no perjudicar la agricultura. Un despacho fechado en San Domingo el 28 de agosto añade que los revolucionarios —algunos encabezados por Horacio Vasquez y otro jefe— ocupan tres poblaciones, entre ellas San Francisco de Macoris y Cotuy, y marchan sobre la capital, donde aún no se ha disparado un solo tiro y el gobierno ha enviado una comisión para conocer sus demandas antes de actuar. El crucero estadounidense New Orleans, el crucero francés Cecille y todos los buques de guerra dominicanos se encuentran en el puerto de San Domingo, donde se informa que Puerto Plata, Santiago y Monte Christi figuran entre las localidades tranquilas y se asegura que los revolucionarios no han proclamado ningún candidato especial.

records.headline: An August 29 dispatch from Santiago in Foster's Daily Democrat reports
records.summary_en: An August 29 dispatch from Santiago in Foster's Daily Democrat reports that General Jiminez, the revolutionary aspirant to the presidency of Santo Domingo, arrived there the previous day with his two sons aboard the south coast boat, but authorities refused to let him land. Greatly annoyed by the refusal, Jiminez declined to grant a newspaper interview, claiming that the press invariably misrepresented him. Authorities likewise denied permission to a large crowd of Dominican sympathizers and refugees who tried to board the steamer to salute him, prompting open expressions of indignation.
records.summary_es: Un despacho fechado en Santiago el 29 de agosto en Foster's Daily Democrat informa que el general Jiminez, aspirante revolucionario a la presidencia de Santo Domingo, llegó allí el día anterior con sus dos hijos en el vapor de la costa sur, pero las autoridades no le permitieron desembarcar. Sumamente molesto por la negativa, Jiminez se negó a conceder una entrevista periodística, alegando que la prensa invariablemente lo tergiversaba. Las autoridades también negaron permiso a una numerosa multitud de simpatizantes y refugiados dominicanos que intentaron subir a bordo del vapor para saludarlo, lo que provocó abiertas muestras de indignación.

records.headline: Reports in the New York Journal and Advertiser state that a Dominican government
records.summary_en: Reports in the New York Journal and Advertiser state that a Dominican government minister, having failed in his mission, has reportedly joined the partisans of revolutionary leader Jiminez. An August 28 dispatch from Puerto Plata via Martinique notes that although Santiago de los Caballeros has not surrendered, its townspeople openly oppose the government; government troops sit entrenched on two hills about eight kilometers outside the city, more than 100 men have deserted to the enemy with arms and supplies, and Dr. Dionicio and many well-equipped residents have left the city to join the insurgents. Advancing rapidly toward Monte Christi while seeking to avoid battle, the insurgents welcome recruits and promise immunity to all who lay down their arms, while farmers amid flourishing crops ask for peace at any price. A separate August dispatch from Santiago de Cuba reports that General Jiminez, revolutionary aspirant to the Dominican presidency, arrived there that day with his two sons on the South Coast boat, was exceedingly annoyed when barred from landing, and refused a press interview while refugees from Santo Domingo tried to board the boat to salute him.
records.summary_es: Informes publicados en el New York Journal and Advertiser señalan que un ministro del gobierno dominicano, tras fracasar en su misión, se habría unido a los partidarios del líder revolucionario Jiminez. Un despacho fechado el 28 de agosto en Puerto Plata vía Martinica indica que, aunque Santiago de los Caballeros no se ha rendido, sus habitantes se oponen abiertamente al gobierno; las fuerzas gubernamentales están atrincheradas en dos colinas a unos ocho kilómetros de la ciudad, más de 100 hombres han desertado hacia el enemigo con armas y suministros, y el Dr. Dionicio junto con numerosas personas bien equipadas han salido de la ciudad para sumarse a los insurrectos. Mientras avanzan rápidamente hacia Monte Christi procurando evitar combates, los insurrectos reciben reclutas y prometen inmunidad a todos los que depongan las armas, en tanto los agricultores, con cosechas florecientes, piden la paz a cualquier precio. Otro despacho de agosto desde Santiago de Cuba informa que el general Jiminez, aspirante revolucionario a la presidencia dominicana, llegó allí ese día con sus dos hijos en el vapor de la costa sur, se mostró sumamente molesto al impedírsele desembarcar y rechazó conceder entrevistas mientras refugiados de Santo Domingo intentaban abordar la embarcación para saludarlo.

records.headline: The New York Journal and Advertiser, continuing its coverage of Dominican
records.summary_en: The New York Journal and Advertiser, continuing its coverage of Dominican affairs, opens mid-statement with references to the town where President Heureaux was assassinated, Santiago fifteen miles away, and Monte Christi in the north, before quoting an unnamed speaker who dismisses reports from Santiago de Cuba as untrue. The speaker notes that Santo Domingo is a south-coast seaport with an army of about 4,000 well-equipped men and argues that the U.S. government would know if trouble had occurred there. The article adds that the recent hurricane broke the cable between Cape Haytien and Puerto Plata, forcing dispatches onto two roundabout substitute routes—either via Halifax, Bermuda, Kingston, St. Thomas, Martinique, Puerto Plata, and overland to Santo Domingo City, or via Lisbon, Para in Brazil, Martinique, and Puerto Plata. General Abelardo A. Moscoso is also quoted as stating the previous day that he opens the absent Dominican consul-general's mail and telegraphic dispatches and has no news of the fall of Santo Domingo.
records.summary_es: El New York Journal and Advertiser, continuando su cobertura de los asuntos dominicanos, inicia a mitad de párrafo con menciones de la localidad donde fue asesinado el presidente Heureaux, de Santiago a quince millas de distancia y de Monte Christi en el norte, antes de citar a un declarante no identificado que descarta como falso el informe procedente de Santiago de Cuba. El declarante señala que Santo Domingo es un puerto marítimo de la costa sur con un ejército de unos 4,000 hombres bien equipados y sostiene que el gobierno de Estados Unidos sabría si allí hubiesen ocurrido disturbios. El artículo añade que el reciente huracán rompió el cable entre Cabo Haitiano y Puerto Plata, obligando a transmitir los despachos por dos extensas rutas sustitutas: ya sea vía Halifax, Bermudas, Kingston, Saint Thomas, Martinica, Puerto Plata y por tierra hasta la ciudad de Santo Domingo, o bien vía Lisboa, Pará en Brasil, Martinica y Puerto Plata. También se cita al general Abelardo A. Moscoso, quien declaró el día anterior que abre la correspondencia y los despachos telegráficos del cónsul general dominicano durante su ausencia y que no tiene noticia alguna sobre la caída de Santo Domingo.

records.headline: The Washington Evening Star, writing editorially on Dominican politics
records.summary_en: The Washington Evening Star, writing editorially on Dominican politics following Heureaux's assassination, observes that while Heureaux lived, his summary methods of discouraging rivals inside San Domingo allowed the exiled Jiminez to pose unchallenged from abroad as leader of the opposition and a martyr to his ambitions. With Heureaux's death opening the field, however, the paper notes that Jiminez finds in exile that other contenders exist. Once the revolutionists overthrow the existing administration and seize the machinery of government, the Star predicts that choosing a new head of state will cause friction, questioning whether Jiminez—who has taken no part in the fighting or dangers—will hold as strong a claim as a successful general in the field. The editorial warns that prolonged strife may follow unless San Domingo brings forward a ruler as capable as Heureaux of holding an administration together against both secret and open opposition.
records.summary_es: El Evening Star de Washington, en un comentario editorial sobre la política dominicana tras el asesinato de Heureaux, observa que, mientras vivió Heureaux, sus métodos sumarios para desalentar rivales dentro de San Domingo permitieron al exiliado Jiminez presentarse sin disputa desde el exterior como líder de la oposición y mártir de sus ambiciones. Sin embargo, ahora que el magnicidio ha abierto el panorama, el diario señala que Jiminez descubre desde el exilio que existen otros aspirantes. Una vez que los revolucionarios derroquen a la administración actual y tomen la maquinaria del gobierno, el Star prevé que la elección de un nuevo jefe de Estado provocará fricciones, y se pregunta si Jiminez —quien no ha participado en las luchas ni en los peligros— tendrá tanto derecho a la preferencia como algún general victorioso en campaña. El editorial advierte que podrían sobrevenir luchas prolongadas a menos que surja en San Domingo un gobernante tan capaz como Heureaux de mantener intacta su administración frente a la oposición secreta y abierta.

records.headline: Reporting an interview in which General Jiminez spoke freely
records.summary_en: Reporting an interview in which General Jiminez spoke freely that day, New Haven's Daily Morning Journal and Courier relates his statement that after the assassination of President Heureaux he cabled his friends in Santo Domingo to take no action until his arrival, and that while the main revolutionary forces complied, his detention by the Americans forced a general outbreak that would likely succeed immediately and certainly within ten days of his arrival. Jiminez stated that cabled word received that day showed the revolutionists holding practically the entire republic except the capital, Santo Domingo, and while calling General Gomez his "particular friend," he denied that Gomez had any involvement in Dominican affairs. He criticized General Wood for halting a recent expedition organized at Baracoa and declined to say whether other expeditions planned to depart. Speaking of Santo Domingo's resources and of popular exasperation with the old government's corruption, Jiminez responded with feeling to a toast to "The future president of Santo Domingo," while a close inspection of his trunks found no arms.
records.summary_es: Al reseñar una entrevista en la que el general Jiminez habló con franqueza ese día, The Daily Morning Journal and Courier de New Haven recoge su declaración de que, tras el asesinato del presidente Heureaux, telegrafió a sus amigos en Santo Domingo para que no hicieran nada hasta su llegada, y que aunque el grueso de las fuerzas revolucionarias acató el pedido, su detención por los estadounidenses precipitó un levantamiento general que probablemente triunfaría de inmediato y con certeza dentro de los diez días posteriores a su llegada. Jiminez afirmó haber recibido ese día informes por cable según los cuales los revolucionarios controlaban prácticamente toda la república salvo la capital, Santo Domingo, y aunque llamó al general Gomez su «amigo particular», negó que este tuviera participación alguna en los asuntos dominicanos. Criticó además al general Wood por impedir la salida de una expedición organizada recientemente en Baracoa y evitó precisar si había otras proyectadas. Tras referirse a los recursos de Santo Domingo y a la exasperación popular ante la corrupción del antiguo gobierno, Jiminez respondió con emoción a un brindis por «El futuro presidente de Santo Domingo», mientras que una revisión minuciosa de sus baúles no halló armas.

records.summary_en: Although he had previously complained of always being misrepresented by the press, General Jiminez spoke freely that day in an interview printed by the Kansas City Journal, stating that after President Heureaux's assassination he cabled his friends in Santo Domingo to do nothing until he arrived. While the main body of revolutionary forces complied, Jiminez asserted that his detention by the Americans precipitated a general outbreak that would probably succeed and would certainly achieve its aim within ten days of his arrival in the country. He said cabled news received that day showed the revolutionists holding practically the entire republic except the capital, San Domingo, and while calling General Gomez his "particular friend," he stated that Gomez had no involvement in Dominican affairs. Jiminez also discussed Santo Domingo's conditions and resources, remarked that the old government's corruption had long made the entire people eager for him to return and lead the insurrection, responded warmly to a toast to "the future president of Santo Domingo," and had his twenty-six trunks closely examined with no arms found.
records.summary_es: Aunque antes había alegado que la prensa siempre lo tergiversaba, el general Jiminez habló con franqueza ese día en una entrevista publicada por el Kansas City Journal, señalando que tras el asesinato del presidente Heureaux telegrafió a sus amigos en Santo Domingo para que no hicieran nada hasta su llegada. Si bien la parte principal de las fuerzas revolucionarias acató el pedido, Jiminez sostuvo que su detención por los estadounidenses desencadenó un levantamiento general que probablemente triunfaría y que sin duda lograría su propósito dentro de los diez días siguientes a su llegada al país. Afirmó que informes por cable recibidos ese día indicaban que los revolucionarios controlaban prácticamente toda la república salvo la capital, San Domingo, y aunque llamó al general Gomez su «amigo particular», precisó que este no tenía participación alguna en los asuntos dominicanos. Jiminez habló además sobre las condiciones y recursos de Santo Domingo, señaló que la corrupción del antiguo gobierno había llevado durante muchos años a todo el pueblo a desear su regreso para encabezar la insurrección, respondió con emoción a un brindis por «el futuro presidente de Santo Domingo», y sus veintiséis baúles fueron examinados minuciosamente sin hallarse armas.
