records.headline: Commenting editorially on what it calls an American "epidemic of expansion,"
records.summary_en: Commenting editorially on what it calls an American "epidemic of expansion," Austin's Hawaiian Weekly warns against extending United States rule over another Antillean island amid the current Dominican crisis. Referring to the shared island in its own phrasing as "Santo Domingo, or Haiti, as perhaps it should be called" and later as "the dual island," the editorial characterizes its history from early Spanish colonization through slave importation, buccaneering, French Revolution-era upheavals, Toussaint L'Ouverture, and the later Dominican Republic as one of almost continuous warfare and bloodshed. Fearing that the crisis may revive the annexation sentiment encouraged under President Grant, the paper hopes such a course will again be opposed as contrary to American traditions, arguing in racialist terms before breaking off that a "dominant race" can exert influence without resorting to the "hazardous expedient of annexation."
records.summary_es: Comentando editorialmente lo que denomina una «epidemia de expansión» estadounidense, Austin's Hawaiian Weekly advierte contra extender el dominio de Estados Unidos sobre otra isla antillana en medio de la crisis actual. Al referirse en sus propios términos a la isla compartida como «Santo Domingo, o Haití, como quizá debería llamarse» y más adelante como «la isla dual», el editorial describe su historia —desde la temprana colonización española, la introducción de esclavos, los bucaneros y las convulsiones de la época de la Revolución Francesa hasta Toussaint L'Ouverture y la posterior República Dominicana— como un escenario de guerra y derramamiento de sangre casi continuos. Ante el temor de que la crisis reavive el sentimiento anexionista alentado por el presidente Grant, el periódico espera que dicha vía vuelva a rechazarse por contraria a las tradiciones estadounidenses y sostiene en términos racialistas, antes de interrumpirse el pasaje, que una «raza dominante» puede ejercer influencia sin recurrir al «peligroso expediente de la anexión».

records.headline: Profiling Dominican presidential aspirant Jiminez, The Maryville Times states
records.summary_en: Profiling Dominican presidential aspirant Jiminez, The Maryville Times states that he was once the wealthiest man in San Domingo until M. Heureaux, upon being elected president, told him the country could not hold two such big individuals, prompting Jiminez to leave. When the Spanish-American War broke out, the exiled capitalist invaded San Domingo with a strong expedition. According to the paper's allegation, after failing as a general he decided to have President Heureaux assassinated, a plot it says was recently carried out as civil war now continues in San Domingo.
records.summary_es: Al trazar el perfil del aspirante presidencial dominicano Jiminez, The Maryville Times señala que alguna vez fue el hombre más rico de San Domingo hasta que M. Heureaux, al ser elegido presidente, le advirtió que en el país no cabían dos figuras tan grandes, lo que llevó a Jiminez a marcharse. Al estallar la guerra hispano-estadounidense, el capitalista exiliado invadió San Domingo con una fuerte expedición. Según alega el periódico, tras fracasar como general resolvió hacer asesinar al presidente Heureaux, plan que afirma se ejecutó recientemente mientras la guerra civil continúa en San Domingo.

records.headline: Reviewing political divisions in the Dominican Republic, the Southern Christian Advocate observes
records.summary_en: Reviewing political divisions in the Dominican Republic, the Southern Christian Advocate observes that the position of President Jiminez, occupying the place of the recently assassinated President Heureaux, remains unsettled. Of the two dominant parties—both styled "Liberals"—the "Young Liberals" seek to come under direct United States influence, whereas the "Old Fogy Liberals" oppose it, a generational split the paper likens to the biblical days of Rehoboam (1 Kings 12:14). Adding geographic notes, it states that the Dominican Republic and Hayti occupy one of the Antilles, with the Dominican Republic much the larger at 18,000 square miles and 250,000 inhabitants (described as chiefly Black and mulatto), and names San Domingo as the capital, whose printed population figure is illegible.
records.summary_es: Al examinar las divisiones políticas en la República Dominicana, el Southern Christian Advocate observa que la situación del presidente Jiminez —quien ocupa el lugar del recientemente asesinado presidente Heureaux— dista mucho de estar consolidada. De los dos partidos dominantes, ambos denominados «Liberales», los «Jóvenes Liberales» desean situarse bajo la influencia directa de Estados Unidos, mientras que los llamados «Liberales Anticuados» («Old Fogy Liberals») se oponen a ello, pugna que el periódico compara con los tiempos bíblicos de Roboam (1 Reyes 12:14). En apuntes geográficos, añade que la República Dominicana y Hayti comparten una de las Antillas, siendo la primera mucho mayor con 18,000 millas cuadradas y 250,000 habitantes —descritos principalmente como negros y mulatos—, y menciona a San Domingo como la capital, cuya cifra impresa de población resulta ilegible.

records.headline: Surveying the geography and society of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Surveying the geography and society of the Dominican Republic, an article in The Bourbon News notes that the country occupies the eastern and larger part of the island of Santo Domingo or Haiti, claims an area of 18,045 square miles with mountain chains and fertile interior plains, and has a population predominantly of mixed Indian, Spanish, and Black heritage alongside some inhabitants of pure African descent and relatively few whites. Spanish is the official language—with French and English spoken in coastal towns—and Roman Catholicism is the state religion alongside tolerated faiths, while agriculture, cattle raising, and timber cutting yield exports of sugar, coffee, tobacco, hides, and cabinet woods, and the capital, Santo Domingo, stands at the mouth of the Ozama River, founded by Bartholomew Columbus. After a column break, the passage condemns an unnamed Dominican president under whom quadrennial elections were a farce, Congress, judges, and governors acted as his creatures, and extravagant habits brought the republic to bankruptcy and ruin.
records.summary_es: Al describir la geografía y la sociedad de la República Dominicana, un artículo de The Bourbon News señala que el país ocupa la parte oriental y más extensa de la isla de Santo Domingo o Haití, reclama una superficie de 18,045 millas cuadradas con cadenas montañosas y fértiles llanuras interiores, y cuenta con una población mayoritariamente de ascendencia mixta indígena, española y negra, junto con algunos habitantes de pura ascendencia africana y relativamente pocos blancos. El español es el idioma oficial —hablándose francés e inglés en los pueblos costeros— y el catolicismo romano es la religión del Estado con tolerancia de otros cultos, mientras la agricultura, la ganadería y el corte de madera generan exportaciones de azúcar, café, tabaco, cueros y maderas preciosas, ubicándose la capital, Santo Domingo, en la desembocadura del río Ozama, fundada por Bartolomé Colón. Tras un salto de columna, el pasaje condena a un presidente dominicano no nombrado bajo cuyo mando las elecciones cuatrienales eran una farsa, el Congreso, los jueces y los gobernadores eran hechuras suyas, y sus hábitos extravagantes condujeron a la república a la bancarrota y la ruina.

records.headline: Concluding a commentary in The Bourbon News, the writer discusses
records.summary_en: Concluding a commentary in The Bourbon News, the writer discusses the prospective election to the presidency of Don Juan Isidro Jimenes, a wealthy native whom Heureaux had expatriated several years earlier and who returned to Santo Domingo leading a powerful band of revolutionists. The article notes insinuations that Heureaux was assassinated by one of Jimenes's henchmen, adding that even the new leader's closest friends have not troubled to deny the rumor. Addressing reports that a bill to annex the Dominican Republic will be introduced in the upcoming session of the United States Congress, the writer warns that its approval by the Senate and President would create "another Philippine elephant," asserting that Dominican hatred of everything American is genuine and deep.
records.summary_es: Al concluir un comentario en The Bourbon News, el autor examina la probable elección a la presidencia de don Juan Isidro Jimenes, acaudalado nativo de la isla a quien Heureaux había expatriado años atrás y que regresó a Santo Domingo al frente de un poderoso contingente revolucionario. El artículo recoge insinuaciones de que Heureaux fue asesinado por uno de los partidarios de Jimenes, y añade que ni siquiera los amigos más íntimos del nuevo caudillo se han molestado hasta ahora en desmentirlas. Ante los rumores de que en la próxima sesión del Congreso de Estados Unidos se presentará un proyecto de ley para anexar la República Dominicana, el autor advierte que su aprobación por el Senado y el presidente acarrearía «otro elefante filipino», asegurando que el odio de los dominicanos hacia todo lo estadounidense es genuino y profundo.

records.headline: Opening mid-sentence on the colonial history of Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: Opening mid-sentence on the colonial history of Santo Domingo, The Nebraska Advertiser describes the city as the oldest European settlement and long the foremost place in the New World, noting its sacking by Sir Francis Drake and the Spanish establishment there of the "audience of Santo Domingo," a high court from which Cortes and other conquerors derived early legal authority until what the paper terms the union of Santo Domingo with Haiti. The article states that thousands of the city's residents are paupers and beggars, and outlines the history of the Dominican Republic following its separation from Haiti by revolution, a subsequent period of Spanish rule, and an annexation treaty with the United States that the American Senate declined to ratify. Under the constitution described as in force, a president is elected every four years by universal suffrage while congress is chosen by restricted suffrage. Prior to the rise of the recently assassinated Ulysses Heureaux, the paper adds, revolutions followed one another while open murder and corruption pervaded the government.
records.summary_es: Comenzando a mitad de frase sobre la historia colonial de Santo Domingo, The Nebraska Advertiser describe la ciudad como el asentamiento europeo más antiguo y durante mucho tiempo el lugar más importante del Nuevo Mundo, señalando su saqueo por Sir Francis Drake y el establecimiento allí por España de la llamada «audiencia de Santo Domingo», alto tribunal del cual Cortes y otros conquistadores derivaron su primera autoridad legal hasta lo que el periódico denomina la unión de Santo Domingo con Haití. El artículo afirma que miles de los habitantes de la ciudad son indigentes y mendigos, y reseña la historia de la República Dominicana tras su separación de Haití mediante una revolución, un período posterior de dominio español y un tratado de anexión con Estados Unidos que el Senado estadounidense se negó a ratificar. Según la constitución descrita como vigente, se elige un presidente cada cuatro años por sufragio universal mientras que el congreso se elige por sufragio restringido. Antes del ascenso del recientemente asesinado Ulysses Heureaux, añade el periódico, las revoluciones se sucedían mientras el asesinato abierto y la corrupción impregnaban el gobierno.

records.headline: The Wichita Daily Eagle reports, in a San Domingo dispatch dated
records.summary_en: The Wichita Daily Eagle reports, in a San Domingo dispatch dated September 15 from the New York Herald's correspondent, that although the recently ended revolution was comparatively bloodless, it caused deep fear after the assassination of President Heureaux ended the eighteen-year "bloody peace" he had maintained. The correspondent contends that no people ever had a juster cause to seize the government by force, charging that Heureaux's crimes, extravagances, and licentiousness wrecked the island and reduced its inhabitants nearly to slavery. Following his death, the Heureaux ministry held together around the aged Vice President Wenceslao Figuereo out of shared emergency interest, yet remained divided by personal ambitions, jealousies, and hatreds that threatened civil war and twenty years of pent-up vengeance. Described as aged, mild, inoffensive, and not unpopular, Figuereo briefly appeared likely to be tolerated before the excerpt breaks off on whether he had the courage to dismiss Heureaux's cabinet.
records.summary_es: The Wichita Daily Eagle informa, en un despacho fechado en San Domingo el 15 de septiembre del corresponsal del New York Herald, que, aunque la revolución recién concluida fue relativamente incruenta, provocó profundo temor después de que el asesinato del presidente Heureaux pusiera fin a los dieciocho años de «paz sangrienta» que había mantenido. El corresponsal sostiene que ningún pueblo tuvo jamás una causa más justa para tomar el gobierno por la fuerza, acusando a Heureaux de haber arruinado la isla y reducido a sus habitantes a una condición cercana a la esclavitud mediante sus crímenes, extravagancias y libertinaje. Tras su muerte, el ministerio de Heureaux se mantuvo unido en torno al anciano vicepresidente Wenceslao Figuereo por interés común ante la emergencia, pero seguía dividido por ambiciones personales, celos y odios que amenazaban con desatar la guerra civil y veinte años de venganzas acumuladas. Descrito como anciano, apacible, inofensivo y no impopular, Figuereo pareció por un tiempo susceptible de ser tolerado antes de que el fragmento se interrumpa al tratar sobre si tenía el valor de destituir al gabinete de Heureaux.

records.headline: Writing from San Domingo on September 15, the Herald's correspondent reports that the assassination of President Heureaux removed
records.summary_en: Writing from San Domingo on September 15, the Herald's correspondent reports that the assassination of President Heureaux removed the hand that had for eighteen years preserved a bloody peace, and that Vice President Figuereo's government weakened as he hesitated to dismiss the Heureaux ministry. Late in August a revolutionary proclamation was issued at San Francisco de Macoris in the interest of Jimenez, telegraph communication was cut, and the correspondent reports that Macoris, Moca and La Vega went over to a revolution headed by Horacio Vasquez, Ramon Caceres and Samuel Mayo.
records.summary_es: Escribiendo desde Santo Domingo el 15 de septiembre, el corresponsal del Herald informa que el asesinato del presidente Heureaux quitó la mano que durante dieciocho años había mantenido una paz sangrienta, y que el gobierno del vicepresidente Figuereo se debilitó al vacilar en destituir al ministerio de Heureaux. A fines de agosto se emitió una proclama revolucionaria en San Francisco de Macorís en favor de Jiménez, se cortó la comunicación telegráfica, y el corresponsal informa que Macorís, Moca y La Vega se pasaron a una revolución encabezada por Horacio Vásquez, Ramón Cáceres y Samuel Mayo.

Within two days, however, the Governor of Concepcion de la Vega, who had escaped with a small retinue, arrived on horseback and brought the news that set everybody by the ears. records.headline: Citing an examination of public records in the Republic of Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: Citing an examination of public records in the Republic of Santo Domingo and earlier reports in the Herald, an account in The Wichita Daily Eagle states that newly uncovered atrocities make Heureaux's previously reported financial plunder of the republic appear mild beside the wholesale murder and butchery that marked the final years of his despotic rule. The writer expresses astonishment that such deeds occurred within sight of the American flag without provoking a single protest in the name of humanity. According to the article, Heureaux's conduct during the last year of his life pointed to a "homicidal mania" in which he brooked no opposition and replaced exile with death so that opponents could never return. Lists and memoranda discovered among his private papers are mentioned as further proof before the passage breaks off mid-sentence.
records.summary_es: Citando una revisión de los registros públicos en la República de Santo Domingo e informes previos en el Herald, una crónica en The Wichita Daily Eagle afirma que las atrocidades recién descubiertas hacen que el saqueo financiero de la república por parte de Heureaux, informado anteriormente, parezca moderado frente a los asesinatos masivos y matanzas que marcaron los últimos años de su gobierno despótico. El autor expresa asombro de que tales hechos ocurrieran a la vista de la bandera estadounidense sin suscitar una sola protesta en nombre de la humanidad. Según el artículo, la conducta de Heureaux durante el último año de su vida apuntaba a una «manía homicida» en la que no toleraba oposición alguna y sustituía el exilio por la muerte para que sus adversarios no pudieran regresar jamás. Se mencionan listas y memorandos hallados entre sus papeles privados como prueba adicional antes de que el pasaje se corte a mitad de oración.

records.headline: Writing on post-revolutionary conditions in Santo Domingo, a correspondent
records.summary_en: Writing on post-revolutionary conditions in Santo Domingo, a correspondent in The Wichita Daily Eagle observes that people connected with Heureaux's administration fear for their lives amid growing popular demands for justice, even though the revolutionists have acted with moderation and the provisional government wishes Heureaux's excesses to end with him. Despite the revolution's popularity, the provisional government is threatened by national bankruptcy and a depreciated currency, and Jimenez has been welcomed in the hope that he will redeem the worthless "Heureaux paper." Although the writer believes Jimenez is personally unable to do so, assistance is expected from the Santo Domingo Improvement Company, which holds $22,000,000 of the republic's bonds and controls customs receipts, leaving the government little choice but to accept its aid or risk an international question and foreign intervention.
records.summary_es: Al escribir sobre las condiciones posrevolucionarias en Santo Domingo, un corresponsal en The Wichita Daily Eagle observa que las personas vinculadas con la administración de Heureaux temen por sus vidas ante el creciente clamor popular de justicia, aun cuando los revolucionarios han actuado con moderación y el gobierno provisional desea que los excesos de Heureaux desaparezcan con él. Pese a la popularidad de la revolución, el gobierno provisional se ve amenazado por la bancarrota nacional y una moneda depreciada, y Jimenez ha sido recibido con la expectativa de que redima el «papel de Heureaux» carente de valor. Aunque el autor considera que Jimenez es personalmente incapaz de lograrlo, se prevé el apoyo de la Santo Domingo Improvement Company, que posee $22,000,000 en bonos de la república y controla las recaudaciones aduaneras, lo que obliga al gobierno a aceptar su ayuda o arriesgarse a un conflicto internacional y a una intervención extranjera.

records.headline: Surveying the Dominican Republic, The Greenville Times opens
records.summary_en: Surveying the Dominican Republic, The Greenville Times opens mid-sentence by reporting that those it calls the bone and sinew of the republic desire the United States either to annex the country or establish a protectorate over it. Occupying the eastern and larger part of the West Indian island of Santo Domingo, the country is crossed by mountain chains enclosing fertile interior plains, and its population consists chiefly of people of mixed Indian, Spanish, and Black heritage, along with some of unmixed African descent and comparatively few whites. Spanish is the official and common language, though French and English are spoken in coastal towns, and Roman Catholicism is the state religion while other faiths are tolerated. Agriculture, cattle raising, and timber cutting form almost the sole industries—exporting sugar, coffee, tobacco, hides, and cabinet woods—and the capital, Santo Domingo, situated at the mouth of the Ozama River, was founded by Bartholomew Columbus and stands as the oldest European city.
records.summary_es: En una reseña sobre la República Dominicana, The Greenville Times comienza a mitad de frase informando que quienes describe como el nervio y sostén de la república desean que Estados Unidos anexe el país o establezca un protectorado sobre él. Ocupando la parte oriental y más extensa de la isla antillana de Santo Domingo, el territorio está atravesado por cadenas montañosas con fértiles llanuras interiores, y su población se compone principalmente de personas de ascendencia mixta indígena, española y negra, junto con algunas de ascendencia africana pura y relativamente pocos blancos. El español es el idioma común y oficial, aunque en los pueblos costeros se hablan francés e inglés, y el catolicismo romano es la religión del Estado con tolerancia hacia otros cultos. La agricultura, la ganadería y el corte de madera constituyen casi las únicas industrias —con exportaciones de azúcar, café, tabaco, cueros y maderas preciosas—, y la capital, Santo Domingo, situada en la desembocadura del río Ozama, fue fundada por Bartholomew Columbus y es la ciudad europea más antigua.

records.headline: Continuing an account of Dominican politics, The Greenville Times discusses
records.summary_en: Continuing an account of Dominican politics, The Greenville Times discusses the presidency of Don Juan Isidro Jimenes, a wealthy native of the island who had been exiled several years earlier by Heureaux and recently returned to Santo Domingo leading a strong revolutionary force. The writer notes that Jimenes currently appears to control affairs and that insinuations linking one of his henchmen to Heureaux's assassination have gone undenied even by Jimenes's closest friends. The article further reports rumors that a bill to annex the Dominican Republic will be introduced at the upcoming session of the American Congress, warning that its approval would bring serious trouble because Dominicans harbor a genuine and deep-rooted hatred for everything American.
records.summary_es: Continuando un relato sobre la política dominicana, The Greenville Times aborda la presidencia de Don Juan Isidro Jimenes, un acaudalado nativo de la isla que había sido desterrado varios años antes por Heureaux y regresó recientemente a Santo Domingo al frente de una poderosa fuerza revolucionaria. El autor señala que Jimenes parece controlar actualmente la situación y que las insinuaciones que vinculan a uno de sus partidarios con el asesinato de Heureaux no han sido desmentidas ni siquiera por sus amigos más íntimos. El artículo recoge además rumores de que en la próxima sesión del Congreso estadounidense se presentará un proyecto de ley para anexar la República Dominicana, advirtiendo que su aprobación acarrearía graves dificultades porque el odio de los dominicanos hacia todo lo estadounidense es genuino y profundo.

records.headline: The Indianapolis Journal prints Associated Press correspondence
records.summary_en: The Indianapolis Journal prints Associated Press correspondence from Santo Domingo, dated October 4, examining the badly muddled condition of Dominican public finances in a country of somewhat less than 500,000 inhabitants. Exact figures cannot be established because state accounts are entangled with the estate of the late President Heureaux and government books were poorly kept. The dispatch breaks the obligations down into two issues of two and three-quarters percent and 4 percent government bonds, an estimated floating debt of about $3,000,000 in high-interest vouchers and open accounts, and a worthless paper currency expected to require three or four million dollars to redeem. Originally issued by a defunct bank backed only by shifting edicts of an overthrown government, that paper currency is supposed to have had something over $200,000 taken up and destroyed before the passage cuts off.
records.summary_es: The Indianapolis Journal publica una correspondencia de la Associated Press fechada en Santo Domingo el 4 de octubre, que examina el grave desorden de las finanzas públicas dominicanas en un país de algo menos de 500,000 habitantes. No es posible obtener cifras exactas porque las cuentas estatales están mezcladas con la sucesión del difunto presidente Heureaux y los libros gubernamentales fueron mal llevados. El despacho desglosa las obligaciones en dos emisiones de bonos gubernamentales al dos y tres cuartos por ciento y al 4 por ciento, una deuda flotante estimada en unos $3,000,000 en comprobantes y cuentas abiertas con altos intereses, y un papel moneda sin valor cuya redención requeriría entre tres y cuatro millones de dólares. Emitido originalmente por un banco desaparecido sin más garantía que los cambiantes edictos de un gobierno derrocado, de ese papel moneda se supone que algo más de $200,000 fue recogido y destruido antes de interrumpirse el pasaje.

records.headline: Two Dominican items appear in this New-York Tribune column
records.summary_en: Two Dominican items appear in this New-York Tribune column, opening mid-article with a report on political confusion in San Domingo, where armed crowds debate paper and silver currency, American money, and public credit while enjoying newly gained freedom of speech and of the press. Many Dominicans hold wages in money that cannot buy basic necessities for their families, with no promise of early relief, and although plots against General Jiminez's program are believed to exist, he retains the vital backing of the business community as well as enthusiastic support from other classes. A second item announces that Emilio Joubert, recently appointed Consul General to the United States by Provisional President Horacio Vasquez of San Domingo, assumed charge of the Dominican consulate in New York the previous day, noting that until seven years earlier he had practiced law in the city of Santo Domingo.
records.summary_es: Dos notas sobre asuntos dominicanos aparecen en esta columna del New-York Tribune, que se inicia a mitad de artículo con un informe sobre la confusión política en San Domingo, donde multitudes armadas discuten sobre papel moneda y plata, dinero estadounidense y crédito público mientras disfrutan de las recién adquiridas libertades de expresión y de prensa. Muchos dominicanos llevan consigo salarios en moneda que no alcanza para comprar artículos de primera necesidad para sus familias, sin promesa de alivio pronto, y aunque se cree que existen intrigas contra el programa del general Jiminez, este conserva el respaldo decisivo del sector comercial así como el apoyo entusiasta de las demás clases. Una segunda nota anuncia que Emilio Joubert, recientemente nombrado cónsul general en Estados Unidos por el presidente provisional Horacio Vasquez de San Domingo, asumió el día anterior la dirección del consulado dominicano en Nueva York, señalando que hasta siete años atrás había ejercido la abogacía en la ciudad de Santo Domingo.

records.headline: Reporting on United States naval deployments, Washington's The Times states
records.summary_en: Reporting on United States naval deployments, Washington's The Times states that a shortage of available officers and bluejackets prevented the Navy Department from manning an additional vessel to protect American interests during internal troubles in Santo Domingo, requiring a ship already assigned elsewhere to cover those waters as well. Earlier in the Dominican revolution, the cruiser New Orleans and the gunboat Nashville had safeguarded American interests in the Dominican Republic, but both warships were subsequently dispatched to the Philippines in response to an urgent request from Admiral Dewey.

En las primeras etapas de la revolución dominicana, el crucero New Orleans y el cañonero Nashville habían resguardado los intereses estadounidenses en la República Dominicana, pero ambos buques de guerra fueron enviados posteriormente a las Filipinas en respuesta a una solicitud urgente del almirante Dewey.

records.headline: A New York dispatch dated October 23 in The Indianapolis Journal reports
records.summary_en: A New York dispatch dated October 23 in The Indianapolis Journal reports that Senor Joubert, the newly appointed consul from Santo Domingo, has taken charge of the Dominican consulate in New York. Speaking on the new government, Joubert denies rumors that General Horacio Vasquez harbors designs on the presidency, stating that Vasquez is in complete accord with newly elected President Jiminez and will loyally support him in the office of vice president. Joubert adds that no revolutionary demonstrations have occurred since the new government was organized, citizens are contented, the island is growing prosperous—with the last Clyde Line steamship from San Domingo unable to load all cargo intended for her—and American money is being imported in large quantities ahead of the newly elected officials' assumption of office in December.
records.summary_es: Un despacho fechado en Nueva York el 23 de octubre y publicado en The Indianapolis Journal informa que el señor Joubert, cónsul recién nombrado de Santo Domingo, ha asumido la dirección del consulado dominicano en Nueva York. Al referirse al nuevo gobierno, Joubert desmiente los rumores de que el general Horacio Vasquez abrigue pretensiones sobre la presidencia, afirmando que Vasquez está en pleno acuerdo con el presidente recién electo Jiminez y lo respaldará con firmeza desde la vicepresidencia. Joubert añade que no se han producido manifestaciones revolucionarias desde que se organizó el nuevo gobierno, los ciudadanos están satisfechos, la isla progresa con rapidez —al punto de que el último vapor de la línea Clyde que zarpó de San Domingo no pudo embarcar toda la carga destinada al buque— y se está importando dinero estadounidense en grandes cantidades antes de que los nuevos funcionarios electos asuman el mando en diciembre.

records.headline: Narrating an expedition aboard the vessel Fanita, The North Platte Semi-Weekly Tribune recounts
records.summary_en: Narrating an expedition aboard the vessel Fanita, The North Platte Semi-Weekly Tribune recounts how the ship stopped at Inagua in the British Bahamas and took on a pilot named Christopher Roberts, who was told she carried general cargo bound for San Domingo. Flying both the American flag and the ensign of the Clyde Line—from which the government had chartered her—the vessel made two stops to pick up co-conspirators, who met below deck at ten o'clock on the final night to plan the next day's attack. Jimenez had sent word to his ally General Garcia, a resident of Monte-Christi, instructing him to have at least a thousand men ready to receive the arms, seize the forts, slaughter the garrison, and march on San Domingo city and Heureaux's palace, but that message never reached Garcia.
records.summary_es: Al narrar una expedición a bordo del buque Fanita, The North Platte Semi-Weekly Tribune relata cómo la embarcación hizo escala en Inagua, en las Bahamas británicas, y embarcó a un práctico llamado Christopher Roberts, a quien se le dijo que llevaba carga general con destino a San Domingo. Enarbolando tanto la bandera estadounidense como la enseña de la línea Clyde —compañía a la cual el gobierno la había fletado—, la nave realizó dos escalas para recoger a conspiradores, quienes se reunieron bajo cubierta a las diez de la última noche para planear el ataque del día siguiente. Jimenez había enviado aviso a su aliado el general Garcia, residente de Monte-Christi, aconsejándole tener al menos mil hombres listos para recibir las armas, avanzar sobre los fuertes, pasar a cuchillo a la guarnición y marchar hacia la ciudad de San Domingo y el palacio de Heureaux, pero ese mensaje nunca llegó a manos de Garcia.

records.headline: Tracing American financial involvement in the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Tracing American financial involvement in the Dominican Republic, The Bottineau Courant recounts how Charles B. Wells, Warner Miller, Willard Brown, Calvin S. Brice, and other prominent capitalists and politicians organized the Santo Domingo Improvement Company to assume European loans, lend further sums to the president, and complete the railroad between Porto Plata and Santiago. Heureaux borrowed heavily from the American concern at ruinous interest incorporated into the national debt, and in 1894 the company bought the French bank of Santo Domingo and reincorporated it as the Banco Nacional de Santo Domingo, holding two-thirds of its stock while Heureaux personally owned the remaining third. Upon Heureaux's assassination a few months earlier, the company held $7,500,000 in 4 percent bonds and $13,825,000 in two and three-quarter percent bonds, alongside roughly $8,000,000 in floating debt—leaving little more than $1,000,000 of a $30,000,000 total traceable to legitimate government expenses—while the company now collects all revenues and supervises state expenditures.
records.summary_es: Al trazar la participación financiera estadounidense en la República Dominicana, The Bottineau Courant relata cómo Charles B. Wells, Warner Miller, Willard Brown, Calvin S. Brice y otros destacados capitalistas y políticos organizaron la Santo Domingo Improvement Company para asumir préstamos europeos, otorgar nuevos empréstitos al presidente y concluir el ferrocarril entre Porto Plata y Santiago. Heureaux tomó préstamos cuantiosos de la empresa estadounidense a intereses ruinosos incorporados a la deuda nacional, y en 1894 la compañía compró el banco francés de Santo Domingo y lo reincorporó como Banco Nacional de Santo Domingo, quedándose con dos tercios de sus acciones mientras el tercio restante pertenecía personalmente a Heureaux. Al ser asesinado Heureaux pocos meses atrás, la compañía poseía $7,500,000 en bonos al 4 por ciento y $13,825,000 en bonos al dos y tres cuartos por ciento, junto con unos $8,000,000 de deuda flotante —de modo que poco más de $1,000,000 de un total de $30,000,000 corresponde a gastos gubernamentales legítimos—, mientras la empresa recauda hoy todos los ingresos y supervisa los gastos públicos.

records.headline: The Bottineau Courant, assessing the prospect of United States intervention
records.summary_en: The Bottineau Courant, assessing the prospect of United States intervention in the Dominican Republic, states that forced American annexation in an emergency would be welcomed by the improvement company because it would bring a profit of at least $5,000,000 to its shareholders. According to the article, patriotic Dominicans place their sole hope of preserving national independence in electing to the presidency Don Juan Isidro Jimenes, a wealthy native exiled years ago by Heureaux who returned to Santo Domingo at the head of a strong revolutionary force and now appears to command the situation, amid undenied hints that one of his henchmen assassinated Heureaux. Reporting rumors that an annexation bill will be introduced in the coming session of the U.S. Congress, the writer warns that approval by the Senate and the President would saddle the country with "another Philippine elephant on our hands."
records.summary_es: The Bottineau Courant, al evaluar la perspectiva de una intervención de Estados Unidos en la República Dominicana, afirma que una anexión estadounidense forzosa en caso de emergencia sería bien recibida por la compañía de mejoras, pues representaría una ganancia de al menos $5,000,000 para sus accionistas. Según el artículo, los dominicanos patriotas cifran su única esperanza de conservar la independencia nacional en elegir presidente a Don Juan Isidro Jimenes, un acaudalado nativo desterrado años atrás por Heureaux que regresó a Santo Domingo al frente de una poderosa fuerza revolucionaria y ahora parece dominar la situación, en medio de insinuaciones no desmentidas de que uno de sus partidarios asesinó a Heureaux. Al recoger rumores de que se presentará un proyecto de anexión en la próxima sesión del Congreso estadounidense, el autor advierte que su aprobación por el Senado y el presidente cargaría al país con «otro elefante filipino entre las manos».

records.headline: Drawing on a letter from Puerto Plata to the New York Sun, The Appeal sketches
records.summary_en: Drawing on a letter from Puerto Plata to the New York Sun, The Appeal sketches the biography of the assassinated Dominican ruler Ulises Heureaux, familiarly called "Lilis," noting that many consider his killing to have freed the Dominican people from twenty years of tyranny. Born in Puerto Plata about forty-six years earlier as the illegitimate son of D'Assas Heureaux, a Haitian mulatto, and Josefa Lebert, a Black woman of St. Thomas, he began as a Dominican soldier, rose to general of division, and first distinguished himself under Gen. Luperon in the restoration wars against the Spaniards. After serving as executive delegate in the Cibao provinces and provisional government delegate in the southern provinces, he became minister of the interior and president of the council of ministers under Merino, assuming sole control of government combinations before winning election as president for 1882 to 1884 and again in 1887.
records.summary_es: Basándose en una carta enviada desde Puerto Plata al New York Sun, The Appeal traza la biografía del asesinado gobernante dominicano Ulises Heureaux, llamado familiarmente «Lilis», señalando que muchos consideran que su muerte liberó al pueblo dominicano de veinte años de tiranía. Nacido en Puerto Plata unos cuarenta y seis años atrás como hijo ilegítimo de D'Assas Heureaux, un mulato haitiano, y de Josefa Lebert, una mujer negra de St. Thomas, comenzó como soldado dominicano, ascendió a general de división y se distinguió por primera vez bajo las órdenes del general Luperon en las guerras de la Restauración contra los españoles. Tras desempeñarse como delegado del Poder Ejecutivo en las provincias del Cibao y delegado del gobierno provisional en las provincias del sur, fue nombrado ministro de lo Interior y presidente del consejo de ministros durante el gobierno de Merino, asumiendo el control exclusivo de las combinaciones políticas antes de ser elegido presidente de 1882 a 1884 y nuevamente en 1887.

records.headline: Describing the espionage network maintained by "Lilis" (Heureaux
records.summary_en: Describing the espionage network maintained by "Lilis" (Heureaux), The Appeal reports that he employed a whole army of spies—including many women, chiefly from the lower classes—both inside the Dominican Republic and abroad in Haiti, Cuba, Porto Rico, St. Thomas, Jamaica, Paris, New York, Turk's Island, and wherever else opponents might travel. Some agents held diplomatic posts abroad in which official representation was largely a sinecure and pay corresponded to the value of their intelligence on the movements of Heureaux's enemies. Although expensive to maintain, this network warned him in time of brewing conspiracies, and when in doubt he pitted one spy against another to verify reports, while none could fathom his politics—likely, the writer remarks, because he had none.
records.summary_es: Al describir la red de espionaje mantenida por «Lilis» (Heureaux), The Appeal informa que empleaba todo un ejército de espías —incluidas muchas mujeres, principalmente de las clases bajas— tanto dentro de la República Dominicana como en el exterior, en Haití, Cuba, Puerto Rico, St. Thomas, Jamaica, París, Nueva York, Turk's Island y cualquier otro punto adonde pudieran dirigirse sus enemigos. Algunos agentes ocupaban cargos diplomáticos en el extranjero cuyas funciones oficiales eran en gran medida una sinecura, recibiendo pago en proporción al valor de sus informes sobre los movimientos de los adversarios de Heureaux. Aunque costosa de sostener, esta red le advertía a tiempo de las conspiraciones en ciernes y, en caso de duda, enfrentaba a un espía con otro para corroborar datos, sin que ninguno lograra descifrar su política, probablemente —observa el autor— porque nunca tuvo ninguna.

records.headline: A post-mortem on Lilís: Heureaux's worldwide spy system, his sharp disposal of political prisoners, his running of congress
records.summary_en: A post-mortem on Lilís: Heureaux's worldwide spy system, his sharp disposal of political prisoners, his running of congress and courts, the paper-money swindle that issued $3.6 million on a $1 million authorization, and the American syndicate arrangement that left the republic bankrupt.
records.summary_es: Una autopsia de Lilís: el sistema de espionaje mundial de Heureaux, su expeditiva eliminación de prisioneros políticos, su manejo del congreso y los tribunales, la estafa del papel moneda que emitió 3.6 millones sobre una autorización de un millón, y el arreglo con el sindicato americano que dejó a la república en bancarrota.

Others have been murdered in the streets at night, and one during carnival time was stabbed to the heart with a dagger, the mask of his assailant allowing him to get away unnoticed and undetected. In Port-au-Prince a political exile was shot through the heart by an unknown assailant, and in Porto Rico a young journalist, whose writings had become especially obnoxious to Lilis, was stabbed in the street, although not killed. Hundreds of similar cases can be cited as instances of the cruelty and despotism of Lilis, his enemies declare. records.headline: The Appeal, examining custom-house administration and currency
records.summary_en: The Appeal, examining custom-house administration and currency issues under "Lilis," reports that although Dominican revenues were managed for bondholders through a board in Santo Domingo, the custom houses yielded as much for Lilis and his followers as for the bondholders, and his joint arrangement with the American syndicate is widely blamed for the Dominican Republic's current bankruptcy. After the vice president reportedly answered Lilis's complaints about his finances by urging more paper money, $3,600,000 in paper was put into circulation on an authorized issue of $1,000,000, becoming worthless paper and provoking a panic that indirectly led Lilis to Moca and his death at the hands of Roman Caceres. The article adds that Lilis's long tenure owed more to heavy debt than fear, relying in every town on three agents—a merchant, a governor, and a commandant—who enriched themselves through custom-house jobbery and favoritism.
records.summary_es: The Appeal, al examinar la administración aduanera y las emisiones monetarias bajo «Lilis», informa que, aunque las rentas dominicanas se manejaban en favor de los tenedores de bonos mediante una junta en Santo Domingo, las aduanas producían tanto para Lilis y sus allegados como para los bonistas, y su acuerdo conjunto con el sindicato estadounidense es considerado generalmente la causa de la actual bancarrota de la República Dominicana. Después de que el vicepresidente supuestamente respondiera a las quejas financieras de Lilis aconsejando emitir más papel moneda, se pusieron en circulación $3,600,000 en billetes sobre una emisión autorizada de $1,000,000, convirtiéndose en papel sin valor y provocando un pánico que llevó indirectamente a Lilis a Moca, donde halló la muerte a manos de Roman Caceres. El artículo añade que la larga permanencia de Lilis en el poder se debió más a su fuerte endeudamiento que al temor, apoyándose en cada pueblo en tres agentes —un comerciante, un gobernador y un comandante— que se enriquecían mediante manejos y favoritismos en las aduanas.

records.headline: Recalling an earlier visit by a French warship to Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: Recalling an earlier visit by a French warship to Santo Domingo, The Appeal relates an anecdote in which President "Lilis" remarked to the visiting admiral on what he called the tenacity of the Black race in never letting go of anything once grasped. Less than two months after Lilis was shot, however, his political opponent at the head of the Liberal party holds power without a shot having been fired, and Jiminez's journey from his landing at Puerto Plata to Santo Domingo city has been a triumphal march while Lilis's boasted following vanished. Ramon Caceres is now celebrated by the public not as an assassin but as a patriot and political redeemer, and the country remains quiet amid expectations of reconstruction and prosperity under Jiminez's administration.
records.summary_es: Recordando la visita años atrás de un buque de guerra francés a Santo Domingo, The Appeal relata una anécdota en la que el presidente «Lilis» comentó al almirante visitante lo que calificó como la tenacidad de la raza negra para no soltar jamás aquello que llegaba a empuñar. Sin embargo, a menos de dos meses de haber sido baleado Lilis, su adversario político al frente del Partido Liberal ocupa el poder sin haber disparado un solo tiro, y el recorrido de Jiminez desde su desembarco en Puerto Plata hasta la ciudad de Santo Domingo ha sido una marcha triunfal mientras el numeroso séquito del que Lilis solía jactarse se desvanecía. Ramon Caceres es hoy aclamado por el pueblo no como un asesino sino como patriota y redentor político, y el país permanece tranquilo ante la expectativa de una etapa de reconstrucción y prosperidad bajo la administración de Jiminez.

records.headline: The Twice-a-Week Courier-Journal, reprinting an account that cites
records.summary_en: The Twice-a-Week Courier-Journal, reprinting an account that cites prior reports in the Herald, describes the fear and apprehension accompanying the comparatively bloodless revolution that followed the assassination of President Heureaux, whose eighteen-year rule had maintained a "bloody peace" in Santo Domingo while reducing the island's inhabitants nearly to slavery through crime, extravagance, and licentiousness. Held together around the aged Vice President Wenceslao Figuereo only by immediate emergency, Heureaux's cabinet was riven by personal ambitions, jealousies, and hatreds that raised fears of civil war and twenty years of buried vengeance. Although Figuereo—described as aged, mild, inoffensive, and not unpopular—might have remained in office until the next regular presidential election had he dismissed the Heureaux ministry, he hesitated weakly until the opportunity passed.
records.summary_es: The Twice-a-Week Courier-Journal, reproduciendo una crónica que cita informes previos en el Herald, describe el temor y la aprensión que acompañaron la revolución relativamente incruenta posterior al asesinato del presidente Heureaux, cuyo dominio de dieciocho años había mantenido una «paz sangrienta» en Santo Domingo mientras reducía a los habitantes de la isla casi a la esclavitud mediante crímenes, extravagancias y libertinaje. Unido en torno al anciano vicepresidente Wenceslao Figuereo únicamente por la emergencia inmediata, el gabinete de Heureaux estaba desgarrado por ambiciones personales, celos y odios que despertaban temores de guerra civil y veinte años de venganzas reprimidas. Aunque Figuereo —descrito como anciano, apacible, inofensivo y no impopular— habría podido continuar en el poder hasta la siguiente elección presidencial ordinaria si hubiese destituido al ministerio de Heureaux, vaciló débilmente hasta dejar pasar su oportunidad.

records.headline: A Santo Domingo letter says the revolution just ended was comparatively bloodless but filled with terror, after the assassination of President Heureaux removed
records.summary_en: A Santo Domingo letter says the revolution just ended was comparatively bloodless but filled with terror, after the assassination of President Heureaux removed the hand that had preserved a bloody peace for eighteen years. It describes Vice President Figuereo's government, held together by the Heureaux ministry, losing its chance by hesitating, and the revolt that began at San Francisco de Macoris in the interest of Jimines spreading as Macoris, Moca and La Vega went over, Santiago surrendered, the wires were cut, and the government suppressed the news and doubled the guards in the capital.
records.summary_es: Una carta de Santo Domingo dice que la revolución recién terminada fue comparativamente sin sangre pero llena de terror, después de que el asesinato del presidente Heureaux apartó la mano que había preservado una paz sangrienta durante dieciocho años. Describe cómo el gobierno del vicepresidente Figuereo, sostenido por el ministerio de Heureaux, perdió su oportunidad por vacilar, y cómo la revuelta que comenzó en San Francisco de Macoris a favor de Jimines se extendió cuando Macoris, Moca y La Vega se pasaron a ella, Santiago se rindió, se cortaron los cables y el gobierno suprimió las noticias y duplicó las guardias en la capital.

records.headline: The Twice-a-Week Courier-Journal, commenting on public sentiment
records.summary_en: The Twice-a-Week Courier-Journal, commenting on public sentiment in Santo Domingo after Heureaux's death, remarks that people in the United States have wondered to hear that a man named Ramon who killed Heureaux in cold blood and cast his body into the street where a mob mutilated it, has become a popular idol and was called to serve as Minister of War. That wonder lessens, the writer suggests, given the admiration fellow citizens accord someone who rid the country of its tyrant, adding that he carries his honors modestly and has just resigned from the Vasques cabinet citing his own unfitness for executive office. At the same time, residents of Santo Domingo, chiefly foreigners, contend that only an iron hand like Heureaux's can govern what they call a thoughtless and revolutionary people who yield only to force.
records.summary_es: The Twice-a-Week Courier-Journal, al comentar el sentimiento público en Santo Domingo tras la muerte de Heureaux, señala que en Estados Unidos ha causado asombro saber que un hombre llamado Ramon, quien mató a Heureaux a sangre fría y arrojó su cuerpo a la calle donde una turba lo mutiló, se ha convertido en ídolo popular y fue llamado a ocupar la cartera de Ministro de Guerra. Ese asombro se atenúa, sugiere el autor, ante la admiración que sus conciudadanos profesan a quien libró al país de su tirano, añadiendo que lleva sus honores con modestia y acaba de renunciar al gabinete de Vasques alegando su propia falta de aptitud para un cargo ejecutivo. Al mismo tiempo, residentes de Santo Domingo, principalmente extranjeros, sostienen que solo una mano de hierro como la de Heureaux puede gobernar a lo que califican de pueblo irreflexivo y revolucionario que únicamente se doblega ante la fuerza.

records.headline: The Indianapolis Journal reports that Mr. Powell has been instructed
records.summary_en: The Indianapolis Journal reports that Mr. Powell has been instructed to proceed from Port-au-Prince to San Domingo to urge the Jiminez government to pay an overdue installment in the arbitration award to the McKay estate arising from the government's absorption of a bridge concession. During this visit, Powell is also looking after broader American interests in San Domingo, including the concession granted to the Weed syndicate to farm the republic's customs revenues for a term of years. Another issue to be presented to the Dominican government stems from the repudiation of debts totaling about $500,000 incurred by the late President Heureaux to Mr. J. Sala of New York, for which claimants seek to hold the government responsible at least for the portion not chargeable to Heureaux personally. Because certain German creditors have also sought to hold the government house occupied by Heureaux as security for debts, the paper notes that Powell may face a difficult task in separating conflicting claims.
records.summary_es: The Indianapolis Journal informa que el Sr. Powell ha recibido instrucciones de trasladarse desde Port-au-Prince a San Domingo para instar al gobierno de Jiminez a pagar un plazo vencido del laudo arbitral a favor de la sucesión McKay, derivado de la absorción gubernamental de una concesión de puente. Durante esta visita, Powell también atiende en general los intereses estadounidenses en San Domingo, incluidos los vinculados con la concesión otorgada al sindicato Weed para recaudar las rentas aduaneras de la república por un período de años. Otro asunto que se presentará al gobierno dominicano surge del repudio de deudas que suman alrededor de $500,000 contraídas por el fallecido presidente Heureaux con el Sr. J. Sala, de Nueva York, por las cuales se procura responsabilizar al gobierno al menos en la parte no imputable personalmente a Heureaux. Dado que ciertos acreedores alemanes también han intentado retener como garantía la casa de gobierno ocupada por Heureaux, el diario señala que Powell podría enfrentar una difícil tarea al deslindar las reclamaciones en conflicto.

records.headline: According to the New-York Tribune, Mr. Powell, the United States minister
records.summary_en: According to the New-York Tribune, Mr. Powell, the United States minister to Hayti and San Domingo, has received instructions to go from Port au Prince to San Domingo to press the Jiminez government for payment of an overdue installment in the McKay estate arbitration award resulting from the government's absorption of a bridge concession. Powell is likewise attending to general American interests in San Domingo during his visit, including the concessions held by the Weed syndicate for farming the republic's customs revenues over a term of years. In addition, the Dominican government will be presented with a claim growing out of the repudiation of debts totaling about $500,000 incurred by the late President Heureaux to J. Sala of New-York, with efforts to hold the government liable at least for the portion not chargeable against Heureaux personally. Certain German creditors have also sought to hold the government house occupied by Heureaux as security for some of his debts, leaving Powell a difficult task in separating these conflicting claims.

records.headline: Opening with a Spanish proverb translated as "He who lives by the sword
records.summary_en: Opening with a Spanish proverb translated as "He who lives by the sword shall die by the sword," the Brookings Weekly Register recounts how President Ulises Heureaux was shot through the heart in Moca, Santo Domingo, on July 26, 1899, by an assailant avenging the assassination of his father at Heureaux's order, an act many say also freed the Dominican people from twenty years of tyranny. Born in Puerto Plata about forty-six years earlier as the illegitimate son of D'Assas Heureaux, a Haytian mulatto, and Josefa Lebert, a Black woman of St. Thomas, Heureaux entered the Dominican army in his youth, rose to general of division, first gained notice under Gen. Luperon, and distinguished himself in the wars of the restoration against the Spaniards. After serving as delegate of the executive power in the provinces of Cibao in 1879 and of the provisional government in the southern provinces in 1880, he was named minister of the interior and president of the council of ministers during Merino's administration. From that point until his death, the article notes before breaking off, he assumed sole responsibility for governing the republic.
records.summary_es: Comenzando con un proverbio en español equivalente a «El que a hierro mata, a hierro muere», el Brookings Weekly Register relata cómo el presidente Ulises Heureaux murió de un disparo en el corazón en Moca, Santo Domingo, el 26 de julio de 1899, a manos de un atacante que vengaba el asesinato de su padre ordenado por Heureaux, acto que según muchos liberó además al pueblo dominicano de veinte años de tiranía. Nacido en Puerto Plata unos cuarenta y seis años antes como hijo ilegítimo de D'Assas Heureaux, un mulato haitiano, y de Josefa Lebert, una mujer negra de St. Thomas, Heureaux sirvió desde muy joven como soldado dominicano, ascendió hasta general de división, se dio a conocer bajo el general Luperon y se distinguió en las guerras de la Restauración contra los españoles. Tras desempeñarse como delegado del poder ejecutivo en las provincias del Cibao en 1879 y del gobierno provisional en las provincias del sur en 1880, fue nombrado ministro del Interior y presidente del consejo de ministros durante la administración de Merino. Desde ese momento hasta el día de su muerte, señala el texto antes de cortarse, asumió él solo la responsabilidad del gobierno de la república.

records.headline: Writing editorially under the heading "No Dominican Cuba," The Jamesburg Record describes
records.summary_en: Writing editorially under the heading "No Dominican Cuba," The Jamesburg Record describes General Jimenez as a "mystery man" surrounded by contradictory reports put forward on equal authority: that he both planned President Heureaux's murder and had no knowledge of it, that he will both use the United States as a filibustering base and scrupulously obey neutrality laws, and that he is both fomenting insurrection in "Dominica" and doing nothing against the lawful government of President Figuero. Such conflicting claims, the paper remarks, leave a casual observer to conclude either that Jimenez has outdone Jekyll and Hyde or that someone is lying. On one point, however, the editorial insists there can be no doubt: there must be no repetition of the Cuban experience between the United States and the Dominican Republic, noting that past Cuban insurrections cost the Federal Treasury millions of dollars to enforce neutrality laws and suppress filibustering.
records.summary_es: En un editorial titulado «Ninguna Cuba dominicana», The Jamesburg Record describe al general Jimenez como un «hombre misterioso» rodeado de versiones contradictorias atribuidas a autoridades equivalentes: que planeó el asesinato del presidente Heureaux y a la vez no tuvo conocimiento alguno de él, que usará a los Estados Unidos como base filibustera y a la vez acatará escrupulosamente las leyes de neutralidad, y que fomenta la insurrección en «Dominica» mientras no hace ni dice nada contra el gobierno legítimo del presidente Figuero. Tales informes opuestos, comenta el periódico, llevan al observador a concluir que Jimenez ha superado a Jekyll y Hyde o que alguien miente descaradamente. En un punto, sin embargo, el editorial sostiene que no cabe duda alguna: no debe repetirse el caso cubano entre los Estados Unidos y la República Dominicana, recordando que las insurrecciones en Cuba costaron millones de dólares al Tesoro Federal para hacer cumplir la neutralidad y reprimir el filibusterismo.

records.headline: Continuing its editorial on the Dominican Republic, The Jamesburg Record declares
records.summary_en: Continuing its editorial on the Dominican Republic, The Jamesburg Record declares that the United States wants no more filibustering "Juntas" and provides asylum rather than a ground for conspiracies, so if Jimenez wishes to wage war against the Dominican Republic he must camp outside the United States and U.S.-controlled West Indian islands. Expressing hope that "Dominica" will not repeat the Cuban conflict through a war of desolation and extermination, the paper warns that neither Jimenez nor anyone else could make a worse mistake than precipitating a "reign of horror" in hopes of provoking American intervention. Although the United States has at times played the "knight-errant," the editorial concludes that Washington will observe neutrality, tolerate no filibusters, and hope against any breach of peace or outrage upon humanity in what it calls "the one remaining independent island in the Great Antilles."
records.summary_es: Continuando su editorial sobre la República Dominicana, The Jamesburg Record declara que los Estados Unidos no quieren más «Juntas» filibusteras y ofrecen asilo pero no espacio para conspiraciones, de modo que si Jimenez desea hacer la guerra contra la República Dominicana deberá establecer su campamento fuera de los Estados Unidos y de las islas antillanas bajo control estadounidense. Expresando la esperanza de que «Dominica» no repita el conflicto cubano mediante una guerra de desolación y exterminio, el diario advierte que ni Jimenez ni nadie podría cometer mayor error que precipitar un «reino del horror» con la esperanza de provocar una intervención estadounidense. Aunque los Estados Unidos han actuado en cierta medida como «caballero andante», el editorial concluye que observarán la neutralidad, no tolerarán a los filibusteros y esperan que no haya quebrantamiento de la paz ni ultraje a la humanidad en lo que denomina «la única isla independiente que queda en las Grandes Antillas».

records.headline: Discussing a pending French claim against Santo Domingo, The Age-Herald reports
records.summary_en: Discussing a pending French claim against Santo Domingo, The Age-Herald reports that an agreement President Heureaux was understood to have arranged to settle the dispute was disregarded by his successor, President Jiminez. The paper notes that the United States could eventually become involved through the "San Dominican syndicate," controlled by New York capitalists, which holds a Dominican government concession entitling it to collect all customs revenues in return for paying interest on the public debt and assisting the city government. Because the current Santo Domingo administration is believed too short of funds to pay the sum demanded by France, a delicate question could arise should French naval commanders attempt to seize the customs revenues, though the State Department has not yet been informed that Jiminez recognizes the New York syndicate's concession from the late President Heureaux as still in force.
records.summary_es: Al abordar una reclamación francesa pendiente contra Santo Domingo, The Age-Herald informa que un acuerdo que según se entendía había dispuesto el presidente Heureaux para resolver el asunto fue desconocido por su sucesor, el presidente Jiminez. El diario señala que los Estados Unidos podrían verse finalmente involucrados por medio del «San Dominican syndicate», controlado por capitalistas de Nueva York, el cual posee una concesión del gobierno dominicano que le da derecho a recaudar todas las rentas aduaneras a cambio de sufragar los intereses de la deuda pública y asistir al gobierno de la ciudad. Dado que se cree que la actual administración de Santo Domingo carece de fondos suficientes para pagar la suma exigida por Francia, podría surgir una cuestión delicada si los comandantes navales franceses intentaran incautar las rentas aduaneras, aunque el Departamento de Estado aún no ha sido informado de que Jiminez reconozca como vigente la concesión otorgada al sindicato neoyorquino por el fallecido presidente Heureaux.

records.headline: A dispatch in The Salt Lake Herald reports that subscriptions
records.summary_en: A dispatch in The Salt Lake Herald reports that subscriptions raised to pay a 280,000-franc claim pressed by the French consul largely cover the required sum, adding that although a French fleet is expected to visit Santo Domingo, the country remains quiet, strong patriotic feeling is expressed, and a United States gunboat has departed. Under a January 6 New York dateline headed "Claim Will Be Settled," General Alejandro "Whozy" Gil, who served for six years as consul general of the Dominican Republic in New York until the assassination of President Heureaux, responded to word that France had ordered its Atlantic squadron to sail for Santo Domingo. He stated the previous night that he had no doubt whatever that the claim would be settled to the French government's complete satisfaction regardless of the intended naval visit.
records.summary_es: Un despacho en The Salt Lake Herald informa que las suscripciones recaudadas para liquidar una reclamación de 280,000 francos exigida por el cónsul francés cubren en gran medida el monto necesario, añadiendo que, aunque se espera la visita de una flota francesa a Santo Domingo, el país permanece tranquilo, se expresa un notable sentimiento patriótico y una cañonera estadounidense ha partido del lugar. Bajo un fechado en Nueva York del 6 de enero titulado «La reclamación será resuelta», el general Alejandro «Whozy» Gil, quien fue cónsul general de la República Dominicana en esa ciudad durante seis años hasta el asesinato del presidente Heureaux, se refirió a la noticia de que Francia había ordenado a su escuadra del Atlántico zarpar hacia Santo Domingo. Declaró la noche anterior que no tenía duda alguna de que la reclamación se resolvería a entera satisfacción del gobierno francés, independientemente de la visita naval prevista.

records.full_text:
MEETS FRENCH ADMIRAL.

Jimenez Confers With Richard—Settlement Expected To-Day.

SPECIAL BY CABLE.
Santo Domingo, Jan. 9.—(Copyright, 1900, by James Gordon Bennett.)—Admiral Richard of the French navy, with his staff, formally called upon President Jimenez this morning. No business was transacted. The French Consul was present. It is rumored on good authority that the French Consul has not been sustained by his Government, and that he has been asked for his resignation.

It is expected that official action will be taken to-morrow. Americans of this place have asked the United States not to allow France to dictate terms to the Dominican Government. An American cruiser is expected to arrive to-day. One is reported to have left Sanchez yesterday.

ORDERS TO THE MACHIAS.
REPUBLIC SPECIAL.
Washington, Jan. 9.—Instructions were to-day cabled to Commander L. C. Logan, commanding the Machias, directing him to promptly return to Santo Domingo.

In compliance with this instruction, it is presumed the Machias has left San Juan bound for the capital of Santo Domingo. Upon his arrival Commander Logan will consult with the American Minister relative to the protection of American interests. It was said at the State Department this evening that no appeal for the intervention of the United States had been received from Santo Domingo and it is hardly likely that this Government will interfere, in view of the fact that the Jimenez Government has collected by popular subscription the money necessary to pay the French claims. It is possible that Minister Powell may act as a mediator between the French fleet and President Jimenez, looking to compliance with the French demand for an apology, but now that the money has been collected [illegible] [illegible] believed that the worst is about over.

records.headline: General Alejandro Woz Gil, who served for six years as consul
records.summary_en: General Alejandro Woz Gil, who served for six years as consul general of the Dominican Republic in New York until the assassination of President Heureaux, is quoted in a New York dispatch dated January 8 in the Canton Weekly Register. Told that the French government had ordered the French Atlantic squadron to sail for Santo Domingo, he declared that he had no doubt whatever that the claim would be settled to France's complete satisfaction irrespective of the squadron's intended visit.

records.summary_en: According to a naval report in The Sun, an American naval commander notified the Navy Department from Santo Domingo City that he was departing in his vessel for San Juan to join the flagship New York, acting on orders sent to him by the Navy Department the previous day. The report states that keeping an American warship at Santo Domingo is no longer necessary because the trouble between France and the Dominican Republic, which had prompted France to send two warships to Santo Domingo City, has ended peaceably.

El reporte señala que ya no es necesario mantener un buque de guerra estadounidense en Santo Domingo debido a que el conflicto entre Francia y la República Dominicana, que había llevado a Francia a enviar dos buques de guerra a la ciudad de Santo Domingo, ha concluido pacíficamente.

records.headline: A January 16 dispatch from Santo Domingo in The Yale Expositor states
records.summary_en: A January 16 dispatch from Santo Domingo in The Yale Expositor states that Admiral Richard of the French navy, after investigating all the facts, found the Dominican government correct in its position on the "Bolsmare-Caccavelli" claim and accepted the terms the government had proposed to the French consul before his protest without demanding money. Having contracted a loan, the Dominican government prefers to pay the claim itself and will thank the public for the popular subscription, which will not be used, while the French consul is expected to be recalled soon. Meanwhile, the French warship Suchet has departed for Haiti to enforce payment of 200,000 francs paid to the late President Heureaux for lands never ceded under a secret boundary settlement.
records.summary_es: Un despacho fechado en Santo Domingo el 16 de enero en The Yale Expositor informa que el almirante Richard, de la marina francesa, tras investigar todos los hechos, halló correcta la postura del gobierno dominicano sobre la reclamación «Bolsmare-Caccavelli» y aceptó sin exigir dinero los términos que el gobierno había propuesto al cónsul francés antes de su protesta. Habiendo contratado un empréstito, el gobierno dominicano prefiere pagar por sí mismo el monto de la reclamación y agradecerá al pueblo de la república la suscripción popular, que no será utilizada, mientras se prevé el pronto retiro del cónsul francés. Entretanto, el buque de guerra francés Suchet partió hacia Haití para exigir el pago de 200,000 francos entregados al fallecido presidente Heureaux por tierras nunca cedidas conforme a un arreglo secreto sobre cuestiones fronterizas.

The Dominican government secured a loan to satisfy the financial claim, releasing citizens from the funds collected by popular subscription. records.full_text:
Attitude of Santo Domingo Correct on Disputed Claim.

Santo Domingo, Jan. 16.—The French admiral finds on investigation of all facts that the Dominican government was correct in its attitude on the Boismare-Caccavelli claim. Admiral Richard of the French navy is not demanding money, but he has accepted the terms which the Dominican government proposed to the French consul before his protest.

The Dominican government, having contracted a loan, prefers to pay the amount of the claim, and will thank the people of the republic for the popular subscription, which will not be used. It is probable that the French consul will be recalled soon.

The French warship Suchet has left for Haiti in order to enforce the payment of 200,000 francs paid to the late President Heureaux for lands never ceded, as provided in the secret settlement of the boundary questions.

records.summary_en: The *Indianapolis Journal* reported on diplomatic friction in Santo Domingo arising from the French consul's abrupt demand on December 5 for immediate installment payments on the Boismare-Caccavelli claims. Dominican citizens held public meetings to protest the consul's haste, while carefully avoiding anti-French hostility. Foreign Minister Henríquez y Carvajal responded to consular complaints on January 4, defending the dignified conduct of the Dominican populace and reaffirming friendship with France.
records.summary_es: El *Indianapolis Journal* informó sobre las tensiones diplomáticas en Santo Domingo surgidas por la abrupta exigencia del cónsul francés el 5 de diciembre para el pago inmediato de cuotas por las reclamaciones Boismare-Caccavelli. Los ciudadanos dominicanos celebraron asambleas públicas para protestar contra la premura del cónsul, evitando con cautela cualquier hostilidad antifrancesa. El ministro de Relaciones Exteriores Henríquez y Carvajal respondió a las quejas consulares el 4 de enero, defendiendo la digna conducta de la población dominicana y reafirmando la amistad con Francia.

This was dated Dec. 5, and the consul added that he expected the payment to be made before the sailing of the French steamer, Dec. 15. Such precipitateness was bitterly resented by the people of the city of Santo Domingo. They held a mass meeting in the public square, and loudly protested, though being careful in their speeches to show that they did not hold France herself responsible for the inconsiderate and, as they declared, too hasty acts of the French minister of foreign affairs. records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* published an interview with Judge Durham, an American attorney and plantation administrator in San Pedro de Macoris, regarding the Dominican Republic's fiscal crisis. Durham recounted providing $12,000 in gold in exchange for Dominican paper currency under President Heureaux to satisfy earlier French demands, and noted local backlash when the American-owned Bass estate refused to donate to a recent indemnity fund. He warned that excessive export taxes and American import duties were ruining Dominican agriculture, while the Improvement Company's monthly government allocation of $60,000 fell far short of public operating costs.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported further statements by Judge Durham concerning the collapse of the Dominican currency system under late President Heureaux. Durham disclosed that Heureaux systematically evaded agreements with the San Domingo Improvement Company by shifting printing plates between American firms to produce excessive quantities of unauthorized paper money. This unchecked currency inflation created widespread commercial distrust, leaving the Improvement Company with large unusable balances and bringing local commerce to an abrupt standstill upon the president's death.

Esta inflación monetaria desmedida generó una desconfianza comercial generalizada, dejando a la Improvement Company con abultados saldos inutilizables y paralizando repentinamente el comercio local tras el deceso del mandatario.
