records.full_text:
FINANCES IN A SNARL. RESTORING SAN DOMINGO'S SHATTERED CREDIT—AN ALMOST HOPELESS TASK.

San Domingo, March 2 (Special).—An interesting talk with Thomas MacLelan disclosed the fact that he is strongly in favor of American occupancy. He is a Scotchman, and is general manager of the railroad running from Sanchez to Las Vegas. There are sixty-three miles of railroad in all, and it is owned by the Baird nobility of Scotland. During the revolution the people of Sanchez tore up the railroad track to keep the insurgents from getting into the city, and the insurgents at Las Vegas tore up that end to keep the soldiers of the Government back, and between the two not much of the railroad was left. The heavy rains carried off most of the bridges and the railroad is laboring under difficulties.

Mr. MacLelan is at the capital asking settlement of the claim for damages arising out of the revolution. He is an able man and has the bluntness characteristic of his people. "I left Scotland thirteen years ago a Monarchist," he said, "and I am more of a Monarchist than ever." Still I recognize that there is no difference between a republic and a monarchy where the government is honest and intelligent. I think Europe for a great many years has recognized the inviolability of the Monroe Doctrine and that the West Indies and Central and South America must yield to American influences. I tell the politicians of my town that the United States will control San Domingo inside of two years and that they will be glad of it, but of course they do not believe me. As I am not an agitator I am allowed to express my opinions with impunity.

THE DOMINICANS NEED A RUDDER.

"What the people need here is a power behind them to maintain order and protect life and property and there will be wonderful progress. What is most exasperating is the failure to meet contracts. When we contract for 18,000 ties we cannot expect to get more than 10,000. When we employ men to do certain things we expect them to be half done. That is the case generally outside. With my employes, there is full service rendered and the men take pride in meeting my expectations. They are sober and industrious when properly trained and render efficient service. Our line passes through the most fertile land in the world, most of it uncultivated and apparently unowned. When we come to build an extension, however, we find half a dozen people with titles to the same property asking damages.

"Sanchez, the town of which I am president, is the most industrious city in the republic, and I think my efforts have led the people to be proud of their thrift and education. We have good schools and are instructing the masses. We are under many disadvantages in the management of our railroad. Every time we pick up a piece of coal we have to pay some kind of a tax on it. There is the import duty, the wharfage, the lighterage, the cartage, and so on until the coal costs us three times the price in the United States, not considering the cost of transportation. These obstacles we have to contend with and still make our road pay."

WHY JUDGE DURHAM SUBSCRIBED.

Judge Durham, at one time United States Consul at San Domingo and later Minister to Hayti and San Domingo under the Harrison Administration, was at the capital at the same time as Mr. MacLelan. Mr. Durham is administrator of the Consuelo sugar estates at Macoris and has claims against the Government arising out of the currency question. When at one time the French claim was being pressed the late President called upon Mr. Durham for assistance in meeting the demands. Mr. Durham knew that a refusal to meet requests of this sort was usually followed by a death or a fire in the sugar cane, and so he gave a draft for $12,000 in gold and took $40,000 of Dominican paper money in exchange. He has the paper money yet. During the recent excitement over the French claim Mr. Durham subscribed $100, Dominican money, to the popular fund, but the heirs of the Bass estate (American), of which he is administrator, cabled to subscribe nothing, probably thinking that $12,000 gold was more than their share. This action has been very unfavorably commented on by the Dominican papers. Judge Durham said:

"I am one of those proverbial Philadelphia lawyers, and I do not see a way out of the present financial difficulties of this Government. All the cultivated soil is taxed away out of sight by the export duties here and the import duties of the United States, and no further taxation is possible. The improvement company has control of the revenues to its loan, and it pays the Government $60,000 a month on its budget, which is not sufficient to meet current expenses. Now, what is the remedy? I confess I do not know; popular loans and subscriptions will soon exhaust the patriotic spirit of the people. The foreign capital that came into this republic came without thought of political intrigue but recognized the fertility of the soil and the possibilities. As a result of that honest investment foreign capital and foreigners bear all the burden of taxation. That is practically an attempt to drive foreign capital out of the republic and to take a step backward in the National progress. Here are some figures on our sugar business. We pay in the way of taxation on 100 pounds of sugar:

Import in New-York............$1 68

Export in San Domingo, including duties, tonnage dues, additional and extra duties, with monument tax for Christopher Columbus...................... 33

Total..........................$2 01

Freight, insurance, commission, lighterage in New-York......................... 33

Grand total...................$2 34

WORKING ON A SMALL MARGIN.

"We sell in New-York for $4 25, so that we have to do business on a margin of less than $2 a hundred pounds, pay for the cultivation of the crop and the gathering of it, take risks on losses at sea and by fire, and compete with Hawaii, Puerto Rico, possibly Cuba, and meet the provisions of the West Indies treaties, the German beet sugar treaty, the American bounties on beet sugar and the Louisiana sugar product. Yet this is the principal product the Government depends upon to meet the demands of the San Domingo Improvement Company in its handling of the revenues. How is the Government going to better this situation? It is absolutely necessary that there be a reduction in this taxation that we may successfully market our product in the United States. At the same time the Government has an equally urgent necessity for increased revenues. The late President had at one time twenty-five clerks employed signing this paper money. The issue was authorized by the San Domingo Improvement Company to the extent of about a million, but when the President began the issue he had control of the plates and went on issuing. The improvement company tried to get control of the plates, but as fast as they traced them the President changed them to some other printing establishment in the United States and the company was unable to control the issue. The company itself had agreed, in order to give them circulation, to accept a certain per cent in customs duties, but so great was the issue that the company found itself in possession of $400,000 of the money that it was unable to dispose of. The abundance of this money created general distrust, and when the President was assassinated there was practically no currency in the island and business was at a standstill.

A NATIVE WHO WOULDN'T ACCEPT GOLD.

"We could buy no meat of any kind for three days, and our people lived on what they could pick from the trees or had in the way of fowl. I called to my office a man who had some cattle to sell and tried to buy them. I laid down a $20 gold piece and offered him all he wanted of them in equal exchange for his cattle. He pulled out of his pocket a Dominican silver dollar and said: 'They tell me this has no silver in it; that it is worthless; how do I know your metal is any more valuable?'

"I said, 'This is gold worth its weight the world over.'

"'How do you know it is? Did you make it?'

"'No,' I said, 'but I tell you it is.'

"'Well, how do I know that you are not mistaken? I thought this silver dollar was silver, but now I find that it is not, and you are just as likely to be wrong as I am. I do not want your money. I know my cattle are real and valuable, and I will keep them.'

"I had to have some meat, and was somewhat nonplussed. My eyes fell on a pile of barbed wire, used everywhere for fencing. I said, 'You know what that is worth a pound?'

"'Yes,' he said.

"'Well, I will trade you that for your cattle.' He jumped at the offer, and for three months we were back to the original savage idea of barter and trade. I had to send to New-York three times for barbed wire to meet the demands. Later I offered $18 worth of barbed wire or $20 in gold in an effort to restore confidence, but it was useless, for the barbed wire always received the preference.

"The labor question is also a serious one here; there is no provision for the future, and nature supplies food practically free, so that when a man works a day he wants to spend his day's wages and enjoy them before he works again. We employ men by the week, paying them every Sunday, and also have piecework, for which we pay every noon, the men getting in from one to five hours. Most of the men prefer to work at the piecework, as they work only a few hours and get a little money daily. At one time a governor of a province was ordered by the President to clear a road from Macoris to intersect the road to the capital. Clearing a road here means cutting out the underbrush low enough and the path wide enough for a horse to get through. The Governor was a man of some energy, and he called out his soldiers, employed his laborers and made them work six days in the week on the road, paying them in full for the week's work. This they considered a great hardship, and he was much hated. A short time after that, in a revolution, he became a political prisoner, and was led captive down to the capital over this same road. This the natives claimed was the act of Providence in retribution.

MONEY OF ALL KINDS DISTRUSTED.

"In the adjustment of wages there is a great difficulty on account of the general distrust in all kinds of money. One man I employed asked $18 a month gold, and I asked him what he meant by gold, and he said he did not know, but that was what everybody asked. Reliable labor is hard to get, and some of the sugar estates adopted the expedient of offering payment in American gold. We met this by offering American gold, Mexican silver or Dominican money—gold at par, Mexican money at 50 cents and Dominican silver at 20 cents. This caused endless financial discussion among the employes, but resulted in their taking gold when paid off on Sunday, changing it for Mexican money Monday at an advantage to us of 6 per cent, and again changing what was left of that to Dominican money on Tuesday at a further discount.

"In our payments for piecework we had a great need for small change, which we could not get in the country. I sent to New-York for 1,000 one cent pieces, which were sent to us new from the mint. We had a great deal of trouble in explaining their value in Mexican and Dominican money, and they were accepted reluctantly. Then there was a great run on the one cent pieces that I could not understand. Employes brought back gold, silver, Mexican money, Dominican money and any other kind and wanted the copper money. I made an inquiry and found that an Arabian pedler had been in town and had mistaken the bright, new copper for gold and had given an employe a shirt and a Dominican dollar in exchange for one of them. I did not want to be a party to a deception of this sort and locked the pennies up, to be used only when necessary.

"What I have stated indicates the popular idea of money and the financial difficulties the Government has to overcome. One remedy is apparent—closer relations with the United States; but just now American intervention is not popular."

records.headline: The Topeka State Journal, describing a financial agreement between
records.summary_en: The Topeka State Journal, describing a financial agreement between the Dominican government and an American improvement company, reports that the arrangement contemplates a three-year period to clear the country's external and floating debt. Originally suggested by the improvement company at President Heureaux's request, the plan provides for the company to take up bond coupons for three years as bonds are presented and issue scrip to holders, giving the administration a respite expected to allow it to meet all obligations or at least accumulate funds guaranteeing prompt payment of all debts. While retaining its agents in the Dominican custom houses, the company will grant the government a larger monthly budget allowance, resolving a longstanding sore point with authorities and the public and leading observers to judge that Santo Domingo has secured favorable terms.
records.summary_es: The Topeka State Journal, al describir un acuerdo financiero entre el gobierno dominicano y una compañía estadounidense de mejoras, informa que el arreglo contempla un período de tres años para liquidar la deuda externa y flotante del país. Propuesto originalmente por la compañía de mejoras a solicitud del presidente Heureaux, el plan dispone que la empresa recoja durante tres años los cupones de los bonos en circulación conforme se presenten y emita certificados a sus tenedores, otorgando a la administración un respiro que permitiría cubrir todas las obligaciones o al menos acumular fondos que garanticen el pronto pago de todas las deudas. Aunque mantendrá a sus agentes en las aduanas dominicanas, la compañía concederá al gobierno una asignación mensual más amplia para su presupuesto, subsanando un viejo motivo de malestar entre las autoridades y la población y llevando a considerar que Santo Domingo ha obtenido condiciones favorables.

records.headline: A June 1 dispatch from Santiago, Cuba, in the Waterbury Evening Democrat reports
records.summary_en: A June 1 dispatch from Santiago, Cuba, in the Waterbury Evening Democrat reports that General Maximo Gomez arrived the previous day from Santo Domingo and spent the day with political leaders of the "black party," who were jubilant at his return. In a bad humor, Gomez flatly refused to be interviewed and declined to speak on either Cuban or Dominican politics. Newspapers supporting the "black party" declared that his return meant the failure of an alleged American, Spanish, and English conspiracy to annex Cuba, and Gomez departed for Havana that evening.
records.summary_es: Un despacho fechado en Santiago de Cuba el 1 de junio en el Waterbury Evening Democrat informa que el general Maximo Gomez llegó el día anterior procedente de Santo Domingo y pasó la jornada con dirigentes políticos del «partido negro», quienes celebraron con júbilo su regreso. De mal humor, Gomez se negó rotundamente a conceder entrevistas y rehusó hablar tanto de política cubana como dominicana. Los periódicos afines al «partido negro» declararon que su retorno significaba el fracaso de una supuesta conspiración de estadounidenses, españoles e ingleses para anexar a Cuba, y Gomez partió esa noche rumbo a La Habana.

Gomez, who was in an ill humor, positively refused interviews and would say nothing regarding Cuban or Dominican politics prior to leaving for Havana. Press organs backing the "black party" assert that his return defeats an alleged American, Spanish, and English plot to annex Cuba.
records.summary_es: Informando desde Santiago de Cuba el 1 de junio, The Denison Review señala que el general Gomez regresó el día anterior desde Santo Domingo y se reunió durante el día con los líderes del llamado «partido negro», quienes celebraron su llegada con entusiasmo. Gomez, quien se encontraba de mal humor, rechazó tajantemente las entrevistas y no quiso pronunciarse sobre la política cubana ni la dominicana antes de salir rumbo a La Habana. Los órganos de prensa que respaldan al «partido negro» sostienen que su retorno frustra una supuesta conspiración de estadounidenses, españoles e ingleses para anexar Cuba.

records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* reported that President McKinley received the credentials of the new Dominican Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary at the White House. In his address, the Dominican minister emphasized the historical friendship between both nations and advocated concluding a reciprocal commercial treaty. President McKinley welcomed the envoy and reciprocated the desire to establish closer, mutually beneficial trade relations between the two republics.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Star* informó que el presidente McKinley recibió en la Casa Blanca las cartas credenciales del nuevo enviado extraordinario y ministro plenipotenciario dominicano. En su alocución, el ministro dominicano destacó la histórica amistad entre ambas naciones y abogó por la concertación de un tratado de reciprocidad comercial. El presidente McKinley dio la bienvenida al enviado y correspondió al deseo de entablar relaciones comerciales más estrechas y mutuamente beneficiosas entre ambas repúblicas.

records.headline: In a June 9 Washington dispatch, the New-York Tribune reports
records.summary_en: In a June 9 Washington dispatch, the New-York Tribune reports that Francisco Vasquez presented his credentials to President McKinley as minister of the Dominican Republic, ending a period of several years during which the country had no minister at Washington and becoming the second new minister received in a week. Vasquez was accompanied to the State Department by Perry Allen, who will serve as counsellor of the Dominican Legation, while Secretary Hay made the introductions. In the speeches exchanged at the ceremony, both President McKinley and Minister Vasquez expressed a mutual desire for a commercial treaty between the United States and San Domingo.
records.summary_es: En un despacho fechado el 9 de junio en Washington, el New-York Tribune informa que Francisco Vasquez presentó sus credenciales ante el presidente McKinley como ministro de la República Dominicana, poniendo fin a varios años sin ministro dominicano en Washington y convirtiéndose en el segundo nuevo ministro recibido en una semana. Vasquez acudió al Departamento de Estado acompañado por Perry Allen, quien actuará como consejero de la legación dominicana, mientras que el secretario Hay realizó las presentaciones. En los discursos pronunciados durante el acto, tanto el presidente McKinley como el ministro Vasquez expresaron el deseo mutuo de concertar un tratado comercial entre los Estados Unidos y San Domingo.

records.headline: A plot to assassinate Ramon Caceres, the governor of Santiago
records.summary_en: A plot to assassinate Ramon Caceres, the governor of Santiago, has been uncovered by authorities, according to a July 26 dispatch from San Domingo in Washington's Evening Star, and twenty-five of the conspirators have been imprisoned. Several military officers are implicated in the conspiracy, and the accused are to be tried by court-martial. The dispatch adds that President Jiminez is touring the interior and that the country as a whole remains quiet.
records.summary_es: Las autoridades descubrieron un complot para asesinar a Ramon Caceres, gobernador de Santiago, y encarcelaron a veinticinco de los conspiradores, según un despacho fechado el 26 de julio en San Domingo y publicado por el Evening Star de Washington. Varios oficiales militares están implicados en la conjura y los acusados serán juzgados por un consejo de guerra. El despacho añade que el presidente Jiminez visita el interior y que el país en general permanece tranquilo.

records.headline: The Times of Washington reports that Salvador Ros of New York
records.summary_en: The Times of Washington reports that Salvador Ros of New York, a Cuban-born naturalized U.S. citizen, appeared the previous day before State Department Solicitor Penfield—in the presence of San Domingo's New York Consul General, Mr. Maxwell—seeking U.S. protection for rights he claims under a Dominican concession. Ros stated that he carried out harbor improvements at San Pedro under a grant from the late Dominican President Heureaux, to be repaid by collecting certain import and export taxes, but Heureaux was assassinated before signing the concession and the Dominican Congress refused to confirm it. Alleging that Dominican authorities now bar him from collecting those taxes, Ros wants U.S. intervention, though the State Department will not take up the matter until formal papers are filed.
records.summary_es: The Times de Washington informa que Salvador Ros, residente en Nueva York y ciudadano estadounidense naturalizado de origen cubano, compareció el día anterior ante el procurador Penfield del Departamento de Estado —en presencia del cónsul general de San Domingo en Nueva York, el señor Maxwell— para pedir protección estadounidense sobre derechos que reclama en virtud de una concesión dominicana. Ros declaró haber realizado mejoras portuarias en San Pedro bajo una concesión del fallecido presidente dominicano Heureaux, pagaderas mediante el cobro de determinados impuestos de importación y exportación, pero Heureaux fue asesinado antes de firmarla y el Congreso dominicano se negó a confirmarla. Alegando que las autoridades dominicanas le impiden recaudar dichos impuestos, Ros solicita el respaldo de los Estados Unidos, aunque el Departamento de Estado no examinará el caso hasta que se presenten los documentos formales.

records.headline: Continuing an account in the New-York Tribune, this passage
records.summary_en: Continuing an account in the New-York Tribune, this passage describes a one-day welcome for the President—marked by American, European, and Dominican flags, speeches, a dinner, and a ball—at a property of a corporation owned in New York, Boston, and Providence, followed at 5 a.m. by an excursion on decorated flatcars as guests of the Samana Bay Fruit Company. The company operates three engines, forty cars, a machine shop, a telephone exchange, and iron fruit-loading piers along a mountain railway overlooking Samana Bay, where company officers' hilltop homes stand and breakfast was served. The writer notes that earlier U.S. Government interest spurred American immigration, including an 1837 settlement of freed American slaves whose English-speaking descendants are reliable workers but too few for local demand, prompting the fruit company's not wholly satisfactory importation of three hundred English-speaking laborers from St. Kitts at wages of sixty cents a day in gold amid minimal living costs.

records.headline: Opening mid-sentence on a report from Cape Haytien of a Dominican
records.summary_en: Opening mid-sentence on a report from Cape Haytien of a Dominican revolution, the New-York Tribune prints a cabled reply declaring that reports of rebellion are "absolutely false" and that the entire country is tranquil. The cable was received at No. 10 Pearl Street by a personal friend of President Jiminez with interests in San Domingo, who had cabled General Jiminez to ask whether the rumor of trouble was true. Recalling that after President Heureaux's assassination a year earlier General Vasquez held the government only until General Jiminez arrived from Cuba despite having ample opportunity to proclaim himself president, the article quotes a friend stating that Vasquez has no presidential ambitions and adds that Dominicans blame unfriendly relations with Hayti for recurring rumors sent to injure their country.
records.summary_es: Comenzando a mitad de frase sobre una noticia procedente de Cape Haytien acerca de una revolución en la República Dominicana, el New-York Tribune reproduce una respuesta por cable que declara que los informes de rebelión son «absolutamente falsos» y que todo el país está tranquilo. El mensaje fue recibido en el número 10 de Pearl Street por un amigo personal del presidente Jiminez con intereses en San Domingo, quien había enviado un cable al general Jiminez preguntando si el rumor de disturbios era cierto. Recordando que tras el asesinato del presidente Heureaux un año antes el general Vasquez asumió el gobierno únicamente hasta la llegada del general Jiminez desde Cuba pese a haber tenido amplia oportunidad de proclamarse presidente, el artículo cita a un amigo según el cual Vasquez carece de ambiciones presidenciales y añade que los dominicanos atribuyen estos rumores frecuentes procedentes de Haití al propósito de perjudicar al país, dado que ambas repúblicas no mantienen relaciones muy amistosas.

records.summary_en: Washington's The Times, beginning with a cabled message stating that reports of rebellion are "absolutely false" and the entire country is tranquil, reports that the dispatch was received in reply to an inquiry by Oscar Huetfinger of 101 Pearl Street, a personal friend of President Jiminez with large interests in San Domingo. The rumors had alleged an uprising led by Vice President Vasquez and Gen. Ramon Caceres of the State of Santiago, but the article notes that Vasquez took temporary control after President Heureaux's assassination a year ago without seizing the presidency while awaiting Jiminez from Cuba, and quotes a friend stating today that Vasquez has no presidential ambition and is among Jiminez's best friends. Dominicans contend that periodic reports of strife coming from Haiti are circulated intentionally to harm the Dominican Republic because the two republics are not on very friendly terms.

Los rumores atribuían un supuesto levantamiento al vicepresidente Vasquez y al general Ramon Caceres, del estado de Santiago, pero el artículo recuerda que Vasquez asumió el mando provisional tras el asesinato del presidente Heureaux hace un año sin proclamarse presidente mientras aguardaba a Jiminez desde Cuba, y cita a un amigo que aseguró hoy que Vasquez no ambiciona la presidencia y es uno de los mejores amigos de Jiminez. Los dominicanos sostienen que los informes periódicos de conflictos procedentes de Haití se difunden con el fin de perjudicar a la República Dominicana debido a las relaciones poco amistosas entre ambas repúblicas.

records.headline: Norfolk's Virginian-Pilot, reprinting an editorial paragraph
records.summary_en: Norfolk's Virginian-Pilot, reprinting an editorial paragraph whose credit line is garbled as "Hartf?rd Contain.," remarks on apparent signs in some quarters of a belief that recent events may permit reviving General Grant's half-forgotten project to purchase Santo Domingo. Although little has been said publicly thus far, the item notes that Charles L. Wells, who holds business interests on the island, has casually remarked that the current leaders of the Dominican Republic are willing and that it would make "a valuable property for our flag."
records.summary_es: El Virginian-Pilot de Norfolk, reproduciendo un párrafo editorial cuya atribución aparece impresa como «Hartf?rd Contain.», señala indicios superficiales en algunos sectores de la creencia de que los acontecimientos recientes podrían permitir revivir el proyecto casi olvidado del general Grant para comprar Santo Domingo. Aunque todavía se habla poco del asunto, la nota apunta que Charles L. Wells, quien tiene intereses comerciales en la isla, comentó casualmente que los actuales gobernantes de la República Dominicana están dispuestos y que sería «una propiedad valiosa para nuestra bandera».

records.summary_en: The *Indianapolis Journal* published a travel account describing the peaceful transition of power following the assassination of President Heureaux and the enthusiastic election of President Juan Isidro Jimenes. The author provided a geographic description of Santo Domingo, noting its fertile soil, moderate tropical climate, and central position among the Greater Antilles. The article observed that despite its rich natural advantages, a century of persistent internal conflict had discouraged foreign capital investment.
records.summary_es: El *Indianapolis Journal* publicó una crónica de viaje que describía la pacífica transición de poder tras el asesinato del presidente Heureaux y la entusiasta elección del presidente Juan Isidro Jimenes. El autor ofreció una descripción geográfica de Santo Domingo, destacando su suelo fértil, su clima tropical moderado y su posición central entre las Grandes Antillas. El artículo observaba que, pese a sus ricas ventajas naturales, un siglo de persistentes conflictos internos había desincentivado la inversión de capitales extranjeros.

San Domingo Is In area almost equal to the State of Indiana, containing 31,000 square miles. It Is sixty miles east of Cuba, seventy miles west of Porto Rico and one hundred miles northeast of Jamaica, so that It Is practically the center of the four great Islands of the West Indias. The center of the island lies about [illegible] miles directly south of Boston. The land in fertility is equal to that of the other islands while the climate is in many respects superior. There is never any high temperature in summer nor low in winter, and the range is between 80 and 90 degrees the year around. Representatives of the San Domingo Improvement Company in New York acknowledged that while annexation might bring economic benefits, the time was not ripe for such a step. records.summary_en: The *Topeka State Journal* reported that the Dominican Congress voted financial compensation for the San Domingo Improvement Company of New York as the government resumed direct control over national customs collection. Under the new arrangement, customs duties were to be received by a mixed commission composed of Dutch, Belgian, American, French, and Dominican representatives. The resumption of national control was greeted with general public satisfaction, and the president received widespread congratulations.
records.summary_es: El *Topeka State Journal* informó que el Congreso dominicano votó una compensación financiera para la San Domingo Improvement Company de Nueva York mientras el gobierno reasumía el control directo de la recaudación aduanera nacional. Conforme al nuevo esquema, los aranceles aduaneros debían ser percibidos por una comisión mixta integrada por representantes holandeses, belgas, estadounidenses, franceses y dominicanos. La recuperación del control nacional fue acogida con general satisfacción pública y el mandatario recibió amplias felicitaciones.

records.summary_en: Washington reported on January 12 that the government would probably take cognizance of the troubles in San Domingo and act as necessary for the protection of American interests, but that the State Department had not yet heard from Consul-General Maxwell on the reports that the Dominican Government had resumed the direction of its own fiscal affairs, terminating the system by which an American syndicate collected the duties and paid the debts of the government. The plan had been adopted some years earlier, and some Belgian bond owners were understood to have objected to it. Representatives of the San Domingo Improvement Company held long conferences with Acting Secretary Hill and Solicitor Penfield concerning the reported repudiation of the company's grant, and a cable message of inquiry was sent to the American representative in San Domingo.
records.summary_es: Washington informó el 12 de enero de que el gobierno probablemente tomaría conocimiento de los problemas en Santo Domingo y actuaría según fuera necesario para proteger los intereses estadounidenses, pero que el Departamento de Estado aún no había recibido noticias del cónsul general Maxwell sobre los informes de que el gobierno dominicano había reasumido la dirección de sus propios asuntos fiscales, poniendo fin al sistema por el que un sindicato estadounidense cobraba los derechos y pagaba las deudas del gobierno. El plan se había adoptado años antes, y se entendía que algunos tenedores de bonos belgas habían objetado a él. Representantes de la San Domingo Improvement Company celebraron largas conferencias con el secretario interino Hill y el procurador Penfield sobre la supuesta rescisión de la concesión de la compañía, y se envió un cable de consulta al representante estadounidense en Santo Domingo.

records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* published an interview with Dominican leader Horacio Vásquez, who described the nation's abundant mineral resources, including deposits of copper, precious metals, and vast salt reserves. Vásquez maintained that political stability had been quickly restored after President Heureaux's assassination through the establishment of a provisional government. He sharply criticized the San Domingo Improvement Company, asserting that it had merely constructed a railroad with Dominican state funds, enriching itself, Heureaux, and local financier Cosme Batlle at the country's expense.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Star* publicó una entrevista con el líder dominicano Horacio Vásquez, quien describió los abundantes recursos minerales de la nación, incluidos yacimientos de cobre, metales preciosos y vastas reservas de sal. Vásquez sostuvo que la estabilidad política se restableció con rapidez tras el asesinato del presidente Heureaux mediante la constitución de un gobierno provisional. Criticó duramente a la San Domingo Improvement Company, aseverando que únicamente había construido un ferrocarril con fondos del Estado dominicano, enriqueciéndose a sí misma, a Heureaux y al financista local Cosme Batlle a expensas del país.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* reported that nationalist pressure compelled President Jimenes to confront the San Domingo Improvement Company and threaten its agent with expulsion after the company challenged Dominican customs authority. Meanwhile, Belgian Foreign Minister de Favereau instructed his consul in Santo Domingo to ensure that bondholder funds in the treasury safe remained strictly protected for European creditors. Additionally, the semi-official Dominican press responded defiantly to rumors that the American gunboat *Scorpion* was en route to coerce the government.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* informó que presiones nacionalistas obligaron al presidente Jimenes a confrontar a la San Domingo Improvement Company y a amenazar a su agente con la expulsión después de que la empresa desafiara la autoridad aduanera dominicana. Mientras tanto, el ministro de Asuntos Exteriores belga, De Favereau, instruyó a su cónsul en Santo Domingo para que garantizara que los fondos de los tenedores de bonos en la caja fuerte de la tesorería permanecieran estrictamente resguardados para los acreedores europeos. Asimismo, la prensa semioficial dominicana respondió con desafío a los rumores de que el cañonero estadounidense *Scorpion* se dirigía a coaccionar al gobierno.

TO PRESENT SAN DOMINGO'S SIDE.

Dr. Francisco Henriquez, Minister of Foreign Affairs of San Domingo, arrived here yesterday on the steamer San Juan from Porto Rico. He comes here as a special commissioner appointed by President Jiminez of the Dominican Republic. His mission is to present to the State Department at Washington San Domingo's case in its controversy with the San Domingo Improvement Company, of this city.

records.summary_en: Dr. Henriquez y Carvajal, the Dominican Foreign Minister, met that day with Acting Secretary of State Dr. Hill, Washington's The Evening Times reports, concerning Santo Domingo's revocation of its contract with the New York improvement company, which had been entrusted with collecting national revenues, making public improvements, and funding the public debt. Henriquez was accompanied by Andre Julio R. Aybar, Santo Domingo's chargé d'affaires in Washington, and Perry Allen of the Dominican Legation. Following the conference, the Dominican Republic acquiesced in Dr. Hill's advice that an equitable basis likely existed for settling the dispute and that negotiations should take place directly between the parties rather than through the U.S. Government.
records.summary_es: El doctor Henriquez y Carvajal, ministro de Relaciones Exteriores dominicano, se entrevistó ese día con el secretario de Estado interino, el doctor Hill, acerca de la revocación por Santo Domingo de su contrato con la compañía neoyorquina de mejoras, encargada de recaudar las rentas públicas, ejecutar obras públicas y consolidar la deuda pública. Henriquez estuvo acompañado por Andre Julio R. Aybar, el encargado de negocios de Santo Domingo en Washington y Perry Allen, de la legación dominicana. Como resultado de la reunión, la República Dominicana aceptó el consejo del doctor Hill de que probablemente existía una base equitativa de arreglo y de que las negociaciones debían llevarse a cabo directamente entre las partes en conflicto y no por intermedio del gobierno de los Estados Unidos.

records.summary_en: A February 27 dispatch from Porto Plata (datelined "Porto, Plata. Hayti.") in The San Francisco Call reports that the Government of Santo Domingo is making warlike preparations following an encounter between Haytian and Dominican guards on the frontier near Dajabon. The Vice President of the republic has set out from Santiago for the scene of the disturbance with a force of cavalrymen, while the Minister of War has sailed from the capital for Monte Cristo aboard a gunboat with additional troops. Great excitement is reported throughout the country.

El vicepresidente de la república partió desde Santiago hacia el lugar de los disturbios con una fuerza de caballería, mientras que el ministro de Guerra zarpó de la capital rumbo a Monte Cristo en un cañonero con más soldados. Se reporta gran agitación en todo el país.

records.headline: Opening mid-sentence with information attributed to persons
records.summary_en: Opening mid-sentence with information attributed to persons recently returned from the island, the Deseret Evening News presents a historical sketch stating that what is known as the Dominican Republic, or Santo Domingo, was once "a province of the republic of Hayti." According to the paper, internal troubles and anarchy resulting from the revolution that overthrew President Boyer after twenty-five years in office—dated in the OCR text as 1841—led the eastern portion of the island to secede and proclaim its independence, which the Haytien government later recognized in a year obscured by conflicting OCR readings. Before breaking off mid-sentence, the article notes that the delicate question of frontier delimitation arose because the Dominican Republic's territory has never been defined.
records.summary_es: Comenzando a mitad de frase con informes atribuidos a personas recién regresadas de la isla, el Deseret Evening News ofrece una reseña histórica según la cual lo que se conoce como República Dominicana, o Santo Domingo, fue alguna vez «una provincia de la república de Haití». De acuerdo con el periódico, los disturbios internos y la anarquía derivados de la revolución que derrocó al presidente Boyer tras veinticinco años en el cargo —fechada en el texto impreso con OCR como 1841— propiciaron la separación de la parte oriental de la isla y la proclamación de su independencia, reconocida posteriormente por el gobierno haitiano en un año afectado por lecturas conflictivas de OCR. Antes de cortarse a mitad de oración, el artículo señala que la delicada cuestión de la delimitación fronteriza surgió porque el territorio de la República Dominicana nunca ha sido definido.

records.headline: Opening mid-article after a reference to 1874, the Western Kansas World explains
records.summary_en: Opening mid-article after a reference to 1874, the Western Kansas World explains that frontier delimitation became an issue because the Dominican Republic's territory has never been defined, and reports that Haytiens regard a recent northern border incident at Phitobert—where Haytien posts  combating cross-border smuggling and brigandage have fended off repeated attacks—as premeditated Dominican provocation endangering relations between the two republics. By mutual consent, the River Massacre separating the Dominican province of Dajabon (or Laxavon) from Haytien territory had long been provisionally accepted as the natural boundary, with the right bank acknowledged as belonging to Santo Domingo and the left bank to Hayti. Before breaking off mid-sentence, the writer recounts that a year or two ago residents on the Dominican right bank conceived the idea of expanding Dominican territory by diverting the river's course.
records.summary_es: Comenzando a mitad de artículo tras una mención de 1874, el Western Kansas World explica que la delimitación fronteriza surgió porque el territorio de la República Dominicana nunca ha sido definido, e informa que los haitianos consideran un reciente incidente en Phitobert, en la frontera norte —donde puestos haitianos establecidos contra el contrabando y el bandolerismo transfronterizos han debido defenderse de repetidos ataques—, como una provocación premeditada dominicana que pone en grave peligro las relaciones entre ambas repúblicas. De mutuo acuerdo, el río Massacre, que separa la provincia dominicana de Dajabon (o Laxavon) del territorio haitiano, había sido aceptado provisionalmente durante mucho tiempo como límite natural, reconociéndose la margen derecha a Santo Domingo y la izquierda a Haití. Antes de interrumpirse a mitad de frase, el autor relata que hace uno o dos años habitantes de la margen derecha concibieron la idea de ampliar el territorio dominicano desviando el cauce del río.

records.summary_en: The New-York Tribune, describing General Gomez's departure in good health aboard the steamer Seguranca amid cheering Cubans on the pier, notes that Gomez bade farewell by embracing Dr. William F. Holcombe, Tomas Estrada Palma, and José Ellis Cambiaso, a grandson of Dominican admiral J. B. Cambiaso and former Chancellor of the Dominican Republic. Cambiaso remarked that many Cubans favored a government modeled on the Swiss Confederation, adding that he believed a confederation of Cuba, San Domingo, and Hayti with a U.S.-style constitution under U.S. government protection would be the best form of government for the peoples of those islands.

Cambiaso comentó que muchos cubanos favorecían un gobierno inspirado en la Confederación Suiza y añadió que, a su juicio, una confederación de Cuba, San Domingo y Haití con una constitución semejante a la de los Estados Unidos y bajo la protección del gobierno estadounidense sería la mejor forma de gobierno para los pueblos de esas islas.

records.summary_en: In an account of the pier-side farewell before the Seguranca steamed away to the cheers of Cubans, Washington's Evening Star reports that General Gomes—who left in the best of health—embraced Dr. William F. Holcombe, Tomas Estrada Palma, and Jose Ellis Cambiaso, identified as a grandson of Dominican admiral J. B. Cambiaso and formerly chancellor of the Dominican Republic. According to Cambiaso, while many Cubans favored a Swiss-style confederation, he considered a confederation of Cuba, San Domingo, and Hayti under U.S. government protection and a constitution modeled on that of the United States to be the best system for those islands' inhabitants.
records.summary_es: En una crónica sobre la despedida en el muelle antes de que el Seguranca zarpara entre aclamaciones de los cubanos, el Evening Star de Washington informa que el general Gomes —quien partió en excelente estado de salud— abrazó al doctor William F. Holcombe, a Tomas Estrada Palma y a Jose Ellis Cambiaso, identificado como nieto del almirante dominicano J. B. Cambiaso y excanciller de la República Dominicana. Según Cambiaso, aunque muchos cubanos preferían un gobierno inspirado en la confederación suiza, él estimaba que una confederación de Cuba, San Domingo y Haití bajo la protección del gobierno estadounidense y con una constitución semejante a la de los Estados Unidos sería el mejor régimen para los habitantes de esas islas.

records.headline: In an item addressing Dominican-Haitian border delimitation
records.summary_en: In an item addressing Dominican-Haitian border delimitation, the Freeland Tribune reports that an incident at Phitobert on the northern frontier has gravely endangered relations between the two republics, with Haitians viewing it as premeditated Dominican provocation. Haitian border posts established to curb cross-border smuggling and brigandage have repeatedly defended against attacks along the frontier. By mutual consent, the Massacre River dividing the Dominican province of Dajabon (or Baxavon) from Haitian territory had long served as the provisional boundary, with the right bank acknowledged as Santo Domingo and the left bank as Haiti. The paper adds that residents on the Dominican side recently attempted to expand their territory by scheming to alter the river's course.
records.summary_es: En una nota sobre la delimitación fronteriza domínico-haitiana, el Freeland Tribune informa que un incidente ocurrido en Phitobert, en la frontera norte, ha puesto en grave peligro las relaciones entre ambas repúblicas, pues los haitianos lo consideran una provocación dominicana premeditada. Los puestos haitianos establecidos para reprimir el contrabando y el bandolerismo transfronterizo han debido defenderse de reiterados ataques a lo largo de la frontera. Por mutuo acuerdo, el río Masacre, que divide la provincia dominicana de Dajabón (o Baxavón) del territorio haitiano, había servido durante mucho tiempo como límite provisional, reconociéndose la margen derecha a Santo Domingo y la margen izquierda a Haití. El periódico añade que habitantes del lado dominicano intentaron recientemente ampliar su territorio planeando alterar el curso del río.

records.headline: The patriots won, the Spaniards were forced to capitulate, and Gomez
records.summary_en: The *Phillipsburg Herald* reviewed the military career of General Máximo Gómez, noting his early service with Spanish forces during the Dominican annexation before becoming a leader in Cuba's ten years' war for independence. In 1887, Gómez returned to Santo Domingo to cultivate tobacco in Guayubín near Monte Cristi, where his widespread popularity quickly aroused political suspicion. Fearing that Gómez harbored presidential ambitions and planned an insurrection, President Heureaux secretly arranged for his arrest and execution.
records.summary_es: El *Phillipsburg Herald* repasó la carrera militar del general Máximo Gómez, destacando su servicio inicial en las fuerzas españolas durante la anexión dominicana antes de convertirse en un caudillo de la guerra de los Diez Años por la independencia de Cuba. En 1887, Gómez regresó a Santo Domingo para cultivar tabaco en Guayubín, cerca de Monte Cristi, donde su inmensa popularidad despertó pronto suspicacias políticas. Por temor a que Gómez albergara ambiciones presidenciales y tramara una insurrección, el presidente Heureaux dispuso secretamente su arresto y ejecución.

records.headline: An unnamed observer in the Phillipsburg Herald, recounting an episode of unwritten
records.summary_en: An unnamed observer in the Phillipsburg Herald, recounting an episode of unwritten history concerning General Gomez ("Don Maximo"), asserts that the Cuban leader never realized how near he came to imprisonment and death in Santo Domingo, from which he was saved only through the intervention of the United States consulate. After being confined to the city and granted a passport, Gomez departed for Haiti and Jamaica before leading Cuban revolutionary forces alongside Maceo. The commentator further states that Gomez was at heart an annexationist who had favored the annexation of Santo Domingo to the United States under the Biaz administration, praising him as the ideal first president for a Cuban republic.
records.summary_es: Un observador no identificado en el Phillipsburg Herald, al relatar un episodio de historia no escrita sobre el general Gómez ("Don Máximo"), afirma que el líder cubano nunca supo cuán cerca estuvo de la prisión y la muerte en Santo Domingo, de las cuales se salvó únicamente gracias a la intervención del consulado de los Estados Unidos. Tras haber tenido la ciudad por cárcel y recibir su pasaporte, Gómez partió hacia Haití y Jamaica antes de encabezar a las fuerzas revolucionarias cubanas junto a Maceo. El comentarista señala además que Gómez era en el fondo un anexionista que había favorecido la anexión de Santo Domingo a los Estados Unidos bajo la administración de Biaz, elogiándolo como el primer presidente ideal para una república cubana.

records.summary_en: A biographical account in the Richmond Dispatch relates that as a young soldier from "Ciebo," Gomez allied with the annexationists and fought alongside the Spaniards during the Dominican War of the Restoration before departing for Havana as a Mariscal de Campo and later fighting in Cuba's Ten Years' War. In 1887, Gomez returned to Santo Domingo, settling in the district of Monte Christi to cultivate tobacco at Guayabin near the Haitian border, where his widespread popularity provoked political jealousy. Suspicious of reports that Gomez was aiming for the presidency and that an uprising was imminent, President General Heureaux planned his imprisonment and execution and ordered him arrested and brought to the capital.

En 1887, Gómez regresó a Santo Domingo, estableciéndose en el distrito de Monte Cristi para cultivar tabaco en Guayabín, cerca de la frontera haitiana, donde su enorme popularidad despertó celos políticos. Receloso ante informes que indicaban que Gómez aspiraba a la presidencia y que una insurrección era inminente, el presidente general Heureaux planeó su encarcelamiento y ejecución y ordenó arrestarlo y trasladarlo a la capital.

President Heureaux accepted the writer's advice, bringing Gomez to the capital, confining him to the city, and soon granting him a passport, which permitted him to travel to Haiti and Jamaica and subsequently lead Cuban forces alongside Maceo. The narrator reflects that Gomez likely never realized how close he came to imprisonment and execution, from which he was saved only through the influence of the United States consulate.

A government gunboat subsequently bombarded the town and landed troops who recaptured Barahona, forcing the insurgents to withdraw to a nearby stronghold. In response to the outbreak, the Dominican minister of war proceeded to the area to restore order, while the Dominican congress decreed martial law throughout the republic and suspended constitutional guarantees.

records.summary_en: The *Arizona Republican* reported that Dominican insurgents captured the southern coastal town of Barahona after heavy fighting that resulted in forty casualties. A government gunboat subsequently bombarded the port and landed forces that successfully recaptured the town, driving the rebels into nearby strongholds. In response to the uprising, the Dominican Congress suspended constitutional guarantees and declared nationwide martial law.
records.summary_es: El *Arizona Republican* informó que insurgentes dominicanos tomaron la localidad costera meridional de Barahona tras intensos combates que causaron cuarenta bajas. Con posterioridad, un cañonero gubernamental bombardeó el puerto y desembarcó tropas que recuperaron con éxito la ciudad, obligando a los rebeldes a replegarse hacia reductos cercanos. En respuesta a la sublevación, el Congreso dominicano suspendió las garantías constitucionales y declaró la ley marcial en todo el territorio nacional.

FROM DULUTH TO THE GULF Funds Raised for a Road to Cut "All Trans-Continental Lines. Duluth, Minn.. March 31. The News- Tribune publishes a statement to the effect that the banques Francaise and Colonial of Paris and Belgium have agreed to take $12,000,000 of the bonds for the building of the Manitoba Gulf railroad on a basis of 95 per cent. The road will run from Duluth to Omaha and Kansas City, cutting every one of the great trans-continental lines. It is the intentions of the promoters to either make connections with the Gould interests or continue the road as an independent line to the gulf. Work will commence immediately.

records.full_text:
THE DOMINICAN REVOLUTION Insurgent Gains—Government Puts Island Under Martial Law.

San Domingo, Republic of Santo Domingo, March 31.—The town of Barahona, on the south coast, was attacked and captured by revolutionists after a severe fight in which forty were killed or wounded. Later a government gunboat bombarded Barahona and landed troops, who retook the town. The revolutionists retired to a stronghold in the neighborhood.

The Dominican minister of war proceeded to Barahona with other troops and will take severe measures to re-establish order. Revolutionary activity is for the present confined to Barahona. The Dominican congress has declared that martial law shall be established throughout the whole republic and that constitutional guarantees be suspended.

records.headline: The gunboat Machias was ordered to proceed to San Domingo City
records.summary_en: The gunboat Machias was ordered to proceed to San Domingo City and Samana Bay to protect American interests during the Dominican outbreak, according to The Washington Times; the Machias, under Commander Henry McCrea, was stationed at San Juan, Puerto Rico. Following the unrest, it was revealed that the Dominican consul general in New York had visited the State Department the prior week, warning that an uprising would likely occur unless liberal tariff concessions were granted to Santo Domingo. The consul argued that proposed U.S. reciprocity with Cuba would severely disadvantage Dominican sugar and provoke rebellion, though the State Department offered no encouragement due to legislative resistance and the Senate's rejection of earlier West Indian reciprocity treaties.
records.summary_es: El cañonero Machias, estacionado en San Juan de Puerto Rico bajo el mando del comandante Henry McCrea, recibió órdenes de trasladarse a la ciudad de Santo Domingo y a la bahía de Samaná para proteger los intereses estadounidenses durante los disturbios dominicanos, según The Washington Times. A raíz de la insurrección, se supo que el cónsul general dominicano en Nueva York había visitado el Departamento de Estado la semana anterior, advirtiendo que probablemente estallaría un levantamiento a menos que se concedieran concesiones arancelarias liberales a Santo Domingo. El cónsul sostuvo que la reciprocidad propuesta entre Estados Unidos y Cuba perjudicaría gravemente al azúcar dominicano y desataría una rebelión, aunque el Departamento de Estado no ofreció aliento alguno ante la resistencia legislativa y la negativa del Senado a ratificar los tratados previos de reciprocidad con las islas de las Indias Occidentales.

records.headline: Under the headline "The Revolt in Hayti," the Evening Star reports
records.summary_en: Under the headline "The Revolt in Hayti," the Evening Star reports mail advices sent from San Domingo City on April 8 by Wm. F. Powell, United States minister to Haiti and the Dominican Republic. Powell stated that the Dominican insurrection was spreading slowly and had reached Azura province, where rumors reported fighting on April 7, prompting the government to dispatch troops and put about 2,400 men into the field with further reinforcements planned. Since sending that written dispatch, Powell telegraphed the State Department to report that the rebellion has been crushed.
records.summary_es: Bajo el titular "The Revolt in Hayti", el Evening Star informa sobre despachos por correo enviados desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo el 8 de abril por Wm. F. Powell, ministro de los Estados Unidos ante Haití y la República Dominicana. Powell comunicó que la insurrección dominicana se propagaba lentamente y había alcanzado la provincia de Azura, donde los rumores indicaban combates el 7 de abril, lo que obligó al gobierno a enviar tropas y disponer de unos 2.400 hombres en campaña, con refuerzos adicionales previstos. No obstante, tras remitir dicho informe por escrito, Powell telegrafió al Departamento de Estado informando que la rebelión ha sido aplastada.

records.headline: Telegraphic communication between Haiti and Santo Domingo has been completely
records.summary_en: Telegraphic communication between Haiti and Santo Domingo has been completely severed following another revolution, reports an April 29 Port-au-Prince dispatch in the Evening Times-Republican. Dispatches received in the Haitian capital from the northern Dominican port of Porto Plata state that Santiago is the center of the revolt, which is led by Vice President Horatio Vasquez (rendered in the text as "Vanquez"). Observers in Port-au-Prince nevertheless believe that Dominican government forces will likely suppress the uprising.
records.summary_es: La comunicación telegráfica entre Haití y Santo Domingo ha quedado completamente interrumpida tras estallar otra revolución, según reporta un despacho del 29 de abril desde Puerto Príncipe en el Evening Times-Republican. Los informes recibidos en la capital haitiana desde el puerto dominicano norteño de Puerto Plata señalan a Santiago como el centro de la revuelta, la cual está encabezada por el vicepresidente Horacio Vásquez (mencionado en el texto como "Vanquez"). No obstante, en Puerto Príncipe se cree que las fuerzas del gobierno dominicano probablemente sofocarán la insurrección.

records.headline: The Wheeling Register publishes an April 28 dispatch from Port -au-Prince
records.summary_en: The Wheeling Register publishes an April 28 dispatch from Port-au-Prince reporting that a new revolution has erupted in Santo Domingo and that telegraphic lines connecting the republic with Haiti have been completely interrupted. Advices arriving from Porto Plata, a northern Dominican seaport, indicate that Santiago is the focal point of the uprising, which is directed by Vice President Horatio Vasques. It is anticipated in Port-au-Prince that the rebellion will be suppressed by Dominican government troops.
records.summary_es: El Wheeling Register publica un despacho del 28 de abril desde Puerto Príncipe que informa sobre el estallido de una nueva revolución en Santo Domingo y la interrupción total de las líneas telegráficas que comunican a dicha república con Haití. Informes procedentes de Puerto Plata, puerto marítimo de la costa norte dominicana, indican que Santiago es el foco del levantamiento, el cual está dirigido por el vicepresidente Horacio Vásquez ("Horatio Vasques"). En Puerto Príncipe se prevé que la rebelión será sofocada por las tropas del gobierno dominicano.

records.headline: Dominican insurgents are positioned near Cotuy and San Domingo
records.summary_en: Dominican insurgents are positioned near Cotuy and San Domingo, the San Antonio Daily Light reports, citing an April 30 dispatch from Cape Haytien, with rumors suggesting they intend to attack both cities the following day. All of the Cibao ("ilm.i") region, with the sole exception of Puerto Plata on the north coast, is in the hands of the revolutionists, while another uprising has erupted in the south. The Dominican government's position appears critical as overland telegraph communication has been cut, leaving news difficult to obtain.
records.summary_es: Los insurgentes dominicanos se encuentran cerca de Cotuy y Santo Domingo ("San Domingo"), informa el San Antonio Daily Light, citando un despacho del 30 de abril desde Cape Haytien, y los rumores sugieren que planean atacar ambas ciudades al día siguiente. Toda la región del Cibao ("ilm.i"), con la única excepción de Puerto Plata en la costa norte, se halla en poder de los revolucionarios, mientras que otro levantamiento ha estallado en el sur. La posición del gobierno dominicano parece crítica debido a que los rebeldes han cortado la comunicación telegráfica terrestre, dificultando la obtención de noticias.

records.summary_en: An Associated Press cable from Cape Haytien in The Guthrie Daily Leader states that Dominican insurgents are operating in the vicinity of Cotuy and Santo Domingo, which they reportedly plan to attack tomorrow. Most of the Cibao region has fallen into the hands of the revolutionists, while another uprising has broken out in the southern part of the Dominican Republic. In consequence, the position of the Dominican government is described as critical.

La mayor parte de la región del Cibao ha caído en manos de los revolucionarios, mientras que otro levantamiento ha estallado en la parte sur de la República Dominicana. En consecuencia, la situación del gobierno dominicano se califica de crítica.

records.headline: Dominican revolutionists are nearing Cotuy and Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: Dominican revolutionists are nearing Cotuy and Santo Domingo, the Rock Island Argus reports, opening mid-dispatch, with intentions to attack both cities the following day. All of the Cibao region except Puerto Plata is in insurgent hands, another revolt has erupted in the south, and land telegraph lines have been severed. Under the subhead "Hold American steamer," the paper further reports that the governor of Puerto Plata prevented the departure of the American steamer Cherokee for Samana despite her commander's protest, and notes that Vice President Vasquez is at the head of the revolution.
records.summary_es: Los revolucionarios dominicanos se aproximan a Cotuy y Santo Domingo, informa el Rock Island Argus, iniciando a mitad de despacho, con la intención de atacar ambas ciudades al día siguiente. Toda la región del Cibao, salvo Puerto Plata, se encuentra en manos insurgentes, otra revuelta ha estallado en el sur y las líneas telegráficas terrestres han sido cortadas. Bajo el subtítulo "Hold American steamer", el periódico reporta además que el gobernador de Puerto Plata impidió la salida del vapor estadounidense Cherokee hacia Samaná a pesar de la protesta de su comandante, y señala que el vicepresidente Vásquez está al frente de la revolución.

Insurgents control the entire Cibao region with the exception of Puerto Plata on the northern coast, while another uprising has broken out in the south, leaving the Dominican government in a highly critical state. With overland telegraphic communication cut by the revolutionists, reliable information remains difficult to secure.

Los insurgentes controlan toda la región del Cibao con la excepción de Puerto Plata en la costa norte, mientras que otro levantamiento ha estallado en el sur, dejando al gobierno dominicano en una situación sumamente crítica. Con la comunicación telegráfica terrestre cortada por los revolucionarios, resulta difícil obtener información fidedigna.

records.headline: Page 1 of The Topeka State Journal carries an April 30 Cape Haytien dispatch
records.summary_en: Page 1 of The Topeka State Journal carries an April 30 Cape Haytien dispatch reporting that General Navarro, sent to reinforce government troops at Guayabin ("Guayanbun"), defected to the Dominican revolutionists and marched against Monte Cristi, prompting Governor Garcia to evacuate his troops and munitions to Puerto Plata. An outbreak also occurred at Sanchez on Samana Bay, while fighting took place yesterday at Sosua ("Pocua" / "Socua"). During the engagement at Sosua, the local agent of the American United Fruit Company was forced to flee his home and seek shelter with his family on coastal rocks, leading the local governor to dispatch reinforcements.
records.summary_es: La primera plana de The Topeka State Journal incluye un despacho del 30 de abril desde Cape Haytien informando que el general Navarro, enviado a reforzar las tropas gubernamentales en Guayabín ("Guayanbun"), se pasó al bando de los revolucionarios dominicanos y marchó contra Monte Cristi, lo que obligó al gobernador García a evacuar sus tropas y pertrechos hacia Puerto Plata. También se produjo un estallido en Sánchez, en la bahía de Samaná, mientras que ayer se libraron combates en Sosúa ("Pocua" / "Socua"). Durante el enfrentamiento en Sosúa, el agente local de la empresa estadounidense United Fruit Company se vio obligado a abandonar su casa y refugiarse con su familia en unas rocas de la costa, lo que motivó al gobernador local a enviar refuerzos.

records.headline: Insurgents led by Vice President Vasquez have advanced to near
records.summary_en: Insurgents led by Vice President Vasquez have advanced to near Cotuy ("Cotyiy") and Santo Domingo, holding nearly all of the Cibao region while a separate uprising erupts in the south, according to dispatches in the Santa Fe New Mexican. In the north, General Navarro defected with his relief force at Guayabin ("Cuaban") and marched on Monte Cristi, forcing Governor Garcia to abandon the city, while outbreaks occurred at Sanchez and a battle was fought at Sosua. Under the subhead "A Clyde Line Steamer Held," an April 30 Cape Haytien dispatch adds that the governor of Puerto Plata detained the Clyde Line steamer Cherokee bound for Samana over her commander's protest.
records.summary_es: Los insurgentes liderados por el vicepresidente Vásquez han avanzado cerca de Cotuy ("Cotyiy") y Santo Domingo, controlando casi toda la región del Cibao mientras estalla un levantamiento aparte en el sur, según despachos en el Santa Fe New Mexican. En el norte, el general Navarro desertó con sus fuerzas de auxilio en Guayabín ("Cuaban") y marchó sobre Monte Cristi, obligando al gobernador García a abandonar la plaza, al tiempo que se producían brotes en Sánchez y se libraba una batalla en Sosúa. Bajo el subtítulo "A Clyde Line Steamer Held", un despacho del 30 de abril desde Cape Haytien añade que el gobernador de Puerto Plata retuvo al vapor Cherokee de la Línea Clyde con destino a Samaná, a pesar de la protesta de su comandante.

records.summary_en: Under the heading "The Dominican Revolution," the Evening Times-Republican publishes an April 30 dispatch from Cape Haitien reporting that insurgents are operating near Cotuy and Santo Domingo, with attacks planned for tomorrow. All of the Cibao region except Puerto Plata has fallen to the revolutionists, another revolt has begun in the south, and land telegraph lines are cut. In addition, the governor of Puerto Plata blocked the American steamer Cherokee from sailing for Samana despite her commander's protest, while the dispatch notes that "Vice Consul Vasquez" heads the revolutionary movement.
records.summary_es: Bajo el encabezado "The Dominican Revolution", el Evening Times-Republican publica un despacho del 30 de abril desde Cape Haitien en el que se informa que los insurgentes operan cerca de Cotuy y Santo Domingo, con ataques planeados para mañana. Toda la región del Cibao, salvo Puerto Plata, ha caído en manos de los revolucionarios, otra revuelta ha comenzado en el sur y las líneas telegráficas terrestres se hallan cortadas. Además, el gobernador de Puerto Plata impidió la salida del vapor estadounidense Cherokee hacia Samaná a pesar de la protesta de su comandante, mientras que el despacho señala que el "vicecónsul Vásquez" encabeza el movimiento revolucionario.

records.headline: News published in The San Francisco Call details the retreat of Dominican forces
records.summary_en: News published in The San Francisco Call details the retreat of Dominican forces under Governor Garcia to Puerto Plata with their munitions, while a revolutionary uprising took place at Sanchez on Samana Bay. During fighting at Sosua, the local agent of the American United Fruit Company and his family were forced to abandon their home and seek refuge on coastal rocks before reinforcements arrived. The paper notes that Vice President Vasquez heads the revolution, and that the governor of Puerto Plata detained the American Clyde Line steamer Cherokee, preventing its departure for Samana over its commander's protest.

Durante los enfrentamientos en Sosúa, el agente local de la empresa estadounidense United Fruit Company y su familia se vieron forzados a abandonar su hogar y buscar refugio en rocas costeras antes de que llegaran refuerzos. El diario señala que el vicepresidente Vásquez encabeza la revolución y que el gobernador de Puerto Plata retuvo al vapor estadounidense Cherokee, de la línea Clyde, impidiendo su salida hacia Samaná a pesar de la protesta de su comandante.

records.headline: Dominican insurgents are threatening Cotuy and Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: Dominican insurgents are threatening Cotuy and Santo Domingo with imminent attack, The Bismarck Daily Tribune reports, having seized control of the entire Cibao region outside Puerto Plata while another rebellion has erupted in the south. With land telegraph lines severed, the Dominican government faces a critical crisis compounded by the defection of General Navarro, who was sent to reinforce Guayuban but joined the revolutionists and advanced on Monte Cristi. In response, Governor Garcia evacuated Monte Cristi with his troops and munitions for Puerto Plata, while fresh outbreaks are noted at Sanchez on Samana Bay and a battle was fought Tuesday at Sosua.
records.summary_es: Los insurgentes dominicanos amenazan a Cotuy y Santo Domingo con un ataque inminente, informa el Bismarck Daily Tribune, habiendo tomado el control de toda la región del Cibao con excepción de Puerto Plata, mientras que otra rebelión ha estallado en el sur. Con las líneas telegráficas terrestres cortadas, el gobierno dominicano afronta una crisis crítica agravada por la deserción del general Navarro, quien fue enviado a reforzar Guayubín pero se unió a los revolucionarios y avanzó sobre Montecristi. En respuesta, el gobernador García evacuó Montecristi con sus tropas y pertrechos hacia Puerto Plata, mientras se reportan nuevos disturbios en Sánchez, en la bahía de Samaná, y un combate librado el martes en Sosúa.

records.headline: Coverage in The Semi-Weekly Messenger highlights the advance of Dominican insurgents
records.summary_en: Coverage in The Semi-Weekly Messenger highlights the advance of Dominican insurgents near Cotuy and Santo Domingo with plans to attack both cities tomorrow, having brought all of the Cibao region outside Puerto Plata under rebel control alongside a new uprising in the south. In Sosua, fighting forced the local agent of the American United Fruit Company and his family to abandon their home and seek refuge on coastal rocks until the governor dispatched reinforcements. A Cape Haytien dispatch adds that Dominican authorities at Puerto Plata prevented the American Clyde Line steamer Cherokee from departing for Samana, drawing a protest from her commander.

En Sosúa, los combates obligaron al agente local de la empresa estadounidense United Fruit Company y a su familia a abandonar su hogar y buscar refugio en rocas costeras hasta que el gobernador envió refuerzos. Un despacho de Cabo Haitiano agrega que las autoridades dominicanas en Puerto Plata impidieron que el vapor estadounidense Cherokee, de la línea Clyde, zarpara hacia Samaná, lo que motivó una protesta de su comandante.

Sent to reinforce government forces at Guayuban, General Navarro joined the insurgents and advanced on Monte Cristi, leading Governor Garcia to retreat to Puerto Plata with his troops and munitions, while unrest is also reported at Sanchez on Samana Bay and a battle occurred at Sosua.

records.newspaper: The Daily Morning Journal and Courier
records.headline: The Daily Morning Journal and Courier prints multiple dispatches
records.summary_en: The Daily Morning Journal and Courier prints multiple dispatches detailing the rapid spread of the Dominican revolution against President Jimenez. A report from Cape Haytien notes that the insurrection's leader, Vice President Horacio Vasquez, has reached Guerra near the capital, with the government's collapse imminent, while Porto Plata remains quiet under Governor General Deschamps, who has resolved to defend the port with concentrated troops and a Dominican war vessel. Further dispatches from San Domingo and Port-au-Prince indicate that lines of communication to the interior are cut and that Vasquez's forces control nearly the entire republic.
records.summary_es: The Daily Morning Journal and Courier publica múltiples despachos que detallan la rápida propagación de la revolución dominicana contra el presidente Jiménez. Un informe procedente de Cabo Haitiano señala que el líder de la insurrección, el vicepresidente Horacio Vásquez, ha llegado a Guerra, cerca de la capital, con la inminente caída del gobierno, mientras que Puerto Plata permanece en calma bajo el mando del gobernador general Deschamps, quien ha resuelto defender el puerto con tropas concentradas y un buque de guerra dominicano. Otros despachos de Santo Domingo y Puerto Príncipe indican que las líneas de comunicación con el interior están cortadas y que las fuerzas de Vásquez controlan casi toda la república.

records.headline: Dispatches compiled in the Wheeling Register trace the rapid
records.summary_en: Dispatches compiled in the Wheeling Register trace the rapid escalation of the Dominican insurrection headed by Vice President Horacio Vasquez. While Governor General Deschamps prepares to defend Porto Plata with concentrated government troops and a Dominican war vessel, rebel forces have seized control of the rest of the republic outside the capital. Wire reports from San Domingo note that communications to the interior have been severed, with Vasquez advancing with a large force and expected to arrive before the capital today.
records.summary_es: Los despachos recopilados en el Wheeling Register relatan la rápida escalada de la insurrección dominicana encabezada por el vicepresidente Horacio Vásquez. Mientras el gobernador general Deschamps se prepara para defender Puerto Plata con tropas gubernamentales concentradas y un buque de guerra dominicano, las fuerzas rebeldes han tomado el control del resto de la república fuera de la capital. Los informes cablegráficos de Santo Domingo señalan que las comunicaciones con el interior han sido cortadas, con Vásquez avanzando con una gran fuerza y previsto a llegar ante la capital hoy.

records.headline: The Evening Times, reporting from Washington, summarizes dispatches
records.summary_en: The Evening Times, reporting from Washington, summarizes dispatches from William F. Powell, United States minister to the Dominican Republic, who reported that the current revolution is led by the Dominican vice president. A second dispatch confirmed the settlement of the Sala & Co. claim for approximately $260,000, which originated from funds loaned to President Hippolyte for weapons and ammunition and which a previous administration had sought to repudiate. In response to these developments, the State Department requested that the Navy dispatch a warship to San Domingo, with the gunboat Machias expected to be assigned to protect American interests.
records.summary_es: The Evening Times, informando desde Washington, resume los despachos de William F. Powell, ministro de los Estados Unidos ante la República Dominicana, quien informó que la actual revolución está encabezada por el vicepresidente dominicano. Un segundo despacho confirmó el arreglo de la reclamación de Sala & Co. por aproximadamente 260.000 dólares, la cual se originó a partir de fondos prestados al presidente Hippolyte para armamento y municiones y que una administración anterior había intentado repudiar. En respuesta a estos sucesos, el Departamento de Estado solicitó que la Armada envíe un buque de guerra a Santo Domingo, esperándose que el cañonero Machias sea asignado para proteger los intereses estadounidenses.

records.headline: The New-York Tribune provides an overview of Dominican affairs
records.summary_en: The New-York Tribune provides an overview of Dominican affairs, reporting that insurgent forces under Vice-President Horacio Vasquez have overrun most of the country and are advancing on the capital as the government prepares its defense. A parallel dispatch reveals that United States Minister William F. Powell has secured a full settlement from the Dominican government for the longstanding Sala claim. The claim originated from war munitions and money supplied to the late President Heureaux by a Frenchman named Sala, whose American widow in New York subsequently pursued the debt with the assistance of the State Department.
records.summary_es: El New-York Tribune ofrece un panorama de los asuntos dominicanos al informar que las fuerzas insurgentes bajo el vicepresidente Horacio Vásquez han dominado la mayor parte del país y avanzan hacia la capital mientras el gobierno prepara su defensa. Un despacho paralelo revela que el ministro de los Estados Unidos, William F. Powell, ha logrado un arreglo definitivo con el gobierno dominicano para la antigua reclamación Sala. Dicha reclamación se originó a partir de municiones bélicas y dinero suministrados al difunto presidente Heureaux por un francés llamado Sala, cuya viuda estadounidense en Nueva York reclamó posteriormente la deuda con la asistencia del Departamento de Estado.

records.headline: Dispatches in the Evening Star, under the heading 'Santo Domingo Reported Taken,' describe
records.summary_en: Dispatches in the Evening Star, under the heading 'Santo Domingo Reported Taken,' describe conflicting developments in the Dominican rebellion. An initial report from Port-au-Prince states that rebel forces under the general commanding the reinforcements at Santiago were defeated by government troops, momentarily strengthening the executive's standing. However, a later dispatch from Jacmel announces that the capital, Santo Domingo, surrendered on Saturday to insurgent forces, forcing President Jiminez to seek asylum in the French consulate, while earlier reports confirmed that Vice President Horatio Vasquez was marching on the capital amidst severed telegraphic lines.
records.summary_es: Despachos en el Evening Star, bajo el encabezado «Se informa de la toma de Santo Domingo», describen acontecimientos contradictorios en la rebelión dominicana. Un informe inicial desde Puerto Príncipe señala que las fuerzas rebeldes bajo el general al mando de los refuerzos en Santiago fueron derrotadas por tropas del gobierno, fortaleciendo momentáneamente la posición del ejecutivo. Sin embargo, un despacho posterior desde Jacmel anuncia que la capital, Santo Domingo, se rindió el sábado ante las fuerzas insurgentes, obligando al presidente Jimenes a buscar asilo en el consulado francés, mientras informes previos confirmaban que el vicepresidente Horacio Vásquez marchaba hacia la capital en medio de líneas telegráficas cortadas.

records.summary_en: The *Minneapolis Journal* reported that Dominican Vice President Horacio Vásquez broke with President Juan Isidro Jimenes over detrimental financial contracts and successfully captured the capital. President Jimenes sought asylum in the French consulate following the city's capitulation, while Governor Deschamps at Puerto Plata refused to yield without direct executive orders. In response to the crisis, the United States Navy dispatched the cruiser *Cincinnati* under rush orders to protect American interests.
