records.headline: The Republic prints two items: a message received from San Domingo
records.summary_en: The Republic prints two items: a message received from San Domingo, dated February 17, says that an American warship bombarded the insurgents at Pajarito, near San Domingo, and then landed marines; the men, however, subsequently re-embarked. Under the head 'Eager for Annexation', special correspondence of the New York Herald and the Republic from San Juan, Porto Rico, dated February 10, reports that a strenuous effort is now being made by the most prominent merchants of Puerto Plata to bring about the annexation of Santo Domingo to the United States, with a view to extricating the country from its chaotic condition; annexation to the United States has long been the cherished dream of the Dominican commercial element, and not much thought is given to the particular form of government the United States would establish, it being immaterial to the business men whether it be annexation or a protectorate, so long as a firm and stable government be established, insuring peace and guaranteeing life and property. Should the American government be ultimately induced to interfere in Dominican affairs, it will be confronted with a situation that it has at no time had to deal with: Cuba, Porto Rico and the Philippines were ruled by an organized government when the United States took charge of them; no such thing will be found in Santo Domingo, as not even when in the enjoyment of undisturbed peace can that country boast of a form of government that could be styled organized or modern.
records.summary_es: El Republic publica dos notas: un mensaje recibido de Santo Domingo, fechado el 17 de febrero, dice que un buque de guerra estadounidense bombardeó a los insurgentes en Pajarito, cerca de Santo Domingo, y luego desembarcó infantes de marina; los hombres, sin embargo, se reembarcaron después. Bajo el titular «Eager for Annexation», la correspondencia especial del New York Herald y el Republic desde San Juan, Puerto Rico, fechada el 10 de febrero, informa que los comerciantes más prominentes de Puerto Plata están haciendo ahora un esfuerzo enérgico por lograr la anexión de Santo Domingo a los Estados Unidos, con miras a sacar al país de su caótica situación; la anexión a los Estados Unidos ha sido durante mucho tiempo el sueño acariciado del elemento comercial dominicano, y no se piensa mucho en la forma particular de gobierno que los Estados Unidos establecerían, pues a los hombres de negocios les es indiferente que sea anexión o protectorado, siempre que se establezca un gobierno firme y estable, que asegure la paz y garantice la vida y los bienes. Si el gobierno estadounidense fuera inducido finalmente a intervenir en los asuntos dominicanos, se enfrentaría a una situación con la que nunca ha tenido que lidiar: Cuba, Puerto Rico y Filipinas eran gobernados por un gobierno organizado cuando los Estados Unidos se hicieron cargo de ellos; no se encontrará tal cosa en Santo Domingo, pues ni siquiera cuando disfruta de una paz sin perturbaciones puede ese país presumir de una forma de gobierno que pudiera calificarse de organizada o moderna.

records.headline: The Argus prints three items: the closing part of the Monte Cristi dispatch
records.summary_en: The Argus prints three items: the closing part of the Monte Cristi dispatch reports that the New York, being in danger, thereupon left Monte Cristo for Puerto Plata; the firing continued for half an hour, after which the gunboat sailed for Puerto Plata; she was hit twice by round shot and apparently by hundreds of bullets, for she stopped and lowered boats, evidently to plug up the holes in her hull; the failure to land the ammunition is a serious blow to General Jiminez. A Washington item reports that drastic measures will be taken by the government to end the anarchy in San Domingo: continued violation of international law, the destruction of American property and disregard of foreign interests has convinced officials that affairs there can best be improved by force; its handling has been turned over to the navy, and Secretary Moody has been sending supplementary instructions to Rear Admiral Wise, commanding the training squadron now in Dominican waters, giving him wide latitude in the course he is to follow. A San Juan, P. R., item reports that the cruiser Dixie took coal here and sailed on rush orders to Santo Domingo, and that the cruisers Montgomery and Detroit, now at Culebra, have been ordered from there to Puerto Plata.

records.headline: The Argus prints the closing part of a Santo Domingo dispatch
records.summary_en: The Argus prints the closing part of a Santo Domingo dispatch and a Washington item: the dispatch reports that the occupation of Pajarito lasted until late this afternoon, when the force withdrew; during the occupation the insurgents withdrew to a great distance; the shells from the cruiser Newark caused some damage in Pajarito and the surrounding country; a protest signed by prominent citizens has been distributed to the public against the action of the United States warship, which is described as an insolent outrage against the liberty of the republic and a disgrace to the national dignity; the Newark left this afternoon for Guantanamo; President Morales arrived here today; the day passed quietly but tonight firing began at the west gate of the city. Under the head 'We Don't Want It', a Washington item of February 21 states that it is authoritatively stated that the question of the annexation of Santo Domingo to the United States has never received the slightest consideration on the part of the United States, and, moreover, the administration is unable to take a position or adopt policies other than the protection of American interests in Santo Domingo, because of the absence of satisfactory information as to conditions there.

records.headline: The Press prints a St. Thomas dispatch of February 23: the United States cruiser
records.summary_en: The Press prints a St. Thomas dispatch of February 23: the United States cruiser Columbia, which left San Domingo yesterday, arrived here this morning and will remain in these waters eight or ten days; she confirms the Washington reports that severe fighting occurred Feb. 16 and 17 outside San Domingo city; the insurgents were completely routed, losing two field pieces, quantities of ammunition and provisions, and four generals and many other officers killed, wounded or made prisoners. San Pedro de Macoris is now the Dominican insurgents' last stronghold. The dispatch appears under the head 'Fighting at San Domingo'.

San Pedro de Macorís es ahora el último baluarte de los insurgentes dominicanos. El despacho aparece bajo el titular «Fighting at San Domingo».

records.headline: The Reporter and Farmer prints the official confirmation of the Pajarito bombardment
records.summary_en: The Reporter and Farmer prints the official confirmation of the Pajarito bombardment: the item confirms the report of the bombardment of the insurgents by the war vessels at a position near the capital city, the landing of marines and bluejackets to punish the revolutionists and their subsequent re-embarkation. According to Capt. Miller's dispatch the affair occurred on a river twenty miles from San Domingo, presumably at Pajarito, the place mentioned in the press dispatches as the locality where the bombardment occurred. The insurgents, who were stationed on the mainland, fired on a United States merchant vessel, believed to be the New York, which was lying in the river; the shots fell so dangerously near the war vessels that the acts of the insurgents were construed by Capt. Miller as an attack on the vessels, and a battery fire was opened on the revolutionists. This was followed by the debarkation of 400 marines and bluejackets from the Columbia and Newark, who made a successful landing ashore; they dislodged the insurgents from their position and chased them into the country; after accomplishing this the marines and bluejackets took again to their boats and returned to their ships. One man, a bugler named Painter, was seriously wounded by the accidental explosion of his firing piece; there were no other casualties. Authoritatively it is stated that the question of the annexation of Santo Domingo to the United States never has received the slightest consideration on the part of the administration.
records.summary_es: El Reporter and Farmer publica la confirmación oficial del bombardeo de Pajarito: la nota confirma el informe del bombardeo de los insurgentes por los buques de guerra en una posición cerca de la ciudad capital, el desembarco de infantes de marina y marineros para castigar a los revolucionarios y su subsiguiente reembarque. Según el despacho del capitán Miller, el hecho ocurrió en un río a veinte millas de Santo Domingo, presumiblemente en Pajarito, el lugar mencionado en los despachos de prensa como la localidad donde ocurrió el bombardeo. Los insurgentes, que estaban apostados en tierra firme, dispararon contra un buque mercante de los Estados Unidos, que se cree era el New York, que estaba en el río; los disparos cayeron tan peligrosamente cerca de los buques de guerra que los actos de los insurgentes fueron interpretados por el capitán Miller como un ataque a los buques, y se abrió fuego de batería contra los revolucionarios. A esto siguió el desembarco de 400 infantes de marina y marineros del Columbia y el Newark, que efectuaron un desembarco exitoso en la costa; desalojaron a los insurgentes de su posición y los persiguieron hacia el interior; tras lograr esto, los infantes de marina y los marineros volvieron a sus botes y regresaron a sus buques. Un hombre, un corneta llamado Painter, resultó seriamente herido por la explosión accidental de su pieza de fuego; no hubo otras bajas. Se ha afirmado autorizadamente que la cuestión de la anexión de Santo Domingo a los Estados Unidos nunca ha recibido la más mínima consideración por parte de la administración.

records.headline: The Press prints a Kingston dispatch of February 24: the German steamer
records.summary_en: The Press prints a Kingston dispatch of February 24: the German steamer Altenburg, Captain Kuhis, from Hamburg and West Indian ports, arrived here today and reported that between San Domingo and Sanchez, Santo Domingo, the Dominican gunboat Presidente hove in sight and fired a shot across her bows; Captain Kuhis, however, refused to stop, and no further interference with the Altenburg was attempted. At Puerto Plata, Santo Domingo, President Morales warned Captain Kuhis against proceeding to Monte Cristi; but the Altenburg went there and landed cargo. Owing to the revolution the steamer did not land anything at San Domingo city. The dispatch appears under the head 'Dominican Gunboat Tried to Hold Up German Merchantman'.

records.headline: The Examiner prints the end of an item: the Morales government
records.summary_en: The Examiner prints the end of an item: the Morales government has won a victory in fighting extended over two days; the siege has been raised and the insurgents are in retreat. The Examiner also prints a Washington statement: close attention is being given by administration officials to affairs in Santo Domingo; a number of warships are being kept in the waters of that country so that American interests may be zealously protected in cases of trouble between the regular government and insurgents; forcible interference in the affairs of the country, however, have been avoided up to this time, so far as news received by the department is concerned. It is authoritatively stated that the question of the annexation of Santo Domingo to the United States never has received the slightest consideration on the part of the administration, and, moreover, the administration is unable to take a position or adopt a policy other than the protection of American interests in Santo Domingo, because of the absence of satisfactory information as to conditions there.
records.summary_es: El Examiner publica el final de una nota: el gobierno de Morales ha ganado una victoria en combates que se extendieron durante dos días; el sitio ha sido levantado y los insurgentes están en retirada. El Examiner también publica una declaración de Washington: las autoridades de la administración están prestando mucha atención a los asuntos en Santo Domingo; se está manteniendo un número de buques de guerra en las aguas de ese país para que los intereses estadounidenses puedan ser celosamente protegidos en casos de problemas entre el gobierno regular y los insurgentes; la interferencia por la fuerza en los asuntos del país, sin embargo, se ha evitado hasta este momento, según las noticias recibidas por el departamento. Se ha afirmado autorizadamente que la cuestión de la anexión de Santo Domingo a los Estados Unidos nunca ha recibido la más mínima consideración por parte de la administración, y que, además, la administración no puede tomar una posición ni adoptar una política distinta de la protección de los intereses estadounidenses en Santo Domingo, por la ausencia de información satisfactoria en cuanto a las condiciones allí.

records.headline: The Tribune prints Señor Joubert's statement and Captain Wainwright's report
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints Señor Joubert's statement and Captain Wainwright's report: Joubert did not consider such action necessary, as the Morales government would, he said, soon restore order. Señor Joubert added: 'President Morales will soon have the rebellion suppressed and the affairs will again assume their normal state. If the reports from San Domingo are true that the rebels have committed outrages against American interests, no one will regret it more keenly than President Morales. He is supported by the best element of the country, and this rebellion is a fight between them and the worst political element, as you would call them here. The President and his government are not only most friendly toward American interests, but it is his first care that all foreign property and life shall be respected and protected.' Under the head 'American Marines in San Domingo', a Washington item of February 20 reports that by order of Secretary Moody the report of Captain Richard Wainwright, commanding the Newark, regarding his recent reconnaissance about San Domingo, was made public at the Navy Department to-day: Captain Wainwright found on his arrival at Sanchez that the daughter and brother-in-law of the American consular agent had been wounded by the same bullet in the fighting there; as it was expected that the attack on February 8 would be repeated the following day, he wrote a letter to the commanders of the government and insurgent forces protesting against further firing in the streets of the city or toward the houses of the inhabitants.

records.headline: The News prints a San Juan dispatch of February 21: the Cuban steamer
records.summary_en: The News prints a San Juan dispatch of February 21: the Cuban steamer Julia, which has arrived here from San Domingo, and the French steamer St. Simon, at this port from Puerto Plata, Santo Domingo, both report that Gen. Jiminez, the Dominican revolutionary leader, has been completely routed, that his whereabouts is unknown, and that his cause is hopeless. The recent fight at Pajarito, near San Domingo, was caused by revolutionists firing on a flag of truce carried by Americans landed from a warship, who were going to consult with persons ashore; the Americans, it is asserted, retaliated and scattered the insurgents. No international complications are expected. The dispatch appears under the head 'Americans Retaliated'.

records.headline: The Herald prints a Washington item bringing official confirmation of the report of the bombardment of the insurgents
records.summary_en: The Herald prints a Washington item bringing official confirmation of the report of the bombardment of the insurgents by the war vessels at a position near the capital city, the landing of marines and bluejackets to punish the revolutionists and their subsequent re-embarkation. According to Capt. Miller's dispatch the affair occurred on a river twenty miles from San Domingo, presumably at Pajarito, the place mentioned in the press dispatches as the locality where the bombardment occurred. The insurgents, who were stationed on the mainland, fired on a United States merchant vessel, believed to be the New York, which was lying in the river; the shots fell so dangerously near the war vessels that the acts of the insurgents were construed by Capt. Miller as an attack on the vessels, and a battery fire was opened on the revolutionists. This was followed by the debarkation of 400 marines and bluejackets from the Columbia and Newark, who made a successful landing ashore; they dislodged the insurgents from their position and chased them into the country; after accomplishing this the marines and bluejackets took again to their boats and returned to their ships. One man, a bugler named Painter, was seriously wounded by the accidental explosion of his firing piece; there were no other casualties. Authoritatively it is stated that the question of the annexation of Santo Domingo to the United States never has received the slightest consideration on the part of the administration.
records.summary_es: El Herald publica una nota de Washington que trae la confirmación oficial del informe del bombardeo de los insurgentes por los buques de guerra en una posición cerca de la ciudad capital, el desembarco de infantes de marina y marineros para castigar a los revolucionarios y su subsiguiente reembarque. Según el despacho del capitán Miller, el hecho ocurrió en un río a veinte millas de Santo Domingo, presumiblemente en Pajarito, el lugar mencionado en los despachos de prensa como la localidad donde ocurrió el bombardeo. Los insurgentes, que estaban apostados en tierra firme, dispararon contra un buque mercante de los Estados Unidos, que se cree era el New York, que estaba en el río; los disparos cayeron tan peligrosamente cerca de los buques de guerra que los actos de los insurgentes fueron interpretados por el capitán Miller como un ataque a los buques, y se abrió fuego de batería contra los revolucionarios. A esto siguió el desembarco de 400 infantes de marina y marineros del Columbia y el Newark, que efectuaron un desembarco exitoso en la costa; desalojaron a los insurgentes de su posición y los persiguieron hacia el interior; tras lograr esto, los infantes de marina y los marineros volvieron a sus botes y regresaron a sus buques. Un hombre, un corneta llamado Painter, resultó seriamente herido por la explosión accidental de su pieza de fuego; no hubo otras bajas. Se ha afirmado autorizadamente que la cuestión de la anexión de Santo Domingo a los Estados Unidos nunca ha recibido la más mínima consideración por parte de la administración.

records.headline: A United States naval report tells of the commander going aboard the Newark to interview General Morales after a charge
records.summary_en: A United States naval report tells of the commander going aboard the Newark to interview General Morales after a charge that Morales had violated asylum granted by the American consular agent at Samana to two men; Morales replied the men were taken not from the consulate but from a farm outside the town belonging to the agent, and the commander warned him to respect the American flag and consulate. The report also covers Morales's decree closing Monte Cristi and Macoris, the firing on the Clyde liner New-York's lighters at Monte Cristi and the agreement to deposit her cargo at Puerto Plata, and the insurgents holding La Vega and the southeastern peninsula while Santo Domingo City is closely invested by about 1,200 men.
records.summary_es: Un informe naval de los Estados Unidos relata que el comandante subió a bordo del Newark para entrevistar al general Morales tras la acusación de que Morales había violado el asilo concedido por el agente consular americano en Samana a dos hombres; Morales respondió que los hombres no fueron tomados del consulado sino de una finca fuera de la ciudad perteneciente al agente, y el comandante le advirtió que respetara la bandera y el consulado americanos. El informe también cubre el decreto de Morales que cerró Monte Cristi y Macoris, los disparos contra las lanchas del vapor New-York de la línea Clyde en Monte Cristi y el acuerdo de depositar su carga en Puerto Plata, y que los insurgentes ocupan La Vega y la península del sureste mientras la ciudad de Santo Domingo está estrechamente sitiada por unos 1,200 hombres.

records.headline: The Freeman prints part of an editorial: it congratulates the government
records.summary_en: The Freeman prints part of an editorial: it congratulates the government upon its determination to avoid all traps laid for it by the various Dominican factions; it has been semi-officially assured that the administration will not be forced into annexing Santo Domingo, no matter what outrages American interests may suffer or what alluring vistas of power and expansion reveal themselves to the gaze of frugal vigilance. It still insists that Haiti and Santo Domingo offer infinitely richer rewards to well directed enterprise than Panama, the Philippines or far Cathay, and still maintains the superior possibilities of opulence awaiting scientific exploitation there; but it has some very formidable contracts on its hands at present, and wisdom counsels at least a temporary hesitation in undertaking new ones. The editorial concludes: 'We find it possible, therefore, to restrain a certain impatience, touching the occupation of Santo Domingo — not permanently, of course, but only until we shall have set these adventures in reasonably smooth running order.'
records.summary_es: El Freeman publica parte de un editorial: felicita al gobierno por su determinación de evitar todas las trampas que le tienden las diversas facciones dominicanas; se le ha asegurado semioficialmente que la administración no será forzada a anexar Santo Domingo, sin importar qué ultrajes puedan sufrir los intereses estadounidenses ni qué atractivas vistas de poder y expansión se revelen a la mirada de la frugal vigilancia. Todavía insiste en que Haití y Santo Domingo ofrecen recompensas infinitamente más ricas a la empresa bien dirigida que Panamá, Filipinas o la lejana Catay, y todavía mantiene las superiores posibilidades de opulencia que esperan allí a la explotación científica; pero tiene entre manos algunos contratos muy formidables en la actualidad, y la sabiduría aconseja al menos una vacilación temporal en emprender otros nuevos. El editorial concluye: «Nos es posible, por tanto, contener una cierta impaciencia en cuanto a la ocupación de Santo Domingo, no permanentemente, por supuesto, sino solo hasta que hayamos puesto estas aventuras en un funcionamiento razonablemente fluido».

records.headline: The Star prints a February 27 cablegram from Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Star prints a February 27 cablegram from Santo Domingo, and a Washington note: United States Minister Powell has been informed that the insurgents at San Pedro de Macoris have seized the tugboat Burro, belonging to the Clyde Line of New York, and armed her. The Clyde Line steamer Cherokee has gone to Azua de Compostela, convoyed by the United States training ship Hartford. Many arrests have been made there, and several politicians were sent out of the country today on board the steamer Julia of the Cuba Line. Edward C. Reed, United States consular agent at San Pedro de Macoris, is said to be in danger, and Minister Powell has taken steps to secure the protection of all interests. The Washington note adds that President Morales of the Dominican Republic has been refused permission to blockade his own ports to keep out the revolutionists, by report to the Navy Department by Captain James K. Miller, commanding the cruiser Columbia. The cablegram appears under the head 'Insurgents Seize a Tugboat'.

Miller, comandante del crucero Columbia. El cablegrama aparece bajo el título «Insurgents Seize a Tugboat».

records.headline: The Bulletin prints a New York item of March 2, in which the Jiminez revolutionists
records.summary_en: The Bulletin prints a New York item of March 2, in which the Jiminez revolutionists are charged with deliberately making war upon Americans: Gen. Francisco Leonto Vasquez, formerly Dominican consul here and a brother of former President Horacio Vasquez of San Domingo, asserts that he has documentary proof that the revolutionists are making war upon Americans in the island in order that the United States government may be moved to interfere and assume a protectorate over the country. Gen. Vasquez, who has just returned from San Domingo, asserts that this policy of the revolutionists explains the killing of the machinist, Johnstone, of the United States gunboat Yankee, and the firing on the Clyde line steamer New York by the revolutionists. That the Dominican insurrectionists are waging a war against Americans and American Interests for the express purpose of causing the intervention of the United States In the affairs of San Domingo was the direct accusation made yesterday by General Francisco Leonte Vasquez, who has just returned to this city from the scene of conflict. He brings with him, he says, documentary proof in substantiation of his assertions, and [in?] these might be found the explanation for the killing of the machinist, Johnson, of the United States gunboat Yankee, and the firing on the Clyde Line steamer New-York by the revolutionists. records.headline: The News-Herald prints a magazine excerpt on Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The News-Herald prints a magazine excerpt on Santo Domingo, drawn from 'Santo Domingo, A Turbulent Republic', by Charles S. Solomon, in the American Monthly Review of Reviews for March: the absence of cold weather, the excerpt says, makes it possible for the insurrectionists to fight season in and season out, sleep in the open, and subsist, if necessary, on the fruit which grows in great variety and abundance in their country. In the Dominican republic, revolutions take the place of elections: not because the people are too impetuous to permit a president to complete his tenure of four years, and not because the conditions have ever been improved as the result of a victorious campaign by some ultra 'patriotic' leader. Solomon, who says he has watched for ten years with political disinterestedness every step made in the politics of Santo Domingo, puts the reasons for the many uprisings that have taken place there in that period in two words, 'political ambition': some supposed misconduct on the part of the government is made the pretext for fighting, he says, done to mislead the people, who blindly follow the standard of the ambitious politician and the manifesto he spreads over the country setting forth the faults of the president whom he wishes to depose and incidentally succeed in office.
records.summary_es: El News-Herald publica un extracto de revista sobre Santo Domingo, tomado de «Santo Domingo, A Turbulent Republic», de Charles S. Solomon, en la American Monthly Review of Reviews de marzo: la ausencia de frío, dice el extracto, hace posible que los insurrectos peleen en toda estación, duerman al aire libre y subsistan, si es necesario, de la fruta que crece en gran variedad y abundancia en su país. En la República Dominicana, las revoluciones ocupan el lugar de las elecciones: no porque el pueblo sea demasiado impetuoso para permitir que un presidente complete su período de cuatro años, ni porque las condiciones hayan mejorado alguna vez como resultado de una campaña victoriosa de algún caudillo ultra «patriótico». Solomon, que dice haber observado durante diez años con desinterés político cada paso dado en la política de Santo Domingo, resume en dos palabras las razones de los muchos levantamientos ocurridos allí en ese período, «ambición política»: alguna supuesta mala conducta del gobierno se convierte en pretexto para pelear, dice, hecho para engañar al pueblo, que sigue ciegamente la bandera del político ambicioso y el manifiesto que difunde por el país exponiendo las faltas del presidente a quien desea deponer y, de paso, suceder en el cargo.

records.summary_en: The Journal prints the end of a Washington item and a New York item of March 2 on Santo Domingo: the Washington item's closing lines say it does not care to create a strong government on the island by taking sides in the factional struggles there, and the whole subject is under serious consideration by the administration, which realizes that foreign interests are looking to the United States to relieve their own governments of the necessity of taking hold in Santo Domingo. The New York item reports that Gen. Francisco Vasquez, formerly Dominican consul here and a brother of former President Horacio Vasquez, asserts that he has documentary proof that the Jiminez revolutionists are deliberately making war upon Americans in the island in order that the United States government may be moved to interfere and assume a protectorate over the country; one letter shown by General Vasquez purports to have been written by General Arias, governor of Monte Cristi, to Jiminez, and declares that they would prefer to cause the loss of Santo Domingo's sovereignty and autonomy than submit to the government in this struggle. General Vasquez, who has just returned from Santo Domingo, asserts that this policy of the revolutionists explains the killing of the machinist Johnston, of the United States gunboat Yankee, and the firing on the Clyde line steamer New York by the revolutionists.

El capitán me informó que la cañonera Presidente le había cerrado el paso a Macorís y no le había permitido entrar, y que se le había dicho que debía dirigirse a este puerto. Inmediatamente después de recibir esta información me comuniqué con el ministro, pidiéndole que se comunicara con el presidente Morales y le informara que yo no reconocería su derecho a bloquear a Macorís y negar la entrada a los buques que enarbolan la bandera de los Estados Unidos. records.headline: The Republic prints an official letter on a bombardment: the letter
records.summary_en: The Republic prints an official letter on a bombardment: the letter, received from San Pedro de Macoris, Santo Domingo, and dated February 29, gives details of the bombardment of San Pedro de Macoris on February 27 by the Dominican warships Presidente and Estrella: the captain of the Presidente, a Spaniard, was killed, and of those on board her only six of the crew escaped without injuries; in all, 74 men were killed and 23 were wounded on the two ships, and the insurgents lost 36 men killed or wounded. The Presidente was driven away at daybreak, February 28, the insurgents having brought up a field piece in the night and unexpectedly opening fire on her. Several defeats of the troops of President Morales, with heavy losses, have been reported lately. General Jose Amador, who was captured at San Antonio de Guerra with quantities of provisions and clothing and $2,000 in cash, is now a prisoner at San Pedro de Macoris.

records.headline: The News prints a signed description of Santo Domingo, its harbors
records.summary_en: The News prints a signed description of Santo Domingo, its harbors, towns and past: Santo Domingo is one of the beautiful islands of the West Indies, lying between Cuba and Porto Rico; in Samana Bay it possesses one of the finest natural harbors in the world, the port President Grant was especially anxious to secure for a coaling station, at present little used. There are a number of small cities in the republic: Santo Domingo the capital, and Puerto Plata the principal port, at about the same number of inhabitants; La Vega about 10,000, Santiago 8,000 and Samana 2,000. The oldest settlement made in the New World was on this island, Columbus himself having founded it, and here the great discoverer was buried for a number of years; it was the capital of the Spanish possessions in the New World. At the end of the eighteenth century Spain ceded the eastern half of the island to France, which held the western half; soon after, the description says, the whole country under Toussaint Louverture gained its independence, and there followed the rebellion of the eastern portion of the island, resulting in the formation of the present Dominican Republic. Outside of the commercial element, there is said to be much opposition to the idea of annexation to the United States.
records.summary_es: El News publica una descripción firmada de Santo Domingo, sus puertos, sus poblaciones y su pasado: Santo Domingo es una de las hermosas islas de las Antillas, situada entre Cuba y Puerto Rico; en la bahía de Samaná posee uno de los mejores puertos naturales del mundo, el puerto que el presidente Grant estaba especialmente ansioso por asegurar para una estación carbonera, en la actualidad poco usado. Existen varias poblaciones pequeñas en la república: Santo Domingo, la capital, y Puerto Plata, el puerto principal, con más o menos el mismo número de habitantes; La Vega, unos 10,000; Santiago, 8,000, y Samaná, 2,000. El asentamiento más antiguo del Nuevo Mundo estuvo en esta isla, fundado por el propio Colón, y aquí estuvo enterrado el gran descubridor durante varios años; fue la capital de las posesiones españolas en el Nuevo Mundo. A fines del siglo XVIII, España cedió la mitad oriental de la isla a Francia, que poseía la mitad occidental; poco después, dice la descripción, todo el país bajo Toussaint Louverture obtuvo su independencia, y siguió la rebelión de la porción oriental de la isla, que dio por resultado la formación de la actual República Dominicana. Fuera del elemento comercial, se dice que existe mucha oposición a la idea de la anexión a los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: The Times prints an item on the Mayflower's return voyage, with Admiral Dewey
records.summary_en: The Times prints an item on the Mayflower's return voyage, with Admiral Dewey and Assistant Secretary Loomis aboard: Admiral Taylor and the other members of the general board of the navy which went to Guantanamo returned with them to Washington this morning on the Mayflower; after visiting the scene of the maneuvers the Mayflower went to Jamaica, Santo Domingo and Cuba before returning to the United States. Mr. Loomis and the naval officers were especially interested in Santo Domingo, which has been the scene of so many revolutions within the last year. The Mayflower stopped at Puerto Plata, Sanchez, Samana, San Pedro, Santo Domingo city and several other Dominican ports, and members of the party found that press reports of the revolutions there have not been exaggerated.

records.headline: The Herald prints the end of a survey of editorial opinion
records.summary_en: The Herald prints the end of a survey of editorial opinion, and the Atlanta Journal, the Buffalo Express, the Macon Telegraph, the Philadelphia Ledger, the New Orleans Times-Democrat and the New York Globe all denounce the annexation idea. The Philadelphia Ledger says that a 'military occupation of Santo Domingo, purely as an exercise of international police power, is the measure suggested by present conditions.' The Philadelphia Record thinks that if we attempt to police the island it will gradually become a ward of our government: 'A government cannot play the role of a big policeman within the limits of another state without becoming the protector of the latter. The sovereignty of a region resides where the power to preserve order resides, and when one takes over the sovereignty the territory usually goes with it.' Russia understood this fully, the Record says, when she undertook to establish settled conditions in and suppress the banditti of Manchuria. A military administrator put 'temporarily' in charge of the administration of Santo Domingo would be likely to undergo a slow and gradual transformation into a subordinate of the bureau of insular affairs in the war department. The Brooklyn Eagle thinks that there is little hope for any of the West Indies 'except as wards of this nation', and the St. Louis Globe-Democrat, which has advocated annexation of Santo Domingo for some time, says that nothing short of American supervision, which will amount to a virtual protectorate, will end the misrule of the island's ambitious politicians and their followers.
records.summary_es: El Herald publica el final de un examen de la opinión editorial, y el Atlanta Journal, el Buffalo Express, el Macon Telegraph, el Philadelphia Ledger, el New Orleans Times-Democrat y el New York Globe denuncian todos la idea de la anexión. El Philadelphia Ledger dice que una «ocupación militar de Santo Domingo, puramente como ejercicio de poder policial internacional, es la medida que sugieren las condiciones presentes». El Philadelphia Record cree que si intentamos vigilar la isla, esta se convertirá gradualmente en pupila de nuestro gobierno: «Un gobierno no puede desempeñar el papel de gran policía dentro de los límites de otro Estado sin convertirse en protector de este último. La soberanía de una región reside donde reside el poder de preservar el orden, y cuando uno asume la soberanía, el territorio suele ir con ella». Rusia lo entendió plenamente, dice el Record, cuando emprendió establecer condiciones de orden y suprimir a los bandidos de Manchuria. Un administrador militar puesto «temporalmente» a cargo de la administración de Santo Domingo probablemente sufriría una transformación lenta y gradual hasta convertirse en subordinado de la oficina de asuntos insulares del Departamento de Guerra. El Brooklyn Eagle cree que existe poca esperanza para cualquiera de las Antillas «excepto como pupilas de esta nación», y el St. Louis Globe-Democrat, que ha abogado por la anexión de Santo Domingo desde hace algún tiempo, dice que nada menos que una supervisión estadounidense, que equivaldrá a un protectorado virtual, pondrá fin al desgobierno de los políticos ambiciosos de la isla y sus seguidores.

records.summary_en: The *New-York Tribune* recounted political maneuvers during President Buenaventura Báez's historical efforts to annex the Dominican Republic to the United States. The account recalled how Báez jailed political opponents to guarantee passage of the treaty until an American politician persuaded him that a small dissenting vote would look less suspicious. It also detailed an earlier attempt to lease Samana Bay surveyed by Captain George B. McClellan, which collapsed when British and French warships arrived to oppose American acquisition.
records.summary_es: El *New-York Tribune* relató las maniobras políticas durante las gestiones históricas del presidente Buenaventura Báez para anexionar la República Dominicana a los Estados Unidos. La crónica recordó cómo Báez encarceló a opositores políticos para asegurar la aprobación del tratado hasta que un político estadounidense lo convenció de que una pequeña votación disidente resultaría menos sospechosa. Detalló asimismo una tentativa anterior para arrendar la bahía de Samaná, inspeccionada por el capitán George B. McClellan, la cual fracasó al llegar buques de guerra británicos y franceses para oponerse a la adquisición estadounidense.

When the report reached the ears of a prominent New-York politician who was at the Dominican Capitol, and who was greatly interested in the treaty, he went at once to Baez and remonstrated:

“Jail methods will ruin the whole business,” he said. “This thing must be done on the square, or it will fall through.” Baez at first shrugged his shoulders, and when he did speak he only said: “But you want it unanimous, don't you? “Not at all. A unanimous vote always creates suspicion. A small minority vote gives a far better impression.” “All right.” said Baez. “You can have that. Anything you want you can have in San Domingo.” Baez summoned several representatives, and there was a hurried conference. The treaty was passed with a “small minority.” Twenty years before the failure of this annexation scheme this government made a treaty with San Domingo to rent in perpetuity the great sheltered Bay of Samana. The father of the present Mayor of New-York accompanied the commission sent to negotiate for the territory, and Captain McClellan, as he was known then, made a survey of that part of the Dominican coast. Just before the treaty could be ratified, however, news of its purpose leaked out. England and France both took alarm, and dispatched warships to Samana Bay. At the sight of European cannon the San Domingo statesmen forgot all about the treaty.

records.headline: The Tribune prints a New York item: General Sanchez sailed yesterday
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints a New York item: General Sanchez sailed yesterday for San Domingo on the Clyde liner New York, on a special mission for his government; General Sanchez said that his mission to Washington had been entirely successful, the principal object of his trip north being to seek the formal recognition of President Morales by the United States, which was accorded. The Dominican diplomat was especially pleased over a tentative promise which, he said, he had obtained from Secretary Hay to assign a minister resident to San Domingo in the near future; at present Minister Powell, Minister to Hayti, with headquarters at Port-au-Prince, is also chargé d'affaires to the Dominican Republic. 'The sending of a minister to my country will develop closer relations with the United States,' said General Sanchez. 'The report that I came here to ask for the establishment of a protectorate over San Domingo was entirely without foundation. Mr. Loomis, on his recent tour of the republic, must have observed that President Morales is thoroughly capable of handling the situation.' In the hold of the steamer were 150,000 cartridges and rifles consigned to the government.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica una nota de Nueva York: el general Sánchez zarpó ayer hacia Santo Domingo en el vapor New York, de la Clyde line, en misión especial de su gobierno; el general Sánchez dijo que su misión a Washington había sido enteramente exitosa, siendo el objeto principal de su viaje al norte buscar el reconocimiento formal del presidente Morales por los Estados Unidos, que fue concedido. records.headline: The Advertiser prints an editorial survey of the island's past
records.summary_en: The Advertiser prints an editorial survey of the island's past and of the Dominican Republic's present troubles: France reconquered the island in 1801, it says, but lost it again two years later; the Dominican Republic was formed in 1844, and the event, instead of giving the eastern half of the island peaceful government, merely provided another stage for melodrama. The republic has a population of somewhat more than 610,000; suffrage is universal in theory, at least, and a president is supposed to be elected once every four years, but the editorial asserts that the people are absolutely incapable of self-rule, and that the president is any man who is able to seize the government by force and to hold it. The present trouble began with an attack by General Morales upon the government of President Wos y Gil, who himself was only the head of a government which had come into power seven months before by overthrowing the administration of President Vasquez. Danger to the lives and property of foreign residents of Santo Domingo has made it necessary for the United States and other countries to send warships and check the fighting, but every one knows, the editorial says, that this is only a makeshift.

La república tiene una población de algo más de 610,000 habitantes; el sufragio es universal en teoría, al menos, y se supone que un presidente es elegido una vez cada cuatro años, pero el editorial afirma que el pueblo es absolutamente incapaz de gobernarse a sí mismo, y que el presidente es cualquier hombre capaz de apoderarse del gobierno por la fuerza y conservarlo. El problema actual comenzó con un ataque del general Morales contra el gobierno del presidente Wos y Gil, que era a su vez solo la cabeza de un gobierno que había llegado al poder siete meses antes derrocando la administración del presidente Vásquez. El peligro para las vidas y las propiedades de los residentes extranjeros de Santo Domingo ha hecho necesario que los Estados Unidos y otros países enviaran buques de guerra y contuvieran los combates, pero todo el mundo sabe, dice el editorial, que esto es solo una medida provisional.

records.headline: The Times prints an item reporting resistance in the interior of Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Times prints an item reporting resistance in the interior of Santo Domingo to the control of the Dominican president: so declares Gen. Juan Isidro Jiminez, deposed president of the little republic, who arrived in New York yesterday on the Red D steamer Philadelphia. General Jiminez sailed from Monte Cristi last week, after the city had surrendered to the government forces. He alleges he is in the United States to rest and is not here for the purpose of buying arms and ammunition to be used in resisting the authority of President Morales. Statements made by General Jiminez in New York yesterday do not agree with reports made to the State Department concerning the conditions in Santo Domingo: it has been reported officially and unofficially many times that President Morales has the situation well under control and is far the strongest man in the republic, a leader who has the support of practically all factions.

records.headline: The Union Times prints an editorial on the state of affairs
records.summary_en: The Union Times prints an editorial on the state of affairs in Santo Domingo: Samana has been invaded by an armed force which dragged refugees from its protection; two American merchantmen, the Cherokee and the New York, have been repeatedly fired upon; the American training ship Yankee has been fired upon, a machinist aboard her being killed; the launch of the American man-of-war Newark has been fired upon, and the Newark has been forced to shell the woods lying across the river from the city of Santo Domingo. Such a state of affairs is simply intolerable. The great danger in which it places the peace of the world is illustrated by an incident that occurred a few weeks ago: supporters of President Morales boarded a German merchantman, then in the harbor of San Pedro de Macoris, and, seizing three refugees, carried them off as prisoners to a Dominican gunboat. Germany is occupied just at this time, but other such affronts, if they are permitted, may bring down upon the island the just wrath of Europe, and force the United States to assert the Monroe doctrine against some great European power. It is a mistake to suppose that Dominican revolutions are slight and bloodless affairs; as a rule, the editorial says, the slaughter is great.

records.headline: The Star prints an item on the movements of the ex-president
records.summary_en: The Star prints an item on the movements of the ex-president: the French trans-Atlantic steamer St. Simon arrived in San Juan, P. R., two days ago, en route to Santo Domingo and Hayti, bringing from the Danish island of St. Thomas Don Juan Isidro Jiminez, ex-president of the former republic. General Jiminez remained in San Juan but a few hours, leaving by train for Mayaguez, where his wife and children have resided ever since the revolution began. After the defeat of his troops before the city of Santo Domingo and their terrible routing in San Pedro de Macoris and La Vega and other serious reverses, General Jiminez took a German steamer at Monte Cristi, the first to leave that port, for St. Thomas, for the purpose of coming to Porto Rico to try and raise funds for the purchase of arms and ammunition. Should he be unsuccessful in raising a sufficient amount here, he will visit the United States for that purpose. He is no longer the man that he was; the months that he has spent in camp in his disastrous campaign have been sufficient to make him twenty years older. He asserts that his defeat was exclusively due to the lack of arms and ammunition, and that if he can but obtain the necessary funds he may yet recuperate all that has been lost.

El general Jiménez permaneció en San Juan solo unas horas, saliendo en tren hacia Mayagüez, donde su esposa e hijos han residido desde que comenzó la revolución. Tras la derrota de sus tropas ante la ciudad de Santo Domingo y su terrible desbandada en San Pedro de Macorís y La Vega y otros graves reveses, el general Jiménez tomó un vapor alemán en Monte Cristi, el primero en salir de ese puerto, rumbo a St. Thomas, con el propósito de venir a Puerto Rico para tratar de recaudar fondos para la compra de armas y municiones. Si no logra recaudar aquí una cantidad suficiente, visitará los Estados Unidos con ese propósito. Ya no es el hombre que era; los meses que ha pasado en campaña en su desastrosa campaña han bastado para envejecerlo veinte años. Afirma que su derrota se debió exclusivamente a la falta de armas y municiones, y que si logra obtener los fondos necesarios aún puede recuperar todo lo perdido.

records.headline: The Tribune prints a San Domingo dispatch of April 18: the members of the government
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints a San Domingo dispatch of April 18: the members of the government this morning attended a memorial service for the generals killed in the revolution of March 23, and for those killed in the present revolution. All the business houses were closed. The United States cruiser Detroit landed a number of officers and 150 men, who were present at the service, carrying American and Dominican flags. The Americans visited the grave of J. C. Johnson, the machinist of the American cruiser Yankee, who was killed by insurgents in February of the present year, and placed wreaths on the grave. President Morales arrived here yesterday. The political situation is better, although towns are still in the hands of the rebels; produce is entering this city, and the country near San Domingo is quiet.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica un despacho de Santo Domingo del 18 de abril: los miembros del gobierno asistieron esta mañana a un servicio fúnebre por los generales muertos en la revolución del 23 de marzo y por los muertos en la revolución actual. Todos los establecimientos comerciales estuvieron cerrados. El crucero estadounidense Detroit desembarcó a varios oficiales y 150 hombres, que estuvieron presentes en el servicio, llevando banderas estadounidenses y dominicanas. Los estadounidenses visitaron la tumba de J. C. Johnson, el maquinista del crucero estadounidense Yankee, muerto por los insurgentes en febrero del presente año, y colocaron coronas sobre la tumba. El presidente Morales llegó aquí ayer. La situación política es mejor, aunque varias poblaciones siguen en manos de los rebeldes; están entrando productos en esta ciudad, y la comarca cercana a Santo Domingo está tranquila.

records.headline: The Tribune prints an editorial on the application of The Hague Peace Tribunal's Venezuelan decision
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints an editorial on the application of The Hague Peace Tribunal's Venezuelan decision to Santo Domingo: United States Minister William F. Powell at Haiti and Santo Domingo was instructed to give notice to the Dominican Republic, and he has given notice, that he will be obliged to seize the custom-houses of that country in the event of any move by a European power or combination of powers to collect claims from Santo Domingo by force. By the terms of the tribunal's findings, the power that makes the first hostile and effective move for the collection of its claims is the one which must receive preferential treatment, and those that peacefully wait in the hope of diplomatically adjusting their claims come in last, and get what is left. Inasmuch as the claims of citizens of the United States amount to far more than the claims of the citizens of other nations, this measure, strictly in accord with the Peace Tribunal's decision in the Venezuelan arbitration case, is merely one of precaution, and is designed to protect the interests of Americans. It is a necessary step under that precedent; but it is a singular thing, the editorial says, that the first great principle announced by that peace tribunal should be one which is a direct incitement to war.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica un editorial sobre la aplicación a Santo Domingo de la decisión venezolana del Tribunal de Paz de La Haya: el ministro estadounidense William F. Powell en Haití y Santo Domingo recibió instrucciones de notificar a la República Dominicana, y lo ha notificado, que se verá obligado a apoderarse de las aduanas de ese país en caso de cualquier movimiento de una potencia europea o combinación de potencias para cobrar reclamaciones a Santo Domingo por la fuerza. Según los términos de la decisión del tribunal, la potencia que haga el primer movimiento hostil y efectivo para el cobro de sus reclamaciones es la que debe recibir trato preferente, y las que esperen pacíficamente con la esperanza de ajustar diplomáticamente sus reclamaciones quedan últimas, y reciben lo que quede. Como las reclamaciones de los ciudadanos de los Estados Unidos ascienden a mucho más que las reclamaciones de los ciudadanos de otras naciones, esta medida, en estricto acuerdo con la decisión del Tribunal de Paz en el caso del arbitraje venezolano, es meramente de precaución, y está destinada a proteger los intereses de los estadounidenses. Es un paso necesario bajo ese precedente; pero es cosa singular, dice el editorial, que el primer gran principio anunciado por ese tribunal de paz sea uno que constituye una incitación directa a la guerra.

records.headline: The Republican prints a description of Santo Domingo, its harbor
records.summary_en: The Republican prints a description of Santo Domingo, its harbor and its past: in Samana Bay it possesses one of the finest natural harbors in the world; it was this port which President Grant was especially anxious to secure as a coaling station. The oldest settlement made in the new world was on this island, Columbus himself having founded it; here the great discoverer was buried, and here for a number of years was the capital of the Spanish possessions in the new world. At the end of the eighteenth century Spain ceded the eastern half of the island to France, which held the western half; soon after the entire country under Toussaint L'Ouverture gained its independence. In 1844 came the rebellion of the eastern portion of the island, resulting in the formation of the present Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: El Republican publica una descripción de Santo Domingo, su puerto y su pasado: en la bahía de Samaná posee uno de los mejores puertos naturales del mundo; fue este puerto el que el presidente Grant estaba especialmente ansioso por asegurar para una estación carbonera. El asentamiento más antiguo del Nuevo Mundo estuvo en esta isla, fundado por el propio Colón; aquí fue enterrado el gran descubridor, y aquí estuvo durante varios años la capital de las posesiones españolas en el Nuevo Mundo. A fines del siglo XVIII, España cedió la mitad oriental de la isla a Francia, que poseía la mitad occidental; poco después, todo el país bajo Toussaint Louverture obtuvo su independencia. En 1844 vino la rebelión de la porción oriental de la isla, que dio por resultado la formación de la actual República Dominicana.

records.full_text:
POWELL SAYS GOODBY Minister to Santo Domingo Takes Leave of President Morales. GIVES HIM SOME GOOD ADVICE Says the United States Will Not Annex Black Republic, but Will Insist That It Behave Itself and Respect Rights of Foreigners.

Santo Domingo, May 4.—United States Minister William F. Powell, who on account of ill health is compelled to return to Port au Prince, has taken leave of provisional President Morales. The president desired that the ceremonies attending the farewell should show the regret of the government and the Dominican people at Mr. Powell's departure, but the minister requested that the ceremony be omitted. The minister, addressing the president, said that the government and people of the United States had a profound interest in the future of Santo Domingo. They hoped revolutions would cease and that the Dominican family would become united. Neither the government nor the people of the United States had the least idea of annexation. They desired that Santo Domingo should remain a sovereign independent power, and in this the republic would have the support of the United States government.

Powell Reasserts Monroe Doctrine.

Mr. Powell said that his government would not consent to any portion of Dominican territory passing under the control of any foreign power. The future of the republic rested largely on the keeping of all obligations toward foreign creditors, on respecting the concessions the government made to foreigners, on developing the country's resources and on the passage of such laws as would bring prosperity. These considerations and the taking of the whole people into the confidence of the government would be the greatest foil and guard against revolution and anarchy. The minister assured the president that the American people would be at his side if he remained steadfast to the principles of a good republic.

Mr. Powell's departure is regretted by all classes.

The United States cruiser Detroit has returned from visiting northern ports. The Dominican warship Independencia has left here with troops for Monte Cristi, which is still in the hands of the revolutionists.

Mr. Powell, who is minister to Haiti as well as to Santo Domingo, is succeeded as minister to the latter country by Thomas C. Dawson of Iowa.

records.headline: The Star prints an editorial survey of Santo Domingo's governments
records.summary_en: The Star prints an editorial survey of Santo Domingo's governments: Santo Domingo has had, first and last, about every form of government, from that of despotic control of delegates from European thrones to the recent reign of terror; it has been an appanage of Spain, of England and of France; for a few weeks the island, now divided between Santo Domingo and Hayti, had a local emperor. Since the formal proclamation of the Republic in 1844 there has been no end of dictators as well as presidents, some of them good, many the reverse; and tyrants have retained the reins of government longer than humane rulers. Since the assassination of President Heureaux in 1899, eight nominal governments, constitutional or provisional, have been set up and overthrown: Vasquez first ousted Figuerado; Jiminez overthrew Vasquez; Vasquez, in his turn, ousted Jiminez; Wos y Gil forced Vasquez out, establishing first a provisional and then a constitutional administration; in a few months this was overthrown by the surviving provisional government of Morales, with Jiminez and Wos y Gil fighting like demons to destroy the Morales regime. But Morales has withstood opposition, and for the moment is able to turn his attention from fighting to governing. Every man's sway has been cursed by insurrections and bloodshed; otherwise, Santo Domingo would have today five or six million happy and prosperous people instead of a bare 500,000. American material interests in San Domingo are very large; half of the sugar estates belong to Americans.

Desde la proclamación formal de la República en 1844 no ha habido fin de dictadores y de presidentes, algunos buenos, muchos lo contrario; y los tiranos han conservado las riendas del gobierno más tiempo que los gobernantes humanos. Desde el asesinato del presidente Heureaux en 1899, ocho gobiernos nominales, constitucionales o provisionales, han sido establecidos y derrocados: Vásquez derrocó primero a Figuerado; Jiménez derrocó a Vásquez; Vásquez, a su vez, derrocó a Jiménez; Wos y Gil obligó a Vásquez a salir, estableciendo primero una administración provisional y luego una constitucional; en unos meses esta fue derrocada por el gobierno provisional superviviente de Morales, con Jiménez y Wos y Gil luchando como demonios por destruir el régimen de Morales. Pero Morales ha resistido la oposición, y por el momento puede dirigir su atención de la lucha al gobierno. Los intereses materiales estadounidenses en Santo Domingo son muy grandes; la mitad de las haciendas azucareras pertenece a estadounidenses.

records.headline: The Pilot prints a description of Santo Domingo, its harbor
records.summary_en: The Pilot prints a description of Santo Domingo, its harbor and its past: it lies between Cuba and Porto Rico; in Samana Bay it possesses one of the finest natural harbors in the world; it was this port which President Grant was especially anxious to secure as a coaling station. The oldest settlement made in the new world was on this island, Columbus himself having founded it; here the great discoverer was buried, and here for a number of years was the capital of the Spanish possessions in the new world. At the end of the eighteenth century Spain ceded the eastern half of the island to France, which held the western half; soon after the entire country under Toussaint L'Ouverture gained its independence. In 1844 came the rebellion of the eastern portion of the island, resulting in the formation of the present Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: El Pilot publica una descripción de Santo Domingo, su puerto y su pasado: está situado entre Cuba y Puerto Rico; en la bahía de Samaná posee uno de los mejores puertos naturales del mundo; fue este puerto el que el presidente Grant estaba especialmente ansioso por asegurar para una estación carbonera. El asentamiento más antiguo del Nuevo Mundo estuvo en esta isla, fundado por el propio Colón; aquí fue enterrado el gran descubridor, y aquí estuvo durante varios años la capital de las posesiones españolas en el Nuevo Mundo. A fines del siglo XVIII, España cedió la mitad oriental de la isla a Francia, que poseía la mitad occidental; poco después, todo el país bajo Toussaint Louverture obtuvo su independencia. En 1844 vino la rebelión de la porción oriental de la isla, que dio por resultado la formación de la actual República Dominicana.

It was announced from Cape Haytien on May 10 that the Haytien authorities had authorized a Dominican cruiser to disembark a strong contingent of troops on Haytien territory for the investment of Monte Cristi, which adjoins Haytien territory, this being made necessary by the fruitlessness of the many bombardments of Monte Cristi by the Dominican gunboat Presidente. records.headline: The Examiner prints advices from San Domingo, under the heads
records.summary_en: The Examiner prints advices from San Domingo, under the heads 'Government Lost 151 in Two Battles' and 'Officers Fled After Fight': severe fighting took place at Navarrete on May 14, and the government troops were defeated, losing 54 men killed and 67 wounded; express trains carrying the wounded arrived at Puerto Plata and Santiago de los Caballeros on May 15. A convoy with 20,000 cartridges, from Puerto Plata to President Morales' forces, fell into the hands of the Dominican insurgents. Dominican government troops, commanded by General Raoul Cabrera, and Dominican revolutionary troops, led by General Pelico Lasala, met at Guayacanes, Santo Domingo, midway between Santiago de los Caballeros and Monte Cristi; in the fighting which followed the government force had 30 men killed or wounded and the revolutionists lost heavily. Five revolutionary generals, including Espaillat, sought refuge in the French and Venezuelan consulates here, and later embarked on the French steamer Olinde Rodriguez, bound for Porto Rico.

records.summary_en: A special cable from Santo Domingo reports that peace has been concluded with the insurgents, that General Cespedes will take charge of the government and that the rebel leader General Rodriguez promises to leave the country, though members of the Jimenez party express dissatisfaction, believing the American gunboats aided Acting President Morales and forced the rebels to capitulate. Rear Admiral Sigsbee telegraphed the Navy Department from Monte Cristi that the custom house there would resume business that day, that all the ports of the Dominican Republic are now open to commerce and that the revolution has ended.
records.summary_es: Un cable especial de Santo Domingo informa que se ha concluido la paz con los insurgentes, que el general Céspedes se hará cargo del gobierno y que el líder rebelde general Rodríguez promete abandonar el país, aunque miembros del partido de Jiménez expresan su descontento, creyendo que los cañoneros estadounidenses ayudaron al presidente interino Morales y obligaron a los rebeldes a capitular. El contralmirante Sigsbee telegrafió al Departamento de Marina desde Monte Cristi que la aduana de allí reanudaría sus operaciones ese día, que todos los puertos de la República Dominicana están ahora abiertos al comercio y que la revolución ha terminado.

records.summary_en: The Star prints a traveler's letter from Santo Domingo's north coast: if the rest of the republic should prove to be as orderly and well kept as Puerto Plata, the writer says, he shall be able to say that the entire country has been most outrageously maligned. From the sea Puerto Plata is first seen as a narrow strip of mottled white, nestling close under a rugged mountain covered with dark green foliage, so steep that it seems as though the venturesome mountain climber could scarcely find a foothold upon its rugged sides. It was on this north coast that Columbus founded the first colony in the new world, and the letter recalls his description of the island upon his return to Spain, when, it is said, crumpling a sheet of paper in his fist, he threw it down, saying, 'The island is like that.'

Desde el mar, Puerto Plata se ve primero como una estrecha franja de blanco moteado, acurrucada junto a una montaña escarpada cubierta de oscuro follaje verde, tan empinada que parece que el aventurero alpinista apenas podría encontrar apoyo en sus escarpados costados. Fue en esta costa norte donde Colón fundó la primera colonia del Nuevo Mundo, y la carta recuerda su descripción de la isla a su regreso a España, cuando, según se dice, estrujando una hoja de papel en el puño, la arrojó al suelo, diciendo: «La isla es así».

records.headline: Writing from Santiago de los Caballeros on June 17, the correspondent says Santo Domingo has had some two hundred
records.summary_en: Writing from Santiago de los Caballeros on June 17, the correspondent says Santo Domingo has had some two hundred revolutions within sixty years of independence and that their battles were long fought with little bloodshed, but that this is no longer the rule. He asserts that more people have been killed in the present revolution than in the war with Spain forty years ago, and gives eyewitness accounts of the battle at Puerto Plata last January, where soldiers on both sides fired their guns off as fast as they could load until their ammunition was gone, and then ran.
records.summary_es: Escribiendo desde Santiago de los Caballeros el 17 de junio, el corresponsal dice que Santo Domingo ha tenido unas doscientas revoluciones en sesenta años de independencia y que sus batallas se libraban durante mucho tiempo con poco derramamiento de sangre, pero que eso ya no es la regla. Afirma que en la revolución actual ha muerto más gente que en la guerra con España de hace cuarenta años, y ofrece testimonios de la batalla de Puerto Plata del enero pasado, donde los soldados de ambos bandos dispararon sus armas tan rápido como podían cargarlas hasta agotar las municiones, y luego huyeron.

records.summary_en: The Tribune prints a Washington item of July 15, under the head 'How Powell Carried His Point': an incident in connection with the disturbed conditions in the Dominican Republic and the firm stand taken by Minister Powell is shown by the current volume on foreign relations, advance sheets of which are now appearing. Mr. Powell had asked the President of San Domingo to rescind an order which prevented a merchant vessel from departing from port and landing her cargo at certain places, and on receiving a reply that the President could not do so, the Minister said: 'Then, your excellency, there is but one course open to you to take. records.summary_es: El Tribune publica una nota de Washington del 15 de julio, bajo el título «How Powell Carried His Point»: un incidente relacionado con las condiciones perturbadas de la República Dominicana y la firme postura adoptada por el ministro Powell se muestra en el volumen actual sobre relaciones exteriores, cuyas entregas anticipadas están apareciendo ahora. El Sr. Powell había pedido al presidente de Santo Domingo que rescindiera una orden que impedía a un buque mercante salir del puerto y desembarcar su carga en ciertos lugares, y al recibir la respuesta de que el presidente no podía hacerlo, el ministro dijo: «Entonces, excelencia, no le queda más que una vía abierta. Ordenaré al capitán dirigirse a esos lugares a desembarcar esta carga, y usted tendrá que hundirla o capturarla, y cuando lo haga aceptará toda responsabilidad futura por su acción». El capitán sacó su buque sin contratiempos.

records.headline: The Star prints two reports from Santo Domingo: an official
records.summary_en: The Star prints two reports from Santo Domingo: an official who had visited the various Dominican ports before presenting his credentials at San Domingo reported to Acting Secretary Loomis in detail, summing up that there is no disturbance in this immediate locality and no likelihood of an immediate outbreak, and that the same is reported to be true throughout the country, except at La Vega, where a revolutionist named Perica has two or three hundred men under arms. Minister Powell reports to the State Department from Port au Prince, under date of July 10, that Jiminez's friends have become quite active again, notwithstanding the agreement made at Monte Cristi; disturbances have occurred at Azua, but they were suppressed through the efforts of Gen. Sanchez, and some troubles at Cibao were also suppressed by the government. It is predicted that Jiminez will again be fighting in a short time, though one report says that he is at Mayaguez, with no intention of re-entering political life.

Se predice que Jiménez volverá a luchar dentro de poco, aunque un informe dice que está en Mayagüez, sin intención de volver a entrar en la vida política.

records.headline: The Star prints the closing part of an item on the arbitration of the claim of a York corporation
records.summary_en: The Star prints the closing part of an item on the arbitration of the claim of a York corporation: the company had extensive financial and property interests in the island, including docks, bridges and a railroad, and the government took this railroad without compensating the company. Through the efforts of Minister Powell, San Domingo about a year ago admitted a liability of $4,300,000 to the company; the method of payment, the time to be allowed and other matters were to be arbitrated. John G. Carlisle was appointed for the company, Senor Galvan, the Dominican consul general, represented his government, and Judge George Gray of Delaware was chosen by them as umpire. These arbitrators have fixed 4 per cent as the amount of interest to be paid by the Dominican government on the principal of $4,300,000; they have provided for monthly payments on the sliding scale and have named Puerto Plata, Sanchez, Samana and Monte Cristi as ports whose customs revenues are to be pledged as securities for the payments.

Por los esfuerzos del ministro Powell, Santo Domingo admitió hace alrededor de un año una responsabilidad de $4,300,000 ante la compañía; el método de pago, el plazo que se concedería y otros asuntos debían ser arbitrados. records.headline: The Star prints a report on the plotting of the Dominican exiles
records.summary_en: The Star prints a report on the plotting of the Dominican exiles against the government of President Morales: the exiles in Mayaguez have succeeded in raising a small loan, and those in Havana and Santiago de Cuba, who are said to have the decided but secret support of the Cuban government, have succeeded in obtaining a loan of some eight or ten thousand dollars. The revolutionists are therefore actively seeking to introduce a large amount of arms and ammunition into the Dominican republic, which they desire to secrete in available localities for use when the proper moment arrives. President Morales' action in appointing the revolutionary chief Demetrio Castillo, who capitulated to the government forces a short time ago, governor of Monte Cristi is most favorable for the revolutionists, as it is asserted that Castillo is secretly in league with his old comrades; President Morales seems to be so far ignorant of these facts, and trusts to the great difficulty the revolutionists experience in raising a decent loan to keep them from immediately renewing their attack upon his government. On the other hand, Morales' government seems to be very unstable: it is practically bankrupt; there is no money in the country, no work, no industry to speak of, very little commerce, and an enormous national debt whose interest is not paid.
records.summary_es: El Star publica un informe sobre las conspiraciones de los exiliados dominicanos contra el gobierno del presidente Morales: los exiliados en Mayagüez han logrado reunir un pequeño préstamo, y los de La Habana y Santiago de Cuba, de quienes se dice que cuentan con el decidido pero secreto apoyo del gobierno cubano, han logrado obtener un préstamo de unos ocho o diez mil dólares. Los revolucionarios buscan por ello activamente introducir una gran cantidad de armas y municiones en la república dominicana, que desean esconder en localidades disponibles para usarlas cuando llegue el momento oportuno. La acción del presidente Morales al nombrar gobernador de Monte Cristi al jefe revolucionario Demetrio Castillo, que capituló ante las fuerzas del gobierno hace poco tiempo, es de lo más favorable para los revolucionarios, pues se afirma que Castillo está secretamente aliado con sus antiguos camaradas; el presidente Morales parece ignorar hasta ahora estos hechos, y confía en la gran dificultad que los revolucionarios experimentan para reunir un préstamo decente para impedir que renueven inmediatamente su ataque contra su gobierno. Por otra parte, el gobierno de Morales parece muy inestable: está prácticamente en bancarrota; no hay dinero en el país, no hay trabajo, no hay industria de que hablar, muy poco comercio, y una enorme deuda nacional cuyos intereses no se pagan.

records.headline: The Times prints an item, under the head 'May Establish Protectorate'
records.summary_en: The Times prints an item, under the head 'May Establish Protectorate', that diplomatists are watching with much interest to see what action the United States will take concerning the Dominican republic as soon as the November election is over; it is freely predicted that revolutions in Santo Domingo will be ended for good and all by the establishment of a sort of protectorate by the United States. United States Minister Dawson's latest reports from Santo Domingo indicate that there is little hope of long continued peace under present conditions; the United States cannot permit the European powers to regulate affairs in the republic because of the Monroe Doctrine, and consequently action on the part of this Government seems imperative.

records.headline: The Times prints an item, under the heads 'Santo Domingo Has a Navy'
records.summary_en: The Times prints an item, under the heads 'Santo Domingo Has a Navy' and 'Republic Buys a Warship': Santo Domingo has purchased a warship. United States Minister Powell, at Haiti, sent the State Department a dispatch this morning announcing that the Dominican Republic has just completed negotiations with Italy for a man-of-war. No details are given as to the size of the vessel or its cost, but Dominicans announce that it is expected in Dominican waters about October 20.

records.headline: The Journal prints a dispatch, under the head 'Dominican Republic'
records.summary_en: The Journal prints a dispatch, under the head 'Dominican Republic', that special advices received at Cape Haytien by the correspondent of the Associated Press from Monte Cristi, republic of Santo Domingo, announce that General Candelaria de Las Rosas, with fifty men, revolted against the government on September 26, in favor of Isidoro Jimires, and started for the interior. The Dominican gunboat Presidente, with 150 troops on board, has sailed from Barahona, on the south coast of San Domingo. Ramon Caceres, vice president of Santo Domingo, has resigned. The dispatch cautions that Isidoro Jimines should not be confounded with General Juan Jimenez, the former president of Santo Domingo, who was recently in New York city.
records.summary_es: El Journal publica un despacho, bajo el título «Dominican Republic», en el que avisos especiales recibidos en Cabo Haitiano por el corresponsal de la Associated Press desde Monte Cristi, república de Santo Domingo, anuncian que el general Candelaria de Las Rosas, con cincuenta hombres, se rebeló contra el gobierno el 26 de septiembre, a favor de Isidoro Jiménez, y partió hacia el interior. La cañonera dominicana Presidente, con 150 tropas a bordo, ha zarpado de Barahona, en la costa sur de Santo Domingo. Ramón Cáceres, vicepresidente de Santo Domingo, ha renunciado. El despacho advierte que Isidoro Jiménez no debe confundirse con el general Juan Jiménez, expresidente de Santo Domingo, que estuvo recientemente en la ciudad de Nueva York.

records.headline: The article describes President Morales arriving at Puerto Plata with five hundred troops aboard his gunboat El Presidente
records.summary_en: The article describes President Morales arriving at Puerto Plata with five hundred troops aboard his gunboat El Presidente, intending to proceed to Monte Cristi, whose authorities had signed a peace compact aboard the American ship Detroit. Those authorities told him by telegraph that he could not land his troops in their territory, and, finding them fully prepared and under arms to resist, he gave up the project and returned to the capital, while the American ship Bancroft sailed away to Porto Rico. The article also charges that Morales broke his amnesty agreements, describing how the surrendered rebel chief Jose Gonzalo was shot in the back by his escort on the road to Santiago, supposedly while trying to escape, and saying such executions have been common under his government.
records.summary_es: El artículo describe al presidente Morales llegando a Puerto Plata con quinientos soldados a bordo de su cañonero El Presidente, con la intención de seguir hacia Monte Cristi, cuyas autoridades habían firmado un acuerdo de paz a bordo del buque americano Detroit. Esas autoridades le dijeron por telégrafo que no podía desembarcar sus tropas en su territorio y, al encontrarlas plenamente preparadas y en armas para resistir, abandonó el proyecto y regresó a la capital, mientras el buque americano Bancroft zarpaba hacia Porto Rico. El artículo también acusa a Morales de romper sus acuerdos de amnistía, describe cómo el jefe rebelde rendido José Gonzalo fue baleado por la espalda por su escolta en el camino a Santiago, supuestamente mientras intentaba escapar, y afirma que ejecuciones como esa han sido comunes bajo su gobierno.
