records.headline: This long feature charges that President Morales used peace compacts arranged with American help, one by Commander Dillingham of the Detroit
records.summary_en: This long feature charges that President Morales used peace compacts arranged with American help, one by Commander Dillingham of the Detroit at Monte Cristi and another in the south aboard the Bancroft, to get the rebels to lay down their arms, conceding anything in the agreements and then keeping none of his promises. It describes the shooting of surrendered rebel chiefs, fighting at La Vega, Moca and Esperanza in which the Minister of War was killed and government troops routed, and Morales's attempt, backed by the Bancroft's investigation, to retake Monte Cristi after claiming its people had broken their compact.
records.summary_es: Este extenso reportaje acusa al presidente Morales de usar acuerdos de paz concertados con ayuda americana, uno por el comandante Dillingham, del Detroit, en Monte Cristi y otro en el sur a bordo del Bancroft, para lograr que los rebeldes depusieran las armas, concediendo cualquier cosa en los acuerdos para luego no cumplir ninguna de sus promesas. I.: a steamer from Puerto Plata, Santo Domingo, reports that the United States has seized the custom-house at Puerto Plata; the Dominican consul has no information of such seizure and discredits the report. records.summary_en: The Tribune prints a Washington item of November 23, under the head 'Peace Expected in San Domingo': prospects for peace in the Dominican Republic for the next few months are improved, according to a report received at the State Department today from Minister Dawson. The Minister reports that Candelario Rosa and all of the insurgents under his command, numbering fifty, have recently surrendered at Barahona, and that they are to be tried by the government. Mr. Dawson says he has been assured that the revolutionists received no reward for their surrender, although the governmental commander at Barahona is said to have given them assurances of personal safety. The representative business men of Monte Christi say they have no thought of insurrection, and point to the fact that General Demetrio Roderiguez has agreed to come to San Domingo for an amicable conference with President Morales. The Minister adds that the discussion about the recent arbitration awards in favor of an American concern is diminishing.

records.headline: The Banner prints an editorial on the American fiscal control of the Dominican ports
records.summary_en: The Banner prints an editorial on the American fiscal control of the Dominican ports: under the award, the United States claims control, through a fiscal agent, of the ports of Puerto Plata, Sanchez, Samana and Monte Cristi; Puerto Plata has already been taken, and the others will be in the near future. The only remaining ports of the republic are Santo Domingo city and Macoris, the receipts from which are pledged in payment of bonds held chiefly by French and Belgian citizens. The revolutions of such frequent occurrence in Santo Domingo are usually due to the efforts of the revolutionists to acquire possession of the ports which will be administered by the government, and American custody of these sources of revenue will therefore effectually prevent further revolution. The assumption that the United States will, after undertaking the administration of the four ports named, go further and assume temporary charge of the entire Dominican administration, with the hope of establishing it on a sound and businesslike basis, is occasioned, the editorial says, by the hopeless insolvency of the present regime, the tyranny of militarism which dominates the republic, and the constant danger that European creditors may be driven to exasperation and their governments feel called upon to do the work which can be better done by the United States.
records.summary_es: El Banner publica un editorial sobre el control fiscal estadounidense de los puertos dominicanos: bajo el laudo, los Estados Unidos reclaman el control, por medio de un agente fiscal, de los puertos de Puerto Plata, Sánchez, Samaná y Monte Cristi; Puerto Plata ya ha sido tomado, y los demás lo serán en un futuro cercano. Los únicos puertos restantes de la república son la ciudad de Santo Domingo y Macorís, cuyos ingresos están dados en garantía de bonos poseídos principalmente por ciudadanos franceses y belgas. Las revoluciones de tan frecuente ocurrencia en Santo Domingo se deben usualmente a los esfuerzos de los revolucionarios por adquirir la posesión de los puertos que serán administrados por el gobierno, y la custodia estadounidense de esas fuentes de ingresos impedirá por tanto efectivamente futuras revoluciones. La suposición de que los Estados Unidos, después de emprender la administración de los cuatro puertos nombrados, irán más lejos y asumirán temporalmente el cargo de toda la administración dominicana, con la esperanza de establecerla sobre una base sólida y práctica, se debe, dice el editorial, a la desesperada insolvencia del régimen actual, a la tiranía del militarismo que domina la república, y al constante peligro de que los acreedores europeos se vean llevados a la exasperación y sus gobiernos se sientan llamados a hacer la obra que los Estados Unidos pueden hacer mejor.

records.summary_en: This feature portrays President Carlos F. Morales ruling Santo Domingo through a secret black list of citizens to be killed or imprisoned, and recounts how, on the eve of his inauguration, he had General Mansueta and Commander Guillhoux taken out at sunrise and shot at the cemetery after they asked for a pardon. It stresses that the execution deliberately violated an amnesty compact signed three weeks earlier aboard the United States cruiser Detroit, in Commander Dillingham's presence, guaranteeing the lives and liberty of rebels who laid down their arms.
records.summary_es: Esta crónica presenta al presidente Carlos F. Morales gobernando Santo Domingo mediante una lista negra secreta de ciudadanos para matar o encarcelar, y relata cómo, en la víspera de su toma de posesión, hizo sacar al amanecer al general Mansueta y al comandante Guillhoux y fusilarlos en el cementerio después de que pidieran un indulto. Subraya que la ejecución violó deliberadamente un pacto de amnistía firmado tres semanas antes a bordo del crucero estadounidense Detroit, en presencia del comandante Dillingham, que garantizaba la vida y la libertad de los rebeldes que depusieran las armas.

records.headline: The Messenger prints an editorial on the American customs administration
records.summary_en: The Messenger prints an editorial on the American customs administration in Santo Domingo: it is said that other ports will soon fall into the hands of fiscal agents of the United States government, for it seems the customs fees at Puerto Plata do not come in fast enough to satisfy the American creditors. Matters have not gotten far enough along yet to discuss the question of permanent occupancy of the island; that point has not been reached yet. Now it is only a question of holding the ports temporarily and administering the affairs of the customs houses for the benefit of the American creditors of this West Indian republic. The Stars and Stripes now flies over one Dominican customs house; that flag will in all probability soon be raised over others. The editorial does not say they should not be pulled down, and is not hankering after the annexation of the Dominican republic, but it has an idea that if the United States government once gets a foothold on this island it will eventually be annexed: 'This land-grabbing is a very insidious disease. It develops rapidly and is an incurable malady.'

records.headline: U. S. Receivership for Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The *Spokane Press* reviewed the history of United States annexation attempts in the Dominican Republic, focusing on President Buenaventura Báez's 1869 pact with President Grant. The treaty failed in the Senate after Senator Charles Sumner denounced Báez as a corrupt despot maintained in power solely by American naval force. The article also noted the short-lived 1872 lease of Samana Bay and President Heureaux's subsequent transfer of national custom houses to an American syndicate in 1893.
records.summary_es: El *Spokane Press* repasó la historia de los intentos de anexión de los Estados Unidos en la República Dominicana, centrándose en el pacto de 1869 entre el presidente Buenaventura Báez y el presidente Grant. El tratado fracasó en el Senado después de que el senador Charles Sumner denunciara a Báez como un déspota corrupto sostenido en el poder únicamente por la fuerza naval estadounidense. El artículo también destacó el efímero arrendamiento de la bahía de Samaná en 1872 y la posterior transferencia de las aduanas nacionales que hizo el presidente Heureaux a un sindicato estadounidense en 1893.

records.full_text:
U. S. RECEIVERSHIP FOR SANTO DOMINGO

The Novel Scheme Which Roosevelt Will Probably Put Into Effect—Island Would Have Been Annexed to This Country in 1869 But for the Opposition of Chas. Sumner.

By Jacob Waldeck.
WASHINGTON, Jan. 10.—Santo Domingo, torn by revolution, misgoverned and despoiled, is soon to feel the chastening influence of "the big stick." A century of turmoil, bloodshed, robbery and disorder is to be terminated by the intervention of the United States.

Officials of the highest rank in the administration say that such action is inevitable. President Roosevelt is said, on the best authority, to hold that view of the case. It is a question of time, but of months, rather than years. American officials and American marines will inaugurate a reign of good order and a season of debt-paying in the country.

They don't call it that in diplomatic language, but the proposed order of things in Santo Domingo seems to be nothing more or less than a receivership. It will be

Something Brand New
in American history. The republic will bear a relation to this country unlike Porto Rico, which was annexed; unlike the Philippines, which were hitched on behind, and unlike Cuba, which is the object of a benevolent guardianship. Santo Domingo is to be regulated. It is to be told to pay its debts and be good.

The plan is to place men in the custom houses to collect the revenue of the country. They are to see that a fair share of this money goes to the creditors, and that public officials, instead of looting the public treasury, conduct the government on an economical basis. One custom house, that of Puerto Plata, is now in the hands of an American as a result of arbitration, last summer, over a claim of $5,000,000 owned by New Yorkers. They advanced a lot of money about 10 years ago and took a blanket mortgage on the government. The proceeds at Puerto Plata are being devoted to their claim.

Opinion as to the new deal is divided among the people. Creditors, business men and most of the people of the cities favor it. Those living in the interior are, as a rule, opposed to foreign interference. So are the insurgent chiefs, who fear that a settled order of things may interfere with the revolution industry and keep them from digging their hands into the treasury.

A Land of Chaos.
In the past the order of things has been very much unsettled. The country has been in a chronic state of revolution. There have been nearly a dozen presidents in five years.

From the standpoint of novelty it would seem that the people ought to welcome a receivership. The country has had autocratic, monarchial and republican forms of government. It has also had no government; there having been prolonged seasons of anarchy. Te people have been ruled by despots, emperors and presidents. Mostly despots, though, for whatever the title of the man who happened to be ruling for a short period, he has usually paid no attention to law. Men whom he hasn't liked he has caused to be shot. Any money lying around that he fancied he has appropriated. If money was scarce he negotiated loans at extravagant rates from foreigners. The lenders got Chadwick rates in the way of interest and bonuses, and could rest serene in the fact that when the day for settlement came their governments would force San Domingo to pay.

Another class of men who may embarrass the administration, when intervention takes place, are now flocking to Santo Domingo. They are "investors." A lot of them, Americans, are going over to the republic from Porto Rico. They

Scent Rich Profits
and are eager to be early on the ground. Tehir option is to pick up property at anarchy rates and sell at prices incident to American rule. Santo Domingo, in its climate and resources, has been described by all travelers who have visited the country as one of the most attractive and richest spots in the world. It has not been developed because for 100 years there has been little or no respect for personal or property rights. As a result of this condition it has been possible for years to buy the best of sugar land and land covered with magnificent forests at a nominal price. A good many Americans have taken advantage of the opportunity. They have made no attempt to develop their holdings, but have patiently awaited the day when order should be restored in the country. Others are now crowding in to get the benefit of the bargains offered. They are confident that this country will, in some form, soon enforce order, and they are equally confident that when the United States finally withdraws it will exact guarantees for the protection of their interests.

Came Close to Annexation.
The question of adding the territory of the republic to the United States has been raised at intervals for half a century. It confronted Lincoln in the closing days of the civil war, but he was busy with bigger problems, and consigned it to a pigeonhole. Grant took it up in 1869. Men contended in those days that Santo Domingo would be a more valuable acquisition than Cuba, Haiti or Porto Rico. The fine climate, valuable forests, rich soil, sparse population and small public debt were all said to be in its favor. At that time the debt to be assumed by this country would have been only $1,500,000. Now it would be $32,000,000, secured by Dominican bonds, while Spain would put in a claim for other millions that, the dons say, they were to receive if the republic should ever, by consent of its people, become annexed to another country.

De B. Randolph Keim, a Pennsylvania editor who is also an official of the bureau of insular affairs, brought the first proposition of annexation to this country. He went to the island in 1869 as the correspondent of a New York newspaper.

President Buenaventura Baez feared that he was going to be displaced by revolutionists. His predecessor had

In a Similar Predicament
given the country to Spain. The latter held it from 1861 to 1865. Baez thought it would be a good scheme to deliver the republic to the United States. He feared to trust a communication on the subject to the mails. Keim was therefore induced to carry the offer to President Grant. The latter received it with the utmost favor. A commission sent by him to the island spent 40 days in investigation and returned with a favorable report. The Dominicans at an election voted in favor of annexation. A treaty was signed Nov. 29, 1869. Grant submitted it to the senate with a favorable recommendation. It was bitterly opposed by Chas. Sumner, chairman of the committee on foreign relations. He denounced Baez as an adventurer and declared that he was held in power by the United States navy. Sumner defeated the treaty. Soon thereafter he was deposed from the chairmanship of the foreign relations committee and otherwise humiliated by his republican colleagues. In 1872, Samana bay, one of the finest harbors on this side of the world, was ceded to a company formed in the United States, but the cession was cancelled in the following year because of the non-payment of rent. When President Heureaux, in 1893, delivered the custom houses to an American company as security for a loan, there was a great outcry soon there was only one president. There was not and has not been, however, much that resembled a civilized governmetn. Now that the cruiser Detroit, Captain Bernard G. Scott, is on guard. It is believed that only the presence of that vessel has prevented the hatching of new revolutions. While there has been quiet, however, there has been no disposition or an inability to pay the debt held by Americans or Europeans. Conditions are intolerable. Unless among Dominicans that it would lead to annexation. In 1891 President Harrison proclaimed a reciprocity treaty with the republie.

The Detroit on Guard.
The navy department has long been keeping a sharp watch on Santo Domingo. About a year ago, when two men were claiming the presidency and two or three revolutions were going on, a naval squadron was sent down there to restore order. Capt. Richard Wainwright brought up the disturbers with a sharp turn and the United States interferes, some foreign power will probably assert its rights. So the United States will step in as the policeman of the occacation.

records.headline: The Tribune prints an editorial on the Santo Domingo settlement
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints an editorial on the Santo Domingo settlement announced by the President's direction today: in ten days agents of the United States will take charge of the fiscal affairs of Santo Domingo, readjust the tariff to provide sufficient revenue for satisfying foreign claims and meeting the expenses of government, administer the custom houses, and endeavor to save the country from irreparable ruin. The experiment is to be tried at the earnest request of President Morales of the Dominican Republic, and is confidently expected to eradicate the restless revolutionary spirit so constantly manifested in the country, and to preserve order and promote prosperity from one end of it to the other. With the chief incentive for instability of government removed by a responsible hand controlling the purse strings, it is believed that an era of peace and industry will speedily be inaugurated. The arrangement has none of the attributes of a treaty, and will not require ratification by the Senate; in fact, it is explained, the United States is doing very little more for Santo Domingo than it did for Japan over thirty years ago, when it loaned experts to that country.
records.summary_es: El Tribune publica un editorial sobre el acuerdo de Santo Domingo anunciado hoy por disposición del Presidente: en diez días los agentes de los Estados Unidos se harán cargo de los asuntos fiscales de Santo Domingo, reajustarán el arancel para proporcionar ingresos suficientes para satisfacer las reclamaciones extranjeras y cubrir los gastos del gobierno, administrarán las aduanas y procurarán salvar al país de la ruina irreparable. records.summary_en: The Advertiser prints the official statement on the Santo Domingo agreement: representatives of this government and Santo Domingo have signed a memorandum of a proposed agreement looking to the American control of fiscal affairs upon the request and with the consent of the Dominican government. 'The United States proposes to guarantee the territorial integrity of the Dominican republic. It is not the purpose of this government to assume a protectorate of Santo Domingo or to interfere with or participate in its domestic affairs any further than collection of its customs revenues, the revision of the tariff laws and the adjustment through properly constituted tribunals or commissions of its foreign claims, as its economic and fiscal organisation on a sound basis may make it essential to do.' President Morales has signed a decree which will be published today, in which the government of the United States is officially asked to take full charge of all the Dominican custom houses, to name all the employes and to collect all the revenues, forty-five per cent of which are to be returned to the Dominican government for its current expenses; the balance is to be used to meet the interest charges on the acknowledged bonded indebtedness and other obligations of the republic, and any surplus will be turned over to the Dominican government. The obligations representing the bonded indebtedness are largely owned by foreign creditors. The government of the United States does not guarantee the debts of Santo Domingo.

records.headline: The Journal prints the official statement on the Santo Domingo agreement
records.summary_en: The Journal prints the official statement on the Santo Domingo agreement: the American control of fiscal affairs is to be upon the request and with the consent of the Dominican government. The United States proposes to guarantee the territorial integrity of the Dominican republic; it is not the purpose of this government to assume a protectorate over Santo Domingo or to interfere with, or participate in, its domestic affairs any further than the collection of its customs revenues, the necessary revision of its tariff laws and the adjustment, through properly constituted tribunals or commissions, of its foreign claims, and its economic and fiscal organization on a sound basis may make it essential to do. The government of the United States does not guarantee the debts of Santo Domingo, or agree to provide for the payment of them, but only promises to try to so organize and adjust the fiscal administration of the country that in time their liquidation may be accomplished automatically, and on a basis of equity toward all creditors. The Journal adds, under the head 'Menace for America', that the unfortunate financial condition of Santo Domingo has more than once in the last decade brought to the United States government questions fraught with imminent peril, and that the government of the United States could not, with due self-respect, allow the impression to deepen and gain currency that the Monroe doctrine can be used as a shield by American republics to deny justice to other governments; many foreign claims are just, beyond peradventure.
records.summary_es: El Journal publica la declaración oficial sobre el acuerdo de Santo Domingo: el control estadounidense de los asuntos fiscales ha de ser a petición y con el consentimiento del gobierno dominicano. Los Estados Unidos se proponen garantizar la integridad territorial de la República Dominicana; no es el propósito de este gobierno asumir un protectorado sobre Santo Domingo ni interferir, ni participar, en sus asuntos internos más allá del cobro de sus ingresos aduaneros, la revisión necesaria de sus leyes arancelarias y el ajuste, por medio de tribunales o comisiones debidamente constituidos, de sus reclamaciones extranjeras, y su organización económica y fiscal sobre una base sana lo haga esencial. El gobierno de los Estados Unidos no garantiza las deudas de Santo Domingo, ni acuerda proveer para el pago de ellas, sino que solo promete tratar de organizar y ajustar la administración fiscal del país de modo que con el tiempo su liquidación pueda efectuarse automáticamente, y sobre una base de equidad hacia todos los acreedores. El Journal añade, bajo el título «Menace for America», que la desdichada condición financiera de Santo Domingo ha traído más de una vez en la última década al gobierno de los Estados Unidos cuestiones cargadas de peligro inminente, y que el gobierno de los Estados Unidos no podría, con el debido respeto de sí mismo, permitir que se profundizara y ganara circulación la impresión de que la doctrina Monroe puede usarse como escudo por las repúblicas americanas para negar justicia a otros gobiernos; muchas reclamaciones extranjeras son justas, sin lugar a dudas.

records.headline: The Bee prints an editorial on the Santo Domingo agreement
records.summary_en: The Bee prints an editorial on the Santo Domingo agreement: a protectorate over that country had doubtless been considered, and such a course would have been entirely satisfactory to the foreign governments having claims against San Domingo, since it would have assured peace in the island and the proper collection and disbursement of its revenues. But it would have been widely regarded, and especially by the republics of this hemisphere, as a prelude of annexation, and undoubtedly would not have been approved by the people of the United States. An agreement has now been reached, by invitation of the government of San Domingo, under which the United States will assist in the administration of the revenues of the island and endeavor to put its fiscal affairs on a sound basis. The announcement of this arrangement explains that the United States proposes to guarantee the territorial integrity of the Dominican republic and does not purpose assuming a protectorate or interfering or participating in its domestic affairs, further than the collection of customs revenues, revision of the tariff and the adjustment of its economic and fiscal organization; neither does the United States assume any responsibility for the foreign obligations of San Domingo, though it will endeavor to have these provided for. It is to be expected that this will be entirely satisfactory to the creditors of the republic, and it should mark the beginning of a period of peace and prosperity for the island.
records.summary_es: El Bee publica un editorial sobre el acuerdo de Santo Domingo: un protectorado sobre ese país había sido sin duda considerado, y tal curso habría sido enteramente satisfactorio para los gobiernos extranjeros que tienen reclamaciones contra Santo Domingo, ya que habría asegurado la paz en la isla y el debido cobro y desembolso de sus ingresos. Pero habría sido ampliamente considerado, y especialmente por las repúblicas de este hemisferio, como un preludio de la anexión, y sin duda no habría sido aprobado por el pueblo de los Estados Unidos. Se ha alcanzado ahora un acuerdo, por invitación del gobierno de Santo Domingo, bajo el cual los Estados Unidos ayudarán en la administración de los ingresos de la isla y procurarán poner sus asuntos fiscales sobre una base sana. El anuncio de este arreglo explica que los Estados Unidos se proponen garantizar la integridad territorial de la República Dominicana y no se proponen asumir un protectorado ni interferir ni participar en sus asuntos internos, más allá del cobro de los ingresos aduaneros, la revisión del arancel y el ajuste de su organización económica y fiscal; tampoco los Estados Unidos asumen responsabilidad alguna por las obligaciones extranjeras de Santo Domingo, aunque procurarán que se provea para ellas. Cabe esperar que esto sea enteramente satisfactorio para los acreedores de la república, y debería marcar el comienzo de un período de paz y prosperidad para la isla.

records.summary_en: The Star reprints a New York Tribune editorial, under the head 'Santo Domingo': it is obviously a golden opportunity for the Dominican republic to find salvation from the evils which afflict it and from the ruin which menaces it, and to place itself upon a plane with the really stable and enlightened states of the world. Without sacrificing its own independence, it gets the full benefit of the experience and the moral influence of the United States. As for this country, it does not appear that it is thus entering into any complications which are likely to prove embarrassing; its hands remain free, it assumes no more responsibility than it has borne for the best part of a century, and, while avoiding entangling technicalities, it is aiding its weaker neighbor in a peculiarly effective and generous way, and it is conforming to its historic Monroe doctrine in a practical way.

Sin sacrificar su propia independencia, obtiene el beneficio pleno de la experiencia y la influencia moral de los Estados Unidos. En cuanto a este país, no parece estar entrando en complicación alguna que pueda resultar embarazosa; sus manos permanecen libres, no asume más responsabilidad de la que ha cargado durante la mejor parte de un siglo, y, evitando tecnicismos enredantes, está ayudando a su vecino más débil de una manera peculiarmente eficaz y generosa, y está conformándose a su histórica doctrina Monroe de una manera práctica.

records.headline: The Press prints an installment of its history of Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Press prints an installment of its history of Santo Domingo, the eastern end of the island again asserted its independence and established the Republic of Santo Domingo. In 1861 affairs in the country were in an even more than usually troubled state; President Santana found it impossible to preserve a semblance of order, and delivered the country to Spain, and Spain remained in control until the Spanish cortes resolved that the Dominicans could have their republic to do with as they pleased, and since that time the country has been independent. As a good example of the uncertainty attending the occupancy of the presidential chair in Santo Domingo, the record of Hon. Buenaventura Baez runs 1849 in, 1853 out, 1857 in, 1858 out, and on through further ins and outs to his banishment from the country. Gen. Ulises Heureaux became president of the republic in 1886 and retained office until 1899; there was a clause in the constitution that no president should serve more than two terms, and Heureaux disposed of that by suspending the constitution. Folks who objected to his exercise of power were sent to prison, and dangerous objectors were shot.
records.summary_es: El Press publica una entrega de su historia de Santo Domingo: el extremo oriental de la isla afirmó de nuevo su independencia y estableció la República de Santo Domingo. En 1861 los asuntos en el país estaban en un estado aun más turbulento que de costumbre; el presidente Santana encontró imposible preservar una apariencia de orden, y entregó el país a España, y España permaneció en control hasta que las Cortes españolas resolvieron que los dominicanos podían tener su república para hacer con ella lo que quisieran, y desde ese tiempo el país ha sido independiente. Como buen ejemplo de la incertidumbre que acompaña la ocupación de la silla presidencial en Santo Domingo, el historial del honorable Buenaventura Báez corre 1849 dentro, 1853 fuera, 1857 dentro, 1858 fuera, y así a través de más entradas y salidas hasta su destierro del país. El general Ulises Heureaux llegó a ser presidente de la república en 1886 y retuvo el cargo hasta 1899; había una cláusula en la constitución según la cual ningún presidente debía servir más de dos períodos, y Heureaux se deshizo de ella suspendiendo la constitución. Las personas que objetaban a su ejercicio del poder eran enviadas a prisión, y los objetores peligrosos eran fusilados.

records.headline: A feature on Santo Domingo under President Morales says the government pays out money daily at Santiago, La Vega
records.summary_en: A feature on Santo Domingo under President Morales says the government pays out money daily at Santiago, La Vega, Moca, Puerto Plata and other towns to maintain peace, while recalcitrant citizens and even suspects are imprisoned, banished or summarily shot. It argues that export duties ruin the sugar planter and discourage production, even though tobacco from the Cibao is shipped to Germany and cocoa, coffee, wax, honey and gold washed from mountain streams all leave the country.
records.summary_es: Un artículo sobre Santo Domingo bajo el presidente Morales dice que el gobierno reparte dinero a diario en Santiago, La Vega, Moca, Puerto Plata y otros pueblos para mantener la paz, mientras los ciudadanos recalcitrantes e incluso los sospechosos son encarcelados, desterrados o fusilados sumariamente. Sostiene que los derechos de exportación arruinan al productor de azúcar y desaniman la producción, aun cuando el tabaco del Cibao se envía a Alemania y el cacao, el café, la cera, la miel y el oro lavado de los arroyos de las montañas salen del país.

records.headline: The Press continues its history of Santo Domingo with the growth of the public debt
records.summary_en: The Press continues its history of Santo Domingo with the growth of the public debt: a small loan was raised when the total debt was only $1,500,000; since then the government, under various leaders who have succeeded him, has learned to borrow, and now the debt is $32,000,000, with a question if even this amount would cover it all. Germany, Spain and Italy have united their claims and have agreed to accept $400,000 in full settlement of them, the Dominican government agreeing by protocols to pay this sum at the rate of $200,000 a year. The French and Belgian bondholders are clamoring for the settlement of their claims at the rate of $300,000 yearly, and the United States has practically seized the northern port of Puerto Plata to collect the $450,000 yearly awarded to the San Domingo Improvement company, an American corporation, while the Morales government is protesting that if deprived of these revenues it will find itself unable to maintain internal peace. A sidebar, under the head 'Dictator and President', traces Horacio Vasquez: he directed the military operations against President Heureaux; after the assassination of Heureaux, General Figueroa became president, but was soon ousted by Vasquez, who took the reins of government as dictator and held the office until Jimenez arrived from Cuba and was proclaimed president. Vasquez became vice president under Jimenez; he soon organized a revolution and deposed Jimenez; then Wos y Gil revolted and deposed Vasquez, and Morales' army put Wos y Gil out of office.
records.summary_es: El Press continúa su historia de Santo Domingo con el crecimiento de la deuda pública: se recaudó un pequeño préstamo cuando la deuda total era de solo $1,500,000; desde entonces el gobierno, bajo varios líderes que lo han sucedido, ha aprendido a pedir prestado, y ahora la deuda es de $32,000,000, con la duda de si siquiera esta cantidad lo cubriría todo. Alemania, España e Italia han unido sus reclamaciones y han acordado aceptar $400,000 en liquidación total de ellas, acordando el gobierno dominicano por protocolos pagar esta suma a razón de $200,000 al año. Los tenedores de bonos franceses y belgas claman por la liquidación de sus reclamaciones a razón de $300,000 anuales, y los Estados Unidos han incautado prácticamente el puerto norteño de Puerto Plata para cobrar los $450,000 anuales adjudicados a la Santo Domingo Improvement Company, una corporación estadounidense, mientras el gobierno de Morales protesta que si se le priva de estos ingresos se encontrará incapaz de mantener la paz interna. Un recuadro, bajo el título «Dictator and President», traza a Horacio Vásquez: dirigió las operaciones militares contra el presidente Heureaux; después del asesinato de Heureaux, el general Figueroa llegó a ser presidente pero pronto fue derrocado por Vásquez, que tomó las riendas del gobierno como dictador y las mantuvo hasta que Jiménez llegó de Cuba y fue proclamado presidente. Vásquez llegó a ser vicepresidente bajo Jiménez; pronto organizó una revolución y depuso a Jiménez; luego Wos y Gil se sublevó y depuso a Vásquez, y el ejército de Morales sacó a Wos y Gil del cargo.

records.summary_en: The *Springfield Weekly Republican* argued that foreign capitalists and commercial planters in the Dominican Republic actively encouraged political unrest to terminate indigenous rule. It cited State Department admissions that American firms had supplied money and weapons to opposing Dominican factions while simultaneously petitioning Washington for naval protection. The editorial noted that President Morales, having secured power through United States naval support, signed the customs receivership agreement to align with foreign property interests.
records.summary_es: El *Springfield Weekly Republican* sostuvo que los capitalistas y hacendados comerciales extranjeros en la República Dominicana fomentaban activamente la inestabilidad política para poner fin al gobierno autóctono. Citó admisiones del Departamento de Estado respecto a que firmas estadounidenses habían suministrado dinero y armas a facciones dominicanas rivales mientras pedían simultáneamente protección naval a Washington. El editorial señaló que el presidente Morales, habiendo asegurado el poder mediante el apoyo naval estadounidense, firmó el acuerdo de administración aduanera para alinearse con los intereses de los propietarios extranjeros.
records.passage: Porto Rico, is significant, for it helps to explain the present situation. The Dominican planters and all the foreign capitalists concerned in the republic have had a strong economic object in bringing the native rule to a close. There is, indeed, reason for thinking that the frequent revolutions of late years have been secretly encouraged, and even fomented in part, by the foreign interests.. For proof of this, we may quote what appeared on March 16 last in the Washington Star, the paragraph having all the appearance of being inspired by the state department. “It is admitted at the ‘state department," said the Star, “that ‘some representations have been made in a ‘forcible way to American firms and indi ‘viduals having an interest in San Domingo ‘that they have small ground for complaint ‘of revolutionary disturbances affecting •their interests unfavorably so long as they themselves are in the. habit of furnishing •arms, ammunition and money to both sides •engaged in this fratricidal strife.” It is necessary to point out, also, that President Morales, now the head of the Dominican government, who has voluntarily, it appears, signed the agreement for the American receivership, represents the property interests of the republic more than his late opponents did. This conclusion is not far-fetched. Morales has been seeking, it might almost be said, American protection ever since his government was firmly established through the armed intervention of the United States navy in the last revolution. records.headline: The Journal prints a description of Santo Domingo: its area
records.summary_en: The Journal prints a description of Santo Domingo: its area, 18,045 square miles, is about equal to that of New Hampshire and Vermont combined, or about one-half that of the state of Indiana. While production at the present time is comparatively small, and confined chiefly to sugar, coffee, cacao, bananas, mahogany and logwood, its possibilities of production are considered very great at such time as the interior may be opened by railways and roads. Marrion Wilcox, an authority on tropical America, is quoted that the island 'excels nearly all others in the world, certainly the neighboring members of the Greater Antilles (Cuba and Porto Rico), in natural fertility and diversity of climate', and that if such a system of highways and railways as the English have constructed in Jamaica were established in Santo Domingo, the long period of political disturbances and revolutions in the Dominican Republic and Republic of Haiti would gradually come to an end. At present the railways of the island have a total length of about 300 miles and are chiefly on the northern coast, extending inland from Samana Bay, one of the finest natural harbors of the West Indies, while another line extends westwardly from Santo Domingo, the capital of the republic, about 100 miles along the southern coast. Santo Domingo, the capital, has a population of 25,000, and is the oldest town of European origin in the New World, having been founded in 1496.

records.headline: The Republican prints a Dominican writer's protest against the Improvement Company debt
records.summary_en: The Republican prints a Dominican writer's protest against the Improvement Company debt: he points out that the much discussed Dominican debt known under the name of the 'Improvement' debt, and which is taken by the American government as a pretext to threaten the Dominican fatherland with criminal aggression, is a matter of the most fraudulent and deceptive character that can be imagined. This Improvement scheme was a senseless scheme on the part of Gen. Heureaux to make money when he was himself in pecuniary difficulties, and in this combination he had some American partners, thus to further his wicked objects and purposes; connected with this criminal matter are also other Dominicans, who, in due time, will have to pay the penalty of their evil acts. The Improvement company was expelled from the country by the government of Gen. Jiminez because it refused to have its accounts audited, most likely because it did not have the necessary books and vouchers. This debt was laid on the shoulders of the San Domingo government after the fall of Gen. Jiminez, and this fraud, with which the American government has been inveigled so as to become its accomplice, forms the real pretext which is being preferred in order to bring about the disintegration of the republic of San Domingo, the much-coveted bay of Samana being occupied, contrary to all rights. The writer goes on to say that if the republic were really owing some American company money it would not be sufficient cause for infringing upon the dignity of the country.

Este esquema de la Improvement fue un esquema insensato de parte del general Heureaux para hacer dinero cuando él mismo estaba en dificultades pecuniarias, y en esta combinación tuvo algunos socios estadounidenses, para promover así sus malvados objetos y propósitos; relacionados con este asunto criminal están también otros dominicanos, que, a su debido tiempo, tendrán que pagar la pena de sus malos actos. La compañía Improvement fue expulsada del país por el gobierno del general Jiménez porque se negó a que sus cuentas fueran auditadas, muy probablemente porque no tenía los libros ni los comprobantes necesarios. Esta deuda fue echada sobre los hombros del gobierno de Santo Domingo después de la caída del general Jiménez, y este fraude, con el cual el gobierno estadounidense ha sido enredado hasta convertirse en su cómplice, forma el verdadero pretexto que se está prefiriendo para lograr la desintegración de la república de Santo Domingo, ocupándose la muy codiciada bahía de Samaná, en contra de todo derecho. records.headline: The Times prints a feature on the island of Santo Domingo: the east
records.summary_en: The Times prints a feature on the island of Santo Domingo: the east and larger part of the island is the Dominican Republic, Santo Domingo; the west part is Haiti. Between the two countries there lies a rough and rugged borderland, a no-man's land, which has been the scene of many bloody battles. Though two-thirds of the island belongs to the Dominican republic, it is the eastern third in which almost the entire population of the country is found; the middle third, known as the 'Despoblado', the Depopulated, is an uninhabited neutral ground, made barren not only by nature, which filled it with inaccessible mountains, but also by warfare, and covered with thick tropical forests.

records.headline: The Times feature continues: Napoleon Bonaparte attempted to regain
records.summary_en: The Times feature continues: Napoleon Bonaparte attempted to regain the island of Santo Domingo for France; an army landed, gaining possession only to be forced to retire later by climatic conditions and disease which killed thousands of the European soldiers. Since the formation of the Dominican Republic in 1844, its history has been one of almost constant revolution; general after general has made a bid for popularity and attempted to overthrow the president in power, and usually these revolutions have been successful; the history of the country reads like a comic opera. Under the head 'Heureaux's Assassination', the feature recounts that General Ulysses Heureaux came into power in 1883 and understood, perhaps better than any other of the presidents, how to keep control of the government in the island: though almost every year of the succeeding fifteen brought out a revolutionary movement, President Heureaux invariably nipped the movement in the bud, and if he caught the leaders he shot them. He managed to defeat all attempts to unseat him, until he was assassinated in 1898; he was popular with the people.
records.summary_es: El reportaje del Times continúa: Napoleón Bonaparte intentó recuperar la isla de Santo Domingo para Francia; un ejército desembarcó, ganando la posesión solo para verse obligado a retirarse luego por las condiciones climáticas y las enfermedades que mataron a miles de los soldados europeos. Desde la formación de la República Dominicana en 1844, su historia ha sido una de revolución casi constante; general tras general ha hecho su apuesta por la popularidad e intentado derrocar al presidente en el poder, y usualmente estas revoluciones han tenido éxito; la historia del país se lee como una ópera cómica. Bajo el título «Heureaux's Assassination», el reportaje relata que el general Ulises Heureaux llegó al poder en 1883 y entendía, quizá mejor que ninguno de los presidentes, cómo mantener el control del gobierno en la isla: aunque casi cada año de los quince siguientes trajo un movimiento revolucionario, el presidente Heureaux invariablemente sofocaba el movimiento en su inicio, y si atrapaba a los líderes los fusilaba. Logró derrotar todos los intentos de desbancarlo, hasta que fue asesinado en 1898; era popular entre el pueblo.

records.summary_en: The Times feature continues: an anecdote of President Heureaux, in which Castillo was sure that the shot had been fired by the president's orders, so when he received an order to come to the capital he made some excuse for not putting in an appearance. Heureaux immediately sent the minister of war word to arrest Governor Estay and to bring him to Santo Domingo; this allayed Castillo's suspicions, and he brought his prisoner to the president. Heureaux invited the two men aboard his yacht and sailed a few miles up the coast; a landing party was called out, and General Castillo was informed that he was to be shot, and a few minutes later he was. The president calmly asked Governor Estay if he had not done the right thing; the governor replied, 'Yes.' Whereupon Heureaux told him that it was his turn next, and in a few minutes Estay was as dead as Castillo.

records.headline: The Times concludes: Santo Domingo asked that it be annexed
records.summary_en: The Times concludes: Santo Domingo asked that it be annexed to the United States, and an investigation was made of affairs on the island, but the Senate refused to take action in the matter. The Monroe Doctrine has become to the United States almost as much an iron-bound law as the Constitution itself; under the circumstances, therefore, to see that Santo Domingo had fair play, and her creditors as well, it was necessary for the United States to take action, otherwise a foreign power must have done so. Santo Domingo's principal creditors are the United States, England, Holland, Belgium, Germany and France.
records.summary_es: El Times concluye: Santo Domingo pidió una vez que fuera anexado a los Estados Unidos, y se hizo una investigación de los asuntos en la isla, pero el Senado se negó a tomar acción en el asunto. La doctrina Monroe se ha convertido para los Estados Unidos en una ley casi tan férrea como la propia Constitución; bajo las circunstancias, por tanto, para ver que Santo Domingo tuviera un trato justo, y sus acreedores también, fue necesario que los Estados Unidos tomaran acción, de otro modo una potencia extranjera habría tenido que hacerlo. Los principales acreedores de Santo Domingo son los Estados Unidos, Inglaterra, Holanda, Bélgica, Alemania y Francia.

records.summary_en: The *Springfield Weekly Republican* detailed the finalized protocol providing for American administration of Dominican customs until foreign creditor claims were settled. The modified convention affirmed the Monroe Doctrine, guaranteed Dominican territorial integrity, and allotted 45 percent of gross customs revenues directly to the Dominican government for its operating budget. The agreement stipulated that future tariff modifications required approval from the President of the United States and prohibited increases in the national public debt.
records.summary_es: El *Springfield Weekly Republican* detalló el protocolo definitivo que establecía la administración estadounidense de las aduanas dominicanas hasta que se saldaran las reclamaciones de los acreedores extranjeros. La convención modificada reafirmaba la Doctrina Monroe, garantizaba la integridad territorial dominicana y asignaba el 45 por ciento de los ingresos aduaneros brutos directamente al gobierno dominicano para su presupuesto operativo. El acuerdo estipulaba que las futuras modificaciones arancelarias requerían la aprobación del presidente de los Estados Unidos y prohibía cualquier incremento de la deuda pública nacional.

The first section is but slightly altered, while the second section is greatly modified, the American government agreeing completely to respect the territorial integrity of San Domingo. The convention or protocol specifically affirms the Monroe doctrine. The customs officials are to be subject to the civil and penal jurisdiction of the Dominican republic without being considered subjects of that government. There is to be paid to the Dominican government 45 per cent of the total gross amount collected in all the custom-houses of the republic, that proportion of the revenues being for the necessities of the administrative budget. The estimate in the protocol of January 20 that this 45 per cent shall be $900,000 for the first year is eliminated, as is. also the agreement “that the extraordinary expenses which may be occasioned in the collection of. the. customs duties shall be made for the account of the creditors of the republic (of Santo Domingo) without assigning to the latter any part thereof.” Any reform of the Dominican tariff is to be subject to approval by the president of the'United States. records.headline: The News prints an editorial on the Dominican receivership
records.summary_en: The News prints an editorial on the Dominican receivership: the temporary control of the finances of the Dominican republic once more brings that restless little West Indian government into public view. It has been apparent for some time that affairs in the republic have reached a critical stage; its chief difficulty, eliminating the ever-present tendency to revolutionize at the slightest pretext, seems to be a wonderful faculty to get into debt and a corresponding incapacity to get out again. The national debt now amounts to a respectable total whose figure is not legible in this printing, and the republic's impatient creditors have long protested that some settlement should be effected; some of them have even declared their willingness to undertake a receivership, promising to wind up the affairs of the improvident republic with amazing celerity. Such a proposition from a foreign power could not be tolerated by the United States; James Monroe would rise in indignation at the mere suggestion, and if there is any adjusting to be done it is the United States' to do it. There does not seem to be the slightest objection to the course, and it is to be most satisfactory to the foreign creditors and to the Dominicans themselves.
records.summary_es: El News publica un editorial sobre la receptoría dominicana: el control temporal de las finanzas de la República Dominicana trae de nuevo a ese inquieto pequeño gobierno antillano a la vista pública. Ha sido aparente por algún tiempo que los asuntos en la república han alcanzado una etapa crítica; su dificultad principal, eliminando la tendencia siempre presente a revolucionar al menor pretexto, parece ser una maravillosa facultad para endeudarse y una correspondiente incapacidad para salir de la deuda. La deuda nacional asciende ahora a un total respetable cuya cifra no es legible en esta impresión, y los acreedores impacientes de la república han protestado por largo tiempo que debe efectuarse alguna liquidación; algunos de ellos han declarado incluso su disposición a emprender una receptoría, prometiendo liquidar los asuntos de la república improvidente con asombrosa celeridad. Tal proposición de una potencia extranjera no podría ser tolerada por los Estados Unidos; James Monroe se levantaría indignado ante la mera sugerencia, y si hay algún ajuste que hacer, corresponde hacerlo a los Estados Unidos. No parece haber la menor objeción al curso, y ha de ser de lo más satisfactorio para los acreedores extranjeros y para los propios dominicanos.

records.headline: This editorial examines the legal basis claimed for American customs operations in Santo Domingo, centered on the arbitration
records.summary_en: This editorial examines the legal basis claimed for American customs operations in Santo Domingo, centered on the arbitration award of July 14, 1904, which authorized the United States Financial Agent to extend his control to Monte Cristi, Sanchez and Samana if the collections at Puerto Plata proved insufficient to meet the monthly installment of $37,500 payable under the award. It reports that Judge Abbott, the Financial Agent, unexpectedly returned to New York saying it had not been necessary to go beyond Puerto Plata for the revenue needed, while Admiral Sigsbee was negotiating with the people of Monte Cristi for their independent adoption of the protocol.

records.headline: The Star prints a passage on the Santo Domingo Improvement Company award
records.summary_en: The Star prints a passage on the Santo Domingo Improvement Company award: when an award and such security are thus obtained, some foreign government complains that the award conflicts with its rights, as a creditor, to some portion of these revenues under an alleged prior pledge, and still other governments complain that an award in any considerable sum, secured by pledges of the customs revenues, is prejudicial to the payment of their equally meritorious claims out of the ordinary revenues, and thus controversies are begotten between the United States and other creditor nations because of the apparent sacrifice of some of their claims, which may be just or may be grossly exaggerated, but which the United States government cannot inquire into without giving grounds of offense to other friendly creditor nations. Still further illustrations might easily be furnished by the hopelessness of the present situation growing out of the social disorders and the bankrupt finances of the Dominican republic, where, for considerable periods during recent years, the bonds of civil society have been practically dissolved. Under the head 'Intervention of Foreign Governments', the passage adds that under the accepted law of nations foreign governments are within their right, if they choose to exercise it, when they actively intervene in support of the contractual claims of their subjects.

records.headline: The Reveille prints a New York item under the head 'Puerto Plata Natives Pleased'
records.summary_en: The Reveille prints a New York item under the head 'Puerto Plata Natives Pleased': the action of the United States government in taking charge of the customs receipts of San Domingo is generally considered by the natives of San Domingo as for the best interests of the country, according to Judge John T. Abbott, who arrived on the Cherokee. Judge Abbott is the representative of the San Domingo Improvement Company, and since last April has been in charge of the customs house at Puerto Plata, under agreement with the Dominican government. Speaking of conditions in San Domingo, Judge Abbott said: 'The United States government took charge of all the ports of San Domingo on Feb. 1, except Puerto Plata and Monte Cristi. The former I still have in charge, while the latter is administered by natives. All the money is turned over to the United States authorities. This arrangement is viewed with satisfaction by the large majority of the natives representing the influential business interests and the landed proprietors. In fact there is very little talk anywhere about the matter. The revolutionary element is not much in evidence.'

El juez Abbott es el representante de la Santo Domingo Improvement Company, y desde abril pasado ha estado a cargo de la aduana de Puerto Plata, bajo acuerdo con el gobierno dominicano. Hablando de las condiciones en Santo Domingo, el juez Abbott dijo: «El gobierno de los Estados Unidos se hizo cargo de todos los puertos de Santo Domingo el 1 de febrero, excepto Puerto Plata y Monte Cristi. El primero todavía lo tengo a mi cargo, mientras el segundo es administrado por naturales. Todo el dinero es entregado a las autoridades de los Estados Unidos. Este arreglo es visto con satisfacción por la gran mayoría de los naturales que representan los influyentes intereses comerciales y los propietarios de tierras. De hecho se habla muy poco en ninguna parte sobre el asunto. El elemento revolucionario no se hace mucho evidente».

records.summary_en: The *Wisconsin Weekly Advocate* published the terms of the treaty signed between United States Minister Thomas C. Dawson and Dominican ministers Juan Francisco Sánchez and Federico Velásquez. Invoking the Monroe Doctrine, the preamble pledged United States assistance in resolving foreign debts while respecting the territorial integrity of the Dominican Republic. Under the first article, the United States agreed to arbitrate all domestic and foreign financial claims and establish joint commissions to determine debt validity and payment schedules.
records.summary_es: El *Wisconsin Weekly Advocate* publicó los términos del tratado firmado entre el ministro de los Estados Unidos Thomas C. records.headline: The Bulletin prints a passage of the President's message on Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Bulletin prints a passage of the President's message on Santo Domingo under the heads 'Condition is Hopeless' and 'Ordinary Diplomacy Inadequate': 'As a result of chronic disorder attended with constant increase of debt the state of things in San Domingo has become hopeless. Unless the United States or some other strong government shall interpose to bring order out of chaos.' The president then refers to the fact that loans of various kinds made to the Dominican government have become the nucleus of the various revolutions there, and continues: 'The ordinary resources of diplomacy and international arbitration are absolutely impotent to deal wisely and effectively with the situation in the Dominican republic, which can only be met by organizing its finances on a sound basis and by placing the custom houses out of the temptation.' It is suggested by the president that if a plan could be adopted in regard to San Domingo similar to that in the Platt amendment for the government of Cuba it would be practicable and a solution to the problem. The message concludes as follows: 'We, on our part, are simply performing in a peaceable manner, not only with the cordial permission but in accordance with the earnest request of the government concerned, part of the international duty which is necessarily involved in the association of the Monroe doctrine.'

records.headline: The Dispatch prints a passage of the President's message on Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Dispatch prints a passage of the President's message on Santo Domingo: the situation in the Dominican republic can only be met by organizing its finances on a sound basis and by placing the custom houses beyond the temptation of insurgent chieftains. Either the United States must abandon its duty, under its traditional policy toward the Dominican people, who aspire to a republican form of government while they are actually drifting into a condition of permanent anarchy, in which case it must permit some other government to adopt its own measures in order to safeguard its own interests, or else it must itself take seasonable and appropriate action. Under the head 'Solution of the Problem', it is suggested by the President that if a plan could be adopted in regard to San Domingo, similar to that in the Platt amendment for the government of Cuba, it would be practicable and a solution to the problem. The message concludes: 'We, on our part, are simply performing in a peaceful manner not only with the cordial acquiescence, but in accordance with the earnest request of the government concerned, part of that international duty which is necessarily involved in the assertion of the Monroe Doctrine. We are bound to show that we perform this duty in good faith and without any intention of aggrandizing ourselves at the expense of our weaker neighbors, or of conducting ourselves otherwise than so as to benefit both these weaker neighbors and those Europeans which may be brought into contact with them.'

records.headline: The Sun prints an analysis of the President's message on Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Sun prints an analysis of the President's message on Santo Domingo: the declaration occurs in the second paragraph, which recites that the government of the United States views any attempt on the part of a foreign government outside of the western hemisphere to oppress the Dominican republic as a manifestation of unfriendly disposition towards the United States. The especial point is made by the president that the government does not propose to take any part of San Domingo or to exercise any other control over the island save what is necessary to its financial rehabilitation in connection with the collection of revenue, a part of which will be turned over to the government to meet the necessary expenses of running it and a part of which will be distributed pro rata among the creditors of the republic upon a basis of absolute equity. Discussing the course aggrieved nations may take against American republics without interference with the Monroe doctrine, the president says that any action may be taken which does not take the shape of interference with their form of government or any disproportionment of their territory under any disguise, but short of this, when the question is one of a money claim, the only way which remains finally to collect is a blockade or a bombardment or a seizure of the custom house, and this means what it is in effect: possession, even though only temporary possession, of the territory. The United States then becomes a party in interest.
records.summary_es: El Sun publica un análisis del mensaje del Presidente sobre Santo Domingo: la declaración ocurre en el segundo párrafo, el cual recita que el gobierno de los Estados Unidos considera cualquier intento de parte de un gobierno extranjero fuera del hemisferio occidental de oprimir a la república dominicana como una manifestación de disposición poco amistosa hacia los Estados Unidos. El presidente hace el punto especial de que el gobierno no se propone tomar parte alguna de Santo Domingo ni ejercer otro control sobre la isla salvo el necesario para su rehabilitación financiera en relación con el cobro de los ingresos, una parte de los cuales será entregada al gobierno para cubrir los gastos necesarios de su funcionamiento y otra parte será distribuida a prorrata entre los acreedores de la república sobre una base de equidad absoluta. Discutiendo el curso que las naciones agraviadas pueden tomar contra las repúblicas americanas sin interferencia con la doctrina Monroe, el presidente dice que puede tomarse cualquier acción que no tome la forma de interferencia con su forma de gobierno ni desproporción alguna de su territorio bajo disfraz alguno, pero fuera de esto, cuando la cuestión es una reclamación de dinero, el único camino que queda finalmente para cobrar es un bloqueo o un bombardeo o una incautación de la aduana, y esto significa lo que es en efecto: posesión, aunque solo posesión temporal, del territorio. Los Estados Unidos se convierten entonces en parte interesada.

records.headline: The Tribune prints a passage of the President's message on Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Tribune prints a passage of the President's message on Santo Domingo: in case the Dominican government should so request, the financial agent of the United States was authorized to have and exercise at any and all of the other ports above described all the rights and powers vested in him by the award in respect of Puerto Plata. Under the award the financial agent could only apply the revenues collected after he had first paid the expenses of collection and certain other obligations styled 'apardos', which constituted prior charges on the revenues assigned; these prior charges are specified in the award. Under the head 'In Possession of Custom Houses', the message continues: the Dominican government defaulted in its payments, and in virtue of the award and the authority conferred by the Dominican government, and at its request, possession was delivered of the custom house of Puerto Plata to the fiscal agent appointed by the United States to collect the revenues assigned by the arbitrators for the payment of the award, and in virtue of the same authority possession of the custom house of Monte Cristi has also been handed over. The president submits a report of Mr. John B. Moore, agent of the United States in this case, and a copy of the award of arbitrators. During the last two years the European claimants, except the English, whose interests were embraced in those of the American companies, have, with the support of their respective governments, been growing more and more importunate in pressing their unsatisfied demands.

records.summary_en: The Censor prints a passage of the President's message on Santo Domingo: 'As the result of chronic disorders, attended with constant increase of debt, the state of things in Santo Domingo has become hopeless, unless the United States or some other strong government shall interpose to bring order out of chaos.' The president then refers to the fact that loans of various kinds made to the Dominican government have become the nucleus of the various revolutions there, and continues: 'The ordinary resources of diplomacy and international arbitration are absolutely impotent to deal wisely and effectively with the situation in the Dominican republic, which can only be met by organizing its finances on a sound basis and by placing the custom house beyond the temptation of insurgent chieftains. Either we must abandon our duty under our traditional policy toward the Dominican people, who aspire to a republican form of government while they are actually drifting into a condition of permanent anarchy, in which case we must permit some other government to adopt its own measures in order to safeguard its own interests, or else we must ourselves take seasonable and appropriate action.' It is suggested by the president that if a plan could be adopted in regard to San Domingo similar to that in the Platt amendment for the government of Cuba, it would be practicable and a solution to the problem.

El presidente se refiere luego al hecho de que préstamos de varias clases hechos al gobierno dominicano se han convertido en el núcleo de las varias revoluciones allí, y continúa: «Los recursos ordinarios de la diplomacia y el arbitraje internacional son absolutamente impotentes para tratar sabia y eficazmente con la situación en la república dominicana, la cual solo puede ser atendida organizando sus finanzas sobre una base sana y poniendo la aduana fuera de la tentación de los jefes insurgentes. O debemos abandonar nuestro deber bajo nuestra política tradicional hacia el pueblo dominicano, que aspira a una forma republicana de gobierno mientras está derivando en realidad hacia una condición de anarquía permanente, en cuyo caso debemos permitir que algún otro gobierno adopte sus propias medidas para salvaguardar sus propios intereses, o si no debemos tomar nosotros mismos acción oportuna y apropiada». Se sugiere por el presidente que si un plan pudiera adoptarse respecto a Santo Domingo similar al de la enmienda Platt para el gobierno de Cuba sería practicable y una solución al problema.

records.headline: The Republican prints a passage on the Santo Domingo Improvement Company award
records.summary_en: The Republican prints a passage on the Santo Domingo Improvement Company award: this situation again reacts injuriously upon the relations of the United States with other nations, for when an award and such security are thus obtained, as in the case of the San Domingo Improvement Company, some foreign government complains that the award conflicts with its rights as a creditor to some portion of these revenues under an alleged prior pledge, and still other governments complain that an award in any considerable sum, secured by pledges of the customs revenues, is prejudicial to the payment of their equally meritorious claims out of the ordinary revenues, and thus controversies are begotten between the United States and other creditor nations because of the apparent sacrifice of some of their claims, which may be just or may be grossly exaggerated, but which the United States government cannot inquire into without giving grounds of offense to other friendly creditor nations. Still further illustrations might easily be furnished of the hopelessness of the present situation growing out of the social disorders and the bankrupt finances of the Dominican republic, where for considerable periods during recent years the bonds of civil society have been practically dissolved. Under the head 'The Dilemma of the United States', the passage adds that under the accepted law of nations foreign governments are within their right, if they choose to exercise it, when they actively intervene in support of the contractual claims of their subjects.
records.summary_es: El Republican publica un pasaje sobre el laudo de la Santo Domingo Improvement Company: esta situación reacciona de nuevo perjudicialmente sobre las relaciones de los Estados Unidos con otras naciones, pues cuando un laudo y tal garantía se obtienen así, como en el caso de la Santo Domingo Improvement Company, algún gobierno extranjero se queja de que el laudo conflige con sus derechos como acreedor a alguna porción de estos ingresos bajo una alegada garantía anterior, y otros gobiernos se quejan todavía de que un laudo en cualquier suma considerable, garantizado por gravámenes de los ingresos aduaneros, es perjudicial al pago de sus reclamaciones igualmente meritorias de los ingresos ordinarios, y así se engendran controversias entre los Estados Unidos y otras naciones acreedoras por el sacrificio aparente de algunas de sus reclamaciones, que pueden ser justas o pueden ser groseramente exageradas, pero que el gobierno de los Estados Unidos no puede investigar sin dar motivos de ofensa a otras naciones acreedoras amigas. Aún podrían darse más ilustraciones fácilmente de la desesperanza de la situación presente que surge de los desórdenes sociales y las finanzas en bancarrota de la república dominicana, donde por períodos considerables durante los años recientes los lazos de la sociedad civil han estado prácticamente disueltos. Bajo el título «The Dilemma of the United States», el pasaje añade que bajo el derecho de naciones aceptado los gobiernos extranjeros están dentro de su derecho, si deciden ejercerlo, cuando intervienen activamente en apoyo de las reclamaciones contractuales de sus súbditos.

records.headline: The Republican prints a passage stating the terms of the Santo Domingo Improvement Company award
records.summary_en: The Republican prints a passage stating the terms of the Santo Domingo Improvement Company award: the Dominican government was to pay the above mentioned sum of $4,500,000, with 4 per cent interest per annum, in monthly instalments of $37,500 each during two years, and of $41,666.66 each month thereafter, beginning with the month of September, 1904, the award to be secured by the customs revenues and port dues of all the ports on the northern coast of Santo Domingo. The award further provides for the appointment of a financial agent of the United States, who was authorized, in case of failure during any month to receive the sum then due, to enter into possession of the custom-house at Puerto Plata in the first instance and assume charge of the collection of customs dues and port dues, and to fix and determine these duties and dues and secure their payment; in case the sum collected at Puerto Plata should at any time be insufficient for the payment of the amounts due under the award, or in case of any other manifest necessity, or in case the Dominican government should so request, the financial agent of the United States was authorized to have and exercise at any and all of the other ports above described all the rights and powers vested in him by the award in respect of Puerto Plata. Under the award the financial agent could only apply the revenues collected toward its payment after he had first paid the expenses of collection and certain other obligations styled 'apardos', which constituted prior charges on the revenues assigned; these prior charges are specified in the award.
records.summary_es: El Republican publica un pasaje que establece los términos del laudo de la Santo Domingo Improvement Company: el gobierno dominicano había de pagar la suma arriba mencionada de $4,500,000, con interés del 4 por ciento anual, en plazos mensuales de $37,500 cada uno durante dos años, y de $41,666.66 cada mes en lo adelante, comenzando con el mes de septiembre de 1904, quedando el laudo garantizado por los ingresos aduaneros y los derechos portuarios de todos los puertos de la costa norte de Santo Domingo. El laudo provee además el nombramiento de un agente financiero de los Estados Unidos, que estaba autorizado, en caso de falta durante cualquier mes en recibir la suma entonces debida, a entrar en posesión de la aduana de Puerto Plata en primer lugar y asumir el cargo del cobro de los derechos aduaneros y portuarios, y a fijar y determinar estos derechos y asegurar su pago; en caso de que la suma cobrada en Puerto Plata fuera en cualquier momento insuficiente para el pago de las cantidades debidas bajo el laudo, o en caso de cualquier otra necesidad manifiesta, o en caso de que el gobierno dominicano lo solicitara así, el agente financiero de los Estados Unidos estaba autorizado a tener y ejercer en todos y cada uno de los demás puertos arriba descritos todos los derechos y poderes que le confiere el laudo respecto a Puerto Plata. Bajo el laudo, el agente financiero solo podía aplicar los ingresos cobrados a su pago después de haber pagado primero los gastos de cobro y ciertas otras obligaciones llamadas «apardos», que constituían cargos anteriores sobre los ingresos asignados; estos cargos anteriores están especificados en el laudo.

records.headline: The Times prints the exchange of notes between Mr. Hay and Minister Leger: Mr. Hay's note
records.summary_en: The Times prints the exchange of notes between Mr. Hay and Minister Leger: Mr. Hay's note declares that the government of the United States of America has no intention of annexing either Haiti or Santo Domingo, and no desire of acquiring possession of them, either by force or by negotiation, and that even if the citizens of either of these republics should solicit incorporation into the American Union, there would be no inclination on the part of the National Government, nor in the sphere of public opinion, to agree to any such proposal: 'Our interests are in harmony with our sentiments in wishing you only continued peace, prosperity, and independence.' Minister Leger, in reply, wrote to Mr. Hay that he was deeply grateful for the sentiments expressed in Mr. Hay's note, and that it would give him great pleasure to convey to his government the views there contained.
records.summary_es: El Times publica el intercambio de notas entre el Sr. Hay y el ministro Leger: la nota del Sr. Hay declara que el gobierno de los Estados Unidos de América no tiene intención de anexar ni Haití ni Santo Domingo, ni deseo alguno de adquirir posesión de ellos, ni por la fuerza ni por negociación, y que aun si los ciudadanos de cualquiera de estas repúblicas solicitaran la incorporación a la Unión Americana, no habría inclinación de parte del Gobierno Nacional, ni en la esfera de la opinión pública, de acceder a propuesta alguna semejante: «Nuestros intereses están en armonía con nuestros sentimientos al desearles a ustedes solo paz, prosperidad e independencia continuadas». El ministro Leger, en respuesta, escribió al Sr. Hay que estaba profundamente agradecido por los sentimientos expresados en la nota del Sr. Hay, y que le daría gran placer transmitir a su gobierno las opiniones allí contenidas.

records.headline: The Courier-Journal prints Minister Leger's reply to Mr. Hay
records.summary_en: The Courier-Journal prints Minister Leger's reply to Mr. Hay: Leger recounts that the government of the United States has neither the intention to annex Hayti nor the Dominican Republic, nor the desire to acquire possession of them by force or by negotiation, and that there was neither on the part of the Federal Government nor in public opinion any disposition to accept, even at their request, the incorporation of these two republics in the American Union; Hay gives him the assurance that American interests are in harmony with American sentiment in wishing for his people a stable peace, prosperity and independence. Under the head 'Returns Thanks', Leger writes that he is most grateful for the good wishes and cannot too sincerely thank the United States for its solicitude. He adds that his compatriots will be especially touched by the interest which President Roosevelt has testified in asking Hay to dissipate, through frank explanations, the anxiety created by erroneous rumors in regard to the character of American relations with the Dominican Republic, and that the Republic of Hayti will learn with pleasure that the United States intends neither to annex the Dominican Republic nor to acquire possession of it.
