records.summary_en: The Evening Star published excerpts from President Taft's message to Congress, reporting that the Dominican customs receivership was operating satisfactorily under the 1907 convention. Taft noted that despite lower customs revenues caused by economic conditions and anticipated tariff revisions, debt service payments were maintained and burdensome private concessions were retired. The message also reviewed U.S. diplomatic interventions regarding corporate claims in Nicaragua and Chile.
records.summary_es: The Evening Star publicó extractos del mensaje del presidente Taft al Congreso, informando que la receptoría de aduanas dominicana operaba satisfactoriamente en virtud de la convención de 1907. Taft destacó que, pese al descenso en los ingresos aduaneros provocado por la coyuntura económica y la expectativa de revisiones arancelarias, se mantuvieron los pagos del servicio de la deuda y se rescataron onerosas concesiones privadas. El mensaje examinó además las intervenciones diplomáticas estadounidenses relativas a reclamaciones corporativas en Nicaragua y Chile.

records.headline: The American customs receivership in the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: The American customs receivership in the Dominican Republic under the convention of February 8 is reviewed in an excerpt from President Taft's message published in The Salt Lake Herald-Republican. Customs collections have proceeded in an uneventful and 'unsatisfactory' manner, with revenues declining because of political and economic instability as well as reduced imports in anticipation of tariff revision. Nevertheless, required convention payments to the United States fiscal agency for bonded railway service have been delivered promptly, and significant headway has been made in adjusting the national debt and acquiring onerous private commercial concessions.
records.summary_es: La receptoría de aduanas estadounidense en la República Dominicana conforme a la convención del 8 de febrero es examinada en un extracto del mensaje del presidente Taft publicado en The Salt Lake Herald-Republican. La recaudación aduanera ha avanzado de manera monótona e 'insatisfactoria' (según aparece impreso en el despacho), habiendo disminuido los ingresos a causa de la inestabilidad política y económica y la reducción de importaciones ante la inminente reforma arancelaria. Sin embargo, los desembolsos estipulados en la convención a la agencia fiscal de los Estados Unidos para el servicio de bonos ferroviarios se han entregado puntualmente, y se registran avances notables en la regulación de la deuda pública y la adquisición de onerosas concesiones comerciales privadas.

records.headline: The collection of the customs of the Dominican republic through the general receiver of customs appointed by the President of the United States in accordance with the convention of February 8, 1907
records.summary_en: The Birmingham Age-Herald reported President Taft's address to Congress affirming the successful operation of the U.S. customs receivership in the Dominican Republic. Taft reported that despite a decline in customs revenues due to economic conditions and tariff anticipation, bond debt payments were fulfilled and progress was made in eliminating commercial monopolies. The message also addressed U.S. diplomatic interventions in contractual claims against Nicaragua and Chile.
records.summary_es: The Birmingham Age-Herald informó sobre el mensaje del presidente Taft al Congreso confirmando el exitoso funcionamiento de la receptoría aduanera estadounidense en la República Dominicana. Taft comunicó que, pese a una disminución en las rentas aduaneras por circunstancias económicas y a la expectativa arancelaria, se cumplieron los pagos de la deuda en bonos y se avanzó en la erradicación de monopolios comerciales. El mensaje abordó asimismo las gestiones diplomáticas de los EE. UU. en reclamaciones contractuales contra Nicaragua y Chile.
records.passage: no negotiations injuriously affecting the situation will be undertaken without consultation. The collection of the customs of the Dominican republic through the general receiver of customs appointed by the President of the United States in accordance with the convention of February 8, 1907, has proceeded in an uneventful and satisfactory manner. The customs receipts have decreased, owing to disturbed political and economic conditions and to a very natural curtailment of imports in view of the anticipated revision of the Dominican tariff schedule. The payments to the fiscal agency fund for the service of the bonded debt of the republic, as provided by the convention, have been made in carrying out the provisions of the convention looking toward the completion of the adjustment of the debt and the acquirement by the Dominican government of certain concessions and monopolies which have been a burden to the Commerce of the country. In short, the receivership has demonstrated its ability, even under unfavorable economic and political conditions, to do the work for which It was intended. This government was obliged to intervene diplomatically to bring about arbitration or settlement of the claim of the Emery company against Nicaragua, which it had long before been agreed should be arbitrated. records.headline: A dispatch in the Evening Journal reports that President Taft nominated
records.summary_en: A dispatch in the Evening Journal reports that President Taft nominated Horace G. Knowles of Delaware to the Senate to become minister resident and consul general to the Dominican Republic. The diplomatic post carries a salary of $10,000 annually and was held by Fenton U. McCreery of Michigan. Knowles was originally appointed minister to Nicaragua by President Roosevelt shortly before the conclusion of his term, but never assumed his functions there owing to political disturbances in that country.
records.summary_es: Un despacho en el Evening Journal informa que el presidente Taft postuló ante el Senado a Horace G. Knowles, de Delaware, para ocupar el cargo de ministro residente y cónsul general en la República Dominicana. La representación diplomática conlleva un sueldo anual de 10 000 dólares y estuvo a cargo de Fenton U. McCreery, de Míchigan. Knowles había sido designado inicialmente ministro en Nicaragua por el presidente Roosevelt poco antes de concluir su mandato, pero nunca llegó a asumir funciones allí debido a los desórdenes políticos en esa nación.

records.headline: Several diplomatic shifts are summarized by The Evening Star
records.summary_en: Several diplomatic shifts are summarized by The Evening Star, noting that Fenton R. McCreery of Flint, Michigan, has been transferred from his post as minister resident and consul general in Santo Domingo—where he served in 1907 —to become minister to Honduras. In his place, Horace G. Knowles of Delaware, who was named minister to Nicaragua in January 1900, has been transferred to Santo Domingo. The notice provides biographical details for Knowles, born in Delaware in 1863 and trained as a lawyer, citing his previous service as consul at Bordeaux and minister to Roumania and Servia.

McCreery, de Flint, Míchigan, ha sido trasladado desde su cargo de ministro residente y cónsul general en Santo Domingo —donde prestó servicios en 1907 — para asumir como ministro en Honduras. En su lugar, Horace G. Knowles, de Delaware, quien fuera nombrado ministro en Nicaragua en enero de 1900, ha sido transferido a Santo Domingo. La reseña aporta antecedentes biográficos de Knowles, nacido en Delaware en 1863 y abogado de profesión, destacando su desempeño previo como cónsul en Burdeos y ministro ante Rumania y Serbia.

records.headline: The diplomatic career of Fenton R. McCreery, of Michigan, is outlined
records.summary_en: The diplomatic career of Fenton R. McCreery, of Michigan, is outlined in a biographical notice in the New-York Tribune, following his appointment as Minister to Honduras. The report notes that McCreery began his service as a clerk in the United States consulate at Valparaiso, Chile, in 18%:, before serving successively as secretary of the legation at Santiago, Chile, and secretary of the legation and embassy in Mexico City. records.headline: A consular report on mining and minerals in the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: A consular report on mining and minerals in the Dominican Republic, prepared by Consul Ralph J. Totten at Puerto Plata, is reviewed in a Washington dispatch published in The Coalville Times. The report identifies gold, silver, iron ore, copper ore, lignite, salt, and petroleum among the country's mineral resources, noting that gold is the only mineral that has been worked to any extent. According to old records cited from 1496, Indians paid tribute in gold under Columbus, with placer workings located in La Vega, the Cibao, San Cristóbal, and Buenaventura. Local residents continue to wash gold from the sands of the Yaque, Verde, and other rivers using primitive apparatus, reportedly securing two or three ounces per week, though modern prospectors report no quartz veins that would pay to work scientifically.
records.summary_es: Un informe consular sobre minería y minerales en la República Dominicana, preparado por el cónsul Ralph J. Totten en Puerto Plata, es reseñado en un despacho de Washington publicado en The Coalville Times. El informe identifica oro, plata, mineral de hierro, mineral de cobre, lignito, sal y petróleo entre los recursos minerales del país, señalando que el oro es el único que ha sido explotado en alguna medida. De acuerdo con antiguos registros citados correspondientes a 1496 (errata 'pear H90'), los indígenas pagaban tributo en oro en la época de Colón, con yacimientos de placer en La Vega, el Cibao, San Cristóbal y Buenaventura. Los pobladores locales continúan lavando oro en las arenas de los ríos Yaque, Verde y otros mediante aparatos primitivos, obteniendo supuestamente dos o tres onzas por semana, si bien los mineros modernos no han localizado vetas de cuarzo cuya explotación resulte rentable a escala científica.

records.headline: New York City Dominicans, a prominent group headed by General Vasquez
records.summary_en: New York City Dominicans, a prominent group headed by General Vasquez, are organizing a political movement to demand governmental reforms from President Caceres, The New-York Tribune reports. Vasquez, former president of Santo Domingo and chief of the 'Horacista' party to which Caceres also belongs, is joined by Dr. Enrique Henriquez, former foreign minister under President Heureaux, and former Dominican congressmen Santiago Guzman Espaillat and Francisco Espaillat de la Mota. In a formal letter to Caceres, Vasquez has demanded the liberation of prisoners and the establishment of constitutional government with guarantees of liberty. Although Vasquez is reported to oppose revolution and no arms have yet been purchased, further action depends on Caceres's response, leaving the local Dominican community in suspense.
records.summary_es: Los dominicanos de la ciudad de Nueva York, un destacado grupo encabezado por el general Vásquez, están organizando un movimiento político para exigir reformas gubernamentales al presidente Cáceres, informa el New-York Tribune. Vásquez, expresidente de Santo Domingo y líder del partido «Horacista» al que también pertenece Cáceres, cuenta con el respaldo del doctor Enrique Henríquez, exministro de Relaciones Exteriores bajo el presidente Heureaux, y de los antiguos congresistas dominicanos Santiago Guzmán Espaillat y Francisco Espaillat de la Mota. En una carta dirigida a Cáceres, Vásquez ha exigido la liberación de prisioneros y el establecimiento de un gobierno constitucional con garantías de libertad. Aunque se señala que Vásquez se opone a una revolución y aún no se han adquirido armas, las medidas posteriores dependerán de la respuesta de Cáceres, manteniendo en gran expectación a la colonia dominicana local.

records.headline: A feature in The Washington Herald recounts the public uproar
records.summary_en: A feature in The Washington Herald recounts the public uproar in the Dominican Republic sparked by the nomination of Amanda Azar, a Syrian resident, as queen of the annual festival in San Pedro de Macoris. Although opposition arose because she was not native-born, Miss Azar gained ardent Dominican champions, prompting torchlight processions, seventeen new cigarette brands named in her honor, and the naming of rum after her. The controversy spread to Santo Domingo, dividing the army and disrupting the police, while cabinet ministers ostracized President Ramon Caceres for remaining neutral. Government officials vied for Miss Azar's hand, leading to intercepted letters, proposals of marriage, an order to rename the Dominican navy 'Amanda', and duels ended only by presidential threats.
records.summary_es: Una crónica en The Washington Herald relata el revuelo público desatado en la República Dominicana tras la postulación de Amanda Azar, una residente de origen sirio, como reina del festival anual en San Pedro de Macorís. A pesar de la oposición inicial por no ser nativa, la señorita Azar consiguió fervientes defensores dominicanos, lo que dio lugar a desfiles con antorchas, diecisiete nuevas marcas de cigarrillos bautizadas en su honor y un ron rebautizado con su nombre. La controversia se extendió a Santo Domingo, dividiendo al ejército y alterando a la policía, mientras los miembros del gabinete dieron la espalda al presidente Ramón Cáceres por negarse a tomar partido. Varios ministros compitieron por la mano de la joven con cartas interceptadas, propuestas de matrimonio, una orden para rebautizar la armada dominicana con el nombre de «Amanda» y duelos que concluyeron únicamente ante las amenazas presidenciales.

records.headline: In San Pedro de Macoris, The Richmond Palladium and Sun-Telegram
records.summary_en: In San Pedro de Macoris, The Richmond Palladium and Sun-Telegram recounts, a sensational civic uproar surrounded the annual festival where Amanda Azar was nominated as queen of the celebration. Opposition arose because she was not Dominican, dividing the citizenry and spreading to Santo Domingo, where the army and police split and cabinet members broke with President Ramon Caceres over his neutrality. Cabinet ministers competed for her hand, with the naval minister ordering the country's single rowboat rechristened Amanda, and several duels taking place until the president threatened the suitors with imprisonment. More than 50,000 votes were ultimately cast, electing the Syrian candidate and sparking street riots in both San Pedro and the capital.

Varios ministros compitieron por casarse con ella, al punto de que el ministro naval ordenó rebautizar Amanda al único bote de remos del país, sucediéndose varios duelos hasta que el presidente amenazó con encarcelar a los pretendientes. Finalmente se emitieron más de 50.000 votos que consagraron a la joven siria como reina electa, desatando disturbios callejeros tanto en San Pedro como en la capital.

records.summary_en: The popular upheaval in the Dominican Republic sparked by the nomination of Amanda Azar as queen of the February 10 festival in San Pedro de Macoris is described in The Americus Times-Recorder. Objections that she lacked Spanish blood and was not native-born divided the local public and spread to Santo Domingo, where the army and police fractured and the cabinet boycotted President Ramon Caceres for staying neutral. Ministers vied for her hand with competing marriage proposals, an order to rename the nation's single rowboat Amanda, and duels halted only by presidential threats of imprisonment in the capital's lock-up. On election day over 50,000 votes were cast, electing the Syrian candidate and provoking street riots across San Pedro and Santo Domingo.

records.headline: The Washington Herald reports an eccentric filibustering scheme
records.summary_en: The Washington Herald reports an eccentric filibustering scheme uncovered in New York, where an arms order was placed by five young American college men—three from Princeton and two from Yale. Their stated objective is to overthrow President Ramon Caceres and transfer the capital of 'Dominica' from Santo Domingo to San Pedro de Macoris in hopes of securing army commands and cabinet posts. The United States Secret Service, fully informed of their plans, considers the group harmless and is permitting them to proceed without interference.
records.summary_es: The Washington Herald da cuenta de un pintoresco plan filibustero descubierto en Nueva York, donde cinco jóvenes universitarios estadounidenses —tres de Princeton y dos de Yale— realizaron un encargo de pertrechos militares. Su propósito confeso es derrocar al presidente Ramón Cáceres y trasladar la capital de «Dominica» de Santo Domingo a San Pedro de Macorís, con la expectativa de obtener puestos de mando en el ejército dominicano y alguna cartera ministerial. El Servicio Secreto de los Estados Unidos, plenamente al tanto de la conspiración, considera inofensivos a los jóvenes y les permite continuar sin interferencias.

records.headline: A travel letter in the Daily Kennebec Journal describes a visit
records.summary_en: A travel letter in the Daily Kennebec Journal describes a visit to the Dominican Republic, depicting it as a rich and fertile country that remains little known and scantily developed. The correspondent characterizes Santo Domingo City, situated at the mouth of the Ozama River, as the oldest European settlement in America, noting its preserved sixteenth-century wall and the 'needle's eye' city gate through which all visitors must enter. The account highlights prominent colonial monuments from the era of Christopher Columbus and Don Diego Columbus, including the ruins of Diego's palace and the cathedral begun in 1514 and completed in 1538. The cathedral is described as containing solid silver altar decorations, artworks accumulated over 400 years, and a monument marking the reputed resting place of Columbus beneath the floor.
records.summary_es: Una carta de viaje en el Daily Kennebec Journal relata una visita a la República Dominicana, describiéndola como un territorio fértil y rico pero escasamente conocido y poco desarrollado. El corresponsal califica a la ciudad de Santo Domingo, situada en la desembocadura del río Ozama, como el asentamiento europeo más antiguo de América, destacando su muralla del siglo XVI bien conservada y la puerta de la ciudad u «ojo de la aguja» por donde deben ingresar todos los visitantes. La crónica resalta los monumentos coloniales de la época de Cristóbal Colón y don Diego Colón, entre ellos las ruinas del palacio de Diego y la catedral comenzada en 1514 y finalizada en 1538. Se describe que la catedral alberga decoraciones de altar en plata maciza, obras de arte acumuladas durante 400 años y un monumento sobre el presunto sepulcro de Colón bajo el suelo de baldosas.

records.headline: The Smyrna Times reports that President Taft announced the appointment of Horace G. Knowles
records.summary_en: The Smyrna Times reports that President Taft announced the appointment of Horace G. Knowles, of Wilmington, as envoy extraordinary and minister to Bolivia. The transfer represents a promotion for Knowles, who has served in Santo Domingo since early this year as minister to the Dominican Republic following earlier diplomatic service in Romania and Serbia. The report credits Knowles with resolving an entangling situation in Santo Domingo and easing friction that threatened relations with the United States. He is expected to return to Wilmington for a vacation before proceeding to South America to assume his new mission in Bolivia.
records.summary_es: El Smyrna Times informa que el presidente Taft anunció la designación de Horace G. Knowles, de Wilmington, como enviado extraordinario y ministro en Bolivia. El traslado representa un ascenso para Knowles, quien ha ejercido en Santo Domingo desde principios de este año como ministro en la República Dominicana tras cumplir misiones diplomáticas previas en Rumania y Serbia. La crónica destaca que Knowles solucionó una situación compleja en Santo Domingo y disipó las tensiones que amenazaban las relaciones con los Estados Unidos. Se prevé que el diplomático regrese a Wilmington para tomarse unas vacaciones antes de viajar a Sudamérica a asumir su nuevo cargo en Bolivia.

records.full_text:
WIPING OUT A REPUBLIC'S DEBT

Honest Administration is Saving Santo Domingo. Honduras Asks for Help

NEW TARIFF LAWS HAVE HELPED COUNTRY

WASHINGTON, Aug. 11—The recent suggestion that this government assume a protectorate over Honduras and enter into a joint protectorate with Great Britian, France and Germany over Liberia, makes a review of this country's protectorate of Santo Domingo of timely interest. It will be recalled that the United States in March, 1905, entered into a treaty with the Dominican Republic to arrange its financial difficulties. The republic owed about $20,000,000, and its foreign creditors were pressing hard. Under a treaty, which the Senate reluctantly ratified, an American collector of customs was appointed for the republic, who received all customs receipts and divided them in the proportion of 45 per cent. for the republic and 55 per cent. for the creditors. Under the old Spanish law, which the Dominican republic never repealed, all expenses of the government are paid them for revenues derived from, imports and exports, property paying no taxes whatever.

In the five years that this government has assumed control of the Dominican custom-houses, the republic's debt has been reduced by $7,000,000 and the government, although receiving only 45 per cent. of the revenues has had more money to expend on administration and on public improvements than ever before when all the receipts went into the national treasury. The reason is not far to seek, for the American administration of the customs is honest. There have been naturally several abortive attempts at revolutions from hungry patriots whose souls shudder at the thought that the country's revenues are going into the country's treasury, but behind the American collector of customs, Mr. W. E. Pulliam, stands the American navy, and the net result of these revolutons has been only a decrease in the population of Santo Domingo, for those revolutionists who are not buried where they fall are safely tucked away in Dominican dungeons.

Result of New Tariff.
So well has Mr. Pulliam administered the revenues of the republic that a year ago last month he submitted a new tariff downward by about 15 per cent. Up to that time the Spanish principal of revenue taxation prevailed—namely, placing the heaviest possible duties on the necessities of life and permitting the luxuries to come in with the lightest possible duty. Mr. Pulliam introduced the American idea of letting the necessities of life come in free of duty, or nearly free, while the burden of taxation rested upon the luxuries. It was stipulated that an annual collection of $2,000,000 must be shown if the new tariff should remain in effect for more than a year. The tariff has now been adopted, and after a few months of a transition period, during which the business men of Santo Domingo adgusted themselves to new conditions, the receipts more than surpassed Mr. Pulliam's expectations. For the past three months the custom receipts have passed each month the quarter-million mark. At this rate the revenues for the current year will be at least $3,000,000, or one million more than the stipulated amount.

With this splended display of what American tariff and honesty will accomplish, it is small wonder that Honduras,, whose foreign creditors are pressing her hard for their money, and that Liberia, which faces dissolution as a republic, have appealed to this country for a similar protectorate. Although the State Department is strongly inclined to accede to both requests, it would be premature to say that the request will be granted. The Senate is bitterly opposed to any more such arrangements, although the example of Santo Domingo is encouraging. In the case of Liberia this country has only a sentimental interest, for Liberia owes its inception to American philanthropists.. It was the legislature of Maryland, whose generous appropriations nearly a century ago founded the Province of Maryland and peopled it with freed men from Maryland. The present republic if Liberia is a development of that settlement, but it is acknowledged on every hand that the republic is a failure. If this country enters into a joint protectorate with Great Britain, France and Germany, it will only mean a postponement of the fatal day.

No more Protectorates.
As for Honduras, a protectorate over that little republic would seem to be a logical corollary of the Monroe Doctrine, but the Senate, as already stated, is so bitterly opposed to any more of these treaties that Secretary Knox is at this moment unable to see his way clear to establishing a protectorate there. The Senate holds that if, following the example in Santo Domingo, this country takes up Honduras, it is only a question of time when an American receiver will be in charge of the customs of every petty republic in Central and South America, a condition not to be regarded with toleration.

records.headline: In an interview published in The Washington Herald, Mrs. Adams describes
records.summary_en: In an interview published in The Washington Herald, Mrs. Adams describes traveling through the Dominican Republic, taking five days on horseback to cross the Cordillera Central to La Vega and Santiago de los Caballeros, which connects by rail with Puerto Plata. She characterizes the people of Santo Domingo as hospitable, industrious, and possessing the courtesy of Spanish-American peoples, praising Dominican history as among the richest in the New World. Noting marked commercial advancement and recent improvements in Santo Domingo, which was founded in 149 as printed in the text, she suggests that planned hotels will make the island a mecca for tourists.
records.summary_es: En una entrevista publicada en The Washington Herald, la señora Adams describe su viaje por la República Dominicana, habiendo tardado cinco días a caballo en cruzar la Cordillera Central hasta llegar a La Vega y a Santiago de los Caballeros, que conecta por ferrocarril con Puerto Plata. Caracteriza a los habitantes de Santo Domingo como hospitalarios, trabajadores y poseedores de la cortesía de los pueblos hispanoamericanos, elogiando la historia dominicana como una de las más ricas del Nuevo Mundo. Tras señalar un marcado avance comercial y mejoras recientes en Santo Domingo, fundada en 149 según se imprime en el texto, sugiere que los hoteles previstos convertirán la isla en una meca para los turistas.

records.summary_en: The rice trade of the Dominican Republic is virtually monopolized by Germany, The Fargo Forum and Daily Republican observes, quoting an item from the Pittsburg Dispatch, citing reports from Commercial Agent Turner in Santo Domingo City. To provide freight for its West Indies route between St. Thomas and Jamaica, the Hamburg-American Line arranged through rates and called at a half dozen Dominican ports. In 1909, the line transported 18,000,000 pounds of rice valued at $801,546 to those Dominican ports.

records.summary_en: The New-York Tribune reports that Dominican residents in New York are excited over the arrival from Puerto Rico of General Eugenio Deschamps, viewed as the harbinger of an insurrection to depose President Ramon Caceres of Santo Domingo. Deschamps, a former vice president under General Wos y Gil and former governor of Puerto Plata, had been exiled in Puerto Rico alongside former Dominican presidents General Carlos Morales and General Juan Isidro Jimenez. The dispatch notes that another opposition leader, General Horacio Vasquez of the Horacista party, is likewise in virtual exile after previously offering conditional support to Caceres.

BLACK REPUBLICS READY FOR WAR Reported that Haiti and Domingo Have Clashed. BOUNDARY DISPUTE SERIOUS Trouble Arose Over Road Which Santo Domingo Is Building and Which Rival Nation Says Crosses Its Territory—Both Sides Sending Troops to the Frontier.

A serious boundary dispute between Santo Domingo and Haiti has broken out and threatens to involve those two countries in war. Information was received at the State and War departments yesterday indicating that an actual conflict between the troops of the two governments had taken place, but this was not verified absolutely.

The War Department received a dispatch from J. H. Edwards, acting general receiver of customs at Santo Domingo, saying that trouble had occurred between Haitian soldiers and Dominican customs and frontier guards near Lake Enriquillo. The dispute, he said, was due to a longstanding controversy over the exact location of the boundary line.

The Dominican cabinet, he said, had a long session to discuss the crisis, and negotiations had begun to avert war. Military preparations, however, were being made, and Dominican troops have been sent from various points to the border.

Wants Dispute Settled.

The Dominican government, he added, hopes for an amicable adjustment of the difficulty, and will insist upon an immediate and definite settlement of the boundary question.

Similar information was received at the State Department from W. W. Russell, American Minister at Santo Domingo. The present trouble, he said, was due to a dispute over the construction of a road between Pedernales and Lake Fondo.

It was reported that a conflict had taken place between the Haitian forces and the Dominican frontier guards. This report, he added, was denied, although the Haitian government admitted sending out an armed force to compel the Dominicans to stop work on the road.

The government of Santo Domingo takes the position that the proposed road does not cross Haitian territory. It considers that Haiti has committed a hostile act, and for this reason is preparing for its own defense by sending troops to the frontier.

SANTO DOMINGO AND HAITI APPEAL TO ARMS Rumor of Fighting on the Border Cabled to State Department.

Rumors of serious fighting on the border between Santo Domingo and Haiti are reported to the State Department in a cablegram dated yesterday from United States Minister Furniss at Port au Prince. He states that the Haitian government, while denying these rumors, is sending soldiers to the border. The Dominican government alleges that Haitian troops under Gen. Ferdinand fired on a Dominican guard at Pedernales. The Dominican republic has requested that the Haitian troops be withdrawn immediately, pending which the Dominican government is also sending troops to the seat of trouble. The President of Haiti, however, looks for an amicable settlement.

Rumor Regarding Collector Beale.

Mr. Furniss refers to the old rumor that Collector Beale had been killed in a collision between the Haitian and Dominican troops at Comendador. That report has been exploded by receipt of reports to the insular bureau of the War Department directly from Mr. Beale of later date than Mr. Furniss' advices.

The auxiliary cruiser Yankton has sailed from San Juan, Porto Rico, for Samana bay, on the north coast of Santo Domingo. The object of her visit is to lay out courses for torpedo practice by the Atlantic fleet within the quiet waters of the bay.

Attracted by the possibilities of the Dominican Republic, Mr. Brown took an active part in developing the country through the extension of its railroads and other industries. He served as a director of the Central Dominican Railway, and held offices as director and treasurer of both the San Domingo Finance Company and the San Domingo Improvement Company.

records.headline: The career of President Caceres of Santo Domingo is reviewed
records.summary_en: The career of President Caceres of Santo Domingo is reviewed in a feature in The Shoshone Journal, following it through a series of political tragedies, beginning in 1884 when his father was executed by order of President Heureaux. After studying and graduating from the Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in Troy, New York, and marrying Lillian Hakes, Caceres returned to Santo Domingo. His political career began in earnest when he avenged his father by assassinating Heureaux on July 28, 1899, facilitating General Jimenez's rise to the presidency. After serving as vice president under President Morales, Caceres was installed in the presidency following Morales's flight from the country in 1905.
records.summary_es: La trayectoria del presidente Cáceres de Santo Domingo es examinada en un artículo en el Shoshone Journal, siguiéndola a través de una serie de tragedias políticas, comenzando en 1884 cuando su padre fue ejecutado por orden del presidente Heureaux. Tras estudiar y graduarse en el Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute en Troy, Nueva York, y contraer matrimonio con Lillian Hakes, Cáceres regresó a Santo Domingo. Su carrera política comenzó formalmente cuando vengó a su padre asesinando a Heureaux el 28 de julio de 1899, lo que facilitó la llegada del general Jiménez a la presidencia. Tras desempeñarse como vicepresidente bajo el presidente Morales, Cáceres asumió la presidencia tras la huida de Morales del país en 1905.

records.headline: Heightened border friction between Haiti and the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Heightened border friction between Haiti and the Dominican Republic is reported by The Montgomery Advertiser, citing the publication Le Cable as urging Haitians to unite against a feared Dominican invasion of territory bequeathed by Dessalines. Under the heading 'Urge Arbitration,' a Washington dispatch dated January 24 states that President Taft instructed Secretary of State Knox to cable United States Minister Russell at Santo Domingo to press for an amicable settlement of the boundary conflict. Citing American obligations under the convention of 1907 and goodwill toward both republics, Knox offered the friendly good offices of the United States after several days without direct word from Russell.

records.headline: The Vilas County News prints a paraphrase of instructions transmitted
records.summary_en: The Vilas County News prints a paraphrase of instructions transmitted by presidential order to United States Minister Russell at Santo Domingo concerning the border dispute with Haiti. The message asserts that no essential difference exists between the Dominican and Haitian proposals, declaring that minor disagreements regarding the status quo and road construction cannot justify delay in submitting the issue to arbitration or any talk of armed conflict. Both governments are urged to unite in a compromise, maintain the status quo, withdraw troops from the border, and halt road work, while Secretary Knox points to American obligations under the convention of 1907.
records.summary_es: El Vilas County News publica una paráfrasis de las instrucciones transmitidas por orden presidencial al ministro estadounidense Russell en Santo Domingo relativas a la disputa fronteriza con Haití. El mensaje sostiene que no existe una diferencia fundamental entre las propuestas dominicana y haitiana, señalando que las desavenencias menores sobre el statu quo y las obras del camino no pueden justificar retrasos en someter el conflicto al arbitraje ni ninguna retórica de enfrentamiento armado. Se exhorta a ambos gobiernos a unirse en un compromiso, preservar el statu quo, retirar las tropas de la frontera y detener las obras viales, mientras el secretario Knox recuerda las obligaciones de los Estados Unidos bajo la convención de 1907.

records.summary_en: The Yorkville Enquirer reported that Dominican authorities arrested former Admiral Catrain as he attempted to sneak aboard a German steamer in Santo Domingo to join an insurrection led by deposed President Morales. Catrain, who had previously commandeered the gunboat *Independencia* during Morales's 1906 ouster before receiving amnesty, was suspected of returning to command a revolutionary vessel. Dominican officials discounted Morales's assertions to his followers that the United States supported his return to power.

Catrain, quien anteriormente había tomado el mando del cañonero *Independencia* durante la caída de Morales en 1906 antes de acogerse a una amnistía, era sospechoso de regresar para capitanear un barco revolucionario. Las autoridades dominicanas desestimaron las aseveraciones de Morales a sus seguidores acerca de que los Estados Unidos apoyaban su retorno al poder.

It is stated that Morales assured his followers that the United States government favors his return to power and will display no undue activity in balking his plans, but this is believed to have been said with a view of raising the courage of such of his supporters as were timorous of success. A fine steam yacht is said to form part of the revolutionary equipment and that a former San Domingan admiral now in Santo Domingo is to assume command. That the Santo Domingan administration gives credence to this statement is obvious from the recent arrest of ex-Admiral Catrain, on attempting to secretly leave Santo Domingo. Catrain, who is a prominent man in Santo Domingan politics and a famous leader, was admiral of the fleet during Morales's presidential term. When the latter was deposed in 1906 Catrain seized the gunboat Independencia and joining Morales's supporters at Monte Cristi attacked Puerto Plata, Samana and Sanchez, but was forced after a brief struggle to surrender. He accompanied Morales into exile, where he remained until an amnesty permitted him to return to Santo Domingo. On January 16 he went on board the German steamer lying in the port of Santo Domingo city and is said to have secreted himself with a view of escaping from the country. records.summary_en: The Yorkville Enquirer commented on Dominican political instability and former President Morales's campaign to regain the presidency by force, arguing that the country needed a strong leader comparable to Mexico's Porfirio Diaz. The article questioned whether Morales could improve upon the incumbent administration or justify plunging the nation into civil war. It noted that if threatened, the Dominican government could invoke a treaty clause originally drafted by Morales himself to request American intervention to protect debt obligations.
records.summary_es: The Yorkville Enquirer comentó sobre la inestabilidad política dominicana y la campaña del expresidente Morales para reconquistar la presidencia por la fuerza, argumentando que el país precisaba de un líder fuerte semejante al mexicano Porfirio Díaz. El artículo cuestionaba si Morales podría mejorar la gestión del gobierno en funciones o justificar que se sumiera a la nación en una guerra civil. Señalaba que, de verse amenazado, el gobierno dominicano podría recurrir a una cláusula del tratado redactada en su momento por el propio Morales para solicitar la intervención estadounidense en salvaguarda de los compromisos de la deuda.
records.passage: beloved by Columbus and the cradle of American civilization, for the first university in the New World was established in Santo Domingo, is at present living in the sixteenth century. Is it to be wondered at under the circumstances that the little republic is a prey to the worst evils that battened upon Europe during that era? Santo Domingo undoubtedly needs a despotic ruler with a determination to make it progress, a man of the Porfirio Diaz type, who will do for it what Diaz has done for Mexico. Whether Morales is capable of doing this or not can not be surmised. His term of office was too short to permit an influence either in pro or in contra, but his passage was marked by undeniable progress. Morales's plans of government, whatever they may be, should he succeed in reaching the presidency, are unknown, but unless he can materially better the present administration he would not be justified in carrying civil war into his country. He is, however, still a long way from the chair and the path to it is rugged and bloody. records.summary_en: Under the historical retrospective rubric 'Fifty Years Ago Today,' The Cairo Bulletin records that on March 21, 1861, the Spanish frigate Blanca was dispatched from Havana to Santo Domingo. The vessel was armed and equipped to uphold the Spanish protectorate recently proclaimed over the Dominican Republic. A parenthetical editorial note adds that Santo Domingo had been nominally independent since 1844, but remained in reality under the absolute rule of dictators.

El buque fue artillado y equipado para sostener el protectorado español proclamado recientemente sobre la República Dominicana. Una nota editorial entre paréntesis añade que Santo Domingo había sido nominalmente independiente desde 1844, pero permanecía en realidad bajo el mandato absoluto de dictadores.

records.headline: The Burlington Weekly Free Press reports on an address delivered
records.summary_en: The Burlington Weekly Free Press reports on an address delivered at a missionary jubilee by Miss Nellie Whlffcti (also referred to as Miss Wh'rfen), a Free Methodist missionary stationed in Santo Domingo. She noted that while a British society had carried on work in Dominican coastal towns over the previous ten years, her mission undertook house-to-house visitation, distributed Spanish translations of the gospels, and held nightly evangelistic services. Describing the populace in stark missionary language, she reported that many converts were nevertheless leading clean lives with Christian devotion and that native workers were going forth in the cause.

Señaló que, mientras una sociedad británica había desarrollado actividades en localidades costeras dominicanas durante los diez años precedentes, su misión realizaba visitas de casa en casa, distribuía traducciones de los evangelios al español y celebraba cultos evangelísticos nocturnos. Aunque describió a la población en severos términos misioneros, informó que numerosos conversos llevaban vidas íntegras con devoción cristiana y que obreros nativos se estaban incorporando a la causa.

records.headline: A dispatch in The Daily Banner reports the arrest of former President Morales
records.summary_en: A dispatch in The Daily Banner reports the arrest of former President Morales and former Vice President Jiminez of Santo Domingo, together with Zenon Torrible, on charges of preparing to organize a military expedition from Puerto Rico against the Dominican Republic; the dispatch came from San Juan. The arrests were prompted by papers and documents seized at a local hotel. Each of the three men was held under a $7500 bond.

Las detenciones fueron motivadas por papeles y documentos incautados en un hotel local. Cada uno de los tres hombres quedó retenido bajo una fianza de $7500.

records.summary_en: Former President Morales and former Vice President Jiminez of Santo Domingo were arrested by federal authorities, according to a San Juan dispatch published in The Washington Herald, along with an associate designated in the dispatch as Senor Torribls, for preparing a military expedition on the island against the Dominican Republic. Seized hotel papers and documents led directly to the arrests. Following the prisoners' arraignment, the hearing was postponed and each man was placed under $7,500 bond.

Papeles y documentos incautados en un hotel condujeron directamente a las detenciones. Tras la comparecencia de los prisioneros, la audiencia fue aplazada y cada hombre quedó sujeto a una fianza de $7,500.

records.summary_en: Charges that Dr. Hollander received salaries and fees from both the United States and Santo Domingo for his services in reorganizing Dominican finances, totaling more than $100,000, are covered by the Evening Star, reporting on congressional hearings. Thomas F. Dawson, former American minister to the Dominican Republic, testified that Hollander arrived in the country bearing letters from President Roosevelt and the State Department. Dawson stated under examination that he had no knowledge Hollander was receiving compensation from the Dominican government while being paid by the United States.

Thomas F. Dawson, exministro estadounidense en la República Dominicana, testificó que Hollander llegó al país con cartas del presidente Roosevelt y del Departamento de Estado. Dawson declaró durante el interrogatorio que desconocía que Hollander recibiera remuneración del gobierno dominicano mientras cobraba de Estados Unidos.

records.headline: An article in The Miller Press highlights the economic advantages of Dominican
records.summary_en: An article in The Miller Press highlights the economic advantages of Dominican cacao, emphasizing that Santo Domingo is closer to New York than any other leading producer, an asset expected to reduce shipping costs once the Panama Canal opens. While bulk cultivation is concentrated in the rainy Cibao region of northern Santo Domingo, the highest-quality beans are grown in the Province of "Setho" near Higuey and around "Salami de la Mar" on Samana Bay. The author notes that Swiss and French planters in those districts obtain premium prices through improved farming techniques, while additional land remains available along the Yuna River near the port of Sanchez.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en The Miller Press destaca las ventajas económicas del cacao dominicano y recalca que Santo Domingo está más cerca de Nueva York que cualquier otro productor destacado, ventaja que se espera reduzca los costos de transporte una vez inaugurado el canal de Panamá. Si bien el cultivo a granel se concentra en la lluviosa región del Cibao en el norte de Santo Domingo, los granos de mejor calidad se cultivan en la provincia de "Setho" cerca de Higüey y en los alrededores de "Salami de la Mar" (según figura en el texto) en la bahía de Samaná. El autor señala que los hacendados suizos y franceses en esos distritos obtienen precios superiores mediante técnicas agrícolas mejoradas, mientras que quedan tierras adicionales disponibles a lo largo del río Yuna, cerca del puerto de Sánchez.

records.headline: The Ordway New Era observes that although Spanish settlers brought
records.summary_en: The Ordway New Era observes that although Spanish settlers brought cacao from Venezuela to Santo Domingo more than two hundred years ago, turning the Dominican Republic into a major world producer, local cultivation remains haphazard and unscientific. The crop is raised largely by smallholders on plots that resemble tangled undergrowth rather than orderly orchards, lacking systematic pruning or selective soil placement. Despite these shortcomings, the article emphasizes that cacao is destined to be the country's primary economic resource, distributing wealth more widely among its people than sugar.
records.summary_es: The Ordway New Era observa que, aunque colonos españoles llevaron el cacao desde Venezuela a Santo Domingo hace más de doscientos años, convirtiendo a la República Dominicana en un gran productor mundial, el cultivo local sigue siendo fortuito y carente de método científico. La cosecha la cultivan mayormente pequeños propietarios en parcelas que parecen maleza enmarañada en lugar de huertos ordenados, sin podas sistemáticas ni selección de suelos. A pesar de estas deficiencias, el artículo subraya que el cacao está destinado a ser el principal recurso económico del país, distribuyendo la riqueza entre su población más ampliamente que el azúcar.

records.headline: A continuing installment in The Ordway New Era details the distribution of Dominican cacao
records.summary_en: A continuing installment in The Ordway New Era details the distribution of Dominican cacao by region, noting that the northern Cibao valley provides the heavy rainfall necessary for high yields. The finest beans come from the Province of Seibo near Higuey and Sabana de la Mar on Samana Bay, where Swiss and French growers secure superior prices that demonstrate the value of better farming methods. The paper reports that settlement land remains available along the Yuna River near Sanchez, and rates standard Dominican cacao on par with Sao Thome while comparing its best fermented grades to the cocoa of Bahia.
records.summary_es: Una entrega consecutiva en The Ordway New Era detalla la distribución del cacao dominicano por región y señala que el valle norteño del Cibao proporciona las copiosas lluvias necesarias para obtener altos rendimientos. Los granos más finos proceden de la provincia de El Seibo cerca de Higüey y de Sabana de la Mar en la bahía de Samaná, donde cosecheros suizos y franceses consiguen precios superiores que demuestran el valor de mejores métodos agrícolas. El periódico señala que aún quedan tierras de colonización disponibles a lo largo del río Yuna, cerca de Sánchez, y sitúa el cacao dominicano regular a la par del de Santo Tomé, al tiempo que compara sus mejores calidades fermentadas con el cacao de Bahía.

records.summary_en: The Wauwatosa News reports on the commercial strengths of Dominican cacao, observing that Santo Domingo's proximity to New York gives it a transportation advantage over competing nations that will expand after the Panama Canal is completed. Production is centered in the northern Cibao district where rainfall is abundant, but the top grades come from the Province of Seibo near Higuey and Sabana de la Mar on Samana Bay. In those areas, Swiss and French estate managers achieve higher prices through improved cultivation, setting an example for local farmers while open land remains available along the Yuna River.
records.summary_es: El Wauwatosa News informa sobre las ventajas comerciales del cacao dominicano y observa que la cercanía de Santo Domingo a Nueva York le otorga una ventaja de transporte sobre los países competidores que aumentará tras la conclusión del canal de Panamá. La producción se centra en el distrito norteño del Cibao, donde abundan las lluvias, pero las calidades óptimas provienen de la provincia de El Seibo, cerca de Higüey y Sabana de la Mar en la bahía de Samaná. En esas zonas, administradores de plantaciones suizos y franceses logran precios más elevados mediante un cultivo perfeccionado, sirviendo de ejemplo a los agricultores locales mientras aún quedan tierras disponibles a lo largo del río Yuna.

records.headline: An article in The Winslow Mail examines the market outlook for Dominican
records.summary_en: An article in The Winslow Mail examines the market outlook for Dominican cacao, arguing that proximity to the huge New York market and the future Panama Canal will provide favorable shipping rates to the West Indies. Cacao farming flourishes across the rainy Cibao region in northern Santo Domingo, though the finest yields come from the Province of Seibo near Higuey and Sabana de la Mar on Samana Bay. European planters from Switzerland and France have raised quality standards and secured better prices in these localities, while fertile acreage open to settlement by purchase lies along the Yuna River near the port of Sanchez.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en The Winslow Mail examina el panorama de mercado para el cacao dominicano, sosteniendo que la cercanía al inmenso mercado de Nueva York y el futuro canal de Panamá brindarán tarifas marítimas ventajosas a las Antillas. La agricultura cacaotera prospera a lo largo de la lluviosa región del Cibao en el norte de Santo Domingo, aunque las cosechas más finas provienen de la provincia de El Seibo, cerca de Higüey y Sabana de la Mar en la bahía de Samaná. Hacendados europeos de Suiza y Francia han elevado los estándares de calidad y obtenido mejores precios en estas localidades, mientras que terrenos fértiles aptos para colonización mediante compra se extienden a lo largo del río Yuna, cerca del puerto de Sánchez.

records.headline: The Vilas County News describes shortcomings in Dominican cacao
records.summary_en: The Vilas County News describes shortcomings in Dominican cacao management, noting that trees are crowded together without proper spacing, soil selection, or pruning, resembling wild undergrowth rather than well-kept orchards. Nonetheless, the writer maintains that cacao will become the backbone of the Dominican economy, distributing earnings far more evenly across society than the sugar trade. The country also benefits from being situated closer to New York than any other major cocoa-producing territory, with anticipated freight advantages once the Panama Canal is operational.
records.summary_es: El Vilas County News describe las deficiencias en el manejo del cacao dominicano, señalando que los árboles crecen apiñados sin una adecuada distancia, selección de suelos ni poda, asemejándose a maleza silvestre en lugar de huertos bien cuidados. No obstante, el articulista sostiene que el cacao llegará a ser la columna vertebral de la economía dominicana, distribuyendo las ganancias de forma mucho más equitativa en la sociedad que el negocio azucarero. El país se beneficia además al encontrarse situado más cerca de Nueva York que cualquier otro gran territorio cacaotero, con ventajas de transporte previstas una vez entre en funcionamiento el canal de Panamá.

records.headline: In a continuation on Dominican cacao, the Vilas County News highlights
records.summary_en: In a continuation on Dominican cacao, the Vilas County News highlights available agricultural land open to purchase along the Yuna River near the port of Sanchez, praising its soil and steady rainfall. Trees in Santo Domingo are reported to bear fruit for sixty years, and in some instances for up to one hundred years. The dispatch notes that ordinary Dominican cacao compares favorably with that of Sao Thome, whereas properly fermented beans rank with high-grade Bahia cacao. Setting up a cacao estate requires relatively small outlays, limited chiefly to land and fencing, because machinery is unnecessary and local labor is inexpensive.
records.summary_es: En una continuación sobre el cacao dominicano, el Vilas County News resalta la existencia de tierras agrícolas abiertas a la compra a lo largo del río Yuna, cerca del puerto de Sánchez, elogiando su suelo y sus lluvias constantes. Se informa que los árboles en Santo Domingo dan fruto durante sesenta años y, en ciertos casos, hasta por cien años. El despacho señala que el cacao dominicano común se compara favorablemente con el de Santo Tomé, mientras que los granos debidamente fermentados se equiparan con el cacao de alta graduación de Bahía. Establecer una finca cacaotera requiere desembolsos relativamente reducidos, limitados principalmente a la tierra y al cercado, ya que la maquinaria resulta innecesaria y la mano de obra local es barata.

records.headline: Dominican cacao enjoys an important geographical advantage
records.summary_en: Dominican cacao enjoys an important geographical advantage, The Willmar Tribune observes, because Santo Domingo is closer to New York than other major producer nations, anticipating lower freight rates following the completion of the Panama Canal. Bulk cultivation takes place in the northern Cibao region under heavy rainfall, while the finest beans are produced in the Province of Seibo near Higuey and Sabana de la Mar on Samana Bay. In those areas, Swiss and French planters obtain higher prices through superior methods, setting a profitable example for native farmers, while additional fertile tracts remain open to purchase along the Yuna River near Sanchez.

El cultivo a granel tiene lugar en la región norteña del Cibao bajo copiosas lluvias, mientras que los granos más selectos se producen en la provincia de El Seibo, cerca de Higüey y Sabana de la Mar en la bahía de Samaná. En esas zonas, hacendados suizos y franceses consiguen precios más altos mediante métodos superiores, brindando un ejemplo rentable para los agricultores nativos, al tiempo que tierras fértiles adicionales permanecen abiertas a la compra a lo largo del río Yuna, cerca de Sánchez.

records.headline: Cacao farming in Santo Domingo places the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Cacao farming in Santo Domingo places the Dominican Republic, an article in The Sea Coast Echo observes, among world leaders, yet methods remain haphazard although Spanish settlers introduced cultivation from Venezuela more than two hundred years ago. Production is primarily conducted by small planters, and even large plantations fail to provide systematic care. Trees are planted without proper spacing, resembling wild undergrowth rather than orderly orchards, while soils are unselected and trees left unpruned. The report maintains that when proper agricultural efforts are applied, the Dominican Republic's cacao output will achieve its true commercial promise.
records.summary_es: El cultivo del cacao en Santo Domingo sitúa a la República Dominicana, observa un artículo en The Sea Coast Echo, entre los líderes mundiales, aunque los métodos siguen siendo fortuitos pese a que colonos españoles introdujeron su producción desde Venezuela hace más de doscientos años. La producción la llevan a cabo primordialmente pequeños agricultores, e incluso las grandes plantaciones no brindan el cuidado sistemático necesario. Los árboles se plantan sin la debida distancia, asemejándose a maleza silvestre en vez de huertos ordenados, al tiempo que los suelos no se seleccionan y los árboles se dejan sin podar. El informe sostiene que, cuando se apliquen los esfuerzos agrícolas adecuados, la producción de cacao de la República Dominicana alcanzará su verdadera promesa comercial.

records.summary_en: The Sea Coast Echo reports, in continuing its account of Dominican cacao, that the finest product originates from the Province of El Seibo around Higuey and Sabana de la Mar, where Swiss and French planters command superior prices through better methods. Available lands well suited to cacao are open to settlement by purchase along both sides of the Yuna River near the port of Sanchez. The dispatch states that some trees in Santo Domingo still bear fruit at all of 100 years old, with an average tree yielding until 60 years old. Standard Dominican cacao compares favorably with that of the Island of Sao Thome, Africa, while carefully fermented beans rank with the best Bahia product, supported by inexpensive local labor.
records.summary_es: The Sea Coast Echo informa, al continuar su reseña sobre el cacao dominicano, que el producto más selecto proviene de la provincia de El Seibo alrededor de Higüey y Sabana de la Mar, donde agricultores suizos y franceses logran precios superiores mediante mejores métodos. Tierras disponibles muy aptas para el cacao se encuentran abiertas a colonización por compra en ambas márgenes del río Yuna, cerca del puerto de Sánchez. El despacho señala que algunos árboles en Santo Domingo aún dan fruto a la edad de 100 años, y que un árbol promedio continúa rindiendo hasta los 60 años. El cacao dominicano estándar resiste una comparación favorable con el de la isla de Santo Tomé, África, mientras que los granos fermentados con esmero se equiparan al mejor producto de Bahía, respaldados por mano de obra local económica.

records.summary_en: The Washington Herald reports that automobile sales in the Dominican Republic remain restricted because few residents can afford them and suitable motoring roads are lacking. Nevertheless, a macadam road of some twenty miles is under construction linking the city of San Cristobal to Santo Domingo, which is described as a well-paved capital of 10,000 inhabitants. records.summary_en: The Evening Capital and Maryland Gazette notes President Taft's appointment of Dr. Charles M. Hathaway, Jr., as United States consul at Puerto Plata, described as the second city in the Dominican Republic in population and foreign trade. The article reviews the historical background of Santo Domingo, noting that the bones of Columbus were buried in the capital and that Columbus named the fertile interior plain the "vega real" (royal plain), whose agricultural yield reaches foreign markets over a railroad to Puerto Plata. In profiling the new consul, the paper outlines Hathaway's schooling in Blakely and Scranton, Pennsylvania, his 1899 graduation and 1902 doctoral degree from Yale University, and his subsequent teaching career at Adelphi College and Columbia University.

records.full_text:
Sugar was the principal crop of the Dominican Republic in 1910, and was the largest and commanded the highest prices in the history of the country. The seven estates located at San Pedro de Macoris alone produced 501,000 bags of centrifugal sugar. In addition to the estates at Macoris, there are three plantations near the capital, one of which produces only for home consumption; one at Ocoa, two at Azua, and two at Puerto Plata. A large amount of American capital is invested in these estates, and most of them are thoroughly equipped with best up-to-date centrifugal sugar machinery and run on modern methods. Encouraged by the large production and high prices of 1909, several estates put in the latest improved machinery. The land under cultivation is being extended yearly, and, although the soil is shallow, it is of such a prolific nature that no fertilization is required, the same land reproducing crops for many years.

The United States took 200,927,359 pounds of sugar from Santo Domingo during 1910, valued at $5,517,202. However, as a great portion of this amount was invoiced to the United States with optional reshipment to Canada and England, the foregoing figures are somewhat misleading. In connection with the sugar industry at Macoris, there was put into operation in 1909 a plant for the production of molasses, the results from which have proved most satisfactory. In 1910, 1,588,934 gallons were exported, for which a very fair price was received. All of the output went to the United States.

records.full_text:
HOW TO STOP WAR U. S. Can Bring Peace to Small Republics, Says Taft. Take Charge of Custom Houses, Is His Plan. REVENUE IS STOPPED. Revolutionists Thus Fail to Get Funds for War. Santo Domingo System Urged for Other Countries.

Sacramento, Oct. 13.—President Taft's first important speech in California was delivered here today from the steps of the state capitol building. The president spoke in behalf of proposed treaties with Nicaragua and Honduras and vigorously defended the policy of the administration which he said "muck raking journals have labelled 'Dollar Diplomacy.'" Broadly speaking President Taft said the proposed treaties with these countries before the senate would secure for them a financial agent in the United States who would settle their existing debts on a just basis and would point the road to peace and prosperity to two republics, rich in natural resources but torn by strife and revolution. The president pointed out the efficacy of a similar arrangement with Santo Domingo where this government collects the customs and sees that foreign debts are paid, exercises a benefit supervision that Mr. Taft said has accrued to the upbuilding of Santo Domingo. Objection to the treaties in the United States senate, the president said, was based largely upon the proposition that they would make entangling alliances with republics in this hemisphere for the promotion of a banking contract since the money for the payment of the debts of the two republics would be furnished by American interests. Another objection discussed by the president was that the Monroe doctrine was sufficient bond between the United States and Latin American countries.

"It is objected that this is 'dollar diplomacy,'" said the president, "and that we ought to have none of it. Give a dog a bad name and you know what follows. To call a piece of statecraft's 'dollar diplomacy' is to invoke the condemnation of the muck raking journals, whose chief capital is in the use of phrases of a lurid character. The United States did not enter into this treaty for the promotion of its own banking business or that of any of its citizens. It was thought advisable to favor a contract with American bankers rather than with foreign bankers because such a contract would tend to keep trade with America. This is the correct object and purpose of diplomatic negotiations."

The Complete Speech.

The speech in full follows:

"My Fellow Citizens: The subject of the ratification of treaties by the senate is frequently confidential, and that prevents public discussion of the pros and cons which might sometimes be useful. Treaties are much less the subject of public consideration than are statutes, because by the Constitution they become the law of the land. In this respect they differ from treaties of other governments, which are only international contracts. Sometimes the senate removes the injunction of secrecy from treaties and the discussion of their merits. It is to certain treaties which I have submitted to the senate which that body has now published and laid before you for consideration and discussion, that I call your attention today. They are the treaties I made with the republic of Honduras and the republic of Nicaragua, for the purpose of securing a loan to each of these Central American republics.

"We have heard a great deal during the past six months in favor of general arbitration treaties for the promotion of the peace of the world. I believe there has been of late more genuine expression of sentiment among all the people of the earth for peace than ever before in the world's history. The craving for some effective means of promoting peace grows not so much out of actual war as out of the desperation with which the great nations are increasing the stupendous burden of armies and armament, making Europe an armed camp, with the growing menace of bankruptcy.

"The fact is that we have had very little war in the last 25 years, and one of the reasons has been the rivalry in preparation for war and the certainty of financial disaster to some nations which must follow.

Substitute Must Be Real.

"Among these great nations there is the conservatism of domestic stability and the law abiding character of the population. Universal treaties of arbitration for such countries are of the highest importance as probably furnishing a means by which all may be induced ultimately to reduce their armaments, when it shall become apparent that arbitration is a real and practical substitute for war.

"I would not therefore minimize the importance of such treaties in the ultimate cause of peace; but I wish to point out that at present wars chiefly arise, not between well ordered nations having well armed, well recruited, and well disciplined forces, but out of internecine strife. They grow out of the rebellion or revolution of part of a people against the constituted authority of the other part. They proceed from the lack of stability of government and cupidity and the ambition of partisan leaders among the people. There are countries where the occupation of a revolutionist has become a profession and the unhappy common people of such a country have no time for peaceful pursuits, and perforce are driven into guerilla warfare for mere self protection. Starvation succeeds plenty in countries as productive as any in the world. The institutions of civil liberty, if they ever were inaugurated under a high sounding constitution, cease to exist, revolutions follow each other in rapid succession, the finances of the government are in hopeless confusion, and it is a stretch of the imagination to call what little authority remains a government at all. Such has been the fate of some of the Central American republics.

"Lying between Mexico on the north and the Isthmus of Panama on the south, they have had the benefit of all the wealth that nature with a generous hand can bestow, and if only peace could be secured for one or two decades, prosperity would ensue. It has been exceedingly difficult, however, to preserve peace, because unscrupulous and ambitious adventurers leading a revolution in one country excite disturbances in another. Honduras and Nicaragua are now the two countries most exposed to these internal dissensions.

Seven Revolutions in Fifteen Years.

"In Honduras there have been seven revolutions in 15 years. Its territory reaches from ocean to ocean, and its neutrality is rarely preserved when its neighbors are at war. These conditions necessitate the keeping up, at great expense, of its army. General arbitration treaties can have little influence over countries subject to these conditions. The shifting of government from one group to another would weaken greatly the practical binding force of such treaties, and the unsettled condition of the population makes it necessary that a more effective method to secure tranquillity and quiet must be found, and thereby the forces among these people making for civilization and progress must be given full opportunity to achieve their beneficent ends.

"Our experience with Santo Domingo, once a volcano of revolution constantly in eruption, suggests a possible and practicable method of meeting the same difficulties that are presented to these Central American republics. A study of the revolutions shows that their first object is the seizure of custom houses through which import taxes are collected. The custom houses are the only sources of revenue at such times, and provide the sinews of war for the professional revolutionist. With these as a basis of operation he moves into the country and ultimately and for the time being secures control of the whole republic. By a very fortunate arrangement, under an order of President Roosevelt, with the consent of Santo Domingo, and under an arrangement with the bondholders of that then failing and unfortunate country, Americans were placed in control of the custom houses and took charge of the collection of the revenues.

Uncle Sam Is Receiver.

"The arrangement was like a receivership, providing for the deposit of a certain proportion of the funds collected in a New York city bank, to be applied to the payment of the national debt, after it had been scaled down to a reasonable figure, with as much as possible of the fraud, waste, and injustice squeezed out. The United States undertook to defend the custom houses against seizure by rebellious Santo Dominicans, and the fact that this government acted as guardian—not of the people, not of the country, but only of the customhouses—was quite sufficient to make this receivership arrangement a complete success.

"Subsequently a treaty with Santo Domingo embodying these features was ratified by the senate, and has now been nearly five years in successful operation. The revenues have been divided, some 40 or 45 per cent applied toward the extinction of the national debt of Santo Domingo, and the remainder of 55 per cent constituted a revenue for the country greater than it ever had before in its history.

"The Santo Dominicans have been well served in the collections of their customs by experienced and honest Americans recommended by this government; revolutions have been prevented because no professional revolutionist believed it possible to oust from the custom houses men who were there by direction and under the protection of the United States. Peace has prevailed; capital has entered after peace; enterprise has followed, and prosperity is the result. We had spent hundreds of thousands of dollars each year in sending fleets of gunboats to protect American and foreign property in Santo Domingo and Haiti against injury from revolutions. Now that source of expense has been reduced to a minimum. Our responsibility, so far as armed interference is concerned, has practically disappeared.

Asks United States to Take Charge.

"The lesson of Santo Domingo has suggested a similar solution of the difficulties of Honduras, Nicaragua, and some of the other countries in Central America. There have been, as I say, seven revolutions in 15 years in Honduras. Her debt, the principal of which was originally $26,000,000 in bonds, has increased by accrued interest to $124,000,000, and her military expenditures each year are $600,000. The government has no money with which to make improvements, to build roads, to do any of the things necessary to progress and civilization. Her people are poor and on the verge of starvation in a land that ought to be blossoming with prosperity, and she has turned to us as a philanthropic guardian of the small countries of our continent to assist in the adjustment of her foreign debt, to improve the collection of her taxes—in a word, to follow the course taken in Santo Domingo. The treaty we have concluded with Honduras provides that we will help her to secure a financial agent in our country who shall settle the existing debt on a just basis, for everyone admits the fraudulent character of part of the debt and its inequity, because so little of it really inured to the benefit of the country.

"By the treaty the government of Honduras undertakes to make a contract providing for the refunding of its present internal and external debt for the adjustment and settlement of claims liquidated and unliquidated, and for the placing of its finances upon a sound and stable basis. Both governments agree to take due note of all the provisions of the contract when made, and to confer in case of difficulties, with a view to the faithful execution of the contract, in order that the benefits to Honduras and the security of the loan may be secured.

Thus War Is Stopped.

"By Article II it is agreed that the loan shall be secured upon the customs of Honduras, and the government of that country agrees not to alter its import or export duties during the existence of the loan without consultation and agreement with the government of the United States. By Article III a full and detailed statement of the operations under the contract is to be submitted by the fiscal agent to the department of state of the United States and to the minister of finance of Honduras at the expiration of each 12 months, and at such other times as may be requested.
