records.full_text:
Pres. Taft's Speech on Arbitration Treaties at Sacramento, Cal.

Following is an abstract of the speech delivered Friday, Oct. 13, at Sacramento, Cal., on the subject of “Arbitration Treaties,” referring specifically to those made with Honduras and Nicaragua:

Arbitration Treaties.

My Fellow Citizens: The subject of the ratification of treaties by the Senate is frequently confidential, and that prevents public discussion of the pros and cons which might sometimes be useful. Treaties are much less the subject of public consideration than are statutes, and yet when ratified they are as binding upon all of us as statutes, because by the Constitution they become the law of the land. In this respect they differ from treaties of other governments, which are only international contracts. Sometimes the Senate removes the injunction of secrecy from treaties and the discussion of their merits. It is to certain treaties which I have submitted to the Senate, and which that body has now published and laid before you for consideration and discussion, that I call your attention to-night. They are the treaties I made with the Republic of Honduras and the Republic of Nicaragua, for the purpose of securing a loan to each of these Central American Republics.

We have heard a great deal during the past six months in favor of general arbitration treaties for the promotion of the peace of the world. I believe there has been of late more genuine expression of sentiment among all the people of the earth for peace than ever before in the world's history. The craving for some effective means of promoting peace grows not so much out of actual war as out of the desperation with which the great nations are increasing the stupendous burden of armies and armament, making Europe an armed camp, with the growing menace of bankruptcy.

The fact is that we have had very little war in the last 25 years, and one of the reasons has been the rivalry in preparation for war and the certainty of financial disaster to some nations which must follow.

Among these great nations there is the conservatism of domestic stability and the law-abiding character of the population. Universal treaties of arbitration for such countries are of the highest importance as probably furnishing a means by which all may be induced ultimately to reduce their armaments, when it shall became apparent that arbitration is a real and practical substitute for war.

I would not therefore minimize the importance of such treaties in the ultimate cause of peace; but I wish to point out that at present wars chiefly arise, not between well-ordered nations having well-armed, well-recruited, and well-disciplined forces, but out of internecine strife. They grow out of the rebellion or revolution of part of a people against the constituted authority of the other part. They proceed from the lack of stability of government and cupidity and the ambition of partisan leaders among the people. There are countries where the occupation of a revolutionist has become a profession and the unhappy common people of such a country have no time for peaceful pursuits, and perforce are driven into guerrilla warfare for mere self-protection. Starvation succeeds plenty in countries as productive as any in the world. The institutions of civil liberty, if they ever were inaugurated under a high-sounding constitution, cease to exist, revolutions follow each other in rapid succession, the finances of the Government are in hopeless confusion, and it is a stretch of the imagination to call what little authority remains a government at all. Such has been the fate of some of the Central American Republics. Lying between Mexico on the north and the Isthmus of Panama on the south, they have had the benefit of all the wealth that nature with a generous hand can bestow, and if only peace could be secured for one or two decades, prosperity would ensue. It has been exceedingly difficult, however, to preserve peace, because unscrupulous and ambitious adventurers leading a revolution in one country excite disturbances in another. Honduras and Nicaragua are now the two countries most exposed to these internal dissensions.

In Honduras there have been seven revolutions in 15 years. Its territory reaches from ocean to ocean, and its neutrality is rarely preserved when its neighbors are at war. These conditions necessitate the keeping up, at great expense, of its army. General arbitration treaties can have little influence over the countries subject to these conditions. The shifting of government from one group to another would weaken greatly the practical binding force of such treaties, and the unsettled condition of the population makes it necessary that a more effective method to secure tranquillity and quiet must be found, and thereby the forces among these peoples making for civilization and progress must be given full opportunity to achieve their beneficent ends.

Our experience with Santo Domingo, once a volcano of revolution constantly in eruption, suggests a possible and practicable method of meeting the same difficulties that are presented to these Central American Republics. A study of the revolutions shows that their first object is the seizure of customhouses through which import taxes are collected. The customhouses are the only sources of revenue at such times, and provide the sinews of war for the professional revolutionist. With these as a basis of operation he moves into the country and ultimately and for the time being secures control of the whole Republic. By a very fortunate arrangement, under an order of President Roosevelt, with the consent of Santo Domingo, and under an arrangement with the bondholders of that then failing and unfortunate country, Americans were placed in control of the customhouses and took charge of the collection of the revenues. The arrangement was like a receivership, providing for the deposit of a certain proportion of the funds collected in a New York City bank, to be applied to the payment of the national debt, after it had been scaled down to a reasonable figure, with as much as possible of the fraud, waste, and injustice squeezed out. The United States undertook to defend the customhouses against seizure by rebellious Santo Dominicans, and the fact that this Government acted as guardian—not of the people, not of the country, but only of the customhouses—was quite sufficient to make this receivership arrangement a complete success. Subsequently a treaty with Santo Domingo embodying these features was ratified by the Senate, and has now been nearly five years in successful operation. The revenues have been divided, some 40 or 45 per cent. applied toward the extinction of the national debt of Santo Domingo, and the remainder of 55 per cent. constituted a revenue for the country greater than it ever had before in its history.

The Santo Dominicans have been well served in the collections of their customs by experienced and honest Americans recommended by this Government; revolutions have been prevented because no professional revolutionist believed it possible to oust from the customhouses men who were there by direction and under the protection of the United States. Peace has prevailed; capital has entered after peace; enterprise has followed, and prosperity is the result. We had spent hundreds of thousands of dollars each year in sending fleets of gunboats to protect American and foreign property in Santo Domingo and Haiti against injury from revolutions. Now that source of expense has been reduced to a minimum. Our responsibility, so far as armed interference is concerned, has practically disappeared.

The lesson of Santo Domingo has suggested a similar solution of the difficulties of Honduras, Nicaragua and some of the other countries in Central America. There have been, as I say, seven revolutions in 15 years in Honduras. Her debt, the principal of which was originally $26,000,000 in bonds, has increased by accrued interest to $124,000,000, and her military expenditures each year are $600,000. The Government has no money with which to make improvements, to build roads, to do any of the things necessary to progress and civilization. Her people are poor and on the verge of starvation in a land that ought to be blossoming with prosperity, and she has turned to us as the philanthropic guardian of the small countries of our continent to assist in the adjustment of her foreign debt, improve the collection of her taxes and—in a word, to follow the course taken in Santo Domingo. The treaty we have concluded with Honduras provides that we will help her to secure a financial agent in our country who shall settle the existing debt on a just basis, for everyone admits the fraudulent character of part of the debt and its inequity, because so little of it really inured to the benefit of the country.

By the treaty the Government of Honduras undertakes to make a contract providing for the refunding of its present internal and external debt, for the adjustment and settlement of claims liquidated and unliquidated, and for the placing of its finances upon a sound and stable basis. Both governments agree to take due note of all the provisions of the contract when made, and to confer in case of difficulties, with a view to the faithful execution of the contract, in order that the benefits to Honduras and the security of the loan may be secured.

By Article II it is agreed that the loan shall be secured upon the customs of Honduras, and the Government of that country agrees not to alter its import or export duties during the existence of the loan without consultation and agreement with the Government of the United States. By Article III a full and detailed statement of the operations under the contract is to be submitted by the fiscal agent to the Department of State of the United States and to the minister of finance of Honduras at the expiration of each 12 months, and at such other times as may be requested. By Article IV—and this is the important article—“The Government of Honduras so long as the loan exists will appoint from a list of names to be presented to it by the fiscal agent of the loan, and approved by the President of the United States of America, a collector general of customs, who shall administer the customs in accordance with the contract, securing said loan, and will give this official full protection in the exercise of his functions. The Government of the United States will in turn afford such protection as it may find requisite.”

A contract for the loan has been made between the Government of Honduras and four of our prominent banking firms—Pierpont Morgan & Co., Kuhn, Loeb & Co., the National City Bank, and the First National Bank of New York—and the Guaranty Trust Co. of New York has agreed to act as fiscal agent of the loan. Under this arrangement the old debt of the Republic, of about $26,000,000, is to be redeemed by the issue of bonds to the amount of $4,500,000. The whole loan is to be $10,000,000, and is to cover this payment of bonds. About $2,500,000 is to be used for internal improvements. The only obligation the United States assumes is to exercise its judgment in recommending collectors of customs, and it reserves the right to protect such collectors. The contract of loan has been examined by the State Department and by experts employed by it, to see whether it is fair to the Government of Honduras. The rate of interest for the bonds is 5 per cent., and the price at which they are to be sold is 88. This is not as high as the Dominican bonds sold under the contract, because when that contract was made the experiment had been actually made and there were already several millions of dollars on deposit in the bank of New York awaiting distribution in liquidation of the debt. The fear of action by the United States, when it has a right to act under such a treaty as this, will reduce the necessity for sending the gunboats we have heretofore had to send every time there was a disturbance in a Central American country. Honduras, stretching from one side of the Isthmus to the other, has been a common camping ground for the revolutionists of the Central American Republics. If we can by such a simple arrangement as this, and by the assumption of such a light responsibility as I have described, put Honduras on her feet, so far as her debts are concerned, and can give her a breathing space in which to develop the wealth which nature has lavished upon her, we can be certain of promoting peace and thrift in a part of the world where peace and due process of law are now unknown.

Nicaragua is a country lying adjacent to Honduras, and its circumstances have been similar to those of Honduras. The treaty with Nicaragua is practically the same as that with Honduras. The approval of these two treaties and a successful administration of the loan contracts will lead to adjustments of the national debts of the other Central American Republics on a basis much more favorable to them and with even less responsibility on the part of the United States.

San Salvador is one of the Central American Republics that has had less revolution and disturbance than any, and its credit has, therefore, been better. The minute, however, that the Honduras treaty was made and the loan effected, subject to ratification by the Senate, the minister of that country advised Mr. Knox that the prospect of putting Honduras on a sound and peaceful basis had enabled his country to reduce its army, thus lessening the cost of its government and increasing its ability to meet its financial obligations.

There is a very decided objection in the Senate to the approval of these treaties. I doubt if I can fairly state their objections. This is due, perhaps, to the depth of my conviction that the treaties ought to be ratified because they are of the utmost importance in the promotion of peace on this hemisphere, in a region where there has been no peace. The general argument seems to be that we ought not to involve ourselves in entangling alliances with Republics in this hemisphere, or to engage in what seems a mere banking arrangement for the promotion of a banking contract. It is objected that this is “dollar diplomacy,” and that we ought to have none of it. Give a dog a bad name and you know what follows. To call a particular piece of statecraft “dollar diplomacy” is to invoke the condemnation of muckraking journals, whose chief capital is in the use of phrases of a lurid character. The United States did not enter into this treaty for the promotion of its own banking business or that of any of its citizens. It was thought advisable to favor a contract with American bankers rather than with foreign bankers, because such a contract would tend to keep trade with America, rather than divert trade to European markets—I mean the trade of these countries. As it is now, a large part of the Honduras trade, both epxort and import, is with the Gulf ports of the United States. Peace and prosperity will largely increase this trade, and with an American loan and our protection of the contract we are sure to retain this trade, which will increase, instead of its going to some other country. This is the correct object and purpose of diplomatic negotiation. Trade is not the chief purpose of the contract, for, as I have already explained, it is to promote peace in this part of the world, a part of the world so near the Panama Canal as to give us an additional geographical reason for desiring to eliminate revolution and warfare. As a matter of fact, it will reduce our naval expenditures by diminishing the number of gunboats we have to maintain in all this region. An examination of our expenditure on this account during the last five years will show that this is considerable.

Another argument against the treaty grows out of the continued discussion of what the Monroe doctrine means. It has been said in favor of such treaties as this that by virtue of the Monroe doctrine all these countries are more or less under our guardianship; that we have guaranteed, in a sense, their integrity against invasion by European countries; and that it is, therefore, our duty, where a European country acting for its own citizens or subjects takes forcible measures to collect their debts from such Republics, to say: “You must keep off and we will undertake properly to adjust your claims.” Now, it is this argument, it seems to me, as much as anything, that has aroused opposition to the treaties, because it proceeds upon premises that are calculated to engender discussion and dispute. Opponents of the argument say that no country has the right to use forcible measures to collect the debts contracted with its citizens by a foreign government, and that the position our Government ought to take is, not to secure payment of the debt, but merely to say, “You can not take forcible measures for this purpose, because it is in violation of the Monroe doctrine,” and that this is far enough for the United States to go.

Further, it is vigorously denied that the Monroe doctrine requires the United States to intervene in debt-collecting expeditions because they do not contemplate the destruction of the Government whose property is seized, but only the forcible collection of the debt. Mr. John Bassett Moore points out that such expeditions in the past have never incurred the condemnation of this Government, or its objection, on the ground that the Monroe doctrine prevented it. He says that doctrine is limited solely to an invasion of the territory of the Governments in this hemisphere with the purpose of changing the form of government. I do not care what is technically included in the Monroe doctrine. Those who look at our position in this hemisphere must recognize that in the brotherhood of the 21 Republics which constitute what is called the “Pan American Union,” the United States is the most powerful, the leading country, and all must hope that through the influence of the United States and the other countries at peace, those Republics at war may be brought to a state of peace. We have progressed beyond the time in civilization when we can stand up and say of our neighbors that we have no interest whether they are at peace or at war. We are neighbors of the Central American Republics. We have always felt it incumbent upon us to help them out of their difficulties, and to intervene and prevent them from cutting each other's throats. Our enormous interest in Panama only accentuates the necessity for our taking care that those countries so near the Isthmus shall not be the scene of warfare which might threaten the usefulness of the canal. For many years it has been our function to intervene here to protect foreign property, and to use our good offices to bring about peace. This is the one spot in the civilized world today where there is more danger of constant war than any other. We are so situated with reference to these five Republics that we are certain to get a large part of the trade which peace and the tranquil development must greatly enlarge. Whether we take formal steps to give us a right to intervene or not, we shall have thrust upon us in almost every quarter the necessity for intervening. Is it not better that we should step in with due authority and act with directness and promptness to suppress war than that we should allow it to go on because we lack authority to interfere; and then, at the extremity, be called in to use force to prevent violation of the rights of foreign nations which always occurs at a certain point in a revolution.

I do not care to discuss the exact boundary lines of the Monroe doctrine. It was announced in a message of President Monroe, and was really directed against the then existing Holy Alliance which it was feared was proposed to assist Spain in the subjugation of her lost colonies in this hemisphere. They had become republics and their independence had been recognized by the United States. There was a reference in the same message to the objection which this country had to colonization on this continent by European countries, but it seems clear that that referred to the settlement by Russian colonists of territory claimed by the United States, and that it was not the declaration of a general principle that mere colonization which did not involve the overturning of established government in this country was objected to by the United States. The Monroe doctrine has been interpreted to be the policy of the United States in conserving the interests of all American Republics where they are liable to possible injury from without. It has been invoked to justify our great and sometimes active interest in the settlement of controversies between the countries of this hemisphere and the countries of Europe, and also the settlement of all controversies between the nations of this hemisphere. The declarations of Mr. Olney at the time of the Venezuelan difficulty were emphatic—some people thought extreme—in reference to the responsibility which the United States thereby assumed for the entire hemisphere, and the rights asserted in the exercise of that responsibility. Certainly it does not involve any extreme view of our friendly relation to these Republics to stand sponsor for them and cooperate with them in securing such loans as are necessary to enable them to pay their debts and to enter a new era of development and prosperity. We do not guarantee the payment of the loans; we simply accept the responsibility of selecting the class of persons to be appointed receivers of taxes, and we undertake to protect those receivers in the discharge of their duties. It happens that this attitude, without further action on our part, enables those countries to make loans on reasonable terms. Now, gentlemen, is it not a good neighborly action for us to allow ourselves to become involved to this slight extent in order to help these struggling sister Republics? Is it not prudent to put those who are certain to be our good customers in a condition where they can increase their business and increase our trade? Is there not an obligation higher than any of these to prevent the recurrence of wars which have deluged with blood that beautiful part of the world and have caused untold misery and unhappiness to hundreds of thousands of God's creatures?

Having taken this step in Santo Domingo, and having shown how successful the method is in suppressing war, in maintaining power, and in securing prosperity, ought we not to extend the same assistance to countries which have an equal right to look to us for aid and protection?

In the promotion of this humane policy the administration has done its part. The treaties with Honduras and Nicaragua have been negotiated and contracts for loans under their provisions have been tentatively approved. All have been submitted to the Senate and are pending there. It is for the Senate to decide whether this, the most effective step in the promotion of peace on this continent, shall be taken; whether the finances of these Republics shall be put on a sound and stable basis, their citizens relieved of the discouraging burden of a debt largely fictitious and greatly disproportionate to their revenues, and the portals of prosperity thrown open to them. Until approved by the upper House of Congress the treaties must remain wholly inoperative.

But if you agree with me that every dictate of prudence, of common sense, of friendship and neighborliness, as well as loyalty to the cause of peace. makes mandatory the approval of these treaties, you will hope and urge as earnestly as I that the Senate, in its wisdom, will give to them its prompt and emphatic approval.

records.headline: Under the subheading "Did It in Santo Domingo," an analytical feature
records.summary_en: Under the subheading "Did It in Santo Domingo," an analytical feature in The Salt Lake Tribune examines how United States supervision stabilized the country following the 1865 withdrawal of Spanish control. The article recounts that the government established after Spanish evacuation was overthrown within a month, and that during the thirty years following, up to and including 1905, the Dominican Republic experienced twenty general revolutions and twenty-five successive administrations. Amid this chronic unrest, internal progress remained paralyzed, leaving not ten miles of roadway across the entire republic while industry lagged and national revenues failed to reach the treasury. During this prolonged turmoil, public debts expanded unchecked, interrupted only by a period of comparative peace from 1888 to 1899.
records.summary_es: Bajo el subtítulo "Lo hizo en Santo Domingo", un artículo de fondo en The Salt Lake Tribune analiza cómo la supervisión de los Estados Unidos estabilizó al país tras el retiro del control español en 1865. El artículo relata que el gobierno establecido tras la evacuación española fue derrocado en menos de un mes, y que durante los treinta años subsiguientes, abarcando hasta 1905, la República Dominicana experimentó veinte revoluciones generales y veinticinco administraciones sucesivas. En medio de esta crónica inestabilidad, el desarrollo interno se mantuvo paralizado, no quedando ni diez millas de carreteras en toda la república mientras la industria decaía y las rentas nacionales no ingresaban a la tesorería. A lo largo de esta prolongada agitación, las deudas públicas crecieron sin control, con la única excepción de un período de relativa paz entre 1888 y 1899.

records.summary_en: The Salt Lake Tribune reviewed the origin of the 1905 Dominican modus vivendi, crediting former American Minister Thomas C. Dawson with devising the administrative revenue plan. Put into effect on April 1, 1905, the agreement placed customs collection under American officials who distributed funds between the government and foreign creditors. The article observed that civil conflicts ceased almost immediately once revolutionists were unable to seize customs houses and revenues.
records.summary_es: The Salt Lake Tribune examinó el origen del modus vivendi dominicano de 1905, reconociendo al exministro estadounidense Thomas C. Dawson la concepción del plan administrativo de recaudación. Puesto en vigor el 1 de abril de 1905, el acuerdo confió el cobro aduanero a funcionarios estadounidenses que distribuían los fondos entre el gobierno y los acreedores extranjeros. El artículo observó que las guerras civiles cesaron casi de inmediato una vez que los revolucionarios se vieron impedidos de apoderarse de las aduanas y de sus caudales.

records.headline: Under the section heading "Did It in Santo Domingo," a feature
records.summary_en: Under the section heading "Did It in Santo Domingo," a feature in The San Francisco Call discusses the impact of United States influence following the withdrawal of Spanish rule from the Dominican Republic in 1865. The report observes that the government established upon Spanish evacuation fell within a month, initiating 30 years of instability up to 1905 during which the country suffered 20 general revolutions and saw 25 administrations take power and collapse. Under these conditions internal improvement proved impossible, leaving fewer than 10 miles of roadway across the republic while national revenues dwindled, public funds failed to reach the treasury, and the public debt mounted continuously.
records.summary_es: Bajo el epígrafe "Lo hizo en Santo Domingo", un artículo especial en The San Francisco Call examina el efecto de la influencia de los Estados Unidos tras la retirada del dominio español de la República Dominicana en 1865. La crónica observa que el gobierno establecido tras la evacuación española cayó en el lapso de un mes, iniciando 30 años de inestabilidad hasta 1905 durante los cuales el país sufrió 20 revoluciones generales y vio asumir y desplomarse a 25 administraciones. En tales circunstancias, el progreso interno resultó imposible, quedando menos de 10 millas de carreteras en toda la república mientras los ingresos nacionales mermaban, los fondos públicos no llegaban a la tesorería y la deuda pública aumentaba sin cesar.

records.headline: A Washington dispatch in The New Haven Union reports that the State Department received
records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch in The New Haven Union reports that the State Department received word from the American chargé d'affaires at Santo Domingo City of the assassination yesterday of President Ramon Caceres. The paper describes the slaying as the latest episode in a cycle of political violence, recalling that after President Heaureaux executed Caceres' father on a flimsy pretext in 1884, the ten-year-old Caceres vowed revenge, ultimately shooting Heaureaux dead 15 years later at a conference in Moca along with an alms-seeking mendicant. Following that killing, Caceres joined the revolutionist leader Morales to mount an uprising against the government. The report adds that Caceres, about 38 years old, had graduated from the Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in Troy, New York, where he married Lillie, the adopted daughter of Mr. and Mrs. J. S. Hakes.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Washington en The New Haven Union informa que el Departamento de Estado recibió aviso del encargado de negocios estadounidense en la ciudad de Santo Domingo sobre el magnicidio de ayer del presidente Ramón Cáceres. El periódico describe el asesinato como el último eslabón de un ciclo de violencia política, recordando que, tras ejecutar el presidente Heaureaux al padre de Cáceres bajo un pretexto endeble en 1884, Cáceres, a la edad de 10 años, juró vengarse, matando finalmente a tiros a Heaureaux 15 años después en una conferencia en Moca junto con un mendigo que pedía limosna. Tras aquel homicidio, Cáceres se unió al caudillo revolucionario Morales para impulsar un alzamiento contra el gobierno. El despacho añade que Cáceres, de unos 38 años de edad, se había graduado en el Instituto Politécnico Rensselaer en Troy, Nueva York, donde contrajo matrimonio con Lillie, hija adoptiva del matrimonio de J. records.headline: A Washington dispatch in The Birmingham Age-Herald reviews the assassination of President Caceres
records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch in The Birmingham Age-Herald reviews the assassination of President Caceres in Santo Domingo and reports apprehension among officials that "Dominica" may enter another troubled chapter in her history. The report recalls that Caceres began his political ascent by killing the dictator Heureux in 1899, an act he claimed was in self-defense, paving the way for General Jiminez to assume the presidency. Caceres served as minister of war under Jiminez, became vice president under Morales, and succeeded Morales as president in December 1905. War Department officials note that this marks the first serious political disturbance in Santo Domingo in four years, a peaceful interval that Secretary Stimson attributes to United States supervision over the island.

La crónica recuerda que Cáceres inició su ascenso político al matar al dictador Heureux en 1899, hecho que afirmó haber ejecutado en defensa propia, abriendo el camino para que el general Jiminez asumiera la presidencia. Cáceres se desempeñó como ministro de guerra bajo Jiminez, pasó a ser vicepresidente con Morales y sucedió a Morales como presidente en diciembre de 1905. Funcionarios del Departamento de Guerra destacan que este acontecimiento representa el primer trastorno político grave en Santo Domingo en cuatro años, intervalo pacífico que el secretario Stimson atribuye a la supervisión ejercida por los Estados Unidos sobre la isla.

records.summary_en: The Birmingham Age-Herald recounts the political succession following President Morales's flight from the country after clashing with his own party and cabinet, which led the ministry to install Caceres in the presidency in December 1903. The account notes that two years later an arrangement was established between the Dominican Republic and the United States appointing an American receiver general of customs for San Domingo. Under this administrative convention, the country's public debt continues to be discharged.

El relato señala que dos años más tarde se concertó un arreglo entre la República Dominicana y los Estados Unidos mediante el cual se designó a un receptor general de aduanas estadounidense para Santo Domingo. Conforme a esta convención administrativa, la deuda pública del país continúa amortizándose.

records.headline: A Washington dispatch in The Sun reports that Francis M. Endicott
records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch in The Sun reports that Francis M. Endicott, Chargé d'Affaires of the American Legation, informed the State Department of the assassination of President Caceres of Santo Domingo, adding that the capital remained quiet without disorder. W. E. Pulliam, General Receiver of Customs, notified the War Department that the attackers were political malcontents and indicated there was no general uprising, with officials attributing the killing to a personal feud. The tragedy represents the first serious disruption in Santo Domingo since the establishment of the United States customs receivership about six years ago. American Minister W. W. Russell plans to cut short his Washington leave to return to his post, the gunboat Wheeling may be dispatched, and the report notes that Caceres, inaugurated on July 1, 1908, had previously killed President Heureaux in revenge for his father's death.

W. E. Pulliam, receptor general de aduanas, notificó al Departamento de Guerra que los agresores eran descontentos políticos e indicó que no había un levantamiento general, atribuyendo los funcionarios el hecho a una disputa personal. La tragedia constituye el primer quebranto grave en Santo Domingo desde el establecimiento de la receptoría de aduanas de los Estados Unidos hace unos seis años. El ministro estadounidense W. W. records.headline: State Department advices reported in The Montgomery Advertiser describe
records.summary_en: State Department advices reported in The Montgomery Advertiser describe the fatal attack on President Caceres outside the American Legation in Santo Domingo City. The opening shots by assailants named as Luis Tejera and Jaime Mote, Jr. were ineffective, but they pursued the wounded president into an adjoining stable and fired again before friends carried him into the legation, where he died at 5:30 o'clock. The attackers fled toward San Cristobal, while Chargé d'Affaires Endicott reported the capital was quiet and patrolled by guards. United States Minister Russell is leaving for Havana to cross Cuba to Guantanamo, where he will board a commercial steamer or an American naval gunboat to reach Santo Domingo.

Los atacantes huyeron con rumbo a San Cristóbal, mientras que el encargado de negocios Endicott informó que la capital permanecía en calma y patrullada por guardias. El ministro estadounidense Russell parte hacia La Habana para cruzar Cuba rumbo a Guantánamo, donde abordará un vapor comercial o un cañonero naval de los Estados Unidos con destino a Santo Domingo.

records.headline: No serious disorders have occurred in the Dominican capital
records.summary_en: No serious disorders have occurred in the Dominican capital, amid intense excitement over the assassination of President Ramon Caceres, a Puerto Plata dispatch published in the Evening Star reports. Caceres was riding along a boulevard when his party was ambushed by gunfire from a side street by a group led by General Luis Tejera, former governor of Santo Domingo City; Caceres fell at the first volley, and Tejera was immediately shot and killed by the president's chief of staff. The cabinet has temporarily assumed executive authority and plans to convene the electoral college at once to choose a successor, with business communities expecting the government party to unite behind former leader General Horacio Vasquez. Dominicans of all political factions share the conviction that the United States will not permit a civil war in the country.
records.summary_es: No se han registrado desórdenes de consideración en la capital dominicana, en medio de la viva agitación por el asesinato del presidente Ramón Cáceres, según un despacho de Puerto Plata publicado en el Evening Star. Cáceres se desplazaba por un bulevar cuando su comitiva fue emboscada desde una calle lateral a tiros por un grupo encabezado por el general Luis Tejera, antiguo gobernador de la ciudad de Santo Domingo; Cáceres cayó en la primera descarga y Tejera fue muerto a tiros en el acto por el jefe de Estado Mayor del mandatario. El gabinete asumió provisionalmente el poder ejecutivo y prevé convocar de inmediato al colegio electoral para elegir un sucesor, previendo los círculos comerciales que el partido gubernamental se cohesionará en torno al general Horacio Vásquez, antiguo jefe de dicha agrupación. Dominicanos de todas las corrientes políticas coinciden en la convicción de que los Estados Unidos no tolerarán una guerra civil en el país.

records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch in The Daily Missoulian reports that President Caceres died at 5:30 o'clock in the American Legation at Santo Domingo half an hour after an attack by Luis Tejera and Jaime Mote, Jr. The initial shots failed, but the assassins pursued the wounded leader into an adjoining stable and fired again before fleeing to San Cristobal, while Chargé d'Affaires Endicott reported the city quiet under guard patrols. American Minister Russell is traveling immediately via Cuba and Guantanamo to reach the Dominican capital. Washington officials recall that Caceres previously shot dictator Hereaux in 1899 in alleged self-defense, warning that Hereaux's relatives long sought vengeance and that rival politicians may exploit the current crisis.

records.headline: A Washington dispatch in the Rock Island Argus reports that President Ramon Caceres of Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch in the Rock Island Argus reports that President Ramon Caceres of Santo Domingo was murdered by malcontents on Sunday, ending a political career that began with an assassination. The dispatch recalls that in 1899 Caceres killed President Hereux, who had executed his father, an act that enabled General Jimenez to assume the presidency. Later, under President Morales, Caceres served as minister of war and suppressed a rebellion launched by the deposed Jimenez. When Morales subsequently clashed with his party and fled the Dominican Republic, the cabinet installed Caceres as president, initiating an administration that lasted four years.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Washington en el Rock Island Argus informa que el presidente Ramón Cáceres de Santo Domingo fue asesinado el domingo por descontentos, poniendo fin a una carrera política iniciada con un magnicidio. La crónica recuerda que en 1899 Cáceres mató al presidente Hereux (según figura impreso), quien había ejecutado a su padre, acontecimiento que facilitó la llegada del general Jiménez a la presidencia. Más tarde, bajo el mandato del presidente Morales, Cáceres se desempeñó como ministro de guerra y sofocó una rebelión promovida por el derrocado Jiménez. Cuando posteriormente Morales se enemistó con su partido y huyó de la República Dominicana, el gabinete instaló a Cáceres como presidente, comenzando una administración que se extendió por cuatro años.

Officials recalled Caceres's rise through cabinet and vice-presidential posts to the presidency in 1905, expressing concern that rival politicians might seize on his death to provoke unrest. records.headline: A special dispatch in The Nome Daily Nugget reports that President Roman Caceres of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: A special dispatch in The Nome Daily Nugget reports that President Roman Caceres of the Dominican Republic was assassinated by political malcontents while returning from a carriage drive, with those accompanying him also killed outright when his carriage was fired upon from ambush. An editorial note adds that the republic, occupying the eastern and larger part of the island of Haiti or Santo Domingo, has an estimated population of about half a million. The paper observes that the slain president was a former general who helped overthrow the government several years earlier and had ruled the republic very ably for nearly six years.
records.summary_es: Un despacho especial en The Nome Daily Nugget informa que el presidente Román Cáceres de la República Dominicana fue asesinado por descontentos políticos mientras regresaba de un paseo en carruaje, muriendo también en el acto quienes lo acompañaban cuando su carruaje fue tiroteado desde una emboscada. Una nota editorial agrega que la república, que ocupa la parte oriental y más grande de la isla de Haití o Santo Domingo, tiene una población estimada de cerca de medio millón de habitantes. El periódico señala que el presidente asesinado era un antiguo general que ayudó a derrocar al gobierno varios años antes y había gobernado la república con gran habilidad durante casi seis años.

records.headline: President Caceres of the Dominican Republic was assassinated
records.summary_en: President Caceres of the Dominican Republic was assassinated yesterday afternoon after leaving the house of an acquaintance in Santo Domingo City, a Washington dispatch to the Daily Kennebec Journal reports. After assailants Luis Tejera and Jaime Mote, Jr. pursued the wounded president into a stable adjoining the American legation, friends carried him into the legation, where he died at 5:30 o'clock, while the assassins fled to San Cristobal. Chargé Endicott reported the city quiet under guard patrols, and Minister Russell prepared to depart from Washington via Cuba for Santo Domingo. Washington officials also recalled that Caceres had killed dictator Heureaux in 1899, raising the possibility of a family vendetta.
records.summary_es: El presidente Cáceres de la República Dominicana fue asesinado ayer por la tarde tras salir de la casa de un conocido en la ciudad de Santo Domingo, según un despacho de Washington para el Daily Kennebec Journal. Después de que los agresores Luis Tejera y Jaime Mote, Jr. persiguieran al presidente herido hasta un establo contiguo a la legación estadounidense, varios amigos lo trasladaron a la legación, donde falleció a las 5:30, mientras los asesinos huían a San Cristóbal. El encargado de negocios Endicott informó que la ciudad se encontraba tranquila bajo patrullas de guardia, y el ministro Russell se disponía a partir desde Washington vía Cuba hacia Santo Domingo. Funcionarios en Washington recordaron asimismo que Cáceres había dado muerte al dictador Heureaux en 1899, planteando la posibilidad de una venganza familiar.

records.headline: A Washington report in the Keowee Courier recounts the death of President Caceres
records.summary_en: A Washington report in the Keowee Courier recounts the death of President Caceres in the American legation after being shot in an adjoining stable, warning under the subhead "May Cause Trouble" that ambitious politicians could exploit the crisis. The dispatch observes that the conditions lead to fears that "Dominica" is entering another troubled chapter in its history, even though War Department officials noted this was the first serious disturbance in Santo Domingo in four years, compared to an earlier average of at least one revolution per annum. Secretary of War Stimson attributed that four-year stability directly to the United States assuming collection of Dominican customs and creating sound financial conditions.

El despacho señala el temor de que «Dominica» entre en otro capítulo turbulento de su historia, a pesar de que funcionarios del Departamento de Guerra indicaron que este era el primer disturbio grave en Santo Domingo en cuatro años, frente al promedio anterior de al menos una revolución por año. El secretario de Guerra Stimson atribuyó esa estabilidad de cuatro años directamente a que Estados Unidos asumió la recaudación de las aduanas dominicanas y estableció condiciones financieras sólidas.

records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch in the New-York Tribune reports that the United States minister to the Dominican Republic, W. W. Russell, left Washington for Hampton Roads to board one of two armored cruisers, the North Carolina and the Washington, sent to Santo Domingo. Although the State Department reported no evidence of revolt, the cruisers were dispatched as a precautionary measure following the assassination of the Dominican president. The paper notes that Navy Department wireless achieved a speed record in relaying sailing orders to the warships while they were at sea with the Atlantic fleet en route to Norfolk.

records.summary_en: A report in The Nome Daily Nugget states that the United States cabinet decided to dispatch the cruisers Washington and North Carolina to Santo Domingo to protect American lives and property following the assassination of President Caceres. The paper reviews earlier American involvement in the republic, asserting that foreign powers look to the United States as a guarantor of Dominican debts. It recalls Minister Powell's intervention over the Improvement company claims, which led to an arrangement dividing customs revenues between foreign debt repayment and the Dominican government.

El periódico repasa la intervención previa de Estados Unidos en la república, afirmando que las potencias extranjeras consideran a Estados Unidos garante de las deudas dominicanas. Recuerda la intervención del ministro Powell sobre las reclamaciones de la compañía Improvement, que condujo a un acuerdo que dividió los ingresos aduaneros entre el pago de la deuda externa y el gobierno dominicano.

records.headline: The Washington Times reports that United States Minister Russell
records.summary_en: The Washington Times reports that United States Minister Russell, currently on leave in the United States, will return immediately to his post in Santo Domingo aboard the cruiser Washington rather than the cruiser Wheeling as originally planned. Accompanied by the cruiser North Carolina, the warship is departing Hampton Roads following cabinet discussions prompted by the assassination of President Caceres. Both the Secretary of State and the Secretary of the Navy deemed the deployment prudent to safeguard American interests in the event of a threatened uprising.
records.summary_es: The Washington Times informa que el ministro de Estados Unidos Russell, actualmente de licencia en Estados Unidos, regresará de inmediato a su puesto en Santo Domingo a bordo del crucero Washington en lugar del crucero Wheeling, como se había planeado originalmente. Acompañado por el crucero North Carolina, el buque de guerra zarpa de Hampton Roads tras deliberaciones del gabinete motivadas por el asesinato del presidente Cáceres. Tanto el secretario de Estado como el secretario de la Marina consideraron prudente el despliegue para proteger los intereses estadounidenses ante la amenaza de un levantamiento.

records.headline: President Caceres died in the American legation thirty minutes
records.summary_en: President Caceres died in the American legation thirty minutes after the attack by Luis Tejera and Jaime Mote, Jr., who pursued him into an adjoining stable after their initial shots failed, a Washington dispatch in the Burlington Weekly Free Press reports. Friends carried the dying president into the legation while the assassins escaped to San Cristobal, with Chargé Endicott reporting the capital quiet and Minister Russell preparing to depart Washington for Santo Domingo. Officials in Washington recalled that Caceres had killed the former dictator Heureaux in alleged self-defense, suggesting relatives sought revenge, and warned that ambitious politicians might exploit the crisis to plunge the republic into another troubled period.
records.summary_es: El presidente Cáceres falleció en la legación estadounidense treinta minutos después del ataque de Luis Tejera y Jaime Mote, Jr., quienes lo persiguieron hasta un establo contiguo tras fallar sus primeros disparos, según un despacho de Washington en el Burlington Weekly Free Press. Amigos llevaron al presidente moribundo a la legación mientras los asesinos escapaban hacia San Cristóbal; el encargado de negocios Endicott informó que la capital permanecía tranquila y el ministro Russell se preparaba para partir de Washington hacia Santo Domingo. Funcionarios en Washington recordaron que Cáceres había matado al antiguo dictador Heureaux en supuesta defensa propia, lo que sugiere que sus parientes buscaban venganza, y advirtieron que políticos ambiciosos podrían explotar la crisis para sumir a la república en otro período turbulento.

records.headline: The Advocate reports from Santo Domingo that the Dominican cabinet
records.summary_en: The Advocate reports from Santo Domingo that the Dominican cabinet has temporarily assumed executive power and plans to convene the electoral college to elect a successor, with business interests expecting the governing party to unite behind General Horatio Vasquez. The dispatch notes that Dominicans believe the United States will not permit a revolution, and it reviews the career of General Ramon Caceres, noting that he entered public life by assassinating President Heureaux at Moca on July 28, 1899, to avenge his father. After helping General Jiminez take power and later serving as minister of war and vice president, Caceres succeeded to the presidency upon the flight of President Morales in December 1905, preceding the 1907 customs receivership convention with the United States.
records.summary_es: The Advocate informa desde Santo Domingo que el gabinete dominicano asumió temporalmente el poder ejecutivo y planea convocar al colegio electoral para elegir un sucesor, mientras los sectores comerciales esperan que el partido de gobierno se una en torno al general Horacio Vásquez. El despacho señala que los dominicanos confían en que Estados Unidos no permitirá una revolución, y repasa la trayectoria del general Ramón Cáceres, recordando que ingresó a la vida pública al asesinar al presidente Heureaux en Moca el 28 de julio de 1899 para vengar a su padre. Tras ayudar al general Jimenes a tomar el poder y luego desempeñarse como ministro de Guerra y vicepresidente, Cáceres asumió la presidencia tras la huida del presidente Morales en diciembre de 1905, antes de la convención de receptoría aduanera de 1907 con Estados Unidos.

records.summary_en: After being pursued into a stable adjoining the American legation and shot, President Caceres died, a Washington report in The Palatka News and Advertiser recounts, with his assassins fleeing to San Cristobal while Chargé Endicott reported the capital quiet under guard patrols. United States Minister Russell prepared to leave his home near Washington to travel via Havana and Guantanamo to Santo Domingo. Reviewing the slain president's past, Washington officials recalled that Caceres had killed the former dictator Heureaux in 1899, prompting fears of retaliation and concerns that "Dominica" is about to enter another troubled chapter in its history.

records.headline: The Putnam Patriot reports under the headline "Domingo's President Slain"
records.summary_en: The Putnam Patriot reports under the headline "Domingo's President Slain" that General Ramon Caceres was assassinated in Santo Domingo City upon leaving the home of Leonte Vasquez, in a Washington dispatch. Two political malcontents, Luis Tejara and Jaime Mote, Jr., fired upon the president, pursued him into a stable adjacent to the American legation, and shot him fatally, with Caceres dying in the legation about half an hour later while the gunmen escaped to San Cristobal. W. E. Pulliam, American collector of customs for the island, stated that the killers were political malcontents and affirmed that no general uprising had taken place.

Dos descontentos políticos, Luis Tejara y Jaime Mote, Jr., dispararon contra el presidente, lo persiguieron hasta un establo contiguo a la legación estadounidense y lo hirieron de muerte, falleciendo Cáceres en la legación cerca de media hora después mientras los atacantes escapaban hacia San Cristóbal. W. E. Pulliam, recaudador estadounidense de aduanas en la isla, afirmó que los agresores eran descontentos políticos y confirmó que no se había producido ningún levantamiento general.

records.headline: General Ramon Caceres, president of Santo Domingo, was assassinated
records.summary_en: General Ramon Caceres, president of Santo Domingo, was assassinated in the capital by political malcontents, The Caucasian reports, ending a four-year administration that had been unsettled by recurring revolutionary conspiracies. Last April, Caceres uncovered a plot led by former president Carlos F. Morales, former vice president Mauricio Jimenez, and General Zenon Toribo, who organized an expedition in Puerto Rico before being arrested in San Juan, acquitted of neutrality violations, and subsequently disappearing. While leaving a friend's residence, Caceres was fired upon by Luis Tejera and Jaime Mote, Jr., pursued into a stable where further shots were fired, and carried by friends to the United States legation.
records.summary_es: El general Ramón Cáceres, presidente de Santo Domingo, fue asesinado en la capital por descontentos políticos, informa The Caucasian, poniendo fin a una administración de cuatro años que se había visto perturbada por recurrentes conspiraciones revolucionarias. En abril pasado, Cáceres descubrió un complot encabezado por el expresidente Carlos F. Morales, el exvicepresidente Mauricio Jiménez y el general Zenón Toribio, quienes organizaron una expedición en Puerto Rico antes de ser arrestados en San Juan, absueltos de violar las leyes de neutralidad y desaparecer posteriormente. Al salir de la casa de un amigo, Cáceres fue atacado a tiros por Luis Tejera y Jaime Mote, Jr., perseguido hasta un establo donde recibió más disparos y trasladado por amigos a la legación de Estados Unidos.

records.headline: The life of recently murdered Dominican president Ramon Caceres
records.summary_en: The life of recently murdered Dominican president Ramon Caceres is recounted in a biographical sketch in the Bridgeton Pioneer, describing him as a six-foot-tall, 250-pound leader whose family held ancestral lands in the interior and who became president in 1900. The article traces his lifelong vendetta against President Ulises Heureaux, whom the paper characterizes as an ex-horse thief who had engineered the fatal shooting of Caceres's father, a former cabinet minister under Luperon. When conspirators gathered at the family plantation to eliminate Heureaux and lots fell upon Caceres's frail cousin Horacio Vasquez, Caceres took the assignment himself, resolving to avenge his father directly.
records.summary_es: La vida del recientemente asesinado presidente dominicano Ramón Cáceres es repasada en una semblanza biográfica en el Bridgeton Pioneer, describiéndolo como un líder de seis pies de estatura y 250 libras cuya familia poseía tierras ancestrales en el interior y quien llegó a la presidencia en 1900. El artículo rastrea su enemistad de por vida contra el presidente Ulises Heureaux, a quien el periódico describe como un antiguo ladrón de caballos que había tramado el asesinato a tiros del padre de Cáceres, exministro de gabinete bajo Luperón. Cuando los conspiradores se reunieron en la plantación familiar para eliminar a Heureaux y la suerte recayó en su frágil primo Horacio Vásquez, Cáceres tomó la misión por su cuenta, resolviendo vengar directamente a su padre.

records.headline: In an article discussing proposed customs conventions for Honduras
records.summary_en: In an article discussing proposed customs conventions for Honduras and Nicaragua modeled on the arrangement in Santo Domingo, The Sun quotes General Edwards on the accomplishments of the Dominican receivership. Edwards states that American administration has done far more than provide a tariff law and stimulate commerce, having transformed a nation plagued by continuous revolutions and worthless bonds into an orderly country able to meet its debt obligations. He reports that the Dominican Republic now collects greater domestic revenue than at any previous time, sees its bonds selling above par alongside leading Latin American nations, and offers security to incoming capital.
records.summary_es: En un artículo que analiza las convenciones aduaneras propuestas para Honduras y Nicaragua siguiendo el modelo de Santo Domingo, The Sun cita al general Edwards sobre los logros de la receptoría dominicana. Edwards afirma que la administración estadounidense ha hecho mucho más que proporcionar una ley arancelaria y estimular el comercio, habiendo transformado una nación azotada por continuas revoluciones y con bonos sin valor en un país ordenado capaz de cumplir con sus obligaciones crediticias. Informa además que la República Dominicana recauda ahora mayores ingresos internos que en cualquier período previo, logra que sus bonos se coticen por encima de la par junto a las principales naciones latinoamericanas y ofrece plena seguridad al capital entrante.

Victoria fue elegido para suceder al general Ramón Cáceres, quien fue asesinado recientemente en la capital.

The item recounts that the earliest of these tragedies took place in 1884, when Caceres's father was executed by order of President Heureaux over suspected sympathy with political dissenters.

El artículo relata que la primera de estas tragedias ocurrió en 1884, cuando el padre de Cáceres fue ejecutado por orden del presidente Heureaux debido a su supuesta simpatía con opositores políticos.

records.headline: Ramon Caceres's subsequent political career in Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: Ramon Caceres's subsequent political career in Santo Domingo and his early ties to the United States are described in a continuing biographical sketch in The Virginia Enterprise. After studying at the Polytechnic Institute in Troy, New York, where he married Lillian, the adopted daughter of Mr. and Mrs. James Hakes, his wife converted her inherited property into cash and accompanied him to the island. Caceres entered national politics by assassinating President Heureaux on July 28, 1899, to avenge his father, facilitating General Jimenez's ascent to the presidency before himself becoming vice president under Morales and ultimately assuming the presidency when Morales fled in 1905.
records.summary_es: La posterior carrera política de Ramón Cáceres en Santo Domingo y sus vínculos iniciales con Estados Unidos son descritos en una semblanza biográfica de continuación en The Virginia Enterprise. Cáceres incursionó en la política nacional al asesinar al presidente Heureaux el 28 de julio de 1899 para vengar a su padre, facilitando el ascenso del general Jimenes a la presidencia antes de convertirse él mismo en vicepresidente bajo Morales y asumir finalmente la presidencia cuando Morales huyó en 1905.

records.summary_en: A Washington report in The Washington Herald states that Dominican government troops have been dispatched to the northern shore to check the advance of former President Morales, who reportedly landed with a few followers. The dispatch adds that the Dominican government is taking strong measures to check the movement.

records.headline: A Washington dispatch to The Sun reports that the American minister
records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch to The Sun reports that the American minister at San Domingo city informed the State Department of a fresh revolutionary movement against the Dominican government. Zenon Torribio, the only uncaptured or unkilled follower of Morales, is leading an expedition organizing in Haitian territory to cross the border near Dajabon. Strong measures are reportedly being taken by the Dominican government to oppose the movement, which is characterized as the latest sequel to the assassination of President Caceres on November 19.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Washington en The Sun informa que el ministro estadounidense en la ciudad de Santo Domingo comunicó al Departamento de Estado sobre un nuevo movimiento revolucionario contra el gobierno dominicano. Zenón Torribio, el único partidario de Morales que no ha sido capturado o muerto, encabeza una expedición que se organiza en territorio haitiano para cruzar la frontera cerca de Dajabón. Según los informes, el gobierno dominicano adopta enérgicas medidas para combatir el movimiento, calificado como la secuela más reciente del asesinato del presidente Cáceres el 19 de noviembre.

records.headline: An account from the Listin, reprinted in The St. Croix Avis
records.summary_en: An account from the Listin, reprinted in The St. Croix Avis, describes the assassination of General Ramon Caceres, President of the Dominican Republic, on Sunday the 19th between 5:30 and 7:00 p.m. While traveling on the road to Haina about three or four kilometers from the city, Caceres was ambushed by a group of armed youths led by General Luis Tejera, suffering almost instantaneous death from revolver and carbine shots. Statements by his military staff chief, Major Ramon A. Perez, and his coachman indicate that the president had taken his customary carriage drive along the western road and was returning past Guibia when an automobile and coach blocked his path outside Pedro Marin's ranch.
records.summary_es: Un relato del Listín, reproducido en el St. Croix Avis, describe el asesinato del general Ramón Cáceres, presidente de la República Dominicana, ocurrido el domingo 19 entre las 5:30 y las 7:00 p. m. Mientras transitaba por el camino hacia Haina a unos tres o cuatro kilómetros de la ciudad, Cáceres fue emboscado por un grupo de jóvenes armados liderados por el general Luis Tejera, sufriendo una muerte casi instantánea por disparos de revólver y carabina. Las declaraciones del jefe de su Estado Mayor militar, el mayor Ramón A. Pérez, y de su cochero indican que el presidente realizaba su acostumbrado paseo en carruaje por el camino del oeste y regresaba pasando por Güibia cuando un automóvil y un carruaje le cerraron el paso frente a la quinta de Pedro Marín.

records.headline: A biographical sketch in The Madison Daily Leader recounts the rise
records.summary_en: A biographical sketch in The Madison Daily Leader recounts the rise and vengeance of Ramon Caceres, the recently murdered president of the Dominican Republic, portraying him as a six-foot-tall figure weighing at least 250 pounds who assumed the presidency in 1900. His father, a cabinet minister under Luperon, had been shot dead on his veranda by order of Ulises Heureaux, then an ambitious general. Conspirators later met on the Caceres plantation to plot Heureaux's assassination by drawing lots; after an initial soldier hesitated and was executed by Heureaux, the second selection fell to Ramon's frail cousin Horacio Vasquez, prompting Ramon to seize the paper and vow to kill Heureaux himself.
records.summary_es: Una reseña biográfica en The Madison Daily Leader relata el ascenso y la venganza de Ramón Cáceres, el recientemente asesinado presidente de la República Dominicana, describiéndolo como una figura de seis pies de estatura y al menos 250 libras de peso que asumió la presidencia en 1900. Su padre, ministro del gabinete bajo Luperón, había muerto baleado en su galería por orden de Ulises Heureaux, entonces un ambicioso general. Más tarde, los conspiradores se reunieron en la hacienda de Cáceres para tramar el asesinato de Heureaux echando suertes; tras vacilar un primer soldado que fue ejecutado por Heureaux, la segunda elección recayó en Horacio Vásquez, el frágil primo de Ramón, lo que motivó a este a arrebatar el papel y jurar que mataría a Heureaux él mismo.

records.summary_en: The recently murdered Dominican president, Ramon Caceres, is profiled in The Madison Daily Leader, describing him as a six-foot-tall man weighing at least 250 pounds who became president in 1900. During the administration of Luperon, his father served as a cabinet minister before being shot dead on his veranda by order of Ulises Heureaux, then an ambitious rising general. Conspirators subsequently assembled on the Caceres plantation to plan Heureaux's assassination by drawing lots; when a soldier hesitated at the crisis, Heureaux detected his expression and killed him, after which the next lot fell upon Ramon's cousin Horacio Vasquez.

Durante la administración de Luperón, su padre ejerció como ministro del gabinete antes de morir baleado en su galería por orden de Ulises Heureaux, entonces un ambicioso general en ascenso. records.headline: The revolt in the Republic of Santo Domingo is spreading rapidly
records.summary_en: The revolt in the Republic of Santo Domingo is spreading rapidly, with insurgents cutting all overland telegraph lines, a special cable from Cape Haitien to The New York Herald reports. General Desiderio Arias, leader of the rebellion, has issued a manifesto from Monte Christi calling upon his countrymen to join his forces, while General Zenon Toribio is engaged in fierce combat along the Haitian border. Presidential candidate Horacio Vasquez, residing in exile in St. Thomas, has reportedly reached an agreement with former Finance Minister Federico Velasquez to ensure a peaceful presidential election, with Vasquez slated for nomination once hostilities end.
records.summary_es: La revuelta en la República de Santo Domingo se extiende con rapidez, habiendo cortado los insurgentes todas las líneas telegráficas terrestres, según un cable especial desde Cabo Haitiano para The New York Herald. El general Desiderio Arias, jefe de la rebelión, emitió un manifiesto desde Monte Cristi convocando a sus compatriotas a sumarse a sus fuerzas, mientras el general Zenón Toribio sostiene intensos combates en la frontera haitiana. El candidato presidencial Horacio Vásquez, exiliado en Santo Tomás, habría llegado a un entendimiento con el exministro de Hacienda Federico Velásquez para asegurar unas elecciones presidenciales pacíficas, previéndose la postulación de Vásquez una vez concluyan las hostilidades.

records.summary_en: The wife of Ramon Caceres converted the estate left by her parents into cash and accompanied her husband to Santo Domingo, the Lincoln County Leader recounts under the heading 'Late Dominican President.' Caceres's political career began when he avenged his father's death by assassinating President Heureaux on July 28, 1899, an act that paved the way for General Jimenez to secure the presidency. Caceres subsequently served as vice-president under President Morales and was installed in the presidency in 1905 after Morales fled the country.

La carrera política de Cáceres comenzó cuando vengó la muerte de su padre asesinando al presidente Heureaux el 28 de julio de 1899, acción que allanó el camino para que el general Jiménez alcanzara la presidencia. Posteriormente, Cáceres ejerció como vicepresidente bajo el presidente Morales y asumió la presidencia en 1905 luego de que Morales huyera del país.

records.headline: A retrospective in the Lincoln County Leader reports that the assassination of President Ramon Caceres of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: A retrospective in the Lincoln County Leader reports that the assassination of President Ramon Caceres of the Dominican Republic by political malcontents in San Domingo city forms the climax to a series of political tragedies. The first of these tragedies occurred in 1884, when Caceres's father was executed by order of President Heureaux because of alleged sympathies with political dissenters. As a boy of ten, Caceres vowed vengeance and later utilized his inheritance to travel to the United States, graduating from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in Troy, New York, and marrying Lillian, the adopted daughter of Mr. and Mrs. James Hakes.

La primera de estas tragedias ocurrió en 1884, cuando el padre de Cáceres fue ejecutado por orden del presidente Heureaux debido a supuestas simpatías con disidentes políticos. Siendo un niño de diez años, Cáceres juró venganza y posteriormente empleó su herencia para viajar a los Estados Unidos, graduándose en el Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute en Troy, Nueva York, y casándose con Lillian, hija adoptiva de los señores James Hakes.

records.headline: In a letter to the editor of The Sun written from Brooklyn
records.summary_en: In a letter to the editor of The Sun written from Brooklyn, a Dominican correspondent explains the distinctions between the two republics sharing the island of Santo Domingo. The writer emphasizes that only Spanish is spoken in the Dominican Republic, settled by Spanish people with some proportion of colored inhabitants, whereas Haiti is populated by descendants of French slaves and speaks Creole French. The author maintains that Dominican society assesses individuals by their moral character rather than skin color, asserting that the proportion of colored residents is no greater than in Cuba, which no observer characterizes as a black republic.
records.summary_es: En una carta al director de The Sun escrita desde Brooklyn, un corresponsal dominicano explica las distinciones entre las dos repúblicas que comparten la isla de Santo Domingo. El autor destaca que solo se habla español en la República Dominicana, colonizada por españoles con cierta proporción de habitantes de color, mientras que Haití está poblada por descendientes de esclavos franceses y habla francés criollo. El autor sostiene que la sociedad dominicana evalúa a los individuos por su solvencia moral y no por el color de su piel, afirmando que la proporción de residentes de color no es mayor que en Cuba, a la que ningún observador califica como república negra.

records.headline: A Santo Domingo dispatch in the Evening Star reports that Secretary of State Knox arrived
records.summary_en: A Santo Domingo dispatch in the Evening Star reports that Secretary of State Knox arrived aboard the cruiser Washington from Venezuela, touring public buildings, ruins, and Spanish forts before attending an official reception. At the presidential palace, President Eladio Victoria made a rare public appearance to receive Knox, who delivered a formal address praising the Dominican Republic as an inspiring example in the struggle for republicanism. Knox affirmed that Dominicans could testify to the unselfish willingness of the United States to assist nations striving for stability and order, stressing that the Monroe Doctrine and the Panama Canal demand close cooperation among all benefiting nations.
records.summary_es: Un despacho desde Santo Domingo en el Evening Star informa que el secretario de Estado Knox llegó a bordo del crucero Washington procedente de Venezuela, recorriendo edificios públicos, ruinas y fuertes españoles antes de asistir a una recepción oficial. En el palacio presidencial, el presidente Eladio Victoria hizo una inusual aparición pública para recibir a Knox, quien pronunció un discurso formal elogiando a la República Dominicana como un ejemplo inspirador en la lucha por el republicanismo. Knox afirmó que los dominicanos pueden dar testimonio de la desinteresada disposición de los Estados Unidos a ayudar a las naciones que procuran la estabilidad y el orden, subrayando que la Doctrina Monroe y el Canal de Panamá exigen una estrecha cooperación entre todas las naciones beneficiarias.

records.headline: The diplomatic tour of Secretary of State Knox brought him to a reception
records.summary_en: The diplomatic tour of Secretary of State Knox brought him to a reception in Santo Domingo, after arriving from Venezuela aboard the cruiser Washington and inspecting historical sites, The Salt Lake Tribune reports. Addressing a gathering at the presidential palace, Knox commended the Dominican Republic as a bright example in the struggle for republicanism that had attracted American assistance, asserting that Dominicans could attest to the unselfish spirit guiding United States policy toward nations seeking stability. Knox emphasized that American responsibilities regarding the Monroe Doctrine and the Panama Canal require close coordination, urging regional governments to be cooperative and unobstructive, after which President Eladio Victoria delivered a cordial welcoming address.
records.summary_es: La gira diplomática del secretario de Estado Knox lo llevó a una recepción en Santo Domingo, tras llegar desde Venezuela a bordo del crucero Washington e inspeccionar lugares históricos, según informa The Salt Lake Tribune. Al dirigirse a los congregados en el palacio presidencial, Knox elogió a la República Dominicana como un brillante ejemplo en la lucha por el republicanismo que había atraído la ayuda estadounidense, asegurando que los dominicanos podían atestiguar el espíritu desinteresado que guía la política de los Estados Unidos hacia las naciones que buscan la estabilidad. Knox recalcó que las responsabilidades estadounidenses respecto a la Doctrina Monroe y al Canal de Panamá demandan una estrecha coordinación, instando a los gobiernos regionales a ser cooperativos y facilitadores, tras lo cual el presidente Eladio Victoria pronunció un cordial discurso de bienvenida.

records.summary_en: A handful of revolutionists along the northwestern border are the exception to the peace reigning throughout the Dominican Republic, The Montgomery Advertiser reports under a Puerto Plata dateline. These insurgents, reportedly including the assassins of the late President Caceres, frequently harass Dominican government forces before retreating across the frontier into Haiti. Several captured rebels were allegedly found in possession of arms and ammunition belonging to government troops, and former provisional President Horacio Vasquez is stated to be leading the uprising.
records.summary_es: Un puñado de revolucionarios a lo largo de la frontera noroccidental es la excepción a la paz que reina en toda la República Dominicana, según informa The Montgomery Advertiser bajo una fecha de Puerto Plata. Estos insurgentes, entre los que supuestamente figuran los asesinos del difunto presidente Cáceres, hostigan con frecuencia a las fuerzas gubernamentales dominicanas antes de replegarse al otro lado de la frontera hacia Haití. Se afirma que varios rebeldes capturados se encontraban en posesión de armas y municiones pertenecientes a las tropas gubernamentales, y se señala al expresidente provisional Horacio Vásquez al frente de la sublevación.

records.headline: Eight millions of dollars of five per cent bonds issued by the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Eight millions of dollars of five per cent bonds issued by the Dominican Republic were guaranteed by the United States, to prevent conflicts under the Monroe Doctrine, an article in The Canon City Record explains; the United States also assumed supervision of island customs collections. Mr. Dye, the former chief of the Philippine constabulary appointed American collector of customs in Santo Domingo, observes that island revenues are increasing slowly, estimating that a generation will elapse before the United States reimburses itself for the funds guaranteed to European bondholders. The article remarks that 'Dominica' is the only government in the Western Hemisphere administered by the colored race.
records.summary_es: Ocho millones de dólares en bonos al cinco por ciento emitidos por la República Dominicana fueron garantizados por los Estados Unidos, para prevenir conflictos derivados de la Doctrina Monroe, explica un artículo en The Canon City Record; los Estados Unidos asumieron también la supervisión de la recaudación aduanera en la isla. El señor Dye, exjefe de la policía de Filipinas nombrado interventor de aduanas de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo, señala que las rentas de la isla aumentan con lentitud y calcula que transcurrirá una generación antes de que los Estados Unidos recuperen los fondos garantizados a los tenedores de bonos europeos. El artículo comenta asimismo que «Dominica» es el único gobierno del hemisferio occidental administrado por la raza de color.

records.headline: Writing from Santo Domingo, the Rock Island Argus reports that Secretary Knox's visit
records.summary_en: Writing from Santo Domingo, the Rock Island Argus reports that Secretary Knox's visit highlighted American efforts to stabilize a struggling republic through customs control. The dispatch states that American financial administration has yielded substantial benefits, enabling the Dominican Republic to service its loan from New York bankers and steadily discharge foreign obligations originally estimated at forty million dollars. Even after deducting 55 per cent of customs receipts for debt liquidation and interest, the republic is receiving greater revenues than under previous regimes, financing improvements such as a seventeen-mile boulevard extending west from the capital.
records.summary_es: Escribiendo desde Santo Domingo, el Rock Island Argus señala que la visita del secretario Knox puso de relieve los esfuerzos estadounidenses por estabilizar a una república en dificultades mediante el control de sus aduanas. El despacho afirma que la administración financiera estadounidense ha producido considerables beneficios, permitiendo a la República Dominicana atender su préstamo con banqueros de Nueva York y saldar gradualmente obligaciones externas calculadas en un principio en cuarenta millones de dólares. Incluso después de deducir el 55 por ciento de los ingresos aduaneros para la liquidación de la deuda y sus intereses, la república percibe mayores rentas que bajo regímenes anteriores, costeando mejoras como un bulevar de diecisiete millas que se extiende al oeste de la capital.

records.headline: A report in the Rock Island Argus observes that physical improvements
records.summary_en: A report in the Rock Island Argus observes that physical improvements in Santo Domingo, including a rebuilt government palace and a new boulevard that spurred the introduction of some thirty-five automobiles, contrast with growing political instability. Visitors to the Dominican Republic report that fresh unrest is brewing, with President Victoria widely viewed as unpopular and his government admitted to be weak. The article notes that following the assassination of President Caceres, Alfredo Victoria assumed control of public affairs at the age of 27 while serving as commander of the army.

Visitantes a la República Dominicana informan que se gestan nuevos disturbios, considerándose ampliamente impopular al presidente Victoria y reconociéndose la debilidad de su administración. El artículo señala que tras el asesinato del presidente Cáceres, Alfredo Victoria asumió el control de los asuntos públicos a la edad de 27 años mientras se desempeñaba como comandante del ejército.

records.summary_en: In remarks reported by the El Paso Herald, Mr. Knox cites the assistance lent by the United States to Santo Domingo in her struggle to extricate herself from foreign debt and political instability. As an illustration of the commercial difference between an indebted country and one made financially sound, he states that Dominican foreign commerce has trebled since that assistance was initiated less than a decade ago. In 190S, the year before the United States extended its aid, total foreign commerce stood at about $6,000,000, whereas by 1911 that figure had jumped to 1 8,000, 8t.
