records.summary_en: The American Falls Press reports that United States officials had hoped the arrangement recently concluded by the special American commission would preserve order for two years until a new election could be held. However, the hurried Thursday night dispatch of the battleship New Hampshire indicates that authorities interpret meager advices from the Dominican Republic as demanding immediate action. Commanded by Captain James H. Oliver, the New Hampshire carries about 900 men, including a company of marines. Pending the battleship's arrival at San Domingo City, American interests are being safeguarded by four gunboats: the Wheeling and Petrel in the capital's harbor, the Nashville at Monte Christi, and the Yankton at Puerto Plata.

Sin embargo, el urgente envío del acorazado New Hampshire en la noche del jueves indica que las autoridades consideran que las escasas noticias procedentes de la República Dominicana exigen una acción inmediata. Al mando del capitán James H. Oliver, el New Hampshire lleva unos 900 hombres, incluida una compañía de infantes de marina. En espera de la llegada del acorazado a la ciudad de Santo Domingo, cuatro cañoneros custodian los intereses estadounidenses: el Wheeling y el Petrel en el puerto de la capital, el Nashville en Monte Cristi y el Yankton en Puerto Plata.

records.summary_en: An architectural note on the west facade of the cathedral of Santo Domingo in the Dominican Republic is published by The Washburn Times under the headline "Columbus' Bones Found Here," where Father Billini discovered the veritable remains of Christopher Columbus in 1877. The item identifies the structure as the first cathedral erected in America, noting that construction began in 1514 and that its early designation was "de los Indios." It adds that the first mass in the New World was celebrated on January 6, 1494, at Isabela on the northern coast of the island.

records.headline: Comment on former Venezuelan president Cipriano Castro's deportation
records.summary_en: Comment on former Venezuelan president Cipriano Castro's deportation appears in The Commoner, which quotes a writer in the New York Weekly People who recalls the legal precedent established when deposed Dominican president General Baez arrived in New York about thirty-odd years ago. Upon landing, Baez was immediately sued for damages by an American citizen who claimed he was outraged in Santo Domingo by the general during his presidency. Represented by William M. Evarts, Baez prevailed on the argument that an official's public acts are reviewable solely by the courts of his own country under its constitution, leaving foreign tribunals without jurisdiction. The court dismissed the suit against ex-President Baez, a ruling the writer invokes to dispute the legal basis for barring and deporting Castro.
records.summary_es: El comentario sobre la deportación del expresidente venezolano Cipriano Castro aparece en The Commoner, que cita a un redactor del Weekly People de Nueva York, quien evoca el precedente jurídico sentado cuando el depuesto presidente dominicano, el general Báez, arribó a Nueva York hace unos treinta y tantos años. Nada más desembarcar, Báez fue demandado por daños y perjuicios por un ciudadano estadounidense que alegó haber sufrido agravios en Santo Domingo a manos del general durante su presidencia. Defendido por William M. Evarts, Báez triunfó con el argumento de que los actos oficiales de un gobernante solo competen a los tribunales de su propio país con arreglo a su constitución, careciendo de jurisdicción las cortes extranjeras. El tribunal desestimó la demanda contra el expresidente Báez, fallo que el articulista esgrime para impugnar los fundamentos jurídicos de la exclusión y deportación de Castro.

records.headline: An article in the Atlanta Georgian recounts a diplomatic controversy
records.summary_en: An article in the Atlanta Georgian recounts a diplomatic controversy caused by a postage stamp issued by the Dominican Republic in 1900 displaying a map of the island. In an effort to emphasize the republic's international prominence through the stamp design, Dominican authorities overstepped the boundary line and appeared to annex a substantial portion of Haitian territory. The Haitian government considered the depiction a serious affront, lodging energetic diplomatic protests against the objectionable labels and reportedly mobilizing troops along the Dominican frontier until the issuing authorities made amends.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en el Atlanta Georgian relata la controversia diplomática originada por un sello postal emitido por la República Dominicana en 1900 que exhibía un mapa de la isla. Con el propósito de destacar la relevancia internacional de la república mediante dicho diseño, las autoridades dominicanas sobrepasaron la línea fronteriza y parecieron anexar una porción considerable de territorio haitiano. El gobierno de Haití consideró la estampa como una grave afrenta, elevando enérgicas protestas diplomáticas contra los objetables sellos y, según se afirmó, movilizando tropas en la frontera dominicana hasta que los emisores presentaron las debidas satisfacciones.

records.headline: All pending disputes between former rebel leader Desidario Arias
records.summary_en: All pending disputes between former rebel leader Desidario Arias and Archbishop Nouel, provisional president of the Dominican Republic, have been settled, the Evening Star reports under the headline "Peace in Santo Domingo," re-establishing permanent peace. The accord was reported to the Navy Department by Commander Long of the warship Des Moines at Monte Christi. The report notes that the prelate, acting in his presidential capacity, had previously pacified other rebel leaders while visiting several ports aboard the American vessel.
records.summary_es: Todas las diferencias pendientes entre el antiguo jefe rebelde Desidario Arias y el arzobispo Nouel, presidente provisional de la República Dominicana, han quedado resueltas, según informa el Evening Star bajo el titular "Peace in Santo Domingo", restableciéndose la paz permanente. El acuerdo fue comunicado al Departamento de la Marina por el comandante Long, del buque de guerra Des Moines, desde Monte Cristi. La crónica añade que el prelado, en el ejercicio de sus funciones presidenciales, ya había pacificado con anterioridad a otros líderes rebeldes al visitar varios puertos a bordo de la nave estadounidense.

records.headline: On the anniversary of Dominican independence, The Bridgeport Evening Farmer observes
records.summary_en: On the anniversary of Dominican independence, The Bridgeport Evening Farmer observes that the support given to the press reflects a people's advancement, asserting that Dominica is far ahead of Haiti in this regard. Although Dominica's population is little more than a third that of its neighbor, the paper reports that Dominica sustains thirty-one newspapers and periodicals—including six dailies and two Santo Domingo evening papers with a combined circulation of 12,000—while Haiti has only five publications and a daily circulation under 7,000 in Port-au-Prince. The article reviews the Dominican Republic's historical separation from Haiti beginning February 27, 1844, and its subsequent status as a Spanish possession from 1861 to 1863, noting that the semi-centenary of the restoration of the republic in 1863 will be celebrated the following August.
records.summary_es: Con motivo del aniversario de la independencia dominicana, The Bridgeport Evening Farmer observa que el respaldo brindado a la prensa refleja el progreso de un pueblo, aseverando que Dominica aventaja con creces a Haití en este aspecto. Aunque la población de Dominica apenas supera un tercio de la de su vecina, el diario reporta que Dominica sostiene treinta y un periódicos y revistas —incluidos seis diarios y dos vespertinos de Santo Domingo con una circulación conjunta de 12.000 ejemplares—, frente a solo cinco publicaciones en Haití y una circulación diaria inferior a 7.000 ejemplares en Puerto Príncipe. El artículo reseña la separación histórica de la República Dominicana respecto de Haití iniciada el 27 de febrero de 1844 y su posterior condición de posesión española entre 1861 y 1863, indicando que el semicentenario de la restauración de la república en 1863 se celebrará en agosto próximo.

records.headline: The Dominican Congress has received numerous reform proposals
records.summary_en: The Dominican Congress has received numerous reform proposals, the Evening Star reports under the heading "Urges Santo Domingo Reforms," designed to eliminate abuses that prompted the Dominican insurrection last year. The measures were outlined in the first message of Archbishop Nouel, provisional president, which was submitted to lawmakers upon convening in ordinary session at Santo Domingo City.

Las iniciativas fueron planteadas en el primer mensaje del arzobispo Nouel, presidente provisional, remitido a los legisladores al iniciar sus sesiones ordinarias en la ciudad de Santo Domingo.

records.headline: The provisional Dominican administration established with United States cooperation
records.summary_en: The provisional Dominican administration established with United States cooperation under Archbishop Nouel has collapsed, a Puerto Plata dispatch in The Washington Herald reports, following his resignation and departure from the country. Revolutionary leaders attributed the government's fall to Nouel's dilatory tactics and his failure to call a popular election pursuant to the agreement reached last autumn with the American commission. Speaking from Puerto Plata, General Horacio Vasquez, former commander-in-chief of the revolutionary forces, asserted that Nouel disregarded his pact, aligned with old political factions, and lost public confidence through delays in establishing constitutional rule. Vasquez cautioned that Congress must not select a provisional president from current candidates in the field, warning of the danger of a coup d'état and renewed revolution in the capital.
records.summary_es: El gobierno provisional dominicano establecido con la cooperación de los Estados Unidos bajo la presidencia del arzobispo Nouel ha colapsado, informa un despacho de Puerto Plata en The Washington Herald, tras su dimisión y salida del país. Los jefes revolucionarios atribuyeron la caída del gobierno a las tácticas dilatorias de Nouel y a su falta de convocatoria a elecciones populares de conformidad con el acuerdo pactado el otoño anterior con la comisión estadounidense. Desde Puerto Plata, el general Horacio Vásquez, antiguo comandante en jefe de las fuerzas revolucionarias, afirmó que Nouel incumplió su pacto, se inclinó hacia viejas agrupaciones políticas y perdió la confianza pública al demorar la instauración del régimen constitucional. Vásquez advirtió que el Congreso no debe elegir un presidente provisional entre los aspirantes que ya se encuentran en campaña, previniendo sobre el riesgo de un golpe de Estado y una nueva revolución en la capital.

records.headline: General McIntyre expressed the view, The Montgomery Advertiser
records.summary_en: General McIntyre expressed the view, The Montgomery Advertiser reports, that if Archbishop Nouel had resigned as unofficially reported, he was practically harassed into doing so by office-seekers; McIntyre had assisted in establishing the provisional Dominican government following the revolution. McIntyre stated that no formal agreement had been made between Nouel and the American commission regarding the calling of a popular election, though he naturally supposed one would be held eventually. The general noted that he saw no reason for United States interference in Santo Domingo on account of Nouel's resignation unless disorders occurred, adding that no official advices concerning the matter had been received that night in Washington.
records.summary_es: El general McIntyre opinó, según informa The Montgomery Advertiser, que si el arzobispo Nouel había renunciado conforme a los informes extraoficiales, prácticamente fue empujado a ello por el hostigamiento de quienes buscaban cargos públicos; McIntyre había participado en el establecimiento del gobierno provisional dominicano después de la revolución. McIntyre puntualizó que no se había concertado ningún acuerdo formal entre Nouel y la comisión estadounidense sobre la convocatoria a elecciones populares, aunque consideraba natural que estas se efectuaran oportunamente. El general señaló que no veía motivo alguno para una intervención de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo con motivo de la dimisión de Nouel, a menos que surgieran desórdenes, agregando que hasta esa noche no se habían recibido avisos oficiales al respecto en Washington.

records.headline: Dominican minister Dr. Peynado received the terse cablegram
records.summary_en: Dominican minister Dr. Peynado received the terse cablegram "Ninguna novedad" from his government's foreign minister, the Evening Star reports under the headline '"Nothing Doing," He Cables'; the cablegram, translated as "nothing doing," came in response to inquiries regarding rumors that Archbishop Nouel had departed the island. Dr. Peynado stated that other sources indicated the provisional president had merely left the capital temporarily to visit another part of the country. The minister affirmed that conditions throughout the Dominican Republic appeared entirely normal.
records.summary_es: El ministro dominicano, doctor Peynado, recibió el escueto cablegrama «Ninguna novedad» de parte del ministro de Relaciones Exteriores de su gobierno, según informa el Evening Star bajo el titular '"Nothing Doing," He Cables'; el cablegrama, traducido al inglés como "nothing doing", llegó en respuesta a consultas sobre rumores de que el arzobispo Nouel había abandonado la isla. El doctor Peynado señaló que otras fuentes indicaban que el presidente provisional solo se había ausentado temporalmente de la capital para realizar una visita a otra región del país. El ministro aseguró que la situación en toda la República Dominicana parecía completamente normal.

records.summary_en: For the protection of American interests, the gunboat Petrel has arrived at Santo Domingo City, capital of the Dominican Republic, a Washington dispatch in The San Francisco Call reports. WASHINGTON, March 11.—"Ninguna novedad," which is Spanish for "nothing doing," was the terse cablegram Dr. Peynado, Dominican minister, received today from minister of foreign affairs of his government in reply to an inquiry concerning the report that Archbishop Nouel, provisional president of the Dominican republic, had left the island.

records.headline: Assistant Secretary of State Adee is the subject of an anecdote
records.summary_en: Assistant Secretary of State Adee is the subject of an anecdote recounted in The News and Citizen, set during an outbreak in Santo Domingo, when the American gunboats Yankton and Wheeling were dispatched to Puerto Plata. Inquired of by a crowd of anxious journalists whether Dominican rebels would dare to attack the Wheeling, Adee quipped that he sincerely hoped not because he was dreadfully fond of wheeling. The report notes that his pun was met with loud amusement by the assembled correspondents.
records.summary_es: El subsecretario de Estado Adee es el tema de una anécdota relatada en el News and Citizen, situada durante un estallido en Santo Domingo, cuando los cañoneros estadounidenses Yankton y Wheeling fueron despachados a Puerto Plata. Al ser interrogado por un grupo de periodistas inquietos sobre si los rebeldes dominicanos se atreverían a atacar al Wheeling, Adee bromeó diciendo que esperaba con sinceridad que no, puesto que era sumamente aficionado al ciclismo ("wheeling"). La nota añade que su juego de palabras fue recibido con grandes risas por los corresponsales congregados.

records.headline: Assistant Secretary of State Osborne, The Evening Star reports
records.summary_en: Assistant Secretary of State Osborne, The Evening Star reports, declared himself thoroughly convinced of the authenticity of Christopher Columbus's remains in Santo Domingo, after examining his bones and a bullet found in the body. Vick, newly appointed receiver of customs for Santo Domingo who accompanied Osborne on the journey, is preparing at his New Jersey home to take up his duties, while Osborne praised the cordial reception extended by President Bordas.

records.headline: Upon returning from a three-week trip to Santo Domingo and Haiti
records.summary_en: Upon returning from a three-week trip to Santo Domingo and Haiti, Assistant Secretary of State John E. Osborne announced that the bones of Christopher Columbus repose in the Cathedral of Santo Domingo rather than in Seville, Spain, The Washington Herald reports. According to Osborne, Dominicans secretly retained Columbus's remains out of love for him, sending only the bones of his son Diego back to Spain, and he identified a lead casket inscribed "Christobal Colon, first admiral and discoverer of America" containing a bullet among the bones. In response, Pan-American Union Director General John Barrett noted that several locations claim the honor and that experts hold widely divergent opinions on the subject.
records.summary_es: Al regresar de un viaje de tres semanas por Santo Domingo y Haití, el subsecretario de Estado John E. Según Osborne, los dominicanos retuvieron secretamente los restos de Colón por el afecto que le profesaban, devolviendo a España únicamente los huesos de su hijo Diego, e identificó un cofre de plomo con la inscripción "Christobal Colon, primer almirante y descubridor de América" que contenía una bala entre los restos. En respuesta, el director general de la Unión Panamericana, John Barrett, señaló que varios lugares se disputan ese honor y que los expertos mantienen posturas divergentes sobre el asunto.

records.headline: The Star prints an account of the question of the remains of Columbus: Mr. Barrett said
records.summary_en: The Star prints an account of the question of the remains of Columbus: Mr. Barrett said that it is a subject of great significance, and that officials of the Dominican republic are very anxious to establish the authenticity of their claim. 'The Pan-American Union has always taken a deep interest in the subject, and we have a number of publications dealing with the claims of different places that the remains of Columbus rest there,' said Mr. Barrett. 'It is a question which has never been finally settled to the satisfaction of every one.' The Dominican minister to the United States is now at Santo Domingo, but before going there he selected a site for the Dominican building at the San Francisco exposition, and the little republic expects to make a good showing at the exposition; officials of the republic are now considering the suggestion that the remains be taken through the Panama canal, and then placed in their building at the exposition. An attempt was made a number of years ago by representatives of the Dominican republic to have their claims investigated by a committee from different American countries, but the claim has never been passed upon by any competent body. Spaniards scout the idea that the remains of Columbus are not in Seville, where a beautiful tomb has been erected; the remains were supposed to have been taken to Seville from Havana, following the Spanish-American war, and the Dominicans claim that the remains taken to Seville were really those of Diego, the son of Columbus.

records.headline: The Star prints a further account of the Columbus remains question
records.summary_en: The Star prints a further account of the Columbus remains question: the late Thomas C. Dawson, formerly United States minister successively to the Dominican Republic, Chile, Colombia and Brazil, wrote an article some time ago in which he said that there could be no doubt but that the remains at Santo Domingo were really those of Columbus; he made this assertion after thoroughly examining all records, and wrote that the remains still rest in the little ancient Dominican city where they were sealed and deposited between the years 1541 and 1544. Señor Don Enrique Deschamps, formerly secretary of the Dominican legation at Washington, and still in the diplomatic service of his country, contributed an article on the question to the September, 1912, issue of the bulletin of the Pan-American Union, in which he reviewed all the authorities on the question, gave pictures of the casket in which the remains were found, and came to the conclusion that there can be no real doubt that Columbus' remains are in the Santo Domingo cathedral. Walker W. Vick, newly appointed collector of customs at Santo Domingo, has let it be known that when he goes to Santo Domingo to take up his new post he is going to make a thorough investigation of the subject.

El señor don Enrique Deschamps, exsecretario de la legación dominicana en Washington, y aún en el servicio diplomático de su país, contribuyó con un artículo sobre la cuestión al número de septiembre de 1912 del boletín de la Unión Panamericana, en el que revisó todas las autoridades en la materia, dio fotografías del féretro en que se hallaron los restos, y llegó a la conclusión de que no puede haber duda real de que los restos de Colón están en la catedral de Santo Domingo. Walker W. Vick, recién nombrado recaudador de aduanas en Santo Domingo, ha dado a conocer que cuando vaya a Santo Domingo a ocupar su nuevo puesto hará una investigación minuciosa del asunto.

records.full_text:
W. W. VICK, NEW PAYMASTER OF SANTO DOMINGO One of President Wilson's Campaign Managers to Continue the Novel Experiment by Which Uncle Sam Administers the Finances of the Republic—Old City Prospers Under the American Receivership

By selecting Walter W. Vick of New Jersey, Wilson campaign worker and secretary of the immigration committee, as Receiver-General of the customs of the Dominican Republic President Wilson assigned him the task of continuing a novel experiment in national finance. Bankruptcies and receiverships are common enough in commercial enterprises, but the Dominican experiment is the first case in which a nation after being plunged into involuntary bankruptcy has accepted a third party, another nation, to act as receiver of its revenues and stand between it and its creditors during the settlement of its outstanding obligations.

The soundness of this commercial practice as applied to governments is shown by the fact that to-day the Dominican Republic has more money to spend for proper purposes than ever before, besides paying the interest on a loan and setting aside each year a sum for the payment of the principal. When the receivership is terminated Santo Domingo is likely to enjoy the distinction of being the only Latin American Government not saddled with a burdensome foreign debt.

The United States Government is the custodian of the Dominican revenues, and stands sponsor not only for the conservation of the public funds but also for the settlement of the republic's debts. This arrangement has lasting force by virtue of a treaty between the United States and the Dominican Republic, in which the conditions of the receivership are set forth. Under this treaty it was that President Wilson appointed Mr. Vick as the representative of the Government of the United States to administer the receivership.

Mr. Vick is not, technically speaking, in any way connected with the Washington Government. His salary is paid by the Dominican Government. The same is true of all the expenses of the receivership. These include the salaries of a number of Americans who serve as his assistants. His own salary is $6,500 a year, and he also gets living quarters.

Mr. Vick is regarded as exceptionally well qualified for the place. His financial abilities and political wisdom were first bought to the attention of President Wilson when he had charge of the Wilson Gubernatorial campaign in Bergen county, New Jersey. During the pre-convention campaign of last year he looked after the Governor's interests in the southern Atlantic States. After the convention at Baltimore he was made assistant secretary of the Democratic National Committee and had charge of the disbursements. More than $3,000,000 passed through his hands in three months. In December he was designated as secretary of the inauguration committee and opened headquarters in Washington, from which he directed the arrangements as the personal representative of the President-elect.

His new appointment involves a radical change. Instead of being in politics he must maintain absolute neutrality in such matters in the Dominican republic. One of the advantages supposed to lie in the American receivership is that the customs revenues are by it removed to neutral hands and are no longer to be preyed upon by aspiring revolutionists or grafting officials. From 1905, when the first temporary arrangement went into effect, until 1912 Santo Domingo had its first long period of freedom from revolution and internal strife. The neutralization of the customs receipts has been regarded as the cause of this peace in the turbulent republic. In 1912 there was continued political disturbance, but even during the revolution the custom houses remained unmolested by either faction in the struggle. It will be Mr. Vick's task to continue this absolute security of the customs receipts and maintain perfect neutrality toward all the contending political factions in the island.

European intervention in Santo Domingo seemed a certainty when President Roosevelt intervened in behalf of the republic. The Dominican Government was saddled with a foreign and domestic indebtedness amounting, with interest, to about $30,000,000. Far from paying the interest the Dominican Government was increasing the debt by about a million dollars a year. As a result of centuries of misrule the revenues were being dishonestly dissipated. A succession of revolutions had reduced the Government simply to a source of graft for which many factions were contending. In this situation the European creditors in 1904 demanded a settlement, and were prepared to take over the revenues of the Government if their demands were not granted. As the Dominicans were unable to do what they asked European intervention seemed certain.

The United States then negotiated the modus vivendi, which was to hold in force while a treaty was being negotiated. The treaty, under which the receivership is now conducted, was ratified by the United States Senate and the Dominican Congress and went into effect July 8, 1907. Meantime under the modus vivendi there had been issued bonds of the Dominican Government to the amount of $20,000,000. This was for the purpose of making a settlement with the foreign creditors and paying for certain public improvements necessary to the utilization of the island resources. Though the nominal debt was $30,000,000 it was scaled down by the United States in making allowance for fraud and dishonest claims to about $17,000,000.

The bonds bear interest at 5 per cent., making the annual charge for the service of the loan $1,000,000 a year. It is provided in the treaty that each month the American Receiver-General shall pay to the Guaranty Trust Company of New York, the fiscal agent of the loan, the sum of $100,000. This is $200,000 in excess of the annual $1,000,000 required, and the balance is applied to the amortization of the bonds. In addition it is provided that whenever the collections for any year shall exceed $3,000,000 half of the surplus shall be applied to the amortization of the bonds.

Highly satisfactory progress has been made toward the repayment of the principal of the $20,000,000 loan, inasmuch as the revenues of the republic have nearly doubled under the American receivership. After the expenses of the receivership have been paid and the interest charges and sinking fund taken care of the Dominican Government gets what is left. Far from being a hardship, the effect of the receivership has been to give to the Dominican Government more money for its own purposes than it ever had before, even in the days when it did not pay a cent on its indebtedness. The first real roads in the republic, outside of the towns, have been built with funds supplied by the receivership, and other public improvements have been made possible.

What the receivership has really done for the Dominican Government is shown by the fact that whereas the customs receipts were only about $2,000,000 a year before the receivership, the receipts for 1912 were $3,642,861. This is the highest figure ever attained, and collections for the first four months of the present calendar year indicate that the total receipts for 1913 will exceed $4,000,000.

W. E. Pulliam, Mr. Vick's predecessor, effected many reforms in the administration of the Dominican customs which will assist Mr. Vick materially when he takes charge. It was found that one reason for the small receipts lay in the dishonesty of the collectors. The men whom the American receiver expelled from the service found difficulty in understanding why there should be any objection to their modest peculations. Similarly, it was found that other men in the customs service were grafting by permitting goods to enter without duty upon payment of tribute to them. This of course, many importers were only too glad to do.

One of the remarkable features of the effects of the receivership is that receipts were increased through the reduction of the customs dues. A cut of 50 per cent. was made in the export duties and a reduction of 15 per cent. in the import duties. The result was to increase both exports and imports.

The former Receiver-General found that while such articles as champagne, silks and automobiles, used solely by the rich, were being admitted practically duty free, the cotton cloths, which are the sole source of clothes for the poorer classes, were being taxed almost 100 per cent. Mr. Pulliam induced the Dominican Government to reverse this arrangement, with salutary effect both upon the condition of the poorer people and upon the state of the treasury.

Though Mr. Vick will be the head of the only non-political Government department in all Latin-America as custodian of the customs receipts, he will really be a tremendous factor in the political stability of the republic. With the American Minister he is the personification of the pledge of the United States that the Dominican Government shall conduct itself honorably in its financial obligations to foreigners. The office of the Receiver-General and the American Legation in Santo Domingo city are the bulwarks of Dominican stability, peace and good government.

As a result of this peculiar relation of the United States to Santo Domingo the Washington authorities have been obliged to take a friendly hand in the settlement of the Dominican political troubles. The rebellion which followed the tyrannical rule of Eladio Victoria and his dictatorlike nephew, Elfredo Victoria—the latter a soldier who got into power in the confusion following the assassination of President Caceres—was really settled through the intercession of the United States. A commission, of which Brig.-Gen. Frank McIntyre, chief of the bureau of insular affairs of the War Department, was one of the members, brought about the compromise by which President Victoria and his nephew retired from the Government and the prelate of Santo Domingo, Archbishop Nouel, came in as temporary President, to hold office until general elections could be held. This compromise was effected last December, but a few weeks ago Archbishop Nouel relinquished his task and went to Europe in search of lost health. Without any turmoil or disorder the Dominican Congress elected Jose Bordas, a Senator who had joined in the rebellion of 1912, to succeed him. Only the influence of the United States kept more trouble from breaking out upon the withdrawal of the Archbishop.

The city of Santo Domingo, the capital of the republic, is full of historical associations. It is the site of one of the first settlements made in the Western Hemisphere by Christopher Columbus. At the entrance to the harbor stands the ancient stone fort and castle erected by his brother, whom Columbus made Governor of the colony. Half a mile further up the Ozama River stands a great tree, to the great trunk of which tradition says Columbus tied his ships.

Just around the corner from the offices which Mr. Vick will occupy are the ruins of a great cathedral, the first stone church ever built in the Western world. Near by, on the old plaza of Santo Domingo, stands the new cathedral, itself centuries old. In it lies a metal casket said to contain the bones of the great Admiral. The Spaniards thought they took the bones of Christopher Columbus to Havana, but there is evidence that they took those of his brother, the former Governor.

records.headline: The Chronicle prints an item on Mr. Vick's visit: his predecessor
records.summary_en: The Chronicle prints an item on Mr. Vick's visit: his predecessor, W. E. Pulliam, should be retained in the position, but Mr. Vick found that the change in the administration of the receivership met with the entire approval of President Bordas of the Dominican Republic and his cabinet. Mr. Vick was very cordially received, both personally and officially, and his five days' stay in Santo Domingo was most pleasant in every way. 'I am delighted with the prospect of an extended stay in the Dominican Republic,' said Mr. Vick. 'It has been called the land of opportunity, and truly so. The climate is delightful, even at this time of the year, and I am looking forward to a real happiness while there. The city of Santo Domingo, the capital of the republic, has about 30,000 inhabitants, and the people are hospitable and genial. I expect to make many strong friendships there. The official relations between the two governments are of the most cordial character.' Mr. Vick will leave New York on August 2, to take up his official residence in Santo Domingo.

El Sr. Vick fue recibido muy cordialmente, tanto personal como oficialmente, y su estancia de cinco días en Santo Domingo fue muy placentera en todos los sentidos. «Me deleita la perspectiva de una estancia prolongada en la República Dominicana», dijo el Sr. Vick. «Ha sido llamada la tierra de la oportunidad, y verdaderamente lo es. El clima es delicioso, incluso en esta época del año, y espero una verdadera felicidad mientras esté allí. La ciudad de Santo Domingo, la capital de la república, tiene unos 30,000 habitantes, y la gente es hospitalaria y afable. Espero hacer muchas amistades fuertes allí. Las relaciones oficiales entre los dos gobiernos son del carácter más cordial». El Sr. Vick saldrá de Nueva York el 2 de agosto para ocupar su residencia oficial en Santo Domingo.

records.summary_en: The Republican comments on the report of Assistant Secretary of State Osborne, who was weeks in Santo Domingo and who declares that the bones of Christopher Columbus, instead of resting at Seville in Spain, are in the cathedral of Santo Domingo, capital of the Dominican Republic: Mr. Osborne knows this because the Dominicans told him; what they told him about their finances, which he went to investigate, will appear later. In 1898, following the Spanish war, when the bodies of Columbus and his son, Diego, were supposed to have been returned from Havana to Seville, their original resting place, only the body of Diego was actually sent, that of Columbus being secretly retained by the Dominicans. On the bottom of the lead casket is the inscription, 'Christobal Colon, first admiral and discoverer of America.' At this rate the shade of the great mariner must be in an unhappy state, uncertain where he saw the light of day and where he was last buried. But Mr. Osborne's report has been received with doubt, very respectfully of course.

records.headline: The Citizen prints an item: that the bones of Christopher Columbus
records.summary_en: The Citizen prints an item: that the bones of Christopher Columbus are now interred in the cathedral of Santo Domingo, the capital of the Dominican Republic, instead of at Seville, Spain, as is generally believed, is the substance of a story which Assistant Secretary of State Osborne has brought back to Washington from his recent trip to that republic. So entirely certain is Mr. Osborne that the story is true that he has suggested that the remains be placed on a battleship and carried through the Panama Canal, as a tribute to the discoverer of the Western Hemisphere. The distinguishing feature of the coffin is the inscription on the bottom, according to Secretary Osborne, containing the name 'Christobal Colon', which is Spanish for Christopher Columbus. He made a special investigation of the facts in the case, and he believes that he can convince both President Wilson and Secretary of State Bryan that the story told to him by the officials of Santo Domingo is true.
records.summary_es: El Citizen publica una nota sobre los huesos del navegante, que están ahora enterrados en la catedral de Santo Domingo, la capital de la República Dominicana, en lugar de en Sevilla, España, como se cree en general, es la sustancia de una historia que el subsecretario de Estado Osborne ha traído de vuelta a Washington de su reciente viaje a esa república. Tan enteramente seguro está el Sr. Osborne de que la historia es verdadera que ha sugerido que los restos sean colocados en un acorazado y llevados a través del Canal de Panamá, como tributo al descubridor del hemisferio occidental. El rasgo distintivo del féretro es la inscripción en el fondo, según el secretario Osborne, que contiene el nombre «Cristóbal Colón». Hizo una investigación especial de los hechos del caso, y cree que puede convencer tanto al presidente Wilson como al secretario de Estado Bryan de que la historia que le contaron los funcionarios de Santo Domingo es verdadera.

records.headline: The Herald prints an item: an automobile containing eight members of the family of the Dominican minister
records.summary_en: The Herald prints an item: an automobile containing eight members of the family of the Dominican minister was stranded during the storm of Thursday at the summer camp and unofficial legation of the Dominican Republic at the crest of the Palisades of the Potomac. One of three tents which compose the camp of the Minister of the Dominican Republic and Mme. Francesco Peynado was blown down by the storm. When the rain and hail and wind first became unusual, members of Dr. Peynado's family became frightened; they entered the automobile and attempted to start for a neighboring farmhouse, but the rain had short-circuited the engine, and the automobile would not start. So bad was the storm that the passengers were afraid to alight from the car; they remained exposed during the storm and later went to a farmhouse. Reconstruction of the camp, which was damaged seriously, began yesterday. The camp of Dr. Peynado is the most palatial the District has contained; although immensely wealthy, Dr. Peynado expressed a preference for camp life during the summer. He had built a camp composed of three tents, and a staff of servants were taken with the family of the minister.

MYSTERY OF THE PLAGUE.
How and Why Did It Disappear Prom
England In 1667?
Why did the plague disappear from
England? Mr. Bernard Shaw lncl
dentally asks this deeply interesting
question In a letter to the Nation, and
we cannot say that we are satisfied
with his answer. He says he “knows"
that plague has been “extirpated" by
•‘common sanitation."
1 Until the recent sporadic Imported
eases, the last recorded cases of plague
In England occurred at Nottingham In
1667. In that year plague vanished ut
terly from England for two and a
I centuries. No one who has examined
the records of the seventeenth century
can believe that It was “extirpated" by
sanitation. Very gradually In the suc
ceeding century and a half plague
withdrew from Europe also
The date of its disappearance from
Constantinople has been fixed at about
the year 1841. It remained endemic
only in a few lonely places In the
world, such as the highlands of west
ern Arabia, Yunnan In China and Mes
opotamia. Sanitation, though an ex
cellent palliative, certainly never drove
the plague from Stamboul and Cairo

records.headline: The Bulletin prints a letter signed S. L. Theobald: he noticed
records.summary_en: The Bulletin prints a letter signed S. L. Theobald: he noticed, in its issue of August 9, a suggestion, attributed to Assistant Secretary of State Osborne, 'that the bones of Christopher Columbus which are at Santo Domingo City be placed aboard the first ship to go through the Panama Canal.' If this is correct, and, as stated, the result of the secretary's visit to the Dominican Republic and Hayti, he is afraid he did not profit by his visit to the islands so far as historical accuracy is concerned. Not since Hispaniola passed into the hands of the French in 1796 have Columbus' bones lain on San Domingan soil, nor have they found a resting place anywhere in the New World since the close of the Spanish-American War, for in 1898 they were transferred from Havana to Seville, where, in the cathedral, they are to be found at the present time.

Desde que La Española pasó a manos de los franceses en 1796, los huesos de Colón no han reposado en suelo dominicano, ni han encontrado lugar de descanso en ninguna parte del Nuevo Mundo desde el fin de la guerra hispanoamericana, pues en 1898 fueron trasladados de La Habana a Sevilla, donde, en la catedral, se encuentran en la actualidad.

records.headline: The Farmer prints a sketch of the island of Santo Domingo: French buccaneers
records.summary_en: The Farmer prints a sketch of the island of Santo Domingo: French buccaneers gained a foothold in the island; in 1795 the flag of France was supreme, but in 1809 the combined Spanish and English forces captured the island and Spanish sovereignty was restored. In 1821 the people of the Spanish part of the island declared their independence, but President Boyer of Hayti was able to extend his dominions to include all of the island. In 1846 the first Dominican Republic was established, and continued until 1861, when the Dominicans, fearing foreign invasion, appealed to Spain for protection. Spain annexed the country, but on August 16, 1863, at Capotillo, a revolution was instituted which resulted in the restoration of the republic. Living side by side on the same island, and presenting many differences to the most casual observer, the people of the Dominican Republic and Hayti are compared by the paper: French is the language of Hayti, while the Dominicans speak Spanish; the Dominicans are better educated, more progressive, less grossly superstitious, and, on the whole, have shown greater capacity for self-government than their neighbors. The newspapers of a country afford the best index to the character and culture of a people, and in this respect the Dominicans are far ahead of the Haytians. There are half a dozen daily papers in the cities of Santo Domingo, Santiago and Puerto Plata, and Santo Domingo also has two literary weeklies, a humorous weekly, and several monthly, professional and literary magazines.
records.summary_es: The Farmer publica un esbozo histórico de la isla de Santo Domingo, donde los bucaneros franceses se afianzaron en la isla; en 1795 la bandera de Francia era suprema, pero en 1809 las fuerzas combinadas españolas e inglesas capturaron la isla y se restauró la soberanía española. En 1821 el pueblo de la parte española de la isla declaró su independencia, pero el presidente Boyer, de Haití, pudo extender sus dominios hasta incluir toda la isla. En 1846 se estableció la primera República Dominicana, que continuó hasta 1861, cuando los dominicanos, temiendo una invasión extranjera, apelaron a España en busca de protección. España anexó el país, pero el 16 de agosto de 1863, en Capotillo, se inició una revolución que resultó en la restauración de la república. Viviendo lado a lado en la misma isla, y presentando muchas diferencias al observador más casual, los pueblos de la República Dominicana y de Haití son comparados por el periódico: el francés es el idioma de Haití, mientras que los dominicanos hablan español; los dominicanos están mejor educados, son más progresivos, menos groseramente supersticiosos y, en conjunto, han mostrado mayor capacidad de autogobierno que sus vecinos. Los periódicos de un país ofrecen el mejor índice del carácter y la cultura de un pueblo, y en este aspecto los dominicanos van muy por delante de los haitianos. Hay media docena de diarios en las ciudades de Santo Domingo, Santiago y Puerto Plata, y Santo Domingo también tiene dos semanarios literarios, un semanario humorístico y varias revistas mensuales, profesionales y literarias.

records.headline: The Sun prints an account of an American colonel: Colonel Betancourt
records.summary_en: The Sun prints an account of an American colonel: Colonel Betancourt, in the Dominican service, served the entire war under the anti-government banner, and that this service was distinguished in character is attested by the bestowal of the full colonel's commission dated from a battlefield; he is the only citizen of the United States who has been so honored in the Dominican Republic for many years, both regulars and rebels in past upheavals, while hating each other, having hated Americans even more and steadfastly refused them either place or recognition as soldiers. At the machete cavalry charge of La Vega, Colonel Betancourt was the only native of the United States to hold a command. The number on each side in the machete duel at La Vega was not over 100, but for cavalry in a tropical country this is sufficient for an encounter of the first magnitude; seventy-five per cent of the combatants on either side were killed or disabled. As he disembarked from the Santo Domingo steamer, the colonel said that he had seen slashing daredevil cavalry work in his time, but the La Vega affair, picayune in numbers as many might have termed the armies, was a stirring sight: 'It was the very saturnalia of battle.'
records.summary_es: The Sun publica un relato sobre un coronel estadounidense: Betancourt, en el servicio dominicano, sirvió durante toda la guerra bajo la bandera antigubernamental, y que ese servicio fue de carácter distinguido lo atestigua la concesión de la comisión de coronel en propiedad fechada desde un campo de batalla; es el único ciudadano de los Estados Unidos que ha sido honrado así en la República Dominicana en muchos años, pues tanto los regulares como los rebeldes en los alzamientos pasados, odiándose entre sí, odiaban aún más a los estadounidenses y les negaban rotundamente todo puesto o reconocimiento como soldados. En la carga de caballería con machetes de La Vega, el coronel Betancourt fue el único oriundo de los Estados Unidos que mantuvo un mando. El número de cada lado en el duelo de machetes de La Vega no pasaba de 100, pero para la caballería en un país tropical esto basta para un encuentro de primera magnitud; el setenta y cinco por ciento de los combatientes de cada lado resultó muerto o incapacitado. Al desembarcar del vapor de Santo Domingo, el coronel dijo que había visto en su tiempo trabajo de caballería osado y de machete, pero que el episodio de La Vega, insignificante en números como muchos lo habrían calificado a esos ejércitos, fue un espectáculo conmovedor: 'Fue la verdadera saturnal de la batalla'.

records.summary_en: Colonel Harry Betancourt, who served under the anti-government banner, recounts the machete cavalry charge at the battle of La Vega, where about a hundred men on each side, half-clad rebels with spurs strapped to naked ankles, fought hand to hand with cane knives in place of sabres. He says seventy-five per cent of the combatants on either side were killed or disabled, that he was the only United States citizen holding a command, and that three battles were fought that day around La Vega, with an interval of two hours between each.

Dice que el setenta y cinco por ciento de los combatientes de cada bando resultaron muertos o incapacitados, que él fue el único ciudadano de los Estados Unidos con un mando, y que ese día se libraron tres batallas alrededor de La Vega, con un intervalo de dos horas entre cada una.

Ever in the van and cheering on his men, no officer of any of the world's armies was ever more courageous. We fought three battles that day about La Vega, actually three battles, with an interval of two hours between each. In each of these encounters Gen. Pichardo received a wound. He fought in the most dangerous spots. He died of his injuries a few days later. "Some of our troopers were boys only 15 years old. Yet they felt the battle power and tingle of the militant demigod. They held themselves stiffly erect, although scores of them had only their horse's backbone for a saddle. Heads high, and with the lofty, confident air of a field marshal, they eagerly and anxiously listened for the command to charge. "Every machete held in the black or brown hand had been sharpened to a razor edge. For two days the sharpening had gone on in our bivouac outside La Vega. When there wasn't anything else to demand the attention of the troopers they fell back to putting a new edge on the machete in their belts. In some cases there was a scabbard, but in most cases there wasn't. The sharp edges of the great knives caused many injuries to the men themselves. records.summary_en: The Times prints an item: the President received the party of Dominican officials visiting Washington at noon today. They were escorted to the White House by the Secretary of State, Mr. Bryan, and afterward went to the Army and Navy Club to be the guests at luncheon of Brig. Gen. records.headline: The Times prints an item under the head 'From Santo Domingo'
records.summary_en: The Times prints an item under the head 'From Santo Domingo': President Wilson received today a party of high officials of Santo Domingo. With them were Secretary Bryan and James M. Sullivan, the new American minister to the Dominican Republic. In the party were the Dominican minister to Washington, the minister of foreign affairs, and the chief justice of Santo Domingo. Following the call, Secretary Bryan and Mr. Sullivan remained behind with the President for final instructions to the new minister regarding the policy of this country in Santo Domingo. The visitors took lunch today as the guests of General McIntyre, chief of the Bureau of Insular Affairs.

records.headline: The Tribune comments editorially on the Monroe doctrine: the United States
records.summary_en: The Tribune comments editorially on the Monroe doctrine: the United States has in pursuance of the Monroe doctrine saved the Dominican Republic from pillage on the part of creditor peoples in Europe. The financial agent which the United States maintains in Santo Domingo has been able to scale down the debt of that Republic to less than half of the preposterous claims made and prepared for enforcement, and our agent there, the collector of the customs revenues, is collecting these revenues honestly and applying them effectively to the payment of interest and to the extinguishment of the principal of its debts. So that the Monroe doctrine is always a help, not a menace.

records.headline: The Forum prints a Washington dispatch of September 8: Puerto Plata
records.summary_en: The Forum prints a Washington dispatch of September 8: Puerto Plata is being shelled by Dominican gunboats, with great danger to American lives and property, according to a report from J. M. Estevan, American vice consul. The gunboat Des Moines is on the way there. The Des Moines is at Guantanamo, coaling for the run to Puerto Plata, where it is due tomorrow. Puerto Plata has been in the hands of Dominican rebels ever since the latest revolution started with the announcement that the governor of that state had seceded from allegiance to the central government. The present danger to Americans and property comes from an attempt of the Dominican government to force the rebel stronghold to capitulate. Until the receipt of today's dispatches, the State Department officials had not thought the flare-up serious. It is supposed the leader of the uprising is Hector Velasquez, one time provisional president of the republic. The American interests in Puerto Plata are small. It is thought a number of Porto Ricans recently entered the business community there.

Puerto Plata ha estado en manos de rebeldes dominicanos desde que comenzó la última revolución con el anuncio de que el gobernador de ese estado se había separado de la obediencia al gobierno central. AMERICANS ARE IN DEADLY PERIL Associated Press, Washington, Sept. 8.—The Puerto Plata in the Dominican republic, where a revolution is in progress, is being shelled by Dominican gunboats, according to reports from the American vice consul today. The American gunboat Des Moines is en route there, as the lives and property of Americans are said to be in danger. records.headline: The Sun prints a Washington dispatch: a vessel will be lent
records.summary_en: The Sun prints a Washington dispatch: a vessel will be lent by the Treasury Department and will proceed at once from San Juan to the Mona Passage, there to act as a relay wireless station between the Dominican capital, the United States gunboat Des Moines and the city of San Juan. The Des Moines is expected to arrive at Puerto Plata to-morrow. According to meager advices received to-day, the Government gunboat is firing shells at the fort in that city now occupied by the provincial rebels. It is said that the lives and property of the Americans there are greatly endangered by the firing. It is likely that when the Des Moines arrives, steps will be taken by her commander to bring about a cessation of any firing dangerous to American interests. James Sullivan, the New York lawyer who has been appointed Minister to the Dominican Republic, was at the State Department to-day and was instructed to sail for Santo Domingo City in a few days, somewhat earlier than he had expected to go. He probably will leave New York Thursday or Friday.

Se espera que la Des Moines llegue mañana a Puerto Plata. Según los escasos avisos recibidos hoy, la cañonera del gobierno está disparando obuses contra el fuerte de esa ciudad, ocupado ahora por los rebeldes provinciales. Se dice que las vidas y las propiedades de los estadounidenses allí corren gran peligro por el fuego. Es probable que, cuando llegue la Des Moines, su comandante tome medidas para lograr el cese de todo fuego peligroso para los intereses estadounidenses. records.headline: The Journal prints a Washington dispatch: hurry orders went
records.summary_en: The Journal prints a Washington dispatch: hurry orders went from here to-day to the cruiser Des Moines, at Guantanamo, Cuba. The cruiser had been preparing to go to Santo Domingo since reports of the latest revolution there were received several days ago. The cruiser is coaling to-day, and is expected to leave for Santo Domingo to-night. Communication between Puerto Plata and the outside world is cut off. Nothing has been received at the State Department since the brief message to-day announcing the bombardment. Under the head 'In Hand of Rebels', the paper adds: Puerto Plata has been in the hands of the Dominican rebels ever since the latest revolution started with the announcement of the governor that the state had seceded from all allegiance to the central government. The present danger to Americans and their property comes from the attempt of the Dominican government to force the rebels' stronghold to capitulate. Until the receipt of to-day's dispatch, State Department officials had not thought the flare-up would be serious. The supposed leader of the uprising is Hector Valesque, one time provisional president of the republic. The Dominican navy consists of two or three converted yachts, armed with six-pounders and machine guns. The Dominican navy's guns could cause enormous damage to an unfortified town like Puerto Plata, especially since it is of wooden construction and might easily be set afire. American interests in Puerto Plata are small, although a number of Porto Ricans recently have entered the business community there, and the warrant for intervention by Commander Long of the Des Moines would be interference by either side with the customs entry. The revolt against President Bordas is understood to be founded upon the objections of Governor Cespedes of the province of Puerto Plata against the attempts of the general government to wrest control of the government railroad from the provincial officers, the railroad having figured frequently in island politics.
records.summary_es: The Journal publica un despacho de Washington: hoy salieron de aquí órdenes urgentes para el crucero Des Moines, en Guantánamo, Cuba. El crucero se preparaba para ir a Santo Domingo desde que hace varios días se recibieron los informes de la última revolución allí. El crucero está carboneando hoy, y se espera que salga esta noche para Santo Domingo. La comunicación entre Puerto Plata y el mundo exterior está cortada. Nada se ha recibido en el Departamento de Estado desde el breve mensaje de hoy que anunció el bombardeo. Bajo el título 'In Hand of Rebels', el periódico añade: Puerto Plata ha estado en manos de los rebeldes dominicanos desde que comenzó la última revolución con el anuncio del gobernador de que el estado se había separado de toda obediencia al gobierno central. El peligro actual para los estadounidenses y sus propiedades proviene del intento del gobierno dominicano de forzar la capitulación de la plaza fuerte de los rebeldes. Hasta la recepción del despacho de hoy, los funcionarios del Departamento de Estado no habían creído grave el brote. El supuesto jefe del alzamiento es Héctor Valesque, en otro tiempo presidente provisional de la república. La marina dominicana consiste en dos o tres yates convertidos, armados con cañones de seis libras y ametralladoras. Los cañones de la marina dominicana podrían causar un daño enorme a una población no fortificada como Puerto Plata, sobre todo siendo de construcción de madera y pudiendo incendiarse fácilmente. Los intereses estadounidenses en Puerto Plata son pequeños, aunque varios portorriqueños han entrado recientemente en la comunidad comercial de allí, y la justificación para la intervención del comandante Long, del Des Moines, sería la interferencia de cualquiera de las partes con la entrada de aduanas. Se entiende que la revuelta contra el presidente Bordas se funda en las objeciones del gobernador Céspedes, de la provincia de Puerto Plata, contra los intentos del gobierno general de arrebatar a los funcionarios provinciales el control del ferrocarril gubernamental, ferrocarril que ha figurado con frecuencia en la política de la isla.

records.headline: The Star prints Washington comment on the Puerto Plata revolt
records.summary_en: The Star prints Washington comment on the Puerto Plata revolt: it will be made known to rebel sympathizers that the Wilson administration is without sympathy with any government not founded upon law and orderly succession. Officials here to-day expressed confidence in the administrative ability and the integrity of President Bordas. They pointed out that one element of strength in his favor is the support of Desiderio Arias, who has been a leading spirit in many previous revolutions. Bordas is an ad interim provisional president, and is serving out that portion of the regular term of the presidency which was unexpired when Archbishop Nouel, provisional president succeeding President Victoria, gave up the office. Governor Cespedes of Puerto Plata province has a strong political following among the people of that province, and likewise commands large financial resources. He has built and equipped a private arsenal at Puerto Plata. It is, therefore, taken for granted that he is prepared to put up a strong fight against the attack being made by the gunboats in the harbor. Former Provisional President Vasquez, whose fortunes are cast with Cespedes in the present attempt to overthrow the regular government, commands equally great influence and resources in the rich farming countries in the interior. As it would be almost impossible to send an army overland to put down this uprising, the authorities in Santo Domingo City are depending altogether on the successful bombardment of Puerto Plata.
records.summary_es: The Star publica comentarios de Washington sobre la revuelta de Puerto Plata: se hará saber a los simpatizantes rebeldes que la administración Wilson no simpatiza con ningún gobierno que no se funde en la ley y la sucesión ordenada. Los funcionarios aquí expresaron hoy confianza en la capacidad administrativa y la integridad del presidente Bordas. Señalaron que un elemento de fuerza a su favor es el apoyo de Desiderio Arias, que ha sido una figura dirigente en muchas revoluciones anteriores. Bordas es presidente provisional interino, y está sirviendo la parte del período regular de la presidencia que quedaba sin expirar cuando el arzobispo Nouel, presidente provisional que sucedió al presidente Victoria, renunció al cargo. El gobernador Céspedes, de la provincia de Puerto Plata, tiene un fuerte seguimiento político entre la gente de esa provincia, e igualmente dispone de grandes recursos financieros. Ha construido y equipado un arsenal privado en Puerto Plata. Por tanto, se da por sentado que está preparado para dar una fuerte pelea contra el ataque que hacen las cañoneras en el puerto. El expresidente provisional Vásquez, cuya suerte está echada con Céspedes en el intento actual de derrocar al gobierno regular, dispone de una influencia y unos recursos igualmente grandes en los ricos países agrícolas del interior. Como sería casi imposible enviar un ejército por tierra para sofocar este alzamiento, las autoridades de la ciudad de Santo Domingo dependen por completo del éxito del bombardeo de Puerto Plata.

records.headline: The Standard prints an item: James M. Sullivan, a Brooklyn lawyer
records.summary_en: The Standard prints an item: James M. Sullivan, a Brooklyn lawyer, is the newly appointed minister to the Dominican Republic and is the man who secured the confession of 'Bald Jack' Rose in the famous Rosenthal murder case. Mr. Sullivan was Rose's attorney. He is a native of Ireland and was born in Killarney in 1873. Mr. Sullivan succeeds William W. Russell at the Dominican post.

The minister and consul will go to Key West, whence they will embark directly for Puerto Plata. Mr. Sullivan will at once take steps to protect the custom houses in the revolutionary section, which, like all of those in the island republic, are operated under American supervision. The cruiser Des Moines arrived at Puerto Plata tonight and reported to the department in a relayed wireless message, the details of which were not made public. With the cruiser Des Moines on the final stage of her run from Guantanamo, Cuba, to Puerto Plata, the seat of the revolutionary outbreak in Santo Domingo, Washington was today still awaiting reports on the bombardment of the town, threatening danger to Americans. records.summary_en: The New Hampshire Farmer and Weekly Union reported that U.S. Minister James M. Sullivan and Consul Charles W. Hathaway departed to inform Dominican insurgents that Washington firmly opposed their rebellion against President Bordas. Sullivan was instructed to protect American-supervised customs houses, supported by the cruiser Des Moines, which arrived at Puerto Plata ready to land marines. The excerpt also detailed the U.S. Senate's passage of the Underwood tariff bill.
records.summary_es: The New Hampshire Farmer and Weekly Union informó que el ministro de los EE. UU. James M. Sullivan y el cónsul Charles W. Hathaway partieron con la encomienda de notificar a los insurgentes dominicanos la firme oposición de Washington a su rebelión contra el presidente Bordas. Sullivan recibió instrucciones de proteger las aduanas bajo control estadounidense, respaldado por el crucero *Des Moines*, que llegó a Puerto Plata preparado para desembarcar infantes de marina. El extracto reseñó asimismo la aprobación en el Senado de los EE. UU. del proyecto arancelario Underwood.
records.passage: WASHINGTON, Sept. 9.—James M. Sullivan, the new American minister to Santo Domingo, and Charles W. Hathaway, consul at Puerto Plata, left Washington late today for Puerto Plata to tell the Dominican revolutionists there in emphatic terms that the United States has no sympathy with their effort to overthrow President Borda's government. They received final instructions at the state department just before their departure. Mr. Sullivan will take steps to protect the customs houses in the revolutionary zone, which like all those in the island republic, are operated under American supervision. The cruiser Des Moines arrived at Puerto Plata late today and should it be necessary there will be no hesitancy in the landing of marines, which besides guarding the customs houses would afford protection to the American consulate and all American interests.

Hathaway, consul at Puerto Plata, left Washington late today for Puerto Plata to tell the Dominican revolutionists there in emphatic terms that the United States has no sympathy with their efforts to overthrow President Bordas's government. They received final instructions at the State Department just before their departure. Mr. Sullivan will take steps to protect the customs houses in the revolutionary zone, which, like all those in the island republic, are operated under American supervision. The cruiser Des Moines was due at Puerto Plata late today, and should it be necessary there will be no hesitancy in the landing of marines, which besides guarding the customs houses would afford protection to the American consulate and all American interests. If hostilities still are in progress, an effort will probably be made to persuade the belligerents to do their fighting outside the city limits.

Commander Long of the cruiser would be warranted in making a move of intervention if the gunboats or the rebels, who hold the port, interfere with the operation of the custom house under American control. The cruiser Des Moines was due at Puerto Plata, where Dominican gunboats had been shelling the rebel city and endangering American lives and property, and marines would be landed if necessary to guard the customs houses, the American consulate and American interests, with an effort to persuade belligerents to fight outside the city limits.
records.summary_es: El Sr. Sullivan tomará medidas para proteger las aduanas en la zona revolucionaria dominicana, todas operadas bajo supervisión estadounidense. El crucero Des Moines debía llegar a Puerto Plata, donde cañoneros dominicanos habían bombardeado la ciudad rebelde y puesto en peligro vidas y propiedades estadounidenses, y se desembarcarían infantes de marina si fuera necesario para custodiar las aduanas, el consulado estadounidense y los intereses estadounidenses, procurando persuadir a los beligerantes de luchar fuera de los límites de la ciudad.
records.passage: Mr. Sullivan will take steps to protect the customs houses in the revolutionary zone, which, like all those in the island republic, are operated under American supervision. The cruiser Des Moines was due at Puerto Plata late Tuesday, and should it be necessary there will be no hesitancy in the landing of marines, which besides guarding the customs houses would afford protection to the American consulate and all American interests. If hostilities still are in progress, an effort will probably be made to persuade the belligerents to do their fighting outside the city limits. News that Dominican gunboats were shelling the rebel city of Puerto Plata, endangering American lives and property, caused hurry orders to go from Washington Monday to the cruiser Des Moines, which had been preparing to sail from Guantanamo, Cuba, for Santo Domingo since reports of the latest revolution there were received several days ago. The cruiser was expected to sail Monday night secretly for Puerto Plata.

records.headline: The Star prints an item: President Bordas of the Dominican Republic cabled
records.summary_en: The Star prints an item: President Bordas of the Dominican Republic cabled the legation here today that the revolution was confined to the cities of Puerto Plata, Samana and Moca; that it was not general in the northern part of the country; and that he had taken personal command of his troops. His message was sent from Santo Domingo City. The revenue cutters Algonquin and Seminole have arrived at Puerto Plata, reinforcing the cruiser Des Moines, which reached that place Tuesday night. The Dominican gunboat Presidente, which had been trying to blockade the port, gave rise to the rumor of a bombardment of Puerto Plata by firing a few shots at the fort at the extreme edge of the town. The gunboat abandoned the blockade, however, and sailed for the southward yesterday. As a result matters have quieted down at Puerto Plata, and the Des Moines will leave the revenue cutters to look after foreign interests there and sail for Santiago, Cuba, to pick up and transport to the Dominican capital American Minister Sullivan, with his secretary and family, next Saturday.

Su mensaje fue enviado desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo. Los guardacostas Algonquin y Seminole han llegado a Puerto Plata, en refuerzo del crucero Des Moines, que llegó a ese lugar el martes por la noche. El cañonero dominicano Presidente, que había estado tratando de bloquear el puerto, dio origen al rumor de un bombardeo de Puerto Plata al disparar unos pocos tiros contra el fuerte situado en el extremo de la ciudad. El cañonero abandonó el bloqueo, sin embargo, y zarpó ayer hacia el sur. Como resultado, las cosas se han calmado en Puerto Plata, y el Des Moines dejará a los guardacostas al cuidado de los intereses extranjeros allí y zarpará hacia Santiago de Cuba a recoger y transportar a la capital dominicana al ministro estadounidense Sullivan, con su secretario y su familia, el próximo sábado.

records.headline: The Advertiser prints an item: the news received by Dominicans
records.summary_en: The Advertiser prints an item: the news received by Dominicans in this city today, which they consider of the greatest importance, is that Ricardo Limardo, Minister of Public Works and Communications in the Bordas government, has resigned and joined the forces of the secession movement in the north. The secessionists in Puerto Plata have formed a provisional government with Horacio Vasques at the head. According to a cable dispatch received by F. Deetjen, the Consul General of Santo Domingo in New York, the Dominican war vessel Jacaqua has left Santo Domingo for Puerto Plata with between 500 and 600 of the best trained soldiers in the country on board. The Consul General said he would not be surprised to learn that President Bordas himself accompanies the expedition. 'My advices,' said Mr. Deetjen, 'are that the representatives of the United States in Santo Domingo are supporting the central government. The United States has agreed to the closing and blockading of the ports which have seceded. The news that the east and south of the country are quiet is confirmed. The secession movement is confined to the north.'

El movimiento secesionista está confinado al norte».

records.summary_en: The Evening Star prints an item: a new State has been formed in the rebellious northern territory by the secessionists, creating an unprecedented situation in the West Indian republic, according to advices received by Dominicans in this city today. The news which they consider of the greatest importance is that Ricardo Limardo, minister of public works and communications in the Bordas government, has resigned and joined the forces of the secession movement in the north. The secessionists in Puerto Plata have formed a provisional government with Horacio Vasquez at the head. According to a cable despatch received by F. Deetjen, the consul general of Santo Domingo in New York, the Dominican war vessel Jacaqua has left Santo Domingo for Puerto Plata with between five and six hundred of the best trained soldiers in the country on board.
records.summary_es: The Evening Star publica una nota: formado por los secesionistas un nuevo Estado en el territorio rebelde del norte, se ha creado una situación sin precedentes en la república antillana, según informes recibidos por los dominicanos de esta ciudad hoy. La noticia que consideran de la mayor importancia es que Ricardo Limardo, ministro de Obras Públicas y Comunicaciones del gobierno de Bordas, ha renunciado y se ha unido a las fuerzas del movimiento secesionista del norte. Los secesionistas de Puerto Plata han formado un gobierno provisional con Horacio Vásquez a la cabeza. Según un despacho por cable recibido por F. Deetjen, cónsul general de Santo Domingo en Nueva York, el buque de guerra dominicano Jacaqua ha salido de Santo Domingo hacia Puerto Plata con entre quinientos y seiscientos de los soldados mejor entrenados del país a bordo.

records.headline: The Watchman and Southron prints a dispatch: the cruiser Des Moines
records.summary_en: The Watchman and Southron prints a dispatch: the cruiser Des Moines was coaling today and was expected to sail tonight directly for Puerto Plata. The cruiser had been preparing to sail from Guantanamo, Cuba, for Santo Domingo since reports of the latest revolution there were received several days ago. In the meantime communication between Puerto Plata and the outside world has been broken and no word has come to the State Department since the brief message early today announcing the bombardment. In order to make certain the re-establishment of communication with the arrival of the Des Moines, the Treasury Department was asked to dispatch the revenue cutter Algonquin from San Juan, Puerto Rico, to Mona Passage, a point on the coast midway between Puerto Plata and Santo Domingo City. The cutter will reach there tomorrow and will serve as a wireless relay station between the Des Moines and the commercial station at Santo Domingo. Long conferences were held today by President Wilson, Secretary Bryan and Assistant Secretary Osborne with James M. Sullivan, the newly appointed American minister to the Dominican Republic. The new minister will sail Friday or Saturday for Santo Domingo City with assurances for President Bordas that he has the moral support of the United States government in his efforts to suppress the Puerto Plata rebellion.

records.headline: The Times prints an item: 'You may say,' declared Secretary of State Bryan
records.summary_en: The Times prints an item: 'You may say,' declared Secretary of State Bryan today, 'that the United States Government has no sympathy for the revolution now in progress in Santo Domingo and that we shall uphold the hands of the Federal President.' Carrying somewhat similar instructions, James M. Sullivan, the new United States minister to the Dominican Republic, is now on his way to his new post from Santiago, Cuba, where he boarded the cruiser Des Moines. Unofficial advices received in Washington are to the effect that the rebels have formed a new State in the rebellious territory, and that Ricardo Limardo, minister of public works and communications in the Bordas administration, has resigned and joined the rebels.

records.headline: The Statesman prints a feature under the head 'Receiver of Revenues of Santo Domingo': Walter W. Vick
records.summary_en: The Statesman prints a feature under the head 'Receiver of Revenues of Santo Domingo': Walter W. Vick, of New Jersey, has been appointed by President Wilson receiver general of the customs of the republic of Santo Domingo, thus continuing a novel experiment in national finance, inaugurated in 1905. It is the first case in which a bankrupt nation has accepted another nation to act as receiver of its revenues and stand between it and its creditors during the settlement of its outstanding obligations. At the present time the Dominican Republic has more money to spend for proper purposes than ever before, while ample provision is being made for wiping out its indebtedness at an early date. The debt of $30,000,000 in 1905 has been reduced to $17,000,000, while customs dues have been reduced, trade increased, misrule brought to an end, and the blessings of peace established in the formerly turbulent country.
records.summary_es: The Statesman publica un reportaje bajo el título 'Receiver of Revenues of Santo Domingo': Walter W. Vick, de Nueva Jersey, ha sido nombrado por el presidente Wilson receptor general de las aduanas de la república de Santo Domingo, continuándose así un experimento novedoso en las finanzas nacionales, inaugurado en 1905. Es el primer caso en que una nación en bancarrota ha aceptado que otra nación actúe como receptora de sus rentas y se interponga entre ella y sus acreedores durante la liquidación de sus obligaciones pendientes. En la actualidad, la República Dominicana tiene más dinero para gastar en fines apropiados que nunca antes, al tiempo que se está proveyendo ampliamente para extinguir su deuda en fecha temprana. La deuda de $30,000,000 en 1905 se ha reducido a $17,000,000, mientras las cuotas aduaneras se han reducido, el comercio ha aumentado, el desgobierno ha llegado a su fin y las bendiciones de la paz se han establecido en el país antes turbulento.

records.headline: The Daily Express prints a dispatch: the Clyde steamer Seminole
records.summary_en: The Daily Express prints a dispatch: the Clyde steamer Seminole was stopped as she was nearing port Monday and boarded by an officer from one of the gunboats and told she could not enter the harbor. The captain of the Seminole replied he would enter anyway. Upon being asked what he would do if he were ordered to remain outside, the captain replied that he would go in and take the boarding officer with him if he did not leave the ship. The officer hurriedly returned to the gunboat and the Seminole entered the port. The blockading boats steamed away. The Seminole had cleared from New York before the blockade of Puerto Plata had been declared, and having no munitions of war aboard and relying upon the presence of the Des Moines, she entered the port without fear of molestation. The captain of the Clyde line steamer Algonquin, on arriving here Tuesday, reported everything quiet in the southern ports which are ostensibly in the hands of the government. With the exception of Monte Cristi and Santiago, the northern part of the island is in the hands of rebels under Gen. Horacio Vasquez, at one time president of the republic. The rebel towns of Sanchez and Samana are barricaded and the inhabitants are ready for a fight. Monte Cristi is reported quiet, though the people there are much excited. It is reported that the revolution has spread to Seibo.
