records.headline: The Star prints an item: Mr. Sullivan reports his safe arrival
records.summary_en: The Star prints an item: Mr. Sullivan reports his safe arrival at Puerto Plata, the center of the latest Dominican revolution; he is the American minister to the Dominican Republic. He was accompanied by Consul Hathaway, who had been in the United States on leave. Mr. Sullivan, in his endeavor to reconcile the warring factions, will follow his instructions from President Wilson and tell the rebels that the United States has no sympathy with the present attempt to overthrow the Bordas government. No official report has been received here of the breaking of the blockade at Puerto Plata by the Clyde liner Seminole with the apparent sanction of the American minister and the commander of the Des Moines. Puerto Plata is in possession of the rebels under Gen. Vasquez, and a blockade was attempted by two Dominican gunboats.
records.summary_es: The Star publica una nota: el Sr. Sullivan informa de su llegada a salvo a Puerto Plata, centro de la última revolución dominicana; es el ministro estadounidense en la República Dominicana. Le acompañaba el cónsul Hathaway, que había estado en los Estados Unidos de licencia. El Sr. Sullivan, en su empeño por reconciliar a las facciones en lucha, seguirá sus instrucciones del presidente Wilson y dirá a los rebeldes que los Estados Unidos no simpatizan con el actual intento de derrocar el gobierno de Bordas. Aquí no se ha recibido informe oficial alguno sobre la ruptura del bloqueo de Puerto Plata por el vapor Seminole, de la Clyde, con la aparente sanción del ministro estadounidense y del comandante del Des Moines. Puerto Plata está en posesión de los rebeldes bajo el general Vásquez, y dos cañoneros dominicanos intentaron un bloqueo.

records.headline: The Times-Dispatch prints a dispatch: ordered to Dominican waters
records.summary_en: The Times-Dispatch prints a dispatch: ordered to Dominican waters to protect American interests, the United States cruiser Des Moines arrived at Puerto Plata today, where two Dominican gunboats were blockading the port. The steamer Seminole, of the Clyde Line, was stopped as she was nearing port yesterday and boarded by an officer from one of the gunboats and told she could not enter the harbor. The captain of the Seminole replied he would enter anyway. Upon being asked what he would do if he were ordered to remain outside, the captain replied that he would go in and take the boarding officer with him if he did not leave the ship. The officer hurriedly returned to the gunboat and the Seminole entered the port. The blockading boats steamed away. The Seminole had cleared from New York before the blockade of Puerto Plata had been declared, and having no munitions of war aboard and relying upon the presence of the Des Moines, she entered the port without fear of molestation. The captain of the Clyde Line steamer Algonquin, on arriving here today, reported everything quiet in the southern ports, which are ostensibly in the hands of the government. With the exception of Monte Cristi and Santiago, the northern part of the island is in the hands of rebels under General Horatio Vasquez, at one time president of the republic. Monte Cristi is reported quiet, though the people there are much excited. It is reported that the revolution has spread to Seybo, and it is expected that that town and La Romana will be attacked.

records.headline: The Herald comments editorially: information laid before President Wilson
records.summary_en: The Herald comments editorially: information laid before President Wilson by State Department officials convinced him that the revolution in Santo Domingo was purely one of greed upon the part of a small group of malcontents, and that the rebellion against the Bordas government was not established on any principle other than that of a desire for office and the proceeds thereof. Consequently, it was determined almost at the outset that everything should be done to discourage the revolutionists. They were at once informed of the disfavor with which the Washington government viewed their attempt to bring on another political upheaval. This declaration of disapproval was soon followed by the double threat of nonrecognition and withholding funds in case the rebels should succeed by force in gaining control of the government authority. Minister Sullivan, recently appointed minister to Santo Domingo, has arrived at Puerto Plata, the stronghold of the revolutionists, and is reiterating to the rebel leaders the determined position of President Wilson. He is backed up by the gunboat Des Moines.
records.summary_es: The Herald comenta editorialmente: la información presentada al presidente Wilson por funcionarios del Departamento de Estado lo convenció de que la revolución en Santo Domingo era puramente una de codicia por parte de un pequeño grupo de descontentos, y de que la rebelión contra el gobierno de Bordas no se fundaba en principio alguno que no fuera el deseo de cargos y de sus provechos. En consecuencia, se determinó casi desde el principio que debía hacerse todo lo posible por desalentar a los revolucionarios. Se les informó de inmediato del desagrado con que el Gobierno de Washington veía su intento de provocar otro trastorno político. Esta declaración de desaprobación fue seguida pronto por la doble amenaza del no reconocimiento y de la retención de fondos en caso de que los rebeldes lograran, por la fuerza, hacerse con el control de la autoridad gubernamental. El ministro Sullivan, recién nombrado ministro en Santo Domingo, ha llegado a Puerto Plata, baluarte de los revolucionarios, y está reiterando a los jefes rebeldes la determinada posición del presidente Wilson. Lo respalda el cañonero Des Moines.

Sullivan, has induced the warring factions in this country to sign a peace pact, and the revolution headed by General Horatio Vasquez against the government of the provisional president, Jose Bordas Valdez, is at an end. The American minister's action is the first successful application of the United States government's new Latin-American policy with regard to the Dominican Republic, which is to the effect that force of arms never again can settle any question in this country. Mr. Sullivan has made it known that the last civil war in this republic has been fought. In the future any uprising, he says, will be stamped as criminal without a conference between the opposing factions.

records.summary_en: The Raymer Enterprise reviewed the history of the Dominican customs receivership, noting that removing customs revenues from political grasp had ended chronic revolutions and established domestic peace between 1905 and 1912. The article recalled that President Roosevelt intervened in 1905 to prevent European creditor nations from seizing Dominican customs to collect $20,000,000 in defaulted debts. records.headline: The Wheeling Intelligencer prints a dispatch: the revolution
records.summary_en: The Wheeling Intelligencer prints a dispatch: the revolution headed by General Horatio Vasquez against the government of Provisional President Jose Bordas Valdez is at an end. The American minister's action is the first successful application of the United States government's new Latin American policy with regard to the Dominican Republic, which is to the effect that the force of arms can never again settle any question in this country. Mr. Sullivan has made it known that the last civil war in this Republic has been fought. In the future any uprising, he says, will be stamped out as criminal without a conference being held between the opposing factions, the United States government supporting the constitutional authority against force regardless of the merits of the issue. The people of Santo Domingo are being instructed that the remedy for future grievances lies in the free ballot at a future election. The American policy, as announced by Mr. Sullivan, has been accepted joyously by all parties, regardless of political affiliations. The American minister arrived at Santo Domingo City from the United States on September 17 and immediately brought about an armistice between the rebels and the government troops fighting in the northern department. Since then negotiations had been in progress continuously with the result that what promised to be the most sanguinary revolution in the history of the Dominican Republic has been averted.

records.full_text:
ADMINISTERING SANTO DOMINGO FINANCES

By selecting Walter W. Vick of New Jersey as receiver-general of the customs of the Dominican republic President Wilson assigned him the task of continuing a novel experiment in national finance. Bankruptcies and receiverships are common enough in commercial enterprises, but the Dominican experiment is the first case in which a nation after being plunged into involuntary bankruptcy has accepted a third party, another nation, to act as receiver of its revenues and stand between it and its creditors during the settlement of its outstanding obligations.

The soundness of this commercial practice as applied to governments is shown by the fact that today the Dominican republic has more money to spend for proper purposes than ever before, besides paying the interest on a loan and setting aside each year a sum for the payment of the principal. When the receivership is terminated Santo Domingo is likely to enjoy the distinction of being the only Latin-American government not saddled with a burdensome foreign debt.

The United States government is the custodian of the Dominican revenues, and stands sponsor not only for the conservation of the public funds, but also for the settlement of the republic's debts. This arrangement has lasting force by virtue of a treaty between the United States and the Dominican republic, in which the conditions of the receivership are set forth. Under this treaty it was that President Wilson appointed Mr. Vick as the representative of the government of the United States to administer the receivership.

Mr. Vick is not, technically speaking, in any way connected with the Washington government. His salary is paid by the Dominican government. The same is true of all the expenses of the receivership. These include the salaries of a number of Americans who serve as his assistants. His own salary is $6,500 a year, and he also gets living quarters.

Mr. Vick is regarded as exceptionally well qualified for the place. One of the advantages supposed to lie in the American receivership is that the customs revenues are by it removed to neutral hands and are no longer to be preyed upon by aspiring revolutionists or grafting officials. From 1905, when the first temporary arrangement went into effect, until 1912 Santo Domingo had its first long period of freedom from revolution and internal strife. The neutralization of the customs receipts has been regarded as the cause of this peace in the turbulent republic. In 1912 there was continued political disturbance, but even during the revolution the custom houses remained unmolested by either faction in the struggle. It will be Mr. Vick's task to continue this absolute security of the customs receipts and maintain perfect neutrality toward all the contending political factions in the island.

European intervention in Santo Domingo seemed a certainty when President Roosevelt intervened in behalf of the republic. The Dominican government was saddled with a foreign and domestic indebtedness amounting, with interest, to about $30,000,000. Far from paying the interest, the Dominican government was increasing the debt by about a million dollars a year. As a result of centuries of misrule the revenues were being dishonestly dissipated. A succession of revolutions had reduced the government agency to a source of graft for which many factions were contending. In this situation the European creditors in 1904 demanded a settlement, and were prepared to take over the revenues of the government if their demands were not granted. As the Dominicans were unable to do what they asked, European intervention seemed certain.

The United States then negotiated the modus vivendi, which was to hold in force while a treaty was being negotiated. The treaty, under which the receivership is now conducted, was ratified by the United States senate and the Dominican congress and went into effect July 8, 1907. Meantime under the modus vivendi there had been issued bonds of the Dominican government to the amount of $20,000,000. This was for the purpose of making a settlement with the foreign creditors and paying for certain public improvements necessary to the utilization of the island resources. Though the nominal debt was $30,000,000 it was scaled down by the United States in making allowance for fraud and dishonest claims to about $17,000,000.

The bonds bear interest at 5 per cent, making the annual charge for the service of the loan $1,000,000 a year. It is provided in the treaty that each month the American receiver-general shall pay to the Guaranty Trust company of New York, the fiscal agent of the loan, the sum of $100,000. This is $200,000 in excess of the annual $1,000,000 required, and the balance is applied to the amortization of the bonds. In addition it is provided that whenever the collections for any year shall exceed $3,000,000, half of the surplus shall be applied to the amortization of the bonds.

Highly satisfactory progress has been made toward the repayment of the principal of the $20,000,000 loan, inasmuch as the revenues of the republic have nearly doubled under the American receivership. After the expenses of the receivership have been paid and the interest charges and sinking fund taken care of, the Dominican government gets what is left. Far from being a hardship, the effect of the receivership has been to give the Dominican government more money for its own purposes than it ever had before, even in the days when it did not pay a cent on its indebtedness. The first real roads in the republic, outside of the towns, have been built with funds supplied by the receivership, and other public improvements have been made possible.

What the receivership has really done for the Dominican government is shown by the fact that whereas the customs receipts were only about $2,000,000 a year before the receivership, the receipts for 1912 were $3,642,861. This is the highest figure ever attained, and collections for the first four months of the present calendar year indicate that the total receipts for 1913 will exceed $4,000,000.

W. E. Pulliam, Mr. Vick's predecessor, effected many reforms in the administration of the Dominican customs which will assist Mr. Vick materially when he takes charge. It was found that one reason for the small receipts lay in the dishonesty of the collectors. The men whom the American receiver expelled from the service found difficulty in understanding why there should be any objection to their modest peculations. Similarly, it was found that other men in the customs service were grafting by permitting goods to enter without duty upon payment of tribute to them. This, of course, many importers were only too glad to do.

One of the remarkable features of the effects of the receivership is that receipts were increased through the reduction of the customs dues. A cut of 50 per cent was made in the export duties and a reduction of 15 per cent in the import duties. The result was to increase both exports and imports.

The former receiver-general found that while such articles as champagne, silks and automobiles, used solely by the rich, were being admitted practically duty free, the cotton cloths, which are the sole source of clothes for the poorer classes, were being taxed almost 100 per cent. Mr. Pulliam induced the Dominican government to reverse this arrangement, with salutary effect both upon the condition of the poorer people and upon the state of the treasury.

Though Mr. Vick will be the head of the only non-political government department in all Latin America as custodian of the customs receipts; he will really be a tremendous factor in the political stability of the republic. With the American minister he is the personification of the pledge of the United States that the Dominican government shall conduct itself honorably in its financial obligations to foreigners. The office of the receiver-general and the American legation in Santo Domingo city are the bulwarks of Dominican stability, peace and good government.

As a result of this peculiar relation of the United States to Santo Domingo the Washington authorities have been obliged to take a friendly hand in the settlement of the Dominican political troubles. The rebellion which followed the tyrannical rule of Eladio Victoria and his dictator-like nephew, Elfredo Victoria—the latter a soldier who got into power in the confusion following the assassination of President Caceres—was really settled through the intercession of the United States. A commission, of which Brig. Gen. Frank McIntyre, chief of the bureau of insular affairs of the war department, was one of the members, brought about the compromise by which President Victoria and his nephew retired from the government and the prelate of Santo Domingo, Archbishop Nouel, came in as temporary president, to hold office until general elections could be held. This compromise was effected last December, but a few weeks ago Archbishop Nouel relinquished his task and went to Europe in search of lost health. Without any turmoil or disorder the Dominican congress elected Jose Bordas, a senator who had joined in the rebellion of 1912, to succeed him. Only the influence of the United States kept more trouble from breaking out upon the withdrawal of the archbishop.

The city of Santo Domingo, the capital of the republic, is full of historical associations. It is the site of one of the first settlements made in the western hemisphere by Christopher Columbus. At the entrance to the harbor stands the ancient stone fort and castle erected by his brother, Diego Columbus, made governor of the colony. Half a mile further up the Ozama river stands a great tree, to the great trunk of which tradition says Columbus tied his ships.

Just around the corner from the offices which Mr. Vick will occupy are the ruins of a great cathedral, the first stone church ever built in the western world. Near by, on the old plaza of Santo Domingo, stands the new cathedral, itself centuries old. In it lies a metal casket said to contain the bones of the great admiral. The Spaniards thought they took the bones of Christopher Columbus to Havana, but there is evidence that they took those of his brother, the former governor.

records.summary_en: The New Hampshire Farmer and Weekly Union reported that Minister Sullivan successfully resolved the Dominican civil conflict, announcing a U.S. policy that rejected armed rebellion in favor of electoral remedies and constitutional governance. Following a battle on October 2, Commander Nulton of the Nashville and Receiver Walter W. Vick transported deadlocked peace envoys from Puerto Plata to Santo Domingo City. Negotiations at the capital concluded with a comprehensive peace accord accepted by all factions.
records.summary_es: The New Hampshire Farmer and Weekly Union informó que el ministro Sullivan resolvió con éxito el conflicto civil dominicano, proclamando una política de los EE. UU. que descartaba la sublevación armada en favor de los cauces electorales y la gobernanza constitucional. Tras un combate librado el 2 de octubre, el comandante Nulton del *Nashville* y el receptor Walter W. Vick trasladaron desde Puerto Plata a la ciudad de Santo Domingo a los delegados de paz cuyas gestiones se hallaban trabadas. Las negociaciones en la capital desembocaron en un amplio tratado de paz aceptado por todas las facciones.

The American policy as announced by Mr. Sullivan has been accepted joyously by all parties regardless of political affiliations. The American minister -arrived at Santo Domingo city from the United States on Sept. 17 and immediately brought about an armistice between the rebels and the government troops fighting in the northern department. Since then negotiations had been in progress continuously with the result that what promised to be the most sanguinary revolution in the history of the Dominican republic has been averted. The last battle was fought on Oct. 2, when the government forces in the vicinity of Puerto Plata attacked the rebels. As a result of the intervention of Commander Louis M. Nulton of the United States cruiser Nashville and Walter W. Vick, general receiver of customs, the revolutionary and governmental peace commissioners which had reached a deadlock at Puerto Plata were urged to come to Santo Domingo city, where the rebels could treat direct with the government and with the friendly co-operation of the American minister. records.summary_en: The Springfield Weekly Republican prints a dispatch: the revolution headed by Gen. Horatio Vasques against the government of Provisional President Jose Bordas Valdez is thus brought to an end. The American minister's action in bringing about a settlement of the differences between the government and the rebels is the first successful administration of the United States government's new Latin-American policy with regard to the Dominican republic, which is to the effect that force of arms can never again settle any question in that country. Mr. Sullivan has made it known that the last civil war in the republic has been fought. In the future any uprising, he says, will be stamped out as criminal without a conference being held between the opposing factions, the United States government supporting the constitutional authority against force regardless of the merits of the issue. The people of San Domingo are being instructed that the remedy for future grievances lies in the free ballot at a future election. The American policy as announced by Mr. Sullivan has been accepted joyously by all parties regardless of political affiliations. The last battle was fought on the 2d, when the government forces in the vicinity of Puerto Plata attacked the rebels.

The people of Santo Domingo are being instructed that the remedy for future grievances lies in the free ballot at an election.

records.headline: The Pinedale Roundup prints a feature: Walter W. Vick, of New Jersey
records.summary_en: The Pinedale Roundup prints a feature: Walter W. Vick, of New Jersey, has been appointed by President Wilson receiver-general of the customs of the republic of Santo Domingo, thus continuing a novel experiment in national finance inaugurated in 1905. It is the first case in which a bankrupt nation has accepted another nation to act as receiver of its revenues and stand between it and its creditors during the settlement of its outstanding obligations. At the present time the Dominican republic has more money to spend for proper purposes than ever before, while ample provision is being made for paying out its indebtedness at an early date. The debt of $30,000,000 has been reduced to $17,000,000, while customs dues have been reduced, trade increased, misrule brought to an end, and the blessings of peace established in the formerly turbulent country.
records.summary_es: The Pinedale Roundup publica un reportaje: de Nueva Jersey, Walter W. Vick ha sido nombrado por el presidente Wilson receptor general de las aduanas de la república de Santo Domingo, continuando así un novedoso experimento en las finanzas nacionales inaugurado en 1905. Es el primer caso en que una nación en bancarrota ha aceptado que otra nación actúe como receptor de sus rentas y se interponga entre ella y sus acreedores durante la liquidación de sus obligaciones pendientes. En la actualidad, la república dominicana tiene más dinero para gastar en fines adecuados que nunca antes, mientras se provee ampliamente para pagar su deuda en una fecha temprana. La deuda de $30,000,000 se ha reducido a $17,000,000, mientras los derechos de aduana se han reducido, el comercio ha aumentado, el mal gobierno ha llegado a su fin, y las bendiciones de la paz se han establecido en el país antes turbulento.

records.headline: This article explains that the United States government is the custodian of the Dominican revenues under a treaty
records.summary_en: This article explains that the United States government is the custodian of the Dominican revenues under a treaty, standing sponsor for the conservation of the public funds and the settlement of the republic's debts, and that President Wilson appointed Mr. Vick to administer the receivership, his salary of $6,500 a year being paid by the Dominican government. It says the removal of the customs revenues to neutral hands gave Santo Domingo its first long period of freedom from revolution, from 1905 to 1912, and recounts how European creditors in 1904 demanded settlement of a debt of about $30,000,000, leading to the modus vivendi, the treaty that took effect on July 8, 1907, and a $20,000,000 bond issue.
records.summary_es: Este artículo explica que el gobierno de los Estados Unidos es el custodio de los ingresos dominicanos en virtud de un tratado, garante de la conservación de los fondos públicos y del arreglo de las deudas de la república, y que el presidente Wilson nombró al señor Vick para administrar la receptoría, con un sueldo de 6.500 dólares al año pagado por el gobierno dominicano. Dice que el traslado de los ingresos aduaneros a manos neutrales dio a Santo Domingo su primer largo período sin revoluciones, de 1905 a 1912, y cuenta cómo los acreedores europeos exigieron en 1904 el arreglo de una deuda de unos 30.000.000 de dólares, lo que llevó al modus vivendi, al tratado que entró en vigor el 8 de julio de 1907 y a una emisión de bonos de 20.000.000 de dólares.

records.headline: The Washington Herald prints an item: James F. Stutesman, of Crawfordsville
records.summary_en: The Washington Herald prints an item: James F. Stutesman, of Crawfordsville, Ind., carrying along with him the title of Commissioner General of the United States Commission of the Panama-Pacific Exposition to Central America and the West Indies, attended a dinner at Santo Domingo given by the President of the Dominican Republic, at which it was suggested by Mr. Stutesman that the bones of Columbus be removed from the cathedral and placed at the bow of the battleship Oregon, which will lead the procession of ships through the Panama Canal to the exposition. Senor Don Francisco J. Peynado, Minister at Washington of the Dominican Republic, endorsed the plan heartily. Then the fun started. There has been controversy for more than twenty-five years as to the resting place of Columbus.

records.summary_en: The Newark Evening Star and Newark Advertiser prints a dispatch of November 21: a five-fold increase in the foreign trade of San Domingo has been one of the beneficial results of the six years' operations of the 'Dominican convention' under which the United States supervises the customs collection of that country, Professor Jacob Hollander, of Johns Hopkins University, told the Clark University conference on Latin America today at Worcester, Mass. Professor Hollander was financial adviser of the Dominican republic from 1908 to 1910. 'The foreign trade of San Domingo for 1911-12, the latest fiscal year for which figures are available,' he said, 'aggregated nearly $20,600,900, as compared with some $6,000,000 for the year preceding the convention. Little short of a revolution, social, political and economic, has been wrought in the country. The people of the island, protected from rapine and bloodshed, are fairly on the way to becoming a decent peasantry, an industrious and stable one, as sub-tropical conditions are likely to evolve.' Professor Philip Brown, of Princeton, former minister to Honduras, advocated a union of the Central American republics and urged that the United States take the initiative in bringing it about. Professor Hiram Bingham, of Yale, and George K. Tucker spoke on the Monroe Doctrine.

records.headline: The Sun prints a dispatch: the Dolphin probably will go to Porto Rico
records.summary_en: The Sun prints a dispatch: the Dolphin probably will go to Porto Rico and take aboard there a number of American officials in Porto Rico who are to join the 'observing' representatives. It is not the present intention that Mr. Bryan's representatives, attached to the Latin American division of the State Department, shall go to Santo Domingo on the Dolphin. They probably will proceed by way of Key West, Havana and Guantanamo, and thence by the gunboat Nashville over to Santo Domingo. Secretary Bryan was most uncommunicative regarding his plans for action in the Dominican republic. It was admitted, however, that this Government is trying to insure the fairness of the elections as a result of assurances given last summer, when through the efforts of the United States the revolution was brought to an end. The plan of having 'observers' has been adopted as the most expedient procedure in view of the short time between now and election day. The fact that the Assembly to be elected is to revise the Constitution, especially with reference to the provisions for elections of a President, gives the coming elections more than usual importance. It is realized that the placing of a few 'observers' in the Dominican provinces will not effect anything like a supervision of the elections by the United States.

El plan de tener 'observadores' ha sido adoptado como el procedimiento más conveniente en vista del corto tiempo entre hoy y el día de las elecciones. El hecho de que la Asamblea que se elegirá deberá revisar la Constitución, especialmente en lo que se refiere a las disposiciones para la elección de un presidente, da a las próximas elecciones una importancia más que ordinaria. Se comprende que la colocación de unos pocos 'observadores' en las provincias dominicanas no logrará nada parecido a una supervisión de las elecciones por parte de los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: The Washington Herald prints an item: the steamer Seminole
records.summary_en: The Washington Herald prints an item: the steamer Seminole, with four passengers and a crew of 100 on board, has been wrecked on a coral reef near Puerto Plata, Santo Domingo. News of the accident was received here today. First news of the wreck was received by the Maritime Exchange, where a bulletin was posted announcing that the steamer was badly damaged. Officials of the Clyde Steamship Company, which owns the Seminole, said that the ship would not be a total loss, according to their dispatches. According to the report of Capt. Carey, commander of the ship, she struck the reef while trying to enter Puerto Plata Harbor. The ship then was beached.

La noticia del accidente se recibió aquí hoy. La primera noticia del naufragio se recibió en la Bolsa Marítima, donde se fijó un boletín que anunciaba que el vapor estaba muy averiado. Funcionarios de la Clyde Steamship Company, propietaria del Seminole, dijeron que el barco no sería una pérdida total, según sus despachos. Según el informe del capitán Carey, comandante del barco, este chocó contra el arrecife al tratar de entrar al puerto de Puerto Plata. El barco fue entonces varado.

records.headline: The Bridgeport Evening Farmer prints a dispatch: the Washington government
records.summary_en: The Bridgeport Evening Farmer prints a dispatch: the Washington government decided to send some observers speaking the language of San Domingo to act as impartial witnesses but not as referees or officials, so that in case of dispute it would have persons to turn to for impartial testimony. The United States does not intend to supervise or interfere with the approaching elections in the Dominican Republic. A special commission from Washington will merely observe the election as 'friendly and impartial spectators.' That was the way President Wilson today outlined informally the mission of State Department officials now on their way to San Domingo. President Wilson made it clear that the United States had used its good offices in persuading the revolutionists to lay down their arms on the promise that everything possible within international right would be done by the United States to insure fair elections. It was pointed out that the commission was unofficial even to the extent of not desiring recognition from the government authorities of the island. The protest from San Domingo, it was explained at the White House today, was founded on the belief that the United States intended a supervision of the election, and now that the notion has been dispelled by the State Department the administration here is confident that there will be no objection to the presence of the American observers.

Los Estados Unidos no tienen la intención de supervisar ni interferir en las próximas elecciones en la República Dominicana. Una comisión especial de Washington se limitará a observar la elección como 'espectadores amistosos e imparciales'. Así fue como el presidente Wilson esbozó hoy informalmente la misión de los funcionarios del Departamento de Estado ahora en camino a San Domingo. El presidente Wilson dejó claro que los Estados Unidos habían usado sus buenos oficios para persuadir a los revolucionarios de que depusieran las armas, con la promesa de que se haría todo lo posible, dentro del derecho internacional, por parte de los Estados Unidos para asegurar unas elecciones limpias. Se señaló que la comisión era no oficial hasta el punto de no desear reconocimiento de las autoridades gubernamentales de la isla. La protesta de San Domingo, se explicó hoy en la Casa Blanca, se fundaba en la creencia de que los Estados Unidos pretendían una supervisión de la elección, y ahora que la noción ha sido disipada por el Departamento de Estado, la administración de aquí confía en que no habrá objeción a la presencia de los observadores estadounidenses.

It was stated today at the Bureau of Insular Affairs that the transfer was not made upon order from the War Department. It is understood that a cousin of the American minister has been appointed to a lucrative position under the Dominican government. The Secretary of State, Mr. Bryan, declined absolutely to comment upon the Dominican situation. It is understood that two officials of the Department of State are soon to leave here for Santo Domingo: Hugh S. Gibson, formerly secretary of the legation at Havana, Cuba, and Jordan Herbert Stabler, of the Bureau of Latin American Affairs. The minister from Santo Domingo, Senor Peynado, conferred with John Bassett Moore, counsellor of the State Department, for several hours today. John T. Mann, who has been removed from the post of director of public works of the Dominican Republic, to which position he was appointed through the direct influence of the State Department under the last administration, called at the State Department Saturday to answer charges.

records.headline: The Evening Star prints an item: Minister Peynado went to the State Department
records.summary_en: The Evening Star prints an item: Minister Peynado went to the State Department today, under instructions from his government, to follow up the verbal statement with a written protest, although it has been declared that these State Department agents are not to 'supervise' the elections. The Dominican officials say they cannot see how a representative of the State Department can visit Santo Domingo for the purpose indicated without some official status, although the State Department officials insist that such is the case. Before the elections occur next Monday the United States Navy will be represented in Dominican waters by at least four vessels, counting as one the Eagle, a survey ship, now at work on the coast of the island. The gunboat Dolphin, which sailed from Washington Saturday, is due at Samana Bay, where the insurgent element has been active in the past, about Wednesday; the Petrel already is in Dominican waters, and the Nashville will pick up the State Department's agents at Santiago, on the south coast of Cuba, tomorrow and convey them to Santo Domingo City. The agents are Jordan H. Stabler and F. A. Sterling of the Latin American bureau of the State Department, and Hugh S. Gibson, formerly secretary of the American embassy at Havana, Cuba. The State Department has made no explanation of the part the officers are to play in assisting the islanders to hold a fair and free election.

records.headline: The Salt Lake Tribune prints a dispatch: Washington, Dec. 8.
records.summary_en: The Salt Lake Tribune prints a dispatch: Washington, Dec. 8. The United States does not intend to supervise or interfere with the approaching elections in the Dominican republic. A special commission from Washington will merely observe the election as 'friendly and impartial spectators.' That was the way President Wilson today outlined informally the mission of State Department officials now on their way to San Domingo. President Wilson made it clear that the United States had used its good offices in persuading the revolutionists to lay down their arms on the promise that everything possible, within international right, would be done by the United States to insure fair elections. The paper also prints an item under the head 'PROTECTORATE IS NOT INTENDED BY THE U. S.': Washington, Dec. 8. President Wilson told callers today that the United States did not wish to establish a protectorate over any country of Central America or over any other part of the globe. Published reports that the United States contemplated a new and far-reaching policy with respect to Central America, especially Nicaragua, brought a prompt denial from the White House.

Así fue como el presidente Wilson esbozó hoy informalmente la misión de los funcionarios del Departamento de Estado ahora en camino a San Domingo. El presidente Wilson dejó claro que los Estados Unidos habían usado sus buenos oficios para persuadir a los revolucionarios de que depusieran las armas, con la promesa de que se haría todo lo posible, dentro del derecho internacional, por parte de los Estados Unidos para asegurar unas elecciones limpias. El periódico publica también una nota bajo el título 'PROTECTORATE IS NOT INTENDED BY THE U. S.': Washington, 8 de diciembre. El presidente Wilson dijo hoy a quienes lo visitaron que los Estados Unidos no deseaban establecer un protectorado sobre ningún país de América Central ni sobre ninguna otra parte del globo. Informes publicados de que los Estados Unidos contemplaban una política nueva y de gran alcance con respecto a América Central, especialmente Nicaragua, provocaron una pronta desmentida de la Casa Blanca.

records.headline: The New Haven Union prints an item: a copy of a message sent
records.summary_en: The New Haven Union prints an item: a copy of a message sent to American Minister Sullivan sets forth in diplomatic language that the watchers sent by the United States are simply to lend moral support to the efforts President Bordas is pledged to make for a fair election. Besides the three officials from the State Department, Hugh S. Gibson, Jordan H. Stabler, and Frederick A. Sterling, about 300 Americans in the Porto Rican public service will be sent to Santo Domingo by Gov. Yager. While there are twelve provinces in the Dominican Republic, there are only 60 polling places, so that a fairly close scrutiny can be made by the Americans. The paper prints Mr. Bryan's message to Mr. Sullivan: 'Please say to President Bordas that the President has planned to send a number of Americans to visit the principal polling places on election day, not as a "commission" for which this Government asks any official recognition, but only as individuals, to lend moral support by their presence to the efforts which President Bordas has so fully pledged himself to make that the elections shall be free and uninfluenced in every respect, and in order that, if any questions should arise as to the good faith of any one concerned, undeniably impartial witnesses may be available to bear testimony as to exactly what happened.'

records.headline: The Salt Lake Tribune prints an item: Washington, Dec. 9. Secretary Bryan today
records.summary_en: The Salt Lake Tribune prints an item: Washington, Dec. 9. Secretary Bryan today declined to comment on a published report that information had been laid before the State Department regarding the conduct of James M. Sullivan of New York, the new minister to the Dominican republic. Charles B. Curtis, former secretary of the legation there, was in the capital recently and is said to have talked with officials about certain negotiations for concessions in Santo Domingo. Mr. Curtis also talked privately with friends, but declined to permit himself to be quoted. Assistant Secretary Osborne of the State Department said today that no charges had been laid before the department and was inclined to discredit statements regarding Minister Sullivan's affairs. Secretary Bryan, however, saying he had not seen all the published reports, refused flatly to discuss the subject. Various reports, however, are being discussed in congressional and diplomatic circles.

Curtis, ex secretario de la legación allí, estuvo recientemente en la capital y se dice que habló con funcionarios sobre ciertas negociaciones para concesiones en Santo Domingo. El Sr. Curtis también habló en privado con amigos, pero se negó a permitir que se le citara. El subsecretario Osborne, del Departamento de Estado, dijo hoy que no se habían presentado cargos ante el departamento y se inclinaba a desacreditar las declaraciones sobre los asuntos del ministro Sullivan. El secretario Bryan, sin embargo, diciendo que no había visto todos los informes publicados, se negó rotundamente a discutir el tema. Varios informes, sin embargo, están siendo discutidos en círculos congresionales y diplomáticos.

records.headline: The Washington Times prints an item: reports current here to the effect
records.summary_en: The Washington Times prints an item: reports current here to the effect that New York capitalists interested in affairs in the Dominican Republic had something to do with the recommendations upon which James M. Sullivan was named by Mr. Bryan as the minister to Santo Domingo. The administration here is stirred up over the gossip. The relationship between Minister Sullivan and T. J. Sullivan, an American promoter interested in a new railroad project on the island, is displeasing to officials here. Friends of the administration insist that in due time the charges will be shown to be false, but it is admitted that Mr. Bryan's refusal to discuss the matter in any particular is complicating matters considerably. As yet no reply has been received by the Department of State to the telegram of explanation sent by Secretary Bryan to President Bordas regarding the mission of the 30 'disinterested, unofficial' observers whom the State Department is sending to the Dominican republic. While it is not thought that President Bordas will refuse permission to these observers to witness the elections, his failure to accept the explanation in any positive way is taken to mean that their presence will not be welcome.

records.headline: The Newark Evening Star and Newark Advertiser prints: Mr. Mann resigned
records.summary_en: The Newark Evening Star and Newark Advertiser prints: Mr. Mann resigned his post because of friction with Minister Sullivan. When asked whether he was investigating Mr. Sullivan's conduct since his arrival in Santo Domingo, Mr. Bryan said no representations had been made which would incline him to make a statement. According to reports, Mr. Mann's resignation is said to have been the result of activities by Sullivan, which made it impossible for him to retain his post. The program then was for Minister Sullivan's friend to get the post, which carries with it great influence over the awarding of contracts for government work in the Dominican republic. It was learned from an authoritative source that Mr. Bryan did not select Mr. Sullivan for the post, as had been supposed, but that the decision to appoint him was reached at the White House without any recommendation from the State Department. It was learned also that Senator Hughes, of New Jersey, was not his political sponsor for the Dominican post. Representative Hamill, of New Jersey, was Sullivan's strongest backer for political preferment. In fact it was said here that the White House named Sullivan chiefly for the purpose of pleasing Mr. Hamill. Senator Martine also spoke a word for Sullivan.

Se supo de una fuente autorizada que el Sr. Bryan no seleccionó al Sr. Sullivan para el puesto, como se había supuesto, sino que la decisión de nombrarlo se tomó en la Casa Blanca sin recomendación alguna del Departamento de Estado. Se supo también que el senador Hughes, de Nueva Jersey, no fue su patrocinador político para el puesto dominicano. El representante Hamill, de Nueva Jersey, fue el partidario más fuerte de Sullivan para el ascenso político. De hecho, se dijo aquí que la Casa Blanca nombró a Sullivan principalmente con el propósito de complacer al Sr. Hamill. El senador Martine también dijo una palabra por Sullivan.

records.headline: The Sun prints an item: the decision to appoint Mr. Sullivan
records.summary_en: The Sun prints an item: the decision to appoint Mr. Sullivan was reached at the White House without any recommendation from the State Department. It was learned also that Senator Hughes of New Jersey was not his political sponsor for the Dominican post. Representative Hamill of New Jersey was Sullivan's strongest backer for political preferment; in fact it was said here today that the White House named Sullivan chiefly for the purpose of pleasing Mr. Hamill. Senator Martine also spoke a word for Sullivan. One interesting fact about the selection is that Sullivan was named without an active endorsement of his candidacy by Senator O'Gorman, from Sullivan's own state, New York. It was learned today that the reported award of a railroad concession in Santo Domingo to T. J. Sullivan was far from an accomplished fact. The project in question is one which has been under discussion in the Dominican republic for years, but still is a long way from realization. Before any concession can be granted under the proposed plan the approval of the State Department will be necessary, as the matter involves an increase of the indebtedness of the Dominican government, over which the United States Government, as receiver, exercises full control.

records.summary_en: The Washington Herald prints an item: Following the recent speech of President Wilson in the South, in which the President asserted that the United States will not seek the acquisition of one foot of South American territory by force of arms, Mr. Vick reported, the honesty of the Wilson policy has been impressed on all Latin-American nations, and especially Mexico, by the way in which the Dominican republic situation has been handled. Prior to his conferences at the White House and State Department, Mr. Vick, it was learned, completed arrangements for a number of Dominican projects of importance. Chief among these was the settlement of his plan to light the Dominican Republic coast so as to make safer the Mona passage to the Panama Canal, a project vitally affecting the American merchant marine and all shipping using the canal. Mr. Vick's plan will be carried through, it was learned. Arrangements also were completed by Mr. Vick for the building of two revenue cutters, to cost $30,000 each. Two new custom-houses, each to cost 150,000, are to be erected in the Dominican Republic as soon as possible, as a result of Vick's trip to Washington. Mr. Vick terminated his stay in Washington with a conference with Secretary of War Garrison, and left the National Capital at midnight. He is to spend the holidays with relatives, and will return to the island after Christmas.

records.headline: The Daily Kennebec Journal prints a feature on the Columbus remains.
records.summary_en: The Daily Kennebec Journal prints a feature on the Columbus remains. A leaden case bore an inscription on the top; it read in Spanish: 'Discoverer of America, First Admiral.' Believing this to be an important find, the Bishop invited all the high officials of the Dominican Republic to be present when the leaden case was opened. Before the President of Santo Domingo, his entire Cabinet, the clergy and many of the foreign Consuls the case was opened. Inside were human bones. On the under side of the lid was an inscription reading: 'Illustrious and Renowned Man, Christopher Columbus.' When the people of Havana heard of this find they at once became indignant and pronounced it a fraud. The remains of Christopher Columbus were in their cathedral, they averred. They dispatched historical students to investigate the matter. These investigators reported in favor of the tomb in the cathedral of Havana. Colmeiro, a member of the Spanish Academy of History, also reported the Santo Domingo case as without authenticity. An official report was made to the King of Spain. Some of the Cuban arguments were that the term 'America' was not in general use as it appeared on the Santo Domingo case, and that if the case had any authenticity it should have had the word 'Indies,' which was the common term for America in Columbus's time. The Dominicans, however, asserted that such a use of the word was not without precedent at the time.

records.summary_en: The Springfield Weekly Republican prints an item: the Dominican government at Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, last week ordered the arrest of a number of persons in connection with a conspiracy, said to have been discovered in the course of the general elections held on Monday and Tuesday. There has been no disorder.

Los candidatos del partido de coalición anunciaron su retiro de la contienda como protesta, y se entiende que los resultados de las elecciones probablemente favorecerán a los candidatos del partido popular. No ha habido ningún desorden.

Sullivan, has induced the warring factions in that country to sign a peace pact, and the revolution headed by Gen. records.headline: The Evening Star prints an extract: the very spirit and letter of the convention of 1907 forecasted a constructive achievement for the sole benefit of a sister republic
records.summary_en: The Evening Star prints an extract: the very spirit and letter of the convention of 1907 forecasted a constructive achievement for the sole benefit of a sister republic, which can be accomplished to the honor and credit of the American government by the sincere conformance of the beneficiary party. The extract gives examples of the very genuine character of the benefits resulting to the Dominican republic through the existence of the receivership. It demonstrates clearly the unlimited possibilities of the future with deterrent influences removed and the pathway to administrative effectiveness cleared of the restraining jungle growth. The process merely entails frank understanding and earnest co-operation by the officials of the Dominican republic. Any suspicion or misconception of the aims and purposes will render nil the effort to regenerate the customs service in keeping with the standard it should maintain. The American personnel, laboring under many discouraging handicaps, is responsible for the rehabilitation evident and should be accorded full measure of credit. The vista of future progress is bright and the natural resources of Santo Domingo almost without parallel. The means of stimulation are readily available to the Dominican government; it is to be hoped the receivership, in its eagerness to accomplish completely its mission and purposes, will be substantially supported and encouraged.

Demuestra claramente las ilimitadas posibilidades del futuro, eliminadas las influencias disuasorias y despejado el camino hacia la eficacia administrativa del restrictivo crecimiento selvático. El proceso solo implica una comprensión franca y una cooperación sincera por parte de los funcionarios de la república dominicana. El personal americano, que trabaja bajo muchas dificultades desalentadoras, es responsable de la rehabilitación ya evidente y se le debe reconocer pleno crédito. Peynado, minister here from the Dominican Republic for two years, has tendered his resignation, and, in spite of his government's cabled reply, urging that he remain here, will leave at the end of this month for Santo Domingo. It is intimated that the minister may be a candidate for president of the island republic in the spring elections.

records.summary_en: The Bridgeport Evening Farmer highlighted the success of President Wilson's Caribbean diplomacy in Santo Domingo, where Minister James M. Sullivan facilitated the end of civil conflict and secured commitments for free elections and civil liberties. A forthcoming constitutional convention planned to enact reforms and select a new president through the ballot. The article also provided a cultural and historical overview of the Dominican Republic, noting its Spanish heritage and multiracial population.

Sullivan facilitó la cesación de la guerra civil y garantizó compromisos de comicios libres y libertades ciudadanas. Una próxima asamblea constituyente contemplaba sancionar reformas y designar un nuevo mandatario por sufragio. El artículo ofreció además un compendio cultural e histórico de la República Dominicana, aludiendo a su legado hispánico y su población mestiza.

The Dominican government promised to accord to all factions the right of free ballot, free press and free speech. The Dominican Republic, or Santo Domingo, as we knew it in the old "geographies," holds great possibilities for development. While French is the official and general tongue of Haiti, the Dominicans speak Spanish, although many natives also have a knowledge of French and English. The population consists of a mixed race of the aborigines, and the first Spanish inhabitants, and of negroes and mulattoes, the last named being in the majority. There are also a considerable number of whites of Spanish descent. Roman Catholicism is the state religion, although other forms of worship are tolerated. records.headline: The Mirror and Farmer prints a profile: Sullivan has nerve
records.summary_en: The Mirror and Farmer prints a profile: Sullivan has nerve, and the Washington government knew it when it picked him as a pacifier. Down where the Morales, the Torribios, the Ariases and the Vasquezes and a long line of other revolutionists have tried since nobody knows when to reduce the population of the Dominican Republic, James M. Sullivan, the new envoy of the Wilson administration, is bringing order out of chaos. Landing at Puerto Plata one September day, Sullivan began telling both sides that they were wrong, kept spreading the gospel of national order and amity and concord, and finally induced Gen. Horacio Vasquez, the revolutionary leader whose pride had been hurt by President Bordas' plan to sell a Puerto Plata and Santiago railroad to interests not pleasing to Vasquez, to lay down arms after a month of gory campaign. Sullivan has a delightful task in maintaining a governmental status quo in a country that has had four presidents since Caceres was elected for a six-year term less than six years ago. And Caceres, by the way, one day fell dead in the American legation.
records.summary_es: The Mirror and Farmer publica un perfil: Sullivan tiene nervio, y el gobierno de Washington sabía que lo tenía cuando lo escogió como pacificador. Abajo, donde los Morales, los Torribios, los Ariases y los Vasquezes y una larga línea de otros revolucionarios han tratado desde nadie sabe cuándo de reducir la población de la República Dominicana, James M. Sullivan, el nuevo enviado de la administración Wilson, está sacando el orden del caos. Al desembarcar en Puerto Plata un día de septiembre, Sullivan empezó a decir a ambos bandos que estaban equivocados, siguió difundiendo el evangelio del orden, la amistad y la concordia nacionales, y finalmente indujo al general Horacio Vasquez, el líder revolucionario cuyo orgullo había sido herido por el plan del presidente Bordas de vender un ferrocarril de Puerto Plata y Santiago a intereses que no agradaban a Vasquez, a deponer las armas tras un mes de campaña sangrienta. Sullivan tiene una tarea deliciosa al mantener un statu quo gubernamental en un país que ha tenido cuatro presidentes desde que Cáceres fue elegido por un período de seis años hace menos de seis años. Y Cáceres, por cierto, un día cayó muerto en la legación americana.

records.headline: The Richmond Virginian prints a dispatch: conditions in Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Richmond Virginian prints a dispatch: conditions in Santo Domingo are becoming so unsettled that the United States gunboat Nashville today was ordered to Puerto Plata, Santo Domingo, from Cape Haitien, Hayti. Revolutionists in the vicinity of Cape Haitien are still operating against the force of the Haitian government, but it was felt that the American warship would be even more needed at the Dominican port than on the Haitian coast. Puerto Plata is in the north of Santo Domingo, and has been for several years the hotbed of Dominican political troubles. It is the headquarters of Desiderio Arias, a chieftain who has been responsible for much of the recent trouble in Santo Domingo, and the district in that vicinity is usually made the field of operations for revolutionary forces.

Puerto Plata está en el norte de Santo Domingo, y ha sido durante varios años el foco de los disturbios políticos dominicanos. Es el cuartel general de Desiderio Arias, un caudillo que ha sido responsable de gran parte de los disturbios recientes en Santo Domingo, y el distrito en esa vecindad suele ser el campo de operaciones de las fuerzas revolucionarias.

records.headline: The Norwich Bulletin prints a dispatch under the head 'Against Insurrectionists'
records.summary_en: The Norwich Bulletin prints a dispatch under the head 'Against Insurrectionists': Washington, April 7. President Bordas of the Dominican republic has left Santo Domingo City for Santiago to take the field against the insurrectionists. Commander Blerer, on the gunboat Wheeling at Santo Domingo City, reported to the navy department today that a Dominican gunboat is carrying General Bordas and two hundred government troops to Puerto Plata, from whence they will go overland to Santiago. Despatches from the commander of the gunboat Nashville at Puerto Plata announced that government troops have driven the rebels under General Arias from Santiago, but that the railroad is not being operated except for a short distance out of Puerto Plata, as the insurrectionists have come down out of Santiago province as far as Biabonico. The government, the report said, has been impressing all available men at Puerto Plata into service to combat the rebels in the interior.

El presidente Bordas, de la república dominicana, ha salido de Santo Domingo rumbo a Santiago para tomar el campo contra los insurrectos. El comandante Blerer, en la cañonera Wheeling en Santo Domingo, informó hoy al Departamento de Marina que una cañonera dominicana lleva al general Bordas y doscientos soldados del gobierno a Puerto Plata, desde donde irán por tierra a Santiago. Despachos del comandante de la cañonera Nashville en Puerto Plata anunciaron que las tropas del gobierno han expulsado de Santiago a los rebeldes al mando del general Arias, pero que el ferrocarril no está operando excepto por un corto tramo desde Puerto Plata, ya que los insurrectos han bajado de la provincia de Santiago hasta Biabonico. El gobierno, según el informe, ha estado reclutando a la fuerza a todos los hombres disponibles en Puerto Plata para combatir a los rebeldes en el interior.

Both armies operating about Puerto Plata have promised to use no artillery near the town, Capt. Eberle said. records.headline: The Washington Herald prints a dispatch: Gen. Bordas, president of San Domingo
records.summary_en: The Washington Herald prints a dispatch: Gen. Bordas, president of San Domingo and leader of the government troops, was immediately cautioned about reckless firing into the town, he having guaranteed the safety of non-combatants. The government troops are entrenching outside of Puerto Plata under cover of rifle fire, Capt. Eberle reported. The Dominican gunboat Jacagua sailed eastward from Puerto Plata; her destination has not been ascertained. Commander Blerer, commanding the gunboat Wheeling, now at Santo Domingo city, reported today that 50,000 rounds of ammunition and a consignment of rifles was forced across the border in spite of the protest and opposition of the customhouse authorities at Commendador. The commander of the border revolutionists at Ouanaminthe has threatened the custom-house at Dajabon with a force of men whose number is not legibly printed. Telegraphic communication with Dajabon is interrupted, and Commander Blerer considers the situation acute. Reports reached here that a small force of revolutionists fired across the river near Old Bridge into San Domingo city Thursday night and then retreated. Lawlessness throughout the country continues to exist.

Las tropas del gobierno se están atrincherando fuera de Puerto Plata bajo la cobertura del fuego de fusilería, informó el capitán Eberle. La cañonera dominicana Jacagua zarpó hacia el este desde Puerto Plata; su destino no ha sido averiguado. La anarquía en todo el país continúa existiendo.

records.headline: Daily Kennebec Journal prints a dispatch: the latest activities of Dominican revolutionists
records.summary_en: Daily Kennebec Journal prints a dispatch: the latest activities of Dominican revolutionists caused no little concern among State and navy department officials. Commander Bierer of the gunboat at Santo Domingo City reported that the rebels had defied American officers in charge of a custom house near Comendador, and forced 50,000 rounds of ammunition across the border from Haiti. At Dajabon, also on the Haitien line, the commander reported, a revolutionary general, with 300 or 400 men, has threatened to attack the custom house and the situation there is 'considered acute.' While this is going on in the North, President Bordas continues his attack upon the rebel stronghold, Puerto Plata, and small revolutionary bands are operating in the vicinity of Santo Domingo City itself. On the night of May 14, the report said, rebels fired about 50 shots across the river at the capital and then disappeared. Captain Eberle of the United States cruiser Washington has been obliged to caution President Bordas to cease reckless firing into Puerto Plata, where the lives of Americans and other non-combatants have been endangered. Gen. Bordas had previously blockaded both Puerto Plata and Montecristi and his forces now are entrenching outside the former town for land attack.
records.summary_es: Daily Kennebec Journal publica un despacho: las últimas actividades de los revolucionarios dominicanos causaron no poca preocupación entre los funcionarios del Departamento de Estado y del Departamento de Marina. El comandante Bierer, de la cañonera en la ciudad de Santo Domingo, informó que los rebeldes habían desafiado a los oficiales americanos a cargo de una aduana cerca de Comendador, y forzaron el paso de 50,000 cartuchos de munición a través de la frontera desde Haití. En Dajabon, también en la línea haitiana, informó el comandante, un general revolucionario, con 300 o 400 hombres, ha amenazado con atacar la aduana y la situación allí es 'considerada aguda'. Mientras esto ocurre en el Norte, el presidente Bordas continúa su ataque contra el bastión rebelde de Puerto Plata, y pequeñas bandas revolucionarias están operando en las cercanías de la propia ciudad de Santo Domingo. En la noche del 14 de mayo, según el informe, los rebeldes dispararon unos 50 tiros a través del río contra la capital y luego desaparecieron. El capitán Eberle, del crucero Washington de los Estados Unidos, se ha visto obligado a advertir al presidente Bordas que cese el fuego imprudente contra Puerto Plata, donde las vidas de los americanos y otros no combatientes han sido puestas en peligro. El general Bordas había bloqueado previamente tanto Puerto Plata como Montecristi y sus fuerzas ahora se están atrincherando fuera de la primera ciudad para un ataque por tierra.

records.summary_en: The Evening Star prints a report: valuable sugar property inland from La Romana, in the Dominican Republic, is without protection, according to a report to the Navy Department today from Commander Bierer on the gunboat Wheeling at Santo Domingo City. records.headline: The Montgomery Advertiser prints reports by American naval commanders
records.summary_en: The Montgomery Advertiser prints reports by American naval commanders: from Puerto Plata, on the northern coast, where President Bordas, commanding the Federal troops, has raised the blockade, Captain Eberle of the cruiser Washington during the night sent a summary of conditions. The steamer Oregon was waiting off Puerto Plata that afternoon. Bordas forces opened artillery fire on rebel headquarters in Puerto Plata, with no injury to foreigners reported. A message from Receiver General Vick stated Sanchez was attacked Wednesday by rebel forces reported marching against the capital. The Castine arrived at Sanchez on Friday afternoon. Between 8 and 10 o'clock that evening, a brisk rifle engagement on the south and west sides of Puerto Plata, with occasional artillery fire by Bordas forces. Commander Carter of the gunboat Castine sent a report from Santo Domingo City: the governor of Samana province, with 100 men, was now there; revolutionists, with about 150 men, were on hills outside of Sanchez; desultory shooting by rebels Thursday and today; government troops did not return fire; no casualties; the railroad open for thirty miles, beyond that revolutionaries in control; no telegraphic communication.

El vapor Oregon esperaba frente a Puerto Plata esa tarde. Las fuerzas de Bordas abrieron fuego de artillería contra el cuartel general rebelde en Puerto Plata, sin que se reportaran daños a extranjeros. Un mensaje del receptor general Vick indicaba que Sanchez fue atacada el miércoles por fuerzas rebeldes que, según se informaba, marchaban contra la capital. El Castine llegó a Sanchez el viernes por la tarde. Entre las 8 y las 10 de la noche de ese día, un enérgico combate de fusilería en los lados sur y oeste de Puerto Plata, con fuego ocasional de artillería por parte de las fuerzas de Bordas. El comandante Carter, de la cañonera Castine, envió un informe desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo: el gobernador de la provincia de Samana, con 100 hombres, estaba ahora allí; revolucionarios, con unos 150 hombres, estaban en las colinas fuera de Sanchez; disparos esporádicos de los rebeldes el jueves y hoy; las tropas del gobierno no devolvieron el fuego; ninguna baja; el ferrocarril abierto por treinta millas, más allá los revolucionarios en control; sin comunicación telegráfica.

records.headline: The Forest City Press prints a dispatch: proposals for a conference of the various factions
records.summary_en: The Forest City Press prints a dispatch: proposals for a conference of the various factions involved in the revolution in Santo Domingo, with a view to bringing about a peaceful settlement, have been made by leaders in the conflict, according to a dispatch to the navy department today from Captain Eberle, of the United States cruiser Washington, now in Dominican waters. Captain Eberle reported that former President Jimenas informed the United States consul yesterday that Generals Arias and Pequers at Puerto Plata had suggested that a conference between Jimenas and General Vasquez be held at Puerto Plata. Captain Eberle also advised the department of reports that Monte Cristi is in military movement against President Bordas, although there has been no fighting. He added that the Monte Cristi communication with the capital had been cut.
records.summary_es: The Forest City Press publica: propuestas para una conferencia de las diversas facciones involucradas en la revolución en Santo Domingo, con miras a lograr un arreglo pacífico, han sido hechas por líderes en el conflicto, según un despacho enviado hoy al Departamento de Marina por el capitán Eberle, del crucero Washington de los Estados Unidos, ahora en aguas dominicanas. El capitán Eberle informó que el ex presidente Jimenas informó ayer al cónsul de los Estados Unidos que los generales Arias y Pequers, en Puerto Plata, habían sugerido que se celebrara una conferencia entre Jimenas y el general Vasquez en Puerto Plata. El capitán Eberle también avisó al Departamento de los informes de que Monte Cristi está en movimiento militar contra el presidente Bordas, aunque no ha habido lucha. Agregó que la comunicación de Monte Cristi con la capital había sido cortada.

records.headline: France and Germany Warn Government to Meet Financial Obligations
records.summary_en: France and Germany have warned Haiti that its customhouses will be seized unless arrangements are made to meet its outstanding financial obligations, according to reports reaching Washington. Secretary of State Bryan said no notice of such a step had reached the United States, but the cabinet discussed the situation at length. Officials noted that no treaty or arrangement would allow the United States to take charge of Haitian customs as it did in Santo Domingo, and pointed out that four American warships were already in Haitian waters while the German cruiser Strassburg lay in Dominican waters, within a few hours' sail of Port-au-Prince. Haiti's minister in Washington, Ulrich Duvivier, protested that his country was not a defaulting debtor and that the debts claimed were indemnities demanded by irresponsible foreigners.
records.summary_es: Francia y Alemania han advertido a Haití que sus aduanas serán embargadas si no se toman medidas para cumplir con sus obligaciones financieras pendientes, según informes llegados a Washington. El secretario de Estado Bryan declaró que no había llegado a los Estados Unidos ninguna notificación de tal medida, pero el gabinete discutió la situación extensamente. Las autoridades señalaron que ningún tratado ni acuerdo permitiría a los Estados Unidos hacerse cargo de las aduanas haitianas como lo hizo en Santo Domingo, e indicaron que cuatro buques de guerra estadounidenses ya se encontraban en aguas haitianas, mientras el crucero alemán Strassburg estaba en aguas dominicanas, a pocas horas de navegación de Puerto Príncipe. El ministro de Haití en Washington, Ulrich Duvivier, protestó que su país no era un deudor moroso y que las deudas reclamadas eran indemnizaciones exigidas por extranjeros irresponsables.
records.passage: serious situation in the island republic, torn within by revolution and besieged by creditors from without, was the subject of a long discussion at today's cabinet meeting. What the attitude of the United States might be was not indicated. Officials pointed out, however, there was no treaty or arrangement under which the United States might assume charge of Haitien customs as it did in the case of Santo Domingo. It also was recalled that the Washington government did not object when a British warship several months ago enforced payment of a Haitian debt. There are four American war vessels in Haitien waters now, including the battleship South Carolina. They have been protecting foreigners in cities around which government and rebel forces have been fighting. The German cruiser Strassburg is in Dominican waters, within a few hours sail of Port-au-Prince. The Haitien minister here, Ulrich Duvivier, earnestly protested today that his country is not a defaulting debtor and that stories of European intervention find their counterpart in reports in foreign newspapers that the United States is contemplating the same act. The minister declared the only “debts" that could be claimed were so-called indemnities demanded by certain irresponsible foreigners whose exploitation and law breaking had brought them to Justice. records.headline: The Times Dispatch prints a long dispatch: the warring forces
records.summary_en: The Times Dispatch prints a long dispatch: the warring forces in the island republic had been sufficiently warned when the American gunboat Machias used her four-inch guns to quiet the artillery of President Bordas, which was bombarding the rebel town of Puerto Plata. Four American naval vessels now are in Dominican waters. They carry a sufficient force to guarantee ample protection to foreign interests. Only a comparatively small number of the republic's inhabitants are said to be involved in the fighting. President Bordas, directing the siege of Puerto Plata, is said to command only about 200 soldiers. Between fighting spells the combatants fraternize. A Dominican gunboat recently destroyed the custom house at Azua, fifty miles west of San Domingo. American officials, charged with collection and administration of Dominican customs, gave warning that such attacks should not be repeated.

records.headline: The Evening Star prints: this government, it is officially declared
records.summary_en: The Evening Star prints: this government, it is officially declared, will not actually intervene so long as the lives and property of foreigners are not recklessly endangered by the contending factions. Administration officials indicated today that they thought the warring forces in the island republic had been sufficiently warned when the American gunboat Machias used her four-inch guns to silence the artillery of President Bordas, which was bombarding the rebel town of Puerto Plata. There is sufficient American naval force in Dominican waters to carry out this government's policy. The big battleship South Carolina, with the equivalent of a regiment of soldiers aboard in her personnel, is alongside the gunboat Machias in the harbor at Puerto Plata. The gunboat Castine is at Santo Domingo City and the gunboat Marietta is at Sanchez, on the northeast coast of the island, with other warships in adjacent waters. Unofficial reports to the State and Navy Departments have long been to the effect that the present political situation may be protracted for several weeks or even months, so long as the government is in receipt of its regular stipend from the American customs collections and the insurgents are in possession of ports that are not blockaded, through which they easily receive all the munitions of war and supplies for which they are able to pay.

Hay fuerza naval americana suficiente en aguas dominicanas para llevar a cabo la política de este gobierno. El gran acorazado South Carolina, con el equivalente de un regimiento de soldados a bordo en su personal, está junto a la cañonera Machias en el puerto de Puerto Plata. La cañonera Castine está en la ciudad de Santo Domingo y la cañonera Marietta está en Sanchez, en la costa nordeste de la isla, con otros buques de guerra en aguas adyacentes. Los informes no oficiales a los Departamentos de Estado y de Marina han sido durante mucho tiempo en el sentido de que la situación política actual puede prolongarse por varias semanas o incluso meses, mientras el gobierno esté recibiendo su estipendio regular de las recaudaciones de las aduanas americanas y los insurgentes estén en posesión de puertos que no están bloqueados y por los cuales reciben fácilmente todas las municiones de guerra y suministros por los que son capaces de pagar.

records.headline: Daily Kennebec Journal prints a dispatch: at the state department
records.summary_en: Daily Kennebec Journal prints a dispatch: at the state department, it is said, the question discussed was how the United States could enter Hayti and manage her finances as the finances of the Dominican Republic are handled. After the departure Tuesday night of the new American minister to Hayti, Mr. Railly-Blanchard, a diplomat of long training and experience, the report was believed that the United States is trying to find a way to have Hayti ask this government to manage her finances. In the Dominican Republic the United States appoints the collector of customs, who takes charge of all revenues, payments on the national debt and maintenance of the customs force. The balance is then turned over to the island government. Despite a series of revolts in Santo Domingo recently, her revenues have not been disturbed, because of the presence of the Americans there. Hayti is now torn by rebellion and her credit is at a low mark.

Although, next to Cuba, the largest of the West Indies, the island which is divided between the Dominican Republic and Hayti is said to be the least known and to offer the greatest possibilities for future development.
