records.headline: Lately the gunboat used her main battery of four-lueli guns to silence President Bordas' batteries
records.summary_en: The U.S. gunboat had lately used her main battery of four-inch guns to silence President Bordas's batteries, which were bombarding the rebel garrison holding the city in violation of the agreement that the lives of foreigners and other non-combatants would not be endangered by artillery fire. A junta commission of legalistas, representing the revolutionists, boarded the vessel and gave assurances of their desire to avoid endangering the safety of Americans, after scattering rebel rifle fire had passed over the ship and some shots struck her. A cable report said Santo Domingo City was still besieged by rebels and that other towns had joined the revolutionist cause, with four separate revolutions raging in the country. From Washington, the little republic was causing grave anxiety: the American minister was returning home after several months of fruitless efforts to restore peace, and the day's reports allowed no improvement in conditions. Bordas, obliged to maintain himself in office by extra-official decrees and partial elections, had been leading his troops in person against the rebellious generals in the northern part of the republic without being able to overcome them, while revolutions had also broken out at Azua, where the government navy found it necessary to destroy the customs house, along the railway between Sánchez and Samaná Bay, at Montecristi and at La Romana, where the agents of extensive American-owned plantations appeared at the State Department seeking protection for their property. Official opinion in Washington was slowly crystallizing into a conviction that only powerful outside influence, probably that of the United States, could terminate the chaotic conditions and set up a stable government: the revolutionists appeared unable to overcome the Bordas government, supported by the monthly proportion of customs receipts handed over by American collectors, but Bordas had not diminished the number of his enemies after a six months' campaign. Mr. Vick, the American collector of customs, had resigned, and Minister Sullivan was returning to the United States, leaving Secretary White in charge of the American legation. The State Department was still reluctant to intervene forcibly, though it was expected that some strong man would be sent to win the confidence of all elements, and meanwhile the navy maintained a considerable fleet in Dominican waters, including the South Carolina at Puerto Plata, the Marietta at Sánchez and the Castine at Azua.
records.summary_es: El cañonero estadounidense había empleado recientemente su batería principal de cañones de cuatro pulgadas para silenciar las baterías del presidente Bordas, que bombardeaban a la guarnición rebelde que ocupaba la ciudad, en violación del acuerdo de no poner en peligro con fuego de artillería las vidas de extranjeros y otros no combatientes. Una comisión de la junta de los legalistas, en representación de los revolucionarios, abordó la nave y dio seguridades de su deseo de no poner en peligro la seguridad de los estadounidenses, después de que fuego disperso de fusilería rebelde pasara sobre el buque y algunos disparos lo alcanzaran. Un despacho por cable decía que la ciudad de Santo Domingo seguía sitiada por los rebeldes y que otras poblaciones se habían unido a la causa revolucionaria, con cuatro revoluciones separadas en el país. Desde Washington, la pequeña república causaba grave preocupación: el ministro estadounidense regresaba a su país tras varios meses de infructuosos esfuerzos por restablecer la paz, y los informes del día no permitían mejora alguna en las condiciones. Bordas, obligado a mantenerse en el cargo mediante decretos extraoficiales y elecciones parciales, llevaba en persona sus tropas contra los generales rebeldes en el norte de la república sin poder vencerlos, mientras también habían estallado revoluciones en Azua, donde la marina gubernamental tuvo que destruir la aduana, a lo largo del ferrocarril entre Sánchez y la bahía de Samaná, en Montecristi y en La Romana, donde los agentes de extensas plantaciones de propiedad estadounidense acudieron al Departamento de Estado en busca de protección para sus bienes. La opinión oficial en Washington cristalizaba lentamente en la convicción de que solo una poderosa influencia exterior, probablemente la de Estados Unidos, podría terminar con las caóticas condiciones y establecer un gobierno estable: los revolucionarios parecían incapaces de vencer al gobierno de Bordas, sostenido por la proporción mensual de los ingresos aduaneros entregada por los colectores estadounidenses, pero Bordas no había reducido el número de sus enemigos tras una campaña de seis meses. El Sr. Vick, colector estadounidense de aduanas, había renunciado, y el ministro Sullivan regresaba a Estados Unidos, dejando al secretario White a cargo de la legación americana. El Departamento de Estado seguía renuente a intervenir por la fuerza, aunque se esperaba el envío de algún hombre fuerte que ganara la confianza de todos los elementos, y entretanto la marina mantenía una flota considerable en aguas dominicanas, incluidos el South Carolina en Puerto Plata, el Marietta en Sánchez y el Castine en Azua.

records.summary_en: Springfield Weekly Republican prints a dispatch: desultory fighting continues around the northern city of Puerto Plata, Dominican republic, where the rebels still hold the city, according to a report from Capt. Russell on the battleship South Carolina. President Bordas's government forces, however, have made new trenches about 600 yards south of the main position of the rebels, have burned the camps recently occupied and are supposed to be moving closer in on the city. Food supplies in the besieged city are scarce.

records.headline: Grand Forks Daily Herald and the Evening Times prints: William E. Pulliam
records.summary_en: Grand Forks Daily Herald and the Evening Times prints: William E. Pulliam, at that time general receiver of Dominican customs, a post which he occupied for six years, having been appointed by President Roosevelt, began one year ago the campaign for a splendid Pan-American tomb and memorial for Christopher Columbus in the city of Santo Domingo, Dominican republic, where his remains are declared now to rest. It is proposed that $500,000 be raised and, if more detailed study makes this seem feasible, to limit each subscription to 50 cents, so that the memorial may represent a great number of the sons and daughters of that New World found by the Genoese. During his residence in Santo Domingo Mr. Pulliam became greatly interested in the controversy which has been waged at various times over the resting place of the remains of Columbus. Both Santo Domingo and Spain claim to have the remains.

records.headline: The Richmond Virginian prints: the sending of 700 marines to Guantanamo
records.summary_en: The Richmond Virginian prints: the sending of 700 marines to Guantanamo, Cuba, was announced tonight by the administration at Washington on July 13, recognizing the necessity of taking some action with regard to conditions in Hayti and Santo Domingo. This force is to be held in readiness for a quick movement into either country. In addition, the gunboat Sacramento, now at Vera Cruz, will proceed to Port Au Prince. The battleship Connecticut is already lying off the Haytien port, while the battleship South Carolina is at Santo Domingo City; the cruiser Washington and gunboat Machias at Puerto Plata, and the gunboats Marietta and Castine are covering other Haytien and Dominican ports. Americans engaged in trade with the two countries, particularly with Santo Domingo, have repeatedly reported to Secretary Bryan the very severe losses they are suffering, owing to the practices of the contending factions.

records.full_text:
FAMINE AND DISEASE Threaten to Dislodge Dominican Rebels at Puerto Plata.

Famine and disease threaten to drive out the Dominican rebels from their stronghold at Puerto Plata, from which President Bordas is unable to dislodge them after several months' campaign. Food and water are scarce and the death rate is increasing daily.

records.headline: Tulsa Daily World prints a dispatch: Vidal has occupied San Cristobal.
records.summary_en: Tulsa Daily World prints a dispatch: Vidal has occupied San Cristobal. He was marching toward the capital when met by Charge White, who, backed by two powerful American warships with marine contingents, secured an agreement to an armistice while the federal officers in San Domingo City communicated Vidal's demands to President Bordas. The wireless outfits of the American vessels were used and at Puerto Plata Captain Eberle of the cruiser Washington submitted the messages to President Bordas in his camp outside the city. So far Mr. White has received no answer, but it is believed Bordas either will make a desperate effort to capture Puerta Plata or to abandon the siege and return south to prevent his own capture. The United States naval transport Hancock is about due at Guantanamo with marines from Vera Cruz. They are to be sent to the Dominican Republic in case of emergency. American Minister Sullivan has arrived in Washington and expects to confer with President Wilson and Secretary Bryan regarding the Dominican situation. It will be determined at this conference whether the Hancock's marines shall be landed and a virtual, though temporary, protectorate established. The transport Prairie sailed today from Vera Cruz for Haiti and the Dominican Republic to strengthen the American forces there.

records.full_text:
mitting the European Governments to acquire a financial or political control of the republic.

In the terms of diplomacy European Governments, particularly the French, German and British, already have let Mr. Bryan know that they are 'uneasy" concerning the Haytian situation. Without formally making any suggestions, they have made it known that they favor the establishment of an international joint commission to take charge of Haytian finances, and thus to run the country. The German Government has made it particularly plain that it wants such a joint financial protectorate, unless the United States will assume the same responsibilities that it has undertaken in Santo Domingo. So disastrous would the United States consider such an outcome that it does not wish even to have the proposal formally presented.

Germany's Eye on Coaling Station.

In addition, however, the Haytian situation contains a possible menace to the naval supremacy of the United States in the region of the Panama Canal. At Mole St. Nicholas, situated twelve hours sail from the American naval base at Guantanamo, on the Windward Passage, in the direct route from Panama to Europe, is an excellent harbor. Germany's need for a coaling station in the Caribbean is so obvious that to appreciate the situation one has only to look at a man and recall that Germany probably will be the principal user of the Panama Canal.

Taking advantage of the troubles of the Haytian Government German interests, which dominate the commercial situation and enjoy a very large degree of influence with the Government, recently sought to get control of the harbor at Mole St. Nicholas for the purpose of establishing a coaling station. It is needless to state that behind the German commercial interests was the Berlin Government, and had the proposal been permitted to go through Germany would have secured the prize long desired—a coaling station for merchant vessels and warships at the gateway to the Panama Canal. Only the influence of the United States prevented the success of the project, but as long as present demoralized conditions in Hayti continue there always will be the danger that a weak, hard pressed Government will barter such privileges in return for such support as will enable it to maintain itself in power.

The German influence already is at work in Hayti, and German merchants in Hayti have placed a loan with the present Government which will entitle them to a voice in the final adjustment of Haytian affairs. Two loans were made this spring on terms so extortionate that had they been made by American bankers present denunciations of American financial operations in Latin America would pale into insignificance.

Zamor Revolution Successful.

The present troubles in the negro republic began with a revolution started last winter against President Oreste by Senator Davilmar Theodore and Charles and Oreste Zamor. The United States supported the Oreste Government and was jockeying to get him in a position where he would invite the United States to assume charge of the Haytian custom houses, thus giving Washington the right to stop the revolution. But Secretary Bryan waited too long and at the critical moment the courage of Oreste failed him and he abdicated. American, British and German marines were landed at Port au Prince to preserve order in the capital.

Meanwhile the Zamor brothers conceived the idea of wresting from Senator Theodore his share in the fruits of victory, turned on his forces, routed them and entered the capital, where Oreste Zamor compelled the Congress by force of arms to elect him President and appointed his brother, Charles, Minister of the Interior. Senator Theodore continued his revolutionary activities and has succeeded in turning the whole northern territory into a state of constant disorder. There sprang up to aid him innumerable bands of "cocos," or mountain banditti, who are raiding throughout the country, making the operation of railroads and the conduct of any industry or commerce virtually impossible.

Meantime the United States, despite its refusal to recognize Huerta and despite the high sounding phrases about non-recognition of revolutionists who sought only their personal aggrandizement, recognized Zamor almost before he was in the Presidential chair. It has since supported Zamor, though fearing to hear any day that his Government has been overthrown.

Secretary Bryan has been converted, by virtue of his contact with the cold facts of the situation, to the conviction that such countries as Hayti are incapable of governing themselves and meeting their just obligations without outside assistance. But he desires that the inevitable American control shall be brought about at the request of the countries concerned, rather than imposed by force upon an unwilling and resisting people. He is seeking so to cultivate their confidence in the good intentions of the United States and appreciation of their own real interests that they will invite Washington to assist them.

Hope Zamor Will Ask Aid.

Consequently the present hope of the Administration in the Haytian situation is that the Zamor Government will ask aid of Washington before conditions come to such a pass that the United States will have to act with or without an invitation. What is desired is control of the Haytian finances—collection of the revenues and also some sort of a check on expenditures, together with an agreement that it shall be the right and privilege of the United States to use its armed forces whenever necessary for the maintenance of orderly government and the security of the Haytian resources.

In other words, an arrangement similar to that existing with Cuba and proposed with Nicaragua is sought with Hayti.

Six Revolutions On in Domingo.

In Santo Domingo the present arrangement lacks what is now considered the necessary feature of any satisfactory control of the disorderly republics of the Caribbean. The United States controls the collection of the revenues, but has no check on the expenditures. The result of American collection of revenues has been to put an end to graft in the customs service; to make the receipts many times larger than before, even though the duties have been reduced; to make considerable progress toward the payment of the national debts, and to give the Dominican Government more money for public improvements and other purposes than it ever had before.

Unfortunately, however, the American receivership has proved so popular to the Dominicans that it has made the control of the Government a more desirable prize than ever, because there is more money to spend and more contracts to award than before the trusteeship. Consequently three years ago, after six years of complete peace, a bloody contest for control of the Government began and has continued ever since, producing an increasing demoralization in Santo Domingo. There are now no less than six revolutions in progress in the island, and it is hardly known each day whether the Bordas Government will be in power the next.

The United States, under the terms of the receivership convention, is obliged to see to it that the required amounts for the interest and payment on the principal of the Dominican debt are taken each month from the Dominican revenues.

The remainder is turned over to the Government for its own needs. The disorderly conditions have reached such a degree and continued so long that the receipts now threaten to fall to a point where, after the required payments are made, there will be nothing left for the Dominicans, and the Government, if it is to live, must either turn to the United States for further aid or else descend to the same confiscatory methods as are employed by the revolutionists and banditti who infest the larger part of Dominican territory.

The third alternative, and one considered quite likely, is that the United States forcibly intervene, take charge of the Government and restore peace.

Incompetents Must Give Way.

The United States hopes, however, just as it hopes in Hayti, that the Government in power in Santo Domingo will throw itself upon the friendship of the United States and ask for aid. This the United States would extend upon condition that the Dominicans consent to some sort of an arrangement which would give the United States a control over expenditures and secure the Government for all time from the plunderings of politicians who seek by armed force to acquire the power of spending the public moneys. If the Dominicans do not adopt this course there is hardly a shadow of doubt that the United States will be compelled forcibly to take charge of the situation.

In both these countries the fundamental principles are the same. There is an absence of any appreciation of the real meaning of constitutional government. Both are and have been for a century or so plundered under the guise of republican institutions; both are in a state of semi-civilization and mediaevalism, with less real popular government than in the most tyrannical empire on earth. The bloody struggles for pure graft have kept both countries in a constant state of upheaval, actually reduced their populations, and kept closed to the world countries admitted to be among the richest in natural resources.

With the opening of the Panama Canal and the natural pressure of the older nations for new fields to develop it is improbable that incompetent peoples will much longer be permitted to despoil a rich area which other peoples are competent and willing to make productive. Upon this natural law, together with its own vital interests, the American policy in Hayti and Santo Domingo is based, and there is absolutely no doubt of the final outcome.

Conditions in Santo Domingo are steadily growing worse, according to a report received to-day from Capt. Eberle, commanding the cruiser Washington at Puerto Plata.

Capt. Eberle reported that news had reached the rebels of the bad conditions at Santo Domingo city and that as a result a conference of all the leaders was held, supposedly with reference to administering a final blow to the Government's power. The rebels learned of the situation in Santo Domingo city through information cabled to them from New York.

The food situation at Puerto Plata has been relieved by the arrival of large quantities of produce and cattle brought in from the surrounding country through the lines of the Government troops.

Desultory fighting still continues about Puerto Plata. Gen. Arias is reported approaching with reenforcements and large quantities of ammunition for the rebels.

Two British schooners have come to Puerto Plata to take off eighty British subjects, residents of Turks Island, who have been reduced to desperate straits by conditions in the Dominican city. The revenue cutter Algonquin is en route to Puerto Plata to get Porto Rican refugees. More than fifty Cubans have asked their Government for aid in returning to Cuba.

records.headline: The Birmingham Age-Herald prints: Minister Sullivan being absent
records.summary_en: The Birmingham Age-Herald prints: Minister Sullivan being absent, Charge d'Affaires White is trying to prevent a clash near the capital, as it would be disastrous to foreigners and the many non-combatants. Following a successful uprising at La Romana, about 50 miles east of the capital, last week, the insurgent general Vidal has occupied San Cristobal and Bani. He was marching toward the capital when met by Charge White, who, backed by two powerful American warships with their marine contingents, secured an agreement to an armistice while the federal officers in San Domingo City communicated Vidal's demands to President Bordas. The wireless outfits of the American vessels were used and at Puerto Plata Captain Eberle of the cruiser Washington submitted the messages to President Bordas in his camp outside the city. So far Mr. White has received no answer, but it is believed Bordas either will make a desperate effort to capture Puerto Plata or to abandon the siege.

records.headline: The Daily Missoulian prints a dispatch: Washington, July 18.
records.summary_en: The Daily Missoulian prints a dispatch: Washington, July 18. While President Bordas of the Dominican republic, with his scanty army, is besieging the northern rebels at Puerto Plata, his hold upon the capital, San Domingo, in the south is weakening, and according to today's advices to the State Department the southern insurgents were already in a position to dictate terms, which may mean the abdication or flight of Bordas. American Charge d'Affaires White, in the absence of Minister Sullivan, has been very active in trying to prevent a clash near the capital, as it would be disastrous to foreigners and the many noncombatants who have flocked into the city. The insurgent general Vidal, having occupied San Cristobal and Bani after driving out the small government garrisons, was marching toward the capital when met by Charge White. The latter had taken counsel with the federal officials left in temporary command by Bordas and was prepared to offer terms for at least a temporary suspension of hostilities. The insurgent leader agreed to an armistice for a few days while the federal officers in San Domingo communicated his demands to President Bordas.

El encargado de negocios americano White, en ausencia del ministro Sullivan, ha estado muy activo tratando de impedir un choque cerca de la capital, pues sería desastroso para los extranjeros y los muchos no combatientes que han acudido en masa a la ciudad. El general insurgente Vidal, habiendo ocupado San Cristóbal y Baní después de expulsar a las pequeñas guarniciones del gobierno, marchaba hacia la capital cuando fue encontrado por el encargado White. Este último había tomado consejo con los oficiales federales dejados en mando temporal por Bordas y estaba preparado para ofrecer términos para al menos una suspensión temporal de las hostilidades. El jefe insurgente aceptó un armisticio por unos días mientras los oficiales federales en San Domingo comunicaban sus demandas al presidente Bordas.

records.headline: The Washington Herald prints a dispatch: Conditions in Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The Washington Herald prints a dispatch: Conditions in Santo Domingo are steadily growing worse, according to a report received today at the Navy Department from Capt. Eberle, commanding the cruiser Washington at Puerto Plata. Mr. Sullivan came on the Clyde liner Seminole and left for Washington, where he will meet officials of the State Department either today or tomorrow and explain some phases of the revolution in Santo Domingo. His activities in influencing the American custom receivership in Santo Domingo have led, it is said, to strong anti-American feeling in the island. The food situation at Puerto Plata has been relieved by the arrival of large quantities of produce and cattle. Desultory fighting still continues about Puerto Plata. Two British schooners have come to Puerto Plata to take off eighty British subjects, residents of Turks Island.

records.headline: The Evening Star prints a dispatch: Charge White had taken counsel
records.summary_en: The Evening Star prints a dispatch: Charge White had taken counsel with the federal officials left in temporary command by Bordas and was prepared to offer terms for at least a temporary suspension of hostilities. The fact that Mr. White has behind him two powerful American warships, with their marine contingents, probably had its effect upon the insurgent leader. At any rate, he agreed to an armistice for a few days while the federal officers in Santo Domingo City communicated his demands to President Bordas. The wireless outfits of the American naval vessels were used in transmitting this information to President Bordas. They afford the only means of quick communication between the north and the south at present, owing to the destruction of the telegraph wires in the interior. At Puerto Plata, Capt. Eberle of the cruiser Washington submitted the messages to President Bordas in his camp outside the city. The United States naval transport Hancock is about due at Guantanamo with nearly 300 marines from Vera Cruz. They are to be sent to the Dominican Republic in case of emergency. Originally it was intended no forward movement should be made by these marines until reinforced by 400 additional men from the Philadelphia navy yard, but as these cannot reach there for two weeks it is probable, if a crisis is reached, the Hancock will be dispatched immediately to Puerto Plata or Santo Domingo City. American Minister Sullivan has arrived in Washington and expects to confer with President Wilson and Secretary Bryan.

records.summary_en: The Anderson Intelligencer prints a dispatch: Two powerful American warships with their marine contingent backed Charge White, who secured an agreement to an armistice while the federal officers in San Domingo City communicated Vidal's demands to President Bordas. The adjutant general, Vidal, has occupied San Cristobal and Bani after a successful uprising at La Romana, about 50 miles east of the capital, last week, and he was marching toward the capital when met by Charge White. The wireless outfits of the American vessels were used and at Puerto Plata Captain Eberle, of the cruiser Washington, submitted the messages to President Bordas in his camp outside the city. So far Mr. White has received no answer, but it is believed that Bordas will either make a desperate effort to capture Puerto Plata or to abandon the siege and return south to protect his own capital. The United States naval transport Hancock is about due at Guantanamo with nearly 300 marines from Vera Cruz. They are to be sent to the Dominican Republic in case of emergency. American Minister Sullivan has arrived in Washington and expects to confer with President Wilson and Secretary Bryan regarding the Dominican situation. It will be determined at this conference whether the Hancock's marines shall be landed and a virtual, though temporary, protectorate established.

Solon Menos, the Haitien minister, conferred today with Secretary Bryan and urged that intervention would result in a number of counter revolutions, necessitate the dissolution of the present government, and even the abdication of the president. "I count on the spirit of justice of the American people," said Minister Menos, referring to intervention, "to restrain them from taking the step which would be so harmful to Haiti." Present mobilization of marines in the vicinity of the islands, the minister explained, had been officially explained by the state department as a precautionary step taken to avert possible trouble, and was not, he felt sure, an indication that plans actually existed for the landing of United States troops at Haiti. records.headline: Springfield Weekly Republican prints: Bordas's hold upon the capital
records.summary_en: Springfield Weekly Republican prints: Bordas's hold upon the capital, San Domingo, in the south is weakening, while President Bordas of the Dominican republic, with his scanty army, is besieging the northern rebels at Puerto Plata, and, according to Saturday's advices to the State Department at Washington, the southern insurgents are already in a position to dictate terms which may mean abdication or flight of Bordas. American Charge d'Affaires White, in the absence of Minister Sullivan, has been trying hard to prevent a clash near the capital, as it would be disastrous to foreigners and the many noncombatants who have flocked to the city. American Minister Sullivan has arrived in Washington and expects to confer with President Wilson and Secretary Bryan regarding the Dominican situation. It will be determined at this conference whether the Hancock marines shall be landed and a virtual, though temporary, protectorate established.
records.summary_es: Springfield Weekly Republican publica: El presidente Bordas sitia a los rebeldes del norte en Puerto Plata, República Dominicana, con su escaso ejército. Su dominio sobre la capital, San Domingo, en el sur se debilita, y, según los avisos del sábado al Departamento de Estado en Washington, los insurgentes del sur ya están en posición de dictar términos, lo que puede significar la abdicación o la huida de Bordas. El encargado de negocios americano White, en ausencia del ministro Sullivan, ha estado tratando arduamente de impedir un choque cerca de la capital, pues sería desastroso para los extranjeros y los muchos no combatientes que han acudido en multitud a la ciudad. El ministro americano Sullivan ha llegado a Washington y espera conferenciar con el presidente Wilson y el secretario Bryan sobre la situación dominicana. records.headline: The Catholic Bulletin prints an item: There is a movement on foot
records.summary_en: The Catholic Bulletin prints an item: There is a movement on foot to raise, by subscriptions limited to fifty cents each from the people of the United States, of the twenty other republics of North, Central and South America and of Canada, the sum of $500,000 for a splendid Pan-American tomb and memorial for Christopher Columbus in Santo Domingo, where his remains are declared to rest. A superb site is available on the coral coast of the Caribbean Sea, where the Dominican Republic about twenty years ago dedicated the Plaza Columbina for the location of a monument to the great discoverer. It is proposed to construct a massive tomb, somewhat similar to the Grant Tomb on the Hudson, for the base, and then to sweep into the air with a superstructure, on the top of which will be placed one of the most powerful lights in the world, to be known as Columbus Light. The plan further provides for an endowment fund for the perpetual maintenance of the light.

records.summary_en: The New Hampshire Farmer and Weekly Union contrasted unrest in the Caribbean, noting that while Dominican disturbances were likely to prompt U.S. armed intervention, the country presented fewer military and diplomatic difficulties than neighboring Haiti. European nations maintained smaller financial interests in Santo Domingo, whereas Haitian instability threatened foreign defaults. The Wilson administration sought guarantees that Haitian customs revenues would be managed to satisfy foreign debts in a manner analogous to the Dominican receivership.
records.summary_es: The New Hampshire Farmer and Weekly Union contrastó las revueltas en el Caribe, observando que, si bien era probable que las perturbaciones dominicanas provocaran una intervención militar estadounidense, dicho país planteaba menores dificultades bélicas y diplomáticas que el vecino Haití. Las naciones europeas conservaban intereses financieros más reducidos en Santo Domingo, al tiempo que la inestabilidad haitiana ponía en riesgo moratorias con el exterior. La administración Wilson demandaba garantías de que los ingresos de las aduanas de Haití fueran administrados para cancelar deudas foráneas de modo análogo a la receptoría dominicana.

The situation in Santo Domingo is not so menacing as that in Haiti. Although there are disturbances in the Dominican republic that will probably lead to armed intervention by the United States, it does not present as difficult a military problem as Haiti, and the political importance is not so great. The European powers are not so much interested in Santo Domingo as they are in Haiti. Solon Menos, the new Haitian minister to Washington, has just presented his credentials to President Wilson and took occasion to assure the President that peace in Haiti was only a matter of a few days. Unfortunately, the President's information, obtained from his own agents in Haiti, do not agree with this prediction. records.headline: Springfield Weekly Republican prints: the cabinet at Washington Tuesday reached
records.summary_en: Springfield Weekly Republican prints: the cabinet at Washington Tuesday reached no definite conclusion in its consideration of the Dominican and Haytian problems. President Bordas is engaged in besieging another faction of the rebels at Puerto Plata, and his absence renders the position of the government doubly precarious. Meanwhile the besieged rebels have managed to secure fresh supplies of ammunition and food and are now said to be in a position to hold out indefinitely. It had been expected that, as a result of Tuesday's meeting, the administration would be able to announce some definite policy in the treatment of the turbulent little republic, but while there was talk of intervention, as a consequence of the apparent incapacity of the Bordas government to restore order, the subject was remanded for further discussion. Herbert M. Johnson of Indianapolis has been designated by the State Department and accepted by the Dominican republic as a financial expert to untangle the complications which involve European interests and threaten American intervention.

records.headline: The Custer Weekly Chronicle prints an editorial: The tremendous operations of this administration
records.summary_en: The Custer Weekly Chronicle prints an editorial: The tremendous operations of this administration in the field of foreign affairs, such as the Mexican matter, the 125,000,000 Colombian surrender and the already discredited Nicaraguan agreement, have obscured for the time the mess into which we have slipped in the island republic. 'Pressed by European powers,' the dispatches say, 'the U. S. has about lost patience with Haiti and San Domingo.' The policy in Santo Domingo of course is 'watchful waiting.' Puerto Plata, one of the chief seaports, is held by the rebels and has been declared under blockade by the Dominican government. Secretary Bryan has recognized the blockade, pronounced the port closed to American vessels and warned commanders of U. S. warships to wait watchfully for the outcome. As a result, American trade has almost ceased and American property interests are in constant danger. Meanwhile, European nations are pursuing a vigorous policy. A short time ago a German merchant vessel steamed into the 'blockaded' port and landed her cargo under protection of the guns of a German cruiser. No one can charge that the Wilson administration is responsible for the revolution, but it is undeniable that some of the deplorable conditions now existing are due to the prostitution of the diplomatic service, under the present regime, to the basest uses of partisan politics.

Puerto Plata, uno de los principales puertos marítimos, está en manos de los rebeldes y ha sido declarado bajo bloqueo por el gobierno dominicano. Como resultado, el comercio americano ha cesado casi por completo y los intereses de propiedad americanos están en peligro constante. Mientras tanto, las naciones europeas siguen una política vigorosa. records.headline: The Tulsa Star prints a dispatch: Reports from Cape Haitien of further
records.summary_en: The Tulsa Star prints a dispatch: Reports from Cape Haitien of further fighting, with added danger to foreigners, were regarded as forecasting prompt action by the marines now being concentrated at Guantanamo. The battleship South Carolina is now at Cape Haitien, but final decision as to whether force is to be used by the American government has been deferred. Not only have the military forces refused to heed the warnings of the American government that fighting should cease, but dispatches Wednesday night from Captain Eberle, of the cruiser Washington at Puerto Plata, San Domingo, reported the failure of attempts to settle the Dominican revolution by diplomacy. The superior Junta of the legalist party has refused to enter into negotiations with the Dominican government. Secretary Daniels decided that the additional 1,400 marines to be sent to Guantanamo, Cuba, for service in Haiti would be embarked from Norfolk, Va., on the transport Hancock, now en route to Hampton Roads from Guantanamo. There are now more than 600 marines at Guantanamo or on ships in Haitien and Dominican waters. Reinforcements could be drawn from Vera Cruz and Mexican gulf waters. There are now some three thousand marines, and another thousand could gather from the warships.

La Junta superior del partido legalista se ha negado a entrar en negociaciones con el gobierno dominicano. El secretario Daniels decidió que los 1,400 infantes de marina adicionales que serán enviados a Guantánamo, Cuba, para el servicio en Haití sean embarcados desde Norfolk, Va., en el transporte Hancock, ahora en ruta a Hampton Roads desde Guantánamo. records.headline: The Evening Star prints a dispatch: The transport Hancock sailed
records.summary_en: The Evening Star prints a dispatch: The transport Hancock sailed yesterday from Guantanamo, Cuba, for Santo Domingo City to reinforce the naval forces of the United States gunboats Castine and Marietta, now in the latter port; she carries a full regiment of United States marines. The Hancock is expected to reach there this afternoon. It is stated that this armed force is sent to the Dominican capital to strengthen the hands of the special commission now on its way there from Havana via Santiago, under orders to propose plans for the re-establishment of peace in the republic. The commission consists of Minister Sullivan, former Gov. Fort of New Jersey and Charles C. Smith of Boston. No orders for landing the marines have been given; their presence in the harbor, however, is expected to be sufficient warning to the Dominicans that the United States is determined that revolutionary disturbances on the island must cease at once.
records.summary_es: The Evening Star publica un despacho: El transporte Hancock zarpó ayer de Guantánamo, Cuba, hacia la ciudad de Santo Domingo para reforzar las fuerzas navales de las cañoneras de los Estados Unidos Castine y Marietta, ahora en este último puerto; lleva un regimiento completo de infantes de marina de los Estados Unidos. Se espera que el Hancock llegue allí esta tarde. Se afirma que esta fuerza armada se envía a la capital dominicana para fortalecer la posición de la comisión especial, ahora en camino allí desde La Habana vía Santiago, con órdenes de proponer planes para el restablecimiento de la paz en la república. La comisión la componen el ministro Sullivan, el ex gobernador Fort de Nueva Jersey y Charles C. Smith de Boston. No se han dado órdenes de desembarcar a los infantes de marina; su presencia en el puerto, sin embargo, se espera que sea advertencia suficiente para los dominicanos de que los Estados Unidos están decididos a que los disturbios revolucionarios en la isla cesen de una vez.

records.headline: The Bridgeport Evening Farmer prints an article: The remains of Christopher Columbus
records.summary_en: The Bridgeport Evening Farmer prints an article: The remains of Christopher Columbus are alleged to rest in the city of Santo Domingo, and a movement has been started to raise a fund of $500,000 to erect a Pan-American tomb and memorial to the discoverer in the capital city of the Dominican republic. The people of the twenty-one republics of the New World and of Canada, Jamaica, Newfoundland and other British possessions have been asked to contribute, but recent events have put a temporary stop to the movement. The project for a Columbus tomb in Santo Domingo originated with the government officials of the Dominican republic about a score of years ago. The scheme progressed so far that a beautiful site in the southern portion of the city, on the Caribbean's coral coast, was dedicated and christened Plaza Columbina. It was planned that the money should be raised by a special tax, but a revolution put a stop to the project. A marble mausoleum was built in the Santo Domingo cathedral, and there rests all that is mortal of Christopher Columbus. The movement for the Pan-American memorial was inaugurated a little more than a year ago by William E. Pullman, then receiver general of Dominican customs.
records.summary_es: The Bridgeport Evening Farmer publica un artículo: Santo Domingo guarda los restos de Cristóbal Colón, según se dice, y se ha comenzado un movimiento para reunir un fondo de $500,000 para erigir una tumba panamericana y un monumento al descubridor en la capital de la república dominicana. Se ha pedido a los pueblos de las veintiuna repúblicas del Nuevo Mundo y de Canadá, Jamaica, Terranova y otras posesiones británicas que contribuyan, pero los acontecimientos recientes han puesto un alto temporal al movimiento. El proyecto de una tumba de Colón en Santo Domingo se originó con los funcionarios del gobierno de la república dominicana hace unos veinte años. El plan avanzó hasta el punto de que se dedicó y se bautizó como Plaza Columbina un hermoso sitio en la parte sur de la ciudad, en la costa coralina del Caribe. Se planeó que el dinero se reuniera mediante un impuesto especial, pero una revolución puso fin al proyecto. Se construyó un mausoleo de mármol en la catedral de Santo Domingo, y allí reposa todo lo mortal de Cristóbal Colón. El movimiento por el monumento panamericano fue inaugurado hace poco más de un año por William E. Pullman, entonces receptor general de las aduanas dominicanas.

records.headline: The Birmingham Age-Herald prints a dispatch: John Franklin Fort
records.summary_en: The Birmingham Age-Herald prints a dispatch: John Franklin Fort, former governor of New Jersey; Charles Smith of Portsmouth, N. H.; and Minister Sullivan are the peace commissioners President Wilson sent to the island, after strong intimations had been given both the Dominican and Haitian governments that unless order was restored on the island the United States would do some police work. News of the success of the special commission sent to the island by President Wilson came today to the State Department and to the Dominican legation, though no details of the agreement were announced. It is understood a provisional president will be named to succeed President Bordas. At the same time the transport Hancock, with a full regiment of marines aboard, was dispatched to Dominican waters to join the half dozen warships already on guard there. At Puerto Plata, the commissioners heard General Bordas's side and also conferred with revolutionary chiefs, including Generals Vasques and Jimenez. The latter accompanied them to San Domingo City, where General Vidal, a leader of the southern revolutionists, joined in the parley. A minister, as he left the State Department today, said the revolution was over, peace was accomplished and they had accepted President Wilson's plan without further bloodshed.
records.summary_es: The Birmingham Age-Herald publica: John Franklin Fort, ex gobernador de Nueva Jersey; Charles Smith, de Portsmouth, N. H.; y el ministro Sullivan son los comisionados de paz que el presidente Wilson envió a la isla, después de que se habían dado fuertes insinuaciones tanto al gobierno dominicano como al haitiano de que, a menos que se restableciera el orden en la isla, los Estados Unidos harían cierto trabajo de policía. Llegó hoy al Departamento de Estado y a la legación dominicana la noticia del éxito de la comisión especial enviada a la isla por el presidente Wilson, aunque no se anunciaron detalles del acuerdo. Se entiende que se nombrará un presidente provisional para suceder al presidente Bordas. Al mismo tiempo, el transporte Hancock, con un regimiento completo de infantes de marina a bordo, fue despachado a aguas dominicanas para unirse a la media docena de buques de guerra ya de guardia allí. En Puerto Plata, los comisionados escucharon la versión del general Bordas y también conferenciaron con jefes revolucionarios, entre ellos los generales Vasques y Jimenez. Este último los acompañó a la ciudad de San Domingo, donde el general Vidal, líder de los revolucionarios del sur, se unió a la conferencia. Un ministro, al salir hoy del Departamento de Estado, dijo que la revolución había terminado, que la paz estaba lograda y que habían aceptado el plan del presidente Wilson sin más derramamiento de sangre.

records.headline: The Irish Standard prints an article: A movement is on foot
records.summary_en: The Irish Standard prints an article: A movement is on foot to raise, by subscriptions limited to fifty cents each from the people of the United States, of the twenty other republics of North, Central and South America and of Canada, the sum of $500,000 for a splendid Pan-American tomb and memorial for Christopher Columbus in Santo Domingo, where his remains are declared to rest. A superb site is available on the coral coast of the Caribbean Sea, where the Dominican Republic about twenty years ago dedicated the Plaza Columbina for the location of a monument to the great discoverer. It is proposed to construct a massive tomb, somewhat similar to the Grant Tomb on the Hudson, for the base, and then to sweep into the air with a superstructure, on the top of which will be placed one of the most powerful lights in the world, to be known as Columbus Light. The plan further provides for an endowment fund for the perpetual maintenance of the light.
records.summary_es: The Irish Standard publica un artículo: Está en marcha un movimiento para recaudar, mediante suscripciones limitadas a cincuenta centavos cada una de parte de los habitantes de los Estados Unidos, de las otras veinte repúblicas de la América del Norte, Central y del Sur y del Canadá, la suma de $500,000 para una espléndida tumba panamericana y un monumento a Cristóbal Colón en Santo Domingo, donde se declara que reposan sus restos. Hay disponible un sitio soberbio en la costa de coral del mar Caribe, donde la República Dominicana dedicó hace unos veinte años la Plaza Columbina para la ubicación de un monumento al gran descubridor. Se propone construir una tumba masiva, algo parecida a la Tumba de Grant en el Hudson, para la base, y luego elevarse en el aire con una superestructura, en cuya cima se colocará una de las luces más potentes del mundo, que se conocerá como la Luz de Colón. El plan dispone además un fondo de dotación para el mantenimiento perpetuo de la luz.

records.headline: The Evening Star prints an anecdote: Count von Bernstorff, the ambassador
records.summary_en: The Evening Star prints an anecdote: Count von Bernstorff, the ambassador, emerging from the elevator, his blue eyes a-twinkle and his 'kaiserlich' mustache partly concealing a smile, he asked the doorkeeper Eddie whether the anteroom was occupied, and on being told that the minister from Santo Domingo was in there, replied, 'Oh, that is all right. We are not at war with the Dominican republic,' and entered and greeted his fellow diplomat cordially. It would have been different had the incumbent of the anteroom been a representative from Great Britain, France, Russia or Belgium, the item notes: diplomatic etiquette forbids even the most formal recognition of the presence of an enemy's official.

No estamos en guerra con la república dominicana», y entró y saludó cordialmente a su colega diplomático. Habría sido diferente si el ocupante de la antesala hubiera sido un representante de Gran Bretaña, Francia, Rusia o Bélgica, señala la nota: el protocolo diplomático prohíbe hasta el más formal reconocimiento de la presencia de un funcionario enemigo.

records.headline: Newark Evening Star and Newark Advertiser prints: Former Governor Fort recounts
records.summary_en: Newark Evening Star and Newark Advertiser prints: Former Governor Fort recounts the peace commission's work in Santo Domingo. Since going there less than two months ago, four distinct revolutions and a number of insurrections of lesser weight have been settled and the leaders brought together in peace and harmony. The first refusals of the government of President Jose Bordas to surrender and submit to a provisional government were met by further demands by former Governor Fort. Bordas, finally realizing that this country meant business, yielded to the demands of the United States after two weeks of parley. The most serious condition found by Governor Fort when he reached the republic was the siege of Puerto Plata, which was held by rebels. President Bordas personally headed the federal troops besieging the city, and government gunboats had effected a full blockade of the port. Negotiations for a discontinuance of hostilities were opened at once, and after two days proved successful. The leaders of the warring factions at Puerto Plata were then taken aboard the steamer Prairie, which cleared for Santo Domingo, where another rebel force under General Vidal was besieging the city. Upon the demand of Mr. Fort hostilities were closed in order that the peace negotiations might be carried on. These were entered into also by President Bordas, who had gone to Santo Domingo in his private yacht. The election will be held under the observation of the United States, with slight modifications over the old Dominican electoral law, he said.
records.summary_es: Newark Evening Star and Newark Advertiser publica: Cuatro revoluciones distintas se han resuelto desde que el ex gobernador Fort fue a Santo Domingo hace menos de dos meses, junto con un número de insurrecciones de menor peso, y los líderes se han reunido en paz y armonía. Las primeras negativas del gobierno del presidente José Bordas a rendirse y someterse a un gobierno provisional fueron respondidas con nuevas exigencias del ex gobernador Fort. Bordas, al darse cuenta finalmente de que este país hablaba en serio, cedió a las exigencias de los Estados Unidos tras dos semanas de negociaciones. La condición más grave que encontró el gobernador Fort al llegar a la república fue el sitio de Puerto Plata, que estaba en poder de rebeldes. El presidente Bordas encabezaba personalmente las tropas federales que sitiaban la ciudad. Las cañoneras del gobierno habían efectuado un bloqueo completo del puerto. Las negociaciones para un cese de hostilidades se abrieron de inmediato y, al cabo de dos días, resultaron exitosas. Los líderes de las facciones en pugna en Puerto Plata fueron llevados entonces a bordo del vapor Prairie, que partió para Santo Domingo, donde otra fuerza rebelde al mando del general Vidal sitiaba la ciudad. records.summary_en: Newark Evening Star and Newark Advertiser prints: Walter W. Vick, of Rutherford, N. J., filed charges against James M. Sullivan, American minister to the Dominican Republic, alleging misconduct in office; the charges will be pigeonholed, it was said at the White House today. The same charges had been thoroughly investigated by ex-Governor Fort, of New Jersey, when he was in Santo Domingo as a member of the President's peace committee, and had been found to be groundless. Mr. Vick was United States general receiver of Dominican customs, and resigned recently on account of the trouble with Minister Sullivan. He was appointed by President Wilson, in whose political behalf he had been active in the presidential campaign of 1912 as assistant secretary of the Democratic National Committee. Clarence D. Baxter, of Paterson, N. J., has been selected by President Wilson to succeed Mr. Vick. The nomination will be sent to the Senate this week. Washington, Oct. 1.

El Sr. Vick era receptor general de los Estados Unidos en las aduanas dominicanas, y renunció recientemente a causa del conflicto con el ministro Sullivan. records.headline: The Guthrie Daily Leader prints a dispatch: An appeal for aid
records.summary_en: The Guthrie Daily Leader prints a dispatch: An appeal for aid for the tobacco interests of the Dominican Republic was made to the State Department today by Doctor Soler, the Dominican minister. He said there was fear that the entire crop, the principal product of the northern part of the island, might be lost, as it had been sold in advance and was to have gone to Hamburg, Germany. No ships can be found to carry it, as it had always been sent in German vessels. The financial stringency already is being felt, the minister explained, and the tobacco cannot be kept long without spoiling. An effort will be made to secure American or other neutral vessels to handle the crop.

records.headline: The Montgomery Advertiser prints a dispatch: Juan Isidro Jimenez
records.summary_en: The Montgomery Advertiser prints a dispatch: Juan Isidro Jimenez, who was proclaimed president of the Dominican Republic yesterday by the National Congress, took the oath of office today. Quiet prevails throughout the country. Jimenez, former president of San Domingo, was driven by a revolution into exile in Porto Rico. A recent election was held under the supervision of an American commission selected by the State Department. On November 25 Secretary of the Navy Daniels, fearing another revolution, sent back to San Domingo 800 marines who shortly before had been relieved of the duty of preserving order there. Opponents of Jimenez, in control of the Dominican Congress, for a time declined to hold a session, and the new president, who was to have assumed office in November, was therefore unable to appear before that body to take the oath.
records.summary_es: The Montgomery Advertiser publica un despacho: Juan Isidro Jimenez, que fue proclamado presidente de la República Dominicana ayer por el Congreso Nacional, prestó hoy el juramento del cargo. Reina la tranquilidad en todo el país. Jimenez, ex presidente de San Domingo, fue expulsado por una revolución al exilio en Porto Rico. Una elección reciente se celebró bajo la supervisión de una comisión americana seleccionada por el Departamento de Estado. El 25 de noviembre, el secretario de Marina Daniels, temiendo otra revolución, envió de vuelta a San Domingo 800 infantes de marina que poco antes habían sido relevados del deber de preservar el orden allí. Los oponentes de Jimenez, en control del Congreso dominicano, por un tiempo se negaron a celebrar sesión, y el nuevo presidente, que debía haber tomado posesión del cargo en noviembre, no pudo por tanto comparecer ante ese cuerpo para prestar el juramento.

records.headline: The Washington Herald prints a dispatch: James M. Sullivan
records.summary_en: The Washington Herald prints a dispatch: James M. Sullivan, minister to Santo Domingo, welcomed the inquiry to be made into his official conduct in dispatches received by President Wilson and Secretary Bryan yesterday. Minister Sullivan declared that his only interest was to serve his government, but that such service had been made difficult by 'sinister influences' in the Dominican republic. In his dispatch to Secretary Bryan he asked when and where the investigation would take place, and urged that it be begun as soon as possible. Secretary Bryan said he had not yet decided anything connected with the investigation.
records.summary_es: The Washington Herald publica un despacho: James M. Sullivan, ministro en Santo Domingo, dio la bienvenida a la investigación que se hará sobre su conducta oficial en despachos recibidos por el presidente Wilson y el secretario Bryan ayer. El ministro Sullivan declaró que su único interés era servir a su gobierno, pero que tal servicio se había hecho difícil por «influencias siniestras» en la república dominicana. En su despacho al secretario Bryan preguntó cuándo y dónde tendría lugar la investigación, e instó a que comenzara lo antes posible. El secretario Bryan dijo que aún no había decidido nada relacionado con la investigación.

records.headline: The Evening Star prints an item under the head 'MAY VISIT SANTO DOMINGO': J. D. Phelan
records.summary_en: The Evening Star prints an item under the head 'MAY VISIT SANTO DOMINGO': J. D. Phelan, senator-elect from California, appointed several days ago to investigate charges against James M. Sullivan, American minister to the Dominican republic, announced yesterday he might visit the island in connection with his inquiry. The State Department, at Mr. Phelan's request, asked Mr. Sullivan whether he desired to appear in person or be represented by counsel at hearings which Mr. Phelan said he thought would start early in January. Persons familiar with affairs in the Dominican republic have been asked to be present at the hearing. Their appearance will be voluntary, as there is no authority to subpoena witnesses or to compel them to testify. Some of the hearings will be here and some in New York. In accordance with a suggestion of Secretary Bryan, in his letter authorizing Mr. Phelan to make the inquiry, the hearings will be public.

Mr. Vick was to be the first witness today.

records.headline: The Chronicle=News prints an item under the head 'PROBE OF MINISTER SULLIVAN CONTINUES': John L. Mann
records.summary_en: The Chronicle=News prints an item under the head 'PROBE OF MINISTER SULLIVAN CONTINUES': John L. Mann, former director of public works of the Dominican republic, testified today that he had been removed from office by the Dominican government at the behest of James M. Sullivan, American minister, in the interests, he believed, of the Banco Nacionale of Santo Domingo, controlled by the Samuel M. Jarvis interests of New York. Mr. Mann appeared as a witness in the inquiry being conducted here by Senator-elect Phelan of San Francisco into Sullivan's fitness to retain his post. He said that after an unsuccessful effort had been made by Sullivan and Mitchell, president of the Banco Nacionale, to get him to transfer government funds to the institution, presumably to save it from insolvency, Sullivan had demanded his removal by Minister of Public Works DeOca, and that his discharge followed on the pretense of irregularities.

records.headline: The Bridgeport Evening Farmer prints an item: The continuation of the inquiry
records.summary_en: The Bridgeport Evening Farmer prints an item: The continuation of the inquiry to determine the fitness of James M. Sullivan, American minister to the republic, heard Farnham, of the National City Bank, as its first witness today before Senator-elect Phelan, of California. The National City Bank, it has been testified, was represented in negotiating the loan by Santiago Michelena, a Santo Domingo banker whose institution was depository of the republic until they were transferred, at the instance of Sullivan, it is alleged, to the Banco Nacionale. Michelena was not in favor with Secretary of State Bryan, it was testified, because Mr. Bryan 'was obsessed with the idea that Michelena represented the money trust.' Farnham began his testimony by saying the National City Bank had no interest in Santo Domingo in any way other than lending $1,500,000 to the government two years ago. This loan, by arrangement with the United States State and War Departments, was being paid off at the rate of $80,000 a month out of the government customs receipts. Farnham said he knew only by hearsay of the reputation of the Banco Nacional and the Jarvis interests controlling it, and that he had no relations with Sullivan. 'There has been talk of the existence of a money trust in New York,' said Commissioner Phelan. 'What do you know about that?' 'The National City Bank does not know that a money trust exists,' remarked Charles H. Strong, the commissioner's attorney.

records.headline: The New Britain Herald prints an item: Farnham began his testimony
records.summary_en: The New Britain Herald prints an item: Farnham began his testimony by saying that the National City Bank had no interest in Santo Domingo in any way, other than in lending $1,500,000 to the government two years ago. This loan, by arrangement with the United States State and War Departments, was being paid off at the rate of $30,000 a month out of the government customs receipts. Farnham said he knew only by hearsay of the reputation of the Banco Nacional and the Jarvis interests controlling it, and that he had no relations with Sullivan. He said that Sir Alexander Baird, representing English capitalists, in the promotion of the Samana railroad in the republic, had approached the National City Bank, seeking financial aid, but that the bank had declined to interest itself in the road. The only relations the bank had with Michelena, he said, was to ask him to present the bank proposition to the government. Farnham denied that there were any plans contemplated by the bank to exploit the island in any way. It was Secretary of State Knox who approved the loan, the witness said. Knox cabled the bank proposal to the then American minister, who presented it to the Dominican government. A copy went to Michelena. The minister and Michelena reported that the government favored their proposition in preference to propositions of other bankers.

records.headline: The Montgomery Advertiser prints an item: Bryne's affidavit
records.summary_en: The Montgomery Advertiser prints an item: Bryne's affidavit continued: 'I told all these things in substance as set forth in this affidavit to Secretary Bryan. I know all the officials of the State Department have been advised of the true conditions in Santo Domingo by many other Americans whose standing and integrity cannot be questioned. The American people, the President of the United States, and the Democratic party have been discredited and dishonored in Santo Domingo by the conduct of Minister Sullivan. The net result in Santo Domingo is that sincere and honest American business men who have invested their money in legitimate enterprises for the development of the Dominican Republic have suffered great loss.' Supplementing his affidavit, Bryne testified that he had asked Secretary Bryan 'most urgently to clean out the situation before it got public and created a scandal.' 'Secretary Bryan said to me,' testified the witness, 'I wish you'd write this out and sign your name to it and leave it here.' Then, keeping his eyes on me, he said, 'Perhaps you wouldn't care to do this.' I said, 'Mr. Bryan, I wouldn't have come here if I wasn't willing to stand by what I've told you.' I said I would be glad to write out a statement, and then he said it would not be necessary. I did everything I could to get Mr. Bryan to take the matter up.' Bryne testified that as far as he knew the alleged conspiracy had not matured, chiefly because of Timothy J. Sullivan's frankness in discussing it.

records.headline: The Evening Star prints an item: W. S. McGunness of Washington
records.summary_en: The Evening Star prints an item: W. S. McGunness of Washington was to be the first witness at this afternoon's hearing of the inquiry by Phelan of California into the conduct of James M. Sullivan, minister to the Dominican Republic. McGunness, who has been active in politics, was expected to tell what he knew of the efforts made in Washington by financiers interested in Santo Domingo to have Sullivan appointed, and the appointment confirmed by the Senate. At yesterday's session Walker W. Vick, former receiver general of Dominican customs and instigator of the present investigation, testified: 'One man told me that he had been promised a postmastership if he would 'get me.'' He intimated that Joseph P. Tumulty, secretary to the President, had been responsible for Secretary Bryan's attitude toward him. This had grown out of rivalry between them for Tumulty's present post, he thought. Earl Harding, a newspaperman, who has been investigating Sullivan in behalf of his paper, testified that he had been told that Tumulty had said that 'the White House regarded Vick as a sore-head and that he would have been removed from his position had he not resigned.' Joseph P. Tumulty, secretary to President Wilson, issued a statement today referring to testimony given yesterday by Walker W. Vick, saying he was ready to testify before Mr. Phelan at any time, either here or in New York.

records.headline: The Washington Herald prints an item: William S. McGinnis testified
records.summary_en: The Washington Herald prints an item: William S. McGinnis testified today before Commissioner Phelan, who is investigating charges against James Mark Sullivan, United States Minister to the Dominican republic, that Beer had captured the finances of Santo Domingo, and was planning to put its officers into Nicaragua. Sullivan was appointed by the efforts of Beer, McGinnis said, and he called him the 'big chief.' When the two met in a Washington hotel, after Sullivan's appointment as Minister, the latter told him: 'Things are going fine, Bill. The big chief will soon be not only financial agent of Santo Domingo, but of Nicaragua as well.' When McGinnis repeated the conversation to Beer, the 'big chief' said, 'for God's sake, keep quiet about that.' On another occasion Beer told him in Washington, 'This Santo Domingo deal has been the dream of my life. There's millions in it. I've been waiting for it for years.' Representative James A. Hamill, of New Jersey, according to the witness, said: 'Beer gets me so worked up over Nicaragua that every morning I wake up thinking I'm going to get $999,000.' McGinnis, formerly assistant superintendent of the railway mail service, told in detail the final steps to put Sullivan into office, even after Secretary Tumulty had told Representative Hamill that the White House heard Beer was interested in the Banco Nacionale of Santo Domingo.

Sullivan fue nombrado por los esfuerzos de Beer, dijo McGinnis, y lo llamó el «gran jefe». Cuando los dos se encontraron en un hotel de Washington, después del nombramiento de Sullivan como ministro, este le dijo: «Las cosas van bien, Bill. El gran jefe pronto será no solo el agente financiero de Santo Domingo, sino también de Nicaragua». Cuando McGinnis repitió la conversación a Beer, el «gran jefe» dijo: «Por el amor de Dios, no hables de eso». En otra ocasión Beer le dijo en Washington: «Este negocio de Santo Domingo ha sido el sueño de mi vida. Hay millones en él. He estado esperándolo por años». El representante James A. records.headline: The Wheeling Intelligencer prints an item: New York, Jan. 19
records.summary_en: The Wheeling Intelligencer prints an item: New York, Jan. 19. Alleged political activities of Congressman James A. Hamill, of New Jersey, W. Beer of New York, and John O. Gray, of Wilmington, Del., in procuring the appointment of James M. Sullivan as minister to the Dominican republic were described today at the investigation which is being conducted by Senator-elect Phelan, of California, into Sullivan's fitness to hold office. W. G. McGunness, of Washington, who described himself as a personal friend of President McKinley and a 'Republican politician,' testified that Beer and Sullivan had promised him the position of director of posts in Santo Domingo in return for his assistance in promoting Sullivan's candidacy. The position was to be a 'sinecure,' said the witness. He described meetings which he said were held between Beer, Hamill and Sullivan in Washington, previous to Sullivan's appointment, the subject of which was ways and means to get the ear of Secretary Bryan. Beer, it has been brought out in previous testimony, was attorney for the Banco Nacional interests, Santo Domingo, who are charged with schemes to exploit public works contracts with the aid of Sullivan.

El puesto iba a ser una «sinecura», dijo el testigo. Se describió a sí mismo como amigo personal del presidente McKinley y un «político republicano». Las supuestas actividades políticas del congresista James A. Hamill, de Nueva Jersey, W. Beer de Nueva York, y John O. Gray, de Wilmington, Delaware, para procurar el nombramiento de James M. Sullivan como ministro en la República Dominicana fueron descritas hoy en la investigación que conduce el senador electo Phelan, de California, sobre la aptitud de Sullivan para ocupar el cargo. Describió reuniones que dijo se celebraron entre Beer, Hamill y Sullivan en Washington, antes del nombramiento de Sullivan, cuyo tema fue los medios para ganarse el oído del secretario Bryan. Nueva York, 19 de enero.

The city was at that time in the possession of revolutionists, and although it was defended by a so-called fort, Baker said it was in no sense fortified, as the entire artillery of the fort consisted of one powder gun.

Davis in the Sullivan investigation an absolute falsehood. Albany, N. Y., Jan. 20. 'The statement of M. E. Davis in the investigation of James M. Sullivan, the American minister to the Dominican republic, that I am interested in Santo Domingo matters is an absolute falsehood,' said former Governor Martin H. Glynn. Beers for years, but I am not interested with him in any enterprise.'

records.headline: The Pierre Weekly Free Press prints an item: Testimony that Secretary of State Bryan
records.summary_en: The Pierre Weekly Free Press prints an item: Testimony that Secretary of State Bryan was informed that James M. Sullivan, American minister to the Dominican republic, figured in an alleged conspiracy to exploit public contracts in that republic, was heard today at the inquiry by Senator-elect Phelan into the minister's fitness. James L. Bryne, of Boston, a construction engineer, testified that he had told Mr. Bryan that the minister's cousin, Timothy J. Sullivan, had told him that the minister had arranged that the Banco Nacional of Santo Domingo should get government contracts and that he, Timothy J., was down in Santo Domingo to manage the construction work and see that Minister Sullivan 'got his bit.' Mr. Bryan, the witness said, asked him to write it out and then said, 'Perhaps you don't care to do this?' Bryne said he would be glad to, and the secretary replied that it would not be necessary. 'I got the impression,' said the witness, 'that the secretary did not want the matter on the records of the state department.' New York, Jan. 18.

records.summary_en: The Review prints: New York. W. Lee Sisson, a construction engineer, who said the late Samuel L. Jarvis, controlling the Banco Nacional of Santo Domingo, had asked him to become president of the construction company, testified that F. J. R. Mitchell, president of the bank, had said to him: 'We'll have to take the minister in with us and I think it advisable to do so, as he can be of considerable service in the way of throwing contracts to us.' The witness said he had objected and that Mitchell had replied: 'Well, the minister insists on it,' and he, Mitchell, suggested that 'we might give him a five or ten per cent interest in the company.' James M. Sullivan, minister to the Dominican republic, whose conduct is under investigation here before Senator-elect Phelan of California, was represented by witnesses as having insisted in sharing profits of a construction company organized to obtain work contracts from the Dominican government.

records.headline: The Sentinel=Record prints an item: Minister Sullivan was charged
records.summary_en: The Sentinel=Record prints an item: Minister Sullivan was charged by G. O. Baker, a construction engineer, with taking no steps to protect his property when the city, in possession of revolutionists, was threatened with bombardment by a Dominican gunboat. Baker said he had a contract to build a power plant in Puerto Plata. He said he formally protested to Minister Sullivan and that Sullivan replied: 'Not only will the United States government not prevent the bombardment, but will encourage it.' A letter written by Sullivan to this effect was put into evidence. A copy of it, he said, had been sent to Secretary Bryan. Baker declared Sullivan generally was held responsible for the revolution and charged with precipitating it through his activity with the lease of a railroad to the government, the terms of which the revolutionists objected to. He said Sullivan had once threatened to get him arrested by the Dominicans and had said to him, 'Don't forget that you're not on American soil.' As evidence of conditions in Santo Domingo, Baker said that on one occasion when all Americans 'had taken to the cellar,' it was reported that Desiderio Arias, revolutionist leader, had recommended that 'it would be a good thing to shoot off three or four good Americans' in order to bring about American intervention.

Baker declaró que Sullivan generalmente era considerado responsable de la revolución y acusado de precipitarla mediante su actividad con el arrendamiento de un ferrocarril al gobierno, cuyos términos objetaban los revolucionarios. records.headline: The Tabor Independent prints an item: Testimony that Secretary of State Bryan
records.summary_en: The Tabor Independent prints an item: Testimony that Secretary of State Bryan was informed that James M. Sullivan, American minister to the Dominican republic, figured in an alleged conspiracy to exploit public contracts in that republic, was heard today at the inquiry by Senator-elect Phelan into the minister's fitness. James L. Bryne, of Boston, a construction engineer, testified that he had told Mr. Bryan that the minister's cousin, Timothy J. Sullivan, had told him that the minister had arranged that the Banco Nacional of Santo Domingo should get government contracts and that he, Timothy J., was down in Santo Domingo to manage the construction work and see that Minister Sullivan 'got his bit.' Mr. Bryan, the witness said, asked him to write it out and then said, 'Perhaps you don't care to do this?' Bryne said he would be glad to and the secretary replied that it would not be necessary. 'I got the impression,' said the witness, 'that the secretary did not want the matter on the records of the state department.' New York, Jan. 18.
records.summary_es: The Tabor Independent publica una nota: James L. Bryne de Boston, un ingeniero de construcción, declaró que había dicho al Sr. Bryan que el primo del ministro, Timothy J. Sullivan, le había dicho que el ministro había arreglado que el Banco Nacional de Santo Domingo obtuviera contratos del gobierno y que él, Timothy J., estaba en Santo Domingo para dirigir el trabajo de construcción y ver que el ministro Sullivan «recibiera su parte». El testimonio de que el secretario de Estado Bryan fue informado de que James M. Sullivan, ministro americano en la República Dominicana, figuraba en una supuesta conspiración para explotar contratos públicos en esa república, se oyó hoy en la investigación del senador electo Phelan sobre la aptitud del ministro. El Sr. Bryan, dijo el testigo, le pidió que lo escribiera y luego dijo: «Quizás no quieras hacer esto». Bryne dijo que con gusto lo haría, y el secretario respondió que no sería necesario. «Tuve la impresión», dijo el testigo, «de que el secretario no quería que el asunto quedara en los registros del Departamento de Estado». Nueva York, 18 de enero.

records.headline: The Evening Journal prints a dispatch: John G. Gray, of Wilmington
records.summary_en: The Evening Journal prints a dispatch: John G. Gray, of Wilmington, a close friend of Secretary Bryan, J. Franklin Fort, former governor of New Jersey, and James K. McGuire, former mayor of Syracuse, were the witnesses who favored Minister Sullivan. Almost the first testimony in favor of James M. Sullivan, minister to Santo Domingo, came in yesterday's hearing before Senator-elect James D. Phelan, President Wilson's commissioner, in the inquiry into the alleged conspiracy to exploit the Dominican republic. New York, Jan. 22. Mr. Gray admitted that he had worked hard to have Sullivan appointed, and said Bryan had been many times a guest at his home in Wilmington. Mr. Gray became incensed at questions by Mr. Strong, the senator-elect's counsel. He objected to what he called a 'political twist' that was given the hearings. 'I don't know why that thing is brought into this inquiry,' stormed Mr. Gray. 'It doesn't belong here. There is some motive behind this investigation that is dragging all this in, and I resent it. It is drawing down this whole inquiry into a field where it doesn't belong. They said I had business interests in San Salvador. That was a fabrication.' He refused to say whether Minor C. Keith was his client or whether Mr. Keith was interested in San Salvador.

records.headline: The Richmond Times-Dispatch prints an item: Jack Rose, gambler
records.summary_en: The Richmond Times-Dispatch prints an item: Jack Rose, gambler and star witness at Police Lieutenant Charles Becker's trial for the murder of Herman Rosenthal, appeared as a witness for James M. Sullivan, American minister to the Dominican Republic, whose fitness to hold office is under investigation. Rose said he had been lecturing young men to live right, and gave Sullivan credit for inducing him to confess all he knew about the Rosenthal murder, and to become the State's witness. Sullivan at that time was his attorney. Rose declared Sullivan had been 'besieged with threats and promises' because of his activity in obtaining the confession, and suggested that 'the present attack' on the minister might be an aftermath of it. Two letters from Sullivan to James K. McGuire were put in evidence, in which Sullivan said that to earn money to go to law school he had, with the brother of the then Mayor of Waterbury, conducted one boxing match in that city. New York, Jan. 23.

Rose dijo que había estado dando conferencias a jóvenes sobre vivir rectamente, y dio a Sullivan el crédito de haberlo inducido a confesar todo lo que sabía sobre el asesinato de Rosenthal, y a convertirse en testigo del Estado. Sullivan en ese tiempo era su abogado. Rose declaró que Sullivan había sido «asediado con amenazas y promesas» por su actividad en obtener la confesión, y sugirió que «el presente ataque» contra el ministro podría ser una consecuencia de ello. Dos cartas de Sullivan a James K. Nueva York, 23 de enero.
