records.summary_en: The Daily Telegram prints an item: M. H. Davis, of New York, a contractor for supplies, testified he had been so informed by Beer while the two were on their way to Santo Domingo, Davis with the expectation of securing government contracts, which he said Beer had represented to him were to be had. That Minister Sullivan had encouraged the Dominican government to bombard the city of Puerto Plata during a revolution in October, 1913, in spite of the fact that it would endanger American property there, was charged in the testimony of E. O. Baker, a construction engineer. Baker had a contract for building a power house in that city for a Boston concern and said he protested to Minister Sullivan, asking intervention against a threatened attack upon the city by a Dominican gunboat patrolling the river. The city was at that time in the possession of the revolutionists, and although it was defended by a so-called fort, Baker said it was in no sense fortified, as the entire artillery of the fort consisted of one one-pounder gun. Sullivan, he said, had insisted that it was a fort and that the gunboat had a right to bombard. Baker said he then entered a protest in writing to the minister. To this Sullivan replied in a letter that was put in evidence, in which occurred the sentence: 'This does not mean that the attack on the town will be stopped by the United States; on the contrary we will encourage it.'

records.summary_en: The Evening Public Ledger prints a dispatch reporting misappropriations in the funds of the Department of Public Works amounting to many thousands of dollars. 'The public works funds of the Dominican Republic are expended under the supervision of the United States Government in its capacity as trustee for the Dominican Republic. American officials are said to be involved in the misappropriations, but no detailed information is obtainable. I am informed from official sources that sufficient evidence has been obtained to begin prosecutions, but that the American Minister, James M. Sullivan, has caused further action in the matter to be postponed. Mr. Sullivan is said to have acted upon instructions from Mr. Bryan, Secretary of State, but it cannot be learned why Washington desired the matter to be kept quiet at this time.' The paper also prints an item under the head 'PRESIDENT KNEW LITTLE OF JAMES M. SULLIVAN': New York, Jan. 23. 'He is the President's friend,' was the way the late Samuel M. Jarvis, the banker, referred to James M. Sullivan, Minister to San Domingo, whose official conduct is being investigated by Special Commissioner James D. Phelan, according to Frank J. R. Mitchell, the principal witness at yesterday's session of the inquiry. Mitchell was made president of the Banco Nacional of the island republic when it was organized by Jarvis.

records.headline: The Sunday Telegram prints a dispatch: Washington, Jan. 23.
records.summary_en: The Sunday Telegram prints a dispatch: Washington, Jan. 23. The reported disappearance of some thousands of dollars of public works funds in Santo Domingo occurred before any of the happenings which led up to the present investigation in New York of James M. Sullivan, American minister to Santo Domingo, according to Secretary Bryan's understanding of the situation. He said today he probably would have a statement to make later in regard to the matter and did not care to discuss it until he could present all the facts in the case. It became known today that Enrique Jimenez, nephew of the new president of the Dominican republic and who recently arrived here as minister, had discussed the alleged shortage with State Department officials. It was understood, however, that the amount which is charged as having been taken from the public fund approximated $8,000.
records.summary_es: The Sunday Telegram publica un despacho: Washington, 23 de enero. La desaparición reportada de algunos miles de dólares de fondos de obras públicas en Santo Domingo ocurrió antes que cualquiera de los sucesos que condujeron a la presente investigación en Nueva York de James M. Sullivan, ministro americano en Santo Domingo, según el entendimiento de la situación del secretario Bryan. Dijo hoy que probablemente haría una declaración más tarde con respecto al asunto y que no deseaba discutirlo hasta que pudiera presentar todos los hechos del caso. Se supo hoy que Enrique Jimenez, sobrino del nuevo presidente de la República Dominicana y que recientemente llegó aquí como ministro, había discutido el presunto faltante con funcionarios del Departamento de Estado. Se entendía, sin embargo, que la cantidad que se acusa haber sido tomada del fondo público se aproximaba a $8,000.

records.headline: The Evening Star prints an editorial on the report of a deficit
records.summary_en: The Evening Star prints an editorial on the report of a deficit in the funds of the Dominican Republic, over which the United States exercises a custodial supervision: The money loss, which would presumably have to be made good by this government, is inconsequential, but the damage to American prestige in the countries of the south and the West Indies would be serious if such a deficit were in fact to have resulted from the carelessness of any official named by the United States. The strictest honesty and the most scrupulous care in safeguarding the financial interests of Santo Domingo are demanded. Especially is it important to maintain a clean slate in this respect, in view of the inquiry now in progress respecting the influences which operated in the selection of representatives of this country in the island republic. The result of the present investigation, directed by the Secretary of State, will be awaited with the keenest interest.

Se demanda la más estricta honestidad y el más escrupuloso cuidado en salvaguardar los intereses financieros de Santo Domingo. Especialmente es importante mantener un historial limpio en este respecto, en vista de la investigación ahora en curso respecto a las influencias que operaron en la selección de representantes de este país en la república insular. El resultado de la presente investigación, dirigida por el secretario de Estado, será esperado con el más vivo interés.

records.headline: The Tulsa Daily World prints an item: Mitchell took the stand
records.summary_en: The Tulsa Daily World prints an item: Mitchell took the stand today at the investigation of the fitness of James M. Sullivan to retain his post as American minister to the Dominican republic. He was asked if he intended to accuse W. W. Russell, Sullivan's predecessor, with dishonesty, when he said in his testimony Friday that had there been an honest American minister at Santo Domingo before Sullivan took the post the Banco Nacional would have received without asking the deposit of customs receipts. Mitchell said he did not mean to imply 'absolute dishonesty,' but that Russell had been unfair to the institution. He said he had based his statement on 'the fact I had been told that Minister Russell had advocated that the Dominican government's loan be given to the National City Bank of New York because it would better suit the Washington government.'

records.headline: The Montgomery Advertiser prints an item: New York, Jan. 27.
records.summary_en: The Montgomery Advertiser prints an item: New York, Jan. 27. John G. Gray of Wilmington, Del., who was influential in obtaining the appointment of James M. Sullivan as minister to the Dominican republic, testified today at the investigation into the fitness of the Minister to hold his post. Mr. Gray said he became attorney for the Banco Nacional of Santo Domingo long after Sullivan was appointed. He 'slipped in,' he said, because the Banco Nacional had been placed in an awkward position through inability to secure payment of loans from the Dominican government. He declared he had not gone to Secretary Bryan in the matter to 'obtain a personal favor,' but that it was a matter of legal right. 'I considered it an honorable matter to take up,' he said, adding that advocacy of Sullivan was an entirely separate matter from his subsequently representing the bank. He said 'unfair imputations' had got into the newspapers to the effect that he had originally sought Sullivan's appointment in behalf of the Banco Nacional's interests.
records.summary_es: The Montgomery Advertiser publica una nota: El testigo John G. Gray declaró hoy en la investigación sobre la aptitud del ministro para ocupar su puesto. El Sr. Gray, de Wilmington, Delaware, que fue influyente en obtener el nombramiento de James M. Sullivan como ministro en la República Dominicana, dijo que se convirtió en abogado del Banco Nacional de Santo Domingo mucho después de que Sullivan fue nombrado. «Se coló», dijo, porque el Banco Nacional había sido puesto en una posición incómoda por la incapacidad de asegurar el pago de préstamos del gobierno dominicano. Declaró que no había ido al secretario Bryan en el asunto para «obtener un favor personal», sino que era un asunto de derecho legal. «Consideré que era un asunto honroso que tomar», dijo, agregando que la defensa de Sullivan era un asunto enteramente separado de su representación posterior del banco. Dijo que «imputaciones injustas» habían llegado a los periódicos en el sentido de que él había buscado originalmente el nombramiento de Sullivan en nombre de los intereses del Banco Nacional. Nueva York, 27 de enero.

records.headline: The Albuquerque Morning Journal prints an item: James M. Sullivan
records.summary_en: The Albuquerque Morning Journal prints an item: James M. Sullivan, American minister to the Dominican republic, denied all the charges of unfitness made against him, chiefly by Walker W. Vick, former receiver general of customs of Santo Domingo, in a statement read in evidence today at the hearings into the charges before Senator-elect Phelan of California. New York, Jan. 28. The statement, received by mail, was supported by documentary evidence and made counter-charges against Vick. Sullivan declared he had been made the victim of a newspaper campaign engineered by Vick to attack his character and conduct, which was unsupported by facts. He said certain newspapers in the United States had 'championed the cause of as audacious a gang of pirates as ever sailed the Caribbean sea.' Sullivan said he had no apology to make for recommending as the depository for the receivership funds the Banco Nacionale, which Vick charges was an untrustworthy institution and which had been accused of seeking the appointment of Sullivan. 'The records of the State Department will show,' he wrote, 'that I never recommended any one bank above another,' except that he preferred some American bank, stating that if the American banks here were not satisfactory the department should urge some responsible bank in America to open a bank here.
records.summary_es: The Albuquerque Morning Journal publica una nota: James M. Sullivan, ministro americano en la República Dominicana, negó todas las acusaciones de ineptitud hechas contra él, principalmente por Walker W. Vick, ex recaudador general de aduanas de Santo Domingo, en una declaración leída como evidencia hoy en las audiencias sobre las acusaciones ante el senador electo Phelan de California. Nueva York, 28 de enero. La declaración, recibida por correo, estaba apoyada por evidencia documental e hizo contraacusaciones contra Vick. records.headline: The New Britain Herald prints an item: A statement by Sullivan
records.summary_en: The New Britain Herald prints an item: A statement by Sullivan, American minister to the Dominican republic, denying all the charges of unfitness made against him, chiefly by Walker W. Vick, former receiver general of customs of Santo Domingo, was read in evidence yesterday at the hearings into the charges before Senator-elect Phelan. The statement, received by mail, was supported by documentary evidence and made counter-charges against Vick. Sullivan declared he had been made the victim of a newspaper campaign engineered by Vick to attack his character and conduct, which was unsupported by facts. He said that certain newspapers in the United States had 'championed the cause of as audacious a gang of pirates as ever sailed the Caribbean.' Sullivan said he had no apology to make for recommending the Banco Nacional as the depository for the receivership funds, which Vick charges was an untrustworthy institution and which has been accused of seeking the appointment of Sullivan in order to exploit the island. 'If Vick was willing to make the change, he would have scarcely acted upon my recommendation,' wrote the minister. 'The fact is that the desire to make further change was born in Vick some months later for reasons best known to himself, and in the campaign he then opened on the Banco Nacional there was no interference from me until I learned of Vick's determination to turn the business over from an American to a British corporation (Royal Bank of Canada).'

records.headline: The Springfield Weekly Republican prints an item: James M. Sullivan
records.summary_en: The Springfield Weekly Republican prints an item: James M. Sullivan, American minister to the Dominican republic, denied all the charges of unfitness made against him, chiefly by Walker W. Vick, former receiver-general of customs of San Domingo, in a statement read in evidence at New York Thursday at the hearings into the charges before Senator-elect Phelan. The statement received by mail was supported by documentary evidence and made counter charges against Vick. Sullivan declared that he had been made the victim of a newspaper campaign engineered by Vick to attack his character and conduct, which was unsupported by facts. He said that certain newspapers in the United States had 'championed the cause of as audacious a gang of pirates as ever sailed the Caribbean.' Sullivan said he had no apology to make for recommending the Banco Nacional as the depositary for the receivership funds which Vick charges was an untrustworthy institution, and which has been accused of seeking the appointment of Sullivan in order to exploit the island. 'If Vick was unwilling to make the change, he would have scarcely acted upon my recommendation,' wrote the minister. 'The fact is that the desire to make further change was born in Vick some months later for reasons best known to himself.'

records.summary_en: The Daily Kennebec Journal prints a dispatch: Witnesses testified today in the inquiry into the conduct and fitness for office of James M. Sullivan, minister to the Dominican Republic, ordered by President Wilson. The witnesses included First Assistant Secretary of State Osborne, Third Assistant Phillips, Assistant Secretary of War Breckinridge, William Walter Smith, former secretary of the legation in San Domingo, W. W. Russell, former minister to Santo Domingo, Capt. E. W. Eberle of the navy, and Frank J. R. Mitchell of the Banco Nacional of Santo Domingo. Most of today's testimony had little to do with Minister Sullivan; it related largely to the circumstances surrounding a loan of $1,500,000 made to Santo Domingo in 1913, through the National City Bank of New York. Frank J. R. Mitchell of the Banco Nacional, one of the unsuccessful bidders for the loan, asserted at a former hearing that he had been informed that Minister Russell had let the Santo Domingo officials know that 'Washington' desired the loan awarded to the National City Bank. This, former Minister Russell flatly denied today.

records.full_text:
'INSIDE INFORMATION' AT SULLIVAN PROBE

Revelations Made by Harry J. Overman, Brother of Senator From South Carolina.

Inside information as to the influences at work on the appointment of American representatives in the Dominican government was brought out yesterday at the first session of the Sullivan hearing here.

Harry J. Overman, file clerk in the office of the Secretary of the Senate and a brother of Senator Lea S. Overman of North Carolina, testified concerning his efforts to obtain appointment as deputy receiver of customs at Santo Domingo under the treaty relations between the Dominican republic and the United States. He declared that he had been urged to apply for the place by a man named Gold, who, he said, suggested that William C. Beer would be a good person to support him for the place. Beer, he said he was told by Gold, could influence Secretary of State Bryan through John H. Grey, of Wilmington, Del.

Md. Overman testified that inasmuch as his own brother was unwilling to use his position to further his candidacy he was compelled to do much of the work himself. He said that he had met Mr. Beer at a hotel in Washington in company with Minister Sullivan.

John E. Osborne, First Assistant Secretary of State, stated that prior to the appointment of Mr. Sullivan, he had gone to Haiti and Santo Domingo on a secret mission for the Government. While there, he stated, he had warned the Dominican government against increasing its indebtedness.

Regarding the Sullivan case, Secretary Osborne said that he knew practically nothing except that he had received personal letters from Mr. Vick, criticising the conduct of the minister.

Others who were present were Joseph P. Tumulty, Secretary to the President; Assistant Secretary of State, Philips; Assistant Secretary of War Breckenridge, and Brigadier General McIntyre, chief of the Bureau of Insular Affairs, War Department.

At the outset of today's session Charles H. Strong, attorney, conducting the examination for Comimssioner Phelan, announced that the entire scope of the investigation was to inquire into the fitness, competence, and conduct of Minister Sullivan.

“The Commissioner intends,” he said, “to run down any legitimate clue bearing on this case without fear or favor for anybody in or out of public office. He means to sift the case to the bottom. Necessarily, inasmuch as the lines upon which this investigation is being conducted are wholly different from court procedure, much hearsay testimony, or even gossip, must creep into the evidence. But as a result of this hearsay evidence we have already been able to unearth things of the utmost importance.”

records.headline: The Montgomery Advertiser prints an item: Washington, Feb. 6
records.summary_en: The Montgomery Advertiser prints an item: Washington, Feb. 6. Testifying today at the investigation into charges against James M. Sullivan, Minister to the Dominican republic, C. H. Albrecht, former vice and deputy consul general to the republic, testified Sullivan had become unpopular with certain factions there because of his conduct in relation to a revolution. He said Sullivan had promised that the United States would guarantee a 'free and fair election' after the revolution and that the people were dissatisfied with the election when it was held. He said he never heard that Sullivan was responsible for 'bloodshed or the destruction of property,' as had been said. Mr. Albrecht said that Sullivan was untiring in his work as minister, and had accomplished many reforms in the conduct of the Department of Public Works.

records.full_text:
BRINGS NEW CHARGE AGAINST SULLIVAN Vick Says Minister Exceeded Authority In Negotiating Dominican Loan

Washington, February 8.—Walter W. Vick, formerly collector general of Dominican customs, made new charges here today in the investigation of the fitness of James M. Sullivan to be minister to the Dominican republic. His testimony today was offered to show that Sullivan, without the knowledge of the government at Washington and without the approval of the Dominican congress, had endeavored to pave the way for negotiations of a $500,000 loan for the Dominican government through banks in the republic.

Vick asserted that W. W. Smith, secretary of legation, first told him of the proposed loan, and that later a Dominican banker showed him a letter from Sullivan which was sent to the three banks in San Domingo city seeking to open negotiations for the loan. A copy of this letter was placed in the record. It set forth that Sullivan had been instructed by his government to arrange the loan, that Dominican bonds would be issued to repay it and that the United States would agree to an extension of the legal limit of the Dominican debt to cover the amount. The recent revolution brought the entire matter to a close, Vick said.

records.summary_en: The Evening Star reported testimony from presidential secretary Joseph P. Tumulty regarding the inquiry into Dominican Minister James M. Sullivan. Tumulty stated he had instructed Customs Receiver Vick to monitor Sullivan following allegations concerning the Banco Nacional and commercial interests, denying that the White House had ever whitewashed the diplomat. While describing Dominican politics as filled with recrimination, Tumulty defended the administration's scrutiny and dismissed personal criticisms between Vick and Sullivan.
records.summary_es: The Evening Star informó sobre la declaración del secretario presidencial Joseph P. Tumulty con relación a la indagatoria en torno al ministro en la República Dominicana James M. Sullivan. Tumulty señaló que había dado instrucciones al receptor de aduanas Vick de vigilar a Sullivan tras imputaciones vinculadas al Banco Nacional e intereses mercantiles, negando que la Casa Blanca hubiese intentado encubrir al diplomático. Al calificar el ambiente político dominicano de plagado de recriminaciones, Tumulty defendió la rigurosidad del gobierno y restó importancia a los agravios personales entre Vick y Sullivan.
records.passage: Asked Vick to Watch Sullivan. "The White House is a great clearing house for rumors," said Mr. Tumulty, "and when these charges began to come in about Mr. Sullivan I heard about the Jarvis interests and the Banco Nacional. I asked Mr. Vick to watch Mr. Sullivan closely and keep the White House advised. I also told him to warn Minister Sullivan that the President would be displeased if he heard of Sullivan growing too close to any interests, and would take such action as became necessary." He was inclined to be suspicious of all charges from the Dominican Republic, because Mr. Vick had told him, in relation to accusations against the latter, that the "atmosphere there was charged with recrimination and throat-cutting." Denies "Whitewashing" Story. Mr. Tumulty denied that the White House had ever exonerated or "whitewashed" Minister Sullivan. He said that J. Franklin Fort, who had headed a commission to settle a Dominican revolution, had told the President that Sullivan was a "big-hearted Irishman," and that there was nothing against him. He declined to express any opinion [illegible] fitness for office, but criticised Vick as a "sorehead." Counsel C. H. records.headline: Commissioner Phelan Tuesday received documentary evidence from state department files
records.summary_en: The Springfield Weekly Republican reported on ongoing proceedings in the Phelan investigation into Minister James M. Sullivan, reviewing personal debts and legal judgments submitted into the record alongside testimonials on his behalf. State Department investigator Harry S. Dickey and former Vice Consul Charles H. Albrecht praised Sullivan's diplomatic rapport, attributing the controversy to personal hostility from former Receiver Walter W. Vick. Representative Hamill also testified, denying any connection to commercial interests in advocating for Sullivan's appointment.
records.summary_es: The Springfield Weekly Republican informó sobre el curso de las actuaciones en la investigación Phelan referente al ministro James M. Sullivan, revisando deudas personales y fallos judiciales incorporados al expediente junto con testimonios a su favor. El investigador del Departamento de Estado Harry S. Dickey y el exvicecónsul Charles H. Albrecht elogiaron el trato diplomático de Sullivan, atribuyendo la polémica a la hostilidad personal del exreceptor Walter W. Vick. El representante Hamill también prestó declaración, negando todo vínculo con intereses comerciales al promover la designación de Sullivan.

Commissioner Phelan Tuesday received documentary evidence from state department files and other sources, including letters from Sullivan's creditors, endeavoring to collect bills through the department. One of the bills for $60.20 from a New Haven clothier, was the subject of a score of letters to President Wilson, Secretary Bryan and other officials. Mr. Strong also put into the record a list of judgments against James M. Sullivan entered in New York courts. Harry S. Dickey, who investigated for the state department the accounts of John L. Mann, former director-general of public works of the Dominican republic, and Charles H. Albrecht, former vice-consul in the republic, were Saturday's witnesses. Both commended the work of Minister Sullivan. “Minister Sullivan,” said Dickey, “is all right. He is a good man for the place. records.headline: The Grangeville Globe prints an editorial asking how Mr. Bryan
records.summary_en: The Grangeville Globe prints an editorial asking how Mr. Bryan, Secretary of State of the United States, has the opportunity of providing 'suitable rewards' for 'workers' in American politics out of the funds belonging to a small foreign nation. To answer this question the paper turns to the story of our relations with San Domingo for the past ten years. On the island of San Domingo (or Santo Domingo) are two small nations, one of these known as the Dominican Republic. In 1904 there was a crisis in that little nation which, strange to say, created complications between the United States and nations in Europe. This crisis all came about because there was a great and unprotected source of wealth in that island, the customs duties of the country. The people of the Dominican Republic, the paper says, had not shown themselves competent to protect their own interests. The money from the customs duties, which ought to have gone to pay the expenses of governing the country, had been going very largely into the pockets of the men who were for the time being in control of the government. Unscrupulous and domineering men were thus always trying to get control of the government in order to make themselves rich, and as a consequence there was an almost constant state of so-called 'revolution.'
records.summary_es: The Grangeville Globe comenta en un editorial cómo el Sr. Bryan, secretario de Estado de los Estados Unidos, tiene la oportunidad de proporcionar «recompensas adecuadas» para «trabajadores» en la política americana con los fondos pertenecientes a una pequeña nación extranjera. Para responder a esta pregunta el periódico se remonta a la historia de nuestras relaciones con San Domingo durante los últimos diez años. En la isla de San Domingo (o Santo Domingo) hay dos pequeñas naciones, una de estas conocida como la República Dominicana. En 1904 hubo una crisis en esa pequeña nación que, cosa extraña, creó complicaciones entre los Estados Unidos y naciones de Europa. Esta crisis se debió por entero a que había una gran fuente de riqueza desprotegida en esa isla, los derechos de aduana del país. El pueblo de la República Dominicana, dice el periódico, no se había mostrado competente para proteger sus propios intereses. El dinero de los derechos de aduana, que debió haber ido a pagar los gastos de gobernar el país, había estado yendo en gran parte a los bolsillos de los hombres que por el momento controlaban el gobierno. Hombres sin escrúpulos y dominantes trataban así siempre de apoderarse del gobierno para enriquecerse, y como consecuencia había un estado casi constante de la llamada «revolución».

records.headline: The Evening Star prints an interview with Senator James D. Phelan of California
records.summary_en: The Evening Star prints an interview with Senator James D. Phelan of California at his apartments in the Shoreham Hotel today, under the heads 'Back From Santo Domingo' and 'Sullivan Inquiry': 'The west is very strong for President Wilson,' said Senator Phelan. He ran as a Wilson man in the campaign last fall, and was elected over his republican and bull moose opponents by a substantial vote. He was selected by the President to investigate the charges made against James M. Sullivan, United States minister to Santo Domingo, and has just returned to this country from a visit to the Dominican republic. He expects to submit his report to Secretary of State Bryan some time next week. Mr. Sullivan has asked to be permitted to submit a brief in his own defense, and Senator Phelan is awaiting the receipt of that brief. If possible, he will leave with the Vice President when the latter goes next week to San Francisco to represent the President at the Panama-Pacific exposition. 'I came back to this country,' said Senator Phelan, 'expecting that an extra session of Congress would be called and that I would be needed in Washington, but it looks now as though the Senate would not meet until next December, or perhaps in October, to consider treaties and cloture.'

records.headline: The Ottumwa Tri-Weekly Courier prints an editorial on the letter of Mr. Bryan
records.summary_en: The Ottumwa Tri-Weekly Courier prints an editorial on the letter of Mr. Bryan, addressed on August 20 last to Walter W. Vick, then receiver general of customs at Santo Domingo. Places in the government service were evidently a little scanty at home; pickings for the faithful must be found elsewhere, where the classified service did not extend, and in what better place than in Santo Domingo, where nobody was watching and where 'our beloved and oppressed brethren' of the Dominican republic might be made to pay the piper. The paper quotes the letter: 'Now that you have arrived and acquainted yourself with the situation, can you let me know what positions you have at your disposal with which to reward deserving democrats? Whenever you desire a suggestion from me in regard to a man for any place down there, call on me. You have had enough experience in politics to know how valuable workers are when the campaign is on and how difficult it is to find suitable rewards for the deserving.' And accordingly, the 'strong, courageous, reliable' Sullivan, who was recommended in the letter, proceeded to 'reform' things by transferring the public funds to a precious group of patriots in control of the Banco Nacional, an institution described by one of the witnesses as 'a joke.'

Newport News, April 12.—One hun
dred and fifty tons of coal, fifty tons of
fresh water and a three days’ supply
of fresh meats, fruits and vegetables
were allotted by Customs Collector
Hamilton, and are now ready to be
loaded on the Kron Prinz Wilhelm, the
German converted cruiser, which
dashed into port yesterday, eluding the
British and French warships. The
Wilhelm left New York August 3. She
armed at sea and sank fourteen mer
chantmen, which, with tbel cargoes,
were valued at *7,000,000.

Captain Thierfelder of the Wilhelm
has not indicated whether he will in
tern or try a dash from the harbor af
ter taking on his supplies. The ma
chinery is in fairly good condition, and
the vessel made twenty-three knots in
the dash through the cordon of allied
warships to enter the harbor.

records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch dated April 13 states that the Navy Department has ordered the cruiser Des Moines to Santo Domingo City from Progreso, Mexico, to join the gunboat Nashville off the Dominican capital. The naval order follows reports from Minister Sullivan of a new revolutionary outbreak in the Dominican Republic. Earlier orders directing a vessel to Port-au-Prince, Haiti, to convey American Minister Bailly-Blanchard to Santiago, Cuba, were canceled.

La disposición naval responde a los informes del ministro Sullivan sobre un nuevo estallido revolucionario en la República Dominicana. Se cancelaron las órdenes previas que disponían el envío de un buque a Puerto Príncipe, Haití, para trasladar al ministro estadounidense Bailly-Blanchard a Santiago de Cuba.

records.headline: A Washington dispatch dated April 13 reports that the Navy Department ordered
records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch dated April 13 reports that the Navy Department ordered the cruiser Des Moines from Progreso, Mexico, to Santo Domingo City, where the gunboat Nashville was already stationed. The two warships were directed to cooperate in protecting American interests following reports from Minister Sullivan of a new revolutionary outbreak in the Dominican Republic. Because the Nashville was required at Santo Domingo, its mission to transport American Minister Bailly-Blanchard from Port-au-Prince to Cuba was reassigned to the gunboat Wheeling.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Washington del 13 de abril informa que el Departamento de la Armada ordenó el traslado del crucero Des Moines desde Progreso, México, a la ciudad de Santo Domingo, donde ya se encontraba el cañonero Nashville. Se dispuso que ambos buques cooperaran en la protección de los intereses estadounidenses tras los informes del ministro Sullivan sobre un nuevo estallido revolucionario en la República Dominicana. Debido a que el Nashville era requerido en Santo Domingo, su misión de trasladar al ministro estadounidense Bailly-Blanchard desde Puerto Príncipe a Cuba fue reasignada al cañonero Wheeling.

records.headline: The Dominican government sent Frederico Velasquez, Jacinto Peynado and Francisco Henriquez as special commissioners
records.summary_en: The Dominican government sent Frederico Velasquez, Jacinto Peynado and Francisco Henriquez as special commissioners to Washington to confer with President Wilson, and officials expected them to protest the recent curtailment of expenditures from the Dominican reserve customs fund. The paper says the United States, as supervisor of Dominican finances, had forbidden further expenditures after the fund was found to be depleted.

El periódico dice que Estados Unidos, como supervisor de las finanzas dominicanas, había prohibido nuevos gastos después de que se descubrió que el fondo se estaba agotando.

records.headline: A report in the Richmond Times-Dispatch lists the Latin American delegates
records.summary_en: A report in the Richmond Times-Dispatch lists the Latin American delegates responding to addresses of welcome, naming Dr. Francisco J. Peynado as the representative for the Dominican Republic. Peynado is included in a roster alongside delegates from fifteen other American republics, including Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Cuba, and Peru; the roster closes with Uruguay, Dr. Pedro Cosio, and Venezuela, Dr. Pedro Rafael Rincones. President Wilson received the delegates at the White House immediately after the morning session. The President stood with Secretary Bryan, Secretary McAdoo and Secretary Daniels, and warmly greeted each delegate as they passed through the Red Room. The President was accompanied by military and naval aides in full dress uniform. The Marine Band played patriotic music as the delegates thronged through the mansion. After passing through the East Room, the Red Room and the Blue Room, the visitors were shown to the historic south portico, and later the President and members of the Cabinet sat with the delegates for a photograph on the lawn.
records.summary_es: Un informe en el Richmond Times-Dispatch enumera a los delegados latinoamericanos que respondieron a los discursos de bienvenida, mencionando al Dr. Francisco J. Peynado como representante de la República Dominicana. Peynado figura en una nómina junto a delegados de otras quince repúblicas americanas, entre ellas Argentina, Brasil, Chile, Cuba y Perú; la nómina se cierra con Uruguay, el Dr. Pedro Cosio, y Venezuela, el Dr. Pedro Rafael Rincones. El presidente Wilson recibió a los delegados en la Casa Blanca inmediatamente después de la sesión de la mañana. El presidente se situó junto al secretario Bryan, el secretario McAdoo y el secretario Daniels, y saludó calurosamente a cada delegado a su paso por el Salón Rojo. El presidente estaba acompañado por edecanes militares y navales con uniforme de gala. La Banda de la Marina interpretó música patriótica mientras los delegados recorrían la mansión. Tras pasar por el Salón Este, el Salón Rojo y el Salón Azul, los visitantes fueron conducidos al histórico pórtico sur, y más tarde el presidente y los miembros del Gabinete posaron con los delegados para una fotografía en el jardín.

records.summary_en: The Washington Herald reports that Secretary of the Navy Daniels has announced the gunboat Nashville was ordered from San Juan, Porto Rico, to San Domingo City to guard American interests in the event of political disturbances in the Dominican Republic. records.headline: An Associated Press dispatch by federal wireless from Washington
records.summary_en: An Associated Press dispatch by federal wireless from Washington in the Honolulu Star-Bulletin reports that James M. Sullivan, United States minister to Santo Domingo, has resigned and his resignation has been accepted. Sullivan had been under charges of incompetence and affiliation with commercial interests seeking to exploit the Dominican Republic after securing his position through the influence of Bryan. Following these allegations, President Wilson appointed United States Senator Jas. D. Phelan of California to investigate the matter, and Phelan reportedly concluded in an unofficial statement that Sullivan was temperamentally unfit, though the report has not yet been made public.

records.summary_en: According to The Bridgeport Evening Farmer, Senator Phelan's report on Minister James M. Sullivan had been before President Wilson and the State Department for several weeks before Sullivan was asked to resign. Sullivan's brief tenure in the Dominican Republic was terminated following charges and countercharges concerning his conduct, including the resignation of Walter W. Vick, United States collector of customs, who cited unsatisfactory working conditions created by the minister. During his investigation in the Dominican Republic and the United States, Senator Phelan took testimony showing that financiers associated with Samuel M. Jarvis of New York—who controlled the Banco National at Santo Domingo City and sought deposits of customs duties collected by the United States—had consulted Secretary Bryan regarding Sullivan's appointment, while other witnesses alleged the minister was interested in local contracts for Americans. Jarvis of New York, who controlled the Banco Nationale at Santo Domingo City and sought deposits of customs dues collected by the United States. Other witnesses gave testimony to show that the minister was interested in securing contracts there for other Americans, though former Governor Forte of New Jersey and additional witnesses testified that Sullivan was big-hearted, good-natured, and honest. records.summary_en: The Madison Daily Leader reports that James M. Sullivan has tendered his resignation as minister to the Dominican Republic to President Wilson, and it has been accepted. Sullivan's resignation is the consequence of an investigation conducted for the State Department by Senator Phelan of California into the minister's fitness for office. Senator Phelan's findings in the inquiry were unfavorable to Sullivan.

Las conclusiones del senador Phelan en la investigación fueron desfavorables para Sullivan.

records.headline: Reviewing the findings of Senator Phelan's investigation, The Washington Times reports
records.summary_en: Reviewing the findings of Senator Phelan's investigation, The Washington Times reports that while no evidence showed Minister Sullivan directly received money for official favors in Santo Domingo or knew of it, evidence demonstrated that a proposal was made to a New York contractor to pay money to a representative of Sullivan's backers to obtain favorable contracts. The report cited specific misconduct by Sullivan, including his relations with the Banco Nacional, hostility toward other banks, unauthorized promises to Dominican revolutionists, participation in Dominican politics, unpaid personal debts, and unauthorized statements to Dominican deputies regarding a proposed loan of $.100,000 in 1914. Senator Phelan concluded that the Dominican government's dependence on the United States for control over Dominican finances was probably responsible for the Dominican Republic's failure to demand Sullivan's recall.
records.summary_es: Al revisar las conclusiones de la investigación del senador Phelan, The Washington Times informa que, aunque ninguna prueba demostró que el ministro Sullivan recibiera directamente dinero por favores oficiales en Santo Domingo o estuviera al tanto de ello, sí hubo pruebas de que se propuso a un contratista de Nueva York pagar dinero a un representante de los patrocinadores de Sullivan para conseguir contratos favorables. El informe señaló faltas específicas de Sullivan, incluidas sus relaciones con el Banco Nacional, hostilidad hacia otros bancos, promesas no autorizadas a revolucionarios dominicanos, participación en la política dominicana, deudas personales impagas y declaraciones no autorizadas a diputados dominicanos sobre un préstamo propuesto de $.100,000 en 1914. El senador Phelan concluyó que la dependencia del gobierno dominicano respecto a Estados Unidos para el control de sus finanzas fue probablemente la causa de que la República Dominicana no exigiera la destitución de Sullivan.

records.summary_en: An editorial note in the Honolulu Star-Bulletin characterizes James Mark Sullivan, the New York lawyer found temperamentally unfit as minister to San Domingo, as a real exponent of shirtsleeve diplomacy. The paper relates an incident where a visiting foreign minister in the Dominican Republic called upon the newly arrived American diplomat and was shocked to find Sullivan lounging comfortably in an armchair without coat or shoes. The commentary observes that this lack of dignity was typical of Sullivan's attitude toward his post, adding that it was to Sullivan that ex-Secretary Bryan addressed his famous letter urging him to look out for positions for deserving Democrats.
records.summary_es: Una nota editorial en el Honolulu Star-Bulletin califica a James Mark Sullivan, el abogado neoyorquino considerado temperamentalmente no apto como ministro en Santo Domingo, como un auténtico exponente de la diplomacia en mangas de camisa. El diario relata un incidente en el cual un ministro extranjero de visita en la República Dominicana acudió a ver al recién llegado diplomático estadounidense y quedó consternado al encontrar a Sullivan descansando cómodamente en un sillón, sin chaqueta ni zapatos. El comentario señala que esta falta de dignidad fue característica de la actitud de Sullivan hacia su cargo, añadiendo que fue a Sullivan a quien el exsecretario Bryan dirigió su famosa carta instándole a buscar puestos para demócratas merecedores.

records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch via federal wireless in The Hawaiian Gazette reports that James M. Sullivan, United States minister to Santo Domingo, has resigned and his resignation has been accepted. Sullivan had been under charges of incompetence and ties to commercial interests seeking to exploit the Dominican Republic after obtaining his post through the influence of William J. Bryan. Following these allegations, President Wilson appointed United States Senator James D. Phelan of California to investigate the matter, and Phelan unofficially reported that Sullivan was temperamentally unfit, though his official report has not yet been released.

records.headline: The Washington Herald publishes excerpts of the findings of fact
records.summary_en: The Washington Herald publishes excerpts of the findings of fact and conclusions from Senator Phelan's investigation regarding James M. Sullivan, United States Minister to Santo Domingo. Phelan concluded that Sullivan lacked the training, education, and experience necessary for a successful administration and did not possess the qualities required for the diplomatic post. The report determined that Sullivan had been actively supported by individuals with large financial interests in Santo Domingo seeking pecuniary profit through an obligated minister, while concealing their motives from the appointing authority. Phelan affirmed there was no evidence Sullivan received money from contractors or participated in graft, but noted that the Dominican Republic's dependence under the convention of 1907 granting U.S. financial control influenced Dominican conduct.
records.summary_es: The Washington Herald publica extractos de las conclusiones fácticas y resoluciones de la investigación del senador Phelan respecto a James M. Sullivan, ministro de Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo. Phelan determinó que Sullivan carecía de la formación, educación y experiencia necesarias para una administración exitosa y no reunía las cualidades requeridas para el puesto diplomático. El informe concluyó que Sullivan contó con el activo respaldo de personas con importantes intereses financieros en Santo Domingo que buscaban beneficios económicos a través de un ministro comprometido, ocultando tales propósitos a la autoridad encargada del nombramiento. Phelan afirmó que no se hallaron pruebas de que Sullivan recibiera dinero de contratistas ni participara en sobornos, pero subrayó que la dependencia de la República Dominicana bajo la convención de 1907, que otorgaba control financiero a Estados Unidos, influyó en la conducta dominicana.

records.headline: The Evening Times-Republican reports on violent uprisings in Port-au-Prince
records.summary_en: The Evening Times-Republican reports on violent uprisings in Port-au-Prince, where the body of General Oscar lay unburied outside the consulate of the Dominican Republic after he faced a firing squad. The governor of Port-au-Prince had sought refuge at the Santo Domingo consulate following his failed defense of the presidential palace, but an enraged mob stormed the diplomatic building, dragged him into the street, and shot him dead. This act of violence erupted following the burial of 160 political prisoners massacred in prison the previous day, prompting relatives of the victims to also storm the French legation, seize President Guillaume, and shoot and mutilate him in the street.

Este acto de violencia estalló tras el entierro de 160 prisioneros políticos masacrados en prisión el día anterior, lo que llevó a familiares de las víctimas a asaltar también la legación francesa, capturar al presidente Guillaume y matarlo y mutilarlo en plena calle.

U. S. CRUISER TO RESCUE Sends Guard Ashore to Protect the Consulate at Cape Haitien CONSUL LIVINGSTON CABLES WASHINGTON Revolutionists Are Menacing the French Representative.

Washington, D. C., July 29.—The French consulate at Cape Haitien, Haiti, is menaced by revolutionists and a guard from the United States auxiliary cruiser Eagle has been landed to protect it. This information was cabled to-day to the state department by American Consul Livingston.

American marines were landed yesterday at Port Au Prince to protect the lives and property of Americans and other foreigners. Rear Admiral Caperton advised the navy department last night that he had sent a force ashore from the Washington. Rear Admiral Benson, acting secretary of the navy, declined to make the message public, but said:

"Caperton now has the situation in hand."

There was no firing at the marines, although disorder continued in the city. It was assumed a guard had been established at the French legation and at other points to protect foreigners.

The mutilated body of President Guillaume, after being dragged through the streets of Port Au Prince, was buried by several women yesterday in a cemetery outside the capital.

Admiral Caperton had reported by wireless while en route from Cape Haitien that the situation at the latter place was "very grave." The state department received messages from Charge D'Affaires Davis telling of the assassination of President Guillaume by a mob which broke into the French legation.

This violation of the diplomatic immunition which foreign legations enjoy would be regarded ordinarily as a serious affront, but in view of the absence of an established government and the generally turbulent conditions, the incident probably will not complicate the situation.

President Wilson has been giving serious consideration to the situation in Haiti for several weeks. Paul Fuller, Jr., sent to investigate conditions there, recently returned with a report that it was impossible for him to negotiate a proposed treaty with President Guillaume because of the latter's fears that the populace would rise against him if he signed it. It is known that the United States attempted to arrange for the administration of the customs in ways analogous to the American control of customs in the Dominican republic.

Sullivan, termed an original "deserving Democrat," as part of the bitterness the "Black Republic" was forced to endure. The paper reports that Dominican exports to the United States nonetheless increased by 60 percent under the Democratic tariff law, driven by sugar shipments jumping from $1,611,161 to $3,367,470 in value, with duty reductions benefiting the American and Federal Sugar Refining Companies. records.newspaper: New Hampshire Farmer and Weekly Union
records.headline: The New Hampshire Farmer and Weekly Union reviews Senator Phelan's report
records.summary_en: The New Hampshire Farmer and Weekly Union reviews Senator Phelan's report on United States Minister Sullivan, asserting that Sullivan demonstrated a complete lack of diplomatic temperament and the qualities required to inspire confidence. Quoting directly from the findings, the article details Sullivan's relations with the Banco Nacional, his hostility toward competing banks, his methods during the revolution at Puerto Plata, his involvement in party politics, his unpaid personal debts, and his obtaining of financial favors for a relative. These actions led to a loss of public confidence that incapacitated Sullivan on the peace commission of 1914 and rendered him powerless to represent the United States. While Phelan's report credits Sullivan's administration with much that was kindly and helpful, the senator concludes that the Dominican government would have demanded his removal were it not afraid of offending the American government, which controls Dominican finances under the convention of 1907.
records.summary_es: El New Hampshire Farmer and Weekly Union examina el informe del senador Phelan sobre el ministro estadounidense Sullivan, afirmando que este demostró una total carencia de temperamento diplomático y de las cualidades necesarias para inspirar confianza. Al citar directamente las conclusiones, el artículo detalla las relaciones de Sullivan con el Banco Nacional, su hostilidad hacia bancos competidores, sus métodos durante la revolución en Puerto Plata, su intromisión en la política partidaria, el impago de deudas personales y la obtención de favores económicos para un pariente. Estas conductas provocaron una pérdida de confianza pública que incapacitó a Sullivan en la comisión de paz de 1914 y lo dejó sin facultades para representar a los Estados Unidos. Aunque el informe de Phelan reconoce que la gestión de Sullivan tuvo mucho de bondadoso y servicial, el senador concluye que el gobierno dominicano habría exigido su destitución de no haber temido ofender al gobierno estadounidense, que controla las finanzas dominicanas en virtud de la convención de 1907.

records.headline: The Perth Amboy Evening News reports that disturbances in Haiti threaten
records.summary_en: The Perth Amboy Evening News reports that disturbances in Haiti threaten to spread across the island into Santo Domingo, where General Blot, former commander of northern Haitian government forces, has departed for Monte Cristi. Authorities believe Blot intends to obtain arms and recruits in the Dominican Republic to resume his struggle for control in Haiti, raising fears that his presence will aggravate local political unrest, as riots have already broken out in several Dominican localities. The dispatch recalls that the cruiser Nashville was sent to Santo Domingo City six weeks earlier during an anticipated disturbance that failed to materialize, before being transferred to operations in Haiti. Observers note that Santo Domingo is currently ruled by a compromise coalition government formed through Washington's influence, which is widely acknowledged as unsuccessful.
records.summary_es: El Perth Amboy Evening News informa que los disturbios en Haití amenazan con extenderse por toda la isla hacia Santo Domingo, adonde el general Blot, excomandante de las fuerzas gubernamentales del norte de Haití, ha partido con rumbo a Monte Cristi. Las autoridades creen que Blot intentará conseguir armas y reclutas en la República Dominicana para reanudar su lucha por el poder en Haití, lo que hace temer que su presencia agrave la agitación política local, habiendo estallado ya disturbios en diversas localidades dominicanas. El despacho recuerda que el crucero Nashville fue enviado a la ciudad de Santo Domingo seis semanas antes ante un previsto conflicto que no llegó a estallar, antes de ser trasladado a operaciones en Haití. Los observadores señalan que Santo Domingo está actualmente gobernado por una coalición de compromiso forjada bajo la influencia de Washington, la cual se reconoce de forma generalizada como un fracaso.

records.headline: A Washington dispatch in The Washington Herald reports that William Worthington Russell of Maryland
records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch in The Washington Herald reports that William Worthington Russell of Maryland will soon return to Santo Domingo as United States Minister, filling the vacancy created by the forced retirement of James J. Sullivan of New York. Two years earlier, Russell had been removed as minister to make way for Sullivan, whom Secretary of State Bryan favored as a "deserving Democrat." The article outlines Russell's extensive diplomatic career, noting that the Annapolis Naval Academy graduate previously served at Caracas, Panama City, Colombia, and Venezuela before holding the post of minister resident and consul general to the Dominican Republic until August 1913.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Washington en The Washington Herald informa que William Worthington Russell, de Maryland, regresará pronto a Santo Domingo como ministro de los Estados Unidos, ocupando la vacante dejada por el retiro forzoso de James J. Sullivan, de Nueva York. Dos años antes, Russell había sido destituido como ministro para dar paso a Sullivan, a quien el secretario de Estado Bryan favoreció por considerarlo un «demócrata merecedor». El artículo reseña la extensa carrera diplomática de Russell, destacando que este graduado de la Academia Naval de Annapolis sirvió previamente en Caracas, la ciudad de Panamá, Colombia y Venezuela antes de ocupar el cargo de ministro residente y cónsul general en la República Dominicana hasta agosto de 1913.

records.headline: The Washington Herald reports that President Wilson has issued
records.summary_en: The Washington Herald reports that President Wilson has issued several recess appointments, designating William W. Russell as United States Minister to the Dominican Republic to succeed James M. Sullivan, who resigned. Russell previously served as minister in Santo Domingo under President Taft before being removed by former Secretary of State Bryan in favor of Sullivan. Sullivan's subsequent resignation followed an investigation conducted by Special Commissioner James D. Phelan into charges of official unfitness originally brought by Walker W. Vick, the former Dominican director of public works.
records.summary_es: The Washington Herald informa que el presidente Wilson ha emitido varios nombramientos durante el receso legislativo, designando a William W. Russell como ministro de los Estados Unidos en la República Dominicana para suceder a James M. Sullivan, quien renunció. Russell se había desempeñado anteriormente como ministro en Santo Domingo bajo la presidencia de Taft antes de ser apartado por el exsecretario de Estado Bryan en favor de Sullivan. La posterior renuncia de Sullivan se produjo tras una investigación realizada por el comisionado especial James D. Phelan sobre acusaciones de ineptitud oficial presentadas originalmente por Walker W. Vick, exdirector de obras públicas de la República Dominicana.

records.headline: In an editorial reprinted from the Providence Journal, the New Britain Herald observes
records.summary_en: In an editorial reprinted from the Providence Journal, the New Britain Herald observes that the selection of William Worthington Russell of Maryland to replace James M. Sullivan as minister to the Dominican Republic brings a vexing chapter to an unusual close. The commentary highlights that Russell was the exact official displaced when Sullivan was originally installed, praising the administration for reversing its initial mistake with admirable candor and completeness. While affirming the recognized prerogative of an incoming executive to reorganize the diplomatic corps along political lines, the editorial notes a growing public sentiment that appointments to foreign service posts should be governed by fitness rather than partisan affiliation.
records.summary_es: En un editorial reproducido del Providence Journal, el New Britain Herald observa que la designación de William Worthington Russell, de Maryland, en reemplazo de James M. Sullivan como ministro en la República Dominicana cierra un enojoso capítulo de manera insólita. El comentario subraya que Russell fue el mismo funcionario desplazado cuando Sullivan fue designado en un principio, elogiando a la administración por corregir su error inicial con admirable franqueza e integridad. Si bien reafirma la prerrogativa reconocida de un poder ejecutivo entrante para reorganizar el cuerpo diplomático con arreglo a criterios políticos, el editorial resalta el creciente consenso público favorable a que las designaciones en el servicio exterior se rijan por la idoneidad y no por la afiliación partidaria.

records.summary_en: Reprinting commentary from the New York World, The Fargo Forum and Daily Republican discusses the reappointment of William W. Russell as minister to the Dominican Republic, viewing it as evidence of improved standards within the State Department under Secretary Lansing. The article notes that although Russell had developed through the diplomatic corps since the Cleveland administration and was himself a Democrat, he was omitted from Secretary Bryan's list of "deserving Democrats." Consequently, he was removed to accommodate James M. Sullivan, whose eventual forced resignation highlighted the flaws of that partisan patronage policy.
records.summary_es: Al reproducir un comentario del New York World, The Fargo Forum and Daily Republican examina la nueva designación de William W. Russell como ministro en la República Dominicana, considerándola una prueba de la mejora de los criterios en el Departamento de Estado bajo el secretario Lansing. El artículo señala que, aunque Russell se había formado en la carrera diplomática desde el gobierno de Cleveland y era él mismo demócrata, fue omitido de la lista de «demócratas merecedores» del secretario Bryan. Por consiguiente, fue destituido para dar cabida a James M. Sullivan, cuya renuncia forzada posterior puso de manifiesto los defectos de esa política de favoritismo partidista.

records.headline: A special feature in The Washington Herald details Dominican trade
records.summary_en: A special feature in The Washington Herald details Dominican trade statistics and agricultural prospects for 1914, noting that the United States handled roughly 75 percent of the nation's commerce, with Germany second. The report illustrates the disruptive impact of the European war: while sugar exports reached $4,948,452 and cocoa $3,896,489, tobacco shipments plummeted from $1,121,775 in 1913 to $394,224 following the closing of the German market, alongside exports of coffee, bananas, and timber. The dispatch emphasizes untapped potential in goat and cattle ranching, observing that the island is free from the fever tick and bovine diseases, and quotes a survey by Karl W. Woodward of the American Forestry Service calculating that forested tracts cover 9,500,000 acres of the republic's total land surface.
records.summary_es: Un reportaje especial en The Washington Herald detalla las estadísticas comerciales y las perspectivas agrícolas dominicanas para 1914, señalando que los Estados Unidos controlaban cerca del 75 por ciento del comercio nacional, con Alemania en segundo término. El informe ilustra el impacto perturbador de la guerra europea: mientras que las exportaciones de azúcar alcanzaron 4,948,452 dólares y las de cacao 3,896,489 dólares, los envíos de tabaco cayeron de 1,121,775 dólares en 1913 a 394,224 dólares tras el cierre del mercado alemán, junto con exportaciones de café, plátanos y madera. El despacho subraya el potencial desaprovechado en la cría de ganado caprino y vacuno, destacando que la isla está libre de garrapatas de la fiebre y enfermedades bovinas, y cita un estudio de Karl W. Woodward, del Servicio Forestal estadounidense, que calcula que las zonas boscosas abarcan 9,500,000 acres de la superficie territorial total de la república.

records.headline: The Washington Herald outlines agricultural and forestry opportunities
records.summary_en: The Washington Herald outlines agricultural and forestry opportunities in northern Santo Domingo, reporting that the soil of the Yaque Valley is exceptionally well suited for cotton cultivation, yielding long-staple varieties with minimal insect or weevil damage across Monte Cristi and Puerto Plata provinces. The article reports that experiments with northern coastal timber, such as "almacigo," show it to be an excellent, lightweight substitute for native basswood, while millions of tons of "baitoa" offer abundant boxwood poised to compete in the American market. In addition, the paper emphasizes the Dominican Republic's vast stands of tropical hardwoods and one of the world's largest primeval tracts of longleaf yellow pine, alongside profitable opportunities in sugar cultivation.
records.summary_es: The Washington Herald describe las oportunidades agrícolas y forestales en el norte de Santo Domingo, e informa que el suelo del valle del Yaque es excepcionalmente propicio para el cultivo del algodón, rindiendo variedades de fibra larga con escasos daños por insectos o gorgojos en las provincias de Monte Cristi y Puerto Plata. El artículo señala que las pruebas con maderas de la costa norte, como el almacigo, demuestran que es un excelente sustituto liviano para el tilo americano, mientras que millones de toneladas de «baitoa» ofrecen madera de cajonería lista para competir en el mercado estadounidense. Además, el periódico destaca las extensas reservas dominicanas de maderas duras tropicales y una de las mayores extensiones vírgenes de pino amarillo de hoja larga existentes en el mundo, junto con oportunidades rentables en el cultivo de azúcar.

records.headline: A Santo Domingo cablegram in the Evening Star reports that President Juan I. Jimenes of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: A Santo Domingo cablegram in the Evening Star reports that President Juan I. Jimenes of the Dominican Republic has appointed Jose Manuel Jimenes as Minister of the Interior. Jose Manuel Jimenes had previously served as minister of public works and minister of the interior in earlier cabinets. The dispatch also announces the appointment of Francisco Herrera as Minister of Finance, noting that quiet prevails throughout the republic.

El despacho anuncia asimismo el nombramiento de Francisco Herrera como ministro de Hacienda, señalando que reina la tranquilidad en toda la república.

records.headline: An editorial in The Wheeling Intelligencer argues that American policy
records.summary_en: An editorial in The Wheeling Intelligencer argues that American policy over the preceding seventeen years—including annexing Puerto Rico, taking the Canal Zone, establishing a protectorate over Cuba, and moving toward the annexation of the entire island of Santo Domingo and Central America—has fostered deep alarm in Latin America. The paper observes that American financial control over the Dominican Republic and Nicaragua appears to other republics as a gradual territorial advance. Rejecting the claim that American benevolence will improve conditions in troubled nations, the editorial asserts that Latin Americans demand the right to govern themselves and fundamentally distrust the motives of the United States.
records.summary_es: Un editorial en The Wheeling Intelligencer sostiene que la política estadounidense durante los diecisiete años anteriores —incluida la anexión de Puerto Rico, la toma de la Zona del Canal, el establecimiento de un protectorado sobre Cuba y los avances hacia la anexión de toda la isla de Santo Domingo y Centroamérica— ha generado una profunda alarma en América Latina. El diario observa que el control financiero que los Estados Unidos ejercen sobre la República Dominicana y Nicaragua es visto por las demás repúblicas como un avance territorial progresivo. Al rechazar la tesis de que la benevolencia estadounidense mejorará las condiciones de países con dificultades, el editorial afirma que los latinoamericanos reclaman el derecho de autogobernarse y desconfían plenamente de los motivos de Washington.

records.headline: Reprinting an account from the New York Telegram, The Detroit Times describes
records.summary_en: Reprinting an account from the New York Telegram, The Detroit Times describes the island shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic, originally named "Isla Española" by its early Spanish discoverers. The article explains that Christopher Columbus established the first European settlement in the New World, called "Isabella" after the Queen of Castile, within modern Dominican territory near the site of Puerto Plata. Although Isabella soon vanished into ruins, the feature observes that the oldest surviving European settlement in the Western Hemisphere is also located in the republic, namely its capital city of Santo Domingo.
records.summary_es: Al reproducir una reseña del New York Telegram, The Detroit Times describe la isla compartida por Haití y la República Dominicana, llamada originalmente «Isla Española» por sus primeros descubridores españoles. El artículo explica que Cristóbal Colón estableció el primer asentamiento europeo en el Nuevo Mundo, llamado «Isabella» en honor a la reina de Castilla, dentro del actual territorio dominicano, cerca del emplazamiento de Puerto Plata. Aunque Isabela pronto quedó reducida a ruinas, la crónica destaca que el asentamiento europeo habitado más antiguo del hemisferio occidental también se localiza en la república, a saber, su ciudad capital, Santo Domingo.

records.headline: The Paris Express surveys key Dominican ports, transport infrastructure
records.summary_en: The Paris Express surveys key Dominican ports, transport infrastructure, and commercial agriculture, noting that cotton yields in the country significantly exceed those of the southern United States. Puerto Plata, with 10,000 to 12,000 residents, is connected by railway southward to Santiago de los Caballeros, La Vega, and Moca in the fertile Cibao region, where cacao and tobacco are cultivated, the latter traditionally marketed in Hamburg. The article describes Samaná Bay as an expansive harbor frequented by the United States North Atlantic squadron, featuring a forty-mile Scottish railway connecting Sánchez to the interior. Additionally, San Pedro de Macorís is highlighted as the center of the sugar trade, backed by millions of dollars in American capital and employing laborers from the English and Danish West Indies.
records.summary_es: El Paris Express pasa revista a los principales puertos dominicanos, su infraestructura de transporte y su agricultura comercial, destacando que el rendimiento del algodón en el país supera con creces al de los estados del sur estadounidense. Puerto Plata, con entre 10,000 y 12,000 habitantes, se comunica por ferrocarril hacia el sur con Santiago de los Caballeros, La Vega y Moca en la fértil región del Cibao, donde se producen cacao y tabaco, este último comercializado tradicionalmente en Hamburgo. El artículo describe la bahía de Samaná como un extenso fondeadero frecuentado por la escuadra estadounidense del Atlántico Norte, con un ferrocarril escocés de cuarenta millas que enlaza Sánchez con el interior. Asimismo, resalta a San Pedro de Macorís como centro del comercio azucarero, financiado por millones de dólares en capital estadounidense y con trabajadores provenientes de las Antillas británicas y danesas.

records.headline: A feature on the Dominican Republic describes the capital's social life, with its clubs, Club Union and Casino de la Juventud
records.summary_en: A feature on the Dominican Republic describes the capital's social life, with its clubs, Club Union and Casino de la Juventud, and frequent entertainments, and says automobiles are plentiful, with the ride from the capital to San Cristobal along the new macadam boulevard most attractive at four dollars an hour. It notes several hotels, of which the Hotel Francis is the best known, a large foreign colony at the capital and in Macoris and Puerto Plata, a trip of about eight or nine days from New York, and a healthy climate with no serious epidemic since the cholera outbreak of the early sixties.
records.summary_es: Un reportaje sobre la República Dominicana describe la vida social de la capital, con sus clubes, el Club Union y el Casino de la Juventud, y sus frecuentes entretenimientos, y dice que los automóviles son abundantes, y que el paseo desde la capital hasta San Cristobal por el nuevo bulevar de macadán es muy atractivo a cuatro dólares la hora. Menciona varios hoteles, de los cuales el Hotel Francis es el más conocido, una numerosa colonia extranjera en la capital y en Macoris y Puerto Plata, un viaje de unos ocho o nueve días desde Nueva York, y un clima saludable sin ninguna epidemia grave desde el brote de cólera de principios de los años sesenta.

records.headline: The Ottumwa Tri-Weekly Courier publishes an editorial arguing
records.summary_en: The Ottumwa Tri-Weekly Courier publishes an editorial arguing that United States acquisitions over the preceding seventeen years in Puerto Rico, Cuba, and the Canal Zone have led Latin American states to suspect Washington intends to annex Central America and the whole island of Santo Domingo. The piece emphasizes that existing American financial supervision over the Dominican Republic and Nicaragua is regarded across the region as a disguised, creeping advance upon local territory. Concluding that Latin American populations place self-determination above foreign governance, the paper warns that neighboring republics thoroughly distrust United States intentions and reject claims of benevolent intervention.
records.summary_es: El Ottumwa Tri-Weekly Courier publica un editorial en el que sostiene que las adquisiciones estadounidenses durante los diecisiete años anteriores en Puerto Rico, Cuba y la Zona del Canal han llevado a los estados latinoamericanos a sospechar que Washington busca anexionarse Centroamérica y la isla entera de Santo Domingo. La nota resalta que la supervisión financiera estadounidense sobre la República Dominicana y Nicaragua se percibe en toda la región como un avance solapado sobre el territorio local. Al concluir que los pueblos latinoamericanos valoran más su libre determinación que el tutelaje extranjero, el diario advierte que las repúblicas vecinas desconfían por completo de las intenciones de los Estados Unidos y rechazan las justificaciones de intervención benevolente.

records.headline: An article in The Monticellonian highlights commercial and agricultural
records.summary_en: An article in The Monticellonian highlights commercial and agricultural developments in the Dominican Republic, noting that domestic cotton cultivation yields far more per acre than in the American South. The report describes the northern port of Puerto Plata, whose railway connects to Santiago de los Caballeros, La Vega, and Moca in the fertile Cibao agricultural region, centers of cacao and tobacco production. It points to Samaná Bay as an exceptional natural harbor frequently used for maneuvers by the United States North Atlantic squadron, with the port of Sánchez serving as a terminal for a forty-mile Scottish railway. In the south, San Pedro de Macorís is identified as the chief sugar port, where modern mills financed by millions in American capital employ workers from the British and Danish West Indies.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en The Monticellonian destaca el desarrollo comercial y agrícola de la República Dominicana, señalando que la producción nacional de algodón genera un rendimiento por acre muy superior al del sur de los Estados Unidos. El informe describe el puerto septentrional de Puerto Plata, cuyo ferrocarril comunica con Santiago de los Caballeros, La Vega y Moca en la fértil región agrícola del Cibao, principales zonas productoras de cacao y tabaco. Señala la bahía de Samaná como un fondeadero natural excepcional empleado con frecuencia para maniobras por la escuadra estadounidense del Atlántico Norte, con el puerto de Sánchez como terminal de un ferrocarril escocés de cuarenta millas. En el sur, identifica a San Pedro de Macorís como el puerto azucarero por excelencia, donde modernos ingenios financiados con millones de dólares de capital estadounidense emplean a obreros de las Antillas británicas y danesas.
