records.full_text:
PROSPEROUS LITTLE REPUBLIC

THAT the European war has disturbed the economic and commercial situation in practically every civilized country in the world is a fact well known to everyone at all conversant with international trade conditions. Naturally the republics of the western hemisphere are no exception. Every one of them has felt the disastrous effects, but not in equal nor even in proportionately equal measure. Nearly all of them have experienced a large diminution in their export trade, and consequently a decrease in purchasing power and a resultant diminution in their imports. One remarkable exception is the Dominican Republic, says the Bulletin of the Pan-American union. That little country enjoys the distinction of having sold more of its products, in point of value, to the outside world during the year 1914 than it did during 1913. The increased value of its exports was only $118,840, but that it should have increased its sales at all is an astounding fact. Its purchases from other nations during the year were considerably less, but the net result is that the country has made a material financial gain.

The Dominican Republic is one of the smallest of the American republics, with an area of about 19,325 square miles. This is nearly equal to the combined areas of New Hampshire and Vermont. It has a population of between six and seven hundred thousand inhabitants. Haiti is the adjoining republic and the two together comprise the island called by the first Spanish discoverers "Isla Espanola" and now sometimes called "Santo Domingo" and sometimes "Haiti." Within the limits of what is now the territory of the Dominican Republic was located by Columbus the first settlement of Europeans in the new world. This settlement was called "Isabella," after the queen of Castile, the friend and patroness of Columbus. The first Spanish settlement, like Jamestown, the first English settlement, no longer exists except as a ruin. In fact, "Isabella" disappeared a few years after its foundation. The modern city of Puerto Plata is located near the former site of the old settlement. The oldest existing settlement of Europeans in the western world is likewise located in the Dominican Republic. This is the capital city, Santo Domingo.

One of World's Richest Spots.

The Dominican Republic, in fact the whole island, is naturally one of the richest spots in the world. The soil is remarkably fertile and produces luxuriously. On the north coast, in the province of Monte Cristi, near the Haitian border, the soil is well adapted for cotton raising, and there is a very considerable acreage devoted to this industry, backed by American and English capitalists. The cotton is of a fine quality, and the yield per acre is much greater than that in our southern states.

Puerto Plata, an important port of the north, is a town of some 10,000 or 12,000 inhabitants, connected by a railway, running south, with the towns of the fertile Caibo region—Santiago de los Caballeros, La Vega, and Moca. These towns are located in the great agricultural regions of the republic, where the famous cacao bean is cultivated. Tobacco also is grown to a considerable extent, and has had until recently a ready market in Hamburg. Other ports of importance are Samana and Sanchez, in the beautiful Samana bay. This bay is famous for its size and picturesque scenery. It is about 25 miles long by 8 miles wide, with a depth of water sufficient to float the largest battleships. Our North Atlantic squadron has frequently gone there for maneuvers. At the entrance to the bay is the town of Samana, and at the head is Sanchez, connected with the interior by the Sanchez & Moca railway, a Scotch enterprise, for a distance of 40 miles.

San Pedro de Macoris is the sugar port of the republic. In and around Macoris there are thousands of acres of land devoted to the raising of sugar cane, and millions of dollars of American capital are invested in this enterprise. The plantations are all equipped with the most modern machinery, and the cane is cultivated and gathered by colored laborers from the English and Danish West Indies.

Relics in the Capital.

Seventy miles from La Romana and 40 miles from Macoris is Santo Domingo City, the capital of the republic. In Santo Domingo we find ourselves in the midst of modern civilization, surrounded by innumerable relics that carry us back to the fifteenth century. Here can be seen the ruins of the first church, San Nicolas, built some time in the early part of 1500, and three or four years ago the mahogany taken from these ruins was in a perfect state of preservation. Here, as claimed by the Dominicans, can be seen the bones of Christopher Columbus, left by mistake by the Spaniards when they evacuated the island, and who removed from the crypt in the cathedral to Havana the remains of a brother of Columbus, thinking they were taking the bones of the great discoverer.

The ruins of the house of Diego Colon, the son of Christopher, are still standing, where, according to history, a court was established whose entertainments rivaled in splendor those we read of in the Arabian Nights. On the bank of the river still stands the massive ceiba tree to which were tied the caravels of Columbus. In Santo Domingo City Columbus was put in chains and sent home to Spain a prisoner in disgrace. The city is built on the west bank of the Ozama river and is under the administration of the department of public works. A magnificent macadam boulevard, bordered on either side with native elms, interspersed with tropical foliage, extends from the center of the city for 20 miles in the direction of Bani, the birthplace of the famous Cuban hero, Maximo Gomez. On this same boulevard can be seen the well-preserved ruins of the Fort San Geronimo, which in early days withstood an attack of the English under Drake. The entrance from the town to this boulevard is through an arch constructed by the government in memory of those who fell fighting for the independence of the country, and the arch bears the inscription "Dulce et Decorum est pro Patria Mori."

Life at the capital, while not as fast and gay as at the larger cities of the South, is still very agreeable. There are two well-equipped and conducted clubs, Club Union and Casino de la Juventud, where there are frequent social entertainments. Automobiles are plentiful and the ride from the capital to San Cristobal along the new macadam boulevard is most attractive. Automobiles can be procured for $4 an hour. There are several hotels in the city, of which the Hotel Francis is the best known. There is quite a large foreign colony at the capital and in Macoris and Puerto Plata. The whole trip from New York, including a stop at all ports, is about eight or nine days.

A very erroneous impression prevails that the climate of Santo Domingo is unhealthy. From its geographical position it cannot be unhealthy. The winds have a clean sweep across the island, and there has been no serious epidemic there since the cholera outbreak some time in the early sixties.

It has a population of between six and seven hundred thousand inhabitants. Haiti is the adjoining republic and the two together comprise the island called by the first Spanish discoverers "Isla Espanola" and now sometimes called "Santo Domingo" and sometimes "Haiti." Within the limits of what is now the territory of the Dominican Republic was located by Columbus the first settlement of Europeans in the new world. This settlement was called "Isabella," after the queen of Castile, the friend and patroness of Columbus. The first Spanish settlement, like Jamestown, the first English settlement, no longer exists except as a ruin. In fact, "Isabeila" disappeared a few years after its foundation. The modern city of Puerto Plata is located near the former site of the old settlement. The oldest existing settlement of Europeans in the western world is likewise located in the Dominican Republic. This is the capital city, Santo Domingo.

One of World's Richest Spots.

The Dominican Republic, in fact the whole island, is naturally one of the richest spots in the world. The soil is remarkably fertile and produces luxuriously. On the north coast, in the province of Monte Cristi, near the Haitian border, the soil is well adapted for cotton raising and there is a very considerable acreage devoted to this industry, backed by American and English capitalists. The cotton is of a fine quality, and the yield per acre is much greater than that in our southern states.

Puerto Plata, an important port of the north, is a town of some 10,000 or 12,000 inhabitants, connected by a railway, running south, with the towns of the fertile Caibo region—Santiago de los Caballeros, La Vega, and Moca. These towns are located in the great agricultural regions of the republic, where the famous cacao bean is cultivated. Tobacco also is grown to a considerable extent, and has had until recently a ready market in Hamburg. Other ports of importance are Samana and Sanchez, in the beautiful Samana bay. This bay is famous for its size and picturesque scenery. It is about 25 miles long by 8 miles wide, with a depth of water sufficient to float the largest battleships. Our North Atlantic squadron has frequently gone there for maneuvers At the entrance to the bay is the town of Samana, and at the head is Sanchez, connected with the interior by the Sanchez & Moca railway, a Scotch enterprise, for a distance of 40 miles.

San Pedro de Macoris is the sugar port of the republic. In and around Macoris there are thousands of acres of land devoted to the raising of sugar cane, and millions of dollars of American capital are invested in this enterprise. The plantations are all equipped with the most modern machinery, and the cane is cultivated and gathered by colored laborers from the English and Danish West Indies.

Relics in the Capital.

Seventy miles from La Romana and 40 miles from Macoris is Santo Domingo City, the capital of the republic. In Santo Domingo we find ourselves in the midst of modern civilization, surrounded by innumerable relics that carry us back to the fifteenth century. Here can be seen the ruins of the first church, San Nicolas, built some time in the early part of 1500, and three or four years ago the mahogany taken from these ruins was in a perfect state of preservation. Here, as claimed by the Dominicans, can be seen the bones of Christopher Columbus, left by mistake by the Spaniards when they evacuated the island, and who removed from the crypt in the cathedral to Havana the remains of a brother of Columbus, thinking they were taking the bones of the great discoverer.

The ruins of the house of Diego Colon, the son of Christopher, are still standing, where, according to history, a court was established whose entertainments rivaled in splendor those we read of in the Arabian Nights. On the bank of the river still stands the massive ceiba tree to which were tied the caravels of Columbus. In Santo Domingo City Columbus was put in chains and sent home to Spain a prisoner in disgrace. The city is built on the west bank of the Ozama river and is under the administration of the department of public works. A magnificent macadam boulevard, bordered on either side with native elms, interspersed with tropical foliage, extends from the center of the city for 20 miles in the direction of Bani, the birthplace of the famous Cuban hero, Maximo Gomez. On this same boulevard can be seen the well-preserved ruins of the Fort San Geronimo, which in early days withstood an attack of the English under Drake. The entrance from the town to this boulevard is through an arch constructed by the government in memory of those who fell fighting for the independence of the country, and the arch bears the inscription "Dulce et Decorum est pro Patria Mori."

Life at the capital, while not as fast and gay as at the larger cities of the South, is still very agreeable. There are two well-equipped and conducted clubs, Club Union and Casino de la Juventud, where there are frequent social entertainments. Automobiles are plentiful and the ride from the capital to San Cristobal along the new macadam boulevard is most attractive. Automobiles can be procured for $4 an hour. There are several hotels in the city, of which the Hotel Francis is the best known. There is quite a large foreign colony at the capital and in Macoris and Puerto Plata. The whole trip from New York, including a stop at all ports, is about eight or nine days.

A very erroneous impression prevails that the climate of Santo Domingo is unhealthy. From its geographical position it cannot be unhealthy. The winds have a clean sweep across the island, and there has been no serious epidemic there since the cholera outbreak some time in the early sixties.

PROSPEROUS LITTLE REPUBLIC

THAT the European war has disturbed the economic and commercial situation in practically every civilized country in the world is a fact well known to everyone at all conversant with international trade conditions. Naturally the republics of the western hemisphere are no exception. Every one of them has felt the disastrous effects, but not in equal nor even in proportionately equal measure. Nearly all of them have experienced a large diminution in their export trade, and consequently a decrease in purchasing power and a resultant diminution in their imports. One remarkable exception is the Dominican Republic, says the Bulletin of the Pan-American union. That little country enjoys the distinction of having sold more of its products, in point of value, to the outside world during the year 1914 than it did during 1913. records.summary_en: An article in The Kansas City Sun notes that Isabella, the first Spanish settlement founded in the New World and named after the queen of Castile, now exists only as a ruin near Puerto Plata, whereas Santo Domingo remains the oldest existing European settlement in the western hemisphere. Describing the Dominican Republic as naturally one of the richest spots in the world, the paper highlights cotton cultivation in the province of Monte Cristi near the Haitian border, where American and English capital supports acreage yielding far more per acre than farms in the American South. The report further details the northern port of Puerto Plata, noting its population of 10,000 to 12,000 and its railway connection southward to Santiago de los Caballeros, La Vega, and Moca in the fertile agricultural interior. In these districts, the article observes extensive production of cacao and tobacco, the latter until recently finding a ready market in Hamburg, while also citing Samana and Sanchez as vital ports on Samana Bay.

El informe detalla además el puerto norteño de Puerto Plata, señalando su población de 10,000 a 12,000 habitantes y su enlace ferroviario hacia el sur con Santiago de los Caballeros, La Vega y Moca en el fértil interior agrícola. records.headline: A feature in The Sun traces the voyage of a merchant vessel
records.summary_en: A feature in The Sun traces the voyage of a merchant vessel following a Dominican government cruiser that transported a volunteer force to preserve order along coastal towns, including Santo Domingo, Macorís, Puerto Plata, Samaná, Sánchez, and Monte Cristi. The account reports that this peacekeeping force proved ineffective, observing that most troops sent to Puerto Plata took refuge in private homes when insurgents fired cannon in the town plaza on August 28. Days prior to the turmoil in Puerto Plata, an uprising of brigands occurred at Sánchez, described as the coastal outlet for timber from Santiago and coffee and cocoa from Moca served by a twenty-five-mile railway built with English capital. The report notes that the Minister of Public Works had advanced into the mountains to suppress the bandits shortly before the line's first passenger train operated on August 21.
records.summary_es: Una crónica en The Sun sigue la travesía de un buque mercante que navegó tras un crucero del gobierno dominicano que transportaba una fuerza de voluntarios para preservar el orden en diversos puertos costeros, entre ellos Santo Domingo, Macorís, Puerto Plata, Samaná, Sánchez y Monte Cristi. El relato informa que esta fuerza de pacificación resultó ineficaz, señalando que la mayoría de las tropas enviadas a Puerto Plata se refugiaron en viviendas particulares cuando los insurgentes dispararon cañones en la plaza de la ciudad el 28 de agosto. Días antes de los disturbios en Puerto Plata, se produjo un alzamiento de bandoleros en Sánchez, descrito como la salida costera para las maderas de Santiago y el café y cacao de Moca mediante un ferrocarril de veinticinco millas construido con capital inglés. La crónica indica que el ministro de Obras Públicas había avanzado hacia las montañas para someter a los bandidos poco antes de que circulara el primer tren de pasajeros de la línea el 21 de agosto.

records.headline: Writing on social conditions in Santo Domingo, The Sun characterizes
records.summary_en: Writing on social conditions in Santo Domingo, The Sun characterizes the Dominican population as predominantly of Spanish descent, comprising white citizens, persons of mixed African heritage, and combinations of European, Indigenous, and African ancestry. The article explains that while pure Black inhabitants are less prominent, significant numbers reside along coastal plantations from Turks Island, the Bahamas, Jamaica, and other West Indian islands, alongside Haitian immigrants near Monte Cristi. Rejecting the label of a black republic, the paper describes the nation as a colored commonwealth where no racial conflict exists, noting that citizens intermarry and hold public office on terms of equality regardless of skin color. The report adds that the national administration has encountered strong opposition in Congress and requires assistance from the United States to suppress recurring revolutions.
records.summary_es: Al escribir sobre las condiciones sociales en Santo Domingo, The Sun describe a la población dominicana como predominantemente de ascendencia española, integrada por ciudadanos blancos, personas con mestizaje africano y combinaciones de ascendencia europea, indígena y africana. El artículo explica que, si bien los habitantes negros puros son menos visibles, un número considerable reside en las plantaciones costeras procedente de las islas Turcas, las Bahamas, Jamaica y otras islas antillanas, además de inmigrantes haitianos cerca de Monte Cristi. Al rechazar la etiqueta de república negra, el diario califica a la nación de comunidad de color donde no existe conflicto racial, señalando que los ciudadanos contraen matrimonio entre sí y ocupan cargos públicos en condiciones de igualdad sin distinción del color de piel. La crónica añade que la administración nacional ha enfrentado una fuerte oposición en el Congreso y requiere ayuda de los Estados Unidos para sofocar las recurrentes revoluciones.

records.headline: An account in The Sun details military impressment abuses in a Dominican port
records.summary_en: An account in The Sun details military impressment abuses in a Dominican port town where the loading of an American steamship was halted after the local governor conscripted two dozen wharf laborers under armed guard. The incident brought port operations to an absolute standstill because the conscripted men included the engineer tasked with operating the harbor crane. Following a sharp protest delivered by the American ship captain through an interpreter and private discussions with a prominent local merchant, the governor consented to release the crane engineer. The report also references President Jimenes expressing satisfaction with President Wilson's diplomatic policy concerning a proposed treaty granting the United States supervision over Dominican constabulary and military forces.
records.summary_es: Un relato en The Sun detalla abusos de reclutamiento forzoso militar en una localidad portuaria dominicana, donde la carga de un vapor estadounidense se paralizó luego de que el gobernador local reclutara a punta de fusil a dos docenas de estibadores del muelle. El incidente detuvo por completo las faenas portuarias debido a que entre los hombres reclutados figuraba el maquinista encargado de operar la grúa del puerto. Tras una enérgica protesta presentada por el capitán del buque estadounidense mediante un intérprete y conversaciones privadas con un destacado comerciante local, el gobernador accedió a liberar al maquinista de la grúa. La crónica menciona asimismo que el presidente Jimenes expresó su satisfacción con la política diplomática del presidente Wilson respecto a un proyectado tratado que otorgaría a los Estados Unidos la supervisión de las fuerzas militares y de policía dominicanas.

records.full_text:
NEW DOMINICAN MINISTER

Senor Armando Perez Perdomo, successor to Doctor Jiminez as minister from the republic of Santo Domingo, recently arrived in Washington and presented his credentials. Before his appointment he was secretary of the treasury in his country.

records.headline: A feature article in The Washburn Times relates that the earliest
records.summary_en: A feature article in The Washburn Times relates that the earliest European settlement founded by Columbus, Isabella, has long disappeared into ruins near Puerto Plata, while Santo Domingo stands as the oldest surviving European city in the Americas. The paper describes the Dominican Republic as naturally among the wealthiest lands in the world, praising its exceptionally fertile soil and extensive cotton acreage in Monte Cristi province near the Haitian border financed by American and British capital. It observes that northern cotton yields per acre far exceed those in the southern United States, and highlights Puerto Plata as a thriving port connected by rail to Santiago de los Caballeros, La Vega, and Moca in the interior agricultural district. In those fertile valleys, the article reports extensive cultivation of cacao and tobacco, while noting Samana and Sanchez as principal ports on Samana Bay.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en The Washburn Times relata que el primer asentamiento europeo fundado por Colón, La Isabela, desapareció hace mucho dejando solo ruinas cerca de Puerto Plata, mientras que Santo Domingo permanece como la ciudad europea más antigua que sobrevive en las Américas. El diario califica a la República Dominicana como naturalmente una de las tierras más ricas del mundo, elogiando su suelo excepcionalmente fértil y las extensas plantaciones de algodón en la provincia de Monte Cristi, cerca de la frontera haitiana, financiadas por capital estadounidense y británico. Señala que el rendimiento de algodón por acre en el norte supera con creces al del sur de los Estados Unidos, y destaca a Puerto Plata como un próspero puerto conectado por ferrocarril con Santiago de los Caballeros, La Vega y Moca en el distrito agrícola del interior. En estos valles fértiles, el artículo da cuenta del amplio cultivo de cacao y tabaco, a la vez que señala a Samaná y Sánchez como los puertos principales en la bahía de Samaná.

records.summary_en: This travel feature describes the Dominican capital as a place where automobiles are plentiful and the ride to San Cristobal along the new macadam boulevard is most attractive, with cars to be had for four dollars an hour. It notes several hotels, of which the Hotel Francis is the best known, a large foreign colony at the capital and in Macoris and Puerto Plata, a trip from New York of about eight or nine days stopping at all ports, and a climate it calls wrongly thought unhealthy, with no serious epidemic since the cholera outbreak of the early sixties.

records.summary_en: Published in the Tensas Gazette, a descriptive sketch notes that the historic settlement of Isabella survives only as a ruin near Puerto Plata, leaving the capital city of Santo Domingo as the oldest extant European settlement in the Western Hemisphere. The article characterizes the Dominican Republic as inherently one of the richest regions in the world, emphasizing its luxurious fertility and productive cotton plantations in Monte Cristi province backed by American and English investors. According to the account, Dominican cotton acreage generates substantially higher yields per acre than fields in the southern United States. The report also highlights the commercial importance of Puerto Plata and its railway link to Santiago de los Caballeros, La Vega, and Moca, noting their abundant harvests of cacao and tobacco, as well as the coastal commerce centered at Samana and Sanchez.

Según el relato, las tierras algodoneras dominicanas generan cosechas por acre considerablemente superiores a las de los campos del sur de los Estados Unidos. records.headline: This descriptive feature presents Santo Domingo City, the capital, seventy miles from La Romana and forty from Macoris
records.summary_en: This descriptive feature presents Santo Domingo City, the capital, seventy miles from La Romana and forty from Macoris, as a place of modern life amid relics of the fifteenth century, including the ruins of the first church, San Nicolas, the bones Dominicans claim are those of Christopher Columbus in the cathedral, and the ruins of the house of Diego Colon, his son. It describes the city on the west bank of the Ozama river, its macadam boulevard, the ruins of Fort San Geronimo, its two clubs, hotels and plentiful automobiles, its large foreign colony, and argues that, contrary to a common impression, the climate of Santo Domingo is healthy.

records.headline: An article in The Daily Journal estimates the population of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: An article in The Daily Journal estimates the population of the Dominican Republic at between six and seven hundred thousand inhabitants, explaining that it shares with neighboring Haiti the island first called Isla Española by Spanish discoverers. The paper relates that Christopher Columbus established the first European settlement in the New World within modern Dominican territory, naming it Isabella in honor of the queen of Castile. While Isabella soon vanished and now survives only as a ruin near Puerto Plata, the account points out that the capital city of Santo Domingo represents the oldest continuously existing European settlement in the Western Hemisphere.
records.summary_es: Un artículo en The Daily Journal estima la población de la República Dominicana entre seiscientos y setecientos mil habitantes, explicando que comparte con la vecina Haití la isla denominada originariamente Isla Española por los descubridores españoles. El diario relata que Cristóbal Colón estableció el primer asentamiento europeo en el Nuevo Mundo dentro del moderno territorio dominicano, bautizándolo como La Isabela en honor a la reina de Castilla. Si bien La Isabela desapareció pronto y hoy solo perdura como ruina cerca de Puerto Plata, el texto destaca que la ciudad capital de Santo Domingo representa el asentamiento europeo continuo más antiguo del hemisferio occidental.

records.summary_en: A historical and geographical sketch in the Walker Lake Bulletin recalls the cathedral crypt in Santo Domingo where the remains of Columbus's brother were mistakenly taken to Havana as the discoverer's bones, and notes that the ruins of the residence of his son Diego Colón still stand. The article explains that Columbus founded Isabella, the hemisphere's earliest European settlement named for the queen of Castile, which today survives only as a ruin near Puerto Plata, while Santo Domingo endures as the oldest inhabited European city in the Americas. Under the heading 'One of World's Richest Spots,' the piece portrays the Dominican Republic as exceptionally fertile and endowed with great natural wealth. It specifically points to Monte Cristi province along the Haitian border, where substantial cotton plantations financed by American and British capital achieve per-acre yields exceeding those of the American South.

El artículo explica que Colón fundó La Isabela, el asentamiento europeo más temprano del hemisferio, llamado así por la reina de Castilla, el cual solo subsiste hoy como ruina cerca de Puerto Plata, mientras que Santo Domingo perdura como la ciudad europea habitada más antigua de las Américas. Bajo el título «Uno de los lugares más ricos del mundo», el escrito presenta a la República Dominicana como un territorio excepcionalmente fértil y dotado de gran riqueza natural. Señala en particular la provincia de Monte Cristi, junto a la frontera haitiana, donde importantes plantaciones de algodón financiadas por capital estadounidense y británico alcanzan rendimientos por acre superiores a los del sur de los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: A syndicated article in the Turner County Herald estimates the population of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: A syndicated article in the Turner County Herald estimates the population of the Dominican Republic at between six and seven hundred thousand inhabitants, observing that it shares the island historically designated Isla Española with neighboring Haiti. The account explains that Christopher Columbus established the earliest European settlement in the Americas within Dominican territory, naming it Isabella after the queen of Castile. Although Isabella soon vanished into ruins near Puerto Plata, the paper notes that the capital city of Santo Domingo remains the oldest extant European settlement in the Western Hemisphere.

El relato explica que Cristóbal Colón estableció el primer asentamiento europeo en América dentro del territorio dominicano, llamándolo La Isabela en honor a la reina de Castilla. Aunque La Isabela pronto quedó reducida a ruinas cerca de Puerto Plata, el periódico señala que la capital de Santo Domingo sigue siendo el asentamiento europeo más antiguo que perdura en el hemisferio occidental.

records.headline: Under the headline 'Severe Earthquake at Santo Domingo,' the Rock Island Argus reports
records.summary_en: Under the headline 'Severe Earthquake at Santo Domingo,' the Rock Island Argus reports that Georgetown University seismographs in Washington recorded two violent earth tremors, the heaviest occurring at 3:21 a.m. eastern time. Father Tondorf, director of the observatory, estimated that the epicenter of the second shock was situated approximately 2,400 miles from Washington and expressed concern that it would inflict heavy destruction in any inhabited area. A concurrent dispatch from Santo Domingo confirms that a severe earthquake shook the Dominican capital at 11:30 p.m. the previous night, though it resulted in no damage.

El padre Tondorf, director del observatorio, calculó que el epicentro del segundo sismo se localizaba a unas 2,400 millas de Washington y expresó su temor de que causara graves destrozos en cualquier zona habitada. Un despacho paralelo desde Santo Domingo confirma que un fuerte terremoto sacudió la capital dominicana a las 11:30 de la noche anterior, aunque no causó daños.

records.headline: An essay published in The Washington Herald examines President Ulysses S. Grant's
records.summary_en: An essay published in The Washington Herald examines President Ulysses S. Grant's administration, focusing on how his determination to annex Santo Domingo alienated influential leaders within his party. Grant's insistence on annexation brought about an open breach with Charles Sumner, the chairman of the Senate Committee on Foreign Affairs, while also driving Horace Greeley, the trenchant editor of the New-York Tribune, into active opposition. The account emphasizes that Sumner represented the elevated traditions of the Republican Party against Grant's pursuit of power, while Greeley's daily editorials mobilized thousands of rural readers against the administration.

El texto destaca que Sumner representaba las tradiciones más elevadas del Partido Republicano frente a la búsqueda de poder de Grant, mientras que los editoriales diarios de Greeley movilizaron a miles de lectores rurales contra el gobierno.

records.headline: Dispatches from Washington and Santo Domingo published in the Daily Kennebec Journal report
records.summary_en: Dispatches from Washington and Santo Domingo published in the Daily Kennebec Journal report on the crisis surrounding the impeachment of General Jiminez. Following the Chamber of Deputies' vote to impeach President Jiminez for alleged constitutional violations in drafting the budget—with a Senate verdict due within 48 hours—the United States dispatched Rear Admiral Caperton with the cruiser Prairie and marines to halt factional moves against the administration. Caperton was ordered to warn leaders behind the impeachment that the United States would not tolerate intrigues, and he subsequently arrived in the quiet capital from Haiti.
records.summary_es: Despachos de Washington y Santo Domingo publicados en el Daily Kennebec Journal informan sobre la crisis en torno al juicio político del general Jiménez. Tras la votación de la Cámara de Diputados para procesar al presidente Jiménez por presuntas violaciones constitucionales en la redacción del presupuesto —con un veredicto del Senado previsto dentro de 48 horas—, Estados Unidos envió al contralmirante Caperton con el crucero Prairie e infantes de marina para detener las maniobras facciosas contra el gobierno. Caperton recibió órdenes de advertir a los dirigentes tras el juicio político que Estados Unidos no toleraría intrigas, arribando posteriormente a la tranquila capital procedente de Haití.

records.summary_en: Writing in the Evening Star, a correspondent reviews the controversial diplomatic career of James M. Sullivan following his resignation as United States minister to the Dominican Republic. An investigation headed by Senator Phelan of California censured Sullivan for official indiscretions—including involvement in contracts concerning fellow Americans in Santo Domingo—while commending certain administrative reforms he enacted. The report details how Sullivan's appointment was credited to former Secretary Bryan, who had inquired of Receiver General Vick regarding posts for deserving Democrats, while Secretary Tumulty disclaimed responsibility for the selection.

El informe detalla cómo el nombramiento de Sullivan se atribuyó al exsecretario Bryan, quien había preguntado al receptor general Vick sobre puestos para demócratas meritorios, mientras que el secretario Tumulty negó su responsabilidad en la designación.

records.headline: A series of dispatches in the Honolulu Star-Bulletin report
records.summary_en: A series of dispatches in the Honolulu Star-Bulletin report on the arrest in Dublin of James Sullivan, former American minister to Santo Domingo, on charges of complicity in the Irish rebellion after having sailed from New York to visit his mother in Limerick. In Washington, Sullivan's wife appealed to Secretary of State Lansing to inquire into his detention by British authorities, while friends in New York maintained his innocence. The dispatches also recount Sullivan's resignation from his Dominican post following an investigation by Senator Phelan of California, who concluded he was temperamentally unfit, alongside brief mention of United States naval and marine operations guarding Dominican customs receipts under a virtual protectorate.

En Washington, la esposa de Sullivan apeló ante el secretario de Estado Lansing para que investigara su detención por las autoridades británicas, mientras amigos en Nueva York sostenían su inocencia. Los despachos relatan asimismo la renuncia de Sullivan a su cargo dominicano tras una investigación del senador Phelan de California, quien concluyó que no era apto temperamentalmente, junto con una breve mención de las operaciones navales y de infantería de marina de Estados Unidos para proteger las rentas aduaneras dominicanas bajo un protectorado virtual.

Para sostener al gobierno, Caperton está autorizado a desembarcar marineros e infantes de marina en Santo Domingo si fuera necesario.

records.headline: Dispatches from Santo Domingo and Washington published in The Laramie Republican report

Jimenez, President of the Dominican Republic, declared the capital in a state of siege and transferred the seat of government to San Geronimo following his impeachment by the Chamber of Deputies on May 2. From Washington, Rear Admiral Caperton was placed under broad instructions to maintain the constitutional government in Dominican waters. American officials emphasized that the United States considers the presidential impeachment to be a disguised rebellion.

Jiménez, presidente de la República Dominicana, declaró la capital en estado de sitio y trasladó la sede del gobierno a San Gerónimo tras ser sometido a juicio político por la Cámara de Diputados el 2 de mayo. Desde Washington, el contralmirante Caperton recibió amplias instrucciones para sostener al gobierno constitucional en aguas dominicanas. Las autoridades estadounidenses subrayaron que Estados Unidos considera el juicio político presidencial como una rebelión disfrazada.

records.headline: A London dispatch in the New Britain Herald reports that James M. Sullivan of New York
records.summary_en: A London dispatch in the New Britain Herald reports that James M. Sullivan of New York, former American minister to Santo Domingo, has been arrested in Dublin on charges of complicity in the Irish rebellion. Sullivan had sailed for Liverpool the previous July ostensibly to visit his mother in Limerick, shortly after being forced to resign his Dominican diplomatic post on July 23 following an official inquiry led by Senator Phelan of California. The investigation censured Sullivan for indiscretions involving contracts with other Americans in Santo Domingo while commending certain administrative reforms. The article notes Sullivan's local Connecticut ties, having worked as a journalist in the state, graduated from Yale Law School, and practiced law there.

La investigación censuró a Sullivan por indiscreciones vinculadas a contratos con otros estadounidenses en Santo Domingo, al tiempo que reconoció ciertas reformas administrativas. El artículo destaca los vínculos locales de Sullivan en Connecticut, donde trabajó como periodista, se graduó de la Facultad de Derecho de Yale y ejerció la abogacía.

records.summary_en: Reporting from Washington, the Evening Public Ledger states that the United States government is awaiting a full report regarding the arrest in Dublin of James Mark Sullivan, formerly American Minister to Santo Domingo, who is charged with complicity in the Irish rebellion. American officials are seriously concerned over the detention, noting Sullivan's prominence in Irish-American circles and warnings that harsh British measures could provoke reprisals, while his friends maintain that his visit was undertaken solely to recover his health after his service in Santo Domingo. The State Department and the White House have received numerous appeals urging intervention, and Sullivan's wife has personally requested official assistance to secure her husband's immediate release.

Las autoridades estadounidenses manifiestan gran preocupación por la detención, destacando la notoriedad de Sullivan en los círculos irlandeses-estadounidenses y las advertencias de que medidas británicas severas podrían suscitar represalias, mientras sus allegados sostienen que su viaje obedeció únicamente a recuperar su salud tras su servicio en Santo Domingo. El Departamento de Estado y la Casa Blanca han recibido numerosos llamamientos solicitando su intervención, y la esposa de Sullivan ha pedido personalmente ayuda oficial para lograr la liberación inmediata de su esposo.

Washington warned Dominican officials that it viewed congressional impeachment proceedings against Jimenes as a veiled revolutionary plot, granting him an eight-day respite to reply. The excerpt also detailed a concurrent constitutional clash in Haiti, where Caperton backed President Dartiguenave against a rebellious parliament.

WASHINGTON, May 5.—Rear Admiral Caperton, commanding the American naval forces in Dominican waters, is under broad instructions to use whatever force is necessary to maintain the constitutional government in the Dominican Republic. The Admiral recently went to the capital with instructions from Washington which declared the United States considered the impeachment of President Jiminez a thinly veiled revolutionary plot. If necessary Admiral Caperton may land bluejackets and marines. PORT AU PRINCE, Haiti, May 5. The Haitian Cabinet has resigned. Parliament has entered a protest with the American Government and Congress against what it declares to be a violation of the rights of the legislative branch of the Government. Jimines, President of the Dominican Republic, declared the capital in a state of siege and moved the seat of government by decree to the suburb of San Geronimo following his impeachment by the Chamber of Deputies on May 2. Despite the political crisis, the dispatch notes that the city remained quiet.

El secretario de lo Interior notificó al Senado que la capital se hallaba en estado de rebelión, impidiendo que el presidente Jimines compareciera a juicio dentro del plazo de cuarenta y ocho horas prescrito por la ley. A pesar de la crisis política, el despacho señala que la ciudad permanecía en calma.

records.headline: A London cable in the Omaha Daily Bee reports that James M. Sullivan of New York
records.summary_en: A London cable in the Omaha Daily Bee reports that James M. Sullivan of New York, formerly American Minister to Santo Domingo, was arrested in Dublin on charges of complicity in the Irish rebellion. Sullivan had sailed from New York the previous July with his family to visit his mother in Limerick, shortly after being forced to resign his post as minister to the Dominican Republic. That resignation followed an inquiry into Dominican affairs by a State Department commission headed by Senator Phelan of California, which found no evidence that Sullivan profited from island contracts but concluded he was guilty of indiscretions unfitting him for his office. The dispatch recalls that Sullivan, formerly an attorney for gambler Jack Rose, owed his appointment to former Secretary of State W. J. Bryan, who had famously asked Receiver General Vick what Dominican positions were available to reward deserving Democrats.

El despacho recuerda que Sullivan, quien había sido abogado del jugador Jack Rose, debió su designación al exsecretario de Estado W. J. records.headline: The Barre Daily Times features dispatches concerning the arrest
records.summary_en: The Barre Daily Times features dispatches concerning the arrest in Dublin of James M. Sullivan, former United States Minister to the Dominican Republic, on charges of complicity in the Irish rebellion. From London, Sullivan's wife reported to the American embassy that the accusations were entirely unfounded, expressing fears that he had been transferred to England where prisoners were being identified only by number. From Washington, the paper reports that the United States government will take no aggressive steps on Sullivan's behalf beyond instructing Ambassador Page to ensure his treaty rights, though Democratic leaders who backed his appointment to Santo Domingo are expected to appeal to President Wilson and Secretary Lansing.
records.summary_es: The Barre Daily Times presenta despachos relativos al arresto en Dublín de James M. Sullivan, exministro de Estados Unidos en la República Dominicana, acusado de complicidad en la rebelión irlandesa. Desde Londres, la esposa de Sullivan declaró ante la embajada estadounidense que las acusaciones carecían por completo de fundamento y expresó su temor de que hubiera sido trasladado a Inglaterra, donde los prisioneros eran identificados únicamente mediante números. Desde Washington, el periódico informa que el gobierno estadounidense no tomará medidas enérgicas en favor de Sullivan más allá de instruir al embajador Page para que garantice sus derechos amparados en tratados, aunque se prevé que líderes demócratas que respaldaron su designación en Santo Domingo apelen ante el presidente Wilson y el secretario Lansing.

records.summary_en: Dispatches to the Ottumwa Tri-Weekly Courier from Santo Domingo state that United States marines were landed from the converted cruiser Prairie to protect the American legation amid a critical situation caused by an attempt to overthrow President Jimines. In response to the crisis, President Jimines ordered the governor of Santo Domingo City to take command of the military forces under General Ferrer and placed the rural guards under officers appointed by the executive.

En respuesta a la crisis, el presidente Jimines ordenó al gobernador de la ciudad de Santo Domingo tomar el mando de las fuerzas militares del general Ferrer y colocó a la guardia rural bajo órdenes de oficiales designados por el ejecutivo.

records.summary_en: Reports published in the Evening times-Republican describe escalating political turmoil in the Dominican Republic. Rear Admiral Caperton advised the Navy Department that the revolt against President Jimenez was grave, noting that he held full authority to land marines or take other necessary steps to preserve order. Meanwhile, a dispatch from Santo Domingo reports that armed hostilities resulting from the attempt to overthrow General Jimenez —which had left several people killed or wounded—were suspended on May 6 as members of the diplomatic corps intervened to seek an amicable settlement.

El contralmirante Caperton comunicó al Departamento de la Marina que la revuelta contra el presidente Jiménez revestía gravedad, señalando que disponía de plena autoridad para desembarcar infantes de marina o tomar las medidas necesarias para mantener el orden. Entre tanto, un despacho desde Santo Domingo reporta que las hostilidades armadas originadas por el intento de derrocar al general Jiménez —que dejaron varias personas muertas o heridas— fueron suspendidas el 6 de mayo mientras miembros del cuerpo diplomático intervenían para procurar un arreglo amistoso.

records.headline: The Daily Journal reports on Dominican mediation efforts alongside
records.summary_en: The Daily Journal reports on Dominican mediation efforts alongside United States naval movements toward the republic. In Santo Domingo, a municipal commission was appointed to persuade President Jiminez and General Arias to settle their conflict, resulting in Arias offering to surrender on condition of the president's resignation, though Jiminez had not yet announced his decision. Meanwhile, a Key West dispatch reports that the American destroyers Walke and Terry have sailed for Santo Domingo, with five more destroyers—the Flusser, Sterett, Reid, Preston, and Ramson—accompanied by the supply ship Panther, scheduled to depart for the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: The Daily Journal informa sobre los esfuerzos de mediación dominicanos junto con los movimientos navales de Estados Unidos hacia la república. En Santo Domingo, se designó una comisión municipal para persuadir al presidente Jiminez y al general Arias de resolver su conflicto, lo que llevó a Arias a ofrecer su rendición a condición de la renuncia del presidente, aunque Jiminez aún no había anunciado su decisión. Entre tanto, un despacho de Cayo Hueso señala que los destructores estadounidenses Walke y Terry zarparon hacia Santo Domingo, y que otros cinco destructores —el Flusser, el Sterett, el Reid, el Preston y el Ramson— junto con el buque de abastecimiento Panther tenían previsto partir hacia la República Dominicana.

records.headline: A London dispatch in The Twin Falls Times, covering the fallout
records.summary_en: A London dispatch in The Twin Falls Times, covering the fallout from the Irish uprising, reports that James M. Sullivan, former minister to Santo Domingo, has been charged with complicity in the Irish rebellion. The article recounts that Sullivan had been forced to resign his diplomatic post following an investigation by a State Department commission headed by Senator Phelan of California. While the Phelan inquiry found no evidence that Sullivan profited from contracts involving Americans in the Dominican Republic, it concluded that his indiscretions unfitted him for the position. The dispatch also recalls that Sullivan's original appointment stemmed from former Secretary of State Bryan's query to Receiver General Vick seeking Dominican offices to reward 'deserving Democrats.'
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Londres en The Twin Falls Times, al cubrir las repercusiones de la sublevación irlandesa, informa que James M. Sullivan, exministro en Santo Domingo, fue acusado de complicidad en la rebelión irlandesa. El artículo relata que Sullivan se vio obligado a dimitir de su cargo diplomático tras una investigación conducida por una comisión del Departamento de Estado presidida por el senador Phelan de California. Si bien la indagatoria de Phelan no halló pruebas de que Sullivan se hubiera beneficiado de contratos que involucraban a estadounidenses en la República Dominicana, concluyó que sus indiscreciones lo inhabilitaban para el puesto. El despacho recuerda asimismo que el nombramiento original de Sullivan se originó en la consulta del exsecretario de Estado Bryan al receptor general Vick solicitando cargos dominicanos para recompensar a 'demócratas meritorios'.

records.headline: Rear Admiral William B. Caperton of the United States Navy arrived
records.summary_en: Rear Admiral William B. Caperton of the United States Navy arrived on the transport Prairie in connection with the escalating crisis threatening the overthrow of President Juan Isidro Jimenez, the St. Croix Avis states, reporting from Santo Domingo. Both the Chamber of Deputies and the Dominican Senate have acted on impeachment charges against Jimenez for violating the constitution regarding the budget, with the constitution requiring his trial before the Senate to begin within forty-eight hours. The report emphasizes that only the American protectorate and Caperton's presence prevented an immediate revolution, as virtually all major political leaders and Congress have aligned against the president.
records.summary_es: El contralmirante William B. Caperton de la Armada de los Estados Unidos llegó a bordo del transporte Prairie en relación con la creciente crisis que amenazaba con derrocar al presidente Juan Isidro Jiménez, según señala el St. Croix Avis informando desde Santo Domingo. Tanto la Cámara de Diputados como el Senado dominicano procedieron con los cargos de juicio político contra Jiménez por violar la constitución en materia presupuestaria, exigiendo la constitución que su juicio ante el Senado se inicie en un plazo de cuarenta y ocho horas. El informe destaca que solo el protectorado estadounidense y la presencia de Caperton evitaron una revolución inmediata, ya que prácticamente todos los principales dirigentes políticos y el Congreso se han alineado contra el presidente.

records.headline: Advices from Washington published in The Johnson City Comet indicate
records.summary_en: Advices from Washington published in The Johnson City Comet indicate that official reports to the State and Navy Departments anticipate the settlement of Dominican unrest through the resignation of President Jimines. The United States Navy had prepared an armed demonstration, ordering a flotilla of destroyers from Florida to reinforce Rear Admiral Caperton aboard the cruiser Prairie at Santo Domingo, though sailing orders for the remaining vessels were canceled once Caperton reported that hostilities had subsided. Admiral Caperton also informed Secretary Daniels by wireless that both President Jimines and General Arias, the rebel leader and minister of war, had reportedly agreed to resign in order to prevent armed American intervention.
records.summary_es: Informes desde Washington publicados en The Johnson City Comet indican que reportes oficiales dirigidos a los departamentos de Estado y de Marina prevén la resolución de los disturbios dominicanos mediante la renuncia del presidente Jimines. La Marina de los Estados Unidos había preparado una demostración armada ordenando una flotilla de destructores desde Florida para reforzar al contralmirante Caperton a bordo del crucero Prairie en Santo Domingo, aunque las órdenes de zarpe para los buques restantes se cancelaron una vez que Caperton informó que las hostilidades habían cesado. El almirante Caperton también comunicó por radio al secretario Daniels que tanto el presidente Jimines como el general Arias, líder rebelde y ministro de Guerra, habrían acordado renunciar para impedir una intervención armada estadounidense.

records.summary_en: The Johnson City Comet reports from Santo Domingo that fully equipped American marines were landed on the outskirts of the city on May 8 due to the serious crisis, while the French armored cruiser Marseillaise arrived in port that morning. Earlier reports indicated that hostilities between the opposing factions of President Jimines and General Arias had subsided after Jimines resigned to avert armed intervention by the United States. records.headline: An editorial in The Twin Falls Times reflects on the Dublin arrest of former Dominican minister
records.summary_en: An editorial in The Twin Falls Times reflects on the Dublin arrest of former Dominican minister and Bryan protégé James M. Sullivan in connection with the Irish rebellion. The editorial recalls how Sullivan was appointed through former Secretary of State Bryan, who notoriously asked Receiver General Vick for customs positions to reward 'deserving Democrats' in a nation described as virtually a ward of the United States. Noting that Sullivan proved completely incompetent, the piece observes that Bryan initially defended his appointee until an official investigation by Democratic Senator James D. Phelan established sufficient evidence of incompetence to induce Sullivan to resign.

records.headline: A Santo Domingo report in the Montpelier Examiner states that hostilities
records.summary_en: A Santo Domingo report in the Montpelier Examiner states that hostilities arising from an attempt to overthrow the regime of General Jimenez, which resulted in several casualties, were suspended on Saturday following diplomatic mediation. American Minister William W. Russell warned that armed intervention would occur within seventy-two hours unless fighting ceased, prompting the municipality to appoint a commission to reconcile President Jimenez and General Arias. General Arias agreed to surrender on condition that the president step down, and the commission conveyed this proposition to President Jimenez, who has resigned his office.
records.summary_es: Un informe de Santo Domingo en el Montpelier Examiner señala que las hostilidades derivadas de un intento por derrocar el régimen del general Jimenez, que dejaron varias víctimas, fueron suspendidas el sábado tras una mediación diplomática. El ministro estadounidense William W. Russell advirtió que se produciría una intervención armada dentro de setenta y dos horas a menos que cesaran los combates, lo que llevó al municipio a nombrar una comisión para conciliar al presidente Jimenez y al general Arias. El general Arias aceptó rendirse bajo la condición de que el presidente dimitiera, y la comisión transmitió esta propuesta al presidente Jimenez, quien ha renunciado a su cargo.

records.headline: In a published letter to the editors of The Pleasantville Press
records.summary_en: In a published letter to the editors of The Pleasantville Press, Mrs. William A. McMahon recounts daily life on a plantation under perpetual sunny skies; the letter is datelined San Isidro, Santo Domingo City, Dominican Republic. She describes Sunday market days when local residents assemble at the plantation camp to sell vegetables and tropical fruits to household servants, remarking that ladies avoid shopping at the bodega except for curiosity strolls, photography, or horseback riding along the road to the capital.
records.summary_es: En una carta publicada dirigida a los editores de The Pleasantville Press, la señora de William A. McMahon relata la vida cotidiana en una plantación bajo cielos continuamente soleados; la carta está fechada en San Isidro, ciudad de Santo Domingo, República Dominicana. Describe los domingos como días de mercado en los que los residentes locales se congregan en el campamento de la plantación para vender vegetales y frutas tropicales a los criados domésticos, señalando que las damas no van de compras a la bodega salvo por paseos de curiosidad, para tomar fotografías o para montar a caballo por el camino hacia la capital.

records.headline: Dispatches in The Ogden Standard from Washington and Santo Domingo report
records.summary_en: Dispatches in The Ogden Standard from Washington and Santo Domingo report that the Arias revolution against former President Jimenez has forced the indefinite postponement of presidential elections, according to Rear Admiral Caperton. In response, the cruisers Tennessee and Salem alongside 400 marines from Haiti have been ordered to Dominican waters. Meanwhile, former Minister of Foreign Affairs Enrique Henriquez departed for the United States to seek the withdrawal of American forces, while seven Dominican provinces repudiated Congress and a force of insurgents assembled in the mountains under General Desiderio Arias.
records.summary_es: Despachos en The Ogden Standard desde Washington y Santo Domingo informan que la revolución de Arias contra el expresidente Jimenez forzó el aplazamiento indefinido de las elecciones presidenciales, según reportó el contralmirante Caperton. En respuesta, los cruceros Tennessee y Salem junto con 400 infantes de marina de Haití han sido enviados a aguas dominicanas. Entretanto, el exministro de Relaciones Exteriores Enrique Henriquez partió hacia los Estados Unidos para solicitar la retirada de las fuerzas estadounidenses, mientras siete provincias dominicanas desconocieron al Congreso y una fuerza insurgente se congregó en las montañas al mando del general Desiderio Arias.

records.summary_en: A Washington report in The Washington Times states that Secretary of the Navy Daniels ordered 300 marines from Norfolk on the cruiser Tennessee and dispatched the cruiser Salem to reinforce operations suppressing the Dominican revolution. Rear Admiral Caperton was authorized to move up to 600 marines from Haiti to Santo Domingo, providing nearly 3,000 men for service. Caperton reported landing marines at Santo Domingo on Monday as revolutionists retreated, while former President Jimenez, ousted in a revolt led by General Arias, faces impeachment proceedings.

records.headline: Dispatches from Washington and Santo Domingo published in The Topeka State Journal report
records.summary_en: Dispatches from Washington and Santo Domingo published in The Topeka State Journal report on the unfolding Dominican crisis. Following the Arias revolution against the Jimenez government, the election of a successor to former President Jimenez has been indefinitely postponed, with Rear Admiral Caperton reporting that holding balloting now is inadvisable. Reinforcements including sixty-four marines on the cruiser Tennessee, accompanied by the cruiser Salem and marines from Haiti, have been ordered to Dominican waters. In Santo Domingo, former foreign affairs minister Enrique Henriquez departed for the United States at the request of several political parties to urge the withdrawal of American armed forces.
records.summary_es: Despachos de Washington y Santo Domingo publicados en The Topeka State Journal informan sobre la crisis dominicana en desarrollo. Tras la revolución de Arias contra el gobierno de Jimenez, la elección de un sucesor para el expresidente Jimenez ha sido aplazada indefinidamente, e informó el contraalmirante Caperton que celebrar votaciones en estos momentos resulta desaconsejable. Refuerzos que incluyen a sesenta y cuatro infantes de marina en el crucero Tennessee, acompañados por el crucero Salem e infantes de marina procedentes de Haití, han sido ordenados hacia aguas dominicanas. En Santo Domingo, el exministro de relaciones exteriores Enrique Henriquez partió hacia los Estados Unidos a petición de varios partidos políticos para instar a la retirada de las fuerzas armadas estadounidenses.

records.summary_en: An account in The Birmingham Age-Herald reports orders directing 214 marines from the Norfolk Navy Yard and Port Royal to proceed to Santo Domingo to help preserve order. Sixty-four men from the battleship Louisiana are scheduled to depart Norfolk Monday aboard the cruiser Tennessee, with an additional 150 embarking at Port Royal, while approximately 400 marines have been dispatched from Haiti. The report notes that unsettled conditions caused by the Arias revolution against the Jiminez government have forced an indefinite postponement of the election to succeed former President Jiminez, as communicated by Rear Admiral Caperton to the Navy Department.

La nota señala que las condiciones de inestabilidad provocadas por la revolución de Arias contra el gobierno de Jiminez han obligado a posponer indefinidamente la elección del sucesor del expresidente Jiminez, según comunicó el contraalmirante Caperton al Departamento de la Armada.

The State Department declared it would not recognize the election of Federico H. Carvajal as provisional president following the impeachment of President Jimenes. American Minister Russell, reporting today that the marines soon would be distributed to strategic points in the republic, said he had received many requests for such action in protection of American sugar plantations and other American Interests. American warships already are stationed at all the important ports. The arrangement for continued cooperation of the American forces in policing Santo Domingo probably will not be as far reaching as that in force in Haiti, officials say, but will be broad enough in scope to prevent any repetition of the present complicated situation. Under a treaty already in force, the United States administers the collection of customs for the Dominican government. It was made clear at the state department today that there was no intention of recognising the election of Frederick H. Carvajal, chosen provisional president of Santo Domingo last week by the Dominican congress, as valid. Minister Russell reported that Enrique Henriques, former American minister, was on his way to Washington to urge Carvajal's recognition. The department holds that the impeachment of President Jiminez was only a political coup and already has informed the Dominican congress that the proceedings cannot be recognised as legal. While Rear Admiral Caperton is not reporting details of his operations, officials here believe he now has the revolutionary movement under General Arias well controlled.

The marine patrol was intended as a preliminary step toward establishing an American-led native constabulary, similar to arrangements under the Haitian treaty. The State Department also announced that it would refuse to recognize the election of Federico H. Carvajal as valid.

POLICING OF THE REPUBLIC State Department Will Not Recognize Newly-Elected President Rear Admiral Caperton at Santo Domingo is taking steps to distribute his landing force of American marines to various points in the little republic, and before they are withdrawn some arrangement probably will be effected through which American officers will be placed in charge of the native constabulary. The broadening out of the marine patrol, officials indicated at Washington Monday, is a step preliminary to establishment of a policing system similar to that recently inaugurated in Haiti under the new Haitian treaty. A complete reorganization of the native troops is contemplated under the plan, and Congress probably will be asked to pass a bill authorizing the navy and marine officers to serve under the Dominican government as officers of the constabulary. The arrangement for continued cooperation of the American forces in policing Santo Domingo probably will not be as far-reaching as that in force in Haiti, officials say, but will be broad enough in scope to prevent any repetition of the present complicated situation. records.summary_en: An article in the Evening Star reports that American warships and marines will remain in Santo Domingo so that the Dominican congress can choose a provisional president to succeed Jimenez unmolested. Although a later dispatch reported that Federico Henrique Carvajal was selected by one branch of congress, the American minister and naval commander were in no hurry to confirm his election. The report recalls that the United States previously supervised Dominican elections and arranged compromise leaders, including the archbishop of the diocese, who soon resigned after finding the presidency inhospitable to a man of peace.

records.headline: A feature in the Evening Star surveys growing American economic
records.summary_en: A feature in the Evening Star surveys growing American economic interests in Santo Domingo, noting capital investments in sugar plantations, the fruit business, timber reserves, and railway construction under dollar diplomacy. Dominican factions are described as nominally friendly toward these investments while demanding assurances that foreign capital will not infringe on national sovereignty. The report observes that ever since President Grant proposed annexing Santo Domingo after recognizing the strategic value of Samana Bay, local politicians have readily warned that the United States intended to seize the country.

Se describe a las facciones dominicanas como nominalmente favorables a estas inversiones, al tiempo que exigen garantías de que el capital extranjero no vulnerará la soberanía nacional. El informe observa que desde que el presidente Grant propuso la anexión de Santo Domingo al reconocer el valor estratégico de la bahía de Samaná, los políticos locales han advertido con facilidad que los Estados Unidos pretendían apoderarse del país.

Dominican rebels who fled Puerto Plata and Monte Cristi upon the marines' approach have entrenched themselves outside the latter town, and a report from Minister Russell indicates the situation is more serious than Washington anticipated. Hirshinger.

records.headline: A State Department dispatch published in the Springfield Weekly Republican relays
records.summary_en: A State Department dispatch published in the Springfield Weekly Republican relays word from Minister Russell in Santo Domingo reporting that the Dominican situation is more serious than initially believed. Russell's dispatch states that after twenty-four hours' notice, marines landed on June 1, taking Monte Christi without resistance but facing two hours of fighting at Puerto Plata. The fatally wounded officer was Captain Herbert J. Hirshinger, commander of the detachment from the battleship Rhode Island, who died Thursday after being shot through the head while directing his men.

Hirshinger, comandante del destacamento del acorazado Rhode Island, quien falleció el jueves tras recibir un disparo en la cabeza mientras dirigía a sus hombres.

records.headline: A special report states that collection of internal revenues
records.summary_en: A special report states that collection of internal revenues in the Dominican Republic is gradually being assumed by resident American customs collectors under an agreement between the State Department and Dominican officials. Charles Baxter, customs collector at Santo Domingo City and director of internal collections under the new arrangement, reports that the inauguration of the system is proceeding successfully. The dispatch notes that the measure establishes what is in effect a commercial protectorate similar to that in Haiti, supplementing the earlier agreement under which the United States already administers Dominican customs.
records.summary_es: Un informe especial señala que la recaudación de las rentas internas en la República Dominicana está siendo asumida gradualmente por los recaudadores de aduanas estadounidenses residentes, en virtud de un acuerdo entre el Departamento de Estado y las autoridades dominicanas. Charles Baxter, recaudador de aduanas en la ciudad de Santo Domingo y director de la recaudación interna bajo el nuevo plan, informa que la inauguración del sistema avanza con éxito. El despacho destaca que la disposición establece en efecto un protectorado comercial similar al de Haití, complementando el convenio previo conforme al cual los Estados Unidos ya administran las aduanas dominicanas.

records.headline: A wireless report from Rear Admiral Caperton to the Navy Department announces
records.summary_en: A wireless report from Rear Admiral Caperton to the Navy Department announces that one American marine was killed and another wounded Tuesday during an engagement with revolutionists near Monte Cristi. The casualties were reported as Private John Acriment of the Twenty-seventh Company of Marines, killed, and Private Albert Vielbaum of the same company, wounded in the upper left arm. Navy officials noted that the name Acriment did not appear on the official Marine Corps roster, suggesting an error in transmission that prompted a records search to determine his correct identity. Private Vielbaum was reported as a 25-year-old native of Aberdeen, Washington, who enlisted in the Marine Corps on September 3, 1912.

Funcionarios de la Armada señalaron que el nombre Acriment no figuraba en la lista oficial del Cuerpo de Infantería de Marina, lo que sugiere un error de transmisión que motivó una búsqueda en los registros para determinar su identidad correcta. Se informó que el soldado Vielbaum es un joven de 25 años oriundo de Aberdeen, Washington, que se alistó en el Cuerpo de Infantería de Marina el 3 de septiembre de 1912.

records.headline: An arrangement for the disarmament of Santo Domingo revolutionists was virtually perfected by a peace conference of the Dominican
records.summary_en: An arrangement for the disarmament of Santo Domingo revolutionists was virtually perfected by a peace conference of the Dominican factions, according to a dispatch from Rear Admiral Caperton, paving the way for a suspension of hostilities while the future form of government was negotiated. Officials regarded it as the collapse of the revolution led by General Arias and expected a new regime with American supervision similar to that in Haiti, including American direction of revenue collection and disbursements.
records.summary_es: Un acuerdo para el desarme de los revolucionarios de Santo Domingo quedó prácticamente perfeccionado en una conferencia de paz de las facciones dominicanas, según un despacho del contralmirante Caperton, lo que allanó el camino para una suspensión de las hostilidades mientras se negociaba la futura forma de gobierno. Los funcionarios lo consideraron el colapso de la revolución dirigida por el general Arias y esperaban un nuevo régimen con supervisión estadounidense similar a la de Haití, incluida la dirección estadounidense del cobro y desembolso de ingresos.

records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch dated July 7 reports that Rear Admiral Caperton advised the Navy Department of arrangements for the peaceful occupation of Santiago, Santo Domingo, by American marines under Colonel Pendleton. Under an agreement negotiated between Colonel Pendleton and the Dominican peace commission, the marines were scheduled to enter the city on the night of July 6 or during July 7. The dispatch notes that the Americans engaged in four fights with revolutionary bands during their overland march, and Admiral Caperton reiterated his prediction of an early restoration of peace across the island republic.

En virtud de un acuerdo negociado entre el coronel Pendleton y la comisión de paz dominicana, estaba previsto que los infantes entraran a la ciudad la noche del 6 de julio o durante el 7 de julio. El despacho señala que los estadounidenses libraron cuatro combates con partidas revolucionarias durante su marcha por tierra, y el almirante Caperton reiteró su pronóstico de un pronto restablecimiento de la paz en toda la república insular.

records.headline: An editorial contends that the self-restraint shown by the United States government
records.summary_en: An editorial contends that the self-restraint shown by the United States government produces contempt rather than respect among Dominicans and Mexicans alike. Writing critically of American intervention in Santo Domingo, the paper asserts that the United States is doing only half the job, arguing that a halfway policy merely irritates while leaving the Dominican Republic a chronic sore spot in American politics. The commentary concludes that establishing an American protectorate and guaranteeing the small republic's debts will alter the Dominican disposition no more than it will alter Dominican skin color.
records.summary_es: Un editorial sostiene que la moderación demostrada por el gobierno de los Estados Unidos produce desprecio en lugar de respeto tanto entre los dominicanos como entre los mexicanos. Al criticar la intervención estadounidense en Santo Domingo, el diario afirma que los Estados Unidos solo están haciendo la labor a medias, argumentando que una política vacilante solo genera irritación y convierte a la República Dominicana en un problema crónico de la política estadounidense. El comentario concluye que establecer un protectorado estadounidense y garantizar las deudas de la pequeña república no cambiará la idiosincrasia dominicana del mismo modo que no cambiará el color de piel dominicano.

records.headline: A photographic report from Puerto Plata documents American marines
records.summary_en: A photographic report from Puerto Plata documents American marines following the capture of a Dominican fort. The accompanying text states that during the final three days of June, American forces under Rear Admiral William B. Caperton pushed an aggressive campaign into rebel territory at 'Puerto Plata, Dominica,' and fought three battles. No Americans were killed, while rebel forces suffered nine killed and numerous wounded. The military operations were undertaken after General Desiderio Arias, leader of the rebel uprising, refused Admiral Caperton's demands to disarm and submit to peace terms.

Caperton emprendieron una enérgica campaña en territorio rebelde en 'Puerto Plata, Dominica', librando tres combates. Ningún estadounidense resultó muerto, mientras que las fuerzas rebeldes sufrieron nueve muertos y numerosos heridos. Las operaciones militares se iniciaron luego de que el general Desiderio Arias, líder de la sublevación rebelde, rechazara las exigencias del almirante Caperton de deponer las armas y someterse a términos de paz.

records.headline: A retrospective article reviewing Admiral Caperton's operations
records.summary_en: A retrospective article reviewing Admiral Caperton's operations recounts that the Dominican crisis erupted six weeks earlier when Minister of War Arias attempted to overthrow President Jiminez. Following Jiminez's resignation, Caperton dispatched the Prairie with a marine battalion under Major N. H. Hall from Port-au-Prince to Santo Domingo City, landing troops after requests from the council of ministers, diplomatic corps, and local citizens. Additional marines arrived under Colonel Kane to secure the capital peacefully as Arias and his revolutionary forces withdrew into the interior toward Santiago. To safeguard foreign lives and property, American landings were also carried out on the north coast at Monte Cristi and Puerto Plata, where marines took the town under heavy fire in an action that claimed the life of Captain H. J. Hirshinger.
records.summary_es: Un artículo retrospectivo que analiza las operaciones del almirante Caperton relata que la crisis dominicana estalló seis semanas antes, cuando el ministro de Guerra Arias intentó derrocar al presidente Jiménez. Tras la renuncia de Jiménez, Caperton despachó desde Puerto Príncipe hacia la ciudad de Santo Domingo el buque Prairie con un batallón de infantes de marina al mando del mayor N. H. Hall, desembarcando tropas tras las solicitudes del consejo de ministros, el cuerpo diplomático y ciudadanos locales. Nuevos infantes de marina llegaron bajo el mando del coronel Kane para asegurar la capital pacíficamente mientras Arias y sus fuerzas revolucionarias se replegaban hacia Santiago en el interior. Para salvaguardar vidas y bienes extranjeros, también se realizaron desembarcos estadounidenses en la costa norte, en Monte Cristi y Puerto Plata, donde los infantes tomaron la plaza bajo intenso fuego en una acción que le costó la vida al capitán H. J. Hirshinger.

records.headline: A historical overview characterizes Santo Domingo as a land of perpetual
records.summary_en: A historical overview characterizes Santo Domingo as a land of perpetual revolt, observing that since its separation from Haiti in 1844 virtually every presidential tenure was begun or ended through revolutionary upheaval. The article notes that the Dominican Republic experienced fewer changes of leadership than neighboring Haiti because several Dominican presidents were formidable strongmen who maintained power through sheer force for lengthy periods. Highlighting General Ulises Heureaux as the nation's last strongman, the text details his 13-year rule beginning in the early '80s, praising his administrative capability and his resolve to govern the country on principles of order and justice.
records.summary_es: Una reseña histórica caracteriza a Santo Domingo como una tierra de perpetua revuelta, señalando que desde su separación de Haití en 1844 prácticamente cada período presidencial se inició o concluyó mediante sublevaciones revolucionarias. El artículo observa que la República Dominicana experimentó menos cambios de liderazgo que el vecino Haití porque varios presidentes dominicanos fueron figuras de gran autoridad que mantuvieron el poder mediante la fuerza durante períodos prolongados. Al destacar al general Ulises Heureaux como el último hombre fuerte de la nación, el texto detalla su mandato de 13 años iniciado a principios de los años ochenta, elogiando su capacidad administrativa y su determinación de gobernar el país bajo principios de orden y justicia.
