records.headline: The Evening Star reports that Rear Admiral Pond informed the Navy Department of extensive Dominican assistance
records.summary_en: The Evening Star reports that Rear Admiral Pond informed the Navy Department of extensive Dominican assistance following the loss of the armored cruiser Memphis. Dominican Secretary of War and Marine Miguel Mascaro and Haitian Minister Felix Magloire helped man lifelines from the ship to the shore, while former Dominican President Dr. Báez and his son opened their hospital and assisted at the American field hospital. Former Foreign Secretary B. Pichardo fed and clothed several crewmen, and Provisional President-elect Henríquez and Archbishop Nouel personally visited Pond to convey their sympathy. Local women tore their skirts to treat scalded sailors, prompting Pond to praise the Dominican people as most sympathetic and kind.
records.summary_es: El Evening Star informa que el contralmirante Pond notificó al Departamento de la Armada sobre la amplia ayuda dominicana tras la pérdida del crucero acorazado Memphis. El secretario dominicano de Guerra y Marina Miguel Mascaro y el ministro haitiano Felix Magloire ayudaron a maniobrar los cabos de salvamento desde el buque a la orilla, mientras que el expresidente dominicano Dr. Báez y su hijo pusieron a disposición su hospital y colaboraron en el hospital de campaña estadounidense. El exsecretario de Relaciones Exteriores B. Pichardo alimentó y vistió a varios marineros, y el presidente provisional electo Henríquez y el arzobispo Nouel visitaron personalmente a Pond para expresarle sus condolencias. Mujeres locales rasgaron sus faldas para atender a marineros quemados, lo que motivó a Pond a elogiar al pueblo dominicano como sumamente compasivo y bondadoso.

records.headline: A descriptive feature in The State Herald reviews the geography
records.summary_en: A descriptive feature in The State Herald reviews the geography and commerce of the Dominican Republic. It notes that the fertile Cibao region connects Santiago de los Caballeros, La Vega, and Moca by railway, supporting major cultivation of cacao and tobacco previously marketed in Hamburg. Samaná Bay, spanning twenty-five miles by four and capable of floating the largest warships, features the port of Samaná at its mouth and Sánchez at its head, linked inland by the forty-mile Scotch-built Sánchez-Moca railway. San Pedro de Macorís serves as the primary sugar port with substantial American investment and West Indian labor, situated forty miles from the capital, Santo Domingo City.

records.full_text:
PROSPEROUS LITTLE REPUBLIC

THAT the European war has disturbed the economic and commercial situation in practically every civilized country in the world is a fact well known to everyone at all conversant with international trade conditions. Naturally the republics of the western hemisphere are no exception. Every one of them has felt the disastrous effects, but not in equal nor even in proportionately equal measure. Nearly all of them have experienced a large diminution in their export trade, and consequently a decrease in purchasing power and a resultant diminution in their imports. One remarkable exception is the Dominican Republic, says the Bulletin of the Pan-American union. That little country enjoys the distinction of having sold more of its products, in point of value, to the outside world during the year 1914 than it did during 1913. The increased value of its exports was only $118,840, but that it should have increased its sales at all is an astounding fact. Its purchases from other nations during the year were considerably less, but the net result is that the country has made a material financial gain.

The Dominican Republic is one of the smallest of the American republics, with an area of about 19,325 square miles. This is nearly equal to the combined areas of New Hampshire and Vermont. It has a population of between six and seven hundred thousand inhabitants. Haiti is the adjoining republic and the two together comprise the island called by the first Spanish discoverers "Isla Espanola" and now sometimes called "Santo Domingo" and sometimes "Haiti." Within the limits of what is now the territory of the Dominican Republic was located by Columbus the first settlement of Europeans in the new world. This settlement was called "Isabella," after the queen of Castile, the friend and patroness of Columbus. The first Spanish settlement, like Jamestown, the first English settlement, no longer exists except as a ruin. In fact, "Isabela" disappeared a few years after its foundation. The modern city of Puerto Plata is located near the former site of the old settlement. The oldest existing settlement of Europeans in the western world is likewise located in the Dominican Republic. This is the capital city, Santo Domingo.

One of World's Richest Spots.

The Dominican Republic, in fact the whole island, is naturally one of the richest spots in the world. The soil is remarkably fertile and produces luxuriously. On the north coast, in the province of Monte Cristi, near the Haitian border, the soil is well adapted for cotton raising, and there is a very considerable acreage devoted to this industry, backed by American and English capitalists. The cotton is of a fine quality, and the yield per acre is much greater than that in our southern states.

Puerto Plata, an important port of the north, is a town of some 10,000 or 12,000 inhabitants, connected by a railway, running south, with the towns of the fertile Caibo region—Santiago de los Caballeros, La Vega, and Moca. These towns are located in the great agricultural regions of the republic, where the famous cacao bean is cultivated. Tobacco also is grown to a considerable extent, and has had until recently a ready market in Hamburg. Other ports of importance are Samana and Sanchez, in the beautiful Samana bay. This bay is famous for its size and picturesque scenery. It is about 25 miles long by 5 miles wide, with a depth of water sufficient to float the largest battleships. Our North Atlantic squadron has frequently gone there for maneuvers. At the entrance to the bay is the town of Samana, and at the head is Sanchez, connected with the interior by the Sanchez & Moca railway, a Scotch enterprise, for a distance of 40 miles.

San Pedro de Macoris is the sugar port of the republic. In and around Macoris there are thousands of acres of land devoted to the raising of sugar cane, and millions of dollars of American capital are invested in this enterprise. The plantations are all equipped with the most modern machinery, and the cane is cultivated and gathered by colored laborers from the English and Danish West Indies.

Relics in the Capital.

Seventy miles from La Romana and 40 miles from Macoris is Santo Domingo City, the capital of the republic. In Santo Domingo we find ourselves in the midst of modern civilization, surrounded by innumerable relics that carry us back to the fifteenth century. Here can be seen the ruins of the first church, San Nicolas, built some time in the early part of 1500, and three or four years ago the mahogany taken from these ruins was in a perfect state of preservation. Here, as claimed by the Dominicans, can be seen the bones of Christopher Columbus, left by mistake by the Spaniards when they evacuated the island, and who removed from the crypt in the cathedral to Havana the remains of a brother of Columbus, thinking they were taking the nones of the great discoverer.

The ruins of the house of Diego Colon, the son of Christopher, are still standing, where, according to history, a court was established whose entertainments rivaled in splendor those we read of in the Arabian Nights. On the bank of the river still stands the massive ceiba tree to which were tied the caravels of Columbus. In Santo Domingo City Columbus was put in chains and sent home to Spain a prisoner in disgrace.

The city is built on the west bank of the Ozama river and is under the administration of the department of public works. A magnificent macadam boulevard, bordered on either side with native elms, interspersed with tropical foliage, extends from the center of the city for 20 miles in the direction of Bani, the birthplace of the famous Cuban hero, Maximo Gomez. On this same boulevard can be seen the well-preserved ruins of the Fort San Geronimo, which in early days withstood an attack of the English under Drake. The entrance from the town to this boulevard is through an arch constructed by the government in memory of those who fell fighting for the independence of the country, and the arch bears the inscription "Dulce et Decorum est pro Patria Mori."

Life at the capital, while not as fast and gay as at the larger cities of the South, is still very agreeable. There are two well-equipped and conducted clubs, Club Union and Casino de la Juventud, where there are frequent social entertainments. Automobiles are plentiful and the ride from the capital to San Cristobal along the new macadam boulevard is most attractive. Automobiles can be procured for $4 an hour. There are several hotels in the city, of which the Hotel Francis is the best known. There is quite a large foreign colony at the capital and in Macoris and Puerto Plata. The whole trip from New York, including a stop at all ports, is about eight or nine days.

A very erroneous impression prevails that the climate of Santo Domingo is unhealthy. From its geographical position it cannot be unhealthy. The winds have a clean sweep across the island, and there has been no serious epidemic there since the cholera outbreak some time in the early sixties.

records.headline: An Atlanta dispatch in The Brunswick News quotes a letter from Captain W. H. Pritchett of the U.S. Marine
records.summary_en: An Atlanta dispatch in The Brunswick News quotes a letter from Captain W. H. Pritchett of the U.S. Marine Corps, stationed at Santiago, Dominican Republic, describing the country's recent three-day election for constitutional convention delegates. Pritchett observes that elections are held over three days to allow ample time for fights and shooting, with continuous gunfire heard in parts of Santiago and brawls breaking out in the crowded central plaza. He explains that political factions take the names of their leaders, with the Aristas opposing and the Horacistas favoring proposed constitutional changes.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Atlanta en The Brunswick News cita una carta del capitán W. H. Pritchett de la Infantería de Marina de EE. UU., destacado en Santiago, República Dominicana, describiendo las recientes elecciones de tres días para delegados a la convención constitucional. Pritchett observa que las elecciones duran tres días para dar tiempo suficiente a peleas y tiroteos, con disparos continuos en zonas de Santiago y riñas en la concurrida plaza central. Explica que las facciones políticas adoptan los nombres de sus caudillos, con los aristas opuestos y los horacistas a favor de las reformas constitucionales propuestas.

records.headline: But after six or seven years of peace trouble broke out
records.summary_en: The *Perth Amboy evening news* reported on U.S. intervention in Santo Domingo, stating that severe unrest in 1914 and 1915 forced the United States to deploy marines and warships to restore quiet. The article asserted that Dominicans reluctantly accepted external peace enforced under the Monroe Doctrine after customs administration alone failed to prevent renewed revolutions. It characterized the military interventions in Santo Domingo, Haiti, and Nicaragua as costly, altruistic sacrifices made for regional security rather than territorial gain.
records.summary_es: El *Perth Amboy evening news* informó sobre la intervención de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo, indicando que los graves disturbios acaecidos en 1914 y 1915 obligaron a Washington a movilizar infantes de marina y escuadras navales para restaurar la calma. El artículo aseveraba que la población dominicana aceptaba a regañadientes una paz exterior impuesta al amparo de la Doctrina Monroe, luego de que la sola administración aduanera resultara ineficaz para evitar la reaparición de revueltas. Calificaba los desembarcos militares en Santo Domingo, Haití y Nicaragua como sacrificios onerosos y altruistas en favor de la seguridad continental antes que en búsqueda de engrandecimiento territorial.
records.passage: still left a greater net Income for the use of the government than It had ever had before. "For a long time it was thought that, deprived of the opportunity of securing customs house revenues through the seizure of ports, revolution could not support themselves. But after six or seven years of peace trouble broke out again, and during 1914 and 1915 it became so serious that the United States was forced to Intervene in behalf of peace and to demand, with marines on shore and naval guns trained and pointed on the ports, that the country return to a state of quiet. And so today the Dominicans, realizing that the Monroe doctrine is determined to afford them protection, from their own excesses, their own bitter passions and blind purposes, have accepted the inevitable and have secured the blessings of peace from without when they could not attain that end themselves. It is a reluctant acquiescence they yield, but a wholesome one, none the less. 'It has not been without effort or without expense, nor yet without the actual sacrifice of blood and life that our country has stepped in to play the role of Good Samaritan to the people of Santo Domingo, Haiti and Nicaragua, who had lost the blessings of peace and were unable to regain them. In Haiti alone we lost one officer and six marines and had a number wounded. But out of this altruistic effort are growing results of which a nation that covets no territory, that seeks only its own security and the welfare of its unfortunate neighbors may well be proud.

records.headline: Quoting the Southwestern Christian Advocate, The Savannah Tribune reports
records.summary_en: Quoting the Southwestern Christian Advocate, The Savannah Tribune reports that local newspapers in Santo Domingo City regularly publish bitter attacks against the United States and the forces of occupation. Major Bearss of the U.S. Marine Corps met with the city governor and ordered the publications halted, warning that the governor would be held responsible if the attacks continued. The governor replied that he was powerless to stop the articles and that restricting press freedoms would be unlawful, after which local papers became even more vehement in their denunciation of American policy.
records.summary_es: Citando al Southwestern Christian Advocate, The Savannah Tribune informa que los periódicos locales de la ciudad de Santo Domingo publican con regularidad duros ataques contra Estados Unidos y las fuerzas de ocupación. UU. se reunió con el gobernador de la ciudad y ordenó el cese de las publicaciones, advirtiendo que el gobernador sería responsabilizado si los ataques continuaban. El gobernador respondió que carecía de poder para frenar los artículos y que restringir la libertad de prensa sería ilegal, tras lo cual los periódicos locales se volvieron aún más vehementes en sus denuncias contra la política estadounidense.

records.headline: The South Bend News-Times reports that the Dominican foreign office
records.summary_en: The South Bend News-Times reports that the Dominican foreign office has unofficially approached U.S. Minister Russell with a proposal to grant a 99-year lease on Samaná Bay to the United States. In return, the American government would assume the Dominican bonded debt, construct an extensive railway line, and pay an annual rental of $100,000. Naval strategists consider the bay the finest landlocked harbor in the Western Hemisphere and indispensable for protecting the Panama Canal. The article recalls that under President Grant, an official commission examined the bay and recommended its acquisition as a harbor capable of sheltering the largest fleets.

records.summary_en: A biographical dispatch in The Crook County Monitor reports that General Juan Isidro Jiménez, former president of the Dominican Republic, is seeking rest for his nerves in the mountains near Wernersville, Pennsylvania. Jiménez had served as president off and on for five years until his resignation on May 8 under pressure from the Dominican Congress. The piece recounts his eventful career commanding armies, defying legislators, assuming office following an assassination, and resisting European pressures. Seeking peace under medical care, the veteran general recently arrived by motor car accompanied by his wife and youthful daughter.

Jiménez había ejercido la presidencia de forma intermitente durante cinco años hasta su renuncia el 8 de mayo bajo presión del Congreso dominicano. La nota reseña su azarosa carrera comandando ejércitos, desafiando a legisladores, asumiendo el cargo tras un magnicidio y resistiendo presiones europeas. En busca de reposo bajo supervisión médica, el veterano general llegó en automóvil acompañado por su esposa y su joven hija.

records.headline: Fully worked out by state and navy department officials after
records.summary_en: The *Ogden standard* reported that Captain Knapp was dispatched to Dominican waters with instructions to institute military rule following the overthrow of President Jiminez by General Arias. Because the United States refused to recognize the administration of Frederico Henriquez, customs revenues had been withheld, leaving native officials unpaid until American officers began disbursing $600,000 in accumulated export duties on December 2. Secretary Daniels emphasized that the military administration would not infringe on civil rights and that Dominican courts would continue to administer municipal laws.
records.summary_es: El *Ogden standard* informó que el capitán Knapp fue despachado a aguas dominicanas con instrucciones de instaurar un régimen militar tras el derrocamiento del presidente Jimenes a manos del general Arias. Debido a que los Estados Unidos no reconocieron el gobierno de Francisco Henríquez y Carvajal (mencionado como Frederico Henriquez), los caudales aduaneros fueron retenidos, quedando sin sueldo los funcionarios del país hasta que los oficiales estadounidenses comenzaron a desembolsar el 2 de diciembre 600.000 dólares en derechos de exportación retenidos. El secretario Daniels enfatizó que el régimen castrense no conculcaría las libertades cívicas y que los tribunales dominicanos seguirían aplicando las leyes locales.
records.passage: fully worked out by state and navy department officials after conferences with Minister Russell, recalled from Santo Domingo for the purpose, and consideration of full reports from the naval officers on the scene. Captain Knapp, recently sent to relieve Rear Admiral Pond in Dominican waters, carried with him complete instructions for his task. The necessity for a drastic step has been considered since the overthrow several months ago by President Jiminez by General Arias, a strongly anti American revolutionist. With Arias in control, the Dominican assembly elected Frederico Enriques president, but the United States refused to recognize the new government and withheld the balance of customs revenues left after the regular payments of interest on the foreign debt. Consequently the native officials and employes will draw their first pay since the downfall of Jiminez when on December 2 the American officers begin to disburse some $600,000 of accumulated export duties. No Infringement on Civil Rights. Secretary Daniels explained today that the form of rule set up by Captain Knapp did not contemplate any infringement of the civil rights or processes of the native government. The marines will maintain order and prevent revolutionary agitation, but the municipal and civil laws will still be administered by Dominican courts. records.headline: A November 30 dispatch from Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: A November 30 dispatch from Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, reports that Capt. H. S. Knapp, commanding the United States forces there, issued a proclamation of military rule declaring on behalf of the American government that the republic has been occupied by military forces. The proclamation gives assurance that the United States has no intention of destroying the republic's independence, but desires to help establish internal order, leaving Dominican laws and courts in force and legal administration under duly authorized Dominican officials supervised by military authorities, while offending members of the American force are to be judged by military officials. Capt. Knapp requested the inhabitants' cooperation in restoring order, established censorship of newspapers, cables, and telegraph lines, and promised that budget payments suspended in August would soon be made, while quiet prevailed in the city the previous night.
records.summary_es: Un despacho fechado el 30 de noviembre en Santo Domingo, República Dominicana, informa que el capitán H. S. Knapp, comandante de las fuerzas de los Estados Unidos allí, emitió una proclama de gobierno militar declarando en nombre del gobierno estadounidense que la república ha sido ocupada por fuerzas militares. La proclama asegura que los Estados Unidos no tienen intención de destruir la independencia de la república, sino que desean ayudar al país a establecer el orden interno, manteniendo vigentes las leyes y los tribunales dominicanos y dejando la administración legal en manos de los funcionarios dominicanos debidamente autorizados bajo el control y la supervisión de las autoridades militares, mientras que los miembros infractores de la fuerza estadounidense serán juzgados por oficiales militares. El capitán Knapp solicitó la cooperación de los habitantes para restablecer el orden, estableció la censura de periódicos, cables y líneas telegráficas, y prometió que pronto se efectuaría el pago del presupuesto suspendido en agosto, mientras la tranquilidad reinaba en la ciudad la noche anterior.

records.headline: According to a report to the Navy Department from Capt. Knapp
records.summary_en: According to a report to the Navy Department from Capt. Knapp, commanding the forces in Haiti and Santo Domingo, a number of men were wounded on both sides in an encounter on Wednesday between American marines and natives at Macoris, Santo Domingo. The dispatch stated that no Americans were killed and only a few marines were injured while investing Macoris, disarming the natives, and establishing themselves under the recently proclaimed military rule, whereas the heaviest losses were suffered by the Dominicans, though their exact numbers were not indicated. Capt. Knapp also reported that his military administration is being received with enthusiasm by most of the islanders, that native officials are being paid their long-awaited salaries out of $800,000 in accumulated export duties held by the American customs receivers, and that government will soon proceed in normal fashion under Navy supervision.
records.summary_es: Según un informe enviado al Departamento de Marina por el capitán Knapp, comandante de las fuerzas en Haití y Santo Domingo, varios hombres resultaron heridos en ambos bandos durante un enfrentamiento ocurrido el miércoles entre marines estadounidenses y nativos en Macorís, Santo Domingo. El despacho señaló que ningún estadounidense murió y que solo unos pocos marines resultaron heridos mientras cercaban Macorís, desarmaban a los nativos y se establecían conforme al gobierno militar recientemente proclamado, mientras que las mayores bajas las sufrieron los dominicanos, aunque no se indicó su número exacto. El capitán Knapp informó además que su administración militar está siendo recibida con entusiasmo por la mayoría de los isleños, que a los funcionarios nativos se les están pagando sus largamente esperados sueldos con cargo a los $800,000 acumulados en derechos de exportación retenidos por los receptores aduaneros estadounidenses, y que en poco tiempo el gobierno funcionará con normalidad bajo la supervisión de la Marina.

records.summary_en: According to a dispatch to the Navy Department from Capt. Harry Knapp, eleven Dominicans were killed and six were wounded, while Capt. J. A. Hughes and ten United States Marine privates were wounded during fighting on November 29 and 30 at Macoris, Dominican Republic, against natives resisting American occupation. In the 31st Company, Capt. Hughes suffered a gunshot wound and fractured left leg, Private Herman S. Clark sustained a compound fracture of the right elbow, and Privates Luther G. Gaskins, William C. Yele, Robert H. Osborn, Robert C. McLennan, Arthur W. Anderson, Sumanter Summer, and Otto E. Hagstrom were less seriously wounded, all in favorable condition. In the 32d Company, Lloyd W. Nicholson sustained a compound fracture of the right elbow and was in serious condition, while Ralph J. Emmel received a slight wound and was in favorable condition.

records.summary_en: The *Presbyterian of the South* reported that Captain Knapp established a military government in Santo Domingo following the overthrow of President Jiminez and Washington's refusal to recognize Frederico Enriquez. Under Knapp's proclamation, the military administration guaranteed monthly loan payments to the Guaranty Trust Company of New York and the payment of salaries for Dominican officials. Secretary Daniels noted that the 1,800 marines would enforce order without infringing upon Dominican civil rights or regular judicial processes.
records.summary_es: El *Presbyterian of the South* informó que el capitán Knapp constituyó un gobierno militar en Santo Domingo tras la deposición del presidente Jimenes y el desconocimiento de Washington hacia Francisco Henríquez y Carvajal (citado como Frederico Enriquez). Mediante la proclama de Knapp, la administración castrense garantizaba los abonos mensuales del empréstito a la Guaranty Trust Company de Nueva York y la cancelación de sueldos a los servidores públicos dominicanos. records.full_text:
SANTO DOMINGO UNDER MARTIAL LAW.

Under instructions from Washington, based on reports of conditions existing in the republic, martial law has been established in Santo Domingo by the American naval and marine force of occupataion. Captain Harry S. Knapp, who is in command of the American forces in Santo Domingo, notified Secretary Daniels that in compliance with these instructions military government was proclaimed by him in that republic.

"An order," said Secretary Daniels, "has been put into effect regarding carrying arms or having them in possession. Payment of salaries of government officials will be resumed immediately. The proclamation is reported by Captain Knapp to have been received favorably, and conditions are reported as being normal, while the great majority of the people regard the proclamation with favor."

It was explained in official circles that it became necessary to set up a military government and martial law in San Domingo in order to enable the Dominican government to pay the interest on its foreign debt in accordance with the treaty of 1907 between this country and Santo Domingo, under which the customs receipts of that country are collected by an American receiver-general of customs, and disbursed in accordance with the terms of that agreement. Part of the collection goes toward the payment of interest and principal on the bonds issued to cover the Dominican foreign debt, and the rest of the receipts go to the Dominican government for its own use.

Reports from Captain Knapp showed that the political situation in Santo Domingo was such that the revenues, collected by the American receiver-general were tied up and could not be disbursed, the result being that, while money was collected and available for paying the interest on the country's foreign debt, these interest payments could not be made safely under the existing political conditions.

Under the military government put into effect by Captain Knapp's proclamation, Captain Knapp will act as military governor, and while so acting not only will provide for the payment of $100,000 a month to the fiscal agent of the loan, the Guaranty Trust Company, of New York, and interest on any other existing foreign obligations, but also will see that the salaries of Dominican government officials and expenses of the government are paid.

Although no publicity had been given to the government's intentions, Captain Knapp's action was the result of plans carefully worked out by State and Navy Department officials after conferences with Minister Russell, who was recalled from Santo Dominga for the purpose, and consideration of full reports from the naval officers on the scene. Captain Knapp, recently sent to relieve Rear-Admiral Pond in Dominican waters, carried with him complete instructions for his task.

The necessity for a drastic step has been considered since the overthrow several months ago of President Jiminez by General Arias, a strongly anti-American revolutionist. With Arias in control, the Dominican Assembly elected Frederico Enriquez president, but the United States refused to recognize the new government.

Secretary Daniels explained that the form of rule set by Captain Knapp did not contemplate any infringement of the civil rights or processes of the native government. The 1,800 American marines now there will maintain order and prevent revolutionary agitation, but the municipal and civil laws will still be administered by Dominican courts.

Captain Knapp was selected for the task because of special fitness growing out of his service on the Neutrality Board. That duty led him into a careful study of the situation in Haiti and Santo Domingo. His report says that probably 90 per cent of the native business men and others who desire permanent peace on the island approve the steps that have been taken and those which are in contemplation.

Upon the election of a president by the Assembly to be chosen in January the United States will ask for the ratification of a treaty similar to that now in force with Haiti, providing for American supervision of Dominican finances and for a native constabulary officered by Americans.

High officials made it plain that the American government was determined that there should be no renewal of the revolutions in Haiti and Santo Domingo, which for years have rendered the island a source of menace to the international relations of the United States because of the foreign capital invested there.

Approximately 1,800 American marines were tasked with maintaining order and supervising native government operations until January elections, including the disbursement of $600,000 in accumulated export duties. The intervention followed the overthrow of President Jiminez by General Arias and Washington's refusal to recognize the newly chosen government of Frederico Enriquez.

records.headline: Gen. Juan Isidor Jiminez served as president of the Dominican
records.summary_en: Gen. Juan Isidor Jiminez served as president of the Dominican Republic, off and on, for five years until he resigned under pressure from his congress on May 8, and is seeking rest for his nerves under the care of doctors and trained nurses in the mountains near Wernersville, Pennsylvania, this profile reports, with his name printed "Juan Tsidor Jiminez". Recalling that the nearly seventy-year-old general led armies, defied a congress, stepped into a presidency vacated by assassination, and more than once shook his fist at Europe, the article describes him arriving up the hill in a big motor car flanked by his wife and his daughter, Carmela Jiminez, and notes that he refuses to discuss Latin-American politics or events in the republic.

records.headline: Within a chronological review of notable events, five entries
records.summary_en: Within a chronological review of notable events, five entries record developments in the Dominican Republic: on May 2, President Jimenez of the Dominican Republic was impeached; on May 6, fighting broke out in Santo Domingo and American marines landed; and on July 1, U.S. marines routed 250 Santo Domingo rebels, killing 27 and losing one man. Later entries note that on October 24 two American officers were killed by Dominican rebels, and on November 29 Capt. H. S. Knapp, U.S.N. commander in Santo Domingo, proclaimed a military government of that country.
records.summary_es: Dentro de un recuento cronológico de acontecimientos destacados, cinco entradas registran sucesos en la República Dominicana: el 2 de mayo, el presidente Jimenez de la República Dominicana fue sometido a juicio político; el 6 de mayo, estallaron combates en Santo Domingo y desembarcaron marines estadounidenses; y el 1 de julio, los marines de los EE. UU. derrotaron a 250 rebeldes de Santo Domingo, matando a 27 y perdiendo a un hombre. Entradas posteriores señalan que el 24 de octubre dos oficiales estadounidenses fueron muertos por rebeldes dominicanos, y que el 29 de noviembre el capitán H. S. Knapp, comandante de la Marina de los EE. UU. en Santo Domingo, proclamó un gobierno militar en ese país.

records.headline: This article reports that Private Hogan of the Fourth Regiment
records.summary_en: This article reports that Private Hogan of the Fourth Regiment, U.S. Marines, left on the Tennessee on May 20 for Santiago and Santo Domingo City to help quell rebellion, taking part on June 3 in a 40-minute battle in which no member of the Fourth Company was wounded while rebel casualties were reported at sixty killed or wounded. After remaining at Santo Domingo until late in the year and surviving the wreck of the ship on the rocks near Santo Domingo, Private Hogan returned to League Island. Speaking of the customs of the islanders (referred to in the text as Haitians), he stated that the rebels are poorly organized, with only officers wearing uniforms or shoes while privates go barefoot, and that because they saw off the front part and forward sight of their rifles their aim in battle is poor, though their sniping causes most of the fatalities among the marines.
records.summary_es: Este artículo informa que el soldado raso Hogan, del Cuarto Regimiento de la Infantería de Marina de los EE. UU., partió en el Tennessee el 20 de mayo hacia Santiago y la ciudad de Santo Domingo para ayudar a sofocar la rebelión, participando el 3 de junio en un combate de 40 minutos en el que ningún miembro de la Cuarta Compañía resultó herido, mientras que las bajas rebeldes se estimaron en sesenta muertos o heridos. Tras permanecer en Santo Domingo hasta finales del año y sobrevivir al naufragio del buque contra las rocas cerca de Santo Domingo, el soldado raso Hogan regresó a League Island. Hablando de las costumbres de los habitantes (llamados haitianos en el texto), afirmó que los rebeldes están mal organizados, pues solo los oficiales usan uniformes o zapatos mientras los soldados rasos van descalzos, y que debido a que recortan la parte delantera y la mira frontal de sus fusiles su puntería en combate es deficiente, aunque sus francotiradores causan la mayoría de las bajas mortales entre los marines.

records.headline: There were assassinations, there were betrayals, there were conspiracies, there
records.summary_en: The *Norwich bulletin* recounted the chronic political instability and recurring civil wars in Santo Domingo that left the republic heavily indebted to foreign creditors. When foreign warships threatened bombardment to enforce debt claims, Dominican authorities entered into an agreement with the United States in 1905 to take over the collection of customs. Under this treaty, American authorities restructured the nation's tariffs to tax luxuries and guaranteed payments to satisfy European claims.
records.summary_es: El *Norwich bulletin* rememoró la crónica inestabilidad política y las constantes guerras civiles en Santo Domingo que abocaron a la república a un pesado endeudamiento con acreedores extranjeros. Al amenazar cañoneros extranjeros con bombardear los puertos para hacer efectivas sus reclamaciones, las autoridades dominicanas celebraron un acuerdo con los Estados Unidos en 1905 para confiarles la recaudación aduanera. Bajo este convenio, los funcionarios estadounidenses modificaron los aranceles nacionales gravando los artículos de lujo y aseguraron pagos para saldar los reclamos europeos.
records.passage: bulletin. "Revolution had followed revolution almost with clocklike regularity. There were assassinations, there were betrayals, there were conspiracies, there were wars within and wars without — war with Haiti over boundary questions and civil war over the control of the government. Debts were piled up without thought of the day of payment or even provisions for meeting the interest charges. "So long and so steady was the orgy of revolution, speculation, debt making and interest-dodging that the nation's credit grew worse than that of its individual citizens. Finally, the day of reckoning came. Foreign warships approached the ports whose harbors had given refuge to the great discoverer Columbus and whose capital city contains what undoubtedly are his ashes, and demanded that the claims of their subjects be satisfied — claims for money advanced, claims for property wantonly destroyed — and they demanded it at the point of big naval guns. "In a predicament from which they were powerless to extricate themselves, the Dominicans were ready enough to negotiate a treaty turning over the control of the country's customs to the United States, if, in return therefor, the United States would protect them from angry European creditors and rejuvenate their treasury. "And so it was that in [illegible] the United States undertook to serve as treasurer of Santo Domingo and to vouch for her debts. The tariff was quickly revised, the American authorities urging that duties be laid on luxuries rather than upon necessities.

records.headline: A night fight between native bandits and American marines in the Dominican republic
records.summary_en: The *New Britain herald* reported that a night skirmish occurred between native bandits and American marines near the Porvenir sugar plantation close to Macoris. Captain Knapp reported that Private J. R. Olson was killed and Corporal George Wilson was shot in the neck during the engagement. Officials believed the marine companies were conducting operations to disarm the local population and enforce the authority of the military government.

El capitán Knapp comunicó que el soldado raso J. R. Olson pereció en el combate y el cabo George Wilson recibió una herida de bala en el cuello. Los mandos militares indicaron que las compañías de infantería de marina adelantaban operaciones para desarmar a la población e imponer la autoridad del gobierno militar.

records.headline: An Associated Press dispatch from Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: An Associated Press dispatch from Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, dated January 23, reports that the American steamer Mariana, trading between San Domingo and Porto Rico, arrived there the previous day from Ponce and reported having sighted a suspicious steamer. The strange vessel was seen near Vieques Island, also known as Crab Island, about 13 miles east of Porto Rico. The dispatch adds that the American Atlantic fleet passed Santo Domingo the previous day.

El buque extraño fue visto en las cercanías de la isla de Vieques, también conocida como Crab Island, a unas 13 millas al este de Puerto Rico. El despacho añade que la flota estadounidense del Atlántico pasó por Santo Domingo el día anterior.

records.summary_en: The *Evening star* reported that despite rumors of policy changes regarding national self-determination, the Navy Department indicated no prospect of an early withdrawal of the 2,000 U.S. marines stationed in Santo Domingo. Retiring Dominican minister Dr. A. Perez Perdomo, removed by the American military commander, stated that any American casualties were caused by patriotic resistance to foreign interference rather than banditry. He strongly rejected the characterization of his fellow countrymen as bandits.
records.summary_es: El *Evening star* informó que, a pesar de los rumores sobre un cambio de política relativo a la autodeterminación de las naciones, el Departamento de la Armada descartó un retiro próximo de los 2.000 infantes de marina estadounidenses destacados en Santo Domingo. El ministro dominicano saliente, Dr. A. Pérez Perdomo, removido por el gobernador militar estadounidense, manifestó que las bajas sufridas por las fuerzas de los Estados Unidos obedecían a la resistencia patriótica frente a la intromisión extranjera y no al bandolerismo. Rechazó categóricamente que se tildara a sus compatriotas de bandoleros.
records.passage: [illegible]ew policy of the Washington government, with respect to the countries named, is based, so the story goes, on the President's recent declaration of his belief "that no nation should seek [to] extend its policy over any other nation or people, but that every people should be left free to determine its own policy, its own way of development, unhindered, unthreatened, unafraid, the little along with the great and powerful." Verification of the above reported plan of action was not obtainable in official quarters. On the contrary, it was indicated clearly in the Navy Department that there was no prospect whatever of the early withdrawal of the American marines from either Santo Domingo or Haiti, where the United States has assumed military control for the preservation of peace and order, much to the gratification, it is said, of the majority of the inhabitants. records.summary_en: According to a January 23 dispatch from Washington, a night fight between native bandits and American marines in the Dominican Republic was reported that day to the Navy Department, leaving one marine dead and another severely injured. Private J. Holson of the Fiftieth Company was killed, while Corporal George Wilson of the Fifty-second Company suffered a gunshot wound in the neck. records.headline: The article, quoting a monthly magazine published by Sr. Ferrara
records.summary_en: The article, quoting a monthly magazine published by Sr. Ferrara, cites its characterization of a third American intervention as the 'diabolic Wilson plan,' which the writer explains was the August 1914 arrangement whereby the United States agreed to protect constitutional government in the Dominican Republic. The quoted magazine article further alleges that the crimes of United States forces in Santo Domingo recall German crimes in Belgium and France and have outraged America and the world. The writer adds that feeling over United States action in the Dominican Republic runs particularly high in eastern Cuba, noting that the independent daily La Independencia in Santiago has devoted columns to the intervention while the American-controlled conservative Havana daily El Mundo points to both the Dominican Republic and Mexico as object lessons for Cuba.

U. S. MARINE DIES IN FIGHT

One American Is Killed and One Severely Wounded by Santo Domingo Bandits.

Washington, Jan. 24.—A night fight between native bandits and American marines in the Dominican republic, resulting in the death of one marine and the severe injury of another, was reported to the navy department.

Captain Knapp, commanding the American cruiser forces, reported the fight occurred Saturday night in the vicinity of the Porvenir sugar plantation, near Macoris, the scene of two similar encounters recently. Private J. R. Olson of the Fiftieth company was killed and Corporal George Wilson of the Fifty-second company was shot in the neck.

records.headline: An Associated Press correspondent writing from Santo Domingo on February 13 reports that peace, expected by everyone
records.summary_en: An Associated Press correspondent writing from Santo Domingo on February 13 reports that peace, expected by everyone to be permanent, has at last been established through the intervention of the United States in a country that has had approximately fifty presidents in seventy years, not one chosen without revolution. Captain Knapp, head of the temporary military government, faces the work of establishing good government, a sound educational system, agriculture and transportation, with an education commission headed by Archbishop Adolfo Nouel already appointed and a great highway of more than 200 miles planned across the Cibao to Monte Cristi.
records.summary_es: Un corresponsal de la Associated Press que escribe desde Santo Domingo el 13 de febrero informa que la paz, que todos esperan permanente, se ha establecido por fin mediante la intervención de los Estados Unidos en un país que ha tenido aproximadamente cincuenta presidentes en setenta años, ninguno elegido sin revolución. El capitán Knapp, jefe del gobierno militar temporal, enfrenta la tarea de establecer un buen gobierno, un sistema educativo sólido, la agricultura y el transporte, con una comisión de educación encabezada por el arzobispo Adolfo Nouel ya nombrada y una gran carretera de más de 200 millas proyectada a través del Cibao hasta Monte Cristi.
records.passage: basis, the evolution of a sound educational system, the development of agriculture and the creation of a system of transportation. In the matter of education a start has been made by the appointment of a commission headed by Archbishop Adolfo Nouel, Catholic primate, Federico Velasquez and other prominent Dominicans, empowered to make an exhaustive study of the educational needs of the people. There is a so-called school system in existence, but those in a position to know say there is not a public school building in the republic and estimates of illiteracy run as high as 90 per cent. Teachers have drawn salaries from the government when they had no pupils to teach and subventions are said to have been granted to private schools which existed only in name. Great Highway Planned. One of the principal public improvements planned by the military government is a great highway crossing the island and connecting Santo Domingo [illegible] Monte Cristi, the most westerly port on the north coast. This proposed highway would be more than 200 miles long and would traverse the vast Cibao region, frequently described as the most wonderful undeveloped agricultural area in the Caribbean. The Cibao country was discovered by Christopher Columbus and still for the most part is virgin soil. In the portions of the Cibao which are under cultivation, the richest products of the island, Cacao and Tobacco, are produced. Many Port Improvements. Many port improvements have also

records.headline: A February 28 dispatch from Puerto Plata reports that extensive repairs
records.summary_en: A February 28 dispatch from Puerto Plata reports that extensive repairs have begun on the state-owned Dominican Central Railroad linking the port with Santiago in the Cibao region, in keeping with the Military Government's desire to place transportation between the two points on a satisfactory footing. With practically no rail freight moved inland from Puerto Plata since August, a year's accumulation of tons of tobacco, coffee, and cacao remains unmoved at Santiago. Engineers are working on two route deviations to reduce the grade from 12 per cent to a maximum of three per cent, eliminating the need for racks, while locomotives and rolling stock are also being restored to usable condition.

Sin que prácticamente ninguna carga haya sido movilizada por ferrocarril tierra adentro desde Puerto Plata desde agosto, toneladas de tabaco, café y cacao acumuladas durante un año permanecen sin moverse en Santiago. Los ingenieros trabajan en dos desviaciones de la ruta actual para reducir la pendiente del 12 por ciento a un máximo del tres por ciento, eliminando la necesidad de cremalleras, al tiempo que las locomotoras y el material rodante también serán puestos en condiciones de uso.

records.headline: A February 28 dispatch from Santo Domingo City reports that nearly
records.summary_en: A February 28 dispatch from Santo Domingo City reports that nearly three months have proved insufficient for the United States Marines of the temporary military occupation to collect all weapons in the Dominican Republic under one of the first orders issued by Captain H. S. Knapp, U.S. Navy, acting head of the temporary government, calling for the voluntary surrender of all arms, ammunition, and explosives. Authorities have not announced the total number of weapons gathered either voluntarily or by Marine searches, though many thousands of revolvers and rifles have been surrendered or seized in certain districts. Observers familiar with the Dominican desire to possess weapons believe complete disarmament will be next to impossible.

Las autoridades no han anunciado el número total de armas reunidas ya sea voluntariamente o mediante registros de los infantes de marina, aunque en ciertos distritos muchos miles de revólveres y rifles han sido entregados o incautados. Personas familiarizadas con el deseo dominicano de poseer armas consideran que lograr un desarme completo será casi imposible.

records.headline: A February 10 dispatch from Puerto Plata states that extensive repairs
records.summary_en: A February 10 dispatch from Puerto Plata states that extensive repairs have been started on the state-owned Dominican Central Railroad between Puerto Plata and Santiago in the Cibao region, in keeping with the military government's aim to bring rail transportation between the two points to a satisfactory condition. Tons of tobacco, coffee, and cacao accumulated over a year remain unmoved at Santiago, as practically no inland rail freight has moved from the port since August and the line has operated profitably on only one or two brief occasions. Engineers are working on two route deviations to cut the grade from 12 per cent to a maximum of 3 per cent and dispense with racks, while locomotives and rolling stock are also being repaired.
records.summary_es: Un despacho fechado el 10 de febrero en Puerto Plata indica que se han iniciado extensas reparaciones en el estatal Ferrocarril Central Dominicano entre Puerto Plata y Santiago, en la región del Cibao, de acuerdo con el propósito del gobierno militar de llevar el transporte ferroviario entre ambos puntos a una condición satisfactoria. Toneladas de tabaco, café y cacao acumuladas durante un año permanecen sin moverse en Santiago, pues prácticamente no se ha transportado carga por ferrocarril tierra adentro desde el puerto desde agosto y la línea solo ha operado de manera rentable en una o dos breves ocasiones. Los ingenieros trabajan en dos desviaciones de la ruta para reducir la pendiente del 12 por ciento a un máximo del 3 por ciento y prescindir de las cremalleras, mientras que las locomotoras y el material rodante también están siendo reparados.

records.summary_en: Opening mid-dispatch with a note that Santiago, Puerto Plata, and the capital are the only cities in the Dominican Republic with electric lighting service, the report outlines public works underway across the country. Immediate projects include rebuilding seven bridges on the Santiago-to-Monte Cristi road that revolutionists burned the previous spring to check advancing United States Marines, while in the south bids have been requested for the first 16 kilometers of a 55-kilometer macadam road from Macoris to Santo Domingo City, connecting with a 12-kilometer road under construction from Macoris to Hato Mayor. In Santo Domingo City, the foundation of a new $50,000 customs house has been laid, work has resumed on a municipal building delayed for nearly ten years by revolutions, and several government buildings are planned to replace rented quarters.

records.headline: A March 6 dispatch from Santo Domingo City reports that the American International
records.summary_en: A March 6 dispatch from Santo Domingo City reports that the American International Corporation, an affiliate of the National City Bank of New York, will soon establish itself in the Dominican capital by purchasing the banking interests of Santiago Michelena, head of the largest banking house there. Although no date has been announced for the transfer of the Michelena bank, which maintains branches in all the principal cities, all details of the purchase have been authoritatively reported as agreed upon, and a formal announcement of the sale is expected shortly.

Aunque no se ha anunciado la fecha en que será traspasado el banco Michelena, el cual cuenta con sucursales en todas las ciudades principales, se afirma de manera autorizada que todos los detalles de la compra han sido acordados y que el anuncio formal de la venta se espera muy pronto.

records.headline: Sugar estates, the largest employers of labor in Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: Sugar estates, the largest employers of labor in Santo Domingo, are seriously handicapped during their harvest by a labor shortage, particularly in the San Pedro de Macoris district, the republic's largest sugar-producing section, Associated Press correspondence from San Pedro de Macoris dated March 9 reports. Estate managers state that they have no more than seventy per cent of the labor needed to handle the crop without loss, even though higher wages than ever before are being paid, with most estates paying cane cutters forty cents a ton and average workers cutting four to six tons daily, and some up to eight tons. Managers add that more Dominicans are working in the cane fields since the temporary United States military occupation because there are no revolutions to draw off or forcibly round up agricultural laborers as recruits.

Los administradores de los ingenios afirman que no cuentan con más del setenta por ciento de la mano de obra necesaria para procesar la cosecha actual sin pérdidas, a pesar de que se están pagando mejores salarios que nunca, pues la mayoría de las fincas pagan a los cortadores de caña a razón de cuarenta centavos por tonelada y un trabajador promedio corta de cuatro a seis toneladas diarias, llegando algunos hasta ocho toneladas. Los administradores añaden que desde la ocupación militar temporal de los Estados Unidos hay más dominicanos trabajando en los cañaverales porque no hay revoluciones que atraigan o recluten por la fuerza a los jornaleros agrícolas.

records.summary_en: An Associated Press dispatch from Santo Domingo City dated February 28 states that nearly three months have not been enough time for the United States Marines of the temporary military occupation to collect all arms in the Dominican Republic pursuant to one of the first orders issued by Captain H. S. Knapp, United States Navy, acting head of the temporary government. While authorities have not announced the total number of weapons voluntarily surrendered or seized in Marine searches, many thousand revolvers and rifles are known to have been gathered in certain districts. Observers familiar with the Dominican desire to possess arms believe complete disarmament will be next to impossible, noting that it had been very common to see gentlemen armed with a revolver at balls or other entertainments.

records.headline: A March 23 dispatch from Puerto Plata reports that extensive repairs
records.summary_en: A March 23 dispatch from Puerto Plata reports that extensive repairs have begun on the state-owned Dominican Central Railroad connecting the port with Santiago in the Cibao region, in accordance with the military government's desire to bring rail transportation between the two points to a satisfactory standard. Practically no rail freight has moved inland from Puerto Plata since August, leaving a year's accumulation of tons of tobacco, coffee, and cacao unmoved at Santiago. Engineers are working on two deviations from the existing route to lower the grade from twelve per cent to a maximum of three per cent and eliminate the need for racks, while locomotives and rolling stock are also to be restored to usable condition.
records.summary_es: Un despacho fechado el 23 de marzo en Puerto Plata informa que se han iniciado extensas reparaciones en el estatal Ferrocarril Central Dominicano, que conecta dicho puerto con Santiago en la región del Cibao, conforme al deseo del gobierno militar de llevar el transporte ferroviario entre ambos puntos a un nivel satisfactorio. Prácticamente ninguna carga se ha movido por ferrocarril hacia el interior desde Puerto Plata desde agosto, dejando sin transportar en Santiago toneladas de tabaco, café y cacao acumuladas durante un año. Los ingenieros trabajan en dos desviaciones de la ruta actual para reducir la pendiente del doce por ciento a un máximo del tres por ciento y eliminar la necesidad de cremalleras, al tiempo que las locomotoras y el material rodante también serán puestos en condiciones de uso.

records.headline: Two picture captions describe views of the Columbus Tower at Santo
records.summary_en: Two picture captions describe views of the Columbus Tower at Santo Domingo, capital of the Dominican Republic, seen both from the city and from the water at the entrance to the port. One caption notes that the gateway in the foreground is of much later construction and remarks that the soldiers pictured show the Spanish strain prevailing in the Republic of Santo Domingo, in contrast to the Republic of Haiti. The second caption states that Santo Domingo is the oldest city and the Columbus Tower the oldest structure of its kind in America.
records.summary_es: Dos pies de grabado describen vistas de la Torre de Colón en Santo Domingo, capital de la República Dominicana, vista tanto desde la ciudad como desde el agua a la entrada del puerto. Uno de los textos señala que el portal en primer plano es de construcción mucho más reciente y apunta que los soldados retratados muestran la ascendencia española que predomina en la República de Santo Domingo, en contraste con la República de Haití. El segundo pie de foto afirma que Santo Domingo es la ciudad más antigua y la Torre de Colón la estructura más antigua de su clase en América.

records.summary_en: The *Omaha daily bee* detailed the natural and mineral wealth of the Dominican Republic, highlighting the gold placers worked in the Cibao range and San Cristobal region. It also pointed to extensive unused forests of valuable timber and mountains of pure rock salt located in Barahona province. The report concluded that the country's lack of coal and poor overland transit routes posed the greatest obstacles to its industrial development.
records.summary_es: El *Omaha daily bee* detalló las riquezas naturales y minerales de la República Dominicana, destacando los placeres auríferos explotados en la cordillera del Cibao y la región de San Cristóbal. Hizo notar asimismo los extensos bosques vírgenes de maderas preciosas y las montañas de sal gema pura ubicadas en la provincia de Barahona. El informe concluía que la escasez de carbón y las deficientes vías de transporte terrestre representaban las principales trabas para el desarrollo fabril del país.
records.passage: with a leaf mold washed down by the rivers from the mountain forests. In this way humus and lime are combined to form a soil of the greatest fertility. The most famous of Dominican resources, and the one about which the American consul receives the most inquiries, is its gold. In the Cibao range and in the San Cristobal region there are placers which have been known and worked for centuries. In the days of the Spanish occupation it is said that the invaders gathered great stores of this treasure by trading with the Indians little silver hawkbells for their fill of gold. Nowadays the peon women wash gold out of these same streams with wooden bowls, making a few dollars a week, and by a law of the land the common people are protected in their right to work these placers. The forest resources are another example of unused wealth. One of the largest Dominican imports is lumber, and yet there are extensive forests of pine, oak and chestnut, as well as mahogany, satinwood, lignum vitae and rosewood. The most serious lack in Santo Domingo is coal, which will probably limit the future industrial development of the island more than anything else. There is an abundance of iron ore and also lead and copper, but no mineral fuel has so far been discovered except lignite. Another striking and so far undeveloped resource is two mountains of rock salt, said to be remarkably pure. They are in Barahona province. records.headline: A large percentage of the Dominicans, then, welcome the American Intervention
records.summary_en: The *Omaha daily bee* reported that many Dominicans accepted American intervention to re-establish law and order, though they remained firmly opposed to annexation. The article analyzed the country's social structure, explaining that approximately twenty elite families controlled virtually all political offices and land while avoiding property taxes. It observed that pervasive political corruption and sinecures had long characterized native governance prior to the American occupation.
records.summary_es: El *Omaha daily bee* informó que numerosos dominicanos aceptaban la intervención estadounidense para restaurar el orden y la ley, aun oponiéndose resueltamente a una anexión. El artículo examinó la estructura social dominicana, señalando que una veintena de familias pudientes acaparaba prácticamente las tierras y los destinos públicos mientras eludía el pago de impuestos prediales. Subrayó que la corrupción inveterada y las prebendas políticas habían sido el rasgo distintivo de la gobernación local con anterioridad a la ocupación estadounidense.
records.passage: him out of his job, so there must be an element of sincerity in his attitude. A large percentage of the Dominicans, then, welcome the American intervention and accept it in a good spirit. They recognize that some stronger power must restore confidence in law and government and initiate the reconstruction of the country. They are not, however, looking toward annexation. Most of them will not hear of this. They are willing for us to help them because they trust the altruism of our motive and the good faith of our professions. It is easy to prove that the Dominicans are a lazy, disorderly people, and also hard to see how they could be anything else under present conditions. As in most small Latin-American countries, there are just two native classes — the very rich and the very poor. The upper class here is said to consist of not more than twenty large families. These hold all the political offices and own nearly all the land. They are wealthy, intelligent and well educated. Every law is designed to benefit them. There is scarcely any tax on land because they own it, but there are two or three taxes on everything else. Political salaries are large and numerous, and many of the political berths include no duties at all. In addition to this, graft in political office was, until the Americans came, the customary and accepted thing. So the upper class might be described as selfish and corrupt and necessarily so. records.summary_en: The *Omaha daily bee* reported that the government of President Jimenez collapsed after its revenues were withheld by American authorities, and Admiral Knapp refused Jimenez's request for a month's salary. Jimenez subsequently departed the country to lecture in Latin America against American despotism in Santo Domingo. The article noted that Knapp's proclamation established a military government intended as a temporary measure, keeping native courts and municipal administrations intact while imposing press censorship.
records.summary_es: El *Omaha daily bee* informó que la administración del presidente Jimenes se desmoronó luego de que las autoridades estadounidenses retuvieran sus fondos fiscales, habiéndose negado el almirante Knapp a pagar a Jimenes un mes de sueldo solicitado. Acto seguido, Jimenes abandonó la nación para dictar conferencias por Hispanoamérica denunciando la opresión estadounidense en Santo Domingo. El artículo apuntaba que la proclama de Knapp fundaba un gobierno militar con carácter provisional, manteniendo operando a los tribunales del país y los cabildos locales pero implantando la censura de prensa.
records.passage: Just exactly what happened to the Jimenez government after this is hard to state in official language, but is sufficiently clear; its political jugular vein has been severed, its golden life blood drained. It did not resign, it did not revolt; simply faded and died. To the cabinet officers was tendered the high and chaste honor of serving on without pay, but they unaccountably failed to respond. President Jimenez sent a messenger to Admiral Knapp to explain that his excellency was in a state of financial need and to request that his salary for one month be paid. This was refused. President Jimenez then sailed away and is said to have taken the lecture platform in other Latin American countries and devoted his abilities to an exposition of the greedy and underhand methods by which the eagle of the north is sinking the talons of despotism into the vitals of free and democratic government in Santo Domingo. The present government in Santo Domingo is based upon a proclamation issued by Admiral (then Captain) Knapp at that time. The essential statements of this document were that the United States navy had assumed governmental power in the republic for the good thereof, and, as a temporary expedient, with an accent on the temporary; that neither municipal nor provincial governments would be interfered with; and that the Dominican judiciary would continue to function. Under the subheading "Changes to Reduce Grade," the report adds that engineers are working on two route deviations to reduce the grade from twelve per cent to a maximum of three per cent and eliminate racks, while locomotives and rolling stock are also to be put in usable condition.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de la Associated Press desde Puerto Plata informa que se han iniciado extensas reparaciones en el estatal Ferrocarril Central Dominicano, que conecta dicho puerto con Santiago en la región del Cibao, conforme al deseo del gobierno militar de colocar el transporte entre ambos puntos sobre una base satisfactoria. Sin que prácticamente ninguna carga haya sido movilizada por ferrocarril hacia el interior desde Puerto Plata desde agosto, toneladas de tabaco, café y cacao acumuladas durante un año permanecen sin moverse en Santiago. Bajo el subtítulo «Changes to Reduce Grade», el informe añade que los ingenieros trabajan en dos desviaciones de la ruta para reducir la pendiente del doce por ciento a un máximo del tres por ciento y eliminar las cremalleras, al tiempo que las locomotoras y el material rodante también serán puestos en condiciones de uso.

records.headline: Opening mid-article with a note that Macoris, Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: Opening mid-article with a note that Macoris, Santo Domingo City, Santiago, and Puerto Plata are the only cities in the Dominican Republic with electric lighting service, the dispatch outlines public improvements and private investments underway following the restoration of order. Immediate projects include rebuilding seven bridges on the Santiago-to-Monte Cristi road burned by revolutionists the previous spring to check advancing United States Marines, requesting bids in the south for the first sixteen kilometers of road connecting with a twelve-kilometer road under construction from Macoris to Hato Mayor, laying the foundation of a new 100,000 customs house in Santo Domingo City, and resuming work on the capital's municipal building after nearly ten years of revolutionary interruptions. In addition, land is being purchased for sugar cane, including several large investments of Puerto Rican capital in sugar lands and preliminary plans by the same interests to establish a bank in the capital with a branch.
records.summary_es: Iniciando a mitad de artículo con la observación de que Macorís, la ciudad de Santo Domingo, Santiago y Puerto Plata son las únicas ciudades de la República Dominicana con servicio de alumbrado eléctrico, el despacho describe las mejoras públicas e inversiones privadas en curso tras el restablecimiento del orden. Entre los proyectos inmediatos figuran la reconstrucción de siete puentes en el camino de Santiago a Monte Cristi quemados por los revolucionarios en la primavera anterior para frenar el avance de los infantes de marina de los Estados Unidos, la solicitud de licitaciones en el sur para los primeros dieciséis kilómetros de carretera que conectarán con una vía de doce kilómetros en construcción de Macorís a Hato Mayor, los cimientos ya tendidos de una nueva aduana de 100,000 en la ciudad de Santo Domingo y la reanudación de las obras del edificio municipal de la capital tras casi diez años de interrupciones por las revoluciones. Asimismo, se están comprando tierras para sembrar caña de azúcar, incluidas varias grandes inversiones de capital puertorriqueño en terrenos azucareros y planes preliminares de esos mismos intereses para establecer un banco en la capital con una sucursal.

records.headline: A dispatch from Puerto Plata, Santo Domingo, dated April 17
records.summary_en: A dispatch from Puerto Plata, Santo Domingo, dated April 17, reports word received there that day that several outlaws had been killed in battle with U.S. and Dominican police under U.S. officers in the interior. The item adds that Americans are preserving order in Santo Domingo.
records.summary_es: Un despacho procedente de Puerto Plata, Santo Domingo, fechado el 17 de abril, informa que ese día se recibió allí la noticia de que varios forajidos habían muerto en combate contra policías estadounidenses y dominicanos bajo el mando de oficiales estadounidenses en el interior. La nota añade que los estadounidenses están manteniendo el orden en Santo Domingo.

records.summary_en: The *Albuquerque morning journal* reported on rising tensions following the landing of U.S. marines in Santo Domingo, including native outrage when marines hung laundry on the historic Conde gate. Snipers frequently fired on marine patrols, prompting street skirmishes and armed retaliation by American forces. The article also reviewed earlier U.S. policy, including the 1914 Wilson plan and the 1915 demand that the Dominican Republic sign a new treaty granting rights similar to those in Haiti.
records.summary_es: El *Albuquerque morning journal* informó sobre la creciente animosidad suscitada tras el desembarco de los infantes de marina estadounidenses en Santo Domingo, incluyendo la indignación popular cuando los soldados colgaron ropa lavada en la histórica Puerta del Conde. Francotiradores tiroteaban con frecuencia las patrullas invasoras, desatando choques callejeros y represalias armadas de las tropas de los Estados Unidos. El artículo repasó además la política previa de Washington, abarcando el plan Wilson de 1914 y la exigencia formulada en 1915 para que la República Dominicana suscribiera un nuevo tratado otorgando atribuciones análogas a las impuestas a Haití.

records.summary_en: Opening mid-sentence and spliced with an adjacent streetcar accident report, this item notes that with the exception of San Pedro de Macoris and Santo Domingo City, Santiago and Puerto Plata are the only cities in the Dominican Republic with electric lighting service. Other public improvements to be undertaken immediately include rebuilding seven bridges on the road from Santiago to Monte Cristi that revolutionists burned the previous spring to check the advance of U.S. Marines. Under the subheading "American Occupation Helped," the passage begins to state that work has commenced or is about to begin in the southern part of the island before breaking off.

Otras mejoras públicas que se emprenderán de inmediato incluyen la reconstrucción de siete puentes en la carretera de Santiago a Monte Cristi que los revolucionarios quemaron la primavera anterior para frenar el avance de los infantes de marina estadounidenses. Bajo el subtítulo «La ocupación estadounidense ayudó», el pasaje comienza a indicar que las obras han comenzado o están por iniciarse en la parte sur de la isla antes de interrumpirse.

records.headline: In a descriptive travel piece on the Caribbean and Colombian
records.summary_en: In a descriptive travel piece on the Caribbean and Colombian ports, the writer notes that Santa Marta on the Colombian coast is the oldest city still standing on either of the American continents, excelled in age only by San Domingo in the Dominican Republic on the island of Haiti. The remainder of the passage describes Cartagena, Barranquilla, the Magdalena River, and average temperatures in the West Indies.
records.summary_es: En una crónica descriptiva de viajes sobre el Caribe y los puertos colombianos, el autor señala que Santa Marta, en la costa colombiana, es la ciudad más antigua aún en pie en cualquiera de los continentes americanos, superada en antigüedad únicamente por San Domingo en la República Dominicana, en la isla de Haití. El resto del pasaje describe Cartagena, Barranquilla, el río Magdalena y las temperaturas promedio en las Antillas.

records.headline: A dispatch from Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic, dated May 28
records.summary_en: A dispatch from Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic, dated May 28, reports that extensive repairs have begun on the state-owned Dominican Central Railroad connecting that port with Santiago in the Cibao region, as the military government seeks to bring transportation between those points to a satisfactory basis. Tons of tobacco, coffee, and cacao have remained unmoved at Santiago while practically nothing has moved inland by rail from Puerto Plata since August. Engineers are working on two route deviations to reduce the maximum grade from 12 percent to 3 percent, eliminating the need for racks, and locomotives and rolling stock are also being repaired on a line that has generally been a heavy expense to the government.
records.summary_es: Un despacho procedente de Puerto Plata, República Dominicana, fechado el 28 de mayo, informa que se han iniciado extensas reparaciones en el Ferrocarril Central Dominicano, propiedad de la república, que conecta dicho puerto con Santiago en la región del Cibao, conforme al deseo del gobierno militar de llevar el transporte entre esos puntos a un nivel satisfactorio. Toneladas de tabaco, café y cacao han permanecido sin moverse en Santiago, mientras que prácticamente nada se ha trasladado tierra adentro por ferrocarril desde Puerto Plata desde agosto. Los ingenieros trabajan en dos desvíos de la ruta actual para reducir la pendiente máxima del 12 por ciento al 3 por ciento, eliminando la necesidad de cremalleras, y también se repararán las locomotoras y el material rodante de una vía que por lo general ha representado un fuerte gasto para el gobierno.

records.headline: Though heavily clipped along the margins, this report in The Butte
records.summary_en: Though heavily clipped along the margins, this report in The Butte Daily Post outlines public works in the Dominican Republic, noting electricity plans for Santiago, Moca, and Puerto Plata and mentioning bridges burned by revolutionists the previous spring to check the advance of U.S. Marines. In the southern part of the island, bids have been requested for the first 16 kilometers of an approximately 56-kilometer macadam road from Macoris to Santo Domingo City, which will connect with a road under construction from Macoris. In addition, a customs house foundation at Santo Domingo has been laid, work has resumed on a new municipal building interrupted frequently by revolutions over nearly 10 years so that it will probably be occupied within six months, and several government buildings are planned to replace rented quarters.
records.summary_es: Aunque presenta fuertes recortes en los márgenes, este reporte en The Butte Daily Post reseña obras públicas en la República Dominicana, señalando planes de electricidad para Santiago, Moca y Puerto Plata y mencionando puentes quemados por revolucionarios la primavera anterior para frenar el avance de los infantes de marina estadounidenses. En la parte sur de la isla, se han solicitado licitaciones para los primeros 16 kilómetros de una carretera de macadán de aproximadamente 56 kilómetros desde Macoris hasta la ciudad de Santo Domingo, la cual conectará con otra vía en construcción desde Macoris. Asimismo, ya se han colocado los cimientos de una aduana en Santo Domingo, se han reanudado las obras de un nuevo edificio municipal interrumpidas frecuentemente por revoluciones durante casi 10 años —el cual probablemente será ocupado dentro de seis meses— y se proyectan varios edificios gubernamentales para sustituir locales alquilados.

records.headline: A feature datelined Santo Domingo City describes the capital of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: A feature datelined Santo Domingo City describes the capital of the Dominican Republic as a clean, attractive town of about 20,000 inhabitants with white, pale blue, and pink flat-roofed houses situated at the mouth of a deep, narrow river. While customs and steamship offices front the river, the main city sits higher behind a high bluff crowned with an old fort over which the U.S. flag is now flying. Although lacking sewerage or a water system, the city has shady plazas and striking buildings, most famously the great weathered stone cathedral housing the bones of Christopher Columbus, altars, statues of popes and saints, and a collection of jewels.
records.summary_es: Una crónica fechada en la ciudad de Santo Domingo describe la capital de la República Dominicana como una población limpia y atractiva de unos 20,000 habitantes, con casas bajas de techos planos pintadas de blanco, azul pálido y rosa, situada en la desembocadura de un río profundo y estrecho. Mientras las oficinas de aduanas y de vapores dan al río, la ciudad principal se asienta a mayor altura, frente a un alto risco coronado por un antiguo fuerte en el que ahora ondea la bandera estadounidense. Aunque carece de alcantarillado o sistema de agua, la ciudad cuenta con plazas sombreadas y edificios llamativos, el más famoso de los cuales es la gran catedral de piedra desgastada que alberga los restos de Cristóbal Colón, altares, estatuas de papas y santos, y una colección de joyas.
