records.headline: Under a Santo Domingo City dateline, this dispatch describes
records.summary_en: Under a Santo Domingo City dateline, this dispatch describes the Dominican capital as a pretty town of low, flat-roofed houses painted white, pale blue, and pink at the mouth of a deep, narrow river serving as a harbor. Above the riverfront customs and steamship offices, the main city is fronted by a high bluff crowned with an old fort from which the U.S. flag flies. Although the city has no water or sewerage system, it is clean and healthy and centers on the weathered stone cathedral holding the bones of Christopher Columbus, altars, statues of popes and saints, and a collection of jewels.
records.summary_es: Bajo datación de la ciudad de Santo Domingo, este despacho describe la capital dominicana como una bonita población de casas bajas de techos planos pintadas de blanco, azul pálido y rosa en la desembocadura de un río profundo y estrecho que sirve de puerto. Por encima de las oficinas ribereñas de aduanas y de vapores, la ciudad principal está precedida por un alto risco coronado por un antiguo fuerte desde el cual ondea la bandera estadounidense. Aunque la ciudad carece de sistema de agua o alcantarillado, es limpia y saludable y tiene como edificio más famoso la catedral de piedra desgastada que conserva los restos de Cristóbal Colón, altares, estatuas de papas y santos, y una colección de joyas.

records.headline: Presenting a statement on the commercial situation of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Presenting a statement on the commercial situation of the Dominican Republic by Chargé d'Affaires Señor Luis Galvan, the article recounts that when the European war began, Dominican commerce initially suffered because its tobacco crop was being shipped to Hamburg and German ports were closed, until new markets were soon obtained and the crisis passed. Galvan states that under the administration of the military officials the Dominican government has attained noticeable development, its finances are on a sounder basis than ever before, and American capital is flowing into the country with full confidence to develop its natural resources.
records.summary_es: Al presentar una declaración sobre la situación comercial de la República Dominicana formulada por el encargado de negocios, señor Luis Galvan, el artículo relata que cuando comenzó la guerra europea el comercio dominicano sufrió inicialmente porque todo el tabaco cosechado allí se enviaba a Hamburgo y los puertos alemanes quedaron cerrados, hasta que pronto se obtuvieron nuevos mercados y pasó la crisis. Galvan afirma que, gracias a la hábil administración de los funcionarios militares, el gobierno de la República Dominicana ha alcanzado un desarrollo notable, sus finanzas se encuentran sobre una base más sólida que nunca y el capital estadounidense fluye hacia el país con absoluta confianza para desarrollar sus recursos naturales.

records.summary_en: A local news item reports that Dean Mitchell has received a letter from Adlai Feather, a University of New Mexico class of '16 alumnus serving in the U.S. Marine Corps in Santo Domingo, who notes that he has visited nearly all the sizable cities in the West Indies. Quoting Feather's letter, the article states that a presidential election is scheduled in the Dominican Republic on November 15, and that if it proves quiet and legal the Marines may be withdrawn within a few months, though he expects considerable boisterousness and jokes that elections are about the only form of athletics that can survive the heat there.

Citando la carta de Feather, el artículo indica que habrá una elección presidencial en la República Dominicana el 15 de noviembre y que, si resulta tranquila y legal, los infantes de marina podrían ser retirados en pocos meses, aunque él espera bastante alboroto y bromea que las elecciones son casi la única forma de atletismo que puede sobrevivir al calor allí.

records.summary_en: A correspondence from Santo Domingo City describes the capital of the Dominican Republic as a clean, attractive tropical town of about 20,000 inhabitants with white, pale blue, and pink flat-roofed houses situated at the mouth of a deep, narrow river. The article notes that customs and steamship offices front the river while the main city sits higher behind a high bluff crowned by an old fort where the American flag is now flying, and that despite lacking a sewerage or water system, the city has shady plazas and striking buildings. Foremost among these is the great weathered stone cathedral holding the bones of Christopher Columbus, decorated inside with altars, statues of popes and saints, and a collection of jewels.

records.summary_en: Opening mid-article, a geographical note explains that the island has been known for most of four centuries as Santo Domingo or Haiti-Santo Domingo and that it is a frequent mistake to call the republic itself Santo Domingo. The writer clarifies that the proper name of the country is the Dominican Republic, whereas Santo Domingo is the name of its capital and largest city. The item further notes that the island is frequently confused with the island of Dominica, a small British island in the Lesser Antilles between Guadeloupe and Martinique named by Columbus upon its discovery on a Sunday.

records.summary_en: Beginning mid-sentence, an explanatory article states that the island may properly be called Santo Domingo—by which name it has been known for most of four centuries alongside Haiti-Santo Domingo—and that the correct name of the country is the Dominican Republic. It points out that Santo Domingo is not the name of a country, but of the capital and largest city of the Dominican Republic. The passage also warns against confusing the island with Dominica, a small British island in the Lesser Antilles about 350 miles southeast of Puerto Rico between Guadeloupe and Martinique that Columbus named on a Sunday.

records.headline: Opening mid-article, a report on professional licensing in the Dominican Republic states
records.summary_en: Opening mid-article, a report on professional licensing in the Dominican Republic states that in addition to passing an examination before the Professional Institute, an applicant must present a duly registered and legalized diploma from a recognized college along with letters of identity and recommendation and a certificate of morality and character. The passage notes that students complete the course at the medical school of the University of Santo Domingo and finish their studies at the University of Paris, whereas nearly all dentists and pharmacists are graduates of United States institutions. No American doctors, dentists, or pharmacists are practicing in the Dominican Republic, where the foreign doctors comprise one Scotch, one Canadian, three Spanish, and three Italian practitioners, and the dentists and pharmacists are almost exclusively Dominicans.

records.headline: Writing from Puerto Plata to counter the impression abroad that the Dominican Republic's climate
records.summary_en: Writing from Puerto Plata to counter the impression abroad that the Dominican Republic's climate is hot, humid, and unhealthful, Consul Arthur McLean states that although tropical, the climate is pleasant and salubrious, tempered by daytime trade winds and refreshing nighttime mountain breezes. Even in summer the temperature seldom reaches 80 degrees F., while coastal towns have a mean annual temperature of about 78 degrees F. and inland temperatures vary with altitude in the central valley of Constanza. Annual rainfall ranges from 15 to 200 inches across different sections: the southern part has a marked distinction between the dry season from September to March and the rainy season from April to August, whereas the northern part has rain more or less all year, heaviest from November to April.
records.summary_es: Al escribir desde Puerto Plata para contrarrestar la impresión en el extranjero de que el clima de la República Dominicana es caluroso, húmedo e insalubre, el cónsul Arthur McLean afirma que, aunque tropical, el clima es agradable y salubre, templado por los vientos alisios durante el día y por las refrescantes brisas de las montañas por la noche. Incluso en verano la temperatura rara vez alcanza los 80 grados F., mientras que las ciudades costeras tienen una temperatura media anual de unos 78 grados F. y en el interior la temperatura varía según la altitud en el valle central de Constanza. Las precipitaciones anuales oscilan entre 15 y 200 pulgadas en distintas zonas: la parte sur presenta una marcada distinción entre la estación seca de septiembre a marzo y la estación lluviosa de abril a agosto, mientras que en la parte norte llueve más o menos todo el año, con mayor intensidad de noviembre a abril.

records.headline: Citing a consular report, an article describes the royal palm
records.summary_en: Citing a consular report, an article describes the royal palm as the most useful tree in the Dominican Republic. Most country houses on the island are built of its bark and roofed with thatch made from its leaves, while the heart of the palm is eaten as a salad delicacy and its berries serve as pig fodder. Additional articles made from the tree on the island include hats, beds, fence posts, brooms, baskets, matting, tobacco-packing screens, and beehives hollowed out of the trunks.
records.summary_es: Citando un informe consular, un artículo describe la palma real como el árbol más útil de la República Dominicana. La mayor parte de las casas campesinas de la isla se construyen con su corteza y se techan con paja hecha de sus hojas, mientras que el palmito se consume en ensalada como un gran manjar y sus frutos sirven de alimento para los cerdos. Otros artículos elaborados con este árbol en la isla incluyen sombreros, camas, postes para cercas, escobas, cestas, esteras, mamparas para empacar tabaco y colmenas hechas con los troncos huecos.

records.headline: Pine in the Dominican Republic is said to be at least as good
records.summary_en: Pine in the Dominican Republic is said to be at least as good as the long-leaf yellow pine of the southern United States, an article reports, with a main pine forest five to twenty miles long extending from about eight miles southwest of San Jose de las Matas to a short distance east and southwest of Jarabacoa, plus scattered pines westward to the Haitian border and eastward of Jarabacoa. Although San Jose de las Matas lies about twenty-five miles from Santiago de los Caballeros—which is linked by rail to its port of Puerto Plata—and Jarabacoa lies about fifteen miles from La Vega—which is connected by rail to its port of Sanchez—a railroad into the pine belt itself would have to be built to get out the timber. The trees are described as very sound, free from windshakes, rich in turpentine, straight, clean, and holding their thickness well up to the first limbs, with some reaching forty-two inches in diameter and few other tree varieties in the belt.
records.summary_es: El pino de la República Dominicana se considera al menos tan bueno como el pino amarillo de hoja larga del sur de los Estados Unidos, según informa un artículo, con un bosque principal de cinco a veinte millas de largo que se extiende desde unas ocho millas al suroeste de San José de las Matas hasta poca distancia al este y suroeste de Jarabacoa, además de pinos dispersos hacia el oeste hasta la frontera haitiana y al este de Jarabacoa. Aunque San José de las Matas se encuentra a unas veinticinco millas de Santiago de los Caballeros —conectada por ferrocarril con su puerto de Puerto Plata— y Jarabacoa está a unas quince millas de La Vega —unida por ferrocarril con su puerto de Sánchez—, sería necesario construir un ferrocarril hasta la propia zona de pinares para extraer la madera. Los árboles se describen como muy sanos, libres de grietas por el viento, ricos en trementina, rectos, limpios y que mantienen bien su grosor hasta las primeras ramas, alcanzando algunos cuarenta y dos pulgadas de diámetro y habiendo pocas variedades de otros árboles en la franja.

records.headline: Opening mid-article on the trade winds and refreshing night
records.summary_en: Opening mid-article on the trade winds and refreshing night mountain breezes, the report states that the island of Santo Domingo offers a wider range of climate than any other part of the Antilles because of its varied relief. While the average annual temperature in coastal towns is muted in print as '7P degrees F.' and inland temperatures drop with elevation—occasionally forming winter ice at 3,500 feet in the central valley of Constanza—annual rainfall ranges from 15 to 200 inches across different regions. The southern section has a dry season from September to March and a rainy season from April to August, whereas the northern half receives rain year-round, heaviest from November to April. Furthermore, the Dominican Republic has never experienced epidemics of cholera or bubonic plague, and yellow fever has not appeared there for many years.
records.summary_es: Iniciándose a mitad de artículo sobre los vientos alisios y las refrescantes brisas nocturnas de las montañas, el informe señala que la isla de Santo Domingo ofrece una mayor variedad climática que cualquier otra parte de las Antillas debido a la diversidad de su relieve. Mientras que la temperatura media anual en los pueblos costeros aparece impresa de forma borrosa como «7P degrees F.» y las temperaturas del interior descienden con la altitud —formándose hielo ocasionalmente en invierno a 3,500 pies en el valle central de Constanza—, la precipitación anual oscila entre 15 y 200 pulgadas según la región. La parte sur presenta una estación seca de septiembre a marzo y una lluviosa de abril a agosto, en tanto que la mitad norte recibe lluvias durante todo el año, con mayor intensidad de noviembre a abril. Asimismo, en la República Dominicana nunca ha habido epidemias de cólera ni de peste bubónica, y hace muchos años que no se registra fiebre amarilla.

records.summary_en: Beginning mid-sentence on daytime trade winds and refreshing night breezes from the mountains, this article notes that the island of Santo Domingo has a wider climatic range than any other part of the Antilles due to its varied topography. Coastal towns average about 79 degrees, while inland elevations are cooler, with winter ice occasionally forming at 3,500 feet in the central Valley of Constanza. Annual rainfall ranges between 15 and 200 inches: the south has distinct dry (September to March) and rainy (April to August) seasons, whereas the northern half receives rain throughout the year, heaviest from November to April. The notice concludes by observing that the Dominican Republic has never had cholera or bubonic plague epidemics and has been free of yellow fever for many years.
records.summary_es: Comenzando a mitad de frase sobre los vientos alisios diurnos y las refrescantes brisas nocturnas de las montañas, este artículo señala que la isla de Santo Domingo posee una gama climática más amplia que cualquier otra parte de las Antillas debido a la diversidad de su relieve. Los pueblos costeros registran una media anual de unos 79 grados, mientras que las zonas altas del interior son más frescas, formándose hielo ocasionalmente en invierno a 3,500 pies de altitud en el central valle de Constanza. La precipitación anual varía entre 15 y 200 pulgadas: el sur tiene estaciones seca (septiembre a marzo) y lluviosa (abril a agosto) bien definidas, en tanto que en la mitad norte llueve más o menos todo el año, con mayor intensidad de noviembre a abril. La nota concluye observando que en la República Dominicana nunca ha habido epidemias de cólera ni de peste bubónica y que hace muchos años que no se registra fiebre amarilla.

records.headline: Opening mid-sentence, this report describes the Yaque, a flat
records.summary_en: Opening mid-sentence, this report describes the Yaque, a flat-bottomed vessel built entirely of Dominican woods—15 feet wide, 60 feet long, drawing 16 inches of water, and powered by twin 30-horsepower duplex marine engines with two 32-inch propellers on a tunnel vacuum system—constructed to make the first attempt at navigating the Yaque River. Its American owners intend to use the boat solely for towing launches of 10 to 40 tons capacity, now under construction at Mao, between the seaport of Monte Cristi and Mao, which lies at the head of navigation 140 miles upriver from the ocean and within 17 miles of Santiago de los Caballeros. The owners expect to develop a large carrying trade in native products from the rich Yaque valley, including dividivi, dyewoods, and hardwoods. At present, transportation between Santiago and Monte Cristi is described as very inadequate, with the highway in poor condition and no railroad yet built, though one is under discussion.
records.summary_es: Iniciándose a mitad de frase, este informe describe el Yaque, una embarcación de fondo plano construida íntegramente con maderas dominicanas —de 15 pies de ancho, 60 pies de eslora y 16 pulgadas de calado, propulsada por dos motores marinos dúplex de 30 caballos de fuerza con dos hélices de 32 pulgadas bajo un sistema de túnel de vacío—, fabricada para realizar el primer intento de navegar el río Yaque. Sus propietarios estadounidenses proyectan destinar el barco exclusivamente al remolque de lanchas de 10 a 40 toneladas de capacidad, actualmente en construcción en Mao, entre el puerto marítimo de Monte Cristi y Mao, situado en el límite navegable a 140 millas por el río desde el océano y a 17 millas de Santiago de los Caballeros. Los armadores esperan desarrollar un amplio comercio de transporte de productos nativos del rico valle del Yaque, tales como dividivi, maderas tintóreas y maderas duras. En la actualidad, los medios de transporte entre Santiago y el puerto de Monte Cristi se describen como muy deficientes, con la carretera en mal estado y sin ferrocarril entre ambos puntos, aunque se discute la construcción de uno.

records.summary_en: Writing from Puerto Plata to counter the impression abroad that the Dominican Republic is hot, humid, and unhealthful, Consul Arthur McLean states that its tropical climate is actually pleasant and salubrious. Summer daytime temperatures rarely reach 90 degrees F., nights are cool year-round thanks to daytime trade winds and nocturnal mountain breezes, and the island of Santo Domingo has a wider climatic range than any other part of the Antilles: coastal towns average about 79 degrees F., while inland altitudes are cooler, occasionally forming winter ice at 3,500 feet in the central valley of Constanza. Annual rainfall varies from 15 to 200 inches, with a distinct dry season (September to March) and rainy season (April to August) in the south and year-round rain in the northern half that is heaviest from November to April; the passage breaks off while noting that there have never been epidemics of cholera or bubonic plague.

Las temperaturas diurnas en verano rara vez alcanzan los 90 grados F., las noches son frescas todo el año gracias a los vientos alisios del día y las brisas nocturnas de las montañas, y la isla de Santo Domingo posee una variedad climática mayor que cualquier otra parte de las Antillas: los pueblos costeros promedian unos 79 grados F., mientras que las alturas del interior son más frescas, formándose hielo ocasionalmente en invierno a 3,500 pies en el valle central de Constanza. La precipitación anual oscila entre 15 y 200 pulgadas, con una estación seca (septiembre a marzo) y una lluviosa (abril a agosto) bien definidas en el sur y lluvias todo el año en la mitad norte, más intensas de noviembre a abril; el pasaje se corta al señalar que nunca ha habido epidemias de cólera ni de peste bubónica.

records.headline: Writing from Santo Domingo to the United States Bureau of Commerce
records.summary_en: Writing from Santo Domingo to the United States Bureau of Commerce on January 26, American Minister William W. Russell reports that this year's tobacco crop is believed to be the largest in the history of the Dominican Republic, estimated at 250,000 to 350,000 bales and probably around 300,000 bales. About half of the crop has been purchased while farmers hold the remainder; prices have had an upward trend, and buyers are now offering $6.50 while growers hold out for $7.00. Fewer than 20,000 bales have been shipped thus far, leaving Puerto Plata overflowing with tobacco and every available space in use for storage.
records.summary_es: Escribiendo desde Santo Domingo al Negociado de Comercio de los Estados Unidos el 26 de enero, el ministro estadounidense William W. Russell informa que se considera que la cosecha de tabaco de este año es la mayor en la historia de la República Dominicana, estimada entre 250,000 y 350,000 pacas y probablemente en torno a las 300,000 pacas. Alrededor de la mitad de la cosecha ha sido comprada mientras los agricultores retienen la otra mitad; los precios han mostrado una tendencia al alza, y los compradores ofrecen ahora $6.50 mientras los cosecheros exigen $7.00. Hasta el momento se han embarcado menos de 20,000 pacas, por lo que Puerto Plata se encuentra abarrotada de tabaco y todo espacio disponible se utiliza para almacenamiento.

records.full_text:
Little-Known Dominican City.

Higuey is one of the principal inland cities of the Dominican Republic. Like its native land, it is quaint, historic, isolated, immensely rich in natural resources, almost poor in actual fact, and practically unknown to the world at large. It lies in the eastern half of the republic, which is the least settled, the least developed and the least known. It is a city of some 2,000 souls, the center of a considerable primitive trade and the site of the most famous shrine on the island.

This latter is the shrine of the Virgin of Alta Gracia, which is visited by devotees from every part of the country. The church which houses the shrine is built in the old Spanish architecture, the quaint and enduring style which has stamped its features on the buildings of a continent, from Patagonia to Colorado.

Dominican pine is described as at least equal to Southern long-leaf yellow pine—sound, free from windshakes, rich in turpentine, straight, and reaching up to forty-two inches in diameter, with few rocks or underbrush and a few walnut trees nearby. records.headline: Opening mid-sentence in a book review column, a notice describes
records.summary_en: Opening mid-sentence in a book review column, a notice describes a work on the history and present condition of Santo Domingo resulting from several trips to the Dominican Republic and Haiti, where the unnamed author served as secretary to the special United States commission investigating Santo Domingo's finances. The volume begins with 'The Days of Conquest' from 1492 to 1533 and traces the main periods of Dominican history to the present. Subsequent chapters cover area and boundaries, topography and climate, minerals, flora and fauna, people, religion, education and literature, transportation and communication, commerce, government, politics, finance, and the future of Santo Domingo.

records.summary_en: The *Richmond times-dispatch* reviewed a book on the history, geography, and administration of Santo Domingo and Haiti written by an author who served with the U.S. financial investigation commission and the Dominican Minister of Finance. The publication traced the republic's development from the Spanish conquest through modern times, detailing its topography, flora, fauna, and population. Additional chapters analyzed Dominican commerce, transportation, national finances, and political prospects.

La obra reconstruía la evolución de la república desde la conquista española hasta la época contemporánea, detallando su topografía, flora, fauna y habitantes. Capítulos complementarios examinaban el comercio dominicano, el transporte, las finanzas públicas y el horizonte político.

records.full_text:
Our Protectorate in the West Indies

No standard American book on Santo Domingo has been published since Mr. Hazard's work (Santo Domingo, Past and Present, with a Glance at Haiti, by Samuel Hazard) which appeared in 1873 and was reviewed by the present writer in the columns of THE SUN. A new one was therefore much needed to bring our knowledge of the country up to date; and this we have in Santo Domingo: A Country with a Future, by Otto Schoenrich, secretary to the United States Commissioner who investigated the financial condition of Santo Domingo in 1905, and subsequently secretary to the Dominican Minister of Finance.

His frequent visits to the island and long sojourn there have made him familiar with the political, social and business conditions which prevail in this "republic of revolutions," as Santo Domingo has aptly been denominated; a title which is becoming less appropriate than it was, however, since the United States Government has consented to supervise the collection of the customs and payment of the foreign debt and has thus really established a sort of American protectorate over two-thirds of the island of Hayti.

America's Stake.

It is vital to the preservation of political liberty in the United States that the countries about the Caribbean Sea should be kept free from the domination of any hostile autocratic power. This truth has been realized more intensely than ever before since Germany has revealed her true attitude toward the rest of the world in the course of the present great war. When therefore the Dominicans found themselves bankrupt and hopelessly at a loss how to adjust their indebtedness it became a matter of the first importance to us that Santo Domingo should seek aid from this country rather than from a Government which might exploit the island not merely to the advantage of Germany but greatly to the detriment of the United States.

By its treatment of Spain after the war of 1898 the United States had shown that a great nation was capable of acting unselfishly and in accordance with altruistic ideals. When Elihu Root was Secretary of State the Dominicans appealed to him to help them settle their national debt. Fearing that any intervention might lead to a scheme for annexation, many members of the Senate opposed any and every scheme for rendering aid. An agreement was finally made, however, between the Government of Santo Domingo and its creditors, whereby the latter agreed to accept specified sums in satisfaction of their claims to be paid out of the customs in instalments, provided the United States would consent to appoint a receiver general to collect the duties and apply them to the liquidation of the indebtedness.

The Senate confirmed a treaty sanctioning this agreement, and since 1907 the customs income of the Dominican Republic has been collected by an American General Receiver, appointed by the President. "The customs receivership," says Mr. Schoenrich, "has continued to render invaluable service. In peace and war its officials have distinguished themselves by a highly efficient, tactful and fearless discharge of their duties. Up to 1913 appointments to the service were determined by the fitness and experience of the appointee rather than by his political antecedents, and the officials appointed possessed unusual qualifications." This reference to 1913, however, must be regarded as an intimation that there has been a falling off in the character of the appointees since that date.

Our Delicate Task.

The relations established by such a fiscal treaty as ours with Santo Domingo are so delicate as to require very careful handling. The purpose of the United States is, or should be, to serve the Dominicans without dominating their Government or wounding their susceptibilities. The revolutionary tendencies of the people render this an exceedingly difficult task.

In 1916 a civil war threatened such disaster to the country that a force of marines was landed from the American cruiser squadron in Dominican waters and order was restored after a brief engagement, in which the Americans suffered a loss of one killed and eight wounded. The Admiral subsequently issued a proclamation declaring Santo Domingo to be under the military administration of the United States, but stating "that the object of the occupation was not to destroy Dominican sovereignty but to restore order; that Dominican laws were to continue in effect, so far as they did not conflict with the objects of the occupation or the decrees of the military Government; that the Dominican courts were to continue in their functions, except that offences against the military Government were to be judged by military courts, and that all the revenues of the Dominican Government were to be paid over to the military Government, which would administer the same."

This was the status quo when the present volume went to press in January, 1918. The affairs of Santo Domingo were being administered by American naval officers, pending a reorganization of the civil Government of the republic.

Columbus's Hispaniola.

Just as all Gaul, in the time of Julius Cæsar, was divided into three parts, so all of the great West Indian island of Hayti is divided into two parts: The French republic of Hayti in the west, dominated by French negroes, and the Spanish republic of Santo Domingo in the east, populated by whites and mulattoes of Spanish descent.

"The area of the island is generally stated at 28,249 square miles, of which Hayti is credited with 10,204 square miles and the Dominican republic with 18,045 square miles." No part of the country, however, has ever been carefully surveyed except the railroad lines and the chief harbors, so these estimates are only approximately correct.

We may fairly consider Santo Domingo as being about as large as Vermont and New Hampshire taken together. The island was discovered on his first voyage by Columbus, who called it La Española (in English, Hispaniola), because the scenery reminded him of Andalusia in Spain; and the Spanish colony which was established there enjoyed great prosperity for about half a century, especially under the administration of Diego Columbus, the son of the great Admiral, who married Maria de Toledo, the beautiful niece of the Duke of Alba, and maintained a sort of vice-regal court in the castle which he built at Santo Domingo city, and which is described as an imposing structure even in its ruins.

France's Foothold.

"About 1508 the island began to be called Santo Domingo, but for almost three centuries royal decrees continued to refer to it as Española. So flourishing was its state at this time that thirteen of its towns were granted coats of arms and three were declared cities. The colony was and for many years continued to be a starting point for voyages of discovery and conquest in the islands and along the shores of the Caribbean Sea." By the peace of Ryswick in 1697 Spain ceded the western part of the island to France, whose colonists had long claimed it, and soon made it the richest country of West Indies.

"Great plantations of tobacco, indigo, cacao, coffee and sugar were established. The country came to be known as the paradise of the West Indies and the wealth of the planters became proverbial." The French Revolution, however, turned this paradise into a veritable hell. The half million of slaves rose against their 30,000 white masters and negro rule was permanently established. "The great plantation homes were burned, the wide estates desolated, white women were ravished and murdered and white men put to death with horrible tortures, while the liberated slaves indulged in orgies at which the beverage was rum mixed with human blood. It was a fearful day of reckoning."

Under Negro Rule.

From this holocaust of blood arose the negro nationality which now constitutes the Republic of Hayti. The Spanish portion of the island fell under the domination of this black republic for twenty-two years, in the early part of the nineteenth century; but the Dominicans declared their independence in 1844, and have maintained it ever since except for a short period (1861-1865), during which they were nominally under the rule of the crown of Spain.

Under the presidency of Gen. Buenaventura Baez in 1871 a strong effort was made to induce the United States to annex the Dominican Republic, but the Senate would not sanction the proposed acquisition, although it was strongly advocated by President Grant. In speculating on what the condition of the country would have been, if annexed to the United States, Mr. Schoenrich says: "The power of the United States would have maintained peace; salutary laws would have educated the people in self-government; liberal tariff concessions would have stimulated agriculture and industry; the influx of a good stock of immigrants would have developed and settled the interior; honest administration would have provided roads and schools; and soon the country would have attained a high degree of development and prosperity."

In the title of his book our author characterizes Santo Domingo as "a country with a future." It is evident that he believes its future will be closely associated with the United States. Irrespective of any question of annexation, he insists it is our moral duty to foster the development of the country and promote the happiness of the people by granting suitable tariff concessions.

Much Natural Wealth.

The lack of a free but stable Government capable of maintaining law and order and thus promoting the general welfare of the inhabitants is the chief reason for the non-development of the rich natural resources of Santo Domingo. With attractive scenery, good harbors, an abundant water supply, a fertile soil, magnificent forests and a healthful climate, the Dominican Republic ought to be one of the most prosperous regions of the New World, as it was one of the earliest to be discovered. What it has needed is "men, high minded men," such as the poet says are necessary to constitute a State. Santo Domingo city, the capital, "had begun to decline almost a hundred years before the Pilgrims landed on Plymouth Rock."

"There are only 144 miles of railroad in the republic, and the other lines of communication overland can be called roads only as a matter of courtesy, being in fact little better than mere trails. This explains why most of the important towns are on the sea coast, where they can be reached by water. One day when travelling on the high road near La Vega the author encountered an old man who was in actual danger of being drowned in the liquid mud; he took a snapshot of the victim while he was being extricated by a good samaritan who was passing by.

Santo Domingo is not only proud of having been discovered and acquired by Christopher Columbus; it also claims to be his burial place. "The same honor is claimed by Spain, but a Dominican would consider it almost treasonable to doubt the justice of the Dominican claim." That the body of Columbus was brought from Spain, where he died, and deposited in the cathedral in Santo Domingo city, where it remained until 1795, is unquestionable.

The doubt arises in reference to the claim of the Spaniards that they removed the remains to Cuba in 1795, whence they were taken back to Spain after the Spanish-American war of 1898. Excavations made in the Dominican Cathedral in 1877 satisfied the Dominicans that the body removed by the Spaniards was really that of Diego Columbus and that the remains of his father were still in the cathedral vault.

Mr. Schoenrich reviews the evidence in detail and concludes that the Dominican contention is correct. It is sustained by a majority of those who have investigated the question, especially those who have personally visited Santo Domingo. "It seems that in spite of the acts of men, fate has permitted the remains of the discoverer of America to repose in the principal cathedral of the island he loved."

23—Revolutions—23.

We have spoken of Santo Domingo as the republic of revolutions. During the seventy years of Dominican independence the country has witnessed twenty-three successful revolutions. Fortunately they have not been very sanguinary as a rule. "In Puerto Plata, it is said that when the Government troops attacked the city in 1904 a fierce battle ensued, which continued from morning till the town was taken by storm in the evening; yet only one man was killed and his death was due to his own carelessness, for he appeared not far from where soldiers of the other side were training a cannon and refused to obey their warning to get out of the way, whereupon the cannon was discharged and his arm shot off, causing a mortal wound." Nevertheless the graves of victims of the numerous revolutions are everywhere to be seen, testifying to the curse of internecine warfare.

Mr. Schoenrich's interesting book shows that Santo Domingo under wise and friendly aid and guidance from the United States may become the most prosperous State in the West Indies.

SANTO DOMINGO: A COUNTRY WITH A FUTURE. By OTTO SCHOENRICH. The Macmillan Company. $3.

records.full_text:
Our Protectorate in the West Indies

No standard American book on Santo Domingo has been published since Mr. Hazard's work (Santo Domingo, Past and Present, with a Glance at Haiti, by Samuel Hazard) which appeared in 1873 and was reviewed by the present writer in the columns of The Sun. A new one was therefore much needed to bring our knowledge of the country up to date; and this we have in Santo Domingo: A Country with a Future, by Otto Schoenrich, secretary to the United States Commissioner who investigated the financial condition of Santo Domingo in 1905, and subsequently secretary to the Dominican Minister of Finance.

His frequent visits to the island and long sojourn there have made him familiar with the political, social and business conditions which prevail in this "republic of revolutions," as Santo Domingo has aptly been denominated; a title which is becoming less appropriate than it was, however, since the United States Government has consented to supervise the collection of the customs and payment of the foreign debt and has thus really established a sort of American protectorate over two-thirds of the island of Hayti.

America's Stake.

It is vital to the preservation of political liberty in the United States that the countries about the Caribbean Sea should be kept free from the domination of any hostile autocratic power. This truth has been realized more intensely than ever before since Germany has revealed her true attitude toward the rest of the world in the course of the present great war. When therefore the Dominicans found themselves bankrupt and hopelessly at a loss how to adjust their indebtedness it became a matter of the first importance to us that Santo Domingo should seek aid from this country rather than from a Government which might exploit the island not merely to the advantage of Germany but greatly to the detriment of the United States.

By its treatment of Spain after the war of 1898 the United States had shown that a great nation was capable of acting unselfishly and in accordance with altruistic ideals. When Elihu Root was Secretary of State the Dominicans appealed to him to help them settle their national debt. Fearing that any intervention might lead to a scheme for annexation, many members of the Senate opposed any and every scheme for rendering aid. An agreement was finally made, however, between the Government of Santo Domingo and its creditors, whereby the latter agreed to accept specified sums in satisfaction of their claims to be paid out of the customs in instalments, provided the United States would consent to appoint a receiver general to collect the duties and apply them to the liquidation of the indebtedness.

The Senate confirmed a treaty sanctioning this agreement, and since 1907 the customs income of the Dominican Republic has been collected by an American General Receiver, appointed by the President. "The customs receivership," says Mr. Schoenrich, "has continued to render invaluable service. In peace and war its officials have distinguished themselves by a highly efficient, tactful and fearless discharge of their duties. Up to 1913 appointments to the service were determined by the fitness and experience of the appointee rather than by his political antecedents, and the officials appointed possessed unusual qualifications." This reference to 1913, however, must be regarded as an intimation that there has been a falling off in the character of the appointees since that date.

Our Delicate Task.

The relations established by such a fiscal treaty as ours with Santo Domingo are so delicate as to require very careful handling. The purpose of the United States is, or should be, to serve the Dominicans without dominating their Government or wounding their susceptibilities. The revolutionary tendencies of the people render this an exceedingly difficult task.

In 1916 a civil war threatened such disaster to the country that a force of marines was landed from the American cruiser squadron in Dominican waters and order was restored after a brief engagement, in which the Americans suffered a loss of one killed and eight wounded. The Admiral subsequently issued a proclamation declaring Santo Domingo to be under the military administration of the United States, but stating "that the object of the occupation was not to destroy Dominican sovereignty but to restore order; that Dominican laws were to continue in effect, so far as they did not conflict with the objects of the occupation or the decrees of the military Government; that the Dominican courts were to continue in their functions, except that offences against the military Government were to be judged by military courts, and that all the revenues of the Dominican Government were to be paid over to the military Government, which would administer the same."

This was the status quo when the present volume went to press in January, 1918. The affairs of Santo Domingo were being administered by American naval officers, pending a reorganization of the civil Government of the republic.

Columbus's Hispaniola.

Just as all Gaul, in the time of Julius Cæsar, was divided into three parts, so all of the great West Indian island of Hayti is divided into two parts: The French republic of Hayti in the west, dominated by French negroes, and the Spanish republic of Santo Domingo in the east, populated by whites and mulattoes of Spanish descent.

"The area of the island is generally stated at 28,249 square miles, of which Hayti is credited with 10,204 square miles and the Dominican republic with 18,045 square miles." No part of the country, however, has ever been carefully surveyed except the railroad lines and the chief harbors, so these estimates are only approximately correct.

We may fairly consider Santo Domingo as being about as large as Vermont and New Hampshire taken together. The island was discovered on his first voyage by Columbus, who called it La Española (in English, Hispaniola), because the scenery reminded him of Andalusia in Spain; and the Spanish colony which was established there enjoyed great prosperity for about half a century, especially under the administration of Diego Columbus, the son of the great Admiral, who married Maria de Toledo, the beautiful niece of the Duke of Alba, and maintained a sort of vice-regal court in the castle which he built at Santo Domingo city, and which is described as an imposing structure even in its ruins.

France's Foothold.

"About 1508 the island began to be called Santo Domingo, but for almost three centuries royal decrees continued to refer to it as Española. So flourishing was its state at this time that thirteen of its towns were granted coats of arms and three were declared cities. The colony was and for many years continued to be a starting point for voyages of discovery and conquest in the islands and along the shores of the Caribbean Sea." By the peace of Ryswick in 1697 Spain ceded the western part of the island to France, whose colonists had long claimed it, and soon made it the richest country of West Indies.

"Great plantations of tobacco, indigo, cacao, coffee and sugar were established. The country came to be known as the paradise of the West Indies and the wealth of the planters became proverbial." The French Revolution, however, turned this paradise into a veritable hell. The half million of slaves rose against their 30,000 white masters and negro rule was permanently established. "The great plantation homes were burned, the wide estates desolated, white women were ravished and murdered and white men put to death with horrible tortures, while the liberated slaves indulged in orgies at which the beverage was rum mixed with human blood. It was a fearful day of reckoning."

Under Negro Rule.

From this holocaust of blood arose the negro nationality which now constitutes the Republic of Hayti. The Spanish portion of the island fell under the domination of this black republic for twenty-two years, in the early part of the nineteenth century; but the Dominicans declared their independence in 1844, and have maintained it ever since except for a short period (1861-1865), during which they were nominally under the rule of the crown of Spain.

Under the presidency of Gen. Buenaventura Baez in 1871 a strong effort was made to induce the United States to annex the Dominican Republic, but the Senate would not sanction the proposed acquisition, although it was strongly advocated by President Grant. In speculating on what the condition of the country would have been, if annexed to the United States, Mr. Schoenrich says: "The power of the United States would have maintained peace; salutary laws would have educated the people in self-government; liberal tariff concessions would have stimulated agriculture and industry; the influx of a good stock of immigrants would have developed and settled the interior; honest administration would have provided roads and schools; and soon the country would have attained a high degree of development and prosperity."

In the title of his book our author characterizes Santo Domingo as "a country with a future." It is evident that he believes its future will be closely associated with the United States. Irrespective of any question of annexation, he insists it is our moral duty to foster the development of the country and promote the happiness of the people by granting suitable tariff concessions.

Much Natural Wealth.

The lack of a free but stable Government capable of maintaining law and order and thus promoting the general welfare of the inhabitants is the chief reason for the non-development of the rich natural resources of Santo Domingo. With attractive scenery, good harbors, an abundant water supply, a fertile soil, magnificent forests and a healthful climate, the Dominican Republic ought to be one of the most prosperous regions of the New World, as it was one of the earliest to be discovered. What it has needed is "men, high minded men," such as the poet says are necessary to constitute a State. Santo Domingo city, the capital, "had begun to decline almost a hundred years before the Pilgrims landed on Plymouth Rock."

"There are only 144 miles of railroad in the republic, and the other lines of communication overland can be called roads only as a matter of courtesy, being in fact little better than mere trails. This explains why most of the important towns are on the sea coast, where they can be reached by water. One day when travelling on the high road near La Vega the author encountered an old man who was in actual danger of being drowned in the liquid mud; he took a snapshot of the victim while he was being extricated by a good samaritan who was passing by.

Santo Domingo is not only proud of having been discovered and acquired by Christopher Columbus; it also claims to be his burial place. "The same honor is claimed by Spain, but a Dominican would consider it almost treasonable to doubt the justice of the Dominican claim." That the body of Columbus was brought from Spain, where he died, and deposited in the cathedral in Santo Domingo city, where it remained until 1795, is unquestionable.

The doubt arises in reference to the claim of the Spaniards that they removed the remains to Cuba in 1795, whence they were taken back to Spain after the Spanish-American war of 1898. Excavations made in the Dominican Cathedral in 1877 satisfied the Dominicans that the body removed by the Spaniards was really that of Diego Columbus and that the remains of his father were still in the cathedral vault.

Mr. Schoenrich reviews the evidence in detail and concludes that the Dominican contention is correct. It is sustained by a majority of those who have investigated the question, especially those who have personally visited Santo Domingo. "It seems that in spite of the acts of men, fate has permitted the remains of the discoverer of America to repose in the principal cathedral of the island he loved."

23—Revolutions—23.

We have spoken of Santo Domingo as the republic of revolutions. During the seventy years of Dominican independence the country has witnessed twenty-three successful revolutions. Fortunately they have not been very sanguinary as a rule. "In Puerto Plata, it is said that when the Government troops attacked the city in 1904 a fierce battle ensued, which continued from morning till the town was taken by storm in the evening; yet only one man was killed and his death was due to his own carelessness, for he appeared not far from where soldiers of the other side were training a cannon and refused to obey their warning to get out of the way, whereupon the cannon was discharged and his arm shot off, causing a mortal wound." Nevertheless the graves of victims of the numerous revolutions are everywhere to be seen, testifying to the curse of internecine warfare.

Mr. Schoenrich's interesting book shows that Santo Domingo under wise and friendly aid and guidance from the United States may become the most prosperous State in the West Indies.

SANTO DOMINGO: A COUNTRY WITH A FUTURE. By Otto Schoenrich. The Macmillan Company. $3.

MARINES KILL HAITI BANDITS U. S. Soldiers of the Sea Battle Outlaws—Three Americans Are Wounded.

Washington, July 30.—Three encounters between United States marines and Dominican and Haitian bandits in Santo Domingo were reported in dispatches to the navy department. Casualties among the marines were one corporal and two privates slightly wounded. About twenty of the bandits were killed, several wounded and others captured.

records.headline: An article on telephone service in the Dominican Republic reports
records.summary_en: An article on telephone service in the Dominican Republic reports that the government owns and operates an 854-mile intertown network connecting twenty-one towns and thirty-four villages, with 276 additional miles proposed. Although the public lines transmitted 116,140 messages the previous year—including 45,242 official communications and the balance private communications—government operation in 1917 resulted in a deficit of $77,842. By contrast, local telephone systems owned by companies or private individuals in Moca, La Vega, La Romana, Salcedo, Monte Cristi, Puerto Plata, San Pedro de Macoris, San Francisco de Macoris, and Santiago de los Caballeros are generally well administered and profitable. Operating from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. with American equipment throughout, these local networks charge a government-capped rate of $3 a month plus $1.50 for branch lines, with discounts for annual advance payment and no limit on messages.

records.summary_en: The *Birmingham age-herald* reviewed a comprehensive historical and descriptive study of Santo Domingo and Haiti written by a former secretary to the 1905 U.S. financial commission and the Dominican Minister of Finance. The work examined the island's history from 1492 to the present, alongside analyses of its geography, minerals, commerce, and municipal administration. It also discussed Dominican political revolutions, public debt, and the fiscal treaty established with the United States.

El libro examinaba los anales de la isla desde 1492 hasta el presente, junto con pormenores de su geografía, recursos minerales, comercio y administración local. Analizaba además las revueltas políticas dominicanas, la deuda pública y el tratado hacendario celebrado con los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: According to a Navy Department dispatch received by his parents
records.summary_en: According to a Navy Department dispatch received by his parents, twenty-one-year-old Marine Corps pharmacist's mate James William Hurley, son of Harry L. Hurley of 625 Columbia Road Northwest, drowned during field operations while crossing the Elbots River at Santiago, Dominican Republic, in August. His body is en route to the United States for burial from his parents' home. Having enlisted in the Navy in May before transferring to the Marine Hospital Corps and training at Quantico, Hurley was sent to St. Thomas Island and then assigned to Fort San Luis at Santiago rather than to France as he had hoped; he is survived by his parents, two sisters, and a younger brother.
records.summary_es: Según un despacho del Departamento de Marina recibido por sus padres, el ayudante de farmacia del Cuerpo de Marines James William Hurley, de veintiún años de edad e hijo de Harry L. Hurley, residente en 625 Columbia Road Northwest, murió ahogado durante operaciones de campaña mientras cruzaba el río Elbots en Santiago, República Dominicana, en agosto. Su cuerpo está en camino hacia los Estados Unidos para ser sepultado desde la residencia de sus padres. Tras alistarse en la Marina en mayo, pasar al Cuerpo Hospitalario de Marines y entrenarse en Quantico, Hurley fue enviado a la isla de Saint Thomas y de allí asignado a la Fortaleza San Luis en Santiago en lugar de ser enviado a Francia como esperaba; le sobreviven sus padres, dos hermanas y un hermano menor.

records.headline: A short geographical item titled 'Next Largest Island' states
records.summary_en: A short geographical item titled 'Next Largest Island' states that the island shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic (referred to as 'The island of Ilaiti-Santo Domingo') is the largest in the West Indies after Cuba. Out of a total area of 29,525 square miles, 10,200 square miles—about one-third—lie in the western section, Haiti, while the remaining 19,325 square miles—two-thirds—are in the eastern portion, the Dominican Republic.
records.summary_es: Una breve nota geográfica titulada «Next Largest Island» señala que la isla compartida por Haití y la República Dominicana (denominada «The island of Ilaiti-Santo Domingo») es, después de Cuba, la más grande de las Antillas. De una superficie total de 29,525 millas cuadradas, 10,200 millas cuadradas —aproximadamente un tercio— corresponden a la sección occidental, Haití, mientras que las 19,325 millas cuadradas restantes —dos tercios— se encuentran en la parte oriental, la República Dominicana.

records.headline: Under the heading 'Can You Read This?', the paper prints a Spanish -language
records.summary_en: Under the heading 'Can You Read This?', the paper prints a Spanish-language notice sent by a brother serving in the U.S. Marines who plays left field for the 'devil dog' team in Santo Domingo City, Dominican Republic. Although the English introduction describes the game as between the American Marines and a team of Spaniards, the Spanish notice itself—headed by the Relief Committee for the Victims of the Puerto Rico Earthquake—announces that Martin Gaudier has completed arrangements for a baseball match between the Marine team and a select team of native players, followed by the Marine batting order and substitutes.
records.summary_es: Bajo el título «Can You Read This?», el periódico reproduce un aviso en español enviado por un hermano que presta servicio en los marines estadounidenses y juega en el jardín izquierdo del equipo de los «devil dogs» en la ciudad de Santo Domingo, República Dominicana. Aunque la introducción en inglés describe el encuentro como un partido entre los marines estadounidenses y un equipo de españoles, el propio aviso en español —encabezado por el Comité de Colectas para las Víctimas del Terremoto de Puerto Rico— anuncia que Martín Gaudier ha concluido los preparativos para un gran partido de béisbol entre el equipo de los marines y una selección de los mejores jugadores nativos, seguido del orden al bate y los sustitutos de los marines.

records.headline: Under a headline announcing a letter home from a U.S. Marine
records.summary_en: Under a headline announcing a letter home from a U.S. Marine in the Dominican Republic, the paper prints a letter dated October 24, 1918, from Santo Domingo addressed 'Dear Uncle.' Writing to family in West Virginia, the Marine hopes the Spanish influenza will not spread there, recalls the Brown Reunion and how Marine training gives one a huge appetite, and expresses pride in being represented by a star on the service flag. Before the window cuts off mid-sentence, he praises the beauty of the tropical sunsets after rain while noting that the rainy season makes camp life less pleasant as sunshine and rain alternate by the minute.
records.summary_es: Bajo un titular que anuncia una carta enviada a casa por un marine estadounidense desde la República Dominicana, el periódico publica una misiva fechada el 24 de octubre de 1918 en Santo Domingo y dirigida a «Dear Uncle». Escribiendo a sus familiares en Virginia Occidental, el marine espera que la gripe española no se propague allí, recuerda la reunión de la familia Brown y cómo el entrenamiento de los marines despierta un gran apetito, y expresa su orgullo de estar representado por una estrella en la bandera de servicio. Antes de que el fragmento se corte a mitad de frase, elogia la belleza de las puestas de sol tropicales tras la lluvia, aunque señala que la temporada lluviosa hace menos agradable la vida en el campamento, pues el sol y la lluvia se alternan de un minuto a otro.

records.summary_en: The *New-York tribune* published the proclamation of the U.S. military occupation in Santo Domingo, which stated that the intervention aimed to restore internal order and treaty compliance rather than end Dominican sovereignty. Dominican statutes and civil courts remained operational for regular matters, while military tribunals were established to try offenses against the occupation or its personnel. The decree also directed that all customs duties and internal revenues be paid directly to the military government.
records.summary_es: El *New-York tribune* publicó el bando de ocupación militar estadounidense en Santo Domingo, en el que se sostenía que la intervención procuraba restaurar el orden interno y hacer cumplir los pactos vigentes antes que menoscabar la soberanía dominicana. El ordenamiento legal ordinario y los tribunales de justicia civil permanecían en funciones, a la vez que se constituían consejos de guerra castrenses para enjuiciar delitos cometidos contra las fuerzas de ocupación o sus efectivos. El decreto disponía asimismo que la totalidad de los gravámenes aduaneros y rentas internas fuesen satisfechos directamente al gobierno militar.
records.passage: This Military Occupation is undertaken with no immediate or ulterior object of destroying the sovereignty of the Republic of Santo Domingo, but, on the contrary, is designed to give aid to that country in returning to a condition of internal order that will enable it to [observe?] the terms of the Treaty aforesaid, and the obligations resting upon it as one of the family of nations. Dominican statutes, therefore, will continue in effect in so far as they do not conflict with the objects of the Occupation or necessary regulations established thereunder, and their lawful administration will continue in the hands of such duly authorized Dominican officials as may be necessary, all under the oversight and control of the United States forces exercising Military Government. The ordinary administration of justice, both in civil and criminal matters, through the regularly constituted Dominican courts will not be interfered with by the Military Government herein established; but cases to which a member of the United States Forces in Occupation is a party, or in which are involved contempt or defiance of the authority of the Military Government, will be tried by tribunals set up by the Military Government. records.full_text:
When "the Inconceivable" Happened in Haiti

PRESIDENT WILSON was recently asked how the formation of the league of nations would affect the application of the Monroe doctrine to the case of a Latin-American republic that might voluntarily return to Spanish allegiance. He is quoted as saying, "It is inconceivable." As a matter of fact this very thing did happen in 1861, when Santo Domingo was restored to Spanish rule for four years.

Up to 1844 the history of what is now the Dominican Republic is the history of Haiti. In that year the Spanish population, under the leadership of Don Pedro Santana, proclaimed its independence and set up a republic. Santana became the first president. Five years later Baez became president and for twelve years he and Santana alternated in the presidency.

In 1861 Santana proclaimed the annexation of the Dominican Republic to Spain. The United States was entering upon the Civil war and had neither the time nor the strength for the prompt and effectual enforcement of the Monroe doctrine. One result was that Napoleon III, counting on the success of the Confederacy, constituted the Republic of Mexico an empire and put Archduke Maximilian of Austria on the throne.

Two years after the Dominican Republic was annexed to Spain its people revolted and restored the republic. In 1865 Spain acknowledged its independence. Incidentally President Grant desired to annex the republic to the United States. A treaty for this purpose was ratified by the Dominican people, but was rejected by the American senate by a tie vote.

At the close of the Civil war in 1865 the United States had both the time and the strength to enforce the Monroe doctrine in Mexico and the French troops withdrew, leaving Maximilian to his fate—execution in 1867 at the hands of the revolutionists. In 1867 Benito Juarez became the first president of the restored Republic of Mexico.

records.summary_en: A historical sketch states that until 1844 the history of the Dominican Republic was that of Haiti, when the Spanish population under Don Pedro Santana proclaimed independence, established a republic with Santana as first president, and saw Baez and Santana alternate in the presidency for twelve years starting five years later. Santana later proclaimed the annexation of the Dominican Republic to Spain while the United States lacked the time and strength to enforce the Monroe Doctrine, and two years after the annexation the Dominican people revolted and restored the republic, with Spain acknowledging its independence. The article also notes that President Grant subsequently desired to annex the republic under a treaty ratified by the Dominican people.

Santana proclamó más tarde la anexión de la República Dominicana a España mientras los Estados Unidos carecían del tiempo y la fuerza para hacer cumplir la Doctrina Monroe, y dos años después de la anexión el pueblo dominicano se rebeló y restauró la república, reconociendo España su independencia. El artículo señala además que el presidente Grant deseó posteriormente anexar la república mediante un tratado ratificado por el pueblo dominicano.

records.headline: An article on the Dominican Republic notes that steamships run
records.summary_en: An article on the Dominican Republic notes that steamships run between New York, Porto Rico, and Santo Domingo, including freighters from New York to Dominican ports via San Juan, Porto Rico. The author states that the country offers abundant well-paying enterprises and laws favorable to foreign investment, while commercial relations, exports, and imports between the Dominican Republic and the United States are increasing rapidly. It also praises the republic's epidemic-free climate and mountain summits such as San Juan de la Maguana and Santo Cerro—where December temperatures match those of New York—and observes that a large number of North American families make their homes in Santo Domingo.

El autor afirma que el país ofrece abundantes empresas rentables y leyes favorables a la inversión extranjera, mientras que las relaciones comerciales, las exportaciones y las importaciones entre la República Dominicana y los Estados Unidos aumentan rápidamente. Asimismo, elogia el clima libre de epidemias de la república y cumbres montañosas como San Juan de la Maguana y el Santo Cerro —donde las temperaturas de diciembre igualan las de Nueva York—, y observa que un gran número de familias norteamericanas residen en Santo Domingo.

records.full_text:
It Happened in Haiti

President Wilson was recently asked how the formation of the league of nations would affect the application of the Monroe doctrine to the case of a Latin-American republic that might voluntarily return to Spanish allegiance. He is quoted as saying, "It is inconceivable." As a matter of fact this very thing did happen in 1861, when Santo Domingo was restored to Spanish rule for four years.

Up to 1844 the history of what is now the Dominican Republic is the history of Haiti. In that year the Spanish population, under the leadership of Don Pedro Santana, proclaimed its independence and set up a republic. Santana became the first president. Five years later Baez became president and for twelve years he and Santana alternated in the presidency.

In 1861 Santana proclaimed the annexation of the Dominican Republic to Spain. The United States was entering upon the Civil war and had neither the time nor the strength for the prompt and effectual enforcement of the Monroe doctrine. One result was that Napoleon III, counting on the success of the Confederacy, constituted the Republic of Mexico an empire and put Archduke Maximilian of Austria on the throne.

Two years after the Dominican Republic was annexed to Spain its people revolted and restored the republic. In 1865 Spain acknowledged its independence. Incidently President Grant desired to annex the republic to the United States. A treaty for this purpose was ratified by the Dominican people, but was rejected by the American senate by a tie vote.

At the close of the Civil war in 1865 the United States had both the time and the strength to enforce the Monroe doctrine in Mexico and the French troops withdrew, leaving Maximilian to his fate—execution in 1867 at the hands of the revolutionists. In 1867 Benito Juarez became the first president of the restored Republic of Mexico.

records.headline: Under a headline referring to the Dominican Republic as "Dominica
records.summary_en: Under a headline referring to the Dominican Republic as "Dominica," an article quotes a Dominican newly arrived at the Hotel Marseilles who states that Santo Domingo, Porto Rico, and Central America offer great natural sources of wealth in a commerce revived by the armistice. He reports growing trade in coffee, sugar, fruits, dyewoods, and rare cabinet woods—noting that the region has all the woods America buys from India and China, though it cannot compete with cheap Oriental labor in rubber and camphor. He adds that the country's greatest present wealth lies in sugar, coffee, fruit, and tobacco, with sugar offering the most money and a crop this year sufficient to supply the world cheaply if properly cared for.

records.full_text:
MARINES TAKE CIVILIZATION TO ISLE OF HAITI

NEW YORK, June 11.—Marines as missionaries! Men of arms teaching the arts of peace!

It is a new idea under the sun and one that the shades of Kubla Khan, Alexander the Great, Caesar, Napoleon and the other great warriors, if they ever could revisit the earth, could scarcely credit.

Yet the United States Marines in Haiti and the Dominican Republic are real and effective missionaries, according to the Rev. Arthur Gray, D. D., Secretary for Latin America of the Board of Missions of the Protestant Episcopal church, who has just returned from a trip to that part of the world.

There are quite a number of Marines in Haiti and the Dominican Republic. They are down there teaching the people how to manage their finances, how to build roads, how to establish schools, how to fight disease—and incidentally, how to preserve law and order so that the national habit of sporadic revolutions may be overcome.

Haiti has long been a country of brigands—of plunderers in high office of the people. One official issued a government loan and, after selling the bonds, skipped out with the proceeds. Foreign buyers of this kind of insecurity got "sore" and a European government was on the point of taking an action which would have resulted in the loss of her autonomy to Haiti if the United States had not stepped in.

By the terms of the treaty of 1915 between Haiti and the United States this country "occupied" Haiti for the purpose of teaching its people to become independent and free from foreign influence. We were given the right to have certain officials at Port-au-Prince, capital of the republic. One of these was a financial adviser through whom, and subject to whose approval, the revenues of the Haitian government are expended. Another is a general of gendarmerie who directs and trains the native constabulary; Commander Gayler of the United States navy is in charge of all public works in Haiti while Commander McClean is in charge of all sanitation. Brigadier General A. W. Catlin, who recently served in France and who is the author of one of the recent war books, "With The Help of God and a Few Marines," is now in charge of the United States forces in Haiti.

Aiding them are a body of United States Marines. A number of these have been appointed officers in charge of the native constabulary. They protect the people from brigands, build roads from one town to another, repair and keep clean the city streets, aid in projects to improve sanitation—particularly by engaging in warfare with the disease-breeding mosquito—and become a sort of Big Brother to the natives.

These marines are missionaries, and prepare the way for the missionaries later sent out by the various churches, by teaching the peoples among whom they are sent that the United States is their friend, has stepped in and been spending money and giving the lives of her sons with no expectation of reimbursement, and familiarizing them with American ideals of law and order, cleanliness and democratic education.

"Only a few years ago and even today," said Dr. Gray, "one can journey through Haiti without seeing any men. The women till the soil and carry the products of the plantations to the markets. The men stay at home keeping carefully within the doors lest they should be impressed into military service by some roving revolutionist. This condition is improving since the United States took hold of Haiti's finances, public works and police in 1915 and the farmer is beginning to appear from his long hiding in his home and beginning to work again.

"In Port-au-Prince docks have been built, the streets have been paved, roads have been built, war has been made on the mosquitoes, dispensaries established, schools cleaned and bettered and disease reduced by the enforcement of quarantine regulations. A surgeon who is a commander in the United States Navy, Commander McClean, is in charge of all sanitation. He has out $1,600 per month for sanitary work among more than 2,000,000 people. He needs trained nurses and pyhsicians to help him preserve the public health. I very much hope that he may obtain both nurses and physicians and thus bring to pass that the nation-wide campaign of the Protestant Episcopal church in developing the spiritual life of the church may not only succeed but may indirectly add to the efficiency of the Missionary Marines.

"I also earnestly hope the work of our church in educating the boys and girls of Haiti will be aided through this campaign. Haiti's great need is education for her people. President Dartenave, his minister of education, and other officials asked me while I was in the island to establish trade schools. Funds have been lacking. If the members of the churches are awake to the needs of the world and the church's opportunity, money will be forthcoming for this work as a result of the nation-wide campaign.

"The church must co-operate with the United States and with the marines in making the Haitiens a strong self-sustaining nation, free from foreign interference. We don't want to keep our troops there a minute longer than necessary and the length of time largely depends upon what the church is willing to do in Haiti and the Dominican Republic. The sooner church workers go south the sooner the marines can come north. The marines cannot come home until the Haitian people have been taught the art of self-control and those other virtues without which a republic will not work. Policemen cannot build character and that is where the church must come in. When she is well established the pioneer missionaries—the marines—can come home."

records.summary_en: The *sun* discussed Dominican efforts to enlist Spanish diplomatic support to secure the withdrawal of U.S. marines, noting historic cultural affinities between the two nations. The piece recalled that Pedro Santana annexed the Dominican Republic to Spain in 1861, which was overturned by a popular revolt that led Spain to recognize Dominican independence in 1865. It added that an 1869 annexation treaty with the United States was ratified by Dominicans but defeated by a tie vote in the U.S. Senate.
records.summary_es: El *sun* trató sobre las gestiones dominicanas dirigidas a concitar el respaldo diplomático de España para lograr la evacuación de las tropas de marina estadounidenses, resaltando los seculares vínculos culturales que unían a ambos pueblos. La nota recordó que Pedro Santana reincorporó la República Dominicana a España en 1861, medida revocada por un alzamiento patriótico que forzó a España a reconocer la emancipación dominicana en 1865. Añadió que el tratado de anexión de 1869 con los Estados Unidos fue respaldado por la población dominicana pero desestimado en el Senado de los EE. UU. por votación empatada.

There has been much disorder in the Dominican Republic, and the United States has kept a force of Marines there to preserve the peace. That the citizens of the Dominican Republic, dissatisfied with the present state of affairs, should seek to enlist the cooperation of Spain to effect our retirement from their country is natural. The sympathy between Spain and the Dominicans has always been strong; in [illegible], seventeen years after the establishment, under Don Pedro Santana, of the Republic, he proclaimed its reannexation to Spain. Two years later there was a revolt against Spanish rule, and in [illegible] Spain again recognized the independence of her former colony. By so doing Spain avoided collision with the Monroe Doctrine, the application of which to foreign adventures in land-grabbing on this continent had been interrupted by the civil war. In [illegible] the Babcock treaty for the annexation of the republic to this country was ratified by the Dominicans, only to be rejected by a tie vote in the Senate of the United States. No complaint can be made if Spanish statesmen offer friendly advice about our conduct in the Dominican Republic. records.headline: This narrative tells how a Puerto Plata senator chosen as president, on trial for one year after the previous president
records.summary_en: This narrative tells how a Puerto Plata senator chosen as president, on trial for one year after the previous president was killed, announced after some ten months that he intended to hold onto the job, sparking a general uprising against him as a usurper and tyrant. As his forces prepared to shell Puerto Plata unless the city surrendered by two o'clock, and Washington had sent two contingents of Marines to Puerto Plata and Monte Cristi to stand by, the American commander warned him that the first gun fired would result in the landing of Marines and a general cleaning out of the belligerents.
records.summary_es: Este relato cuenta cómo un senador de Puerto Plata escogido como presidente, a prueba por un año tras la muerte del presidente anterior, anunció después de unos diez meses que pretendía quedarse en el puesto, lo que desató un levantamiento general contra él como usurpador y tirano. Mientras sus fuerzas se preparaban para bombardear Puerto Plata si la ciudad no se rendía a las dos en punto, y Washington había enviado dos contingentes de marines a Puerto Plata y Monte Cristi para estar listos, el comandante americano le advirtió que el primer cañonazo disparado provocaría el desembarco de los marines y una limpieza general de los beligerantes.

records.headline: One year was the limit if he failed to "make good
records.summary_en: The *Richmond planet* recounted the outbreak of civil war in Santo Domingo after a provisional president, appointed for a one-year trial term, issued a manifesto ten months later refusing to relinquish office. The declaration provoked widespread public outrage, prompting citizens to take up arms under the banner of liberty to remove the administration. While the president armed supporters with government artillery, fighters in Puerto Plata organized resistance, plunging the country into open conflict.
records.summary_es: El *Richmond planet* relató el estallido de la guerra civil en Santo Domingo después de que un presidente provisional, designado para un período de prueba de un año, emitiera un manifiesto diez meses después negándose a dejar el cargo. La declaración provocó una indignación pública generalizada, lo que llevó a los ciudadanos a alzarse en armas bajo el estandarte de la libertad para deponer a la administración. Mientras el presidente armaba a sus partidarios con artillería gubernamental, combatientes en Puerto Plata organizaron la resistencia, sumiendo al país en un conflicto abierto.
