records.full_text:
OUR QUEER PRIVATE WAR IN HAYTI AND SAN DOMINGO

Hand grenades and machine guns are to be used in subjugating the Dominican and the Haytian. Within the very near future 2,500 additional United States marines are to be sent to San Domingo. They will be armed with grenades and the latest machine guns. They will co-operate with the 3,000 marines now in that “republic” in the hope that before the citizens of the United States really learn what is going on the trouble can be brought to an end.

There have been marines in San Domingo for three years. There have been, too marines in Hayti for as long. How long they will remain there is a problem that no one can answer now.

We'll be here for a hundred years at the rate things are progressing now, remarked a high military official to the writer a short time back.

Few in the United States know that we really have “wars” with the Dominicans and the Haytians. The strictest of censorships is maintained, newspaper accounts of happenings on the island—both “republics” are on the same island—cannot be sent through the mails, officers who have served down there dare not talk of what they have seen or what they experienced. Privates who have served in these sub-tropical places know little of what is going on on the inside and when they do “kick out” and return home their stories are not always wholly coherent or credible.

Some day the history of the United States occupation of Hayti and San Domingo will be written. The names of the American boys who have fallen victims to the bullets or knives or machetes of natives will be made known. The almost unbelievable hardships suffered by our troops will be described and then we will ask one another, “What was it all about anyhow?”

The Domincans have not been conquered; nor have the Haytians. Both peoples make an outward show of friendliness; also they spit at a United States uniform after first assuring themselves that the wearer of that uniform is ignorant of the saliva expelling process.

HATRED FOR AMERICANS.

Domincans hate the Americans; so do the Haytians. Nothing pleases the citizen of either country more than to take a shot at the wearer of Uncle Sam's livery, provided of course, the shooter is behind an adobe wall or a tree or in the window of a house. Few snipers though take advantage of this “house” business; the risk is too great.

Neither the Dominican nor the Haytian is a good shot. They shoot from the hip and take a chance. It's good for the United States marines that such is the case, else there would have been—would be in the future—more of them killed or wounded.

There are high offices in the marine service now stationed in these “Spiggoty” countries who would give nearly all they possesss to be permitted to tell their stories. They would tell the results of their personal observations during the time they have been there.

These men woud tell of “leathernecks” who have gone insane while out in the brush searching for the will-of the wisp bandits who infest the country. They would describe the restraints that have been heaped on the sea soldiers, these being forced to “treat the natives with forbearance and kindliness, no matter what happens” as ordered by Admiral Knapp, until recently Military Governor of San Domingo. They would tell too, of the utter uselessness of the marines being in San Domingo a country that under existing conditions is to Americans an inferno of heat and loneliness and madness

And the worst of it all is that few of the “leathernecks”—this meaning officers as well as buck privates—know what it is about. They do not know why they are in San Domingo. They—that is, some of them—have a vague idea that they are in this land to enforce the payment of a debt said to be owing to their country, the United States. They recall snatches of talk they have heard of some $20,000,000 due to Uncle Sam from the Domincans; and they know too, that the United States government is in charge of the customs on the island.

Still, if the military establishment in San Domingo was merely for the purpose of collecting a bad debt, why it is asked is there such a rigid censorship maintained? In their balmiest days the censors who flaunted the people of the States in regard to the happenings of the great war in Europe had nothing on the gentlemen who are in charge at San Domingo—in Hayti.

Hundreds of letters written by enlisted men to their folks back in the States never get further than the censor's wastebasket. They are keenly or wholly macerated before going that far.

Readers of the Herald will recall the interview given out by the late Theodore Roosevelt along in November of last year, which had to do, according to the former President with “President Wilson's private wars in San Domingo and Hayti.” Every effort I understand was made to keep this statement away from the islands.

And these efforts almost succeeded—almost but not quite. A copy of a Washington daily newspaper used in packing merchandise reached Puerto Plata just before Christmas, the man getting it advertising the fact that “Teddy had gone after the President. This article was widely read and commented upon.

Most of the officers who were in San Domingo when I was on the island were of the old stock of marines—fighting men every man of them. They couldn't understand why, when there were real doings over on “the other side” they were shunted down into the midst of a flock of “spiggoties” with nothing but bush fighting and bush whacking to relieve the monotony.

At one time it had been possible for the fighters to “go out on a jam and then shoot up a section of what ever town they happened to be stationed in. But this sort of pleasure is boreo” to amass a skinful of bad rum denied them now; less than a year ago a “no booze” order was promulgated from Washington. Rum is the chief aim of the Domincans. A license to dispose the fiery stuff costs something like $50 a year. Before one can seil cigars one must first pay the $400 license fee demanded. They grow what many consider the best tobacco in the world in San Domingo, too.

One buck private one who had been reduced from a top sergeancy for a reason that I will tell later on told me:—

“Why, there used to be lots of fun here. We had all night liberty and as soon as a fellow got away from the fort he could go down town, get properly jingled and then start shooting up the town. We never shot to hit any of the 'Spigs' but we did like to chase them inside of their houses. Then we would shoot up the electric lights which are lighted only when the moon is not shining. Sometimes one of the natives would take a shot at us; and then we would sure have a golrious time!”

SOME AMAZING TALES.

The marine came from a town within twelve miles of Pittsburgh. When I met him he was serving his third “hitch.” He was a rather talkative person and possessed a deadly hatred for Dominicans and things Dominican. And the same applied to Hayti and Haytians. He was with Butler and Waller when Hayti was first in would certainly stir up the good folks vaded; and the tales he told of what happened in that Negro republic of the States were they made public.

Here is one story told to me by a marine and which is offered here for what it is worth:

“I had a buddy,” said my friend, 'of whom I thought the world. We went through all the rough stuff in Hayti—and let me tell you it was some rought after we started to clean up. We worked together all the time we slept together and we fought for each other. I tell you, I thought more of that buddy than I did of any other living thing.

During the raid we made through Hayti when lots of our fellows were bumped off we made an agreement that if the Haytians got one of us the other would not rest until he had taken his revenge—had venged his pal's death.

And what made me go crazy after my friend was picked off in Puerto Prince by a skulking assassin was the fact that we had gone through hell and had come through alive. But an 'amigo' hiding behind the walls of an adobe shack got Tommie and then,—well I didn't care what became of me!

“That night I picked up a few tumblers of rum and after thinking the matter over decided I was going to start a little war of my own. You know how they do down in these countries; how they plaster on the talcum powder an inch thick and then start on their parades around the town square or plaza. Sometimes there is a band concert, and sometimes there isn't. But concert or no the natives keep milling and milling and milling, getting up a sweat the stench of which turns the stomach of any honest to goodness American who happens near them.

“The moon wasn't shinning the night I selected for action,” continued Jack the Avenger so I was in luck. I had determined to get as many blacks as it was possible to get before they got me. I firmly expected to go along with them; but I didn't care.

“At first I considered the idea of picking them off with a rifle. This would be too slow I decided; a machine gun would be better. And a chine gun it was.

“I got eighty-nine of them before a marine officer laid me out with a bump on the head, using his revolver to hand out the bump. There was excitement to peddle and for a time it looked as though there was going to be hell in general. You know we really were at war with those Haytians; they were killing us and we were killing them. I guess I was a bit hasty; but—well it was all in the game.

I was court martialled of course. But the action against me wasn't very spirited. Our fellows knew that the Haytians were taking advantage of every opportunity to bump off marines and that the greatest treachery was in evidence on their part at all times. That's why I guess I was let off with a mere reduction to the ranks.”

HE KILLED FIVE.

This same marine it was who killed five Domnicans in the streets of Santiago some time after his being transferred to that city. These victims were prisoners and were being used on street work near the fort which houses the American forces there.

Our friend was in charge of a bunch of six prisoners and was given a job of filling in a cut near the road leading up to the fort. Of the six 'Spigs' five wore political prisoners—men who had been found bearing arms or having arms in their homes. They had been acting ugly for some time and their guard was ordered to be on the quivive.

The break camp after the felons started to work. They went with a rush down San Luis street.

The marine said never aword. Swinging his automatic pistol from its holster at his side he began picking off the fugitives. Five shots were fired—five that's all. Five Dominicans were buried the next day.

It must not be understood that the Dominicans and marines are at it, all the time. Such is not the case. A month, two months may pass and there won't be a happening to disturb the serenity of the situation.

Again, it may be that there will be a spell during which the “bandits” as they are teremd, will evince all kinds of activity keeping the American fighters as well as their supporters the Guardia Naconal on the jump continuously.

For somehow or other, the Dominicans cannot reconcile themselves to the idea that they are getting a “square deal.” They resent the presence in their midst of an armed force representing an alien nation. They are intensely patriotic and belive they should be permitted to work out their own salvation.

“What mattres it” they argue. “if we do have our revolutions and kill one another off? Others spring up to take the places of the ones killed in battle. We have been happy in our ignorance for years; we have been patriotic; our sons and daughters have been brought up and educated. Why, then, should we be forced to suffer the presence of these armed men from the United States a country with which we are not at war?”

Peculiarly enough one cannot find any person in authority in the States who will admit that the government of Uncle Sam is “at war” with the Dominican government. Here's the way the matter was explained to me by a high official down in the island:

“At war? certainly not. The marines go everywhere and when they land, such a procedure does not mean that the United States has declared war upon the country invested. Of course, if the army landed men in a foreign country that would be different. But the marines—oh, my no! We're not at war with San Domingo!

According to the statement of a high Dominican official to the writer, the United States to use the vernacular, “pulled a boner” when the occupation of San Domingo was effected. Here's the story as I heard it.

REASON FOR THE “WAR.”

The President of the island was helped to glory by some of his over zealous fellow countrymen and a successor was needed.

At that time San Domingo had a “House and a “Senate.” The Senator representing Puerto Plata was well liked throughout the island and was the especial pet of his hometown people. Immediately he was selected to take the place of the murdered President. There were four years of the latter's term remaining.

The Puerto Plata man was not selected for these four years; rather he was placed in office on trial. He was given to understand that his tenure of office would depend upon himself. One year was the limit if he failed to “make good.” If, at the end of that year his administration of affairs had been satisfactory he would be reappointed for the remaining 3 years. However, Dominicans are all ambitious. Give them a taste of power and they are willing to fight for a mouthful of the same.

And so it was with the President by accident. After being in office for something like ten months he issued a manifesto announcing that he intended hanging onto the job and that he defied the powers of light and darkness—this meaning all of San Domingo—to oust him.

That defiance was the spark that ignited the train leading to the magazine. Immediately the Dominicans were up in arms.

“Can it be said,” they asked, “that this bad man whom we were gracious enough to permit to serve us shall now appoint himself our master. We the free people of San Domingo? Let it not be so. Down with the tyrant! Viva Libertad!”

First of all the usurper gathered about him a few hundred of his backers and proceeded to arm them. There was in the government arsenal a few pieces of antiquated artillery, among the lot two or three six pounders. The Puerto Platans, patriots and fighters, willing to brawl at the drop of a cigarette butt, were not slow in picking up the gauge of battle. They, too had arms—and what Dominican didn't? And so the war was on.

Some word of the threatening outbreak had reached Washington and orders had been despatched to the marine commander at Guantanamo, Cuba, to proceed forthwith to the Dominican coast and to stand by, ready for eventualities. Two separate contigents of “leathernecks” were sent—one to Puerto Plata and another to Monte Christi the latter city being the closest to the States and immediate to the Haytian coast.

The army of the President was encamped on a hill back of Puerto Plata when the United States forces drew into the harbor at that place. The usurper had issued an ultimatum giving the citizens of the city until two o'clock of that afternoon to surrender. A refusal on their part meant according to the President that the city would be shelled from the guns then in hand.

The American commander was apprised of these conditions. He despatched a courier to the President stating that the first gun fired would result in the landing of marines and the general cleaning out of the belligerents.

A HARD BLOW.

This was a body blow. The Dominicans had heard of the work of the marines in Hayti, their neighboring republic and they didn't hanker very keenly after any of the same.

But these island people are not given to showing the white feather. They are brave to foolishness; life to them means little as long as their honor remains unsullied and they are fighting for what they believe to be just and right.

And so it was with the man who wanted to remain as President. While he knew that he wouldn't stand as much chance as a wax cat in a certain warm climate, he nevertheless hesitated over agreeing to the terms offered by the representative of Uncle Sam—these being unconditional surrender.

Just there fate took a hand. The guns which were mounted to cover the city of Puerto Plata had not been fired for some time. The soldiers were aching to start something and they could not understand why the President did not order the war to begin.

One man after imbiding more than an ordinary man's share of rum began to cry. With tears coursing down his jetty cheeks he begged to know why this and that was so and why there had been no opportunity for himself and his mates to show their bravery, their skill with the big guns.

This thought became an obsession with the lachrymose one.

“By Cristofer Colon!” he ejaculated, “must I, whose forebears landed in this paradise of a land with the great discoverer stand by and listen to the orders of the Yankee dogs from another land? Let it not be so!”

A few minutes later this man had “begun the war.” Under cover of darkness he sidled up to one of the largest guns loaded the same with an explosive shell and bing! a house or two in the city had been unroofed and confusion came.

Hardly had the echo of this shot died away when the war ship in the harbor hopped into action. A slavo of six pounders was sent back into the hills and then to quote one of the marines who took part in the fracas, “there was hell to pay.”

Strangely enough—or was it strange?—the partiots who had been opposing the usurper's advance, turned in against the Yankees immediately the latter showed their teeth. Commanding the harbor at Puerto Plata is an old fort, a relic of Spanish days—a fort that is probably two hundred years old. It still is trong and formidable if well manned; and thither rushed the Dominicans to oppose the landing of the Americans.

LANDING THE MARINES.

Unfortunately the harbor is wide open, and prior to a year ago it was necessary to anchor at least a half mile out because of the shallow water. And this is what the marines were up against. As their boats left the war ship they were shining marks for the natives of the fort, and the fact that only a few of the Yanks were hit was due more to the poor aim of their enemies than to lack of opportunity to pick them off.

One thing that worried the American commander was the sight of a great gun mounted on a small hillock at the sea side of the fort. This looked as big as a six inch piece and as minute succeeded minute and there was no great shell sent hurling in their direction the Americans wondered why.

Orders were given the gunners aboard the war ship to “get that big gun,” and although a score or more efforts were made the big gun is still there. Afterward this gun was found to be of ancient vintage and out of commission.

At first the American commander was anxious to wound as few of the Dominicans as possible. Orders were to “shoot high” and the marines obeyed.

But the going became hotter and hotter until finally the gunners were instructed to place a few shells inside the fort. This they did with neatness and despatch and soon the fracas was terminated.

When the Yankee forces invested the city they at once took possession of the fort. Thier presence sent the Dominicans into a wild rage. Still the natives were helpless opposed to a superior force and a force that was armed with modern guns, with field pieces and with machine guns to peddle. What could they do?

In the meantime the force that had landed at Monte Christi was indulging in a forced march through the hills and over almost impassable roads to the direction of Santiago. They marched night and day resting only when the men were too tired to keep going. They reached their objective two or three days after Puerto Plata had been taken, and there was little or no trouble experienced in including the officials of the city to surrender.

This Santiago place is one of the show places of the island. In the business section of the city there is hardly a building that doesn't show the scars of battle. The old cathedral said to have been erected more than one hundred years ago flanks the public park on the south, while on the north is the barracks of the Guardian Nacional, a body composed of natives and performing functions something like those which fall to the lot of the New York or Pennsylvania State Constabulary. On the west of the park is the Governor's Palace and the City Hall. On the east is another church.

Most of these biuldings are built of wood and adobe, or concrete. The outer layer is of this plaster stuff and there is hardly a square foot of either the cathedral the barracks or the church that doesn't show signs of bullets and heavier shot. The cathedral in particular is riddled.

So, after taking the island San Domingo City, in the South, the capital of the republic having fallen without trouble the Americans had a proposition on thei rhands. Communication was had with Washington at once. The exact situation was made clear to the officials and instructions were asked for.

In the meantime some of the better class of Dominicans began to take heart. They were satisfied that their big brother of the North would see justice was meted out to them and that they would be permitted to select their President and to administer their own affairs. The usurping President would surely get what was coming to him. In fact, a demand was formally made that he who by this time was under the protection of the Stars and Stripes be turned over to his fellow countrymen that he might be properly punished.

Imagine then the disgust, the rage the manical fury of the islanders when came from Washington instructions to the American commander to see to it that the pretender to the Presidency be placed back in power, and held there by force of arms if necessary.

For that is exactly what happened the man who failed of the trust reposed in him; the man who treacherously betrayed his friends, his fellow countrymen and his country was thrust down the throats of a protesting people and held fast there by superior force.

The excuse has since been made so I was informed, that this “President” person had promised to see that the $20,000,000 of debt claimed by the United States would be paid. However, something must have happened for there is now no President in San Domingo, no Senators and not representatives. The United States military force is the “whole works.”

(N. Y. Herald, Sept. 14, 1919.)

records.headline: A feature on the American occupation reports that 2,600 additional United States Marines, armed with hand grenades
records.summary_en: A feature on the American occupation reports that 2,600 additional United States Marines, armed with hand grenades and the latest machine guns, are to be sent to San Domingo to cooperate with the 3,000 Marines already there, where Marines have been stationed for three years under a strict censorship that keeps news of the fighting from the United States. It says Dominicans hate the Americans and take shots at the uniform when they can do so safely, that officers would tell of leathernecks driven insane searching the brush for bandits, and that few of the Marines know why they are there beyond a vague idea of a debt of some $20,000,000 and the United States being in charge of the customs.
records.summary_es: Un reportaje sobre la ocupación americana informa que 2,600 infantes de marina adicionales de los Estados Unidos, armados con granadas de mano y las ametralladoras más recientes, serán enviados a Santo Domingo para cooperar con los 3,000 infantes de marina ya allí presentes, donde los marines llevan tres años estacionados bajo una censura estricta que impide que las noticias de la lucha lleguen a los Estados Unidos. Dice que los dominicanos odian a los americanos y disparan contra el uniforme cuando pueden hacerlo sin riesgo, que los oficiales contarían de marines enloquecidos buscando bandidos entre la maleza, y que pocos de los marines saben por qué están allí más allá de una vaga idea de una deuda de unos $20,000,000 y de que los Estados Unidos están a cargo de las aduanas.

records.headline: A Latin American personal column opens with the end of a notice
records.summary_en: A Latin American personal column opens with the end of a notice stating that a representative to Haiti is recovering from an illness, and reports that Dominican Republic President Federico Henriquez y Carvajal left the previous week for Santiago de Cuba with his daughter, Luz Henriquez, after spending a few days in Washington. The column also notes that M. M. Morillo, Charge d'Affaires of Santo Domingo in Havana, has left the city for Cuba.

La columna señala además que M. M. Morillo, encargado de negocios de Santo Domingo en La Habana, ha salido de la ciudad rumbo a Cuba.

records.headline: Under the protection of United States Marines, 600 rudimentary schools
records.summary_en: Under the protection of United States Marines, 600 rudimentary schools have been opened in the rural districts of the Dominican Republic, where approximately half of the children are receiving instruction, a dispatch from Puerto Plata reports. Prior to the pacification of the country by the Marines, there were virtually no schools for the poorer classes, and bandit-infested roads and trails often deterred parents from sending their children where schools did exist. Every village with a school is now guarded by Marines or by the Marine-commanded native Guardia, and special protection provided to students and teachers during the school season has led parents to send their children in greater numbers than ever before.
records.summary_es: Bajo la protección de los infantes de marina de los Estados Unidos, se han abierto 600 escuelas rudimentarias en los distritos rurales de la República Dominicana, donde aproximadamente la mitad de los niños recibe instrucción, según un despacho procedente de Puerto Plata. Antes de la pacificación del país por los infantes de marina, prácticamente no existían escuelas para las clases más pobres, y los caminos y senderos infestados de bandidos a menudo disuadían a los padres de enviar a sus hijos allí donde sí había escuelas. Cada aldea que cuenta con una escuela está ahora resguardada por infantes de marina o por la Guardia nativa comandada por ellos, y la protección especial brindada a alumnos y maestros durante el período escolar ha llevado a los padres a enviar a sus hijos en mayor número que nunca.

records.summary_en: According to an October 2 dispatch from Puerto Plata, 600 rudimentary schools have been opened in the rural districts of the Dominican Republic under the protection of United States Marines, teaching about half of the children. Before the Marines pacified the republic, the poorer classes had practically no schools, and parents were frequently afraid to send their children along bandit-infested roads and trails. Now every village with a school is guarded by Marines or the native Guardia under Marine command, and special protection afforded to children and teachers during the school season has resulted in higher school attendance than ever before.
records.summary_es: Según un despacho de Puerto Plata fechado el 2 de octubre, se han abierto 600 escuelas rudimentarias en los distritos rurales de la República Dominicana bajo la protección de los infantes de marina de los Estados Unidos, en las cuales se enseña a cerca de la mitad de los niños. Antes de que los infantes de marina pacificaran la república, las clases más pobres prácticamente no contaban con escuelas, y los padres con frecuencia temían enviar a sus hijos por caminos y senderos infestados de bandidos. Ahora cada aldea donde se ubica una escuela está custodiada por infantes de marina o por la Guardia nativa bajo mando estadounidense, y la protección especial otorgada a niños y maestros durante la temporada escolar ha dado como resultado una asistencia mayor que nunca.

records.headline: Henriquez said, "concerns only the collection of revenue for the payment
records.summary_en: The *Evening star* reported that Dr. Francisco Henriquez y Carvajal rejected assertions that the United States exercised a protectorate over the Dominican Republic, declaring that no treaty akin to the Platt Amendment existed. Henriquez explained that the 1907 convention was limited strictly to customs administration for debt repayment and, as President Roosevelt affirmed, conferred no authority for military intervention. He maintained that the agreement was temporary and would naturally expire once the foreign debt was fully discharged.
records.summary_es: El *Evening star* informó que el Dr. Francisco Henríquez y Carvajal rechazó las afirmaciones de que Estados Unidos ejerciera un protectorado sobre la República Dominicana, declarando que no existía ningún tratado similar a la Enmienda Platt. Henríquez explicó que la convención de 1907 se limitaba estrictamente a la administración aduanera para el pago de la deuda y que, como afirmó el presidente Roosevelt, no confería autoridad para una intervención militar. Sostuvo que el acuerdo era temporal y que expiraría de manera natural una vez que la deuda externa quedara totalmente saldada.

He declares there is no such treaty and that he would not favor any treaty similar to that with Cuba under the Platt amendment. "The financial convention of 1907 between the United States and Santo Domingo," Dr. Henriquez said, "concerns only the collection of revenue for the payment of the public debt, which is supervised by both American and Dominican officials. Mr. Roosevelt more than once referred to this convention, pointing to the fact that it does not imply any right of intervention in Santo Domingo. 'The interference of our government is minimized,' said Mr. Roosevelt, when recommending the treaty to the Senate, 'so that we shall only act in conjunction with the Santo Domingo authorities to secure the proper administration of the customs, and, therefore, to secure the payment of just debts.' That convention is transitory, and shall end when the foreign debt of Santo Domingo is totally paid, which will be a few years hence." records.headline: An obituary reviewing the diplomatic career of Mr. Handley notes
records.summary_en: An obituary reviewing the diplomatic career of Mr. Handley notes that after holding consular posts in Africa, Trinidad, and Matanzas, Cuba, he served as United States consul at Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic, from June 5 to November 16, 1905. Following his service in Puerto Plata, he became consul general at Boma in the Belgian Congo until December 1910, served three years as consul at Naples, and then spent six years as consul general at Callao-Lima, Peru. He married the daughter of former Colombian minister Dr. Ricardo Becerra in June 1910 and is survived by his widow and his sister, Mrs. F. D. McKenny of Washington.
records.summary_es: Una nota necrológica que repasa la carrera diplomática del Sr. Handley señala que, tras ocupar cargos consulares en África, Trinidad y Matanzas, Cuba, se desempeñó como cónsul de los Estados Unidos en Puerto Plata, República Dominicana, desde el 5 de junio hasta el 16 de noviembre de 1905. Después de su servicio en Puerto Plata, pasó a ser cónsul general en Boma, en el Congo Belga, hasta diciembre de 1910, sirvió durante tres años como cónsul en Nápoles y luego pasó seis años como cónsul general en El Callao-Lima, Perú. Contrajo matrimonio con la hija del exministro colombiano Dr. Ricardo Becerra en junio de 1910 y le sobreviven su viuda y su hermana, la Sra. de F. D. McKenny, de Washington.

records.headline: Under the subhead "Question of Finland, Luxemburg and Dominica,"
records.summary_en: Under the subhead "Question of Finland, Luxemburg and Dominica," a report on an international labor conference in Washington states that a newly appointed committee on the admission of new states failed to reach an agreement regarding the applications of Finland, Luxemburg, and the Dominican Republic. Because these three countries are not listed in the annex to the Covenant of the League of Nations, the committee scheduled another meeting for the following morning to rule on the legal phases of the question.
records.summary_es: Bajo el subtítulo «Question of Finland, Luxemburg and Dominica», un informe sobre una conferencia internacional del trabajo en Washington señala que un comité recién nombrado sobre la admisión de nuevos Estados no logró llegar a un acuerdo respecto a las solicitudes de ingreso de Finlandia, Luxemburgo y la República Dominicana. Debido a que estos tres países no figuran en el anexo del Pacto de la Sociedad de las Naciones, el comité programó otra reunión para la mañana siguiente con el propósito de pronunciarse sobre los aspectos jurídicos de la cuestión.

records.headline: A dispatch datelined Puerto Plata, San Domingo, reports that 600
records.summary_en: A dispatch datelined Puerto Plata, San Domingo, reports that 600 rudimentary schools have been opened in the rural districts of the Dominican Republic under the protection of United States Marines, teaching approximately half of the children. Prior to the pacification of the republic by the Marines, the poorer classes had practically no schools, and bandit-infested roads and trails often deterred parents from sending their children to existing schools. Every village with a school is now guarded by Marines or by the Marine-commanded native Guardia, and special protection during the school season has led parents to send their children to school in greater numbers than ever before.
records.summary_es: Un despacho fechado en Puerto Plata, San Domingo, informa que se han abierto 600 escuelas rudimentarias en los distritos rurales de la República Dominicana bajo la protección de los infantes de marina de los Estados Unidos, donde recibe enseñanza aproximadamente la mitad de los niños. Antes de la pacificación de la república por los infantes de marina, las clases más pobres prácticamente carecían de escuelas, y los caminos y senderos infestados de bandidos a menudo disuadían a los padres de enviar a sus hijos a los planteles existentes. Cada aldea donde hay una escuela está ahora custodiada por infantes de marina o por la Guardia nativa comandada por ellos, y la protección especial durante la temporada escolar ha llevado a los padres a enviar a sus hijos a la escuela en mayor número que nunca.

records.headline: Tulio M. Cestero, former Dominican minister to France, Spain
records.summary_en: Tulio M. Cestero, former Dominican minister to France, Spain, and Italy who was sent to the United States as a special commissioner to request the withdrawal of American military rule from the Dominican Republic, criticizes U.S. administration and customs control in the country. Cestero charges that American officers who do not know the language of the natives enforce their personal will rather than the laws of the country. The report adds that complaints accuse the military government of violating the 1907 convention between the United States and the Dominican Republic, alleging that the republic is losing money through the handling of its financial affairs while outsiders profit from the sale of Dominican bonds in the United States.

Cestero denuncia que oficiales estadounidenses que desconocen el idioma de los nativos imponen su voluntad personal en lugar de aplicar las leyes del país. El informe añade que las quejas acusan al gobierno militar de violar la convención de 1907 entre los Estados Unidos y la República Dominicana, alegando que la república pierde dinero mediante el manejo de sus asuntos financieros mientras extranjeros se benefician con la venta de bonos dominicanos en los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: After visiting his home in Washington, Mr. Miller is preparing
records.summary_en: After visiting his home in Washington, Mr. Miller is preparing to sail shortly for a new post in Santo Domingo following six years in the Dominican customs service as inspector, assistant auditor, and secretary. The article notes that the Dominican customs receivership was established under the 1907 American-Dominican convention when a loan was negotiated to relieve the Dominican Republic's financial difficulties, and that annual customs receipts of about $5,000,000 are partly applied in monthly installments through the Guaranty Trust Company of New York to liquidate the fiscal debt. Headquartered in Santo Domingo City under General Receiver C. H. Baxter of New Jersey, the customs service employs mostly Dominicans with Americans holding the executive positions.

El artículo señala que la receptoría de aduanas dominicana fue creada bajo la convención domínico-estadounidense de 1907 cuando se negoció un préstamo para aliviar las dificultades financieras de la República Dominicana, y que las recaudaciones aduaneras anuales de unos $5,000,000 se destinan en parte, mediante abonos mensuales a través de la Guaranty Trust Company de Nueva York, a liquidar la deuda fiscal. Con sede central en la ciudad de Santo Domingo bajo la dirección del receptor general C. H. Baxter, de Nueva Jersey, el personal del servicio aduanero está integrado mayoritariamente por dominicanos, con estadounidenses en los cargos ejecutivos.

records.headline: Colonel Campbell B. Hodges of the War Department's Bureau of Insular Affairs
records.summary_en: Colonel Campbell B. Hodges of the War Department's Bureau of Insular Affairs has returned from inspecting the United States-administered customs service of the Dominican Republic, having visited every seaport of entry and three land ports along the Haitian border. The report notes an increase in 1919 customs collections over 1918 and states that a new tariff effective January 1 materially reduced rates on many items while making all agricultural machinery and implements duty-free. Hodges also reported that several large areas have been opened for sugar cultivation and that other industries are developing in Santo Domingo.
records.summary_es: El coronel Campbell B. Hodges, del Negociado de Asuntos Insulares del Departamento de Guerra, ha regresado de una inspección del servicio de aduanas de la República Dominicana administrado por los Estados Unidos, tras haber visitado todos los puertos marítimos de entrada y tres puertos terrestres a lo largo de la frontera haitiana. El informe señala un incremento en las recaudaciones aduaneras de 1919 respecto de 1918 e indica que un nuevo arancel que entró en vigor el 1 de enero redujo sustancialmente las tasas sobre numerosos artículos al tiempo que declaró libres de derechos toda la maquinaria e implementos agrícolas. Hodges informó además que se han abierto varias zonas extensas para el cultivo de azúcar y que se están desarrollando otras industrias en Santo Domingo.

records.headline: The Willmar Tribune reports that James A. Ostrand, formerly
records.summary_en: The Willmar Tribune reports that James A. Ostrand, formerly a judge of the Supreme Court of the Philippine Islands and recently appointed Chief Justice of the Dominican Republic, has been visiting his mother, Mrs. Carl O. Peterson, in Willmar during the past week and expects to arrive at his new post about July 1. A graduate of the Minnesota University Law School who spent about twenty years in the Philippines, Judge Ostrand was selected for the Dominican position because of his mastery of Spanish, while his son, James Ostrand, Jr., has entered the Willmar schools and will reside there with his grandmother.

records.headline: Our Caribbean Empire
records.summary_en: The *Milwaukee leader* reported sharp criticisms of the U.S. military occupation in Haiti and Santo Domingo, citing findings by Judge Otto Schoenrich and Archbishop Adolfo Nouel. The article reported allegations of despotic military rule, the dissolution of legislative assemblies, arbitrary provost court trials, and the suppression of civil liberties. It also claimed that debt disbursements to native bondholders were suspended under the occupation while New York bankers acquired the depreciated securities.

El artículo dio cuenta de denuncias de un régimen militar despótico, la disolución de asambleas legislativas, juicios arbitrarios ante cortes marciales y la supresión de las libertades civiles. También afirmó que durante la ocupación se suspendieron los pagos de la deuda a los tenedores de bonos nacionales, mientras banqueros de Nueva York adquirían los títulos depreciados.

records.full_text:
OUR CARIBBEAN EMPIRE

The average citizen of the United States is blissfully ignorant of the extent to which this government has established a colonial empire in the Caribbean regions. In Nicaragua the government is practically in the hands of the United States marines. The natives complain not merely that they are ruled without their consent but that they are subject to the whims of our navy department which in this matter is responsible neither to congress nor the people. The American government is also charged with unwarranted interference in Guatemala, Costa Rica and Honduras. At a recent conference at Clark university, Judge Otto Schoenrich, a conservative citizen, born in America, who has held high judicial posts in Porto Rico and is familiar with all the Caribbean countries, read a paper reviewing the record of the American administration of the two island republics, Santo Domingo and Haiti. The first, it will be recalled, is Spanish-speaking and predominantly white; the second French-speaking and Negro. In 1916 our navy took over the government of Santo Domingo, and administers it through the marines against the wishes of the people. “Law and order” have been established. Roads have been built and a beginning has been made at popular education. The reason for our intervention was the failure of the Dominican government to live up to its agreement in the matter of its foreign debt. Foreign bondholders now get their interest regularly! Judge Schoenrich, however, charges that in accomplishing these things the United States government has maintained a censorship so rigid as to apply to every public statement “from the utterances of the chief justice to an advertisement for a servant girl.” Until recently the words, national, revolution, freedom of thought and speech could not appear in a Dominican publication. One unfortunate bookseller was originally sentenced to five years in prison for circulating a speech by the speaker of the Porto Rican house of representatives. Later his sentence was graciously commuted to banishment. Judge Schoenrich also reports serious charges of torture in connection with the administration of the provost courts.

In the neighboring republic of Haiti conditions are even more unsatisfactory. There we intervened on the nominal authority of a treaty, but the Haitian congress only ratified that treaty with 23 reservations which we ignored. In 1916 marines dispersed the congress and in 1917 dispersed a constituent assembly. Tell it not to Trotzky! Judge Schoenrich says there are three governments: the Haitian, the government of the American treaty officials, and the government of the American military. The first is impotent, the second inefficient, and the third indifferent. In the interior districts of the island the officers of the marines exercise despotic powers and the natives charge that a marine can do no wrong to a Haitian. From Haiti also come ugly stories of torture, autocratic and unjust trials of civilians by provost court, and denials of civil liberty. A few months ago armed Haitians, either bandits or revolutionists according to the point of view, actually marched on the capital city where there was vigorous fighting before they were dispersed. The Haitian debt was largely held by the people, who, lacking proper banking facilities, put their savings into national bonds. Under American occupation payment on these was suspended although it was guaranteed in the treaty. The people sold their holdings at low prices. The bonds, it is believed, are now held by New York bankers, and negotiations are under way looking to their payment at par.

It is only fair to say that such criticisms as these were vigorously attacked at the Clark university conference by defenders of the American regime. They are, however, supported by other testimony. Archbishop Nouel of Santo Domingo in a letter to the American minister (we go through the farce of maintaining a minister plenipotentiary in a country ruled by an American rear admiral) complains not only of torture, of the denial of liberty, but of a faulty system of taxation and waste in its expenditure. Emphatically the situation requires investigation. The navy department is ruling three republics without their consent primarily in the interests of their American creditors, with a blissful irresponsibility even as regards congress or the American public. Supposing that conditions in Nicaragua, Santo Domingo, and Haiti prior to our intervention were as bad as their critics assert—it is a sorry world if we can discover no way of helping to educate “backward” people without subjecting them to flagrant economic and political imperialism.

Porto Rico welcomed American annexation and her case is not on all fours with her neighbor’s. Nevertheless, our territorial rule leaves something to be desired. During the year 1917-’18 only 142,846 children out of 427,668 of school age were actually enrolled in the public schools. The total wealth of the island is in the hands of 15 per cent of the population; 14 per cent is in the hands of native Porto Ricans; 67 per cent in the hands of Americans. Wages, housing, and health conditions are wretched. The extension of this sort of thing in Mexico and the Caribbean countries is not our idea of civilizing people.—The World Tomorrow.

records.headline: The military Government has set the country an unassailable example of good government
records.summary_en: The *Richmond times-dispatch* published a report by Military Governor Rear Admiral Thomas Snowden detailing administrative progress in Santo Domingo. Snowden reported that internal revenue collections had increased from $700,000 to approximately $3,500,000 annually and that regressive taxes were replaced with direct property taxes. He stated that the republic's floating debt was cleared, the 1908 loan was on course to be retired thirty years early by 1926, and administrative savings were funding new schools, highways, and sanitation projects.

Declaró que la deuda flotante de la república había sido liquidada, que el empréstito de 1908 estaba encaminado a cancelarse con treinta años de anticipación para 1926 y que los ahorros administrativos financiaban nuevas escuelas, carreteras y obras sanitarias.

records.headline: Brigadier General Logan Feland of the Marine Corps, commanding
records.summary_en: Brigadier General Logan Feland of the Marine Corps, commanding the marine brigade in the Dominican Republic, has been ordered to Washington to take charge of the planning section of the Marine Corps staff. The notice recalls that Feland rendered efficient service in France during the World War, receiving the Distinguished Service Cross and the Croix de Guerre and being named an officer of the Legion of Honor.
records.summary_es: El general de brigada Logan Feland, del Cuerpo de Marines, comandante de la brigada de marines en la República Dominicana, ha recibido órdenes de trasladarse a Washington para hacerse cargo de la sección de planificación del estado mayor del Cuerpo de Marines. La nota recuerda que Feland prestó un servicio eficiente en Francia durante la Guerra Mundial, por el cual recibió la Cruz por Servicio Distinguido y la Cruz de Guerra y fue nombrado oficial de la Legión de Honor.

records.summary_en: The *Pine Bluff daily graphic* reported that Julio M. Cestero of the Dominican junta issued a statement asserting that Dominican citizens never sought U.S. intervention and continually demanded the return of their national sovereignty. In a concurrent release, Secretary of State Colby defended American policy, stating that military intervention in Haiti was prompted by chronic bloodshed and the 1915 lynching of President Guillaume Sam in the French legation. Colby maintained that the United States acted under the Monroe Doctrine to restore order and preempt European military intervention.

records.summary_en: A biographical sketch notes that when President Jiminez was organizing his cabinet, there was strong popular demand for General Camacho to serve as Minister of War. Offered that post and other prominent offices, including the governorship of Santo Domingo, capital of the Dominican Republic, Camacho instead chose the post of Consul General at New York. The item adds that President Jiminez has been dead for more than four years and that the Dominican Republic is currently under a military administration.

La nota añade que el presidente Jiminez lleva muerto más de cuatro años y que en el presente la República Dominicana se encuentra bajo una administración militar.

records.summary_en: The *Pulaskian* reported that Secretary of State Colby defended American Caribbean policy against political attacks by Senator Harding, maintaining that interventions in Haiti and Santo Domingo were undertaken solely to assist local populations. Colby confirmed that the State Department was continuing to withhold salaries from Haitian officials until they ceased obstructing the bilateral treaty. Simultaneously, Dominican representative Julio M. Cestero protested that the Dominican people never requested American occupation and consistently demanded the restoration of their freedom and sovereignty.
records.summary_es: El *Pulaskian* informó que el secretario de Estado Colby defendió la política caribeña de Estados Unidos frente a los ataques políticos del senador Harding, sosteniendo que las intervenciones en Haití y Santo Domingo se llevaron a cabo únicamente para auxiliar a las poblaciones locales. Colby confirmó que el Departamento de Estado seguía reteniendo los salarios de los funcionarios haitianos hasta que cesaran de obstruir el tratado bilateral. Al mismo tiempo, el representante dominicano Julio M. Cestero protestó que el pueblo dominicano jamás solicitó la ocupación estadounidense y reclamó de manera constante el restablecimiento de su libertad y soberanía.

records.headline: A report notes that at the request of both the army and navy
records.summary_en: A report notes that at the request of both the army and navy, the American Red Cross is continuing its peacetime relief operations in insular possessions and foreign territories where the United States maintains armed forces, including Haiti, the Dominican Republic, the Philippines, Hawaii, the Canal Zone, and China. The article states that soldiers and marines in these outlying districts are often engaged in quelling uprisings and suppressing marauding bandits under extreme hardships, with little entertainment or recreation. It adds that in Haiti alone there are some fifty outposts of up to 100 men each on constant patrol duty, and that a large share of the marines in Haiti and Santo Domingo are serving back in the hills out of communication with the outside world except for the occasional visit of a supply truck.

El artículo indica que los soldados y marines en estos distritos apartados participan con frecuencia en sofocar levantamientos y reprimir a bandidos merodeadores bajo extremas privaciones, con poco entretenimiento o recreación. Añade que solo en Haití hay unos cincuenta puestos avanzados de hasta 100 hombres cada uno en constante servicio de patrulla, y que una gran parte de los marines en Haití y Santo Domingo prestan servicio en las montañas, incomunicados del mundo exterior salvo por la visita ocasional de un camión de suministros.

records.summary_en: The *Springfield weekly Republican* reported that the State Department credited U.S. treaty officials with restoring public order, increasing revenues, and advancing road and telegraph construction in Haiti. The department also refuted claims of favoritism toward the National City Bank of New York, stating it received only standard commercial support abroad. The statement noted that U.S. authorities had actually required modifications to the bank's agreement to eliminate monopolistic privileges in the National Bank of Haiti.

El departamento también refutó las acusaciones de favoritismo hacia el National City Bank of New York, declarando que únicamente recibió el respaldo comercial habitual en el extranjero. La declaración indicó que las autoridades estadounidenses habían exigido modificaciones al convenio bancario a fin de eliminar privilegios monopolísticos en el Banco Nacional de Haití.

The account observes that troops in these outlying districts frequently face extreme hardships while quelling uprisings and suppressing marauding bandits in countries offering little entertainment or recreation. In Haiti alone numerous outposts are constantly on patrol, and roughly 50 per cent of the marines in Haiti and Santo Domingo serve in the hills where they depend on occasional supply trucks for communication with the outside world.

records.headline: A report on American armed forces abroad states that the American Red
records.summary_en: A report on American armed forces abroad states that the American Red Cross, acting at the request of the army and navy, is continuing its operations with peacetime troops in foreign territories and insular possessions, where it had previously confined its post-armistice relief program to the continental United States. The article lists Haiti, the Dominican Republic, the Philippines, Hawaii, the Canal Zone, and China as stations where United States soldiers and marines are maintained to protect American interests or as a disciplinary measure, often engaging in combat to quell uprisings and suppress marauding bandits. It notes that about 50 per cent of the marines in Haiti and Santo Domingo serve back in the hills with little recreation and no outside contact save the occasional supply truck, while Haiti alone has some fifty outposts of 50 to 100 men each on constant patrol.
records.summary_es: Un informe sobre las fuerzas armadas estadounidenses en el exterior indica que la Cruz Roja Estadounidense, actuando a petición del ejército y de la marina, continúa sus operaciones con las tropas en tiempos de paz en territorios extranjeros y posesiones insulares, tras haber limitado su programa de asistencia posterior al armisticio al territorio continental de los Estados Unidos. El artículo enumera a Haití, la República Dominicana, las Filipinas, Hawái, la Zona del Canal y China como estaciones donde se mantienen soldados y marines de los Estados Unidos para proteger los intereses estadounidenses o como medida disciplinaria, participando a menudo en combates para sofocar levantamientos y reprimir a bandidos merodeadores. Señala que alrededor del 50 por ciento de los marines en Haití y Santo Domingo sirven en las montañas con poca recreación y sin contacto exterior salvo la visita ocasional del camión de suministros, mientras que solo en Haití hay unos cincuenta puestos avanzados de 50 a 100 hombres cada uno en patrulla constante.

records.headline: Under military occupation the United States has restored order
records.summary_en: Under military occupation the United States has restored order in Santo Domingo, rehabilitated its finances, established public sanitation, and begun training Dominicans to carry on the government when the American Navy withdraws, a dispatch reports. Quoting a report obtained on October 8 by Commander Reynolds Hayden, U.S. Navy Medical Corps, a member of the staff of the Military Governor of Santo Domingo, the article notes that when the temporary government was installed the Dominican treasury account was overdrawn and salaries and supply bills were heavily in arrears, whereas the military government has paid off all the indebtedness, met all expenses including large repayments on the bonded debt, and accumulated a substantial surplus in the treasury by August 1, 1920. Hayden adds that the country's $20,000,000 bonded debt is expected to be paid thirty-three years before it falls due, while the military government is also expanding general education, sanitation, roads, mails, telegraphs, and port improvements.
records.summary_es: Bajo la ocupación militar los Estados Unidos han restablecido el orden en Santo Domingo, rehabilitado sus finanzas, establecido la sanidad pública e iniciado la capacitación de los dominicanos para dirigir el gobierno cuando se retire la Marina estadounidense, según un despacho. Citando un informe obtenido el 8 de octubre del comandante Reynolds Hayden, del Cuerpo Médico de la Marina de los Estados Unidos y miembro del estado mayor del gobernador militar de Santo Domingo, el artículo señala que cuando se instaló el gobierno provisional la cuenta del gobierno dominicano estaba sobregirada y había grandes atrasos en salarios y cuentas de suministros, mientras que el gobierno militar ha pagado toda la deuda, cubierto todos los gastos incluidos grandes abonos a la deuda en bonos, y acumulado un importante superávit en el tesoro para el 1 de agosto de 1920. Hayden añade que se espera pagar la deuda en bonos de $20,000,000 del país treinta y tres años antes de su vencimiento, al tiempo que el gobierno militar también amplía la educación general, la sanidad, las carreteras, el correo, los telégrafos y las mejoras portuarias.

records.headline: A geographical and historical article explains that while the Republic of Haiti occupies
records.summary_en: A geographical and historical article explains that while the Republic of Haiti occupies the western third of the island, possibilities of confusion are increased because the island is also known as Santo Domingo and San Domingo, names applied to the Dominican Republic occupying the eastern two-thirds. It notes that "Haiti," an aboriginal term meaning "high land," is widely used for the island that Christopher Columbus named Hispaniola ("Little Spain") and referred to as a "Garden of Eden" when he landed on December 6, 1492, at a spot he called "the Vale of Paradise." The passage also recounts the wreck of Columbus's flagship Santa Maria near present-day Cape Haitien on Christmas Eve, 1492, and the construction from its timbers of the Fort of Navidad, the first European structure in the Western Hemisphere.
records.summary_es: Un artículo geográfico e histórico explica que, mientras la República de Haití ocupa el tercio occidental de la isla, las posibilidades de confusión aumentan porque la isla también se conoce como Santo Domingo y San Domingo, nombres aplicados a la República Dominicana, que ocupa los dos tercios orientales. Señala que «Haití», un término aborigen que significa «tierra alta», se emplea ampliamente para designar la isla que Cristóbal Colón llamó Hispaniola («Pequeña España») y a la que se refirió como un «Jardín del Edén» cuando desembarcó el 6 de diciembre de 1492 en un punto que denominó «el Valle del Paraíso». El pasaje también relata el naufragio de la nave capitana de Colón, la Santa María, cerca del actual Cabo Haitiano en la Nochebuena de 1492, y la construcción con sus maderas del Fuerte de la Navidad, la primera estructura europea en el hemisferio occidental.

records.headline: After a turbulent history, during which the native Indians were exterminated
records.summary_en: The *Evening star* published a historical overview of the Dominican Republic, detailing its initial settlement by Spain, the eradication of indigenous inhabitants, and the importation of enslaved Africans. The article described how an eighteenth-century uprising abolished slavery and expelled colonizers, followed by shifts between Spanish and Haitian rule until the Dominican Republic secured independence in 1844. It observed that despite preserving Spanish language and institutions, the nation experienced frequent political coups and revolutions throughout its history.
records.summary_es: El *Evening star* publicó una reseña histórica de la República Dominicana, detallando su colonización inicial por parte de España, la desaparición de los pobladores indígenas y la importación de africanos esclavizados. El artículo describió cómo un levantamiento en el siglo XVIII abolió la esclavitud y expulsó a los colonizadores, seguido de sucesivas alternancias entre el dominio español y el haitiano hasta que la República Dominicana consolidó su independencia en 1844. Observó que, a pesar de conservar la lengua y las instituciones españolas, la nación experimentó frecuentes golpes políticos y revoluciones a lo largo de su historia.
records.passage: the country of which it was the capital, setting up there a court of such regal splendor that it aroused the envy of the Spanish king. Slaves Seize Power. "Santo Domingo seemed destined to become the bustling metropolis of a western empire. But it became the victim of exploitation. After a turbulent history, during which the native Indians were exterminated and thousands of African slaves were imported, the latter, assisted by mulatto freemen, rose, in the last years of the eighteenth century, abolished slavery, and drove their oppressors from the island. Though the land of the Dominican Republic reverted for a while to Spanish control, and later was conquered by the Republic of Haiti, with which it shares the island, it established its independence in 1844 and has retained its individuality since. "The territory which now constitutes the Dominican Republic has been subject at different periods to a number of nations. It has been twice under the rule of Spain and has been controlled at other times by French, English and Haitians. The Spanish influence has been the strongest, and the language of Spain and many of its customs and institutions are those of the Dominicans of today. "The Dominican Republic is peopled largely by mulattoes. While it has not been as badly torn by revolution as the 'black republic' to the west, its history has by no means been one of peaceful development, and assassinations and coups have played their part in determining the succession of its rulers. records.headline: A Washington dispatch states that in four years of military occupation
records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch states that in four years of military occupation, the United States has restored order, rehabilitated finances, established public sanitation, and begun training Dominicans to carry on the government when the American Navy withdraws. Citing an October 3 report by Commander Reynolds Hayden of the U.S. Navy Medical Corps, a staff member of the military governor of Santo Domingo, the article notes that the Dominican government account was overdrawn by $14,234.33 when the temporary government was installed, whereas the military government has paid all 1916 indebtedness, met all government expenses, and held $3,200,000 in the treasury on August 1, 1920. The report adds that the country's $20,000,000 bonded debt due in 1958 is expected to be paid in 1925, and that the military government is extending general education and sanitation while creating communications, roads, mills, telegraphs, and port improvements.
records.summary_es: Un despacho desde Washington afirma que, en cuatro años de ocupación militar, Estados Unidos ha restablecido el orden, rehabilitado las finanzas, establecido la sanidad pública e iniciado la capacitación de dominicanos para dirigir el gobierno cuando se retire la Armada estadounidense. Citando un informe del 3 de octubre del comandante Reynolds Hayden, del Cuerpo Médico de la Armada de Estados Unidos y miembro del estado mayor del gobernador militar de Santo Domingo, el artículo señala que la cuenta del gobierno dominicano tenía un sobregiro de $14,234.33 cuando se instaló el gobierno temporal, mientras que el gobierno militar ha pagado todo el endeudamiento de 1916, cubierto todos los gastos gubernamentales y mantenía $3,200,000 en el tesoro el 1 de agosto de 1920. El informe añade que se espera que la deuda en bonos del país de $20,000,000, con vencimiento en 1958, quede saldada en 1925, y que el gobierno militar está ampliando la educación general y la sanidad al tiempo que crea comunicaciones, caminos, molinos, telégrafos y mejoras portuarias.

records.headline: In a first-person account under the subheading "Stories of Eyewitnesses,"
records.summary_en: In a first-person account under the subheading "Stories of Eyewitnesses," the writer states that U.S. Marines who have served in Haiti and in San Domingo readily recount what they learned there. During a stay at Santiago de los Caballeros in San Domingo, the author met a talkative marine on his third enlistment who had been through most of the trouble in Haiti and boasted of his experiences. The writer recalls the marine saying that his unit was ordered up a valley near Port au Prince with orders to kill and burn everything they came across.
records.summary_es: En un relato en primera persona bajo el subtítulo «Relatos de testigos presenciales», el autor afirma que los infantes de marina estadounidenses que han prestado servicio en Haití y en San Domingo cuentan sin reparos lo que conocieron allí. Durante una estancia en Santiago de los Caballeros, en San Domingo, el autor conoció a un locuaz infante de marina en su tercer período de alistamiento que había vivido la mayor parte de los disturbios en Haití y alardeaba de sus experiencias. El escritor recuerda que el infante de marina dijo que a su unidad se le ordenó subir por un valle cerca de Port au Prince con órdenes de matar y quemar todo lo que encontraran a su paso.

records.headline: Writer David J. Davies argues
records.summary_en: Writer David J. Davies argues that the secrecy surrounding the conduct of United States marines in Hayti and San Domingo is lifting, as Major-General George Barnett's letter calling for a full investigation focuses public attention on the occupation. He recounts stories told by marines who served in both republics, including a former steel worker he met at Santiago de los Caballeros who boasted of orders to kill and burn everything in a valley near Port au Prince and of natives being killed for the fun of it.
records.summary_es: El escritor David J. Davies argumenta que el secreto que rodea la conducta de los infantes de marina de los Estados Unidos en Haití y Santo Domingo se está levantando, a medida que la carta del mayor general George Barnett pidiendo una investigación completa centra la atención pública en la ocupación. Relata historias contadas por infantes de marina que sirvieron en ambas repúblicas, incluido un ex trabajador del acero que conoció en Santiago de los Caballeros y que se jactaba de órdenes de matar y quemar todo en un valle cerca de Puerto Príncipe y de nativos asesinados por diversión.
records.passage: [illegible] The statement in Col. Russell's letter that only twelve marines have been killed during the occupation of Hayti is at variance with the stories of the marines who served there with Waller and Butler and appeared to know whereof they spoke. I can recall the night we stopped at Monte Christi en route for Puerto Plata on our way from the States. A sergeant coming aboard with other officers reported that on the night before a party of marines had been waylaid and seven of them killed. There was in the party the wife of a Major, but she had escaped unhurt. Doubtless the marines — officers as well as men — suffered great provocation — not "doubtless"; they did! Little wonder then that their morals as well as their morale suffered to that extent that the Navy Department felt impelled to despatch a special agent to the island in an effort to work out the salvation — physical and spiritual — of [illegible] there. That special agent was a Pittsburgher. His report submitted after several months in Hayti caused a furor of doubt and excitement in official circles. At once preparations were made to ameliorate conditions, and beginning late in 1918 some improvements were worked out. Young men who went to Hayti clean and wholesome remained clean and wholesome only for a brief, brief time. Many of them left there wrecks of their former selves; they were in such condition as to be better dead. Others — and many of them — were sent home raving maniacs. records.headline: Mr. Knowles charged that Santo Domingo's territorial integrity
records.summary_en: Mr. Knowles charged that Santo Domingo's territorial integrity and political independence had been completely destroyed by American occupation forces acting under the direct orders of President Wilson and his Secretary of the Navy, the article states, reporting on his speech. Knowles alleged that American marines committed numerous atrocities and murders, recounted the forcible expulsion by the American admiral of the constitutionally chosen Dominican president, the dissolution of the Dominican Congress, and the unseating of every civil government official, and contended that martial law and censorship were no less severe than what the Germans inflicted upon the Belgians. He further declared that a reign of terror had existed in Santo Domingo for the past four years, calling the invasion unwarranted and charging that the Wilson administration had scrapped the Monroe Doctrine.
records.summary_es: El Sr. Knowles denunció que la integridad territorial y la independencia política de Santo Domingo habían sido completamente destruidas por las fuerzas de ocupación estadounidenses bajo las órdenes directas del presidente Wilson y su secretario de Marina, según señala el artículo al informar sobre su discurso. Knowles alegó que los infantes de marina estadounidenses cometieron numerosas atrocidades y asesinatos, relató la expulsión forzosa por el almirante estadounidense del presidente constitucionalmente elegido de la República Dominicana, la disolución del Congreso dominicano y la destitución de todos los funcionarios del gobierno civil, y sostuvo que la ley marcial y la censura no eran menos severas que las infligidas por los alemanes a los belgas. Declaró además que durante los últimos cuatro años había existido un régimen de terror en Santo Domingo, calificando la invasión de injustificada y acusando a la administración de Wilson de haber desechado la Doctrina Monroe.

records.headline: According to a military personnel notice, several U.S. Marine Corps officers
records.summary_en: According to a military personnel notice, several U.S. Marine Corps officers stationed in Santo Domingo and Haiti have been ordered home while others have been ordered to those countries. Major E. H. Ellis of the 2d Brigade in the Dominican Republic is assigned to marine headquarters in the city while Major F. D. Gilmore is ordered to the 2d Brigade, and Captains R. E. Messersmith and A. H. Page are assigned to duty in Santo Domingo while Captain W. A. Worton is ordered from there to Portsmouth, New Hampshire. In addition, Captain O. H. Hine at marine headquarters has been assigned to duty with the 1st Brigade in Haiti.
records.summary_es: Según un aviso de personal militar, varios oficiales del Cuerpo de Infantería de Marina de Estados Unidos destacados en Santo Domingo y Haití han recibido órdenes de regresar al país, mientras que otros han sido destinados a esas naciones. El mayor E. H. Ellis, de la 2.ª Brigada en la República Dominicana, es asignado al cuartel general de la Infantería de Marina en la ciudad, mientras que el mayor F. D. Gilmore es destinado a la 2.ª Brigada; asimismo, los capitanes R. E. Messersmith y A. H. Page son asignados al servicio en Santo Domingo, en tanto que el capitán W. A. Worton recibe órdenes de trasladarse desde allí a Portsmouth, New Hampshire. Además, el capitán O. H. Hine, en el cuartel general de la Infantería de Marina, ha sido asignado al servicio con la 1.ª Brigada en Haití.

records.summary_en: An article reports that in four years of military occupation in Santo Domingo, the United States has restored order, rehabilitated finances, established public sanitation and compulsory education, and begun training Dominicans to run the government when the American Navy withdraws. It quotes a report by Commander Reynolds Hayden of the U.S. Navy Medical Corps, a member of the staff of the military governor of Santo Domingo, before cutting off mid-sentence as he explains that the military government was established in November four years earlier because of seriously disturbed conditions dangerous to Dominicans and foreigners and repeated failures of the Dominican authorities.

records.headline: Opening mid-sentence, this article states that during its military occupation
records.summary_en: Opening mid-sentence, this article states that during its military occupation the United States has put the republic of Santo Domingo on its feet, restored order, rehabilitated finances, established public sanitation, and begun training Dominicans to carry on the government when the American Navy withdraws. It quotes an October 3 report by Commander Reynolds Hayden of the U.S. Navy Medical Corps, a member of the staff of the military governor of Santo Domingo, noting that the Dominican government account was overdrawn by $14,234.33 when the temporary government was installed, whereas the military government has since paid all 1910 indebtedness, met all government expenses, and held $3,200,000 in the treasury on August 1, 1920. Hayden's report adds that the country's $20,000,000 bonded debt due in 1938 is expected to be paid in 1925, and that the military government is extending education and sanitation while creating communications, roads, mills, telegraphs, and port improvements.
records.summary_es: Iniciándose a mitad de oración, este artículo afirma que durante su ocupación militar Estados Unidos ha puesto en pie a la república de Santo Domingo, restablecido el orden, rehabilitado las finanzas, establecido la sanidad pública y comenzado a capacitar a dominicanos para dirigir el gobierno cuando se retire la Armada estadounidense. Cita un informe del 3 de octubre del comandante Reynolds Hayden, del Cuerpo Médico de la Armada de Estados Unidos y miembro del estado mayor del gobernador militar de Santo Domingo, en el que se señala que la cuenta del gobierno dominicano tenía un sobregiro de $14,234.33 cuando se instaló el gobierno temporal, mientras que desde entonces el gobierno militar ha pagado todo el endeudamiento de 1910, cubierto todos los gastos gubernamentales y mantenía $3,200,000 en el tesoro el 1 de agosto de 1920. El informe de Hayden añade que se espera que la deuda en bonos del país de $20,000,000, con vencimiento en 1938, sea pagada en 1925, y que el gobierno militar está ampliando la educación y la sanidad al tiempo que crea comunicaciones, caminos, molinos, telégrafos y mejoras portuarias.

records.headline: This historical sketch recounts that Christopher Columbus's body
records.summary_en: This historical sketch recounts that Christopher Columbus's body was brought from Spain to the island of his early triumphs and placed beside his son Diego, and that later examinations of the Santo Domingo cathedral burial vaults indicated that the casket taken to Havana when Spain transferred sovereignty to France in 1796—and a century later to Spain—contained the ashes of Diego instead. The article describes how Diego Columbus established a court of regal splendor in Santo Domingo that aroused the Spanish king's envy, and how the city, though seemingly destined to become a bustling metropolis, became the victim of exploitation. After the extermination of the native Indians and the importation of thousands of African slaves, the slaves and mulatto freemen rose at the end of the eighteenth century, abolished slavery, and drove out their oppressors, before the land of the Dominican Republic briefly reverted to Spanish control and was later conquered by the Republic of Haiti, where the passage cuts off.

El artículo describe cómo Diego Colón estableció en Santo Domingo una corte de esplendor regio que despertó la envidia del rey español, y cómo la ciudad, aunque parecía destinada a convertirse en una bulliciosa metrópoli, fue víctima de la explotación. Tras el exterminio de los indígenas nativos y la importación de miles de esclavos africanos, los esclavos y los libertos mulatos se sublevaron a finales del siglo XVIII, abolieron la esclavitud y expulsaron a sus opresores, antes de que el territorio de la República Dominicana volviera por un tiempo al dominio español y fuera luego conquistado por la República de Haití, punto en el que se corta el pasaje.

records.headline: Opening mid-sentence on Spain's 1795 transfer of sovereignty
records.summary_en: Opening mid-sentence on Spain's 1795 transfer of sovereignty to France, this historical account states that later examinations of the cathedral burial vaults indicated that the casket borne from Santo Domingo to Havana at the end of the eighteenth century, and a century later to Spain, contained the ashes of Diego Columbus rather than his father. It notes that Diego Columbus set up a court of regal splendor in Santo Domingo that aroused the envy of the Spanish king, and recounts how the city suffered exploitation, the extermination of the native Indians, the importation of African slaves, and a late-eighteenth-century uprising by slaves and mulatto freemen that abolished slavery. The article concludes that although the land of the Dominican Republic reverted for a while to Spanish control and was later conquered by the Republic of Haiti, with which it shares the island, it established its independence in 1844 and has retained its individuality ever since.
records.summary_es: Comenzando a mitad de frase sobre la transferencia de soberanía de España a Francia en 1795, este relato histórico señala que exámenes posteriores de las bóvedas funerarias de la catedral indicaron que el féretro llevado desde Santo Domingo a La Habana a finales del siglo XVIII, y un siglo después a España, contenía las cenizas de Diego Colón en lugar de las de su padre. Apunta que Diego Colón instaló en Santo Domingo una corte de esplendor regio que despertó la envidia del rey español, y relata cómo la ciudad sufrió la explotación, el exterminio de los indígenas nativos, la importación de esclavos africanos y un levantamiento a finales del siglo XVIII de esclavos y libertos mulatos que abolió la esclavitud. El artículo concluye que, aunque el territorio de la República Dominicana volvió por un tiempo al control español y más tarde fue conquistado por la República de Haití, con la que comparte la isla, estableció su independencia en 1844 y ha conservado su individualidad desde entonces.
