records.headline: This historical feature relates that Christopher Columbus's body
records.summary_en: This historical feature relates that Christopher Columbus's body was brought from Spain to the island of his early triumphs, and that although the Spaniards were thought to have removed his remains when transferring sovereignty to the French in 1795, later examinations of the cathedral burial vaults indicated that the casket borne from Santo Domingo to Havana and a century later to Spain contained the ashes of his son Diego instead. While Columbus did not live to see much of Santo Domingo's early growth, Diego Columbus engraved the family name deeper on the capital and country by setting up a court of regal splendor that aroused the Spanish king's envy. After describing how the native Indians were exterminated and thousands of imported African slaves, assisted by mulatto freemen, rose in the late eighteenth century to abolish slavery and drive out their oppressors, the passage notes that the land of the Dominican Republic reverted for a while to Spanish control and was later conquered by the Republic of Haiti, where the text breaks off.
records.summary_es: Este artículo histórico relata que el cuerpo de Cristóbal Colón fue llevado desde España a la isla de sus primeros triunfos y que, aunque se pensaba que los españoles habían retirado sus restos al transferir la soberanía a los franceses en 1795, exámenes posteriores de las bóvedas funerarias de la catedral indicaron que el féretro trasladado desde Santo Domingo a La Habana y un siglo más tarde a España contenía en realidad las cenizas de su hijo Diego. Aunque Colón no vivió para ver gran parte del crecimiento temprano de Santo Domingo, Diego Colón grabó más profundamente el apellido familiar en la capital y en el país al establecer una corte de esplendor regio que despertó la envidia del rey español. Tras describir cómo los indígenas nativos fueron exterminados y miles de esclavos africanos importados, ayudados por libertos mulatos, se levantaron a finales del siglo XVIII para abolir la esclavitud y expulsar a sus opresores, el pasaje señala que el territorio de la República Dominicana volvió por un tiempo al control español y más tarde fue conquistado por la República de Haití, punto en el que se interrumpe el texto.

records.headline: A December 4 dispatch from Havana reports that Venezuelan writer
records.summary_en: A December 4 dispatch from Havana reports that Venezuelan writer and poet Horatio Blanco Fombona landed at Santiago, Cuba, the previous day after reportedly being expelled from the Dominican Republic following his arrest in Santo Domingo the previous month by American military authorities. According to a dispatch to the newspaper El Mundo, American authorities deported him for alleged newspaper activities tending to incite the native population to mutiny against American authority. While imprisoned in Santo Domingo, Fombona undertook a hunger strike to protest his detention and the class of food provided.
records.summary_es: Un despacho del 4 de diciembre desde La Habana informa que el escritor y poeta venezolano Horatio Blanco Fombona desembarcó la víspera en Santiago de Cuba tras haber sido presuntamente expulsado de la República Dominicana luego de su arresto en Santo Domingo el mes anterior por las autoridades militares estadounidenses. Según un despacho enviado al periódico El Mundo, las autoridades estadounidenses lo deportaron por supuestas actividades periodísticas tendientes a incitar a la población nativa a amotinarse contra la autoridad estadounidense. Mientras estuvo preso en Santo Domingo, Fombona inició una huelga de hambre en protesta por su detención y por la clase de comida suministrada.

records.headline: Citing the "Review," the article reports a Protestant program
records.summary_en: Citing the "Review," the article reports a Protestant program contemplating the expenditure of more than a million dollars over the next five years and the employment of thirty foreign and fifty native workers in the Dominican Republic. The plan provides for an "institutional" church, an industrial school, a hospital, and a bookstore in the capital city of Santo Domingo, similar proselytizing facilities in Santiago, and "institutional" churches and hospitals at five other locations. The report adds that Rear Admiral Snowden, who according to the "Review" approved these plans for Protestant propaganda, had refused the previous January to grant demands by Archbishop Adolfo A. Nouel and other prominent Dominicans for modifications to the military dictatorship governing the republic since the 1916 American occupation, prompting the archbishop and his associates on the Consulting Board to resign, with their correspondence published in The Nation on July 17, 1920.

El plan prevé una iglesia «institucional», una escuela industrial, un hospital y una librería en la ciudad capital de Santo Domingo, instalaciones similares de proselitismo en Santiago, e iglesias «institucionales» y hospitales en otros cinco lugares. He states that only a limited number of diplomatic functionaries in direct contact with the Navy Department possess knowledge of the question, and that without a casual allusion by President-elect Harding, the "tombstone of silence" would still weigh on the Dominican people. The former president and his nephew assert that reports of ill treatment of Dominicans by United States marines are "absolutely true," express conviction that the liberty and sovereignty of Santo Domingo will be restored, and announce plans to visit Rio Janeiro, Buenos Aires, and Pacific coast cities.

records.headline: Opening mid-sentence on the withdrawal from the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Opening mid-sentence on the withdrawal from the Dominican Republic under the Christmas Eve proclamation issued at Santo Domingo by direction of President Wilson, this item reports that Secretary Daniels conferred that day with State Department officials regarding the membership of a commission to revise Dominican laws and frame new statutes enabling the Dominicans to govern their country. Rear Admiral Thomas Snowden, Naval Governor of Santo Domingo, will appoint the commission upon recommendations from Washington, and Daniels stated that the withdrawal of American forces will begin after the Dominican Congress approves the new statutes and puts them into effect.
records.summary_es: Comenzando a mitad de frase sobre el retiro de la República Dominicana bajo la proclama de Nochebuena emitida en Santo Domingo por instrucción del presidente Wilson, esta nota informa que el secretario Daniels conferenció ese día con funcionarios del Departamento de Estado respecto a la integración de una comisión encargada de revisar las leyes dominicanas y redactar nuevos estatutos que permitan a los dominicanos gobernar su país. El contralmirante Thomas Snowden, gobernador naval de Santo Domingo, nombrará la comisión por recomendación de Washington, y Daniels declaró que el retiro de las fuerzas estadounidenses comenzará después de que el Congreso dominicano apruebe los nuevos estatutos y los ponga en vigor.

records.headline: The possibility that the island of Haiti might become a pawn
records.summary_en: The *Springfield weekly Republican* discussed prospective U.S. withdrawal from Santo Domingo, observing that wartime strategic concerns and foreign debt disputes had prompted military guardianship over the island of Hispaniola. Acting Secretary of State Davis noted that the occupation grew out of the 1907 convention establishing an American customs receivership and barring unauthorized debt expansion. The article observed that Dominican authorities later violated the convention by increasing public debt to finance the suppression of domestic rebellions.
records.summary_es: El *Springfield weekly Republican* analizó la proyectada retirada de Estados Unidos de Santo Domingo, observando que las preocupaciones estratégicas en tiempos de guerra y las disputas por la deuda externa habían motivado la tutela militar sobre la isla de La Española. El secretario de Estado interino Davis señaló que la ocupación derivó de la convención de 1907, la cual estableció la receptoría general de aduanas estadounidense y prohibió el aumento no autorizado de la deuda. El artículo indicó que las autoridades dominicanas violaron posteriormente dicha convención al incrementar la deuda pública para financiar la represión de rebeliones internas.
records.passage: steps looking to its withdrawal suggests an experience in guardianship of an interesting sort. The public would like to hear more about it. It is more than a coincidence, of course, that the period of military occupation has been commensurate with the latter half of the war and the early stage of international adjustment. The possibility that the island of Haiti might become a pawn in the great game explains in part, no doubt, the relation of the United States toward the island's two little republics during the past few years. It was important that they should be assured stable and responsible government of some sort in view of foreign claims upon their resources and foreign appreciation of their strategic location. The present status of Santo Domingo, or the Dominican Republic, is a direct outgrowth, however, of conditions existing long before the war. It was in 1907, in the administration of President Roosevelt, that a treaty was concluded, as Acting Secretary of State Davis explains, by which Santo Domingo agreed to the appointment of an American receiver-general of customs for the purpose of meeting the obligations of the national debt and also agreed that the debt should not be increased without the approval of the United States. This course was held to be desirable because of the danger of European intervention prompted by the Dominicans' failure to pay the interest on their foreign loans. records.summary_en: The *Evening star* reported that the United States initiated steps toward withdrawing forces from Santo Domingo and establishing a native governing commission to restore self-government. The report recounted that naval officers instituted military rule in 1916 after provisional president Francisco Henriquez y Carvajal refused terms of a proposed treaty. Under the occupation, Dominican school enrollment grew from 18,000 to 100,000 pupils, and gross annual revenues expanded from $4,600,000 to over $7,000,000.
records.summary_es: El *Evening star* informó que Estados Unidos inició medidas destinadas a retirar sus tropas de Santo Domingo y establecer una comisión de gobierno nativa para restaurar el autogobierno. La crónica relató que oficiales de la armada impusieron el régimen militar en 1916 luego de que el presidente provisional Francisco Henríquez y Carvajal rechazara las condiciones de un tratado propuesto. Durante la ocupación, la matrícula escolar dominicana aumentó de 18 000 a 100 000 alumnos, y los ingresos fiscales brutos anuales se incrementaron de 4 600 000 dólares a más de 7 000 000 de dólares.
records.passage: into Domingo and the United States landed naval forces to prevent further bloodshed. Dr. Henriquez y Carvajal was elected provisional president, but the United States refused to recognize his government until he agreed to the provisions of the proposed treaty of 1915. He refused, and the United States declined to pay to his government the revenues collected under the treaty of 1907. This condition continued until the United States directed the naval officer in charge of the naval forces in Dominican waters to assume direction of affairs, and in 1916 a temporary military government was proclaimed. At that time there were 18,000 children attending school in Santo Domingo. Now there are 100,000 pupils, and the gross revenues of the republic have increased from about $4,600,[illegible] to more than $7,000,000. The United States has begun steps toward a withdrawal of its forces in Santo Domingo and the appointment of a governing commission of Dominicans, the ultimate [illegible] will be the restoration of self-government in Santo Domingo. Although the government of Haiti is directly under Haitians, the United States has maintained a military force there to insure order since July 28, 1915. For the first time in more than a century tranquillity and security of life and property exist in Haiti. records.headline: A group of prominent Spaniards—including former Premier Count
records.summary_en: A group of prominent Spaniards—including former Premier Count Romanones, former Minister of Public Works Francisco Cambo, and Professor Miguel Unamuno of Salamanca University—has addressed a message to President Harding protesting the U.S. troop occupation of Santo Domingo and the suppression of rights and liberties there. The signers invoke the ideals of the United States in favor of the Dominican Republic, stating that the triumph of those ideals would win the United States a new title of respect and the admiration of humanity. The report recalls that Count Romanones, Cambo, and other prominent men of Spain sent a similar address to President Wilson in September 1919 suggesting that the time was propitious to withdraw U.S. troops and restore the regime annulled by the military occupation.
records.summary_es: Un grupo de prominentes españoles —entre ellos el ex primer ministro conde de Romanones, el exministro de Obras Públicas Francisco Cambo y el profesor Miguel Unamuno de la Universidad de Salamanca— ha dirigido un mensaje al presidente Harding en protesta por la ocupación de Santo Domingo por tropas estadounidenses y la supresión de derechos y libertades allí. Los firmantes invocan los ideales de los Estados Unidos en favor de la República Dominicana, afirmando que el triunfo de esos ideales ganaría para los Estados Unidos un nuevo título de respeto y la admiración de la humanidad. La nota recuerda que el conde de Romanones, Cambo y otros hombres prominentes de España enviaron un mensaje similar al presidente Wilson en septiembre de 1919 sugiriendo que el momento era propicio para retirar las tropas estadounidenses y restaurar el régimen anulado por la ocupación militar.

records.headline: Steps for withdrawing American control over the government of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Steps for withdrawing American control over the government of the Dominican Republic are under consideration by Secretary Hughes, and President Harding is expected to issue a statement on the matter soon. Withdrawal plans prepared under President Wilson's direction—announced on December 24 and providing for a commission of Dominicans to confer with an American technical adviser on details including a new constitution—are understood to be subject to some modification. Although that commission is understood to be already at work under the island republic's naval government, the nature of the modifications under consideration was not disclosed.
records.summary_es: El secretario Hughes estudia medidas para el retiro del control estadounidense sobre el gobierno de la República Dominicana, y se espera que el presidente Harding emita pronto una declaración sobre el asunto. Se entiende que los planes de retiro preparados bajo la dirección del presidente Wilson —anunciados el 24 de diciembre y que contemplaban una comisión de dominicanos para conferenciar con un asesor técnico estadounidense sobre detalles que incluían una nueva constitución— serán modificados en cierta medida. Aunque se tiene entendido que dicha comisión ya está trabajando bajo el gobierno naval de la república isleña, no se reveló la naturaleza de las modificaciones en estudio.

records.headline: An April Associated Press dispatch from Washington reports that Secretary Hughes
records.summary_en: An April Associated Press dispatch from Washington reports that Secretary Hughes is considering steps for the withdrawal of American control over the Dominican Republic's government and that President Harding is expected to issue a statement soon. According to the dispatch, the withdrawal plans prepared under President Wilson's direction and announced on December 24 last—which included appointing a commission of Dominicans to work out details, including a new constitution, with an American technical adviser—are to be modified somewhat. The commission is understood to be already working under the naval government of the island republic, and the nature of the proposed modifications was not disclosed.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de abril de la Associated Press desde Washington informa que el secretario Hughes está considerando medidas para el retiro del control estadounidense sobre el gobierno de la República Dominicana y que se espera que el presidente Harding emita pronto una declaración. Según el despacho, los planes de retiro preparados bajo la dirección del presidente Wilson y dados a conocer el 24 de diciembre pasado —que incluían el nombramiento de una comisión de dominicanos para elaborar detalles, incluida una nueva constitución, junto con un asesor técnico estadounidense— serán modificados en cierta medida. Se entiende que la comisión ya trabaja bajo el gobierno naval de la república isleña, y no se reveló la naturaleza de las modificaciones propuestas.

records.headline: A Washington dispatch dated April 22 reports that two U.S. Marine Corps
records.summary_en: A Washington dispatch dated April 22 reports that two U.S. Marine Corps airplanes, having departed on March 29, arrived safely at Bolling Field from Fayetteville, North Carolina, completing a 5,000-mile round-trip aerial journey to the Dominican Republic and back. Escorted from Fayetteville to Washington by three other Marine Corps planes, the expedition had originally intended to blaze an air trail from Washington to the Virgin Islands, but an outbreak of bubonic plague at San Juan, Puerto Rico, caused the fliers to turn back from Santo Domingo.

Escoltada desde Fayetteville hasta Washington por otros tres aviones del Cuerpo de Marines, la expedición tenía originalmente el propósito de abrir una ruta aérea desde Washington hasta las Islas Vírgenes, pero un brote de peste bubónica en San Juan, Puerto Rico, hizo que los aviadores regresaran desde Santo Domingo.

records.headline: It is frequently said that a revolution would follow the departure
records.summary_en: The *Dearborn independent* argued that an immediate withdrawal of American marines from Haiti would quickly lead to revolution and governmental collapse. The article contrasted the French colonial period's agricultural prosperity with the nation's condition following Toussaint L'Ouverture's uprising and Jean-Jacques Dessalines's 1804 declaration of independence. It asserted that more than a century of post-independence conflict and despotic leadership had ruined the country's plantations and civil institutions.

Aseguró que más de un siglo de conflictos y caudillismos despóticos posteriores a la independencia habían arruinado las plantaciones y las instituciones civiles del país.

For more than a century the Haytian mass have followed the African instinct back to barbarism. Previous to 1804 by fifty years their land under the French had become the richest area in the West Indies. Great plantations of sugar and coffee covered the land. Beautiful cities, built after the French plan, graced the seaports, which were constantly filled with craft carrying the products to Europe. Napoleon looked upon his West Indian possession as the richest under the flag of France. When Toussaint L'Ouverture, an ex-slave, led a revolt against the French land and slave owners in 1798, there started a period of terror which ended in 1804 when Dessalines, the successor of L'Ouverture stood on the seashore at Gonaives, tore the French tricolor into three pieces, cast away the white and ordered the red and blue bars to be fastened together as the flag of independent Hayti. The whites had been expelled. Generations of despotism, revolution and strife have followed. The great plantations of the French, their rich architectural dwellings both in city and country have gone the way of ruin. The ruling class one finds today in Hayti is gathered in the cities. records.headline: Opening mid-sentence on the question of withdrawing the U.S. military occupation of Santo
records.summary_en: Opening mid-sentence on the question of withdrawing the U.S. military occupation of Santo Domingo, this report states that the U.S. government intends to withdraw its force of 2,148 American Marines as soon as a government can be firmly established in the Dominican Republic. The republic is currently under the authority of an American military governor and is without its own president. A complete policy on the withdrawal of the occupation of Santo Domingo has been decided upon by Secretary of State Hughes and awaits only formal approval by President Harding before being announced in a few days.
records.summary_es: Iniciando a mitad de oración sobre la cuestión del retiro de la ocupación militar estadounidense de Santo Domingo, este informe señala que el gobierno de los Estados Unidos tiene la intención de retirar su fuerza de 2,148 marines estadounidenses tan pronto como pueda establecerse firmemente un gobierno en la República Dominicana. En la actualidad, la república se encuentra bajo la autoridad de un gobernador militar estadounidense y carece de su propio presidente. El secretario de Estado Hughes ha decidido una política completa sobre el retiro de la ocupación de Santo Domingo, la cual solo aguarda la aprobación formal del presidente Harding antes de ser anunciada en pocos días.

records.headline: President Wilson near the close of his second administration
records.summary_en: The *Evening star* reported that President Harding, Secretary Hughes, and Secretary Denby approved a proclamation establishing procedures for withdrawing the military government from the Dominican Republic. The plan directed primary assemblies to convene within a month to choose electors, who would elect senators and deputies and nominate judges under the Dominican constitution. Delegates appointed by the military governor would then negotiate an evacuation convention to ratify military government acts, validate a $2,500,000 public works loan, and extend customs receivership duties.
records.summary_es: El *Evening star* informó que el presidente Harding, el secretario Hughes y el secretario Denby aprobaron una proclama que establecía el procedimiento para retirar el gobierno militar de la República Dominicana. El plan ordenaba convocar asambleas primarias en el plazo de un mes para designar electores, quienes elegirían a senadores y diputados y nominarían jueces conforme a la constitución dominicana. Delegados designados por el gobernador militar negociarían luego una convención de evacuación para ratificar las disposiciones del gobierno militar, convalidar un préstamo de 2 500 000 dólares para obras públicas y prorrogar las funciones de la receptoría de aduanas.

records.headline: This financial notice, opening mid-sentence on a Dominican bond
records.summary_en: This financial notice, opening mid-sentence on a Dominican bond issue payable in U.S. gold coin in New York free of Dominican taxes, explains that a sinking fund will retire at least one-quarter of the bonds annually at 105 and interest through semi-annual drawings by lot beginning December 1, with any remaining bonds paid at 105 and interest at maturity. Approved by the U.S. government under the 1907 American-Dominican convention and by the U.S. military government of Santo Domingo, the bonds are secured by customs and other revenues, extend the duties of the general receiver of Dominican customs, and bind any Dominican government to accept the issue as a legal, irrevocable obligation. Proceeds will mainly fund the completion of essential public works—such as roads, port improvements, and schools—under American engineers' supervision, along with retiring certificates of indebtedness, while funds used for supplies and equipment will be spent in the United States.
records.summary_es: Esta nota financiera, que se inicia a mitad de oración sobre una emisión de bonos dominicanos pagaderos en moneda de oro de los Estados Unidos en Nueva York y libres de impuestos dominicanos, explica que un fondo de amortización retirará al menos una cuarta parte de los bonos anualmente a 105 más intereses mediante sorteos semestrales a partir del 1 de diciembre, pagándose los bonos restantes a 105 más intereses al vencimiento. Aprobados por el gobierno estadounidense bajo la convención domínico-americana de 1907 y por el gobierno militar de los Estados Unidos en Santo Domingo, los bonos están garantizados por las rentas aduaneras y otros ingresos, extienden las funciones del receptor general de aduanas dominicanas y comprometen a cualquier gobierno de la República Dominicana a aceptar la emisión como una obligación legal e irrevocable. Los fondos se destinarán principalmente a concluir obras públicas esenciales —como carreteras, mejoras portuarias y escuelas— bajo la supervisión de ingenieros estadounidenses, así como a retirar certificados de deuda, mientras que la parte empleada en suministros y equipos se gastará en los Estados Unidos.

records.headline: The U.S. military government of Santo Domingo announced the issuance
records.summary_en: The U.S. military government of Santo Domingo announced the issuance on behalf of the Dominican Republic of a closed issue of $2,500,000 of four-year customs administration 8 per cent sinking fund gold bonds, which were purchased by the Equitable Trust Company of New York and Speyer & Co. and offered for public subscription. Lieutenant Commander Arthur H. Mayo, Supply Corps, U.S. Navy, administering the Department of Finance and Commerce for the military government, states that the bonds are dated June 1 and running for four years, secured by customs and other revenues, and carry a sinking fund to redeem at least one-quarter of the loan annually through semi-annual drawings in New York by the Equitable Trust Company as fiscal agent. In approving the issue, the State Department authorized a clause securing the consent of the United States before the passage cuts off.

records.summary_en: Information furnished by Lieutenant Commander Arthur H. Mayo, Supply Corps, U.S. Navy, the officer administering the Department of Finance and Commerce for the U.S. Military Government, states that the Dominican bond issue has been approved by the U.S. government under the American-Dominican Convention of 1907 and by the U.S. Military Government of Santo Domingo, with unretired bonds payable at maturity at 105 and accrued interest. The bonds include a clause binding any government of the Dominican Republic to accept and validate the issue as a legal, binding, and irrevocable obligation and extending the duties of the General Receiver of Dominican Customs under the 1907 convention to the issue. Until all the bonds are redeemed, the Dominican Republic agrees not to increase its public debt or modify its customs duties without prior U.S. consent, and its customs revenues will continue to be collected by a General Receiver appointed by and responsible to the U.S. president.

records.headline: A June 21 dispatch from Santo Domingo reports that an enormous demonstration
records.summary_en: A June 21 dispatch from Santo Domingo reports that an enormous demonstration was held there on Sunday supporting the unconditional withdrawal of U.S. military forces and asking that Santo Domingo assume no further obligations beyond the 1907 customs convention. Leaders of the demonstration handed the military governor a letter addressed to President Harding embodying the people's protests. The archbishop, supreme court members, lawyers, and university faculties participated in the meeting, which demanded the refusal of the United States' offer of conditional withdrawal.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de Santo Domingo del 21 de junio informa que el domingo se celebró allí una enorme manifestación en apoyo del retiro incondicional de las fuerzas militares estadounidenses y para pedir que Santo Domingo no asuma más obligaciones que las de la convención aduanera de 1907. Los dirigentes de la manifestación entregaron al gobernador militar una carta dirigida al presidente Harding que recogía las protestas del pueblo. El arzobispo, miembros de la Suprema Corte, abogados y las facultades universitarias participaron en el acto, en el cual se exigió rechazar la oferta estadounidense de un retiro condicional.

records.headline: An Associated Press dispatch dated June 20 from Santo Domingo reports
records.summary_en: An Associated Press dispatch dated June 20 from Santo Domingo reports that a large demonstration was held there the previous day calling for the unconditional withdrawal of U.S. military forces and urging that Santo Domingo take on no obligation beyond the 1907 convention for U.S. assistance with customs revenues. The demonstration's leaders delivered a protest letter addressed to President Harding to the military governor. Participating in the meeting were the archbishop, members of the supreme court, lawyers, and university faculties, who demanded that the American offer of conditional withdrawal be refused.

records.summary_en: The *New York herald* reported that the U.S. government conditioned the withdrawal of troops from the Dominican Republic on guarantees that developmental loans and obligations would be respected. During the occupation, the United States oversaw the construction of schools and highways funded through a $2,500,000 loan. Officials warned that American marines would remain and military rule would continue unless the Dominican government provided binding assurances that these financial commitments would be fulfilled.
records.summary_es: El *New York herald* informó que el gobierno estadounidense condicionó la retirada de tropas de la República Dominicana a garantías de que se respetarían los empréstitos y obligaciones de fomento. Durante la ocupación, Estados Unidos supervisó la construcción de escuelas y carreteras financiadas mediante un préstamo de 2 500 000 dólares. Las autoridades advirtieron que los infantes de marina estadounidenses permanecerían y el régimen militar continuaría a menos que el gobierno dominicano brindara seguridades vinculantes de que se cumplirían dichos compromisos financieros.
records.passage: [illegible] by which American troops are to be withdrawn. The Government finds itself in the position of the person who has adopted a ward, has given to it a rudimentary education and has incurred obligations for its further improvement, and desires to assure itself that these obligations will be observed. It might happen that the ward would prove unwilling to carry out the terms of these obligations. That is the situation in which the Government of the United States finds itself. During its occupation the United States started the construction of schools, roads and other improvements, and negotiated a minimum loan of $2,500,000 to insure the completion of those improvements for the advantage of the Dominican people. Before evacuating the republic the Government of the United States wants assurance doubly sure that those obligations will be taken care of. Without such assurances the American marines will remain in the island and the present military Government will continue. It was explained that the proclamation is not in answer to the recent protest made by the Dominicans to the terms of evacuation, but merely to clarify the situation. records.headline: Quoting Dominican President Henriquez on the 1916 U.S. intervention
records.summary_en: Quoting Dominican President Henriquez on the 1916 U.S. intervention, the article recounts that American battleships entered Santo Domingo harbor without notice and landed an armed force that ousted him and his Cabinet, dissolved Congress, banned elections, muzzled the press, and seized the national treasury. The commentary states that Woodrow Wilson's actions contradicted his prior assurances against territorial conquest and provoked protests across the South American press. It adds that the Harding administration inherited the task of dispelling the resulting doubts among Latin American republics.
records.summary_es: Citando al presidente dominicano Henríquez sobre la intervención estadounidense de 1916, el artículo relata que acorazados estadounidenses entraron sin previo aviso en el puerto de la ciudad de Santo Domingo y desembarcaron una fuerza armada que lo destituyó a él y a su gabinete, disolvió el Congreso, prohibió las elecciones, amordazó a la prensa e incautó el tesoro nacional. El comentario señala que las acciones de Woodrow Wilson contradijeron sus garantías previas contra la conquista territorial y provocaron protestas en toda la prensa sudamericana. Añade que la administración Harding heredó la tarea de disipar las dudas resultantes entre las repúblicas latinoamericanas.

the minds of our sister republics by the high-handed proceedings of
a chief executive whose practice it was to act "in his own name and
his own proper authority," without consulting the wishes of the
American people or their representatives in Congress.

records.headline: William E. Pulliam has been appointed receiver general of customs
records.summary_en: William E. Pulliam has been appointed receiver general of customs for the Dominican Republic at the request of Santo Domingo officials who recalled his earlier service from 1908 to 1913. Originally recommended by the Governor General of the Philippines at President Roosevelt's request, Pulliam was replaced by President Wilson in 1913, and residents of Santo Domingo had urged his reappointment since the Harding administration took office.

La misma nota señala que un equipo de nativos derrotó a los marines estadounidenses con marcador de 12 a 0 en un partido de béisbol jugado ese día.

records.headline: A December 14 dispatch from Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: A December 14 dispatch from Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, reports that witnesses testifying before the U.S. Senate committee investigating the American military occupation of Santo Domingo and Haiti alleged atrocities against prisoners. Specific allegations included cutting off prisoners' ears, pouring salt into their wounds, and slashing a prisoner with a knife from throat to abdomen. The committee, chaired by Senator McCormick of Illinois, expected to finish its local hearings in time to sail for the United States on Friday.
records.summary_es: Un despacho del 14 de diciembre desde Santo Domingo, República Dominicana, informa que testigos que declararon ante la comisión del Senado de Estados Unidos que investiga la ocupación militar estadounidense de Santo Domingo y Haití denunciaron supuestas atrocidades contra prisioneros. Las acusaciones específicas incluían cortar las orejas a los prisioneros, echar sal en sus heridas y acuchillar a un prisionero desde la garganta hasta el abdomen. La comisión, encabezada por el senador McCormick de Illinois, esperaba concluir sus audiencias locales a tiempo para zarpar hacia Estados Unidos el viernes.

records.summary_en: President Harding has appointed William E. Pulliam as receiver general of Dominican customs. Pulliam was originally named to the post by President Roosevelt and continued in the office under President Taft. He is scheduled to depart shortly for Santo Domingo, the capital of the Dominican Republic.

The committee proposed appointing a presidential High Commissioner with envoy extraordinary powers to direct all civilian and military U.S. officials in Haiti. It also advised issuing a new loan to discharge European debt obligations and resolve valid claims held by Haitian citizens against their government.

records.summary_en: The *New-York tribune* reported that while a Senate committee recommended extending Cuban tariff preferences to the Dominican Republic, the Haiti-Santo Domingo Independence Society fiercely condemned the committee's preliminary report. The society denounced the findings as an imperialist endorsement of armed intervention and treaty imposition on smaller republics. It contended that maintaining military garrisons and puppet executives did lasting damage to American prestige throughout Latin America.

La sociedad denunció las conclusiones como un respaldo imperialista a la intervención armada y a la imposición de tratados a repúblicas más pequeñas. Sostuvo que el mantenimiento de guarniciones militares y gobernantes títeres causaba un perjuicio duradero al prestigio estadounidense en toda América Latina.

McCormick stated that the committee's findings on marine atrocity allegations in Haiti would be made public around February 1, with a separate report on Santo Domingo forthcoming. He also urged the immediate appointment of a High Commissioner to unite diplomatic, treaty, and military authorities under single leadership.

To offset revenue declines caused by the post-war trade depression, the committee advised issuing a new loan to consolidate two outstanding short-term debts. McCormick reported that outside of localized banditry in the east, the military administration had established unprecedented domestic peace while modernizing municipal sanitation, docks, and public education.

Knowles alleged that a $2,500,000 loan was floated without Dominican consent at high interest rates through New York banking syndicates that received large discounts. He also announced plans to file charges against Military Governor Admiral Samuel S. Robison for intimidation, while asserting that the naval financial officer's personal accounts were exempt from audit.

records.headline: An editorial contrasts another population with the Dominican
records.summary_en: An editorial contrasts another population with the Dominican Republic, describing Dominicans as among the most intelligent and cultured peoples of Latin America and fully competent to administer their own affairs, while hoping the U.S. Senate Committee will recommend steps toward that outcome. The paper notes receiving several copies of the Santo Domingo daily Listin Diario and praises its impartial reporting and courteous treatment of the U.S. Senate Commission. Calling the Dominican Republic one of the world's richest nations in natural resources—capable of ranking next to Cuba and surpassing Porto Rico in annual trade if developed—the editorial advocates a reciprocal tariff and commercial privileges between the United States and Santo Domingo and wishes the republic a prosperous New Year.
records.summary_es: Un editorial contrasta a otra población con la República Dominicana, describiendo a los dominicanos como uno de los pueblos más inteligentes y cultos de América Latina y plenamente competentes para administrar sus propios asuntos, al tiempo que espera que el Comité del Senado de los Estados Unidos recomiende pasos hacia ese resultado. El periódico señala haber recibido varios ejemplares del diario de Santo Domingo Listin Diario y elogia sus informes imparciales y su trato cortés hacia la Comisión del Senado de los Estados Unidos. Calificando a la República Dominicana como uno de los países más ricos del mundo en recursos naturales —capaz de ubicarse después de Cuba y superar con creces a Porto Rico en volumen comercial anual si se desarrolla—, el editorial aboga por un arancel recíproco y privilegios comerciales entre los Estados Unidos y Santo Domingo y desea a la república un próspero Año Nuevo.

records.headline: Archbishop Nouel of Santo Domingo states that both he and the Dominican people
records.summary_en: Archbishop Nouel of Santo Domingo states that both he and the Dominican people unanimously desire to see the Dominican Republic restored to full liberty, independence, and sovereignty. He declares that the American occupation was unjustified, lacked any basis in right and justice, and diminished rather than increased friendly feeling between Dominicans and the people of the United States, adding that South and Central American archbishops and bishops he met in Rome the previous year unanimously agreed and warned that their countries should prepare because nobody knew whose turn would come next. Noting that most American citizens were until recently uninformed about events in Haiti and Santo Domingo over the last five years, the article quotes Nouel's message questioning how a nation that shed its blood in defense of liberty could deprive a small liberty-loving people of the independence they had held for almost a century.
records.summary_es: El arzobispo Nouel de Santo Domingo afirma que tanto él como el pueblo dominicano desean unánimemente ver a la República Dominicana restituida en el pleno goce de su libertad, independencia y soberanía. Declara que la ocupación estadounidense fue injustificada, careció de toda base en el derecho y la justicia, y disminuyó en lugar de aumentar el sentimiento de amistad entre los dominicanos y el pueblo de los Estados Unidos, añadiendo que los arzobispos y obispos de América del Sur y Central con quienes se reunió en Roma el año anterior coincidieron unánimemente y advirtieron que sus países debían prepararse porque nadie sabía a quién le tocaría el próximo turno. Señalando que la mayoría de los ciudadanos estadounidenses estuvieron hasta hace muy poco desinformados sobre los acontecimientos en Haití y Santo Domingo durante los últimos cinco años, el artículo cita el mensaje de Nouel cuestionando cómo un pueblo que derramó su sangre en defensa de la libertad podía privar a un pequeño pueblo amante de la libertad de la independencia que había poseído durante casi un siglo.

records.headline: A reader letter signed "A Constant Reader" criticizes several statistical and geographical errors
records.summary_en: A reader letter signed "A Constant Reader" criticizes several statistical and geographical errors in a recent publication, first noting that sovereignty over the Isle of Pines belongs to Cuba rather than the United States. The writer then points out that Santo Domingo (Dominican Republic) is erroneously labeled on the map as "Dominica" and assigned a heavily inflated population figure, remarking that such a number would not be reached even if all the cats and dogs on the island were counted. According to the letter, the republic's actual population is around 700,000, as shown in The World Almanac.
records.summary_es: Una carta de un lector firmada "A Constant Reader" critica varios errores estadísticos y geográficos en una publicación reciente, señalando primero que la soberanía sobre la Isla de Pinos pertenece a Cuba y no a los Estados Unidos. El autor indica luego que Santo Domingo (República Dominicana) aparece erróneamente rotulado en el mapa como "Dominica" y con una cifra de población muy inflada, comentando que dicho número no se alcanzaría ni siquiera incluyendo a todos los gatos y perros de la isla. Según la carta, la población real de la república es de alrededor de 700,000 habitantes, tal como figura en The World Almanac.

records.summary_en: The *Chicago whip* reported on continued resistance to the U.S. occupation of Haiti, mocking claims of mutual devotion between Haitians and military authorities while officials acknowledged that ending martial law would spark immediate revolt. The paper published a statement by Haitian Hague delegate Pierre Hudicourt, who traveled to Washington to formally protest the occupation before the Senate. Hudicourt condemned the invasion as an assault on national sovereignty driven by foreign commercial interests and urged the American public to demand military withdrawal.

records.summary_en: The *Milwaukee leader* asserted that the Dominican Republic was peaceful and paying foreign debts ahead of schedule when American naval forces seized Santo Domingo City in 1916. The report stated that President Jimenez resigned rather than accept American armed support against congressional impeachment proceedings. After Congress elected Francisco Henriquez y Carvajal and he rejected an American treaty identical to Haiti's, U.S. naval commanders landed marines and extinguished the constitutional Dominican government.

Not an American dollar or an American life was even threatened when the fleet ordered to San Domingo City by Secretary Daniels, in agreement with Secretary of State Lansing, committed its act of war or piracy by seizing the capital city and suppressing the Dominican government. When the Dominican congress began proceedings for impeachment of President Jimenez, the American representative offered armed support to Jimenez against the congress. Jimenez resented the insult, and resigned at once. Then the minister of war was escorted to the American legation and offered a "corrupt proposal" if he would support for the presidency a man picked by the American representative. Mitchell, the Red Cross announced an appropriation of $2,000 for food, medicines, and other relief for smallpox victims in the republic. records.headline: Eugene H. Hathaway, director general of posts and telegraphs of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Eugene H. Hathaway, director general of posts and telegraphs of the Dominican Republic and former supervisor of the U.S. Post Office Department's rural free delivery service, died in Santo Domingo City on March 3 after an illness of several months. Born in Wellesley, Massachusetts, on March 21, 1849, Hathaway previously worked as a gold mine superintendent in Sonora, Mexico, a Chicago newspaper correspondent during the Spanish-American War, and head of the postal service in Porto Rico for nine years before accepting his Dominican post in 1917. He was the father of Eugene P. D. Hathaway, and his funeral services took place in Wellesley on Sunday.
records.summary_es: Eugene H. Hathaway, director general de correos y telégrafos de la República Dominicana y exsupervisor del servicio de entrega rural gratuita del Departamento de Correos de los Estados Unidos, falleció en la ciudad de Santo Domingo el 3 de marzo tras una enfermedad de varios meses. Nacido en Wellesley, Massachusetts, el 21 de marzo de 1849, Hathaway trabajó anteriormente como superintendente de una mina de oro en Sonora, México, corresponsal periodístico de Chicago durante la guerra hispano-estadounidense y jefe del servicio postal en Puerto Rico durante nueve años antes de aceptar su cargo dominicano en 1917. Era padre de Eugene P. D. Hathaway, y sus servicios funerarios se celebraron en Wellesley el domingo.

records.full_text:
THE U. S. OCCUPATION OF HAITI

THE tenth session of the Popular Government League Forum recently held in Washington dealt with the American invasion and occupation of the Dominican Republic, which occupies the eastern two-thirds of the Island of Haiti. The island won its independence from France in 1804. Since 1884 the Dominican Republic has been recognized in international law as a free and sovereign State.

Hon. Horace G. Knowles, of New York, former minister to the Balkan states by appointment of Roosevelt, later as minister to Santo Domingo by appointment of President Taft, and later still to Bolivio, was the speaker of the occasion. Although Mr. Knowles' address was given in a calm, dispassionate manner, the Forum was moved to its depths. A mass of official documents at hand was read or offered to prove every statement he made. For more than an hour after the address two-thirds of the audience remained questioning him and discussing the various phases of the occupation.

Mr. Knowles declared that in repudiating the action of the government toward the Dominican Republic he considered himself serving his own country more than he was the Dominicans, on the grounds that the honor and pledged word of the United States was at stake in this issue, and the hour was at hand whether we would uphold the principles on which this nation was founded and which its people cherish, or ruthlessly disregard its obligations and become an imperialism comparable with the old monarchies of Europe.

The following is a condensed summary of the case as presented by Mr. Knowles:

The Invasion.

In May of 1916, when the Dominican Republic was at peace with the world, while it was a party to two existing treaties with the United States and in direct violation to one of them, and without the slightest attempt to appeal to or use diplomatic means or submitting any question in dispute to The Hague tribunal, President Wilson ordered a part of the United States Navy, without any notice to the Dominican Government, to go secretly to Santo Domingo to seize the government and proceed to subjugate the people. This was done without consulting or informing Congress, without a declaration of war.

American battleships entered the roadstead of Santo Domingo City, and under the cover of long range guns landed a force of marines and took possession. This was a paramount act of war. A little later the United States presented to the Dominican president, Francisco Henriquez y Carvajal, a treaty which completely destroyed the liberty, independence and sovereignty of his nation, putting it under the absolute control of the United States. It was an exact duplicate of the treaty which had just been forced upon the helpless Haitian government by guns and bayonets. President Henriquez refused to accept the demand, whereupon the American admiral, acting, of course, under orders from Washington, proceeded to use pressure and force. The military force was increased, and on November 29, 1916, nearly seven months after the invasion, a proclamation of occupation was issued and the admiral declared himself military governor of the country.

Wholesale Atrocities.

Following orders from Washington, the President and his ministers of state were forced out of office; the government treasury was seized; the national congress dismissed; elections prohibited; thousands of marines were spread over the country, with unlimited authority over the natives; public meetings were banned; a censorship of tongue, press, mail and telegraph of the severest kind was established; a reign of intense terror was inaugurated; destructive bombs were dropped from airplanes upon towns and hamlets; every home was searched for arms; homes were burned; natives were killed; tortures and cruelties were committed; "Butcher" Weiler's horrible concentration camps were established, and the brutal methods of Weiler, that did so much to bring about our war with Spain, were imitated.

Repressions and oppressions followed in succession. Persons making protest were fined and imprisoned; bullets and bayonets followed any attempt at resistance or defense. Those who criticized the action of the military government or used patriotic expressions were severely punished by fines and imprisonment. Hundreds of capable native government employes were dismissed, and their families distressed, and their places taken by men sent from the States. The Dominican treasury being tapped to pay all their traveling and incidental expenses. Their foreign indebtedness has been greatly increased, against their protest and in violation of the treaty of 1907. For five years this policy has continued. Thousands of natives have had their homes burned over their heads and in sheer terror have fled to the forests. Those of them who have attempted resistance in self-defense of their lives and their country have been designated "bandits" by the occupation.

Alleged Reasons.

The official reasons set up by the United States Government for this invasion of Santo Domingo were, first, violation of the Roosevelt-Dominican treaty of 1907, and second, to restore peace and order to the country.

Mr. Knowles denied that the Dominicans had violated the treaty, but that the United States had openly and flagrantly violated it. Even had the treaty been violated by the Dominicans and denied, the United States had not the right to set itself up as the judge of the point in dispute. And further, had there been such violation and no denial, the United States, by resolution which it offered and which was adopted by the Second International Peace Conference at The Hague in 1907, was precluded from using force in such occasion.

As to the second reason, Mr. Knowles made a number of startling disclosures. There was on revolution in the capital or disorder in the country as charged, but that the representatives of the United States were endeavoring to encourage and provoke a revolution. He produced documentary proof to show that the resignation of President Jimenez was caused by acts of government agents and further that deception was used in land troops. The United States claims that it landed troops for the purpose of guaranteeing a free and deliberate election of a new president by the Dominican Congress, but as a matter of fact it arrested Dominican congressmen and used armed force to compel them to vote for a president picked by the agents of the United States.

Further, that an attempt was made in the American Legation to bribe the Dominican Minister of War to use his influence and power with members of congress to force the election of a certain man for president.

Specifically, the treaty of 1907 was to provide for a loan of $20,000,000 and to protect the bondholders. There has been no default in the payment of interest and amortization, and never for a moment had the bondholders' interest been in danger. Contrariwise, the reports of the Navy Department show that overpayment has been made to such an extent that the entire loan will be paid in 1925, instead of 1958, or 33 years before it is due.

Mr. Knowles solemnly insisted that the life or property of any American had never been in danger, and throughout the history of the republic only one American has been killed in Santo Domingo, that by pure accident, for which the Dominicans paid the heirs $30,000.

Harding Follows Wilson.

Mr. Knowles showed that the subjugation of Santo Domingo followed promptly upon the like subjugation of the Republic of Haiti, which was described to the Forum at the previous session by Dr. Pierre Hudicourt, of Port au Prince, the whole being a campaign evidently designed for complete conquest of the whole island. That the secret and under reason for this conquest, when all things are considered, was to open these islands

records.headline: A smallpox epidemic is raging in Santo, Moca, and La Vega in the Dominican
records.summary_en: A smallpox epidemic is raging in Santo, Moca, and La Vega in the Dominican Republic, cabled reports from Washington to the American Red Cross and the Navy Department state. Red Cross field director S. A. Mitchell telegraphed from Santo Domingo that there are 22,000 cases and 225 deaths in one week in those localities, though U.S. Marines stationed in Santo Domingo are unaffected. records.headline: The Federal Council of Churches of Christ in America, the Home Mission
records.summary_en: The Federal Council of Churches of Christ in America, the Home Mission Council, and the Committee on Co-operation in Latin America have submitted a recommendation to the Senate committee preparing a report on the U.S. occupation of Haiti and the Dominican Republic. The church organizations ask that complete administrative independence be restored in Haiti and Santo Domingo as soon as possible on moral and humanitarian rather than political and financial grounds. The protest follows President Harding's refusal to provide the Senate with instructions given to General John H. Russell regarding control over civil and military officials in the occupied republics.

Las organizaciones eclesiásticas solicitan que se restablezca la completa independencia administrativa en Haití y Santo Domingo lo antes posible por razones morales y humanitarias, más que políticas y financieras. La protesta sigue a la negativa del presidente Harding de entregar al Senado las instrucciones dadas al general John H. Russell sobre el control de los funcionarios civiles y militares en las repúblicas ocupadas.

records.summary_en: A bond issue by the United States Military Government of Santo Domingo on behalf of the Dominican Republic is expected within a few days. The coupon rate will be 5 or 5 1/2 per cent.

records.headline: Secretary of State William H. Seward under President Johnson negotiated
records.summary_en: Secretary of State William H. Seward under President Johnson negotiated with Latin American powers for a U.S.-controlled isthmian canal and attempted to secure a footing in Santo Domingo for a naval station, The New York Herald notes in a historical review of U.S. foreign policy. The article adds that President Grant, convinced that American interest lay in the Pacific and determined to protect the approaches to a future American canal by securing a foothold in the West Indies, conceived in 1869 the policy of annexing the Dominican Republic, to which Secretary Fish somewhat reluctantly agreed.
records.summary_es: El secretario de Estado William H. Seward, bajo la presidencia de Johnson, negoció con potencias latinoamericanas para lograr un canal ístmico controlado por los Estados Unidos e intentó asegurar un punto de apoyo en Santo Domingo para una estación naval, según señala The New York Herald en una reseña histórica de la política exterior estadounidense. El artículo añade que el presidente Grant, convencido de que el interés estadounidense residía en el Pacífico y decidido a proteger los accesos a un futuro canal estadounidense asegurando una posición en las Indias Occidentales, concibió en 1869 la política de anexión de la República Dominicana, a la cual el secretario Fish accedió con cierta reticencia.

records.headline: Continuing its assessment of President Grant's Caribbean policy of 1869
records.summary_en: Continuing its assessment of President Grant's Caribbean policy of 1869, The New York Herald states that Grant conceived and Secretary Fish somewhat reluctantly agreed to the policy of annexing the whole or part of the Dominican Republic to protect a future canal. Although the writer characterizes Grant's diplomacy as crude and his agent Babcock as shady, the article contends that had Sumner and his friends shared Grant's foresight, the United States could have established itself in the West Indies thirty years before the Spanish war of 1898.

Aunque el autor califica la diplomacia de Grant de rudimentaria y a su agente Babcock de dudoso, el artículo sostiene que si Sumner y sus amigos hubieran compartido la previsión de Grant, los Estados Unidos habrían podido establecerse en las Indias Occidentales treinta años antes de la guerra con España de 1898.

records.headline: Testimony regarding abuses during the U.S. occupations of Haiti
records.summary_en: Testimony regarding abuses during the U.S. occupations of Haiti and the Dominican Republic, including the torture of Cayo Baez with red-hot machetes to force him to reveal an ammunition arsenal he had never heard of, after which he was left for dead but recovered, The Milwaukee Leader recounts. The article also reports that editor Horacio Blanco Fombona was imprisoned, fined, had his magazine suspended, and was expelled from Santo Domingo, subsequently writing a pamphlet titled 'In the Clutch of the Eagle's Claws.' Concluding that both the Republic of Haiti and the Dominican Republic are entitled to complete independence, the piece asks whether President Warren G. Harding will honor his fall 1920 campaign promise made in Marion, Ohio.
records.summary_es: Testimonios sobre abusos cometidos durante las ocupaciones estadounidenses de Haití y la República Dominicana, incluida la tortura de Cayo Baez con machetes al rojo vivo para obligarlo a revelar un arsenal de municiones del que nunca había oído hablar, tras lo cual fue dado por muerto pero se recuperó, según relata The Milwaukee Leader. El artículo también informa que el editor Horacio Blanco Fombona fue encarcelado, multado, vio suspendida su revista y fue expulsado de Santo Domingo, escribiendo posteriormente un folleto titulado «In the Clutch of the Eagle's Claws». Al concluir que tanto la República de Haití como la República Dominicana tienen derecho a la plena independencia, la nota pregunta si el presidente Warren G. records.headline: Archbishop Adolfo Alejandro Nouel of the Dominican Republic

Pulliam, the American receiver of Dominican customs, strongly endorsing the project to erect a great lighthouse or pharos at the entrance of the harbor of San Domingo as a memorial to Christopher Columbus, a Washington dispatch dated May 4 reports. The project had gained considerable headway a few years earlier before being suspended during the war.

records.headline: Word has reached Washington of the wedding on April 18 in the Dominican Republic of Lieutenant Fellows of the United States Marine
records.summary_en: Word has reached Washington of the wedding on April 18 in the Dominican Republic of Lieutenant Fellows of the United States Marine Corps, son of Mrs. C. Viola Fellows of Washington, and Miss Lillian Alice Watkins, daughter of Dr. and Mrs. Victor E. Watkins. Held at sunset in the garden of the bride's parents' estate at La Romana overlooking the Caribbean Sea, the ceremony was attended by Rear Admiral Samuel S. Robison, U.S. Military Governor of the Dominican Republic, and Mrs. Robison; Brigadier General Harry Lee, commanding the 2nd Brigade of U.S. Marines, on whose staff the bridegroom serves; American Minister William Russell; the American consul and his wife; and other naval, marine, and civilian guests.

records.full_text:
THE AMERICAN EMPIRE

(Continued from page 1)

Hitherto the goal of every revolutionist had been the nearest customhouse; now Americans held all customhouses and gave would-be revolutionists sharply to understand that American marines would deal with any interference there in summary fashion. The warning was a great check on revolutions; Santo Domingo became quieter than it had ever been in its history; the natives began to develop the remarkable resources of the republic, and prosperity increased by leaps and bounds. Not only was the republic able to pay its debts, but—unheard-of event!—there was a large cash balance in the treasury!

Meanwhile in the neighboring Republic of Haiti things continued to go from bad to worse, and in the spring of 1914 it looked as if a crisis had arrived similar to that in the Dominican Republic nine years before. At the very moment when our hands were full with what seemed like ly to be war with Mexico the British government presented an ultimatum to Haiti over unsatisfied claims for damage; and a few days later German financial interests concluded the preliminaries of a loan to the Haitian customhouses and the right to build a commercial coaling station at the best harbor of Haiti, Mole-Saint-Nicholas. The second event was only the last of a number of moves that had made Germany paramount in the financial and business life of Haiti, and it might have been the cause of serious friction between America and Germany if the Great War had not broken out when it did and entirely changed the situation.

The lesson was not lost upon our government, which saw that conditions in Haiti had reached such a pass that intervention was inevitable. Accordingly in 1915 after a particularly atrocious outburst of revolutionary anarchy American marines landed on the island, and American control was established over the republic. In November of that year the Haitian government ratified a treaty with the United States that established a virtual American protectorate over the country. To be sure, the forms of native government were preserved, but all real power lay in the hands of the American "advisers" who controlled the various branches of the administration. The presence of a strong force of marines assured American control, and presently the marines were supplemented with a "gendarmery," recruited among the natives and officered by Americans. Then the Americans proceeded to pacify the country, which they did not without considerable fighting. The numerous "generals," bandits and "bad men" who had so long terrorized Haiti naturally would not allow their careers to be cut short without protest. Taking to the bush, known as cacos, began guerrilla warfare, those rebellious gentlemen, who were and the fine fighting qualities of our marines were never better displayed than in the way they hunted the cacos through tangled forest and over trackless mountains until they had captured or exterminated them.

Long before Haiti was pacified we had undertaken a similar task in the Dominican Republic. We have already mentioned the agreement of 1905, which gave the United States a certain degree of financial control, and the improvement that followed. For a time things ran smoothly; but presently the very prosperity of the country incited fresh political troubles. The lure of the tempting cash balances in the treasury was too much for the appetites of hungry "generals;" revolutionary disturbances broke out, and the Dominican government was soon unable to live up to obligations. According to the terms of the 1905 agreement, which was virtually limited to a control of custom receipts, the United States was unable to cope with the situation. Accordingly in 1916 direct intervention took place. Strong forces of marines occupied the capital and the principal strategic points, the recalcitrant Dominican government was abolished, and a United States military government was set up. As in Haiti, a certain amount of fighting took place in the remote districts, but the Dominican rebels were easier to handle than the Haitian cacos. A native constabulary officered by Americans soon supplemented the marines, and before long the Dominican Republic was pretty thoroughly pacified. Thus by 1917 both parts of the island of Santo Domingo had become American protectorates, occupied and effectively controlled.

The results of American control have proved strikingly favorable. Both Haiti and the Dominican Republic are enjoying unprecedented prosperity. Municipal governments, sanitation, good roads, schools and other innovations together with the blessings of peace, order and prosperity are teaching the Haitians and the Dominicans the value of a regulated, civilized life; and in time those lessons should have salutary results. Of course our administration has not been perfect. Mistakes have been made—mistakes that the small class of noisy politicians and would-be revolutionists who are forever declaiming about their "lost liberties" and inciting the ignorant masses against American rule have capitalized. But no such arguments as they present should blind us to the fact that American control should continue for at least a generation if Santo Domingo is not to relapse into the morass of poverty and misgovernment from which we dragged it a few years ago. The outstanding lesson that the history of the island teaches is that the people have been incapable of self-government. The educated, well-intentioned upper class is too few in numbers and too lacking in strong moral fibre to keep the reins of government in its own hands. Even if it were placed in control, the ever-watchful "generals" and their brutal "armies," composed of the desperadoes of the country districts and the vicious rabble of the towns, would supplant it as soon as we had evacuated the island. The sole motive of those agitators, who are absolutely without principle, is their lust for power and plunder; and, since the country is too poor to satisfy the appetites of all of them at the same time, there would always be a gang of "outs" envious of the "ins" and determined to sate their appetites at any price. In other words, the wretched cycle of revolutions would soon be in full swing once more.

Of course that does not mean that as conditions improve we should not grant larger measures of self-government and restrict the sphere of our direct control. In the Dominican Republic a step in that direction seems about to be made; our government has recently announced that in the near future it will restore native administration and do away with direct military rule. But plainly the United States must retain supreme authority and oversight for a long time to come. When there has grown to manhood a new generation born and bred in an atmosphere of peace, order and good government—a generation having a certain amount of education, familiar with the benefits of civilized life and imbued with an intelligent appreciation of the value of security and prosperity—the situation may be altered.

The article depicted Haiti's post-colonial history as an imitation of French royalty plagued by endless civil wars that destroyed colonial plantations and towns. records.full_text:
THE AMERICAN EMPIRE

[Selected]

In none of the lands that America has guided and protected during the last generation is more interesting than the great island often called Haiti, but more correctly known as Santo Domingo—the island which lies between Cuba and Porto Rico. It is unquestionably the finest of the West Indies—a land of lofty mountains clothed with splendid forests and a rich variety of minerals; a land of spacious plateaus and fertile plains that are capable of producing the finest of sugar, tobacco and other tropical products. Santo Domingo would appear predestined by nature to be the richest and most prosperous of the West Indies. As a matter of fact it lost its early prosperity long ago, and for more than a century has been sunk in a backwardness and misery from which, under recent American guidance, it is only now beginning to emerge. The story of the turbulent past of Santo Domingo and of its new start is a story well worth telling.

As its double name suggests, the island of Santo Domingo, which has an area of some thirty thousand square miles (about half the area of New England), is divided politically into two distinct nations. The western third forms the republic of Haiti; the eastern two-thirds constitutes the Dominican Republic. Haiti is a nation of Negroes; it has only a few mulattoes and no native whites. The people speak a corrupt French and look to France for their culture. The Dominican Republic, on the other hand, is a Spanish-speaking land, much like Cuba and Porto Rico. It has a considerable white or near-white upper class, a peasantry of mixed blood (Indian, white and African) and relatively few full-blooded Negroes.

Christopher Columbus discovered Santo Domingo, and the island was the first Spanish colony in the New World. It had a fine start, for at first the whole colonizing energy of Spain flowed into that relatively small insular area. Within thirty years multitudes of colonists had covered the land with towns of stone. Even now, after four centuries of decay, Santo Domingo, the capital city, still shows those stately mansions proudly described by an early Spanish historian as “so fair and large that they may well receive any lord or noble of Spain.”

During those thirty years the blood of a million Indians paid for the ingots of gold and silver that amazed the Spanish court. But at the end of that exciting period the bloodshed ceased. Mexico and Peru were conquered, the mines of Santo Domingo became insignificant beside the mines of the mainland, and the Indian workers were dead. The restless, fortune-hunting conquistadores who had made up the bulk of the population of Santo Domingo flocked away to the more tempting Spanish Main; and depopulated Spanish Santo Domingo almost sank into oblivion.

So matters stood for perhaps a hundred years. Then, just about the time when our ancestors were settling the Atlantic seaboard of North America, the coming of the French revived the prosperity of Santo Domingo. The Spaniards had colonized only the eastern part of the island—the part now known as the Dominican Republic; they had left the western part, which is today known as Haiti, virtually uninhabited, and the deserted coasts became the haunt of the famous buccaneers. The buccaneers were mainly French, and in time France claimed the region they had occupied, introduced respectable immigrants and made it a colony known as the French part of Santo Domingo. Like the Spaniards, the French devoted themselves to agriculture, and soon showed what marvelous productiveness the island had. During the eighteenth century French Santo Domingo was by far the most flourishing colony in the West Indies. Covered with fine plantations and cultivated to the very mountain crests, the French part of Santo Domingo, though only a trifle larger than the state of Massachusetts, furnished not only France but half Europe with sugar, coffee and other tropical products.

In order to obtain the labor necessary for so many plantations the French brought in multitudes of Negro slaves, who soon vastly outnumbered the white population. When the French Revolution convulsed France and its colonies, the Negroes of French Santo Domingo took advantage of the situation, revolted and after a long struggle succeeded in expelling the whites. Then they declared their independence, and in the year 1804 set up the republic of Haiti, the old Indian name for the land. About twenty years later the eastern part of the island threw off Spanish rule and became the Dominican Republic.

But independence meant neither peace nor prosperity. Having gained their freedom, the Haitians and the Dominicans began to misuse it. Both peoples showed from the first an utter lack of capacity for orderly self-government. The “Black Republic” of Haiti quickly degenerated into an absurd burlesque of France. The government sedulously copied French political forms; and the republic was sometimes styled a kingdom, sometimes an empire. One of the rulers of Haiti especially distinguished himself by creating a whole nobility headed by four princes and fifty-nine dukes; innumerable marquises, counts and barons completed the pompous galaxy that surrounded the “imperial” throne. Meanwhile Haiti itself went to rack and ruin. An endless succession of black and mulatto “generals” at the head of tatterdemalion “armies” fought ferociously for the spoils of office and kept the land plunged in a horrid and interminable anarchy. Revolution succeeded revolution and in those senseless civil wars the fine, well-constructed towns that the French had left were destroyed and replaced by squalid shacks, and the broad plantations and shaded highroads of the countryside again became bush and forest.

In the Spanish (Dominican) Republic colonial prosperity was destroyed because the Haitians repeatedly invaded and conquered it. How the Haitians ruled their own country suggests how they ruled the Dominicans; and finally, when the Dominicans at last succeeded in expelling them, the Dominican Republic continued to flounder in the bog of misgovernment and revolution.

By the beginning of the present century things had become so bad that European intervention seemed certain. Both republics had piled up huge foreign debts that they could not pay. Some of the creditors were Americans, but most of them were Europeans, particularly Englishmen, Frenchmen and Germans.

Now, it soon became clear that, whatever the United States might think or might not be inclined to do to protect its own injured citizens, the European powers were determined to see that their subjects obtained redress. In the year 1904 at least two European powers told our government that they were going to intervene in the Dominican Republic if something was not speedily done. The European powers were not giving us the option either of cleaning up the mess in the Dominican Republic or of standing aside and seeing Europeans come over and do it and thus violate the Monroe Doctrine, one of the corner stones of our foreign policy.

Faced with that critical situation, President Roosevelt succeeded in 1905 in getting the Dominican government to sign an agreement that permitted the United States to adjust the Dominican debt and to administer the customs for the benefit of creditors. The effects of American intervention were instantly felt. an agreement that permitted the United States to adjust the Dominican debt and to administer the customs for the benefit of creditors. The effects of American intervention were instantly felt.

Hitherto the goal of every revolutionist had been the nearest customhouse, because the customs were almost the only source of revenue. If a revolutionist could seize a customhouse, he could maintain an army. But when the United States took charge of the customhouses, the customs officials turned over 45 per cent of the revenue to the Dominican government for its current expenses and applied the remaining 55 per cent to paying the foreign debt. At once the customhouses ceased to be prizes for revolutionists, because an American collector with American naval forces behind him was in charge. Revolutions promptly stopped, and for nearly ten years the Dominican Republic enjoyed unprecedented peace and prosperity. The country developed rapidly; roads, harbors, schools and public buildings were constructed, and the public debt was steadily reduced.

Then came the World War. The withdrawal of American naval vessels to European waters was the signal for fresh revolutions. A series of uprisings threatened to undo all that had been accomplished. In 1916 the United States intervened with armed force. American marines landed, deposed the revolutionary government and set up a military administration headed by an American naval officer. Under American military rule the republic was completely disarmed, banditry was suppressed, and order was firmly established.

Meanwhile, across the border in Haiti, conditions had gone from bad to worse. Between 1908 and 1915 seven presidents were successively overthrown, assassinated or driven into exile. When the World War broke out, German influence in Haiti was strong, and there was danger that Germany might seize a naval base on the island. In July, 1915, after a particularly shocking massacre of political prisoners, American marines landed at Port-au-Prince. A treaty was negotiated between the United States and Haiti under which the United States assumed control of the finances and police of the republic.

Under American supervision the gendarmery was organized, public works were pushed forward, and the country was cleared of the cacos, or mountain bandits, who had terrorized the population for generations. Today both republics on the island of Santo Domingo are peacefully developing their immense natural resources under American guidance and protection.

records.summary_en: The *Evening star* detailed an agreement between Dominican leaders and American authorities to establish a provisional government preparatory to ending the military occupation. Under the arrangement, executive departments would be transferred to Dominican ministers, expenditures would follow established budgets, and American troops would concentrate into select centers while the national police preserved order. Full American evacuation was conditioned on a newly elected constitutional government ratifying executive orders and the 1918 and 1922 bond issues.

La evacuación estadounidense definitiva quedaba condicionada a que un nuevo gobierno constitucional electo ratificara las órdenes ejecutivas y las emisiones de bonos de 1918 y 1922.
