records.headline: The U.S. State Department has announced a tentative plan for the withdrawal of American
records.summary_en: The U.S. State Department has announced a tentative plan for the withdrawal of American military forces from Santo Domingo, reached after months of talks in Washington with a group of Dominican leaders acting on their own initiative, the Associated Negro Press reports in a July 21 dispatch from Washington. According to the department's statement, the evacuation program will be implemented as soon as it is determined whether a majority of the Dominican people approve of it. Former Latin American division chief Sumner Welles of New York has been appointed commissioner to the Dominican Republic with the rank of envoy and minister, and will depart immediately for the island to gauge public opinion on the withdrawal plan.
records.summary_es: El Departamento de Estado de los Estados Unidos ha anunciado un programa tentativo para la evacuación de las fuerzas militares estadounidenses de Santo Domingo, acordado tras meses de conversaciones en Washington con un grupo de líderes dominicanos que acudieron por iniciativa propia, según informa la Associated Negro Press en un despacho del 21 de julio desde Washington. Según el comunicado del departamento, el programa de evacuación se llevará a cabo tan pronto como se determine si cuenta con la aprobación de la mayoría del pueblo dominicano. El exjefe de la división latinoamericana Sumner Welles, de Nueva York, ha sido nombrado comisionado en la República Dominicana con rango de enviado y ministro, y partirá de inmediato hacia la isla para conocer la opinión de la población sobre el plan de retirada estadounidense.

records.summary_en: Reporting from Washington on July 20, this item states that the U.S. State Department has announced a tentative plan for the evacuation of American military forces from Santo Domingo, agreed upon in conferences with Dominican leaders who have spent several months in Washington on their own initiative. records.headline: Referencing a U.S. Senate committee investigation of conditions
records.summary_en: Referencing a U.S. Senate committee investigation of conditions in Santo Domingo that recommended continuing the U.S. military government, an investor writes to the New-York Tribune and asks that the answer not be published in the investors' column for fear an unfavorable comment would further depress the bond's price. In its reply, the paper advises that the Dominican Republic bond is a sound investment despite its decline from the offering price. Although not a U.S. government obligation, the bond's security is strengthened by direct American involvement, a guarantee from the military government of Santo Domingo that any Dominican government will accept it as a binding and irrevocable obligation, and customs revenues managed by a U.S. presidential appointee that have averaged nearly two and a half times the debt's interest and sinking fund requirements over the past six years. The reply attributes the price decline to criticism of the American position in the Dominican Republic, such as a speech by Senator Borah cited in the reader's letter.
records.summary_es: Haciendo referencia a una investigación de un comité del Senado de los Estados Unidos sobre las condiciones en Santo Domingo que recomendó continuar el gobierno militar estadounidense, un inversionista escribe al New-York Tribune y solicita que no se publique la respuesta en la columna de inversionistas por temor a que un comentario desfavorable deprima aún más el precio del bono. En su respuesta, el periódico aconseja que el bono de la República Dominicana es una inversión sólida a pesar de su caída respecto al precio de oferta. Aunque no es una obligación del gobierno estadounidense, la seguridad del bono se ve reforzada por el interés directo de los Estados Unidos, una garantía del gobierno militar de Santo Domingo de que cualquier gobierno dominicano lo aceptará como una obligación legal, vinculante e irrevocable, y recaudaciones aduaneras administradas por un funcionario nombrado por el presidente de los Estados Unidos que han promediado durante los últimos seis años prácticamente dos veces y media el servicio de intereses y fondo de amortización de la deuda de la República. La respuesta atribuye la baja en el precio a las críticas contra la posición estadounidense en la República Dominicana, como un discurso del senador Borah citado en la carta del lector.

records.headline: the committee found that, on the whole, American administration In Haytl
records.summary_en: The *Pleasantville press* reported that a Senate committee led by Senator Medill McCormick described the American record in Haiti as one of both achievement and failure, admitting instances of military cruelty and administrative mistakes. The committee maintained that intervention was necessary to defend the Monroe Doctrine against European threats following the collapse of Haitian credit and public order. It concluded that under the bilateral treaty, the occupation had successfully established national peace, financial solvency, and security.
records.summary_es: El *Pleasantville press* informó que una comisión del Senado encabezada por el senador Medill McCormick describió la trayectoria estadounidense en Haití como una mezcla de logros y desaciertos, reconociendo episodios de crueldad militar y fallas administrativas. La comisión sostuvo que la intervención fue indispensable para defender la Doctrina Monroe de amenazas europeas tras el descalabro del crédito y del orden público en Haití. Concluyó que, en el marco del tratado bilateral, la ocupación había logrado instaurar la paz nacional, la solvencia económica y la seguridad.
records.passage: In the report signed by Senator McCormick, Republican, Illinois, chairman, and Senators Oddie, Republican, Nevada; Pomerene, Democrat, Ohio, and Jones, Democrat, New Mexico, who have held protracted hearings and who recently toured Hayti and Santo Domingo. The committee found that, on the whole, American administration in Hayti had been of great benefit to the Haytians and was so regarded by a vast majority. The American record, however, was described as one both of "failure" and achievement. There had been some "blunders" and a few instances of cruelty against natives by members of the military force. "In brief, under the treaty between Hayti and the United States," the report said, "the peace of the republic, the solvency of its government and the security of its people have been established for the first time for many years." In justification of American intervention, the report said that "the chronic anarchy into which Hayti had fallen, the exhaustion of its credit, the threatened intervention of the German government and the actual landing of the French naval forces, all imperiled the Monroe doctrine and led the government of the United States to take the successive steps set forth to establish order in Hayti, to help institute a government as nearly representative as might be, and to assure the collaboration of the governments of the United States and Hayti for the future maintenance of peace and the development of the Haytian people." The campaign for a Columbus lighthouse memorial in Santo Domingo—where many historians contend Columbus's remains rest—was initiated by William E. Pulliam, receiver general of Dominican customs, and had been temporarily suspended during the World War.

records.headline: Associated Press dispatches dated October 7 from Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: Associated Press dispatches dated October 7 from Santo Domingo and Port-au-Prince report that American aviator Lieutenant Hinton, flying from New York to Rio de Janeiro in the hydroplane Sampaio Correia II, arrived at Santo Domingo at 3 o'clock that afternoon. Hinton had resumed his flight from Port-au-Prince at 11:30 o'clock after a delay of several weeks to install new engines, following an overland and sea route of seventy-seven miles across three lakes to Barahona on the southwestern Dominican coast and eighty-five miles over water to Santo Domingo. Major Francis T. Evans piloted Hinton's craft in a Marine airplane.
records.summary_es: Despachos de la Associated Press fechados el 7 de octubre desde Santo Domingo y Puerto Príncipe informan que el aviador estadounidense teniente Hinton, en vuelo de Nueva York a Río de Janeiro en el hidroavión Sampaio Correia II, llegó a Santo Domingo a las 3 en punto de esa tarde. Hinton había reanudado su viaje desde Puerto Príncipe a las 11:30 luego de una demora de varias semanas para instalar nuevos motores, siguiendo una ruta terrestre y marítima de setenta y siete millas a través de tres lagos hasta Barahona, en la costa suroeste dominicana, y ochenta y cinco millas por mar hasta Santo Domingo. El mayor Francis T. Evans guió el aparato de Hinton en un avión de la Infantería de Marina.

records.headline: President Harding sent a message through American Commissioner Sumner Welles
records.summary_en: President Harding sent a message through American Commissioner Sumner Welles to Juan Bautista Vicini Burgos on the occasion of his taking the oath of office as Provisional President of the Dominican Republic. In the message, Harding conveyed the good will of the United States government and people, expressed hope for the successful functioning of the provisional government and for the country's peace and prosperity, and offered personal congratulations. An accompanying Associated Press dispatch from Santo Domingo dated October 21 reports that Vicini Burgos took the oath of office before the Supreme Court of Justice that morning, ending the regime of the American occupation.
records.summary_es: El presidente Harding envió un mensaje por intermedio del comisionado estadounidense Sumner Welles a Juan Bautista Vicini Burgos con motivo de su juramentación como presidente provisional de la República Dominicana. En el mensaje, Harding transmitió la buena voluntad del gobierno y del pueblo de los Estados Unidos, expresó la esperanza en el buen funcionamiento del gobierno provisional y en la paz y prosperidad del país, y le ofreció sus felicitaciones personales. Un despacho adjunto de la Associated Press desde Santo Domingo fechado el 21 de octubre informa que Vicini Burgos prestó juramento ante la Suprema Corte de Justicia esa mañana, poniendo fin al régimen de la ocupación estadounidense.

records.summary_en: According to an authoritative statement reported by The Washington Times, the State Department had not yet received a request from Dominican citizens asking that American Commissioner Sumner Welles be permitted to stay in the Dominican Republic until a constitutional president is installed. Although press dispatches from Santo Domingo reported that several prominent Dominicans had sent such a plea, it had not arrived by the time the State Department closed for the day, and Welles had been scheduled to depart Santo Domingo for Haiti on Friday.

records.headline: Reptile expert G. K. Noble of the American Museum of Natural
records.summary_en: Reptile expert G. K. Noble of the American Museum of Natural History, accompanied by Mrs. Noble, is in the Dominican Republic hunting for snakes, lizards, and frogs. He particularly hopes to study the rhinoceros iguana, found mainly in the arid southwestern region near a dead sea more than a hundred feet below sea level, and the giant tree frog, which is confined to the island and has been taken only in the Central Cordillera and the Quita Espuala mountain range in the northeast. Because the life history of the giant tree frog is completely unknown, the expedition must work during the height of the rainy season to gather scientific data and exhibition specimens.
records.summary_es: El experto en reptiles G. K. Noble, del Museo Americano de Historia Natural, acompañado por la señora Noble, se encuentra en la República Dominicana cazando serpientes, lagartos y ranas. Espera estudiar en particular la iguana rinoceronte, que se halla principalmente en la árida región suroeste cerca de un mar muerto a más de cien pies bajo el nivel del mar, y la rana arborícola gigante, que está circunscrita a la isla y solo ha sido capturada en la Cordillera Central y en la sierra de Quita Espuala en el noreste. Debido a que el ciclo de vida de la rana arborícola gigante es completamente desconocido, la expedición deberá trabajar durante el apogeo de la temporada de lluvias para reunir datos científicos y ejemplares de exhibición.

records.summary_en: To commemorate the completion of the new highway, Episcopal missionaries in the Dominican Republic led by Archdeacon William Wyllie and his wife under Bishop Charles B. Colmore, D.D., have secured land to establish a new church at Puerto Plata within a few months. Mrs. Wyllie was the first woman to travel over the new road from Santo Domingo City to Puerto Plata and just passed through New York on her return to "Dominica" (the Dominican Republic) after attending the Episcopal General Convention in Portland, Oregon. Alongside her missionary duties, she manages the U.S. Government Hospital in "Dominica," has attended the births of the many children born there since the start of the American occupation, and served as the only nurse on the island when the influenza epidemic broke out.

records.headline: A former engineer on a Scotch tramp ship in West Indian waters
records.summary_en: A former engineer on a Scotch tramp ship in West Indian waters now serving in missionary work is credited with extensive knowledge of the Dominican coast, frequently guiding vessels through dangerous reefs into port during coastal missionary trips. On the island itself, a newly opened road built largely by U.S. Marines connects Santo Domingo City on the south with Puerto Plata on the north. Freight that previously required a ten-to-twelve-day voyage around the south, east, and northern ends of the island can now travel over the new highway to Puerto Plata for shipment in a few hours, while Episcopal missionaries in the Dominican Republic are commemorating the road.

records.headline: In commemoration of the newly completed highway in the Dominican
records.summary_en: In commemoration of the newly completed highway in the Dominican Republic, Episcopal missionaries under Right Reverend Charles B. Colmore, D.D., Episcopal Missionary Bishop of Porto Rico and the Dominican Republic, are establishing a church at Puerto Plata to link the two sections of the country. Archdeacon William Wyllie and his wife have led the movement to build the new edifice, and Mrs. Wyllie was the first woman to travel the new highway from Santo Domingo City to Puerto Plata. Having just passed through New York on her way back to "Dominica" (the Dominican Republic) from the Episcopal General Convention in Portland, Oregon, Mrs. Wyllie also manages the U.S. government hospital in "Dominica," has attended the births of all the army children born there since the start of the American occupation, and was the only nurse on the island when the influenza epidemic broke out.

Colmore, D.D., obispo misionero episcopal de Porto Rico y la República Dominicana, están estableciendo una iglesia en Puerto Plata para enlazar las dos secciones del país. El arcediano William Wyllie y su esposa han encabezado el movimiento para levantar el nuevo edificio, y la señora Wyllie fue la primera mujer en recorrer la nueva carretera desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo hasta Puerto Plata. Tras pasar recientemente por Nueva York en su viaje de regreso a «Dominica» (la República Dominicana) procedente de la Convención General Episcopal en Portland, Oregón, la señora Wyllie también dirige el hospital del gobierno de los Estados Unidos en «Dominica», ha asistido en el nacimiento de todos los hijos de militares nacidos allí desde el inicio de la ocupación estadounidense y fue la única enfermera en la isla cuando se desató la epidemia de influenza.

records.summary_en: Following the State Department's agreement to withdraw American military forces from San Domingo, the provisional government of the Dominican Republic will assume administrative powers from the date of its installation. It will legislate to regulate the holding of elections, reorganize provincial and municipal government and enable the Dominican people to amend the constitution as they deem appropriate, and from that date it will be alone responsible for its acts, ending seven years of American military government.
records.summary_es: Tras el acuerdo del Departamento de Estado de retirar las fuerzas militares estadounidenses de Santo Domingo, el gobierno provisional de la República Dominicana asumirá los poderes administrativos desde la fecha de su instalación. Legislará para regular la celebración de elecciones, reorganizará los gobiernos provinciales y municipales y permitirá al pueblo dominicano enmendar la constitución como lo considere apropiado, y desde esa fecha será el único responsable de sus actos, poniendo fin a siete años de gobierno militar estadounidense.
records.passage: follows the agreement of the state department in Washington to withdraw the American military forces from San Domingo. The provisional government from that date will be alone responsible for its acts. The American military government has been in the Dominican republic for seven years, marines first coming because of disorders. records.headline: The American occupation of Santo Domingo lasted for seven years, and while there has been much criticism of the government for its Dominican policy
records.summary_en: The *Birmingham age-herald* commented that the planned withdrawal of American troops after seven years proved the success of the U.S. mission to stabilize the Dominican Republic and prepare it for self-government. The editorial cited extensive road construction, suppression of banditry, sanitary improvements, and fiscal reforms as permanent benefits of the occupation. It argued that the impending military evacuation refuted accusations that the United States harbored imperialistic designs in Santo Domingo.
records.summary_es: El *Birmingham age-herald* comentó que la planeada retirada de las tropas estadounidenses tras siete años demostraba el éxito de la misión de Estados Unidos para estabilizar la República Dominicana y prepararla para el autogobierno. El editorial citó la extensa construcción de caminos, la supresión del bandolerismo, las mejoras sanitarias y las reformas fiscales como beneficios permanentes de la ocupación. Sostuvo que la inminente evacuación militar refutaba las acusaciones de que Estados Unidos albergaba designios imperialistas en Santo Domingo.
records.passage: result of the state department's decision to withdraw American troops from the Dominican republic. The American occupation of Santo Domingo lasted for seven years, and while there has been much criticism of the government for its Dominican policy, the task of restoring order and placing the Dominican people in a position to govern themselves has apparently been accomplished. Furthermore, by the building of roads, the protection of private property, the breaking up of banditry, sanitation and government economies, the republic and its people are in far better case than they otherwise would have been. The withdrawal of American troops should put an end to the accusations that the United States was pursuing a high-handed and imperialistic policy in its treatment of Santo Domingo. records.headline: Ten to twelve days are cut off the journey from Santo Domingo City
records.summary_en: Ten to twelve days are cut off the journey from Santo Domingo City to New York by a new highway of about 150 miles built by American Marines when not occupied maintaining order in the Dominican Republic. The road places Puerto Plata on the north and Santo Domingo City on the south in close touch with coastwise shipping on both the Atlantic and the Caribbean, allowing freight and passenger traffic that previously required a ten-to-twelve-day trip around the island's south, east, and northern ends to reach Puerto Plata for shipment in a few hours. In commemoration of the highway's completion, missionaries of the Episcopal Church in the Dominican Republic are undertaking work on the island, where the Church of San Nikolo founded by Columbus at Santo Domingo City still stands.
records.summary_es: De diez a doce días se reduce el viaje desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo hasta Nueva York por una nueva carretera de unas 150 millas, construida por infantes de marina estadounidenses cuando no estaban ocupados manteniendo el orden en la República Dominicana. La vía pone a Puerto Plata en el norte y a la ciudad de Santo Domingo en el sur en estrecho contacto con la navegación de cabotaje tanto en el Atlántico como en el Caribe, permitiendo que el tráfico de carga y pasajeros que antes requería un recorrido de diez a doce días alrededor de los extremos sur, este y norte de la isla llegue a Puerto Plata para su embarque en pocas horas. En conmemoración de la conclusión de la carretera, los misioneros de la Iglesia Episcopal en la República Dominicana llevan a cabo labores en la isla, donde aún se conserva la iglesia de San Nikolo fundada por Colón en la ciudad de Santo Domingo.

records.summary_en: The post of the 44th Company of U.S. Marines—one of the Marine Corps' few mounted companies—on the east side of the road opposite the small town of Chicharrones, twenty-one kilometers from the seaport of San Pedro de Macoris in the eastern part of the island of Santo Domingo, is described by Joe Loyd of Hot Spring County, writing from the Dominican Republic. He notes that Chicharrones consists of only two bodegas, a bakery shop, and about twenty-five small houses, while the company is made up of strong, sturdy young Americans between eighteen and thirty years of age selected from Marine Corps recruiting stations.

records.headline: An Army flight itinerary to Porto Rico and back traces stages
records.summary_en: An Army flight itinerary to Porto Rico and back traces stages from Arcadia, Florida, through Havana, Camaguey, and Guantanamo in Cuba, then 225 miles to Port-au-Prince, Haiti, 150 miles to San Domingo in the Dominican Republic, and 250 miles to San Juan, Porto Rico, before returning along the same route to Arcadia and proceeding to Jacksonville, Fort Bragg, Fayetteville, and Bolling Field in Washington, D.C. records.summary_en: The *Alexandria gazette* reported that disagreements over a newly drafted electoral law delayed Dominican congressional elections and the scheduled withdrawal of American troops. Opponents contended the statute was overly complicated for the public, prompting efforts to amend the law to satisfy competing political factions. Special Commissioner Sumner Welles prepared to return to Santo Domingo to help mediate disputes and facilitate the transition to constitutional government.

records.summary_en: Final arrangements are nearly complete for Edwin Keller to travel to West Indian markets as San Antonio's first overseas trade envoy. records.headline: U.S. officials and Dominicans who have their country's best
records.summary_en: U.S. officials and Dominicans who have their country's best interest at heart hope full government control can be returned to the Dominicans as soon as possible without undue delays, The Evening star comments. Calling the intervention in Santo Domingo a thankless job that has drawn criticism in Europe and Latin America as a form of "imperialism," the paper states that before withdrawing, the United States will ensure that Dominican independence, territorial integrity, public order, and the security of life and property are adequately safeguarded. If those assurances fail after withdrawal, the United States may be forced to interfere again, whereas if the Dominican Republic governs itself without the periodic upheavals of past administrations, the intervention will be justified.

Calificando la intervención en Santo Domingo como una tarea ingrata que ha suscitado críticas en Europa y América Latina como una forma de «imperialismo», el periódico afirma que, antes de retirarse, Estados Unidos se asegurará de que la independencia dominicana, la integridad territorial, el orden público y la seguridad de la vida y la propiedad estén adecuadamente salvaguardados. Si esas garantías fracasan tras la retirada, Estados Unidos podría verse obligado a intervenir nuevamente, mientras que si la República Dominicana se gobierna a sí misma sin las conmociones periódicas de las administraciones pasadas, la intervención quedará justificada.

records.full_text:
Pickpocket or Parson?

SCENE: A street corner with a lot of doubtful customers hanging around.

A woman, passing by, drops her pocketbook.

Behind her a man of winning mien—perhaps a person, perhaps a pickpocket—the crowd can't tell—stoops and picks it up.

For a minute he stops and turns the object over in his hand.

"Say, cull," says one of the gang, "whatcher go'nter to with it?"

"Give it back to the lady," says the queer-acting man.

And he starts walking after the lady, but so haltingly that his actions belie his words.

"Like fun he is!" mutters the gang. "Watch 'im go south with it."

DURING the Spanish-American war Uncle Sam picked up the Philippines.

"What are you going to do with them?" asked a skeptical world.

"Give them their freedom," said Uncle Sam, looking them over.

"Like fun he will!" leers the knowing old world. "Watch him go south with them."

THE United States today is on trial for its honor. For decades we have been telling the world how honest we are. And now we have got to make good or admit we are no better than the rest—just a great, big, powerful empire whose morals are molded to conform to the dollar.

The whole world is watching to see what we will do next.

"You say you are not imperialistic," it jeers. And it sticks its tongue in its cheek and looks at the Philippines and Porto Rico and Hawaii and Guam and the Virgin Islands; at our virtual protectorate over Cuba and the Republic of Panama; at our control of the customs of the Dominican Republic and Haiti, and our occupation of the latter country by marines; at our hegemony, as they call it, over Central and much of South America.

And reviewing it all, it asks insinuatingly:

"What are you up to in all those places?"

"Just protecting the interests of the unfortunate peoples," we say.

"Oh!" says the world, winking prodigiously.

WELL, a showdown is approaching. The Philippines may well be the test case. And the case of the Philippines is this:

Congress officially promised the Filipinos their freedom as soon as they proved they could govern themselves. Gov. Gen. Harrison from 1916 to 1921 gave them a chance, and they did a pretty good job. And President Wilson in 1920 told Congress the time had about come for America to make good her promise.

Then bang! Something happened. It was Gen. Leonard Wood. He arrived in the islands and as governor general, instead of giving the Filipinos more freedom, took what they had away.

Now the islanders have put the whole thing squarely up to President Harding, meantime refusing to co-operate with Gen. Wood. They have gone out on strike.

CHEATING the Filipinos won't hurt the Filipinos much. But it will hurt us a lot. By cheating the Filipinos we will destroy our own great influence for good in the world. We will destroy the faith an otherwise well-nigh hopeless old earth still somehow manages to retain in us—faith which may yet save mankind from perdition.

We know what the people of this country would do about it. Wood would get his orders, and he would get them right.

But what will the government do? Let it not forget the world, not merely the Philippines, is waiting to hear the answer.

records.headline: The Navy Department ordered an investigation into reports of an uprising
records.summary_en: The Navy Department ordered an investigation into reports of an uprising in the Dominican Republic linked to the departure of the cruiser Rochester, flagship of the special service squadron commanded by Rear Admiral John H. Dayton, from Panama to Santo Domingo. According to Navy Department officials, the vessel's movement from Colon was not caused by any disturbance in the Dominican Republic, and no official advices had been received of any trouble involving the Marines stationed there. Marine Corps administrative officers and Dominican diplomatic representatives in Washington also discounted the reports, noting they would have been notified immediately of any untoward incidents.
records.summary_es: El Departamento de Marina ordenó una investigación sobre los informes de un levantamiento en la República Dominicana vinculados a la salida del crucero Rochester, buque insignia del escuadrón de servicio especial comandado por el contralmirante John H. Dayton, desde Panamá hacia Santo Domingo. Según funcionarios del Departamento de Marina, el movimiento del buque desde Colón no fue motivado por ningún disturbio en la República Dominicana, y no se habían recibido informes oficiales de ningún problema que involucrara a los infantes de marina destacados allí. Oficiales administrativos del Cuerpo de Marines y representantes diplomáticos dominicanos en Washington también descartaron los informes, señalando que habrían sido notificados de inmediato sobre cualquier incidente adverso.

records.summary_en: The *Evening star* reported official statements declaring that the United States did not seek permanent dominion over Santo Domingo, but was actively preparing to evacuate its forces following free elections scheduled for mid-September. The statement explained that American policy in Haiti similarly aimed only to establish stability and competent self-governance following decades of revolution. U.S. authorities emphasized that they harbored no territorial ambitions on the island and would welcome the day American troops could safely withdraw.
records.summary_es: El *Evening star* informó sobre declaraciones oficiales en las que se afirmaba que Estados Unidos no buscaba una dominación permanente sobre Santo Domingo, sino que preparaba activamente la evacuación de sus tropas tras las elecciones libres programadas para mediados de septiembre. El pronunciamiento explicaba que la política estadounidense en Haití aspiraba igualmente a restablecer la estabilidad y un gobierno autónomo competente tras décadas de revoluciones. Las autoridades de Washington hicieron hincapié en que carecían de ambiciones territoriales en la isla y celebrarían el momento en que los efectivos estadounidenses pudieran retirarse de forma segura.
records.passage: THE EVENING STAR, WASHINGTON, D. C., FRIDAY, AUGUST 31, 1923. is that instead of using this opportunity, as has falsely been charged, to establish a permanent control of Santo Domingo, the government of the United States has been solicitous to arrange for the termination of the occupation and the withdrawal of its forces and has devoted its endeavors, earnestly and effectively, to the assistance of the Dominican people in establishing a sound basis for an independent government. It is expected that elections in which the authorities of the United States will not intervene will be held about the middle of September and in due course the permanent government will be established. "In order to understand conditions in Haiti it should be recalled that since the republic of Haiti gained its independence it has been the scene of almost continuous revolution. This is true of its recent history as well as of the earlier years. By the Associated Press.

MINNEAPOLIS, Minn., August 31.—The Monroe doctrine was defined here last night by Secretary Hughes as embodying a policy vitally related to national safety, inimical to no just interest in Latin America or elsewhere, and imposing no barrier to wider international co-operation in the promotion of peace and understanding.

Speaking before the American Bar Association, the Secretary declared that while the doctrine in no way established a "protectorate" over other American republics, American rights and obligations not specifically outlined by Monroe in his famous message had sometimes made intervention in some Latin American states an absolute necessity. He recalled that the right to intervene in Cuba is a matter of record in the treaty of 1904, although he added that the United States would rather, if possible, continue in its present role of "friendly adviser."

Called Defensive Policy.

"Taking the doctrine as it has been and as it is believed to remain," said Mr. Hughes, "I desire to comment upon certain points which, as I believe, deserve special emphasis at this time.

"First. The Monroe doctrine is not a policy of aggression; it is a policy of self-defense. It was asserted at a time when the danger of foreign aggression in this hemisphere, a firm basis of independent national life, and we were menaced by threats of old world powers directed against republican institutions. But the achievements of the century have not altered the scope of the doctrine or changed its basis. It still remains an assertion of the principle of national security. As such, it is obviously not exclusive.

"Second, as the policy embodied in the Monroe doctrine is distinctively the policy of the United States, the government of the United States reserves to itself its definition, interpretation and application. This government has welcomed the recognition by other governments of the fact and soundness of this policy and of the appropriateness of its application from time to time.

Makes Own Interpretation.

"But the United States has not been disposed to enter into engagements which have the effect of submitting to any other power or to any concert of powers the determination either of the occasions upon which the principles of the Monroe doctrine shall be invoked or the measures that shall be taken in giving it effect. As President Wilson observed: 'The Monroe doctrine was proclaimed by the United States on her own authority. It always has been maintained and always will be maintained upon her own responsibility.'

"This implies neither suspicion nor estrangement. It simply means that the United States is asserting a separate national right of self defense, and that in the exercise of this right it must have an unhampered discretion.

"Third. The policy of the Monroe doctrine does not infringe upon the independence and sovereignty of other American states. Misconception upon this point is the only disturbing influence in our relations with Latin American states. The declaration of our purpose to oppose what is inimical to our safety does not imply an attempt to establish a protectorate any more than a similar assertion by any one of the great southern republics of opposition to conduct on the part of any of the others endangering its security would aim at the establishment of a protectorate.

No Overlordship Desired.

"I utterly disclaim, as unwarranted, the observations which occasionally have been made implying a claim on our part to superintend the affairs of our sister republics, to assert an overlordship, to consider the spread of our authority beyond our own domain as the aim of our policy, and to make our power the test of right in this hemisphere. I oppose all such misconceived and unsound assertions or intimations.

"They do not express our national purpose; they belie our sincere friendship; they are false to the fundamental principles of our institutions and of our foreign policy which has sought to reflect, with rare exceptions, the ideals of liberty; they menace us by stimulating a distrust which has no real foundation. They find no sanction whatever in the Monroe doctrine. There is room in this hemisphere, without danger of collision, for the complete recognition of that doctrine and the independent sovereignty of the Latin American republics.

"Fourth. There are, indeed, modern conditions and recent events which cannot fail to engage our attention. We have grown rich and powerful, but we have not outgrown the necessity, in justice to ourselves and without injustice to others, of safeguarding our future peace and security. By building the Panama canal we have not only established a new and convenient highway of commerce, but we have created exigencies and new conditions of strategy and defense. It is for us to protect that highway.

May Need New Canal.

"It may also be necessary for us at some time to build another canal between the Atlantic and the Pacific oceans, and to protect that. I believe that the sentiment of the American people is practically unanimous that in the interest of our national safety we could not yield to any foreign power the control of the Panama canal or the approaches to it or the obtaining of any position which would interfere with our right of protection or would menace the freedom of our communications.

"So far as the region of the Caribbean sea is concerned, it may be said that if we had no Monroe doctrine we should have to create one. And this is not to imply any limitation on the scope of the doctrine, as originally proclaimed and as still maintained, but simply to indicate that new occasions require new applications of an old principle which remains completely effective. What has taken place of late years in the region of the Caribbean has given rise to much confusion of thought and misapprehension of purpose.

"As I have said, the Monroe doctrine as a particular declaration in no way exhausts American right or policy; the United States has rights and obligations which that doctrine does not define. And in the unsettled condition of certain countries in the region of the Caribbean it has been necessary to assert these rights and obligations as well as the limited principles of the Monroe doctrine.

Intervention in Cuba.

"In 1898 the United States intervened in Cuba in the cause of humanity and because of a condition of affairs at our very door so injurious to our interests that it had become intolerable. In view of the distress, miseries, and barbarities that existed, our action, as John Bassett Moore has said, 'was analogous to what is known in private law as the abatement of a nuisance.'

"In the settlement that followed the establishment of Cuban independence, Cuba agreed 'that the United States may exercise the right to intervene for the preservation of Cuban independence, the maintenance of a government adequate for the protection of life, property and individual liberty, and for discharging the obligations with respect to Cuba imposed by the treaty of Paris on the United States, now to be assumed and undertaken by the government of Cuba.'

"Cuba also agreed not to enter into any treaty with any foreign power which would tend to impair her independence, 'nor in any manner authorize or permit any foreign power or powers to obtain by colonization or for military or naval purposes or otherwise lodgment in or control of any portion of said island.' There were also restrictive provisions as to the contracting of debts."

Holds Special Position.

"The United States thus holds a special position in relation to Cuba, but it should be pointed out and clearly understood that, while in view of this position, we have acted as the friendly adviser of the Cuban government, our action has been solely for the purpose of aiding in maintaining the independence and stability of Cuba and thus not to create but to preclude the necessity of intervention under the treaty by encouraging the Cuban people to eliminate waste and corruption, to reduce public expenses to the normal requirements of government, and to secure the just and efficient administration which will safeguard the desired independence of Cuba and promote the prosperity which, with their abundant natural resources, the Cuban people are entitled to enjoy.

"It is impossible for me to review in any detail the events which led to the occupation of Santo Domingo and Haiti. In Santo Domingo, during the forty years prior to 1907, there had been sixteen revolutionary movements, and complete political and economic demoralization had resulted. A military government was established in 1916 and until recent months was continued in the interest of public order. This occupation was due to the demonstration, to use the phrase of President Roosevelt, of an impotence resulting in the lessening of the ties of civilized society and thus requiring intervention.

U. S. Will Withdraw.

"But the point that I desire to make is that instead of using this opportunity, as has falsely been charged, to establish a permanent control of Santo Domingo, the government of the United States has been solicitous to arrange for the termination of the occupation and the withdrawal of its forces and has devoted its endeavors, earnestly and effectively, to the assistance of the Dominican people in establishing a sound basis for an independent government. It is expected that elections in which the authorities of the United States will not intervene will be held about the middle of September and in due course the permanent government will be established.

"In order to understand conditions in Haiti it should be recalled that since the republic of Haiti gained its independence it has been the scene of almost continuous revolution. This is true of its recent history as well as of the earlier years. The government of the Untied States is seeking to make its relation to Haiti beneficial to Haitian people; it has no other aim but to establish peace and stability. It does not seek to acquire or to control the territory of Haiti, and it will welcome the day when it can leave Haiti with the reasonable assurance that the Haitians will be able to maintain an independent government competent to keep order and discharge its international obligations.

Wants Republic Stable.

"The disturbed conditions and revolutionary tendencies in some of the Central American republics have given great solicitude to the government of the United States, and its efforts have been directed to the promotion of tranquillity and stability. This is in the interest of the maintenance of the unimpaired integrity and sovereignty of these republics.

"Fifth. It is apparent that the Monroe doctrine does not stand in the way of the pan-American co-operation; rather it affords the necessary foundation for that co-operation in the independence and security of American states. With the aim of furthering this pan-American co-operation there have been five pan-American conferences, the last of which was recently held in Santiago. The best results of these conferences are not found in any formal acts or statements, but in the generation of helpful and friendly influences which draw peoples together through a better mutual understanding.

"The essential condition of co-operation is peace, and this government is constant in its endeavors to promote peace in this hemisphere by using its good offices, whenever they are welcome, in eliminating the causes of strife, and in making provision for the settlement of disputes that cannot be adjusted by diplomacy. Almost all the boundary disputes in Latin America have been settled, and those that remain are in process of adjustment.

Wide Liberty of Action.

"Finally, it should be observed that the Monroe doctrine is not an obstacle to a wider international co-operation, beyond the limits of pan-American aims and interests, whenever that co-operation is congenial to American institutions. From the foundation of the government we have sought to promote the peaceful settlement of international controversies. Establishment of a permanent court of international justice, which might make available the facilities of a permanent tribunal (instead of the less satisfactory provision of temporary tribunals of arbitration) to governments desiring to submit their controversies to it, has been a distinct feature of the policy of the government of the United States for many years. We are also interested in measures of conciliation and in the facilities of conference.

"Our attitude is one of independence, not of isolation. Our people are still intent upon abstaining from participation in the political strife of Europe. They are not disposed to commit this government in advance to the use of its power in unknown contingencies, preferring to reserve freedom of action in the confidence of our ability and readiness to respond to every future call of duty. They have no desire to put their power in pledge, but they do not shirk co-operation with other nations whenever there is a sound basis for it and a consciousness of community of interest and aim.

Ready to Co-Operate.

"Co-operation is not dictation, and it is not partisanship. On our part it must be the co-operation of a free people drawing their strength from many racial stocks, and a co-operation that is made possible by a preponderant sentiment permitting governmental action under a system which denies all exercise of autocratic power. It will be the co-operation of a people of liberal ideals, deeply concerned with the maintenance of peace and interested in all measures which find support in the common sense of the country as being practicable and well designed to foster common interests.

"To such aims the Monroe doctrine is not opposed, and with the passing of 100 years it remains a cherished policy, inimical to no just interest and deemed to be vitally related to our own safety and to the peaceful progress of the peoples of this hemisphere."

Zeballos Promises Speech.

Dr. E. S. Zeballos of Argentina, president of the International Law Association, commended the address of Mr. Hughes on the Monroe Doctrine. Lord Birkenhead, former lord chancellor of Great Britain, declared it "an admirable presentation."

Dr. Zeballos, who followed closely every utterance of the Secretary of State, showed his approval by joining the applause frequently.

"Mr. Hughes' address was very favorable to the South American countries," he told the Associated Press at its conclusion. "It was the first utterance of the new administration, and it confirmed the Harding Administration policies."

"The position of the United States, as Mr. Hughes outlined it, is fully in accord with that desired by the South American republics. Mr. Hughes is to be congratulated by South America."

Taft on Judicial Ethics

Adoption of a code of ethics for the legal profession should be preceded by thorough consideration by the parties affected, Chief Justice William Howard Taft declared today when presenting to the Bar association the report on judicial ethics. Justice Taft, as chairman of the committee which prepared the report, presented it with the recommendation that the committee be continued while action on the canons and ethics be postponed. His recommendations were adopted.

The day was devoted to presentation of reports of sections and committees, reading of three committee reports and an attempt to change the constitution to permit change in the selection of the general council.

Commenting on the special committee's report on judicial ethics, Justice Taft declared that adoption of the code of ethics for judges which he outlined should be preceded by thorough consideration by the members of the judiciary. He recommended that the committee's recommendations be reported to the judicial section of the Bar association, and that the chairman of this section, Justice Pierce Butler of the United States supreme court, be authorized to appoint a committee of from three to five judges to consider the recommendations.

"Taking the doctrine as it has been and as it is believed to remain," said Hughes in his address, "I desire to comment upon certain points which, I believe, deserve special emphasis at this time.

"First: The Monroe doctrine is not a police of aggression; it is a policy of self-defense. "Third: The policy of the Monroe doctrine does not infringe upon the independence and sovereignty of other American states. Misconception upon this point is the only disturbing influence in our relations with Latin-American states. The declaration of our purpose to oppose what is inimical to our safety does not imply an attempt to establish a protectorate any more than a similar assertion by anyone of the great southern republics of opposition to conduct on the part of any of the others endangering its security would aim at the establishment of a protectorate.

records.headline: An editorial column in The Washington daily news quotes an assessment
records.summary_en: An editorial column in The Washington daily news quotes an assessment from the Guardian stating that the Dominican Republic placed its customs under United States control in 1907 and Nicaragua in 1911, while American Marines have occupied the Dominican Republic since 1916 and Nicaragua since 1912. The quoted piece adds that recent years have seen American capital flooding Latin America with varying degrees of control, naming Haiti, Santo Domingo, Bolivia, and other republics across the region, and concluding that only Chile, Uruguay, and Argentina are strong enough to receive U.S. capital on independent terms like Canada. The columnist remarks that this view offers food for thought as the United States attempts to settle a dispute with Cuba.
records.summary_es: Una columna editorial en The Washington daily news cita una evaluación del Guardian que afirma que la República Dominicana puso sus aduanas bajo el control de Estados Unidos en 1907 y Nicaragua en 1911, mientras que los infantes de marina estadounidenses han ocupado la República Dominicana desde 1916 y Nicaragua desde 1912. El texto citado añade que en los últimos años el capital estadounidense ha inundado América Latina con diversos grados de control, nombrando a Haití, Santo Domingo, Bolivia y otras repúblicas de la región, y concluyendo que solo Chile, Uruguay y Argentina son lo suficientemente fuertes como para recibir capital estadounidense en términos independientes como Canadá. El columnista señala que esta perspectiva invita a la reflexión mientras Estados Unidos intenta resolver una disputa con Cuba.

records.headline: After a heavy sea shifted their cargo and sprung a leak that filled
records.summary_en: After a heavy sea shifted their cargo and sprung a leak that filled the holds with 19 feet of water on the fourth day, the crew of a schooner abandoned ship in an 18-foot lifeboat south of San Pedro de Macoris, Dominican Republic. Taking sea biscuit, canned beef, and four casks of water, the crew rowed in shifts through squalls and high seas for four days and nights toward San Pedro de Macoris. There the American consul took charge of the men and sent them to San Domingo City, where they boarded the Hancock County as passengers.
records.summary_es: Después de que un mar grueso desplazara su carga y abriera una vía de agua que llenó las bodegas con 19 pies de agua al cuarto día, la tripulación de una goleta abandonó el barco en un bote salvavidas de 18 pies al sur de San Pedro de Macorís, República Dominicana. Llevando galletas marineras, carne enlatada y cuatro barriles de agua, la tripulación remó por turnos a través de chubascos y mar gruesa durante cuatro días y noches hacia San Pedro de Macorís. Allí el cónsul estadounidense se hizo cargo de los hombres y los envió a la ciudad de Santo Domingo, donde abordaron el Hancock County como pasajeros.

records.headline: Citing the paper L'Echo, the Evening star reports its assertion
records.summary_en: Citing the paper L'Echo, the Evening star reports its assertion that Haiti and Santo Domingo are exasperated to the point of revolution by American activities. Under the subheading "Little Family Matters," L'Echo states that a telegram from Panama recently reported that the Dominican Republic had revolted and nineteen American sailors had been killed, adding that nothing more had been heard since from Santo Domingo because American information bureaus had been discreet. The quoted paper concludes that the United States will probably find means to quickly teach obedience to the Dominican patriots.

El periódico citado concluye que Estados Unidos probablemente encontrará los medios para enseñar rápidamente obediencia a los patriotas dominicanos.

records.headline: M. we started to motor the two hundred miles through the mountains
records.summary_en: The *Ventnor news* published a first-hand travel narrative praising the stabilization of Santo Domingo under the U.S. Marine Corps, highlighting administrative order and revenue collection. The author described motoring two hundred miles from Monte Cristi through Santiago to Santo Domingo City over modern mountain highways recently constructed by American military engineers. The account commended the marines for modernizing infrastructure, civilizing the region, and establishing public safety.
records.summary_es: El *Ventnor news* publicó una crónica de viaje testimonial que elogiaba la estabilización de Santo Domingo bajo el Cuerpo de Marines de Estados Unidos, destacando el orden administrativo y la recaudación fiscal. El autor describió su trayecto en automóvil de doscientas millas desde Monte Cristi pasando por Santiago hasta la ciudad de Santo Domingo a través de modernas carreteras de montaña recién construidas por ingenieros militares estadounidenses. El relato alabó a los marines por modernizar la infraestructura, pacificar la región y establecer la seguridad pública.

It has been reported by those who have investigated the agricultural possibilities of Haiti that shrubs and small trees shoot up out of the walls ruined buildings, nourished only by the mortar between the bricks, the air, the dew and the rain; that a riot of vegetation is seen in the uncultivated portions of the country, and that neglected fields are speedily covered with a thick growth of tropical verdure. All tropical fruits, flourish, -- the orange, the shaddock, the pineapple, the mango, the alligator pair, the plaintain, and the fig banana. It is claimed that Haiti is one of the best banana countries in the tropics. Although Haitian cotton brings a much higher price on the Enropean market than ordinary cotton' the cultivation of this plant has been sadly neglected. Sugar cane flourishes whether it is cultivated or not, and grows on almost indefinitely without being replanted, reproducing itself year after year.

The great staple product of Haiti is coffee. It supplies the bulk of the revenues of the government, and the mergre demands of the simple peasantry which constitutes about 95 percent of the population. Women and children gather it and take it to the seaport towns on their heads and on the backs of burros. Although an effort is now being made by the American government to make a market for this coffee in the United States, practically all of it is shipped to European countries. The cultivation of coffee, however, not unlike cotton, has been greatly neglected by the natives, except in small patches around the cottages. Most of the crop is the result or the reproduction from fallen berries, and the crop has varied from year to year only through influences like a variation in rainfall.

Since the American intervention in 1915 there has been a revival in agricultural pursuits and a careful survey has been made of the need of agricultural instruction. Highways are being constructed and reforms established that will rapidly develop Haiti morally, socially, politically and economically. According to the select committee that made an inquiry into the American occupation and administration of Haiti and the Dominican Republic, few of the Haitians had ever seen a plow before the American intervention. The peasant class had never seen and did not know how to use a shovel, and when a load of road-building machinery, including 60 wheelbarrows, was docked, the natives carried them on their heads, instead of wheeling them to the place where the road-building was in progress.

There can be no question as to the benefit to Haiti of a temporary American occupation. With the development of her natural resources; with the establishment of thoroughly equipped public schools; with the revival of agricultural pursuits, the building of a railroad, the construction of hospitals and the suppression of the revolutionary propensities of the political leaders, Haiti will eventually be the garden spot of our western civilization.

records.full_text:
Haiti Progressing Toward Self-Rule, Lejeune Declares

WASHINGTON—Progress in the rehabilitation of Haiti and the Dominican republic under the tutelage of the United States marine corps is recorded by Maj.-Gen. John A. Lejeune, commandant, in his annual report to Secretary Denby.

The last year, the general asserts, "there has been no call for the services of marines for expeditionary duty."

The achievements of the marine corps in Haiti, Gen. Lejeune states, "constitute one of the bright pages in American history." A people "torn with revolution and misery have been rescued," he says, and "today peace, personal liberty and prosperity prevail such as never known before."

The native gendarmerie of Haiti, the general notes, have taken the places of marines "with marked success." There were no reports of banditry during the entire year.

In the Dominican republic, Gen. Lejeune explains, the country is entering upon a period of self-government "in accordance with the Dominican-American plan of evacuation."

records.headline: The daily worker reports that the March election in Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: The daily worker reports that the March election in Santo Domingo will be the first since American Marines occupied the country, asserting that military control was withdrawn on condition that the Dominican government accept U.S. fiscal and political control, which the paper equates with the National City Bank of New York. According to the article, a constituent assembly is to be called to revise the constitution under threat that U.S. troops will return if it does not comply with American demands. The paper adds that deposed president Henriquez y Carvajal finds it safer to remain in Havana, while his sons and close relatives stay in Mexico or Cuba despite the "freedom" granted by the United States.
records.summary_es: The daily worker informa que las elecciones de marzo en Santo Domingo serán las primeras desde que los infantes de marina estadounidenses ocuparon el país, afirmando que el control militar fue retirado con la condición de que el gobierno dominicano aceptara el control fiscal y político de Estados Unidos, lo cual el periódico equipara con el National City Bank de Nueva York. Según el artículo, se convocará una asamblea constituyente para revisar la constitución bajo la amenaza de que las tropas estadounidenses regresarán si no cumple con las exigencias norteamericanas. El periódico añade que el presidente depuesto Henríquez y Carvajal considera más seguro permanecer en La Habana, mientras que sus hijos y parientes cercanos permanecen en México o Cuba a pesar de la «libertad» concedida por Estados Unidos.

Washington's proposals for withdrawal require recognition of all acts of the military government, including the 1918 bond issue and the 1922 customs loan, and an assurance that the customs tariff will not be changed during the life of the 1922 loan without Washington's consent; after the convention is ratified, United States military forces will leave the republic.

records.summary_en: Acting on the request of Central American powers, the United States government ordered Sumner Welles, American commissioner to the Dominican Republic, to proceed immediately to Tegucigalpa to act as mediator. A State Department communication stated that Welles was directed to offer the friendly assistance of the United States government in establishing peace in Honduras. Welles departed San Domingo on Wednesday aboard the United States scout cruiser Richmond and will fly by airplane from Amapala to Tegucigalpa as soon as the ship reaches port.

An attache of the American legation in Tegucigalpa is said to have proceeded to La Libertad, Salvador, a cable station, in order to communicate with the government at Washington. A dispatch from Amapala says additional reinforcements for the provisional government forces, who are besieged in Tegucigalpa, have managed to slip through the revolutionary lines and enter the capital. Other dispatches are to the effect that none of the political parties in Honduras cares to shoulder the responsibility of intervening with Sumner Welles, representing the American government, in an endeavor to bring about peace between the discordant factions.

records.headline: President and Mrs. Coolidge hosted a large luncheon at the White House
records.summary_en: President and Mrs. Coolidge hosted a large luncheon at the White House in honor of General Horacio Vasquez, president-elect of the Dominican Republic, who arrived in Washington on Saturday. The gathering, the first of a series of entertainments planned for the visiting president-elect, included Cabinet secretaries, Supreme Court justices, military commanders, Third Assistant Secretary of State J. Butler Wright, Sumner Welles of the State Department, Dr. Leo S. Rowe, Dominican Minister Emilio C. Joubert, and members of General Vasquez's party, Senor Ariza and Senor Ricart. Dr. Rowe will also host a luncheon at the Pan-American Union.

Joubert y los miembros de la comitiva del general Vasquez, el señor Ariza y el señor Ricart. El doctor Rowe también ofrecerá un almuerzo en la Unión Panamericana.

records.summary_en: General Vasquez, on a semi-official tour of the United States prior to his inauguration, arrived in Washington yesterday afternoon accompanied by Orme Wilson, Jr., and by Joseph Flack, secretary of the U.S. Legation in Santo Domingo, who will act as his aide during his stay. At Union Station he was met by Third Assistant Secretary of State J. Butler Wright, American Commissioner to the Dominican Republic Sumner Welles, Admiral Edward W. Eberle, and Brigadier General Samuel D. Rochenbach, while a Fort Myer cavalry troop saluted, the Army band played the Dominican national anthem and the Star-Spangled Banner, and a salute of twenty-one guns was fired at the Washington Navy Yard as the party drove to the Hotel Hamilton. General Vasquez received a formal reception from the Secretary of State at 11 o'clock this morning and will be honored at a luncheon tomorrow at 1 o'clock by Pan-American Union director Dr. Leo S. Rowe.

records.headline: But all agree that Santo Domingo should have Its trial at domestic tranquillity
records.summary_en: The *Evening star* assessed the outlook for stability in Santo Domingo following the evacuation of American troops, noting general agreement that the nation deserved its opportunity for independent self-government. The article reviewed the background of intervention, recalling that the 1916 marine occupation followed decades of civil strife and the 1905 crisis when foreign creditors threatened naval force over unpaid debts. It described how the United States helped arrange a $20,000,000 refunding loan backed by an American receiver-general collecting customs to make monthly debt payments.
records.summary_es: El *Evening star* evaluó las perspectivas de estabilidad en Santo Domingo tras la evacuación de las tropas estadounidenses, destacando el consenso general de que la nación merecía su oportunidad de autogobierno independiente. El artículo recapituló los antecedentes de la intervención, recordando que la ocupación de los marines en 1916 siguió a decenios de contiendas civiles y a la crisis de 1905, cuando acreedores extranjeros amenazaron con recurrir a la fuerza naval por deudas impagas. Describió cómo Estados Unidos facilitó la gestión de un empréstito de refinanciamiento de 20 000 000 de dólares respaldado por un receptor general estadounidense encargado de recaudar las rentas aduaneras para efectuar pagos mensuales de la deuda.
records.passage: to support his government, or will it be undermined and hampered by political conspiracies and insurrections like those of the past? There are some familiar with the West Indies who feel a good deal of doubt on this question. But all agree that Santo Domingo should have its trial at domestic tranquillity — its chance to make good as an independent, responsible nation. When United States marines were landed on the island in 1916 it was to restore order out of a political and economic chaos that had lasted for many long years. As early as 1905 repeated revolutions had left the affairs of the Dominican government in such a hopeless state that the United States was compelled to come to its assistance in order to preserve the Monroe doctrine. A large group of foreign creditors, each ready to present his bill with a gunboat, clouded the horizon. Another large group of native creditors, each planning to enforce his claims against the government by insurrection, agitated the country's interior. Clearly something had to be done to reestablish Dominican credit, and the United States did it. Through its offices the republic was enabled to secure a loan of $20,000,000 with which to refund its foreign debts. This was arranged by a bond issue, with the understanding that the bonds were to be paid off in monthly installments from the customs revenues. Although Dominican authorities promised fiscal restraint and agreed not to increase public debt without U.S. consent, recurring revolutions diverted revenues into military operations and generated massive unpaid debts. The article explained that the resulting financial collapse and threats to custom houses prompted the United States to deploy marines in 1916.

Aunque las autoridades dominicanas prometieron moderación presupuestaria y convinieron en no aumentar la deuda pública sin el consentimiento de Estados Unidos, sucesivas revoluciones desviaron los fondos hacia gastos bélicos y generaron deudas impagas colosales. Dominican Promises In this agreement, moreover, the Dominicans promised a wise and efficient administration of their treasury. They were to pay back the salaries of civil employes regularly. In addition to back pay, and any surplus was to be used for the building of public works. They were not to increase the public debt without consulting the United States. But the continued outbreak of revolutions made it impossible to keep this promise. Great sums were expended for military preparations instead of public improvements, and other sums disappeared without any explanation as one faction after another came into control of the treasury. In order to make up deficits, stamps, stamped paper and other government securities were recklessly issued. Thus, within a few years, the republic was again burdened with an enormous interior debt which made the position of the custom-houses extremely unsafe. records.headline: Vasquez as president of the Dominican Republic brings to a successful end the long struggle of more than eight years by the people of Santo Domingo to regain their sovereignty and independence
records.summary_en: The *Evening star* reported that the inauguration of General Horacio Vasquez brought a successful conclusion to over eight years of Dominican efforts to recover their national sovereignty from American military rule. The article recounted how sustained Dominican resistance and an advocacy campaign begun in 1920 by former minister Horace G. Knowles spurred a U.S. Senate investigation that culminated in an evacuation agreement. Full sovereignty was restored with the March 15 presidential election, and transports were carrying the remaining 1,800 marines back to the United States.
records.summary_es: El *Evening star* informó que la toma de posesión del general Horacio Vásquez puso un término exitoso a más de ocho años de gestiones dominicanas por recuperar su soberanía nacional frente al régimen militar estadounidense. El artículo relató cómo la sostenida resistencia dominicana y la campaña iniciada en 1920 por el exministro Horace G. Knowles impulsaron una investigación del Senado estadounidense que culminó en un acuerdo de evacuación. La plena soberanía se restableció con las elecciones presidenciales del 15 de marzo, y buques de transporte conducían a los 1 800 infantes de marina restantes de regreso a Estados Unidos.
records.passage: then engaged in an enthusiastic demonstration in honor of the new president. Ends Long Struggle. The inauguration of Gen. Vasquez as president of the Dominican Republic brings to a successful end the long struggle of more than eight years by the people of Santo Domingo to regain their sovereignty and independence, which they have contended was taken away from them by the United States when their country, under orders from Washington, was placed under the control of a large military force. After the setting up by the United States of a military government, the Dominicans made repeated efforts to bring about a withdrawal of the forces. In 1920 Horace G. Knowles, former American minister, started a campaign to secure sovereignty for the Dominicans. Subsequently, the United States Senate authorized a special committee to inquire into the occupation and administration of the country, and such a committee proceeded to Santo Domingo, setting up a court of investigation. The committee's return to Washington was followed by an agreement for the withdrawal of the American forces from the country. The full and complete sovereignty of Santo Domingo was restored and, for the first time in about ten years, an election was held March 15 last, Gen. Vasquez being elected president. There remain in Santo Domingo about 1,800 marines and officers. The evacuation has begun and transports are taking the troops to the United States as speedily as possible. SUBMARINE RAMS YACHT. S-29 in Trial Cruise Sinks Sailing Vessel. PROVINCETOWN, Mass., July 12.

records.summary_en: The Dispatch-News reports that the United States is withdrawing from Santo Domingo following the inauguration of General Horatio Vasquez as President of the Dominican Republic. With the American flag lowered and the Dominican emblem flying in its stead, United States Marines are boarding transports after eight years of intervention. The paper remarks that it took eight years to put affairs in order for the Dominicans to govern alone again, adding that they never ceased protesting throughout that period.

Con la bandera estadounidense arriada y el emblema dominicano ondeando en su lugar, los infantes de marina de Estados Unidos están subiendo a los transportes después de ocho años de intervención. El periódico comenta que tomó ocho años poner los asuntos en orden para que los dominicanos intentaran gobernarse solos nuevamente, y añade que en ningún momento durante esos ocho años dejaron de protestar.

Dr. Rowe stated that the recently completed evacuation of the Dominican Republic should be followed as soon as possible by the evacuation of Haiti.

records.headline: The Evening Star reports that Senor Ariza, recently promoted
records.summary_en: The Evening Star reports that Senor Ariza, recently promoted after a few weeks as charge d'affaires to Minister from the Dominican Republic, presented his credentials to President Coolidge within the past two weeks. Described as a prominent figure from San Domingo, Senor Ariza's principal duty in Washington is to help resolve the longstanding differences between the United States government and that of his country. Having already made progress in this work, he plans to sail for his homeland in September to spend about a month conferring with the Dominican executive and state department officials, and then escort Senora de Ariza back to Washington around October 25.
records.summary_es: El Evening Star informa que el señor Ariza, recientemente ascendido tras unas semanas como encargado de negocios a ministro de la República Dominicana, presentó sus credenciales al presidente Coolidge en las últimas dos semanas. Descrito como una figura destacada de San Domingo, el deber principal del señor Ariza en Washington será ayudar a resolver las diferencias que han existido durante varios años entre el gobierno de Estados Unidos y el de su país. Habiendo logrado ya avances en esta tarea, tiene la intención de zarpar hacia su patria en septiembre para permanecer alrededor de un mes en conferencias con el ejecutivo de la República Dominicana y los funcionarios de su departamento de Estado, y además acompañar a la señora de Ariza de regreso a Washington hacia el 25 de octubre.

records.headline: Messages exchanged between officials of Santo Domingo and the United States marked
records.summary_en: Messages exchanged between officials of Santo Domingo and the United States marked the opening by All America Cables, Inc., of a new cable service between the two countries. President Coolidge sent the first message over the wire to Dominican President General Horatio Vasquez congratulating him on the work bringing the two nations into closer telegraphic union, while the president of the municipal government of Santo Domingo sent the first message in the opposite direction to Mayor Hylan of New York City expressing hope that the line will unite the two peoples. The cable route opens for public patronage tomorrow and features an automatic receiving, sending, and relay station at the Santo Domingo terminal.
records.summary_es: Mensajes intercambiados entre funcionarios de Santo Domingo y de Estados Unidos marcaron la inauguración por parte de All America Cables, Inc., de un nuevo servicio de cable entre ambos países. El presidente Coolidge envió el primer mensaje por la línea al presidente de la República Dominicana, el general Horatio Vasquez, felicitándolo por la obra que acerca a ambas naciones en una unión telegráfica más estrecha, mientras que el presidente del gobierno municipal de Santo Domingo envió el primer mensaje en dirección opuesta al alcalde Hylan de la ciudad de Nueva York expresando la esperanza de que la línea una a los dos pueblos. La ruta de cable se abrirá al público mañana y contará en la terminal de Santo Domingo con una estación automática de recepción, transmisión y retransmisión.

records.headline: Discussing the traditional foreign policy of the United States
records.summary_en: Discussing the traditional foreign policy of the United States as one of independence and collaboration rather than alliance, the writer cites the U.S. Senate's resistance to the annexation of the Dominican Republic alongside its declaration against annexing Cuba and its actions regarding the Panama Canal. According to the passage, these Senate actions reflected the judgment of the American people, who opposed assuming political responsibilities in Europe or Asia and resented great-power intervention in the Caribbean area.

Según el pasaje, estas medidas del Senado reflejaron el criterio del pueblo estadounidense, que se oponía a asumir responsabilidades políticas en Europa o Asia y rechazaba la intervención de las grandes potencias en la región del Caribe.

records.full_text:
The Day in Washington

The house passed a bill to promote production and conservation of helium.

A bill for a new American embassy and consulate general in Tokio passed the house.

The senate rejected a proposal to withhold funds to maintain marines in Haiti.

A senate elections sub-committee recommended the seating of Senator Mayfield, democrat, Texas.

The senate called on Secretary Hughes for information on the Paris reparations agreement.

Heber H. Votaw, brother-in-law of the late President Harding resigned as superintendent of prisons.

The naval bill, containing a request that President Coolidge call an arms conference, passed the senate.

Members of the senate foreign relations committee and others were invited to a night dinner at the White House.

The senate ratified treaties with the Dominican republic on evacuation of American troops and refunding of the Dominican debt.

Senator Shipstead, farmer-labor, Minnesota, charged the increased prices for stocks and bonds were the result of a “stock gambling boom.”

Senator McKellar, democrat, Tennessee, presented a resolution asking President Coolidge to investigate whether England violated the arms treaty in building the battleships Rodney and Nelson.

Justice department took steps to subpoena Senator Wheeler, democrat, Montana, to appear before a grand jury here in connection with the home state indictment against him.

records.summary_en: The *Omaha morning bee* reported details of the treaty ratified by the U.S. Senate refunding the Dominican national debt of $25,000,000. The pact authorized the U.S. president to appoint a general receiver to collect all Dominican customs duties, applying proceeds to receivership expenses, interest, and sinking fund amortization before remitting any surplus to the Dominican government. Under an additional article, the Dominican Republic was prohibited from increasing its public debt without American consent until all refunding bonds were fully paid.
records.summary_es: El *Omaha morning bee* reportó detalles del tratado ratificado por el Senado de Estados Unidos para el refinanciamiento de la deuda nacional dominicana por 25 000 000 de dólares. El pacto autorizaba al presidente estadounidense a nombrar un receptor general para recaudar todos los derechos aduaneros dominicanos, aplicando lo recaudado a los gastos de la receptoría, intereses y amortización del fondo de amortización antes de transferir cualquier remanente al gobierno dominicano. Conforme a un artículo adicional, se prohibía a la República Dominicana aumentar su deuda pública sin consentimiento estadounidense hasta que la totalidad de los bonos de refinanciamiento quedara saldada.

TREATY WITH DOMINICAN REPUBLIC RATIFIED

WASHINGTON, Jan. 24, (AP)—The Senate today ratified the treaties with the Dominican Republic, confirming the evacuation of American military forces and providing for the refunding of the Dominican debt.

records.summary_en: The *Pocahontas times* published a geographical and historical overview of Hispaniola, noting that Haiti occupied 10,204 square miles with a population of 2,506,000 while the Dominican Republic held the remainder of the island with 708,000 residents. The article recounted Haiti's successful revolution against French colonial rule to establish independent governance. It added that American troops had been stationed in Haiti since the 1915 assassination of its president following the reported execution of 156 political prisoners.

records.headline: Agreement With Finns Reached On U. S. Trade
records.summary_en: The United States and Finland have agreed, by an exchange of notes, to grant each other most-favored-nation treatment on customs duties and other charges relating to commerce, the State Department announced. As it applies to import and export duties, the agreement becomes operative on May 17; in all other matters it takes effect after notification that Finland has passed the necessary legislation. The State Department noted that similar exchanges of notes have recently been concluded with Brazil, Czechoslovakia, the Dominican Republic, Estonia, Greece, Guatemala, Nicaragua and Poland.

En lo que respecta a los derechos de importación y exportación, el acuerdo entrará en vigor el 17 de mayo; en los demás asuntos, surtirá efecto tras la notificación de que Finlandia ha aprobado la legislación necesaria.
