records.headline: 11.—The hurricane which swept Porto Rico Thursday night with undetermined damage
records.summary_en: The *Indianapolis Times* reported that a severe hurricane was advancing toward the Dominican Republic and Haiti after striking Puerto Rico with winds up to 100 miles per hour. The storm had caused one fatality and injured several others in San Juan before entering the passage toward Hispaniola. The report noted that this disturbance was separate from a deadly cyclone that destroyed the city of Belize.
records.summary_es: El *Indianapolis Times* informó que un fuerte huracán avanzaba hacia la República Dominicana y Haití tras azotar a Puerto Rico con vientos de hasta 100 millas por hora. La tempestad había ocasionado una muerte y varios heridos en San Juan antes de enfilar por el canal hacia La Española. El despacho precisó que este temporal era independiente del mortífero ciclón que arrasó la ciudad de Belice.
records.passage: Haiti in Line of Storms By United Press WASHINGTON, Sept. 11. — The hurricane which swept Porto Rico Thursday night with undetermined damage was reported by the weather bureau today to be approaching Haiti and the Dominican republic with undiminished violence. Dispatches received here said one person was killed and several were injured in San Juan Thursday night. Extent of damage in the interior of Porto Rico was unknown. Meantime, unofficial reports to the Tropical Radio Company said the city of Belize, British Honduras, had been destroyed by a hurricane Thursday night. The reports said 150 persons had been killed. The Belize hurricane was a disturbance far removed from that which hit Porto Rico. The weather bureau believes the former hurricane has about spent its force. It was centered today in the extreme southern part of the Gulf of Mexico. Warnings were sent by the bureau to Belize Thursday night that the city was in danger, but communications were interrupted. The bureau has charted the progress of the Belize disturbance for several days and added to the current hurricanes that one which reached San Juan shortly before midnight. The San Juan disturbance was about half-way between Porto Rico and Haiti today. Estimates of the violence of the hurricane varied from 70 to 100 miles an hour. Wind velocity of the storm which struck Belize was fifty miles an hour when last reported to the weather bureau. United States Consul Taggart was injured slightly. records.headline: A United Press dispatch from Washington reports that the hurricane
records.summary_en: A United Press dispatch from Washington reports that the hurricane that struck Porto Rico the previous night was approaching Haiti and the Dominican Republic with undiminished violence. Quoting a Weather Bureau hurricane warning, the article states that the tropical disturbance had passed near San Juan about 10 p.m., was moving westward over the Mona Passage, and was expected to reach the eastern end of the island and pass near the city of Santo Domingo that afternoon or early evening. The dispatch also notes storm damage and casualties in San Juan and mentions that a separate disturbance at Belize, British Honduras, had diminished in intensity.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de la United Press desde Washington informa que el huracán que azotó a Puerto Rico la noche anterior se aproximaba a Haití y a la República Dominicana con violencia no disminuida. Citando un aviso de huracán del Negociado del Tiempo, el artículo señala que la perturbación tropical había pasado cerca de San Juan alrededor de las 10 p. m., se desplazaba hacia el oeste sobre el Canal de la Mona y se esperaba que alcanzara el extremo oriental de la isla y pasara cerca de la ciudad de Santo Domingo esa tarde o a primeras horas de la noche. El cable también reseña daños y víctimas por la tormenta en San Juan y menciona que otra perturbación en Belice, Honduras Británica, había disminuido de intensidad.

records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* reported that the Dominican Republic suspended principal amortization payments on its foreign debt while maintaining interest payments, diverting customs revenues to internal operational expenses. The article noted that American private investments totaled nearly $70,000,000 alongside over $17,000,000 in Dominican government bonds.

records.full_text:
DOMINICANS HALT PAYMENT ON LOANS

The State Department announced today that the Dominican Republic has suspended further payment on foreign loans as a "drastic emergency step." Although American long-term investments are believed to have absorbed virtually all outstanding Dominican governmental securities, the department announced the United States plans no action for the present.

The republic will continue, however, to pay interest on foreign loans. Certain customs revenues, which previously had been applied to the payment of the principal of this indebtedness, will be for the present diverted to the government's own maintenance.

Held Violation of Pact.

The suspension is said to constitute a violation of a "convention" of the treaty between the United States and the republic, whereby increases in Dominican national indebtedness must be approved by the United States and a customs receiver is kept there to protect the interests of foreign investors.

The Commerce Department estimated at the end of 1930 that American long-term investments in Dominican governmental securities were $17,367,000.

$69,822,000 Private Investment.

The Dominican government recently fixed its outstanding foreign debt at $17,283,000. Private American direct investments in the republic at the end of last year were placed by the Commerce Department at $69,822,000.

Failure of the Dominican Republic to negotiate further loans from American bankers is held responsible in official circles for the deferment of amortization payments.

records.summary_en: This article, reprinting commentary from La Opinion of Santo Domingo, reflects on the abduction of Colonel Lindbergh's young son, attributing the crime to the customs and temperament of a cosmopolitan American population that lacks uniform policies for dealing with crime. The Santo Domingo paper argues that unlike early pioneers who braved the wilderness for faith and principles, many recent immigrants who had become "persons non gratae" in their homelands came to North America solely for material advantage and easy wealth without regard to method.

LOUISVILLE, Ky., May 7 (AP) — John [illegible] Lautz, 20, was accidentally killed here late today in carrying pictures of the Kentucky Derby to Bowman field. His motorcycle, in which he was carrying Harry Hall, an Associated Press staff photographer, crashed into a telephone pole on Bardstown road. Lautz' skull was fractured and he died soon after being taken to a hospital. It was not known at first how seriously either of the men was injured. After Lautz had been taken to a hospital, Hall, with a broken arm and two broken ribs, jumped into a taxicab and rushed to the airport in time to catch a plane for Chicago in order not to miss sending the picture of the Derby winner by telephoto. He left for Chicago before learning of Lautz' death.

BATTLE SUCCESSES Nicaraguan Rebel Leader Contributes Article to Honduran Paper. By the Associated Press. TEGUCIGALPA, Honduras, June 15. — Augusto Sandino, Nicaraguan insurgent leader, contributed an article under his own signature to a newspaper here today in which he asserted that in the month of April his men had fought nine battles against the Nicaraguan national guard. Seven United States Marines serving with the guard were killed, he said, and in all the dead numbered 131. Thirty of the guards were wounded and the insurgents captured 29 rifles, seven machine guns and 19,000 cartridges, Sandino wrote. He asserted the only candidate for the Nicaraguan presidency acceptable to him is Gen. Horacio Portocarrero. "Nicaragua will be freed only by the bullets and blood of our people," he wrote, "we will oppose by force of arms whatever election farce may be attempted with the aid of foreign supervision."

RADICALISM SPREADING OVER LATIN REPUBLICS

Virtually All of Central and South American Nations Have Had Recent Red Manifestations.

BY GASTON NERVAL.

PROBABLY of very few countries in the Western Hemisphere could be said what Gov. Roosevelt said of the United States and its behavior through the present world-wide economic crisis.

“The great social phenomenon of this depression,” stated the Governor in his acceptance speech of the Democratic presidential nomination, “unlike others before it, is that it has produced but a few of the disorderly manifestations that too often attend upon such times. Radicalism has made few converts * * *.”

The other American republics have been less fortunate. Either because their traditional social structure is a semi-feudalism in which there is the material for a clean-cut class struggle, or because their inhabitants are biologically more inclined to change, revolution and disorder, the Latin nations on the other side of the Rio Grande have witnessed an impressive growth of radical tendencies in the last few years.

Communists of Russian type may not be numerous in Latin America, but the number of radicals and discontented laborers—faced with unemployment or pitifully low wages—who are willing to follow Communist leaders and agitators has increased notably as a result of the economic distress and the political upheavals of the past two years.

Chile Indicates Trend.

The recent disturbances in Chile and the establishment there of the first Socialist republic in the New World are only an indication of the trend of political thought in the southern continent. But they do not tell the whole story. The real significance of the Chilean upheaval will be appreciated only when it begins to reflect in other Latin American countries.

When the news of the Socialist revolt in Chile reached Washington I did not hesitate to say that the major danger lay in the propagation of similar conditions in the neighboring countries, and thence to the rest of the Latin American continent. It was easy to see that the success of the Chilean movement would have a great influence in encouraging the activities of radicals throughout Latin America. Leaders of the Left who had been playing up what they called the failure of capitalism, as shown by the world depression, and promising the setting up of a new and happier order of things, were bound to profit by the psychological influence, if nothing else, of the successful Chilean outbreak upon the masses of other Latin American republics.

Since then, cable dispatches from the Latin capitals have confirmed that fear and given an impression of continental-wide unrest and radical agitation south of the Rio Grande.

In Argentina, Socialists and Communists have long had a part in internal politics. The former constitute one of the largest and most influential sectors of public opinion, but it is from the latter that any threat of disorder comes. In fact, this menace has become so grave recently, with the recurrence of strikes and labor disturbances, that the more moderate Socialist elements have been forced to abandon their opposition to the conservative rule of President Justo and pledge themselves to support him in the event of any major Communist uprising. In the capital and in other regions of the country there is the added danger of a well organized group of anarchists, largely immigrants, who have transplanted to Argentina the methods of European nihilists.

In Other Countries.

In Brazil, although the governmental elements still have a firm control of the situation, unrest has been spreading rapidly. Following a conference of administration officials and military leaders from various parts of the country, the Government announced a few weeks ago it would take “the most energetic measures to preserve internal peace and principally to combat attempts to corrupt the Brazilian family by preaching discontent.” The Third October Club, a political organization, had just adopted a resolution urging the government to incorporate some of the principles advocated by the Socialist Republic of Chile in its original program.

In Bolivia, Peru and Ecuador, heirs to the glories of the ancient Inca Empire, Communist propagandists have been making considerable strides in their efforts to convince the native Indian classes that they deserve a better treatment from their white and mestizo brothers, who have monopolized the government since the Spanish conquistadores first landed in America. The aboriginal Indians still form a large part of the population of Bolivia, Peru and Ecuador, and the slowly and subtle, but tenacious, way in which red agitators are gaining them to their cause with the promise of a re-distribution of land, is causing great alarm to the authorities of those countries.

In Peru the problem has taken more definite form. There is an organized Communist group. And there is another supposedly non-Communist entity, the Apra party, which, while denouncing the Moscow tactics and denying any connection with Soviet plans, preaches a philosophy and follows a program almost equally radical. The Apristas made an impressive showing in the last presidential elections and since then have seen their prestige increased by the difficulties the Sanchez Cerro government has encountered in weathering the economic crisis. Last May a radical uprising started in Callao, the chief Peruvian port, the paternity of which was attributed alternately to Communists and Apristas. Geographical proximity and the co-operation long existing between Chilean and Peruvian radical leaders strengthen now the likelihood of new disturbances.

Colombia has been one of the very few Latin American countries to escape the wave of revolutionary fever which has swept that continent in recent months. That, however, does not mean that the Colombian authorities do not have a Communist problem to deal with. Press dispatches have reported raids of Communists on small towns in the interior of the country, where they attempted to establish their own form of government. Although these endeavors did not meet with much success, they have been sufficient to prove the growth of radical theories among the native population.

North of Panama, Communist elements have lately caused trouble for several of the Central American governments. With the exception of Nicaragua, where the presence of United States Marines may have had some influence in discouraging them, they have appeared at one time or another in all the other States of Central America. And even in Nicaragua, if the unpopular resistance of President Moncada to the candidacy of the liberal leader, Dr. Sacasa, finally results in a new civil war, as it is feared, the Communists across the border may find a splendid opportunity to step into Nicaragua and profit by the convulsion.

It is in El Salvador that Communists agitators have so far proven more successful in Central America. Under the regime of President Araujo they were not seriously opposed, for they, themselves, had lent support to Araujo's election. However, when President Araujo was forced to flee the country by a military coup d'etat and Vice President Martinez became head of the government, Salvadorian Communists intensified their subversive activities until they finally succeeded in starting an uprising of considerable proportions. We all know how much blood and material losses that uprising, only a few months ago, meant. British and American warships stood by, while it lasted, ready to take off foreigners in danger. Only the energy and promptness with which the Salvadorian authorities proceeded, and the overwhelming support they received from all social and political sectors to put down the Communists revolt, prevented its propagation to the rest of the country. The peril, however, has not disappeared entirely, and Salvadorians claim that it will last, and grow worse, so long as the State Department refuses to extend recognition to the constitutional government of President Martinez.

Communists in Guatemala have been the object of an intensive round-up by the authorities. Sixty-five of the agitators were arrested within a fortnight, including the Salvadorian imbroglio. And from time to time, the cable brings reports of new red plots discovered by the Guatemalan police.

Outbreak in Costa Rica.

Until recently Costa Rica was thought to be immune to the advances of radical propagandists. The very liberal and democratic institutions of the little but progressive republic were considered a barrier to the dissemination of doctrines of discontent and violent change. Two weeks ago, however, the first Communist riot took place in San Jose, the capital, after a meeting of the “General Union of Workmen and Communists.” Fifty-eight manifestants were arrested after their leader had solemnly announced, “This episode opens the Communists' fight in Costa Rica, and we will win or die.”

In the latest Honduran uprising and even in the various Cuban riots intended to overthrow President Machado, Communists' hands have been found at work. It is only natural that radical leaders encourage and take advantage of any internal political conflict, to make gains during the storm.

In Mexico, where the first seeds of Latin American radicalism were sown, a revival of the Communist spirit has lately made itself felt in certain regions of the country. Here, however, the problem is rather different, as it is the authorities of some Mexican states and not the people who are leading the trend to the left. The States of Hidalgo and Vera Cruz recently passed almost confiscatory laws against large foreign industrial interests, “in the benefit of the community.” Though the action of the federal government at Mexico City prevented a conflict with foreign interests, the popularity of such radical measures seems to be increasing in the neighboring republic along with the progress of the economic crisis.

In contrast with these dark reports from all over the continent, a dispatch from Santo Domingo, printed a few days ago in the metropolitan papers, announces that the position of President Trujillo's government is every day stronger in the Dominican Republic and that domestic unrest has disappeared in the island. The dispatch adds that governmental finances in the Dominican Republic are sound, and that, when most of the Latin American nations have been forced to suspend payments on their debts, that country has until now faithfully kept its foreign obligations and, stranger still, maintained a balanced budget.

Which goes to show, as I have many times said in these columns, that internal political unrest and governmental finances are closely interrelated in Latin America.

(Copyright, 1932.)

records.full_text:
THIS IS NEWS

At least one solvent country has been discovered in these days of unbalanced budgets and record breaking deficits. At Santo Domingo the Treasury of the Dominican Republic has announced that the government of President Trujillo has rigidly maintained its budget during the first six months of 1932, and that payment on foreign and other debts has been promptly met. The administration of this Carribean country is looked upon as a model by our State Department.

records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* reported favorably on conditions in the Dominican Republic on the eve of its sixty-ninth national anniversary, noting that President Trujillo's government had strengthened internal order and foreign credit. In contrast to political instability and financial defaults across much of Latin America since 1930, the commentary noted that the Dominican Republic maintained a balanced budget and steady governance. This administrative stability was credited with bolstering public support at home and prestige abroad.

En contraste con la inestabilidad política y las cesaciones de pagos en gran parte de América Latina desde 1930, el comentario destacó que la República Dominicana mantenía un presupuesto equilibrado y una gobernabilidad firme. Se atribuyó a esta estabilidad administrativa el haber afianzado el respaldo popular en el país y el prestigio en el extranjero.

records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* published a profile of Dominican President Rafael Trujillo on the republic's sixty-ninth national anniversary, recounting his rise from enlistment during the U.S. Marine Corps occupation to top commander of the Dominican Army within a decade. The article highlighted his friendly relations with the United States and his employment of American technical advisers to overhaul national finances and develop natural resources. It also commended Trujillo's programs to diversify Dominican agriculture beyond its four traditional export crops.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Star* publicó una semblanza del presidente dominicano Rafael Trujillo con motivo del sexagésimo noveno aniversario nacional de la república, relatando su ascenso desde que se alistó durante la ocupación del Cuerpo de Marines de Estados Unidos hasta convertirse en comandante en jefe del ejército dominicano en el lapso de una década. El artículo destacó sus relaciones cordiales con Estados Unidos y la contratación de asesores técnicos estadounidenses para sanear las finanzas nacionales y explotar los recursos naturales. Asimismo, elogió los planes de Trujillo encaminados a diversificar la agricultura dominicana más allá de sus cuatro cultivos tradicionales de exportación.

But the efficiency of his administration and his successful conduct of the political and economic problems of the Dominican Republic are not the only things which make President Trujillo outstanding among the statesmen of the day. Probably the youngest elected Chief Executive of an independent nation, yet the story of his life is full of human interest, and should be particularly appealing to American readers, for President Trujillo started his military career in the ranks of the United States Marine Corps. Since he joined the Marines — while they were on duty in the Dominican Republic — Gen. Trujillo was promoted in the short period of 10 years from the lowest to the highest rank in the Dominican Army. It is probably his contacts with Americans that have made him such an admirer and good friend of the United States as he has proven himself to be. records.headline: Mrs. Miller recently inherited a Santo Domingo placer concession

Following several months of negotiations confirming her rights and securing promises of cooperation from officials and business people, Mr. Salsman and his staff plan to depart after the autumn tropical rains subside to investigate and prospect the estate. records.headline: Systematic efforts to build a pan-American memorial lighthouse
records.summary_en: Systematic efforts to build a pan-American memorial lighthouse to Christopher Columbus began in 1914 under William E. Pulliam, an American then serving as receiver of Dominican customs, who enlisted editors and publicists across North and South America and urged the United States House Committee on Foreign Affairs to participate. International support crystallized in 1923 at the fifth International Conference of American States in Santiago de Chile, which unanimously adopted Dominican delegate Julio M. Cestero's resolution recommending that all American republics cooperate in erecting a monumental Columbus lighthouse on the coast of Santo Domingo, capital of the Dominican Republic. On June 27, 1927, the United States Congress ratified the action.

records.headline: The Evening Star highlights the proposal to build a memorial
records.summary_en: The Evening Star highlights the proposal to build a memorial lighthouse honoring Christopher Columbus at Santo Domingo, capital of the Dominican Republic, a project endorsed by the International Conference of American States and advanced by the governing board of the Pan-American Union. In October 1931, an international jury awarded the prize for the structure's design—intended as a guide to both sea and air voyagers—to J. L. Gleave of Manchester, England. National Columbus lighthouse committees are being formed in several countries with world-wide aid invited, though no fundraising campaign will be launched for the present.

En octubre de 1931, un jurado internacional otorgó el premio por el diseño de la estructura —concebida como guía para navegantes marítimos y aéreos— a J. L. Gleave, de Mánchester, Inglaterra. Se están formando comités nacionales pro faro de Colón en varios países y se ha invitado a colaborar a todo el mundo, aunque por el momento no se realizará ninguna campaña de recaudación de fondos.

records.headline: Through the Pan-American Union at Washington, the 21 independent
records.summary_en: Through the Pan-American Union at Washington, the 21 independent republics of the New World are working with the United States to build a colossal memorial lighthouse at Santo Domingo in the Dominican Republic, described as the first permanent Christian settlement in the New World, to honor Christopher Columbus; twenty of the republics emerged from Spain's colonial empire. Special Columbus ceremonies were held on Wednesday at the Pan-American Union, and on Tuesday President Hoover sent a tribute to the country's Italian-Americans honoring the explorer and his native land of Italy.

El miércoles se celebraron ceremonias especiales en honor a Colón en la Unión Panamericana, y el martes el presidente Hoover envió un tributo a los italoestadounidenses del país en homenaje al explorador y a su Italia natal.

records.summary_en: The *Washington Daily News* reported on a large diplomatic reception held in Washington to celebrate the birthday of Dominican President Rafael Trujillo, organized by Minister Despradel. The article described Trujillo as a military ruler with marine training who prioritized government funds for his armed forces and diplomats over teachers and bondholders. Trujillo sent his personal greetings to the assembled guests through a large ornamental cake fashioned to resemble a radiogram.

Trujillo transmitió sus saludos personales a los invitados congregados mediante un gran pastel ornamental moldeado a semejanza de un radiograma.

records.full_text:
TINY REPUBLIC—HUGE LIST

The tiny Dominican Republic received a full column of publicity in Washington society columns yesterday when Minister Despradel gave a huge tea at the Hotel Mayflower.

There was Chinese tea in the Chinese Room for Orientals (altho no Chinese were present) and rum for President Trujillo's special reserve in adjoining alcoves for Occidentals.

It took the services of a corps of diplomats to protocol the guest list. Everybody was invited except Mrs. Dolly Gann, the Vice President's sister, a fact that occasioned some surprise in view of the cordial relations between Mr. Gann and the Dominican Government.

Minister Despradel—a famous mathematician—calculated that 400 persons easily could squeeze into the Chinese Room. Flowers and punch bowls occasioned some slight inconvenience, but guests sniffed at the former and emptied the latter.

The distinctly military mass formation of the party recalled the fact that it was given in honor of the birthday anniversary of President Rafael Trujillo, formerly of the U. S. Marines, a gentleman who pays first his army—then his diplomats—occasionally his school teachers—not his bondholders.

Trujillo's interest in the party was attested by a huge creation of vari-hued icings, moulded in the format of a radiogram from him conveying greetings to all present.

records.headline: Mr. Gleave, the 25-year-old architect whose design for the Columbus Memorial
records.summary_en: Mr. Gleave, the 25-year-old architect whose design for the Columbus Memorial to be erected in Santo Domingo won an international competition with a $25,000 prize announced at Rio de Janeiro the previous October, sailed from San Juan for New York after spending two weeks in Santo Domingo, the St. Croix Avis reports, quoting the Porto Rico Progress. Making his first visit to the United States after traveling directly to Santo Domingo on a French liner, Gleave is heading to Washington to consult with the Pan American Union committee in charge of erecting the memorial. He will also supervise the construction of a replica at next year's Chicago fair to house the Dominican exhibit, where J. H. Cerecedo of San Juan, now residing in Chicago, will serve as Commissioner of the Dominican Republic.

Asimismo, supervisará la erección de una réplica en la feria de Chicago del próximo año que albergará la exhibición dominicana, donde J. H. records.full_text:
WHAT LIGHTHOUSE?

DR. LEO ROWE, genial director of the Pan American Union, yesterday entertained at luncheon in honor of a distinguished architect, Mr. J. L. Gleave of Manchester, England.

Mr. Gleave was awarded first prize for his design of the Columbus memorial lighthouse to be erected at Santo Domingo.

Early to arrive, dressed in a black coat and striped trousers, was the Minister of Santo Domingo, Mr. Despradel. In spite of the fact that he had already eaten bananas at dinner the preceding night, more bananas at breakfast, he still ate a third portion at Dr. Rowe's lunch.

Lamb stew and cream puffs were favored by Mr. Espaillat, the Dominican attache, who is dieting.

Everyone at the luncheon talked about the celebrated lighthouse designed by Architect Gleave.

"Have you started to build it yet?" a guest asked him.

"No," said Mr. Gleave.

"When will you start?" persisted the guest.

Architect Gleave glanced across at Dr. Rowe.

"Dr. Rowe will have to answer that," he replied.

"Oh," said Dr. Rowe, interrupted in the midst of a lamb chop, "we will start to build the lighthouse as soon as we get the money."

NOTE:—The Dominican government is reported to have spent $200,000 on the lighthouse project,

records.headline: Plans for the upcoming Chicago exposition were discussed yesterday
records.summary_en: Plans for the upcoming Chicago exposition were discussed yesterday in a conference between Pan-American Union Director General Dr. L. S. Rowe and Dr. J. M. Cerecedo, Dominican Republic consul in Chicago and a native of Puerto Rico with United States citizenship who has been designated exposition commissioner for both Santo Domingo and Puerto Rico. Cerecedo stated that he aims to promote the industrial, trade, and tourist possibilities of Puerto Rico and Santo Domingo to the American public, noting that both islands possess rich agricultural resources, rapidly developing industries, and three annual grapefruit crops for New York and other Eastern markets. He added that Santo Domingo has ideal soil for agriculture and vast virgin forests offering trade opportunities in mahogany and other forest products.
records.summary_es: Los planes para la próxima exposición de Chicago fueron abordados ayer en una conferencia entre el director general de la Unión Panamericana, doctor L. S. Rowe, y el doctor J. M. Cerecedo, cónsul de la República Dominicana en Chicago y nativo de Puerto Rico con ciudadanía estadounidense que ha sido designado comisionado ante la exposición tanto por Santo Domingo como por Puerto Rico. Cerecedo declaró que su objetivo es dar a conocer al público estadounidense las posibilidades industriales, comerciales y turísticas de Puerto Rico y Santo Domingo, señalando que ambas islas cuentan con ricos recursos agrícolas, un rápido desarrollo industrial y tres cosechas anuales de toronja destinadas a Nueva York y otros mercados del Este. Añadió que Santo Domingo posee suelos ideales para la agricultura y extensos bosques vírgenes que ofrecen grandes posibilidades para el comercio de caoba y otros productos forestales.

Su esposa estuvo con él al final y su cuerpo será enviado a Santo Domingo.

records.full_text:
HAVANA HIGH POINTS

By Local Cuban Consulate

Reconstruction work has commenced in the town of Santa Cruz del Sur, which was destroyed during the last storm, at a point approximately three kilometers from the coast.

According to news received, Cuban avocado pears have been declared duty free in the United States.

The sugar crop will not begin until February 15 of the present year.

The postal treaty between Cuba and the Dominican Republic was signed on the 20th day of December, Dr. Orestes Ferrara, secretary of state, representing Cuba, and Mr. Osvaldo Bazil, Dominican minister to Cuba, representing the dominican republic.

It has been announced that the racing season on the Marianao race tracks of Marianao, Havana, will begin on January 21 under the auspices of the Cuban-American Jockey Club which has taken the place of the Havana-American Jockey Club.

The president of the republic, General Gerardo Machado, has denied the news published in the United States regarding an economic project calling for the emission of $70,000,000 and a loan.

The department of agriculture is organizing expositions of live stock, aviculture and agriculture, to be celebrated in the Exposition Park, in the "Lutgardita" subdivision, from February 20 to 26.

According to estimates which have been published, exportation of coffee in 1932 amounted to 3,000,000 "kilos," part of which went to the United States.

The government has acquired four new cruising planes to be used for military aviation purposes and already four lieutenants of the aviation corps have left for the United States with the sole object of bringing said planes to Cuba.

records.headline: Pulliam is returning to his job in Santo Domingo, and “on account of his very able record and capable work, is being retained by this Administration in recognition of his merit."
records.summary_en: An effort to remove William E. Pulliam as collector of customs in the Dominican Republic failed, and the State Department announced that Pulliam is returning to his job in Santo Domingo and is being retained in recognition of his merit and capable work. The decision is described as a rebuke to the regime of President Rafael Trujillo, after Dominican Minister Despradel and Counselor Espaillat had represented that Pulliam was persona non grata. Pulliam served as collector from 1907 to 1913 and from 1921 to the present, and his honesty is widely praised.
records.summary_es: Fracasó un intento de remover a William E. Pulliam como recaudador de aduanas en la República Dominicana, y el Departamento de Estado anunció que Pulliam regresa a su puesto en Santo Domingo y es mantenido en reconocimiento a su mérito y su capaz labor. La decisión se describe como un desaire al régimen del presidente Rafael Trujillo, después de que el ministro dominicano Despradel y el consejero Espaillat representaran que Pulliam era persona non grata. Pulliam fue recaudador de 1907 a 1913 y desde 1921 hasta el presente, y su honestidad es ampliamente elogiada.

The State Department announced that Mr. Pulliam is returning to his job in Santo Domingo, and "on account of his very able record and capable work, is being retained by this Administration in recognition of his merit." This is what is undiplomatically termed "a sock in the eye" at the regime of President-Dictator Rafael Trujillo. Not long ago, Minister Despradel and Counselor Espaillat of the Dominican Legation here, went to the State Department and represented that Mr. Pulliam was "persona non grata" in Santo Domingo. NOTE — Mr. Pulliam has been Collector of Customs in the Dominican Republic from 1907 to 1913 and from 1921 to the present date. His honesty and his vigor in prosecuting political plundering are widely praised. records.summary_en: The Washington daily news notes that Dominican Minister of Foreign Affairs Max Henriquez Urena is visiting Washington, ostensibly on vacation, though some observers suggest there is a business angle to the trip. Sus actividades incluyen una cena ofrecida por el ministro dominicano Despradel y una probable fotografía con el director general de la Unión Panamericana, Dr. Leo Rowe, en el patio de la Unión, mientras que cualquier asunto oficial solo es conocido por Urena y su jefe, el presidente y dictador Trujillo.

records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* shared a private letter from an American resident in the Dominican Republic describing a luncheon given by sugar estates for President Rafael Trujillo on May 3. Following the meal, Trujillo lowered the presidential flag and personally hoisted the United States flag before 450 guests. The observer characterized the ceremony as a notable Pan-American gesture demonstrating Trujillo's continued goodwill toward the United States.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Star* difundió una carta privada de un residente estadounidense en la República Dominicana que describía un almuerzo ofrecido por haciendas azucareras al presidente Rafael Trujillo el 3 de mayo. Al término de la comida, Trujillo arrió la bandera presidencial e izó personalmente la enseña de Estados Unidos ante 450 comensales. El observador calificó la ceremonia como un notable gesto panamericano que demostraba la constante buena voluntad de Trujillo hacia Estados Unidos.
records.passage: tiny Dominican Republic, alternately torn by revolution and hurricane, which shares, with its sister republic of Haiti, possession of the Caribbean Island of Santo Domingo, is still our friend. His assurances on this score are contained in a letter recently received by a prominent Washingtonian from an American friend in the Island Republic. The latter writes: "On May 3 the Sugar Estates gave a luncheon and reception to the President of the Dominican Republic. After lunch President Trujillo went to the flag pole, pulled down the presidential flag and hoisted the United States flag — the only United States flag among the hundreds of Dominican banners. This was done in the presence of 450 guests and caused some emotion. Some Pan-American gesture!" records.summary_en: In a stamp column, the Evening star reports that the Dominican Republic has maintained daily internal airmail service since February 20, when Capt. Frank A. Felix Miranda of the national army made the inaugural flight in a Bellanca plane, N. C. 252-M. The flight carried 166 pieces of mail from Santo Domingo City to Santiago, dropping a sack of 132 pieces at La Vega and another of 73 pieces at Moca en route, without using a distinctive stamp or charging an extra rate.

El vuelo transportó 166 piezas de correspondencia desde la ciudad de Santo Domingo hasta Santiago, dejando en ruta una saca de 132 piezas en La Vega y otra de 73 piezas en Moca, sin emplear un sello distintivo ni cobrar tarifa adicional.

Curtis Considers New Job; Brother-in-Law Loses One

Ex-Vice President Ponders Offer of Job to Represent Notorious 'Goat Gland Doctor' in Mexican Radio Case

By GEORGE ABELL

FORMER Vice President Charlie Curtis is considering a visit to Mexico City to represent Dr. William Brinkley, "goat gland doctor" and former candidate for the governorship of Kansas, in a radio litigation case.

If Charlie decides to go, he will leave some time next week.

"There's nothing definite yet. I won't know until Monday," he said yesterday. "People have been calling up all day to ask me about it."

Despite the fact that Charlie is now president of the New Mexico Gold Producers Corporation he is keeping up his law practice with great enthusiasm. Recently he confided that he had never enjoyed himself more.

"I like to be busy," he explained. "And now I always have a lot to do."

Dr. Brinkley, known thruout the U. S. as the "goat gland doctor," has attracted much notoriety because of his unorthodox political and medical views. His campaign for the governorship of Kansas, in 1932, was sensational. He ran up a huge number of votes and was very nearly elected, but lost his license to operate a radio station in this country.

At present the goat gland specialist operates a huge radio station in Mexico and the litigation which Charlie may participate in concerns Brinkley's efforts to strengthen his network. Stations as far north as New York have complained against Brinkley's tactics.

TRUJILLO TACTICS

CHARLIE'S brother-in-law, Mr. Edward Everett Gann, has lost one job because of the change in administration.

During the Hoover-Curtis regime Mr. Gann served (for a reported fee of $400 a month) as Washington representative of the Trujillo government at Santo Domingo. Dictator Trujillo is now said to be seeking a Democratic connection in the person of Joe Davies, Washington lawyer.

Davies served as Federal Trade Commissioner under the Wilson Administration, acted as counsel for the Mexican government in 1920 and for Peru in the Tacna-Arica controversy. He is now serving as counsel for Sen. James J. Davis in lottery charges against the Senator.

Davies recently returned from a visit to Santo Domingo, making the trip by plane. He was accompanied by his daughter and Senor Ulises Espaillat, counselor for the Dominican Legation here.

Newspapers in Santo Domingo made much of Davies' visit as "an influential Democrat at Washington", and of the reception given him by President Trujillo. They reported Davies as saying Trujillo has many friends in Washington, "especially among the Marines, having been at one time an officer in that branch of the U. S. military."

(Trujillo never was a U. S. Marine officer, but during the military occupation of the republic, while many Dominicans were resentful and humiliated, he enlisted in the Guardia Nacional Dominicana which was officered by the U. S. Marines.)

Diplomatic opinion here is that even if Counselor Espaillat is successful in the present instance, he will not be rewarded by the coveted post of Dominican Minister to Washington.

The recent reappointment of William Pulliam as Collector General of Customs in Santo Domingo—after Espaillat had declared him "persona non grata" there—has proved a severe blow to many political aspirations.

Quoting the *Express*, the article suggested that Haiti could follow the example of the neighboring Dominican Republic, which was progressing under President Trujillo after overcoming years of internal conflict. records.headline: The practice among certain Dominican families of sending a servant
records.summary_en: The practice among certain Dominican families of sending a servant or young boy to borrow newspapers subscribed to by friends and neighbors in order to read them free of charge is growing, the Evening star describes, quoting La Opinion of Santo Domingo. The commentary complains that this custom annoys subscribers who have barely glanced at the front page and often either never receive their paper back or get it returned soiled, tattered, and disarranged.

El comentario se queja de que esta práctica molesta a los suscriptores que apenas han ojeado la primera página y que a menudo no reciben de vuelta su ejemplar o lo recuperan sucio, roto y desordenado.

records.summary_en: The *Washington Times* reported that Mrs. H. F. Arthur Schoenfeld, wife of the U.S. Minister to the Dominican Republic, was visiting Washington and staying at the Wardman Park Hotel. Her visit was scheduled to last a few weeks before she traveled to join the legation in Santo Domingo.

records.headline: At the request of Dominican President General Raphael Trujillo
records.summary_en: At the request of Dominican President General Raphael Trujillo, Major Thomas E. Watson and First Lieutenant Gregon A. Williams of the U.S. Marine Corps have been assigned to Santo Domingo City to reorganize the Dominican army. Both officers are personal friends of Trujillo currently serving in the Division of Operations and Training at Marine Corps Headquarters in the Navy Department. Trujillo once served as a private in the Dominican National Guard company of Lieutenant Williams—who gave him his first promotion to corporal—and later served as a captain under Major Watson, who was his commanding officer from 1920 to 1923. Watson, born in Oskaloosa, Iowa, on January 18, 1892, entered the Marines in 1916 for expeditionary duty in Santo Domingo and also served in Nicaragua, while Williams, born in Carrollton, Illinois, on January 8, 1896, has been a Marine officer since January 1923 with service in Nicaragua and China.
records.summary_es: A petición del presidente dominicano, general Raphael Trujillo, el mayor Thomas E. Watson y el primer teniente Gregon A. Williams, del Cuerpo de Marines de los Estados Unidos, han sido asignados a la ciudad de Santo Domingo para reorganizar el ejército dominicano. Ambos oficiales son amigos personales de Trujillo y prestan servicio actualmente en la División de Operaciones y Entrenamiento del Cuartel General del Cuerpo de Marines en el Departamento de Marina. Trujillo sirvió anteriormente como soldado raso en la compañía de la Guardia Nacional Dominicana del teniente Williams —quien le otorgó su primer ascenso a cabo— y más tarde sirvió como capitán bajo el mando del mayor Watson, quien fue su oficial comandante de 1920 a 1923. Watson, nacido en Oskaloosa, Iowa, el 18 de enero de 1892, ingresó en los Marines en 1916 para servicio expedicionario en Santo Domingo y también sirvió en Nicaragua, mientras que Williams, nacido en Carrollton, Illinois, el 8 de enero de 1896, es oficial de los Marines desde enero de 1923 con servicio en Nicaragua y China.

records.full_text:
NEW DEAL ACCORDED HAITI HAILED BY LATIN AMERICA Resentment Over Past Military Policy of United States Fades on Advent of New Course.

BY GASTON NERVAL.

THROUGHOUT Latin America the "executive agreement" recently concluded between the Governments of the United States and Haiti has received enthusiastic approval. To understand this enthusiasm, although the agreement is only the first step to end American intervention in the island republic and does not correct all of the objectionable practices allied with intervention, one must bear in mind the high lights of Haitian-American relations in the past quarter of a century, and compare the methods then prevailing with the liberal and considerate treatment involved in the new agreement.

Despite the fact internal political disturbances had always been more or less chronic in Haiti, it was only after the establishment of United States financial interests in the country that they aroused concern in Washington. Soon after the appearance of the National City Bank in Haitian finances, in 1910, the State Department began to show anxiety for the instability of the Haitian authorities and to devise means to insure the safety of American investments.

Control Sought.

It was, precisely, at that time that the ultimate transformation of the Monroe Doctrine had taken place. The Roosevelt corrollary had definitely converted the old declaration, in the eyes of public opinion as well as in the understanding of many statesmen unfamiliar with its original meaning, into a policy which precluded any kind of European interference and which intrusted the United States with the protection of European lives and property in revolution-torn Latin American countries. The policy of the "big stick" had already been announced by Theodore Roosevelt and realistic obligations of "dollar diplomacy" had been avowedly praised by Taft and Knox.

Following the Dominican precedent, the State Department decided that the best way to bring about domestic tranquility, protect American interests and avoid possible European complications, was to secure control of the Haitian customs house, main source of the national revenue, and supervise the government finances. Suggestions to this effect became quite insistent after the outbreak of the World War.

After six of these overtures had failed, while one revolutionary regime succeeded another, the State Department advanced the peculiar doctrine that the United States, in view of "its tacitly conceded obligations as the nearest friend of Haiti in her relations with the rest of the world"—an obvious reference to the Monroe Doctrine—"would feel at liberty thereafter to insist that revolutionary movements cease and that all subsequent changes in the government of the republic be effected by the peaceful processes provided in the Haitian constitution."

Pressure Attempted.

When President Theodore was quietly elected in Haiti, the Secretary of State offered to extend him recognition in exchange for a convention conceding customs control, settlement of all outstanding questions between the government, the bank and the American railroad, and an agreement never to lease to any European power any portion of Haitian territory for naval or coaling purposes. This having proved of no avail, a method of pressure which had already been used in the neighboring Dominican republic, was attempted. The bank, controlled by the National City Bank, withheld all government funds, upon the advice of the American Minister that this course might persuade the Haitian authorities to turn over the customs houses.

Such expectation did not come true, and, several days later, fearing that the government might try forcibly to take its funds, the bank decided to transfer them to a safer haven, its home office in New York. For this purpose, a contingent of United States Marines landed in the Haitian capital, "proceeded to the vaults of the National Bank of Haiti and in broad daylight forcibly seized $500,000 and carried it aboard the gunboat Machias. The money was transported to New York and deposited in the vaults of the National City Bank."

Landing Force Ordered.

Soon afterward the disorder following the overthrow of President Guillaume Sam offered an opportunity for more drastic action. When the deposed Chief Executive was dragged out of the French legation, at Port au Prince, and murdered by a mob infuriated by his massacre of political prisoners, Admiral Capperton of the United States Navy received instructions from Washington to land forces "at the request of the State Department."

Admiral Capperton complied magnificently. He occupied the Haitian capital and reported that the situation was controlled by a committee of prominent citizens acting "practically" under his directions. He "persuaded" the Chamber of Deputies to postpone presidential elections, ordered the treasury service restored to the National Bank and suggested the sending of a regiment of Marines, in addition to that already landed, to suppress native rebel bands, "if the United States desires to negotiate treaty for financial control of Haiti." The admiral knew the plans of the State Department and, in his frank military language, did not attempt to conceal them. But he advocated the use of bayonets to obtain that which the diplomatic endeavors of the American charge d'affaires or the financial pressure of the National City Bank had been unable to accomplish.

U. S. Friend Elected.

Even for this, however, it was necessary to set up a local government favorable to the United States with which to negotiate. With the open and avowed support of the American forces of occupation, M. Dartiguenave, who had promised to support "any terms proposed by the United States," was elected President, while United States Marines stood at the doors of the legislative chamber and Admiral Capperton's chief of staff circulated among the Congressmen.

Immediately afterward the State Department notified the new President that it expected the signing of the proposed treaty "without modification." When the Haitian secretary of foreign affairs contended that the new government might have to resign rather than accept such imposition, the Secretary of State replied that if the treaty were not accepted "the United States would have either to set up a military government * * * or permit the control of the government to pass to some other political faction which would fall in with the American plans."

Customs Houses Taken.

At the same time Admiral Capperton was ordered to strengthen his hold on the country. In less than two weeks his forces took over the customs houses at the 10 leading ports of Haiti, the government being thus deprived of its chief source of income. Finally, after martial law had been formally declared by Admiral Capperton, he reported: "Treaty situation at present looks more favorable than usual. This has been effected by exercising military pressure at propitious moments."

Presently the treaty was accepted and signed by the government, but further pressure, military as well as financial, was required before the Haitian Senate consented to ratify it. It only did so when Admiral Capperton personally and dramatically declared before the cabinet that the United States had the intention to retain control in Haiti until ratification had been obtained.

Provisions of Treaty.

What were the provisions of this treaty for which the United States spared neither diplomatic nor military pressure? Here are the most important: (a) Appointment, upon the nomination by the President of the United States, of a general receiver to collect, receive and apply all customs duties, and of a financial adviser to be attached to the ministry of finance; (b) prohibition to increase the public debt without permission from the President of the United States; (c) prohibition to surrender any portion of the national territory by sale, lease or otherwise, or jurisdiction over such territory, to any foreign government; (d) creation of a native constabulary officered by Americans; (e) authorization for the United States to aid in the preservation of Haitian independence and the maintenance of a government adequate for the protection of life, property and individual liberty.

Under this semi-protectorate, the government of Haiti in the years to follow became a unique four-headed aggregation of powers: The military government, the treaty officials, the native government and the Minister of the United States

In 1918 the Haitian authorities agreed to sumbit all proposed legislation to the United States legation for approval. The year before the treaty had been extended to 1936. In 1920, upon disagreements on financial matters between the American adviser and the Haitian government, the former employed, again, the old recourse of withholding the salaries of the President and his cabinet and the principal executive officers. Several times popular opposition to the American occupation was quelled by the use of military force.

"New Deal" Arrives.

Until the "executive agreement," signed recently—justly considered the first tangible expression of the "new deal" in inter-American relations—the condition of Haiti had improved little from the restrictions upon national sovereignty involved in the treaty which the United States Navy secured for the State Department under President Dartiguenave.

As to the merits or disadvantages of American control of the island republic, this is not the place to discuss them. The material benefits must be paired against the humiliation inherent in lack of political self-determination, the complete subservience to American financial interests—which, until not long ago, had the active co-operation of the State Department in strengthening their ever-expanding net—the curtailment of individual liberty and the abuses unavoidable in military rule by foreigners.

The recent agreement tends to terminate these things. This, alone, even if it were not sufficient to heal completely the wound and remove resentment for past mistakes, is enough to win the praise of governments and public opinion on the other side of the Rio Grande. Latin Americans can better appreciate the change because they have not forgotten the methods of the past.

records.headline: Quoting a statement by Mr. Buell, the Evening Star examines
records.summary_en: Quoting a statement by Mr. Buell, the Evening Star examines the assignment of U.S. Marine Corps Major Watson to assist Dominican President Trujillo in training his army. Buell notes that Trujillo's administration has repeatedly been accused of atrocities comparable to those of the Machado regime in Cuba, and characterizes Trujillo as a dictator planning for reelection in 1934. Although sending Watson—a former American naval attaché in the Dominican Republic—appears harmless on the surface, Buell warns that it will strengthen Trujillo against domestic opposition and that Navy Secretary Swanson is unintentionally underwriting dictatorship there. Buell urges that if the State Department was not consulted on the appointment, the matter should be reopened and Major Watson kept home.

Buell señala que el gobierno de Trujillo ha sido acusado en numerosas ocasiones de las mismas atrocidades que el régimen de Machado en Cuba, y caracteriza a Trujillo como un dictador que planea reelegirse en 1934. Aunque el envío de Watson —quien ya sirvió como agregado naval estadounidense en la República Dominicana— parece inocente en la superficie, Buell advierte que fortalecerá la posición de Trujillo frente a la oposición local y que el secretario de Marina Swanson está respaldando inconscientemente la dictadura allí. Buell insta a que, si el Departamento de Estado no fue consultado sobre el nombramiento, se reabra la cuestión y el mayor Watson permanezca en su país.

records.headline: The United States Geographic Board has approved the name Hispaniola
records.summary_en: The United States Geographic Board has approved the name Hispaniola for the Caribbean island that includes the Dominican Republic and Haiti. As reported in the Nogales International, the name Hispaniola was widely used for three centuries after Columbus discovered the island, though in recent years the entire island has frequently been called Santo Domingo—after the Dominican capital—or Haiti, the republic on the west. The board notes that no island name is needed when addressing mail, as "Dominican Republic" and "Haiti" are each sufficient for their respective republics.

La junta señala que no es necesario incluir el nombre de la isla en la correspondencia postal, pues basta con indicar «Dominican Republic» o «Haiti» para cada una de las repúblicas.

RUM, PERHAPS ROMANCE?

THE new Haitian Minister to the United States, M. Albert Blanchet, arrived here last night to take up the duties of the post he held from 1920 to 1922. He replaces the brilliant French linguist, Dantes Bellegarde, who resigned in vigorous protest over the new Haitian financial policy.

Coming direct from Port-au-Prince, Envoy Blanchet knows all about "rum and communism." He will tell United States tariff officials of the superior qualities of Haitian rum and seek preferential duties on its import.

Perhaps he will also tell the story of how "Communists" are dealt with in Haiti. It involves the settlement of an old dispute between that country and the Dominican Republic over the rights to a large tract of land lying along the border of the two republics.

Dominican President-Dictator Trujillo on Oct. 18 made a secret offer to the Haitian President to relinquish his country's claims to the disputed territory in return for certain personal favors in the interest of his tottering regime.

A few days ago five exiled Dominicans, well known political enemies of Trujillo's administration, were deported by official order from their refuge in a small border town of Haiti.

The stigma of "communism" was attached by deporting with them one Serge Jakimoff, a Russian laborer.

records.headline: Pan-American Delegates Ready for Conference Opening Today
records.summary_en: One hundred delegates from the American nations gathered in Montevideo for the opening of the Pan-American Conference on economic and peace questions, with the Gran Chaco war between Bolivia and Paraguay and the monetary and debt situations among the subjects expected to be taken up. Cuba's delegation said its program rested on the complete independence of all American countries and freedom from intervention, while Haiti's delegate, Pierre Paul, charged that the United States had for eighteen years supported unjustifiable intervention in Haiti and said he would introduce a resolution establishing the principle of non-intervention. Secretary of State Cordell Hull visited the heads of delegations, including that of the Dominican Republic, and discussed the question of American financial control in Haiti with the Haitian delegation.

La delegación de Cuba declaró que su programa se basaba en la independencia integral de todos los países americanos y en la libertad frente a la intervención, mientras que el delegado de Haití, Pierre Paul, denunció que los Estados Unidos habían sostenido durante dieciocho años una intervención injustificable en Haití y anunció que presentaría una resolución que estableciera el principio de no intervención. records.headline: Having obtained permission the previous day to enter the Dominican
records.summary_en: Having obtained permission the previous day to enter the Dominican Republic, Colonel and Mrs. Lindbergh were indicated to be planning a stop at Santo Domingo, about 300 miles away, on their route to Miami, though Colonel Lindbergh did not specify his immediate destination before taking off. At 10 a.m., the fliers reported their position ten miles south of Cape Engaño on the northeastern tip of the Dominican Republic, approximately 145 miles from San Juan and apparently heading toward Santo Domingo.
records.summary_es: Habiendo obtenido permiso el día anterior para ingresar a la República Dominicana, se indicó que el coronel y la señora Lindbergh podrían hacer una escala en Santo Domingo, a unas 300 millas de distancia, en su ruta hacia Miami, aunque el coronel Lindbergh no especificó su destino inmediato antes de despegar. A las 10 a. m., los aviadores informaron su posición a diez millas al sur de Cabo Engaño, en el extremo noreste de la República Dominicana, a unas 145 millas de San Juan y aparentemente en dirección a Santo Domingo.

records.headline: The couple intended to fly to Santo Domingo in the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: The couple intended to fly to Santo Domingo in the Dominican Republic the next morning as the next leg of their cruise, Pan-American Airways officials stated, after Colonel and Mrs. Lindbergh landed their seaplane following a six-hour, 20-minute flight from Trinidad over the Caribbean Sea. Lindbergh himself declined to comment on their plans and refused requests for a press interview. As the seaplane came down on the waterfront at San Juan, a great cheer went up from thousands of Puerto Ricans and Americans gathered to greet them and welcome “Lindy and Anne” back to American territory.
records.summary_es: La pareja tenía la intención de volar a Santo Domingo, en la República Dominicana, a la mañana siguiente como próxima etapa de su travesía, según informaron funcionarios de Pan-American Airways, después de que el coronel y la señora Lindbergh amerizaran en su hidroavión tras un vuelo de seis horas y 20 minutos desde Trinidad sobre el mar Caribe. El propio Lindbergh declinó hacer comentarios sobre sus planes y rechazó las solicitudes de entrevista de la prensa. Cuando el hidroavión descendió sobre el frente marítimo de San Juan, una gran aclamación se elevó de los miles de puertorriqueños y estadounidenses congregados para saludarlos y dar la bienvenida a «Lindy y Anne» de vuelta a territorio americano.

records.headline: According to the Douglas Daily Dispatch, the Dominican consul
records.summary_en: According to the Douglas Daily Dispatch, the Dominican consul signed papers granting the Lindberghs permission to fly to Santo Domingo. Although Colonel Lindbergh did not confirm the schedule, it was indicated that unless plans changed, the fliers would depart at 9 a.m. the following day for Santo Domingo City, the capital of the Dominican Republic, located about 300 miles due west. On the fliers' arrival, a crowd of more than a thousand gathered at the airport, and as the plane came down in the channel, after encircling the port, whistles of harbor craft sounded a raucous welcome.
records.summary_es: Según el Douglas Daily Dispatch, el cónsul dominicano firmó los documentos que autorizan a los Lindbergh a volar a Santo Domingo. Aunque el coronel Lindbergh no confirmó el itinerario, se indicó que, salvo un cambio de planes, los aviadores partirían a las 9 a. m. del día siguiente hacia la ciudad de Santo Domingo, capital de la República Dominicana, situada a unas 300 millas al oeste. A la llegada de los aviadores, una multitud de más de mil personas se congregó en el aeropuerto, y cuando el avión descendió en el canal, tras sobrevolar el puerto en círculo, las sirenas de las embarcaciones del puerto sonaron en una estruendosa bienvenida.

records.headline: An Associated Press dispatch from San Pedro, Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: An Associated Press dispatch from San Pedro, Dominican Republic, dated December 15 reports that Pan-American Airways announced the landing of Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh at 10:40 a.m. Eastern Standard Time after a flight from San Juan, Puerto Rico. Located on the southern coast of the Dominican Republic east of Santo Domingo and roughly 225 miles west of San Juan, San Pedro was chosen for its airport facilities, according to Pan-American officials. The couple planned to remain there for the day before continuing toward Miami and New York the next day.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de la Associated Press fechado el 15 de diciembre en San Pedro, República Dominicana, informa que Pan-American Airways anunció el aterrizaje del coronel y la señora Charles A. Lindbergh a las 10:40 a. m., hora estándar del Este, tras un vuelo desde San Juan, Puerto Rico. Situado en la costa sur de la República Dominicana, al este de Santo Domingo y a unas 225 millas al oeste de San Juan, San Pedro fue elegido por sus buenas instalaciones aeroportuarias, según indicaron funcionarios de Pan-American. La pareja planeaba permanecer allí durante el día y reanudar su viaje hacia Miami y Nueva York al día siguiente.

records.headline: A United Press dispatch from Santo Domingo dated December 16
records.summary_en: A United Press dispatch from Santo Domingo dated December 16 reports that Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh took off from San Pedro de Macoris and appeared over the Dominican capital forty-five minutes later, at 7:19 a.m. Before heading north on their homeward flight, the couple circled wide over Santo Domingo in their monoplane and dipped their wings in salute to crowds gathered in the streets and on rooftops. Although Colonel Lindbergh declined to state their destination, it was believed to be either Havana or directly to Miami.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de la United Press fechado el 16 de diciembre en Santo Domingo informa que el coronel y la señora Charles A. Lindbergh despegaron de San Pedro de Macorís y aparecieron sobre la capital dominicana cuarenta y cinco minutos después, a las 7:19 a. m. Antes de dirigirse al norte en su vuelo de regreso a casa, la pareja trazó amplios círculos sobre Santo Domingo en su monoplano e inclinó las alas en saludo a las multitudes congregadas en las calles y azoteas. Aunque el coronel Lindbergh declinó indicar su destino, se creía que era La Habana o directamente Miami.

records.headline: In a December 15 dispatch from Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: In a December 15 dispatch from Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, the Douglas Daily Dispatch reports that Colonel and Mrs. Lindbergh arrived in their hydro-monoplane at 10:45 a.m. after a two-hour, 300-mile flight from San Juan, Puerto Rico. U.S. Minister H. F. Arthur Schoenfeld and Mrs. Schoenfeld met the fliers at the Pan-American Airways harbor, brought them into the capital—where they called on President Trujillo at the palace—and entertained them that evening. Positioned 900 miles from the United States, the Lindberghs planned to depart at 7 a.m. the next day on the final leg of their journey toward Miami, likely by way of Havana.
records.summary_es: En un despacho del 15 de diciembre desde Santo Domingo, República Dominicana, el Douglas Daily Dispatch informa que el coronel y la señora Lindbergh llegaron en su hidromonoplano a las 10:45 a. m. tras un vuelo de dos horas y 300 millas desde San Juan, Puerto Rico. El ministro de los Estados Unidos, H. F. Arthur Schoenfeld, y la señora Schoenfeld recibieron a los aviadores en el puerto de Pan-American Airways, los trasladaron a la capital —donde visitaron al presidente Trujillo en el palacio— y los agasajaron esa noche. Situados a 900 millas de los Estados Unidos, los Lindbergh planeaban partir a las 7 a. m. del día siguiente en el último tramo de su viaje hacia Miami, probablemente pasando por La Habana.

records.headline: The political and economic achievements of Dominican President Trujillo's administration
records.summary_en: The political and economic achievements of Dominican President Trujillo's administration have replaced domestic opposition with a strong movement favoring his continuance in office after his current term ends, the Evening Star reports in a review of political developments over the past two years. In neighboring Haiti, domestic peace also remained uninterrupted during the year ending that day, and President Vincent strengthened his support by concluding an executive agreement with the United States aimed at ending American interference and asking President Roosevelt for its immediate fulfillment.
records.summary_es: Los logros políticos y económicos del gobierno del presidente dominicano Trujillo han hecho que la oposición interna dé paso a un fuerte movimiento a favor de su permanencia en el poder cuando concluya su mandato actual, según informa el Evening Star al reseñar los acontecimientos políticos de los últimos dos años. En la vecina Haití, la paz interna también se mantuvo ininterrumpida durante el año que termina ese día, y el presidente Vincent aumentó su respaldo al concluir un acuerdo ejecutivo con los Estados Unidos tendiente a suprimir la injerencia estadounidense y solicitar al presidente Roosevelt su cumplimiento inmediato.

records.headline: An Associated Press dispatch from Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: An Associated Press dispatch from Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, dated March 7 reports that the airliner American Clipper, carrying Mrs. Franklin D. Roosevelt and her party through the West Indies from Miami to San Juan, Puerto Rico, took off at 9:30 a.m. Eastern Standard Time from the San Pedro de Macoris airport after a 35-minute stopover. During the flight, Mrs. Roosevelt read, wrote, sent a cable to her husband, and conversed at length with Professor Rexford G. Tugwell, who was also traveling to Puerto Rico to study its problems. As the airliner departed the harbor, three squads of three U.S. Marine planes escorted the Clipper in close formation for 15 minutes before turning back across a Haitian lake.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de la Associated Press fechado el 7 de marzo en Santo Domingo, República Dominicana, informa que el avión de pasajeros American Clipper, que transportaba a la señora Franklin D. Roosevelt y su comitiva por las Indias Occidentales desde Miami hacia San Juan, Puerto Rico, despegó a las 9:30 a. m., hora estándar del Este, del aeropuerto de San Pedro de Macorís tras una escala de 35 minutos. Durante el vuelo, la señora Roosevelt leyó, escribió, envió un cable a su esposo y conversó extensamente con el profesor Rexford G. Tugwell, quien también viajaba a Puerto Rico para estudiar sus problemas. Al salir el avión del puerto, tres escuadrillas de tres aviones cada una del Cuerpo de Marines de los Estados Unidos escoltaron al Clipper en formación cerrada durante 15 minutos antes de dar la vuelta sobre un lago haitiano.

records.headline: The Indianapolis Times reports that the wife of the U.S. President set
records.summary_en: The Indianapolis Times reports that the wife of the U.S. President set an ambitious program for her twenty-four hours visit to the Virgin Islands to inquire into island development, education, homeless youths, illiteracy, economic plans, the bay rum industry, and homesteading. After departing Port-au-Prince at 6:30 a.m. the previous day, Mrs. Roosevelt traveled to San Pedro, the Pan-American Airways port in the Dominican Republic, where she was received by President Rafael Trujillo. From San Pedro she proceeded to San Juan and, after an hour, flew on to St. Thomas.
records.summary_es: The Indianapolis Times informa que la esposa del presidente estadounidense fijó un ambicioso programa para su visita de veinticuatro horas a las Islas Vírgenes con el fin de indagar sobre el desarrollo insular, la educación, los jóvenes sin hogar, el analfabetismo, los planes económicos, la industria del bay rum y el asentamiento agrícola. Tras partir de Puerto Príncipe a las 6:30 a. m. del día anterior, la señora Roosevelt viajó a San Pedro, puerto de Pan-American Airways en la República Dominicana, donde fue recibida por el presidente Rafael Trujillo. Desde San Pedro prosiguió hacia San Juan y, tras una hora, voló hacia Saint Thomas.

records.headline: An Associated Press dispatch from San Pedro de Macoris, Dominican
records.summary_en: An Associated Press dispatch from San Pedro de Macoris, Dominican Republic, dated March 15, reports that Mrs. Franklin D. Roosevelt and her party were blocked by a Thursday rainstorm over Haiti while traveling in a Pan-American Airways flying boat and returned to the San Pedro de Macoris airport after flying 120 miles west. The plane had arrived at 7:05 E.S.T. from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and took off shortly afterward on its return flight to Miami before a heavy downpour reduced visibility over the mountains of Haiti, which occupies the western half of the island where the Dominican Republic is situated. Taking no chances, the pilot turned back as Mrs. Roosevelt concluded the West Indian tour she had begun from Washington on March 5 to gather first-hand information on health and economic conditions in Puerto Rico.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de la Associated Press desde San Pedro de Macorís, República Dominicana, fechado el 15 de marzo, informa que la señora Franklin D. Roosevelt y su comitiva fueron bloqueadas el jueves por una tormenta de lluvia sobre Haití mientras viajaban en un hidroavión de Pan-American Airways y regresaron al aeropuerto de San Pedro de Macorís tras volar 120 millas hacia el oeste. El avión había llegado a las 7:05 E.S.T. procedente de San Juan, Puerto Rico, y despegó poco después en su vuelo de regreso a Miami antes de que un fuerte aguacero redujera la visibilidad sobre las montañas de Haití, país que ocupa la mitad occidental de la isla donde está situada la República Dominicana. Sin correr riesgos, el piloto dio media vuelta mientras la señora Roosevelt concluía la gira por las Indias Occidentales que había iniciado desde Washington el 5 de marzo para obtener información de primera mano sobre las condiciones sanitarias y económicas en Puerto Rico.

records.summary_en: When reduced visibility over the mountains of Haiti—the western half of the island on which the Dominican Republic is situated—blocked her flight, pilot Charles Dewey decided to turn back to San Pedro de Macoris. Upon returning to San Pedro de Macoris aboard the plane Caribbean Clipper, Mrs. Roosevelt remained calm, had lunch, and made no comment on the delay. Airline officials monitoring the weather map by wireless reported that there was no storm area, advised waiting until the clouds cleared before resuming the flight, and estimated that perhaps 20 minutes of rain would be encountered in the valley beyond Barahona. The party had departed San Juan at 6 a.m. expecting to reach Miami late that day on the longest day's oceanic flying of the First Lady's 10-day Puerto Rican and Virgin Islands trip.

records.headline: The homeward flight of Mrs. Franklin D. Roosevelt and her party
records.summary_en: The homeward flight of Mrs. Franklin D. Roosevelt and her party following an inspection tour of the West Indies is reported in two March 15 Associated Press dispatches in the McAllen Daily Monitor. A wireless message received in Miami stated that the airliner carrying Mrs. Roosevelt from San Juan, Puerto Rico, to Miami was forced back to San Pedro, Dominican Republic, by unfavorable weather after passing westward from that city. An accompanying dispatch from San Pedro de Macoris noted that the party had arrived there at 7:05 E.S.T. aboard the airliner American Clipper after leaving San Juan at 6 a.m. on the approximately 1,045-mile journey to Miami.
records.summary_es: El vuelo de regreso de la señora Franklin D. Roosevelt y su comitiva tras una gira de inspección por las Indias Occidentales es informado en dos despachos de la Associated Press del 15 de marzo en el McAllen Daily Monitor. Un mensaje inalámbrico recibido en Miami indicó que el avión de pasajeros que transportaba a la señora Roosevelt desde San Juan, Puerto Rico, hacia Miami se vio obligado a regresar a San Pedro, República Dominicana, debido al mal tiempo tras pasar al oeste de dicha ciudad. Un despacho adjunto desde San Pedro de Macorís señaló que la comitiva había llegado allí a las 7:05 E.S.T. a bordo del avión American Clipper tras salir de San Juan a las 6 a. m. en el trayecto de aproximadamente 1,045 millas hasta Miami.

records.headline: Generalissimo Rafael L. Trujillo was re-elected president of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Generalissimo Rafael L. Trujillo was re-elected president of the Dominican Republic in the previous day's voting, while Jacinto B. Peynado was elected vice president, according to election returns reported in a May 17 Associated Press dispatch from Santo Domingo. The general election also chose 12 Senators, 33 Deputies, 12 Governors, municipal governments, and 33 members of an assembly to revise the national constitution.

En las elecciones generales también se eligieron 12 senadores, 33 diputados, 12 gobernadores, gobiernos municipales y 33 miembros de una asamblea encargada de revisar la constitución nacional.

records.headline: A United Press dispatch from Port-au-Prince, Haiti, dated June
records.summary_en: A United Press dispatch from Port-au-Prince, Haiti, dated June 26, reports semi-official disclosures that former Cuban President Gerardo Machado, sought for extradition by the Cuban government, has been located on a farm 16 miles from the city of Santo Domingo. The farm is owned by Dominican Republic President Rafael Trujillo. Machado was understood to have reached Santo Domingo aboard a small commercial steamer from the southern United States, though the information was not officially verified.

La finca es propiedad del presidente de la República Dominicana, Rafael Trujillo. Se tenía entendido que Machado había llegado a Santo Domingo a bordo de un pequeño vapor comercial procedente del sur de los Estados Unidos, aunque la información no fue verificada oficialmente.
