records.headline: The State Department announced yesterday that the United States had agreed
records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* reported that the State Department agreed to terminate the U.S. customs receivership in the Dominican Republic, restoring duty collections of roughly $4,000,000 annually to Dominican authorities. In exchange, the Dominican Republic granted the United States a first lien on its total revenues, estimated at $12,000,000, to guarantee the servicing of $15,400,000 in external debt. The treaty was negotiated in Ciudad Trujillo by U.S. Ambassador Hugh Wilson and Dominican Foreign Minister Arturo Despradel, ending the 1924 convention.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Star* informó que el Departamento de Estado acordó extinguir la receptoría aduanera estadounidense en la República Dominicana, devolviendo a las autoridades dominicanas la recaudación de tributos, estimada en unos 4.000.000 de dólares anuales. Como contraparte, la República Dominicana concedió a Estados Unidos un gravamen preferente sobre la totalidad de sus rentas fiscales, calculadas en 12.000.000 de dólares, para afianzar el servicio de 15.400.000 dólares de deuda externa. El tratado fue pactado en Ciudad Trujillo por el embajador estadounidense Hugh Wilson y el canciller dominicano Arturo Despradel, poniendo término a la convención de 1924.
records.passage: Terminated by U. S. By the Associated Press. The State Department announced yesterday that the United States had agreed to terminate its receivership of the Dominican Republic customs revenues and restore to that nation the privilege of handling collection of the approximately $4,000,000 annual intake from duties. In turn, the Dominican government agreed to give the United States first lien on total revenues of the Dominican government, a figure roughly estimated at $12,000.000. The department announced that the agreement was reached in Ciudad Trujillo by a United States commission headed by Ambassador Hugh Wilson and a Dominican commission headed by Arturo Despradel, Minister of Foreign Affairs. The agreement, embodied in a convention, terminates the convention of 1934 by which the United States assumed general receivership of customs in order to guarantee the servicing of the Dominican Republic's external debt of 1922 and 1928, computed at $15,400,000. records.headline: The Minister of the Dominican Republic and Señora de Pastoriza
records.summary_en: The Minister of the Dominican Republic and Señora de Pastoriza are scheduled to host a reception on Monday afternoon from 5 to 7 o'clock in honor of Gen. Rafael Trujillo, generalissimo of the Dominican Republic, who is visiting Washington on a special mission. The gathering will take place in the minister's apartment at 2101 Connecticut Avenue. The report recalls the large and brilliant receptions held for Trujillo during his visit several months earlier, noting that the upcoming Monday party will be on a smaller scale.

El agasajo se llevará a cabo en el espacioso apartamento que ocupan el ministro y la señora de Pastoriza en el 2101 de Connecticut Avenue. La crónica evoca las concurridas y brillantes fiestas ofrecidas en honor de Trujillo durante su visita efectuada pocos meses atrás, señalando que la reunión del próximo lunes será a menor escala.

records.headline: Former Dominican President Gen. Rafael Trujillo attended a Latin American musical concert
records.summary_en: Former Dominican President Gen. Rafael Trujillo attended a Latin American musical concert at the Pan American Union as the guest of the Dominican Minister and Señora de Pastoriza. The event drew an audience of approximately 4,000 people, including members of the diplomatic corps, British Ambassador the Marquess of Lothian, and National Symphony Orchestra conductor Dr. Hans Kindler. Pan American Union Director General Dr. Leo S. Rowe, who inaugurated the concert series, visited patrons in the boxes during intermission.

El director general de la Unión Panamericana, Dr. Leo S. Rowe, bajo cuya gestión se inauguró la serie de conciertos, saludó a los asistentes en los palcos durante el intermedio.

records.headline: Gen. Rafael Trujillo, former president of the Dominican Republic
records.summary_en: Gen. Rafael Trujillo, former president of the Dominican Republic on a special mission to Washington, hosted a luncheon aboard his yacht Ramfis at the Navy Yard in honor of yard commandant Rear Admiral George Pettengill. The vessel had been moored at the yard for nearly a week, and guests included several naval commanders and Marine Barracks commandant Lt. Col. L. L. Whaley. The previous evening, Trujillo entertained Major General Commandant of the Marine Corps Gen. Thomas Holcomb and other senior military officers at dinner aboard the yacht.
records.summary_es: El general Rafael Trujillo, expresidente de la República Dominicana en misión especial en Washington, ofreció hoy un almuerzo a bordo de su yate Ramfis en el Astillero Naval en honor del comandante del recinto, contraalmirante George Pettengill. La nave había permanecido atracada en el astillero durante casi una semana, y entre los invitados figuraron varios oficiales navales y el comandante del cuartel de infantería de marina, teniente coronel L. L. Whaley. La noche anterior, Trujillo agasajó a bordo del yate en una cena al mayor general comandante del Cuerpo de Infantería de Marina, general Thomas Holcomb, junto con otros altos mandos militares.

records.headline: Leopold Stokowski's All-American Youth Orchestra arrived in New York
records.summary_en: Leopold Stokowski's All-American Youth Orchestra arrived in New York on Tuesday aboard the liner Argentina following an acclaimed tour of South America. During its homeward voyage, the vessel made a special stop at Trujillo City in the Dominican Republic, where the ensemble performed before an audience of 28,000 people. The orchestra consists of eighty young men and twenty young women chosen through nationwide competition across all U.S. states, with an average age of twenty-three.
records.summary_es: La Orquesta Juvenil Panamericana de Leopold Stokowski llegó a Nueva York el martes a bordo del transatlántico Argentina tras una aclamada gira por Sudamérica. Durante su travesía de regreso, el barco realizó una escala especial en Trujillo City, en la República Dominicana, donde la agrupación tocó ante un público de 28.000 personas. La orquesta está integrada por ochenta hombres jóvenes y veinte mujeres jóvenes seleccionados mediante concurso en todos los estados del país, con una edad promedio de veintitrés años.

records.headline: The election of Mr. Vance to an office in Hispanic American law
records.summary_en: The election of Mr. Vance to an office in Hispanic American law coincides with broader efforts to strengthen cultural cooperation among Western Hemisphere nations. Prior to his legal career in Washington, he served for six years as deputy general receiver of customs in the Dominican Republic and subsequently practiced law in Santo Domingo. Appointed law librarian of Congress in 1924, Vance has made multiple official visits to Spain and Latin America on behalf of the Library of Congress.
records.summary_es: La elección del señor Vance para un cargo en el ámbito del derecho hispanoamericano coincide con esfuerzos más amplios para estrechar la cooperación cultural entre las naciones del hemisferio occidental. Antes de su trayectoria jurídica en Washington, ejerció durante seis años como receptor general adjunto de aduanas en la República Dominicana y posteriormente ejerció la abogacía en Santo Domingo. Designado bibliotecario de leyes del Congreso en 1924, Vance ha realizado múltiples visitas oficiales a España y América Latina en representación de la Biblioteca del Congreso.

records.headline: Señora de Brea Messina, daughter of former Dominican President Gen. Rafael Trujillo
records.summary_en: Señora de Brea Messina, daughter of former Dominican President Gen. Rafael Trujillo and wife of Dr. Ramón A. Brea Messina, the Dominican Minister to Mexico, was honored at a diplomatic luncheon hosted by Señorita Bernardino. Educated in Paris at the Collège Féminin de Bouffémont, Señora de Brea Messina is fluent in several languages, was presented at the British royal court, and attended the coronation of King George VI in 1937. Guests attending the Washington function included Señora de Pastoriza, wife of the Dominican Minister, Señora de Vega, wife of the first secretary of the Dominican legation, and diplomatic wives representing Panama, Ecuador, El Salvador, Honduras, Cuba, and Peru.

Brea Messina, ministro de la República Dominicana en México, fue honrada en un almuerzo diplomático ofrecido por la señorita Bernardino. Educada en París en el Collège Féminin de Bouffémont, la señora de Brea Messina domina varios idiomas, fue presentada ante la corte británica y asistió a la coronación del rey Jorge VI en 1937. Entre las invitadas al agasajo en Washington figuraron la señora de Pastoriza, esposa del ministro dominicano, la señora de Vega, esposa del primer secretario de la legación dominicana, y esposas de miembros del cuerpo diplomático de Panamá, Ecuador, El Salvador, Honduras, Cuba y Perú.

records.headline: Datelined Ciudad Trujillo, Dominican Republic, October 10
records.summary_en: Datelined Ciudad Trujillo, Dominican Republic, October 10 (UP), a news dispatch reports that nine fugitives from the penal colony in French Guiana arrived today aboard the sailing vessel Remember from Georgetown, British Guiana. The men replenished their food provisions in the Dominican capital before setting sail, apparently bound for Miami, Florida. The report appears alongside news of four separate Devil's Island escapees detained after arriving in St. Thomas, Virgin Islands, in an open boat seeking to reach Canada.
records.summary_es: Con fecha de Ciudad Trujillo, República Dominicana, 10 de octubre (UP), un despacho noticioso informa que nueve fugitivos de la colonia penal de la Guayana Francesa llegaron hoy a bordo del velero Remember procedentes de Georgetown, Guayana Británica. Los individuos se abastecieron de provisiones de alimentos en la capital dominicana antes de zarpar, aparentemente con rumbo a Miami, Florida. La crónica aparece junto a la noticia de otros cuatro evadidos de la Isla del Diablo que fueron detenidos tras arribar a Santo Tomás, Islas Vírgenes, en un bote abierto buscando llegar a Canadá.

records.summary_en: A dispatch from Washington reports that Secretary of State Hull and Dominican Ambassador Extraordinary Dr. Rafael Trujillo signed a convention returning to Santo Domingo the right to collect its own customs. The item notes that an American force had been in charge of receiving customs since Dec. 27, 1939. That arrangement had been instituted so the United States could supervise the settlement of debts owed to American bondholders and claims brought by American nationals against the Dominican Republic.

Dicho acuerdo se había instituido para que los Estados Unidos pudieran supervisar el pago de las deudas a los tenedores de bonos estadounidenses y las reclamaciones presentadas por ciudadanos estadounidenses contra la República Dominicana.

records.full_text:
Many Undefined Laws Add to President's War Powers

(Fifth Article in a Series of Six)

By LUDWELL DENNY

Despite the President's dictatorial domestic powers in an emergency, it is commonly assumed that Congress at least has an over-balancing check on the Executive in foreign affairs.

Does not the Constitution give Congress the sole right to declare war, the Senate the right to ratify treaties and confirm diplomatic appointments, and the House the power of initiating appropriations necessary for foreign adventures and war-making?

These much-advertised checks exist—on paper. On the record, however, they have rarely been effective in a crisis.

UNDEFINED POWERS

There are many reasons. One is the undefined Commander-in-Chief powers in the Constitution. Another reason is that a President cannot conduct foreign relations without creating situations and trends that largely determine eventual peace or war. Congress then must recognize an accomplished and irreparable fact, whether Congress or the country likes it or not.

Congressional confirmation and appropriation become ineffective "checks" when Presidents use their own private Col. Houses, or better still, use the transoceanic telephone; and when they spend money without authorization. As for treaty ratification, if the President calls it an "executive agreement" (or leaves it as an unwritten understanding), Congress has no check.

PAST EXAMPLES

Here is the way it has operated:

By extending or withholding his favor, he has virtual life-or-death power over certain Latin American governments. He can keep alive a foreign government at war—as China today. Theodore Roosevelt in a deal with Japan revoked United States recognition of Korean independence.

Examples of executive agreements more important than most treaties: The 1917 Lansing-Ishii Agreement recognizing Japan's special interests in the Orient, which Harding reversed and F. D. R. is continuing to reverse. Theodore Roosevelt's application, in the Dominican Republic, of provisions of a protectorate treaty after the Senate refused to ratify. The 1905 Roosevelt-Japanese secret agreement.

Some of these single-handed executive agreements make foreign alliances: The Japanese-Anglo-American alliance of 1905. Our present far-reaching alliance with Canada, and our presumptive alliance with Britain (terms unknown).

CAN WAGE WAR

The President can send expeditionary forces and fight wars overseas without a congressional declaration of war or consultation. For many years this was almost a habit in Caribbean countries. Wilson waged undeclared war in Siberia.

The President can even conquer foreign territory and rule it thru his own agents or with native puppets—as in the past in Haiti, the Dominican Republic and Nicaragua. Or he can do it with a phony revolution, as T. R. took Panama from Colombia.

CAN'T ALWAYS STOP HIM

And he can act when Congress has tried to stop him—as when Wilson armed merchant ships, and (so congressmen contend) when F. D. R. traded destroyers to Britain.

When President Polk sent troops into disputed territory, the Mexican War resulted almost automatically. William McKinley sent the battleship Maine to Havana, when he knew this "unfriendly" act might precipitate a Spanish-American War. It did.

F. D.'s PLEDGE

Franklin Roosevelt's single-handed commitment to Canada will put us into war with Germany, if Hitler is foolish enough to attack our neighbor or a British government which retreats there. That is the specific Roosevelt pledge. And certainly the White House decision to send or not to send our fleet to British waters in the Far East, in defiance of the new Japanese-German-Italian alliance, may determine war or peace.

The record shows, therefore, that the presidency is a constitutional dictatorship in any self-proclaimed emergency both in domestic and foreign affairs, even to the ultimate degree of pledging war and making war.

AN INCOMPLETE LIST

When the Senate, alarmed by the snowballing of Rooseveltian authority, asked the Attorney General to inform it of the source and extent of the President's emergency and war powers, he gave as an incomplete list 100 laws.

Congress, theoretically, could repeal all of those grants. But that would not change the situation basically. As the Attorney General reminded the Senate:

"You are aware, of course, that the Executive has powers not enumerated in the statutes—powers not derived by statutory grants, but from the Constitution. It is universally recognized that the constitutional duties of the Executive carry with them the constitutional powers necessary for their proper performance.

"These constitutional powers have never been specifically defined and, in fact, cannot be, since their extent and limitations are largely dependent upon conditions and circumstances."

TURN TO HISTORY

Unlimited and undefined powers are dictatorial. This is not only theory but historic fact.

Lincoln (not Congress) freed the slaves. He increased the Army and Navy beyond the legal limits. He suspended writs of habeas corpus and declared martial law. He spent millions of dollars without appropriations.

This was Lincoln's justification: "I felt that measures, otherwise unconstitutional, might become lawful by becoming indispensable to the preservation of the Constitution thru the preservation of the nation."

Woodrow Wilson, as a generation still living cannot forget, in a war crisis assumed even greater dictatorial powers than Lincoln.

NEXT: "Dictatorship" and the Third Term.

records.full_text:
Hugh Wilson to End Diplomatic Career On December 31 Former Envoy to Reich Is Praised by Hull on Announcing Retirement

Hugh R. Wilson, veteran career diplomat, who has been a special assistant to the Secretary of State since he resigned as Ambassador to Germany soon after the European war began, plans to retire December 31.

The State Department announced his retirement last night, making public a letter by Secretary of State Hull praising Mr. Wilson's services and saying "certain important and confidential work" which he had undertaken "has now been satisfactorily completed."

Mr. Hull's letter did not indicate the nature of the work to which he referred. Mr. Wilson recently negotiated a new customs treaty with the Dominican Republic which is understood now to be ready for submission to the Senate for ratification. His work at the State Department also has been concerned with special problems arising from the war in Europe.

Mr. Wilson, who is 55 years old, entered the foreign service in 1911 and has held posts in Lisbon, Guatemala, Buenos Aires, Vienna, Berne and Tokio, as well as Berlin. He also served as chief of the Division of Current Information and as an Assistant Secretary at the State Department.

As a protest against Nazi anti-Semitic and other policies, Mr. Wilson was called home from Berlin "for report and consultation" in November, 1938. The German Ambassador was recalled to Berlin soon thereafter. There has been no indication that a new Ambassador to Germany would be appointed.

More Diplomats Accept Invitations To Aviation Ball

The Charge d' Affaires of the Cuban Embassy and Senora de Baron, the Ambassador of Colombia, Senor Dr. Gabriel Turbay and the Minister of Costa Rica and Senora de Fernandez are among the latest Pan-American diplomats to accept invitations to the Pan-American Aviation Day ball, to be held tomorrow night at the Mayflower Hotel. A special invitation has been sent to Gen. Rafael Trujillo of the Dominican Republic. Gen. Trujillo is now in New York.

Members of the "Escuadrilla de Aviacion Interamericana de Cuba" also have been invited. This group is scheduled to take part in the Havana celebration of Pan-American Aviation Day and the plan is to have them fly here in time to be honor guests at the Washington celebration.

Embassies and Legations of the Latin American republics are to supply decorations emblematic of their countries for use at the celebration here. A general Pan-American motif of decoration will be used.

records.headline: A report on European refugee resettlement in the New World highlights
records.summary_en: A report on European refugee resettlement in the New World highlights the growing community at Sosua, which has expanded to more than 1.000 persons. Officials explain that two-thirds of the colonists are young men in their early twenties who are in need of wives for companionship and domestic support. The enterprise was launched by the Dominican Republic Settlement Association with $10,000,000 in capitalization after the republic agreed to accept 100.000 refugees, with Generalissimo Rafael Trujillo contributing an estate of 65.000 acres along with buildings and equipment. The colonists have already cleared 3.000 acres for agricultural production and established an independent dairy industry.

records.headline: A correspondent describes life at the American Legation in the Dominican Republic

The dispatch remarks on the legation's domestic staff, highlighting a Danish chief cook who had worked at the New York World's Fair before traveling to the Dominican Republic to seek employment when his United States visa expired. The writer adds that the Scottens anticipate taking leave in Washington in the spring and are preparing to receive their first Washington visitor, Mrs. Marian Warburg, at the end of the month.

La crónica resalta al personal de servicio de la legación, haciendo mención especial de un jefe de cocina danés que había trabajado en la Feria Mundial de Nueva York antes de viajar a la República Dominicana en busca de empleo al expirar su visado estadounidense. El autor agrega que los esposos Scotten esperan tomar una licencia en Washington durante la primavera y se preparan para recibir a fines de mes a su primera visitante de Washington, la señora Marian Warburg.

records.headline: A news item datelined Ciudad Trujillo reports on ceremonies
records.summary_en: A news item datelined Ciudad Trujillo reports on ceremonies held at the National Palace marking the first anniversary of the agreement between the Dominican Republic and the Dominican Republic Settlement Association. On that occasion, the president of the settlement association announced a financial gift from the Rosenwald family to support the refugee colony at Sosua. He further disclosed that 1.000 additional settlers are scheduled to be brought to the settlement during the current year, following conferences held in New York with Archduke Otto of Austria.

En dicha ocasión, el presidente de la asociación de asentamiento anunció una donación económica de la familia Rosenwald para apoyar la colonia de refugiados en Sosúa. Asimismo, reveló que está programada la llegada de 1.000 colonos adicionales al asentamiento durante el presente año, tras reuniones sostenidas en Nueva York con el archiduque Otón de Austria.

records.headline: An article records that in 1933 Mr. Newman stepped away from his advertising
records.summary_en: An article records that in 1933 Mr. Newman stepped away from his advertising and public relations practice to serve as economic adviser to the Dominican Republic during debt rearrangement proceedings before the State Department and the Foreign Bondholders' Protective Council. Following the successful outcome of the negotiations, then-President Trujillo awarded him the Order of Merit of Juan Pablo Duarte, recognized as the highest decoration granted by Santo Domingo. Mr. Newman traveled by air to the Dominican Republic two years ago to formally accept the honour.
records.summary_es: Un artículo consigna que en 1933 el señor Newman se apartó de sus actividades de publicidad y relaciones públicas para desempeñarse como asesor económico de la República Dominicana durante las negociaciones de reestructuración de la deuda ante el Departamento de Estado y el Foreign Bondholders' Protective Council. Tras el exitoso resultado de las gestiones, el entonces presidente Trujillo le confirió la Orden del Mérito de Juan Pablo Duarte, reconocida como la máxima condecoración otorgada por Santo Domingo. El señor Newman viajó por vía aérea a la República Dominicana hace dos años para aceptar formalmente el galardón.

records.headline: Following an appointment to the diplomatic post of Minister
records.summary_en: Following an appointment to the diplomatic post of Minister to the Dominican Republic, Señora de Garland and her three children will remain in Washington until June so the younger children can complete the academic year. The eldest son attends George Washington University, the elder daughter is in high school, and her six-year-old sister attends grade school. The family will reside at their apartment at 3024 Tilden Street until June, when they are scheduled to sail for San Domingo.
records.summary_es: Tras el nombramiento para el cargo diplomático de ministro en la República Dominicana, la señora de Garland y sus tres hijos permanecerán en Washington hasta junio con el fin de que los más jóvenes concluyan el curso académico. El hijo mayor asiste a la George Washington University, la hija mayor cursa la secundaria y su hermana de seis años asiste a la escuela primaria. La familia residirá en su apartamento del 3024 de la calle Tilden hasta junio, fecha en la que tienen previsto zarpar con rumbo a Santo Domingo.

records.headline: A Washington correspondent provides an architectural and social
records.summary_en: A Washington correspondent provides an architectural and social account of the renovated American Legation in Ciudad Trujillo, noting drawing room floors constructed from diverse native Dominican woods alongside fine furnishings arranged by Mrs. Ann Scotten. At a luncheon held in the residence, guests included Dr. Dana Munroe of Princeton University, who was in the Dominican Republic conducting an economic survey for the Brookings Institution. The gathering also included the Dominican Minister of Foreign Affairs and Señora Despradel, legation architect and constructor Señor Alfonseca and his wife, and Colonel and Mrs. Murray Jacoby, who were staying at Sans Souci as guests of General Trujillo.
records.summary_es: Una corresponsal de Washington ofrece un relato arquitectónico y social de la renovada legación de los Estados Unidos en Ciudad Trujillo, destacando los pisos del salón elaborados con diversas maderas nativas dominicanas junto al refinado mobiliario dispuesto por la señora Ann Scotten. En un almuerzo celebrado en la residencia, entre los invitados figuraron el doctor Dana Munroe de Princeton University, quien se encontraba en la República Dominicana realizando un estudio económico para la Brookings Institution. La reunión contó además con la presencia del ministro de Relaciones Exteriores dominicano y la señora Despradel, del arquitecto y constructor de la legación, señor Alfonseca, y su esposa, y del coronel Murray Jacoby y su esposa, quienes se hospedaban en Sans Souci como invitados del general Trujillo.

records.headline: A society letter from Ciudad Trujillo details diplomatic entertainments
records.summary_en: A society letter from Ciudad Trujillo details diplomatic entertainments surrounding United States Minister Robert Scotten. An afternoon reception brought together the French Minister and Mme. Henriot, the Peruvian and Colombian chargés d'affaires, General Trujillo's sister-in-law Señora de Trujillo, and numerous prominent Dominican guests. Later that evening, Third Secretary and Mrs. William Belton hosted an outdoor courtyard supper for an American contingent that included Minister and Mrs. Scotten as well as First Secretary and Mrs. Edward Lawton.
records.summary_es: Una carta social desde Ciudad Trujillo detalla los agasajos diplomáticos en torno al ministro de los Estados Unidos, Robert Scotten. Una recepción vespertina reunió al ministro francés y madame Henriot, a los encargados de negocios de Perú y Colombia, a la señora de Trujillo, cuñada del general Trujillo, y a numerosos destacados invitados dominicanos. Más tarde esa misma noche, el tercer secretario y la señora de William Belton ofrecieron una cena en un patio exterior para una delegación estadounidense que incluía al ministro y la señora de Scotten, así como al primer secretario y la señora de Edward Lawton.

records.headline: Peruvian Ambassador Señor de Freyre y Santander hosted a diplomatic
records.summary_en: Peruvian Ambassador Señor de Freyre y Santander hosted a diplomatic dinner at his embassy on Scott Circle in Washington to honor Señor Garland, the newly named Peruvian Minister to the Dominican Republic, and Señora de Garland. Among the guests in attendance were Señora de Pastoriza, whose husband, the Dominican Minister, was then visiting Trujillo City, as well as the Bolivian Minister and Señora de Guachalla. The report details a full calendar of upcoming farewell entertainments for the Garlands, including an evening party scheduled to be co-hosted by Señora de Pastoriza.

Entre los asistentes se encontraban la señora de Pastoriza, cuyo esposo, el ministro dominicano, se hallaba entonces de visita en Ciudad Trujillo, así como el ministro de Bolivia y la señora de Guachalla. El reporte detalla un nutrido calendario de próximas reuniones de despedida para los esposos Garland, incluida una fiesta nocturna programada en conjunto por la señora de Pastoriza.

records.full_text:
By the Way—

By Beth Blaine

La Cumbre, Dominican Republic: High on a mountain peak 2,500 feet above sea level, overlooking—on one side, the blue Atlantic, and on the other a valley rich with beautiful royal palm trees, is La Cumbre, the residence of Mr. and Mrs. Edwin Kilbourne. At night one may see in the distance, way down the valley, the twinkling lights of the city of Santiago, 15 miles away, and by day a panorama of sea and tropical mountains that is so beautiful it leaves one breathless. The house itself is of stone, painted white, with eaves and shutters a wonderful shade of Madonna blue. Built to fit its lofty mountain perch, it is one room deep—but long enough to include on the first floor, a sitting room, dining room, kitchen and library, and at either end guest rooms and bath. The furniture is comfortable and attractive—much of it made from the native Dominican woods. There is a small outside guest house for the Kilbournes' young daughter and her English governess, and further from the house proper a playhouse (for the grownups) with a ping-pong table, an enormous open fireplace (it's very cool this far up in the mountains, at times), bridge tables, books and an excellent radio.

The gardens surrounding La Cumbre have been planned and executed with the greatest care and thought, and their leafy flowery beauty is difficult to describe on paper. All about the place (so that one may make a circular tour) are footpaths, made from native stones, leading down to the croquet lawn (where the grass is emerald green) through arches of flaming hibiscus trees, on down to the lily pond with its large overhanging fern trees and its magnificent pink and mauve and crimson water lilies. (There are, also, as Herman, the faithful major domo, points out, some "wild fish" here!) Past the orchard of native fruit trees—mangoes, bread fruit, banana, orange and grapefruit and avocado—orchid and vanilla plants twisted about their trunks—on through the flower garden with its gardenia bushes in full bloom and the colorful creeping portulaca, on to the vegetable garden, filled to overflowing with the most luscious vegetables—and a strawberry patch where one may pluck strawberries ten months of the year instead of for a few short weeks in season as at home.

Mrs. Kilbourne, a lovely dark-eyed Dominican, is the former Senorita Ana Rosa Santoni and she and her husband divide their time between La Cumbre and the other sugar plantations—where they also have houses. One at Consuelo by the river, and two by the sea, Barahona and Montellana.

Most of the plantations have their own golf courses—so that with the wonderful sea bathing and golf one has plenty of outdoor life. Mr. Kilbourne, who has his own plane, told us, by the way, that his last pilot was the famous Tex Anding, who left the Dominican Republic to enlist with the British R. A. F.

Back to the American Legation in Trujillo City, by motor—over one hundred and twenty miles of smooth well-kept roads, winding through the beautiful mountainous country of the island. Arriving in time for a swim and then tea with the American Naval Attache and Mrs. John Butler. The Butlers' house is the one occupied by the former secretary of the Legation and Mrs. Eugene Hinckle (now en poste in Berlin, Germany) and is of pink stucco with an adorable little private swimming pool painted brilliant green. We had tea and cocktails on the cool veranda and then home to change for dinner and bridge with the Scottens and Mr. and Mrs. Forrest Wiggs, a very nice English couple; the Theodore Rimingtons (he's also an Englishman) and Oliver Newman, formerly one of the Commissioners of the District of Columbia, now in the Dominican Republic representing the American Bondholders.

records.headline: An account of a formal evening in Ciudad Trujillo portrays a multi-lingual
records.summary_en: An account of a formal evening in Ciudad Trujillo portrays a multi-lingual gathering conducted in Spanish, French, and English with guests dressed in tropical white dinner jackets. The hostess placed Señor Paino Pichardo, head of the Dominican party, at her right, and Señor Andrés Pastoriza, Dominican Minister to Washington, on her left. Minister Pastoriza was on a brief visit to the country after traveling down with General Rafael Trujillo on his private yacht, while Señora de Pastoriza remained in Washington. The assembly also included Señora Clarita Pichardo, the Ernest Matiss couple, diplomatic representatives from Peru and Colombia, and Deputy Bonetti-Burgos from La Vega.

records.headline: Beth Blaine writes from Ciudad Trujillo regarding the entertainment
records.summary_en: Beth Blaine writes from Ciudad Trujillo regarding the entertainment provided by First Secretary of the United States Legation and Mrs. Edward Lawton, under the column heading 'By the Way.' The Lawtons regularly charter a small launch to take friends up the picturesque Yabacao River for evening picnic suppers to view the countryside at sunset. The author notes that outings typically embark at 4:30 before the rapid tropical twilight sets in, though sudden heavy downpours had twice prevented scheduled departures.
records.summary_es: Beth Blaine escribe desde Ciudad Trujillo, bajo el título de columna «By the Way», sobre las atenciones brindadas por el primer secretario de la legación de los Estados Unidos y la señora de Edward Lawton. Los esposos Lawton suelen alquilar una pequeña lancha para llevar a sus amistades por el pintoresco río Yabacao a disfrutar de cenas campestres al atardecer y contemplar el paisaje. La autora destaca que las excursiones suelen zarpar a las 4:30 antes de que caiga el rápido crepúsculo tropical, si bien repentinos y torrenciales aguaceros habían impedido en dos ocasiones las salidas programadas.

CUIDAD TRUJILLO, Dominican Republic: The first secretary of
the United States Legation and Mrs. Edward Lawton have a charming
and informal way of entertaining here (in addition to the delightful small
dinners they give). They charter a small launch, gather a few congenial
friends, and take them up the beautiful Yabacao River to see the lovely
interior country and have a picnic supper.
The party usually starts at 4:30, in time to see the sunset and then
home by the light of the moon. There is no twilight in the tropics—only
a magnificent swiftly dying sun, whose flaming glory is gone almost in
a matter of moments—then dusk and the moon and the stars. For this
reason, it’s important to start on time, or the darkness overtakes one be
fore scarcely any of the picturesque river country has been seen. Twice
we were asked to go on such excursions, and both times, just before we
were about to start, it poured!

records.summary_en: The *West Virginia Digest* profiled newly elected Haitian President Élie Lescot, outlining his earlier service as Haiti's Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary to Ciudad Trujillo. In that post, Lescot helped negotiate the settlement of the border dispute between Haiti and the Dominican Republic, earning the Dominican decoration of Juan Pablo Duarte. He subsequently served as a delegate to the Buenos Aires peace conference before becoming Haitian Minister to the United States in 1937.
records.summary_es: El *West Virginia Digest* perfiló la biografía del recién electo mandatario haitiano Élie Lescot, reseñando su desempeño diplomático anterior como enviado extraordinario y ministro plenipotenciario de Haití en Ciudad Trujillo. En aquella misión, Lescot facilitó las gestiones conciliatorias del pleito limítrofe entre Haití y la República Dominicana, lo que le valió la condecoración dominicana de la Orden de Juan Pablo Duarte. Con posterioridad asistió como delegado a la conferencia de paz de Buenos Aires antes de asumir como ministro plenipotenciario de Haití ante los Estados Unidos en 1937.
records.passage: the early age of twenty-seven he was elected to Legislative Assembly where he served with distinction for three years. At the close of this experience he entered the judiciary finally winning promotion to the cabinet portfolio of Secretary of Public Education and Agriculture in the administration of President Borno. President Vincent made him Secretary of Justice and of the Interior and later sent him to Ciudad Trujillo, the Dominican Republic, as Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary of the Haitian government. He settled the vexing boundary dispute between Haiti and Santo Domingo, receiving from the Dominican government the cross of the "Gran Oficial del Orden de Merito de Juan Pablo Duarte." President Vincent bestowed upon him the title of "Grand officier de l'Ordre Honneur et Merite" for achievements as Secretary of the Interior. He also was among the Haitian delegates to the Inter-American Conference for the Maintenance of Peace at Buenos Aires. In April, 1937, M. Lescot presented his credentials to President F. D. His activities in the United States have been unprecedented in promoting and cementing better economic relations between his country and the United States as well as increasing the exchange of cultural amenities, and a practical program of exchange of college students for the purpose of a reciprocal assimilation of language and customs. records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* assessed the military vulnerabilities of Hispaniola, noting that the island's extensive coastline could offer bases to enemy forces threatening U.S. naval installations at Guantanamo Bay and Puerto Rico. While the Dominican Republic possessed a larger army than Haiti, it lacked airplanes, anti-aircraft weaponry, and artillery capable of resisting naval or aerial invasion. The article highlighted substantial pro-Axis sentiment in Santo Domingo, with British diplomats estimating that 75 percent of the populace favored Germany, though American observers believed sympathies were evenly divided.

records.full_text:
Haiti's Fifth Column Problem

By C. Leigh Stevenson.

PORT AU PRINCE, Haiti.—If the United States gets into war, Haiti will declare war on Germany as promptly as she did in 1917. It isn't that the government of Haiti plans any active support for American arms. She has little to offer in the way of soldiers, nothing in the way of military equipment and virtually no money.

The declaration of war is considered essential to control the fifth column. There are Germans and Italians here. They are active, and openly pro-Axis and unless Haiti does announce herself on the side of the United States there will be no legal excuse for herding the enemy aliens into concentration camps.

The camps, not large ones because Haiti is a small republic and the number of Axis sympathizers is proportionately small, have been designated. All that will remain to be done will be to send the soldiers out to round up the suspects and escort them to the place of detention and there they will remain until peace is restored to this world.

No other republic in this part of the world has worked out its plans in such full detail.

The coastline is extensive. There are numerous bays and inlets and it could be valuable as a base for an enemy force seeking to paralyze the United States Navy based at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, or to raid the defense base at Puerto Rico.

The Haitians aren't trained strategists. Uncle Sam's experts say the establishments in Cuba and Puerto Rico effectively safeguard Haiti and Santo Domingo from attack. The Haitians feel no such assurance. They have a little army, equipped with rifles and a small cannon or two.

At the other end of the island the Dominican Republic has a larger army and a better one. It has no planes, no anti-aircraft guns, no artillery good enough to stand off an invasion from the sea, to say nothing of invasion from the air.

In Santo Domingo, as a matter of fact, the pro-Axis element is large, much more so than in Haiti, where the link with France makes for pro-British sympathy. Members of the British Legation in Santo Domingo say that 75 per cent of the people in that republic are hoping for a German victory. Americans who are in close touch with the people say that sympathy is divided equally.

Serious-minded Haitians are convinced that Germany knows all she needs to know about Haiti. They believe that many resident Germans and Italians have their posts assigned to them. These Haitians insist that it will be important to break the pattern by getting these people segregated and under guard. Informed spokesmen say Haiti would round up its aliens tomorrow if the United States were to initiate such action in the United States.

Farewell Parties Held for Retiring Dominican Envoy

The Ambassador of Ecuador, Capt. Colon Eloy Alfaro, entertained at luncheon today in honor of the retiring Minister of the Dominican Republic and Senora de Pastoriza, who will leave shortly for their native country. Senor Pastoriza has been appointed Minister of Communications of his country.

Another farewell party for the popular Pastorizas was a cocktail party yesterday with Assistant Secretary of State Adolf A. Berle, jr., as the host. Also sharing honors at the party attended by officials and members of the diplomatic corps were Senor de Pastoriza's successor, Senor J. M. Troncoso and his attractive wife.

In the absence of Mrs. Berle, who is still at her summer home at Great Barrington, Mass., Mrs. Laurence Duggan and Mrs. Fletcher Warren were hostesses for Mr. Berle.

records.full_text:
Freighter Reported Sinking in Hurricane In Caribbean Sea

BULLETIN.

HAVANA, Cuba (AP).—The National Observatory reported today that a Caribbean storm of cyclonic proportions was centered about 300 miles south of Ciudad Trujillo, Dominican Republic, and was moving west-northwest toward the Gulf of Mexico at a rate of 360 miles a day.

By the Associated Press.

JACKSONVILLE, Fla., Sept. 25.—Coast Guard headquarters reported today that the S. S. Libby Maine in the Caribbean Sea had sent out distress calls, saying she had been hit by a "hurricane" and was "sinking." She asked immediate aid.

The ship gave its position as latitude 14 degrees and 20 minutes north and longitude 70 degrees and 10 minutes west.

The Libby Maine had reported earlier that her steering gear was out of order and she was being buffeted by a tropical storm about 200 miles south of Haiti.

The Coast Guard at San Juan, Puerto Rico, advised headquarters here that it had dispatched the cutter Analga to the position given by the Libby Maine. There was no information here about the number of persons aboard.

About the same time the Weather Bureau here received an advisory from its bureau at San Juan, Puerto Rico, saying "delayed ship reports indicate the tropical disturbance in the Caribbean Sea was centered at 7 a.m., E. S. T., about latitude 13 degrees and 30 minutes north and longitude 69 degrees and 30 minutes west, moving westward with increasing intensity."

Lloyd's shipping register lists the Libby Maine as a 1,811-ton freighter built in 1918 and operating out of San Francisco, by the firm of Libby, McNeill & Libby.

Other American Republics Express Support of U. S.

By the Associated Press.

The State Department said last night all other American republics had been informed of the "treacherous attacks" by Japan on the United States and that the United States had received "very heartening messages of support" from other American republics.

Jesus Maria Troncoso, Minister of the Dominican Republic, said his country's Congress would go into session at noon today and "give its support to whatever declaration is made by the United States Congress."

3 Latin Legations Raised to Embassies

By United Press

In a series of nominations sent to the Senate today, President Roosevelt raised the legations in Bolivia, Ecuador and Paraguay to embassy status.

He nominated Pierre de L. Boal of Pennsylvania, present Minister to Nicaragua, as Ambassador to Bolivia; Boaz Long of New Mexico, present Minister to Ecuador, as Ambassador to the same country; Wesley Frost of Kentucky, present Minister to Paraguay, as Ambassador to the same nation; Arthur Bliss Lane of New York, present Minister to Costa Rica, as Ambassador to Colombia, filling the vacancy left by the assignment of Spruille Braden as Ambassador to Cuba; Robert M. Scotten of Michigan, now Minister to the Dominican Republic, as Minister to Costa Rica, replacing Mr. Lane; Avra M. Warren of Maryland, chief of the State Department visa division, Minister to the Dominican Republic, replacing Mr. Scotten, and James B. Stewart of New Mexico, consul general at Zurich, as Minister to Nicaragua, succeeding Mr. Boal.

records.headline: Two submarines sank the 4,015-ton British steamship MacGregor
records.summary_en: Two submarines sank the 4,015-ton British steamship MacGregor in the Caribbean, 15 miles off the northern Dominican coast, the newspaper Nacion reports in a story relayed by an Associated Press dispatch from Ciudad Trujillo. The Dominican coast guard reportedly rescued 30 survivors, while one crewman was lost.
records.summary_es: Dos submarinos hundieron el vapor británico MacGregor, de 4.015 toneladas, en el Caribe, a 15 millas de la costa norte dominicana, según informa el periódico Nacion en una información transmitida por un despacho de Associated Press desde Ciudad Trujillo. Según se informó, el cuerpo de guardacostas dominicano rescató a 30 sobrevivientes, mientras que un tripulante se perdió.

records.headline: An official announcement from Ciudad Trujillo states that the British merchant
records.summary_en: An official announcement from Ciudad Trujillo states that the British merchant ship MacGregor was sunk on Friday off the Dominican coast by two enemy submarines. One man from the crew of 31 was killed in the attack, which occurred off Old Cape Frances with submarine shellfire heard in the village of Cabrera. Two coast guard ships were sent immediately to the area but failed to locate the enemy raiders. The MacGregor was a 2,408-ton vessel built in 1918, and its cargo was not disclosed.

Dos embarcaciones del cuerpo de guardacostas fueron enviadas de inmediato a la zona, pero no lograron localizar a los atacantes enemigos. El MacGregor era un buque de 2.408 toneladas construido en 1918, y su cargamento no fue revelado.

records.headline: The United States Navy announced the purchase of the 968-ton
records.summary_en: The United States Navy announced the purchase of the 968-ton yacht Ramfis from Generalissimo Rafael Trujillo, commander in chief of the Dominican Republic army, for $180,000. Originally constructed at a cost of $850,000, the yacht has been renamed the U.S.S. Marcasite and assigned to the patrol fleet. President Roosevelt sent a personal letter of thanks to Trujillo for making the vessel available. Measuring 285 feet in length with a 32-foot beam, the ship was built in Neponset, Massachusetts, in 1928 and was formerly owned by Julius Fleischmann under the name Camargo.

March 6.—The $6,000,000 submarine Amberjack, latest of such craft built for the United States Navy, slipped from the ways at the Electric Boat Co. shipyard into the fog-shrouded waters of the Thames River today less than 10 months after her keel had been laid. Diplomatic Nominations Confirmed by Senate

By the Associated Press.

The Senate confirmed yesterday nominations of several men for diplomatic posts. They were:

Pierre De L. Boal of Pennsylvania to be Ambassador to Bolivia; Arthur Bliss Lane of New York to be Ambassador to Colombia; Boaz Long of New Mexico to be Ambassador to Ecuador; Wesley Frost of Kentucky to be Ambassador to Paraguay; Robert M. records.headline: Senorita Fior d'Oro Trujillo, daughter of the former Dominican President
records.summary_en: Senorita Fior d'Oro Trujillo, daughter of the former Dominican President and Senora de Trujillo, was married yesterday to Dr. Maurice Marshall Berck at the Hotel Pierre in New York. The Dominican Minister and Senora de Troncoso were unable to attend the ceremony because the minister's wife is recovering in the hospital from a recent operation. Dr. Francis P. Conway of New York served as best man, and the bride was unattended. Following a wedding trip north for winter sports, the couple will make their home in New York, where Dr. Berck is on the surgical staffs of Mount Sinai and Gouverneur hospitals.
records.summary_es: La señorita Fior d'Oro Trujillo, hija del expresidente dominicano y de la señora de Trujillo, contrajo matrimonio ayer con el Dr. Maurice Marshall Berck en el Hotel Pierre de Nueva York. El ministro dominicano y la señora de Troncoso no pudieron asistir a la ceremonia debido a que la esposa del ministro se recupera en el hospital de una reciente operación. El Dr. Francis P. Conway de Nueva York fue el padrino de bodas y la novia no llevó cortejo. Después de un viaje de bodas al norte para practicar deportes de invierno, la pareja residirá en Nueva York, donde el Dr. Berck forma parte del personal quirúrgico de los hospitales Mount Sinai y Gouverneur.

records.headline: For the first time in Dominican Republic history, women will run
records.summary_en: For the first time in Dominican Republic history, women will run as candidates in elections to the Senate and Chamber of Deputies following recent constitutional reforms that granted women the right to vote. The names of women seeking congressional seats will be announced at an upcoming National Convention in Ciudad Trujillo. The general elections are scheduled for May 16, with Generalissimo Dr. Rafael L. Trujillo Molina standing as the Dominican Party candidate for the presidency.

Los nombres de las mujeres que aspiran a escaños en el Congreso se anunciarán en una próxima convención nacional en Ciudad Trujillo. Las elecciones generales están programadas para el 16 de mayo, con el generalísimo Dr. Rafael L. Trujillo Molina como candidato del Partido Dominicano a la presidencia.

records.summary_en: In Ciudad Trujillo, the capital and modern port of the Dominican Republic, stand the ruins of the colonial settlement of Santo Domingo, named by Columbus as the first European city in the New World. Part of an informational series prepared for the Pan American Union, the text notes that the Dominican Republic is about one-third the size of neighboring Florida but three times as densely populated. Four wooded mountain ranges cross the nation, led by the Central Cordillera, which acts as the chief watershed and contains the highest peak in the West Indies.

Como parte de una serie informativa preparada para la Unión Panamericana, el texto señala que la República Dominicana tiene alrededor de un tercio del tamaño de la vecina Florida pero una densidad de población tres veces mayor. Cuatro cordilleras boscosas atraviesan la nación, encabezadas por la Cordillera Central, que sirve como principal cuenca hidrográfica y alberga el pico más alto de las Antillas.

records.headline: With fertile valleys and Monte Trujillo—at 10,417 feet the highest
records.summary_en: With fertile valleys and Monte Trujillo—at 10,417 feet the highest peak in the West Indies—the Dominican Republic has established agriculture as the solid foundation of its economy. Sugar, which formed the primary colonial plantation crop of Santo Domingo, continues to hold first place in national prosperity, representing close to three-quarters of the value of Dominican industries. In response to past lessons regarding reliance on a single crop, the Dominican government has advanced a planned agricultural economy that has steadily increased the production and trade value of cocoa, coffee, molasses, starch, corn, bananas, and tobacco.

El azúcar, que constituyó el principal producto de plantación colonial de Santo Domingo, continúa ocupando el primer lugar en la prosperidad nacional, representando cerca de tres cuartas partes del valor de las industrias dominicanas. Frente a las lecciones del pasado sobre la dependencia de un solo cultivo, el gobierno dominicano ha impulsado una economía agrícola planificada que ha incrementado de manera constante la producción y el valor comercial del cacao, café, melaza, almidón, maíz, guineos y tabaco.

records.headline: Official sources in Ciudad Trujillo announced that the 1,161 ton
records.summary_en: Official sources in Ciudad Trujillo announced that the 1,161-ton Dominican Republic steamship San Rafael was recently torpedoed by an enemy submarine while returning home from Tampa, Florida, by way of Kingston, Jamaica. Eight survivors reached Cayman Brac, an island northwest of Jamaica, in a lifeboat and reported that the entire crew had abandoned ship into lifeboats when attacked. Thirty crewmen, including the captain, remained missing, though survivors were hopeful they would be located by Caribbean air search patrols because the boats were well provisioned.

Ocho sobrevivientes llegaron en un bote salvavidas a Caimán Brac, una isla al noroeste de Jamaica, e informaron que toda la tripulación se había lanzado a los botes salvavidas al producirse el ataque. Treinta tripulantes, incluido el capitán, continuaban desaparecidos, aunque los sobrevivientes abrigaban la esperanza de que patrullas aéreas de búsqueda en el Caribe pudieran localizarlos gracias a que los botes estaban bien abastecidos.

records.summary_en: The Spanish-speaking Dominican Republic occupies two-thirds of the island of Hispaniola but maintains only half the population of neighboring Haiti. While both nations have histories marked by revolution and bloodshed, each is progressing in civilization, with the Dominican Republic particularly renowned for supplying the finest mahogany on the market. In the capital, Trujillo City—established in 1493 as the oldest European settlement in the Western world—the Cathedral of Santo Domingo enshrines the remains of Christopher Columbus.

Dominicans Co-operating, Newman Tells President

Former District Commissioner Oliver P. Newman, now representing a Dominican Republic bondholders committee, reported to President Roosevelt today that there is complete co-operation by the Dominican Republic with the United States in defense of the Caribbean area.

An old friend of the President, Mr. Newman is in Washington on a month's furlough. He was a member of the Board of Commissioners here from 1913 to 1917.

As he was leaving the White House, Mr. Newman told reporters the American War Relief Committee in the little island territory has raised $15,000 for contribution to the Red Cross and allied agencies.

Mr. Newman said that Dominican customs collections in the last year have been enough to service the government bonds and to make a small extra payment to coupon holders. He emphasized, however, that the shipping problem is a serious one for the ordinary commerce and economy of the island.

records.headline: A historical column recounts a report published in June 1892
records.summary_en: A historical column recounts a report published in June 1892 alleging that Samana Bay, terminus of the Sanchez-La Vega Railway in the Dominican Republic, had been ceded to the United States. In response to the rumors, the German consul at Port-au-Prince was instructed to confer with representatives of France and England to safeguard the autonomy of Santo Domingo, causing great anxiety in Haiti. The commentary observes that such alarm proved unnecessary, noting that Santo Domingo and Haiti have both remained independent nations ever since 1844.

Ante dichos rumores, el cónsul alemán en Puerto Príncipe recibió instrucciones de consultar con representantes de Francia e Inglaterra para salvaguardar la autonomía de Santo Domingo, lo que causó gran inquietud en Haití. El comentario añade que tal alarma resultó infundada, señalando que tanto Santo Domingo como Haití han permanecido como naciones independientes desde 1844.

records.full_text:
Delegates Arriving
For Inter-American
Economic Parley

Welles to Be Keynoter
At Conference Here
Opening Tuesday

By HAROLD B. ROGERS.

As distinguished delegations of finance ministers, heads of central banks, and technical experts from the other American republics continued to arrive over the week-end, plans were being put into final shape for the first Inter-American Conference on Systems of Economic and Financial Control, to open Tuesday at the Pan American Union.

Under the agenda for the conference, which was authorized by the January meeting of Foreign Affairs Ministers at Rio de Janeiro, two different committees will be set up among the delegates. One will consider “international transactions” the other “domestic transactions,” as protection against Axis influence.

The first and last sessions of the conference will be public meetings, but the intervening technical sessions, under present plans probably will be behind closed doors, unless other public sessions “are agreed upon and so ordered by the delegates.” The conference may last about 10 days.

Republics Each Have One Vote.

Each of the 21 republics will have but one vote, regardless of the size of their various delegations.

“Proposals, reports, and projects,” it is provided in the agenda, “shall be considered approved when they have obtained the affirmative vote of an absolute majority of the countries represented at the respective meeting.”

The conference is only one of the several new inter-American developments which have grown out of the second World War to help the American republics present a more united front to the aggressor nations of Germany, Japan and Italy.

Authorized specifically by the Rio Conference of Foreign Ministers, this new gathering is operating under sponsorship of the Inter-American Financial and Economic Advisory Committee. This committee was set up in 1939 and has been regularly functioning since the outbreak of the second World War. At its headquarters in the Pan American Union, this committee, headed by Undersecretary of State Welles, has been holding regularly scheduled meetings and has prepared a comprehensive background of data, which according to experts, should provide much material of value for the forthcoming meeting.

Welles to Be “Keynoter.”

Mr. Welles, who will deliver the opening “keynote” address to the conference, and Dr. Leo S. Rowe, director general of the Pan American Union, who will welcome the delegates, will be followed by a spokesman for the Latin American group. This spokesman will be selected at a preliminary meeting of the delegates tomorrow. There was no official indication today as to who this spokesman may be.

Problems to be considered by the conference, involving the severance of commercial and financial ties between the Western Hemisphere and the Axis powers, are considered by officials to be virtually parallel to the vital issues of breaking diplomatic relations with the Axis, which absorbed major public attention at the Rio conference.

By the terms of two financial and economic resolutions at Rio, it was explained last night by one official, economic intercourse between the American republics and the Axis powers is to be cut; and transactions by nationals of Axis states, likely to benefit members of the tripartite pact (Germany, Italy and Japan) are to be placed under rigid control and supervision.

Other inter-American measures have been adopted to meet economic problems arising out of the war. The Inter-American Development Commission has set up national commissions in each of the Latin-American countries and is especially interested in the development of new industries in each country for which there may be markets in the other republics.

Commission’s Duties.

The Inter-American Maritime Technical Commission, created only a few months ago, is designed primarily to supervise the operation of the immobilized vessels taken over in ports of the American republics. The Office of Co-ordinator of Inter-American Affairs and the Board of Economic Warfare have wide authority and operate extensively in Latin-American affairs.

Over all the American representatives in these agencies, the State Department has exercised a guiding hand, though allowing to some far-reaching autonomy, within the limits of the general international policies laid down by the administration. The Inter-American Defense Board recommends defense measures.

The new program of international solidarity in the economic sphere aimed at by the Rio conference, according to Dr. Rowe, “was nothing short of pooling the resources of the American continent for the winning of the war, and at the same time adopting measures to protect the economic and financial structure of all the republics. The motive that guided the (Rio) delegates,” he added, “was not the selfish interest of any individual state, but the safety and welfare of the entire Western World.”

Many foreign delegations already have arrived and established headquarters. Some are in hotels, others are understood to be established in connection with their embarries or legations. Some of the delegates are ambassadors or ministers.

Brazilian Group Arrives.

Among the first to arrive recently was the group from Brazil. This delegation is headed by Francisco Alves dos Santos, jr., director of exchange, Bank of Brazil. With his technical adviser, Achilles Moreaux of the Bank of Brazil, and other experts he is at the Shoreham Hotel.

Delegates from the other republics, according to the official list, are as follows: Argentina, Eduardo Gagneaux, assistant general manager, Central Bank of Argentina; Bolivia, Humberto Cuenca, general manager, Central Bank of Bolivia; Chile, Pedro Enrique Alfonso, former Minister of Finance; Colombia, Alberto Bayon, chief, Office of Exchange and Import Control; Costa Rica, Paul Gurdian, former Minister of Foreign Affairs and former Minister of Finance; Cuba, Ramiro Guerra Sanchez, representative of Cuba on the Inter-American Financial and Economic Advisory Committee; Dominican Republic, Harry E. Henneman, speci[illegible] representative of the Ministry of Finance and Commerce; Ecuador, Eduardo Icaza, president, Central Bank; El Salvador, Carlos Adalberto Alfaro, charge d’affairs of El Salvador here; Guatemala, Luis Beltranena, dean, School of Economic Scieinces, University of Guatemala; Haiti, Abel La Croix, Minister of Finance; Honduras, Julian R. Caceres, Minister of Honduras here; Mexico, Eduardo Villaseñor, director, Bank of Mexico; Nicaragua, Leon De Bayle, Minister of Nicaragua here; Panama, Ricardo Marciacq, comptroller general of the Republic; Paraguay, Harmodio Gonzalez, manager, Bank of the Republic; Peru, Manuel Gallagher; Uruguay, Roberto E. MacEachen, Minister of Uruguay to Cuba; Venezuela, Diogenes Escalante, Ambasador of Venezuela here.

Ten of the Central American and Caribbean countries have declared war on the Axis, and all other Latin American republics have broken diplomatic relations with the Axis except Argentina and Chile. The United States delegate will be Edward H. Foley, general counsel of the Treasury Department. He will be assisted by advisers from both the Treasury and State Departments and by L. records.headline: A submarine believed to have shelled Curacao oil refineries
records.summary_en: A submarine believed to have shelled Curacao oil refineries sank the Dominican schooner Nueva Altagracia on June 16, eighty-five miles northeast of Curacao, according to reports in Ciudad Trujillo. Capt. Jose Hernandez stated that the submarine halted his vessel, took him and his crew of seven aboard, seized their food stores, and blew up the schooner with explosives. Two hours later, the eight men were transferred to the Dominican sloop Comercio, which was forced by the submarine to jettison half its cargo to accommodate them before conveying them to Curacao. The crew members remained in Curacao while Capt. Hernandez arrived in San Pedro de Macoris on Saturday, noting that the submarine bore "SV-59" on its damaged conning tower.
records.summary_es: Un submarino que presuntamente bombardeó refinerías de petróleo en Curazao hundió la goleta dominicana Nueva Altagracia el 16 de junio, a ochenta y cinco millas al noreste de Curazao, según despachos en Ciudad Trujillo. El capitán José Hernández declaró que el submarino interceptó su embarcación, los llevó a él y a sus siete tripulantes a bordo, confiscó sus provisiones de alimentos y destruyó la goleta con explosivos. Dos horas más tarde, los ocho hombres fueron transferidos a la balandra dominicana Comercio, a la que el submarino obligó a arrojar al mar la mitad de su cargamento para hacerles lugar antes de trasladarlos a Curazao. Los tripulantes permanecieron en Curazao mientras el capitán Hernández llegó el sábado a San Pedro de Macorís, señalando que el submarino llevaba "SV-59" en su dañada torre de mando.

records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* reported that Representative Hamilton Fish denied being questioned by the Internal Revenue Bureau regarding a $25,000 credit he received from Dominican dictator Rafael L. Trujillo in 1939. Fish stated that he acted solely as an agent in oil speculations, explaining that $12,500 was lost and the remaining $12,500 was returned to Trujillo. Fish added that tax officials had advised him the agency transaction did not need to be declared on his income tax return.
records.summary_es: El *Evening Star* informó que el legislador Hamilton Fish desmintió haber sido interrogado por la Oficina de Rentas Internas en torno a una partida de 25.000 dólares transferida por el dictador dominicano Rafael L. Fish alegó que se limitó a desempeñarse como comisionista intermediario en especulaciones petrolíferas, precisando que se esfumaron 12.500 dólares y se reembolsó a Trujillo el restante de 12.500. Fish arguyó asimismo que las autoridades impositivas le dictaminaron que dicha intermediación no requería ser asentada en su balance tributario anual.

Mr. Fish discussed over the long distance telephone, from his office at 111 Broadway, New York, the copyrighted account of his dealings with Gen. Trujillo published in the Washington Post today. "There are four points," said Mr. Fish, "in connection with this matter. "First, no representative of the Internal Revenue Bureau has approached me to discuss this credit of $25,000. records.summary_en: Official disclosures indicated that Representative Hamilton Fish was under investigation by the Justice Department regarding a secret $25,000 sum received in 1939 from General Rafael Trujillo, described as military dictator of the Dominican Republic. records.full_text:
Was He True to Trujillo? $25,000 Fee Probe 'Hooks' Ham Fish

Rep. Hamilton Fish (R., N. Y.) today was disclosed as being under official investigation by the Justice Department on the ground that he received a secret $25,000 feet in 1939 from Gen. Rafael L. Trujillo, military dictator of the Dominican Republic.

The fee was received in July, 1939, a week after Mr. Fish made an about-face, eulogizing the dictator for inaugurating a "golden age" in Dominican affairs, and a few weeks before he visited Germany where he was wined and dined by big shot Nazis on his way to Oslo, Norway. A clerk in his office recently was sentenced for perjury in connection with the Justice Department's investigation of isolationist and Nazi propaganda.

The fee came to the attention of the Justice Department about six weeks ago at the time the District grand jury on Axis agents was questioning George Jamhar Djamgaroff, a White Russian who claims to have turned down a $200,000 offer to handle Nazi propaganda here in 1935.

OLD FRIENDS

Mr. Djamgaroff and Rep. Fish had been old friends since the Congressman in 1932 interceded for the Russian when the latter's immigration standing was in question. With the passage of the foreign agent registration act, Mr. Djamgaroff three years ago registered with the American State Department as the $50,000-a-year agent of the Dominican Republic.

ASKED TO EXPLAIN

Rep. Fish, presumed to be in New York, currently is explaining to the Bureau of Internal Revenue how he came to "overlook" the alleged $25,000 fee in 1939 when his total reported income from all other sources was only $22,000, the department said. The sequence of events leading up to and following the alleged fee, were:

Dec. 21, 1937—Commenting on reports that several thousand Haitians had been massacred by Trujillo's soldiers, Rep. Fish told the House: "This is the most outrageous atrocity ever perpetrated on the American continent . . . I should like to see the Government of the United States withdraw our recognition of the Dominican Republic."

Jan. 4, 1938—Fish inserted a magazine story in the Congressional Record describing the massacre.

A GOODWILL TOUR

March, 1939—Mr. Djamgaroff, as Dominican agent, arranged to have several American newspapermen and congressmen make a "goodwill tour" of the Dominican Republic. Mr. Fish went along; discovered that Trujillo had retired as "president" but was keeping the reins of government as generalissimo of Dominican army.

July, 1939—Gen. Trujillo, "perpetrator of most outrageous atrocity," returned goodwill visit "as a private citizen," but was a guest of honor at a Pan American Society banquet in New York on July 12. While pickets paraded outside the Biltmore Hotel with banners repeating Gen. Hugh Johnson's description of Gen. Trujillo as a "blood-spattered bully," Rep. Fish was quoted as telling Gen. Trujillo:

"General, you have created a golden age for your country . . . and I am proud and happy to repeat at this time to a United States audience, you will go down in the history of your country as a builder greater than all the Spanish conquistadores together."

Sails for Europs a few days later—The $25,000 is alleged to have been deposited to Rep. Fish's order in the National City Bank of New York as part of a $300,000 credit established in this coutry for Gen. Trujillo thru the Dominican Legation in Washington.

A few weeks later—Rep. Fish sailed for Europe to attend the Interparliamentary Union at Oslo, pausing in Berlin for enthusiastic write-ups in German press, a conversation with the Foreign Minister Von Ribbentrop, whose private plane flew him to Oslo.

HID OIL COMPANY PROFIT

Sept., 1939 — Rep. Fish returned to America and became a leader of the isolationists. Justice Department operatives have been seeking to establish that while he then used his office as headquarters for the National Committee to Keep America Out of War, he instructed the National City Bank how to dispense the $25,000; that at this point the bank was instructed to transfer more than $2000 to his Washington bank to be followed by an equal sum a month later.

It is also alleged by the Justice Department that more than $8000 found its way to an oil company, the Nepaug Oil Co., of Houston, Tex., whose president, David D. McDaniels, is said to have had dealings with Rep. Fish.

At about the same time, the National City Bank is alleged to have been directed to transfer $12,500—half of the total fee—back to Gen. Trujillo.

Rep. Fish was (and is) ranking Republican member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, which passes on legislation affecting other governments.

records.headline: Publicist George Jamhar Djamgaroff issued a personal statement
records.summary_en: Publicist George Jamhar Djamgaroff issued a personal statement highlighting his promotion of the Columbus Memorial in Santo Domingo as a symbol of Western Hemisphere peace and unity. He noted that in 1939 he arranged for a congressional delegation, including Representative Hamilton Fish, to visit the Dominican Republic, after which Fish accepted $25,000 from President Trujillo for oil investments. Djamgaroff condemned press reports that characterized Trujillo as a dictator, asserting that such claims against an allied wartime leader were unfounded and urging newspapers to adopt voluntary self-censorship.
records.summary_es: El publicista George Jamhar Djamgaroff emitió una declaración personal en la que destacó su labor de promoción del Faro a Colón en Santo Domingo como símbolo de paz y unidad en el hemisferio occidental. Señaló que en 1939 organizó una delegación del Congreso, de la cual formó parte el representante Hamilton Fish, para visitar la República Dominicana, tras lo cual Fish aceptó $25,000 del presidente Trujillo para inversiones petroleras. Djamgaroff censuró los reportajes periodísticos que calificaban a Trujillo de dictador, afirmando que tales acusaciones contra un mandatario aliado en tiempo de guerra carecían de fundamento e instando a los periódicos a adoptar una autocensura voluntaria.

records.summary_en: The *Evening Star* reported on statements by Dominican Minister Dr. Jesús María Troncoso, who expressed confidence that anti-submarine measures would soon reopen sea lanes for Dominican sugar shipments to Britain while expanding food exports to Puerto Rico. Troncoso asserted that Dominican economic warfare was its main Allied war contribution, defended strong Dominican leaders by comparing them to President Andrew Jackson, and denied that the country was run by a dictatorship. He also praised the agricultural settlement for European refugees established following the 1938 Évian Conference.

The agricultural settlement was tested on a scientific basis, with a group of refugees from Europe selected for youth and health and character.

records.headline: Conflicting historical claims over the burial site of Christopher Columbus
records.summary_en: Conflicting historical claims over the burial site of Christopher Columbus were reviewed, noting that both Spain and the Dominican Republic assert his remains lie within their borders. While Spaniards place his tomb in the Cathedral of Seville, Dominicans maintain he is entombed in the Cathedral at Santo Domingo. Although Italian authorities had previously claimed Columbus was buried in Genoa, Italy abandoned those claims upon entering the war, with the Rome press dismissing his heritage.

Mientras que los españoles sitúan su tumba en la catedral de Sevilla, los dominicanos sostienen que está sepultado en la catedral de Santo Domingo. Aunque las autoridades italianas habían afirmado con anterioridad que Colón fue inhumado en Génova, Italia desistió de dichos reclamos tras su entrada en la guerra, desestimando la prensa de Roma su legado.

records.headline: A commentary on a Brookings Institution report states that the refugee
records.summary_en: A commentary on a Brookings Institution report states that the refugee settlement at Sosua, established on land donated by dictator Trujillo, has reached its absorptive capacity and cannot accommodate additional colonists beyond those already settled. Highlighting a unit cost of $3,000 per male settler and demographic changes showing white population decline since 1783, the study asserts that the surrounding population will inevitably engulf the settlement, noting that two of twenty marriages recorded among colonists in the past two years were with native women. The author concludes that the findings doom the Dominican project as a large-scale Jewish settlement or homeland, arguing that mass colonization in Santo Domingo was unviable from the outset.

Al subrayar un costo unitario de $3,000 por colono masculino y cambios demográficos que reflejan una disminución de la población blanca desde 1783, el estudio afirma que la población circundante terminará inevitablemente por absorber el asentamiento, destacando que dos de los veinte matrimonios registrados entre los colonos en los últimos dos años fueron con mujeres nativas. El autor concluye que estos hallazgos condenan al fracaso el proyecto dominicano como asentamiento judío a gran escala o patria judía, sosteniendo que la colonización masiva en Santo Domingo resultaba inviable desde el principio.

records.summary_en: A geographical feature in the Evening Star notes that nearly twice as many Haitians inhabit the western portion of Hispaniola as Dominicans in the east. The island discovered by Columbus in 1492 was formerly divided between Spain and France, shared by the Haitian Republic and Spain in the early 1800s, and placed entirely under Haitian rule between 1822 and 1844, when the Dominican Republic was established. The article explains the varied names used for the territory, noting that Columbus called it Española, while Santo Domingo served as the name of both the eastern nation and its capital.
records.summary_es: Una reseña geográfica en el Evening Star señala que casi el doble de haitianos habita la parte occidental de La Española en comparación con los dominicanos en el este. La isla descubierta por Colón en 1492 estuvo dividida anteriormente entre España y Francia, fue compartida por la República de Haití y España a principios del siglo XIX y quedó totalmente bajo control haitiano entre 1822 y 1844, año en que se proclamó la República Dominicana. El artículo explica las diversas denominaciones utilizadas para el territorio, indicando que Colón la llamó Española, mientras que Santo Domingo sirvió como nombre tanto del país oriental como de su capital.

records.headline: A profile describes the Dominican Republic as the cradle of the New World
records.summary_en: A profile describes the Dominican Republic as the cradle of the New World, noting that Spain established its first American colonial settlements there. The capital, Santo Domingo, founded in 1496 by Bartholomew Columbus and now named Trujillo City in honor of the republic's President, contains colonial stone buildings that survived the 1930 hurricane alongside modern paved thoroughfares. The country has settled European refugees under the requirement that they avoid competing with staple exports including sugar, cacao, coffee, and tobacco. The city preserves Spanish traditions and takes pride in the sixteenth-century cathedral believed to house the remains of Christopher Columbus.
records.summary_es: Una reseña describe a la República Dominicana como la cuna del Nuevo Mundo, destacando que España estableció allí sus primeros asentamientos coloniales en América. La capital, Santo Domingo, fundada en 1496 por Bartolomé Colón y llamada ahora Ciudad Trujillo en honor al presidente de la república, conserva edificaciones coloniales de piedra que sobrevivieron al huracán de 1930 junto a modernas vías pavimentadas. El país ha acogido a refugiados europeos bajo la condición de que no compitan con exportaciones fundamentales como el azúcar, el cacao, el café y el tabaco. La urbe mantiene tradiciones españolas y se enorgullece de su catedral del siglo XVI, en la que se cree que reposan los restos de Cristóbal Colón.

records.headline: Señorita Minerva Bernardino, who writes for "La Nación" in Ciudad
records.summary_en: Señorita Minerva Bernardino, who writes for "La Nación" in Ciudad Trujillo, Dominican Republic, was among the guests at a reception held at the Friendship estate for members of the American Newspaper Women's Club. Bernardino attended alongside Bolivian writer Carmen B. de Lozada and other Latin American correspondents belonging to the Inter-American Commission of Women. The event was hosted by Mrs. McLean together with club presidents Alice Eversman of the Evening Star and Christine Sadler of the Washington Post.
