records.headline: An editorial notes that members of the new Dominican governing
records.summary_en: An editorial notes that members of the new Dominican governing authority are widely respected and have pledged to stage free elections within 12 or 18 months, while observing that practically nobody in Santo Domingo appears to bemoan the coup or the fall of Dr. Juan Bosch. The piece states that many Dominicans view the ousted president as having failed to utilize his authority effectively, causing internal party divisions and lacking leadership for democratic reforms. Pointing to the public apathy surrounding Bosch's removal, the editorial argues that deploying American armed forces, the fleet, or the Marines to restore a leader whom the Dominican people appear ready to do without would be entirely misguided.
records.summary_es: Un editorial señala que los integrantes de la nueva autoridad gobernante dominicana son ampliamente respetados y se han comprometido a celebrar elecciones libres dentro de 12 o 18 meses, observando al mismo tiempo que prácticamente nadie en Santo Domingo parece lamentar el golpe o la caída del doctor Juan Bosch. El artículo afirma que muchos dominicanos consideran que el presidente derrocado no supo aprovechar su autoridad, provocó divisiones dentro de su propio partido y careció de liderazgo para impulsar reformas democráticas. Al señalar la apatía pública ante la destitución de Bosch, el editorial sostiene que desplegar fuerzas armadas estadounidenses, la flota o los infantes de marina para restituir a un gobernante de quien el pueblo dominicano parece dispuesto a prescindir resultaría un absoluto despropósito.

records.headline: A commentary on strategic materials stockpiling notes that the aluminum
records.summary_en: A commentary on strategic materials stockpiling notes that the aluminum industry requires approximately fourteen million tons of bauxite annually, highlighting substantial deposits in British Guiana, Haiti, and the Dominican Republic. The analysis warns that access to these mineral resources could be jeopardized if Marxist factions led by Cheddi Jagan take complete control in British Guiana or if Castroites succeed in Haiti and Santo Domingo. The column stresses that United States industrial supply faces comparable foreign vulnerabilities regarding tungsten from South Korea and cobalt from the Congo.
records.summary_es: Un comentario sobre la acumulación de materiales estratégicos señala que la industria del aluminio requiere anualmente cerca de catorce millones de toneladas de bauxita, destacando importantes yacimientos en la Guayana Británica, Haití y la República Dominicana. El análisis advierte que el acceso a estos recursos minerales podría verse comprometido si facciones marxistas lideradas por Cheddi Jagan toman el control total de la Guayana Británica o si los castristas se imponen en Haití y Santo Domingo. La columna subraya que el suministro industrial de Estados Unidos afronta vulnerabilidades externas comparables en relación con el tungsteno de Corea del Sur y el cobalto del Congo.

records.headline: Dr. Diego Bordas arrived in St. Thomas overnight en route to Puerto Rico
records.summary_en: Dr. Diego Bordas arrived in St. Thomas overnight en route to Puerto Rico and Guadeloupe after being released on Monday and given only 30 minutes to leave the Dominican Republic following six days in prison. Bordas stated he would join deposed President Juan Bosch in Pointe-à-Pitre, Guadeloupe, noting that the president had refused to resign and was removed from the Santo Domingo palace on Saturday night and transported to Guadeloupe aboard a Dominican navy frigate. Following his meeting with Bosch, Bordas intends to travel to Washington.

Bordas manifestó que se reuniría con el derrocado presidente Juan Bosch en Pointe-à-Pitre, Guadalupe, señalando que el mandatario se había negado a renunciar y fue sacado del palacio de Santo Domingo el sábado por la noche y trasladado a Guadalupe a bordo de una fragata naval dominicana. Tras su reunión con Bosch, Bordas planea viajar a Washington.

records.headline: A dispatch from Santo Domingo describes grassroots community
records.summary_en: A dispatch from Santo Domingo describes grassroots community development work in the capital's impoverished slums, where worker Mr. Hernandez observes that a new sense of optimism is lifting the heavy burden of defeatism among local residents. A primary focus of the effort is the barrio of Ensanche Luperon, characterized by Hernandez as one of the hardest areas to reform. In three small blocks of mangled shacks, approximately 3,000 squatters—predominantly peasant families migrating from rural areas in search of unavailable work—reside in tightly packed shelters constructed of scrap lumber and palm leaves.
records.summary_es: Un despacho desde Santo Domingo describe la labor de desarrollo comunitario de base en los barrios marginales de la capital, donde el trabajador Sr. Hernández observa que un nuevo sentido de optimismo está disipando la pesada carga de derrotismo entre los vecinos. Uno de los puntos centrales del esfuerzo es el barrio de Ensanche Luperón, calificado por Hernández como uno de los sectores más difíciles de transformar. En tres pequeñas manzanas de casuchas precarias, aproximadamente 3.000 ocupantes irregulares —en su mayoría familias campesinas que emigraron de zonas rurales en busca de trabajo inexistente— habitan refugios apiñados construidos con tablas de desecho y hojas de palma.

records.headline: Residents of Haiti and the Dominican Republic, the two nations
records.summary_en: Residents of Haiti and the Dominican Republic, the two nations sharing the island of Hispaniola, were warned to evacuate immediately as Hurricane Flora advanced with winds expected to buffet both countries. The Weather Bureau urged people living west of Santo Domingo City to flee beaches and coastal lowlands at once before rising storm waters cut off escape routes. Forecasters warned that torrential rains over Haiti and the western Dominican Republic posed a serious danger of destructive flooding along all major rivers and streams as the storm progressed northwest at approximately 9 miles per hour.
records.summary_es: Los habitantes de Haití y la República Dominicana, las dos naciones que comparten la isla de La Española, recibieron la advertencia de evacuar de inmediato ante el avance del huracán Flora, cuyos vientos amenazaban a ambos países. La Oficina Meteorológica instó a las personas que viven al oeste de la ciudad de Santo Domingo a abandonar de inmediato las playas y las zonas costeras bajas antes de que la crecida de las aguas bloqueara las rutas de escape. Los meteorólogos advirtieron que las lluvias torrenciales sobre Haití y el oeste de la República Dominicana representaban un grave peligro de inundaciones destructivas en los principales ríos y arroyos mientras la tormenta avanzaba hacia el noroeste a unas 9 millas por hora.

records.summary_en: A wirephoto caption reports that Carmen Bosch, wife of deposed President Juan Bosch of the Dominican Republic, boarded a plane in San Juan, Puerto Rico, bound for Santo Domingo. She was accompanied by Puerto Rican Bar Association president Manuel Abreu Castillo and Puerto Rican House of Representatives speaker Santiago Polanco Abreu. Mrs. Bosch returned to ascertain her husband's fate following his overthrow and the installation of a three-man civilian junta.

Estaba acompañada por el presidente del Colegio de Abogados de Puerto Rico, Manuel Abreu Castillo, y el presidente de la Cámara de Representantes de Puerto Rico, Santiago Polanco Abreu. La señora Bosch regresó para averiguar el destino de su esposo tras su derrocamiento y la instalación de una junta civil de tres hombres.

records.headline: A UPI report from Santo Domingo indicates that armed leftist
records.summary_en: A UPI report from Santo Domingo indicates that armed leftist groups were prepared to stage an uprising against the Dominican Republic's civilian junta as soon as their leaders issued orders. Speaking at a clandestine meeting on the outskirts of Santo Domingo, an insurgent spokesman stated that authorities had failed to arrest a single member of their group and confirmed they possessed weapons. The representative explained that fighters held back on the first day of the coup that ousted former president Juan Bosch to avoid needless casualties, adding that Communists had urged an immediate strike against the generals who deposed the president and established the three-man regime.
records.summary_es: Un despacho de UPI desde Santo Domingo indica que grupos armados de izquierda estaban preparados para sublevarse contra la junta civil de la República Dominicana tan pronto como sus líderes dieran la orden. En una reunión clandestina en las afueras de Santo Domingo, un portavoz insurgente afirmó que las autoridades no habían logrado detener a ningún miembro de su organización y confirmó que contaban con armamento. El representante explicó que los combatientes no entraron en acción el primer día del golpe que derrocó al expresidente Juan Bosch para evitar bajas innecesarias, agregando que los comunistas habían instado a asestar un golpe inmediato contra los generales que depusieron al mandatario e instalaron el régimen de tres hombres.

records.headline: After surviving eight hours adrift in a lifeboat during Hurricane
records.summary_en: After surviving eight hours adrift in a lifeboat during Hurricane Flora, six Dominican Republic seamen arrived safely in St. Thomas. Their 50-foot freighter Carmon Julia, returning to its home port of Santo Domingo from Curaçao under Captain Antonio Bernard, was broken in half by 20-foot waves approximately 150 miles south of Santo Domingo on Wednesday night at 10:30 p.m. Crew members Antonio Bernard, Jose Dmitro, Miguel Kamone Sosar, Elias Jackson, Eliah Fromota, and Ramone Queto escaped into a lifeboat and endured rough seas until they were rescued on Thursday morning by the British tanker Elobo.

records.headline: An editorial in The Daily News discusses controversy over statements
records.summary_en: An editorial in The Daily News discusses controversy over statements attributed to the Governor of the Virgin Islands concerning political turmoil in the Dominican Republic following the overthrow of President Juan Bosch. Endorsing comments by exiled Dominican cabinet officer Dr. Diego Bordas that Latin America is closely watching United States policy, the paper expresses concern that the territorial governor may have spoken on the crisis without serious deliberation. The editorial defends the integrity of reporting by UPI and El Mundo while questioning whether personal ties or friendships in Santo Domingo unsympathetic to Bosch prompted the governor's regrettable remarks.
records.summary_es: Un editorial de The Daily News aborda la controversia en torno a las declaraciones atribuidas al gobernador de las Islas Vírgenes sobre la agitación política en la República Dominicana tras el derrocamiento del presidente Juan Bosch. Al respaldar las declaraciones del ministro del gabinete dominicano en el exilio, doctor Diego Bordas, respecto a que América Latina observa de cerca la política de Estados Unidos, el diario expresa preocupación de que el gobernador territorial haya opinado sobre la crisis sin una deliberación seria. El editorial defiende la integridad de la cobertura de UPI y El Mundo, preguntándose si vínculos personales o amistades en Santo Domingo contrarias a Bosch motivaron los lamentables comentarios del gobernador.

records.headline: A traveler, Mrs. Arensberg, reported on witnessing the military coup
records.summary_en: A traveler, Mrs. Arensberg, reported on witnessing the military coup in the Dominican Republic that deposed the Bosch government nine months after its election by a 60 per cent majority. Two days before the overthrow, a general strike had closed one television and four radio stations, leaving only the government station broadcasting amid what she described as a tense atmosphere. She learned that the director of Radio Santo Domingo had been jailed and the facilities commandeered for announcements by the military junta. Following delays at a tightly guarded airport, she arrived in the United States, where word was received that Free Cuba Radio and Free Russia broadcasts had resumed.

Dos días antes del derrocamiento, una huelga general había cerrado una estación de televisión y cuatro de radio, dejando únicamente la emisora estatal transmitiendo en medio de lo que describió como una atmósfera tensa. He explained that the facility was planned for the Dominican government rather than a foreign oil company, estimating that an Esso-Standard contract would have generated a profit of $300 million for Standard, Texaco, and Shell over 20 years. records.headline: Following the coup that overthrew the elected government in the Dominican
records.summary_en: Following the coup that overthrew the elected government in the Dominican Republic, the military authorities declared a state of siege after university students clashed with police in Santo Domingo. The demonstrators attempted to march on the presidential palace to protest the ouster of President Juan D. Bosch. Police fired machine guns and used tear gas against students who threw stones, resulting in the arrest of about 50 students.

La policía disparó ametralladoras y empleó gases lacrimógenos contra los estudiantes que arrojaban piedras, lo que resultó en el arresto de unos 50 estudiantes.

records.headline: A political analysis reports that while most American officials
records.summary_en: A political analysis reports that while most American officials regretted the fall of the fragile democratic government in the Dominican Republic, Senator Gruening, Democrat of Alaska, proposed returning deposed President Juan Bosch to Santo Domingo aboard an American warship. Seeking a middle course, the United States administration attempted to balance using aid and diplomacy to discourage military coups without permanently refusing to engage with de facto military governments once established. The commentary notes debate between liberals urging punitive policies and conservatives warning that unstable civilian administrations risked Communist subversion.

En busca de un rumbo intermedio, la administración de Estados Unidos intentó equilibrar el uso de la ayuda y la diplomacia para desincentivar los golpes militares sin negarse permanentemente a tratar con los gobiernos militares de facto una vez establecidos. El comentario destaca el debate entre liberales que pedían políticas punitivas y conservadores que advertían que los gobiernos civiles inestables corrían el riesgo de caer ante la subversión comunista.

records.headline: An editorial reviewing statements by Representative Selden argues
records.summary_en: An editorial reviewing statements by Representative Selden argues against American efforts to crush the military regime that ousted Juan Bosch in Santo Domingo. The piece asserts that both Bosch and Honduran President Villeda Morales led weak governments that temporized in the face of internal Communist threats, citing Selden's remark that democracy was doomed by its weak servants rather than strong enemies. While endorsing the suspension of aid and diplomatic recognition to encourage democratic commitments from the military rulers, the editorial cautions against forcing their collapse, arguing that such an outcome could produce a Castro-style regime.

records.full_text:
Actress Remembers Turning Point

By HAL BOYLE

NEW YORK (AP)—Ever afterward the girl would remember this moment as the turning point in her life.

She was tall and slender and 17 years old. She had green-blue eyes and reddish gold hair, and the freckles on her fair skin shone like tiny doubloons scattered by wastrel elves.

She walked hesitantly into the room where a number of men were drinking cocktails and smoking.

"Say the Lord's Prayer," brusquely commanded producer Gabriel Pascal.

"Our Father, who art in heaven," began the girl. For a moment, frightened, she paused then went on. "Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come, thy will be done..."

The room became silent except for her voice. When she had finished, the men exchanged glances.

Then Pascal signed the girl, who had been living on $10 a week in a London YWCA, to her first movie role—as the Salvation Army lass in Bernard Shaw's "Major Barbara."

Deborah Kerr, now an international film star who has six times been nominated for academy awards, recalled the incident during a stopover on her way to Mexico to make her 28th picture, "Night of the Iguana," in which she will co-star with Richard Burton and Ava Gardner.

"I was so unnerved that I was afraid I'd forget the words of the prayer," she said.

Miss Kerr carries herself with an air of aristocratic grace and elegance that is rescued from aloofness by an easy warmth and those down-to-earth freckles, which she doesn't mind at all.

"If you have freckles, you might as well relax and enjoy them," she remarked. "There's nothing you can do about them."

The major tensions that afflict many actresses seem to have passed Deborah by:

"But my biggest fault probably is fretting over trifles," she said.

"I'm terribly indecisive — perhaps because I was born in September under the zodiac sign of Libra."

Miss Kerr has wide-ranging interests—painting, the piano, poetry, and studying cook books. Her favorite food is "spaghetti with anything," and her greatest unachieved ambition is "to be able to cook marvelously."

Deborah is somewhat apologetic over being so distressingly normal.

"I have a happy life," she said. "Perhaps I should be a bit more of a kook, but I'm afraid I'm too old to start."

She said that her philosophy stems from her aunt, who on giving birth to a child at the age of 46 and being asked what it was like, replied, "Never make heavy weather of anything, dear."

"Now doesn't that sound terribly British and nautical?" asked Deborah, smiling. "But it's a good phrase to live by."

records.full_text:
Dominican Ex-Presidents Join Forces; Seek Support

By VIRGINIA PREWETT

WASHINGTON (NANA) — Ex-President Juan Bosch's forces in the Dominican Republic for the first time are acquiring partial army support. This has come through a quiet agreement with former president Dr. Joaquin Balaguer, who has a respectable army following and who now swings his influence to the Bosch cause.

Till this development, the Bosch camp lacked a real handhold on the power apparatus in Santo Domingo, though Bosch won the 1962 election by more than 60 per cent of the popular vote. The apparatus consists mainly of the militarized police the army and the air force.

The pro-Balaguer officers include a few at top levels and many lower officers in control of troops. Balaguer was made president of his country by the late dictator Rafael Trujillo in Aug. 1960, but tried to become independent of the Trujillo dynasty after the dictator's assassination in May, 1961.

Balaguer's army friends asked him to send them an advisor on ways to effectively support the "constitutional" cause led by Bosch. On Oct. 17, Balaguer, who is in New York, sent to Santo Domingo by air the secretary general of his reform party, Nicolas Silfa. Silfa was turned back from the airport because his name is blacklisted by the junta, but the two maintain contact with the Dominican Republic.

Serves As Link

Silfa was ex-Pres. Bosch's U.S. representative for many years before he broke with Bosch and realigned with Balaguer. Now he serves as link between the two ex-presidents.

The new Balaguer-Bosch alignment comes at a time when the power apparatus in Santo Domingo is splitting up. Brig. Gen. Elias Wessin y Wessin is challenging for supreme control a combination headed by Gen. Antonio Imbert, one of the men who assassinated Trujillo, and Gen. Belisario Peguero, commander of the Dominican militarized police.

The Dominican police, involved in the grim chores of political repression at present, number from 13,000 to 15,000 men. The army is stronger than the police only because it has planes and tanks. General Peguero has a palace guard who include many former low-echelon Trujillo enforcers. He is not popular however, with his own higher officers.

Line-Up Of Power

Wessin Y Wessin controls more officers than General Imbert, who attained his rank only last year as a reward for eliminating Trujillo. However, Imbert has a long-standing pact with Peguero which gives him a strong leverage in the power game.

records.headline: A company spokesman tracking the historical cultivation of bananas
records.summary_en: A company spokesman tracking the historical cultivation of bananas stated that the Caribbean served as an important way station during their journey from southern Asia to Central and South America. Father Tomás de Berlanga, a Spanish priest, brought banana plants to Santo Domingo in what is now the Dominican Republic. Other travelers subsequently transported the plants from Santo Domingo across Latin America.

Fray Tomás de Berlanga, un sacerdote español, llevó plantas de plátano a Santo Domingo, en lo que hoy es la República Dominicana. Posteriormente, otros viajeros transportaron las plantas desde Santo Domingo hacia el resto de América Latina.

records.headline: A political commentator criticizes liberals and State Department factions
records.summary_en: A political commentator criticizes liberals and State Department factions for continuously assailing the Trujillo regime in the Dominican Republic until it was brought down. While acknowledging grounds for criticizing the dictatorship, the author contends that the United States and Dominican populations acted out of fear of communism and argues that the successor government deserves American assistance rather than sending aid to foreign leftist and neutralist regimes. The column asserts that the same principles apply to the situation in Honduras.

La columna afirma que los mismos principios se aplican a la situación de Honduras.

records.summary_en: The Guatemalan government announced that it has resumed full diplomatic relations with the Dominican Republic on Thursday night. Formal ties had been broken in April, 1962, when the Dominican government recalled its ambassador following student demonstrations in Santo Domingo that accused Guatemalan President Miguel Ydígoras Fuentes of repressive actions. records.summary_en: The State Department announced that the United States has granted diplomatic recognition to the Dominican Republic and Honduras following consultations with hemisphere governments and commitments to election timetables. Under the schedule established by the Dominican civilian junta, an elected government is slated to assume power on August 16. The resumption of formal relations follows punitive measures enacted after the late September coup against President Juan Bosch, which had suspended diplomatic ties and halted promised aid mounting to 155 million.

Según el calendario fijado por la junta civil dominicana, un gobierno electo tiene previsto asumir el poder el 16 de agosto. La reanudación de relaciones formales se produce tras las medidas punitivas adoptadas después del golpe de finales de septiembre contra el presidente Juan Bosch, las cuales habían suspendido los lazos diplomáticos y paralizado la ayuda prometida que ascendía a 155 millones.

records.headline: Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: George L. Rosenblatt's travel feature opens on Santo Domingo, the oldest city in the New World, founded by Christopher Columbus's brother Bartholomew, with the celebrated founding date set at August 4, 1496. A few hours' stroll through the Colonial Zone shows the firsts of the hemisphere: the first cathedral, the first hospital, the first university and the first commercial street. Foremost among the sights is the Cathedral of Santa María la Menor, the first cathedral established in the New World, which the article presents as the last resting place of Christopher Columbus, whose ornate tomb stands inside the cathedral and whose coffin is traditionally opened to view on Columbus Day.
records.summary_es: El reportaje de viajes de George L. Rosenblatt se abre con Santo Domingo, la ciudad más antigua del Nuevo Mundo, fundada por Bartolomé, hermano de Cristóbal Colón, con la fecha de fundación celebrada fijada el 4 de agosto de 1496. Unas pocas horas de paseo por la Zona Colonial muestran las primicias del hemisferio: la primera catedral, el primer hospital, la primera universidad y la primera calle comercial. Entre los lugares se destaca la Catedral de Santa María la Menor, la primera catedral establecida en el Nuevo Mundo, que el artículo presenta como el último descanso de Cristóbal Colón, cuya tumba adornada se encuentra dentro de la catedral y cuyo ataúd se abre tradicionalmente a la vista el Día de Colón.
records.passage: this hemisphere. The Cathedral of Santa Maria la Menor was the first built in While the precise locale of the great explorer's burial is questioned, the most convincing arguments have been in favor of the ornate tomb inside the Santo Domingo cathedral. It has been suggested, for example, that a bone from his skeleton or similar relic may have been buried in Seville, Spain, thus giving rise to claims that Seville is Columbus' eternal home. But one knowledgeable guide in Seville says that Santo Domingo is where Christopher Columbus is buried. If you happen to be here on Columbus Day (Oct. 12), you may be able to glimpse Old Chris, since the coffin traditionally is opened to view on the anniversary of his discovery of the New World. These most Columbian of relics were brought to Hispaniola in the mid-1540s from Spain, where Columbus died in 1506, then were buried in a secret vault within the cathedral. Within a block of the cathedral are the Ozama Fort and its component Tower of Homage, both built in the first decade of the 1500s. The grounds of the fortress are spacious and parklike, quite a contrast to the narrow, steep [illegible] spiral stairway that takes visitors through a dim, chimneylike passage to the tooth fringe of the walls. To the east is the Rio Ozama and the port of Santo Domingo, where a freighter may moor so close to the shore that it almost seems tied to the fortress itself. records.headline: Santo Domingo
records.summary_en: In the next stretch of George L. Rosenblatt's Santo Domingo feature, the walk continues to the Ozama Fort and its Tower of Homage, both built in the first decade of the 1500s, a short block from the cathedral. From the top of the tower visitors can scan a panorama of the old city: the Ozama River and the port to the east, the bridges to the north, the harbor mouth where the Ozama empties into the Caribbean Sea to the south, and the rooftops of the old city to the west. The feature then passes the Casa de Bastidas, a sprawling sixteenth-century home now a museum and crafts outlet, and notes the sun clock on Calle Las Damas, an eighteenth-century device that still keeps fairly good time.
records.summary_es: En el siguiente tramo del reportaje de George L. Rosenblatt sobre Santo Domingo, el paseo continúa hacia la Fortaleza Ozama y su Torre del Homenaje, ambas construidas en la primera década del siglo XVI, a una manzana de la catedral. Desde lo alto de la torre los visitantes pueden contemplar un panorama de la ciudad vieja: el río Ozama y el puerto al este, los puentes al norte, la desembocadura del puerto donde el Ozama desemboca en el mar Caribe al sur, y los tejados de la ciudad vieja al oeste. El reportaje pasa luego por la Casa de Bastidas, una amplia casa del siglo XVI hoy convertida en museo y tienda de artesanías, y menciona el reloj de sol de la calle Las Damas, un artefacto del siglo XVIII que todavía da la hora con bastante exactitud.

records.summary_en: The final stretch of George L. Rosenblatt's page-one feature carries the walk north along Calle Las Damas to the Columbus Castle, built by Christopher Columbus's son Diego and now a museum of sixteenth-century court life. Descending the stairs at the northern edge of the castle, the reader reaches La Atarazana, the oldest shopping street in the New World, which dates from the 1500s. The feature pauses at the Casa de Bastidas, with its shaded garden courtyard, and at the eighteenth-century sun clock on Las Damas, described as simple and more remarkable for having survived intact than for any intrinsic quality.

records.summary_en: In this continuation of George L. Rosenblatt's Santo Domingo feature, the walk resumes on La Atarazana, where a lunch at the Fonda de la Atarazana ends in a tropical downpour that traps the writer in the restaurant, watching the rain on the brick tiles of the patio. The feature continues to the Casa del Cordón, built in 1503 and believed to be the first stone house in the Americas, and to Puerta del Conde, where the flag of the Dominican Republic first flew in 1844. Through the gate stands the shrine of La Trinitaria, where the three Founding Fathers — Juan Pablo Duarte, Francisco del Rosario Sánchez and Ramón Mella — are entombed. The writer closes with his impressions of the Dominican people, whom he finds gentle and unobtrusive, and with a long taxi ride driven by Victor, a man who spoke no English but with whom he talked baseball, and who charged about eleven dollars for a two-hour excursion.

records.chapter_en: Annexation to Spain and the Restoration War
records.chapter_es: La anexión a España y la Guerra de la Restauración
records.full_text:
ARRIVAL OF THE EAGLE. HIGHLY IMPORTANT FROM ST. DOMINGO. The Entire Spanish Province in a Blaze. Complete Destruction of Puerto Plata by the Insurgents. Signal Advantages Gained by Them at Azua. THE WHOLE COAST TO BE BLOCKADED. IMPORTANT FROM VENEZUELA. Capture of Puerto Cabello by Falcon. &c., &c., &c.

ARRIVAL OF THE EAGLE.

HIGHLY IMPORTANT FROM ST. DOMINGO.

The Entire Spanish Province in a Blaze.

Complete Destruction of Puerto Plata by the Insurgents.

Signal Advantages Gained by Them at Azua.

THE WHOLE COAST TO BE BLOCKADED.

IMPORTANT FROM VENEZUELA.

Capture of Puerto Cabello by Falcon.

&c., &c., &c.

The steamship Eagle, Captain Adams, from Havana 24th inst., via Delaware Breakwater 29th, where she put in for coal, arrived at this port at an early hour this morning. Her news is important, as will be seen by our correspondence.

The following are the passengers by the Eagle:—

J de Esoards (French Consul), lady and two children; Miss Martine, Mrs B Levy, four children and two servants; Gustavus Pessel and lady, F W Wagner, N A Normand, Manuel Pontes, Thos Gonzales, J del Casal, Marcos Lasa, Lorenzo H de Alva, Manuel H de Alva, Mrs S Mathews, Miss J Jameiquin, Miss M Fesser, Miss M Morney, M Sabonim, lady and two children; Mrs L P de Serrano and daughter, and Dr O'Donnell and son.

Our Havana Correspondence.

HAVANA, Oct. 24, 1863.

Spread of the Dominican Revolution—Destruction of Puerto Plata—A New Captain General Arrived There—The Wounded Spaniards at Santo de Cuba—Generous Conduct of the Creoles—Spanish Victory at Santa Cruz—A Glance at the Situation—The Learning of the New York Tribune—News from Venezuela, &c., &c.

In former letters I have endeavored to prove that if the revolution in St. Domingo was really confined to the one province of Ciboa, it had no chance of success. This I think is undeniable. But if it should appear that it was spreading rapidly, those chances are naturally increased. That such is the case is now unquestionable. Not only has it spread beyond the limits of its cradle, Cibao, where it certainly was at first confined, but, since the beginning of the present month, has assumed such proportions that it may now be said the entire country is in a blaze.

It is extremely difficult to get not simply details but leading facts, nor do the newspapers as yet admit the whole truth. We know, however, enough through such sources to warrant us in believing that the insurrection is spreading, for we have in the first place the proclamation of the Captain General, Don Felipe Rivero of Lemoyne, declaring the blockade of the entire coast, in the preamble to which he states that "several provinces of the Spanish part of the Island of St. Domingo have declared themselves in rebellion, &c." In the next place, we have the very important news that the town of Puerto Plata has been completely destroyed. At first we were told the suburbs had been burned. We now know not a single building remains.

Through private sources, I learn that a day or two after the insurgeints were defeated near the town of Azua, they returned, attacked the garrison unawares and gained signal advantages, even capturing some artillery. It is also asserted, on what I believe to be good authority, that St. Domingo city is ripe for revolt, with the probability that by this time it has risen against the Spanish rule.

Our latest dates from the capital are to the 9th inst., brought to Santiago de Cuba by the war steamer Velasco, but a tithe of the news will never be known. In the attack on Puerto Plata the insurgents had thirty killed, and lost six or seven in prisoners, among them an officer. Spanish loss not stated. These, to the number of twelve or fifteen hundred, are posted in an entrenched camp, fortified with twelve pieces of cannon. Considering that the insurgents succeeded in their design, which was the destruction of the town, their loss has been very insignificant, while they probably inflicted equally as heavy a one on their enemies.

The new Captain General of St. Domingo arrived in Puerto Rico from Spain on the 15th inst., whence he proceeded on the 18th to take charge of his onerous office. This officer is General Don Carlos Vargas, the same who left Havana in the Spanish expedition to Vera Cruz, as second in command to General Gassett, and is one of those most distinguished for their gallantry in the Morocco war. His predecessor, General Rivero, who will not I am sure cry salt tears at his removal, is to return to Madrid to occupy a high post.

The insurgents had sent a flag of truce to the Spaniards at Puerto Plata, asking for medicines and provisions for the sick and wounded who fell into their hands at Santiago, and who were receiving every care and attention at their hands. This fact is additiodal proof that the insurrection is well organized and led, and gives us reason to hope that the war will be conducted humanely.

One hundred and fifty six sick and wounded were carried to Santiago de Cuba on board the Velasco, where they were received with every mark of attention by the people, the members of the volunteer companies vieing with each other in rendering the most friendly services, carrying the unfortunates to the hospitals on their shoulders, and supplying their every want in a manner highly creditable to the generous and charitable character for which the people of Santiago are remarkable. This little incident is worthy of notice, for the volunteers there are mainly composed of natives, many of those most conspicuous in their attentions to the wounded Spaniards, being members of the wealthiest Creole families of that section. I doubt very much if such a fact could be chronicled in any other part of the island. The ladies of Santiago have also shown their kind solicitude for the sufferers by making lint, and bandages, and sending them quantities of every thing they might require. These noble hearted Santiaguenses have even sent delicacies and hospital stores to Puerto Plato, for which General Gandara thanks them in the warmest terms, as well he may.

This general left Santiago for Puerto Plata with the last batch of reinforcements sent from Cuba on board the war steamer Santa Lucia, and on arriving at that place was fired upon by a masked battery which the insurgents had succeeded in planting near the Spanish camp. The Santa Lucia returned the fire, and, as a matter of course, you are prepared to find the Spanish bulletins declare that the rebels were routed ignominiously. In bulletins "our side" invariably wins. That you know from your experience at home. However General Gandara did not land his troops at Puerto Plata, but put to sea again and went to the capital, where they were, by all accounts, just as much needed.

Since writing the above news has been received of a victory gained by Santana, on the 17th inst., at a place called Santa Cruz, in which that individual claims to have made five hundred prisoners and taken a couple of pieces of artillery. I do not know where to locate this Santa Cruz if not in the province of Seibo, some distance to the northeast of the capital, and a still greater distance from Santana's headquarters at Arroyo Vermejo, where he also claims to have whipped the rebels a few days previously. If this conjecture be right, it shows clearly that the insurrection exists in every part of the country, as a glance at the map will disclose. This being the case, let us consider the resources of the Dominicans for carrying on a war with their powerful enemy.

The population of the Spanish part of the island may be estimated at not more than two hundred thousand souls, which might furnish a fighting force of twenty-five to thirty thousand men. It would not be safe, however, to calculate on their furnishing so large a number; for in the war with Hayti for their independence in the year 1844, after the most strenuous exertions, they did not turn out more than half the smaller number. The estimate of fourteen thousand insurgents in Cibao alone, which I mentioned in a former letter, is therefore either very much exaggerated or else armed men from other parts of the country have been flocking there in considerable numbers.

This population of two hundred thousand souls, is scattered over a territory of, I should think, about eighteen thousand square miles, calculating the Spanish part at two-thirds of the entire island; for in the absence of more positive information there is no other way to arrive at an approximation to the truth than by close guessing, and all the information we have in regard to the island is exceedingly meagre. For a guerilla war no country is better adapted, being traversed in every portion by ranges of hills and mountains, some of which rise to the height of six thousand feet. It is besides well watered and generally heavily timbered, to say nothing of the dense undergrowth which

could afford impenetrable concealment to guerrillas. In fact, the insurgents seem to have adopted the plan suggested by Mackenzie in his "Notes on Hayti," by following which, he says, the natives would be invincible, namely, to abandon the coast and destroy all the towns. So far, they have obeyed this suggestion to the letter. Two of their most important towns have been laid in ashes, and we may expect to hear that Azua de Compostela has shared their fate. Yet there is one great difficulty in the way of Dominican success. With a world of mineral and other wealth at their feet, the Dominicans are among the poorest people on the globe, a fact which says nothing in their favor. Under these circumstances, and in this material, unromantic age, the prospects of their being able to negotiate a loan in Paris, London, or even New York, are absurdly small. To carry on war they must have powder, lead and iron; but if they have no money to buy these articles with, how are they to get them? This is a great obstacle. The blockade of their coast is nothing. Blockades have been run before now. But the want of money, the sinews of war, overwhelms all calculation, or rather reduces the question to so plain a point as to remove all doubt.

Spain will be obliged to send an army of fifty thousand men and spend millions of dollars; but she has the men, and if she have not the money, can borrow it from her friends.

The only question for Spain really is, is it worth her while to conquer St. Domingo? Judging from the history of the past, I am convinced it would be a useless conquest, unless a large European immigration could be coaxed to settle there. Never while the sun shines will the Dominicans be induced to develop the resources of their country by voluntary labor. Their own leaders found it necessary to establish a compulsory system of labor, which differed very little indeed from slavery. President Boyer tried the voluntary system and abrogated the laws of Christophe and Petion; but he soon found it utterly useless, and was obliged to re-enact the severe laws of his predecessors. This is an indisputable fact, and the whole modern history of St. Domingo lies snugly in it. The labor laws of Christopher cost him his life. The opposite system, with which Boyer inaugurated his rule, induced the lazy, indolent, labor hating Dominicans to submit themselves to him, and both sections of the island became united in one common republic in the year 1821. The return of the general government to the forced system induced the Dominicans to rebel, or secede, whichever you choose, and they gained their point. Since that time the country has not improved, one may very well imagine, but has, if anything, deteriorated, much to the disgust of the few educated, intelligent Dominicans who went about the world for years begging for some one to take charge of their country. Spain was disposed to undertake the business, but insists point blank that the Dominicans must work. The Dominicans will fight first. Work they will not. Let philosophers, like those of the New York Tribune, whose article on the bloody struggle in Dominica (!) amused and instructed me very much, for I did not know there was any struggle going on in that island. Let those philosophers or any others rant over St. Domingo as much as they know how, but the real kernel of Dominican hostility to the Spaniards is their constitutional dislike to earn their bread by the sweat of their brow.

At the same time I do not think the Spaniards have any right to force them to work, or to govern them in any way, shape or form. They have no business whatever in St. Domingo. The people of that country have a "natural and inalienable right" to go to the devil their own road, and no one has any right to interfere. Yet while I do not sympathize with the Spaniards, because I think them in the wrong, I certainly feel no sympathy in my bosom for the Dominicans, whose noblest motive in this, as in all other wars, is the unrestrained indulgence of their sloth and licentiousness.

We have had no news from Mexico lately.

From Venezuela we learn that the troops of Falcon attacked Puerto Cabello successfully and occupied the town on the 5th inst., the discomfited garrison taking refuge on board their fleet and making off to Ciudad Bolivar. This is highly important. We should now very much like to know if the escaped garrison will be the nucleus for another army opposed to Falcon, and if the civil war is to break out as bad as ever.

The scarcity of paper on the United States has caused a slight improvement in exchange, when by all the rules of commerce it ought to be further depressed. New York is quoted at 35 to 36 dis. It had been 38. The Corsica leaves this evening.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
Interesting from Santo Domingo.

THE BAEZ PARTY REDUCED TO THE LAST STRAITS—POSITION OF HIS FORCES AT SAN DOMINGO CITY AND SAMANA—WANT OF PROVISIONS—GENERAL PALMADTIER AT POINT OF DEATH—NAVAL NEWS—GERMAN IMMIGRANTS DYING OF HUNGER, ETC.

By the schooner Brontes, from Puerto Platto, we have received files of the Gaceta Oficial of the Dominican republic to the 31st of January, and a letter from our correspondent at St. Jago de los Caballeros, the provisional seat of government.

OUR DOMINICAN CORRESPONDENCE.

ST. JAGO, Jan 19, 1858.

Return of our Exiled Correspondent—Position of the Contending Parties—Formation of the New Constitution—Hopes of Recognition by Foreign Governments—War Vessels Fitting Out—Trade, &c., &c.

It is a long time since I had the pleasure to address you, but it has been owing to the political affairs of this country; in consequence of which I have been an exile, travelling in Curracoa and Turks' Islands. But now that I am settled again, you will receive my letters as regularly as before.

Enclosed you will find a file of the Official Gazette, by which you will perceive that Baez is confined to the old city of San Domingo, and that the gallant and good patriot, Santana, is at the head of a large army, besieging said city, where foreign provisions are very scarce, and none at all of the domestic. Besides, Baez is in a very hopeless position, having but very few soldiers, and these deserting almost daily, three by three and five by five, and sometimes in larger numbers.

The representatives appointed to revise the constitution by the different conventions of all the counties of the republic, met on the 7th of December last, at Moca, a small village twelve miles from this city, in order to make a new constitution, which is already drawn up, and now in the printing office. The debates will begin in a few days, and there is every reason to expect that the new political basis of this unfortunate country will be very liberal, the penalty of death for political faults being forever abolished, religious tolerance being established, harmonizing the democratic principles with the strength of the executive power, and granting several advantages to foreigners; not only to those belonging to friendly nations, but to the citizens and subjects of the countries at peace with the republic

We entertain the hope that as soon as the new authorities or powers of the State be regularly established, all the nations which have representatives in this country will recognise our new government, such a course being consonant with international practice, not forgetting that the will of the people, particularly in the republics, is the true sovereign; and that the whole population of this country having raised against Baez and his minions, has reason to expect from every civilized nation that their new rulers be recognized by them as the true and legitimate magistrates. Such is the inference naturally drawn from the relation given to General Bido on the 5th inst., by the Azuans, who at that date deserted from the old capital, and amongst whom, we see with satisfaction, was the valiant Captain Baldomero Victorino.

According to that account, Baez prohibited that the condition which Samana at present is in be spoken of at St. Domingo, the best proof that the brave Generals at the head of the army besieging that peninsula, cannot be taxed with exaggerating the reports they addressed to our government of the victories obtained by them over the troops of Palmantier. No other reason can be assigned for this extraordinary prohibition. In consequence of the official communications, in which the commander-in-chief of the rebels at Samana reports the repeated defeats our valiant troops caused to him, Baez came to the conviction that the surrender or capture by force of that place is inevitable. It is for this reason that he in advance imposed silence with regard to the war which Generals Puello and Mella are carrying on against Palmantier, in order that when victory crowns our troops nobody may learn of it or be astonished at the silence on that point, Baez having in advance put a curb into the mouth of the citizens and monopolized the bad news he is receiving from Samana.

But this is not the only reason which confirms us in our conviction relative to the speedy termination of the exceptional state of things wherein the country finds itself. As our readers will learn from the communication addressed by Gen. Bido, under date of the 7th inst., to the provisional government, the disaffection amongst the people of St. Domingo, and more particularly amongst the small force of troops Baez has under his command in that city, is going on increasing. When the Azuans left that city there were but eight head of cattle, a number not sufficient to provide the entire population of St. Domingo with meat, which is also wanted by the inhabitants of San Carlos and Pajarito, who, unfortunately for them, since the end of July, find themselves confined within the old capital, and the troops of the garrison, who, although small in number, must have their part of the provisions. The stock of hogs reported by the deserters of Baez will last for about two weeks; but will the poor be able to buy this meat at a cost of $65 the pound? This is impossible. Besides, the great majority of the population, and of the inhabitants of the two localities above mentioned, are composed of very poor people, who live partly by their labor (and to-day they did not find any) and others on their small farms which they at present are not allowed even to visit. As to the cocoa nuts, what kind of food can they get out of them? We do not see that they can be of any other use than to furnish them with sweetmeats or a certain quantity of oil.

To the above must be added those military persons who, as accomplices of Baez, are very much frightened at the idea that our flotilla might cut off their retreat. Poor cowards they are. Their conscience warns them that the day of expiation for their numberless villainies is close at hand, and that it must take place in a just proportion with the evils they inflicted on their country.

What is still worse, of the three war ships sent by Baez to Samana he has not had any news, although over two months have elapsed since the first two left St. Domingo and one month since the last of them sailed. Thus Baez has at present no ship left at his disposal, since those three were the only vessels he had. They are named El Libertador, La Australia and El Cirus, El 19 de Marzo having been delivered up to the provisional government by her commander, and La Merced having been sunk some two months and a half since by the well directed balls of the besieging army before Pajarito.

As regards Samana, the position in which the deluded soldiers who form the battalion under the command of the rebel Palmantier find themselves, is not any better. According to the report of the German immigrant alluded to by the commander of Puerto Plata in his despatch of the 12th inst. Palmantier was so seriously ill when the former left that place that he was not even able to speak; and there is no doubt but that the population of that peninsula find themselves in a very bad situation as far as provisions are concerned, a chicken being sold for five pesos, as is stated by the same individual.

This latter, with whose misfortunes we sincerely sympathize, adds that of his companions immigrants like himself, eight died in St. Domingo and six in Samana, one of sickness and the others by famine. The unfortunates! In September last, two or three of them had asked from General Santana permission to work in the fields agreeably to the contract on the stipulation of which they had left the shores of France; the libertador gave them the permission, and kept even for some days in the neighborhood of St. Domingo, a drove of beasts ready, with which he intended to send them to the provisional government, to be provided by the latter with land, and to be established thereon. Why have they not accepted the benevolent offer of General Santana? Nobody knows. It is much to be wondered at that the French Consul in St. Domingo, under whose protection those unfortunates had been in that city, did not take the necessary measures to prevent them from perishing by hunger.

records.chapter_es: Una república en busca de reconocimiento
records.full_text:
Affairs in the Dominican Republic.

CITY OF ST. DOMINGO, July 12, 1848.

Omission in a former Letter Supplied—Recent Legislative Enactment for the Encouragement of Mining Operations—Another Remodeling the Monetary System—Public Excitement Incidentally Connected with the Latter, and the Cause of it.

In the synopsis which I gave, in a former communication, of the principal articles of the Dominican constitution, I omitted to notice one to which recent occurrences have attracted much attention and given considerable prominence. By its terms, the President is empowered, during the continuance of the actual war with the Haytien republic, growing out of the separation from her, and until peace is established, to freely organise the army and navy, mobilize the National Guards, and take all measures he may deem proper for the defence and security of the nation, and in consequence, to issue all orders and decrees proper for those ends, without being subject to any responsibility whatever.

I now supply this omission, to illustrate some future details.

The gold mines of St. Domingo are celebrated in the early history of the new world, as being the incentive that gave the first impulse to Spanish adventure and enterprise in America. These have remained unwrought, to any considerable extent, for a long series of years; and the government has heretofore refused to permit the working of them, from the fear, it is said, of stimulating the cupidity of their enemies, and also, perhaps, of foreign nations. Besides those of gold, there are also, as I have mentioned on a former occasion, mines of copper, and very probably of silver also, within the territory of the republic. By an act of Congress, passed at the recently closed session, and approved the 16th of May last, it is declared that the working of the "minerals," or mines of every description that are found on the public lands, is open and free to every individual who may choose to engage in it. Arrangements for this purpose must be made by those intending to avail themselves of the privilege with the Minister of Finance—Ministro de Hacienda—who is authorized, under contracts of lease or otherwise, to stipulate, in behalf of the public treasury, for the payment of a per centage by the operators—never to exceed the maximum of five per cent of the metal wrought.

The terms of the act specify individuals only. Whether the privilege conferred by this enactment would be extended to organized companies, formed to carry on mining operations on an extensive scale, in the usual way, and such as there have heretofore and recently been attempts made to organize in the United States and elsewhere, with a view to operations here, may possibly, under the peculiar circumstances of the case, and the present tone of public feeling, admit of some doubt; though I incline strongly to the belief that no opposition to such a plan of operations would be officially interposed.

The most important measure that came before the Congress at its late session, and which engrossed a much greater share of its attention than any other, was the monetary system—the devising of ways and means to place the currency on a better basis, and to restore the circulating medium of the country to a better credit and condition. This I have heretofore shown, had depreciated to fifteen for one dollar specie, and the tendency has since been very slightly downwards. At last the Congress, after protracted discussions, in the course of which were successively examined and rejected several different schemes, agreed upon a system which they embodied in an act approved on the 19th day of June last. It is entitled, in substance, an act to provide for the deficit in the treasury, occasioned by the insufficiency of the public imposts, and by the consequent depreciation of the government paper.

By it, the Executive is first directed to have the hard money now accumulated in the treasury, and the future additions thereto, to the amount, in all, of one hundred thousand dollars, converted into milled coin of the United States, of the several denominations of five, ten, and twenty five cent pieces, provisionally, until such time as Dominican silver can be minted. It proceeds to direct that all old silver, wrought or unwrought, which the inhabitants may see fit to deliver into the Treasury Department, shall be sent abroad to the United States, or elsewhere, and its value returned to the owners in coined money, at the rate of ninety-five cents per ounce troy, of the metal delivered, and of the same quality of fineness.

To provide for the replacement of the present depreciated government paper money, which it is contemplated to call in and cancel, the Executive is authorised to have prepared, and to issue a new emission of paper money, based on the credit of the National Treasury, to the amount of $250,000, in bills of the nominal value of one dollar each, and which the public treasury is to guarantee for forty cents, hard money; and also, the further emission of 150,000 bills of the nominal value of two dollars each, and guaranteed in like manner and rates. The whole of both which emissions are to be ready for issuing, at latest, by the first of January, 1849. He is also further directed to have prepared an additional quantity of 375,000 bills of the denominations of one and two dollars, to be laid by in reserve in the treasury department, to be used for the purpose of expanding the monetary circulation as soon as the condition of mercantile affairs and the state of the country, require it.

To hasten the withdrawal of the present issue from circulation as soon as the sum of $25,000, in coin is imported, as before provided, dues accruing to the treasury shall commence to be paid, half in the new small coin and half in the present currency, the latter at the rate of ten dollars to one, while the old paper thus called in is to be cancelled in due form. And the act goes on to declare that a portion of this new coin, which will thus find its way into the treasury, may from time to time be appropriated, in sums not exceeding five thousand dollars at any one time, to the purchase of old silver at the rate before designated, and which shall be coined in like manner. After proceeding to many specific details—of no particular interest to my present purpose—the act finally empowers the President to raise, by a loan, foreign or domestic, on credit or by mortgage of the national property, the further sum of 100,000 to 150,000 dollars, to be appropriated, when obtained, to the withdrawal and cancellation of the same amount of the present circulation.

It will be observed that the foregoing act fixes the value of the old emission, to be allowed at the treasury, at ten for one; which is, in fact, the rate at which it has all along been received for the custom-house dues that were payable in that currency; while, as has been before seen, the market value of the same currency has been only fifteen for one, with a downward tendency. Now, however plausible the charge may at first appear, that the government, by receiving their own paper only at a great discount off from its ostensible value, though it be still a less one than is exacted in the market, repudiates a large portion of her debt in this form, it must in justice be remarked, that this issue never did circulate at par from the beginning; and much, if not most of it, went into circulation with no higher intrinsic value attached to it than its authors now allow for it on its return. For any slight practical repudiation there may be in it, there are still, in extenuation, the mitigating circumstances of overruling necessity, and the high examples of greater and far more wealthy nations.

As to the question of what will be practically effected under this scheme, that is quite another affair; and I confess myself unable to discover what is at last to guaranty the new paper circulating medium that is to be issued at market value, at the rate per nominal dollar prescribed by the act—in other words, to save it from the fate of the old emission. With a nearly empty treasury, and with governmental expenditures that each year more than consume the annual revenue, what can save it from a rapid depreciation—if not nominal, at least actual, in the shape of enhanced prices of all commodities of consumption? No great results can, I fear, be anticipated from the coining—in other words, sale of the old silver to be found here. The Haytiens made too clean a sweep for that, when they got possession. And as to the authorized loan, still less, it is to be feared, can be hoped for or realized from that. No; evade the issue as they may, vainly attempt to do—beat about and try to shun the real rock of difficulty as long and perseveringly as they please—still this government must, at last, adopt the only effectual means of removing it. They will be broken in pieces upon it. An efficient and extensive system of agricultural improvements must be instituted, and its growth fostered, as the only sure basis for monetary and every other kind of stability and prosperity pertaining to the state; and this can only be effected, as is, in effect, admitted by almost everybody, by foreign immigration. Ah! but the danger of the overthrow of our state religion—the subversion or seizure into their hands of the government by a horde of foreign adventurers!—we are afraid of them! And so the only remedy for a great evil, or train of evils, is shunned, and mere airy schemes, based on nothing but a gossamer tissue of financial devices, are elaborated with careful ingenuity and patient toil, to end in nothing.

The hard money alluded to in the beginning of the above act, and on which all the legislative deliberations had been based, was the sum of 58,000 dollars, reserved in the chest of the department for this purpose, which surplus had occurred, notwithstanding the fact of the government expenditures surpassing in amount its revenues, by the disbursements being mostly made in the paper currency, while a considerable portion of the gold of several years' accrual from import duties has been retained in the treasury.

Some unfavorable rumors having got abroad, the Congress, on completing their labor of devising and drafting the new monetary system, appointed a committee to proceed and examine the condition of the strong chest; when lo! a large deficit was discovered. The city was soon all in an uproar. Every body accused the minister of having converted the funds to his private purposes, and some went so far as to implicate the President himself in their suspicions. The lower house demanded an account of the minister; which, on the refusal of that officer to submit, any farther than to declare that it had been appropriated to the legitimate purposes of the government, that body proceeded to impeach him. The upper house, however, on examining into the case, refused to ratify the measure, as was necessary to render it effectual as an impeachment, and so it fell through. The President, who had been absent from the city for a long while, on account of his health, returned highly incensed at the proceeding of the House, and threatened to banish certain members who had been most active in the measure. But the affair was finally compromised by the House receding from the ground they had taken, and acknowledging they had acted with precipitation. Another ground of irritation was also embraced in this rather singular compromise, or "making up." Some of the same active and bold members had somewhat warmly discussed the propriety of defining and limiting the, in some respects, dictatorial power conferred on the President by the article of the constitution herein before noticed. They maintained that the executive had, on several occasions, in practice, given a somewhat latitudinarian construction to its provisions, which, they contended, were intended to apply for certain purposes only, to particular times and emergencies. And so ended, at least for the present, this serious misunderstanding between the two branches of the government, and which, for some days, threatened the most disastrous consequences. During this period the public excitement was intense. Nearly all business was suspended by day, while the streets and places of public resort were deserted by night. Rumors of plots and conspiracies for putting the obnoxious functionaries out of the way, and substituting others in their stead, were constantly rife, and everything seemed ripe for intestine commotion and revolution. A portion of the residents were apprehensive, and, I think, not without some good reason, that, in such a case, scenes similar to those which have, of late, been enacted at the Haytien end of the island, would be reproduced here, or, quite as likely, the far more appalling tragedies so frequently enacted in that portion of the island near the close of the last century.

But the tempest, which at one time seemed to be so fast gathering to a head, to sweep down, like the hurricanes of these latitudes, with desolating violence on this city, has happily completely dissipated itself; and our political heavens again wear, in their usual degree, an aspect of serenity, at least, though it may be, not of tropical brilliancy and splendor.

The President still holds firmly his uncurtailed authority; and it may, after all, I think, be well questioned whether this rule of the strong hand, at least, in cases of moment and emergency, is not the best for this people; and, indeed, the only one for which they are, as a body, as yet prepared. Nor do I believe an instance can be pointed to, where President Santana has abused it to the purposes of cruelty or revenge; nor, after fully weighing, as well as I am able, in my own mind, the various conflicting rumors, charges and assertions, on the one side or the other, am I much more inclined to believe that he has perverted it to purposes of extortion or peculation of any kind.

And, in regard to the charge of embezzlement made against the minister, and at one time certainly almost universally believed, I confess, that on sifting the evidence against him carefully and dispassionately, it certainly appears exceedingly vague and flimsy. His own general statement of the character of the appropriation is plausible and rational; and I am very much mistaken if the financial report of that minister, and any corresponding investigation, that may then be instituted to verify or falsify it, do not prove the correctness of this favorable conjecture. Time will disclose the positive or probable truth, and then, verémos.
