WASHINGTON. Annexation of San Domingo, and the Authors of the Scheme. General Babcock Warned Against General Cazeneau. How General Cazeneau Made Himself Generally Useful. Pre-emption Claims on the Bay of Samana. Senator Sumner's Resolution Explained.

[FROM AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.]

WASHINGTON, Dec. 10.

The singular pertinacity with which the President insists upon the annexation of the Dominican portion of the Island of San Domingo—for, although the message speaks of the annexation of the whole Island, it can scarcely be possible the President means to swallow up the Haytian portion of it without at all consulting the Haytian Government—has brought the question again before the country, and this time, it is believed, the plan hit upon will not fail. General Benjamin F. Butler, the Presidential organ in the House, will introduce the annexation resolutions next week; and, as a bare majority of each house will be sufficient, it is supposed the effort will be crowned with success.

It must not, however, be assumed that the opponents of the measure in the Senate will not make a struggle, as well because of the want of merit of the proposition itself, as because of the blow the procedure inflicts upon the Senate in its executive capacity. I have little faith, however, in the efforts of the opposition, pitted, as they are, against the extraordinary personal exertion which the President is making. More as a matter of record, therefore, than with any expectation that Congress will resist the blandishments or the powers of the Executive, the following history of the matter is briefly given:

For more than twenty years Washington has been periodically visited by a certain General Cazeneau and his clever wife, who, under the nom de plume of "Flora Montgomery," was a contributor to the Democratic Review in John L. O'Sullivan's time, and to the Democratic press generally. The particular hobby of Mr. and Mrs. Cazeneau was the annexation of the Dominican portion of San Domingo, where they had resided under Pierce's administration in some sort of official capacity, Cazeneau having been sent to the island by both Pierce and Buchanan as a sort of combined consul and secret agent. During the rebellion Washington missed the Cazeneaus, who were then busy paying court to Jeff. Davis and his government at Richmond, where they enjoyed a high measure of favor from their activity in the "lost cause." Shortly after the collapse of the Confederacy, we again heard of the Cazeneaus working away in San Domingo, and making propositions to Mr. Seward looking to the fulfilment of their favorite scheme of annexation. The matter fell through at that time, and was again revived upon General Grant's accession to office. The result was the drawing up of a convention under the auspices of General Babcock, one of the President's young military Secretaries, with the aid of Admiral Porter, as wet nurse, and the valuable assistance of Cazeneau as interpreter. That treaty was presented to the Senate last session, and, as your readers know, came to grief by the aid of Mr. Sumner's opposition—the treaty receiving just one-half the votes of the Senate, whilst two-thirds was requisite.

Thus far I have only stated what is generally known. Now for details. When Mr. Fish gave General Babcock his instructions to visit Baez, the President of the Dominican Republic, he particularly warned him against having anything to do with Cazeneau, as a dangerous man, mixed up in his private schemes and speculations, and who only wanted to make a cat's-paw of the United States, so as to realize on the vast concessions of lands in the Bay of Samana and elsewhere which it was known with certainty he had secured. Thus warned, Babcock was sent down, like a good boy, with a bag full of gold from the secret service fund of the State Department, to treat with Baez, and to avoid the naughty but clever Cazeneau. I have no reason to doubt but that Babcock left Washington a good and virtuous young man. He may have been seasick, and his bowels troubled, but, assuredly, his conscience was at rest, although his dreams may have been disturbed with visions of the astute and diplomatic Cazeneau, against whose wiles and interference Mr. Fish had warned him. But, alas, on reaching the island and seeking Baez, an unlooked-for difficulty arose. Baez could speak no English, Babcock was all in the dark as regarded Spanish. Like Tom Hood's English soldier in Paris, after Waterloo, Babcock was astonished to find the ignorance of Baez in not understanding the American tongue, while his surprise was great to hear even the little children speaking Spanish. In this emergency the inevitable Cazeneau put in an appearance, and, being equally conversant with the Spanish and the English, proffered his services as interpreter, and they were gladly accepted—all Mr. Fish's warnings to the contrary notwithstanding.

Behold, then, the unsophisticated young warrior, Babcock, in the hands of two such experts as Cazeneau and Baez, and wonder no longer at the result. In all the interviews between Babcock and Baez—the busy B's—Cazeneau did the translating. What he told to Baez as Babcock's speech, Heaven, Cazeneau, and Baez only know; for certainly Babcock didn't; and equally ignorant was the American military "gent" as to what reply the hybrid San Dominican vouchsafed. Cazeneau was master of the situation, and said what he liked. One thing is certain, however, Babcock liked the looks of the place—of the Bay of Samana especially—and American naval officers here, who have visited the bay, assert that he has entered pre-emption claims for large blocks of land surrounding that magnificent water, and that they are now duly labeled, "Babcock," "Porter," "David A. Porter," "Grant," etc. It would be uncharitable to suppose that all this land is not to be paid for by the parties whose names now figure on the signboards affixed to the property in question, after the annexation is accomplished, and I therefore disdain any injurious reflections while mentioning an undoubted and indisputable fact, vouched for by respectable naval officers.

But all this is of secondary importance. There are questions underlying any mere consideration as to the manner in which this annexation job has been worked at, or the individuals, if any there be, who are pecuniarily interested in it. And, in this connection, Mr. Sumner's resolution of inquiry is exceedingly suggestive, as a little explanation will suffice to show. That resolution reads:

"Resolved, That the President of the United States be requested to communicate to the Senate (if, in his opinion, not incompatible with the public interests) copies of all papers and correspondence relating to the proposed annexation of the Dominican portion of the island of San Domingo, or the purchase of any part thereof, including the original and all subsequent instructions to any agent or Consul of the United States, with the correspondence of such agent or Consul; also, any protocol or convention signed by such agent or Consul; also, an account of the debt and liabilities of the Dominican Government, especially its obligations to the neighboring Republic of Hayti; also the provisions of the existing Constitution of Dominica, so far as the same relate to the sale or transfer of the national domain; also any treaty with Hayti or France by which Dominica is affected; also, any communication from the neighboring Republic of Hayti or from our Minister there relating to the proposed annexation; also, instructions to the commander of our naval squadron in the waters of the island since the commencement of the late negotiations, with the reports and correspondence of such commander; also, any information tending to show what European power, if any, proposes to acquire jurisdiction of any part of the island, and if so, of what part; also, any information as to the position of President Baez, under whom the treaty of annexation was negotiated, and the extent to which he has been maintained in power by the presence of United States vessels-of-war; also, any information with regard to the sentiments of the people in Dominica, and the reported pendency there of civil war; also, any information with regard to any claim of jurisdiction by the Republic of Hayti over the territory of Dominica."

Mr. Sumner, of course, in drawing up the above resolution, framed it not as a roving inquiry after facts unknown to him, but to elicit facts of which he has full cognizance. Whether the President will deem it "compatible with the public interests" to communicate the required information, remains to be seen. In the meantime, I will endeavor to throw some light upon it.

The Republic of Dominica, although territorially embracing two-thirds of the island, has a population variously estimated at from 200,0000 to 250,000, nearly all hybrids, Spanish and negro. General Grant sets the population at less than 100,000, but all other authorities place it at the higher figures. Hayti has a population of about 600,000, nearly all pure blacks, or with French blood intermingled. Hayti has paid France an indemnity of 60,000,000 francs, a moiety of which sum the Haytians claim as due them by the San Dominicans; and by treaty between Hayti and San Domingo, it is provided that neither party shall alienate any portion of the territory. This fact is perfectly well known to the government here. I have before me a letter dated the 5th of February, 1868, addressed to "Hon. W. H. Seward, Secretary of State," by Louis Achille da Pitti-Fernandi, Consul of Hayti at New York, in which, by order of his government, he protests against any sale or transfer of any portion of the island; giving, among other reasons, the statement that he protests "in consequence of the existence of a treaty between the Government of Hayti and San Domingo, by which it is provided that no part of the island can be alienated by either of the two governments." In this letter the Haytian Consul also urges that at all events a vote of the inhabitants should be had—a plebiscite—and that at that time it was evident the population of Dominica was opposed to the annexation.

Upon the revival of the proposition by General Grant, the form of a plebiscite was had, but it is alleged that it was a perfect farce, the soldiers of Baez seizing and imprisoning every one who voted against annexation. Besides, it must be remembered that the Dominicans are at this time engaged in a civil war, General Cabral, the former President, heading the insurgents and having possession of all the country, outside of the towns and fortified places. If we annex the Dominican portion of the island, we take it with its debt of 30,000,000 francs, gold, due to Hayti as its portion of the French indemnity, and we take with it its own debt of about eight million dollars,—in all, about fourteen million dollars,—and, above all, we assume its civil war. It has been said that a man who buys a lawsuit is a fool. What shall be said of a country which buys several millions of debt, a civil war, and a difficulty with the copartners in the non-alienation of the soil which must lead to contention, and in the end the absorption of the whole island, with its hybrid and African population of people, none of whom speak our language, and all of whom are of essentially different races from those of the United States?

We are much too well informed in this country to require any information or lessons from any other people, or we might perhaps pause and reflect over very recent Spanish experience in this same Dominican Republic. At the request of one of the insurgent parties there—for it must be understood revolts like earthquakes are natural with that species—the Spanish Government undertook to establish a protectorate, simply with a view of enabling the Spanish population to sustain themselves against the Haytians. After two years experience, the loss of ten thousand soldiers, mostly by disease incident to the climate, and an expense of millions of dollars, the Spaniards were glad to withdraw, never having succeeded in having their authority recognised or respected beyond the reach of their guns or the tramp of their soldiers.

What are the facts as regards the so-called sentiments of the people of San Domingo in favor of annexation to the United States? Mr. Sumner shadows them in his resolution. Respectable naval officers, now here, who were attached to our men-of-war in Samana Bay, openly declare that but for the presence of our armed ships, Baez could not maintain his power a single day, and that the vote there on the annexation proposition was the veriest farce upon a free expression of opinion. Nor is there any fact to support the assertion that any European power desires, or, at all events, has given any evidence of an intention of effecting a foothold in San Domingo. Well aware that the United States will not permit any European power to obtain a fresh foothold on this continent, or any of its islands, no nation of the Old World is foolhardy enough to wish to throw down the gauntlet. The assertion to the contrary is mere smoke, under the cover of which it is supposed the American project can be more easily effected.

What sort of a population are we about to annex and ennoble with the title of American citizens?—and what sort of a country are we called upon to settle? The one a hybrid people of a race essentially different from our own; the other a tropical climate unsuited for American immigration. We are essentially Anglo-Saxons, and the immigrants from Saxon countries intermingle with us as our own blood, capable of learning the duties as well as the privileges of a republic based upon general education, labor, and obedience to the laws. Is it to such a republic we are to invite the hybrids of the tropics?—must we record that self-interest, pecuniary benefits, or a subserviency to the will of the "Powers that be," will force upon us a brotherhood such as now inhabits Dominica, and accustomed to a government which seems to have been permitted to exist only to make such governments as that of Mexico respectable by comparison? ALPHA.

records.full_text:
OUR QUEER PRIVATE WAR IN HAYTI AND SAN DOMINGO

Hand grenades and machine guns are to be used in subjugating the Dominican and the Haytian. Within the very near future 2,500 additional United States marines are to be sent to San Domingo. They will be armed with grenades and the latest machine guns. They will co-operate with the 3,000 marines now in that “republic” in the hope that before the citizens of the United States really learn what is going on the trouble can be brought to an end.

There have been marines in San Domingo for three years. There have been, too marines in Hayti for as long. How long they will remain there is a problem that no one can answer now.

We'll be here for a hundred years at the rate things are progressing now, remarked a high military official to the writer a short time back.

Few in the United States know that we really have “wars” with the Dominicans and the Haytians. The strictest of censorships is maintained, newspaper accounts of happenings on the island—both “republics” are on the same island—cannot be sent through the mails, officers who have served down there dare not talk of what they have seen or what they experienced. Privates who have served in these sub-tropical places know little of what is going on on the inside and when they do “kick out” and return home their stories are not always wholly coherent or credible.

Some day the history of the United States occupation of Hayti and San Domingo will be written. The names of the American boys who have fallen victims to the bullets or knives or machetes of natives will be made known. The almost unbelievable hardships suffered by our troops will be described and then we will ask one another, “What was it all about anyhow?”

The Domincans have not been conquered; nor have the Haytians. Both peoples make an outward show of friendliness; also they spit at a United States uniform after first assuring themselves that the wearer of that uniform is ignorant of the saliva expelling process.

HATRED FOR AMERICANS.

Domincans hate the Americans; so do the Haytians. Nothing pleases the citizen of either country more than to take a shot at the wearer of Uncle Sam's livery, provided of course, the shooter is behind an adobe wall or a tree or in the window of a house. Few snipers though take advantage of this “house” business; the risk is too great.

Neither the Dominican nor the Haytian is a good shot. They shoot from the hip and take a chance. It's good for the United States marines that such is the case, else there would have been—would be in the future—more of them killed or wounded.

There are high offices in the marine service now stationed in these “Spiggoty” countries who would give nearly all they possesss to be permitted to tell their stories. They would tell the results of their personal observations during the time they have been there.

These men woud tell of “leathernecks” who have gone insane while out in the brush searching for the will-of the wisp bandits who infest the country. They would describe the restraints that have been heaped on the sea soldiers, these being forced to “treat the natives with forbearance and kindliness, no matter what happens” as ordered by Admiral Knapp, until recently Military Governor of San Domingo. They would tell too, of the utter uselessness of the marines being in San Domingo a country that under existing conditions is to Americans an inferno of heat and loneliness and madness

And the worst of it all is that few of the “leathernecks”—this meaning officers as well as buck privates—know what it is about. They do not know why they are in San Domingo. They—that is, some of them—have a vague idea that they are in this land to enforce the payment of a debt said to be owing to their country, the United States. They recall snatches of talk they have heard of some $20,000,000 due to Uncle Sam from the Domincans; and they know too, that the United States government is in charge of the customs on the island.

Still, if the military establishment in San Domingo was merely for the purpose of collecting a bad debt, why it is asked is there such a rigid censorship maintained? In their balmiest days the censors who flaunted the people of the States in regard to the happenings of the great war in Europe had nothing on the gentlemen who are in charge at San Domingo—in Hayti.

Hundreds of letters written by enlisted men to their folks back in the States never get further than the censor's wastebasket. They are keenly or wholly macerated before going that far.

Readers of the Herald will recall the interview given out by the late Theodore Roosevelt along in November of last year, which had to do, according to the former President with “President Wilson's private wars in San Domingo and Hayti.” Every effort I understand was made to keep this statement away from the islands.

And these efforts almost succeeded—almost but not quite. A copy of a Washington daily newspaper used in packing merchandise reached Puerto Plata just before Christmas, the man getting it advertising the fact that “Teddy had gone after the President. This article was widely read and commented upon.

Most of the officers who were in San Domingo when I was on the island were of the old stock of marines—fighting men every man of them. They couldn't understand why, when there were real doings over on “the other side” they were shunted down into the midst of a flock of “spiggoties” with nothing but bush fighting and bush whacking to relieve the monotony.

At one time it had been possible for the fighters to “go out on a jam and then shoot up a section of what ever town they happened to be stationed in. But this sort of pleasure is boreo” to amass a skinful of bad rum denied them now; less than a year ago a “no booze” order was promulgated from Washington. Rum is the chief aim of the Domincans. A license to dispose the fiery stuff costs something like $50 a year. Before one can seil cigars one must first pay the $400 license fee demanded. They grow what many consider the best tobacco in the world in San Domingo, too.

One buck private one who had been reduced from a top sergeancy for a reason that I will tell later on told me:—

“Why, there used to be lots of fun here. We had all night liberty and as soon as a fellow got away from the fort he could go down town, get properly jingled and then start shooting up the town. We never shot to hit any of the 'Spigs' but we did like to chase them inside of their houses. Then we would shoot up the electric lights which are lighted only when the moon is not shining. Sometimes one of the natives would take a shot at us; and then we would sure have a golrious time!”

SOME AMAZING TALES.

The marine came from a town within twelve miles of Pittsburgh. When I met him he was serving his third “hitch.” He was a rather talkative person and possessed a deadly hatred for Dominicans and things Dominican. And the same applied to Hayti and Haytians. He was with Butler and Waller when Hayti was first in would certainly stir up the good folks vaded; and the tales he told of what happened in that Negro republic of the States were they made public.

Here is one story told to me by a marine and which is offered here for what it is worth:

“I had a buddy,” said my friend, 'of whom I thought the world. We went through all the rough stuff in Hayti—and let me tell you it was some rought after we started to clean up. We worked together all the time we slept together and we fought for each other. I tell you, I thought more of that buddy than I did of any other living thing.

During the raid we made through Hayti when lots of our fellows were bumped off we made an agreement that if the Haytians got one of us the other would not rest until he had taken his revenge—had venged his pal's death.

And what made me go crazy after my friend was picked off in Puerto Prince by a skulking assassin was the fact that we had gone through hell and had come through alive. But an 'amigo' hiding behind the walls of an adobe shack got Tommie and then,—well I didn't care what became of me!

“That night I picked up a few tumblers of rum and after thinking the matter over decided I was going to start a little war of my own. You know how they do down in these countries; how they plaster on the talcum powder an inch thick and then start on their parades around the town square or plaza. Sometimes there is a band concert, and sometimes there isn't. But concert or no the natives keep milling and milling and milling, getting up a sweat the stench of which turns the stomach of any honest to goodness American who happens near them.

“The moon wasn't shinning the night I selected for action,” continued Jack the Avenger so I was in luck. I had determined to get as many blacks as it was possible to get before they got me. I firmly expected to go along with them; but I didn't care.

“At first I considered the idea of picking them off with a rifle. This would be too slow I decided; a machine gun would be better. And a chine gun it was.

“I got eighty-nine of them before a marine officer laid me out with a bump on the head, using his revolver to hand out the bump. There was excitement to peddle and for a time it looked as though there was going to be hell in general. You know we really were at war with those Haytians; they were killing us and we were killing them. I guess I was a bit hasty; but—well it was all in the game.

I was court martialled of course. But the action against me wasn't very spirited. Our fellows knew that the Haytians were taking advantage of every opportunity to bump off marines and that the greatest treachery was in evidence on their part at all times. That's why I guess I was let off with a mere reduction to the ranks.”

HE KILLED FIVE.

This same marine it was who killed five Domnicans in the streets of Santiago some time after his being transferred to that city. These victims were prisoners and were being used on street work near the fort which houses the American forces there.

Our friend was in charge of a bunch of six prisoners and was given a job of filling in a cut near the road leading up to the fort. Of the six 'Spigs' five wore political prisoners—men who had been found bearing arms or having arms in their homes. They had been acting ugly for some time and their guard was ordered to be on the quivive.

The break camp after the felons started to work. They went with a rush down San Luis street.

The marine said never aword. Swinging his automatic pistol from its holster at his side he began picking off the fugitives. Five shots were fired—five that's all. Five Dominicans were buried the next day.

It must not be understood that the Dominicans and marines are at it, all the time. Such is not the case. A month, two months may pass and there won't be a happening to disturb the serenity of the situation.

Again, it may be that there will be a spell during which the “bandits” as they are teremd, will evince all kinds of activity keeping the American fighters as well as their supporters the Guardia Naconal on the jump continuously.

For somehow or other, the Dominicans cannot reconcile themselves to the idea that they are getting a “square deal.” They resent the presence in their midst of an armed force representing an alien nation. They are intensely patriotic and belive they should be permitted to work out their own salvation.

“What mattres it” they argue. “if we do have our revolutions and kill one another off? Others spring up to take the places of the ones killed in battle. We have been happy in our ignorance for years; we have been patriotic; our sons and daughters have been brought up and educated. Why, then, should we be forced to suffer the presence of these armed men from the United States a country with which we are not at war?”

Peculiarly enough one cannot find any person in authority in the States who will admit that the government of Uncle Sam is “at war” with the Dominican government. Here's the way the matter was explained to me by a high official down in the island:

“At war? certainly not. The marines go everywhere and when they land, such a procedure does not mean that the United States has declared war upon the country invested. Of course, if the army landed men in a foreign country that would be different. But the marines—oh, my no! We're not at war with San Domingo!

According to the statement of a high Dominican official to the writer, the United States to use the vernacular, “pulled a boner” when the occupation of San Domingo was effected. Here's the story as I heard it.

REASON FOR THE “WAR.”

The President of the island was helped to glory by some of his over zealous fellow countrymen and a successor was needed.

At that time San Domingo had a “House and a “Senate.” The Senator representing Puerto Plata was well liked throughout the island and was the especial pet of his hometown people. Immediately he was selected to take the place of the murdered President. There were four years of the latter's term remaining.

The Puerto Plata man was not selected for these four years; rather he was placed in office on trial. He was given to understand that his tenure of office would depend upon himself. One year was the limit if he failed to “make good.” If, at the end of that year his administration of affairs had been satisfactory he would be reappointed for the remaining 3 years. However, Dominicans are all ambitious. Give them a taste of power and they are willing to fight for a mouthful of the same.

And so it was with the President by accident. After being in office for something like ten months he issued a manifesto announcing that he intended hanging onto the job and that he defied the powers of light and darkness—this meaning all of San Domingo—to oust him.

That defiance was the spark that ignited the train leading to the magazine. Immediately the Dominicans were up in arms.

“Can it be said,” they asked, “that this bad man whom we were gracious enough to permit to serve us shall now appoint himself our master. We the free people of San Domingo? Let it not be so. Down with the tyrant! Viva Libertad!”

First of all the usurper gathered about him a few hundred of his backers and proceeded to arm them. There was in the government arsenal a few pieces of antiquated artillery, among the lot two or three six pounders. The Puerto Platans, patriots and fighters, willing to brawl at the drop of a cigarette butt, were not slow in picking up the gauge of battle. They, too had arms—and what Dominican didn't? And so the war was on.

Some word of the threatening outbreak had reached Washington and orders had been despatched to the marine commander at Guantanamo, Cuba, to proceed forthwith to the Dominican coast and to stand by, ready for eventualities. Two separate contigents of “leathernecks” were sent—one to Puerto Plata and another to Monte Christi the latter city being the closest to the States and immediate to the Haytian coast.

The army of the President was encamped on a hill back of Puerto Plata when the United States forces drew into the harbor at that place. The usurper had issued an ultimatum giving the citizens of the city until two o'clock of that afternoon to surrender. A refusal on their part meant according to the President that the city would be shelled from the guns then in hand.

The American commander was apprised of these conditions. He despatched a courier to the President stating that the first gun fired would result in the landing of marines and the general cleaning out of the belligerents.

A HARD BLOW.

This was a body blow. The Dominicans had heard of the work of the marines in Hayti, their neighboring republic and they didn't hanker very keenly after any of the same.

But these island people are not given to showing the white feather. They are brave to foolishness; life to them means little as long as their honor remains unsullied and they are fighting for what they believe to be just and right.

And so it was with the man who wanted to remain as President. While he knew that he wouldn't stand as much chance as a wax cat in a certain warm climate, he nevertheless hesitated over agreeing to the terms offered by the representative of Uncle Sam—these being unconditional surrender.

Just there fate took a hand. The guns which were mounted to cover the city of Puerto Plata had not been fired for some time. The soldiers were aching to start something and they could not understand why the President did not order the war to begin.

One man after imbiding more than an ordinary man's share of rum began to cry. With tears coursing down his jetty cheeks he begged to know why this and that was so and why there had been no opportunity for himself and his mates to show their bravery, their skill with the big guns.

This thought became an obsession with the lachrymose one.

“By Cristofer Colon!” he ejaculated, “must I, whose forebears landed in this paradise of a land with the great discoverer stand by and listen to the orders of the Yankee dogs from another land? Let it not be so!”

A few minutes later this man had “begun the war.” Under cover of darkness he sidled up to one of the largest guns loaded the same with an explosive shell and bing! a house or two in the city had been unroofed and confusion came.

Hardly had the echo of this shot died away when the war ship in the harbor hopped into action. A slavo of six pounders was sent back into the hills and then to quote one of the marines who took part in the fracas, “there was hell to pay.”

Strangely enough—or was it strange?—the partiots who had been opposing the usurper's advance, turned in against the Yankees immediately the latter showed their teeth. Commanding the harbor at Puerto Plata is an old fort, a relic of Spanish days—a fort that is probably two hundred years old. It still is trong and formidable if well manned; and thither rushed the Dominicans to oppose the landing of the Americans.

LANDING THE MARINES.

Unfortunately the harbor is wide open, and prior to a year ago it was necessary to anchor at least a half mile out because of the shallow water. And this is what the marines were up against. As their boats left the war ship they were shining marks for the natives of the fort, and the fact that only a few of the Yanks were hit was due more to the poor aim of their enemies than to lack of opportunity to pick them off.

One thing that worried the American commander was the sight of a great gun mounted on a small hillock at the sea side of the fort. This looked as big as a six inch piece and as minute succeeded minute and there was no great shell sent hurling in their direction the Americans wondered why.

Orders were given the gunners aboard the war ship to “get that big gun,” and although a score or more efforts were made the big gun is still there. Afterward this gun was found to be of ancient vintage and out of commission.

At first the American commander was anxious to wound as few of the Dominicans as possible. Orders were to “shoot high” and the marines obeyed.

But the going became hotter and hotter until finally the gunners were instructed to place a few shells inside the fort. This they did with neatness and despatch and soon the fracas was terminated.

When the Yankee forces invested the city they at once took possession of the fort. Thier presence sent the Dominicans into a wild rage. Still the natives were helpless opposed to a superior force and a force that was armed with modern guns, with field pieces and with machine guns to peddle. What could they do?

In the meantime the force that had landed at Monte Christi was indulging in a forced march through the hills and over almost impassable roads to the direction of Santiago. They marched night and day resting only when the men were too tired to keep going. They reached their objective two or three days after Puerto Plata had been taken, and there was little or no trouble experienced in including the officials of the city to surrender.

This Santiago place is one of the show places of the island. In the business section of the city there is hardly a building that doesn't show the scars of battle. The old cathedral said to have been erected more than one hundred years ago flanks the public park on the south, while on the north is the barracks of the Guardian Nacional, a body composed of natives and performing functions something like those which fall to the lot of the New York or Pennsylvania State Constabulary. On the west of the park is the Governor's Palace and the City Hall. On the east is another church.

Most of these biuldings are built of wood and adobe, or concrete. The outer layer is of this plaster stuff and there is hardly a square foot of either the cathedral the barracks or the church that doesn't show signs of bullets and heavier shot. The cathedral in particular is riddled.

So, after taking the island San Domingo City, in the South, the capital of the republic having fallen without trouble the Americans had a proposition on thei rhands. Communication was had with Washington at once. The exact situation was made clear to the officials and instructions were asked for.

In the meantime some of the better class of Dominicans began to take heart. They were satisfied that their big brother of the North would see justice was meted out to them and that they would be permitted to select their President and to administer their own affairs. The usurping President would surely get what was coming to him. In fact, a demand was formally made that he who by this time was under the protection of the Stars and Stripes be turned over to his fellow countrymen that he might be properly punished.

Imagine then the disgust, the rage the manical fury of the islanders when came from Washington instructions to the American commander to see to it that the pretender to the Presidency be placed back in power, and held there by force of arms if necessary.

For that is exactly what happened the man who failed of the trust reposed in him; the man who treacherously betrayed his friends, his fellow countrymen and his country was thrust down the throats of a protesting people and held fast there by superior force.

The excuse has since been made so I was informed, that this “President” person had promised to see that the $20,000,000 of debt claimed by the United States would be paid. However, something must have happened for there is now no President in San Domingo, no Senators and not representatives. The United States military force is the “whole works.”

(N. Y. Herald, Sept. 14, 1919.)

records.full_text:
Our Dominican Correspondence.

City of St. Domingo, July 15, 1848.

Decree for the Organization of the Civic Guard—Requisition on Foreigners to Enroll themselves therein—Subsequent Modification of it in Regard to this Class of Residents—The Question of the Lawfulness of such a Requisition, under the Law of Nations, Briefly Considered—Steps taken to Obtain the Recognition of the Republic—A Ground of Difficulty in this Matter Stated.

A measure of some interest to foreigners resident here—United States citizens, as well as others—and on which action has just now begun to be taken, seems to demand some notice at the hand of your correspondent, if from no other American quarter.

Acting under the general authority conferred upon him by the article of the constitution noticed in my last letter, the President of this republic promulgated on the 22d of February last, a decree for the more effectual organization and enrollment of the civic guard, or militia, of the State. This document commences by declaring that all those persons who at the sound of the tocsin of alarm, by the proper authorities, shall not present themselves to take arms, shall be considered as suspected persons, and treated and punished as such, as the law or circumstances shall require. It further declares that foreigners who have entered the country, shall also form part of the civic guard after three months' residence therein. They, as well as the citizens, are allowed to choose in what arm to serve; their uniform and arms to be furnished at their own expense.

It is decreed that the civic guard shall appear under arms to pass review once every three months—namely, the first Sundays (the regular parade day) in January, April, July, and October respectively, and in all cases provided for by the laws, which includes the obligatory liability to march to the frontier, or into cantonment, in case of apprehended invasion; and, in short, to serve in any emergency, as militia may be required to do.

After entering into some details, which are unimportant to my present purpose, the decree proceeds to prescribe specific penalties for non-compliance with its requirements. Any member of the guard who shall not appear at the prescribed reviews, is to suffer, for the first delinquency, arrest and imprisonment—an arrest of twenty-four hours; for a second, double that length of time, and a very small pecuniary fine; and, for the third, in addition, he shall suffer the penalty of being incorporated into the troops of the line. No distinction is here made between citizens and mere foreign residents, who do not enjoy the rights pertaining to that character.

The promulgation of this decree caused great excitement among the foreign residents, who are almost exclusively of European origin; and the consular representative of France—the only European one here, and under whose protection most of the foreign residents from the old world range themselves—protested against its provisions as applicable to them, and, moreover, directed them not to comply with the mandate. The United States commercial agent, also, who resides at Puerto Plata, on the north side of the island, took ground against it; and besides sending for his deputy here, at the capital, for a list of whatever American citizens were resident here, he also sent directions to him to protest to the government against the requisitions of the decree, in case an intention on the part of the authorities to enforce it against citizens of the United States, should be manifested.

The opposition made to the right of enforcing this decree against foreign residents, made by the French functionary, had the effect to induce the President to modify its terms in reference to this class of the population, which he did in a supplemental decree, dated the 29th of March. In this latter, he states that the same penalties cannot be applied to foreigners who are required to enroll themselves in the civic guard; as to the natives,—nacionales—inasmuch, as by not being in the enjoyment of political rights, (in other words, not being citizens,) the former cannot be made to constitute a part of the permanent army. On this account, the penalty against them will be, for the first and second delinquencies, arrest and imprisonment in the Consistorial House—los arrestos en la casa Consistorial—and the small prescribed fines; and for the third, deprivation, or the withholding of patents, that is, licence to trade, &c., and of the right to exercise their profession or industry for the space of two years. The foreigners are further allowed by its provisions, to form a company by themselves, which shall constitute part of a battalion. And lastly, they are not to be required to march to the frontier, or other cantonment, even though occasion should arise for the mobilization, or calling forth and marching, of the civic guard. But they are required on such occasions only, to take arms in the place of their residence, and place themselves at the service of the government for the purpose of protecting their own (or its, as the peculiar construction of the Spanish language allows it with equal propriety to be translated, though the understanding of its meaning by the public here, is in accordance with the former construction,) interests and the public security. But whenever any of this company become citizens, they are to be transferred to other companies of the civic guard.

I have thus given a summary of the requisitions of the original decree, in connection with that of the subsequent and materially modified explanatory one, for the sake of preserving the historical connection of events and of illustrating the course of things here, and not for the purpose of casting odium or reproach on this government for an act which, though a flagrant contravention of personal rights of foreign residents, under the law of nations, was yet essentially modified on protest being made against it. But even as the law now stands, the decree, having all the binding force of one, there are, I conceive, serious objections to it on the same ground.

It is, I take it, a well settled, undisputed principle of what is called the private law of nations, that the foreign residents of a country, who have not acquired the rights and privileges of citizenship, according to its laws, while they owe the same obedience that natives do to the general municipal local laws, are, however, entirely exempt, of right, from all military service whatever; and that, in all cases of public disturbance or commotion—intestine or from without—they have the indefeasible right to stand neutral, and, in this character, to place themselves under the protecting folds of their country's flag at the consulate or embassy, as the case may be. The decree in question violates this principle. Undoubtedly, this government has the right to say, that foreigners resident in the country shall not be allowed to carry on trade or follow any other particular calling, unless they will serve in the militia. This is an act of sovereignty which, as such in the abstract, cannot, I suppose, be called in question, though its exercise is certainly contrary to the liberal spirit and enlightened practice of modern times. But to subject foreigners to arrest and fine—which latter, no matter how small, necessarily carries with it as a sanction the power to enforce its payment, either by imprisonment or the seizure and confiscation of property under process of law, to satisfy a claim to the State, the legality of which is altogether denied—is as manifest a violation of individual right, under the law of nations, if I am right in my view of the subject, as was the original decree, though by no means to the same objectionable extent. The representative of France is understood to have acquiesced in the terms of the supplementary decree, and this morning there was a general meeting of the foreign residents for the purpose of organizing their company by enrollment and the choosing of officers. Your correspondent, Mr. Herald, of course looked in on them. Uncle Sam was unrepresented, at least by any of his legitimate boys, whose number, at present here, lacks one, to tell the truth, of being sufficient to form a trio. If, instead of the form of a penalty—sanctioned decree or law—the call upon the foreigners had been in the form of an invitation and appeal to their chivalry or public spirit, our venerable and beloved uncle would certainly have been represented at the meeting by those "of his own flesh and blood." But it is, I believe, a characteristic trait of that worthy gentleman's male representatives, abroad as well as at home, that they won't be driven into a thing which cannot be rightfully required of them, though they may be led into it by reasonable request or solicitation. Like old Sir John—though, to say the truth, more ready generally to back their words by acts than was that worthy—"if reasons were as plenty as blackberries, they wouldn't give one on compulsion."

Notwithstanding the directions acknowledged to have been given, as before stated, no official opposition to the operation of this decree has, as yet, been made here in behalf of the United States' citizens. The writer contents himself, for the present, with this simple statement of the fact, reserving to himself the right to comment on it and its attendant circumstances in full, should occasion hereafter arise to call forth such comment.

The truth is, the United States ought to be represented here at the capital and principal port by an agent appointed directly by the department at Washington, and in immediate communication with it, and not by a deputy of the one so appointed and resident at Puerto Plata, which port, for all practical purposes, is farther removed from the capital than is Castine, in the State of Maine, from Corpus Christi, Texas. Nor are the facilities for secure and independent communication between this city and Puerto Plata as great as those, for the same purpose, between this and the port of New York.

Further, the interests of American citizens who may from time to time be temporarily resident here, ought to be more frequently and carefully looked to by the United States government than they have heretofore been. No American vessel of war has touched here for several years. Let the head of the navy department order one to do so; let him instruct her commander to enquire after resident American citizens and their interests, and whether any among them are denied any rights or exemptions which the law and usage of nations guaranty to the foreign residents of a country. Such a step, with such instructions faithfully carried out—as they certainly would be, if committed to any officer of the American navy—would have a most salutary and abiding effect. Such a visit, so far from creating ill feeling, the writer knows would be considered complimentary, while it would show that the American government is jealous of any infringement of the rights and privileges secured to its citizens by the code of nations, the nice prescriptions and distinctions of which, it is to be feared, the Spanish States of the new world do not always regard with the most scrupulous care.

This republic, now—since the 27th of February last—in the fifth year of its existence, has not yet been recognised by any nation. Soon after the establishment of the present government, a commissioner was sent to Washington, for the purpose of obtaining its recognition by the United States. He did not, however, succeed in effecting the object of his mission.

Since that time, this government has sent commissioners to Europe, to endeavor to obtain the recognition of the new republic by the courts of Spain, France, and Great Britain. The aim has ever been to first obtain its recognition by the first of these three governments. This is regarded as a very desirable, if not, indeed, a necessary preliminary to obtaining that of the other two, on account of the old unextinguished and unrenounced title to the crown of Spain to the territory of this, her ancient colony.

To make this clearly intelligible, it may be well to remark that, by the treaty of Basle, some half century since, the territory of the old Spanish portion of the island, now embraced within, and co-extensive with, the limits of this republic, was ceded to France, as I have stated in a former letter, who held possession until the year 1809 or 1810, when Spain again resumed her ancient title and possession, in virtue of the treaty of Paris, and continued thenceforward to hold it under the rule of royal governors appointed by the Crown, until the 30th of November, 1821, on or about which particular date the Spanish Governor was deposed in a popular insurrection, put on board a vessel, and sent home to Spain. The home government seems to have been too much occupied with other affairs to resent or notice this; at all events, this was the last governor sent out to rule the colony, and the inhabitants who had, on his expulsion, formed a provisional government, after much intestine and party strife, at last hoisted the Colombian flag. But that South American republic declining to receive within its territorial limits the proffered island colony, the inhabitants were again thrown back on their own governmental resources and abilities, and after many scenes of anarchy, they—or a faction of them, at least, for the thing is a matter of dispute here—invited Boyer to come and take possession of the country, which that dignitary responded to by marching his army to this city, as has been stated in a former letter, in the year 1822. The occupation by Hayti, thus commenced, continues the chain of overriding titles, by occupancy, down to the year 1844, the era of its separation from that republic, and of its erection into the present independent Dominican republic.

This brief historical recapitulation—in some respects more complete than the account I have previously given—shows the foundation and present state of the old Spanish title to the territory of this republic; a title which has been so long and so frequently over-ridden without protestation, by supervening ones, as to be now buried, one would suppose, almost beyond the power or reach of resurrectionary resuscitation. I have said, without protestation. That is not altogether correct for the whole of the above period, as will appear by the following historical anecdote, which I have from good authority, and repeat, partly to preserve a historical fact of which there is, I believe, no record existing, on this side of the ocean at least, save among the musty public archives at Port au Prince, and partly to illustrate the political astuteness of the shrewd Haytien chief, Boyer. In or about the year 1827, the King of Spain sent an envoy, one Senor De Castro, to Port au Prince, to formally demand of President Boyer the surrender to the Spanish crown of this part of the island, at that time constituting, as has been seen, a part of the Haytien republic. To his demand, made at an interview held for that purpose, the cunning black chief replied that he had taken possession of it, at the solicitation of its inhabitants; but that he was willing and disposed to refer the question back to them, whether they would remain as they were, an integral portion of the Haytien republic, or return under the dominion of the crown of Spain. If they should decide by their popular voice, in favor of the latter course, he had no objection to their adopting it. No decided offence could be taken at a so seemingly fair proposition; while, at the same time, the envoy knew as well as President Boyer did, what would be the result if the matter were to be submitted to this method of decision; for a large majority of the present citizens were recently emancipated slaves, and those who sympathized with them from being of the same color and of a similar class; and these would, of course, have an equal voice with other classes of citizens, in deciding the question, which, to the emancipated portion of them, would be no less than a question of continued freedom, or return to servitude under Spanish masters. The envoy hereupon took his leave, and the demand was prosecuted no further.

The last despatches, within the writer's knowledge, received by this government from their commissioners in Europe, were of the date of November last, from Madrid, in which they express themselves as entertaining strong hopes of obtaining the recognition of the republic. It had, in fact, some time previous, been expressly promised by the Spanish minister; but his displacement very soon after, and the successive changes that rapidly followed each other, of a similar kind, had thus far delayed and prevented the termination of the negotiation.

As to the recognition of this republic by the government of the United States, that is a question for the authorities at Washington, in their wisdom, to determine for themselves. I do not feel called upon, nor indeed am I disposed at present, to state what the opinion of so humble an individual as myself may be on this subject. I have thus far contented myself mainly with stating facts and circumstances of various kinds, leaving those who may read them—be they in authority or otherwise—to draw their own conclusions on this as on other points. There, at least, so far as regards this particular question, I shall stop for the present. Hereafter, I may perhaps present my views, whatever they may be, on the point in consideration, supported by as good reasons as a somewhat favorable and tolerably well improved opportunity for arriving at correct conclusions will have enabled me to bring together.

records.summary_en: The newspaper reported that when Santo Domingo faced an imminent crisis and appealed to the United States for protection during an ongoing annexation negotiation, the U.S. Administration notified Haytian authorities that an invasion would be regarded as unfriendly to the U.S. until Congress decided on the treaty. Additionally, the President sent American warships into Dominican waters at the request of the Dominican Government, which successfully prevented conflict and kept the peace between Hayti and Santo Domingo without firing a shot or landing sailors on Haytian territory.
records.summary_es: El periódico refirió que, al afrontar Santo Domingo una crisis extrema y acudir en demanda de auxilio a los Estados Unidos durante las tratativas de anexión, el gobierno de Washington advirtió a las autoridades de Haití de que cualquier invasión sería juzgada como un acto inamistoso contra los Estados Unidos hasta tanto el Congreso se pronunciase sobre el tratado. Asimismo, el mandatario destacó buques navales estadounidenses en aguas dominicanas a instancias del gobierno de Santo Domingo, logrando disuadir las hostilidades y preservar la paz entre ambas naciones insulares sin haber efectuado un solo disparo ni desembarcado marinería en suelo haitiano.

records.full_text:
THE SAN DOMINGO QUESTION.

WHAT PRESIDENT GRANT HAD TO DO WITH IT.

To the Editors of the Boston Daily Advertiser:

The annexation of San Domingo is not at present a party question. The Philadelphia platform did not endorse it. The Cincinnati and Baltimore did not oppose it. The New York Tribune has heretofore favored it. Other Liberal and Democratic papers have been neutral in regard to it.

* * * * * * * * *

In his farewell speech on the Presidential election, Senator Sumner made the following specific charges against the President:

1. That he had perpetrated an outrage upon Hayti and menaced her independence with war, in violation of international law.

2. That he kept our navy hovering on the Haytian coast "like a hawk sailing in air," and has employed United States ships of war, at great expense, in maintaining "the usurper Baez" in power, thus acting in flagrant violation of the Federal Constitution.

3. That, through his agents, he has connived at and prolonged the imprisonment of Mr. Hatch, "an American citizen," and that Hatch was "immured" because it was feared that, if released, he would write against annexation.

4. That he has insulted Frederick Douglass, first because Mr. Douglass was excluded from the Commissioners' table on board of a Potomac steamer, and again because Mr. Douglass was omitted from an invitation to a dinner given to the Commissioners at the Presidential mansion.

The facts are briefly these:

Spanish Santo Domingo comprises two thirds (22,000 square miles) of the island.—The Government de facto, through its Minister Plenipotentiary, formaily applied to President Grant three years ago; proposing annexation to the United States as a territory, upon the sole condition of our assuming its national indebtness, which was estimated as a million and a half dollars. The President, before entertaining the proposition, sent down his private secretary, Gen. Babcock, ann honorable and reliable man, to ascertain the competency and stability of the Dominician Government, the sentiment of the Dominican people in regard to annexation, the amount of the debt, and the value of the territory. Being fully satisfied upon all these points, two treaties were negotiated by the State Department—one for the lease of the peninsula and magnificent Bay of Samana at a rent of $150,000 a year, the other for the annexation of the whole country; the former to terminate upon the ratification of the latter, and both subject to the approval of Congress. The matter was brought before Congress in due time, and an annexation was recommended by the President, sustained by facts and arguments which have since been reiterated and sustained by the report of the Commissioners appointed to investigate the subject.

These negotiations were frank and explicit. So far from shunning publicity, the President called in person upon Senator Sumner at his own house, and in presence of Colonel Forney, asked for his co-operation. Mr. Sumner returned an evasive answer, which both the President and Col. Forney understood to be affirmative and favorable. Soon afterwards, without previous remonstrance, without any effort to induce the Administration to forego or modify its plans, Senator Sumner publicly assailed the Administration and the President as guilty of a violation of all laws, human and divine.

1. The alleged outrage upon Hayti occurred as follows: No sooner was it known that a negotiation for annexation was pending than preparations were made by the Haytian authorities to invade their feeble neighbor, instigated to this course by the deplomatic representatives of certain European Powers, who were jealous of American suprmacy. Hayti, which comprises less than one-third of the island (10,000 square miles,) has repeatdly sought to subjugate the whole (32,000 square miles.) She feared that Santo Domingo would forever escape from her clutches. The population of Hayti (500 000) is four fold that of Santo Domingo (125,000,) and is governed by a military despotism under the forms of a republic. Hayti was possessed of an armed steamer. The seaports of Santo Domingo, protected by only two small schooners, were liable too bombardment. The crisis was iminent, and the Government of Santo Domingo appealed to our Government for protection against a danger growing out of this very negotiation. Congress was not in session at the time.

What did the Administration do? Just this: In the interest of peace and humanity it notified the Haytian authorities that a preliminary treaty of annexation had been negotiated, and that, until Congress should have expressed its decision, an invasion of the Dominician territory by any foreign Power would be regarded as an act unfriendly to the United States.

Was this an outrage? Was it a violation of international law? So far from it, any fair-minded man, no matter what his views concerning annexation may be, would say that it was a duty. To have done less or to have done otherwise, under the circumstances, would have been a base desertion of the gallant little nation whose only crime was its aspiration to merge itself in the great American Republic.

2. With a sagacious knowledge of human nature, the President prevented any necessity of forcible intervention, and kept the peace between Hayti and Santo Domingo, by sending several American vessels of war (which would otherwise have been cruising at equal expense in the Mediterranean or upon the South American coast) not into Haytian, but into Dominician waters, at the request of the Dominician Government. Not a gun was fired, not a sailor was landed upon Haytian territory. Nor was the Dominician Government, which Senator Sumner so insultingly terms "the usurper Baez," upheld by our fleet. No American interference in the internal affairs of Santo Domingo was offered, nor would it have been welcomed.—The presence of American vessels was valued only as an evidence of sympathy and as a guaranty against foreign invasion; their subsequent withdrawal in deference to the clamor of the opposition was followed by no popular uprising. The Government of President Baez, after the lapse of years, is to-day stronger and more popular than ever. Was it a violation of international law for the Russian fleet to visit the harbor of New York? Just as much so, and no more, was the weicome presence of American ships of war in the Bay of Mansanillo and the port of Santo Domingo!

3. The Congressional committee of investigation have demonstrated that Mr. Hatch, though a native of Connecticut, afterwards claimed that he was a naturalized subject of Spain. Being a resident of Santo Domingo he was subject, as such, to Dominician laws, and was legally tried and sentenced to death for actual participation in civil war and revolution. Nevertheless, at the intercession of the American Consul, his sentence was commuted to imprisonment, and he was finally released at the request of our Government. The Dominician authorities frankly avow that his imprisonment was prolonged by them because they did not choose to be subject to his calumnies. This they had a perfect right to do, nor had we any right to insist upon his release.

The appointment of Mr. Douglass as a Secretary of the Commission was an honor, not an insult. Every one who accompanied the Commissioners will testify that he was treated by the Commissioners with the consideration and respect to which he is so justly due. He was one of the five or six gentlemen who dined with the Commissioners at the Captain's table on board the Tennessee, to which most of the correspondents and members of the scientific corps could not be admitted for want of room. While on the island Mr. Douglass resided with the Commissioners, and accompanied them upon the most intimate and confidential footing. Just before reaching Washington the Captain of a Potomac steamer, over whom the Commissioners had no control, refused to allow Mr. Douglass a seat at his table, whereupon the Commissioners and every member of their party, with one exception, resented the insult by leaving the table.—That exception, by a singular coincidence, was a reporter of the New York Tribune, who retained his seat. But no one charges the Tribune with having insulted the colored race in the person of Mr. Douglass.—The only reason why Mr. Douglass was not invited by the President to dine with the Commissioners was that Mr. Douglass was not one of the Commissioners. But let Mr. Douglass speak for himself. He says:

"I never was received by any gentleman in the United States with more kindness, more cordiality, I may say with more confidence—never felt more at home in the presence of any gentleman—than I have in the presence of this true and steady man. You know what he is to-day what he was yesterday and what he will be to-morrow, for he does not turn with every wind of doctrine, and for that reason we want him."

Since Mr. Sumner has made so great a mistake in the case of Mr. Douglass, the public may well pause before crediting the other charges which are contradicted by the three Commissioners—viz: Dr. Samuel G. Howe, Hon. B. F. Wade and Hon. A. D. White—also by Hon. Allen C. Burton, Frederick Douglass, General Sigel, Major Hazzard, Dr. Necomb and many other gentlemen who acocmpanied the Commission. Such charges, if made by men of less eminence, would be severely characterized. As it is, they constitute a case of misconception and consequent misstatement unparalleled in our political history.

The great grossness of the charges will create a reaction of the public mind. I confess that my own regard for the character and services of President Grant is stirred into enthusiasm by my keen sense of the scandalous injustice of aspersions which he has too much self-respect and reticence to deny. But above all, I feel indignant at the opprobrium which has been cast upon the Government and people of San Domingo, who deserve better treatment from the friends of the colored race.

Respectfully,

HENRY B. BLACKWELL.

Boston, September 10, 1872.

records.full_text:
Interesting Intelligence from Hayti and St. Domingo.

By Captain McIntyre, of the schooner Enterprise, arrived on Monday night, in eleven days, from Cape Haytien, we have been furnished with the following items of news:—

The Emperor of the Republic of Hayti had issued an edict, to take effect on the 5th instant, that no foreign merchant should do business unless he paid a license of $1800, Spanish, per year, in place of $900, as heretofore; or any foreign clerk, unless he paid $1000. No vessel was allowed to take cargo, unless she had discharged her cargo at that port. The export duty on coffee and logwood was $50, Haytien money, per 1000 pounds, instead of $5, as heretofore; and in the same ratio on all merchandise. He has fixed a price on all goods imported and exported. He was raising an army to march against the Spanish part of the island. Business was very dull.

We learn from Capt Morton, of the schooner Jane and Eliza, which arrived yesterday from Port au Prince, (having left that port on the 20th ult..) that the government had just paid to the French a portion of the interest of the indemnity.

A meeting was to take place, to take into consideration the better mode of equalising the distribution of coffee. Export duties are to be increased on coffee and logwood. American provisions are getting scarce. The articles of British manufacture having been burnt by the disastrous fire on the 14th, the articles of first necessity, such as checks, osnaburgs, and finer goods, were on the decrease and scarce.

The Haytien squadron left on the 20th, destination unknown, supposed to be for Jacmel.

Capt. M. also informs us, that the Emperor was to have marched on the 18th, with his whole army, for the Spanish part of the Island.

The French frigate Naide was lying at Port au Prince, waiting orders. The British brig of war Persian, was to sail for the city of St. Domingo on the 20th ult.

PROCLAMATION.

Buenaventura Baez, President of the Dominican Republic, to the Haytiens!

HAYTIENS!—The new President of the Republic of Dominica addresses you, in the name of his fellow-citizens, and in the common interest of all. It is now nearly six years ago that we separated from you, and declared ourselves independent; and this separation, in spite of false assurances to the contrary, is destined to be an eternal one. We may yet live as good neighbors, though under different banners. We have invited you to do this, by proposing a peace, which is necessary to all our interests; but those who rule over you have rather preferred to force you to leave your homes to fight against us, and doomed you to be shot, as many of you as were unwilling. Recollect your sufferings in the last campaign, which our brave Santanna terminated so gloriously, and consider what confidence can you have in men who called your defeat a victory! We have never attacked you; we have contented ourselves with defending ourselves against aggression, in the hope that you would imitate our moderation. But patience becomes sometimes exhausted; and since you would not have peace, now, then, in your turns, support all the sufferings of war on your own soil—on your properties—on your persons. When we wish to attack you, we know well our advantages and your weakness. We can hurt you as much as will suit you, both by sea and on your rivers. While we only have three cities on our coast—Saint Domingo, Puerto Plata, and Samona, cities well fortified and secure from attack—your shores are covered with innumerable villages, villas, plantations, towns, and cities, built of wood, without any defence offering themselves an easy prey to flames and pillage. Your cities are going to disappear, and their inhabitants to be driven into the woods. Haytiens! Our fleet, well armed, well equipped, well commanded, having numerous troops on board, has set sail to pillage your coast and intercept your shipping. Watch, then, night and day. Watch on the North, on the West, on the South. Drive your wives and children into the morasses; abandon your fields, to keep guard on the tops of the rocks—your guns in your hands in the wind and the rain—and then when you go home you will find your houses burnt down. You know all these sufferings already. You suffer already, dreadfully by this war. To it you owe the odious monopoly which ruins you, and the tyranny you labor under. See, then, what you will still suffer, if you continue this war. Haytiens! We might live in peace and happiness, each on our own territory, making a mutual exchange of our cattle and tobacco for your coffee; but your rulers will not have it so. Well, then, be it so! Let all the horrors of war fall upon their heads, and upon yours, who will not force them to better measures.

By the President, BUENAVENTURA BAEZ.

Minister of War, J. E. AYBAR.

St. Domingo, Nov. 16, 1849,
