records.full_text:
Affairs in San Domingo.

OUR SAN DOMINGO CORRESPONDENCE.

SAN DOMINGO, April 27, 1857.

Collision of American and Dominican Vessels—Arrest of the American Captain—His Sentence and Abandonment of his Schooner—A Call on the United States Cabinet.

We have an excellent case on account of the interference of this government with us. They abuse the Yankees here with impunity, and this is an excellent chance for redress.

It appears that some seven weeks since the American schooner Charles Hills, Captain Smith, bound from Mayaguez for this port, during the night came in collision with the Dominican packet schooner and stove her badly. The American schooner came in here, and when ready for sea was refused a pass and the captain summoned to appear before a court. He was sentenced to pay the sum of $3,300 for “wilfully running into and damaging the Dominican packet.”

Now, every one knows that the captain was right, being on the starboard tack and on a wind, whereas the other had his larboard tack aboard and from the wind; therefore he should have kept off and not crossed the bows of the American. This any Marine Court would allow, but here he was condemned without a trial, and not being able to pay was sentenced to a year's imprisonment. He (Captain Smith,) has abandoned his vessel to the Dominican government, and looks at home for redress. It is one of the most urgent cases ever heard of, and a complete burglary and robbery on their part. They even now laugh at our threats. Only to think of it. A petty government like this. It is too bad. I am in hopes for a time to come to correct all.

We have received the Gaceta Oficial of Santo Domingo to May 4.

The American schooner Charles Hill, Captain Albert Smith, had come in collision with the Dominican packet schooner named the Nineteenth of March; and the Charles Hill having run in to San Domingo was detained, and the captain sentenced to pay $3,100 for wilfully running into and damaging the Dominican packet. We find the following documents, in reference to the case, published under the head of “official:”—

THE UNITED STATES COMMERCIAL AGENT TO THE MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS.

COMMERCIAL AGENCY OF THE UNITED STATES, CITY OF SAN DOMINGO, March 13, 1857.

SIR—You will find herewith the protest of Mr. Albert Smith, Captain of the American schooner Charles Hill, against the Dominican authorities, and which is to lead the way to proceedings for illegal and unjust detention. I am, sir, &c. JONATHAN ELLIOTT.

To the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Dominican Republic.

THE DOMINICA MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS TO THE AMERICAN COMMERCIAL AGENT.

Mr. AGENT—My government has been ignorant of your return and entering on the discharge of your functions. Entrusted ad interim to Mr. Jacob Pereyra on account of your not having notified my government thereof in an official manner. Nevertheless, on receiving your note of the 18th, accompanied by the protest of Capt. Smyth, I have brought it to the notice of the government, for the proceedings to which it may give rise.

It is proper for me to say that if the Captain had only availed himself of the means of conciliation to which he was invited, it is more than probable that that question would have had a solution as speedy as it would have been peaceable, but being obstinate in his refusal, it became necessary to submit the matter to the common tribunals, to be decided by them in conformity with the laws.

I also believe that it would have been more effectual for him to show before the tribunal, which had charge of the matter, the illegal proceedings and injustices of which the captain complains, that being impartially examined they might be redressed or declared null. I am, &c. FELIX M. DELMONTE.

SAN DOMINGO, March 16, 1857.

THE UNITED STATES COMMERCIAL AGENT TO THE DOMINICAN MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS.

SENOR MINISTER:—The tribunal of the first instance, of this district, has granted judgment against Capt. Albert Smith of the American schooner Charles Hill, for injury done to the Dominican packet 19th of March, in a collision, amounting, with cost, to some $3,160, and from which decision the Captain will not appeal.

I desire now to know, and beg of you to inform me, whether the American schooner Charles Hill and its crew will be detained, or its voyage prevented in this port, to the injury and loss of its owners, until such time as the Captain shall have complied with the judgment, or until the same shall have been exacted? JONATHAN ELLIOTT.

To the MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS.

THE DOMINICAN MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS TO THE AMERICAN COMMERCIAL AGENT.

SAN DOMINGO, March 27, 1857.

SIR—I have the honor to acknowledge the receipt of your official note of this day, in which, after assuring me that Capt. Smith will not avail himself of the resource of appeal which the laws permit him to do, you ask to be informed whether his voyage, or that of his crew, will be prevented before the execution of the sentence of the tribunal of first instance.

I assure you that the government has no other action over matters submitted to the tribunals than the interest of having the laws fulfilled, or distributing justice impartially, without meddling in any manner in decrees or their execution. Therefore, the tribunal alone is able to answer the question submitted by you, in determining whether it will accept bail. I am, &c. FELIX M. DELMONTE.

To the COMMERCIAL AGENT OF THE UNITED STATES.

THE COMMERCIAL AGENT DEMANDS RESTITUTION, ETC.

COMMERCIAL AGENCY OF THE UNITED STATES, April 17, 1857.

SIR:—It was brought to my notice yesterday that Mr. Albert Smith, captain of the American schooner Chas. Hill, of Portsmouth, was to be condemned on the 18th to two years imprisonment in the public prison of this city, against which sentence and proceedings I solemnly protest as unjust.

The accusation against the Captain for having wilfully injured the Dominican packet “19th of March” is irrational.

The schooner Charles Hill has been anchored here six weeks, and as it has not been copper fastened, it is so much injured that it will require a large outlay to repair it.

Consequently, as commercial agent of the United States, I ask in the name and on the belief of the owners or shippers of the said vessel the sum of $5,000 from the government of the Dominican republic, to be paid or secured before the 22d inst., and also the freedom of the vessel and its crew to depart hence on that date.

The undersigned regrets extremely the occurrence of this thing, and his being forced to this disagreeable duty, and takes this occasion to express to the honorable Minister, &c., JONATHAN ELLIOTT.

THE MINISTER'S REPLY.

Mr. AGENT—My government has seen with extreme regret your note of 17th inst., substantially affirming that the proceeding against Captain Albert Smith, who through recklessness, negligence, or some other unfavorable cause, ran into and injured the Dominican packet, is unreasonable, and that the detention of the vessel is, in your judgment, equal to a loss of $500.

Neither the fact itself nor the consequent detention of the vessel can be unreasonable without acknowledging a theory fatal to all nations. 1st. That wrongs committed at sea do not constitute crime nor carry responsibility for the losses occasioned; and 2d, That the republic has no jurisdiction to take cognizance of these acts.

In reference to the first it does not even admit of discussion, and the second contains the first, because in denying jurisdiction to the republic, it must be denied to every government, and therefore there being no jurisdiction anywhere in the world to decide these controversies would establish impunity.

If the act had taken place on the coasts of the republic, in one of her ports both vessels rode for the first time since the event, and the aggrieved party presented its formal complaint, it is evident that the jurisdiction is in this republic and in no other, and that the government in having submitted the question to the tribunals has done wrong to no one.

To disregard, as Captain Smith has disregarded, the right of appeal—to resort to the extraordinary course of international resources—and that against the government which invited him several times to the frankest settlement, is to reveal the desire of recurring to force, and not to the means which universal reason has accepted and sanctioned. Such a fatal precedent being permitted, it would be impossible for the civil power to decide questions between two foreigners.

If the act in question had occurred between an American and an English vessel, the American Captain denying the jurisdiction, and the English captain demanding justice, how could he evade the international demand? In no way, because the one would be described as abuse of power or the other a denial of justice.

After these observations you will admit that your demand is not founded in reason. The government regrets that your pretensions are not acceptable, and trusts to the enlightenment and rectitude of the government of the United States for the approval of its moderate and just proceedings in the present question.

SAN DOMINGO, April 21, 1857.

The commercial agent of the United States, in another letter of April 23, notified the Minister that at noon that day the schooner Charles Hill would be abandoned to the authorities.

records.headline: HAYTI.
records.summary_en: According to *The Liberator*, Boyer agreed to pay France an indemnity of 150,000,000 francs to prevent further bloodshed, after which France and other European powers acknowledged Haiti's independence, though U.S. recognition was blocked by the influence of slaveholders. Around the time Herard was elected president of the island, the Spanish part declared independence from the legitimate government, and subsequent presidents—Guerrier and Perriot—failed to bring the revolters back to their allegiance. Additionally, when Dominican agents were dispatched to the U.S. government for aid about two years prior, the application was coldly received by Mr. Upshur.
records.summary_es: A juicio de *The Liberator*, Boyer consintió en abonar a Francia una indemnización de 150.000.000 de francos para evitar nuevos derramamientos de sangre, tras lo cual Francia y otras naciones europeas admitieron la independencia haitiana, si bien el reconocimiento estadounidense fue frustrado por la influencia de los propietarios de esclavos. Coincidiendo con la proclamación de Hérard como mandatario insular, la sección española proclamó su separación del gobierno legítimo, y los presidentes que le sucedieron —Guerrier y Pierrot— no consiguieron restituir a los sublevados a su antigua subordinación. Se recordaba asimismo que, cuando emisarios dominicanos fueron destacados unos dos años antes ante el gobierno estadounidense en demanda de socorro, la pretensión fue acogida con frialdad por el Sr. Upshur.

From the Boston Journal.

HAYTI.

Mr. Sleeper—Since the return of Mr. Hogan from his secret mission to St. Domingo, a strong disposition has been manifested to learn the result of his researches.

The Washington correspondents of several northern journals, with a view of gratifying curiosity, have drawn largely upon what they understand to be the substance of his report. These communications have given an impression that a splendid arrangement for 'mutual benefit,' is nearly completed with the Eastern part of St. Domingo. One writer expresses surprise that Mr. Hogan should have found in that region a population of 190,000, including 130,000 whites.

His astonishment is certainly natural, for the majority of those 190,000 are men in buckram suits and Kendal green.

According to the census taken in 1825, the eastern division contained less than 65,000, all told: at this moment, it may possibly number 80,000, including 5 or 6,000 whites.

Another writer, in alluding to the mission, luxuriates upon the idea of annexing the whole island. He considers it the most delightful country which the sun has shown upon since the garden of Eden went out of cultivation, and descants philosophically upon the 300 millions of pounds of coffee which we might wring out of its soil. But before we proceed to acknowledge the independence of the Dominicans or to reckon the precise value of 300 million pounds of coffee, perhaps it may be well to turn over a few pages of the checkered history of St. Domingo, and learn something of the relations which subsist between the parties.

Possibly nothing injurious may immediately grow out of this tampering with the enemies of a friendly foreign power; but that an effort will be made hereafter to carry out the views of the secret agent, there exists not a doubt.

In the absence of a stronger arm, (which might, perhaps, draw a 'shining blade for Greece,' but decline a cause not tinged with romance,) we dip our 'tea-spoon in Niagara,' and proceed to notice briefly some of the peculiarities which mark this business; and a few of the calumnies and misrepresentations which have been circulated in relation to an unoffending government, and a harmless and afflicted people

In the first place, there is no ground for the common opinion, that the Dominicans were originally annexed to the government of the French part—against their consent. It is not true that they were conquered, beaten down, trampled upon, and crushed, before they were united with the Haytiens; the very reverse of all this was the case, as we shall attempt to show.

In 1821, at the time of Christophe's death, Boyer was called to the Presidency by the united voices of the Haytiens. At that period, the Spanish part of the Island was independent, but its situation was most precarious. The war between Spain and her revolted provinces in South America was at its height and the Columbian privateers which thronged the Caribbean seas were continually plundering the people along the shores of the Spanish part; moreover, there were many persons in that division of the Island, who were inclined to favor an union with the patriots of South America—but by far the greatest number opposed this suggestion. Such was the state of things at the commencement of Boyer's government. After maturely reflecting upon the difficulties by which they were surrounded, the feeble government of the Spanish part sought protection in an union with the Haytiens, and Boyer was formally solicited by them to grant his consent to the annexation of the Eastern part to the Republic of Hayti. The request was complied with, and the Eastern portion became a part and parcel of that Republic, as much so as Massachusetts now is of this Union. Thus it appears that the Dominicans adopted the Haytien Government, not only voluntarily but joyfully. Shortly after this, the French (with an overwhelming force in the harbor of Port au Prince) demanded an indemnity for the property sacrificed in the Revolution. The people of the country had 'supped full of horrors,' and Boyer, to prevent further bloodshed and destruction of property, agreed to the payment of 150,000,000 of francs; the independence of Hayti was then acknowledged by France and other European powers. A vigorous attempt was made to obtain a similar acknowledgement from the United States, but the interest of slaveholders prevailed against it, and nothing was effected.

About three years since, Herard was elected President of the Island. This was the signal in the Spanish part for a separation from the legitimate Government, and they declared themselves independent of it. It does not appear that this movement was caused by the election of Herard, or from a conviction that his course would be a bad one—for what his policy would be was not known. It proved, however, disastrous enough, although some of his worst acts were consequent upon the rebellion, and not the cause of it; still it has been urged by many that Herard's impolitic course was the great cause of discontent. If it were so, it may be asked why Guerrier and Perriot, his successors and opposites in everything, have been unable to induce the revolters to return to their allegiance.

About two years since, agents were despatched by the Dominicans to our Government for aid of some sort. The application was coldly received by Mr. Upshur, which, considering the influences by which he was surrounded, was somewhat remarkable. After the death of Mr. Upshur, the application was renewed, and the nullifiers of the Spanish part found a kindred spirit in Mr. Calhoun, the successor of Mr. Upshur. To Mr. Calhoun belongs the distinguished honor of sending a secret agent to a small discontented portion of another republic, to ascertain whether the dissolution of an Union, contrary to the Constitution of the country, and in opposition to nine-tenths of its inhabitants, was an act which this Government ought to encourage, in order to prove that blacks are not competent to maintain their rights even in their own country, if indeed they are supposed to have any rights anywhere. To be sure, we are told of the advantages to be derived from a trade with the 80,000 Dominicans, provided we acknowledge her independence—but who believes this to have been an incentive to our Government in this movement? The commerce of our country has long had little of its care—had it been otherwise, millions of dollars might have been saved in our trade by making the slight concession to the Haytien Government which was asked for during the administration of General Jackson. It is notorious that for the last twenty-four years, goods imported into Hayti in American vessels have been subject to and have actually paid an extra duty of ten per cent, beyond that charged by vessels of other nations. The interest of the country has been thus sacrificed to gratify the refined notions of our Southern brethren.—'Aristocratic England' could acknowledge the independence of Hayti, and by so doing, compass an immense trade, which naturally belonged to us—but 'Democratic America' had 'a peculiar institution' * to which the commerce of the country was made subservient. Does any one imagine the prospect of future business with eighty thousand Dominicans induced the secret mission? Why, an untrammeled trade with one million of Haytiens, under a regular government, had not been deemed worthy of the slightest consideration.

* Although we cannot but feel that Slavery speaks to this Republic as prophetically as did the ghost of Cæsar to the ill-starred Brutus, yet we allude to its existence amongst us, only incidentally, being well satisfied that a few demagogues, who rejoice in Slavery at home, and forge fetters for other lands, do not represent our Southern brethren any nearer than the rabid 'one idea' Abolitionist does the people of New England.

But we are told that the Haytiens are cruel, blood-thirsty and barbarous—Christophe is held up as an evidence of the fact. It is true that the black chief was a great rascal—so was Napoleon, in about the same way; the former, however, merely sprinkled the avenue to his citadel with blood, to perpetuate his rule in his own country, whilst the latter waded through seas of slaughter to subjugate other nations. Napoleon was of course the most popular man, for it is a great and philanthropic truth that

'One murder makes a villain—
Millions, a hero.'

The Haytiens universally hold in utter detestation the memory of the villain; whilst the refined French almost forget Heaven in the remembrance of the hero.

The successor of Christophe, as has been stated, was Boyer, the first President of the Island. It does not suit those who consider a colored Republic an anomaly, to speak of his Government. The truth is, that, during his administration of twenty years, there was less taking of responsibility on the part of the Executive, less corruption amongst the officers, less plundering of the treasury, and a more hearty contempt for repudiation, than was seen in this country during the same period. Why, then, it may be asked, has not the Island prospered in a greater degree? Why is not the French indemnity entirely paid? Let it be remembered, that the country has suffered, in many ways, from its efforts to meet its obligation to the French honorably. They did not over estimate their ability, at the time the debt was contracted; but, since that period, the produce of the Island has declined in value at least two-thirds. Moreover, the losses, (both public and private,) by fires in the principal towns, have been immense. Added to these, the earthquake of 1842 deluged and completely destroyed the Cape, and nearly every town in the North. These calamities could not all have been avoided. The President might, perhaps, have checked the decline of Coffee throughout the world, and forbade the fires, but he could not veto the earthquake.

On the score of indolence, the Haytiens may be justly chargeable, but in no greater degree than the inhabitants of the other islands. We must not go within the tropics, amongst the children of the sun, to find the characteristics of the New-Englander and the Scotchman. It is very true that the capabilities of Hayti have not been taxed to the utmost; the resources of such countries are never fully developed by voluntary labor. How much rice would the Carolinians 'wring' from their swamps with their own hands?

As regards the other, and more important attributes of the people, in the interior, (who have been denounced as 'blood-thirsty barbarians,') it may safely be affirmed that the peasantry of the Island, particularly in the North, will compare favorably with the cultivators of any country, for mildness, hospitality, and freedom from vice. Their opportunities, however, for religious and moral teaching have been slender—circumstances have deprived them of these blessings, except in a very limited degree.

Our missionaries have gladdened nearly every benighted spot,

'From Greenland's icy mountains
To India's coral strand.'

But it is a melancholy fact that Hayti has been overlooked. A million of people at our very door-stone have been permitted to grope in comparative darkness.* How far this neglect is to be attributed to the contemptuous tone of our Government toward these Islanders, may be inferred by those who are familiar with American missionaries.

In the present state of things, a manifest disposition on the part of the United States to aid the Dominicans would lead to difficulty. Not only would the measure be considered by the world as anti-republican, ungenerous and unjust, but on the miserable score of policy, it would prove perplexing and dangerous in the extreme. It is well known that the French King entertains the best feelings towards the Haytiens, and that the most liberal indulgence as to the payment of the indemnity has lately been granted by him, with the kindest expressions of good will. France will not allow us to tamper with her debtor with impunity; and by an ill-timed, impertinent interference with another Government, destroy her chance for the recovery of her claim. A difference with the French, however, is less to be shunned than the foul dishonor which would attach itself to the act of robbing a Government less powerful than our own, of the fairest portion of its territory.
